metadata.title: Complete Catalogue of the BSI IT-Grundschutz Compendium 2023

controls.title: Assumption of overall responsibility for information security by management (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution's management has only acknowledged responsibility for information security verbally or informally. The assumption of responsibility is not documented and is not actively communicated, which leads to ambiguity among employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, responsibility is often only mentioned reactively in the event of a security incident or an external audit. There are no formal documents such as a letter of appointment for the Information Security Officer (ISO) or an official policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews managers and determines whether they understand and exercise their responsibility for information security. It is checked whether a formal assignment of overall responsibility is missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The overall responsibility for information security is formally assigned to the institution's management, e.g., in its rules of procedure. However, management only assumes this responsibility passively and delegates the tasks completely without active steering or control.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The assignment of responsibility is recorded in an official document. Management approves budgets but does not proactively intervene in the design of the security process and only irregularly requests information on its status.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews documents such as the rules of procedure to verify the formal assignment of responsibility. Interviews are conducted to check the extent to which management actively steers and controls the security process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution's management MUST assume overall responsibility for information security within the institution. This MUST be clearly recognizable to all stakeholders. The institution's management MUST initiate, steer, and control the security process. The institution's management MUST define the responsibilities for information security and equip the responsible employees with the necessary competencies and resources. The institution's management MUST be regularly informed about the status of information security as well as potential risks and consequences due to a lack of security measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The assumption of responsibility is documented by a security policy signed by management. Regular meetings (e.g., quarterly) between management and the ISO are established to discuss status and risks. The results of these meetings are documented in minutes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the signed security policy. Minutes of the management meetings on information security are reviewed. Interviews with employees confirm that the role of management in the security process is clear and known.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution's management actively sets an example for information security ('Tone at the Top'). It critically questions the status reports received, demands deeper analyses in case of deviations, and consistently follows up on the implementation of risk treatment measures. Compliance with security policies is also demonstrated at the management level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Management actively participates in important awareness measures. Decisions on risk treatment are not only documented but also provided with a clear justification for the chosen option (e.g., acceptance, mitigation). A dedicated risk committee chaired by a member of the institution's management is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the minutes of the risk committee and the documented risk decisions for their plausibility. It is checked whether management carries out a clear prioritization based on business risk when allocating resources for security measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information security objectives are fully integrated into the superordinate business objectives and the strategic planning of the institution. The performance in the area of information security is part of the target agreements and performance appraisals for upper management. Management actively promotes a positive security culture and proactively invests in future security technologies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The annual business reports include information on the information security situation. The achievement of objectives is measured using Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), which are visualized in a management dashboard. Management initiates and finances research projects to defend against future threats.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the strategic planning documents and the management's target agreements for the integration of security objectives. The existence and use of a KPI dashboard are verified. The effectiveness of the security culture is assessed through employee surveys and the analysis of security incidents.

controls.title: Definition of security objectives and strategy (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some disconnected and undocumented security objectives exist, which were mostly formulated reactively. A comprehensive security strategy is completely missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Objectives like 'install antivirus protection' or 'operate a firewall' exist, but there is no documentation on how these objectives contribute to protecting business processes. The objectives are not measurable or time-bound.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews with management and IT managers, the auditor determines that no formalized and documented security objectives or strategy exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: General security objectives and a basic strategy are recorded in a document. However, they lack a direct link to the specific business objectives and processes of the institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document titled 'Security Strategy' exists. It lists generic objectives like 'ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability'. However, it lacks concrete specifications on how this is to be achieved in the context of the specialized tasks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the strategy document and assesses whether the objectives and the strategy are tailored to the specific needs of the institution or only contain general phrases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution's management MUST initiate and establish the security process. For this, the institution's management MUST define and document appropriate security objectives and a strategy for information security. Conceptual requirements MUST be developed and organizational frameworks MUST be created to enable the proper and secure handling of information. The institution's management MUST support, be responsible for, and regularly review the security strategy and objectives for their topicality, appropriateness, and effective implementation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security strategy and the objectives derived from it are documented in the security policy. The objectives are formulated in such a way that they establish a clear link to business processes or specialized tasks. An annual process for reviewing and adapting the strategy and objectives is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and content of the documented security strategy and objectives. It is checked whether a process for regular review is established by inspecting the minutes of review meetings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security objectives are formulated according to the SMART method (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound). The security strategy is explicitly linked to the overall business objectives and derives its priorities from them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each security objective, specific metrics (KPIs) are defined to measure success. For example, the objective 'reduce phishing incidents' is made measurable by the metric 'click rate in internal phishing simulations'. The strategy includes a concrete implementation plan (roadmap).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor evaluates the formulated security objectives based on the SMART criteria. The existence of KPIs and a roadmap is checked. The link between the security strategy and the business objectives is traced using strategic planning documents.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security strategy is a dynamic, living construct that is continuously adapted to the changing threat landscape, new technologies, and business strategies. The process for defining security objectives is fully integrated into the annual strategic planning cycle of the entire institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The strategy is informed by a threat intelligence program. Scenario analyses and wargaming are used to validate and refine the strategy. The security strategy is positioned as an enabler for new digital business models.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a formal process for integrating threat intelligence into strategic planning. Evidence of conducted wargaming and scenario analyses is checked. The role of information security in the development of new business areas is assessed through interviews with management and a review of project documents.

controls.title: Creation of an information security policy (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A draft of an information security policy exists, but it has not been approved by management or communicated to employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A file, e.g., 'policy_draft.docx', is located on a network drive, but its status is unclear and it is not being applied.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds the draft but notes that it is not signed by management and is not known to employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general information security policy has been approved and communicated. However, it is generic and not specifically tailored to the business objectives and risks of the institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A template for a security policy was adopted from the internet without significant adaptation. It contains general statements but no concrete security objectives relevant to the institution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reads the policy and finds that it has no specific references to the processes, specialized tasks, or organizational structure of the institution.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution's management MUST adopt a high-level information security policy. This MUST describe the importance of information security, the security objectives, the key aspects of the security strategy, and the organizational structure for information security. A clear scope of applicability MUST be defined for the security policy. The information security policy MUST explain the security objectives and the relationship of the security objectives to the business objectives and tasks of the institution. The institution's management MUST communicate the policy to all employees and other members of the institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is signed by the institution's management and published on the intranet. New employees are notified of the policy upon hiring. The content is checked for comprehensibility for all employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the policy signed by management. It is checked whether the content required in the text (importance, objectives, strategy, organization, scope, relation to business objectives) is present. Random interviews with employees confirm the awareness of the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The information security policy is updated regularly, at least annually, and in the event of significant changes in the organization or the threat landscape. A formal process exists for managing exceptions to the policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security concept defines a process for the annual review of the policy. Versions of the policy are archived. A form for requesting exceptions is provided, and the approval process for it is defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the change log and the policy archive to verify the regularity of updates. The exception handling process is examined, and approved exceptions are reviewed on a sample basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The effectiveness of the policy is actively monitored using metrics (e.g., by reducing incidents attributable to policy violations). Employees' acknowledgment and understanding of the policy are regularly checked, for example, through short tests as part of awareness campaigns.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Key figures on policy compliance are collected and listed in the management report. A Learning Management System (LMS) is used to automate and document the distribution of the policy and the execution of comprehension tests.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the management reports for key figures on the effectiveness of the policy. The results of the comprehension tests from the LMS are reviewed. The process for measuring effectiveness is assessed for its appropriateness.

controls.title: Appointment of an Information Security Officer (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The information security tasks are performed informally by an IT employee in addition to their other duties, without a formal appointment as Information Security Officer (ISO).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no letter of appointment or an adjusted job description. The person has no dedicated time for ISO tasks and often only acts reactively.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through inspection of the organizational chart and job descriptions, as well as through interviews, that no formal ISO role is filled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A person has been formally appointed as ISO. However, the ISO does not have sufficient resources, authority, or a direct reporting line to management to effectively fulfill the role.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a letter of appointment. However, the ISO is positioned low in the hierarchy of the IT department and has difficulty enforcing security-related decisions outside of IT. No separate budget is available for security projects.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the appointment, but checks through interviews with the ISO and other managers whether the actual powers and resources are sufficient for the performance of the tasks. The organizational chart is used to analyze the reporting line.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution's management MUST appoint an ISO. The ISO MUST promote information security within the institution and help steer and coordinate the security process. The institution's management MUST provide the ISO with adequate resources and the opportunity to report directly to them if necessary. The ISO MUST be involved at an early stage in all major projects and in the introduction of new applications and IT systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The appointment is made by a formal letter of appointment. The role, tasks, and powers of the ISO are clearly defined in the security policy or a job description. Early involvement in projects is ensured by a corresponding regulation in the project management process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the letter of appointment and the definition of the ISO role. It is verified that the ISO has adequate resources (time, budget, training). Based on project documentation, it is checked on a sample basis whether the ISO was involved at an early stage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The independence of the ISO is ensured by organizationally separating the role from IT management to avoid conflicts of interest. The ISO has its own budget, approved by management, for security initiatives, training, and external consulting services.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ISO reports directly to a member of the institution's management or to a staff unit of the management. Budget planning for information security is an integral part of the institution's annual planning process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the organizational chart to assess the reporting line and independence of the ISO. The budget plans are reviewed to verify the existence of a dedicated security budget.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The ISO function is performed by a team (Information Security Management Team, ISMT) with different specializations (e.g., for technology, GRC, awareness). The ISO and their team are firmly integrated into all strategic decision-making processes of the institution, including outside of IT projects (e.g., in M&A, introduction of new business areas).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ISMT is formally established, with its members and tasks defined. The ISMT is a permanent member of the Architecture Board and the Change Advisory Board. The security assessment is a mandatory gate check in all important corporate processes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and composition of the ISMT. Based on minutes of strategic committees, the actual involvement of the ISO/ISMT in decision-making processes is checked. The process documentation is analyzed for the integration of security gate checks.

controls.title: Contract design for the appointment of an external Information Security Officer (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An external service provider is entrusted with ISO tasks on an informal basis or by a handshake agreement. A detailed contract is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The engagement is made orally or by a simple email. Rights, obligations, and especially confidentiality are not regulated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that there is no written contract with the external ISO that regulates the essential aspects of the cooperation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standard service contract is used that only describes the ISO tasks in general terms. Specific regulations on confidentiality, reporting, or a controlled termination of the relationship are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A general framework agreement for consulting services is used. A specific confidentiality agreement (NDA) for the deep insights that an ISO receives is missing. The handover of documents and knowledge at the end of the contract is not regulated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract and finds that essential clauses specific to the ISO role (e.g., detailed task description, confidentiality, handover process) are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If the role of the ISO cannot be filled by an internal employee, the institution's management MUST appoint an external ISO. The contract with an external ISO MUST include all tasks of the ISO as well as the associated rights and obligations. The contract MUST include a suitable confidentiality agreement. The contract MUST ensure a controlled termination of the contractual relationship, including the handover of tasks to the client.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated contract for the external ISO services is drawn up. This contract lists the services to be provided in detail (e.g., creation of reports, participation in meetings, advice on projects). A separate, strict confidentiality agreement is signed. The contract contains a termination clause with a defined handover phase.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the contract with the external ISO for completeness of the required clauses: detailed tasks, rights and obligations; confidentiality agreement; regulation on contract termination and task handover.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The contract with the external ISO includes clear Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for essential tasks. This includes, for example, response times for security incidents, deadlines for the delivery of reports, and availability for consultations. The contract also regulates liability issues.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Measurable SLAs are defined in the contract, e.g., 'response to critical incidents within 2 hours', 'quarterly report by the 5th working day of the following quarter'. Compliance with the SLAs is regularly reviewed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract for the presence of SLAs and liability clauses. The documentation for verifying SLA compliance (e.g., time sheets, activity logs) is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The performance of the external ISO is regularly evaluated based on the contractually agreed SLAs and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). The contract contains clauses that allow for an independent audit of the external ISO's service by third parties. Clear escalation paths exist for non-performance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Annual review meetings are held with the service provider, during which performance is formally assessed. The institution reserves the right to have the working methods of the external ISO audited to ensure the quality and conformity of their work.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the annual review meetings. It is checked whether the contract contains an audit right for the institution. The process for evaluating the service provider's performance is examined for its effectiveness.

controls.title: Building a suitable organizational structure for information security (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Apart from the (possibly only informal) role of the ISO, there is no other defined organizational structure for information security. Responsibilities are unclear.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All information security inquiries end up with the ISO or in the general IT department, regardless of the topic. There are no specialized contacts or committees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that no document exists that describes an organizational structure for information security, and that employees cannot name clear contacts for security issues.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some roles for information security are named (e.g., IT Security Officer, Data Protection Officer). However, their tasks, competencies, and communication channels are not clearly delineated, which leads to gaps or overlaps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An organizational chart for security exists, but the role descriptions are vague. The collaboration between the roles is based on informal agreements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing role descriptions and identifies ambiguities and conflicts in responsibilities through interviews with the role holders.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A suitable overarching organizational structure for information security MUST be in place. For this purpose, roles MUST be defined that take on concrete tasks to achieve the security goals. Furthermore, qualified persons MUST be appointed to whom sufficient resources are available. The tasks, roles, responsibilities, and competencies in security management MUST be comprehensibly defined and assigned. There MUST be effective deputy arrangements for all important functions. Communication channels MUST be planned, described, established, and made known.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A security organization chart with clear roles (e.g., CISO/ISO, security analysts, emergency team) and their detailed job descriptions is created and communicated. A deputy is designated for each role. A communication matrix defines who informs whom and under what circumstances.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the organizational structure, including role descriptions, substitution rules, and the communication matrix. Interviews with role holders and their deputies confirm that they are aware of their tasks and responsibilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is regularly reviewed, at least annually, whether the organizational structure for information security is still appropriate and needs to be adapted to new framework conditions. An interdisciplinary body (e.g., an information security steering committee) is established to make strategic decisions and promote cooperation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IS steering committee with representatives from management, IT, HR, legal, and key business areas is established. This committee meets regularly (e.g., quarterly). The process for reviewing the organizational structure is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the rules of procedure and the minutes of the IS steering committee. It is checked whether the annual review of the organizational structure has taken place and been documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security organization is fully integrated into the institution's overarching Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) framework. The roles and responsibilities are mapped in a GRC tool and directly linked to the associated policies, controls, and risks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC tool is used to manage the organizational structure. Changes to processes or systems automatically trigger a review of the assigned security roles and tasks. Cooperation between information security, data protection, business continuity, and physical security is systematically managed through common processes and tools.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor gains access to the GRC tool and verifies the mapping of the organizational structure and its connection to other GRC objects. The functionality of the integrated processes (e.g., joint risk management) is checked.

controls.title: Definition of Security Measures (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security measures are implemented ad hoc and reactively, often as a direct response to a security incident or a single threat. There is no systematic process for defining the measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After a ransomware attack, a new backup solution is procured. However, there is no comprehensive plan that defines what other measures (such as network segmentation or awareness training) would also be necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that the selection of implemented security measures is not based on a protection needs assessment or risk analysis and is inconsistent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic set of standard security measures (e.g., virus scanners, firewalls) is applied to all systems. However, these measures are not adapted to the specific protection needs of individual applications or data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All servers and clients receive the same basic configuration, regardless of whether they are publicly accessible, process critical data, or are used only for testing purposes. The selection of measures is based on general 'best practices' rather than on an internal analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a basic level of protection is in place, but notes that there is no differentiation of measures according to protection needs. It is checked whether additional measures have been taken for systems with high protection needs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of the security process, comprehensive and appropriate security measures MUST be defined for all information processing. The selection of measures is based on the security objectives and a structured analysis of the protection requirements of the processed information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on the protection needs assessment, catalogs of measures are defined for different protection classes (e.g., 'normal', 'high'). When introducing new systems, the appropriate package of measures is selected and implemented based on the data classification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the protection needs assessment process and the resulting catalogs of measures. On a random basis, it is checked for selected IT systems whether the implemented measures correspond to the determined protection needs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All security measures SHOULD be systematically documented in security concepts. The security measures SHOULD be updated regularly to respond to new threats or changed framework conditions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For critical applications or systems, dedicated security concepts are created that describe the threat analysis, the protection needs assessment, and the selected measures in detail. There is an annual review process for these concepts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing security concepts for their completeness and quality. It is checked whether a process for regular updating of the concepts exists and is adhered to by reviewing the revision history of the documents.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection, implementation, and monitoring of security measures are fully integrated into a risk management process. The effectiveness of each important security measure is continuously monitored through technical metrics. The measures are dynamically adjusted based on the results of the monitoring and current threat intelligence.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC tool is used to link measures with risks and assets. A SIEM system collects log data to measure the effectiveness of controls such as firewalls or access restrictions. Automated playbooks (SOAR) adjust configurations when anomalies are detected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the risk management process and its connection to the selection of measures. The process of continuous effectiveness measurement is reviewed by evaluating data from the SIEM or other monitoring tools. The automation of responses is verified using SOAR playbooks and their execution logs.

controls.title: Integration of employees in the security process (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are informed once about the most important security rules (e.g., password policy) upon hiring. After that, no further awareness or training measures take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A leaflet is handed out upon hiring. There are no regular awareness campaigns or training on current threats.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the onboarding documents. Interviews with employees who have been with the company for a longer time confirm that no regular awareness measures take place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Annual, general security training sessions are held for all employees. However, these are not tailored to specific roles, tasks, or current threats.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual online training is mandatory for all employees. The content is identical each year and only covers basic topics.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the completion of the annual training based on certificates of participation. The training content is checked to see if it is current and relevant for different target groups.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees MUST be integrated into the security process. For this, they MUST be informed about the background and the threats relevant to them. They MUST know and implement security measures that affect their workplace. When introducing security policies and tools, employees MUST be adequately informed on how to use them. Employees MUST be made aware of the consequences of violating security requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A basic awareness program is established that covers the mentioned points. This can be done through a combination of intranet articles, regular emails, and training sessions. The acknowledgment of important policies is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the content of the awareness program. Random surveys of employees show whether they are familiar with the measures relevant to them and the consequences of violations. The documentation of policy acknowledgment is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees SHOULD be enabled to actively participate in shaping security. Therefore, employees SHOULD be involved at an early stage when security measures are to be planned or organizational regulations are to be designed. The awareness program is target-group-specific and addresses current threats.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separate, in-depth training sessions are conducted for target groups with increased risk (e.g., admins, HR department, managers). A clearly defined channel (e.g., an email address or a ticket system) is established through which employees can report security concerns or suggestions for improvement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the training plans and content for target-group specificity. It is verified that a reporting channel for security concerns exists and is known. The processing of received reports is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A continuous program to promote a positive security culture is established. This program uses gamification, regular phishing simulations with direct feedback, and rewards proactive security behavior. The effectiveness of the program is measured by metrics and continuously improved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A phishing simulation platform is used to simulate realistic attacks and measure click rates. Employees who correctly report phishing emails receive positive feedback or small rewards. The results are used to plan future awareness measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the results and methodology of the phishing simulations. It is checked whether a system for rewarding security-conscious behavior exists. The process for measuring and improving the security culture is evaluated for its effectiveness.

controls.title: Integration of information security into organization-wide processes (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information security is considered almost exclusively a technical topic and is only taken into account in the context of IT projects. It plays no role in business processes such as human resources management or procurement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When procuring new software, IT is consulted for a technical review, but there are no security requirements in the procurement process itself, e.g., regarding contracts with the supplier.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes central business processes (e.g., hiring, procurement, development process) and finds that no security steps or requirements are defined therein.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In some central processes (e.g., in change management), there is a formal 'security approval' step. However, this is often treated merely as a checkbox without a substantial review.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the change management tool, there is a mandatory field 'ISO approval'. The ISO often gives this a blanket approval because there is insufficient information for a security assessment or a lack of time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews change tickets and checks whether the security approvals are provided with a traceable justification or audit documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information security MUST be integrated into all business processes and specialist tasks. It MUST be ensured that all necessary security aspects are considered not only in new processes and projects, but also in ongoing activities. The Information Security Officer (ISO) MUST be sufficiently involved in security-relevant decisions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The most important business processes are identified and analyzed to insert security-relevant control points. For example, the hiring process is supplemented with mandatory security training and the signing of a non-disclosure agreement. The ISO has veto power in the change management process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the process documentation for the integration of security control points. The actual involvement of the ISO in decisions is verified using logs and tickets (e.g., from change management).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information security SHOULD also be coordinated with other areas in the institution that deal with security and risk management (e.g., Business Continuity Management, physical security, compliance). Regular coordination meetings are held and the processes are aligned with each other.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A joint risk management board is established, in which the ISO, BCM officer and other security functions are represented. The risk analyses from the various areas are consolidated to obtain a holistic view of the risk situation. Emergency plans from IS and BCM are coordinated with each other.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the joint risk board. The process documentation and the results of the risk analyses from the various areas are checked for consistency and coordination.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security requirements are integrated into the entire lifecycle of processes, applications, and systems according to the 'Security by Design' principle. Automated workflows ensure that security checks at critical process gates (e.g., before a go-live) are performed in a mandatory and traceable manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Fixed security tests (e.g., static code analysis, penetration tests) are embedded in the software development life cycle (SDLC). The approval of a new release is technically coupled with the successful execution of these tests. A GRC tool controls the workflow and documents the approvals in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the process definition of the SDLC and checks the integration of the security tests. The automation of the security gates is verified based on the tool configuration (e.g., in the CI/CD or GRC tool). The results of the security tests for recent releases are reviewed.

controls.title: Creation of a security concept (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only individual, disconnected documents exist that cover parts of a security concept, such as a list of IT systems or a network diagram. A coherent overall structure is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Various documents are located on different drives and are often outdated. There is no comprehensive description of the security process or the measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that there is no central, structured security concept that covers the entire information network.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single, highly abstract security concept document exists. It describes the general objectives, but lacks detailed, actionable measures derived from a protection needs assessment or risk analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The document corresponds to a template but has not been filled with specific content for the information network. The measures described are very general (e.g., 'A firewall is used').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the security concept and determines that it does not contain any concrete measures tailored to the information network or a traceable derivation of the measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the defined scope (information network), an appropriate security concept SHOULD be created as the central document in the security process. A decision SHOULD be made as to whether the security concept should consist of one or several sub-concepts, which are created successively in order to first establish the required security level in selected areas.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A clear structure for the security concept (and possible sub-concepts) is defined, e.g., based on BSI Standard 200-2. The concept is created for the defined information network and approved by management. It contains a description of the scope, the results of the structural analysis and protection needs assessment, as well as a description of the procedure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether an approved security concept exists for the information network. The structure and basic content (scope, structural analysis, protection requirements) are checked for completeness and appropriateness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the security concept, concrete security measures appropriate to the information network under consideration MUST be derived from the institution's security objectives, the identified protection requirements, and the risk assessment. The measures provided for in the security concept MUST be implemented in practice promptly, which MUST be planned and controlled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security concept contains an implementation plan for the defined measures, including responsibilities and deadlines. The derivation of the measures from the risk analysis is clearly traceable. The progress of implementation is monitored regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the traceability of the measure derivation in the security concept. The existence and current status of the implementation plan are verified. Random checks are carried out to see whether planned measures have been implemented on schedule.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security concept is a 'living document' that is managed in a central GRC tool. It is dynamically linked to the asset inventory list, the risk register, and the implementation plans. Changes to the IT environment or the risk situation automatically trigger a review and potential adjustment of relevant parts of the concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC tool is used to manage the ISMS. The security concept is structured modularly within it. When a new critical system is entered into the CMDB, a workflow for creating or adapting the corresponding sub-concept is automatically triggered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is given read access to the GRC tool. The dynamic linking of concept elements with assets and risks is checked. Using an example (e.g., decommissioning a system), it is verified whether the process for adapting the concept functions as defined.

controls.title: Maintaining information security (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Reviews of information security only take place reactively, for example, after a serious security incident. There is no plan for regular reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Concepts and policies are created, but are not subsequently checked for their timeliness or effectiveness. They become outdated and no longer reflect reality.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that important security documents are outdated and that there is no process or plan for their regular review.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a plan for annual reviews. However, these reviews are superficial and are carried out by people who are themselves responsible for the audited areas (lack of independence).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT administrator checks the firewall rules he configured himself. The results are recorded informally and deficiencies are not systematically tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the reviews carried out were not performed by independent persons. The audit documentation is insufficient and there is no systematic deficiency management.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security process, security concepts, guidelines, and organizational structure SHOULD be regularly reviewed and updated for effectiveness and appropriateness. Security audits SHOULD be carried out regularly, whereby it SHOULD be regulated which areas are to be reviewed, when, and by whom. Reviews SHOULD be carried out regularly (at least annually) and on an ad-hoc basis by qualified and independent persons. The results SHOULD be documented in a traceable manner and, based on this, deficiencies should be eliminated and corrective measures taken.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal audit plan is created that defines the audit areas, intervals, and the responsible auditors. Independence is ensured by having auditors not audit their own areas. For identified deficiencies, an action plan with responsibilities and deadlines is created, the implementation of which is tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the internal audit plan for completeness and appropriateness. The qualification and independence of the auditors are assessed. Using audit reports and action plans, random checks are carried out to determine whether the process from audit to deficiency remediation is functioning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The audit process is controlled by a multi-year, risk-based audit plan. Identified deficiencies are recorded in a central tracking system (finding management system). In the case of serious deficiencies, a root cause analysis is carried out to identify and remedy systemic weaknesses.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An audit plan for the next 3 years is created, which audits high-risk areas more frequently. A module in the ticket system or a GRC tool is used for the management of audit findings. A formal process for root cause analysis is defined and applied.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the multi-year audit plan and its risk-based derivation. The use and functionality of the finding management system are checked. The documentation of performed root cause analyses is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The audit process is supported by automated tools for continuous compliance checking and vulnerability analysis (Continuous Auditing). The results of the audits and the metrics obtained flow directly back into the risk management process to dynamically adapt the security strategy and controls.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools for configuration checking (e.g., CIS-CAT) and vulnerability scanners are used to automatically detect deviations from security baselines. The results are visualized in a dashboard and automatically trigger tickets for critical deviations. The results are incorporated into the annual reassessment of risks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and results of the automated testing tools. The process of how the results of the continuous audit are incorporated into risk management is verified. The degree of automation of the process is assessed. The automated check can be verified by querying the API of the testing tool.

controls.title: Management reports on information security (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Management is only informed orally and irregularly about the state of information security, usually only when an incident has occurred.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are no formal reports. Information is passed on through 'informal channels', which is not audit-proof.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with management and the ISO that no regular, formal reporting process exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Management receives reports, but they are very technical, merely list operational details, and lack a management-level summary, risk assessment, or clear recommendations for action.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The report consists of an export of firewall log statistics or a list of applied patches. The link to business risk is missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the management reports and assesses whether they are understandable and relevant for decision-making for the target audience (management).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution's management SHOULD be regularly informed about the state of information security. For this purpose, management reports SHOULD be written that contain the essential relevant information (current threat landscape, effectiveness and efficiency of the security process, problems, successes, opportunities for improvement). The reports SHOULD contain clearly prioritized proposed measures with realistic estimates of the implementation effort. The management reports and the management decisions based on them SHOULD be archived in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A fixed template for the quarterly security report is created. The ISO collects the information and prepares it for management. The reports are stored in an audit-proof system. Management's decisions are recorded in the meeting minutes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the management reports of the last periods for completeness of the required content. The minutes of the management meetings are inspected to understand the resulting decisions. The audit-proof archiving is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management reports contain meaningful Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and Key Risk Indicators (KRIs), which are presented over time to identify trends. The reports include a concise executive summary that translates technical risks into business impacts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A set of 5-10 relevant KPIs (e.g., 'number of critical vulnerabilities', 'click rate in phishing simulation', 'time to resolve incidents') is defined and compared in each report with the values from previous periods. Diagrams are used to visualize trends.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the selection and quality of the KPIs/KRIs used. It is checked whether the reports contain trend analyses and an executive summary. The correctness of the underlying data is verified on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reporting system is largely automated through a management dashboard and provides management with a near real-time updated view of the security situation. The reports contain benchmarking data that allow comparison with industry peers or recognized standards.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC or SIEM tool is used to automatically aggregate KPIs from various sources (e.g., vulnerability scanner, ticketing system) and display them in a dashboard. Management has direct access to this dashboard. External data sources or surveys are used for benchmarking.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is given access to the management dashboard and checks its functionality and the correctness of the data aggregation. The origin and relevance of the benchmarking data are assessed. The automated check can be performed via a query of the dashboard API.

controls.title: Documentation of the security process (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Important documents such as the security concept exist, but are outdated and not centrally located. Many decisions are made verbally and not documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Documents are located on the local hard drives of individual employees. There is no version control.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor cannot find important documents or can only find outdated versions. There is no evidence for important decisions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The essential documents of the security process are created and stored in a central location. However, a regulated process for the creation, approval, versioning, and archiving of documents is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All documents are stored in a shared folder on a network drive. However, there is no uniform naming convention or approval process, which leads to confusion about the validity of versions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds the documents but notes that there is no clear process for document control. It is often unclear which is the currently valid, approved version of a document.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security process workflow SHOULD be documented. Important decisions and work products (security concept, policies, investigation results) SHOULD be sufficiently documented. There SHOULD be a regulated procedure for the creation and archiving of documentation. Regulations SHOULD exist to maintain currency and confidentiality. The current version SHOULD be accessible at short notice and all previous versions SHOULD be centrally archived.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy for document control is created. This defines templates, naming conventions, an approval workflow (review, approval), rules for access rights, and a process for archiving. A central, access-protected storage location (e.g., a SharePoint or Wiki) is used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy on document control. Using random samples, it is verified whether the process (creation, approval, versioning, archiving) is being followed for important security documents and whether the current version is easy to find.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A document management system (DMS) is used to manage all security documents. The DMS enforces the defined lifecycle of the documents, including versioning, access control, and automated review workflows.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A DMS like SharePoint with activated content management features or a dedicated DMS is configured. For each document type, a workflow is defined that, for example, automatically prompts the document owner for a review after one year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is given read access to the DMS. The configuration of the workflows and permissions is checked. The revision history of a document is traced in the system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security documentation is integrated into a central knowledge base or a GRC tool. The relationships between documents (e.g., between a policy, a concept, and a related procedure) are explicitly mapped. This enables automated impact analysis in case of changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a GRC tool, the guideline is linked to the implementing policies, and these in turn are linked to the relevant controls and assets. If the guideline is changed, the tool can automatically identify all dependent documents and controls that require a review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the linking of the documents in the GRC tool. A change scenario is simulated to test the functionality of the impact analysis.

controls.title: Economic use of resources for information security (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Resources for information security are only provided reactively and without strategic planning or budgeting. Investments are often made based on fears or aggressive sales pitches rather than on an analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After a media report about a new wave of attacks, an expensive tool is purchased ad hoc, without checking whether the available funds would be better used for basic organizational measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that there is no formal budget process for information security and that investments made are not justified by a risk or needs analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an annual budget for information security. However, the allocation of funds within this budget is not clearly justified, and it is not measured whether the investments achieve the desired benefits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A flat-rate budget is carried over each year. There is no process to justify the expenses or to evaluate the 'Return on Security Investment' (ROSI).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a budget but cannot find any documentation that makes the budget decisions traceable or measures the success of the investments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security strategy SHOULD consider economic aspects. When security measures are defined, the resources required for them SHOULD be quantified. The resources planned for information security SHOULD be provided on time. In case of peak workloads or special tasks, additional internal staff SHOULD be deployed or external expertise SHOULD be brought in.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the annual budget process, the ISO reports its resource requirements (personnel, licenses, projects) based on the implementation plan of the security concept. The costs for each measure are estimated. A process for commissioning external service providers when needed is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the budget planning for information security and compares it with the requirements from the security concept. It is checked whether the approved funds were made available on time and whether a process for procuring external expertise exists and is used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal cost-benefit analysis is performed for significant security investments. The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) of a security solution, including personnel and maintenance costs, is considered in the investment decision.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before acquiring a new security system, various alternatives (including open source) are evaluated. The evaluation includes a TCO calculation over 3-5 years and a qualitative assessment of the benefits (e.g., risk reduction, efficiency gain).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of recent investment decisions and checks whether a cost-benefit analysis and a TCO consideration have been carried out.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The resource allocation process is directly linked to the risk management framework. Investments are clearly prioritized to mitigate the greatest risks to the institution's business objectives. The effectiveness of the spending is systematically measured and reported via security metrics and KPIs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The risk register is used to identify the top risks. The security budget is specifically targeted at measures to address these top risks. The management report contains key figures that show the effect of the investments on the risk situation (e.g., 'reduction of the expected loss amount through investment X').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor traces how the priorities in the risk register were incorporated into the budget planning. The metrics presented in the management report on the effectiveness of the spending are checked for their correctness and meaningfulness.

controls.title: Creation of target-group-specific security policies (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is only a single, very general, and highly abstract guideline on information security. Detailed, topic-specific policies are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employee questions on specific topics such as 'Use of private devices' or 'Cloud services' cannot be answered based on policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that no binding policies exist for essential security topics (e.g., passwords, email usage, mobile devices).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are some topic-specific policies (e.g., a password policy). However, these are written as 'one-size-fits-all' documents for the entire institution and are not tailored to the different needs and knowledge levels of various target groups (e.g., admin vs. end user).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The password policy mandates the same complexity for all accounts, although technical service accounts have different requirements than personalized user accounts. The policies are often formulated in very technical terms and are difficult for non-IT employees to understand.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing policies and assesses whether they are understandable and practical for the respective recipients. It is checked whether unnecessary, sweeping restrictions exist for certain groups.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the general requirements, there SHOULD also be target-group-oriented security policies that cover the relevant security topics as needed. A process is established to identify the need for such policies and to create them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Dedicated policies are created for specific target groups or topics, e.g., a 'Secure Software Development Policy' for developers, a 'Policy for Handling Personal Data' for the HR department, and a 'Policy for the Use of Mobile Devices' for all employees with a company mobile phone.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether appropriate, target-group-specific policies exist for the most important target groups (e.g., administrators, developers, external parties) and risk areas (e.g., cloud usage, home office). The content is assessed for its relevance and comprehensibility for the respective target group.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A clear framework for policy management is established, which governs the entire lifecycle of all policies (creation, review, approval, communication, review, decommissioning). The policies are formulated in understandable language and presented in a visually appealing way to increase acceptance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 'Policy on Policies' document is created. For important policies, short summaries (one-pagers) or explanatory videos are also created for easier comprehension and made available via the intranet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the framework for policy management. The existence and quality of supporting communication materials (such as summaries or videos) are assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Acknowledgement and understanding of the relevant policies are demonstrably ensured and documented for each employee. Wherever technically possible and reasonable, the requirements from the policies are enforced by technical controls and their compliance is monitored automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Learning Management System (LMS) is used to manage the distribution of policies and conduct comprehension tests. The requirements from the password policy are technically implemented in the systems (e.g., Active Directory). An MDM solution enforces the security configuration on mobile devices according to the corresponding policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the evidence of policy acknowledgment in the LMS. The technical configuration of systems (e.g., AD GPOs, MDM profiles) is checked to see if it correctly and completely implements the requirements of the corresponding policies. The automated check can be performed via a script (e.g., `Get-GPOReport`).

controls.title: Taking out insurance (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The topic of cyber insurance was discussed internally, but no concrete steps were taken to obtain offers or take out a policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are meeting notes or emails on the subject, but no formal decision or further activities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that despite discussions, no systematic review of taking out a cyber insurance policy has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general business liability insurance policy is in place. However, it is unclear or has not been checked to what extent this insurance also covers damages from cyber incidents. A dedicated cyber insurance policy does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The existing insurance policies have not been specifically analyzed for coverage of cyber risks (e.g., ransomware, data breaches, business interruption due to IT failure).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing insurance policies and determines that explicit coverage for cyber risks is missing or the coverage amounts are insufficient.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be examined whether insurance can be taken out for residual risks. It SHOULD be checked regularly whether the existing insurance policies are appropriate for the current situation. This process is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the risk analysis, residual risks that are candidates for insurance coverage (risk transfer) are identified. Offers for cyber insurance are obtained and evaluated. The decision (to take out a policy or not) is documented. Existing policies are reviewed annually for their timeliness and appropriateness.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the risk analysis documentation for the identification of residual risks. It is checked whether a conscious and documented decision was made about taking out insurance. The process for the annual review of the policies is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated cyber insurance policy has been taken out. The coverage amounts, exclusions, and especially the obligations (requirements for the institution's security level) of the policy were carefully reviewed by security and legal experts before conclusion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before taking out the insurance, a self-assessment is carried out to ensure that all security measures (obligations) required by the insurance company are met. The result of this assessment is documented. Unclear clauses are clarified with the insurer or a specialized broker.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the cyber insurance policy. The documentation of the review of the obligations before conclusion of the contract is checked. It is verified on a random basis whether the required security measures are actually implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cyber insurance is an integral part of emergency management. The process for reporting a claim to the insurer is described in detail in the incident response plan and has been tested. There is a continuous dialogue with the insurer to ensure that the security level meets the requirements and to potentially optimize premiums.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The incident response plan contains a chapter 'Communication with the Cyber Insurer' including contact details, reporting deadlines, and required information. As part of emergency drills, reporting the claim to the insurer is also simulated. The results of audits and penetration tests are proactively shared with the insurer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the incident response plan for the integration of insurance communication. Emergency drill logs are reviewed to verify the testing of the reporting process. The communication history with the insurer is checked for proactive exchange.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: (Information) security management refers to the planning, steering, and control task required to establish and continuously implement a well-thought-out and effective process for ensuring information security. A functioning security management system must be embedded in the existing management structures of every institution. Therefore, it is practically impossible to specify an organizational structure for security management that is directly applicable to every institution. Instead, adjustments to specific circumstances will often be necessary.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is to show how a functioning Information Security Management System (ISMS) can be set up and further developed during ongoing operation. To this end, the module describes the steps of a systematic security process and provides guidance on creating a security concept.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The ISMS.1 Security Management module must be applied once to the information network.
The module is based on the BSI Standards 200-1 "Information Security Management Systems" and 200-2 "IT-Grundschutz Methodology". It summarizes the most important aspects of security management from these standards.
Regular security reviews should be conducted within the institution. Detailed requirements for this are not found in this module, but in the DER 3.1 Audits and Reviews module. Furthermore, all employees of the institution as well as all relevant external parties should be systematically made aware of security risks and trained on information security issues in a target-group-specific manner. Detailed requirements for this can be found in the ORP.3 Information Security Awareness and Training module.
This module also does not cover specific aspects of personnel or organization. These requirements are addressed in the ORP.2 Personnel and ORP.1 Organization modules, respectively.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Lack of personal responsibility in the security process
parts.prose: If the roles and responsibilities in the security process are not clearly defined in an institution, it is likely that many employees will reject or forget their responsibility for information security by referring to higher hierarchical levels. As a result, security measures are not implemented, as they almost always initially represent an additional effort in the usual workflow.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Lack of support from institutional management
parts.prose: If the security officers are not fully supported by the institution's management, it can be difficult to demand the necessary measures. This is especially true for individuals who are above the security officers in the line structure. In this case, the security process cannot be fully implemented.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Inadequate strategic and conceptual guidelines
parts.prose:
In many institutions, a security concept is created, but its content is often known to only a few people within the institution. This leads to requirements being consciously or unconsciously disregarded in areas where organizational effort would be necessary.
Even if the security concept contains strategic objectives, these are often viewed by the institution's management as merely a collection of declarations of intent. Frequently, insufficient resources are then made available for implementation. It is also often wrongly assumed that security is automatically established in an automated environment.
Without strategic guidelines, incidents are often handled in an unstructured manner. As a result, only partial aspects can be improved at best.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Insufficient or misguided investments
parts.prose:
If the institution's management is not sufficiently informed about the security status of all business processes, IT systems, and applications, as well as existing deficiencies, not enough resources will be allocated for the security process, or they will not be used appropriately. In the latter case, this can lead to an excessively high security level in one area being contrasted by serious deficiencies in another.
It is also frequently observed that expensive technical security solutions are used incorrectly and are therefore ineffective or even become a source of danger themselves.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Insufficient enforceability of security measures
parts.prose: To achieve a consistent and appropriate level of security, different areas of responsibility within an institution must cooperate. However, a lack of strategic guidelines and unclear objectives can sometimes lead to different interpretations of the importance of information security. This can result in the necessary cooperation not materializing, for example, because the task of 'information security' is seen as unnecessary or at least not a priority. Thus, security measures might not be implemented.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Lack of updates in the security process
parts.prose: New business processes, applications, and IT systems, as well as new threats, permanently influence the status of information security within an institution. If an effective review concept is lacking, which also strengthens awareness of new threats, the security level decreases. Real security then gradually turns into a dangerous false sense of security.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Violation of legal regulations and contractual agreements
parts.prose:
If an institution's information, business processes, and IT systems are inadequately secured, for example through insufficient security management, this can lead to violations of legal provisions related to information processing or existing contracts with business partners. Which laws must be observed in each case depends on the type of institution or its business processes and services.
Depending on the locations of an institution, different national and international regulations may also need to be observed. If an institution has insufficient knowledge of international legal requirements, e.g., regarding data protection, information obligations, insolvency law, liability, or information access for third parties, this increases the risk of corresponding violations. This can result in legal consequences.
In many industries, it is common for customers to require their suppliers and service providers to comply with certain quality and security standards. If a contracting party violates contractually agreed security requirements, this can lead to contractual penalties, contract terminations, or even the loss of business relationships.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Disruption of business operations due to security incidents
parts.prose: Security incidents can be triggered by a single event or a chain of unfortunate circumstances. They can lead to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information and IT systems being compromised. This then quickly has a negative impact on the essential specialized tasks and business processes of the affected institution. Even if not all security incidents become public, they can still lead to negative effects in relationships with business partners and customers. Legal requirements could also be disregarded. It is not the case that the most severe and far-reaching security incidents were caused by the largest security vulnerabilities. In many cases, a chain of small causes leads to major damage.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Uneconomical use of resources due to insufficient security management
parts.prose:
Insufficient security management can lead to wrong priorities being set and investments not being made in the areas that bring the greatest value to the institution. This can lead to the following errors:
• Investments are made in expensive security solutions without a foundation of necessary organizational regulations. Unclear responsibilities and accountabilities can lead to serious security incidents despite expensive investments.
• Investments in information security are made in a few areas of an institution that are particularly aware of information security. Other areas, which may be more important for fulfilling professional tasks and achieving business goals, are neglected due to scarce resources or lack of interest from those in charge. Investments are then made unevenly in sub-areas, while security risks that are particularly significant for the overall system are ignored.
• The one-sided increase in the protection of individual basic values can even reduce overall protection, for example, by encrypting information, which increases confidentiality but can reduce availability.
• A heterogeneous and uncoordinated use of security products can lead to high financial and personnel resource deployment.

controls.title: Definition of responsibilities and regulations (B) [Institutional management]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Rough assignments of responsibility exist only for the areas considered most critical, and are often communicated only verbally. Some basic security regulations are documented, but they are outdated, incomplete, and not actively communicated or maintained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, responsibilities are typically assigned informally or reactively when a problem occurs. Existing documents are often orphaned and do not reflect the current organizational structure. A central overview or a systematic approach is completely lacking.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly interviews employees from various departments about their security responsibilities. It is checked whether basic security documentation exists, even if it is outdated. The absence of any documentation or the complete lack of employee awareness of responsibilities would indicate non-fulfillment of this stage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The most important tasks and functions are assigned to organizational units or roles, but a clear, fine-grained demarcation between the functions is often missing. A basic set of security regulations exists, but it is only updated sporadically or in case of major incidents. Changes are communicated, but without a fixed process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Responsibilities are roughly outlined in organizational charts or function descriptions. Security regulations are stored as static documents on the intranet, and their timeliness is not systematically monitored. Changes are usually announced via email to all employees, without follow-up.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests organizational charts and basic security policies. It is checked whether the most important responsibilities (e.g., IT manager, data protection officer) are named. It is checked on a random basis whether basic regulations for topics such as password security or email usage exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Within the institution, all relevant tasks and functions MUST be clearly defined and demarcated from one another. Binding regulations for information security MUST be established across the board for the various operational aspects. The organizational structures and binding regulations MUST be revised on an ad-hoc basis. The changes MUST be communicated to all employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is implemented by creating and maintaining an ISMS role concept and a comprehensive but understandable set of policies. Revisions take place at least annually or in the event of significant organizational changes. The announcement is made via official channels such as the intranet, and acknowledgment is confirmed by new employees as part of the onboarding process.

parts.name: assessment-method
