parts.prose: The auditor requests the current set of information security policies and the associated role concept. It is checked whether a documented process for regular revision and communication of changes exists. Employees are randomly asked whether they know the regulations relevant to them and where they can find them.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined regulations and responsibilities are subject to an annual, formal review and approval process by the institutional management. A documented process for announcing changes to all affected organizational units is enforced and acknowledgment is actively tracked, for example, through mandatory read receipts in a learning management system (LMS).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A workflow tool or a GRC tool is used to manage the lifecycle of policies. This includes creation, review, approval, distribution, and decommissioning. Read receipts are automatically requested and their status is monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the minutes of the annual management review for the security policies. The technical records or reports from the system for tracking read receipts for a recently changed policy are examined. An automated check could verify the configuration of the GRC tool for compliance with the defined review cycle.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities and regulations are stored in an integrated management system (e.g., GRC tool) and dynamically linked to business processes, risks, and technical assets. Revisions are automatically triggered by organizational or technical changes (e.g., introduction of a new system). The effectiveness of the regulations is measured and continuously improved through regular, partially automated audits and key performance indicators (KPIs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The GRC tool is linked to the HR system and the CMDB. If an employee's role changes in the HR system, their responsibilities and applicable policies are automatically updated. Effectiveness is assessed, for example, by measuring the number of security incidents in relation to a specific regulation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the links stored in the GRC tool between roles, regulations, and assets. Reports and dashboards that display the KPIs for the effectiveness of the regulations are examined. An automated test could send a query to the GRC API to verify that all assets have an assigned owner and all roles have corresponding regulation assignments.

controls.title: Assignment of responsibilities (B) [Institution management]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities are only defined for a few, obviously critical assets, such as the central email server or the main firewall. The documentation of these responsibilities is incomplete, inconsistent, and stored in various non-centralized locations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Responsibilities are often only kept in the minds of long-term administrators. If documentation exists, it is usually a simple text or spreadsheet file on a local drive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects five critical systems and asks who is responsible for their security. The consistency and availability of the answers are assessed. It is checked whether a written assignment exists for these systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities are defined for most IT systems and applications at the department level, but not always for individual persons or specific assets. Employees know their general tasks, but not the specific security responsibilities for the assets assigned to them. An inventory list exists, but it does not contain explicit owners.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Responsibility is implicitly attributed to the department that primarily uses a system (e.g., 'The accounting department is responsible for the financial system'). Information about responsibilities is passed on orally to new team members.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the central inventory list and checks whether responsibilities are noted there. Department heads are interviewed to understand how responsibilities are handled within the team.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all business processes, applications, IT systems, rooms and buildings, and communication links, it MUST be defined who is responsible for them and their security. All employees MUST be informed, in particular about what they are responsible for and what associated tasks they perform.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central inventory list (asset register), e.g., in the form of a maintained spreadsheet or a simple database, is kept. In this list, a unique owner (asset owner) and, if applicable, a technical administrator are entered for each asset. Responsibilities are formally communicated as part of the onboarding process and during role changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the central inventory list and checks on a random basis whether owners have been named for all asset categories (systems, applications, rooms). Interviews are conducted with some named owners to check whether they are aware of their role and tasks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The assignment of responsibilities is an integral part of the on- and offboarding process as well as internal transfers. There is a regular, documented review process (e.g., annually) in which all asset owners formally confirm the currency of their responsibilities. For all critical responsibilities, deputy arrangements are also defined and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HR department and IT work with a common checklist for entries and exits, which includes the item 'Assignment/return of asset responsibilities'. The asset register is expanded to include fields for 'Deputy' and 'last confirmed on'. A script or calendar reminder triggers the annual review process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation for onboarding, offboarding, and the review of responsibilities. Minutes from the last review round are inspected. Using a recently departed employee as an example, the offboarding process is checked for the correct transfer of responsibilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities are stored and dynamically managed in a central configuration management system (CMDB) or GRC tool. Changes to systems (e.g., new servers in the CMDB) or personnel (e.g., departmental change in the HR system) automatically trigger a workflow to review and adjust assigned responsibilities. The performance of tasks by the responsible parties is monitored through technical audits and metrics (e.g., 'number of assets without a confirmed owner').

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CMDB is integrated with the HR system and the ticketing system. If an asset owner leaves the company, a ticket is automatically created for their supervisor to name a successor. As long as no successor is named, no change (change request) can be approved for the respective asset.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the management system's dashboard, which displays key figures on asset responsibilities. The workflow for reassigning responsibilities is tested. An automated test could query the CMDB via API for assets whose assigned owner is marked as 'inactive' in the HR system.

controls.title: Supervision or escorting of external persons (B) [Employees]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: External persons are registered at the reception and receive a visitor badge. However, escorting them into the building is not consistently implemented and depends on the respective employee. There are no special regulations in sensitive areas.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The reception staff maintains a manual visitor list. Whether the visitor is picked up and escorted after registration is not checked. Each employee decides for themselves how closely they escort a visitor.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor observes how visitors are handled at the reception. They conduct random walk-throughs to determine whether external persons (identifiable by their visitor badges) are moving around the office areas alone.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a written instruction that visitors must be escorted by employees. However, supervision in sensitive areas, such as server rooms, is only carried out sporadically or is not understood as an active, continuous task. Employees are generally aware of the rule, but implementation is inconsistent.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The regulation is part of the general house rules. There is no separate, stricter regulation for access to sensitive areas regarding supervision. Maintenance personnel from external companies, for example, are often left alone in the server room.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the house rules or corresponding instructions. Logs of external persons' access to sensitive areas (e.g., server room) are checked and compared with the attendance times of the internal escorts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: External persons MUST be escorted to the premises by employees. The institution's employees MUST supervise external persons in sensitive areas. Employees SHOULD be encouraged not to leave external persons unsupervised on the institution's premises.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A clear and binding visitor policy is documented and known to all employees. Sensitive areas are clearly defined (e.g., data center, archives, development departments). The policy stipulates that the escort must keep an eye on the external person during the entire stay in the sensitive area.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the visitor policy and checks whether it contains a clear instruction for escorting and supervision in sensitive areas. Employees are interviewed to see if they know the policy. It is checked whether access logs for sensitive areas document the presence of an internal escort.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The visitor process is supported by an electronic visitor management system that manages visitor registrations, the assignment of escorts, and the logging of entry and exit times. Regular awareness training for employees and random, unannounced checks are conducted to ensure compliance with the escort duty.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Visitors register in advance via a web portal, and the internal contact person is automatically notified. A photo is taken at reception, and a visitor badge with a photo and validity period is printed. The security staff conduct weekly patrols.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the functionality of the visitor management system demonstrated and checks the log data. The documentation of the awareness measures (e.g., intranet articles, emails) and the conducted patrols are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access for external persons to high-security areas is technically linked to the presence of their registered escort (e.g., through two-person access controls or mantrap systems). In these areas, compliance with the escort duty is supported by video surveillance, which triggers an alarm if a single person with visitor status is detected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Card readers are installed at the doors to data centers that require two valid cards (visitor and escort) to be swiped within a short time window. The video analysis software is configured to sound an alarm if a badge 'tagged' as a visitor appears in the camera's field of view without an escort's badge.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the effectiveness of the two-person access control by trying to gain access with only one card. The alarm logs of the video surveillance are checked for corresponding incidents and their processing. An automated test could verify the configuration of the access control system for the correct implementation of the two-person rule for the defined areas.

controls.title: Segregation of duties between incompatible tasks (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The principle of segregation of duties is only implemented to a limited extent in areas where it is explicitly required by law or regulation, such as in financial accounting (four-eyes principle for payments). In IT administration and development, the principle is not systematically observed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Segregation of duties is seen as a bureaucratic hurdle. Administrators often have development, test, and production access simultaneously. Small teams often lead to one person holding many incompatible roles without this being recognized as a risk.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the payment authorization process. It is checked whether IT administrators have the ability to extend their own permissions or to log and delete their own activities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fundamental separation between development, test, and operations teams or roles exists. However, control functions, such as approving changes or reviewing log data, are often performed by the same people who carry out the operational activity. Deputy arrangements often de facto negate the segregation of duties.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are separate user accounts for administrative and regular activities. However, a developer can move their own code into production after having 'self-inspected' it. If an approver is on vacation, the applicant grants the approval themselves 'by proxy'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the permissions of developers and administrators on the various system environments (development, test, production). Samples from the change management process logs are checked to see if the requester and approver are identical.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The tasks and the required roles and functions MUST be structured in such a way that incompatible tasks such as operational and controlling functions are distributed among different people. For incompatible functions, a segregation of duties MUST be defined and documented. Deputies MUST also be subject to the segregation of duties.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list or matrix of incompatible functions (Segregation of Duties - SoD matrix) is defined and documented. Examples are: request vs. approval, development vs. release for operation, administration vs. auditing. The assignment of permissions in IT systems is manually checked against this matrix. For deputies, it is clearly regulated that they may not represent the tasks of the person whose actions they control.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the SoD matrix and the process documentation for authorization assignment. Using examples (e.g., 'setting up a new user,' 'changing a firewall rule'), the process is traced. It is checked how the deputy arrangements ensure the segregation of duties.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The concept for segregation of duties (SoD matrix) is formalized and systematically supported by a defined process when assigning permissions. Compliance with the segregation of duties is reviewed regularly, at least semi-annually, through a manual or semi-automated analysis of the assigned permissions, and the result is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Identity and Access Management (IAM) system is used to manage roles and permissions. Before assigning a new role, it is checked manually or via a script whether an SoD conflict would arise. A script regularly extracts the permissions from the target systems and compares them against the SoD matrix.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the reports from the last SoD audits and checks how identified conflicts were handled. The process for approving permissions in the IAM system is examined. An automatic check could be a script that reads the permissions from a critical system and checks them against a digital SoD matrix.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The segregation of duties is preventively enforced by technical systems (e.g., an IAM or GRC tool). Requests for permissions that violate the digitally stored SoD matrix are automatically blocked or forwarded to an escalated approval process. Regular, fully automated audits continuously check the existing permissions for SoD conflicts and report them on a dashboard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system has implemented the SoD matrix as a rule set. When requesting a new role via a self-service portal, the system checks for conflicts in real time. If a conflict is unavoidable (e.g., in very small teams), a justified exception must be approved by the CISO and be accompanied by compensatory controls (e.g., enhanced monitoring).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to request a combination of conflicting roles for a user in the IAM system for testing purposes and verifies that the request is blocked or escalated. The SoD conflict dashboard is analyzed. It is checked whether the corresponding compensatory controls are implemented and effective for all approved exceptions.

controls.title: Contact person for information security questions (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is informally known who to ask at the IT helpdesk for general IT problems. However, a dedicated, officially designated contact person specifically for information security questions does not exist or is not known to most employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Security questions, if they are asked at all, are directed to the general IT support, which handles them based on their level of knowledge and available time. There is no guaranteed processing or escalation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly interviews employees to ask who they would contact with a question about the secure configuration of their laptop or how to handle a suspicious email. The answers are checked for consistency and the presence of a clear point of contact.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An Information Security Officer (ISO) or a similar role is formally appointed. However, the contact details and the exact responsibilities of this person are not easily accessible to employees or are difficult to find, for example, in a comprehensive organizational manual.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The appointment of the ISO was made primarily for compliance reasons. There is no active communication of their role and availability to the organization. The contact details are buried on a subpage of the intranet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the ISO's letter of appointment. Then, the ISO's contact information is searched for on the intranet or in the official communication media to assess its findability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In every institution, there MUST be contact persons for security questions who can answer both seemingly simple and complex or technical questions. The contact persons MUST be known to all employees of the institution. Information in this regard MUST be available and easily accessible to everyone in the institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One or more persons (e.g., the ISO, an IT security team) are officially designated as contact persons. Their names, photos, contact details (phone, email), and a brief description of their responsibilities are published on a prominent and easily findable page on the intranet (e.g., under 'Security' or 'Help').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the intranet page for existence, timeliness, and easy findability of the information about the security contacts. It is checked on a random basis whether the specified contact options (e.g., email address) are functional.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated and central communication channel, such as a ticketing system or a functional email address (e.g., security@company.com), is established for security inquiries. This ensures tracking, categorization, and adherence to defined service times. The contact persons regularly participate in further training to keep their expertise up to date.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate queue for information security is set up in the IT Service Management tool. Incoming requests are automatically recorded and assigned to a processor. Participation in training courses and conferences is specified for the security team in the annual training plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has reports from the ticketing system shown to them to analyze the number, type, and processing times of security inquiries. The training records of the contact persons for the last year are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A self-service portal with a searchable knowledge base (FAQ) for common security questions is established to help employees quickly and independently solve standard problems. For complex or urgent inquiries, a qualified team of specialists (e.g., a Security Operations Center - SOC) is available with guaranteed availability, potentially around the clock.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The self-service portal is integrated into the intranet. It contains instructions, short videos, and checklists on topics such as 'Recognizing Phishing,' 'Creating Secure Passwords,' or 'Using Wi-Fi in a Hotel.' The availability of the SOC is ensured via a hotline and a ticketing system and is contractually defined in SLAs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the quality and timeliness of the knowledge base. The SLAs for the SOC are reviewed and verified through test calls or tickets at various times. Usage statistics of the portal are analyzed to evaluate its acceptance and effectiveness.

controls.title: Asset and device management (S) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the most important IT devices such as servers and laptops are recorded in a simple list. Other security-relevant assets such as UPSs, network components, or fire extinguishers are not inventoried. Regular needs planning does not take place; assets are procured reactively when they fail.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The inventory list is an Excel spreadsheet that is maintained manually and only when devices are first issued. There is no process for decommissioning and secure disposal.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the inventory list and compares it with the devices actually present in an office space. They ask how old, decommissioned laptops are handled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An inventory of most IT devices takes place, but it is often not up-to-date because changes are not promptly recorded. a simple procurement process exists, but without a formal, security-related approval procedure. A basic process for erasing data carriers is in place, but it is not documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The inventory list is updated quarterly or semi-annually. Procurement is approved by the department head without involving IT security. Hard drives are overwritten once with standard software before disposal.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the inventory list with the results of a network scan to identify discrepancies. The procurement process for a new IT system is traced. Evidence of the erasure of data carriers from decommissioned devices is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All devices and assets that have an impact on information security SHOULD be available in sufficient quantity. There SHOULD be suitable testing and approval procedures before the devices and assets are used. Devices and assets SHOULD be listed in suitable inventory lists. To prevent the misuse of data, the reliable erasure or destruction of devices and assets SHOULD be regulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Inventories are maintained for all relevant asset classes (IT hardware, software, security-relevant infrastructure such as UPSs). A documented procurement process ensures that new devices are reviewed by IT security before deployment. There is a binding policy that describes the process for secure deletion (in accordance with BSI specifications) and disposal of devices and data media.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the inventories and the device disposal policy. The documented process for the procurement and approval of a new device is examined. Documentation of the deletion for recently disposed devices is requested on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The inventories are consolidated in a central database (e.g., CMDB) and are regularly checked for their up-to-dateness and completeness by automated discovery tools (e.g., network scanners, agents). The entire lifecycle of each asset, from procurement through maintenance and changes to disposal, is fully documented. Maintenance intervals (e.g., for UPS batteries) are actively monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CMDB tool is used that is automatically populated with data by nightly scans and agents installed on the clients. Each asset receives a unique inventory number (as a barcode label). For security-relevant assets, maintenance plans are stored that automatically create tickets for technicians when they are due.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the CMDB and the connected scan tools. The documented lifecycle of a specific server from acquisition to the present day is examined. The maintenance logs for critical infrastructure components for the last 12 months are reviewed. An automated check could search the CMDB for assets without a current scan timestamp.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Asset management is fully integrated into an integrated IT Service Management (ITSM) system. This system controls and automates processes such as patch management, license management, and capacity planning based on CMDB data. The destruction of data media is carried out exclusively by certified service providers whose destruction certificates are digitally archived and linked to the respective assets in the CMDB.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If a client agent reports an outdated software version, the ITSM system automatically creates an update ticket. The license management tool compares the installed software with the procured licenses and reports under- or over-licensing. The serial numbers of the destroyed hard drives on the service provider's certificate are scanned and assigned to the corresponding asset record in the CMDB.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the integration between CMDB and patch management by tracing the process from vulnerability detection to patch deployment. Destruction certificates are requested on a random basis and compared with the decommissioned assets in the CMDB. A report on the license compliance status is requested.

controls.title: Security during relocations (S) [IT Operations, Building Services]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relocation is planned primarily from a logistical perspective (e.g., hiring a moving company, ordering boxes). Specific information security risks, such as the protection of data media during transport or access control at the old and new locations during the relocation phase, are not systematically considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department is responsible for dismantling and setting up its own systems, but there is no overall security planning. Data media are transported together with the devices in unsealed boxes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews the relocation project manager about specific security measures in the relocation concept. It is checked whether there were instructions on how to handle sensitive documents or data media during the relocation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic checklist for the IT relocation exists. It mainly covers technical aspects such as backing up configurations and data before dismantling. Physical security during transport is only mentioned peripherally. A completeness check after the relocation is only carried out superficially by visual inspection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A backup of all servers is created before the relocation. Employees are instructed to back up their personal data. After the relocation, it is checked whether all large devices (servers, printers) are in the right place. Smaller components or individual hard drives are not explicitly inventoried.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the relocation checklist and assesses its level of detail regarding information security. It is asked how it was ensured that no data media or devices were lost during the relocation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before a relocation, security policies SHOULD be developed or updated in a timely manner. All employees SHOULD be informed about the relevant security measures before, during, and after the relocation. After the relocation, it SHOULD be verified whether the transported goods have arrived completely and undamaged or unchanged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A relocation concept is created that includes a separate section on information security. This section regulates responsibilities, secure transport (e.g., escorting the transporter), control of external personnel, and access regulations. After the relocation, a formal inventory is carried out based on the existing inventory list.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the relocation concept and reviews the section on information security. The documentation of the inventory carried out after the relocation is reviewed. It is checked how the employees were informed about the security measures (e.g., via email, in meetings).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A detailed relocation and security plan is created that defines specific protective measures for different asset classes (e.g., sealed and tamper-evident transport containers for servers, only encrypted laptops in transit). External moving companies are contractually obligated to comply with the security policies and their personnel undergo a reliability check. The relocation is accompanied by internal security personnel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The server racks are transported in lockable, sealed roll containers. The seal numbers are logged before and after transport. Employees of the moving company must sign a confidentiality declaration. The truck with critical IT systems is escorted by a security service vehicle.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract with the moving company and checks the security clauses contained therein. The logs of the seal numbers and the documentation of the personnel checks are reviewed. The deployment plan of the security personnel during the relocation is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire relocation of critical assets is continuously monitored by security personnel and technical means. The transport vehicles and critical containers are equipped with GPS trackers whose position is tracked in real time. At the new location, a complete re-inventory and a technical functional and integrity check of all IT systems are carried out before they go back into production. The relocation is accompanied by an independent external audit.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the security control center, the truck's route is tracked live on a digital map. An alarm is triggered in the event of unplanned stops or deviations from the route. At the new location, all systems are checked for physical manipulation (broken seals, additional components). System scans are performed to check software integrity before the systems go back online.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the GPS tracking and the alarm logs. The documentation of the technical integrity checks (e.g., hash value comparisons of system files) at the new location is reviewed. The final report of the external relocation audit is analyzed.

controls.title: Policy for secure IT use (S) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are some disjointed, verbal or emailed instructions on IT use (e.g., 'do not send private emails'). A formal, comprehensive, and binding policy does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instructions are given reactively when misconduct has occurred. New employees do not receive structured instruction on the permitted and prohibited use of IT.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for an official 'Acceptable Use Policy' or a usage policy for IT. New employees are asked what instructions they have received regarding IT use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An IT use policy exists, but it is often outdated, too technical, or formulated in an incomprehensible way. Acknowledgment by employees upon hiring is not systematically required or tracked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is part of a bundle of documents that new employees receive, but it is not explicitly discussed. The document is rarely updated and does not reflect new technologies (e.g., cloud use, social media).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the IT use policy and assesses its currency and comprehensibility. The onboarding process is checked to see if the confirmation of acknowledgment is part of the personnel file.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy SHOULD be created that transparently describes for all employees which framework conditions must be observed for IT use and which security measures must be taken. The policy SHOULD cover security objectives, terms, roles, contact persons, and specific rules of conduct. Every new user SHOULD confirm their acknowledgment in writing. The policy should be freely accessible to all employees for reference.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A clear, understandable 'Acceptable Use Policy' (AUP) is created and published in a prominent place on the intranet. It is part of the hiring documents, and the signature for acknowledgment is filed in the personnel record. The policy covers topics such as password use, email traffic, internet use, and handling mobile devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the AUP and checks its content and availability. Personnel files of recent employees are spot-checked to see if the confirmation of acknowledgment is present. An automated test could check if the link to the AUP on the intranet is accessible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy is reviewed and updated at least annually or in the event of significant technological changes. All employees must re-confirm their acknowledgment of the current version, e.g., via an online portal or a learning management system. The contents of the policy are actively kept in mind through regular, target-group-specific awareness measures (e.g., newsletters, phishing simulations).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual process for reviewing the AUP is defined in the ISMS. After an update, a campaign is launched in which all employees receive an email with a link through which they must read the amended policy and digitally confirm their acknowledgment. The status is tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation and the logs of the annual reviews. The report of the last confirmation campaign is analyzed (e.g., who has not yet confirmed?). Examples of the implemented awareness measures are requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the policy is monitored and enforced by technical means wherever possible and reasonable (e.g., through web content filters, data loss prevention systems, configuration baselines for endpoints). Detected deviations from the target state lead to automated notifications to the user and/or the security department. The policy has a modular structure, and role-specific appendices define specific rules for different user groups (e.g., administrators, external parties).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A DLP system blocks the sending of emails with documents classified as 'internal' to external addresses. A web filter prevents access to websites categorized as dangerous or undesirable. The AUP consists of a general part and specific appendices for roles that are automatically assigned during the granting of permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the configuration of the technical control systems (DLP, web filter) demonstrated and reviews their rule sets. Alarm and event logs from these systems are analyzed for relevant incidents and their handling. It is checked whether the role-specific policies are correctly assigned to the corresponding user groups.

controls.title: Prohibition of carrying mobile phones (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The risk posed by carrying mobile phones into meetings is vaguely known. However, there is no official regulation, only occasional, informal requests from meeting leaders to put phones away.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The issue is handled on a case-by-case basis at the personal discretion of the organizer. There is no uniform procedure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks employees whether there are rules for handling mobile phones in confidential meetings. It is observed whether phones are left openly on the table in meetings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A regulation prohibiting mobile phones in confidential meetings exists on paper, e.g., as part of a general security policy. However, it is not actively communicated or enforced in practice.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The rule is contained in a long policy document, but most employees are not aware of it. Meeting invitations do not include a notice about the ban.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the relevant policies for such a clause. It is checked whether invitations to meetings marked as 'confidential' refer to the ban.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Mobile phones SHOULD NOT be brought to confidential meetings and conversations. Invitations to such meetings and the start of these meetings must explicitly state this prohibition.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a clear policy that mandates this ban for meetings with a 'confidential' or higher protection requirement. The calendar templates for confidential meetings include a standard notice about the carrying ban. The organizer is responsible for reminding participants at the beginning of the meeting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the policy on handling mobile devices. Random calendar invitations for confidential meetings are checked for the corresponding notice. If necessary, the auditor participates in such a meeting to observe whether the notice is given.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For meetings with high protection requirements, compliance with the ban is actively monitored. Secure and easy-to-use storage options for mobile phones (e.g., lockable compartments, 'mobile phone garages') are provided in front of the respective meeting rooms. The ban is permanently indicated in the rooms by clearly visible pictograms and signs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before entering the meeting room, there is a cabinet with small, numbered lockers. The organizer or an assistant actively asks participants to deposit their devices there. Compliance is ensured through social control and the active request.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the meeting rooms declared as highly secure and their surroundings for the presence of signage and storage facilities. It is observed whether participants use the lockers before a meeting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In high-security areas and meeting rooms, the ban on carrying mobile phones is technically enforced and monitored. If necessary, this is checked using mobile phone detectors that trigger an alarm when active transmitting or receiving devices are detected. Access to these areas is only possible after surrendering all private electronic devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A permanently installed or mobile radio frequency (RF) detector is operated in the room. The system is calibrated to react to typical mobile phone signals (GSM, UMTS, LTE, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth) and trigger a silent alarm to security personnel or a visible alarm in the room. Alternatively, checks are carried out before entering the room.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the functionality of the mobile phone detector demonstrated. This involves attempting to bring an active mobile phone into the room and verifying that the alarm is triggered. The system's alarm logs are checked for past events and their handling. An automated test could query the configuration and online status of the detector via an API.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: Every institution needs a responsible department to steer and regulate general operations and to plan, organize, and execute administrative services. Most institutions have an organizational unit for this purpose, which controls the interplay of the various roles and units with the corresponding business processes and resources. Information security aspects must be introduced and bindingly defined at this overarching level.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module lists general and overarching requirements in the area of organization that contribute to increasing and maintaining the level of information security. In this context, information flows, processes, role distributions, as well as the structural and procedural organization must be regulated.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The ORP.1 Organisation module must be applied to the information network at least once. If parts of the information network are assigned to another organisational unit and are therefore subject to different framework conditions, the module should be applied to each unit separately.

The module forms the overarching basis for implementing information security in an institution. It does not cover specific aspects of personnel, employee training, identity and authorisation management, or requirements management. These aspects are covered in the modules ORP.2 Personnel, ORP.3 Information Security Awareness and Training, ORP.4 Identity and Access Management, and ORP.5 Compliance Management (Requirements Management).

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Missing or inadequate regulations
parts.prose:
A lack of regulations can lead to massive security vulnerabilities if, for example, employees do not know how to react to incidents. Problems can also arise from regulations being outdated, impractical, or written in an incomprehensible way.

The importance of these overarching organisational regulations increases with the complexity of the business processes and the scope of information processing, but also with the protection requirements of the information to be processed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Non-observance of regulations
parts.prose:
All employees must be made aware of the applicable regulations and these must be available for reference. Experience shows that it is not enough to simply establish security rules. Communicating them to employees is fundamentally important so that the guidelines can also be put into practice by all concerned in their daily work.

If regulations are disregarded by employees, the following security vulnerabilities can arise, for example:

• Confidential information is discussed within earshot of unauthorised persons, for example in conversations during breaks in meetings or via mobile phone calls in public environments.
• Documents are published on a web server without checking whether they are actually intended and approved for publication.
• Due to incorrectly administered access rights, employees can change data without being able to assess the seriousness of this integrity violation.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Missing, unsuitable, or incompatible operating resources
parts.prose:
If required operating resources are available in insufficient quantities or are not provided on time, disruptions can occur in the institution. It can also happen that unsuitable or even incompatible operating resources are procured, which consequently cannot be used.

Example: The storage space of hard disks in clients and servers as well as mobile data carriers is constantly increasing. It is often forgotten to procure IT components and data carriers that offer sufficient capacity for regular data backup.

The functionality of the operating resources used must also be guaranteed. If maintenance work is not carried out or is carried out inadequately, this can result in high levels of damage.

Examples:

• The capacity of the batteries of an uninterruptible power supply (UPS system) was not checked in time. If the capacity or the acid level is too low, the UPS system can no longer bridge a power failure for a sufficient length of time.
• The fire extinguishers were not maintained in time and therefore no longer have sufficient pressure. Their extinguishing performance is therefore no longer guaranteed in the event of a fire.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Threat from external personnel
parts.prose:
With external personnel, it cannot generally be assumed that they will handle the information and information technology accessible to them in accordance with the regulations of the host institution.

Visitors, cleaning and third-party personnel can endanger internal information, business processes and IT systems in various ways, ranging from improper handling of technical equipment, to attempting to "play" with IT systems, to the theft of documents or IT components.

Examples:

• Unaccompanied visitors can access documents and data carriers or have access to devices, damage them or spy on sensitive information.
• Cleaning staff can accidentally disconnect plugs, let water run into devices, misplace documents or dispose of them with the waste.

controls.title: Regulated onboarding of new employees (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The onboarding of new employees is sporadic and unstructured. Only some employees receive security-relevant information, mostly orally and without traceable documentation. There is no uniform process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, onboarding is often handled by the immediate team, without central guidelines from HR or IT security. Important regulations, such as the IT acceptable use policy, may not be communicated at all or only with a delay.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews a sample of recently hired employees about what information and instructions they received upon hiring. It is checked whether there is any documented evidence of completed onboarding, with the expectation that it will be incomplete or non-existent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic onboarding process that applies to all new employees. The most important regulations and contact persons are named. However, the process is not formalized, and it is not systematically checked whether all information has been understood.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, a standard presentation or a set of documents is handed out to new employees. A contact person is named, but their tasks in the onboarding process are not clearly defined. The documentation of the onboarding is inconsistent.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies whether all new employees receive a basic onboarding. It is checked whether standard documents are provided and a contact person is named. It is expected that there are no formal checklists or confirmations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The HR department and supervisors MUST ensure that employees are onboarded into their new roles at the beginning of their employment. Employees MUST be informed about existing regulations, instructions, and procedures. The process is defined and repeatable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined onboarding plan is created, which specifies the relevant stations, contact persons, and content to be conveyed. The handover of information is documented, for example, by the employee's signature on a receipt confirmation for the IT usage policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the onboarding plans and the associated documentation for a sample of new employees. It is checked whether the defined process is consistently followed and whether all employees have demonstrably been informed about the relevant regulations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined onboarding process is supported by the consistent use of a checklist, which is signed off by employees and supervisors. In addition, each new employee is assigned a dedicated contact person ('buddy' or 'mentor'), whose role and tasks are clearly defined. The onboarding process SHOULD be established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The checklist is centrally managed by the HR department and is accessible to supervisors. The role of the buddy is formalized, and buddies receive a brief introduction to their tasks. The checklist covers administrative, professional, and security-relevant aspects.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the completed onboarding checklists for completeness and correct signing. A sample of new employees and their buddies are interviewed to evaluate the effectiveness of the buddy program.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire onboarding process is integrated into the HR management system and largely automated. New employees go through interactive e-learning modules on information security, the completion of which is linked to the activation of IT permissions. The effectiveness of the process is monitored and continuously improved through regular feedback from new employees and key performance indicators (KPIs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Learning Management System (LMS) is used for security training. The link to the Identity and Access Management (IAM) system ensures that access is only granted after successful completion of the mandatory training. Feedback is collected via automated surveys and analyzed centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the LMS and the IAM system to verify the coupling of training to permissions. Reports from the HR system and the evaluations of the feedback surveys are reviewed to understand the continuous improvement process.

controls.title: Regulated procedure for employee departures (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When employees leave, only the most obvious measures, such as returning keys or laptops, are carried out sporadically. There is no uniform process, which often results in former employees still having active IT accounts or access rights.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process is left to the direct supervisor, who acts without central guidelines or support. The IT department is often not informed or informed too late about the departure date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares a list of recently departed employees with the list of active user accounts in Active Directory. It is expected that active accounts of former employees will be found. A survey of supervisors shows that no standardized procedure exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic offboarding process exists. IT accounts are usually deactivated and physical assets such as laptops and ID cards are reclaimed. However, the transfer of knowledge and the updating of documentation are not systematically regulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HR department informs the IT department about the departure. There is a simple checklist for the return of hardware. The handover of projects and knowledge is the sole responsibility of the departing employee without formal control.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies whether user accounts have been deactivated and the most important assets returned for departed employees. It is checked whether there is basic communication between HR and IT. It is expected that proof of knowledge transfer will be missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When employees leave the institution, their successor MUST be briefed in a timely manner. All documents, keys, devices, as well as ID cards and access authorisations received by departing employees in the course of their work MUST be collected. Furthermore, emergency and other operational plans MUST be updated and all affected parties MUST be informed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized offboarding form is used to document all steps: return of assets, handover of tasks and knowledge, revocation of permissions, and a reminder of the confidentiality obligation. The supervisor is responsible for implementation and documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the completed offboarding forms for a sample of departures. It is verified whether all defined steps, especially the return of assets and the revocation of permissions, were documented in a timely and complete manner.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined offboarding process is supported by a detailed checklist. The handover SHOULD ideally be carried out by the departing employee; if this is not possible, detailed documentation MUST be created. Special care SHOULD be taken to ensure that no conflicts of interest arise, and if necessary, non-compete clauses and cooling-off periods SHOULD be agreed upon. A dedicated contact person in the HR department SHOULD support the process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The offboarding checklist is a central document that is jointly processed by HR, the supervisor, and IT. For positions with increased risk, exit interviews are conducted as standard to identify potential conflicts of interest. The legal framework for cooling-off periods is reviewed and applied.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the offboarding checklists for completeness and the collaboration of the involved departments. It is analyzed whether measures to avoid conflicts of interest (e.g., minutes of exit interviews) have been taken and documented for critical positions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The offboarding process is fully integrated into the HR and IAM system. The departure date triggers an automated workflow that deactivates all permissions (physical and logical) at the exact time of departure, tracks the return of assets, and digitally archives the handover protocols. An automated analysis checks for unusual activities of the departing employee in the last weeks before departure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A workflow management tool, connected to HR, IAM, and asset management systems, controls the process. SIEM rules are used to detect data exfiltration or other anomalous behaviors from accounts that are about to be deactivated. The entire process is seamlessly and audit-proof documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the workflow tool and the logs of the automated permission revocations. The SIEM alerts and the subsequent responses for a sample of departures are checked. The audit-proof nature of the digital archives is verified.

controls.title: Definition of substitution rules (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Substitution rules exist only informally and for a few, selected key personnel. In the absence of other employees, work processes regularly come to a standstill because tasks cannot be taken over.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Teams arrange substitutions ad-hoc and without formal instruction. There is no central overview of critical functions and their substitution. Knowledge is often tied to individuals (knowledge silos).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks team leaders and employees how substitution is handled in case of absence. It is expected that no written or systematic regulations can be presented and that process interruptions during vacation or illness are considered normal.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A substitute is named for most roles. However, the substitution rules are not detailed, and it is not systematically ensured that the substitute has the necessary knowledge and required permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A substitute is entered in team lists or out-of-office notices. However, an orderly handover or training of the substitute usually does not take place. Permissions for the substitution case are often requested ad-hoc.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews team documentation and absence calendars for named substitutes. Interviews determine whether the named substitutes would actually be able to take over the tasks and whether they have the necessary permissions. Gaps in preparation are expected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Supervisors MUST ensure that substitution rules are implemented in ongoing operations. For this, it MUST be ensured that there are practicable substitution rules for all essential business processes and tasks. In these rules, the scope of tasks for the substitution MUST be clearly defined in advance. It MUST be ensured that the substitute has the necessary knowledge for this.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For critical functions, a list of tasks is created that must be taken over in the event of a substitution. The supervisor determines who will take over the substitution and ensures appropriate documentation or briefing. The necessary permissions are defined in advance and can be activated if required.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: For a sample of essential business processes, the auditor requests the documentation of the substitution rules. It is checked whether the scope of tasks is clearly defined and whether measures to ensure knowledge (e.g., documentation, training records) exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The substitution rules are proactively managed. If the designated substitute cannot be sufficiently trained, it MUST be checked how to train them or whether sufficient documentation is enough. If, in exceptional cases, it is not possible to appoint an internal substitute, a decision MUST be made early on whether external personnel can be brought in. The rules are reviewed regularly, e.g., annually, for currency and practicability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A qualification and training plan is created for substitutes in critical roles. The decision to use external personnel is formally documented and budgeted. The review of the substitution rules is part of the annual management reviews.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the regular reviews of the substitution rules. It is checked whether there are documented decisions on the training of substitutes or the use of external personnel. The qualification plans for substitutes are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Substitution rules are stored in a skill management system that actively matches the qualifications of employees and potential substitutes and identifies training needs. For highly critical roles, there are at least two named and fully qualified substitutes (N+1 redundancy principle). The activation of substitution permissions is automated and time-limited via the IAM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The skill management system is linked to the HR and training database. The IAM system supports 'firefighter' roles or temporary privilege escalations, the use of which is logged and monitored. Regular, unannounced tests of the substitution rules (e.g., during a planned vacation) ensure functionality.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the skill management system and the reports on qualification gaps. The logs of the automated permission activations in the IAM system are checked. Proof of conducted tests of the substitution rules and their results are requested.

controls.title: Definition of regulations for the use of external personnel (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: External personnel are deployed without clear security guidelines. There are no uniform rules for briefing, supervision, or offboarding. The handling of external personnel is left to the respective department.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Externals often receive uncontrolled access to internal systems and information. There is no formal briefing on internal policies. After the end of the contract, accounts and access rights often remain active.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews departments that work with external personnel about the applicable processes and rules. It is expected that no or only informal rules exist. A comparison of active user accounts with the list of current external employees is likely to reveal orphaned accounts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are basic regulations for the use of external personnel. They are contractually obligated to comply with laws and regulations. A basic briefing takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Standard contractual clauses are used. External personnel receive a brief induction from the department. The accounts are usually deactivated manually after the end of the contract, but without a formal offboarding process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contracts with service providers for basic security clauses. It is checked on a random basis whether a briefing has taken place and whether the accounts were deactivated after the end of the contract.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If external personnel are employed, they MUST be obligated, like all internal employees, to comply with applicable laws, regulations, and internal rules. Long-term external personnel MUST be briefed on their tasks like internal employees. If the external personnel leave the institution, work results MUST be properly handed over and access rights MUST be returned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a defined process for the entire lifecycle of external personnel (onboarding, management, offboarding). This process is managed by the HR department or a central coordination office. All external employees must verifiably acknowledge the institution's security policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the process documentation for the use of external personnel. Using a sample, the entire process from hiring to departure is checked, including the evidence of acknowledgment of the policies and the logged return of permissions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined process is extended. External personnel who are employed for a short term or on a one-off basis MUST be supervised in security-relevant areas. A substitution rule MUST also be introduced for long-term external personnel. Compliance with the regulations is checked regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For short-term assignments, there is a clear visitor and escort policy. For long-term external employees, substitution rules are established and documented analogously to internal employees. Compliance with the rules is verified by spot checks by the internal contact person or the security department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the regulations for the supervision of short-term external personnel and the documentation of substitution rules for long-term external personnel. Evidence of performed checks and their results is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of external personnel is managed via an automated system (e.g., an Identity and Access Management system with functionality for external parties). Permissions are granted according to the principle of least privilege and have a fixed expiration date. The activities of external personnel in sensitive systems are intensively monitored, and deviations from expected behavior automatically trigger alarms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system automatically provisions and deprovisions external accounts based on contract data from the procurement system. The roles and permissions for external personnel are severely restricted and clearly defined. SIEM use cases are specifically tailored to monitor the activities of external personnel.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the IAM system for managing external personnel, especially the automatic expiration dates and the defined roles. The SIEM rules and the associated alarms for external personnel accounts are reviewed. The effectiveness of the monitoring is verified using examples.

controls.title: Confidentiality agreements for the use of external personnel (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Confidentiality agreements (NDAs) with external personnel are only concluded in exceptional cases or for very critical projects. A systematic requirement does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision to conclude an NDA is at the discretion of the individual department or project manager. There is no standard template.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a sample of projects with external involvement and checks whether NDAs exist. It is expected that this will only be the case for a small proportion of cases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a standard template for confidentiality agreements. This is generally used for external personnel who are active for a longer period or in sensitive areas. However, its use is not mandatory for all external personnel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The legal or HR department provides an NDA template. The departments are instructed to use it, but compliance is not consistently tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a standard template for NDAs exists. Using contract documents, random checks are performed to see in which cases the template was used. Inconsistencies in application are expected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before external persons receive access to confidential information, confidentiality agreements MUST be concluded with them in writing. These agreements MUST take into account all important aspects for the protection of the institution's internal information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A binding process is established that ensures no external employee gains access to systems or data before a valid, signed confidentiality agreement is in place. The HR or purchasing department is responsible for the administration and archiving of these documents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the signed confidentiality agreements for a sample of external employees. It is checked whether these were signed before access was granted and whether the templates used cover all necessary protection aspects. The 'no NDA, no access' process is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The standard confidentiality agreement is regularly reviewed (e.g., annually) by the legal department for up-to-dateness and legal effectiveness and adapted if necessary. There are different, adapted NDA templates for different protection requirement classes of information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process for the regular review of NDA templates is defined and documented. The selection of the appropriate template is based on a classification of the information to which the external employee will have access. This classification is carried out by the information owner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation on the revision of the NDA templates. It is checked whether a process for selecting the correct template based on data classification exists and is applied. This is verified using project and contract documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for concluding confidentiality agreements is fully digitized and automated. The signing is done via a qualified electronic signature. The validity of the NDA is stored in the IAM system, and access to information is automatically blocked if the NDA expires or is revoked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document management system with workflow functions and an interface to a service for qualified electronic signatures is used. The IAM system reads the metadata (e.g., validity date) of the NDAs from the DMS and controls access permissions based on this.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the digitized workflow from sending to archiving the NDA. The configuration of the interface between the DMS and IAM system is checked. Test cases are used to verify that an expired NDA leads to the automatic revocation of access.

controls.title: Tasks and responsibilities of employees (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Tasks and responsibilities are only vaguely defined. Employees are not aware of their specific responsibilities for information security. Regulations are only communicated verbally and incompletely.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Job descriptions are very general or outdated. Security-related tasks are not explicitly named. The awareness that information security is part of every task is largely absent.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions employees about their tasks and their responsibility regarding information security. It is expected that the answers will be vague and limited to general statements. Written, detailed job descriptions cannot be provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Tasks and responsibilities are documented in basic form in job descriptions. Employees are encouraged to comply with internal regulations, but they are not always aware of the specific regulations and the legal framework in detail.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every employee has a job description. General obligations to comply with policies are set out in the employment contract. However, there is no systematic communication of the specific policies relevant to the role.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews job descriptions and employment contracts. It is checked whether basic responsibilities are defined. Interviews are used to determine whether employees know the most important policies for them.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees MUST be obliged to comply with applicable laws, regulations, and internal rules. Employees MUST be aware of the legal framework of their activities. The tasks and responsibilities of employees MUST be documented in a suitable manner. Employees MUST be made aware of the need to protect the institution's information security outside of working hours and off the business premises.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Detailed, up-to-date job descriptions or role profiles are available and accessible to all employees. As part of the onboarding process and through regular training, it is ensured that employees are familiar with the regulations relevant to them. The commitment to compliance is documented (e.g., by signing a declaration of commitment).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the corresponding job descriptions and evidence of the commitment to comply with the regulations for a sample of roles. It is checked whether the documentation clearly describes the security-relevant tasks and responsibilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Tasks and responsibilities, especially those with a security relevance, are regularly reviewed and updated if necessary (e.g., annually or in case of organizational changes). All employees are explicitly informed that information received during work is intended for internal use only. Targeted awareness measures are carried out to strengthen security awareness for activities outside the company premises (e.g., in the home office, when traveling).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process for the regular review of job descriptions is established and linked to the annual HR cycle. Specific awareness campaigns (e.g., on phishing, secure mobile working) are carried out and their participation is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the reviews of job descriptions. The content and participant lists of the awareness campaigns are checked. Interviews are used to evaluate the employees' awareness of information protection in mobile working.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Roles, tasks, and responsibilities are stored in a central Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC) tool or an HR system and are directly linked to the assigned permissions in the IAM system (Role-Based Access Control). Any change to a role automatically triggers a review of the permissions and the necessary training. Compliance with the duties is monitored through technical controls and regular, automated reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An RBAC model is fully implemented. The GRC tool manages the rule set and the assignment to roles. The IAM system technically implements the permissions. Regular 'User Access Reviews' are initiated automatically, in which supervisors must confirm the permissions of their employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the role model defined in the GRC tool and its technical implementation in the IAM system. The logs of the automated 'User Access Reviews' are evaluated. Test cases are used to check whether a role change triggers the correct workflow for adjusting rights and training.

controls.title: Qualification of personnel (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The qualification of the personnel is checked upon hiring, but is not systematically developed thereafter. Training takes place only sporadically and in an uncoordinated manner. There is a risk that employees work with outdated knowledge.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no central training budget or program. Further training is the employee's own initiative. Security-relevant training is missing or not mandatory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions employees and managers about the training opportunities and qualification processes. It is expected that no systematic approach can be proven. Certificates or training records are only available in isolated cases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Required qualifications for positions are defined in the job advertisement. There is an annual budget for further training, but no structured plan to specifically close knowledge gaps. General security awareness training is offered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Job advertisements contain requirement profiles. Employees can apply for training within a budget. Participation in an annual security training is recommended, but not always tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews job advertisements for defined qualifications. It is checked whether a training budget exists and how it is used. The auditor verifies whether general security training exists and what the participation rate is.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees MUST be regularly trained or further educated to ensure that no employee works with outdated knowledge. When filling positions, the required qualifications and skills MUST be precisely formulated. It MUST be ensured that positions are only filled by employees who are qualified for them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The required qualifications and training needs are defined for each role. In the hiring process, the qualifications of applicants are systematically checked. There is an annual, mandatory training plan for security-relevant topics, the implementation of which is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the qualification profiles for a sample of roles. The process for checking applicant qualifications is analyzed. The training plans and proof of participation for the mandatory security training courses are inspected and checked for completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees SHOULD be given the opportunity to pursue further training within their field of activity during their employment. Subsequently, it SHOULD be checked whether applicants for the position actually possess the required qualifications. Training needs are determined and planned not only on a general basis, but also individually in the context of employee appraisals.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Individual development plans are an integral part of the annual employee appraisals. The hiring process may include practical tests or case studies to verify actual skills. There is a central range of further training courses from which employees and managers can choose.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews anonymized records of employee appraisals or development plans to verify the process of individual needs assessment. The hiring process is analyzed to determine if and how practical qualification checks are conducted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A skill management system is used to record the qualifications of all employees, compare them with the requirements of the roles, and proactively identify training needs. The system is linked to a Learning Management System (LMS) that offers personalized learning paths. The success of training measures is measured and included in the performance appraisal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The skill management system is integrated into the central HR system. The LMS offers a mix of e-learning, in-person training, and certification programs. Competence acquisition is demonstrated through tests or the attainment of certificates and is incorporated into strategic personnel planning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the skill management system and the competence models defined therein. Reports on identified skill gaps and the resulting training measures are reviewed. The link between proven learning success and personnel development is verified using process documentation and system data.

controls.title: Verification of employee trustworthiness (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The trustworthiness of applicants is not systematically checked. Information in the resume is generally accepted without verification. A check only takes place in individual cases if there is justified suspicion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The focus in the application process is exclusively on professional qualifications. There are no instructions or tools for HR managers to assess trustworthiness.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions HR managers about the process for reviewing application documents. It is expected that no systematic verification steps exist to verify information or assess trustworthiness.

parts.name: statement
