parts.prose: Application documents such as diplomas and certificates are checked for completeness and obvious inconsistencies. A more in-depth verification of the resume does not take place as a standard procedure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: HR managers conduct a visual inspection of the submitted documents. Conspicuous gaps in the resume are addressed in the job interview. However, there is no process to actively verify the information provided (e.g., by contacting previous employers).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process instructions for the application process. It is checked whether a basic review of the documents is planned. It is expected that there is no requirement for active verification of information.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: New employees SHOULD be checked for their trustworthiness before they are hired. As far as possible, all those involved in the personnel selection process SHOULD check whether the applicants' information relevant to assessing their trustworthiness is credible. In particular, it SHOULD be carefully checked whether the submitted resume is correct, plausible, and complete.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a defined process step in the hiring procedure to verify the information in the resume and the certificates. This may include checking educational institutions or obtaining references (with the applicant's consent). HR managers are trained to look for inconsistencies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the process documentation for the hiring procedure. Based on personnel files, a random check is performed to see if and how the trustworthiness check was documented (e.g., notes on the check, references obtained).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for checking trustworthiness is risk-based. For positions with increased protection needs or extensive authorizations, more intensive checks are carried out. Conspicuous information in the resume SHOULD be systematically checked, e.g., through targeted inquiries with previous employers or educational institutions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a classification of positions according to their risk profile. Depending on the risk level, different depths of checks are defined (e.g., simple check, extended check with references, background check). The process is documented and all involved parties are trained accordingly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the classification of the positions and the associated, defined verification procedures. Using examples of high and low classified positions, it is compared whether the corresponding checks have been carried out and documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For positions with very high risk, the trustworthiness check (background screening) is carried out by a specialized, external service provider as standard, as far as legally permissible. The results are documented and demonstrably influence the hiring decision. The process is regularly reviewed for its effectiveness and legal conformity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Framework agreements exist with service providers for background checks. The process is clearly defined, including obtaining the necessary consents from applicants. The results of the check are stored securely and access to them is strictly regulated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contracts with the external service providers and their certifications (e.g., in the area of data protection). The process of commissioning and the handling of the results are checked. The legal admissibility and the obtaining of consent are verified on a random basis.

controls.title: Security Screening (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A security screening is only considered in absolute exceptional cases. There is no established process and no clear criteria for when such a screening is required.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The need for a security screening is discussed on an ad-hoc, project-related basis, but is rarely implemented due to a lack of knowledge about the process and the legal basis (e.g., Security Screening Act).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks those responsible for high-security areas if and how security screenings are conducted. It is expected that no formal process exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The need for security screenings for handling classified information or for activities in high-security areas is known. Initial, informal checks are carried out, but they do not meet the standard of the Security Screening Act (SÜG).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A police clearance certificate is required for certain roles. However, this does not constitute a full security screening. The exact requirements of the SÜG are not fully implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks for which roles extended reliability checks (such as requesting a clearance certificate) are performed. It is determined that these do not meet the requirements of an SÜG screening.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the high-security area, an additional security screening SHOULD be carried out in addition to the basic check of the trustworthiness of employees. It is defined for which activities or information such a screening is required.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: It is specified in a policy which roles, areas, or information classes require a security screening. The process for initiation and processing is described, but may not yet be fully compliant with the SÜG.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the policy on security screening. It is checked whether the criteria for the necessity of a screening are clearly defined. Using random samples, it is checked whether the defined process has been initiated for the corresponding employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If employees work with information classified according to the classified information protection regulations, the respective employees SHOULD undergo a security screening according to the Security Screening Act (SÜG). In this regard, the Information Security Officer SHOULD involve the institution's classified information protection officer or security representative.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process according to SÜG is established. The role of the classified information protection officer is named and filled. This person works closely with the CISO and the HR department to initiate, manage, and document the screenings. The employees are informed about the process in advance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation for security screenings according to SÜG. The cooperation between CISO, classified information protection officer, and HR is verified using records or communication evidence. It is checked whether the affected employees have demonstrably undergone an SÜG screening.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of security screenings (initial screening, update, repeat screening) is managed in a central system. The results of the screening are directly linked to Identity and Access Management, so that access to VS-classified information is only possible with a valid screening. There is a defined process for the event that a security screening is negative or is not extended.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized software or a module in the HR system is used to manage security clearances. The system monitors the validity periods and automatically initiates the processes for re-screening. In the event of a negative or expired check, the IAM system automatically revokes the corresponding authorizations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the security clearance management system and its configuration. The technical coupling to the IAM system is verified. Using test cases, the process for an expired or negative check is traced, including the automatic revocation of authorizations.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: The personnel of a company or public authority play a decisive role in the success or failure of the institution. The employees have the important task of implementing information security. The most elaborate security precautions can come to nothing if they are not put into practice in everyday work. The fundamental importance of information security for an institution and its business processes must therefore be presented to the personnel in a transparent and comprehensible manner.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to show what "personnel-related" security measures the human resources department or supervisors must take to ensure that employees handle the institution's information responsibly and thus behave in accordance with the guidelines.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The ORP.2 Personnel module is to be applied once for the information network.
The module deals with the requirements that must be observed and fulfilled by the human resources department or the supervisors of an institution. Personnel requirements that are tied to a specific function, such as the appointment of the system administrator of a LAN, are listed in the modules that deal with the respective subject area. The ORP.2 Personnel module does not cover specific aspects of employee training or the management of identities and authorisations. These aspects are dealt with in the modules ORP.3 Awareness and Training for Information Security and ORP.4 Identity and Access Management.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Staff absence
parts.prose: The absence of personnel can lead to certain tasks no longer being performed or not being performed in a timely manner.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficient knowledge of regulations
parts.prose: Simply defining regulations does not guarantee that they will be observed and that operations can function without disruption. All employees must be aware of the applicable regulations, especially those in official functions. Damage that occurs because existing regulations are not known should not be excused with statements such as: "I didn't know I was responsible for that" or "I didn't know how to proceed."

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Carelessness in handling information
parts.prose: It is often observed that while institutions have many organisational and technical security procedures, they are circumvented by the careless behaviour of employees. A typical example of this is a note on the monitor on which access passwords are written.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Insufficient qualifications of employees
parts.prose: Many disruptions and errors can occur in the daily IT operations of an institution. If the responsible employees are not sufficiently qualified, sensitised, and trained, e.g. they have an outdated level of knowledge for their tasks, they might not identify security-relevant events as such, and attacks could go undetected. Even if the employees are sufficiently qualified, sensitised, or trained for the concerns of information security, it still cannot be ruled out that they will not recognise security incidents. In some situations, such as staff shortages or resignations, it may happen that employees have to temporarily take over the tasks of other employees. Errors can arise here if employees do not have the necessary qualifications or are insufficiently trained to take on the task.

controls.title: Raising Information Security Awareness among Institutional Management

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The need for information security is recognized by individual members of the institutional management, but there is no formal resolution to support awareness measures. Support is sporadic and reactive to individual incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, there are typically no dedicated resources for management awareness. The topic is only addressed when there is an acute reason, e.g., a successful phishing attack on an executive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with various members of the institutional management whether there is a basic but inconsistent understanding of security risks. Minutes of management meetings are reviewed to verify that the topic of information security is not discussed regularly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institutional management has formally recognized the importance of information security and approved the implementation of an awareness program. However, support is rather passive and limited to the release of budgets.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a year, as part of budget planning, an item for security training is approved. Management expects a brief report on the measures taken but shows little active engagement beyond that.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of an official document (e.g., a management resolution) that confirms support for the training program. The financial resources provided are checked. Interviews reveal the management's knowledge of the program, but also their lack of active participation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Institutional management MUST be made sufficiently aware of security issues. Security campaigns and training measures MUST be supported by the institutional management. Before starting an awareness and training program, the support of the institutional management MUST be obtained. All supervisors MUST support information security by setting a good example and demanding compliance with the regulations from their employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The support is documented by a formal resolution of the institutional management. Supervisors are instructed in their role as role models and multipliers and, if necessary, receive separate briefings tailored to their leadership role. Compliance with security regulations is made a topic in employee appraisals.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks for the presence of a management resolution to support the program. Through random interviews with supervisors and employees, it is verified that the role model function is being fulfilled and that compliance with security rules is actively communicated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institutional management actively participates in awareness measures, e.g., through personal addresses at events or written forewords in newsletters. The effectiveness of the security culture is regularly reported to the management using key figures, which they actively evaluate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ISO prepares a quarterly report on the security situation and the progress of the awareness program. This report contains key figures such as phishing rates or the number of reported incidents and is discussed in the management committee. The communications department is involved to make the active participation of the management visible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews evidence of management's active participation in campaigns (e.g., videos, emails, intranet articles). Minutes of management meetings are reviewed to verify the regular discussion of security metrics.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information security is a firm and strategic component of institutional management. The promotion of a positive security culture is anchored in the target agreements of the executives. The management proactively requests resources and initiates strategic security projects based on threat analyses and program feedback.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The target agreement systems for executives are supplemented by the HR department with measurable criteria for security culture (e.g., reduction of incidents in the area of responsibility). The management uses a dedicated security dashboard with real-time KPIs for strategic decisions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the target agreement documents of executives. In interviews with the institutional management, their strategic vision for information security and their knowledge of current threats and internal key figures are assessed. The existence and use of a management dashboard for security is verified.

controls.title: Briefing of staff on the secure use of IT

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal briefing on the secure use of IT systems is only provided for selected groups of people, such as administrators. There is no structured instruction for the general staff. Guidelines are outdated or not easy to find.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The briefing is often limited to handing over access data and a verbal reference to the IT department in case of problems. Existing guidelines are usually only available on the intranet and are not explicitly mentioned during hiring.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews a random sample of employees hired in the last six months about their IT security briefing. It is checked whether the provided guidelines are up-to-date and easily accessible to a normal user.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All new employees receive a standardized initial briefing on IT security basics as part of their hiring process. General guidelines are provided that cover basic usage.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The briefing is typically carried out through a short presentation by the IT department on the first day of work or through a standard document (e.g., "IT User Regulations"), the acknowledgment of which must be signed. There is no role-specific differentiation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the onboarding documents for new employees for the standardized briefing component. It is checked whether a signed acknowledgment of the IT guidelines is available for all employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees and external users MUST be instructed and made aware of the secure use of IT, ICS, and IoT components, insofar as this is relevant to their work contexts. For this purpose, binding, understandable, and up-to-date guidelines for the use of the respective components MUST be available. If a system is used in a way that contradicts the interests of the institution, this MUST be communicated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The briefing is an integral part of the onboarding process and is documented. The guidelines are maintained centrally and versioned in a location accessible to all (e.g., intranet portal) and are actively communicated in the event of significant changes. Externals receive a customized version of the guidelines.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the documented process for briefing staff and externals. The timeliness and clarity of the guidelines are checked. Random checks on recently briefed employees verify whether the core content has been understood.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The initial briefing is supplemented by regular, mandatory refresher courses. The provided guidelines and instructions are tailored to specific roles and contain practical examples and instructions for daily work. Understanding is checked through simple tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the general briefing, there are specific modules for target groups such as personnel with access to sensitive data or for mobile work. The refresher course is conducted annually via an e-learning tool with a final quiz. The results are recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the role-specific training materials and the records of participation in the refresher courses. The results of the comprehension tests are evaluated on a random basis to assess their effectiveness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The briefing and training is an interactive and continuous process that is anchored throughout the employee life cycle. It includes role-based learning paths and practical exercises, such as phishing simulations. The effectiveness of the training is continuously measured and the content is dynamically adapted to new threats and technologies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Learning Management System (LMS) is used to manage the learning paths. When a role changes, new, relevant training modules are automatically assigned. The results of phishing simulations flow directly into individualized short training sessions for affected employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and content of the LMS. The coupling between HR processes (e.g., role change) and the training system is verified. The effectiveness is assessed by analyzing trend data (e.g., click rates in phishing simulations over time).

controls.title: Conception and planning of an awareness and training program for information security

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Ad-hoc awareness measures are carried out, usually in response to current events (e.g., a warning in the newsletter). There is no overall concept or annual plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Planning is limited to the next quarter or is purely event-driven. There is no analysis of target groups or the specific risks of the institution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and by reviewing the measures taken that they are uncoordinated and reactive. The absence of a planning document or concept is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a simple annual plan for security training. This plan lists generic topics (e.g., 'Secure Passwords', 'Phishing') and is aimed at all employees equally. A rough distinction is made between general users and IT staff.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The plan is created by the ISO and is based on general best practices. It includes a schedule and the intended formats (e.g., e-learning, poster campaign). A in-depth analysis of target groups or risks is missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the annual plan and compares it with the measures actually implemented. It is checked whether the plan is based on generic assumptions and no specific target group analysis is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A target-group-oriented awareness and training program SHOULD be created. This SHOULD be based on a target group analysis to focus the measures on specific requirements and backgrounds. The program SHOULD provide all information and skills necessary for implementing the applicable security regulations, and it SHOULD be regularly reviewed and updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: First, an analysis is performed to identify different target groups (e.g., management, developers, assistants, production) and their specific information needs. Based on this, an annual program with different modules, formats, and learning objectives is created. The program is reviewed annually for its relevance and effectiveness.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and quality of the target group analysis. The training program is analyzed to determine whether it addresses the identified needs. Furthermore, the process for regular review and updating of the program is verified (e.g., through minutes of review meetings).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training program is based on the results of the institution's own risk management processes. A mix of different didactic methods (e.g., e-learning, workshops, simulations) is planned to appeal to different learning types. The plan includes clear key performance indicators (KPIs) for measuring success.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The top risks identified in risk management (e.g., ransomware via phishing, data leakage via social engineering) are translated into concrete learning objectives for the relevant target groups. The plan specifies that success is measured, for example, by the click rate in phishing simulations or the number of reported security incidents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the content of the training program with the documented results of the risk analysis. The methodological diversity of the program is evaluated, and the definition of the KPIs is checked for their appropriateness and measurability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The design of the program is a dynamic, continuous process. The plan is continuously adapted based on the external threat landscape (threat intelligence), internal incident analyses, audit results, and employee feedback. The planning is fully integrated into the HR lifecycle and uses gamification approaches to increase motivation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cross-functional team (ISO, HR, Communications, Works Council) meets quarterly to adapt the plan. Current attack vectors are analyzed and promptly implemented into new micro-learnings or warning messages. A point system or badges reward particularly security-conscious behavior.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the agile planning process by inspecting protocols, ticket systems, or other artifacts. It is checked how quickly and effectively new threats or internal incidents are responded to with adjustments in the training plan. The effectiveness of the gamification elements is evaluated.

controls.title: Conducting awareness and training on information security

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Trainings are offered only irregularly and on a voluntary basis. Participation is not tracked, and the content only reaches a small part of the workforce.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, lunch sessions or optional webinars are offered, the existence of which is only communicated via the newsletter. There is no obligation to participate.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the announcements for the training sessions and the (mostly non-existent) participant lists. Interviews with employees confirm the voluntary and sporadic nature of the measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An annual, mandatory security training is conducted for all employees. This usually consists of a standardized measure, such as an e-learning module.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All employees receive an automatic invitation to the annual security awareness training. The HR department or the supervisor is responsible for ensuring participation, which is often done through manual list comparisons.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the annual mandatory training and checks the participant lists for completeness. It is noted that the training is identical for all employees (one-size-fits-all).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees SHOULD be trained on information security topics according to their roles and responsibilities. The training SHOULD be conducted systematically according to the planned, target-group-oriented program.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on the training program, the identified target groups are invited to the trainings relevant to them. Participation is mandatory and is tracked centrally, e.g., in a Learning Management System (LMS). Supervisors receive reports on the training status of their teams.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the trainings conducted with the training plan. Based on participant lists and system logs, it is verified that the right employees have participated in the trainings intended for them. The process for tracking participation is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The trainings are conducted using a didactic mix to increase effectiveness. In addition to e-learnings, interactive workshops, live demonstrations, and regular awareness campaigns (e.g., phishing simulations, posters) are implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Phishing simulations are conducted quarterly. Developers receive a bi-annual workshop on Secure Coding. Management receives an annual presentation on the current threat landscape. These measures supplement the basic e-learnings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews artifacts from the various training formats (e.g., workshop materials, phishing simulation reports, posters). It is assessed whether the method mix is appropriate for the respective target groups and topics.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The execution of the trainings is highly automated and personalized. The learning experience is interactive and engaging. The results from attack simulations lead to an immediate, automated assignment of in-depth learning content for affected employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A security awareness platform is used that integrates phishing simulations, e-learning, and reporting. If an employee clicks on a phishing link, they are immediately directed to a learning page and automatically assigned a short training module on the topic. The execution is continuously optimized based on effectiveness measurements (A/B testing of campaigns).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the security awareness platform and the degree of automation. The workflow from simulation through detection to personalized follow-up training is reviewed. Reports on effectiveness measurement and optimization are inspected and evaluated.

controls.title: Training on the procedure according to IT-Grundschutz

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Information Security Officer (ISO) has familiarized themselves with IT-Grundschutz through self-study. There is no formal training or certification.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The knowledge is based on reading the BSI websites and the Grundschutz building blocks. There is a lack of structured methodological training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In an interview with the ISO, the auditor determines that although basic knowledge is present, methodological knowledge for implementing IT-Grundschutz (e.g., structural analysis, protection needs assessment) is incomplete. There are no training certificates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The ISO has participated in a basic training course on IT-Grundschutz, for example by completing the BSI online course or attending an introductory event.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ISO can present a certificate of participation for the BSI online course or a comparable basic training. The institution has facilitated the participation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the proof of completion of the basic training. In an interview, it is verified whether the basic concepts and methodology of IT-Grundschutz have been understood.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information Security Officers SHOULD be familiar with IT-Grundschutz. If a training need has been identified, a suitable IT-Grundschutz training SHOULD be planned and conducted, in which the procedure is practiced using practical examples. It SHOULD be checked whether the ISO should qualify as a BSI IT-Grundschutz Practitioner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The training need of the ISO is formally identified. The institution plans and finances the participation in an official training to become a BSI IT-Grundschutz Practitioner with a licensed training provider. The planning considers the BSI online course as preparation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the process for identifying the training need. It is checked whether a plan for a qualifying training exists or has already been carried out. The selection of the training provider is checked for its BSI licensing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The ISO has successfully completed the training to become a BSI IT-Grundschutz Practitioner with an exam and holds the corresponding certificate. They keep their knowledge up-to-date by regularly participating in professional events, webinars, or BSI events.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ISO's certificate is on file. In the annual training plan, budgets are planned for participation in conferences (e.g., BSI Security Congress) or update trainings. The ISO subscribes to relevant newsletters and professional media.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the valid certificate for IT-Grundschutz Practitioner. Evidence of continuous professional development is reviewed (e.g., certificates of attendance, travel expense reports for conferences).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The ISO or the head of the IS management team holds the advanced certification as a BSI IT-Grundschutz Consultant. The institution actively promotes further training in related or specialized subject areas (e.g., ISO/IEC 27001, ICS security, cloud security). Knowledge is systematically shared and documented within the team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an IS management team in which competencies are bundled and further developed. Internal knowledge sessions are held regularly. The institution uses an ISMS tool that methodologically supports the application of IT-Grundschutz.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the advanced certificates (Consultant certificate). The process of internal knowledge management in the security team is reviewed (e.g., by inspecting an internal wiki or minutes of team meetings). The team's qualification is assessed in relation to the complexity of the information network.

controls.title: Measurement and evaluation of learning success

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The success of training measures is measured exclusively by quantitative participation numbers. It is not checked whether the content has been understood or leads to a change in behavior.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After a training session, only a list of participants is archived. There are no tests, surveys, or other feedback mechanisms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes that the only available metrics are participant lists. Interviews confirm that no qualitative success measurement takes place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: At the end of e-learning modules, simple comprehension tests (quizzes) are conducted to check immediate knowledge acquisition. The results are collected but not systematically evaluated to improve the program.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The e-learning tool automatically generates a report with the quiz results. This is noted and filed by the ISO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports from the comprehension tests. It is noted that while the data is collected, it is not used for trend analysis or to identify knowledge gaps in specific target groups.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Learning success SHOULD be measured and evaluated on a target-group basis to determine the extent to which the described objectives have been achieved. The measurements SHOULD consider both quantitative (participation) and qualitative (comprehension, behavioral change) aspects. The results SHOULD be incorporated into the improvement of the training offerings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple set of key performance indicators (KPIs) is defined, e.g., participation rate per department, average score in the final test, results from feedback forms. These KPIs are evaluated annually, and the results are summarized in a report that serves as the basis for planning for the next year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the definition of the KPIs and the data collection process. The evaluation report from the previous year is reviewed, and it is checked whether the findings contained therein have demonstrably been incorporated into the planning for the following year.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Advanced methods such as phishing simulations are used to measure learning success and behavioral change. The results (e.g., click rate, reporting rate) are systematically collected and analyzed. Other data sources, such as helpdesk requests or audit findings, are also used to assess program effectiveness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The click and reporting rates of phishing simulations are recorded per target group and monitored over time. A decreasing number of helpdesk tickets for forgotten passwords can be seen as an indicator of the effectiveness of the password training. The results are regularly reported to management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports of the phishing simulations and the trend analyses. The process for correlating training measures with other data sources (e.g., ticketing system) is checked. The management reports on effectiveness are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive metric framework is implemented that continuously measures the effectiveness of the awareness program and correlates it with real security incidents. The data analysis is partially automated to identify risk groups and accelerate the feedback loop for program improvement. A/B tests are used to optimize the effectiveness of different campaigns.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A security dashboard visualizes the KPIs in real time. It is analyzed whether departments with more intensive training show a lower number of security incidents. Before rolling out a new campaign, different versions are tested on test groups to determine the most effective variant.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the KPI framework and the dashboard for their significance and technical implementation. The process for correlating training data with incident data is verified. The methodology and results of the A/B tests are checked.

controls.title: Special training for exposed persons and institutions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general awareness that certain individuals (e.g., the management) are particularly at risk. However, only informal, unstructured advice is given to these individuals, usually in response to high-profile attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CISO forwards a warning about CEO fraud to the management without offering dedicated training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In interviews with exposed individuals, the auditor determines that no formal training tailored to their role has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A group of exposed individuals is defined (e.g., senior management, their assistants). This group receives a one-time, standardized special training on typical risks such as CEO fraud or travel security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a year, a workshop is held for the defined group of individuals, covering general risks for executives. Participation is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the definition of the group of exposed individuals and checks the documents and participant lists of the special training.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Highly exposed individuals SHOULD receive in-depth training regarding potential threats as well as appropriate behaviors and precautionary measures. A process is established to identify these individuals and regularly offer them training.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on a risk assessment, exposed individuals and roles (e.g., management, R&D leadership, system administrators with extensive rights) are identified. A recurring, mandatory training program is established for this group, addressing their specific threat situation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the process for identifying exposed individuals. The training plans and content for this group are evaluated to determine whether they address the specific risks. The regular and mandatory participation is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training for exposed individuals is highly personalized and based on the individual's or role's risk profile. It includes interactive elements and practical exercises, such as simulated spear-phishing attacks or social engineering attempts by phone.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the training, the person's public online profile is analyzed to demonstrate realistic attack vectors. The training is conducted as personal coaching or in a small group and covers specific scenarios (e.g., protecting research data at conferences).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the personalized training concepts and the results of the practical exercises. The relevance and effectiveness of the training are assessed in confidential interviews with the trained individuals.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training and protection concept for exposed individuals is a continuous, dynamic process based on person-specific threat intelligence. It also includes the private environment (e.g., securing the home network, social media behavior of the family) and advanced topics such as counter-surveillance measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution commissions specialized external service providers for coaching and threat analysis. Regular, unannounced, and sophisticated attack simulations are conducted. The individuals are provided with technical tools for secure communication.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contracts and reports of the external specialists. The methodology of the person-specific threat analysis is evaluated. The appropriateness and effectiveness of the entire protection concept, including technical and private aspects, is assessed.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Employees are an important success factor for a high level of information security in an institution. It is therefore important that they know the security objectives, that the security measures are understandable, and that each individual employee is willing to implement them. The prerequisite for this is that there is a security awareness within the institution. In addition, a security culture should be established and brought to life in day-to-day work.
Employees must be made aware of relevant threats and know how they can affect their institution. They must know what is expected of them in terms of information security and how they should react in security-critical situations.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module describes how to build and maintain an effective information security awareness and training programme. The aim of the programme is to raise employees' awareness of security risks and to provide them with the necessary knowledge and skills for security-conscious behaviour.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The ORP.3 Awareness and Training for Information Security module is to be applied once for the information network.
This module formulates requirements for awareness and training on information security that concern the working environment in the institution, the teleworking workplace, and mobile working.
The ORP.3 Awareness and Training for Information Security module describes the procedural, technical, methodological, and organisational requirements for awareness and training on information security. Further training topics are planned, designed, and carried out by the human resources department or the continuing education management.
Many of the other IT-Grundschutz modules describe specific training content on the topics considered there. This module deals with how a systematic approach can be efficiently designed in the areas of awareness and training on information security.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient knowledge of regulations
parts.prose: Simply establishing information security regulations does not guarantee that they will be observed. All employees, especially those elected to a function, must also be aware of the applicable regulations. In many security incidents, non-compliance with regulations is not the sole cause of the incident, but it is one of the reasons for its occurrence. Security vulnerabilities due to insufficient knowledge of regulations can jeopardise the confidentiality, availability and integrity of the information being worked with. The fulfilment of tasks and the handling of business processes and professional tasks can be restricted as a result.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficient awareness of information security
parts.prose: Experience shows that it is not enough to simply order security measures. Employees should understand the meaning and purpose of the measures, as they might otherwise be ignored in everyday work. If employees are insufficiently sensitised to information security topics, the institution's security culture, security objectives and security strategy may be jeopardised.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Ineffective awareness and training activities
parts.prose:
The activities carried out for awareness and training are not always as successful as desired. The reasons for this can be:
• a lack of management support,
• unclear objectives,
• poor planning,
• lack of performance monitoring,
• lack of continuity, and
• insufficient financial or human resources.
If no suitable measures are taken to ensure the success of the activities carried out, the objective of the respective training activity can often not be achieved. If the institution carries out insufficient awareness and training activities for its employees, aspects of information security can be endangered, which directly restricts the fulfilment of tasks.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Inadequate training of employees on security functions
parts.prose: Frequently, employees do not use newly introduced security programs and functions because they do not know how to operate them and consider it too time-consuming to familiarize themselves with them in their daily workflow. Furthermore, a lack of training after the introduction of new software can lead to employees operating or configuring it incorrectly, unnecessarily delaying workflows. Therefore, the procurement and installation of (security) software is not sufficient. Especially with critical IT systems and applications, incorrect operation can have existence-threatening consequences.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Undetected security incidents
parts.prose: In the daily operation of IT and ICS components, many disruptions and errors can occur. Security incidents may not be identified as such by personnel, and cyber-attacks or attempted attacks may go undetected. Security incidents and technical errors are sometimes not easy to distinguish. If users and administrators are not specifically trained and sensitized to recognize security incidents and react to them appropriately, security vulnerabilities can remain undiscovered and be exploited. If security incidents are detected too late or not at all, effective countermeasures cannot be taken in time. Small security gaps in the institution can grow into critical threats to integrity, confidentiality, and availability. This can hinder business processes, cause financial damage, or lead to regulatory and legal sanctions.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Disregard of security measures
parts.prose: A wide variety of reasons, such as carelessness or haste, can lead to confidential documents being left openly at workstations or e-mails not being encrypted. Such supposedly minor oversights can cause damage that would not normally happen with well-trained employees.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Carelessness in handling information
parts.prose:
It is often observed that while a variety of organizational and technical security procedures are established in institutions, they are circumvented by the careless handling of employees. A typical example is the almost famous sticky notes on monitors with login passwords written on them. Similarly, hard drive encryption does not protect a laptop on the go from confidential information being read by a neighbor on a train, for instance. The best technical security solutions are of no help if printouts with confidential information are left at the printer or end up in freely accessible waste paper containers.
If employees handle information carelessly, established information security processes become ineffective. Unauthorized persons could, for example, exploit carelessness in handling information to conduct targeted industrial espionage.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Lack of acceptance of information security policies
parts.prose: There can be various reasons why employees do not implement information security policies. These include, for example, a lack of a security culture in the institution or a lack of a role model function by the institution's management. However, excessive security requirements can also lead to employees rejecting security measures. Problems can also arise from the fact that certain authorizations or even the provision of specific hardware or software are seen as a status symbol. Restrictions in these areas can meet with great resistance.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Social Engineering
parts.prose:
Social engineering is a method to gain unauthorized access to information or IT systems by "prying" on employees. In social engineering, the attacker usually establishes direct contact with a victim, e.g., by phone, e-mail, or social networks. Social engineering attacks are often multi-stage. By pretending to have insider knowledge and simultaneously appealing to helpfulness, the attacker can expand their knowledge in further steps. If employees are not sufficiently aware of this type of attack, they could be manipulated through clever communication into acting improperly. This can lead to them disclosing internal information, their IT systems becoming infected with malware, or even transferring money to alleged business partners.
For example, in so-called "CEO fraud," employees who are authorized to transfer money on behalf of the institution are presented with a fictitious order from management. They are supposed to carry out transactions for a supposedly urgent and confidential business deal that is extremely important for the continued existence of the institution.

controls.title: Regulation for the creation and deletion of users and user groups (B) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There MUST be a defined process for creating and deleting user accounts and groups. Each account MUST be uniquely assigned to a person. Inactive accounts SHOULD be deactivated after a defined period. The creation and deletion of accounts and groups MAY ONLY be performed by separate administrative roles. Default accounts (e.g., guest accounts) MUST be deactivated or deleted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process for managing user accounts (Joiner, Mover, Leaver) is documented and known to all responsible administrators. Administration is carried out via dedicated admin accounts, not via the administrators' personal accounts. The deactivation of inactive accounts is supported by a regularly executed script that reports accounts based on the last logon date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor ensures that a documented policy for the user account lifecycle exists. It is checked on a random basis whether newly created accounts followed the process and whether accounts of departed employees were deactivated promptly. The configuration is checked to see if default and guest accounts are deactivated. This can be checked automatically with: `Get-AdUser -Filter * -property LastLogonDate | where { $_.LastLogonDate -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-90) -and $_.enabled -eq $true}` (Example for Active Directory and 90 days of inactivity).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The user account management process is largely automated. The deactivation of inactive accounts is automatic. Regular, logged recertifications of all accounts and groups are carried out by the respective business owners.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Identity Management (IDM) system is used to automate the Joiner-Mover-Leaver process. The IDM is linked to the HR system, so that personnel changes automatically lead to account adjustments. Deactivation and deletion processes are multi-stage (deactivation -> archiving -> deletion).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the IDM system and its integration with the HR system. The logs of the automated deactivation runs and the completed recertification campaigns are reviewed. It is checked whether a workflow for the approval of accounts and groups exists and is being followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of identities (including digital certificates and service accounts) is fully automated and managed by a central, highly integrated Identity and Access Management (IAM) system. The system continuously monitors the validity of accounts and groups and adjusts them in real time if necessary. Anomalies in the account creation process trigger automatic alerts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system is integrated not only with the HR system but also with the Physical Access Control System and other central services. The creation of accounts follows a strict approval workflow with a four-eyes principle for privileged accounts. The deletion of accounts is linked to an audit-proof archiving process for relevant data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration and process logs of the IAM system. It is checked whether the integrations with surrounding systems (HR, etc.) are robust and secure. The effectiveness of the automated controls and alarms is checked through test cases (e.g., simulating a delayed report from HR). The audit-proof nature of the logs and archives is verified.

controls.title: Provisioning, modification, and revocation of permissions (B) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Permissions MAY ONLY be granted according to the principle of least privilege and the need-to-know principle. When personnel changes occur, permissions that are no longer needed MUST be removed. Requests for permissions that go beyond the standard MAY ONLY be granted after additional justification and review. File system permissions SHOULD be restrictive. All permission changes MUST be made via administrative roles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A basic role-based access control (RBAC) concept is used for standard employees. Requests for additional rights are made via a ticketing system and require the approval of the supervisor and, if applicable, the data owner. NTFS permissions are assigned at the group level instead of the user level to simplify administration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the authorization concept. Spot checks of users (especially after a change of department) are carried out to ensure that old permissions have been revoked. Requests in the ticket system are checked for compliance with the approval process. File system permissions on an important share are examined for overly permissive entries (e.g., 'Everyone').

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A detailed RBAC model is implemented and centrally managed. Regular, semi-automated permission recertifications are performed, where managers must confirm the permissions of their employees. The assignment of permissions is largely automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IAM system is used to manage roles and to automate the assignment of rights for joiners, movers, and leavers. Recertification campaigns are controlled and logged via the IAM system. Reports on the current permission landscape can be generated at any time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the RBAC model in the IAM system. The logs of the last recertification campaign are reviewed to assess the completeness and the response of the approvers. It is verified that the mover process in the IAM system correctly performs the automatic adjustment of permissions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dynamic, attribute-based access control (ABAC) system complements or replaces the RBAC model. Access decisions are made in real time based on user attributes, resource properties, and the context of the request. The verification of permissions is fully automated and continuous.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central 'Policy Decision Engine' is used to enforce ABAC policies. This is integrated with all critical applications and data stores. The policies are managed and versioned as code ('Policy as Code'). The system can grant 'Just-in-Time' permissions for a limited period.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the defined ABAC policies and their implementation as code. Test scenarios are conducted to validate the correct real-time decision-making of the Policy Engine (e.g., blocking access from an untrusted device). The logs of access decisions are examined for anomalies.

controls.title: Documentation of user IDs and rights profiles (B) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be documented which user IDs, user groups, and rights profiles are created and permitted. This documentation MUST be regularly reviewed to ensure it reflects the actual status and meets current requirements. The documentation MUST be protected from unauthorized access and SHOULD be included in the data backup procedure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The documentation is maintained in a central database or a protected area on the intranet (e.g., Wiki). The review takes place as part of a semi-annual manual audit, where the documented information is compared with the live system (e.g., Active Directory). Access to the documentation is restricted to administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation and checks its access rights. The date of the last review is verified. Random samples of entries from the documentation are compared with the actual configurations in the target systems to assess their timeliness and correctness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documentation of user IDs, groups, and rights profiles is largely automated through an IAM system or specialized reporting tools. The regular review is supported by automated comparisons between the target concept (in the documentation) and the actual state (in the systems).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Scripts or reporting tools (e.g., PowerShell scripts for Active Directory, reports from the IAM tool) are used to generate nightly reports on all accounts, group memberships, and assigned roles. These reports are versioned and archived to track changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automation scripts used or the configuration of the reporting tools. The generated reports from the last few weeks are reviewed for completeness and correctness. The process for handling deviations reported by the automated comparisons is evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documentation is an integral part of a central IAM system or a CMDB and is updated in real time. Every change to accounts, groups, or roles is automatically logged and documented. The review is a continuous process where deviations from the defined baseline are immediately reported and tracked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system serves as the 'Single Source of Truth' for all identity and permission information. It provides a live dashboard with the current status. Changes can only be made through defined workflows in the IAM system, which ensures consistency between documentation and reality. The data is forwarded to a SIEM system for correlation and anomaly detection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses the live dashboard of the IAM system to audit the current state of permissions. The configuration of the continuous monitoring and alerting rules is reviewed. It is tested whether a manual change made bypassing the system (if possible) is correctly detected and reported as a deviation.

controls.title: Separation of duties and functions (B) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The incompatible tasks and functions defined by the institution MUST be separated by the identity and authorization management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Separation of Duties (SoD) policy is created that defines critical task conflicts (e.g., 'may not create users and assign permissions at the same time'). This policy is used as a basis for review during the manual assignment of permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the SoD policy. Spot checks of the permissions of administrators and other privileged users are carried out to check whether they violate the defined SoD matrix. This is done by manually analyzing the assigned roles and permissions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SoD policy is stored in the IAM system. The system preventively blocks the assignment of conflicting permissions. Automated reports on compliance with the SoD rules are regularly generated and reviewed by an independent body (e.g., information security).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM tool used is configured with the SoD matrix. If an administrator attempts to assign a conflicting permission, the system blocks the action and requires a documented exception process. Monthly SoD reports are automatically generated and distributed to the responsible auditors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the SoD matrix implemented in the IAM system. It is tested whether the system correctly prevents the assignment of a conflicting role. The reports from recent months and the handling of reported exceptions are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SoD controls are comprehensive and also cover complex, cross-application conflicts. The system performs not only preventive but also detective controls in real time and reports violations immediately. The SoD policy is reviewed and refined annually as part of a risk assessment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system has an advanced SoD module that is capable of detecting conflicts across system boundaries (e.g., a person who places an order in the ERP system and approves the same order in the finance system). The SoD analysis is part of the continuous monitoring in the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the completeness and timeliness of the SoD matrix, especially with regard to cross-application processes. Complex test cases are constructed to validate the effectiveness of the SoD controls. The alerts and the response to SoD violations in the SIEM system are analyzed.

controls.title: Assignment of access rights (B) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process MUST be defined for which access rights are granted to or revoked from which persons. The issuance and revocation of access media (e.g., chip cards) MUST be documented. Compromised access media MUST be replaced. Users SHOULD be trained and temporarily blocked during long absences.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The issuance of chip cards is documented in an Excel list that contains the employee's name, the card number, and the assigned access zones. Applications and returns are recorded in writing. If a card is lost, it is manually blocked in the access control system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of card issuance and compares it with the active cards in the access control system on a random basis. The process for blocking a lost card is checked. It is also checked whether the access rights of recently departed employees have been revoked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The physical access control system is integrated with the HR system. The joiner-mover-leaver process automatically triggers the granting, adjustment, or revocation of access rights. Access logs are regularly checked for anomalies (e.g., access attempts outside business hours).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An interface between the HR system (e.g., SAP HR) and the access control system (e.g., Kaba exos) is operated. The access rights are based on roles (e.g., 'Data Center Admin', 'Office Employee') that are stored in the HR system. The logs are sent to a central log management system for analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the interface between the HR and access control systems. The process for a department change is tested to see if the access rights are correctly adjusted. The evaluation of the access logs and the response to detected anomalies are assessed.

controls.title: Assignment of access permissions (B) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process MUST be defined for which access permissions (e.g., VPN) are granted to or revoked from which persons. The issuance and revocation of access means (e.g., tokens) MUST be documented. Compromised access means MUST be replaced. Users SHOULD be trained and temporarily blocked during long absences.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: VPN access is granted upon request via a ticket system and requires the approval of the supervisor. The assignment to specific VPN profiles (e.g., 'Standard User', 'Admin Access') is documented. If a hardware token is lost, the associated account is blocked in the VPN system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the remote access policy. The tickets for assigning VPN access are checked for compliance with the approval process. The list of active VPN users is compared with the list of current employees to find orphaned accounts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The assignment of access rights is integrated into the central IAM system and is based on the role concept. The Joiner-Mover-Leaver process automatically adjusts access rights. Access logs are collected centrally and automatically monitored for suspicious activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VPN system is connected to the central authentication service via RADIUS or SAML. Assignment to VPN groups is done automatically based on membership in Active Directory groups, which are managed by the IAM system. VPN logs are sent to a SIEM, which alerts on multiple failed login attempts or logins from unusual locations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the VPN system's connection to the central authentication service. The automated rules in the SIEM for monitoring VPN access are reviewed. It is verified that the access rights of recently departed employees have been revoked automatically and in a timely manner.

controls.title: Assignment of access rights (B) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process MUST be defined for which access rights (to data and applications) are granted to or revoked from which persons. If chip cards or tokens are used, their issuance and revocation MUST be documented. Users SHOULD be trained for correct handling. In the case of long absences, the rights SHOULD be temporarily suspended.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access to file shares and applications is controlled via an approval process in the ticket system, which requires the consent of the data owner. Implementation is done by manually assigning users to Active Directory groups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented approvals for access to a critical application. The membership in the corresponding AD groups is checked and compared with the list of approved users. The permission structure of an important file share is analyzed for compliance with the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access rights management is carried out via a central IAM system that enforces a role-based access control (RBAC) model. Regular, system-supported recertification campaigns are conducted, in which data owners review and confirm the access rights to their resources.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IAM tool is used to manage the entire lifecycle of access rights. Users can request access via a self-service catalog, which then goes through a defined approval workflow. The results of the quarterly recertification campaigns are logged in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the roles and approval workflows configured in the IAM system. The logs of the last recertification campaign are checked for completeness and timely processing by the approvers. It is verified that rejected or unconfirmed accesses were automatically revoked.

controls.title: Regulation of password use (B) [Users, IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST regulate the use of passwords in a binding manner. Passwords MUST NOT be reused. Easily guessable passwords MUST NOT be used. Passwords MUST be kept secret and MUST ONLY be entered unobserved. They MUST NOT be stored on function keys. A password MAY ONLY be written down for emergency backup purposes and must then be stored securely. The use of a password manager SHOULD be considered; synchronization features via third-party providers MUST be disabled. A password MUST be changed if it is compromised or suspected of being compromised.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A password policy is created, communicated to all employees, and published on the intranet. The policy contains clear rules for creating, using, and storing passwords. The use of a specific password manager approved by IT operations is recommended.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the password policy and checks whether it covers all required aspects and whether it has been communicated to the employees. As part of interviews, employees are randomly asked about their understanding of the password rules. The configuration of the approved password manager is checked for the deactivation of insecure synchronization functions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the password policy is enforced by technical measures. This includes enforcing a password history to prevent reuse, and checking new passwords against a list of known weak and compromised passwords. The use of a centrally managed password manager is mandatory for all employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Active Directory is configured to enforce a password history of at least 12 passwords. A service like 'Have I Been Pwned' (as a local instance or via a secure API) is integrated to check new passwords upon creation. An enterprise password manager (e.g., Bitwarden, 1Password) is centrally deployed and configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the password policy settings in Active Directory (or a comparable service). The implementation of the check for compromised passwords is verified. It is checked whether all employees have licenses for the enterprise password manager and whether its use is monitored.

controls.title: Identification and authentication (B) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to all IT systems and services MUST be secured by appropriate identification and authentication of the accessing entity (user, service, system). Pre-configured authentication credentials (e.g., default passwords) MUST be changed before productive use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All production systems require authentication, usually by username and password. A checklist for commissioning new systems includes an item for changing all default credentials. This also applies to service accounts and API keys.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly selects several IT systems (servers, network components, applications) and verifies that access without authentication is not possible. The commissioning logs are checked to see if the change of default passwords has been documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is provided by a central identity provider (IdP) for most applications (Single Sign-On). Two-factor authentication (2FA) is mandatory for all users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central IdP such as ADFS, Azure AD, or Keycloak is used. Applications are connected to the IdP via standards such as SAML or OpenID Connect wherever possible. All user accounts in the IdP are configured for 2FA use (e.g., via an authenticator app) and its use is enforced.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the IdP and the list of connected applications. It is checked whether the 2FA requirement is technically enforced for all user accounts. The login process for various applications is tested on a sample basis to verify the correct SSO and 2FA functionality.

controls.title: Protection of user accounts with extensive permissions (S) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: User accounts with extensive permissions (e.g., administrator accounts) SHOULD be protected with multi-factor authentication (MFA). Cryptographic certificates, chip cards, or tokens can be used as factors, for example.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy requires the use of MFA for all accounts that are members of privileged groups (e.g., 'Domain Admins', 'Enterprise Admins'). Implementation is done by configuring the central authentication service, which enforces MFA for these user groups. A TOTP-based authenticator app is used as the second factor.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the list of privileged groups and their members. Then, the configuration of the authentication service is checked to ensure that the MFA requirement is correctly and unavoidably configured for these users. A test login with an admin account is performed to verify the MFA prompt.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all administrative access, phishing-resistant MFA methods, such as hardware tokens (FIDO2), are used. Privileged access is made via a dedicated Privileged Access Workstation (PAW) to reduce the attack surface.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All administrators are equipped with FIDO2 security keys (e.g., YubiKeys). The authentication policies are adapted so that only these strong authenticators are accepted for administrative logins. Administrators are only allowed to perform administrative tasks from hardened and strictly monitored PAWs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the authentication policies for the exclusive admission of FIDO2 keys for admin accounts. The configuration and patch level of the PAWs are checked. It is verified that administrative logins from non-PAW systems are successfully blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All privileged access is handled via a Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution. This enforces MFA, credential vaulting, Just-in-Time (JIT) access, and records all administrative sessions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM solution (e.g., CyberArk, Delinea) is implemented. Administrators never authenticate directly to the target systems, but always to the PAM solution. The PAM solution establishes the connection to the target system without the administrator knowing the target system's password. Every session is recorded as a video, and the executed commands are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration of the PAM solution, including the access policies and the connection to the target systems. It is randomly checked whether session recordings are complete and tamper-proof. The process for requesting and approving JIT accesses is analyzed.

controls.title: Resetting passwords (S) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An appropriately secure procedure SHOULD be defined and implemented for resetting passwords. The IT operations staff who can reset passwords SHOULD be trained accordingly. For higher protection needs, a strategy SHOULD be defined in case the responsibility for transmission cannot be assumed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented process for resetting passwords by the IT helpdesk is established. This process requires clear identification of the caller, e.g., by asking for the employee ID and the name of the supervisor. The new, temporary password is communicated to the user on a separate, agreed-upon channel (e.g., by phone) and must be changed at the first login.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process for resetting passwords. The helpdesk tickets are randomly checked to see if the identification process has been documented and followed. It is verified that the system configuration forces a change of the temporary password at the first login.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A secure Self-Service Password Reset (SSPR) portal is provided for all users. Registration for SSPR requires multi-factor authentication. Resetting passwords via the helpdesk is only possible in justified exceptional cases and follows a strict protocol.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SSPR service such as Azure AD or a specialized IAM tool is implemented. Users must register in advance by providing, for example, an alternative email address, a phone number for SMS codes, and security questions. The use of the portal is logged and monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the SSPR portal, particularly the security requirements for registration and use. The portal's logs are examined for suspicious activities (e.g., multiple failed attempts for one account). The exception process for helpdesk resets is reviewed for its security and frequency of use.

controls.title: Development of an authentication concept for IT systems and applications (S) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An authentication concept SHOULD be created. It SHOULD define the functional and security requirements for authentication for each IT system and application. Authentication information MUST be stored cryptographically securely and MUST NOT be transmitted unencrypted over insecure networks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An overarching authentication concept is created and approved as a document. It defines standards such as the mandatory use of modern hashing algorithms (bcrypt, Argon2) for password storage and the exclusive transmission of credentials over TLS-encrypted connections.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the authentication concept and assesses its completeness and appropriateness. During the audit of applications, it is verified on a random basis whether the requirements defined in the concept (e.g., secure password storage) have been implemented, for example, by inspecting the configuration files or databases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The authentication concept is detailed and defines specific requirements based on the protection requirement assessment of the respective application. It mandates the connection to a central authentication service. The concept is an integral part of the Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC).

parts.name: guidance
