parts.prose: The concept includes a matrix that prescribes the required authentication strength (e.g., password, MFA, smart card) for different protection requirement classes (low, normal, high). Compliance with this concept is a mandatory criterion when developing or procuring new software.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the detailed authentication concept. The process for developing new software is examined to ensure that the concept is considered in the design and testing phases. The configuration of multiple applications with different protection requirements is checked for correct implementation of the conceptual specifications.

controls.title: Appropriate selection of authentication mechanisms (S) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Identification and authentication mechanisms appropriate to the protection requirements SHOULD be used. Authentication data SHOULD be protected at all times. After unsuccessful login attempts, there SHOULD be an increasing time delay. The total number of attempts SHOULD be limited, after which the user ID is locked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An account lockout policy is configured for all externally accessible services (e.g., lockout for 15 minutes after 5 failed attempts). The configuration is documented and standardized.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the account lockout policies on several systems (e.g., Active Directory, VPN gateway, web applications). An attempt is made to trigger an account lockout through repeated incorrect entries to test the effectiveness of the measure. The AD policy can be checked automatically with `Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The authentication mechanisms can detect and respond to attacks such as password spraying and credential stuffing. The account lockout policies are intelligent and do not prematurely lock accounts during distributed attacks. Users are informed about their account lockout through a secure channel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Intrusion Detection/Prevention System (IDS/IPS) or a Web Application Firewall (WAF) is used to analyze login attempts. Rules are configured to alert on a high number of login failures from a single IP address (brute-force) or for many different accounts (password spraying) and to block the source IP.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and the alerting rules of the IDS/IPS or the WAF. The logs are checked for detected attacks and the triggered responses. The effectiveness of the notification process for users in case of an account lockout is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is risk-adaptive. Based on context factors such as location, device, time of day, and user behavior, the required authentication strength is dynamically adjusted. Logins classified as high-risk are blocked and trigger a security alert.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A modern Identity Provider (e.g., Azure AD with Conditional Access, Okta) that supports risk-based authentication is used. Policies are defined, e.g., 'If login is from outside the country AND the user is privileged, then require FIDO2 MFA and block if not met'. Impossible travel scenarios are automatically detected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configured risk-based access policies in the Identity Provider. Various scenarios (e.g., login via Tor network, from a non-compliant device) are played out to test the correct response of the system. The logs of the risk engine and the triggered alarms are checked.

controls.title: Contingency planning for the identity and access management system (H) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be checked to what extent a failed IAM system is security-critical. Provisions SHOULD be made to remain operational in the event of a failure. In particular, the authorization concept provided for in the contingency plan (e.g., with emergency accounts) SHOULD remain applicable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system is classified as a critical system in the Business Continuity Plan (BCP). A recovery plan for the IAM system is documented. There are defined 'Break-Glass' emergency accounts that are managed outside the IAM system, with their passwords stored securely in a vault.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the BCP and the recovery plan for the IAM system. It is checked whether the documentation for the emergency accounts exists and whether the process for their use is clearly defined and approved. It is verified that the passwords of the emergency accounts are changed regularly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The IAM system is designed to be redundant to ensure high availability. The recovery plan is tested regularly. The use of emergency accounts is technically monitored and automatically triggers an alert.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system's servers are configured as a cluster and the database is replicated. As part of the annual disaster recovery test, a failover of the IAM system to a secondary site is performed. The emergency accounts are configured so that every login sends an email to the security team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the highly available architecture of the IAM system. The logs from the last DR tests are checked to verify compliance with RTO/RPO values. It is tested whether logging in with an emergency account triggers an alert as intended.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The IAM system is designed as a geo-redundant, fault-tolerant service with automatic failover. The recovery time objective (RTO) is near zero. Even in the event of a total failure of the primary data center, authentication is still possible for users without any noticeable interruption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system is distributed across multiple, geographically separate data centers (Active/Active configuration). A global load balancer distributes requests to the available sites. System integrity and availability are continuously monitored, and failover is fully automatic without human intervention.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the architecture of the geo-redundant service. An unplanned outage of one site is simulated to test the automatic and uninterrupted functioning of the failover. The configuration of the global load balancer and the monitoring systems is checked.

controls.title: Multi-factor authentication (H) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A secure multi-factor authentication (MFA), e.g., with cryptographic certificates, smart cards, or tokens, SHOULD be used for authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: MFA is enforced for all users with access to externally accessible services or to internal applications classified as critical. A TOTP-based authenticator app (e.g., Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator) is used as the second factor.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies the applications classified as critical and checks whether access to them is protected by MFA as defined. The configuration of the authentication service is analyzed to ensure that the MFA requirement is technically implemented. Random login tests are performed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: MFA is mandatory for all users for all logins. Phishing-resistant authentication factors such as FIDO2 security keys are preferably used, especially for privileged users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The authentication policy enforces MFA for all user accounts without exception. Administrators and management are equipped with FIDO2 hardware tokens. For standard users, push notifications are an option in addition to TOTP apps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the global MFA policy in the authentication service. It is checked whether exceptions exist and whether they are sufficiently justified and approved. The assignment and lifecycle of the hardware tokens are monitored.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is passwordless by default using phishing-resistant MFA methods. The authentication strength is dynamically adapted to the risk of the respective login attempt (risk-adaptive authentication).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: FIDO2 security keys or Windows Hello for Business are introduced as the primary login method for all users, making passwords obsolete for daily use. The identity provider's risk-based access engine is used to enforce additional verification steps for higher-risk logins (e.g., from an unknown device).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of passwordless authentication and risk-adaptive policies. It is tested whether login attempts under different risk conditions are handled as expected. The acceptance and use of passwordless methods by users is assessed.

controls.title: Four-eyes principle for administrative tasks (H) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative activities SHOULD only be possible to be performed by two people (four-eyes principle). For MFA, the factors SHOULD be distributed between the two people. For passwords, they SHOULD be split into two parts, with each person receiving one part.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the most critical administrative accounts (e.g., root access to the CA, domain admin password for emergencies), the password is split and stored in two separate, sealed envelopes in a safe. Its use requires the presence of both individuals and documented approval.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy on the four-eyes principle and the list of affected accounts. The secure storage of the password parts in the safe is inspected. The logs of the use of these accounts are checked for compliance with the four-eyes principle and for correct documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The four-eyes principle is enforced for critical changes through technical measures. Changes to systems must be initiated by one person and approved by a second, independent person before they become effective.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In critical systems (e.g., firewall management, IAM system), a 'maker-checker' principle is configured. An administrator ('maker') can prepare a change (e.g., a new firewall rule), but it only becomes active after a second, authorized administrator ('checker') has reviewed and approved it in the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the 'maker-checker' workflow in the relevant systems. The change log is examined to verify that all critical changes were processed by two different people. It is tested whether an administrator can approve a change they prepared themselves.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administrative sessions on critical systems require real-time dual-control approval via a PAM solution. High-impact cryptographic operations require the involvement of multiple people through the use of threshold cryptography (e.g., Shamir's Secret Sharing).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM solution is used that requires a just-in-time request by an administrator and real-time approval by a second one for access to critical systems. For the management of the root CA keys, a Hardware Security Module (HSM) solution is used that enforces (M of N) authentication for critical operations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration of the PAM solution, particularly the dual-control workflows. The configuration of the HSM and the regulation for storing the key shares are checked. The logs of critical administrative sessions and cryptographic operations are analyzed for correct compliance with the multi-person principle.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Access to an institution's resources requiring protection must be restricted to authorized users and authorized IT components. Users and IT components must be unequivocally identified and authenticated. The management of the information necessary for this is called identity management.
Authorization management is about whether and how users or IT components are allowed to access and use information or services, i.e., whether they are to be granted or denied entry, access, or access rights based on their permissions. Authorization management refers to the processes required for the assignment, revocation, and control of rights.
The transitions between the two terms are fluid, which is why this module uses the term Identity and Access Management (IAM). For better understanding, this module uses the term "user ID" or "ID" synonymously for "user account," "account," "login," and "account." In this module, the term "password" is used as a general term for "passphrase," "PIN," or "password."

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of the module is to ensure that users or IT components can only access the IT resources and information that they need for their work and for which they are authorized, and to deny access to unauthorized users or IT components. To this end, requirements are formulated with which institutions should build a secure identity and authorization management system.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose: The ORP.4 Identity and Access Management module is to be applied once for the information network.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Missing or inadequate processes in identity and access management
parts.prose:
If processes in identity and access management are inadequately defined or implemented, it is not guaranteed that access is restricted to the necessary level, thus violating the need-to-know or least-privilege principles. IT operations may not receive information about personnel changes, so that, for example, accounts of departed employees are not deleted. These can thus continue to access sensitive information.
It is also possible that employees who have been transferred to a new department retain their old permissions and thus accumulate extensive overall permissions over time.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Lack of a central deactivation option for accounts
parts.prose: In institutions, employees often have accounts for various IT systems, such as production, test, quality assurance, or project systems. These are usually in different areas of responsibility and are often managed by different administrators. This can lead to the situation where the same and a unique ID is not used on all IT systems and there is no central overview of the accounts on the individual IT systems. In such a scenario, it is not possible to deactivate all accounts of the affected employees in a single step in the event of an attack or a password theft. Also, in this scenario, when employees leave the institution, all accesses cannot be blocked in a single step.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Unsuitable management of entry, access, and access rights
parts.prose: If the allocation of entry, access, and access rights is poorly regulated, it quickly leads to serious security vulnerabilities, e.g., through uncontrolled growth in the allocation of rights. During the introduction of identity management systems or revisions, it often turns out that different people in a wide variety of organizational units are responsible for granting permissions. This can lead to users receiving permissions on demand or, conversely, only being able to obtain them through unnecessarily complicated means. As a result, on the one hand, a lack of permissions can hinder daily work, and on the other hand, permissions can be granted without requirement, thus posing a security risk.

controls.title: Identification of the framework conditions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only a few, obvious legal requirements (e.g., from the GDPR) are sporadically recorded. Contractual, industry-specific, or internal requirements are largely ignored. Documentation is incomplete and not maintained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The collection is mostly reactive, for example, when a new law is discussed in public. The information is collected in unsystematic formats such as simple text files or emails.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews with management and the legal department (if any), the auditor determines that there is no systematic process for identifying requirements. A random check of contracts and internal policies shows that the resulting information security requirements are not documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a list of the most important legal and contractual requirements. However, this list is not systematically maintained or analyzed for its impact on information security management. The documentation is stored centrally, but not versioned or structured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The list is maintained in a spreadsheet. Responsibility for maintaining the list is assigned to a role (e.g., the Information Security Officer), but there is no defined process for regular review and updates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the relevant framework conditions and checks their completeness at a basic level. It is checked whether a central document exists. By interviewing the person in charge, it is determined that there is no formal process for updating and that the last revision was some time ago.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All legal, contractual, and other requirements with an impact on information security management MUST be identified and documented. The legal, contractual, and other requirements relevant to the individual areas of the institution SHOULD be compiled in a structured overview. The documentation MUST be kept up to date.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirements are recorded in a central database or a structured document management system. For each requirement, the source, relevance to the institution, and the affected areas are documented. A process is defined that prescribes an annual review and update of the entire documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the documented overview of requirements presented to them and checks it for structure, completeness, and up-to-dateness. It is verified that a defined process for identification and updating exists. New legal changes or contract conclusions are used on a random basis to check whether the resulting requirements were promptly incorporated into the documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for identifying and documenting requirements is formalized and integrated into the institution's management system. The requirements are not only listed, but also assigned to the respective assets, processes, and protective measures. Information sources such as legal newsletters or industry associations are actively used to be proactively informed about changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool or a specialized compliance management tool is used to manage requirements and link them to internal controls. Responsibilities for monitoring specific legal areas (e.g., data protection, financial law) are clearly defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the links between requirements, assets, and controls in the tool used. It is checked whether the process for proactive monitoring of changes is documented and functioning, e.g., by providing proof of subscribed information services and the resulting activities. It is checked whether the assigned responsibilities are being fulfilled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process of identifying requirements is largely automated. The GRC tool used is automatically updated with new and amended regulations via external feeds from legal databases. AI-supported analysis helps to assess the relevance of new regulations for the institution. The assignment to internal controls is automatically suggested and only needs to be confirmed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Interfaces between the GRC tool and external providers of legal information (e.g., LexisNexis, Wolters Kluwer) are implemented. The workflow for assessing and implementing new requirements is fully mapped in the tool and actively monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the automated feeds and the logs of the GRC tool to verify the complete and timely adoption of legal changes. The effectiveness of the AI-supported relevance assessment is checked through random samples. An automated audit trail in the tool can prove compliance with the process.

controls.title: Observance of the framework conditions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Requirements are only considered reactively and ad hoc when planning new systems or processes, usually only when a problem occurs. There are no defined responsibilities for compliance; this is left to the respective project team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The topic of compliance is sometimes mentioned in project meetings, but there are no formal review steps or checklists. Decisions are made without formal approval from a compliance function.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the project documentation of recently completed projects and finds that no explicit check for compliance with security or compliance requirements has taken place. Interviews with project managers confirm the lack of a formal process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When designing new applications and systems, compliance with the known main requirements (e.g., data protection) is generally checked. However, this is done unsystematically and is highly dependent on the initiative of individual employees. If violations are identified, measures are taken, but there is no formal process for correction.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Project managers are instructed to 'think about security' in new projects. There may be a simple checklist, but its use is not enforced or verified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the concept documents for selected new systems shown to them and looks for explicit chapters or documents on compliance. It is checked whether responsibilities for compliance with requirements are at least known informally. Examples of how identified violations have been handled are requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements identified as security-relevant MUST be incorporated into the planning and design of business processes, applications, and IT systems, or when procuring new components. Managers who bear legal responsibility for the institution MUST ensure compliance with legal, contractual, and other requirements. The responsibilities and accountabilities for compliance with these requirements MUST be defined. Suitable measures MUST be identified and implemented to prevent violations of relevant requirements. If such violations are detected, appropriate corrective actions MUST be taken to remedy the deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 'Security by Design' process is established. For all new projects, systems, and procurements, a security and compliance check is a fixed milestone in the process. The results of this check are documented and must be approved before implementation. There is a documented incident response process that also covers the handling of compliance violations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the process for observing the requirements is documented and known to all relevant employees. Using random samples (e.g., new applications, major procurements), it is checked whether the prescribed compliance checks have been carried out and documented. It is checked whether the responsibilities (e.g., in role descriptions) are clearly defined. The auditor examines the logs of detected violations and their remediation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The 'Security and Compliance by Design' process is formalized and supported by standardized templates and checklists based on the central list of requirements. Adherence to the process is actively monitored. For significant changes and projects, formal approval by the Information Security Officer and the Compliance Officer is mandatory.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process is integrated into the institution's project management or ticketing system. For example, a ticket for a new project cannot move to the implementation phase until the 'compliance check' milestone has been marked as 'completed' by the responsible parties. The checklists are regularly updated to reflect new requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the enforced workflows in the project management or ticketing system. It is verified that the used checklists are up-to-date and cover all relevant requirement areas. The logs of the approval processes for several projects are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The verification of requirements is largely automated and integrated into the development and operational processes (CI/CD pipeline). 'Policy as Code' is used to automatically check compliance requirements (e.g., for cloud configurations). Deviations lead to automatic alerts or block the deployment. Corrective actions are automatically tracked and escalated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools such as Open Policy Agent (OPA), terraform-compliance, or Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) are used. The defined policies are versioned and subject to an approval process. A central dashboard visualizes the compliance status of all systems in real time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the 'Policy as Code' definitions and their coverage of the relevant requirements. The logs of the automated checks in the CI/CD pipeline are reviewed. The auditor verifies the functionality of the alerting and escalation process for detected deviations. The integrity of the real-time dashboard is checked.

controls.title: Conception and Organization of Compliance Management

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance is understood as a purely legal topic and is handled in isolation from IT and information security. There is no designated role for compliance management and no established processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Inquiries on compliance topics are forwarded ad hoc to the management or an external law firm. There is no internal structure or organization for this topic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By reviewing the organizational chart and conducting interviews, the auditor determines that no role or department for compliance management exists. There is no evidence of organized cooperation between the legal and IT departments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a named person responsible for compliance topics (Compliance Officer). However, their tasks and the cooperation with the Information Security Officer (ISO) are not formally defined. An exchange only takes place when needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The role of the Compliance Officer is roughly outlined in a job description. The cooperation with the ISO is reactive, e.g., when the ISO has a question about a legal requirement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the job description of the Compliance Officer. Through separate interviews with the Compliance Officer and the ISO, the extent and regularity of cooperation are determined. The auditor asks for minutes of joint meetings, which typically do not exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process SHOULD be established in the institution to identify all relevant legal, contractual, and other requirements with an impact on information security management. Appropriate processes and organizational structures SHOULD be established to ensure an overview of the various legal requirements for the individual areas of the institution, based on the identification and observance of the legal framework. For this purpose, responsible persons for compliance management SHOULD be appointed. Compliance officers and information security officers SHOULD exchange information regularly. They SHOULD jointly integrate security requirements into compliance management, translate security-relevant requirements into security measures, and monitor their implementation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A concept for compliance management is documented. It describes the processes, the organizational structure, and the roles (e.g., Compliance Officer). Regular (e.g., quarterly) coordination meetings between the Compliance Officer and the ISO are firmly scheduled in the calendar. The results of these meetings are recorded in minutes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the compliance management concept and reviews it for completeness regarding processes, structures, and roles. The minutes of the coordination meetings between Compliance and ISO for the last 12 months are reviewed for content and tracking of action items. It is verified that the defined responsibilities are known to the respective persons.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal Compliance Management System (CMS) is established and documented. There is a compliance committee or a similar body in which, in addition to the Compliance Officer and the ISO, representatives from relevant departments and management are also represented. Joint risk analyses are conducted to identify overlaps and gaps between compliance and security risks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The charter of the compliance committee is documented and approved by management. The committee meets regularly, and its decisions are binding. The results of the joint risk analyses are incorporated into the institution's central risk treatment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the charter and minutes of the compliance committee. The documentation of the joint risk analyses is reviewed, and their results are compared with the institution's risk treatment plan. Interviews are conducted with committee members to assess its effectiveness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Compliance Management System is fully embedded in an Integrated Management System (IMS) that also includes information security, quality management, and other areas. A GRC tool supports the processes throughout. The effectiveness of the CMS and the cooperation is measured and continuously improved using Key Performance Indicators (KPIs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The GRC tool maps the common workflows, manages the central requirements and control catalog, and generates automatic reports and dashboards for the management level. KPIs could be, for example, 'number of compliance violations per quarter' or 'turnaround time for assessing new legal requirements'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the GRC tool and the IMS documentation. The defined KPIs and the associated reports and dashboards are checked for their meaningfulness and correctness. The continuous improvement process is verified based on documented measures and their effectiveness check. It is checked whether the system is externally certified (e.g., according to IDW PS 980).

controls.title: Exception approvals

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Exceptions to regulations are granted informally and mostly verbally. There is no documentation, no risk assessment, and no time limit.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An employee asks their supervisor if they can deviate from a security policy and receives verbal approval. There is no central body that has an overview of granted exceptions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: When auditing other controls, the auditor identifies obvious deviations from policies. When asked, reference is made to an informal approval for which no written proof exists. Interviews confirm the absence of a process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Exception approvals are requested and approved in writing (e.g., via email). However, there is no standardized process, no formal risk assessment, and no central recording of exceptions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The approval process is not clearly defined; sometimes the supervisor approves, sometimes the IT department. The emails with the approvals are stored decentrally in the mailboxes of the participants.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for examples of exception approvals. Emails are presented that do not contain a structured justification or risk analysis. A complete list of all current exceptions cannot be provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If it is necessary in individual cases to deviate from established regulations, the exception SHOULD be justified and approved by an authorized body after a risk assessment. There SHOULD be an approval procedure for exception approvals. An overview of all granted exception approvals SHOULD be created and maintained. A corresponding procedure for documentation and a review process SHOULD be established. All exception approvals SHOULD be time-limited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process for exception approvals is documented. This process requires a written request with a justification and a documented risk assessment. The approval is granted by a defined authorized body (e.g., the ISO). All exceptions are recorded in a central list (e.g., a table) with justification, approver, and an expiration date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documented process for exception approvals and the central list of exceptions. It is checked whether the list is complete and up-to-date. On a sample basis, it is verified for some exceptions whether the process was followed (request, risk assessment, approval, time limit).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for exception approvals is integrated into the IT Service Management system (e.g., as a separate ticket type). Requests are submitted via a standardized form that enforces the entry of a risk assessment and possible compensating measures. The central list is regularly (e.g., quarterly) reviewed by management or a security committee.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A workflow for exception approvals is stored in the ticketing system, which automatically forwards the requests to the correct authorized body. The system sends automatic reminders before an exception expires. The regular reviews are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configured workflow in the ticketing system. It is checked whether the form contains all necessary fields. The minutes of the management reviews of the exception list are reviewed. It is checked whether the automatic notifications for expiring exceptions are configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of exception approvals is managed in a GRC tool. The system links the exception directly to the risk in the risk register and adjusts the risk assessment accordingly. The effectiveness of compensating measures is actively monitored. A dashboard provides an up-to-date overview of all exceptions and the associated overall risk at all times.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technical systems (e.g., vulnerability scanners, CSPM tools) can be configured to consider approved exceptions in their checks to avoid false alarms. The approval workflow in the GRC tool can be multi-stage depending on the risk level of the exception.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the link between exceptions, risks, and compensating controls in the GRC tool. The monitoring of the effectiveness of the compensating measures is checked. The real-time dashboard is evaluated for its correctness and meaningfulness. It is checked whether technical control systems interpret the exception list correctly.

controls.title: Regular reviews of compliance management

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No review of compliance management takes place. Action is only taken reactively when external auditors (e.g., certified public accountants, regulatory authorities) make findings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are no internal plans or activities to review compliance processes. There is a reliance on external bodies to point out problems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for internal audit plans or reports on compliance management and finds that none exist. It is checked whether findings from external audits have led to improvements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance management is reviewed informally at irregular intervals. The reviews are not systematic, the scope is not defined, and the results are not formally documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The compliance officer occasionally holds talks with specialist departments to see if 'everything is running smoothly'. The findings are kept in mind or in personal notes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the compliance officer about reviews that have been carried out. No formal reports or evidence of a systematic approach can be provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A procedure SHOULD be established on how compliance management and the resulting requirements and measures are regularly reviewed for their efficiency and effectiveness (see also DER.3.1 Audits and Reviews). It SHOULD be regularly checked whether the organizational structure and the processes of compliance management are appropriate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an annual internal audit plan that also includes the review of the Compliance Management System (CMS). The review is conducted using a predefined checklist. The results, findings, and recommendations for improvement are documented in an audit report and presented to management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the audit plan and the audit reports of recent years for the CMS. It is checked whether the audits took place as planned. The content of the reports and the follow-up of the findings are analyzed. It is checked whether the audits were carried out by sufficiently qualified personnel.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The review of compliance management is carried out through regular, formal internal audits conducted by an independent body (e.g., Internal Audit). In addition, a self-assessment process is established in which the specialist departments regularly assess their own compliance. The results from all reviews are consolidated and prepared for a formal management review.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Internal Audit uses recognized auditing standards (e.g., from DIIR or IIA) to conduct the audits. Web-based questionnaires are used for the self-assessments. The management review is a firmly established, documented process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the independence of the auditing body. The methodology and documentation of the self-assessments are analyzed. The minutes and the resulting action plans of the management review are inspected to assess the effectiveness of the improvement process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Compliance Management System is continuously monitored (Continuous Auditing). Key controls are tested automatically, and the results are displayed in a real-time dashboard. In addition, the CMS is regularly certified by external, specialized auditors (e.g., according to IDW PS 980). The results feed directly into a continuous improvement process, which is measured by KPIs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC tool is used for continuous auditing. It automatically tests, for example, configurations, permissions, or adherence to process steps. The KPIs for the effectiveness of the CMS are also recorded and visualized by the tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and logic of the automated control tests in the GRC tool. The external audit reports and certificates are reviewed. The functioning of the KPI-based improvement process is checked by analyzing the development of KPIs over time and the measures based on them.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
In every institution, there are relevant legal, contractual and other requirements, such as internal guidelines, that must be observed. Many of these requirements have a direct or indirect impact on information security management.

The requirements differ depending on the industry, country and other framework conditions. In addition, a public authority, for example, is subject to different external regulations than a public limited company. The institution's management level must ensure compliance with the requirements through appropriate monitoring measures.

Depending on its size, an institution may have various management processes that deal with different aspects of risk management. These include information security management, data protection management, compliance management and controlling. The various units should work together in a spirit of trust in order to leverage synergies and resolve conflicts at an early stage.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of the module is to show how responsible parties can get an overview of the various requirements for the individual areas of an institution. For this purpose, suitable security requirements are to be identified and implemented in order to avoid violations of these specifications.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module ORP.5 Compliance Management (Requirements Management) must be applied once to the entire information network.

The obligation of employees to comply with the legal, contractual and other requirements identified in this module is not part of this module, but is dealt with in module ORP.2 Personnel.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Violation of legal requirements
parts.prose: If information security is implemented incorrectly or only sparsely, institutions can violate legal regulations or contractual agreements. Institutions must also observe many different industry-specific, national, and international legal frameworks. As this can be very complex, users may unintentionally violate legal requirements or even knowingly accept doing so. For example, many cloud service providers offer their services in an international environment. This often subjects the providers to different national legislations. Cloud users frequently focus only on low costs and misjudge the legal frameworks to be observed, such as data protection, information obligations, insolvency law, liability, or information access by third parties.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Unauthorized disclosure of information
parts.prose: Incorrect employee behavior can lead to the impermissible disclosure of information that requires protection. For example, confidential information might be discussed within earshot of unauthorized individuals, such as during conference breaks or on mobile phone calls in public areas. It is also conceivable that a department head suspects an employee of collaborating with a competitor. To prove this, they ask the IT department for an "off-the-record" look at the employee's emails. The IT department complies with the request without obtaining the necessary approvals.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Insufficient identification check of communication partners
parts.prose: In personal conversations, on the phone or in e-mails, many employees are willing to disclose far more information than they would in a letter or in a larger group, for example. In addition, the identity of communication partners is usually not questioned, as this is perceived as impolite. Likewise, authorisations are often not sufficiently checked, but are implicitly derived from the (claimed) role. For example, employees may receive an e-mail from alleged acquaintances of their superiors with whom the rapid transfer of an outstanding amount was supposedly agreed. Or a stranger in work clothes with a tool case is granted access to the data centre after mentioning something about "water pipes".

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Unintentional disclosure of internal information
parts.prose: When information is passed on, it often happens that other details are transmitted accidentally along with the desired content. This can cause confidential information to fall into the wrong hands. This could be, for example, old files or residual information on data carriers that have been passed on. Users could also transmit incorrect data or send it to the wrong recipients.

controls.title: Selection of suitable cryptographic methods

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cryptographic methods are only used for selected, particularly critical systems. The selection of algorithms and key lengths is done on an ad-hoc basis, often based on the default settings of the respective software and without a formal, documented assessment or consideration of current security recommendations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In practice, this means that outdated or known insecure algorithms (e.g., MD5, SHA-1 for signatures) may still be in use in some areas, as there is no proactive process for review and updating. The selection is made by individual administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through spot checks that cryptographic methods are used inconsistently. It is checked whether a central policy or documentation for the selection of cryptographic methods exists. The absence of such a policy and the use of outdated algorithms in some systems indicate this level of maturity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic, informal list of recommended cryptographic methods and key lengths exists, which is used for new systems. However, existing systems are not systematically checked against it. The selection is based on generally known standards; a specific adaptation to the protection period of the data does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, a list from a trusted source (e.g., BSI or NIST) is adopted once and distributed as an internal recommendation. However, there is no process for regularly updating this list or for checking conformity across the entire IT landscape.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of recommended cryptographic methods. By questioning administrators and inspecting the configurations of newer systems, it is verified that this list is generally followed. At the same time, it is found that no process exists for reviewing older systems or for updating the list.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Suitable cryptographic methods MUST be selected. It MUST be ensured that established algorithms are used that have been intensively studied by the professional community and have no known security vulnerabilities. Likewise, currently recommended key lengths MUST be used. These selection criteria are documented in the cryptography concept and are mandatory for all systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection is based on the specifications of the cryptography concept, which explicitly refers to recognized technical guidelines (e.g., BSI TR-02102). For each new system or application, it is documented which methods and key lengths were selected based on these specifications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies, using the cryptography concept, that clear specifications for the selection of algorithms and key lengths exist. It is checked on a sample basis for several systems whether the used methods and lengths comply with the documented specifications and whether these selection decisions are traceable.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined standards, the planned operational life of the cryptographic method is systematically considered when selecting the key length. For a longer planned operational life, longer key lengths SHOULD be used proactively. The process for selecting and reviewing cryptographic methods is carried out regularly, e.g., annually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of system planning, the lifespan of data and applications is estimated. Based on this, the required key length is determined and documented according to current forecasts (e.g., from BSI TR-02102). There is a planned process to review the crypto inventory for the appropriateness of the methods.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the process for selecting the key length considers the lifespan of the data. Based on project or system documentation, it is checked whether this consideration has taken place and is traceable. Furthermore, it is verified that a regular review process for the used methods is established.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of cryptographic methods is a dynamic, proactive process that is integrated into risk management. The organization continuously monitors research in the field of cryptography and post-quantum cryptography. The systems in use are designed for crypto-agility to enable a fast and automated exchange of algorithms and keys.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Automated tools are used to scan the IT landscape and compare the used crypto implementations with current threat data and recommendations. For critical new developments, post-quantum methods are already being evaluated or used (hybrid approach). Policies are enforced via central configuration management systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and functionality of the automated scanning tools. It is checked whether the cryptography concept and risk assessments are based on current research findings. The ability to automatically exchange a cryptographic algorithm system-wide is proven by a test or a demonstration. An automated check could be a script that queries configurations on all systems and validates them against a central policy for crypto-agility.

controls.title: Data backup when using cryptographic methods

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cryptographic keys are backed up sporadically, but often without sufficient protection against unauthorized access. In some cases, the keys are stored unencrypted on the same data carrier or in the same backup set as the corresponding encrypted data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A typical example is a backup script that backs up an encrypted directory and places the associated key file unprotected in the same backup archive. Restoration of long-term archives is not tested.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects backup archives and configurations on a sample basis. It is checked whether key files are backed up separately from the data and with appropriate access restrictions. The discovery of unprotected keys in the backups confirms this level of maturity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic procedure for backing up long-lived cryptographic keys separately from the data, e.g., on another server or an external medium. However, this process is manual, not standardized for all systems, or fully documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators manually copy important key files to a designated, access-protected network drive or a USB stick that is kept in a safe. However, there is no guarantee that this is done for all relevant keys and that the offline media are still readable.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews administrators about their procedures for key backup and requests proof of the backed-up keys. It is checked whether the procedure is documented and whether a complete list of keys to be backed up exists. Gaps in documentation and coverage indicate this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In data backups, cryptographic keys MUST be stored or kept by IT operations in such a way that unauthorized persons cannot access them. Long-lived cryptographic keys MUST be kept offline, outside of the IT systems in use. IT operations MUST ensure that information stored in encrypted form can still be accessed even after long periods. These processes are documented in the cryptography concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Keys are backed up in a dedicated, encrypted repository that is physically and logically separated from the production systems and their backups. For long-lived keys, offline media (e.g., USB sticks, LTO tapes) are used, which are stored in a secure location (e.g., a safe in a different fire compartment). The process is described in the backup concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the defined processes for key backup using the backup and cryptography concepts. The implementation is checked by inspecting access to the key repository and the physical storage location of the offline media. It is checked whether processes exist to ensure access to long-term data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For long-term storage of encrypted information, it SHOULD be regularly checked whether the cryptographic algorithms and key lengths used are still suitable for the respective information. Hardware or software used with cryptographic functions SHOULD also be archived for the duration of the archiving period. Recovery tests of archived data and keys are performed periodically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual process is established to review the long-term archives. This involves checking whether the encryption is still considered secure. Virtualized instances of the required software or the original hardware are kept together with the keys to ensure readability. The successful execution of recovery tests is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the regular reviews and recovery tests for long-term archives. It is checked whether a process for archiving the required crypto software/hardware exists and is implemented. The presence of test reports and an inventory of archived software is an indicator for this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The backup and archiving of keys is carried out exclusively via dedicated, high-availability Hardware Security Modules (HSM) or a central Key Management System (KMS). The entire process of reviewing algorithms, archiving, and periodic recovery tests is automated and logged in a tamper-proof manner. Data in long-term archives is proactively re-encrypted to newer, stronger algorithms as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A KMS manages the entire lifecycle of the keys. Backups of the KMS are automatically and securely stored in encrypted form at geographically separate, secure locations. An automated script attempts to restore a sample of archived data quarterly and raises an alarm in case of errors. A process for 'crypto-migration' of archives is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the architecture and configuration of the central KMS/HSM. The logs of the automated recovery tests and the key backups are analyzed. It is checked whether a documented and tested process for re-encrypting long-term archives exists. An automated test could query the KMS API to verify the backup status and geographical redundancy.

controls.title: Appropriate key management

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no formal, documented key management. Keys are generated ad-hoc as needed, rarely or never changed, and often stored unprotected on the systems. A systematic process for deleting or replacing compromised keys is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators use the standard tools of the operating system (e.g., ssh-keygen) for key generation. The keys are stored in the users' home directories without additional passphrases. Default keys of devices are not changed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and system checks that no key management concept exists. They search for default keys or very old, unprotected private keys on the systems. The absence of processes for the entire key lifecycle is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic, but undocumented procedures for key generation and storage are in place. The renewal of keys and certificates is mostly manual and reactive, e.g., shortly before or after their expiration. The authenticity of public keys from external partners is not systematically checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an informal checklist for setting up new servers, which includes the generation of new SSH keys. Certificate expirations are tracked via administrators' calendar entries. Public keys are exchanged via email and accepted without further verification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the informal processes explained to them. It is checked whether there have been repeated outages due to expired certificates. The method for exchanging public keys is analyzed (e.g., by checking email traffic) to uncover missing integrity checks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In a suitable key management system, it MUST be defined how keys and certificates are generated, stored, exchanged, and deleted or destroyed. It MUST also be specified how the integrity and authenticity of the keys are ensured. Secret keys MUST be stored securely and protected from unauthorized access. When public keys of third parties are used, it MUST be ensured that the keys are authentic. Time-limited keys or certificates MUST be renewed in a timely manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: These requirements are documented in the cryptography concept or a dedicated key management policy. The policy describes the tools to be used, the protection mechanisms for stored keys (e.g., passphrases, file permissions), and the process for verifying external keys (e.g., comparing the fingerprint over a second channel). A process for monitoring expiration dates is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the key management concept for completeness regarding the entire lifecycle. Random checks are performed to verify whether private keys are protected according to the policy, whether external public keys have been verified, and whether the process for renewing certificates is functioning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cryptographic keys SHOULD always be generated with suitable key generators and in a secure environment. Default keys SHOULD be replaced. A key SHOULD preferably serve only one purpose; in particular, different keys SHOULD be used for encryption and signing. The exchange SHOULD be carried out using methods considered secure. Keys SHOULD be changed sufficiently frequently. A procedure SHOULD be defined for the event of a private key compromise, and all generated cryptographic keys SHOULD be securely stored and managed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Key generation takes place on dedicated, hardened systems or directly on hardware modules. The separation of keys (e.g., one key pair for encryption, another for signatures) is technically enforced. A documented emergency plan for key compromise (including revocation and replacement) exists and is regularly practiced. A central inventory (crypto-cadastre) is used to manage all keys.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the implementation of the advanced measures. It is checked whether default keys on devices have been replaced and whether keys are used for different purposes. The emergency plan for key compromise is checked for completeness and feasibility. The existence and up-to-dateness of the key inventory is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of all cryptographic keys is managed by a central, automated Key Management System (KMS) or by Hardware Security Modules (HSM). Processes such as key generation, rotation, revocation, and destruction are fully automated. Key usage is monitored and logged in real-time to detect misuse.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An enterprise KMS is implemented and all applications and systems are connected to it. The KMS enforces policies such as key length, rotation intervals, and usage purpose. Application secrets such as API keys are also managed centrally and dynamically. Alerts from the KMS are automatically fed into the SIEM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration and the operating processes of the central KMS. It is checked whether all critical systems are connected to the KMS. The automation of the lifecycle processes (e.g., automatic rotation) is verified based on configuration and logs. An automated test could query the KMS API to validate the compliance of the managed keys with the corporate policies.

controls.title: Secure deletion and destruction of cryptographic keys

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Key files that are no longer needed are only deleted using standard operating system functions. No special procedures for securely overwriting the data are used, which means the keys potentially remain recoverable. A process for this does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator deletes a private key file that is no longer needed with the `rm` command under Linux or by moving it to the Recycle Bin under Windows. No `shred` or `sdelete` is used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews administrators about their procedure for deleting keys. They may attempt to recover deleted key files on test disks with forensic tools to demonstrate the inadequacy of the process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal instruction to use secure deletion tools for key files on hard disk drives (HDDs). However, this instruction is not formally documented and does not take into account the specifics of modern storage media such as SSDs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators are encouraged to use tools like `shred`. For SSDs, where overwriting does not work reliably, or for keys in memory, there are no specific instructions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether employees are aware of the instruction for secure deletion. It is analyzed whether the methods used are suitable for the existing storage types (especially SSDs). The absence of a formal, media-specific policy indicates this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Private keys that are no longer needed SHOULD be securely deleted or destroyed. The procedures and methods used to delete or destroy private keys that are no longer needed SHOULD be documented in the cryptographic concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cryptographic concept or a deletion policy describes the tools (e.g., `sdelete`, `shred`) and processes to be used for the secure deletion of keys on various storage media. The process is part of the offboarding of systems or applications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the cryptographic concept that documented procedures for the secure deletion of keys exist. It is checked on a random basis during the decommissioning of systems whether these procedures are demonstrably applied (e.g., through logs or tickets).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documented methods for deletion and destruction are tailored to the different types of storage media (HDD, SSD, HSM, Smart Cards, main memory). The successful destruction of keys is logged and is part of the formal decommissioning process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy specifies: multiple overwrites for HDDs, the ATA Secure Erase command for SSDs, a factory reset for HSMs, and physical destruction for smart cards. The execution is recorded in an asset management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the deletion policy contains media-specific instructions. It is verified using the logs in the asset management or ticket system that the destruction of keys is traceably documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The destruction of keys is an automated and enforced part of the key lifecycle managed by a Key Management System (KMS). For physical data carriers (such as HSMs or hard drives) that contained keys, a logged physical destruction process (e.g., shredding) is established, which is verified by multiple people.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a key in the KMS reaches its end of validity, it is automatically marked as 'destroyed' and is no longer cryptographically recoverable. Hardware that is decommissioned is handed over to a certified disposal service provider for verifiable destruction. The entire process is integrated into asset management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the KMS configuration regarding automatic key destruction. In addition, the contracts and destruction certificates of the external service provider are reviewed. An automated test could query the KMS API to confirm that expired keys have the status 'destroyed' and are not recoverable.

controls.title: Definition of criteria for the selection of hardware or software with cryptographic functions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of cryptographic hardware or software is made opportunistically and ad hoc. The main criteria are often only immediate availability, cost, or the administrator's personal preferences, without a structured evaluation of security functions or interoperability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A development team chooses an open-source crypto library because it is easy to integrate, without checking its security, maintenance status, or potential licensing issues.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and examination of the software inventory list that a variety of different crypto products are in use without any discernible strategy. The absence of a documented requirements or evaluation matrix for procurements confirms this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When selecting crypto products, a basic checklist is used that focuses mainly on functional requirements and costs. Non-functional requirements such as security, usability, legal frameworks, or interoperability are not systematically considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the procurement of a new disk encryption solution, a list of 'must-have' features (e.g., 'supports Windows 10', 'central management') is created. The product that checks the most boxes and is the cheapest is selected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the evaluation documents for recently procured crypto products. It is analyzed whether the criteria go beyond purely functional aspects. The absence of security or legal aspects in the evaluation indicates this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The cryptographic concept SHOULD define the criteria and requirements based on which hardware or software with cryptographic functions is selected. Aspects such as functional scope, interoperability, cost-effectiveness, security against misuse and malfunction, technical, personnel and organizational aspects, lifespan of the methods, legal frameworks, and data protection SHOULD be considered and documented in the cryptographic concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized requirements catalog for the procurement of crypto products is established as an appendix to the cryptographic concept. Every procurement process must go through this catalog and the decision must be documented. The specialist departments, the data protection officer, and IT security are involved in the process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and completeness of the criteria catalog in the cryptographic concept. Based on recent procurement processes, it is checked whether this catalog was demonstrably used and whether the decision was transparently documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When making a selection, certified hardware or software with cryptographic functions, whose certification covers the relevant aspects of cryptography, SHOULD generally be preferred. The selection process includes a formal risk assessment of the candidate products, especially with regard to international legal aspects such as export and import restrictions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Products with certifications such as Common Criteria (CC) or FIPS 140-2 are given higher weight in the evaluation. For products intended for international use, an explicit review by the legal department regarding cryptography regulations in the target countries is conducted and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether certifications are demonstrably considered in the selection process and reflected in the decision matrix. It is verified whether a documented legal review of export/import regulations is available for internationally used software.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection process is deeply integrated into the overarching procurement and risk management processes. It includes not only the review of certificates but, for critical components, also the execution of independent security tests (e.g., penetration tests, code reviews). The security of the manufacturer's supply chain is also evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before procuring a new HSM, a specialized external service provider is commissioned to conduct a penetration test of the product. In addition, the manufacturer must disclose and prove its processes for secure software development (Secure SDLC). These results are a decisive factor in the purchasing decision.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests reports from independent security tests or code reviews for selected crypto products. It is checked whether the evaluation of supply chain security is part of the procurement process and how the results have influenced the selection decision. Little can be checked automatically here; it is a procedural audit.

controls.title: Creation of a cryptographic concept

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no central cryptographic concept. Specifications for cryptography, if they exist at all, are only found in fragments in other documents (e.g., individual system documentation) or as unwritten knowledge with individual administrators.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installation guide for a new web server states that a TLS certificate must be set up, but there is no company-wide specification as to which certificates, key lengths, or cipher suites to use.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the central cryptographic concept. If none can be provided, this maturity level is reached. The inconsistent and non-uniform application of cryptography is confirmed by examining various system configurations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic document exists, which typically contains a list of allowed cryptographic algorithms and key lengths. However, it does not cover the entire lifecycle and all relevant organizational aspects such as key management, configuration guidelines, key backup, or emergency processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a one-page 'Crypto Policy' that states: 'For TLS, version 1.2 with AES-256 must be used'. How to manage, secure, or handle the keys in an emergency is not described.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the submitted document and compares its contents with the comprehensive requirements for a cryptographic concept. Specific questions are asked about the uncovered areas (e.g., 'What happens in the event of a key compromise?') to highlight the gaps.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the institution's general security concept, a cryptographic concept for hardware and software with cryptographic functions SHOULD be created. The cryptographic concept SHOULD describe how data backups of cryptographic keys are performed, how key management is designed, and how the crypto inventory is compiled. Furthermore, it SHOULD describe how it is ensured that cryptographic functions are securely configured and correctly used, including all technical specifications.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A comprehensive cryptographic concept document is created and approved by management. It contains dedicated chapters on the required aspects (key management lifecycle, backup, configuration guidelines, etc.) and refers to the associated processes and responsibilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reads the cryptographic concept and checks it for completeness based on the points mentioned in the requirement. It is checked whether the document has been approved, versioned, and communicated to the relevant employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To select suitable cryptographic methods, the consideration of BSI TR-02102 SHOULD be specified in the cryptographic concept. The cryptographic concept SHOULD be known to all who use cryptographic methods, and it SHOULD be binding for their work. In particular, IT operations SHOULD implement the specifications. Any change to or deviation from the cryptographic concept SHOULD be coordinated with the ISO and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cryptographic concept is actively communicated, e.g., through regular training for administrators and developers. Compliance with the specifications becomes part of the target agreements for IT operations. a formal change process for the cryptographic concept is established, which requires approval by the ISO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the cryptographic concept is actively managed. Evidence of training or communication measures is requested. The change management system is used to check whether changes to the concept or approved deviations are correctly documented and approved by the ISO.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The crypto concept is a 'living document' that is dynamically adapted to new threats and technologies. The policies and configuration specifications it contains are technically enforced wherever possible by automated configuration management and policy enforcement tools (e.g., 'Policy as Code'). Compliance with the concept is monitored continuously and automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Configuration baselines for TLS, SSH, etc. are stored as code in a configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible, Puppet) and are rolled out to all systems. An automated compliance scanning tool checks the systems against these baselines daily and reports deviations to the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the 'Policy as Code' artifacts and the configuration of the automation tools. The reports from the compliance scanning tools are evaluated to assess the effectiveness of enforcement and monitoring. An automated test could query a server's configuration via script and validate it against the policy defined in the code.

controls.title: Response to practical weakening of a cryptographic algorithm

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Known vulnerabilities in cryptographic algorithms are only responded to reactively, typically only after the vulnerability has been exploited in a high-profile manner. There is no proactive process for reviewing the deployed algorithms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After a vulnerability like 'Heartbleed' was in the news, there is a panicked check to see if one is affected. There is no regular monitoring of security warnings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor searches the crypto inventory or system configurations for evidence of algorithms that have long been considered weakened or obsolete (e.g., SSLv3, RC4). Their continued use without a migration plan is an indicator of this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal awareness of cryptographic vulnerabilities, e.g., from reading IT news. However, a review of one's own inventory is carried out irregularly and is not scheduled. A response process is not documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department knows that they should disable TLS 1.0/1.1 and has this on an internal to-do list, but without a firm deadline or project plan. Implementation happens 'when there is time for it'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the administrators about their process for staying informed about new vulnerabilities. It is checked whether there are documented plans and deadlines for replacing known weak algorithms. The absence of formal plans indicates this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD review at least annually, based on the crypto inventory, whether the cryptographic algorithms and associated parameters in use are still sufficiently secure and have no known vulnerabilities. A process SHOULD be defined and documented in the crypto concept for the event that vulnerabilities in cryptographic algorithms occur. It SHOULD be ensured that the weakened algorithm is either secured or replaced by a suitable alternative.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual review meeting is firmly scheduled in the calendars of the ISO and IT Operations. The crypto inventory is checked against current recommendations (e.g., BSI TR-02102). The crypto concept includes a chapter on 'Incident Response for Crypto Weaknesses' that describes the steps from identification to assessment to migration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the minutes of the annual crypto reviews. The crypto concept is checked for the existence of the defined response process. Using an example (e.g., a recently disclosed vulnerability), it is simulated or checked whether the process was followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The review process is supported by semi-automated tools that compare the crypto inventory or live systems with vulnerability databases. The defined response process includes a communication plan for internal and external stakeholders and is integrated into the general incident and change management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A vulnerability scanner is configured to specifically search for weak cipher suites and crypto protocols. The results automatically generate tickets in the change management system. In the event of replacing a widely used algorithm, a communication template for customers is available.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and reports of the vulnerability scanner. It is checked whether the response process is demonstrably integrated into the established ITIL processes (Incident, Change). The existence of communication plans is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution has established processes and technologies to achieve crypto-agility. The identification and replacement of weakened cryptography are highly automated.
