Monitoring relies on specialized threat intelligence feeds that proactively provide information about potential future weaknesses (e.g., through advances in quantum computing).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration of crypto parameters is done centrally via a configuration management tool, which allows for the replacement of a cipher suite on thousands of servers within hours. The organization is a member of an Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) and automatically evaluates its crypto warnings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the ability for rapid, automated crypto-migration through a demonstration or analysis of automation scripts. It is checked which threat intelligence sources are used and how their information is processed. An automated test could query the configuration of all web servers and measure the time it takes to disable a specific cipher suite system-wide.

controls.title: Creation of a crypto inventory

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no central directory (inventory) of the cryptography in use. Information about it, if any, is only available decentrally with the respective system administrators as unwritten knowledge.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When the ISO asks where disk encryption is used, emails have to be sent to all administrators to laboriously compile the information. A complete and accurate answer is hardly possible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the crypto inventory to be presented. If none can be provided, this maturity level is met. The organization's inability to provide timely and accurate information about the use of a specific crypto algorithm confirms this.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple list, usually in the form of a spreadsheet, exists, but it is often incomplete, not updated regularly, and covers only a partial aspect (e.g., only SSL/TLS certificates, but not disk encryption or VPNs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The network team maintains an Excel spreadsheet with all public web server certificates and their expiration dates. However, the BitLocker encryption used by the server department is not recorded in it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the crypto inventory and compares its content with reality on a random basis. It is checked whether the inventory is up-to-date and covers all essential crypto applications (TLS, VPN, email encryption, disk encryption, etc.). Significant gaps indicate this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each group of IT systems, the following information SHOULD be recorded in the crypto inventory: purpose of use (e.g., disk encryption), responsible person/team, cryptographic algorithm used, hardware or software used with cryptographic functions, and security-relevant parameters used (e.g., key lengths). The maintenance of the inventory is a defined process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The crypto inventory is maintained as a structured database or wiki page. For each entry, the required fields are mandatory. Updating the inventory is an integral part of the process for commissioning new systems or applications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the crypto inventory and checks whether the required information fields for the entries are consistently maintained. Based on the documentation of recently introduced systems, it is verified whether the process for updating the inventory is being followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The crypto inventory is maintained in a central database, ideally as part of the Configuration Management Database (CMDB). The process for updating the inventory is integrated into the formal IT change management process. The completeness and accuracy of the inventory are audited regularly, e.g., annually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the CMDB, there is a dedicated object type 'Crypto Application'. No change request for a new system is approved without the creation or update of the corresponding crypto entry. An annual internal audit checks the CMDB data against the actual configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of the crypto inventory into the CMDB and the change management process. The records of the regular audits on the data quality of the inventory are reviewed. The CMDB API can be queried automatically and compared with the results of a network scan to find deviations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The crypto inventory is largely generated and kept up-to-date automatically through the use of network and system scanning tools. It is dynamically linked to the risk and vulnerability management systems to provide a real-time view of the organization's cryptographic security posture.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool such as a Certificate Lifecycle Management or a Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) continuously scans all systems and cloud environments. It detects deployed crypto protocols, certificates, and configurations and automatically populates the CMDB. If a new web server with a weak TLS profile is detected, a high-priority vulnerability finding is automatically generated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the architecture and reliability of the automated scanning and inventory tools. The integration with vulnerability management is checked by tracking a finding from detection to remediation. An automated test could deploy a new resource with a known crypto configuration and check if it appears correctly in the inventory within a defined time.

controls.title: Testing of hardware with cryptographic functions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cryptographic hardware is put into operation without specific functional tests of its cryptographic capabilities. It is assumed that the hardware works 'out of the box' as advertised by the manufacturer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A new Hardware Security Module (HSM) is installed in the rack, connected to the network, and powered on. If the management interface is reachable, the installation is considered successful, without a single key operation having been tested.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the test records for the commissioning of crypto hardware. If none exist, this maturity level is met. It is checked whether the commissioning checklists include an item for functional tests of the cryptography.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before production deployment, basic functional tests are performed manually to ensure core functionality (e.g., a key can be generated, a text can be encrypted and decrypted). However, there is no formal, documented test plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After installing the HSM driver, the administrator executes the supplied example commands to see if a key operation works in principle. The result is not logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the administrators about their testing activities during commissioning. A standardized test plan is requested. If tests are only carried out informally and without documentation, this maturity level is applicable.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The crypto concept SHOULD define test procedures for hardware with cryptographic functions. Before hardware with cryptographic functions is used, these defined procedures should be used to test whether the cryptographic functions are working correctly. The successful execution of the tests is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized test plan for crypto hardware is part of the crypto concept. This plan includes a series of defined test cases (e.g., generation of RSA and ECC keys, signature creation/verification, encryption/decryption). The results are recorded in a commissioning log.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the documented test procedures in the crypto concept. Commissioning logs are used to check on a random basis whether these test plans have been followed and the results documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If an IT system that uses crypto hardware is changed (e.g., through a driver or firmware update), it SHOULD be tested again to see if the crypto hardware used is still functioning properly (regression test). The configuration of the cryptographic hardware SHOULD be regularly checked for conformity with the specifications.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After every firmware update of the HSM or the operating system of the connected server, the standardized functional test is executed again. In addition, a configuration audit script is run quarterly, which compares the HSM settings (e.g., activated algorithms) with the target specifications from the crypto concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines change management logs to see if regression tests were performed after relevant changes. The logs of the regular configuration audits are requested and analyzed. An automatic check can query the current configuration of the hardware API and compare it with a golden baseline.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automated test suites are used to comprehensively validate the crypto hardware. This includes not only functional tests, but also performance tests under load and basic checks for vulnerabilities to side-channel attacks. The self-tests provided by the hardware (power-on self-tests) are enabled and their results are centrally monitored and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CI/CD pipeline automatically runs a series of crypto tests against reference hardware with every change to the connected software. The HSMs are configured to enter an error state and send an alert to the SIEM system in the event of a failed self-test.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and logs of the automated testing and monitoring systems. It is checked whether the hardware self-tests are active and whether the alarms in the SIEM are processed correctly. The robustness of the test suite is assessed.

controls.title: Physical security of hardware with cryptographic functions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Special cryptographic hardware (e.g. HSMs, smart cards) is treated like any other IT component and is not subject to any special physical protection measures. It is located in generally accessible office environments or unlocked server racks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A network HSM is installed in an open rack in a server room to which many employees and external service providers have access. USB crypto tokens are left unsecured on the desk.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the locations of the crypto hardware and assesses the physical protection measures on site. The absence of dedicated locks, safes, or access restrictions for the hardware itself is an indicator of this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The crypto hardware is located in a generally secured area, such as a locked server room, which is subject to general access controls. However, there are no specific protective measures for the hardware within this room.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HSM is housed in a rack in a server room that is accessible with a key card. Within the room, however, the rack itself is not locked and the HSM can be easily removed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the crypto hardware is located in a generally access-protected room. However, it is determined that within the room, no further measures (e.g., lockable rack) exist to protect against unauthorized physical access by authorized persons.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The crypto concept SHOULD specify how IT operations ensure that hardware with cryptographic functions cannot be physically accessed without authorization. This specification describes the basic required protective measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The crypto concept stipulates that HSMs and other critical crypto hardware must be housed in lockable server racks or dedicated safes within the server room. The key to these racks/safes is kept separately and access to it is logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the corresponding specifications in the crypto concept. During an inspection, it is checked whether the hardware is actually housed in locked racks or safes and whether a process for managing and logging access to the keys exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to locked enclosures, further protective measures are taken. Physical access is strictly limited to a minimum number of people and every access opening is logged and reviewed. Tamper-evident seals are applied to the hardware to detect unnoticed opening attempts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Only two named administrators have the key to the HSM rack. Every opening is recorded in the logbook with the date, time, and reason. The integrity of the seals attached to the housing screws is checked and documented at every opening and additionally on a quarterly basis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the access logs for the crypto hardware and compares them with the change tickets. The existence and condition of the tamper-evident seals and the logs of their inspection are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The crypto hardware is housed in a high-security environment (e.g., a certified bank vault or a dedicated cage in the data center). Access requires two-factor authentication (e.g., card and biometrics) and is continuously monitored by video. The hardware itself has active tamper detection and response mechanisms (e.g., deletion of keys in case of unauthorized opening), which are centrally monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HSMs are located in their own cage, which can only be entered using a 2-person rule with biometric control. The tamper detection integrated in the HSM is activated and sends a critical alarm to the SIEM if triggered, which initiates an automatic security process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the high-security environment and the configuration of the access control system. The video surveillance recordings and the alarm logs from the SIEM regarding tamper detection are analyzed. The configuration of the tamper-response mechanisms in the HSM is checked.

controls.title: Emanation security

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The risk of compromising electromagnetic emanations (TEMPEST) is not considered or assessed in any way. The topic is not known or is considered irrelevant.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Highly sensitive cryptographic operations take place on standard hardware in a normal office room with outside windows, without any consideration for emanation security.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by questioning the CISO or IT management that the topic of emanation security has not been addressed so far. A risk assessment on this topic does not exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general awareness of the risk of emanation security, but no formal or documented assessment is carried out to determine whether measures are necessary. There is a reliance on general physical security measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When planning a new server room, the topic is mentioned briefly, but dismissed with the argument that the room has no outside windows and the walls are made of concrete. No measurement or detailed analysis is carried out.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In interviews, the auditor finds that although the topic is known, no formal risk assessment or documentation exists. Decisions are made based on assumptions and not on facts or analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of the risk analysis, it SHOULD be checked and documented whether additional measures regarding emanation security are necessary. This check is a defined part of the risk management process for systems with high protection requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The risk management manual contains a checklist that includes the item 'Check the need for emanation protection'. For systems classified as very critical, this item is processed and the decision (measures required / not required) is documented with a justification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the risk management documentation for systems with high protection requirements and verifies whether the check on emanation security has been demonstrably and comprehensibly documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal, detailed check of emanation security SHOULD be carried out in particular when classified government information (CI) of the classification levels CONFIDENTIAL or higher is processed. Measures taken regarding emanation security SHOULD be documented in the crypto concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When planning a classified information workstation, a TEMPEST assessment is carried out as standard. Possible measures, such as the selection of specially shielded hardware or the definition of minimum distances to unsecured areas, are implemented and recorded in the system documentation and the crypto concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In the case of systems that process classified information, the auditor verifies that a specific TEMPEST assessment has taken place. The implementation of the resulting measures is checked on site and in the documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the formal assessment, active protective measures are implemented. This can include the use of specially certified, low-emanation hardware (TEMPEST-certified), shielded racks, or the construction of shielded rooms (Faraday cages). The effectiveness of the measures is checked by specialized on-site measurements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the processing of data with the highest protection requirements, a data center area is converted into a Faraday cage. After the IT installation, a specialized service provider carries out an acceptance measurement to certify compliance with the shielding requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documents and the acceptance certificates for the implemented emanation protection measures. Compliance with the relevant national standards (e.g., of the BSI) is checked. An automated check is not possible here; it is an audit of the physical and technical documentation.

controls.title: Cryptographic replacement hardware

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No special replacement hardware is kept for cryptographic components. In the event of a failure, re-procurement is subject to standard procurement times, which can lead to long downtimes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The central HSM fails. The manufacturer has a delivery time of four weeks. During this time, all applications dependent on the HSM are unavailable.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the contingency plan for the failure of critical crypto hardware and about the inventory of spare devices. The absence of both indicates this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Replacement hardware is kept on hand for some common, low-cost crypto components such as smart card readers or USB tokens. However, for expensive, specialized hardware such as HSMs, there is no replacement; reliance is placed on service contracts with the manufacturer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are some spare tokens for 2-factor authentication in the IT warehouse. For the failed HSM, there is a '48h on-site service' contract.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the spare parts concept and the service contracts. It is assessed whether the recovery times from the service contracts correspond to the availability requirements of the dependent processes. Often, a discrepancy can be identified (e.g., critical process requires 4h recovery, contract offers 48h).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware with cryptographic functions (e.g. hardware tokens for two-factor authentication) SHOULD be in stock. The crypto concept SHOULD document which hardware with cryptographic functions has replacement hardware available and how it is replaced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on a criticality analysis, a decision is made as to which hardware (e.g. HSMs, tokens) spare devices are kept in stock for. The crypto concept contains a list of this hardware as well as a step-by-step guide for the replacement process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the list of replacement hardware to be kept in stock from the crypto concept with the actual inventory. The replacement instructions are checked for completeness and clarity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The spare hardware in stock is not only stored, but is also pre-configured ('Cold Standby') and regularly tested (e.g. annually) to ensure its functionality. The documented replacement process is practiced regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The spare HSM in the safe already has the current firmware and a basic configuration loaded. Once a year, it is taken out of the safe, started up, and a functional test is performed. The replacement process is part of the annual IT emergency drill.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the logs of the regular tests of the spare hardware and of the emergency drills. It is checked whether the configuration of the spare hardware is up to date.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all critical cryptographic functions, a fully redundant, high-availability hardware architecture ('Hot Standby') is implemented, which enables automatic failover in the event of a failure without manual intervention. Replacing a defective component is an interruption-free routine procedure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HSMs are operated as a geo-redundant cluster. If one HSM fails at one location, the other HSMs seamlessly take over operation. The defective device can be replaced during ongoing operation. The failover is regularly tested automatically.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the high-availability crypto cluster. The configuration of the failover mechanism and the logs of the automated failover tests are checked. The effectiveness can be demonstrated by an announced test (e.g., disconnecting a cluster node from the network).

controls.title: Tamper detection for hardware or software with cryptographic functions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No specific measures are taken to detect tampering with crypto components. Reliance is placed on general protective measures such as virus scanners, which are not designed for targeted attacks on crypto libraries.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A new version of a crypto library is installed without checking its integrity (e.g. hash value, digital signature).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about processes and tools for monitoring the integrity of crypto components. The absence of such specific measures indicates this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of crypto software is manually checked during installation by comparing hash values. For hardware, a visual inspection for obvious physical damage is performed during commissioning. Continuous monitoring does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrator checks the SHA256 hash of the download before installing OpenSSL. After installation, the integrity is no longer checked. A new HSM is checked for scratches or opened seals before installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the integrity check is part of the installation instructions. However, it is noted that no regular or continuous monitoring of integrity takes place during operation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware and software with cryptographic functions SHOULD be monitored for tampering attempts. The methods and frequency of this monitoring are documented in the crypto concept or a relevant operating instruction.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The crypto concept stipulates that File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) must be set up for all critical crypto libraries. For hardware, a regular, logged inspection for physical tampering is planned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the specifications for tamper detection in the crypto concept. It is checked whether the defined monitoring measures (e.g. FIM tool, inspection logs) are actually implemented and operated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) continuously monitors all critical crypto software components and configuration files and raises an alarm in case of changes. For hardware, tamper-evident seals are used, the condition of which is logged regularly and after every physical access. Hardware self-tests, which also check integrity, are activated and their logs are centrally collected and evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An FIM agent runs on all servers that provide crypto functions. Changes to OpenSSL libraries or the SSH configuration trigger an alert in the SIEM. The condition of the seals on the HSM is documented in the ticket system during each maintenance. HSM log files are sent to a central syslog server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the FIM tool and the alerts in the SIEM. The logs of the physical inspections and the centrally collected hardware logs are reviewed. An automated check could change an unimportant file in the monitored directory to see if an alarm is triggered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware with certified physical and logical tamper detection and response mechanisms (e.g., FIPS 140-2 Level 3/4) is used. These mechanisms are actively monitored, and an alarm triggers an automated incident response process. For software, Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) is used to detect and block tampering at runtime.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HSMs used are FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified. An attempt to open the housing leads to the immediate deletion of all keys and an alert. Critical applications are instrumented with a RASP module that detects attempts to patch crypto functions at runtime and terminates the process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the certification of the hardware and the configuration of the active tamper response. The effectiveness of the RASP is evaluated by analyzing the configuration and the triggered alerts. The incident response process, which is triggered by a tamper alarm, is checked for its functionality.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Cryptography is a widely used means of ensuring information security in terms of the protection goals of confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. For example, it makes it possible to encrypt information in such a way that its content is unreadable without the corresponding key. In symmetric methods, the same key is used for encryption and decryption, whereas in asymmetric methods, one key is used for encryption and another for decryption.
In a wide variety of IT environments, such as client-server environments, locally stored information and information to be transmitted between communication partners can be effectively protected by cryptographic methods. Cryptographic methods can be implemented in hardware or software components (hereinafter referred to as hardware or software with cryptographic functions).
The sole technical use of cryptographic methods is not sufficient to guarantee the confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of the information. In addition, organizational measures are required. To effectively protect information, it is necessary to address the topic of cryptography holistically within the framework of a crypto concept.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module describes how a crypto concept should be created and how it can be used to cryptographically secure information in institutions.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The CON.1 Crypto Concept module is to be applied once to the information domain. This module deals with organizational and technical requirements for hardware or software with cryptographic functions, as well as cryptographic methods. The core IT tasks associated with the operation of hardware or software with cryptographic functions are not addressed. For this, the requirements of the modules from the OPS.1.1 Core IT Operations layer must be met.
How applications (e.g., end-to-end encryption for emails), individual IT systems (e.g., laptops), or communication links can be cryptographically secured is also not the subject of this module. These topics are covered in the corresponding modules of the APP Applications, SYS IT Systems, and NET Networks and Communication layers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Inadequate key management for encryption
parts.prose:
Inadequate key management could lead to the disclosure of unencrypted information during attacks. For example, due to a lack of regulations, encrypted information and its corresponding keys might be located on the same data medium or transmitted unencrypted over the same communication channel. In these cases, with symmetric methods, any person who can access the data medium or the communication channel can decrypt the information.
Inadequate or missing key management can also threaten the availability of applications, for example, if cryptographic functions become unusable after the validity period of keys or certificates has expired.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Violation of legal frameworks when using hardware or software with cryptographic functions
parts.prose:
When institutions use hardware or software with cryptographic functions, they must comply with various legal frameworks. In some countries, for example, cryptographic methods may only be used with government approval, which significantly restricts the use of hardware or software with strong cryptographic functions. This can mean that recipients in such countries cannot read encrypted data records because they are not allowed to use the required hardware or software with cryptographic functions. In the worst case, recipients would even be committing a criminal offense if they were to use the required hardware or software with cryptographic functions without authorization. Or this situation tempts the people involved in the communication to exchange the information unencrypted, which in turn can lead to a multitude of threats to the confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of the exchanged information.
A situation may even arise where the legal provisions of one country stipulate that appropriate cryptography must be used, while the provisions of another country prohibit this or provide for a state-sanctioned decryption capability. For example, European data protection regulations may require that appropriate cryptographic methods be used to protect personal data. If communication is to take place from such a European country to another country where the use of cryptography is highly regulated and not approved in the specific case, then legal communication between two people from the respective countries is not possible.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Loss of confidentiality or integrity of information due to misconduct
parts.prose:
If cryptographic functions are not used or not used correctly, they cannot provide the intended protection for information. For example, if an institution uses hardware or software with cryptographic functions that is very complicated to operate, users might forgo encrypting the information and transmit it in plain text instead. As a result, the transmitted information can be read during an attack.
If hardware or software with cryptographic functions is operated incorrectly, this can also lead to confidential information being intercepted during attacks, for example, if it is transmitted in plain text because the plain text mode was accidentally activated.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Vulnerabilities or errors in hardware or software with cryptographic functions
parts.prose:
Vulnerabilities or errors in hardware or software with cryptographic functions compromise the security of the cryptographic methods used. They can, for example, lead to the protected information being read.
For example, a variety of cryptographic methods rely on random number generators to generate secure keys, e.g., for a communication link. Even if such a method is considered fundamentally and conceptually secure, an error in the hardware or software implementation can lead, for example, to predictable random numbers being generated and thus the associated cryptographic keys being reconstructed. This allows encrypted information to be spied on, which in turn can have far-reaching consequences.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Failure of hardware with cryptographic functions
parts.prose: Hardware with cryptographic functions (e.g. smart cards for drive encryption) can fail due to technical defects, power outages or deliberate destruction. As a result, already encrypted information could no longer be decrypted as long as the required hardware is not available. As a consequence, entire process chains can come to a standstill, e.g. if other applications are dependent on the information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Insecure cryptographic algorithms
parts.prose: Insecure or outdated cryptographic algorithms can be broken with little effort in an attack. For encryption algorithms, this means that it is possible to determine the original plaintext from the encrypted text without any additional information being available in the attack, such as the cryptographic key used. If insecure cryptographic algorithms are used, attackers can bypass the cryptographic protection and thus access sensitive information of the institution. Even if an institution exclusively uses secure (e.g. certified) hardware or software with cryptographic functions, the communication can still become insecure. This is the case, for example, if the communication partner uses cryptographic methods that are not state-of-the-art.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Errors in encrypted information or cryptographic keys
parts.prose:
If information is encrypted and the ciphertext is subsequently changed, the encrypted information may no longer be decrypted correctly. Depending on the mode of operation of the encryption routines, this can mean that only a few bytes or all of the information is lost. If no data backup is available, such information is lost. This circumstance can also be exploited in attacks by changing only a minimal part of the ciphertext, causing the encrypted information to be completely lost.
An error in the cryptographic keys used can have an even more critical effect. Even changing a single bit of a cryptographic key means that all information encrypted with it can no longer be decrypted.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Compromise of cryptographic keys
parts.prose: The security of cryptographic methods depends critically on how confidential the used cryptographic keys remain. Therefore, an attack will usually try to obtain or determine the keys used. This could be achieved, for example, by reading volatile memory or finding unprotected keys that are stored, for example, in a data backup or a configuration file. If the keys used and the crypto method used are known, the information can be decrypted relatively easily.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Forged certificates
parts.prose:
Certificates are used to bind a public cryptographic key to a person, an IT system, or an institution. This binding of the key is in turn cryptographically secured by means of a digital signature, often from a trusted third party.
Certificates are used by third parties to verify digital signatures of the person, IT system, or institution identified in the certificate. Alternatively, the key stored in the certificate can be used for an asymmetric encryption method to encrypt the information for the certificate holder.
If such a certificate is forged, digital signatures are incorrectly verified and assigned to the person, IT system, or institution in the certificate. Or information is encrypted with a possibly insecure key and sent.

controls.title: Authentication in web applications (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is only implemented for individual, particularly critical functions of the web application. There is no central concept, and the implementation is inconsistent.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, only the administration area is protected by a password, while other areas with sensitive data, such as user profiles, are accessible without authentication.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether functions that process sensitive data or perform critical actions can be called without prior authentication.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All protected functions and content require authentication. A basic authentication method, usually username and password, is used. However, there are no measures to protect against brute-force attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple login form is placed in front of all protected areas. The password reset function exists, but does not proactively inform the user about the change that has been made.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is verified that all routes defined as protected require authentication. An attempt is made to simulate a brute-force attack by repeatedly entering an incorrect password and to check whether countermeasures are effective.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The developers MUST ensure that users can authenticate themselves to the web application securely and appropriately. An appropriate authentication method MUST be selected and the selection process documented. A central authentication component SHOULD be used. If authentication data is stored on a client, the user MUST explicitly consent ('opt-in'). The web application MUST immediately inform users when their password has been reset.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For implementation, an established standard component from a framework (e.g. Spring Security, ASP.NET Core Identity) is used. The password reset function sends a notification email to the user's stored address. The 'Stay logged in' function is only activated after explicit consent from the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The documentation of the selection process for the authentication method is checked. The configuration of the central authentication component is analyzed. It is tested whether a notification is sent when a password is reset and whether storing authentication data on the client requires explicit consent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined requirements, the web application MUST set and implement limits for failed login attempts to make brute-force attacks more difficult. After a defined number of failed attempts, the account is temporarily locked. Password policies (minimum length, complexity) are enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A mechanism for counting login failures per user account is implemented in the authentication component. For example, after five failed attempts, the account is locked for 15 minutes. When creating and changing passwords, complexity rules are validated on the server side.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether the set limits for failed logins are effective by intentionally entering several wrong passwords. It is verified that the account is temporarily locked. An attempt is made to set a password that is too short or too simple to test the implementation of the password policies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is secured by a second factor (MFA). Login attempts are monitored for anomalous behavior (e.g., impossible travel scenarios, logins from known malicious IP addresses). Passwords are checked against lists of known compromised passwords upon entry.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MFA solution using TOTP (e.g., Google Authenticator) or FIDO2/WebAuthn is implemented. The login logs are sent to a SIEM system where rules for anomaly detection are configured. An API like HaveIBeenPwned is used to check passwords.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether MFA is enforced for all or at least for privileged accounts. The configuration of the anomaly detection in the SIEM is analyzed. An attempt is made to use a known compromised password, and it is checked whether the system prevents this.

controls.title: Access Control in Web Applications (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access control is only implemented in a rudimentary way. Typically, a distinction is only made between anonymous users and logged-in users, without finer-grained permission levels.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application only checks if a valid session exists. Every logged-in user has the same rights as any other logged-in user, including administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether a normal user can impersonate an administrator, e.g., by calling an administrative URL. It is verified whether all logged-in users can access all data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Role-based access control is in place. However, the check only occurs at the URL level (e.g., access to '/admin'), but not at the level of individual data objects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Roles like 'USER' and 'ADMIN' are defined. A normal user cannot call the '/admin' URL. However, they may be able to edit another user's data by manipulating an ID in another URL (e.g., '/users/123/edit').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: As a normal user, an attempt is made to access data for which there is no authorization by manipulating URL parameters (e.g., IDs) (Insecure Direct Object Reference).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Developers MUST use an authorization component to ensure that users can only perform actions for which they are authorized. Every access to protected content and functions MUST be controlled. The authorization component MUST consider all resources and content. There MUST be access control for URL calls AND object references.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central authorization component is used. Every request to the business logic checks not only the user's role but also their permission for the specific data object (e.g., 'can user A edit document B?'). This is enforced server-side on every access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether access control is enforced centrally and server-side. Code reviews or penetration tests are used to verify that both URL-based and object-based access control are correctly implemented and that faulty access attempts are rejected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access control is based on an explicitly defined and documented authorization concept. Access decisions are logged centrally to be able to trace unauthorized access attempts. The 'need-to-know' principle (least privilege) is consistently implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The authorization concept is versioned as part of the software documentation. Every rejected access request generates a log entry with details about the requesting user, the target resource, and the timestamp. New user roles are created with minimal rights by default.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The documented authorization concept is checked against the technical implementation. The log files are examined for entries on access denials. It is checked whether the default rights assignment follows the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access control is attribute-based (ABAC) and allows for dynamic and context-sensitive decisions (e.g., based on time of day, location, or transaction risk level). Changes to permissions are reviewed and approved according to the four-eyes principle. The effectiveness of access control is continuously verified through automated tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ABAC framework like OPA (Open Policy Agent) is used to manage access rules centrally and declaratively. Changes to these rules require a pull request review by a second person. Integration tests that specifically check authorization scenarios are run in the CI/CD process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The configuration of the ABAC system is checked. The process for changing authorization rules is examined for compliance with the four-eyes principle. The test coverage for the access control logic is verified in the CI/CD system.

controls.title: Secure Session Management (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Session IDs are used, but they are predictable (e.g., sequential) and are not renewed. There is no logout mechanism.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application uses a simple session ID consisting of an ascending number. Once logged in, the session remains valid forever until the browser is closed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Several sessions are created in succession and the session IDs are checked for predictability. It is verified that there is no function to explicitly end the session.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Session IDs are generated randomly. A logout function is available, but the session ID is not renewed after login, which makes the application vulnerable to session fixation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application uses the default session management of a web framework that generates random IDs. There is a logout button. However, session regeneration after login has not been explicitly activated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A session is created before login, then the login is performed, and it is checked whether the session ID remains the same. This indicates a session fixation vulnerability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Session IDs MUST be generated randomly and with sufficient entropy. After an account has logged in, an existing session ID MUST be replaced with a new one. Sessions MUST have a maximum validity period (timeout). Inactive sessions MUST automatically become invalid after a certain time. A web application MUST offer the option to explicitly terminate an existing session. After the session is invalid, all session data MUST be invalid and deleted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The secure session management functions of the framework used are utilized and correctly configured. This includes session regeneration after login, configuration of session timeouts for inactivity and an absolute lifetime, and implementation of a logout function that invalidates the session server-side.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The configuration of the session management in the framework is checked. It is tested whether the session ID changes after login. It is checked whether a session expires after the configured inactivity period and whether the logout button terminates the session server-side.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined requirements, session cookies are set with the 'Secure' and 'HttpOnly' attributes to protect them from theft through Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and transmission over unencrypted connections.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the configuration of the web server or application, it is ensured that all session cookies are delivered with the 'Secure' (send only over HTTPS) and 'HttpOnly' (not readable by JavaScript) flags.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The browser's developer tools are used to check whether the session cookie set by the server contains the 'Secure' and 'HttpOnly' attributes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The session is bound server-side to other client characteristics, such as the User-Agent string and the IP address. If these characteristics change during a valid session, the session is invalidated as a precaution to make session hijacking more difficult.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When the session is created, the client's User-Agent and IP address are stored server-side. With each subsequent request with this session ID, the current values are compared with the stored ones. In case of a discrepancy, the session is terminated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A valid session is established. Subsequently, an attempt is made to access the application with the same session ID but via a proxy (different IP) or with a different User-Agent. It is checked whether the application denies access and invalidates the session.

controls.title: Controlled Inclusion of Content in Web Applications (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The application redirects users to external websites without any checks or warnings. URLs for redirection are taken directly from request parameters.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A login function redirects the user to a URL passed in the `redirect_url` parameter after successful login. An attacker can insert a malicious URL here.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether redirection functions exist that derive the target URL from a parameter. It is tested whether a redirection to any external domain is possible (Open Redirect).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Redirections to external websites are possible, but the user is warned by an intermediate page before leaving the site. However, there is no allow list for permitted redirection targets.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the user is redirected to an external page, a message like 'You are now leaving our website. Continue to [external_url]?' appears. The URL itself, however, is not validated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is verified whether the warning message is displayed for all external redirections. It is checked whether the application uses an allow list or allows any URL after the warning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that a web application only includes and delivers intended data and content. The targets of a web application's redirection function MUST be sufficiently restricted so that it only redirects to trusted websites. If the trust domain is left, the web application MUST inform the user.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Redirection URLs are validated against a server-side managed allow list (whitelist) of permitted domains and paths. The redirection is only performed if the target URL is on this list. For targets that are not on the own domain, an information page is displayed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The implementation of the redirection function is analyzed via code review to ensure that a server-side allow list is used. An attempt is made to bypass the validation (e.g., with `example.com.evil.com`) and it is checked whether the redirection is prevented.

controls.title: Upload Functions (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users can upload files, where the filename and path can be controlled by the client. There is no check of the file type or content.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An upload script takes a filename as a parameter (e.g., `upload.php?filename=../../config.php`) and saves the uploaded file under this name. This allows for path traversal attacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: An attempt is made to upload a file with a relative path (`../`) to overwrite existing files on the server. An attempt is made to upload an executable file (e.g., `.php`, `.jsp`) and execute it later.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The upload path is fixed on the server side and cannot be influenced by the user. A basic check of the file extension is carried out to prevent the upload of executable scripts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application checks if the filename ends with `.jpg` or `.png`. However, an attacker could try to upload a file `shell.php.jpg`, which some server configurations would still execute as a PHP script.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: An attempt is made to bypass the file extension check, e.g., by using double extensions, case variations (`.JpG`), or null byte injection in the filename.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Developers MUST ensure that users can only save files in the specified path and cannot influence the storage location. Developers MUST integrate functions into the web application that allow uploads to be configured during the web application's operation (e.g., allowed file types).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Uploaded files are stored in a dedicated directory outside the web root. The filename is regenerated server-side (e.g., from a hash value) to avoid conflicts and attacks. The original filename is stored separately. The allowed file types are validated not by the extension, but by the MIME type and the file's magic byte.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked that uploaded files are stored in a directory that is not directly accessible via the web. It is verified that the filename is generated server-side. An attempt is made to upload a file with a wrong extension but correct content (e.g., a PHP file disguised as a `.jpg`) and it is checked whether the content validation detects this.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined requirements, all uploaded files are scanned for malware server-side with an up-to-date virus scanner before they are further processed or offered for download.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After upload, the file is temporarily stored in a quarantine zone. From there, a server-side scan is initiated with a tool like ClamAV. Only if the scan is successful is the file moved to the final directory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A test file with an EICAR test signature is uploaded. It is checked whether the application correctly blocks the upload and generates a corresponding log entry.

controls.title: Protection against unauthorized automated use of web applications (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic but easily bypassable protection mechanisms against automated use are in place, e.g., a simple, client-side validated CAPTCHA.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CAPTCHA is displayed in the login form, but the check to see if it was solved correctly only takes place in the client's JavaScript. An attacker can simply send the request directly to the server and bypass the client-side check.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A request that calls a protected function (e.g., login) is sent directly to the server using a tool like Burp Suite or `curl`, without the CAPTCHA parameters. It is checked whether the request is still successful.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Developers MUST implement security mechanisms that protect the web application from automated access. The implementation MUST consider how these affect the usage possibilities of legitimate accounts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Server-side protection mechanisms are implemented at critical endpoints (e.g., login, registration, password reset). This can be a server-side validated CAPTCHA (e.g., Google reCAPTCHA v2/v3) or a rate-limiting mechanism that limits the number of requests per IP address and time interval.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether the CAPTCHA mechanism is validated server-side. A script is used to call a function repeatedly, and it is checked whether access is blocked or slowed down after a certain number of requests (e.g., HTTP status code 429 Too Many Requests).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The protection mechanism is adaptive. For example, it is only activated when a suspicious access pattern is detected, so as not to impair usability for normal users. The thresholds for rate-limiting are different per function and are configurable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CAPTCHA is only displayed after three failed login attempts from the same IP address. The rate-limiting for the login function is stricter than for the search function. These thresholds can be adjusted in a configuration file.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Several failed login attempts are made to check if the adaptive protection mechanism (CAPTCHA) is triggered. The configuration is analyzed to verify the different thresholds for different functions.

controls.title: Protection of confidential data (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Confidential data is transmitted via HTTP POST. However, passwords are stored server-side in plain text or with an insecure hash function (e.g., MD5 without salt).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HTML form uses `method="POST"`. On the server, the received password is written directly to the database or hashed with `md5($password)`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The database structure and user management code are analyzed to determine how passwords are stored. It is checked whether outdated hash algorithms are used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Developers MUST ensure that confidential data is transmitted from clients to servers only using the HTTP POST method. Developers MUST ensure through directives in the web application that no sensitive data is cached on the client side. All access credentials for the web application MUST be protected server-side from unauthorized access using secure cryptographic algorithms (Salted Hash). The web application's source code files MUST be protected from unauthorized retrieval.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All forms containing confidential data use `method="POST"`. HTTP headers like `Cache-Control: no-store` are set. Passwords are hashed with a modern, adaptive algorithm like Argon2 or bcrypt and an individual salt per user. The web server is configured to block direct access to source code files (e.g., `.php`, `.py`, `web.config`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The HTML code of forms is checked for the use of `method="POST"`. The HTTP response headers are examined for caching directives. The password processing code is checked for the use of strong hashing algorithms with salt. An attempt is made to access source code files directly via the browser.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined requirements, confidential form data is masked in the display (e.g., password input). The web application SHOULD prevent confidential data from being unexpectedly stored by the web browser by setting `autocomplete="off"` for corresponding fields.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For passwords, `input type="password"` is used. For sensitive fields like credit card numbers or passwords, the attribute `autocomplete="off"` or more specific values like `autocomplete="new-password"` are set in the HTML form to prevent automatic saving by the browser.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether passwords and other sensitive data are masked during input in the browser. The HTML source code of the form fields is checked for the presence of the `autocomplete="off"` attribute or suitable alternatives.

controls.title: Comprehensive input validation and output encoding (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Input validation takes place exclusively on the client side (e.g., with JavaScript). Output data is written directly to the web page without encoding.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A form checks in the browser whether an email address contains an '@' character. An attacker can bypass this check and send arbitrary data to the server. This data is then output directly in the HTML response, leading to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: An attempt is made to send a request with invalid data directly to the server to bypass client-side validation. An attempt is made to inject HTML and JavaScript code into input fields and check if it is executed on output.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Server-side input validation is present, but it is based on a blacklist, i.e., it attempts to filter known dangerous characters (e.g., `<script>`). This approach is often incomplete.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A server-side script removes the word `<script>` from all inputs. An attacker can easily bypass this, e.g., by using `<sCrIpT>` or by using event handlers like `onerror`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Various bypass techniques for the implemented blacklist filter are tested to identify XSS vulnerabilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Developers MUST treat all data passed to a web application as potentially dangerous and filter it appropriately. All input data, data streams, and secondary data MUST be validated server-side. The validation should be based on a whitelist. Output data MUST be encoded in such a way that malicious code is not interpreted or executed on the target system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each input field, an expected format is defined server-side (e.g., 'may only consist of digits', 'must be a valid email address'). All inputs that do not conform to this format are rejected. Before outputting to an HTML page, all data is context-sensitively encoded (e.g., `>` becomes `>`) to prevent XSS. Standard framework functions (e.g., Twig, Jinja2, React) are used for this purpose.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The implementation of the server-side whitelist validation is checked via code review. Test data that is just outside the specification is entered to test the strictness of the validation. It is checked whether the output encoding is context-sensitive and consistently applied to all user-controlled data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to validation and encoding, a Content Security Policy (CSP) is used to drastically reduce the impact of any remaining XSS vulnerabilities by preventing the execution of unauthorized JavaScript in the browser.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A restrictive `Content-Security-Policy` HTTP header is sent by the server. For example, it only allows the execution of scripts that originate from its own domain and prohibits inline scripts and `eval()`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The `Content-Security-Policy` header sent by the server is analyzed. It is checked how restrictive the policy is and whether it effectively protects against typical XSS attacks. It is checked whether the application works without CSP violations in the browser console.

controls.title: Protection against SQL Injection (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: SQL queries are created by directly concatenating strings with user input. There are no protective measures against SQL injection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The code contains queries like `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '` + userId + `'`. An attacker can inject SQL code here, e.g., `' OR 1=1 --`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: An attempt is made to enter SQL-specific characters such as the single quote (') or SQL keywords into all input fields that interact with the database in order to provoke errors or unexpected behavior that indicate an SQL injection vulnerability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An attempt is made to prevent SQL injection by manually escaping critical characters (e.g., the single quote). This approach is error-prone and often incomplete.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before insertion into the SQL query, every `'` in the user input is replaced with `''`. This does not protect against all types of SQL injection, especially if the input is expected in a numeric context.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Advanced SQL injection techniques that go beyond simple single quotes are tested to check the effectiveness of manual escaping. The source code is examined for places where the escape function was forgotten.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If data is passed to a database management system (DBMS), stored procedures or prepared SQL statements (parameterized queries) MUST be used. If these are not supported by the deployment environment, the SQL queries MUST be secured separately.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Parameterized interfaces provided by the respective database interface or framework (e.g., PDO in PHP, JDBC PreparedStatement in Java) are used for all database queries. User input is never concatenated directly into SQL strings but is always passed as separate parameters.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: All source code that interacts with the database is code-reviewed to verify that only parameterized queries or stored procedures are used. Any form of string concatenation with user input in SQL queries is reported as a critical vulnerability.

controls.title: Restrictive Disclosure of Security-Relevant Information (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In case of an error, detailed error messages and stack traces are output to the user. These often contain sensitive information about the internal system architecture.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The debug mode is activated in the application or web server configuration, which leads to the display of verbose error pages.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: An attempt is made to intentionally provoke errors through invalid input. It is checked whether the resulting error messages disclose sensitive information such as database table names, file paths, or internal function names.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Developers MUST ensure that web pages, responses, and error messages from web applications do not contain information that could give attackers clues on how to bypass security mechanisms. This includes version numbers, internal paths, database schemas, or detailed error messages.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Only generic error messages are displayed to the user (e.g., 'An unexpected error has occurred. Please try again later.'). Detailed error information is written exclusively to server-side log files. HTTP headers such as 'Server' or 'X-Powered-By' that indicate the technologies used are suppressed or anonymized.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Errors are provoked and it is checked that the error messages displayed to the client are generic. The server-side logs are checked for completeness of the error information. The HTTP response headers are examined for unnecessary information disclosure.

controls.title: Web Application Software Architecture (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The software architecture is documented, but the documentation is only updated sporadically and is often not up-to-date. Security mechanisms are not explicitly identified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an architecture diagram in a wiki that reflects the state of a year ago. New components or changes to security features have not been added.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The existing documentation is compared with the actual code and the running application to identify deviations and outdated information.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Developers SHOULD document the software architecture of the web application with all its components and dependencies. The documentation SHOULD be updated during the development process. It SHOULD be designed in such a way that it can be used during the development phase and decisions are traceable. The documentation SHOULD describe which components implement which security mechanisms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The architecture is maintained using a 'Documentation-as-Code' approach. Diagrams are generated from text files using tools like PlantUML or Mermaid, which are versioned along with the source code. The documentation clearly assigns which component is responsible for authentication, authorization, validation, etc.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The revision history of the documentation and the code is compared to check if they are updated synchronously. The documentation is checked for completeness and traceability, especially regarding the description of security components.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The architecture documentation is extended with data flow diagrams and threat modeling (e.g., using STRIDE) for the critical components. Security-relevant design decisions are explicitly justified and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A threat modeling workshop is conducted for each new critical function. The results, including the identified threats and the planned countermeasures, become part of the architecture documentation. Data flows, especially of sensitive data, are visualized.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The threat modeling documentation is reviewed. It is verified that adequate countermeasures for the identified threats are provided in the architecture. The data flow diagrams are checked for plausibility and correctness.

controls.title: Verification of Essential Changes (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If important settings are to be changed with the application (e.g., changing the email address or password), developers SHOULD ensure that the changes are re-verified by entering the password. If this is not possible, the web application SHOULD ensure that users authenticate in another suitable way.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a user tries to change their email address or password, they are prompted to re-enter their current password to confirm the action. This prevents someone who has temporary access to a logged-in computer from changing critical account settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: An attempt is made to change critical account settings such as the password or email address in an active session. It is checked whether the application requires re-authentication (e.g., password entry) before the change takes effect.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to re-authentication, users SHOULD be informed about security-critical changes via communication channels outside the web application.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After a successful and verified change of the password or email address, the application automatically sends a notification email to the *old* and the *new* email address. This email informs the user about the change that was made.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A critical account change is performed. It is checked whether a notification is sent to the stored contact addresses (e.g., via email) informing about the change.

controls.title: Error Handling (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unexpected errors lead to the application crashing or put it in an inconsistent state. Error messages are not logged centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An unhandled exception in a function causes the entire application process to terminate and become unavailable to all users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: An attempt is made to provoke unhandled exceptions through unexpected input or by calling functions in the wrong order. It is observed whether the application remains stable or crashes. It is checked whether errors are recorded in a log file.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If errors occur during the runtime of a web application, they SHOULD be handled in such a way that the web application remains in a consistent state. The web application SHOULD log error messages. If an initiated action causes an error, the web application SHOULD cancel this action. In the event of an error, the web application SHOULD deny access to a requested resource or function.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All potentially failing operations are encapsulated in try-catch blocks. In case of an error (catch block), initiated transactions are rolled back to maintain data consistency. The error is logged server-side with all relevant details (stack trace, context), and a generic error message is displayed to the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The error handling logic is analyzed via code review. It is checked whether database transactions are correctly rolled back in case of an error. It is verified that errors are logged centrally and with sufficient detail, while the user only receives a generic message.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Previously reserved resources SHOULD be released as part of error handling. The error SHOULD be handled by the web application itself as much as possible, rather than relying on the runtime environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Constructs like `try-finally` or `try-with-resources` (in Java) are used to ensure that resources such as file handles or network connections are properly closed and released even in the event of an error. This prevents resource leaks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code is checked for the correct use of resource management constructs. Long-term load tests are performed, during which errors are deliberately injected to observe whether resource usage (e.g., memory, handles) increases over time.

controls.title: Secure HTTP Configuration in Web Applications (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some security-relevant HTTP headers are set, but not consistently or not restrictively enough. Cookies are used without security settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `X-Content-Type-Options` header is set, but a `Content-Security-Policy` header is missing. Cookies are created without the `secure`, `httponly`, and `samesite` attributes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The HTTP headers sent by the application and the cookies set are analyzed using the browser's developer tools or a specialized tool. It is checked which security-relevant headers are missing or insufficiently configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To protect against clickjacking, cross-site scripting, and other attacks, appropriate HTTP response headers SHOULD be set. At a minimum, the following HTTP headers SHOULD be used: Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Type, X-Content-Type-Options, and Cache-Control. Cookies SHOULD generally be set with the secure, SameSite, and httponly attributes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web application or web server is configured to send the required HTTP headers with secure, restrictive values. The Content Security Policy (CSP) is defined to prohibit inline scripts and only allow content from trusted sources. All cookies are set by default with the `secure`, `httponly`, and `samesite=strict` or `samesite=lax` attributes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A comprehensive check of all HTTP headers sent by the application is performed, e.g., using online scanners like `securityheaders.com`. It is verified that all required headers are present and securely configured, and that all cookies have the necessary security attributes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The HTTP headers used SHOULD be tailored to the web application and be as restrictive as possible. The Content Security Policy is not only set but actively maintained and adapted to new functionalities of the application.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CSP is defined granularly to allow only the exact scripts, styles, and sources required. Instead of using wildcards, specific hosts are listed. Changes to the CSP are part of the regular development process when new third-party resources are integrated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The CSP is checked for overly permissive directives such as `unsafe-inline`, `unsafe-eval`, or wildcards in `script-src` or `style-src`. It is verified that the policy is precisely tailored to the application's needs.

controls.title: Prevention of Cross-Site Request Forgery (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some measures against CSRF are in place, e.g., the exclusive use of POST requests for state-changing operations, but an anti-CSRF token is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All actions like 'Delete' or 'Save' are handled via POST requests. However, an attacker can still create a malicious website containing a form that automatically sends a POST request to the vulnerable application.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A web page is created that sends a form to a state-changing endpoint of the target application. It is checked whether the action is executed successfully when a user logged into the target application visits the malicious page.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The developers SHOULD equip the web application with security mechanisms that allow distinguishing between intended page views and unintentionally forwarded commands from third parties. At a minimum, it SHOULD be checked whether a secret token (anti-CSRF token) is required in addition to the session ID to access protected resources and functions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application implements the Synchronizer Token Pattern. For each user session, a random, secret token is generated. This token must be sent with every state-changing request (e.g., POST, PUT, DELETE) as a hidden parameter in the form or as an HTTP header. The server validates on each request that the submitted token matches the token stored in the session.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether all forms that trigger state-changing actions contain an anti-CSRF token. An attempt is made to send a request without a token or with an incorrect token, and it is verified that the server rejects the request with an error.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the anti-CSRF token, the `SameSite` attribute for cookies is consistently set to `Strict` or `Lax`. This provides an additional layer of protection against CSRF that is enforced by modern browsers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All cookies, especially the session cookie, are set with the `SameSite=Strict` attribute. This instructs the browser not to send the cookie with cross-site requests, which prevents most CSRF attacks from the outset.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Using the browser's developer tools, it is checked whether all cookies set by the application contain the `SameSite` attribute with a secure value (`Strict` or `Lax`).

controls.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) SHOULD be implemented. Users are offered the option to additionally secure their account with a second factor.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the account settings, the user can optionally activate MFA via a TOTP application (such as Google Authenticator or FreeOTP). After activation, upon login, the user is prompted for the 6-digit code from the app in addition to entering their password.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether the functionality to activate MFA is present and functional in the account settings. After activation, the login process is tested to verify that the second factor is correctly requested and validated.

parts.name: statement
