parts.prose: The collection of influencing factors is carried out for all IT systems, but primarily focuses on technical aspects such as storage volume and change rates. The requirements of the business owners are collected but not systematically recorded or prioritized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard questionnaire is used to collect technical data from the system owners. The results are recorded in a simple list or table, but there is no formal coordination with the business departments regarding availability or confidentiality requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds documented collections of technical influencing factors for most systems. However, interviews with business owners make it clear that their specific requirements (e.g. maximum downtime) have not been fully captured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations MUST collect the framework conditions for data backup for every IT system and application. To do this, the business owners MUST define their requirements. At a minimum, the following points MUST be coordinated: data to be backed up, storage volume, change volume, change times, availability requirements, confidentiality requirements, integrity needs, legal requirements, requirements for deletion and destruction, and responsibilities. The influencing factors MUST be documented in a traceable manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Structured interviews with business owners and system administrators are conducted to collect the information. The results are recorded in a standardized document per system or application. This document serves as direct input for the creation of data backup plans. New requirements are captured as part of the change management process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly verifies for several critical systems that the documentation of the influencing factors exists and is complete. They check whether the documented requirements (e.g., RPO) have been demonstrably confirmed by the respective business owners (e.g., by signature or ticket approval).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for collecting influencing factors is formalized and integrated into IT Service Management. There is a fixed, regular review cycle (e.g., annually) to update the requirements for all systems, even if no changes have been reported. The results are stored in a central database (e.g., CMDB).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The influencing factors are maintained as attributes of Configuration Items (CIs) in the CMDB. Changes to systems or applications in the change management process automatically trigger a workflow to review the associated data backup requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the process for collecting and reviewing the influencing factors is defined in the process manual of the ISMS or IT operations. They check the CMDB for completeness of the requirement data and verify, based on change tickets, that the review process is followed when changes are made.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The collection and updating of influencing factors is largely automated. The system correlates data from the Business Impact Analysis (BIA), the risk management tool, the CMDB, and legal databases to dynamically determine and adjust protection and availability requirements. Changes in business processes automatically trigger a reassessment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool is used to model the dependencies between business processes, applications, and IT systems. BIA results (RPO, RTO) are directly incorporated into the configuration of the backup system to ensure compliance with the requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration and workflows of the GRC tool. They have it demonstrated how a change in the criticality of a business process in the BIA automatically affects the data backup requirements of the supporting IT system and triggers an adjustment of the backup plan.

controls.title: Defining the procedures for data backup

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no uniformly defined procedures. Data backup is performed individually on each system at the discretion of the respective administrator. Usually, only full backups are created, without considering efficiency or RPO.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators use different tools and scripts. Backup media are labeled and stored ad hoc. There are no regulations for retention or transport.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By interviewing various administrators and reviewing backup logs, the auditor determines that there are no consistent procedures. The backup methods (e.g., time, frequency) differ significantly between similar systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic data backup procedures (type, frequency) are defined for all systems, but they are generic and not tailored to the specific requirements of individual systems. Data backups are stored on separate storage media.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An organization-wide policy mandates daily backups for all servers, for example, regardless of their criticality or data change rate. A single standard storage medium (e.g., external hard drives) is used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds a general policy on data backup. They determine that although the procedures are implemented, they do not take into account the specific influencing factors identified in CON.3.A1 (e.g., different RPOs).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations MUST establish procedures on how data is to be backed up. For the data backup procedures, the type, frequency, and timing of data backups MUST be determined based on the collected influencing factors and in coordination with the business owners. It MUST be defined which storage media are used and how the transport and retention modalities are designed. Data backups MUST always be stored on separate storage media.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procedures are described in detail in a central document (e.g., the data backup concept). For different system categories (defined by criticality and RPO), this document specifies whether full, incremental, or differential backups are used, which backup windows apply, and which storage media are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the defined procedures are documented and based on the results of CON.3.A1. They randomly check the configuration of the backup system to ensure that the defined procedures (e.g., backup type and frequency) are correctly implemented for selected systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procedures are refined and optimized. Particularly sensitive storage media for data backup are only connected to the network during data backup and data recovery (air-gap principle). In virtual environments, snapshot technology is additionally used to create quickly restorable intermediate versions. The choice of backup method is explicitly optimized for RPO/RTO and storage efficiency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Backup systems are configured so that the connection to the backup targets is only active for the duration of the backup job. For virtual machines, hourly snapshots are created and retained for 24 hours, while tape backup only occurs nightly. Combined strategies (e.g., weekly full, daily differential) are used to optimize backup windows and recovery times.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the implementation of the offline connection of the storage media by checking the network configuration and the backup scripts. They check the configuration of the virtualization platform for the existence of and compliance with the snapshot policies. They have the rationale for the chosen backup strategy (e.g., differential vs. incremental) explained.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The backup strategy is dynamic and automated. The backup system automatically selects the optimal backup method and schedule based on real-time data change rates and system criticality (from the CMDB). Immutable storage (Immutable Storage/WORM) is used for critical data backups to ensure maximum protection against manipulation and ransomware.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Modern backup solutions are used that integrate with the CMDB and monitoring systems. Policies define that systems with high data change rates are automatically switched to continuous data protection (CDP). The backup repositories are configured on storage systems with WORM functionality or in a cloud with Object Lock.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the configuration of the automation workflows in the backup system demonstrated. They verify the configuration of the storage system to ensure that immutability is correctly activated for critical backups and test this with a simulated deletion attempt.

controls.title: Creation of data backup plans

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data backup plans exist only as informal notes or comments in backup scripts. The knowledge about the execution and recovery is person-dependent and not documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator has written a shell script that performs a backup. The necessary steps for recovery are not recorded anywhere and are only known to this administrator.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the data backup plan for a specific system. The response is that there is none or only a script without further documentation can be provided. An interview with another administrator confirms that they would not be able to perform the recovery.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Simple, documented data backup plans exist for each system. These describe the basic backup process, but lack details on specific parameters, error handling, or the recovery sequence for complex systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each backup job, a Word document is created that describes what data is backed up and how to start the recovery in a normal case. Information on retention periods or the protection of backups is missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds documents for most systems that are labeled as data backup plans. Upon review, they find that essential information (e.g., recovery sequence for an application with a database) is missing, which would complicate recovery in an emergency.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations MUST create data backup plans for each IT system or group of IT systems. These MUST specify the requirements to be met and contain at least a brief description of: which IT systems and data are backed up, the order of restoration, how backups are created and restored, how long they are retained, how they are protected from unauthorized access, which parameters are to be selected, and which hardware and software are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized template for data backup plans is used, which covers all required points. The completed plans are stored in a central location accessible to operations staff (e.g., Wiki, SharePoint).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly selects several data backup plans and checks them for completeness against the required points using a checklist. They verify whether the plans are up-to-date and correspond to the actual configuration of the backup system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data backup plans are subject to version control and are stored in a highly available repository. They contain detailed troubleshooting instructions for common problems and are directly linked to the system's entry in the CMDB.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The data backup plans are managed in a Git repository, which allows tracking of all changes. Each plan includes a 'Troubleshooting' section that describes solutions for known error messages. In the CMDB, each CI is linked to its corresponding backup plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the version history of a data backup plan to understand the change management process. They have someone demonstrate the direct jump from the CMDB to the correct data backup plan for a selected system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data backup plans are 'executable documentation'. The plan is a configuration file for an automation engine (Infrastructure as Code) that orchestrates the entire backup and recovery process. This ensures that the plan is always up-to-date and directly testable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Ansible, Puppet, or Terraform are used to define the configuration of the backup jobs. The recovery process is also mapped as code, which can build a complete environment including network and dependencies in a sandbox on demand. The plans are part of the CI/CD pipeline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the code and configuration files in the repository that represent the data backup plan. They have someone demonstrate the execution of an automated restore test that is initiated directly from the plan defined in the repository.

controls.title: Regular data backup

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data backups are performed irregularly and often manually, whenever an administrator remembers to do so. Employees are not formally informed about their data backup responsibilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrator manually starts the backup jobs at the end of the week. When they are on vacation, no backups are made. There is no formal assignment of responsibilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the backup logs or the timestamps of the backup files and finds large, irregular gaps. Interviews with employees show that they have no knowledge of specific tasks in the backup process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data backups are set up as scheduled tasks and run automatically. However, failed backups are only detected if an administrator actively checks the logs. Employees have been instructed but do not have clear, written instructions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cron job or a scheduled task starts the backups every night. Failed jobs do not send a notification. The IT staff knows where to find the logs, but there is no firm rule on how often they must check them.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor confirms that the backup jobs are automated. However, they find failed jobs in the logs over several days that have not been fixed. Written work instructions for the staff are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Regular data backups MUST be created in accordance with the data backup plans. All employees MUST be informed about the data backup regulations. They MUST also be informed about their tasks in the creation of data backups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The execution of data backups is controlled by a central backup system that runs the jobs according to the plans. Every employee with tasks in the backup process (e.g., tape rotation) receives written work instructions. The general workforce is informed about the basic backup regulations (e.g., storage locations) through a policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration of the backup jobs with the specifications from the data backup plans. They check whether the responsible employees have received the relevant instructions and know their content. They verify that general information is available to all employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The backup system automatically generates notifications for errors, which are logged and tracked in a ticketing system. There is a defined process for resolving backup errors within a specified timeframe. Employees receive regular refresher training on their backup tasks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup system is integrated with the monitoring and ticketing system. A failed job automatically creates a medium-priority ticket assigned to the backup team. A brief training on backup processes is conducted annually for the relevant employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the alerting configuration demonstrated to them. They analyze the ticketing system for backup-related incidents and check their processing time. They review the training materials and participant lists of the refresher courses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data backup process includes automated pre- and post-checks to ensure data consistency (e.g., checking databases before and after the backup). The success of data backups is a Key Performance Indicator (KPI) on an IT operations dashboard, which is regularly reviewed by management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before backing up a database, it is put into backup mode and checked for consistency via a script. After the backup, the backup is automatically checked for readability (restore simulation). The success rate of backups is reported weekly in an IT management meeting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the backup scripts for the existence of consistency checks. They have the IT operations dashboard shown to them and check the KPIs for backup quality over a longer period. They review the minutes of the management meetings in which these KPIs were discussed.

controls.title: Secure storage of storage media for data backups

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Backup media are stored separately from the IT systems, but in an unsecured location, such as in a desk drawer in the same room.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The external hard drive for the backup is disconnected from the server after the backup and placed on the administrator's desk.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor finds that backup media are located in unsecured, freely accessible places. There is no separation from fire compartments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Backup media are stored spatially separated from the secured IT systems in a locked cabinet. However, the environmental conditions are not controlled, and it may be in the same fire compartment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup tapes are stored in a lockable file cabinet in an office space located in the same building and fire compartment as the data center.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the storage location is locked. However, based on the building plans, they determine that there is no separation of fire compartments. Measuring devices for temperature or humidity are not present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The storage media for the data backup MUST be stored spatially separated from the secured IT systems. The storage location is access-secured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The storage media are stored in a fireproof data safe in another part of the building. Access to the room and the safe is restricted to a few, authorized persons and is logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the storage location. They verify that it is physically separated from the production IT systems. They check the access control mechanisms and the corresponding logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The storage media are kept in a different fire compartment. The storage location is air-conditioned so that the data carriers can be stored according to the manufacturer's specifications and the data backup concept. Access to the location is logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A special room in another building or fire compartment is used as a backup archive. This room has its own air conditioning system that keeps temperature and humidity in the optimal range. Access is via an electronic locking system with logging.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies, using building and fire protection plans, that the storage location is in a different fire compartment. They check the air conditioning records and the access logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: At least one copy of the critical data backups is outsourced to a certified, external service provider for data archiving. The physical security and environmental conditions of the external storage location are regularly checked through audits (e.g., according to ISO 27001).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a contract with a specialized service provider for the external storage of backup media. The service provider offers secure transport and air-conditioned, fire-protected storage. The provider's current certificate is requested and checked annually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract with the external service provider and the corresponding SLAs. They check the provider's current certificates and audit reports. They verify the logs of media storage and retrieval.

controls.title: Protection of data backups

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No specific measures are implemented to protect data backups from being overwritten. The reliance is on administrators working carefully.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup software is configured to overwrite media without prompting. There are no file system permissions that prevent this.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During a review of the backup software configuration, the auditor finds that no protection mechanisms against overwriting are activated. A test shows that a backup can be easily overwritten.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After writing, the backup files are set to 'read-only' at the file system level. This provides basic protection, but it can be easily bypassed by an administrator.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A post-backup script runs the `chmod 444` or `attrib +r` command for all new backup files.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the permissions of the backup files and confirms the read-only protection. However, they also verify that an administrator with standard permissions can easily remove this protection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The created data backups MUST be adequately protected against unauthorized access. In particular, it MUST be ensured that data backups cannot be intentionally or unintentionally overwritten. IT systems used for data backup should only permit write access to the storage media for authorized data backups or administrative activities. Alternatively, the storage media should only be connected to the IT systems for authorized activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup server uses special accounts with restricted rights for the backup jobs. Administrators must log in with a separate, privileged account to access backup data or configuration. For backups on external media, physical separation (air gap) is used as a protective measure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the permission structure on the backup server. They verify that standard user accounts have no access to the backup data. They examine the processes for connecting and disconnecting external backup media.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Strict role-based access control (RBAC) is implemented on the backup server. Administrative tasks require a separate, privileged account, the use of which is heavily logged and monitored. Access to backup data is actively monitored for suspicious activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On the backup server, roles such as 'Backup Operator' (can start/stop jobs, change media) and 'Backup Administrator' (can change configuration, delete data) are defined. Every administrative action is sent to a central SIEM system for monitoring.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the RBAC configuration and the assigned roles. They analyze the logs in the SIEM system for access events and verify that suspicious patterns (e.g., mass deletions) lead to alerts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Immutable storage (WORM functionality) is used for the backup repositories. This technically ensures that for a defined retention period, data backups cannot be changed or deleted, even by a compromised administrator account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backups are stored on a storage system with hardware WORM functionality or in an S3 bucket with 'Object Lock' activated in compliance mode. The retention period is set to a value that is longer than the typical dwell time of ransomware before its activation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the immutability setting on the storage system or in the cloud account. They attempt to delete a backup file marked as immutable using a privileged account and ensures that the action fails.

controls.title: Regular testing of data backups

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Recovery tests are not performed proactively, but only reactively after an actual data loss has revealed a problem with a data backup.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no plan or process for restore tests. It is assumed that the backup software "will just work".

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the records of the last recovery tests. None can be provided, or the only existing records are from actual emergencies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Simple recovery tests are performed occasionally. Typically, this involves testing only the recovery of a single file to check the readability of the medium. A full system recovery is not tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a quarter, an administrator restores a random file from a backup and checks if it can be opened. The test is not formally documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds out through interviews that such simple tests take place. However, there is no evidence, and it is confirmed that the recovery of a complex application or an entire server has never been practiced.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be regularly tested whether the data backups are working as intended, especially whether backed-up data can be restored flawlessly and in a reasonable amount of time. The tests and their results are documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an annual test plan that specifies which systems are to be tested and when. The tests include both the recovery of individual files and the full recovery of selected, non-critical systems. The results, including the time required, are recorded in a log.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the test plan and the corresponding test records for the last test cycle. They check whether the tests were conducted as planned and whether the results (including recovery time) meet the requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal test plan for recoveries exists and is executed regularly (e.g., quarterly). The tests cover various critical systems in rotation and include full system recovery tests in an isolated test environment. The test results are documented, and identified deficiencies are tracked and resolved via a ticketing system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated test environment (sandbox), separated from the production network, has been established. Every quarter, a different critical business application (e.g., an ERP system) is fully restored in this sandbox. A test record is created and stored in the ISMS tool. Discovered issues lead to the creation of change requests.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the test environment demonstrated to them. They check the test records of the last few quarters and verify that critical and complex systems were also tested. They track an issue identified in a test through the ticketing system to its verifiable resolution.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Recovery tests are largely automated. A system automatically provisions an isolated environment, restores a random or critical system from the last backup, performs automated integrity and functional tests, and reports the success as well as the time required. This provides continuous verification of recoverability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Modern backup software with 'Automated Restore Testing' or 'SureBackup' functionality is used. Weekly, a random server is selected, started in a sandbox, booted up, and checked for service availability and data integrity. The results are displayed on a dashboard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration of the automated restore tests. They analyze the reports from the past weeks and months on the dashboard to evaluate the success rate and recovery times. They have such an automated test started live for a selected system.

controls.title: Development of a data backup concept

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD create a data backup concept that covers at least the following points: definitions of essential aspects of data backup, a requirement-specific threat landscape, the identified influencing factors for each IT system or group, the data backup plans for each IT system or group, and relevant results of emergency management, in particular the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) for each system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central 'Data Backup Concept' document is created and maintained. It serves as an umbrella document that defines the strategy, responsibilities, and general regulations, and refers to the detailed data backup plans (from CON.3.A4). The concept is coordinated with the department heads and emergency management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the data backup concept and checks it for completeness based on the required outline points. They verify that the contents are consistent with other documents, such as the results of the Business Impact Analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data backup concept is formally approved by management, is subject to version control, and is reviewed at least annually or in the event of significant changes. It is explicitly linked to the higher-level Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plan. The concept itself is also backed up to ensure it is available in an emergency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The concept is managed in a document management system with an approval workflow and versioning. There is a planned annual review task in the ISMS tool. A copy of the concept is kept at an external, secure location (e.g., cloud storage or with the emergency officer at their home).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the approval record and version history of the concept. They verify the existence and the process for the annual review. They inquire about the storage location of the emergency copy of the concept and check its availability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data backup concept is an active, 'living' document integrated into a GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool. Changes to the Business Impact Analysis, risk assessments, or IT architecture automatically trigger a review process and a possible update of the data backup concept and the subordinate plans.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RPOs and RTOs defined in the concept are directly linked to business processes and IT systems in the GRC tool. A change in the criticality of a process leads to an automatic notification for the person responsible for backups to review and, if necessary, adapt the backup strategy for the supporting systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the workflow demonstrated in the GRC tool: How does a change in the BIA lead to a review task for the data backup concept? They check whether the backup requirements stored in the tool align with the actual configuration of the backup system.

controls.title: Procurement of a suitable data backup system

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before a data backup system is procured, IT operations SHOULD create a requirements list to evaluate the products available on the market. The procured data backup systems SHOULD meet the requirements of the institution's data backup concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on the data backup concept, a detailed catalog of requirements (specification sheet) is created. This includes functional (e.g., support for specific operating systems) and non-functional (e.g., performance, scalability, security) requirements. Vendor offers are systematically evaluated against this catalog.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: For a recent procurement, the auditor requests the requirements list and the evaluation matrix for the various products. They compare the requirements with the specifications from the data backup concept to verify alignment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before the final decision, a formal market analysis is conducted, and a proof-of-concept (PoC) is performed in the own environment for the 2-3 best candidates. This is to verify the vendors' performance and feature promises before the purchase.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The top candidates from the bid evaluation are invited to install their system in a test environment. During the PoC, real backup and restore scenarios are executed, and performance is measured. The results of the PoC are a decisive criterion for the award.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the PoC documentation, including the test plan and the results records. They check whether the test results provide a comprehensible justification for the purchase decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection process includes a thorough security assessment of the backup product itself (e.g., its vulnerability management process, secure coding practices, support for hardened configurations) and its long-term strategic alignment with the organization's technology roadmap.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the procurement process, information on the manufacturer's Secure Development Lifecycle processes is requested. The product undergoes a penetration test. An assessment is made of how well the product fits into the existing and planned system landscape (e.g., cloud strategy, automation tools).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the product's security assessment, such as penetration test reports or manufacturer questionnaires. They have the strategic classification of the product explained to them based on the institution's IT roadmap.

controls.title: Prerequisites for online data backup

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If online storage is to be used for data backup, the following points SHOULD be contractually regulated as a minimum: contract design, data storage location, service level agreements (SLA), especially with regard to availability, suitable authentication methods for access, encryption of data on the online storage, and encryption during transport. In addition, the backup system and network connection SHOULD be designed in such a way that the permissible backup and recovery times are not exceeded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before signing a contract with a cloud backup provider, a checklist of the required points is processed. The contract is legally reviewed. It is ensured that the provider guarantees compliance with the GDPR (e.g., storage location in the EU). The necessary bandwidth is calculated and tested in advance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the contract with the online backup provider and compares it with the checklist of required regulatory points. They check the configuration of the backup software to ensure that transport encryption is enabled. They review measurements of the backup performance to verify compliance with the time windows.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution enforces client-side encryption before data is sent to the provider to ensure that the provider itself does not have access to the decryption keys (zero-knowledge principle). The provider's security certifications (e.g., ISO 27001, BSI C5) are checked, and the right to audit the provider is contractually agreed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup software is configured to encrypt the data with its own key before uploading. This key is securely managed in its own infrastructure. The provider's valid certificates are requested and checked annually. An audit clause is included in the contract.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the client-side encryption. They review the provider's current certificates and the contract clause on the right to audit. They check the concept for the secure management of the own encryption keys.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A multi-cloud backup strategy is pursued, in which encrypted data backups are replicated to a second, independent online provider to mitigate the risk of failure or lock-in with a single provider. The provider's resilience and disaster recovery capabilities are regularly tested as part of their own DR exercises.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup software is configured to replicate a copy to a secondary provider in a different region after a successful backup to the primary cloud provider. An annual DR test simulates a recovery from the secondary provider.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the replication jobs to the second provider. They review the logs of the DR exercises that prove the successful test of the recovery from the secondary provider.

controls.title: Use of cryptographic methods in data backup

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To ensure the confidentiality of the backed-up data, IT operations SHOULD encrypt all data backups. It SHOULD be ensured that the encrypted data can be restored even after a long period of time. Cryptographic keys used SHOULD be protected with a separate data backup.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The encryption function of the backup software is enabled for all jobs. The generated keys or passphrases are stored in a password manager or an encrypted document. This is in turn backed up separately and stored in a secure, separate location.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of all backup jobs and ensures that encryption is consistently enabled. They have the process for backing up and storing the cryptographic keys explained to them and check its implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated Key Management System (KMS) or a Hardware Security Module (HSM) is used to manage the lifecycle of the backup encryption keys. Key rotation policies are enforced. The strength of the cryptographic algorithms and key lengths follows the current recommendations (e.g., BSI TR-02102).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup software is integrated with a central KMS. The KMS enforces that new keys are generated for the backups every 1-2 years, while the old keys remain available for restores. Only algorithms such as AES-256 are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the KMS and its connection to the backup system. They check the configured crypto policies (algorithms, key lengths, rotation intervals) for compliance with external specifications. They check the logs of the KMS.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire backup process is cryptographically secured end-to-end. The data is already encrypted on the client before transmission (client-side encryption) and remains encrypted during transport and storage on the backup medium. Key management is handled by a highly available, audited HSM cluster. Regular 'crypto-agility' exercises are conducted to test the ability to migrate to new cryptographic algorithms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup agents on the source systems encrypt the data directly before it is sent over the network. The keys for this are obtained from a redundant HSM cluster. As part of the DR tests, a scenario is also played out in which a cryptographic algorithm is considered broken and all systems have to be switched to a new algorithm.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network traffic during a backup to verify the end-to-end encryption. They check the configuration and audit logs of the HSM cluster. They review the logs of the crypto-agility exercises.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Institutions are storing more and more data and at the same time are increasingly dependent on it. If data is lost, e.g. due to defective hardware, malware, or accidental deletion, serious damage can occur. This can affect classic IT systems, such as servers or clients. But routers, switches, or IoT devices can also store information worthy of protection, such as configurations. Therefore, the term IT system in this module includes all forms of IT components that store information worthy of protection.

Regular data backups can minimize the effects of data loss. A data backup should ensure that, with a redundant data stock, the operation of the information technology can be resumed shortly after parts of the actively used data stock are lost. The data backup concept thus also plays a central role in contingency planning. The essential requirements of contingency planning, such as the maximum permissible data loss (Recovery Point Objective, RPO), should be taken into account in the data backup concept.

A complete data backup concept includes not only the aspect of how data backups are created preventively (backup), but also how created data backups are restored on the original system (restore). A wide variety of solutions can be used for a data backup, such as:

• Storage systems,

• Tape drives,

• Mobile removable media (USB sticks or external hard drives),

• Optical data carriers, and

• Online solutions.

These solutions are summarized below as storage media for data backup. In contrast, data mirroring via RAID systems is not understood as data backup, as the mirrored data is changed simultaneously. This means that while data mirroring via a RAID system can prevent failure due to a hardware defect of individual data carriers, it cannot protect against unintentional overwriting or infection with malware.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to show how institutions can create a data backup concept and how they can use it to adequately secure their data against data loss.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The CON.3 Data Backup Concept module must be applied once to the entire information network.

The module describes fundamental requirements that contribute to an appropriate data backup concept. It does not cover requirements for the retention and preservation of electronic documents for long-term storage. These can be found in module OPS.1.2.2 Archiving.

This module also does not cover system-specific and application-specific properties of data backups. The system-specific and application-specific requirements for the data backup concept are supplemented in the corresponding modules of the NET Networks and Communication, SYS IT Systems, and APP Applications layers.

For the deletion and destruction of data backups, the CON.6 Deletion and Destruction module must be considered.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Lack of data backup
parts.prose: If data is lost and has not been backed up beforehand, this can have existence-threatening consequences for an institution. Data can be lost, for example, through malware, technical malfunctions, or a fire, but also if employees intentionally or unintentionally delete data.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Lack of restoration tests
parts.prose: Regularly backing up data does not automatically guarantee that it can be restored without problems. If it is not regularly tested whether data can be restored, it may be that the backed-up data cannot be restored.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Inappropriate storage of the storage media for the data backups
parts.prose: The storage media for data backups contain numerous pieces of information worthy of protection of the institution, regardless of whether they are classic tapes or modern storage systems. If the storage media for data backups are stored in an insecure location, they may be accessed during an attack and information worthy of protection may be stolen or manipulated. Likewise, storage media for data backups can become unusable due to unfavorable storage or climatic room conditions. Then the information stored on them is no longer available.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Missing or insufficient documentation
parts.prose:
If data backup measures, and especially the measures for restoration, are not documented or are poorly documented, this can significantly delay the restoration. As a result, important processes, e.g. in production, can also be delayed. It is also possible that a data backup can no longer be restored at all and the data is therefore lost.

If the information for restoration is only available digitally, there is a risk that it will also be lost in the event of major damage (such as ransomware), and the restoration will then be endangered.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Disregard of legal regulations
parts.prose: If legal requirements, such as data protection laws, are not observed during data backup, fines may be imposed on the institution or claims for damages may be asserted.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Insecure providers for online data backups
parts.prose:
If institutions outsource their data backup online to a third-party institution, attacks on this institution can also affect the data of their own institution. As a result, this can lead to the leakage of data worthy of protection.

Furthermore, there is a risk that unfavorable contractual conditions will lead to data backups not being available at short notice. In an emergency, they cannot be restored within a defined time frame.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Insufficient storage capacities
parts.prose: If storage media for data backup do not have sufficient free capacity, more recent data may no longer be backed up. It is also possible that the data backup software used automatically overwrites old and possibly still required data backups. If the responsible persons are not informed about this, for example because monitoring is inadequate, data may be lost completely. It would also be possible that in an emergency, only outdated versions are available.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Inadequate data backup concept
parts.prose:
If an appropriate concept is not created for data backup measures, the functional requirements for the affected business processes could be disregarded. For example, if the recovery time or data backup intervals are not taken into account, this could lead to the data backups not being suitable for restoring the lost data in an appropriate manner in the event of data loss.

In addition, a storage medium for a data backup can itself become a preferred attack target if valuable data from all business processes of the institution is stored on it in a concentrated manner.

Furthermore, organizational deficiencies can lead to the data backup becoming unusable. For example, if it is encrypted and the key for decrypting the data backup is also affected in the event of data loss, the data cannot be restored. This could be the case, for example, if it was not thought to keep the key stored separately.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Insufficient data backup speed
parts.prose: In addition to the storage space required for the data backup, the time required to perform a data backup also increases. In the worst-case scenario, this can mean that a data backup has not yet been completed when a new data backup begins. This in turn can lead to various problems. In some circumstances, the data backup that has not yet been completed is terminated. This would mean that complete data backups would no longer be made from then on. Alternatively, the data backup solution could try to perform the new data backup in parallel with the old one. As a result, this could lead to the data backup system eventually failing under the increasing load.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.10. Ransomware
parts.prose: A special form of malware is ransomware, which encrypts data on infected IT systems. After encryption, a ransom is demanded so that the victim can decrypt the data again. Without data backups, the encrypted data is often lost or can only be ransomed for the demanded fee. However, even after paying a ransom, it is not guaranteed that the data can be restored. Many variants of ransomware search for network drives with write access, on which all data is also encrypted. This can result in the loss of all encrypted information since the last data backup, even if a ransom was paid. Not only the originally infected IT system would be affected, but also centrally stored information that many IT systems are allowed to access. If the storage media for data backup are not sufficiently secured, there is an additional risk that they themselves will be affected by a ransomware attack and the information stored on them (data backups) will be encrypted.

controls.title: Regulation for the deletion and destruction of information (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Rudimentary, informal instructions for deleting data exist only for individual, particularly critical business processes or IT systems. A comprehensive regulation valid for the entire institution is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Regulations often exist only in the form of email instructions or verbal agreements and are not centrally documented. Compliance with legal retention periods is only checked reactively upon request.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through random checks in various departments that there are no consistent and documented deletion concepts. Interviews with subject matter experts confirm the lack of a central regulation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general, company-wide policy for deletion and destruction is in place. This defines basic retention periods for common document types such as invoices and personnel files. However, specific regulations for individual specialized procedures or IT systems have not been developed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A basic policy has been created and published on the intranet. Coordination with the data protection officer for general personal data has taken place, but not for special data categories.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the general deletion policy. However, interviews with subject matter experts reveal that this policy is not specific enough for their particular systems and data and is therefore only partially implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST regulate the deletion and destruction of information. For each specialized procedure and each business process, the subject matter experts MUST define which information must be deleted and disposed of under which conditions. Legal provisions (e.g., minimum and maximum retention periods) MUST be observed. Regulations concerning personal data MUST be coordinated with the data protection officer. The regulations for deletion and destruction MUST be defined for all IT systems, specialized procedures, and business processes before they go live.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A deletion concept is created that contains specific deletion rules and periods for each specialized procedure. These rules are recorded in the procedural documentation. Coordination with the data protection officer is carried out as a standard part of the data protection impact assessment process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether documented deletion rules exist for a representative selection of specialized procedures. They check the records of the coordination with the data protection officer and verify that these rules were defined before the systems went into production.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The deletion rules are documented in a central deletion concept that is linked to the data classification policy. There is an established process that periodically reminds subject matter experts to review and confirm their deletion rules. The implementation of the deletion periods in the IT systems is technically checked on a random basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A ticket system is used to control the review process for deletion rules. Technical scripts are used to check in databases or file systems whether data that has exceeded its retention period has actually been deleted or marked for deletion.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the records of the review process (e.g., tickets). They have the results of the technical checks of the deletion implementation presented to them and verify them through their own queries on selected systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The deletion and retention management is fully integrated into the lifecycle of information and IT systems. Deletion rules are centrally managed in a tool and are largely automated on the target systems. Automated workflows control deletion requests, approvals, and logged execution. Deviations are automatically detected and reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Information Lifecycle Management (ILM) or Data Governance tool is used. This tool is connected to the leading systems (e.g., ERP, DMS) and enforces the deletion rules automatically. A central dashboard visualizes the status of data retention and upcoming deletions throughout the institution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the central management tool and the associated audit logs. They verify the end-to-end automation of the process, from rule definition and approval to technical deletion, and checks the response to automatically generated deviation messages.

controls.title: Proper deletion and destruction of assets and information worthy of protection (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an instruction to shred paper documents. However, there are no guidelines for digital data carriers; they are often disposed of without secure deletion. A central, secure collection point is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are paper shredders in the offices. Decommissioned hard drives or USB sticks are disposed of with normal electronic waste after users have been asked to delete their data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the disposal containers and finds inadequately destroyed digital data carriers. Interviews with employees confirm the lack of a process for digital media.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic process for the destruction of paper and common digital data carriers (HDDs, CDs) is documented. A central collection point in a lockable room has been set up. The employees are informed about this process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A written work instruction describes how to dispose of data carriers. There is a locked container in the basement into which data carriers are thrown for later destruction.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the work instruction and inspects the collection point. They determine that the process exists but contains no specific regulations for e.g. SSDs or data backup tapes, and there is no logging of the destruction.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before sensitive information and data carriers are disposed of, they MUST be securely erased or destroyed. The process for this MUST be clearly regulated and also take data backups into account. The responsible employees MUST be informed of their duties. The location of destruction facilities or central collection points MUST be clearly regulated and secured against unauthorized access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed policy for deletion and destruction is created, covering different data carrier types and the respective procedures. A central, access-controlled collection point is set up. The disposal of data backup media is explicitly regulated. The responsible employees receive verifiable instruction.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the policy and the documentation of the employee instructions. They inspect the physical security of the collection point (e.g., locked door, defined group of people with access) and checks whether the process for data backups is defined.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire process of deletion and destruction is logged. A certificate of destruction is created and archived for each data carrier. The security of the collection point is regularly checked, and there are clear regulations for the transport of data carriers for external destruction.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list (e.g., in a spreadsheet or a ticket system) is maintained, in which the serial number of each destroyed data carrier, the date, and the responsible person are recorded. Sealed security containers are used for transport.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the destruction logs and compares them on a sample basis with the inventory of decommissioned devices. They review the logs of the security checks of the collection point and the regulations for secure transport.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire process, from the decommissioning of a device to the certified destruction of the data carrier, is tracked seamlessly in a central system. The collection point is secured by multi-level access controls and video surveillance. The destruction is secured and verified by the four-eyes principle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An asset management system is used to track the status of data carriers from 'in operation' to 'scheduled for destruction' to 'destroyed'. Each status change requires confirmation. On-site destruction is carried out and logged jointly by two authorized employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the logs of the asset management system to verify the complete traceability. They check the video surveillance recordings and the access logs of the collection point, as well as the logs created according to the four-eyes principle.

controls.title: Selection of suitable methods for erasing or destroying data carriers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data erasure tools available in the institution (e.g., the standard paper shredder) are used for all data carriers without checking whether they are suitable for the respective data carrier type or protection requirement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple particle-cut shredder is also used for the destruction of CDs or ID cards, although it is not designed for this. Hard drives are formatted by default, regardless of whether they are HDDs or SSDs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that the tools and procedures used do not match the media to be destroyed (e.g., remnants of CDs in the paper shredder). Interviews show that there is no process for selecting suitable procedures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A one-time basic analysis was carried out to define a standard procedure and tool for each of the most common data carrier types (paper, HDD, CD). However, this selection is not regularly reviewed for its up-to-dateness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on a recommendation, a shredder of a certain security class and a software for overwriting HDDs were procured. These procedures are documented in a guide.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the guide and the availability of the specified tools. However, they find that there is no process for reviewing the procedures and that newer media types such as SSDs are not considered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD check whether the minimum requirements (from CON.6.A12) are sufficient for the data carriers actually used and the protection requirements of the information. Based on this, it SHOULD determine and provide suitable procedures and tools for erasing or destroying each type of data carrier. The procedures SHOULD be known to the responsible employees. It SHOULD be checked regularly whether the procedures still comply with the state of the art.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A matrix is created that assigns one or more approved erasure or destruction methods and the tools to be used for them (software, degausser, shredder) to each data carrier type (HDD, SSD, LTO tape, smartphone, paper, etc.). This matrix is published on the intranet and is part of the training materials.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procedure matrix and checks whether suitable procedures are defined for all data carrier types in use. They interview employees to ensure that the procedures are known and check whether a process for regular review of the procedures exists (e.g., annual review note).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of erasure and destruction procedures is directly linked to the protection requirement assessment and data classification. For data with high protection requirements, stricter procedures (e.g., higher security levels according to ISO/IEC 21964) are generally applied. The regular review of the procedures is a firmly established, documented process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procedure matrix contains columns for different protection requirement levels. Before a data carrier is destroyed, its classification is checked to select the correct procedure. The annual review of the procedures is carried out as a formal project with a protocol and action tracking.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly selects decommissioned data carriers with high protection requirements and verifies, based on the destruction logs, that the correct, stricter procedure was applied. They review the protocols of the annual procedure reviews.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection and execution of the appropriate procedure is largely automated. The asset management system automatically suggests the correct destruction procedure based on the stored data classification. The effectiveness of the tools used (e.g., residual magnetism after degaussing) is periodically checked in a laboratory environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a device is decommissioned in the asset management system, the system automatically generates a work order that specifies the exact procedure (e.g., 'Overwrite with DoD 5220.22-M, 3 passes' or 'Destroy according to ISO/IEC 21964, level E-5'). Specialized measuring devices are used for random checks of the destruction results.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration in the asset management system to check the correct assignment of classification to procedure. They review the reports of the periodic effectiveness checks of the destruction tools.

controls.title: Creation of a policy for the deletion and destruction of information (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are several, partly outdated work instructions for specific deletion or destruction activities. A consolidated, overarching, and up-to-date policy is not available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One guide describes the operation of the paper shredder, another an old version of a deletion software. The documents are stored in different places and are not managed centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In their research, the auditor finds contradictory and outdated documents on the subject. Interviews confirm that there is no central, recognized binding policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic policy on deletion and destruction exists. It was created once and made available to all employees, but is not actively communicated or regularly checked for compliance and up-to-dateness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PDF document with the policy is available on the intranet. An initial email pointed to the policy. Since then, there have been no further activities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds the policy on the intranet. However, interviews with new employees show that they are not aware of the policy. The document has not been updated for several years.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regulations for deletion and destruction SHOULD be documented in a policy. The policy SHOULD be known to all relevant employees and cover all data carriers, applications, and IT systems used. It SHOULD be checked regularly and on a random basis whether employees adhere to the policy. The policy SHOULD be updated regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An official policy on deletion and destruction is created, approved, and actively communicated to all relevant roles (employees, IT operations, data protection officers). The policy is reviewed in a regular cycle (e.g., annually) and updated as needed. Acknowledgment is documented, e.g., when hiring new employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence, content, and approval status of the policy. They verify the process for dissemination and regular updating (e.g., by reviewing the version history and review protocols). Compliance with the policy is checked through interviews and random checks during the inspection of workplaces.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the policy is actively monitored through planned, regular checks, and the results are documented. The policy is part of regular security training, and understanding is verified. The policy contains clear references to the underlying detailed technical work instructions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual audit plan provides for the review of compliance with the deletion policy in selected departments. The results are incorporated into the CIP (Continuous Improvement Process). The annual security awareness campaign includes a module on secure deletion, possibly with a short test.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit plans and the reports of the internal controls. He checks the training materials and the results of the comprehension tests. He follows the references in the policy and ensures that the technical instructions are consistent and up-to-date.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy is implemented as a 'living document' in a digital management system. Parts of the policy compliance are monitored automatically (e.g., by checking system configurations for automatic deletion). Deviations from the policy lead to automatic notifications to the security officers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool is used to manage the policy and link it to technical controls. Configuration management tools automatically check whether, for example, temporary directories are cleared at system startup, as required by the policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the GRC tool and the reports of the automated compliance checks. He examines the processing of automatically generated tickets that indicate policy deviations.

controls.title: Deletion and destruction of data carriers by external service providers (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: External service providers are commissioned for disposal, but there are no contractual agreements that specify security requirements for data destruction. The company relies on the service provider's standard processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The local disposal company is commissioned to collect containers with electronic waste. The order only mentions 'proper disposal'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contracts with disposal service providers and notes the absence of clauses on data security and secure destruction.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Contracts with external service providers require the destruction of data carriers. A general certificate of destruction is required, but the exact procedures and security standards are not specified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The contract contains a clause that obliges the service provider to 'securely destroy all provided data carriers in accordance with data protection regulations'. The service provider provides a blanket certificate for each pickup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the contract and the received certificates. He determines that the requirements are not specific enough to ensure compliance with internal security levels (e.g., no specification of the destruction standard).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When external service providers are commissioned, the process for deletion and destruction MUST be sufficiently secure and traceable. The procedures used by the service providers MUST at least meet the institution's internal requirements. The companies commissioned with deletion and destruction SHOULD be checked regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before commissioning, a service provider is carefully selected (e.g., based on certifications). The contract specifies the applicable standards (e.g., ISO/IEC 21964), the security levels, and the obligation to create detailed destruction certificates per data carrier or batch. A Data Processing Agreement (DPA) is concluded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the contracts and DPAs with the service providers for the required specifications. He checks the received destruction certificates for completeness and plausibility. He verifies whether a process for reviewing the service provider is defined (even if it has not yet been carried out).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution conducts regular reviews of the contracted service providers, which may also include on-site audits. The entire chain of custody from pickup to destruction is secured by security measures such as sealed containers and documented handovers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a year, an audit is conducted at the service provider's premises to inspect their processes. The handover of the data carriers is documented by means of a detailed protocol signed by both parties. The transport containers are sealed before pickup, and the seal number is recorded in the protocol.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit reports of the service provider reviews as well as the handover protocols, including the seal numbers. He checks whether the integrity of the seals is checked and documented upon arrival at the service provider.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only certified specialist companies are used for data destruction. The destruction takes place, especially for data with high protection needs, directly on-site at the institution under the supervision of its own employees (mobile shredder). The effectiveness of the destruction by the service provider is checked by our own random checks of the destroyed material.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A service provider is commissioned to come to the company premises with a truck that has a high-performance shredder. A security employee of the institution supervises the entire destruction process. Alternatively, forensic samples are taken from data carriers declared as deleted before they are sent to the service provider.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contracts for on-site destruction and the corresponding supervision protocols. He reviews the reports on the random quality checks of the destruction result.

controls.title: Minimum requirements for deletion and destruction procedures (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only some of the minimum requirements are implemented. For example, paper is shredded, but digital data carriers are only deleted using the operating system's standard deletion function (simple deletion).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a paper shredder. For hard drives, the 'format c:' command is used without secure overwriting. Smartphones are not reset to factory settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines decommissioned devices and finds with simple recovery tools that data is recoverable. He notes that there are no tools for secure overwriting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All explicit MUST requirements are generally implemented, but with the simplest available means. The SHOULD requirements are not taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A freeware deletion software is used for single overwriting of hard drives. Smartphones are reset to factory settings, but the setup process is not run again. Paper is destroyed according to the required level P-3.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a basic procedure exists and is applied for each media type in accordance with the MUST requirements. However, he notes that further recommendations (SHOULD) are not implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST use at least the following procedures: Digital rewritable data carriers MUST be completely overwritten with random values if they are not encrypted. Encrypted data carriers MUST be deleted by securely deleting the key. Optical data carriers MUST be destroyed according to O-3, paper according to P-3 (ISO/IEC 21964-2). IoT devices MUST be reset to factory state and access data changed. Smartphones MUST be reset to factory settings. Integrated data carriers MUST be securely erased or removed and destroyed according to E-3/H-3.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Verified software tools (e.g., DBAN, `shred`) are used to overwrite HDDs. For SSDs, the manufacturer-specific Secure Erase command is used. For the destruction of paper and optical media, devices are procured and used that demonstrably achieve the required security level. Detailed instructions for resetting smartphones and IoT devices exist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existing tools (hardware and software) and instructions for compliance with all mentioned minimum requirements. He has the process demonstrated on a sample device.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All MUST and SHOULD requirements are consistently implemented. Smartphones and smart devices are generally encrypted (SHOULD) and after resetting, the setup process is carried out to complete the deletion process (SHOULD). The choice of procedures is adapted to the protection needs of the data, with the minimum requirements representing the lower limit.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Mobile Device Management (MDM) solution is used to enforce encryption on smartphones and to trigger the 'Factory Reset' remotely. The process for decommissioning devices includes an explicit step to check the protection requirement in order to apply a procedure with higher security than the minimum, if necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the MDM system. He checks the process documentation and the destruction protocols to ensure that the SHOULD requirements are implemented and that procedures appropriate to the protection needs are selected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution uses procedures that exceed the minimum requirements and follow a defense-in-depth strategy. For example, data carriers are first cryptographically erased (if encrypted), then overwritten with random data, and finally physically destroyed. The successful deletion is technically verified after each step.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated deletion workstation or a degausser is used. After overwriting a hard drive, a sector dump is read out to verify that no original data remains. The data carrier is then destroyed in a high-performance shredder.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation, which prescribes a multi-stage deletion/destruction. He requests to see the verification protocols of the individual steps and inspects the shredded material to confirm compliance with the highest security level.

controls.title: Destruction of defective digital data carriers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Defective data carriers are sent to the manufacturer for repair or under warranty without any special security measures. On-site physical destruction does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defective hard drive is removed from a server and sent back to the supplier in the original packaging to receive a replacement device.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the RMA (Return Material Authorization) processes and finds that no security precautions are taken for the data on the defective devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general instruction to physically destroy defective data carriers (e.g., with a hammer) before they are disposed of. However, no specific security level is maintained. In cases of warranty, an attempt is made to delete the data if this is still possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Defective hard drives are drilled through several times before disposal. In warranty cases, a standard format is attempted. Contracts with service providers do not contain any specific clauses.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that rudimentary destruction takes place, but it does not comply with a standardized security level, and thus data fragments could remain recoverable. They verify that RMA contracts do not contain any security clauses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If defective digital data carriers with information worth protecting cannot be securely erased, they SHOULD be destroyed at least in accordance with security level 3 of ISO/IEC 21964-2. Alternatively, in the event that defective data carriers are replaced or repaired, it SHOULD be contractually agreed with the service providers that they will securely destroy or erase the data carriers and that the procedures meet at least the internal requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process is defined: First, it is checked whether secure erasure is possible. If not, the data carrier is destroyed internally with a suitable shredder according to the required security level. For warranty cases, there are standard contractual clauses that oblige the service provider to perform certified destruction and offer this as an option for return.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process description for handling defective data carriers. They inspect the standard contractual clauses for repair and warranty cases and check the destruction certificates issued by service providers for such cases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution keeps its own equipment (e.g., a degausser) on hand to securely erase even defective magnetic data carriers on-site before they leave the premises.
