In warranty cases, an option is preferred where the defective data carrier can be retained for a fee and destroyed internally ('Keep Your Hard Drive' options).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A degausser is procured to degauss defective hard drives and tapes. The purchasing department is instructed to negotiate and conclude 'Keep Your Hard Drive' clauses as standard in support contracts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and use of the degausser and inspects its usage logs. They check the service contracts of servers and storage systems for the presence of 'Keep Your Hard Drive' clauses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Defective data carriers with highly sensitive data never leave the institution under any circumstances. They are invariably physically destroyed on-site, even if this voids warranty claims. The destruction process is secured by the four-eyes principle and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A clear instruction in the security policy stipulates that data carriers from a certain classification level (e.g., 'secret') must always be destroyed on-site in the event of a defect. A high-performance shredder that also reliably destroys SSDs and other flash media is available in a secure area.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy and the destruction logs for defective data carriers with high protection requirements. They check whether the logs were signed by two people and whether there have been no warranty cases for such data carriers since the rule was introduced that required a return.

controls.title: Destruction of data media at a high security level (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD determine the required security level for the destruction of data carriers in accordance with ISO/IEC 21964-1 based on the protection needs of the data to be destroyed. The data carriers SHOULD be destroyed in accordance with the assigned security level according to ISO/IEC 21964-2.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A table is created that maps the internal protection requirement categories ('normal', 'high', 'very high') to the corresponding material classifications and security levels of ISO/IEC 21964. When decommissioning a data carrier, the required security level is determined based on its classification and the destruction procedure is selected accordingly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the mapping table from protection requirement to ISO security level. They randomly select data carriers with high protection requirements and check, based on the destruction logs, whether the correct, higher security level was applied.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for determining and applying the higher security level is formally documented and integrated into the decommissioning processes. The destruction at a higher level is verified by the four-eyes principle and recorded in a detailed log that describes the achieved particle size or degree of destruction.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decommissioning form contains a mandatory field for determining the destruction security level. The destruction itself is carried out by one person and monitored and confirmed by a second person. The log is archived together with a photo of the destroyed material.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the decommissioning forms and the associated destruction logs signed by two people. They compare the documented results (e.g., photos) with the requirements of the respective security level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For data carriers with very high protection requirements, a security level is generally chosen that is above the formally determined minimum requirement to ensure a security margin. The destruction takes place in a specially secured area. The effectiveness of the destruction process is regularly audited by an external, qualified body.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy stipulates that for data in the highest protection requirement category, the highest technically possible security level of the available equipment (e.g., P-7 for paper) must always be used. An external auditor is commissioned annually to review the destruction process and certify its compliance with the standard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy, the destruction logs, and the certificates from the external auditor. They verify that a 'Defense-in-Depth' approach is consistently pursued for the most sensitive data during destruction.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Deletion and destruction are an essential part of the lifecycle of information on data carriers. In this module, the term data carrier includes analog data carriers such as paper or films, as well as digital data carriers such as hard drives, SSDs, or CDs.

If data carriers are decommissioned, the information they contain could be disclosed if the data carriers have not been securely deleted or completely destroyed beforehand. In addition to clients and servers, this can affect all IT systems, such as IoT devices (e.g., smart TVs), on which supposedly only insignificant information is stored. However, IoT devices are often connected via WLAN and store the necessary access credentials for this. These access credentials can, in turn, be sensitive information themselves and must not be accessible to unauthorized persons.

Ordinary deletion processes using operating system functions generally do not result in the secure deletion of information in a way that prevents the data from being reconstructed. Securely deleting information therefore requires special procedures. However, data carriers can only be effectively and securely deleted in their entirety, and this is usually only possible for individual files with limitations.

In addition, there are legal provisions, such as the German Commercial Code or data protection laws, which have far-reaching consequences for the deletion and destruction of documents. On the one hand, these result in retention periods for business transactions, balance sheets, or contracts, for example, which prohibit premature deletion. On the other hand, these legal provisions give rise to legal claims for the secure and timely deletion of data, for example, when personal data is affected.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module describes how information in institutions is securely deleted and destroyed and how a corresponding, holistic concept for this is created.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose: The module CON.6 Deletion and Destruction is to be applied once for the entire information network. The module contains general procedural, technical and organizational requirements for deletion and destruction. The module only deals with the secure deletion and destruction of complete data carriers, as the secure deletion of individual files is only possible to a limited extent in most cases.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Missing or insufficiently documented regulations for deletion and destruction
parts.prose: If there are no secure processes and procedures for deleting and destroying information and data carriers, or if they are not applied correctly, it is not guaranteed that confidential information will be securely deleted or destroyed. This makes it impossible to foresee where this information will remain and whether it will be accessible to third parties. This danger is particularly high for digital data carriers and IT systems that are to be decommissioned, as it is not always immediately apparent what (residual) information is on them. This information could be read by unauthorized third parties. If this is particularly sensitive information, such as personal data worthy of protection under Article 9 of the GDPR or trade secrets, this can result in high fines.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Loss of confidentiality due to residual information on data carriers
parts.prose:
Most applications and operating systems do not securely and completely irreversibly delete files by default. Only the references to the files are removed from the file system's management information, and the blocks belonging to the files are marked as free. However, the actual content of the blocks on the data carriers remains and can be reconstructed with appropriate tools. This means that the files can still be accessed, for example, if these data carriers are passed on to third parties or disposed of improperly. This could lead to confidential information falling into the hands of unauthorized persons.

Swap files, swap partitions, or 'hibernate files' (files for hibernation mode) also sometimes contain confidential data, such as passwords or cryptographic keys. However, this data and its contents are often not protected. They can be read, for example, if the data carriers are removed and reinstalled in other IT systems.

During the ongoing operation of many applications, files are also created that are not needed for productive operation, such as the browser history. These files can also contain security-relevant information. If swap files or temporary files are not securely deleted, sensitive information, passwords, and keys can be misused by unauthorized persons to gain access to other IT systems and data, to gain a competitive advantage in the market, or to specifically spy on user behavior.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Inappropriate involvement of external service providers in deletion and destruction
parts.prose:
If data carriers are deleted or destroyed by external service providers, the information on them could be disclosed if it is not sufficiently regulated how the external service providers are involved in the process of deletion and destruction.

For example, attackers can steal data carriers from insufficiently secured collection points or obtain residual information if service providers do not delete or destroy data carriers sufficiently securely.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Inappropriate handling of defective data carriers or IT devices
parts.prose:
If a defect occurs in a data carrier, this does not necessarily mean that the data on it is irreversibly damaged. In many cases, the data, or at least parts of it, can be recovered with special tools. If defective data carriers or IT devices are now simply disposed of without the data on them being deleted or destroyed, the data could be disclosed during the disposal process.

Data from defective data carriers could also be disclosed in warranty or guarantee cases or for repair orders. For example, a defective hard drive can be sent to the manufacturing company as a warranty case. The company identifies a defect in the controller and replaces the defective model with a new one for the customer. At the same time, the defective controller is replaced with a new one, and the originally defective hard drive is only quickly and thus insecurely erased. The hard drive then re-enters the market. Throughout this entire process, sensitive information can be disclosed, as it is still on the hard drive.

groups.title: CON.7 Information security for international travel

controls.title: Security policy for information security during international travel (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An informal leaflet or checklist with basic security recommendations for international travel exists. However, these documents are not mandatory and are only distributed to travelers sporadically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The creation of the leaflet is done ad-hoc, often by a single department such as the HR department, without formal coordination with IT security. It is typically sent as an email attachment when a trip is scheduled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews a selection of employees who have recently traveled to ask if they have received security information. It is also checked whether such a document exists, even if it has not been formally approved.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic security policy for international travel is in place and accessible to all employees, for example, on the intranet. It covers essential points such as handling company data and reporting losses but is kept general.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy was created once and published on the intranet. Employees are informed of the policy's existence in a general email and are responsible for reading it before a trip.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and accessibility of the policy on the intranet. In spot checks, employees' knowledge of the existence of this policy is queried.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All aspects relevant to information security in connection with activities abroad MUST be considered and regulated. The security measures taken in this context MUST be documented in a security policy for information security during international travel. This security policy or a corresponding leaflet with security measures to be observed MUST be handed over to employees operating transnationally. In addition, a security concept for the handling of portable IT systems on international travel MUST be created, which adequately details all security requirements and measures. The implementation of the security concept MUST be reviewed regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal security policy is developed, approved by management, and is part of the official company policies. Handing out the policy is integrated as a fixed component in the travel preparation process. The security concept for mobile IT systems is maintained by the ISO and, if necessary, individually adapted, e.g., for travel to high-risk areas.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a formal, approved security policy exists and whether a process is established that ensures all travelers receive the document. Additionally, the existence and level of detail of the security concept for portable IT systems are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy for international travel is integrated into the travel booking process. Employees must actively confirm they have read and understood the policy before the final booking. The policy and the associated security concept are reviewed and updated annually and on an ad-hoc basis (e.g., after security incidents).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The internal travel booking portal is configured so that a checkbox to confirm acknowledgement of the travel policy must be checked. The ISO conducts regular reviews of the documents, incorporating findings from current threat landscapes and internal incidents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the technical integration of the confirmation in the booking process. Additionally, the logs of the reviews of the policy and the concept are inspected to assess the regularity and quality of the updates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policies and concepts are dynamic and are individually adapted for each trip based on destination, duration, and purpose. An automated system generates trip-specific security instructions and technical specifications. Compliance is actively monitored, and for travel to high-risk areas, explicit approval by the ISO is required.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system connected to the travel booking portal and a threat intelligence database automatically creates customized security documents. For high-risk travel, a workflow is triggered that requires manual review and approval by the ISO before the trip is approved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration and logic of the automated system for creating the trip-specific instructions. Using examples of high-risk travel, the documented approval process by the ISO is reviewed.

controls.title: Employee awareness training on information security for international travel (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Awareness training is unstructured and ad-hoc, for example, through a brief email from the supervisor with general advice before an important trip. There is no formal training program.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: It is at the discretion of individual managers to inform their employees about potential risks. No central materials or resources are provided.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts interviews with employees and managers to determine if and how awareness training on travel security takes place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general presentation on information security, which also includes a chapter on security while traveling, is available on the intranet. Employees are informed about this and are required to review the content independently.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HR or IT department creates a one-time PowerPoint presentation and makes it available for download. No active training or comprehension check takes place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and content of the presentation on the intranet. Spot checks are carried out to determine whether employees are aware of the existence of these materials.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users MUST be made aware and trained in the responsible use of information technology and portable IT systems during international travel. Users MUST be aware of the dangers that can arise from the inappropriate handling of information, the improper destruction of data and data carriers, or from malware and insecure data exchange. Furthermore, the limits of the security measures used MUST be pointed out. Users MUST be enabled and encouraged to prevent loss or theft and to seek professional advice in case of irregularities. Employees SHOULD be informed about the legal requirements of individual travel destinations regarding travel security. For this purpose, the Information Security Officer MUST inform themselves about the legal requirements within the scope of information security and raise awareness among employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Regular, documented training sessions (e.g., annually) are conducted for all traveling employees. The training content is created by the ISO and includes technical aspects as well as rules of conduct and country-specific legal information (e.g., on data protection, IT security laws). A contact person is designated for queries during the trip.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the training documents, participant lists, and training schedules. In addition, the ISO's documentation regarding research on legal requirements is audited. Interviews with trained employees are used to randomly check their understanding of the content taught.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Participation in a special travel security training is mandatory for all employees who travel internationally. The training is role-based and concludes with a short test to check understanding. The training materials are updated annually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An e-learning module on travel security is developed. Completion of the module is stored in the travel booking system as a prerequisite for booking an international trip.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the technical coupling of the training obligation to the booking process. The training content and test results are analyzed to evaluate the quality and effectiveness of the awareness measure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Awareness is raised through interactive, adaptive e-learning modules that are tailored to the respective travel destination. For travel to high-risk areas, personal, mandatory security briefings by the ISO are also required. The effectiveness of the awareness-raising is continuously monitored through simulated social engineering attacks during the trip.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The e-learning system pulls information about the travel destination and dynamically generates relevant training content. The process for personal briefings is formalized. The organization conducts targeted but harmless test attacks (e.g., phishing emails related to the destination) to test the travelers' vigilance and provide further training if necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the concepts and results of the dynamic training sessions and simulated attacks. It is verified that the personal briefings have demonstrably taken place for high-risk trips and that the findings from the tests are used to improve the awareness measures.

controls.title: Identification of country-specific regulations, travel and environmental conditions (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The responsibility for identifying country-specific regulations and conditions lies entirely with the traveling employee. The institution does not provide any central support or information for this.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees use public sources such as the websites of the Foreign Office to inform themselves independently. There is no institutionalized process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks travelers how they informed themselves about the conditions in the destination country and determines that there is no organized approach on the part of the institution.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The HR department provides a generic travel checklist that, in addition to points such as visa and vaccinations, also contains the general note 'Check local laws and conditions'.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard checklist is provided to all travelers at the time of booking. The actual research remains the responsibility of the employee.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and distribution of the checklist. It is checked whether the checklist offers specific help beyond the general note.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before starting a trip, the applicable regulations of the individual countries MUST be checked by the information security management or the HR department and communicated to the respective employees. The institution MUST create, implement, and communicate suitable regulations and measures that enable the appropriate protection of internal data. The individual travel and environmental conditions MUST be taken into account. In addition, employees MUST familiarize themselves with the climatic conditions of the travel destination before starting the trip and clarify what protective measures they need for themselves and what is necessary for the information technology they are carrying.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined process, supported by the ISO and the HR department, ensures that country-specific dossiers (e.g., on legal, technical, and climatic specifics) are created and maintained for common travel destinations. This information is proactively provided to the traveler as part of the travel preparation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the process for identifying and communicating country-specific regulations is documented. The created dossiers for various countries are randomly checked for up-to-dateness and completeness. It is verified that travelers have demonstrably received this information.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution subscribes to a professional travel information service provider that supplies up-to-date data on legal, technical, and physical risks for various countries. This information is made available on the intranet and integrated into the travel approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The data from the external service provider is integrated into the institution's travel portal via an interface. When a travel destination is selected, the relevant risk information and rules of conduct are automatically displayed to the booker.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract with the information service provider and checks the integration of the data into the internal systems. The up-to-dateness and relevance of the provided information are assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated risk management system maintains a detailed and continuously updated risk profile for each potential travel country. Based on the travel destination, a mandatory set of technical measures (e.g., use of rental hardware), rules of conduct, and briefing requirements is automatically generated and assigned to the traveler.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The risk management system is linked to external threat intelligence feeds and the internal travel booking system. The process is fully automated. If a risk threshold is exceeded, a manual review and approval by the institution's crisis management team is automatically triggered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration, data sources, and logic of the risk management system. High-risk scenarios are used to check the correct triggering of automated measures and escalation paths.

controls.title: Use of privacy screen filters (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some employees use privately procured privacy screen filters. There is no institutional requirement or provision.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of privacy screen filters is based on the personal initiative and security awareness of individual employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through observation and questioning that there is no uniform regulation or provision of privacy screen filters.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution recommends the use of privacy screen filters on trips and provides them on request via IT support.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Privacy screen filters are kept in stock in the IT warehouse. Employees must actively ask for one to receive it. The recommendation is noted in the travel policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that privacy screen filters are available from IT support and that the recommendation for their use is communicated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users MUST ensure, especially when abroad, that no sensitive information can be spied on when working with mobile IT devices. For this purpose, an appropriate privacy screen MUST be used that covers the entire screen of the respective device and makes it difficult to spy on information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of a privacy screen filter is mandatory for all travelers when working in public or semi-public areas (e.g., train, plane, hotel lobby). The filters are issued with the laptops by default or must be requested before the trip.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the corresponding regulation in the security policy. By interviewing travelers and inspecting the IT issuance processes, it is verified that the employees are equipped with privacy screen filters and are informed about the mandatory use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Privacy screen filters are mandatory for all company-owned laptops used for international travel. The IT department centrally procures and installs the filters. Compliance is checked as part of the device check-out process for the trip.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All laptops intended for travel are preemptively equipped with suitable privacy screen filters. The IT travel checklist includes a checkpoint 'Privacy screen filter present and intact'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects a sample of the laptops intended for travel for the presence of privacy screen filters. In addition, the IT support checklists for device issuance are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For international trips where sensitive data is handled, only devices with integrated, hardware-based privacy protection (e.g., HP Sure View, Lenovo Privacy Guard) are used. The activation of the privacy protection in public environments is mandatory for users and is practiced in training sessions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the procurement process for laptops, the function of an integrated privacy screen is defined as a criterion for devices intended for travelers. The awareness training includes a dedicated module on the correct use of this function.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement policies and the technical specifications of the laptop models used for travel. In interviews, the users' knowledge of the activation and purpose of the function is verified.

controls.title: Use of screen/code lock (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The screen lock is configured on some devices, but with long timeouts and simple PINs like '1234'. There is no uniform policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration of the screen lock is left to the individual user. The operating system's default settings are often retained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects a sample of devices and finds inconsistent and often insecure screen lock configurations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a requirement to use a screen lock. However, the complexity of the code or password and the duration until automatic activation are at the user's discretion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A written instruction in the security policy requires the use of the screen lock. However, no technical means are used for verification or enforcement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the instruction in the policy and interviews a random sample of users about their implementation of the requirement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A screen or code lock that prevents third parties from accessing data on mobile devices MUST be used. Users MUST use an appropriate code or a secure device password for this purpose. The screen lock MUST activate automatically after a short period of inactivity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy defines clear requirements for password complexity (length, character types) and sets a maximum time for the automatic lock upon inactivity (e.g., maximum 15 minutes). Users are instructed to make these settings manually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the policy clearly defines the requirements for password and lock time. On a sample of devices, it is manually checked whether the settings comply with the specifications.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The screen lock policy (timeout, password complexity) is technically enforced via a central management solution (MDM/EMM). The time until automatic lock is set to a short period (e.g., 1-5 minutes).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM software (e.g., Microsoft Intune, Jamf) is used to roll out a configuration policy on all managed mobile devices that enforces the screen lock according to ISB specifications. Deviations from the configuration are reported.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the MDM policy and its assignment to the corresponding device groups. The compliance rate of the devices is checked using the MDM dashboard. An automated scan of device compliance can be performed: `Get-MobileDevice -Filter {ClientType -eq 'EAS'} | Get-MobileDeviceMailboxPolicy | Select-Object Name, AllowSimpleDevicePassword, MaxInactivityTimeDeviceLock`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multi-factor authentication (e.g., PIN and biometrics) is required to unlock the device. The screen lock policy is enforced via MDM, and any attempt to tamper with it is logged and triggers an alert to the security team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM policy is configured to require both a complex password and the use of a biometric feature (fingerprint, face recognition). The device compliance policies in the MDM are linked with 'Conditional Access' rules, so that non-compliant devices lose access to corporate resources. Tampering attempts are reported to a SIEM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the MFA requirement in the MDM policy and the configuration of the alerting rules for tampering attempts. The effectiveness of the 'Conditional Access' rules is verified by a test with a simulated non-compliant device.

controls.title: Timely loss reporting (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees MUST immediately report to their institution if information, IT systems, or data carriers have been lost or stolen. For this purpose, there MUST be clear reporting channels and contact persons within the institution. The institution MUST assess the possible effects of the loss and take appropriate countermeasures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A reporting form for the loss of IT equipment is provided on the intranet. A central email address and a telephone number for IT support are communicated as the primary reporting channels. A simple, manual process for assessing the incident and initiating standard countermeasures (e.g., password reset) is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the reporting channels and contact persons are documented and made known to all employees. Based on past loss reports (if any) or a test case, it is checked whether the defined process for assessment and response is followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A 24/7 hotline is set up for reporting lost devices. The reporting process automatically triggers a documented incident response workflow that includes remote wipe of the device, resetting passwords of associated accounts, and a formal impact analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The 24/7 hotline is implemented by an external service provider or an internal on-call duty. In the MDM system, an automated workflow is configured that locks and wipes the device upon receipt of an authorized loss report. The steps are defined in an incident response plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract with the hotline service provider or the internal on-call schedule. The configuration of the automated workflow in the MDM and the associated incident response plan are checked for completeness and correctness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The incident response process for device loss is highly automated. The remote wipe is executed immediately upon reporting. The process includes automated notification of all relevant stakeholders (e.g., Data Protection Officer, management) based on the classification of the data likely to have been on the device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ticketing system that receives the loss report is connected via API to the MDM and the SIEM system. A playbook in a SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) platform orchestrates the entire process, from remote wipe to blocking user accounts to creating notifications according to a predefined matrix.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the SOAR playbook and the associated configurations and interfaces. The correctness of the notification matrix is verified. The execution of an end-to-end test of the automated process is observed.

controls.title: Secure remote access to the institution's network (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To provide employees on international trips with secure remote access to the institution's network, a secure remote access solution, e.g., a Virtual Private Network (VPN), MUST have been set up beforehand by IT operations. The VPN access MUST be cryptographically secured. Furthermore, users MUST have appropriately secure credentials. Employees MUST use the secure remote access for any communication possible through it. It MUST be ensured that only authorized persons are allowed to access IT systems. Mobile IT systems MUST be protected by a restrictively configured personal firewall against direct connection to the internet, as far as possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A VPN server is configured with current encryption protocols (e.g., IKEv2/IPsec or OpenVPN). Authentication is done via username and a complex password. The configuration files for the VPN client are provided to the users. The personal firewall on the end devices is configured to block incoming connections by default.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the VPN server for the use of strong cryptography. The password policies for VPN users are checked. The configuration of the personal firewall on an example client is inspected to verify the restrictive setting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VPN access requires multi-factor authentication (MFA). The configuration of the VPN client as well as the personal firewall policies are centrally managed via management software and enforced on the end devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VPN gateway is integrated with a RADIUS server or a cloud identity provider (e.g., Azure AD, Okta) to enforce MFA. The VPN client software and firewall rules are distributed and configured on the devices via an MDM or endpoint management system to prevent manual misconfigurations by users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of MFA for VPN access. The management policies in the MDM/endpoint management system for the VPN client and the firewall are checked. The compliance reports from the system are used to verify the comprehensive implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of a traditional VPN, a Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) solution is used. Before granting access, the security state of the end device (Device Health) is checked. All data traffic is logged and analyzed for anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A ZTNA solution (e.g., Zscaler Private Access, Cloudflare Access) is implemented. Policies are defined that only allow access to specific applications from compliant devices (current OS, active antivirus, encrypted hard drive, etc.). All access logs are forwarded to a SIEM system for correlation and anomaly detection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the ZTNA policies, particularly the criteria for the device compliance check. It is tested whether a non-compliant device is correctly denied access. The configuration of the log forwarding to the SIEM and the analysis and alerting rules set up there are reviewed.

controls.title: Secure use of public Wi-Fi networks (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As a matter of principle, it MUST be regulated whether mobile IT systems are allowed to access the internet directly. For access to the institution's network via publicly accessible Wi-Fi networks, users MUST use a VPN or comparable security mechanisms. When using Wi-Fi hotspots, security measures MUST also be taken.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy mandates the use of the provided corporate VPN as soon as a connection is established with an untrusted network (such as public Wi-Fi in hotels, airports, or cafes). Users are trained accordingly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the policy requires the mandatory use of VPN for public Wi-Fi. In interviews with travelers, their knowledge and behavior regarding this rule are reviewed. The VPN server logs can be randomly checked for usage from external IP addresses to verify compliance.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The end device is configured with an 'Always-On' VPN, which automatically establishes a secure tunnel as soon as an internet connection is detected in an untrusted network. Direct internet access is blocked by the firewall policy when the VPN is not active.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VPN client software is configured via central endpoint management to run in 'Always-On' mode and knows a list of trusted networks (e.g., the corporate Wi-Fi). Outside of these networks, the client forces all data traffic through the VPN tunnel. The personal firewall on the client is configured to only allow outbound traffic to the VPN gateway.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration profiles for the VPN client and the firewall in the endpoint management system. On a test device, it is verified that when connected to a public Wi-Fi, data traffic is correctly routed through the tunnel and direct connections to the internet are blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The device uses an 'Always-On' VPN in combination with a client that actively warns about malicious Wi-Fi networks (e.g., 'Evil Twin' attacks). All DNS queries are routed through a secure, encrypted DNS service (DNS-over-HTTPS or DNS-over-TLS) to prevent manipulation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the 'Always-On' VPN, an endpoint protection solution is used that includes a network threat protection feature. The operating system or browser settings are centrally configured to use a specified, trusted DoH/DoT resolver.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the endpoint protection solution and the DNS settings via the central management system. In a test environment, a simulated 'Evil Twin' attack is carried out to verify the correct detection and warning by the client.

controls.title: Secure handling of mobile storage media (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When using mobile storage media, users MUST first ensure that they are not infected with malware. Before passing on mobile storage media, users MUST also ensure that they do not contain any sensitive information. If it is no longer used, the storage medium MUST be securely erased, especially if it is passed on to other people. To do this, the storage medium MUST be overwritten using a sufficiently secure method specified by the institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy defines the process for handling mobile storage media. It requires that all external storage media be scanned with the antivirus software installed on the endpoint device before use. For secure erasure, a specific software tool (e.g., `shred` on Linux, `Cipher.exe` on Windows) and a procedure (e.g., single overwrite) are specified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and content of the policy on handling mobile storage media. Interviews are conducted to assess users' knowledge of these procedures. It is checked whether the named software tools are available on the client systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of unapproved USB devices is blocked by technical means at the endpoint. All USB storage devices issued by the company are hardware-encrypted. A dedicated, isolated kiosk system is provided for secure data transfer from external media.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The endpoint protection software is configured to block access to all removable media unless their serial number is on a whitelist. The IT department exclusively procures hardware-encrypted USB drives (e.g., FIPS 140-2 certified). A separate computer with no network access and up-to-date antivirus software serves as an airlock for data from external sources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the endpoint protection policy regarding device control. An attempt is made to use an unapproved USB stick on a protected computer. The existence and correct isolation of the kiosk system is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of any removable media is disabled by default. Exceptions are granted only in justified individual cases and exclusively for specific, approved, and hardware-encrypted devices. All file transfers to and from removable media are logged and monitored. Secure erasure is performed with certified tools, and a certificate of destruction is created.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy for blocking removable media is strictly enforced. A formal process for requesting and approving exceptions is implemented in the ticket system. The endpoint protection software logs all file access on approved removable media and forwards the logs to a SIEM. For destruction, tools are used that comply with standards from e.g., BSI or NIST, and the process is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the documented exception process and the corresponding approval tickets. The log configuration of the endpoint protection and the corresponding analysis rules in the SIEM are verified. The documentation of the secure erasure (destruction protocols) is checked on a random basis.

controls.title: Encryption of portable IT systems and storage media (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To prevent sensitive information from being viewed by unauthorized third parties, employees MUST ensure before traveling that all sensitive information is secured according to internal guidelines. Mobile storage media and IT systems SHOULD be encrypted by users or IT operations before travel. The cryptographic keys MUST be stored separately from the encrypted device. When encrypting data, the legal regulations of the destination country SHOULD be observed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The travel policy stipulates that the hard drives of laptops and external storage media carried on trips must be encrypted. Instructions for activating built-in tools like BitLocker (Windows) or FileVault (macOS) are provided to users. Users are instructed to store recovery keys securely and separately from the device and to inform themselves about any import restrictions for encryption technology in the destination country.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the policy and the provided instructions. Interviews and manual inspection of a sample of devices are used to verify whether encryption is enabled and whether users know how to manage their recovery keys.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hard drive encryption is mandatory for all company-owned laptops and is technically enforced via a central management tool (e.g., MDM, GPO). The recovery keys are stored centrally in a secure repository under the control of the IT department (Key Escrow).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Using Microsoft Intune or Group Policies in Active Directory, BitLocker activation is enforced on all Windows clients. The policy is configured so that the recovery keys are automatically saved in Azure AD or Active Directory. Access to these keys is restricted to authorized IT administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the encryption policy in the management tool. The compliance reports are reviewed to verify comprehensive implementation. The process for secure recovery of a key by an authorized administrator is checked. An automated scan of device compliance can be performed: `manage-bde -status` on the clients or via the central console.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all portable devices, hardware-based encryption with FIPS 140-2 (or higher) certification is used. For travel to high-risk countries where there may be a legal obligation to disclose keys, a procedure exists whereby travel is only undertaken with 'clean', minimally provisioned devices and data access is exclusively via secure remote connections.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During procurement, only devices with Self-Encrypting Drives (SED) and corresponding certification are considered. A pool of special 'travel laptops' is maintained, which do not store permanent data and are securely erased and re-imaged after each trip. Data access for these devices is exclusively via a VDI or ZTNA solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement policies and the technical specifications of the devices used. The process for providing and returning the special travel laptops is checked. It is verified that these devices are technically configured to not allow local data storage.

controls.title: Use of anti-theft devices (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To protect mobile IT systems outside the institution, users SHOULD use anti-theft devices, especially where there is high public traffic or a high turnover of users. The procurement and deployment criteria for anti-theft devices SHOULD be adapted to the institution's processes and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In its travel policy, the institution recommends the use of physical locks such as Kensington locks. These are issued by IT support upon request. The criteria for when to use such a lock (e.g., in a hotel room, in conference rooms) are described in the policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the recommendation and the deployment criteria are documented in the policy. It is checked whether IT has the corresponding locks ready for issue. Interviews are conducted to assess employee awareness of this recommendation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All laptops issued for travel are equipped with a suitable cable lock by default. The travel policy mandates the compulsory use of these locks in public areas and hotel rooms. The awareness training includes corresponding application examples.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department centrally procures cable locks and issues them as a standard part of the laptop accessories for travelers. The mandatory use is clearly formulated in the travel policy. The process of issuing devices to travelers includes checking for completeness of accessories, including the lock.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the mandatory issuing of cable locks by inspecting the IT processes and checklists. It is checked whether the mandatory use is anchored in the policy and the training materials.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to physical locks, the devices are equipped with anti-theft software that allows for tracking as well as remote locking and wiping. The use of physical locks is mandatory and is checked on a random basis for particularly valuable devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An endpoint management solution with an integrated anti-theft function (e.g., Absolute, Prey) is installed and configured on all travel laptops. The process for activating remote locking/wiping is part of the incident response plan for device loss.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the anti-theft software on the devices. The corresponding part of the incident response plan is reviewed for completeness and feasibility. It is tested whether the remote control functions work as intended.

controls.title: Secure destruction of sensitive materials and documents (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST show employees ways to appropriately and securely destroy documents requiring protection. Users MUST comply with these regulations. They MUST NOT dispose of the institution's internal documents before they have been securely destroyed. If this is not possible on-site or if the documents or data carriers contain particularly sensitive information, they MUST be kept until return and then destroyed appropriately.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy contains a clear section on the disposal of documents while traveling. It promotes the 'leave nothing behind' rule. All paper documents and notes requiring protection created or received during travel must be brought back for secure destruction in the institution's shredders. Employees are instructed accordingly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the corresponding instruction in the security policy and the training materials. Interviews are conducted to check the employees' awareness of this regulation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For longer stays abroad, e.g., in a branch office, the institution organizes a secure on-site destruction facility. This can be achieved by commissioning a certified service provider or by providing a cross-cut shredder (according to DIN 66399 protection class 2, security level P-4 or higher).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution has framework agreements with international disposal service providers or equips its foreign branches with appropriate shredders. For individual travelers, portable shredders can be provided as travel equipment if required.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the contracts with disposal service providers or the procurement records and specifications of the shredders provided on-site. It is checked whether a process exists to organize this service for longer stays.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The principle of 'paperless travel' is enforced. All necessary information is made available and processed exclusively digitally on a secure end device. Printing while traveling is technically prevented or only possible on approved, secure printers. For the rare case that paper is generated, a portable high-security shredder is provided as standard travel equipment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Printer drivers are removed from the travel laptops or printing is blocked via an endpoint protection policy. All relevant documents are made available to travelers via a secure, encrypted platform (e.g., SharePoint with appropriate access permissions).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the technical implementation of the print block on a travel laptop. The configuration of the secure document platform is checked. The standard equipment for travelers is checked for the presence of a shredder.

controls.title: Taking necessary data and data carriers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before starting a trip, users SHOULD check which data is not absolutely necessary on the IT systems during the trip and delete it securely. If it is necessary to take data requiring protection on a trip, this SHOULD only be done in encrypted form. Furthermore, it SHOULD be regulated in writing which mobile data carriers may be taken on trips abroad and which security measures must be considered. Employees SHOULD be aware of and comply with these regulations before starting their trip. The technical security requirements SHOULD be based on the protection needs of the data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy for data minimization during travel is created. It contains a checklist that guides users to review their local data and delete anything unnecessary. The policy mandates that all data carried must be stored on an encrypted drive or in an encrypted container (e.g., with VeraCrypt). The list of permitted data carriers (e.g., only company-owned, encrypted USB sticks) is also part of the policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the data minimization policy and the associated checklist. Interviews are used to conduct spot checks on users' understanding and implementation of this rule. It is checked whether the encryption requirement is consistent with CON.7.A10.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal data minimization policy is established and actively communicated. Before starting a trip, employees must justify in a form why they are taking sensitive data with them. The IT department provides tools that make it easy to create an encrypted container for travel-specific data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process is integrated into the travel booking system where travelers must declare the necessity of taking along data requiring protection. The IT department provides a script or an easy-to-use software that creates an encrypted container on the user's laptop and securely removes it again after the trip.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the process for declaring data and the associated forms or system workflows. The provided tools for creating encrypted containers are checked for their functionality and security.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution provides 'clean' travel laptops with a minimal operating system and application set. No permanent company data is stored on these devices. Access to all necessary data is exclusively via a secure connection (e.g., VDI, ZTNA) to the corporate network. This enforces data minimization by design.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A pool of dedicated travel laptops is maintained. These are configured as thin clients and only allow access to a virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) or specific applications via a ZTNA solution. After each trip, the device is reset (wiped) and re-provisioned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the travel laptops and the VDI/ZTNA environment. It is checked whether the devices actually do not allow local storage of company data. The process for returning and re-provisioning the devices is reviewed.

controls.title: Cryptographically secured email communication (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Email-based communication SHOULD be cryptographically secured in accordance with the institution's internal guidelines. The emails SHOULD also be appropriately encrypted or digitally signed. Public IT systems, such as in hotels or internet cafés, SHOULD NOT be used to access emails. When communicating via email services, e.g., webmail, IT operations SHOULD clarify in advance which security mechanisms are implemented by the provider and whether they meet internal security requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy mandates that emails with content requiring protection must be end-to-end encrypted (e.g., using S/MIME or PGP). Instructions for setup and use are provided. The use of webmail in internet cafés is explicitly prohibited. Before using external mail services while traveling, the IT department conducts a risk assessment of the provider.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the corresponding specifications in the policy and the provided instructions. The risk assessments carried out for external mail services are reviewed. Interviews are used to query users' knowledge of the encryption obligation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An email gateway automatically encrypts emails based on predefined rules (e.g., keywords, recipient domain). S/MIME or PGP is centrally rolled out to the devices of all travelers, and its use for sensitive communication is mandatory. Access to webmail from untrusted networks is technically blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An email gateway (e.g., Secure Email Gateway) is configured with rules that, for example, automatically enforce encryption if 'confidential' is in the subject line. The certificates for S/MIME are centrally managed and distributed to the end devices. Conditional Access policies block access to Exchange Online / webmail from unknown locations or non-compliant devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the email gateway and the Conditional Access policies. The processes for central certificate management are reviewed. It is tested whether an email with the corresponding keyword is correctly encrypted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All outgoing emails are automatically digitally signed. Encryption is enforced by the gateway for any communication that is classified as sensitive. The system prevents sending if a secure channel to the recipient cannot be established. Key and certificate management is fully automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The email gateway is configured to prevent the sending of unencrypted sensitive emails (hard fail rule). The certificate management is integrated into the institution's PKI and ensures automatic renewal and distribution of certificates. Integration with a DLP (Data Loss Prevention) system ensures reliable classification of email content.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the gateway configuration, especially the 'hard' rule for blocking sending. The degree of automation of certificate management is checked. The rules of the DLP system for data classification are analyzed.

controls.title: Emanation security of portable IT systems (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before the start of the trip, it SHOULD be determined what level of protection the individual pieces of information processed on the employee's mobile data carrier or client abroad have. The institution SHOULD check whether the information carried has special protection needs and, accordingly, use data carriers and clients with low or secure emanation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process is established whereby trips involving the processing of classified or otherwise highly sensitive information are subject to a special risk assessment by the ISO. As a result of this assessment, the requirement to use emanation-proof hardware can be formulated. Procurement is carried out on a project-specific basis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the process for risk assessment of trips with highly sensitive data. It is checked whether the option to request emanation-proof hardware is part of this process. If applicable, the procurement documents for such hardware are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For trips to high-risk areas, a formal TEMPEST risk analysis is carried out as a standard procedure. Based on this analysis, specific, certified low-emanation hardware is procured and made available to the traveler.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ISO maintains a list of high-risk countries. When traveling to these countries, a TEMPEST analysis is automatically initiated. The institution keeps a small number of laptops with a basic certification for emanation security available for such cases or has a framework agreement with a specialized supplier.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the list of high-risk countries and the associated process for TEMPEST analysis. It is verified whether appropriate hardware is available or can be procured. The certificates of the hardware used are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution maintains a pool of certified, radiation-proof (TEMPEST) travel hardware. The use of this hardware is mandatory for any travel involving the processing of classified information. The traveler receives specific training on how to handle the hardware to maintain its protective properties.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated stock of TEMPEST-approved laptops and accessories is managed by IT. The process for requesting and issuing these devices is formalized and linked to the classification of the data to be processed. A special handling procedure (e.g., transport in shielded bags) is defined and trained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the inventory of TEMPEST hardware and the associated certificates. The issuing and return process is checked. The training materials for special handling are reviewed and the users' knowledge is verified on a random basis.

controls.title: Integrity protection through checksums or digital signatures (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users SHOULD use checksums during data transfer and data backup to be able to verify the integrity of the data. Better still, digital signatures SHOULD be used to preserve the integrity of sensitive information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution trains its employees in the manual use of tools for creating and verifying hash values (e.g., `sha256sum`) for important files. For official documents, the use of digital signatures (e.g., in PDF documents) is recommended and instructions are provided.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the training materials and instructions. In interviews, the users' knowledge of the procedures for integrity checking is randomly queried.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of digital signatures for all official documents and archives with sensitive data is mandated by a policy. The software used for file transfer during travel automatically calculates and verifies checksums for all transfers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Certificates for creating digital signatures are centrally provided for the relevant employees. The file-sharing or synchronization solution used is configured to ensure the integrity of the transferred files by default using hash values.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy on the use of digital signatures and the certificate provisioning process. The configuration of the file transfer software is checked for automatic integrity verification.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) system is installed on the travel devices. This creates a baseline of critical system and application files and continuously monitors them for unauthorized changes. All changes are logged and trigger a real-time alarm. Digital signatures are integrated into all workflows with sensitive data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An endpoint protection solution with FIM functionality is used on the travel laptops. The FIM policy is centrally defined and rolled out to the devices. The FIM logs and alarms are forwarded to a central SIEM for analysis and correlation. The use of digital signatures is technically enforced in document management systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the FIM configuration policy and the baseline of the monitored files. The alarm rules in the SIEM are checked. In a test, a protected file is modified to verify correct detection and alarming.

controls.title: Use of pre-configured travel hardware (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To prevent third parties from intercepting the institution's sensitive information on trips abroad, the IT department SHOULD provide employees with pre-configured travel hardware. This travel hardware SHOULD, based on the principle of least privilege, only provide the functions and information that are absolutely necessary to carry out business activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For travel to certain high-risk areas, IT support can provide a laptop with a reduced software set and minimal data on request. This process is manual and is only carried out when required.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the process for requesting and providing special travel hardware. Using a case study, the configuration of such a device is checked for compliance with the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a dedicated pool of hardened 'travel laptops'. These devices have a minimal OS image, application whitelisting, enhanced security configurations, and no administrative rights for the user. The devices are securely wiped and re-provisioned after each trip.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department maintains a standard image for travel laptops that contains only essential, approved software. The process for issuing, returning, and reimaging these devices is formalized and documented. The use of these devices for travel to high-risk countries is mandatory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the master image for the travel laptops and the configuration of the application whitelisting. The documented lifecycle process (issuing, return, wipe) is checked for compliance.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The travel hardware is a thin client or a device designed exclusively for accessing a VDI/DaaS environment. No company data is ever stored on the device itself. The integrity of the device is checked before establishing a connection using a hardware root of trust (e.g., TPM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution uses a VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) solution. The travel laptops are thin clients that only contain the operating system and the VDI client. The connection to the VDI is protected by a device health attestation check, which validates the state of the TPM and the boot process. The entire lifecycle of the devices is automated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the VDI solution and the configuration of the thin clients. The policies for device health attestation are reviewed. It is tested whether a manipulated device is correctly prevented from establishing a connection.

controls.title: Restricted permissions on trips abroad (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before the start of a trip, it SHOULD be checked which permissions employees really need to carry out their daily business abroad. It SHOULD be checked whether access rights can be revoked by the IT department for the duration of the user's trip to prevent unauthorized access to the institution's information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of travel preparation for high-risk areas, IT support, together with the traveler's supervisor, carries out a manual review of the user's permissions. Superfluous group memberships or access rights are manually removed for the duration of the trip and restored upon return. This process is documented via a ticket.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the documented process for temporary rights reduction. The correct execution of the manual process is verified on the basis of completed tickets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal process is implemented in which the traveler's standard user account is temporarily deactivated before a high-risk trip. Instead, a new, separate account with minimal, travel-specific permissions is provisioned. This process is controlled via an Identity and Access Management (IAM) system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system has predefined roles or profiles for travelers. As part of the travel workflow, a temporary travel account with the appropriate role is automatically created and the normal account is locked. After the travel date, the process is automatically reversed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the travel roles in the IAM system and the automated workflow for provisioning and de-provisioning the temporary accounts. The permissions of the travel roles are checked for compliance with the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Just-in-Time (JIT) Access system is used. The travel account has no permissions by default (Zero Standing Permissions). Permissions for access to specific systems or data are granted dynamically for a short, predefined period on request, requiring supervisor approval and MFA. All privileged sessions are recorded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Privileged Access Management (PAM) or a JIT-capable IAM solution is used. The travel account is by default in a group with no rights whatsoever. The user must request access to a required resource for a limited period of time (e.g., 2 hours) via a self-service portal. After approval, the account is temporarily added to the corresponding permission group and then automatically removed again.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the JIT system, the approval workflows, and the defined time limits. The logs of granted access and the session recordings are randomly checked. It is tested whether the revocation of the permission works correctly after the time has expired.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Business travel has become a daily routine in many institutions. To be able to work outside the regular work environment, it is necessary to carry not only paper documents but also information technology, such as notebooks, smartphones, tablets, removable hard drives, or USB sticks. However, on business trips, especially abroad, there are numerous threats and risks to information security that do not exist in normal business operations.
Each trip must be assessed individually, as a new threat situation arises from the combination of the purpose of the trip (business meeting, conference, congress, etc.), its duration, and destination, also with regard to protecting business-critical information.
The threat level is particularly high when traveling. This is due, for example, to communication over public networks that are not under the control of one's own institution. This makes threats relevant again, against which the institution may have already secured itself. In addition, the risk on trips abroad is often significantly higher than on domestic trips, depending on the destination country.
Protecting corporate and official information is not always easy to achieve due to constantly changing travel destinations, as well as regulatory and legal requirements. For example, legal requirements can tighten entry controls and thus affect the protection of data confidentiality. This results in individual information security requirements depending on the type and duration of the trip, as well as the destination. Political, social, religious, geographical, climatic, legal, and regulatory particularities of individual travel destinations play a decisive role here.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose:
This module describes the protection of all information carried on trips abroad, both in electronic and physical form, with regard to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Confidential information that traveling employees carry in their minds is also a subject of this module. It outlines appropriate regulations and measures for handling sensitive information and data on trips abroad. Basic framework conditions, such as from the areas of IT, data protection, and law, must be taken into account.
In this module, threats and requirements of specific scenarios are highlighted that are directly related to the secure use of information technology, the information, and the devices used on trips abroad.
This module serves as a guide for those responsible within an institution to establish appropriate security measures for information security on trips abroad. It outlines the essential principles that must be considered in this context. Many of the mentioned threats also apply to domestic travel or generally when processing information in environments not under the control of one's own institution.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module CON.7 Information Security on Trips Abroad is to be applied to the information network when employees travel abroad or work abroad temporarily and carry or process particularly sensitive information.
The module generally covers the requirements that contribute to an adequate protection of information on trips abroad. The protection of confidentiality and integrity of sensitive information during travel has the same importance as at the institution's headquarters.
Threats and requirements affecting the local information network are not considered here.
Since the module CON.7 Information Security on Trips Abroad specifically addresses the procedural, technical, and organizational requirements specific to business work while traveling, requirements of the layers NET Networks and Communication, SYS IT Systems, and APP Applications are not considered. All necessary modules, especially SYS.2.1 General Client, NET.3.3 VPN, and SYS.3.2.2 Mobile Device Management (MDM), must be considered separately.
Furthermore, the requirements from the thematically similar modules INF.9 Mobile Workstation and OPS.1.2.4 Teleworking must be observed and implemented.
Within this module, there are also overlaps with other modules and subject areas that are not considered here:
• Fulfillment of data protection requirements,
• Preventive measures for information protection (including technical requirements for portable IT systems, e.g., protection against compromising emanations or eavesdropping), and
• Personnel security.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Eavesdropping and spying on information/Industrial espionage
parts.prose: Espionage refers to attacks aimed at collecting, evaluating, and processing information about institutions, people, products, or other target objects. Especially when traveling abroad, there are unknown sources of danger over which the own institution's information security management has no influence. In principle, there are many dangers in foreign rooms and foreign IT environments due to the targeted eavesdropping of conversations, lines, telephone calls, or data transmissions. This can be problematic, especially abroad, due to corresponding legal possibilities and difficult for travelers to assess. The threats can affect public places and spaces, conditions in other institutions, but also the institution's own representative offices abroad. Devices, such as mobile phones, can also be used to secretly record or listen to conversations. In addition, many IT systems are equipped with microphones and cameras by default, which can be attacked and then exploited. Furthermore, in certain countries, there may be restrictions on entry and exit that override or contradict the regulatory requirements of the country of origin and the institution's security requirements. For example, access to data stored on notebooks and other portable IT systems may be required. In this context, confidential and personal data can not only be viewed but also copied and stored. Since this information could also be, for example, strategy papers or strictly confidential drafts of an institution, potential misuse must always be expected when an inspection takes place (industrial espionage). When traveling abroad, there is not only the risk that information can be eavesdropped on in a technically complex way. Often, sensitive data can be spied on more easily by optical, acoustic, or electronic means, as the usual standards for information security regulations often cannot be applied abroad. This affects, for example, the general security level of a country as well as the local conditions that travelers must inevitably use.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Disclosure and misuse of sensitive information (electronic and physical)
parts.prose: When exchanging information, it can happen that in addition to the desired information, sensitive information is also unintentionally transmitted. This can happen both when sending information electronically and during a phone call or when personally handing over data carriers. On trips abroad, secure information exchange is sometimes made even more difficult due to technically insecure conditions. In addition, it can happen that business travelers leave confidential documents, both physical and electronic, openly visible in public spaces or in their hotel room out of carelessness. Communication with unknown IT systems and networks always poses a potential threat to one's own end device. For example, confidential information can also be copied. On the other hand, foreign data carriers can also contain malware. Here there is a risk that important data will be stolen, manipulated, encrypted, or destroyed. Likewise, the integrity and availability of IT systems can also be impaired. This aspect is favored by the fact that data exchange abroad often takes place via insecure media.
