However, employees are not always aware of this important aspect.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Impersonating a false identity
parts.prose: When communicating while traveling, there is an increased risk of attackers attempting to fake a false identity or take over an authorized identity, both personally and electronically, for example through masquerading, various types of spoofing, hijacking, or man-in-the-middle attacks. In this process, users can be deceived about the identity of their communication partner to such an extent that they disclose information worthy of protection. An attacker can obtain a false digital identity, for example, by spying on a user ID and password, manipulating the sender field of a message, or by manipulating an address on the network. In foreign business relationships, employees do not always know their contact persons personally. Therefore, it can happen that strangers introduce themselves with the name of the contact persons, and the employees trust them and pass on valuable information. The security requirements for confidentiality and integrity can never be fully met in non-institutional, especially foreign, buildings and rooms. Therefore, there is always a residual risk that devices that would normally be classified as secure could also be manipulated. This includes, for example, the caller ID on a telephone or the fax ID of a fax sender, through which a false identity can be faked and information can be obtained.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Lack of security awareness and carelessness in handling information
parts.prose: It is often observed that while institutions have organizational regulations and technical security procedures for portable IT systems and mobile data carriers, these are not sufficiently observed and implemented by employees. For example, employees often leave mobile data carriers unattended in meeting rooms or train compartments. Furthermore, gifts in the form of data carriers, such as USB sticks, are accepted by employees and carelessly connected to their own notebooks. This poses a risk of the notebook being infected with malware, leading to the theft, manipulation, or encryption of sensitive data. In public transport or during business dinners, it is also repeatedly observed that people have open conversations about business-critical information. This can then be easily overheard by outsiders and potentially used to the serious disadvantage of the employees or their institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Violation of local laws or regulations
parts.prose: When traveling abroad, it is particularly important to take into account the different laws and regulations of the destination country, as these can differ massively from the national legal situation. Relevant laws and regulations of the destination country, e.g., on data protection, information obligations, liability, or information access for third parties, are often unknown to travelers or are misjudged. This can lead to violations of a multitude of laws not only abroad but also at home, for example, when personal data of domestic customers is transferred unprotected over public networks during a business trip abroad.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Coercion, blackmail, kidnapping, and corruption
parts.prose: Abroad, different security risks often apply due to political and social circumstances. The security of information, as well as the safety of the travelers themselves, could be endangered during trips abroad by coercion, blackmail, or kidnapping. For example, employees could be threatened with violence to force them to hand over sensitive data. In doing so, they are coerced into circumventing or disregarding security policies and measures. The focus is often on high-ranking executives or employees who hold a special position of trust. Attacks primarily aim to steal or manipulate sensitive information to disrupt business processes or to enrich themselves and others. Political, ideological, and economic goals of the attackers play a major role here. In addition to the threat of violence, there is also the possibility of bribery or corruption. For instance, travelers are specifically offered money or other advantages to induce them to disclose confidential information to unauthorized persons or to commit security breaches. In general, coercion, blackmail, kidnapping, and corruption disrupt or undermine information security regulations.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Information from an unreliable source
parts.prose: In the context of activities abroad, travelers may be intentionally fed false or misleading information to deceive them. As a result of this deception, false statements could be included in business-critical reports. This can lead, among other things, to business-relevant information being based on a false data basis, calculations yielding incorrect results, and wrong decisions being made based on them.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Theft or loss of devices, data carriers, and documents
parts.prose: Especially when traveling abroad, it must be expected that mobile devices can be easily lost or stolen. The smaller and more desirable these devices are, the higher this risk. In addition to the purely material damage from the immediate loss of the mobile device, further financial damage can arise from the disclosure of sensitive data, e.g., emails, meeting notes, or addresses. Furthermore, the reputation of the institution can be damaged.

controls.title: Definition of roles and responsibilities

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Roles and responsibilities for the software development process are only informally named for individual, critical projects. There is no continuous or formal documentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Responsibilities are often assigned verbally within the project team. One person, usually the project manager, is de facto responsible for everything, without specific roles such as 'security officer' formally existing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews project members to determine whether they are aware of their responsibilities in the development process. It is checked whether there are any written records of roles at all, even if this is only in meeting minutes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic roles such as 'developer' and 'project manager' are defined for development projects. A person with overall responsibility for the development process has been appointed. However, specific roles for security or architecture are still missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The role definitions are contained in a general project management policy, but do not explicitly cover all the specialist topics mentioned in the requirement (e.g. requirements engineering, information security).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a person with overall responsibility has been officially appointed and whether basic roles are documented. It is verified whether the appointed persons are aware of their basic roles.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A person with overall responsibility SHOULD be appointed for the software development process. In addition, the roles and responsibilities for all activities within the scope of software development SHOULD be defined. The roles SHOULD cover the following topics: requirements engineering, software design and architecture, information security in software development, software implementation, and software testing. For each development project, a person responsible for information security SHOULD be appointed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The roles and responsibilities are documented in a matrix (e.g. RACI matrix) and are part of the development policy. For each project, a person responsible for information security is explicitly appointed and documented at the beginning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and completeness of the documented roles and responsibilities. Random checks are carried out in several projects to verify whether the roles, especially those for information security, are actually filled and known to the project members.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined roles and responsibilities are reviewed regularly, at least annually, for relevance and appropriateness and are adjusted as necessary. There are defined deputy regulations for all critical roles, including those for information security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The review of roles is part of an annual review process of the development guideline. The roles are stored in a central ALM (Application Lifecycle Management) tool and are assigned to projects.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the annual reviews of the role definitions. It is checked whether deputies have been demonstrably appointed for critical roles in ongoing projects.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Roles and responsibilities are deeply integrated into an ALM (Application Lifecycle Management) tool. Permissions within the development tools (e.g., code repositories, CI/CD pipelines) are automatically granted and enforced based on the assigned roles. Changes to roles or responsibilities trigger an automated review and approval workflow.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The roles are managed via an Identity and Access Management (IAM) system and synchronized with the development tools. A 'Security Champion' program is established to embed security expertise decentrally in the development teams.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the IAM and ALM system to verify the automated assignment of permissions based on the defined roles. An audit trail of changes to role assignments and the associated approvals is checked. The existence and activity of the 'Security Champion' program is reviewed.

controls.title: Selection of a process model

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process model is only selected for individual, particularly critical software development projects. There is no company-wide specification, and compliance is not consistently ensured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection is often made ad hoc by the respective project team, without formal documentation or justification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks on a random basis whether a process model is mentioned at all in project documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A generic process model (e.g. Waterfall) is defined for all projects, but it is not specifically adapted to the project requirements or security aspects. A rough schedule exists, but it integrates security requirements only superficially.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A company-wide template for a project plan is used, but it is rarely adapted. Security requirements are listed as a separate item on a checklist but are not deeply integrated into the phases.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether the standard process model is documented and whether the corresponding standard document templates are used in projects.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A suitable software development process model MUST be defined. Based on the selected process model, a schedule for the software development MUST be created. The client's security requirements for the procedure MUST be integrated into the process model. The selected process model, including the defined security requirements, MUST be adhered to.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Depending on the project type, a suitable model (e.g. V-Model XT, Scrum) is selected and documented. The schedule contains explicit milestones or phases for security activities such as threat modeling or security tests. Compliance is monitored through regular project meetings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the defined process model and the associated schedule. It is verified that the plan explicitly considers security requirements. Compliance with the plan is checked on a random basis using project documentation and artifacts (e.g. test reports).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined process model is regularly reviewed for its suitability and adapted if necessary. The personnel SHOULD be trained in the methodology of the chosen process model. Security requirements are explicitly embedded as part of the 'Definition of Done' or as acceptance criteria in each phase.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Agile models such as Scrum or Kanban are used with dedicated security stories in the backlogs. Training on the applied methodology is demonstrably conducted for all team members and its success is evaluated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the training records of the employees. Project backlogs or phase plans are reviewed for the explicit integration of security requirements and their acceptance criteria. Minutes from retrospectives or review meetings are examined for discussions on process improvement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of the process model is made dynamically based on a risk and complexity analysis of the respective project. 'Secure Development Lifecycle' (SDL) frameworks such as Microsoft's or OWASP SAMM are systematically adapted and applied. The processes are supported by tools (e.g. ALM tools) and compliance is monitored automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ALM (Application Lifecycle Management) tool such as Jira, Azure DevOps or GitLab is used to enforce the chosen process model. Security gates (e.g. mandatory SAST scans) are integrated into the CI/CD process and prevent progress if defined quality and security standards are not met.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the ALM tool and the CI/CD pipeline to check the automated process enforcement and the configuration of the security gates. Dashboard reports that visualize compliance with the SDL process in real time are checked.

controls.title: Selection of a development environment

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Developers select their development environments and tools individually and without central guidelines or criteria. A formal selection or documentation does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each developer installs and configures their own IDE, compiler, and libraries. This often leads to compatibility issues ('works on my machine').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions developers about the tools they use and checks if there is a uniform basis. The lack of any documentation on the selection of development tools is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a recommended standard development environment (e.g. a specific IDE and compiler version), but there are no formal selection criteria. The use of the recommendation is not checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A wiki entry lists the recommended tools. However, there is no process to ensure that new projects also implement these recommendations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a list of recommended tools exists. Spot checks with developers and in project documentation show the degree of deviation from the recommendation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A list of mandatory and optional selection criteria for a development environment MUST be created by those responsible for software development. The development environment MUST be selected based on the specified criteria.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection criteria are documented in a checklist. Criteria include technical requirements (e.g. supported programming languages), license costs, support availability, and basic security aspects (e.g. known vulnerabilities). The decision for a specific environment is logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and appropriateness of the list with selection criteria. It is verified whether the selection of the currently used development environment is documented and is traceable based on the criteria.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection criteria for the development environment are extended to include explicit security criteria, such as the support of static code analysis (SAST) plugins or the origin of the manufacturer. The selected development environment is centrally provided and configured to ensure uniformity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized development environment is provided as a virtual machine image or as a Docker container. This ensures that all developers work with identical tools and configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the security criteria in the selection list. It is verified if and how the development environment is provided centrally (e.g. by checking the configuration scripts for the VM image or Dockerfile).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The provided development environment is hardened and its integrity is checked regularly and automatically. The selection and updating of tools and libraries follows a defined process that includes a security check (e.g. for known vulnerabilities) before they are released to developers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal repository (e.g. Artifactory, Nexus) is used to provide only approved and tested versions of libraries and tools. The development environments (containers/VMs) are regularly updated with the latest security patches and redeployed. Integrity is ensured through digital signatures or hash checks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process for releasing new tools and libraries, including the security test reports. The configuration of the internal repository is examined. It is checked whether mechanisms for integrity verification of the development environments are implemented and whether the corresponding logs are analyzed.

controls.title: Secure system design

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Individual aspects of secure system design, such as input data validation, are implemented ad hoc by individual developers. There are no overarching design principles or guidelines.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One developer implements input validation for a form, while another forgets to do so on a similar form. Security aspects are not addressed in the design document, if one exists.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts random code reviews to identify inconsistencies in the implementation of security measures like input validation. It is checked whether system design documents contain security considerations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a checklist with basic security rules for system design, but it is not enforced for every project. Input data validation is known as a basic rule but is mainly implemented on the client side.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A wiki page lists 'Security Best Practices'. Developers are encouraged to follow them. The system design document has an optional section for security.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence of the checklist or the best practice documentation. Code reviews are used to verify whether basic rules like server-side validation are consistently implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The following fundamental rules of secure system design MUST be considered in the software to be developed: Input data MUST always be checked and validated before further processing. In client-server applications, the data MUST always be validated on the server. The default settings MUST be preset in such a way that secure operation is enabled. In the event of errors, sensitive information MUST NOT be disclosed. The software MUST be able to run with the lowest possible privileges. Sensitive data MUST be transmitted and stored in encrypted form. Trusted mechanisms MUST be used for authentication. Passwords MUST be stored using a secure hashing method. Security-relevant events MUST be logged. The system design MUST be documented and reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: These fundamental rules are part of a mandatory coding guideline. Central libraries are provided for input validation. The system design is recorded in a standardized documentation format (e.g., with UML diagrams) and subjected to a peer review before implementation begins.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the coding guideline for the completeness of the required fundamental rules. The system design documentation and the protocols of the associated reviews are examined. Compliance with the rules (e.g., server-side validation, password hashing, error handling) is verified through random code reviews.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the fundamental rules, principles such as 'Defense-in-Depth' and 'Fail-Secure' are systematically applied in the system design. Information that is not relevant for production operation (e.g., comments with credentials for the development environment) SHOULD be removed from delivered program code and delivered configuration files. Compliance with the design specifications is supported by automated linting and code analysis tools in the build process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A build script is implemented that automatically removes debug information, comments, and unneeded configuration files before creating the final artifact. Static code analysis tools (SAST) are configured with rule sets that check for compliance with secure design principles.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the SAST tools and the build scripts. The delivered software artifact is analyzed to ensure that it contains no irrelevant information. The design documentation is checked for the consideration of 'Defense-in-Depth' concepts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secure system design is based on formal threat modeling (e.g., according to STRIDE). Reusable, tested, and hardened security components (e.g., for authentication, encryption) are provided in a central library, and their use is mandatory for all developments. The design is not only peer-reviewed but also formally approved by a security team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The results of the threat modeling are directly incorporated as requirements into the system design. A company-wide library of security components exists, and its integration into the CI/CD pipeline is checked. The design approval is a firmly defined quality gate in the development process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the threat modeling protocols and compares them with the implemented system design. The source code of the central security library and the process for its maintenance and release are reviewed. The protocols of the formal design approvals by the security team are verified.

controls.title: Use of external libraries from trusted sources

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Developers download external libraries from any sources on the internet without checking their trustworthiness or integrity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Libraries are sourced directly from forums, personal GitHub repositories, or via unsecured HTTP connections. A list of used libraries is not centrally maintained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the build configuration files (e.g., pom.xml, package.json) for references to non-official repositories. Developers are asked how they integrate external dependencies into their projects.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a requirement to source external libraries only from official repositories (e.g., Maven Central, npmjs). However, there are no further checks of the libraries or their integrity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Developers are instructed to use the default repositories of their build tools. However, the integrity check (e.g., checking GPG signatures), which is often offered by the tools, is not activated or its results are ignored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the build tools to ensure that only official repositories are configured. It is checked whether there are processes in place to react to warnings during the integrity check.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If external libraries are used in the development and implementation process, they MUST be sourced from trusted sources. Before external libraries are used, their integrity MUST be ensured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Trusted sources are defined as official package repositories (e.g., Maven Central, PyPI). Integrity is ensured by checking checksums (SHA-256) or, if available, digital signatures of the artifacts. This process is configured and enforced in the build system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a list of sources classified as trustworthy exists. The configuration of the build systems is checked to see if the integrity check (checksums/signatures) is activated and if a build is aborted in case of a failed check.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All external libraries are sourced through an internal repository manager (proxy). Only tested and approved libraries are made available in the internal repository. An automated vulnerability analysis (Software Composition Analysis - SCA) is performed before approval.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like Nexus Repository or Artifactory is used as a proxy for external repositories. The build systems are configured to only access this internal proxy. An SCA tool (e.g., OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk) is integrated into the approval process for new libraries.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the internal repository manager and the build systems. The process documentation for the release of new libraries is checked, and reports from the SCA scans are viewed on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of external libraries is actively managed. This includes continuous monitoring of all used libraries for newly discovered vulnerabilities (also in production), assessing license compliance, and establishing a process for quickly updating or replacing vulnerable components. A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is automatically created and maintained for each application.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SCA tool is integrated into the CI/CD pipeline and blocks builds if new high-severity vulnerabilities are found in a dependency. An automated process exists that informs developers about vulnerable libraries in their code and ideally creates update pull requests (e.g., via Dependabot/Renovatebot). SBOMs are generated in CycloneDX or SPDX format.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline for the integration and rules of the SCA tool. It is verified whether SBOMs are available and correct for all current releases. The process for handling newly discovered vulnerabilities is tracked using concrete examples (e.g., tickets, pull requests).

controls.title: Conducting software tests during development

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Software tests are conducted in an unstructured manner and mostly manually by the developers themselves ('dev testing'). There is no test strategy or test cases. Security tests do not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The developer superficially tests the function they created to see if it works in the 'happy path'. The tests are not documented or repeated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks developers about their testing procedures. The lack of test documentation, test code (unit tests), or testing tools is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unit tests are written during development to check the functionality of individual components. However, there are no requirements for test coverage and no systematic integration tests. Security tests are limited to simple, known cases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Developers are encouraged to write JUnit or similar tests. The tests are checked in with the source code, but their execution is not mandatory in the build process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the code repository for the existence of test code. It is analyzed whether the execution of tests is part of the build process and whether there are metrics for code coverage, even if they are not enforced.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Even before the software is tested and released in the release process, software tests MUST be carried out during development and the source code MUST be inspected for errors. The development-accompanying tests MUST cover the functional and non-functional requirements of the software. The software tests MUST also cover negative tests. In addition, all critical limit values of the input and the data types MUST also be checked. The software MUST be tested in a test and development environment that is separate from the production environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A test strategy is defined that specifies different test types (unit, integration, system tests) and their scope. Test cases, including those for negative scenarios and boundary value analysis, are created and managed. The tests are conducted in a dedicated test environment. Code reviews (e.g., four-eyes principle) are mandatory before merging code.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the test strategy and the documentation of the test cases. It is verified whether a separate test environment exists and is used. The auditor checks the protocols of test runs and code reviews (e.g., in the form of pull requests in the version control system).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In this process, the subject matter experts of the client or the commissioning department SHOULD already be involved. Test data SHOULD be carefully selected and protected for this purpose. Furthermore, an automatic static code analysis SHOULD be performed. It MUST be tested whether the system requirements for the intended software are sufficiently dimensioned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Business departments are actively involved in the creation of acceptance tests. A process for generating anonymized and pseudonymized test data is established. A SAST (Static Analysis Security Testing) tool is run regularly, e.g., on every commit. Load and performance tests are conducted to check the dimensioning of the system requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews logs or tickets that prove the involvement of the business departments in testing. The test data generation process is reviewed. The configuration and reports of the SAST tool are analyzed. The results of the load and performance tests are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The test activities are fully integrated into a CI/CD (Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery) pipeline. Each build automatically goes through a chain of tests, including unit, integration, SAST, DAST (Dynamic Analysis Security Testing), and acceptance tests. A build fails if predefined quality and security criteria (e.g., test coverage, number of critical vulnerabilities) are not met. A 'Test-Driven Development' (TDD) or 'Behavior-Driven Development' (BDD) methodology is applied.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Jenkins, GitLab CI, or Azure DevOps pipeline is implemented that orchestrates the entire testing process. SAST and DAST tools are seamlessly integrated. A test dashboard visualizes the results and metrics (code coverage, load times, security findings) for each build in real time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline and the integrated testing and analysis tools. The quality gates and the corresponding thresholds are verified. The auditor analyzes the test dashboards and historical data to assess the consistent application and effectiveness of the testing process.

controls.title: Provision of patches, updates, and changes

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Patches and updates are only deployed reactively when a critical error occurs in the production environment. There is no proactive process for identifying or distributing updates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a user reports a problem, a hotfix is created and manually applied to the production system. There is no plan for regular updates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the ticket system for bug fixes and compares this with the release history. The absence of an update plan or process is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a process to provide patches for known bugs. Security-critical patches for the company's own software are created as needed. However, there is no systematic process for updates of external libraries.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Minor bug fixes and new features are bundled into releases at irregular intervals. Information about the need to update external libraries often only reaches developers by chance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the release notes for the type of changes (bug fixes, features). It is checked whether a basic process for creating and distributing patches is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that security-critical patches and updates for the developed software are provided by the developers in a timely manner. If security-critical updates are provided for used external libraries, the developers MUST adapt their software accordingly and in turn provide corresponding patches and updates. For the installation, update, or patch files, checksums or digital signatures MUST be provided by the developer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process for monitoring security advisories for all used external libraries is established. There are defined Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for the delivery of security patches. For each release, SHA-256 checksums are generated and published along with the release.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process for monitoring vulnerabilities and the defined SLAs. It is verified whether checksums or signatures have been published for current and past releases. It is checked on a random basis whether known vulnerabilities in libraries were responded to with a patch in a timely manner.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for providing patches and updates is largely automated. There is a defined release cycle (e.g., monthly patch days). The integrity of the provided files is ensured by digital signatures (e.g., with GPG) instead of just checksums.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CI/CD pipeline is used to automatically build, test, and sign patches and updates. A Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tool continuously monitors dependencies and automatically creates tickets or pull requests when updates are required.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline with regard to automated signing. It is checked whether the published artifacts have valid digital signatures. The configuration of the SCA tool for automatic notification is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully automated process is established that identifies vulnerable libraries, rebuilds and tests the software with the patched version, and creates a pull request for review by a developer. The patch and update process is part of a comprehensive vulnerability management program that tracks and optimizes metrics such as 'Time to Remediate'.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Dependabot or Renovatebot are configured to automatically create pull requests for security updates. The CI pipeline automatically runs a full suite of regression and security tests after the update. The vulnerability management dashboard provides real-time metrics on the patch status of the entire software portfolio.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the automation tools (e.g., Dependabot) and the associated CI pipeline jobs. The history of automatically created and merged pull requests for security updates is checked. The metrics and reports of the vulnerability management program are evaluated.

controls.title: Source code version control

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Source code is stored locally on developers' computers or in shared network folders. There is no systematic version control. Changes are managed by manually copying files and renaming folders (e.g., `project_final_final2.zip`).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This method inevitably leads to conflicts, data loss, and a lack of traceability as to who made which change and when. A backup is not guaranteed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the developers how they store their code and share it with colleagues. Inspecting developer workstations or network shares for the presence of versioned zip files or folders confirms this state.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A version control system (e.g., Git, SVN) is used to store the source code. However, there are no clear rules for its use, such as branching strategies or commit messages. Access to the repository is not or only inadequately regulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central Git repository exists, but all developers work directly on the main branch (e.g., `main` or `master`). Commit messages are often meaningless ('update', 'fix'). Anyone with network access can access the repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a version control system is in use. The commit history is examined for the use of branches and the quality of commit messages. The repository's access permissions are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The source code of the development project MUST be managed using a suitable version control system. The institution MUST regulate access to the version control system and define when changes to the source code should be saved by the developers as a separate version in the version control system. It MUST be ensured that all changes to the source code can be tracked and reverted through the version control system. The version control system MUST be included in the data backup concept. Version control MUST NOT be performed without data backup.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central version control system like Git (with GitLab, GitHub, or Bitbucket) is used. There is a documented branching strategy (e.g., GitFlow). Access to repositories is regulated on a role-based basis (e.g., read vs. write access). The repository is backed up daily.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the version control system, including access permissions. The branching strategy is checked for its documentation and compliance (based on the commit history). The data backup concept is reviewed for the inclusion of the version control system and the logs of the backups performed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Changes to the main branch (production branch) are protected and can only be made via pull or merge requests with mandatory review (four-eyes principle). Important branches are protected from accidental deletion or 'force-pushes'.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In GitLab or GitHub, the main branches are configured as 'protected branches'. It is enforced that at least one other developer must approve a pull request before it can be merged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the repository settings, especially the branch protection rules. Randomly selected closed pull requests are checked to see if the review process was followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The review process for pull requests is enhanced by automated checks (status checks). A merge is only possible if all status checks are successful, e.g., the build runs without errors, all tests are successful, the test coverage meets a minimum level, and a security scan does not yield any critical findings. Commits must be digitally signed to unequivocally prove authorship.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CI pipeline is integrated with the version control system and reports the results of the checks back to the pull request. The repository settings enforce the success of these checks. Developers are instructed and technically guided to sign their commits with GPG keys, which is also displayed as 'verified' in the repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the branch protection rules for the mandatory execution of status checks. The configuration of the CI pipeline is analyzed to see which checks are performed. The commit history is checked for the use of signed commits.

controls.title: Creation of a policy for software development

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no formal policies for software development. The approach is based on unwritten rules and the individual preferences of the developers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New developers learn the 'rules' through word of mouth from experienced colleagues. This leads to highly inconsistent results and code styles.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the development policy to be presented. If none can be provided, the requirement is not met. Code reviews typically show a high variance in code quality and structure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a simple coding style guideline that defines basic naming conventions and formatting rules. Further specifications, especially regarding security, are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A wiki document describes how variables should be named and code indented. Compliance is left to the individual developer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence of the style guideline. Code reviews are used to randomly check the extent to which these simple rules are followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A software development policy SHOULD be created and kept up-to-date. The policy SHOULD contain, in addition to naming conventions, specifications for elements that may or may not be used. The relevant requirements from this module SHOULD be incorporated into the policy. The policy SHOULD be mandatory for the developers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal, versioned policy is created that includes topics such as secure coding practices (based on OWASP Top 10), forbidden functions (e.g., `strcpy`), and specifications for error handling and logging. The policy is demonstrably communicated to all developers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence, completeness, and timeliness of the policy. It is checked whether the relevant requirements from CON.8 (e.g., A5, A6, A7, A10) are addressed in it. The auditor verifies that the policy has been communicated to the developers (e.g., through training records or read receipts).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the development policy is supported by automated tools. Static code analysis tools (SAST) and linters are configured with rule sets that correspond to the policy's specifications and are integrated into the development process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A linter profile (e.g., for ESLint, Checkstyle) and a SAST rule set (e.g., for SonarQube) are centrally defined and must be used in all projects. The tools run automatically with every commit or pull request.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the analysis tools and compares the active rules with the policy's specifications. The tools' reports and the CI pipeline configuration are reviewed to verify the integration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The development policy is a 'living document' that is continuously evolved based on findings from security audits, penetration tests, and new threat analyses. The enforcement of the policy is fully automated and implemented as a Quality Gate in the CI/CD pipeline, which blocks a build or deployment in case of violations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a formal process for updating the policy. The configuration of the analysis tools is stored and versioned in the version control system as 'Configuration as Code'. The CI/CD pipeline aborts a build if the linter reports errors or the SAST tool finds new critical vulnerabilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process for updating the policy and the history of changes. The CI/CD pipeline configuration is checked to verify that violations of the policy actually lead to a build failure. The 'Configuration as Code' for the tool rules is inspected.

controls.title: Detailed documentation

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Documentation, if any, is only created in the form of comments in the source code. There is no separate project or operational documentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Knowledge about the software architecture and operation exists only in the minds of the original developers. Onboarding new employees is extremely time-consuming.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the documentation. If only the source code is referenced, the requirement is not met. The absence of documents such as an architecture overview, installation guide, or user manual is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic project documentation is created, but it is often not kept up-to-date. Operational documentation exists, but it only describes the basic installation steps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At the beginning of the project, an architecture document is created, but it is not synchronized with the actual changes in the code during development. There is a simple 'README' file for the installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the existing documentation with the current state of the software to identify discrepancies. It is checked whether the operational documentation is sufficient to put the software into operation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Sufficient project, functional, and interface documentation SHOULD be created and kept up-to-date. The operational documentation SHOULD include specific security instructions for installation and configuration for administration, as well as for the use of the product. The software development SHOULD be documented in such a way that experts can understand and further develop the program code with the help of the documentation. The documentation SHOULD also cover the software architecture and threat modeling.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Templates are used for the required documentation types (architecture document, operating manual, user manual). Updating the documentation is part of the 'Definition of Done' for new features. The operating manual contains a dedicated 'Security Instructions' section with instructions for hardening and secure configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence, completeness, and timeliness of the required documentation. The 'Security Instructions' section in the operating manual is specifically checked. Random checks are performed to see if changes in the code have also been reflected in the documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documentation is maintained as 'Docs-as-Code' along with the source code in the version control system. The creation of the documentation (e.g., in the form of HTML pages) is part of the automated build process. The aspects of documentation SHOULD be considered in the software development process model.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Documentation is written in a simple markup language like Markdown or AsciiDoc. A static site generator (e.g., MkDocs, Antora) creates a searchable website from it, which is updated with every release. Changes to the documentation go through the same review process as code changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the documentation files are present and versioned in the code repository. The CI/CD pipeline configuration is checked for the job to create the documentation. It is verified whether documentation changes are part of the pull request reviews.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Parts of the documentation, especially interface documentation (API documentation), are automatically generated directly from the source code and comments. The documentation is interactive and offers the possibility to try out API endpoints directly. There are automated tests that ensure that code examples in the documentation are correct and executable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Frameworks like Swagger/OpenAPI are used to define REST APIs and generate interactive documentation from them. Tools like Javadoc or Doxygen are used to extract code documentation. A script in the CI pipeline executes the code snippets from the documentation to validate their correctness.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the tools for automatic documentation generation. The generated API documentation is checked for interactivity and completeness. The CI pipeline is examined for the existence of tests for the documentation code examples.

controls.title: Information security training for the development team

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no formal information security training sessions for the development team. Knowledge is passed on informally and reactively, usually after a security incident has occurred.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A developer reads a blog article about a new vulnerability and tells their colleagues about it in the coffee room. There is no structured program.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the training plan and training records for the development team. The absence of such documents is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: New developers receive one-time, general information security training as part of their onboarding. There are no further or role-specific training sessions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All new employees must complete a web-based training on 'Security Awareness', which, however, does not specifically address the risks of software development.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the onboarding documents and the participation certificates of the general security training. It is checked whether the content is relevant for developers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The developers and the other members of the development team SHOULD be trained on general information security aspects and on the aspects specifically relevant to them. This includes: requirements analysis, project management, risk management or threat modeling, quality management, models and methods for software development, software architecture, software testing, change management, as well as information security, security requirements, and security aspects in special areas.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual training plan is created for the development team. The training covers core concepts of secure development (e.g., OWASP Top 10) and is conducted by internal or external experts. Participation is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the training plan, training materials, and attendance lists. It is verified that the training content covers the required aspects and is tailored to the target audience of developers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training program is role-specific. Backend developers receive different training than frontend developers or DevOps engineers. The success of the training is checked through knowledge tests or practical exercises.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A learning platform is used that provides different training modules for different roles. After completing a module, a test must be passed. Capture-the-Flag (CTF) events or hackathons are regularly held to apply the knowledge in practice.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the role-specific training plans and the results of the knowledge tests. The organization and results of practical exercises such as CTFs are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A 'Security Champion' program is established, in which selected developers receive in-depth security training and act as first points of contact and multipliers for security in their teams. The training program is continuously adapted based on new threats, internal pen test results, and the needs of the teams. Gamification elements are used to increase motivation for continuous further education.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Security Champions receive a dedicated time budget for further education and supporting their teams. The results of security tests flow directly into the creation of new training content (e.g., 'Lesson of the Week'). A learning platform awards badges and points for completed courses and successful participation in security events.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation and activities of the 'Security Champion' program through interviews and inspection of communication channels. The process for adapting the training content is reviewed. The effectiveness of the program is evaluated based on metrics such as a decreasing number of security findings in the respective teams.

controls.title: Appropriate governance of software development

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Software development is managed ad-hoc, without a defined project management model. Planning is informal and not documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Requirements are passed on to developers by word of mouth or email. Project progress is not transparent.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the project plan and status reports. If these do not exist, the requirement is not met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple project management model is used, which, however, mainly focuses on time and resource planning. Aspects such as risk management or quality objectives are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Gantt chart is used for time planning. There are regular status meetings where progress is discussed. However, quality and security aspects are not a fixed part of the agenda.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the project plans and the minutes of the status meetings. It is verified whether risks or quality objectives are addressed therein.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For software development, a suitable governance or project management model SHOULD be used based on the selected process model. The governance or project management model SHOULD be integrated into the software development policy. In doing so, the required qualifications of personnel and the coverage of all relevant phases during the software lifecycle SHOULD be given special consideration. A suitable risk management process SHOULD be established for the process model. Furthermore, suitable quality objectives SHOULD be defined for the development project.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A project management framework (e.g., PRINCE2, Scrum) is selected and made mandatory for the projects. A risk register is maintained and regularly reviewed. Measurable quality objectives (e.g., maximum number of critical errors, code coverage target) are defined at the beginning of the project and their achievement is tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the development policy for the integration of the project management model. The existence and maintenance of the risk register as well as the documentation and tracking of quality objectives are reviewed. Project plans are examined for consideration of personnel qualifications and coverage of the entire lifecycle.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Software development management is supported by an ALM (Application Lifecycle Management) tool. Risk management and the tracking of quality objectives are integrated into the tool. The defined processes are mapped in the tool and their compliance is monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool such as Jira or Azure DevOps is used to manage requirements, tasks, risks, and test results. Dashboards are configured to visualize the project status, risk situation, and the achievement of quality objectives in real time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the ALM tool. It is checked whether the processes defined in the model (e.g., risk assessment) are mapped in the tool. The dashboards and reports are evaluated to verify active control and monitoring.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of software development is data-driven. Metrics from all phases of the lifecycle (e.g., Lead Time, Cycle Time, defect density, results of security scans) are automatically collected and used for continuous process improvement. Risk management is proactive and uses insights from threat modeling to identify and mitigate risks early on.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ALM tool is integrated with all other development tools (version control, CI/CD, test tools) to ensure a continuous data flow. 'Value Stream Mapping' analyses are performed to identify bottlenecks and potential for improvement in the development process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the integration of the toolchain and the automated metric collection process. It is analyzed how the collected metrics and risk analyses are demonstrably used for process control and improvement (e.g., by analyzing logs from retrospectives or management reviews).

controls.title: Selection of trustworthy development tools

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only development tools (compilers, IDEs, build tools) from established and well-known manufacturers are used. The tools are obtained from official sources and their integrity is verified by checksums.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of approved tools and manufacturers is maintained. Before use, the checksum of the download is compared with the one published by the manufacturer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the list of approved tools. It is randomly checked whether the integrity verification process is documented and followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Sufficient security requirements for their tools SHOULD be imposed on the manufacturing companies of hardware or software. This includes the demand for secure development processes (e.g., proof of an SDL) and the timely provision of security patches for the tools themselves.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When procuring commercial development tools, security requirements are formulated as part of the tender or contract. For open-source tools, the maturity of the project is assessed (e.g., community size, response time to security issues).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews procurement documents and contracts for the stated security requirements. For used open-source tools, the documentation of the project evaluation is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For software development, only tools with proven security properties SHOULD be used. This can be demonstrated, for example, by a formal certification (e.g., according to Common Criteria) or an independent security analysis of the tool. The configuration of the tools themselves is hardened and checked for compliance with internal security policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools that have a security certification are preferred. The configuration of IDEs, compilers, and build tools is centrally managed and rolled out to ensure that security-relevant options (e.g., stack protection, ASLR) are enabled by default.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the certificates or reports of the independent security analyses of the tools used. The centrally managed configuration of the tools is checked for the implementation of hardening measures and secure default settings.

controls.title: Regular security audits for the development environment

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The development environment and the test environment are subjected to a security audit in the event of significant changes or a concrete suspicion of security problems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An audit is manually performed by a security team, for example, when a new central tool is introduced. The audit consists of a configuration review and a vulnerability scan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports of the event-driven security audits and the follow-up on the deficiencies identified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Regular security audits of the software development environment and the software test environment SHOULD be conducted. This is done at fixed intervals, e.g., annually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual audit plan is created. The audit includes the review of access rights, the configuration of servers and tools, patch levels, and compliance with security processes (e.g., version control, backup).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit plan and the audit reports from the last periods. It is verified that the identified findings are addressed in a remediation process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regular security audits are supplemented by continuous, automated compliance checks. In addition, periodic penetration tests of the development infrastructure are carried out by independent third parties to uncover undetected vulnerabilities and attack vectors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An automated tool for checking system configurations (Configuration Management Database, CMDB, or Security Posture Management, CSPM) is used to detect deviations from the hardened baseline in real time. An external penetration test is commissioned every two years.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and reports of the automated compliance tool. The reports of the external penetration tests and the action plan for remedying the vulnerabilities found are analyzed.

controls.title: Regular integrity check of the development environment

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of critical components of the development environment (e.g., build server, code repository) is manually checked on an ad-hoc basis, e.g., after a security incident or if there is a suspicion of compromise.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator manually calculates the hash values of critical binary files and compares them with a reference list.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of manual integrity checks, if they were performed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of the development environment SHOULD be regularly checked with cryptographic mechanisms in accordance with the state of the art. The checksum files and the verification program itself SHOULD be sufficiently protected against manipulation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An integrity monitoring tool (e.g., AIDE, Tripwire) is installed on critical systems in the development environment. The tool is configured to perform a daily check and trigger an alarm in case of deviations. The configuration and reference database of the tool are stored on a read-only medium or a separate, secured server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the integrity monitoring tool. It is verified how the reference database is protected. The logs and alarms of the tool are checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity check is fully automated and integrated into the central security monitoring (SIEM). Important indications of a loss of integrity SHOULD not be lost in a flood of irrelevant warnings (false positives). The configuration of the checks is fine-tuned to report only relevant changes. Integrity is additionally strengthened by hardware-based mechanisms (e.g., Trusted Platform Module - TPM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The alarms from the integrity tool are sent to a SIEM system and correlated with other events there. There is a defined process for analyzing and handling integrity alarms to quickly identify and suppress false alarms. A 'Measured Boot' sequence with a TPM is used on build servers to ensure the integrity of the entire software chain from the bootloader to the application.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the SIEM rules for integrity alarms and the documented incident response process. It is checked whether the configuration of the integrity tool is optimized to reduce false positives. If TPMs are used, their configuration and integration into the boot process is verified.

controls.title: Checking of external components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: External components and libraries are integrated into projects without any check for security or compatibility.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A developer finds a library that solves a problem and integrates it immediately. Potential risks such as vulnerabilities, outdated code, or license conflicts are not considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the list of dependencies of a project (e.g., `pom.xml`, `package-lock.json`) and asks the developers if a process for reviewing these components exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of external components is ensured by comparing checksums upon integration. However, outdated versions are not systematically identified or updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Build tools like Maven or Gradle automatically check the checksums of downloaded artifacts. However, there is no process to regularly check if the used library versions are still up to date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the build tool for the activation of checksum verification. A manual analysis of the dependencies for outdated versions reveals the gaps in the process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unknown external components (or program libraries) whose security cannot be ensured by established and recognized peer reviews or comparable means MUST be checked for vulnerabilities. All external components MUST be checked for potential conflicts. The integrity of external components MUST be verified by checksums or cryptographic certificates. Furthermore, outdated versions of external components SHOULD NOT be used in current development projects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process for the selection and approval of external components is defined. This includes checking for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) using online databases, a basic compatibility check, and integrity verification. There is a policy that prohibits the use of libraries that have not received an update in more than a year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation for the approval of external components. The logs of these checks are reviewed on a random basis. The list of project dependencies is analyzed to verify compliance with the policy regarding outdated versions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The verification of external components for known vulnerabilities is performed by an automated Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tool. This tool is integrated into the build process and warns about the use of vulnerable or outdated components.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SCA tool like OWASP Dependency-Check is run as part of the CI build. The build is marked with a warning if components with vulnerabilities above a certain threshold or outdated components are found.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the SCA tool and its integration into the CI pipeline. The reports of the SCA scans are analyzed, and it is checked how the generated warnings are responded to.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The verification of external components is a quality gate in the CI/CD pipeline. A build or a deployment is blocked if components with critical vulnerabilities, license conflicts, or those marked as 'outdated' are found. For particularly critical or untrustworthy components, a manual code analysis is performed by the security team before they are approved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SCA tool is configured to fail the CI/CD run if the defined policies are violated. A 'whitelist' of approved components and versions exists, which is managed in an internal repository manager. The process for manual code analysis is formally defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline to verify that it fails in case of violations (blocking). The configuration of the internal repository manager and the process documentation for manual code analyses are reviewed. Reports of completed manual analyses are inspected.

controls.title: Threat Modeling

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Threats are not systematically analyzed. Security measures are implemented reactively after a vulnerability has been exploited or a security problem becomes known.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The team informally discusses possible problems, but there is no structured process to identify, assess, or document threats.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for documents or records that prove a threat analysis has been performed. The absence of such artifacts is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For new, larger projects, an informal risk analysis is conducted in the form of a brainstorming session. The results are recorded in a simple list but are not systematically assessed or tracked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a workshop at the beginning of the project, potential threats are collected. The list is stored in the project wiki, but there is no formal process to derive countermeasures or to monitor their implementation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether lists of identified threats exist. It is analyzed whether these threats have been assessed and whether concrete software requirements have been derived from them.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the design phase of software development, threat modeling SHOULD be performed. For this purpose, potential threats SHOULD be identified based on the security profile, the requirements catalog, and the planned operational environment or deployment scenarios. The threats SHOULD be assessed in terms of their likelihood of occurrence and impact.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An established threat modeling method (e.g., STRIDE) is used. The process is moderated in a workshop with developers, architects, and security experts. The results (identified threats, risk assessment, planned countermeasures) are documented and added to the backlog as requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the threat modeling performed. It is verified whether the methodology was applied correctly and whether the results are comprehensible. It is checked on a random basis whether the derived countermeasures were actually implemented as requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Threat modeling is a fixed, repeatable process for all new features or significant changes, not just for new projects. The results of the modeling are recorded and managed in a tool that facilitates the tracking of threats and countermeasures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized tools for threat modeling (e.g., Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, OWASP Threat Dragon) are used. The threat models are versioned and maintained along with the architecture documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether threat modeling is also performed for changes to existing software (e.g., based on logs). The use of specialized tools and the versioning of the models is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Threat modeling is partially automated by automatically analyzing architecture diagrams (e.g., from 'Infrastructure as Code' descriptions) and comparing them with known threat patterns. The results of the threat modeling are used to automatically generate test cases for security tests (e.g., for penetration tests).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool is used that can parse IaC templates (e.g., Terraform, CloudFormation) and generate a data flow diagram with potential threats from them. From the identified threats, test scenarios for DAST tools or manual test plans are derived directly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and results of the tools for automated threat analysis. The process for generating test cases from threat models and the corresponding test logs are analyzed to trace the continuous chain from threat to test.

controls.title: Secure Software Design

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The software design focuses exclusively on functionality. Security aspects are not proactively considered in the design.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The architecture is designed to meet the functional requirements. Security functions, if any, are added later in response to problems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the design and architecture documents for consideration of security aspects. If these are completely missing, the requirement is not met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic security functions such as authentication and authorization are considered in the software design. However, there is no overarching secure architecture or systematic application of security design principles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The architecture documentation includes a chapter on user management. However, principles like 'Least Privilege' or 'Defense in Depth' are not consistently applied to all parts of the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the design goes beyond basic security functions and whether security design principles are known and at least partially applied.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The software design SHOULD consider the requirements catalog, the security profile, and the results of the threat modeling. As part of the secure software design, a secure software architecture SHOULD be developed, on the basis of which the application's source code is to be developed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The design process includes an explicit step in which the results of the threat modeling are translated into concrete architectural decisions and security controls. The software architecture is documented (e.g., using the C4 model) and reviewed by a peer or architect before implementation begins.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether there is a traceable link between the identified threats and the countermeasures taken in the software design. The software architecture documentation and the architecture review logs are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When designing the software architecture, established security design principles are systematically applied (e.g., Least Privilege, Defense in Depth, Fail Secure, Separation of Duties). The design considers maintainability and modifiability to facilitate future security adjustments.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The architecture policy requires the application of security design principles. The design is laid out for loose coupling and high cohesion to simplify the replacement of components. Established and secure architecture patterns (e.g., Backend-for-Frontend) are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the architecture documentation for the explicit application and justification of security design principles. It is assessed to what extent the architecture supports maintainability and future adjustments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Future standards and attack techniques SHOULD be considered as much as possible, so that the software to be developed can also be easily maintained in the future. The software design is reviewed and approved in a formal process by a dedicated security team or a security architect. Reference architectures are provided for various types of applications that already implement secure design patterns.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The company maintains a technology radar and a process for monitoring security trends to proactively consider future requirements in the design. For common use cases (e.g., web application with database, microservice), documented and tested reference architectures exist that serve as templates for new projects.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the formal architecture approvals by the security team. The existence, quality, and use of the provided reference architectures are verified. It is checked whether a process for technology and threat monitoring is established and whether its results are incorporated into the architectural guidelines.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Many institutions face challenges that they can no longer adequately solve with a standard, off-the-shelf software product. They require software solutions tailored to their individual requirements. Examples include highly specific software solutions for industry-specific applications (such as controlling production plants) or IT applications adapted to their own business processes (such as content management systems or identity management systems). Legacy systems that are no longer maintained by the original manufacturer can also be custom-developed further.

Here, (individual) software can be developed by the institution itself or by a third party. Software development plays a central role when program code is developed or adapted from the institution's requirements. It is essential that information security is considered throughout the entire software development process and not just in a later phase. Only in this way can the information security of the software solution to be developed be sustainably guaranteed.

Software can be developed within classic, self-contained projects, or as a continuous activity without a fixed end. In practice, project management tools are very often used in both cases to coordinate and manage software development. Therefore, this module uses the term 'project' frequently and does not consistently differentiate between project-based and continuous development, as the associated procedures and tools are similar.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
