The necessary system accesses for IT operations (e.g., root access to the server) and for business application administration (e.g., admin access to the application interface) are explicitly documented and limited to the necessary minimum.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the operating manual and the RACI matrix for a selected specialized application. They check the technically implemented permissions for IT operations and business application administration and compare them with the documentation. It is checked whether the documented interface processes (e.g., 'How does the business admin request an OS patch?') are being followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The separation of administrative tasks between IT operations and business application administration is technically enforced. The business application administrator has no way to access the operating system level. The system administrator has no way to access the application data (e.g., through database encryption where the key is only held by the business application administration). All interactions at the interfaces between IT operations and business application administration are logged and monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application is operated in a way that allows for a strict 'Separation of Duties'. For example, business application administration is handled via a dedicated web interface or an admin tool that does not allow shell access. The database is transparently encrypted (TDE) and IT operations have no access to the decryption keys. Requests from the business department to IT operations run through a ticket system with defined, automated workflows.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the technical architecture of the application and its operating environment. They attempt to access application data as a system administrator and the operating system as a business application administrator. The logs of the interface communication are checked for completeness and compliance.

controls.title: Documentation of IT administration activities (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a requirement that administrative changes must be documented in a ticket system or a logbook. The documentation includes at least a description of the change made.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every administrator is instructed to create a ticket for every change or at least to document it afterwards. However, the quality and level of detail of the documentation depend on the discipline of the individual administrator.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation for a recently performed change. They assess whether documentation exists and whether it describes the basic change.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Performed IT administration activities SHOULD be documented in a traceable manner. It SHOULD be checked what the basic requirements are for the documentation of IT administration activities. It SHOULD be identified which goals are to be achieved with the documentation. Based on these requirements and goals, it SHOULD be bindingly defined which steps are to be documented and in what level of detail. The documentation SHOULD at least indicate what changes were made, when the changes were made, who made the changes, on what basis or for what reason the changes were made, and to what extent and for what reason there were deviations from specified standards or configurations. Documentation in the context of an IT administration activity SHOULD be included in standard workflows. It SHOULD be regulated what options are to be used if IT administration activities are carried out unscheduled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The change management process requires that every administrative change be documented in a ticket. The ticket template contains mandatory fields for all required information (Who, What, When, Why, etc.). For emergency changes, there is a defined process for subsequent documentation. The documentation is regularly reviewed as part of change audits.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the documented change management process and the associated ticket templates. They select several completed changes (including emergency changes) on a random basis and check the completeness and quality of the documentation against the defined requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documentation of administrative changes is largely automated. When using Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC), the commit of the configuration change in the code repository serves as the primary documentation. The execution logs of the automation tools are automatically linked to the corresponding change ticket.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Git repository is used for managing configurations (e.g., Ansible Playbooks, Terraform code). The Git commit log, including the link to the ticket ID, serves as the change history. A CI/CD pipeline executes the changes and automatically attaches the execution log to the ticket in Jira.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor traces a change from the request in the ticket, through the code commit in Git, to the automated deployment and logging in the CI/CD pipeline. They verify that the change defined in the code exactly matches the implemented change on the system.

controls.title: Advanced security measures for administrative access (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative access is restricted by firewall rules to specific source IP addresses or networks. It is ensured that administrative interfaces are not accessible unprotected from the internet.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Rules are implemented on the network firewalls and the host-based firewalls of the servers that allow access to administrative ports (such as 22, 3389) only from the IP addresses of the administrators' workstations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rules for administrative services. They perform a port scan from an unauthorized network (e.g., guest WLAN) on a server to check if the administrative ports are accessible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to administrative surfaces and interfaces SHOULD be restricted to IT systems used for IT administration. Therefore, networks used for IT administration SHOULD be separated from production networks of components to be administered through filtering and segmentation measures (out-of-band management). Where out-of-band management is not possible, software interfaces and physical interfaces for IT administration SHOULD be secured by additional measures and only be accessible to persons authorized for their use. For this purpose, two-factor authentication SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate management VLAN is set up. All management interfaces of the servers, network components, and other devices are exclusively connected to this VLAN. Access to this VLAN is highly regulated. In addition, two-factor authentication is enforced for all administrative logins (e.g., via SSH, RDP, VPN).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network architecture and the VLAN configuration. They check the firewall rules between the management VLAN and other networks. It is verified that a login to an administrative interface is not possible without the second factor.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administrative access is exclusively via a hardened Bastion Host or Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution located in the management network. Direct connections from workstation networks to the management network are completely prohibited. Access to the PAM system itself is protected by multi-factor authentication and strict access controls.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators connect exclusively to the PAM system. This system is the only one allowed to establish connections to the management interfaces of the target systems (Jump Host architecture). The use of dedicated Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for accessing the PAM system is enforced.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the entire access chain: from the PAW through the PAM system to the target system. They analyze the firewall rules and the PAM configuration to ensure that no bypass possibilities exist. The hardening of the PAWs and the PAM system itself is audited.

controls.title: Role and authorization concept for administrative access (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a document that describes the existing administrative roles and their main responsibilities. The process for assigning roles is informal but is generally tied to approval by a supervisor.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of admin roles is maintained in a wiki. The assignment is made via an email from the supervisor to the IT team, which then manually implements the permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the document with the role descriptions. They randomly check for an administrator whether their assigned role can be traced back to an approval by the supervisor.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There SHOULD be an appropriate role and authorization concept for administrative access. It SHOULD specify fundamental guidelines, at least on how administration roles are requested and assigned, what types of administration roles exist, what types of permissions are granted in the context of administration roles, and how permissions necessary for IT administration are granted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal, versioned role and authorization concept has been adopted and is known to all administrators. It describes in detail the entire lifecycle of a permission: from the definition of the role, through the application and approval process (e.g., via an ITSM tool), to regular review (recertification) and revocation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the formal role and authorization concept. They check whether the processes described therein (application, approval, review) are technically and organizationally implemented. The lifecycle of an exemplary permission assignment is traced using tickets and logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The role and authorization concept is fully mapped and automated in an Identity and Access Management (IAM) system. The assignment of roles is done just-in-time and is linked to a need (e.g., an approved ticket). Access reviews are automatically initiated, and the results are used for the automatic correction of permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IAM system centrally manages all administrative roles and permissions. The process from application to revocation is a continuous digital workflow. The system automatically detects orphaned or unused permissions and suggests their revocation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is granted read access to the IAM system to analyze the configuration of the role model and the workflows. They check the logs of the automated access reviews and the resulting permission changes. It is verified that the entire process is logged in an audit-proof manner.

controls.title: Reviewing IT administration activities (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrators are instructed to check the changes they have made for correct function. This check is performed by the administrator themselves and is not documented separately.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After an administrator changes a firewall rule, they test for themselves whether the connection works as desired. This is part of good professional practice, but not a formal process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks administrators how they ensure the correctness of their changes. It is accepted if they describe an informal self-test process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before an IT administration activity is carried out, it SHOULD be checked whether the reason for and the nature of the activity are plausible in the context of the underlying task. After an IT administration activity has been carried out on a component, it SHOULD be checked whether the configuration and the status of the component correspond to the desired target state. If additional quality assurance of the executed administration task is necessary, it SHOULD not be carried out by the same person who performed the corresponding activities. For IT administration activities with potentially far-reaching consequences, it SHOULD be checked whether these activities could restrict the availability of the IT administration itself. In this case, appropriate precautions SHOULD be taken to enable a rollback of the IT administration activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The change management process specifies for which change categories a four-eyes principle (implementation by person A, review by person B) is required. A rollback plan is created before implementation. The successful review is documented in the change ticket and is a prerequisite for closing the ticket.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a critical change and checks in the corresponding ticket whether the rollback plan is documented and whether the review was carried out and proven by a second, qualified person.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The review of administrative activities is automated. After each configuration change by an automation tool, a series of tests (test suite) is automatically executed to verify the state and functionality of the system. In case of deviations from the target state, the change is automatically rolled back and an alarm is triggered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CI/CD pipeline for Infrastructure-as-Code is used. After the 'Deploy' step, a 'Test' step automatically follows, which uses tools like 'Serverspec' or 'InSpec' to check the system's compliance with the defined target state. If the test fails, the previous configuration state is automatically restored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the CI/CD pipeline and the test and rollback steps it contains. They ask to be shown the logs of a deployment to verify the automatic execution of the tests and the results. The quality and coverage of the test suite are evaluated.

controls.title: Time windows for major IT administration activities (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general rule has been established that service-impacting changes should take place outside of core business hours. These time windows are generally known but not formally defined for each application.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an unwritten rule in the team that restarts or major updates to servers are carried out in the evening or on weekends. The exact time is coordinated within the team at short notice.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the administration team about practices regarding maintenance windows. They compare the timestamps of critical changes in the logs with the core business hours.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For IT administration activities with potentially far-reaching consequences, maintenance windows SHOULD be coordinated by the IT operations team. If the IT operations team specifies time windows for IT administration activities, these MUST be adhered to.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the change management process, explicit maintenance windows are defined for all critical IT services and coordinated with the business departments. Any planned, potentially disruptive change must be scheduled for one of these windows. Compliance is checked in the change process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the documentation of the agreed maintenance windows. They check in the change tickets of critical changes whether the implementation took place within the agreed time window.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with maintenance windows is technically enforced. Automation tools are configured to only allow the execution of changes marked as critical within the predefined time windows. Unscheduled changes require an escalated emergency approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The automation platform (e.g., Ansible Tower) or the ITSM tool checks before executing a change whether the current time is within the maintenance window defined for the affected service. If this is not the case, execution is blocked unless the change has been explicitly marked as an emergency change with special approval.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the automation platform to verify the technical enforcement of the maintenance windows. The logs are checked for attempts to execute changes outside the windows, as well as for the correct handling of the emergency process.

controls.title: Configuration Backup (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a process for regular backups of server systems, which also includes the configuration files. Before major manual changes, a manual backup of the configuration file to be changed is created.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The central backup software backs up the complete virtual machines or file systems. Before an administrator changes e.g. the `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`, they copy it to `sshd_config.bak`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the central backup solution. He questions administrators about their procedure for manual configuration changes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All configurations SHOULD be backed up through regular backups at the application level and at the IT system level. An additional backup SHOULD be made before IT administration activities with potentially far-reaching consequences. For backups, it SHOULD be ensured that they can be restored in case of failure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to system backups, there are dedicated processes to automatically and regularly back up application configurations (e.g., from databases) and the configurations of network devices and firewalls. The change process stipulates that an unscheduled backup of the affected system or configuration must be performed before any critical change. Recoverability is tested regularly (restore tests).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration of the configuration backup systems (e.g. for network devices). In critical change tickets, it is checked whether the required pre-backup is documented. Logs of the last restore tests are requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Configurations are managed as code in a versioned repository (Infrastructure-as-Code). Every change is a commit and therefore implicitly a backup and part of a complete history. A rollback to any previous version is possible with a simple 'revert' command.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Configurations of servers, cloud resources, and network devices are managed with tools like Ansible, Terraform, and Git. The 'main' branch always represents the production state. Before a change, a new branch is created. The change is merged through a pull request with a mandatory review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the IaC workflow. He checks the Git history for completeness and traceability. He has someone demonstrate how a rollback to a previous configuration version is performed.

controls.title: Replacement for central IT administration tools (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In case of failure of a central administration tool (e.g. vCenter), there is a documented emergency guide that describes how to access individual components directly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The emergency manual describes how to connect directly to an ESXi host via SSH if the vCenter is unavailable. The necessary passwords for this are stored in a password safe.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to be shown the emergency guide for the failure of a central administration tool. He checks whether the instructions are plausible and the necessary access data are available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For central IT administration tools, alternatives SHOULD be available that can be used for administration if necessary. For this purpose, jump systems with access to corresponding administration networks SHOULD be available. If such alternatives are not available, access and direct access to the IT to be administered SHOULD be possible for IT administration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Central administration tools (e.g. PAM system, vCenter, automation platform) are designed to be redundant (e.g. as a cluster). In addition, there is a documented and regularly tested 'break-glass' process that allows direct access to the target systems via a separate jump system in an emergency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the architecture documentation for redundancy of the central administration tools. He has the 'break-glass' process explained to him and requests evidence of its last test as part of an emergency drill.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Central administration tools are designed to be highly available across multiple locations or availability zones. The failover between instances is automatic and is permanently monitored. The 'break-glass' process is also automated and triggers special alarms and a high-priority monitoring process upon activation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The vCenter is configured as an HA cluster. The PAM system runs in an active/passive cluster with automatic switchover. Activating a 'break-glass' account requires the approval of two people via the system and immediately leads to a P1 alert in the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the high-availability architecture and the configuration of the cluster systems. He checks the monitoring and alerting configuration for the failover. The logs of the 'break-glass' process are checked for correct triggering, approval, and alerting.

controls.title: Logging of administrative activities (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging is enabled on most systems and the logs are kept for a defined period. There are no central protective measures that prevent administrators from deleting or changing the local logs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Standard logging is enabled on the servers. The log files are stored locally and are rotated and deleted after 30 days. An administrator with root or admin rights can edit or delete these files.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the logging configuration and the existence of the log files on a server. He verifies that an administrator with their assigned rights could manipulate the log files.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative activities SHOULD be logged. The log files SHOULD be kept protected for an appropriate period of time. The executing administrators SHOULD have no possibility to change or delete the recorded log files. Log data SHOULD be checked regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All relevant logs are sent in real-time to a central, write-protected log management system (e.g. a syslog server or a SIEM solution). On this central system, the administrators of the source systems have no write or delete rights. The information security team performs regular, random, or automated checks of the logs for anomalies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the log forwarding on a source system and the permission structure on the central log management system. He verifies that an administrator cannot manipulate the centrally collected logs. Evidence of the regular review of the log data is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of the log files is ensured by cryptographic methods (e.g. hashing, signatures). All administrative sessions are routed through a PAM system, which performs a complete and tamper-proof recording of all commands and actions (session recording). The log data is reviewed in real time by a SIEM with automated correlation rules and alarm triggering.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The central log management system uses WORM storage (Write Once, Read Many) or blockchain-based technologies to guarantee the immutability of the logs. The PAM system used records all keystrokes and the screen output of administrative sessions. The SIEM correlates the PAM logs with network and application logs to detect complex attack patterns.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the mechanisms for protecting log integrity. He has an administrative session recorded in the PAM system shown to him. In the SIEM, the configuration of the correlation rules and the triggered alarms related to administrative activities are analyzed.

controls.title: IT administration according to the four-eyes principle (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be regulated which administration tasks require an additional person to monitor the execution. This person SHOULD also have the necessary qualifications in the context of the IT administration activities to be performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The change management process defines a list of particularly critical changes (e.g. 'change to the central firewall', 'update of the domain controller') that must be carried out according to the four-eyes principle. This means that a second qualified person is present during the implementation (physically or via screen sharing) and monitors the steps. The implementation according to the four-eyes principle is documented in the change ticket and confirmed by both persons.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of changes that require a four-eyes principle. He selects a corresponding change and checks the ticket for proof that a second person was present and confirmed the implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The four-eyes principle is technically enforced (Dual Control). Critical commands or actions can only be executed if a second, authorized person approves the action in real time via a technical system (e.g. a PAM system).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Privileged Access Management (PAM) system is used with a 'Dual Control' function. If an administrator wants to execute a command defined as critical (e.g. 'shutdown') on a production server, the execution is paused. A second administrator receives a notification and must explicitly approve the command in the PAM console before it is executed. The entire process is logged in a tamper-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the 'Dual Control' function in the PAM system. He has the process demonstrated live. The logs are checked to see if critical commands were executed without the required second approval.

controls.title: Continuous logging of administrative activities (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For IT components with high protection requirements, all administrative activities are logged centrally and in a tamper-proof manner. It is ensured that the logging covers all relevant levels (operating system, database, application).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Detailed logging profiles are activated for systems classified as having high protection requirements. All logs (system logs, database audit logs, application logs) are sent to a central SIEM system to which administrators do not have write access. The logs are regularly checked for completeness and anomalies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a system with high protection requirements and checks the logging configuration at all levels. They compare the logs in the SIEM with the actions performed according to the change tickets to verify completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For IT components with high protection requirements, all administrative activities in all areas SHOULD be logged. Every administrative action SHOULD be fully traceable. The performing administrators SHOULD not be able to influence the type and scope of the logging.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logging configuration is centrally managed and enforced via a configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible, Puppet). Any deviation from the target configuration on an end system is automatically detected and corrected or triggers an alert. Additionally, session recording is enforced for all administrative sessions on these systems to ensure complete traceability of actions not directly logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration in the configuration management tool and the monitoring rules for logging. They request a complete session recording of an administrative activity and compare it with the generated text logs to verify end-to-end logging.

controls.title: Use of highly available IT administration tools (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Critical, central administration tools (e.g., PAM, vCenter, central log servers) are designed redundantly within one location (e.g., as an active/passive cluster).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The vCenter runs in HA mode. The PAM system consists of two servers in a cluster with manual or semi-automatic failover. Redundancy is tested regularly during planned maintenance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture documentation and the configuration of the cluster systems. Logs from past failover tests are requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administration tools SHOULD be designed redundantly. It SHOULD be ensured that in the event of a failure, all administrative tasks can still be performed without significant restrictions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All central and critical administration tools are designed as highly available, geo-redundant clusters across at least two locations. Failover in the event of a failure is fully automatic and is monitored 24/7. Functionality is proven through regular, planned failover tests.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the geo-redundant architecture and the configuration of the automatic failover mechanisms. They request the logs of the last failover tests and analyze the monitoring data to assess the switchover times and reliability.

controls.title: Monitoring of IT administration tools (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For critical IT administration tools, basic availability and performance parameters (e.g., reachability, CPU load) are recorded in a central monitoring system. If thresholds are exceeded, the administration team is notified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The central monitoring system (e.g., Nagios, Zabbix) monitors the basic health of the administration tools via ping and SNMP. In case of a failure or high load, an email is sent to the responsible team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the monitoring checks for the administration tools and the associated alerting rules in the monitoring system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For IT administration tools, key figures for availability SHOULD be identified. These key figures SHOULD be continuously monitored. Tolerable limit values for these key figures SHOULD be defined. If these are not met, the responsible teams SHOULD be automatically notified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Comprehensive Application Performance Monitoring (APM) is used for all critical administration tools. Not only system metrics but also application-specific transactions (e.g., 'login time', 'number of managed sessions') and their response times are monitored. The thresholds are defined based on Service Level Objectives (SLOs). Alerting is automated and integrated into the ticketing system to automatically create an incident in case of a disruption.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the APM system and the defined key figures and SLOs. They check the historical performance data and the triggered alerts to assess the effectiveness of the monitoring and compliance with service levels.

controls.title: Security monitoring of administrative activities (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logs of administrative activities are sent to a central log management system. There, rule-based searches are performed to identify known suspicious activities (e.g., multiple failed login attempts).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a SIEM or log management system, basic correlation rules are defined for administrative logs. For example, an alert is triggered if an administrator account logs in from two different geographical locations within a short period of time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the configuration of the correlation rules for administrative events in the SIEM. They check whether alerts have been triggered and appropriately handled in the past.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If an IT system is used for central detection and automated real-time verification of event messages, event data on administrative activities SHOULD be evaluated there. For this purpose, existing IT monitoring systems and critical administration tools SHOULD be integrated into this IT system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An advanced SIEM system with User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) functions is used. All administrative logs, including recordings from the PAM system, are analyzed in real time. The system learns the normal behavior of each administrator and alerts on significant deviations (anomalies), even if they do not match any known rule. Critical alerts lead to the automatic blocking of the affected account.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the UEBA functions in the SIEM. They request to see the learned behavior profiles of administrators. They check the logs of anomaly-based alerts and the subsequent responses, including automatic account lockouts.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
IT administration refers to activities, mainly within IT operations, for which administrative rights are required and which change the configuration of IT components. Administrators not only ensure that the IT components remain available, but also implement information security measures and check whether they are effective.
The activities of administrators include setting up, configuring, checking and modifying an institution's existing IT. This also includes specialized administration, i.e. the IT administration of applications for whose operation the corresponding specialist department is responsible instead of the IT operations organizational unit.
Administrative rights for IT components (i.e. in particular for IT systems, IT services, applications, IT platforms and networks) are privileged rights that can include not only logins but also access over the network and physical access. Therefore, both administrative rights at the organizational level and the administration tools themselves are an attractive target for attackers. The proper and traceable execution of all administrative activities and the protection of the necessary tools are essential for the security of IT administration.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to establish information security as an integral part of proper IT administration. By implementing this module, the institution ensures on the one hand that the IT administration activities required for the security of the information domain are carried out properly and systematically. On the other hand, the institution also reacts to the special threats that inevitably arise from handling privileged rights and from access to areas of the institution that are worthy of protection.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module OPS.1.1.2 Proper IT Administration must be applied once to the entire information network.
To create an IT-Grundschutz model for a specific information network, the entirety of all modules must be considered as a matter of principle. As a rule, several modules are to be applied to the topic or target object.
This module covers
• overarching requirements for the administration process, both for IT operations and in specialized administration,
• requirements for administrative activities, and
• requirements for handling administrative permissions, i.e. privileged physical entry, logins and access.
The following contents are also important and are dealt with elsewhere:
• remote administration of IT systems via external interfaces and remote maintenance of devices and components by the manufacturing or supply companies (see OPS.1.2.5 Remote Maintenance)
• patch and change management (see OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management)
• the protection of administration tools (see NET.1.2 Network Management and OPS.1.1.7 System Management)
• the proper management of users and permissions (see ORP.4 Identity and Authorization Management)
• special requirements in the event that IT administration is carried out by third parties (see OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing and OPS.3.2 Offering Outsourcing)
• aspects for the IT administration of industrial IT (see modules from the IND Industrial IT area)
This module does not cover
• the general aspects of IT operations such as inventory, commissioning and decommissioning of IT components, and the basic framework conditions for administrators (see OPS.1.1.1 General IT Operations)
• briefing of staff on general IT security regulations to be observed (see ORP.3 Information Security Awareness and Training)
• the continuous training of staff and the associated awareness of threats and security measures (see ORP.2 Personnel and ORP.3 Information Security Awareness and Training)

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficiently regulated responsibilities
parts.prose:
IT administration comprises diverse tasks on a wide variety of components in different areas. If there are no regulations on responsibilities or processes, or if the regulations and processes are not known to the responsible parties, this can have various possible consequences. Required administration tasks may not be carried out at all or by the wrong department, which may not be aware of all the details to be considered. It is also possible that counteracting measures are carried out by different departments. This can result in IT systems being available only to a limited extent or not at all.
If it is not taken into account when defining responsibilities that different IT administration activities, e.g. between application operation and system operation, are inseparably linked, related tasks may not be carried out properly.
If administrators are given too many rights because responsibilities are not regulated, they may be able to view confidential information that they are not allowed to see. This is particularly the case if too many administrative accounts with overly extensive rights are set up for convenience, in the worst case even across organizational units.
In addition, an excessive number of administrators can lead to a loss of control if it is not clearly regulated who is responsible for which tasks. In this case, all information security objectives are at risk.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Inadequate documentation
parts.prose:
Documentation can be inadequate if information about IT components (e.g. about configuration or access rights) has not been recorded or has been recorded incompletely. Even if the documentation is not updated as part of IT administration activities, the documentation is inadequate because it no longer corresponds to the actual state.
Inadequate documentation can lead to misconfigurations or generally faulty IT administration. This can significantly jeopardize all information security objectives.
In addition, emergency management can also be considerably impaired because information first has to be collected for time-critical tasks or the tasks cannot be carried out as planned due to the discrepancy between the documentation and the actual state. This can lead to an emergency not being dealt with quickly enough and the availability of IT components being impaired for longer.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Misuse of privileged permissions by administrators
parts.prose:
Overly broad administrative permissions can be used for sabotage or to spy on information that can be used as a starting point for attacks. This jeopardizes all information security objectives.
Privileged physical entry, logins and access can also be misused if the processes for the departure of internal or external administrators are inadequate and departing personnel can therefore continue to access IT components. In this case, too, all information security objectives are at risk.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Disclosure of sensitive information to unauthorized persons
parts.prose: IT administration access can be used to access sensitive information, e.g., documentation required for IT administration or the configurations of IT systems. If IT administration access is inadequately secured, unauthorized persons can also gain access to sensitive information. Beyond the loss of confidentiality, this information can also be manipulated or used for further attacks, which significantly jeopardizes all information security objectives.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Staff shortage of core competence holders
parts.prose:
If the necessary knowledge is not redundantly available among administrators in all areas, a corresponding IT administration activity could not be carried out if key competency holders are unavailable. If, in addition, the documentation for the work steps to be carried out is inadequate, the IT administration activity cannot be carried out by other administrators without further risks. This can lead to malfunctions not being rectified. As a result, the availability of IT systems is not (sufficiently) guaranteed and vulnerabilities cannot be rectified, which facilitates attacks.
This situation can also arise if there are no designated deputies with a corresponding level of authorization for IT administration activities or if designated deputies or even the emergency access do not have the required administrative permissions.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Insufficient availability of administrators
parts.prose:
If there is a shortage of administrative staff, e.g. due to inadequate personnel planning, overbooking or a pandemic, required administrative tasks may not be performed if there is no time. Under certain circumstances, mistakes may also be made in IT administration due to lack of time. Both can lead to insufficient availability of IT systems or to an increased attack surface and thus to the endangerment of all information security objectives.
Staff shortages can also result in administrators being inadequately trained for their tasks due to a lack of time, which can also lead to certain IT administration activities not being carried out correctly in case of need or in an emergency.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Inadequate securing of administration tools
parts.prose:
Administration tools provide extensive access to an institution's IT. If these tools are inadequately secured, it can lead to the administration tools themselves being compromised in terms of all information security objectives. They can be used to sabotage IT administration or to enable unauthorized IT administration.
If access to administration tools is gained during an attack, extensive permissions can be obtained. These permissions can be abused for all types of attacks, which also compromises all information security objectives.
One cause for the inadequate security of administration tools can be, for example, their insufficient separation from other applications. This insufficient separation is possible at all levels. It can arise, for example, from using text editors or SSH clients for IT administration that are also used in a non-administrative context.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Failure of the administration option
parts.prose:
If administration capabilities fail and there is no redundancy or other alternatives due to poor planning, IT administration activities of this kind cannot be performed until the failure is resolved. In the worst case, this can result in the entire IT being restricted or unavailable/non-functional.
Administration tools can also fail due to the administration of the tool itself, e.g., through misconfiguration, an applied patch, or a change introduced by an IT administration activity.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Misguided administration
parts.prose: If the IT administration is misguided, for example, by introducing false information, the IT administration can be induced to react incorrectly. For example, administrators can be falsely informed outside of the regulated process that an IT system has failed, which prompts them to restart it. In this way, information, hardware, or software can be manipulated, whereby their availability and integrity are no longer guaranteed. In addition, sensitive information can also be disclosed in this way.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.10. Faulty administration
parts.prose:
Human errors can never be ruled out and can have far-reaching consequences in IT administration. Additionally, they are exacerbated by some of the previously mentioned threats.
The tools used in IT administration allow for very extensive changes to IT components with little effort. Depending on the error, all information security objectives can be significantly compromised. Errors are particularly encouraged by working on different topics in parallel, where, for example, different input windows or console outputs can be confused.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.11. Disruption of IT by IT administration activities
parts.prose: Even if IT administration activities are carried out without errors, the institution's IT can still be disrupted. For example, if specified maintenance windows for IT administration activities are not adhered to, the availability of the administered IT can be disrupted. In addition, IT administration activities carried out correctly within the maintenance window can also lead to disruptions later on, for example, if the administrability of the corresponding components is impaired by unforeseen interactions.

controls.title: Concept for Patch and Change Management (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are isolated, informal instructions on how to handle patches, but they mainly focus on reacting to incidents that have already occurred. A comprehensive, proactive concept for changes is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instructions are often communicated only verbally or by email for specific emergencies. There is no central documentation or standardized process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews with administrators, the auditor determines that there is no formal, documented strategy for patch and change management. The review of change tickets (if any) shows a lack of consistent planning and approval.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic concept for patch management exists and is documented. It describes the planning and implementation of patches. However, aspects of general change management as well as formal approval and fallback procedures are only superficially covered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document describes the process for regular security patches (e.g., on Patch Day). However, changes to configurations or applications are still handled on an ad hoc basis. Fallback plans are limited to the instruction 'to have a backup'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing patch management document. In the sample check of changes, it is found that while patches are planned, other changes and the associated approvals and fallback plans are not consistently documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When IT components, software, or configuration data are changed, there MUST be requirements for this that also consider security aspects. These MUST be recorded and followed in a concept for patch and change management. All patches and changes MUST be appropriately planned, approved, and documented. When patches are installed and changes are made, fallback solutions MUST be available. For major changes, the ISO MUST also be involved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal document 'Concept for Patch and Change Management' is created, approved by management, and made available to all relevant employees. Changes are requested via a ticket system and go through a defined approval workflow. A fallback plan must exist for every change.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the concept for patch and change management and checks its completeness and approval. Using a sample of recently implemented changes, it is verified whether the planning, approval, documentation, and fallback plan have been implemented in accordance with the concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the defined concept, patches and changes SHOULD be adequately tested in a representative test environment beforehand. It is ensured that the target security level is maintained during and after the changes. In particular, the desired security settings SHOULD also be retained and their configuration verified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate test environment that mirrors the production environment is established. Before a change is released, a successful test run must be logged in this environment. Configuration management tools are used to check compliance with security baselines before and after a change.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and use of a test environment. For a sample of changes, the test logs are checked. A technical audit is used to verify that configuration changes have not negatively affected the security settings (e.g., through a configuration scan).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire patch and change management process is largely automated and integrated into the ISMS. The concept is regularly reviewed and improved based on key figures and audits. Automated tests and configuration checks are an integral part of every change workflow to ensure continuous compliance with security policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ITSM tool controls the entire workflow from request to documentation. CI/CD pipelines are used for software changes, which include automated security, configuration, and functional tests. A failure of the tests automatically prevents deployment. The effectiveness of the process is measured by SLAs and KPIs (e.g., 'Time-to-Patch').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the ITSM tool and the automation pipelines. Dashboard evaluations of KPIs and SLAs are reviewed. The auditor verifies that a faulty change in testing is automatically stopped and not rolled out to production.

controls.title: Definition of Responsibilities (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal responsibility for installing patches, which usually lies with one or a few central administrators. Responsibilities for approving changes or coordinating with business departments are not defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator decides independently which patches are to be installed. Business departments are not informed or are only informed sporadically.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines in interviews that there is no documented assignment of responsibilities and that decisions are made by individuals without a defined process or coordination.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The responsibility for the technical implementation of patches and changes is defined and documented for IT operations. However, the responsibility for the business approval by the business departments is still unclear.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: It is clear within the IT department who implements patches and changes. However, approval is often given by the IT manager without formal involvement of the affected business department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds documented responsibility within the IT team. However, when reviewing change tickets, it becomes clear that business approvals are missing or were not granted by the responsible business managers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities for patch and change management MUST be defined for all organizational areas. This includes both technical implementation and business responsibility. The defined responsibilities MUST also be reflected in the authorization concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of responsible persons (e.g., change manager, technical implementers, business owners per application/system) is created and maintained. The corresponding permissions for approving or implementing changes are set up in the ticket system and on the target systems according to the authorization concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of responsibilities. They compare the defined responsibilities with the rights stored in the ticket system and in the system permissions for a sample of employees. It is checked whether changes were only approved and implemented by the defined responsible persons.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined responsibilities also include defined deputy regulations to ensure the ability to act at all times. The responsibilities are reviewed regularly, at least once a year, for their timeliness and adjusted if necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The list of responsible persons is extended to include a column for deputies. The corresponding permissions are also set up for the deputies. An annual review process is scheduled in the calendar of the process owner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the list of responsibilities and checks whether deputies have been appointed. They request proof of the last annual review of responsibilities (e.g., meeting minutes or a confirmed review ticket).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities are detailed in a comprehensive RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) for all aspects of patch and change management. The assignment of responsibilities and the associated permissions are managed automatically based on information from an HR system and a CMDB.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A RACI matrix is created as part of the concept for patch and change management. The synchronization of roles and permissions in the ITSM tool is linked to the HR system (for personnel changes) and the CMDB (for system responsibility).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the RACI matrix for completeness and logic. They have the automated process for managing permissions demonstrated and verify its correct function by simulating a personnel change (e.g., a change of department).

controls.title: Configuration of autoupdate mechanisms (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Autoupdate mechanisms are activated or deactivated on individual systems on an ad hoc basis, depending on the default setting of the software or at the discretion of the administrator. There is no uniform strategy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The autoupdate of the web browser is active on some workstations, while it is mostly deactivated on servers. There is no deliberate, documented decision.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through a random check on various systems that the configuration of autoupdate mechanisms is inconsistent and that there is no underlying rule or documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic, company-wide rule for handling autoupdate mechanisms (e.g., 'all autoupdates are to be deactivated'), but it is not differentiated or aimed at a secure configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple policy states that all autoupdate functions should be deactivated to maintain control. However, this is done manually and is not checked, which leads to inconsistencies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing policy. However, a technical check shows that the rule is not consistently implemented on all systems and that no measures have been taken to secure the mechanisms (if they are active).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The patch and change management strategy MUST define how to handle integrated update mechanisms (autoupdate) of the software in use. In particular, it MUST be specified how these mechanisms are to be secured and appropriately configured if they are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate chapter on autoupdates is added to the concept for patch and change management. It specifies for which software classes (e.g., browsers, operating systems) autoupdates are permitted and how they are to be configured (e.g., only download updates, but do not install). Implementation is carried out centrally via GPOs or an MDM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the corresponding section in the concept. They then verify by inspecting the GPO/MDM configuration that the defined rules for autoupdate mechanisms are technically implemented and enforced.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The handling of autoupdate mechanisms is systematically checked and evaluated when introducing new software or components. The defined configuration of the autoupdate mechanisms is regularly checked for compliance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The software introduction process is extended to include an 'autoupdate behavior' checkpoint. Regular configuration scans (compliance scans) check whether the autoupdate settings on all systems comply with the policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the software introduction process. They review the results of the last compliance scans to verify continuous compliance with the autoupdate policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The strategy for autoupdates is differentiated according to the criticality of the systems and the trustworthiness of the source. For critical systems, updates via autoupdate mechanisms are only downloaded to an internal test repository and centrally approved after testing. The integrity of the communication of the autoupdate clients is actively monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system like WSUS or a comparable third-party tool is used to manage updates centrally. Autoupdates on the clients are configured to only retrieve updates from this internal server. Network firewall rules prevent clients from communicating directly with external update servers. Deviations trigger an alarm in the SIEM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the central update server (e.g., WSUS) and the corresponding client configurations (GPOs). They verify the firewall rules that prevent direct communication with external update servers. It is checked whether failed or unauthorized update attempts are logged in the SIEM.

controls.title: Regular updating of IT systems and software (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Updates are applied irregularly and mostly only reactively when problems occur. A systematic evaluation or prioritization of patches does not take place. There are systems whose support has expired.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators install patches when they have time or a user reports a problem. There is no inventory list that tracks the support status of products.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines, through a network scan or a manual check of systems, that many devices are missing critical patches and that software with expired manufacturer support is in use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a fixed rhythm for installing patches (e.g., monthly Patch Day). All available patches are installed in this process, but without a thorough assessment of their relevance or urgency. The handling of unsupported software is not regulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every second Wednesday of the month, the patches provided by Microsoft are distributed to the Windows systems. A prioritization based on CVSS scores or documentation of the decision does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the patch rhythm. However, they find that there is no documentation on the evaluation and prioritization of patches. The decision not to apply a patch is not justified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the patch and change management concept, patches MUST be evaluated promptly after release and prioritized according to their criticality. A decision MUST be made on whether to install the patch. If a patch is not installed, the decision and the reasons for it MUST be documented. If hardware or software products are used that are no longer supported by the manufacturer, it MUST be checked whether they can still be operated securely. If this is not the case, these products MUST NOT be used anymore.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process is established in which all new patches are evaluated based on sources such as manufacturer information, CVSS score, and internal criticality ratings. The decision is documented in a ticket system. An inventory list is maintained that contains the support end date for all products. A formal risk assessment is carried out for products after their end of support.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the change tickets for recently released patches and checks the documented evaluation and prioritization. They request the inventory list and check the process for handling obsolete software using a specific example.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In principle, patches SHOULD be installed promptly after release, especially those that fix known vulnerabilities. After installation, it SHOULD be checked whether the patch has been installed promptly and successfully on all relevant systems. Distribution tools that provide a success status are used for this purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Service Level Objectives (SLOs) are defined for fixing vulnerabilities of different criticality levels (e.g., critical vulnerabilities within 7 days). A central patch management tool is used that generates detailed reports on the installation status on all clients. Failed installations are automatically retried and escalated to an administrator after several failed attempts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the defined SLOs. They review the reports from the patch management tool to verify compliance with the deadlines and the success rate of installations for a sample of critical patches. They check the escalation process for failed installations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire vulnerability and patch management process is automated. This includes subscribing to threat intelligence feeds, automatic reconciliation with the CMDB, risk assessment, creation of change requests, and deployment. Unsupported software is automatically detected, and the affected systems are isolated until a solution is found.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A vulnerability management tool is integrated with the patch management system and the ticketing system. Detected vulnerabilities automatically trigger workflows. For systems with end-of-life software, network isolation rules are automatically activated via a Network Access Control (NAC) system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the automated workflow from the detection of a vulnerability to the deployment of the patch demonstrated. They check the configuration of the NAC system and verify that a test device with outdated software is correctly isolated. They can validate this on a test device using `nmap --script vulners <host>` followed by `sudo arpspoof`.

controls.title: Handling of Change Requests (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Change requests are communicated informally via email or orally. There is no central recording or documentation, and a security review is not planned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A user directly asks an administrator to change a configuration. The administrator does this without a ticket and without a formal review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and analysis of system logs that changes have been made for which there are no documented requests or approvals.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All Requests for Changes (RfCs) are recorded in a ticketing system. However, a formal check for security aspects by subject matter experts only takes place sporadically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A ticket is created for every change. However, approval is often given as a blanket approval by the supervisor, without a security expert or the subject matter expert checking the details.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the ticketing system and confirms that RfCs are being recorded. However, a sample of the tickets shows that documented security reviews are missing in most cases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All Requests for Changes (RfCs) SHOULD be recorded and documented. The change requests SHOULD be checked by the respective subject matter experts for patch and change management to determine whether information security aspects have been sufficiently considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized form for RfCs is introduced in the ticketing system, which also includes fields for describing the security implications. Each RfC is assigned to a defined subject matter expert who must check the security aspects and document their approval before implementation can begin.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks a sample of RfCs in the ticketing system. They verify that the requests are documented in a standardized way and that a traceable check and approval by the designated subject matter expert has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The check of security aspects is supported by a standardized checklist to ensure a consistent and traceable review. For high-risk changes, the Information Security Officer (ISO) is mandatorily involved in the approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A security assessment checklist is integrated into the RfC form in the ticketing system. A workflow automatically routes RfCs classified as 'high risk' to the ISO for approval.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the security assessment checklist. For an RfC classified as high-risk, they check whether the ISO has demonstrably reviewed and approved the change.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The collection and categorization of change requests is largely automated. The check of security aspects is supported by automated analyses that detect and flag potential policy violations or security risks (e.g., opening of insecure ports) at the time of the request.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ITSM tool is integrated with a configuration management and a security policy system. If an RfC requests a change to a firewall rule that violates the security policy, the request is automatically blocked or flagged with a warning and escalated for manual review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the automated analysis process demonstrated. They create a test RfC that requests a known insecure configuration and verify that the system correctly classifies the request as risky and triggers the defined escalation path.

controls.title: Coordination of Change Requests (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Changes are coordinated within the IT team, but affected business departments or end users are not informed or are only informed after implementation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The server team informs the network team about a planned change, but the business department whose application is affected is not told.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds through interviews with business department heads that they are regularly surprised by IT changes that affect their processes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Affected target groups are informed about planned changes, but there is no formal process through which they can provide verifiable feedback or raise objections.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An email about a planned change is sent to a large distribution list. It is assumed that no response means consent.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor sees evidence of informing the target groups (e.g., emails) but cannot find any proof of a structured feedback or approval process by these groups.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The coordination process associated with a change SHOULD consider all relevant target groups and the impact on information security. The target groups affected by the change SHOULD be able to comment on it in a verifiable manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each change, the affected stakeholders (e.g., application owners, department heads, end-user groups) are identified. They are asked for their comments and approval via the ticketing system. Their consent is documented in the ticket before the change is implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In a sample of changes, the auditor checks whether the relevant target groups were correctly identified and whether their verifiable consent is available in the ticketing system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For coordinating changes with significant impact, a Change Advisory Board (CAB) is convened, in which all relevant stakeholders are represented. In addition, there SHOULD be a defined procedure for accelerating the handling of important change requests (emergency changes), e.g., through an Emergency CAB (eCAB).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Regular CAB meetings are held for standard changes. A separate, fast-track process for emergency changes is defined, which allows for approval by a small, predefined group of decision-makers (eCAB).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the CAB meetings. They check the process for emergency changes and verify that it was only used for actual emergencies and that subsequent documentation and review in the regular CAB has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The identification of relevant target groups and stakeholders for a change is automated based on a comprehensive and up-to-date Configuration Management Database (CMDB) that maps dependencies between IT services, applications, and business processes. The coordination is supported by collaborative tools.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a change is requested for a server, the ITSM tool automatically determines via the CMDB which applications are running on the server and which business processes they support. The responsible application and process owners are then automatically included in the approval workflow.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the quality and currency of the CMDB. They have it demonstrated how, for a test RfC for a critical component (e.g., a central database server), the correct stakeholders are automatically identified and notified.

controls.title: Integration of Change Management into Business Processes (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT changes are planned purely from a technical perspective, without considering business cycles such as month-end closings or important production phases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A critical update for the ERP system is installed on the last working day of the month, which leads to disruptions in the accounting department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews with business departments and analysis of incident reports, the auditor identifies cases where IT changes have led to foreseeable conflicts with business processes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal agreement with the business departments about the timing of changes. However, a systematic process for considering the current business situation is lacking.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT administrator calls the controlling department and asks if it is okay to perform an update 'next week'. A shared calendar or formal maintenance windows do not exist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor sees notes in change tickets like 'spoke with department' but finds no systematic planning or formal approval of the timing by the business process owners.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The change management process SHOULD be integrated into the business processes or functional tasks. For planned changes, the current situation of the affected business processes SHOULD be considered. All relevant business departments SHOULD be informed about upcoming changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central calendar for maintenance windows and 'change freezes' (e.g., during the year-end closing) is introduced and maintained. When planning any change, the timing must be coordinated with this calendar and the affected business department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the calendar for maintenance windows and change freezes. For a sample of changes, they check whether the chosen timing was determined in accordance with the specifications and in coordination with the business department.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There SHOULD be an escalation level whose members belong to the management level of the institution. In cases of doubt, these members SHOULD be able to decide on the priority and scheduling of a hardware or software change, especially if there are conflicts between IT requirements and business processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Change Advisory Board (CAB) is designated as the formal escalation body. If IT and the business department cannot agree on a date, the CAB decides. The members of the CAB include representatives from IT and business department management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the composition and mandate of the CAB. They review minutes to verify how conflicts in scheduling have been handled in the past.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of changes is fully integrated into the strategic and operational planning of the business units. The impact of changes on business process KPIs is assessed in advance and is part of the decision-making basis. Communication is automated and tailored to the respective target groups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ITSM tool is linked to the business process management systems. A 'Forward Schedule of Change' (FSC) is published and is visible to everyone. The assessment of an RfC includes a formal Business Impact Analysis (BIA).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the Business Impact Analysis process for changes. They verify the existence and use of the Forward Schedule of Change and check how the impact on business KPIs was assessed in a specific change case.

controls.title: Secure Use of Patch and Change Management Tools (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Various scripts and tools are used ad hoc to distribute patches and changes. No security review or uniform configuration of these tools is performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator uses a self-written PowerShell script to distribute software. The passwords contained in the script are in clear text.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and system analysis that no standardized tools are used and the scripts and tools used have fundamental security deficiencies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central tool for patch management is used. However, there are no formal requirements for its selection or a specific policy for its secure configuration and use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A WSUS server is used to distribute Windows updates. However, it is operated with the default settings, and access to it is not particularly restricted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the use of a central tool. However, they find that no documentation on requirements definition or a hardening policy for this tool exists. A review of the configuration shows insecure settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Requirements and framework conditions SHOULD be defined according to which tools for patch and change management are selected. In addition, a specific security policy SHOULD be created for the tools used, which describes their hardening and secure use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before purchasing a management tool, a requirements catalog is created that also queries security features. A hardening guide is created and implemented for the selected tool (e.g., SCCM/MECM). This regulates, for example, access, securing communication, and logging.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the requirements catalog and the security policy for the tool used. They check the configuration of the tool and the associated servers on a random basis against the specifications of the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the tools used is regularly checked for compliance with the security policy (compliance scan). Access to the tools is strictly controlled according to the principle of least privilege and via role concepts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Automated configuration scans (e.g., using DSC - Desired State Configuration) are used to detect and report deviations from the hardening policy. Specific administrator roles (e.g., 'Patch-Deployer', 'Software-Packager') with different permissions are defined in the management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the results of the last compliance scans for the management infrastructure. They check the role concept and verify that administrators only have the permissions necessary for their tasks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The tools for patch and change management and their infrastructure are themselves integrated into the complete security management process. This includes that they are regularly patched themselves and their integrity is continuously monitored. All administrative accesses and actions in the tools are forwarded to a central SIEM system for monitoring and anomaly detection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The servers of the management infrastructure are treated as Tier-0 systems and protected with the highest security precautions. The configuration integrity of the servers and the management software is monitored using File Integrity Monitoring (FIM). Detailed audit logs are sent to the SIEM, where special rules check for suspicious activities (e.g., rolling out an unapproved package).
