parts.prose: An XDR platform collects and analyzes data from EDR agents, network sensors, and cloud APIs. The SOC team uses this platform to conduct hypothesis-based threat hunting (e.g., 'Search for all Powershell processes that establish network connections'). The results of the BAS tests are used to identify gaps in detection and to improve the configuration of the XDR solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the XDR platform and the configuration of the connected data sources. Examples of conducted threat hunting searches and their results are demonstrated. The reports from the BAS tool and the improvement measures derived from them are reviewed.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: Malware is software that usually executes malicious functions on an IT system without the user's knowledge and consent. These malicious functions can cover a wide field, ranging from espionage to extortion (so-called ransomware) to sabotage and destruction of information or even devices. Malware can basically be executed on all operating systems and IT systems. In addition to classic IT systems such as clients and servers, this also includes mobile devices such as smartphones. Network components such as routers, industrial control systems and even IoT devices such as networked cameras are also often at risk from malware today. Malware on classic IT systems usually spreads via email attachments, manipulated websites (drive-by downloads) or data carriers. Smartphones are usually infected by installing malicious apps, and drive-by downloads are also possible. In addition, open network interfaces, incorrect configurations and software vulnerabilities are common gateways on all IT systems. In this module, the term 'antivirus program' is used. 'Viruses' is used as a synonym for all types of malware. 'Antivirus program' therefore means a program to protect against any type of malware.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module describes requirements that must be met and implemented in order to effectively protect an institution against malware.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module OPS.1.1.4 Protection against Malware must be applied once to the information network.
This module describes the general requirements for protection against malware. Specific requirements for protecting certain IT systems of the institution from malware can be found, if necessary, in the respective modules of the SYS IT Systems layer. If an identified malware leads to a security incident, the requirements of module DER.2.1 Handling of Security Incidents should be taken into account. The requirements of module DER.2.3 Cleanup of Major Security Incidents help to remove identified malware and restore a clean state.
The anti-virus programs used within the scope of this module should also be considered in patch and change management (OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management). Furthermore, the topic of protection against malware should also be taken into account within the scope of module ORP.3 Information Security Awareness and Training and CON.3 Data Backup Concept.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Software vulnerabilities and drive-by downloads
parts.prose: If IT systems are not adequately protected against malware, software vulnerabilities can be exploited in attacks to execute malicious code. This can happen, among other things, if patches are not applied promptly and protection mechanisms of application programs, such as browsers, are not configured correctly. In the case of so-called drive-by downloads, for example, it is sufficient to visit a website laden with malicious code. A vulnerability in the browser or in an installed plug-in, such as Java or Adobe Flash, can then be exploited to infect the IT system and give attackers extensive control and access to an institution's network. IT systems that are not updated regularly, such as many smartphones, are particularly at risk here.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Extortion by Ransomware
parts.prose: A widespread type of malware is so-called ransomware. It encrypts the data of the infected IT system and often also other data that is accessible via network shares, for example. As a rule, the attackers use encryption methods that cannot be reversed without knowledge of the key, and use this to extort large sums of money from their victims. If there is no effective protection against malware and no additional precautions, such as data backups, have been taken, the availability of information can be severely restricted, data can be lost, and massive financial and reputational damage can occur.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Targeted attacks and social engineering
parts.prose: Institutions are often attacked with custom-made malware. For example, executives are tricked into opening malicious email attachments using social engineering methods. Custom-made malware can also often not be detected immediately by anti-virus programs. An institution's HR department can also be a target, for example, by sending job applications infected with malware electronically. If the attackers have managed to infect an IT system in this way, they can spread within the institution and, for example, view, manipulate, or destroy information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Botnets
parts.prose: Through malware, an institution's IT systems can become part of so-called botnets. Attackers, who often control thousands of systems in such a botnet, can use them, for example, to send spam or launch distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks on third parties. Even if one's own institution may not be immediately harmed, this can still have a negative impact on the availability and integrity of one's own services and IT systems and can even lead to legal problems. For example, if an institution's email server gets on a blocklist, it may no longer be possible to send and receive emails.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Infection of production systems and IoT devices
parts.prose: In addition to classic IT systems, devices that do not look like obvious targets at first glance are also increasingly being attacked by malware. In an attack, for example, a surveillance camera accessible via the Internet could be infected to spy on the institution. But a networked light bulb or a coffee machine with app control can also serve as an entry point into the institution's network or as part of a botnet if these devices are not adequately protected against malware. Networked production systems or industrial controls can also be manipulated or even destroyed by malware, which can lead to failures and many other hazards for the institution and its employees, e.g. through fires.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for logging (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are only isolated, informal instructions for logging on critical systems. A formal, overarching security policy for logging is missing, which leads to inconsistent and incomplete logging in the information network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In practice, this means that individual administrators configure logging settings at their own discretion. These are not documented centrally anywhere and vary greatly between systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with various administrators that there is no uniform procedure for logging. A random check of system configurations confirms the inconsistent and often inadequate settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic policy on logging is available, often as part of a general IT security policy. It contains general statements on the necessity of logging but does not define specific details such as events to be logged, retention periods, or responsible roles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a document that mandates logging, but it lacks concrete instructions for the administrators. The implementation is therefore often based on the default settings of the respective systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the general IT security policy and finds the section on logging. However, upon reviewing the implementation, it is found that the specific configurations cannot be derived from the policy and show no evidence of uniform planning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the institution's general security policy, a specific security policy for logging MUST be created. This security policy MUST clearly describe requirements and specifications on how, where, and what to log. The policy MUST be created by the ISO together with the responsible department heads, be communicated to all relevant employees, and be regularly checked for correct implementation. Changes to or deviations from the policy MUST be coordinated with the ISO and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The specific logging policy is published as a separate, controlled document in the ISMS tool or on the intranet. It contains concrete tables that define which event classes (e.g., login, configuration change, error) are to be logged per system type and for how long the logs must be retained. The responsibilities for implementation and control are clearly named.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the specific security policy for logging and checks its content for completeness and comprehensibility. It is verified that the policy has been approved by the relevant roles (ISO, department heads). Interviews with administrators ensure that the policy is known and serves as a working basis. The documentation of the last reviews of the policy implementation is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined logging policy is supplemented by further specifications. The type and scope of logging are clearly based on the protection needs of the respective information and IT systems. The policy is integrated into the formal ISMS review process and is reviewed regularly, at least annually, and adapted if necessary. The results of the review are tracked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy contains a matrix that links protection requirement categories (e.g., normal, high) with specific logging levels (e.g., standard, verbose). The review of the policy is created and scheduled as a recurring task in the organization's GRC tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the logging requirements for a system with a high protection need with those for a system with a normal protection need and verifies that the requirements in the policy are appropriate for the protection need. The minutes of the last ISMS management reviews are inspected to understand the formal review process of the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logging policy is a dynamic document that adapts to new threats and technologies. Changes in the IT landscape or new findings from threat analysis lead to an automated review and adaptation workflow. Compliance with the policy is continuously monitored through automated configuration and compliance scans.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 'Policy as Code' approach is used. The logging policy is stored in a machine-readable format (e.g., YAML) in a Git repository. Changes go through a review and approval process. Automated scripts (e.g., via Ansible or DSC) implement the policy on the target systems and continuously check for compliance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the 'Policy as Code' workflow, including the commit history and approval steps. The dashboard of the automated compliance tool is reviewed to assess the current compliance status of the information network in real time. The response to automatically detected deviations is examined.

controls.title: Configuration of logging at system and network level (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging is only enabled on a few systems classified as particularly critical. The configuration usually corresponds to the manufacturer's default settings. A functionality check is only performed on an ad-hoc basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, an administrator enables the Security Event Log on the domain controller, but on most other servers and clients, logging remains in its default state or is disabled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a sample of 10 servers and finds that an advanced logging configuration has been implemented on only 2 of them. On the remaining systems, the log files are empty or contain only minimal information.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A logging function is enabled on most IT systems and applications. However, the configuration is not specifically adapted to the organization's requirements but uses general profiles. Functionality is checked manually at irregular intervals.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Group Policy Object is used to enable a basic audit policy on all Windows servers. However, there is no comparable central specification for Linux systems or network components.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that logging data is being collected on a majority of the systems. However, a deeper analysis shows that important security-relevant events (e.g., detailed process creation) are not being captured because only the basic configuration is active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All security-relevant events from IT systems and applications defined as relevant in the logging policy MUST be logged. If a logging function is available, it MUST be used. The manufacturer's specifications MUST be observed. At appropriate intervals defined in the policy, random checks MUST be carried out to verify that logging is still functioning correctly. If a system cannot log events, additional IT systems (e.g., for logging network events) MUST be integrated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logging configuration is carried out systematically based on the specifications from the logging policy. Documented standard configurations exist for the most important system types (Windows, Linux, firewalls). The regular check is performed using a checklist, and the results are recorded. To ensure logging for a system without its own log function, the network traffic of this system is routed via a port mirror to a Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS), which logs the events.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a system, compares its logging configuration with the policy specifications, and verifies compliance. The logs of the last functional tests are inspected. It is checked whether compensation measures such as network logging have been implemented for systems without native logging. Automatic check: `auditctl -l` on Linux systems or `Get-AuditPolicy` in PowerShell on Windows systems can be used to check the audit rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logging configuration on all systems is centrally managed and enforced via configuration management tools. The functional check of the logging is automated and performed daily. The results are collected centrally, and deviations trigger an alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Playbooks in Ansible or manifests in Puppet define the exact logging configuration for each system type. A central script connects to all systems daily, checks if the logging service is running and if new log entries have been generated in the last hour, and reports the result to a monitoring system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the playbooks of the configuration management system and verifies that they implement the policy's specifications. The dashboard of the monitoring system is viewed to check the results of the automated functional tests of the last 30 days.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logging configuration is managed as 'Policy as Code'. Any deviation from the defined baseline is not only alerted, but leads to an automatic correction (self-healing). The scope of logging is dynamically adjusted: upon detection of suspicious activity on a system, its logging level is automatically raised to 'verbose' to gather more detailed data for analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Puppet or Chef are operated in enforcing mode to immediately correct configuration drift. A SOAR platform receives alarms from the SIEM and, for certain events (e.g., multiple failed logins), automatically executes a playbook that tightens the audit configuration on the affected system via an API call.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor triggers a configuration change on a system as a test and observes how the configuration management system automatically reverts the change within a few minutes. A simulated attack is launched to verify that the logging scope on the target system is dynamically increased as expected.

controls.title: Time synchronization of IT systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Time synchronization is only set up manually on a few central servers, such as domain controllers. There is no company-wide strategy or monitoring, which leads to significant time discrepancies between different systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When installing a server, the time is set manually once. The configuration of an NTP client is often forgotten. The date and time format in log files varies depending on the operating system and application.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the system time of a sample of systems with a reference time and finds significant deviations. When comparing log files from two different systems concerning the same event, the timestamps are not correlatable.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Most IT systems are configured to get their time from an internal or external time source. However, there is no central monitoring of the synchronization status, and the time format in log files is not strictly standardized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Windows clients get their time from the domain controller by default. Other systems (Linux, network components) are manually configured to use a public NTP server. There is no dedicated internal NTP service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that most systems have an NTP client configuration. However, a query of the synchronization status (`w32tm /query /status` or `ntpq -p`) on sample systems shows that some systems have not had a successful synchronization for a long time.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system time of all logging IT systems and applications MUST always be synchronized. It MUST be ensured that the date and time format of the log files is uniform. For this purpose, a reliable, central time source is used for the entire information network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two dedicated internal servers are configured as NTP servers (Stratum 2), which get their time from a trusted external source (e.g., PTB). All systems in the network are configured via configuration management (e.g., GPO for Windows, Ansible for Linux) to use only these internal NTP servers. The default time format for all logs is set to ISO 8601 (e.g., `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ`) in the logging policy and enforced during log forwarding configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the central NTP servers and the NTP client configuration on a representative selection of systems. It is verified that all systems use the correct internal time sources. Log files from different sources are analyzed to confirm the uniformity of the date and time format. Automatic check: A script can be run on all systems to check the NTP configuration (`/etc/ntp.conf`, `w32tm /query /configuration`) and the current synchronization status (`ntpstat`, `w32tm /query /status`) and compare it with the central specification.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The central NTP infrastructure is designed to be redundant. The synchronization status of all clients is actively monitored by a central monitoring system. An alarm is automatically triggered in case of a time deviation of more than one second.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At least two, ideally three, internal NTP servers are operated. The monitoring system (e.g., Nagios, Zabbix) checks the time offset of each client to the reference server every five minutes. If the threshold is exceeded, a ticket is created in the ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the redundancy of the NTP infrastructure. The dashboard of the monitoring system is viewed to analyze the historical time deviation of the clients and to verify the alarm configuration. As a test, the time on a system is manually changed to check the correct triggering of the alarm.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The internal NTP infrastructure uses authenticated NTP to prevent manipulation of time data during transmission. Time synchronization is treated as a critical service, whose availability and accuracy are defined and continuously verified by SLAs. The log ingestion process automatically normalizes timestamps to UTC to eliminate time zone issues.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NTP servers and clients are configured with symmetric keys to authenticate the NTP packets. A log processing pipeline (e.g., Logstash or Fluentd) contains a filter that analyzes each incoming timestamp, converts it to UTC, and stores it in the uniform ISO 8601 format before the log entry is indexed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the NTP authentication keys on the servers and a sample of clients. The configuration of the log processing pipeline is analyzed to confirm the correct normalization of the timestamps. To do this, test logs with different time zones and formats are fed in and the result is checked in the central log database.

controls.title: Compliance with legal frameworks (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general awareness of data protection, but no specific processes related to log data. The deletion of log data is done ad hoc, usually when disk space is running low, without considering retention requirements or privacy rights.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators manually delete old log files from the server when low disk space warnings occur. There is no documentation of these operations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews administrators about the process for deleting log data and finds that there is no formal process. A review of the log servers shows inconsistent retention periods that are not based on legal requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic data deletion concept exists, which also includes log data. However, implementation is manual and not systematic. The legal requirements (e.g., GDPR, co-determination) are known but not fully implemented in technical and organizational measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a policy stating that system logs should be deleted after 90 days. An administrator has a recurring calendar reminder to perform this process manually. The co-determination rights of the employee representation were not formally considered when logging was introduced.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the deletion concept. A check of the log servers shows that the manual deletion is not always performed reliably. It is checked whether documented coordination with the employee representation and the Data Protection Officer exists, which is often not the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When logging, the provisions of current federal and state data protection laws MUST be observed. Any personal or co-determination rights of employee representations MUST be respected. Logging data MUST be deleted according to a defined process that considers legal retention periods and the right to erasure. It MUST be technically prevented that logging data can be deleted or modified in an uncontrolled manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed logging and deletion concept was created and approved in coordination with the Data Protection Officer and the employee representation. This document defines the exact retention period for each data type. Deletion is carried out by automated scripts running on the central log management system. Permissions for the log data are set so restrictively that administrators have no delete or write permissions (see A10).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the logging and deletion concept and checks the documented coordination with the Data Protection Officer and the employee representation. The configuration of the log management system is checked to verify the automated deletion according to the defined periods. An attempt is made to modify or delete a log file as an administrator to test the effectiveness of the protective measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for handling personal data in log files is fully documented and also includes procedures for anonymization or pseudonymization wherever possible and reasonable. The deletion process is not only automated but also logged in an audit-proof manner. Regular, documented reviews with the Data Protection Officer take place to ensure ongoing compliance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the log processing pipeline, filters are used to replace sensitive data such as usernames or IP addresses with a hash value (pseudonymization) or a placeholder (anonymization) before storage, provided the data is not needed for analysis. Each deletion operation of the automated system generates its own log entry, which is stored immutably.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the log processing pipeline to verify the anonymization and pseudonymization rules. The logs of the automated deletion processes are reviewed. The minutes of the regular coordination meetings with the Data Protection Officer are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the legal framework is continuously monitored using automated tools. Data lifecycle management is fully automated and includes classification at creation, application of retention policies, and verifiably secure deletion. Every access to log data, especially data with personal reference, is logged in detail and automatically analyzed for anomalies (e.g., an administrator accessing an unusually large number of log records).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC tool is used to map legal requirements to technical controls and continuously monitor their effectiveness. The log data is archived on WORM (Write-Once, Read-Many) storage to guarantee integrity and compliance with retention periods. A Data Access Governance (DAG) tool monitors and analyzes all access to the log database.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the dashboard of the GRC tool to assess the compliance status. The configuration of the WORM storage is checked. The reports from the DAG tool are analyzed to understand the monitoring of data access. A test access by an authorized user is performed to verify that this access is correctly logged and analyzed.

controls.title: Establishment of a central logging infrastructure (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single server is used as a log collector for a few critical systems. This server is not a dedicated infrastructure, is not located in a secure network segment, and is not sufficiently dimensioned for the amount of data generated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An existing file server is additionally configured as a syslog server to receive the firewall logs. It is not specially hardened or monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies the log collector and determines that it also provides other services. A network analysis shows that the server is in the normal server LAN and is reachable from many other systems. The disk capacity is nearly exhausted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated central log server exists, and most systems send their logs to it. However, the infrastructure is not designed as a fault-tolerant cluster, it may lack sufficient storage, and it is not located in a properly isolated network segment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A single virtual machine is operated as a dedicated log server. All systems are configured to send their logs there. There is no redundancy for the server or the storage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a central log server exists and receives logs from many sources. However, the analysis of the server architecture shows that it is a single point of failure. The firewall rules for the server are checked and assessed as too permissive.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All collected security-relevant logging data SHOULD be stored in a central location. For this, a central logging infrastructure in the form of a log server cluster SHOULD be established and placed in a dedicated, protected network segment. This infrastructure SHOULD also log general operational events. The infrastructure SHOULD be sufficiently dimensioned, consider a scalability option, and be supported by sufficient technical, financial, and personnel resources.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A log server cluster (e.g., based on the Elastic Stack) is set up. The components (Logstash, Elasticsearch, Kibana) run on multiple virtual machines. The infrastructure is located in its own management VLAN, which only administrators and the log-providing systems can access. The storage capacity is designed for 12 months of data growth, and the budget includes funds for an expansion.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture concept of the logging infrastructure. The network and firewall configuration of the dedicated segment is checked. The utilization of CPU, RAM, and storage of the log servers is analyzed to assess sufficient dimensioning. It is checked whether corresponding resources for operation and further development are planned in the budget and personnel planning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The central logging infrastructure is designed as a fault-tolerant cluster (e.g., Elasticsearch, Splunk) in a dedicated, hardened network segment with strict access controls. Capacity and performance are actively monitored, and there are clear plans and processes for scaling.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Elasticsearch cluster consists of at least three master nodes and multiple data nodes to ensure fault tolerance. Capacity monitoring checks disk utilization, indexing rate, and search latency. If disk capacity exceeds 80%, a process to procure more storage is automatically initiated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the cluster configuration and health (`GET /_cluster/health`). The dashboards for capacity and performance monitoring are reviewed. The documented scaling process is checked for plausibility and feasibility.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A highly available, geographically distributed logging infrastructure is implemented. It uses a tiered storage model (Hot, Warm, Cold) to optimize cost and performance. The entire infrastructure is managed via 'Infrastructure as Code', which enables rapid scaling and recovery. Log sources use a preceding, robust message broker to prevent log losses in case of central infrastructure failures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The log cluster is distributed across two data centers. Log data from the last 30 days is kept on fast SSDs (Hot), older data is automatically moved to slower HDDs (Warm) and after 90 days, it's moved to S3-compatible object storage (Cold). The entire environment is described in Terraform code. All systems send their logs to an Apache Kafka cluster, which buffers the data before it is collected by the log ingestion pipeline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the Terraform code to understand the architecture and redundancy. The configuration of the Index Lifecycle Management (ILM) policies for the tiered storage is checked. As a test, a part of the central log processing is stopped to verify that the logs are buffered in the Kafka cluster and are not lost.

controls.title: Archiving of logging data (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Archiving is performed manually and sporadically for some selected log data. There is no clear policy that governs the process or compliance with legal requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator occasionally copies the web server's log files to an external hard drive to free up space on the server. There is no check for the integrity or completeness of the copy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews the administrators about the archiving process and determines that there is no formalized procedure. The analysis of existing archives shows gaps and inconsistencies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a process to move old log data from the central server to more cost-effective long-term storage. This is often done through a manual or semi-automated script.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a month, an administrator runs a script that compresses all log files older than 90 days and moves them to a NAS system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the script and the process documentation. A check of the script's execution logs shows that the process is not always executed successfully or on time.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging data SHOULD be archived. The legally prescribed regulations and retention periods SHOULD be taken into account. The archiving process must be defined and reliable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The central log management system is configured to automatically offload data older than the defined hot/warm phase to a dedicated archive storage (e.g., an S3-compatible object storage). The retention periods are defined per log source in the logging policy and configured in the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the archiving policies in the log management system and compares them with the specifications from the logging policy. A sample of archived data is checked for completeness and compliance with the deadlines. The process for restoring archived data for analysis is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The archiving process is fully automated. Archived logs are indexed to allow for later searchability. Before archiving, integrity checks (e.g., by creating hash values) are performed on the log data, and these checksums are stored securely to allow for later verification.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The log management system (e.g., Elastic Stack with ILM) not only moves the data but also creates searchable snapshots. Before the snapshot is created, a hash value (e.g., SHA-256) is calculated for the data to be archived and stored along with the snapshot in a separate, secure directory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the process for searching in archived data demonstrated. A sample of archived data is restored and its hash value is recalculated. This is compared with the stored hash value to verify integrity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully automated, policy-based data lifecycle management is implemented. Log data is stored on WORM (Write-Once, Read-Many) storage for archiving to guarantee integrity and meet strict legal or forensic requirements. The process for restoring archived data for analysis purposes is fully documented and tested regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The log management system automatically moves data to an S3 bucket for which 'Object Lock' is enabled in compliance mode. This ensures WORM capability. At least once a year, a 'Disaster Recovery' test is conducted in which a simulated security incident requires the restoration and analysis of archived data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the 'Object Lock' configuration on the S3 bucket. An attempt is made to modify or delete an archived file to test the WORM functionality. The logs of the last disaster recovery tests are reviewed to assess the practical suitability of the recovery process.

controls.title: Provision of logging data for evaluation (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Analysts have read access to the raw, unprocessed log files on the central collection server. Each analysis is completely manual and requires the use of command-line tools like `grep` or `awk`.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An analyst connects to the log server via SSH and manually searches the syslog files for a specific IP address. The results are difficult to correlate and interpret.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the process for analyzing a security incident demonstrated and finds that it is completely manual and very time-consuming. There are no tools for visualization or correlation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic log viewer is available that offers simple filtering and search functions over the collected raw data. However, no normalization, aggregation, or correlation of the data takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple web front-end like `lnav` or a Graylog installation without configured extractors is used. Analysts can search for keywords but must interpret the different log formats themselves.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses the log viewer tool and finds that a search for an IP address in the firewall logs returns a different field format than in the Windows Event Logs, which makes correlation difficult.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The collected logging data SHOULD be filtered, normalized, aggregated, and correlated. The processed data SHOULD be made available in a suitable manner for analysis. To enable automated analysis, the logging applications SHOULD have appropriate interfaces for the analysis programs. The original, unmodified data SHOULD also be retained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM solution (e.g., Elastic SIEM, Splunk) is used. For each log source, parsers (extractors) are configured to convert the raw logs into a uniform schema (e.g., Elastic Common Schema). This normalizes fields like `source.ip` or `user.name` across all log sources. The raw logs are archived on separate storage before being processed. The SIEM provides an API through which other tools can access the normalized data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the parsing rules for various important log sources and verifies that they correctly convert the data into the common schema. A test analysis of a cross-cutting incident (e.g., a user clicks on a phishing link, leading to malware execution) is performed in the SIEM to evaluate the correlation capabilities. The availability and documentation of the API are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIEM system is used to automatically normalize, aggregate, and correlate logs from all relevant sources. It has predefined dashboards and alerting rules for common security events. The security requirements observed during evaluation are defined in the logging policy and are taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SIEM is equipped with rule sets for detecting common attack techniques (e.g., based on the MITRE ATT&CK Framework). There are dashboards for monitoring authentication events, network traffic, and endpoint activities. Alerts are automatically generated and sent to the security team's ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the correlation rules and alerts in the SIEM. The effectiveness of the dashboards is evaluated by running through typical analysis scenarios. It is checked whether the access rights to the evaluation functions comply with the policy's specifications.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIEM is enhanced with SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) functions. Data enrichment with threat intelligence, user information, and asset data occurs in real time. Machine learning models (UEBA) are used to detect anomalies and complex attack patterns that rule-based correlations would miss.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When processing a log, the source IP address is automatically checked against multiple threat intelligence feeds. UEBA models create a baseline of normal behavior for each user and system and raise an alarm in case of significant deviations. An 'impossible travel' alert (logins from geographically distant locations in a short period of time) automatically leads to the user account being locked by a SOAR playbook.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the data enrichment and UEBA modules. The effectiveness is tested by simulating an anomaly scenario (e.g., a user accesses sensitive data at an unusual time). The SOAR workflow for automated response is reviewed to ensure its reliability and correctness.

controls.title: Access protection for logging data (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to log files is restricted to the group of administrators, but they have full read, write, and delete permissions. A separation of duties is not implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The log files are located in `/var/log` and are only readable and writable by `root`. All system administrators can log in as `root` and thus have full control over the logs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor logs in with a normal administrator account and verifies that they can modify or delete log files.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic file system permissions are used to make direct modification more difficult (e.g., by setting the 'append-only' attribute). However, a privileged administrator (root) can easily bypass these protective measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrator uses the `chattr +a` command for important log files. This prevents overwriting, but not deletion by the `root` user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the file system attributes (`lsattr`) of the log files. Then, as `root`, it is verified that the attribute can be removed and the file can still be deleted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that the performing administrators who manage the systems do not themselves have permission to modify or delete the recorded logging data. This requires a technical separation of duties.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The log data is sent from the source systems to a central log server. The system administrators do not have login credentials on this log server. The log server itself is managed by a separate, small team of log management administrators. The system administrators can only view the logs of their systems via a web interface (e.g., Kibana) with read-only permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the access permissions on the central log server and verifies that the group of system administrators has no login rights there. The authorization concept of the log management front-end (e.g., Kibana Roles) is analyzed to ensure that system administrators only have read rights to the data relevant to them. A test with a system administrator account is performed to confirm the lack of write/delete permissions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Role-based access control (RBAC) is strictly enforced in the central logging system. All access to log data, including read access, is itself logged (read-access logging) and regularly reviewed on a random basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Different roles (e.g., 'Security Analyst', 'Windows Admin', 'Auditor') with different permissions for data and dashboards are defined in the SIEM. The SIEM is configured to log every search query performed with username and timestamp. Once a week, the security manager reviews the access logs for unusual activities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the RBAC model and its implementation in the SIEM. The access logs (audit logs) of the SIEM itself are requested and checked for completeness and significance. The process for reviewing these logs is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Log data is written to WORM-compliant (Write-Once, Read-Many) storage, which makes subsequent modification technically impossible, even for the most privileged administrator. Access control is managed via a separate, dedicated identity management system with mandatory multi-factor authentication for all users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The log database writes its data blocks to an S3 bucket with 'Object Lock' enabled or to a specialized hardware appliance. Access to the SIEM front end requires login via a central IdP (e.g., Azure AD, Okta) with MFA. Even the log management administrators can no longer change data that has already been written.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the WORM configuration of the storage system by attempting to delete a log file with the highest possible permissions. The login process is tested to confirm the enforcement of MFA. The configuration in the IdP is checked to verify the correct connection of the SIEM application.

controls.title: Increasing Logging Scope (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For applications or IT systems with high protection requirements, more events SHOULD be logged so that security-related incidents can be traced as completely as possible. To be able to evaluate the data in real time, it SHOULD be stored centrally at shorter intervals. Logging SHOULD enable evaluation across the entire information network. Applications and IT systems for which central logging is not possible SHOULD NOT be used if they have high protection requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For servers in the DMZ, the audit policy enables logging of process creation, command line arguments, and network connections. These systems are configured to send their logs immediately (without local buffering) to the central log server. The selection of new systems for the high-security area includes the ability to forward logs via standard protocols such as Syslog or the Elastic Winlogbeat protocol as a hard criterion.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the audit configuration of a high-protection server with that of a standard server and verifies the increased level of detail. The configuration of the log shipper on the high-security server is checked to confirm real-time transmission. The procurement process for new IT systems is analyzed to check whether logging capability is a firm selection criterion.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The scope of logging is increased not only in quantity but also in quality. This includes logging DNS requests, changes to file integrity, and the use of specialized agents (EDR). The log transmission intervals are in the sub-second range (near real-time). The central analysis platform has specific, high-precision detection rules that are tailored to this detailed data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) agent that collects detailed telemetry data is rolled out on all critical servers and endpoints. A File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) tool such as Wazuh or Tripwire monitors critical system files and configurations. The SIEM contains correlation rules that, for example, correlate a suspicious DNS request with the subsequent creation of a process by the same host.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the installation and configuration of the EDR agent and the FIM tool on a high-security system. A test change is made to a monitored file to check the alarm in the SIEM. The specific correlation rules for the detailed endpoint data are analyzed for their logic and effectiveness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging is performed at the highest possible level of detail, e.g., by capturing system calls (syscalls). The log data is streamed in real time and continuously analyzed by automated threat-hunting playbooks. Any system that cannot meet these strict logging requirements is automatically isolated from the high-security network segment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like osquery or eBPF-based agents are used to capture in-depth system activities. The data is fed into a streaming data bus (e.g., Kafka). A downstream analytics platform continuously searches for Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) and attacker Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs). A Network Access Control (NAC) system automatically revokes network connectivity from systems whose logging agent no longer reports.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the syscall capturing agent and the threat-hunting playbooks. A known but harmless TTP is simulated on a test system to verify that the playbook detects it correctly. The logging agent on a test system is stopped to check if the NAC system reacts as expected and isolates the system.

controls.title: Encryption of logging data (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To transmit logging data securely, it SHOULD be encrypted. All stored logs SHOULD be digitally signed to ensure their integrity. Archived logging data stored outside the logging infrastructure SHOULD also always be stored encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All communication between the log shippers (e.g., Beats) and the central log ingestion platform (e.g., Logstash) is secured with TLS 1.2 or higher. After processing, the log batches are signed with a private key of the log server before being stored in the database. The archive storage (e.g., S3 bucket) is configured with server-side encryption (SSE).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the log shippers and the ingestion platform to verify TLS encryption. A network analysis with Wireshark can confirm this. The process for signing and later verifying the signatures is analyzed. The encryption settings of the archive storage are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire log transmission is encrypted with strong, modern ciphers (e.g., TLS 1.3). Logs are digitally signed upon receipt by the central collector. All storage (hot and archive storage) is encrypted, e.g., through disk encryption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The TLS configuration enforces the use of TLS 1.3 with Forward Secrecy. Transparent disk encryption (e.g., LUKS for Linux, BitLocker for Windows) is enabled at the operating system level on the log servers and the archive storage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the TLS configuration files for the enforced protocol versions and cipher suites. The status of the disk encryption is verified on the servers using operating system tools (`lsblk`, `manage-bde -status`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: End-to-end encryption is used: logs are encrypted on the source system before transmission. They are stored in this encrypted format on the central server and only decrypted in memory when needed for analysis by authorized users. Digital signatures are already applied on the source system. The key management system for the encryption is a dedicated, hardened Hardware Security Module (HSM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A log shipper with an encryption function is used. The data is encrypted with a public key of the log management system. Only the analysis component has access to the corresponding private key, which is securely stored in an HSM. This means that even the administrators of the log server cannot read the raw data. The signatures are also created on the client with a per-client key.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the log shipper on a source system to verify encryption before sending. The key management architecture and the integration of the HSM are reviewed. A network capture is taken to confirm that the transmitted data is encrypted. The process for authorized decryption during analysis is checked.

controls.title: High-availability logging infrastructure (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A high-availability logging infrastructure SHOULD be built. This means that the infrastructure is designed in such a way that the failure of a single component does not lead to the failure of the entire service.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logging infrastructure (e.g., Elastic Stack) is operated as a cluster. There are multiple instances of the data collection (Logstash) and data processing components (Elasticsearch Data Nodes). A load balancer distributes the incoming logs to the Logstash instances. The Elasticsearch data is replicated across multiple nodes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture diagram and the configuration of the cluster. The state of the cluster (`/_cluster/health`) is checked to ensure that it is stable and all shards are replicated. The failure of a single component (e.g., a Logstash node) is simulated to verify that log processing continues.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logging infrastructure is distributed as an active-active cluster across at least two data centers or availability zones. It has redundant components and automatic failover functions. The Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) are defined and regularly tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Elasticsearch cluster is configured as 'Cross-Cluster Replication' across two data centers. In the event of a data center failure, operation can switch completely to the other. The RTO is set to 15 minutes and the RPO to 0 (no data loss). A failover test is conducted every quarter.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the Cross-Cluster Replication. The documentation of the defined RTO/RPO targets and the logs of the last failover tests are inspected. A planned failover is performed during the audit to verify the automatic switchover and compliance with the RTO.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The infrastructure is designed as a multi-region setup with auto-scaling and self-healing functions. It is designed to withstand the failure of an entire region without data loss or significant service degradation. The log sources use an upstream, high-availability message broker to ensure that no logs are lost, even if the entire central infrastructure is temporarily unavailable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The infrastructure runs in a public cloud (e.g., AWS, Azure) and spans multiple geographic regions. Auto-scaling groups automatically adjust the number of processing and storage nodes to match the load. All systems send their logs to a geo-replicated Apache Kafka cluster, which serves as a robust buffer. If an entire region fails, the remaining regions seamlessly take over processing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the cloud architecture, including the configuration of auto-scaling groups, multi-region deployments, and the Kafka cluster. A 'Chaos Engineering' experiment is conducted, in which entire availability zones or services are deliberately shut down to test the resilience and self-healing capabilities of the system under real conditions and to verify that no data is lost.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
To ensure reliable IT operations, IT systems and applications should log either all or at least selected operational and security-relevant events, i.e., automatically save them and make them available for analysis. Logging is used in many institutions to detect hardware and software problems as well as resource bottlenecks in a timely manner. But security problems and attacks on the operated network services can also be traced using logging data. Likewise, such data can be used to secure evidence through forensic investigations after an attack on IT systems or applications has become known.
In every information network, logging data is generated locally by a variety of IT systems and applications. However, to obtain a complete overview of an information network, the logging events generated by various IT systems and applications can be sent to a dedicated logging infrastructure and stored there centrally. Only in this way can the logging data be selected, filtered, and systematically analyzed at a central location.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of the module is to securely collect, store, and make all relevant data available for analysis in a suitable manner, so that as many security-relevant events as possible can be logged.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module OPS.1.1.5 Logging is to be applied once to the entire information network.
This module exclusively considers overarching aspects that are necessary for appropriate logging. The logging of specific IT systems or applications is not dealt with here, but is described in the respective modules of the IT-Grundschutz Compendium.
In many operating systems or applications, logging functions are already present or can be integrated using additional products. To secure these functions and the stored logging data, the underlying operating system must be protected. However, this is not part of this module. For this, the operating system-specific modules must be implemented, e.g., SYS.1.2.3 Windows Server.
Prior to logging security-relevant events, it is important that responsibilities and competencies are clearly defined and assigned. In particular, the principle of separation of duties should be observed. This topic is not part of this module but is dealt with in the ORP.1 Organisation module.
This module must also be distinguished from the detection of security-relevant events (see DER.1 Detection of Security-Relevant Events) and the response to security incidents (see DER.2.1 Handling of Security Incidents). Both aspects are not dealt with or are only touched upon in this module.
Also described elsewhere are the analysis of logging data and their long-term, secure, unchangeable, and reproducible storage (see DER.1 Detection of Security-Relevant Events or OPS.1.2.2 Archiving).
Requirements on how to handle personal data are described in the CON.2 Data Protection module.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Missing or insufficient logging
parts.prose:
In an information network, there are often IT systems or applications where logging has not been enabled in the default settings. Also, some IT systems or applications may not be able to log at all. In both cases, important information can be lost and attacks may not be detected in time. This is also possible if logging is used for individual IT systems or applications, but the logging data is not consolidated at a central location. In information networks without central logging, it is difficult to ensure that the relevant log information from all IT systems and applications is retained and analyzed.
Furthermore, logging data must contain meaningful information. Which events are logged depends, among other things, on the protection requirements of the respective IT systems or applications. If this is disregarded, for example by only reverting to the default settings of the IT systems or applications for logging, this can lead to particularly relevant security events not being logged. Thus, attacks may not be detected.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Incorrect selection of relevant log data
parts.prose:
Log data often provide important information that helps to detect security incidents. A particular challenge is to filter out the relevant messages from the large amount of different log events. This is because many log events are only for informational purposes and distract from the really important messages. If too many log events are selected, the wealth of information is difficult to evaluate and requires a great deal of time.
Furthermore, log events can be discarded or overwritten if the memory or hard disk capacity of the IT system or the logging infrastructure is insufficient. If too few or not sufficiently relevant log events are recorded as a result, security-critical incidents could go undetected.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Missing or faulty time synchronisation in logging
parts.prose: If time is not synchronised on all IT systems in an information network, the logging data may not be able to be correlated with each other, or the correlation may lead to incorrect statements. The reason for this is that the different timestamps of events do not have a common basis. A lack of time synchronisation thus makes it difficult to evaluate collected logging data, especially if it is stored on a central log server. Furthermore, faulty or missing time synchronisation can lead to the logging not being able to be used for the preservation of evidence.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Poor planning in logging
parts.prose: If logging is not planned sufficiently, IT systems or applications may not be monitored, and security-relevant events may not be detected and handled appropriately. Data protection breaches could also not be traced.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Loss of confidentiality and integrity of log data
parts.prose: Some IT systems in an information network generate log data such as login names, IP addresses, email addresses, and computer names, which can be assigned to specific individuals. Such information can be copied, intercepted, and manipulated if it is not transmitted in encrypted form and stored securely. This can lead to attackers accessing confidential information or, through manipulated log data, security incidents being deliberately concealed. Likewise, if attackers obtain a large amount of log data, they can use this information to uncover the internal structure of the information network and thus target their attacks more precisely.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Misconfigured logging
parts.prose:
If logging in IT systems is misconfigured, important information is either recorded incorrectly or not at all. It is also possible that too much or incorrect information is logged. For example, personal data could be logged and stored without authorization. The institution could thereby violate legal requirements.
Misconfigured logging can also result in log data being in inconsistent or proprietary formats. This can make the logs difficult to analyze, and security incidents may go undetected.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Failure of data sources for log data
parts.prose: If IT systems in an information network no longer supply the necessary log data, security incidents can no longer be adequately detected. The cause of such data source failures can be errors in hardware and software or incorrectly administered IT systems. Especially if it is not noticed that data sources have failed, this can lead to a false picture of the security situation in the institution. As a result, attackers can, for example, remain undetected for a very long time and exfiltrate institution-critical information or manipulate production systems.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Insufficiently dimensioned logging infrastructure
parts.prose: Due to complex information networks and diverse attack scenarios, the demands on logging are increasing, as a great deal of log data must be stored and processed. Furthermore, it is common during security incidents to increase the intensity of logging. However, if the logging infrastructure is not designed for this, log data may be stored incompletely. Thus, security-relevant events can no longer be analyzed or can only be analyzed inadequately, and security incidents remain undetected.

controls.title: Planning of software tests

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Test planning only takes place sporadically for individual, particularly critical software projects. There is no established process; planning is done ad-hoc and is usually not documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Test planning is discussed informally between the project manager and the developers. No formal documents are created. Test cases focus on core functionality and are not selected systematically.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks by interviewing project managers and developers whether any form of test planning takes place at all. It is checked on a random basis whether comprehensible, albeit informal, planning artifacts exist for completed projects.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic but simple process for planning software tests exists. The planning covers the essential functional requirements, but does not systematically consider all environments or negative test cases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple template for a test plan is used. The test cases are selected to cover the 'happy paths' of the main functions. The test environment is generic and does not represent all production configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a test plan based on a basic template is created for all new software versions. It is verified that the plans cover the basic functions, even if advanced aspects are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The framework conditions for software tests MUST be defined within the institution before the tests, in accordance with the protection requirements, organizational units, technical possibilities, and test environments. The software MUST be tested based on the requirements of the requirements catalog (and, if applicable, the specifications). The test cases MUST be selected in such a way that they check all functions of the software as representatively as possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal test planning process is established and documented. Test plans are created for all software introductions and major changes. The selection of test cases is based on a risk analysis and the specified requirements to ensure representative coverage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a documented test planning process exists and is being followed. It is verified that test plans are created based on protection requirements and requirements catalogs and that the selection of test cases ensures representative coverage of the functions. This is checked using project documents and test plans.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The test planning systematically considers negative tests to check the software's robustness against unexpected inputs and states. The test environment is selected to representatively cover all device models and operating system environments used in the institution. The compatibility of the software with the used system configurations is specifically tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The test plans contain dedicated sections for negative tests, compatibility tests, and tests on different target platforms. There is an inventory of the production hardware and software configurations, which serves as a basis for designing the test environment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the test plans explicitly provide for negative and compatibility tests. It is verified that the test environments reflect the diversity of the production environments. This is checked by reviewing the test plans and the documentation of the test environments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The test planning process is fully integrated into the CI/CD process. Test environments are automated and dynamically provisioned using Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) to ensure an exact copy of the production environment. The selection and prioritization of test cases is supported by analysis tools that consider code changes and risk profiles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: IaC tools like Terraform or Ansible are used to provision the test environments. Static and dynamic code analysis tools contribute to the risk-based test case selection. The entire planning process is managed and documented via a central ALM (Application Lifecycle Management) tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline and the IaC scripts to verify the automated provisioning of test environments. The configuration of the analysis tools for test case selection is checked and it is demonstrated that the process is continuously mapped in an ALM tool.

controls.title: Execution of functional software tests

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Functional tests are only carried out as informal 'smoke tests' to check whether the software starts and the most basic function is present. The tests often take place in the development environment and potentially affect other development work.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Developers conduct short, undocumented tests on their own machines after compilation. A dedicated test phase or environment does not exist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by interviewing the developers that no systematic functional tests are taking place. There are no test logs or other evidence of structured test execution.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Functional tests are performed manually and cover the most important use cases. The tests are carried out in a separate test environment to avoid directly endangering the production operation, but the isolation is not always fully guaranteed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Testers work through a checklist of test cases. The test environment is a long-lived, shared environment that may differ from the production environment. Results are recorded in a simple table or document.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks for the existence of test checklists and simple result logs. It is verified that a dedicated test environment exists, even if its configuration is not strictly controlled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Functional software tests MUST be used to verify the proper and complete functioning of the software. The functional software tests MUST be carried out in such a way that they do not affect production operations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Functional tests are systematically carried out on the basis of the previously created test plans in a dedicated test environment separate from production operations. The execution and the results are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether functional tests take place in an isolated environment to rule out any impact on production operations. It is verified on the basis of test logs that the tests defined in the test plan to check functionality have been carried out in full.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A significant portion of the functional tests, especially regression tests, is performed automatically. The test execution is integrated into a test management tool that ensures traceability from requirements to test cases and results.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Test automation frameworks such as Selenium, Cypress, or Playwright are used. A test management tool like Jira with Xray/Zephyr or a dedicated tool is used to control and document the test process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the test automation framework and the test scripts. The test management tool is inspected to check the linking of requirements, test cases, and automated test results.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The execution of functional tests is fully integrated into the CI/CD pipeline. Every commit automatically triggers a series of tests. A failure of critical tests automatically prevents the further delivery of the software (build-breaker). The test environments are ephemeral and are created new for each test run and identical to production.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: CI/CD tools such as Jenkins, GitLab CI, or GitHub Actions control the test execution. Container technologies (e.g., Docker) and IaC scripts are used to create ephemeral, production-like test environments on-demand and destroy them again after the test.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline to verify that tests are automatically executed with every commit and that a failure stops the build. The scripts for creating the ephemeral test environments are checked for their correctness and correspondence with the production environment.

controls.title: Evaluation of the test results

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evaluation of the test results is done verbally and informally. There is no written documentation of the results or identified errors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The tester tells the developer directly whether the test was successful or not. Errors are discussed and fixed ad-hoc, without formal recording.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor can determine through interviews that no formal evaluation process exists. No documents such as test reports or error logs can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The results of the software tests are documented in a simple form, e.g., in a table. The evaluation is limited to a 'Pass/Fail' rating.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Excel spreadsheet or a simple text document is used to record the results of the performed test cases. Identified errors are recorded in a separate list.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and completeness of the results documentation on a random basis. It is verified that simple logs exist for test runs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The results of the software tests MUST be evaluated. The evaluation MUST be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal test report is created for each test run. This report documents the tests performed, the results achieved, and any deviations that occurred. The evaluation is stored centrally and is accessible to the project stakeholders.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether documented evaluations (test reports) are available for all relevant test cycles. It is verified that these reports contain a comprehensible presentation of the results and deviations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evaluation of the test results SHOULD include a target-actual comparison with the defined specifications from the requirements catalog or specifications. Deviations and errors are systematically recorded in an issue tracking system, prioritized, and their resolution is tracked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The test evaluation takes place in a test management or ALM tool. Each error is created as a ticket (e.g., in Jira or Azure DevOps), linked to the failed test case, and assigned to a developer. The test report contains a detailed analysis of the deviations from the specifications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the test evaluation contains an explicit comparison with the specifications. By inspecting the issue tracking system, it is verified that errors are systematically recorded, prioritized, and tracked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evaluation of test results is fully automated. Test dashboards visualize the quality status of the software, test coverage, and error trends in real time. In the event of failed tests, tickets are automatically created in the issue tracking system, enriched with all relevant information (logs, screenshots), and assigned to the responsible team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Analysis and reporting tools such as Grafana, SonarQube, or the reporting functions of test management tools are used to create live dashboards. The integration between the test automation framework and the issue tracking system ensures automatic ticket creation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the reporting and dashboard tools. The integration between the test framework and the issue tracker is reviewed to verify the automated creation and enrichment of defect tickets. The correctness and up-to-dateness of the dashboards are checked on a random basis.

controls.title: Software Release

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The software is released informally through a verbal agreement or a brief email, often directly by the development department. The business department is not involved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A developer informs IT operations that a new version is ready for installation. There is no formal release process or release document.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with business and IT managers that no established release process exists. No release documents can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a simple release process in which the responsible business unit accepts the software after a brief demonstration. The release is documented via email.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After completion of the tests, the new functionality is shown to the business owner. The release is made via a confirming reply email, which is archived.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether releases in the form of emails or simple protocols are available for software installations. It is verified that a business acceptance has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The responsible business unit MUST release the software as soon as the software tests have been successfully completed. The release MUST be documented in the form of a release declaration. The releasing organizational unit MUST verify that the software has been tested according to the requirements, that the results match expectations, and that legal and organizational specifications have been met.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal release process is defined. The business owner receives the test report for review. The release is granted by signing a standardized release document, which confirms that all tests were successful and the requirements are met.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and completeness of the signed release declarations for all software versions put into production. It is verified that the release was granted on the basis of the documented test results and in consideration of all relevant specifications.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The release process is supported by a workflow system. The release is multi-stage and involves not only the business department but also IT operations and the Information Security Officer (ISO). There are defined criteria for the release, including a maximum permissible number of open defects of certain priority levels.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A workflow in a ticket system or ALM tool controls the release process. The release criteria (e.g., 'no open critical defects') are stored in the system. All involved roles (business department, IT operations, ISO) must give their approval digitally.
