parts.prose: Upon reaching 85% fill level, the storage system automatically mounts another, already prepared storage LUN and expands the file system. Upon reaching 90%, a purchase requisition for new hardware is triggered in the ERP system via an API interface.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the automation rules for storage expansion and the procurement workflows. The successful automatic execution of these processes is verified using the system logs.

controls.title: Regular review of the archiving processes

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A review of the archiving processes only takes place reactively when a serious error or data loss has occurred.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After an incident, a 'post-mortem' analysis is conducted, but there are no proactive, planned audits to prevent such incidents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds no plans or reports on regular reviews. Only in the documentation of incidents are there indications of procedural weaknesses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Informal reviews of the archiving processes are carried out occasionally, for example in the context of team meetings. However, the results are not systematically documented or followed up.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a year, the team talks about 'what's going well and what's not' with archiving. However, the points discussed are not formally recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds occasional mentions of archiving in meeting minutes but cannot identify a structured review process or documented results.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be regularly checked whether the archiving processes are still functioning correctly and properly. For this purpose, a checklist SHOULD be created that contains questions about responsibilities, organizational processes, the use of archiving, the redundancy of archive data, administration, and the technical assessment of the archive system. The audit results SHOULD be documented in a comprehensible manner and compared with the target state. Deviations SHOULD be investigated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual self-assessment is conducted using a standardized checklist. The results, including the identified deviations, are documented in a review report. A corrective action is defined for each deviation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the review checklist and inspects the review reports from recent years. It is checked whether the reports are complete, contain a target-actual comparison, and whether the identified deviations have been followed up (e.g., by inspecting related tickets).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reviews are regularly carried out by an independent body, for example by internal audit or an external auditor. Identified deficiencies are recorded in a central system for tracking measures (issue tracker), assigned with responsibilities and deadlines, and their resolution is actively monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An external audit for the archiving process is commissioned every two years. The results are fed as 'findings' into the organization's GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool, where their resolution is managed until completion.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit reports of the independent body. Using the GRC tool or ticket system, it is verified that all findings have been recorded, processed, and closed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The review process is supported by automated tools (Continuous Auditing). These permanently check compliance with the defined processes and configurations. Deviations from the target state are detected and reported in real time, which allows for immediate correction.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A compliance-as-code tool continuously checks whether the technical settings of the archive system (e.g., encryption, logging) comply with the policies. A process mining tool analyzes the log data and detects when the defined archiving workflows are not being followed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and reports of the continuous auditing tools. The rule base (e.g., the codified policies) is checked and verified against live data to ensure that deviations are detected correctly and in a timely manner.

controls.title: Regular observation of the market for archive systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The market for archive systems is only considered when a new acquisition or replacement is imminent. Proactive or regular observation does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Action is only taken when the manufacturer announces the end-of-life for the current product. Technological developments or new security vulnerabilities in other products are ignored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During interviews, the auditor discovers that there is no process for market observation. Decisions are made purely reactively.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsible employees informally keep up to date with market developments, for example by reading professional journals or websites. However, the findings are not systematically collected or evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Some administrators have subscribed to newsletters from manufacturers or professional magazines. However, the knowledge gained is only shared sporadically within the team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor cannot prove a formal process, but determines in discussions that the employees have a certain degree of current market knowledge.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The market for archive systems SHOULD be monitored regularly and systematically. Criteria such as changes in standards, technological changes by manufacturers, published security vulnerabilities, and the loss of security suitability of cryptographic algorithms SHOULD be observed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One or more employees are explicitly tasked with monitoring the market based on the specified criteria. The results are summarized in a short report at regular intervals (e.g., semi-annually) and discussed within the team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the responsibility for market observation is clearly regulated. The existence and completeness of the regular reports are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Market observation is documented in formal, regular reports that are presented to the responsible management level. This includes subscribing to analyst reports (e.g., Gartner, Forrester) and relevant threat intelligence feeds.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The team creates a quarterly management summary on market trends and risks. The organization obtains threat intelligence data that also includes vulnerabilities in archiving software.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the management reports and the sources used for observation (e.g., invoices for analyst subscriptions, configuration of the threat intelligence platform).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organization actively participates in relevant user groups, standardization bodies, and professional conferences. The insights gained are formally and systematically integrated into the strategic IT planning process and risk management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees regularly attend conferences and report on them afterwards. The organization is a member of a relevant standardization organization. The findings are used to proactively adapt the IT roadmap and the risk assessment of the archive system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks evidence of active participation in external bodies (e.g., membership certificates, travel expense reports for conferences). Minutes from the strategy or risk management committee are used to verify that the information obtained has been incorporated and considered.

controls.title: Regular renewal of cryptographically secured data in archiving

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cryptographically secured data is no longer considered after its creation. Once signed or encrypted, its state is no longer checked, even if the algorithms used become known to be insecure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The motto is 'fire and forget'. The need for a crypto-agile strategy is not known.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that the archive contains data with outdated signatures (e.g., SHA-1) and there is no process to rectify this situation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an awareness that cryptographic methods can age. However, a renewal of the cryptographic protection is only considered reactively when an algorithm is publicly declared broken.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: They wait for an official warning from the BSI or another body before considering a migration of the signatures. This is not done proactively.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds no proactive process. In interviews, employees confirm that they would wait for external warnings before taking action.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The field of cryptography SHOULD be continuously monitored to assess whether an algorithm is still reliable and sufficiently secure. Archive data secured with cryptographic methods that will no longer be suitable for protection in the foreseeable future SHOULD be re-secured in a timely manner using appropriate methods.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined process for monitoring cryptographic standards (e.g., by regularly checking publications from the BSI or BNetzA) is established. A plan for the so-called re-signing or re-encryption of archive data is created and maintained in order to be able to react in a timely manner when necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the process for crypto-monitoring and the plan for renewing cryptographic measures. It is checked whether the organization is capable of identifying the algorithms used in the archive and renewing them if necessary.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal crypto-agility policy is established. It defines which algorithms with which parameters are considered 'secure', 'at risk', or 'insecure' and specifies timeframes for migration. A planned, recurring process performs the renewal of the cryptographic protection (e.g., re-signing) long before the old methods are considered insecure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy stipulates that all signatures must be renewed every 5 years, regardless of the state of the algorithm. An annual process identifies all data that needs to be re-signed in the coming year and plans its execution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the crypto-agility policy. System logs and archive data are used to verify that the process for regularly renewing signatures or encryption is being carried out as planned.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The cryptographic renewal process is fully automated. The archive system maintains an inventory of all cryptographic metadata (algorithms used, key strengths, creation dates). Based on the crypto-agility policy, the system automatically flags and renews objects that require renewal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The archive system checks the crypto inventory daily. If it determines that a signature will reach its defined validity period in 6 months, a re-signing job is automatically queued. The successful renewal is logged in an audit-proof manner (e.g., in an Evidence Record according to BSI TR-ESOR).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the automated crypto-renewal process and the inventory. The logs are used to track the complete and correct execution of the automated jobs. A `get-crypto-inventory --status expiring` command is executed and its result is checked.

controls.title: Regular renewal of technical archive system components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware and software components of the archive system are only replaced when they fail or no longer function (break-fix).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A server is operated until it can no longer be switched on. An operating system is used until the archive software no longer starts on it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through an inventory check, the auditor finds that numerous components (hardware and software) are being operated far beyond their manufacturer-declared 'End of Life'.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic lifecycle plan for the components exists. However, it is not strictly followed, and renewals are often postponed for budget or time reasons.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a list with the planned replacement dates for servers and software, but the actual implementation often lags years behind this schedule.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds a lifecycle plan but, when comparing it with the inventory, discovers significant deviations and excessive replacement cycles.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Archive systems SHOULD be kept up-to-date technologically over long periods. New hardware and software SHOULD be thoroughly tested before being installed in a live archive system. When new components are put into operation or new file formats are introduced, a migration plan SHOULD be created. It SHOULD describe all changes, tests, and expected test results. The conversion of individual data SHOULD be documented (transfer record).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A lifecycle management process is established. New components are tested for compatibility and security in a separate test environment before being deployed in the production system. A detailed migration plan is created for each migration (e.g., to a new server or a new file format) and its execution is logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the lifecycle management process. Migration plans and the corresponding test and execution logs (including transfer records) for recently performed renewals are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The technology lifecycle management process is formalized and backed by long-term budget planning for regular renewals. All new components undergo a formal security assessment before procurement and extensive testing in a dedicated, production-like test environment before commissioning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT strategy and budget planning provide for a complete renewal of the archive hardware every 5 years. Every new software version must successfully pass a standardized test protocol in the staging environment before rollout.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the medium-term budget planning in relation to the archive system. The logs of the security assessments and the acceptance tests in the test environment are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Technological renewal is part of a continuous improvement process. Modern deployment strategies such as canary releases or blue-green deployments are used for introducing new components to ensure a seamless transition without downtime. The migration processes are largely automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A new archive backend is built in parallel to the old one (blue-green). After successful tests, traffic is gradually switched to the new system. Scripts automate the transfer of data and configurations from the old to the new system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture and automation scripts for zero-downtime deployments and migrations. Logs are used to reconstruct how the last major renewal was performed using these techniques.

controls.title: Selection of a suitable archive system

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of an archive system is based on subjective criteria such as price or a single outstanding feature, not on a systematic requirements analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The system is selected because it was the cheapest provider or because a sales representative gave a good presentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds no documented requirements analysis or a comprehensible catalog of criteria on which the procurement decision was based.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection is based on a list of functional requirements. However, security requirements are not defined or are insufficiently defined and evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A requirements specification with the desired functions was created. However, the requirement 'secure' was not further specified (e.g., what encryption, what logging functions, etc.).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the requirements specification and finds that important non-functional requirements, especially in the area of information security, are missing or formulated too vaguely.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A new archive system SHOULD always be selected based on the specifications described in the archiving concept. It SHOULD meet the requirements formulated therein.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed catalog of requirements is created, which derives all functional and non-functional requirements from the archiving concept (incl. security requirements). The selection decision is made and documented based on the degree of fulfillment of these requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the catalog of requirements used for the selection with the specifications in the archiving concept. It is checked whether the selection decision was documented in a comprehensible manner.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection process includes a formal Request for Proposal (RFP) and a 'Proof-of-Concept' (PoC) phase. In the PoC phase, the shortlisted candidates are installed in a test environment and intensively tested against the requirements catalog.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The top 2 vendors must install their system in the organization's test environment for four weeks. A standardized test plan is executed and the results are evaluated. The result of the PoC is decisive for the final selection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the tender documents, the test plans for the PoC, and the final evaluation reports. It is checked whether the process was fair and comprehensible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection process includes an in-depth review of the security architecture of the candidate systems. This can also include the analysis of manufacturer security certifications (e.g., Common Criteria), conducting own penetration tests, or, if possible, a source code analysis before a final decision is made.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the final contract is signed, an external service provider is commissioned to conduct a penetration test against the PoC installation of the favored system. The manufacturer must also disclose its security development processes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports of the security analyses and penetration tests that were carried out as part of the selection process. It is checked whether the critical vulnerabilities identified there were demonstrably rectified before going live.

controls.title: Use of suitable archive media

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unsuitable storage media from the consumer sector (e.g. simple USB hard drives, consumer SSDs) are used for archiving without considering longevity, reliability, or data integrity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Archive data is stored on external hard drives that were bought in an electronics store and are not designed for continuous operation or long-term storage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inventory of the archive media, the auditor determines that consumer hardware without guarantees for longevity or data integrity is being used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Storage media from the enterprise segment are used (e.g. server hard drives). However, the selection is not specifically tailored to the requirements of the archive (e.g. access frequency, data volume, long-term stability).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The same high-performance but expensive enterprise SSDs are used as for the production databases, although slower but more durable and cheaper media would be sufficient for the archive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that although high-quality media are used, the selection is not based on an economic or technical requirements analysis for archiving.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Suitable media SHOULD be selected and used for archiving. Aspects such as the data volume to be archived, the average access times, and the average number of simultaneous accesses to the archive system SHOULD be taken into account. The archive media SHOULD also meet the requirements for long-term archiving with regard to auditability and lifespan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The storage media are selected on the basis of a documented analysis of the specific requirements. Media are selected that are explicitly certified by the manufacturer for long-term archiving and the determined access patterns (e.g. LTO tapes for infrequent access, nearline SAS hard drives for more frequent access).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the requirements analysis for the storage media. It is checked whether the specifications of the media used (e.g. manufacturer data sheets) match the documented requirements for lifespan and auditability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A tiered storage concept is used that combines different media types (e.g. SSDs, HDDs, tapes, cloud storage) to optimally meet the requirements of different data classes in terms of performance, cost, and longevity. The media are explicitly certified for long-term archiving.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Data from the last 12 months is stored on a fast hard disk storage. Older data is automatically migrated to a more cost-effective LTO tape archive. This process is described in the archiving concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the documented tiered storage concept and verifies its technical implementation. It is checked whether the media used have corresponding certificates for long-term archiving.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of storage media is based on a formal risk analysis and a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) consideration. For data with the highest integrity requirements, non-rewritable media (WORM - Write Once, Read Many) are generally used to prevent manipulation at the media level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A WORM-capable storage system or WORM tapes are used for audit-proof accounting records. The decision for a specific technology is supported by a documented analysis that considers acquisition, operating, and migration costs over the entire lifecycle.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the risk and TCO analysis. It is technically verified that for the data declared as WORM, non-rewritable storage areas or media are actually used and that a subsequent change or deletion before the end of the retention period is not possible.

controls.title: Regular functional and recovery tests for archiving

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Functional or recovery tests are only performed reactively after a problem or failure has occurred. There are no proactive, planned tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One relies on the system to work. The process is only investigated when a user cannot restore a document.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds no plans or logs for regular tests. Incident logs can serve as evidence of reactive action.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic functional tests are carried out occasionally (e.g. whether the web interface is accessible). However, the actual recovery of archived data or the readability of media is not tested or only very rarely.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitoring system checks via ping whether the archive server is online. Whether the data on the tapes can still be read is not checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that only superficial availability tests are taking place. There is no evidence of successful end-to-end recovery tests of archive data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Regular functional and recovery tests SHOULD be carried out for archiving. The archive data carriers SHOULD be checked at least once a year to see if they are still readable and intact. Suitable processes SHOULD be defined for troubleshooting. Furthermore, the hardware components of the archive system SHOULD be regularly checked for their proper function. It SHOULD be checked regularly whether all archiving processes are functioning without errors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A test concept is created that provides for regular (at least annual) tests. These include checking media readability, random recovery and verification of archive data, and checking the hardware diagnostic functions. The test results are logged, and a troubleshooting process is defined for any errors found.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the test concept and the test logs from the last year. It is checked whether all required test types (media, recovery, hardware, process) were covered and carried out regularly. The existence and application of the troubleshooting process is verified using examples.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All tests are carried out on the basis of detailed test plans. The execution, the results, and any deviations are formally documented. Identified errors are recorded in a ticket system and their resolution is tracked until completion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a detailed schedule for the annual recovery test. The test is logged and the results report is countersigned by the ISO. Any irregularity found during the test leads to the creation of a ticket, which is only closed after a successful re-test.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the test plans and the corresponding, detailed result logs. The systematic tracking and resolution of errors discovered during the tests is traced using the ticket system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The functional and recovery tests are highly automated. In a dedicated, isolated test environment (sandbox), complete recovery simulations are carried out regularly and automatically without affecting the production system. The results are automatically evaluated and reported to a monitoring system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every night, a selection of archive data from the previous day is automatically restored in a sandbox environment. A script checks the restored files for completeness and integrity (hash comparison). If successful, the status in the monitoring is set to 'green'; if not, an alarm is triggered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the automated test environment and the test scripts. The logs and history in the monitoring system are analyzed to confirm the continuous and successful execution of the tests. A `get-automated-recovery-dashboard` is executed.

controls.title: Appropriate use of cryptographic methods in archiving

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy is defined that mandates the use of cryptographic methods (encryption, signatures) for archiving. The algorithms and key lengths used comply with general recommendations but are not necessarily aligned with the highest standards for long-term preservation of evidentiary value.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The archive data is encrypted with AES-256 and signed with RSA-2048. This is a solid basic configuration, but it does not take into account the special requirements of standards such as BSI TR-ESOR.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the crypto policy and the technical configuration of the archive system. It is determined that a fundamentally sound cryptography has been implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To be able to cover long retention periods, archive data SHOULD only be secured with cryptographic methods based on current standards and norms. This includes compliance with the requirements of relevant institutions such as the BSI or the Federal Network Agency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cryptographic methods used strictly adhere to the respectively valid versions of the Technical Guidelines of the BSI (e.g., TR-02102 for crypto-mechanisms, TR-03125 for preservation of evidence) and the algorithm catalogs of the BNetzA. This is ensured during the configuration of the system and the selection of signature cards.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration of the cryptographic methods used (algorithms, key lengths, modes, curves) exactly with the current specifications of the mentioned standards and norms. It is checked whether qualified time stamps from a trustworthy provider are used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to strict adherence to current standards, cryptographic operations and the management of the associated keys are protected at the highest level through the use of Hardware Security Modules (HSM). To safeguard against future threats, Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) methods are evaluated and, where appropriate, used as a hybrid approach.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All signatures and encryptions in the archiving process are performed within a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 (or higher) certified HSM. The private keys never leave the HSM. For particularly sensitive data, a hybrid encryption is used that combines a classic algorithm (e.g., AES) with a PQC algorithm (e.g., Kyber).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration and configuration of the HSM. It is checked whether the keys were demonstrably generated in the HSM and are marked as non-exportable. The configuration of the hybrid encryption approach is analyzed.

controls.title: Transfer of paper data to electronic archives

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A defined process for replacement scanning is implemented. This includes logging of the scans performed, quality controls (e.g., for readability and completeness), and secure destruction of the originals after a security period has expired.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a procedural instruction for scanning. After scanning, an employee randomly checks the quality of the scan. The originals are kept for 30 days and then destroyed by a certified service provider.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procedural instruction and the logs of the scans performed and the destruction. The appropriateness of the quality controls is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If paper documents are digitized and transferred to an electronic archive, it SHOULD be ensured that the digital copy corresponds to the original document in terms of image and content. This requires comprehensive quality assurance measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The scanning process includes technical measures to ensure pictorial and content consistency. This includes the use of calibration targets, automatic detection of double-sheet feeds, and a 100% visual inspection of each individual scan by an employee (this does not mean the four-eyes principle, but a complete check).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the scanning software and the process instructions for quality assurance. The performance of the complete visual inspection is proven on the basis of logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process of replacement scanning is carried out strictly in accordance with the requirements of a recognized guideline such as BSI TR-03138 RESISCAN. This includes detailed, complete procedural documentation, the protection of the integrity and authenticity of the scan data through qualified electronic signatures or seals, and audit-proof logging of the entire process to give the digital copy the same or a higher evidentiary value than the original.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A certified scanning solution is used. Each scanned document or scan batch is provided with a qualified electronic seal and a qualified time stamp immediately after its creation. The entire process from preparation through scanning to destruction is documented in a tamper-proof scan log.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the entire scanning process against the requirements of BSI TR-03138. This includes checking the procedural documentation, the technical configuration (e.g., integration of the seal), the certificates used, and the complete, tamper-proof logging.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Archiving plays a special role in the document management process. On the one hand, it is expected that digital documents are available until the end of a specified retention period. On the other hand, their confidentiality and integrity must be preserved. Additionally, the context must be maintained so that the respective stored transaction is reconstructible.
Throughout the entire duration of long-term storage, appropriate measures for information preservation and, if necessary, measures for preserving evidentiary value must therefore be implemented.
In German information technology usage, the term 'electronic archiving' is sometimes used synonymously with 'electronic long-term storage'. For better understanding, this module therefore generally only speaks of 'archiving' or 'digital long-term archive'. An IT procedure for the retention of electronic documents is referred to as an 'archive system', 'digital archive', or 'long-term storage'. The retention period of the documents is determined by legal and other requirements as well as the purpose of the data.
The term 'documents' used in this module includes data and digital documents, unless they are explicitly used in another meaning.
From a legal perspective, the term 'archiving' in Germany is specified and defined by the archival laws of the federal government and the states. 'Archiving' in the legally correct sense only concerns records of public administration. It refers to the fact that documents of an authority, as soon as they are no longer needed for its purposes, are to be sorted out and kept for an unlimited time by a competent state institution (Federal Archives) (cf. §§ 1 and 2 BArchG). This type of archiving is to be distinguished from the time-limited retention discussed in this module.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The module describes how digital documents can be archived for the long term, securely, immutably, and reproducibly. It defines requirements for securely planning, implementing, and operating an archive system.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The storage of paper documents is not considered in this module, but requirements are set for how they can be digitized and archived.
The module OPS.1.2.2 Archiving is to be applied once to the information domain if long-term archiving of electronic documents is performed. Long-term archiving may be required due to external or internal regulations, or a system for long-term archiving of electronic documents may already be in operation.
The module does not cover archiving for an unlimited period in the sense of the archival laws of the federal government and the states.
This module describes security measures with which electronic documents can be stored and preserved for long-term storage within applicable retention periods. Measures for operational data backup are not covered in this module. Requirements for this are presented in CON.3 Data Backup Concept.
A digital long-term storage consists of individual components, e.g., a database. However, how to operate such components securely in detail is also not the topic of this module. For this, the requirements from the corresponding modules, such as APP.4.3 Relational Databases, SYS.1.1 General Server, and SYS.1.8 Storage Solutions, must also be taken into account.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Obsolescence of archive systems
parts.prose:
Archived data is typically intended to be stored for a very long period. During this time, however, the underlying technical system components, storage media, and data formats can age physically or technically and thus become unusable. For example, compatibility problems with the data formats used may arise over time.
If this aging process is not addressed, it is to be expected in the long term that, for example, archived raw data will no longer be readable from the archive media. Archived data can also be altered by physical errors on the archive system and media.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Inadequate classification criteria for archives
parts.prose: Electronic archives can contain very large amounts of data. The individual data records are stored according to specific classification criteria, which are distinguished between index data of the business applications and index data of the archive system. If unsuitable classification criteria are used, archived documents may no longer be retrievable or only with great effort. It is also possible that the semantics of the documents cannot be clearly determined. An unsuitable or limited selection of classification criteria could also defeat the purposes of retention, e.g., the ability to provide evidence to third parties.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Unauthorized archive access due to insufficient logging
parts.prose: Unauthorized archive access is usually detected using log files. However, if logging is not extensive enough, such access might not be discovered. As a result, attackers could gain unnoticed access to the information stored there and, for example, copy or modify it.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Inadequate transfer of paper data to an electronic archive
parts.prose: When documents are scanned, the appearance or semantics of the captured data can be falsified. Documents can also be lost in the process. This can lead to the information in the document being misinterpreted and miscalculated, for example, if important parts of the document or the document stack are forgotten during scanning.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Insufficient renewal of cryptographic procedures in archiving
parts.prose: Cryptographic procedures used, for example, for signatures, seals, timestamps, technical evidence records, or encryption must be regularly updated to the current state of the art to maintain their protective effect. If this is not done, the integrity of the document can no longer be guaranteed, for example, due to an outdated, insecure signature. Furthermore, the file may not be admitted as evidence in court, even if the document is still completely correct. The confidentiality of an encrypted document is also lost in this way.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Insufficient audits of archiving
parts.prose: If the archiving process is audited too infrequently or inaccurately, this can lead to malfunctions not being detected. This can cast doubt on the integrity of the archived documents themselves. This can result in legal and economic disadvantages for the institution: For example, a file may not be admitted as evidence in court under certain circumstances because it cannot be ruled out that it has been manipulated.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Violation of legal frameworks when using archiving
parts.prose: When archiving electronic documents, various legal frameworks must be observed. Failure to comply can have civil or criminal consequences, e.g., regarding minimum retention periods arising from tax, budgetary, or other reasons.

controls.title: Regulations for teleworking (B) [Supervisors, HR department]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are only isolated, informal instructions for teleworking. A simple leaflet with basic information may exist, but it is neither comprehensive nor legally binding. Important aspects such as availability or how to handle security-related incidents are not regulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The regulations are often limited to an email from the supervisor granting permission for teleworking without providing further security instructions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By interviewing employees and supervisors, the auditor determines that there are no formal, consistent regulations for teleworking and that it is handled on an ad-hoc basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic, standardized regulation for teleworking that is given to all relevant employees. This regulation covers the most important organizational and technical aspects, but does not address all contentious points or special cases. It is not systematically updated on a regular basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard template for a teleworking agreement is used. This is handed out once when the teleworking place is set up. The security measures are described in a general document.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a standard teleworking regulation and checks on a random basis whether new teleworkers have received it. It is checked whether the regulation contains basic security measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All relevant aspects of teleworking MUST be regulated. For informational purposes, teleworkers MUST be provided with the applicable regulations or a dedicated leaflet explaining the security measures to be observed. All contentious points MUST be regulated either by company agreements or by individual agreements between the employee and the institution, made in addition to the employment contract. The regulations MUST be updated regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A comprehensive teleworking policy is created and maintained. It is made available to all employees on the intranet. Individual agreements are managed by the HR department as an addendum to the employment contract. A review of the regulations is initiated manually when needed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the official teleworking policy for completeness. He checks whether contentious points have been clarified by company agreements or individual agreements by inspecting the documentation of the HR department. In addition, it is checked whether a process for the regular updating of the policy is defined and when the last update took place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regulations for teleworking are not only documented, but also actively communicated and their acknowledgement is tracked among employees. A formalized process ensures that the regulations are reviewed and updated at least annually and in the event of relevant changes (e.g., after security incidents). The responsibility for updating is clearly assigned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New teleworkers must confirm their acknowledgement of the policy in writing or electronically. The CISO or information security officer is responsible for the annual review process. Changes are provided with a changelog and proactively communicated to all teleworkers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the formalized review process by inspecting the logs of the last reviews. It is checked whether the proofs of acknowledgement from the employees are complete. `Get-PolicyAcknowledgement -Policy 'Telearbeit' -User * | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne 'Acknowledged' }`

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regulations for teleworking are integrated into a GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool or a digital policy management system. Employees must recertify the policies annually via the system. Updates are distributed automatically and acknowledgement is enforced. The effectiveness of the regulations is continuously assessed using metrics (e.g., number of reported incidents from teleworking stations) and used to improve the regulations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC tool is used to manage the entire lifecycle of the teleworking policy, from creation to distribution and confirmation to review. Dashboards visualize the compliance status in real time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses the reporting functions of the GRC tool to verify compliance with the policy lifecycle. It is checked whether defined metrics for measuring effectiveness exist and how they lead to the adaptation of the regulations. An automated audit trail from the GRC tool serves as the primary proof.

controls.title: Security requirements for the teleworking computer (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are only general, non-binding recommendations for the security of teleworking computers, such as 'use a virus scanner'. There is no defined and verifiable technical configuration. Use for private purposes is not regulated and is tolerated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees are often allowed to use their private devices (BYOD) without any technical security provided by the institution. Recommendations are sent in an email.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews and review of IT policies, the auditor determines that no mandatory technical requirements are defined for teleworking computers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic checklist of technical requirements is defined (e.g., current operating system, activated virus scanner, firewall). Access to the computer is protected by a password. Compliance is checked during setup but not continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before being granted access to the corporate network, an IT employee manually checks against a checklist to see if the computer meets the basic requirements. It is assumed that the user will maintain this state.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks for the existence of the checklist for technical requirements. The documentation for the initial setup of telework computers is randomly checked to ensure the audit has been carried out.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security requirements that an IT system for telework must meet MUST be defined. It MUST be ensured that only authorized persons have access to the telework computers. Furthermore, the telework computer MUST be secured in such a way that it can only be used for authorized purposes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard hardening document for telework computers is created and applied. Access is regulated by personal user accounts with strong passwords. Use for authorized purposes is implemented through a software usage policy and administrative rights restriction.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the defined security requirements (e.g., hardening specifications) shown to them. It is checked whether a process for setting up user accounts exists and how authorization is carried out. The regulations for the use of software and administrative rights are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined security requirements are centrally managed by a client management system (MDM/UEM) and their compliance is continuously monitored. Deviations from the target state (e.g., disabled firewall) are automatically reported or corrected. Use for authorized purposes is enforced through technical measures such as application whitelisting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UEM (Unified Endpoint Management) solution such as Microsoft Intune or JAMF is used to distribute configuration profiles to telework computers and to check their compliance status. Application Control Policies (e.g., via AppLocker) prevent the execution of unauthorized software.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is granted read access to the client management system to view the configuration profiles and compliance policies. A report on the compliance status of all telework computers is analyzed. `(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections` can be checked on a client to see the application whitelisting rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The telework computer is integrated into a Zero Trust architecture. Access to corporate resources is granted dynamically for each request based on device health, user identity, and context. Hardware-based security features (e.g., TPM, Secure Boot) are mandatory and used for device attestation. Usage is restricted to a hardened, centrally managed operating system image.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Microsoft's Conditional Access is used in conjunction with Intune and Entra ID to check the device state. A TPM chip is used for storing BitLocker keys and for Health Attestation. All telework computers are provisioned with a hardened image via a standardized process such as Windows Autopilot.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the Conditional Access Policies and the Health Attestation Services. It is verified that all telework computers have TPM 2.0 and that Secure Boot is active. An automated report from the UEM solution, which shows the compliance status of all security-relevant hardware and software features, is used as proof.

controls.title: Awareness and training of employees (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Awareness of the dangers of teleworking is only raised sporadically, for example through an occasional email with general security tips. No formal training takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a current phishing attack becomes known, the IT department sends a circular email to all employees, which also reaches teleworkers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by interviewing employees that there are no regular or mandatory training sessions on security in teleworking.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees receive a one-time briefing or a leaflet on the most important security risks when setting up their telework station. Participation is documented, but there are no regular repetitions or further measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the onboarding process, a 30-minute presentation is given that also covers telework-specific risks. Alternatively, a PDF guide is handed out.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies on the basis of onboarding checklists or participant lists that new teleworkers receive basic security training.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on a guide, employees MUST be made aware of the dangers associated with teleworking. They MUST also be instructed in the institution's corresponding security measures and trained in their use. The training and awareness measures for employees SHOULD be repeated regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed guide to telework security is created and available on the intranet. Mandatory initial training is conducted for all teleworkers. The recommendation for regular repetition is implemented by a reminder in the ISB's annual plan, who then manually organizes a new training session.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the guide and the training materials. It is checked on the basis of participant lists whether all teleworkers have taken part in the initial training. It is checked whether there is a plan for repeating the training sessions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training and awareness measures are mandatory and repeated annually. The content is regularly updated to address new threats. The effectiveness of the awareness is checked through regular phishing simulations, the results of which are used for targeted follow-up training.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An e-learning platform is used for the annual, mandatory security training. A tool for phishing simulations is used to test awareness. Employees who fall for the simulations automatically receive additional short training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports from the e-learning platform to verify the participation rate in the annual training sessions. The results of the phishing simulations and the resulting follow-up training measures are reviewed to assess effectiveness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training program is role-based and adaptive. Employees with access to particularly sensitive data receive in-depth training. The program learns from user behavior (e.g., in phishing tests, reported incidents) and individually adapts the training content. Gamification elements are used to increase motivation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An advanced security awareness platform is used that creates individual learning paths based on risk scoring and role profiles. Positive security behaviors (e.g., successfully reporting a phishing attempt) are rewarded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the security awareness platform to understand the logic of the role-based and adaptive training assignment. Reports are evaluated that show the individual development of employees and the reduction of the human risk factor over time.

controls.title: Creating a security concept for teleworking (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic document that lists the most important security rules for teleworking. However, this document does not contain a formal description of protection goals, no analysis of protection needs, and no systematic risk assessment. It is more of an extended policy than a complete concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A chapter in the general IT security policy is dedicated to teleworking. It describes the VPN solution to be used and the password policy for remote access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the document and determines that essential elements of a security concept such as protection needs assessment and risk analysis are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A security concept for teleworking SHOULD be created that describes security objectives, protection needs, security requirements, and risks. The concept SHOULD be regularly updated and revised. The teleworking security concept SHOULD be aligned with the institution's overall security concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standalone security concept for teleworking is created as a Word or PDF document. It follows a standard structure (e.g., BSI Standard 200-2) and describes the specific threats (e.g., theft of the laptop, insecure Wi-Fi) and the resulting requirements and measures. It is updated manually as needed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security concept for teleworking and checks whether the required content (objectives, protection needs, requirements, risks) is present. It is checked whether the document is versioned, when the last update took place, and whether there are references to the higher-level ISMS concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The teleworking security concept is subject to a formal approval and review process that takes place at least annually. The risk analysis defined in the concept is systematically carried out and the resulting measures are tracked. The concept is directly linked to the implemented technical and organizational controls.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The concept is managed in the intranet or a document management system. The review and approval process is controlled by a workflow. The measures from the risk analysis are recorded in a ticket system (e.g., Jira) and their implementation is monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the logs of the review and approval process. He checks the documentation of the risk analysis and randomly follows up on the implementation of the resulting measures in the ticket system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security concept is a 'living document' that is managed in a GRC tool. Risks are continuously assessed, and the concept dynamically adapts to changes in the threat landscape or business processes. The effectiveness of the measures defined in the concept is measured using Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and visualized in a dashboard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC tool is used to integrate the security concept, risk analysis, control implementation, and audit management. Automated threat intelligence feeds are incorporated into the risk assessment. KPIs could be: 'Number of security incidents at teleworkstations per month' or 'Compliance rate of telework computers'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is granted read access to the GRC tool. He analyzes the historical data of the concept, the continuous risk assessment, and the KPI dashboards to verify the dynamic adaptation and effectiveness measurement.

controls.title: Regulation of the use of communication options in teleworking (S) [IT operations, employees]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal list of approved communication tools (e.g., email, a specific messenger). However, there are no clear rules for their secure use, especially with regard to the exchange of sensitive data. Private use is not explicitly regulated and is often tolerated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A guide to teleworking mentions that Microsoft Teams and Outlook are to be used for communication. There are no further specifications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews that although preferred tools are known, there are no binding rules for their use or a clear separation between private and business use defined.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be clearly regulated which communication options may be used for telework and under which conditions. The business and private use of internet services during telework SHOULD be regulated. It SHOULD also be clarified whether private use is generally permitted or prohibited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A written policy for the use of communication tools is created. It lists permitted tools (e.g., email, Teams, internal telephone system) and prohibited tools (e.g., private messengers for business purposes). The policy includes a clear section that regulates private use (e.g., 'permitted to a limited extent, as long as professional activities are not affected').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy for the use of communication tools and checks whether the use of internet services and private use are regulated clearly and unambiguously. It is checked whether this policy has been made known to all teleworkers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regulations for the use of communication options are technically enforced. Only approved cloud services and communication platforms are accessible from telework computers. To prevent the leakage of sensitive data, Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies are applied to approved channels such as email and collaboration tools.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A web proxy or Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) solution is used to block access to unapproved web applications. DLP policies in Microsoft 365 are configured to, for example, prevent files marked as 'confidential' from being sent to external addresses.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the web proxy or CASB. They check the established DLP policies and their logs for effectiveness. `(Get-DlpCompliancePolicy -Identity 'PolicyName').Rules.ContentContainsSensitiveInformation`

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All business communication channels are centrally managed, encrypted, and monitored for security anomalies. The use of private communication tools for business purposes is completely blocked technically. Data usage policies are dynamically enforced based on data classification, user role, and context (e.g., location, device security).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A comprehensive SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) solution is implemented, integrating network and security functions. Communication is monitored by a SIEM solution that detects suspicious patterns. Access to data in collaboration tools is regulated by granular, attribute-based access controls (ABAC).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture and configuration of the SASE solution. The SIEM rules for monitoring communication are checked. The effectiveness of the dynamic ABAC policies is tested on a random basis by attempting to access protected data with different user and context attributes.

controls.title: Information flow between employees and the institution (S) [Supervisors, Employees]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Regular team meetings are established (e.g., weekly) to exchange essential information. Important security updates or organizational changes are distributed to everyone via email. However, there are no central, fixed rules for availability or for handling problems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each team leader is instructed to hold a weekly team meeting in which teleworkers also participate. The IT department sends out informational emails as needed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews calendar entries or minutes of team meetings to confirm their regularity. It is checked whether important information has been communicated via email.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A regular internal exchange of information between employees and the institution SHOULD be ensured. All employees SHOULD be promptly informed about changed security requirements and other security-relevant aspects. All colleagues of the respective employees SHOULD know when and where they can be reached. Technical and organizational telework regulations for task management, security incidents, and other problems SHOULD be regulated and communicated to the employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy on information flow for telework is created. It specifies: fixed availability times, the use of calendars to display presence and absence, and a defined process for reporting security incidents via the IT helpdesk. Important information is communicated via an email distribution list and in regular meetings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the information flow policy. They randomly check the calendars of teleworkers for maintained availability times. It is verified whether a documented process for incident reporting exists and is known.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central communication platform (e.g., an intranet portal or a dedicated Microsoft Teams channel) is established as the binding 'Single Source of Truth' for all important information. The presence status is automatically integrated from the calendar into the communication tools. There is a formalized and tested process for reporting and handling incidents, specifically tailored to the needs of teleworkers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A corporate wiki (e.g., Confluence) is used for the central documentation of all policies and guidelines. The status integration between Outlook Calendar and Teams is activated for all employees. Regular exercises for reporting security incidents remotely are conducted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the central platform exists and is actively used. They check the configuration of the status integration. The documentation of the conducted incident handling exercises is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Communication is multi-channel and automated where appropriate. A dedicated, monitored emergency communication channel exists for urgent security warnings. A comprehensive, searchable knowledge base for telework-specific questions and problem-solving is actively maintained and used by employees. The effectiveness of the information flow is evaluated using metrics (e.g., read receipts, access to the knowledge base).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to Teams and email, a mobile app is used for push notifications for critical security warnings. The knowledge base is coupled with a chatbot that automatically answers initial inquiries. Analytics tools measure the interaction rates with important communications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the communication channels, including the emergency channel. They check the usage statistics of the knowledge base and the chatbot. The reports on the interaction rates are evaluated to assess the effectiveness of the information flow.

controls.title: Support and maintenance concept for teleworkstations (S) [IT Operations, Employees]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general IT support that is also responsible for teleworkstations. A contact point has been designated. However, there is no specific concept that addresses peculiarities such as remote maintenance, device transport, or guaranteed response times. Support is provided on a 'best-effort' basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Teleworkers contact the central IT helpdesk with problems. Remote maintenance is carried out ad-hoc using any remote desktop tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By reviewing support tickets and interviewing employees, the auditor determines that no formalized concept for the support of teleworkstations exists and that support is provided reactively.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A special support and maintenance concept SHOULD be created for teleworkstations. It SHOULD regulate the following aspects: contact person in IT operations, maintenance schedules, remote maintenance, transport of IT equipment, and the introduction of standard telework computers. To ensure employees remain operational, contact persons for hardware and software problems SHOULD be designated for them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document 'Telework Support Concept' is created. It names the responsible support group, describes the process for secure remote maintenance (e.g., via a specific tool), regulates the logistics for repairs, and defines a standard laptop for telework to simplify support.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the support and maintenance concept presented to them and checks whether the required aspects (contact person, remote maintenance, transport, etc.) are regulated therein. It is checked whether the designated contact persons and processes are known within the company.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The support concept includes defined Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for response and resolution times for problems at teleworkstations. Remote maintenance is carried out exclusively via a secure, centrally managed tool that records (audits) sessions. A standardized process for replacing defective hardware is established to minimize downtime (e.g., through advance replacement).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the IT Service Management tool (e.g., ServiceNow), SLAs for telework tickets are defined and monitored. A tool like BeyondTrust or TeamViewer (Enterprise version) with an audit log function is used for remote maintenance. A small pool of replacement devices is kept on hand.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the SLA reports from the ITSM tool. They check the configuration and audit logs of the remote maintenance tool. The process for hardware replacement is traced using exemplary cases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Support for teleworkstations is proactive. Client management tools continuously monitor the status of endpoints and automatically fix many problems before the user notices them (self-healing). A self-service portal allows employees to solve common problems themselves, request software, and track the status of their support requests. All support and maintenance activities are seamlessly and audibly logged in a central system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UEM solution with proactive remediation scripts (e.g., Intune Proactive Remediations) is used. The ITSM tool offers an extensive self-service portal with an integrated knowledge base and automated workflows for standard requests (e.g., password reset).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the proactive remediation scripts and their execution logs. They test the functionality of the self-service portal. The complete audit trails of all support activities in the ITSM system are checked on a random basis.

controls.title: Conducting a requirements analysis for the teleworkstation (S) [IT Operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A uniform standard hardware and software package is provided for all teleworkers, regardless of their specific role or tasks. An individual analysis of requirements does not take place. The protection requirement of the processed information is not explicitly assessed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department has defined a 'telework kit' (laptop, monitor, docking station) that everyone receives. A standard software image is installed on the laptop.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By reviewing the procurement and deployment processes, the auditor determines that a 'one-size-fits-all' approach is being followed without an individual requirements analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before a teleworkstation is set up, a requirements analysis SHOULD be conducted. This SHOULD indicate, for example, which hardware and software components are needed for the teleworkstation. The requirements for the respective teleworkstation SHOULD be coordinated with the IT managers. It SHOULD always be determined and documented what protection level is required for the information processed at the teleworkstation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before setting up a teleworkstation, the supervisor, together with the employee, fills out a requirements analysis form. This form records the required software and the type of data to be processed (e.g., 'public', 'internal', 'confidential'). The form is reviewed and archived by the IT department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the template for the requirements analysis. On a sample basis, for newly set-up teleworkstations, they check whether the form has been filled out and archived and whether the protection requirement of the data is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements analysis is a formalized, documented process based on employee role profiles and their data access rights. The results of the analysis, particularly the determined protection requirement, are directly incorporated into the configuration of security measures for the workstation (e.g., activation of disk encryption, assignment of stricter access policies). The analysis is repeated when an employee's role changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirements analysis is part of the digital onboarding process in the HR system. Depending on the role and the specified data classification, tickets are automatically created for the provisioning of appropriate hardware and software, as well as for the configuration of specific security settings (e.g., via assignment to a specific device group in the UEM).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the documented requirements analysis process. They trace the process for an exemplary employee from role definition to the concrete technical security configuration of the endpoint device and check whether the configuration corresponds to the protection requirement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements analysis is fully integrated into an automated Identity and Access Management (IAM) process. Based on an employee's role and projects, the required hardware, software, and access rights are dynamically assigned and revoked according to the need-to-know principle. The determination of protection requirements is directly linked to the organization's data classification scheme and automatically triggers the application of corresponding protection profiles (e.g., encryption, DLP, access controls).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central IAM system is the authoritative source. Changes in the HR system (e.g., department change) automatically trigger a workflow in the IAM system, which adjusts the workstation and permissions via interfaces to the UEM and ticketing system. Data classification tools scan data and automatically set protection requirement flags that are read by the security systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and workflows in the IAM system. They check the audit logs to trace the automatic assignment and revocation of resources. It is checked whether the active protection profiles on the endpoints match the classification of the data processed there.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: Teleworking is understood as any activity supported by information and communication technology that is carried out wholly or partly outside the business premises and buildings of the institution. In home-based teleworking, employees work alternately at their workplace on the institution's premises and at their home office on a regular basis, either for days or hours at a time.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of the module is to protect information that is stored, processed, and transmitted during teleworking. For this purpose, typical threats are identified and special requirements for secure teleworking are defined.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module OPS.1.2.4 Telework is to be applied for each teleworking workplace.

This module focuses on the form of telework that is carried out in the home environment (home-based telework). It is assumed that there is a secure telecommunications connection between the teleworking workplace and the institution, which allows for the appropriate exchange of information and access to data on the institution's server. The requirements of this module cover the following three areas:

•
the organization of telework,

•
the employees' workplace PCs, and

•
the communication link between teleworking computers and the institution.

Security requirements for the infrastructure of the teleworking workplace are not considered in this module but are described in module INF.8 Home Workplace. Requirements for a non-permanently established workplace are to be found in module INF.9 Mobile Workplace.

Detailed recommendations on how IT systems can be configured and secured are not covered within this module. They can be found in SYS.2.1 General Client as well as in the operating system-specific system modules. Other security aspects relevant to telework, such as for WLAN, are considered in the modules of the sub-layers NET.2 Wireless Networks or NET.4 Telecommunications.

If data that has been modified during telework is not immediately stored on the institution's IT systems, it must be regulated how a data backup is performed. Requirements for this can be found in module CON.3 Data Backup Concept.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Missing or inadequate regulations for the teleworking workstation
parts.prose: The use of a teleworking workstation requires supplementary organizational agreements between employees and managers. They also need instructions on how to act in the event of security-related incidents at the teleworking workstation. If, for example, confidential information falls into the hands of third parties, this can result in serious damage to the institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Unauthorized private use of the official teleworking computer
parts.prose: In the home environment, it is easier to use unchecked and unapproved hardware or software, and thus malware, for example, can get onto the teleworking computer through careless actions. This could compromise confidential information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Delays due to temporarily limited availability of employees
parts.prose: If employees do not have fixed working hours at the teleworking workstation and no fixed times are agreed upon when they must be available, the workflow can be delayed as a result.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Insufficient integration of employees into the information flow
parts.prose: Since employees are not in the institution every day, they have less opportunity to participate in the direct exchange of information with managers and colleagues. It is therefore possible that teleworkers may not receive information, especially information passed on verbally, or may receive it with a delay. This can disrupt workflows and operational processes and limit the productivity of the employee.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Non-compliance with security measures
parts.prose: At the teleworking workstation, for example, a lack of control options can lead to employees not implementing recommended or ordered security measures, or not implementing them in full. For example, confidential information could fall into the hands of third parties.

controls.title: Planning the Use of Remote Maintenance (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of remote maintenance is ad hoc and without formal planning. There is no documented overview of which systems are remotely maintained or who is responsible for them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, remote maintenance is usually only used when an immediate problem occurs that would prevent an on-site visit. Decisions are made by individual administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the administrators if a plan for remote maintenance exists. The absence of any written planning or a consistent procedure confirms this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is basic, informal planning in the form of a list of remotely maintained systems. Responsibilities are named, but organizational and detailed technical aspects are not systematically considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple list of the systems to be maintained is kept in a wiki or a shared file. The basic responsibility (e.g., 'Server Team') is known, but not differentiated per system or use case.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documents. They check whether a list of systems exists and whether basic responsibilities have been clarified. It is determined that a detailed technical and organizational plan is missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of remote maintenance MUST be adapted to the institution. Remote maintenance MUST be planned according to needs with regard to technical and organizational aspects. At a minimum, it MUST be considered which IT systems are to be remotely maintained and who is responsible for them.

parts.name: guidance
