parts.prose: A formal document 'Remote Maintenance Concept' is created. This document lists all IT systems approved for remote maintenance, names the responsible administrators or teams, and describes the basic organizational framework (e.g., approval processes).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the remote maintenance concept. It is checked whether it clearly names the remotely maintained systems and the responsible persons or roles. This can be verified by inspecting the document and interviewing the IT operations staff.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The remote maintenance plan is a formally approved and versioned document. It defines not only the systems and responsibilities, but also specific security requirements for the connections and tools. The plan is reviewed regularly, at least annually, and updated as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The remote maintenance concept is integrated into the institution's ISMS. Changes to the concept follow the established change management process. The review of the concept is filed as a periodic task in the ITSM tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the remote maintenance concept and checks its version history and approval records. It is verified that a process for regular review is established, e.g., by inspecting meeting minutes or tickets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The remote maintenance planning is fully integrated into the Asset and Configuration Management (CMDB). The approval of a system for remote maintenance is an attribute in the CMDB based on a formal risk assessment. The planning is continuously validated and updated through automated system discovery and configuration checks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system in the CMDB is marked with the 'remote maintenance enabled' flag. This flag can only be set after an approval workflow. Automated scripts regularly check if remote maintenance access (e.g., firewall rules) is active only for flagged systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the process in the CMDB demonstrated. An automated query is used to check whether the configuration of the remote maintenance systems (e.g., firewalls, PAM system) matches the approvals stored in the CMDB.

controls.title: Secure Connection Establishment for Remote Maintenance of Clients (B) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On some client systems, the remote maintenance software is configured to allow connections to be established without user interaction or consent. A uniform regulation is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators install the remote maintenance software with default settings that often allow unattended access to simplify administration. This is done inconsistently across the client fleet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a sample of client systems and checks the configuration of the remote maintenance software. It is found that on some systems, user consent is not required to establish a connection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The remote maintenance software is generally set up to inform the user of an incoming connection attempt, e.g., through a pop-up window. However, consent can be passive, for example, through a timeout.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default software configuration, which displays a notification, is rolled out to all clients. However, it is not ensured that an explicit, active action by the user is required.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the connection setup demonstrated on a typical client. It is observed that although a notification appears, the connection is established automatically after a certain time even without clicking 'Accept'.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When accessing client desktop environments via remote maintenance, the remote maintenance software MUST be configured to establish a connection only after explicit consent from the user.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: By means of a central administrative policy (e.g., GPO or MDM policy), the configuration of the remote maintenance software is enforced on all clients. The setting that requires explicit user consent (e.g., actively clicking a 'Yes' button) is enabled and cannot be changed by the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the central configuration policy (GPO, MDM) for the remote maintenance software. Additionally, on a sample of clients, it is verified that the setting is active and a connection is not possible without a user click. This can be verified through a test setup `gpresult /scope computer /r` (for GPO) or by querying the MDM configuration on the client.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The consent dialog box displays detailed information to the user, such as the name of the requesting administrator and the associated support case ticket number. The consent is logged centrally and in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The remote maintenance software is integrated with the ITSM/ticketing system. The connection request transmits the ticket ID. The consent dialog queries and displays this information. The result (accepted/rejected) is stored in the client's system log and centrally on the remote maintenance server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has a remote maintenance session demonstrated and checks whether the context-related information is displayed in the consent dialog. Afterwards, the central log files are inspected to verify the log entry for the consent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: User consent requires additional authentication. The administrator provides the user with a session-specific code via a second channel (e.g., telephone), which the user must enter. The user can revoke the session at any time with a prominently placed 'End Session' button, which disconnects the connection immediately and without further inquiry.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A remote maintenance solution that supports a 'Session PIN' or a similar function is used. The process is documented in the work instructions for IT support. The client software is configured so that the session control window always remains in the foreground.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor validates the process through a live demonstration. A check is performed to see if the connection fails without the correct PIN. Furthermore, the function for immediate session termination by the user is tested. The software's configuration settings are reviewed to verify the permanent visibility of the control window.

controls.title: Securing remote maintenance interfaces (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Remote maintenance interfaces are largely unrestricted and open. Sessions are not consistently terminated. Remote maintenance software is installed on many systems, even when not needed, and encryption is only used sporadically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Remote maintenance software is part of the standard client image. Firewall rules for remote maintenance are very broad (e.g., 'any' to 'any' for the remote maintenance port). Administrators regularly forget to log out after the session.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a network scan to identify open remote maintenance ports. The firewall configuration is checked and assessed as too permissive. A sample of systems is checked for unnecessarily installed remote maintenance software.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are basic restrictions for remote maintenance access, e.g., through perimeter firewall rules. Sessions are usually terminated manually. External connections are encrypted, but internal ones often are not.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On the central firewall, the remote maintenance port is open only for specific source IP ranges (e.g., of the external service providers). However, there are no further restrictions within the LAN. The administrators are instructed to terminate sessions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the perimeter firewall. During the examination of internal network traffic (e.g., via port mirroring), unencrypted remote maintenance traffic is detected. Active but unused sessions are found on servers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Possible access points and communication links for remote maintenance MUST be restricted to the necessary minimum. All remote maintenance connections MUST be terminated after remote access. It MUST be ensured that remote maintenance software is only installed on IT systems where it is needed. Remote maintenance connections over untrusted networks MUST be encrypted. All other remote maintenance connections SHOULD be encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specific firewall rules are created that only allow remote maintenance access from dedicated admin networks or jump servers. The remote maintenance software is installed on an as-needed basis via software distribution. A policy is established that mandates encryption for external connections and recommends it for internal ones. Terminating the connection after the session ends is stipulated in the administrators' work instructions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the firewall rules for specificity. The software distribution policies are checked to verify the as-needed installation. A sample of internal and external remote maintenance connections is checked for the use of encryption. For example, using `netstat -anp | grep <port>` to see the connection and `tcpdump` to see if the traffic is encrypted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All remote maintenance connections, both internal and external, must be strongly encrypted. Access is restricted to authorized devices by Network Access Control (NAC). Unused sessions are automatically terminated server-side by an automatic timeout. The installation of remote maintenance software is centrally monitored via an inventory system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The remote maintenance servers and clients are configured to only accept TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites. An NAC solution enforces that only managed devices with an up-to-date patch level can establish remote maintenance connections. The remote maintenance server is configured to automatically disconnect sessions after 30 minutes of inactivity.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the remote maintenance server with regard to the encryption settings and the session timeout. The NAC policies are reviewed. An inventory report is requested to verify the installation of the remote maintenance software.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A zero-trust network approach is implemented. Each remote maintenance access is explicitly authenticated and authorized per session. Using micro-segmentation, the remote maintenance interfaces on each system's host firewall are isolated so that only the jump server can access them. The installation of remote maintenance software is controlled and monitored by an application whitelisting solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM (Privileged Access Management) solution serves as a policy enforcement point for all access. Host-based firewalls (e.g., nftables on Linux, Windows Defender Firewall) are rolled out via configuration management to open the remote maintenance port only for the IP address of the PAM system. AppLocker or a similar tool prevents the execution of unapproved remote maintenance applications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the PAM solution and the centrally managed host firewall policies. An attempt is made to establish a connection from an unauthorized system, which must fail. The application whitelisting rules are checked.

controls.title: Use of online services (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Various administrators and teams use different, unverified online services for remote maintenance at their own discretion. There is no central policy or risk assessment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a user has a problem, the administrator instructs them to use any freely available online remote maintenance service to provide quick help. Security aspects such as encryption are not checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks various administrators which tools they use. The analysis of DNS or proxy logs shows connections to a variety of different online remote maintenance services.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A specific online service is used for remote maintenance, but there is no formal policy governing its use. It is superficially checked whether the service is encrypted (e.g., HTTPS), but true end-to-end encryption is not verified. Automatic connections at system startup are not explicitly prohibited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department has informally agreed to use a well-known online service. Its client software is installed when needed. The default configuration, which may allow automatic connections, is retained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the policy on the use of online services, which does not exist. It is checked whether client systems try to establish a connection to the online service after a restart (e.g., by checking autostart entries and network traffic).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD specify the circumstances under which online services may be used for remote maintenance where the connection is established via an external server. The use of such services SHOULD generally be limited to as few cases as possible. The IT systems SHOULD NOT establish automated connections to the online service. It SHOULD be ensured that the online service used encrypts the transmitted information end-to-end.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy is created that limits the use of online remote maintenance services to the support of external users. A specific service is selected whose manufacturer guarantees end-to-end encryption. The client software is configured so that it does not start automatically and does not establish persistent connections.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy on the use of online services. The configuration of a sample client is checked to ensure that no automatic connections are established. The manufacturer's documentation on end-to-end encryption is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A specific online service, audited and approved by the CISO, is mandatory in the policy. Technical controls (e.g., proxy and DNS filters) prevent the use of other services. The assurance of end-to-end encryption is validated by independent test reports or certifications (e.g., according to BSI TR-02102).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The URL of the permitted service is entered on the proxy whitelist. All other services in the "Remote Maintenance" category are blocked. Before selecting the service, a market analysis is conducted and the security documentation of the providers is compared.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the web proxy or DNS filters. An attempt is made to use an unapproved service, which must fail. The CISO's approval documentation and the external audit reports for the selected service are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of external cloud-based remote maintenance services is generally prohibited. Instead, a self-hosted gateway solution (on-premises) is operated, which offers similar functionality but keeps all communication and control within one's own security domain. All connections through the gateway are inspected and logged at the protocol level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An on-premises version of a remote maintenance solution or an open-source product like Apache Guacamole is installed on hardened servers in a DMZ. All remote maintenance traffic is routed through this gateway and monitored by a Web Application Firewall (WAF) or an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the architecture and configuration of the self-hosted gateway solution. The log files of the gateway and the monitoring systems are checked for completeness and significance. Egress firewall rules are checked to ensure that no direct connections to external remote maintenance services are possible.

controls.title: Creation of a remote maintenance policy (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no written regulations for remote maintenance. The procedure is based exclusively on orally transmitted, informal practices within the IT team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New administrators learn the remote maintenance procedure by watching and asking more experienced colleagues. There is no documentation they can refer to.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the remote maintenance policy to be presented. The employees interviewed confirm that no such written policy exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are some written regulations and instructions for remote maintenance, but they are scattered across various documents and knowledge bases and are not consolidated into a single, official policy. Not all parties involved are aware of all relevant regulations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One team has stored instructions for its specific remote maintenance tool in a wiki, while another team maintains its rules in a shared text document. There is no overarching policy approved by management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor collects the various existing documents and finds that they are inconsistent and incomplete. Interviews with employees from different teams show that knowledge of the regulations is patchy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD create a remote maintenance policy that documents all relevant regulations for remote maintenance. The policy SHOULD be known to all responsible parties involved in the design, setup, and operation of remote maintenance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central policy document "P-RemoteMaintenance" is created that covers all aspects (permitted tools, authentication requirements, logging, etc.). This document is published on the intranet, and all members of the IT department are informed about it via email.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the remote maintenance policy and checks it for completeness. By interviewing responsible employees, it is checked on a random basis whether the policy and its contents are known.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The remote maintenance policy is a formally approved, versioned, and controlled document within the ISMS. There is a documented process to communicate the policy and its changes to all relevant employees. The employees' acknowledgement of the policy is documented in a verifiable manner, e.g., through a read receipt.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is managed in a document management system (DMS) with an approval workflow. After each significant change, a training or information campaign is launched, and participation or acknowledgement is recorded in a learning management system (LMS) or via email confirmation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy in the DMS and checks the version history and the approval records. The evidence for communication and acknowledgement (e.g., extract from the LMS, list of read receipts) is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The remote maintenance policy is integrated into automated processes. Access to remote maintenance tools is technically granted only after the administrator has confirmed the current version of the policy in a system. Key elements of the policy (e.g., permitted protocols, MFA usage) are enforced by technical configuration requirements and permanently checked by automated audits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system checks whether the "Policy-RemoteMaintenance-V3-confirmed" attribute is set for the user before granting remote maintenance access. Configuration management tools (e.g., Ansible, Puppet) roll out configurations that comply with the policy's specifications. A compliance scanner checks the configurations against the policy requirements daily.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the automated process in the IAM system demonstrated to them. The configuration templates in the configuration management tool are compared with the policy. The results of the automated compliance scans are evaluated. An `osquery` or `ansible --check` can check this automatically.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
The term remote maintenance refers to a time-limited access to IT systems and the applications running on them, which is carried out from another IT system. The access can be used, for example, to carry out configuration, maintenance, or repair work.
Remote maintenance can be done in different ways. In the case of remote maintenance of clients, the keyboard and mouse signals of IT systems are often transmitted from the administrators to a remote IT system. The remote IT system transmits the screen output to the administrators' IT system. The administrators perform actions on the remote IT system as if they were on site themselves (active remote maintenance). In the case of remote maintenance of servers, the input and output of the console are often transmitted.
In passive remote maintenance, only the screen contents of an IT system are transmitted to the administrators. Administrators give instructions to the users on site, which are carried out by them and observed by the administrators. However, in practice, this procedure usually proves to be very time-consuming and cumbersome, which is why IT operations are often given full access via the IT system.
Since many IT systems are outside the reach of their administrators (e.g., in remote data centers, industrial plants, or an external location without IT staff), remote maintenance is used in many institutions. Remote maintenance often involves accessing internal IT systems and applications of an institution via insecure networks. Due to the far-reaching intervention possibilities in these IT systems and applications, the security of remote maintenance components is of particular importance.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to protect the information that is stored, processed, and transmitted during remote maintenance, as well as to protect the remote maintenance interfaces of IT systems. For this purpose, requirements are placed on remote maintenance that relate equally to the functions of active and passive remote maintenance.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module is to be applied to all target objects in the information domain where remote maintenance is used.
This module looks at remote maintenance primarily from the perspective of IT operations and provides guidance for administrators on how remote maintenance can be used. The security aspects of the communication links and authentication mechanisms used, as well as the security of the remote maintenance access points, are important components of this module. Nevertheless, it does not cover all relevant aspects of the business processes associated with remote maintenance. In particular, the modules OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management, ORP.3 Information Security Awareness and Training, CON.1 Crypto-Concept, and CON.3 Data Backup Concept must also be considered. Likewise, the specifications of the NET Networks and Communication layer must be implemented if they are directly related to remote maintenance.
If remote maintenance is carried out by external service providers, the OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing module must also be observed. If cloud-based remote maintenance products are used, the general requirements from the OPS.2.2 Cloud Use module must also be met.
Requirements for securing remote maintenance by means of firewalls are not part of this module. Requirements for this can be found in the NET.3.2 Firewall module.
Fundamental aspects of IT administration are also not considered in this module. They can be found in the OPS.1.1.2 Orderly IT Administration module. Requirements for system management are also not considered. These can be found in the OPS.1.1.7 System Management module.
The focus of the module is not on remote maintenance in the industrial environment. Requirements for this can be found in the IND.3.2 Remote Maintenance in the Industrial Environment module.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficient knowledge of remote maintenance regulations
parts.prose: Administrators who set up and use remote maintenance are dependent on regulations that specify how remote maintenance should be used. For example, it is necessary to specify how remote maintenance applications should be configured. Otherwise, remote maintenance can create additional risks for the internal network. If the parties involved are not informed of the regulations for remote maintenance, dangers arise for IT operations. For example, a remote maintenance interface could be set up and an authentication method with an insecure password could be allowed instead of a secure, certificate-based method.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Missing or insufficient planning and regulation of remote maintenance
parts.prose: If remote maintenance is not carefully planned, established, and regulated, the security of all of an institution's IT systems can be compromised. If, for example, insecure communication protocols, encryption algorithms, or authentication mechanisms are used, security vulnerabilities can arise. An inadequately secured remote maintenance interface can also lead to the compromise of a coupled network of a third party.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Inappropriate use of authentication in remote maintenance
parts.prose:
Different authentication mechanisms can be used for remote maintenance. If an insecure authentication method is used, unauthorized third parties can gain administrative privileges on remote maintenance systems or for remote maintenance tools. This allows them to access an institution's IT systems and cause extensive damage.
An example of this is a login procedure that uses only a short password. In an attack, this password can be guessed in a short time, thus gaining access to the institution's IT systems.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Faulty remote maintenance
parts.prose: To ensure the security and functionality of IT systems and applications that can only be accessed remotely, professional and regular remote maintenance is required. If such IT systems and applications are not properly configured and maintained via remote access, they may become unusable in the worst-case scenario. If remote maintenance processes do not run correctly, this can lead to malfunctions of individual operating system components. Furthermore, delayed or faulty IT system maintenance can create security vulnerabilities.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Use of insecure protocols in remote maintenance
parts.prose: Communication over public and internal networks using insecure protocols poses a potential threat. If, for example, outdated versions of IPSec, SSH, or SSL/TLS are used to establish a tunnel between two networks or endpoints, it cannot be guaranteed that this tunnel is sufficiently secure and that the information transmitted within it is adequately protected. In an attack, vulnerabilities in these protocols can be exploited to inject content into protected connections. Protocols that transmit information in cleartext are generally considered insecure.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Lack of regulations for third-party use of remote maintenance access
parts.prose: If IT systems are remotely maintained by third parties without a contractual basis, the responsibilities for remote maintenance may not be clearly regulated. This can, for example, lead to the circumvention of role separation or to open remote maintenance access points not being documented.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Use of online services for remote maintenance
parts.prose:
In addition to remote maintenance where a direct data connection to the respective institution is established, online services can also be used. In this case, the IT systems to be administered connect to the servers of online services, and administrators can access these IT systems, for example, via a web browser.
If the communication is not end-to-end encrypted, the online services could eavesdrop on the data exchange. Additionally, the IT systems could be administered by unauthorized persons by altering the data connection. If the IT systems automatically establish a data connection to the online service at system startup, the IT system could be accessed directly without the knowledge of the IT system's users or the responsible administrators.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unknown remote maintenance components
parts.prose:
Many IT systems contain components that offer integrated functions for remote maintenance. Often, however, these functions are poorly documented and are not considered during the procurement and operation of IT systems.
Integrated remote maintenance components have extensive access to the IT systems in which they are installed. This access often directly affects other components of the IT system and can thus bypass the operating system's security mechanisms. Additionally, integrated remote maintenance functions can contain vulnerabilities that facilitate unauthorized access to the IT system.

controls.title: Planning of NTP deployment

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: NTP is used ad-hoc only for individual systems considered critical. There is no formal plan, and the configuration is not documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Configuration is done manually on the respective systems, often by different administrators without a uniform procedure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the administrators if and how NTP is used. A random check is performed to see if an NTP configuration is present on some systems. The lack of documentation is noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic plan that specifies which systems require NTP. However, this plan is incomplete and does not go into details such as server selection, operating modes, or specific application requirements. The documentation is superficial.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of standard NTP servers (e.g., from the internet) is used for all clients. The operating modes are mostly left at their default values.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the NTP plan and compares it with the configuration of some systems. It is checked whether the basic specifications (e.g., which systems use NTP) have been implemented. Gaps in planning and documentation are noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The IT operations MUST create a documented plan on where and how NTP is used. It MUST be determined which applications rely on accurate time information, and the accuracy requirements MUST be defined. It MUST be specified which NTP servers are used by which NTP clients and whether the client-server or broadcast mode is used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NTP plan is an official document that is maintained as part of configuration management. It contains a list of authorized internal and external NTP servers, an assignment of client groups to servers, and the defined operating modes for different network segments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the NTP plan and verifies its completeness. It is checked on a random basis on several clients and servers whether the configuration corresponds to the specifications of the plan. This includes the configured servers, the operating mode, and application-specific requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The NTP plan is complete, reviewed regularly, and updated as needed. It explicitly considers fallback scenarios for the failure of time sources and the effects of network segmentation on NTP communication. The documentation is detailed and accessible to all relevant employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The plan is implemented using a configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible, Puppet) to ensure consistent configuration on all systems. Changes to the plan go through a formal approval process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies not only the existence and implementation of the plan, but also the process for its review and update. It is checked whether the fallback scenarios defined in the plan are technically feasible and have been tested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The time synchronization concept is fully integrated into a central configuration management database (CMDB). Compliance with the plan is continuously and automatically monitored. The concept proactively considers future growth and changing application requirements and is part of the overall IT architecture planning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An automated system checks the NTP configuration of all connected systems against the specifications in the CMDB daily. Any deviation triggers an alert or an automated correction workflow.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the reports from the automated monitoring system. It is checked how deviations are responded to. In addition, the integration of the NTP concept into the CMDB and the architecture processes is evaluated.

controls.title: Secure use of external time sources

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: External NTP servers from the internet are used without any assessment of their reliability or trustworthiness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators select any easily found public NTP servers and configure them on the systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through configuration review that arbitrary external NTP servers are being used and that there is no documentation on the evaluation of these sources.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A list of well-known public NTP pools (e.g., pool.ntp.org) is used, assuming their general reliability. However, the terms of use of these services are not explicitly checked or observed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard configuration for all clients points to a general NTP pool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies the use of public NTP pools and asks whether the terms of use are known and whether a reliability assessment has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If time information is obtained from external NTP servers, the IT operations MUST assess their reliability and document this. It MUST be ensured that only servers classified as reliable are used. The IT operations MUST know and observe the terms of use of the external NTP servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of approved external NTP servers (e.g., from PTB, NIST, or other national institutes) is maintained. The assessment of reliability and the acknowledgement of the terms of use are recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation for the evaluation of external time sources. It is checked whether the servers configured on the systems match the list of approved servers and whether the terms of use are documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evaluation of external NTP servers is repeated periodically to capture changes in their reliability or terms of use. A diversified set of external sources (e.g., from different countries or from different providers) is used to avoid a single point of failure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The list of external NTP servers is reviewed at least annually. The internal NTP servers are configured to use a mix of these sources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the process for the regular review of external time sources and checks the configuration of the internal servers for the use of a diversified set of sources.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution minimizes its dependence on external third parties by operating its own Stratum 1 servers, which are synchronized with highly trustworthy sources (e.g., GPS, DCF77). If external servers are still used, their performance (jitter, offset, availability) is continuously monitored to detect deviations immediately.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Own GPS or DCF77 receivers are connected to the internal Stratum 1 servers. A monitoring tool like Nagios or Zabbix with NTP plugins permanently monitors the quality of the external and internal time sources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the physical Stratum 1 time sources. The reports from the monitoring system are reviewed to verify the continuous quality control of the time sources.

controls.title: Secure configuration of NTP servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: NTP servers run with default configurations that potentially allow any client to query the status or change settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NTP service is installed and started without modifying the provided configuration file.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration files of NTP servers and finds that no restrictive settings have been made. A test with `ntpq -c peers <server>` from an unauthorized client is successful.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are basic restrictions in place, such as disabling remote configuration from untrusted networks, but not granularly for specific clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the configuration file, `disable monitor` and `restrict default noquery nomodify` are set, but access for the internal network is permitted wholesale.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that basic security measures are present in the configuration, but no granular access control for status information or configuration changes is implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The NTP server MUST be configured so that unauthorized clients cannot change any settings. Access to status information MUST be restricted to trusted clients (e.g., monitoring systems). Internal NTP servers MUST be configured to obtain time information from reliable external or higher-level internal servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NTP configuration (e.g., `ntp.conf`) uses `restrict` statements to precisely control access. Only the IP addresses of the monitoring systems are allowed to query status, and only authorized administration hosts are allowed to make configuration changes. The `server` or `pool` statements refer to the approved, upstream time sources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the `restrict` statements in the NTP configuration and compares the entered IP addresses with the list of authorized systems. It is checked whether the configured upstream servers correspond to the time source plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The NTP server configuration is hardened. Unnecessary NTP control messages are disabled. Access control is secured not only via IP addresses but also via NTP authentication mechanisms (e.g., symmetric keys) for administrative access and the exchange of status information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the `restrict` statements, `keys` and `trustedkey` are used to secure the query of status information by the monitoring system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the implementation of NTP authentication. It is checked whether the keys are stored securely and whether the clients (e.g., the monitoring system) are also configured for authenticated communication.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The NTP server configuration is managed via a configuration management system, with all changes logged and audited. Any deviation from the secure baseline configuration triggers an alarm. All administrative access is protected by strong authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Ansible playbooks or Puppet modules define the hardened state of the NTP configuration. A regular compliance check (e.g., using InSpec or OpenSCAP) checks the live configuration against the baseline. Changes are only possible through the automated process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration templates in the configuration management system as well as the reports of the compliance checks. The process for managing configuration changes and the response to detected deviations is assessed.

controls.title: Ignoring unsolicited time information

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some clients are configured to accept unsolicited NTP packets (e.g., in broadcast mode) in certain subnets, while others are not. There is no uniform regulation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In some network segments where the configuration is considered simple, broadcast mode is used without considering the security implications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During a random check of client configurations, the auditor discovers that different modes are used and some clients are configured to receive broadcast packets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All clients are generally configured to only query their designated servers. However, no specific configuration is applied to explicitly block unsolicited broadcast or multicast packets.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The clients are operated in client-server mode, but no additional measures are taken to prevent the acceptance of broadcast packets if they reach the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the clients are operating in client-server mode, but notes that there are no explicit configurations (e.g., `disable broadcast`) to prevent the acceptance of unsolicited packets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations MUST configure all NTP clients to discard time information that they receive unsolicited from other IT systems (e.g., NTP broadcast or multicast packets).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All NTP clients are explicitly configured for client-server mode. In the configuration of the NTP daemon, the acceptance of broadcast packets is explicitly disabled (e.g., by `disable broadcastclient` in chrony or corresponding `restrict` rules in ntpd).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration files of the NTP clients and verifies that the acceptance of unsolicited packets is explicitly disabled. This can be done automatically through a configuration scan that searches for the corresponding directive.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to configuring the clients, network firewalls are configured to block NTP broadcast and multicast traffic from untrusted segments to enforce the policy at the network level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access Control Lists (ACLs) are implemented on the firewalls and routers between the network segments, which block NTP packets to broadcast (255.255.255.255) or multicast addresses.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks not only the client configurations but also the rules of the network firewalls and routers to ensure that the blocking of NTP broadcast/multicast traffic is effective.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The compliance of client and network configurations is checked automatically. An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is configured to trigger an alarm for any NTP broadcast or multicast traffic in segments where it is not explicitly permitted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IDS like Suricata or Snort is equipped with rules that look for NTP broadcast packets (port 123). In case of a match, a ticket is automatically created in the security team's system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the IDS configuration and its associated alerting rules. It is checked whether alarms have occurred in recent months and how they were responded to. As a test, an NTP broadcast packet can be generated to verify detection.

controls.title: Use of Client-Server Mode for NTP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only some clients use client-server mode. Others, especially in networks classified as non-critical, still use broadcast mode as it is easier to configure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no clear guideline, so the choice of mode is left to the respective administrator.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through random checks that both client-server and broadcast modes are used in a mixed fashion in the network.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Most systems are configured for client-server mode, but some legacy systems or special network segments (e.g., OT) may still use broadcast mode.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an informal policy to prefer client-server mode, but there is no formal process for exceptions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that client-server mode is the rule, but finds undocumented exceptions. It is checked whether the reasons for these exceptions are comprehensible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a policy that prescribes client-server mode as the standard for time synchronization. All NTP servers and clients SHOULD be configured accordingly, so that servers only send time information upon active request from clients. Deviations (e.g., the use of broadcast mode in isolated OT networks) are documented and risk-assessed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default images and configuration templates for new systems exclusively provide for client-server mode. A justified request must be submitted and approved for any exception.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the NTP operations policy. The configuration of servers and clients is checked on a random basis. In case of deviations, the corresponding documentation and risk assessment are requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Client-server mode is mandatory for all systems. Broadcast mode is explicitly forbidden and blocked at the network level, unless there is a documented and approved exception. Server configurations are hardened to respond only to explicit requests from known clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Network ACLs block NTP broadcast traffic at VLAN boundaries. NTP servers are configured with `restrict` statements that only allow requests from authorized client networks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the client configurations and the network ACLs. It is checked whether the server configurations effectively restrict access to known clients.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The exclusive use of client-server mode is enforced by automated configuration management and continuous monitoring systems. Any attempt by a system to send or receive NTP broadcasts triggers an automated security alarm and/or a remediation action.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM system correlates data from network sensors (IDS) and configuration audit tools. If a system is detected sending broadcast packets, it can be automatically moved to a quarantine network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the rules and actions in the SIEM and automation system. The end-to-end process from detecting a deviation to responding to it is assessed.

controls.title: Monitoring of IT systems using NTP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the basic reachability of the NTP servers (e.g., via ping) is monitored. Logs from NTP clients or servers are not collected or evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple monitoring tool checks every five minutes whether the NTP server responds to a ping.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that only a ping check exists and that there is no specific monitoring of the NTP service or the logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The availability of the servers and a basic check of the NTP service are performed. Client logs are generated locally on the systems but are not centrally collected or regularly reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The monitoring also checks if the NTP process is running on the server. The log files on the clients are only manually inspected in case of an error.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the server monitoring. It is checked on a random basis on clients whether logs are being generated, and it is determined that no central collection or evaluation is taking place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD monitor the availability, capacity, and system time of the internal NTP servers. IT systems that use NTP SHOULD be configured to log critical events. These include unexpected system or NTP service restarts, NTP errors, and unusual time information (e.g., large time jumps). These logs SHOULD be collected centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central monitoring system (e.g., Zabbix, Prometheus) actively queries the status of the NTP servers (offset, jitter, stratum). At the same time, the system and NTP logs of all clients and servers are sent to a central log management system (e.g., Graylog, ELK stack).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration of the monitoring system and the log management system. It is verified that the relevant metrics of the servers are monitored and that the defined events from the clients are logged and centrally collected. It can be automatically checked whether log forwarders for the corresponding log files are configured on clients.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The centrally collected logs are actively monitored. Automated alarms are configured for critical events such as significant time deviations, service outages, or frequent restarts. Baselines for normal operation (e.g., normal jitter) are established, and deviations from them are reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Dashboards and alerting rules are created in the log management system. An alarm is triggered, for example, if a server's time offset exceeds 50 milliseconds or a client reports a time jump of more than one second.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configured dashboards and alerting rules. The process for handling alerts is examined. Based on historical data, it is assessed whether the thresholds for the alerts are set appropriately.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The monitoring is integrated into a SIEM system. Correlation rules are used to detect complex attacks, such as slow, stealthy time manipulations over a long period. Automated responses are triggered for specific alerts, e.g., isolating a client that repeatedly reports incorrect time information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM rule correlates NTP log entries from multiple clients. If multiple clients simultaneously report a specific server as unreliable, this server is automatically removed from the clients' configuration and a technician is notified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the complex correlation rules and the configured automated responses in the SIEM. The effectiveness of these rules is assessed based on simulated attack scenarios or past real incidents.

controls.title: Secure configuration of NTP clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Clients use default settings that may accept arbitrary time updates, including large and incorrect ones, especially at system startup.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NTP client software is operated without adjusting the configuration file.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the client configurations are not hardened and contain no precautions against large time jumps.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some basic client settings are configured, e.g., entering multiple servers. However, the behavior on restart or in case of large time jumps is not explicitly defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each client is configured with two or three internal NTP servers, but other parameters like `maxpoll` or `iburst` are not adjusted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that multiple servers are configured, but notes that no explicit policies for handling errors or large time discrepancies have been implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD establish a documented configuration policy for NTP clients. This SHOULD define how clients react to significantly deviating time information, especially after a reboot. Thresholds for significantly deviating time information SHOULD be defined. Furthermore, it SHOULD be ensured that clients can still synchronize even when a server requests them to reduce queries (KoD packets).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a standard configuration (e.g., for `chrony.conf`) that sensibly sets options like `maxchange`, `makestep`, and `iburst`. This configuration is used for all clients and ensures that large time jumps only occur at startup and within a defined threshold.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the configuration policy for NTP clients and compares it with the live configurations. It is checked whether the parameters for controlling time jumps and handling rate limiting are set correctly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The client configuration is hardened. It specifies a pool of multiple trusted servers. The client is configured to never make large time jumps during operation, but to slowly adjust the clock (`slewing`), unless this is explicitly required after a reboot. The configuration is deployed and enforced via a configuration management tool.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the ntpd configuration, the `-x` option is used to prevent time jumps. Ansible or a similar tool ensures that this configuration is consistent across all clients.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration in the configuration management tool and checks on the clients whether the resulting process parameters (e.g., via `ps aux | grep ntpd`) contain the desired options. It is examined how deviations from the configuration are handled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The behavior of the clients is dynamically monitored. Any client that accepts a time change outside the defined thresholds or does not synchronize correctly triggers an alarm. The configuration is part of a 'Golden Image' and is automatically checked for compliance with every system change.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM monitors the NTP client logs for messages about large time jumps ('time reset'). A compliance scan checks the NTP configuration file at every system startup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the alerting rules in the SIEM and the configuration of the compliance scan. It is analyzed whether the monitoring is complete and whether alerts are responded to appropriately.

controls.title: Use of secure protocols for time synchronization

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No secure protocols for time synchronization are used. The possibility is not considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Time synchronization is done exclusively via unsecured NTP (UDP Port 123).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by reviewing the configurations that no mechanisms such as NTS or NTP with symmetric keys are in use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic evaluation of secure time protocols was conducted, but no implementation was carried out due to perceived complexity or lack of system support.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an internal document that describes the pros and cons of NTS, but it concludes that an introduction is currently not feasible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the evaluation document and questions the reasons for non-implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD check whether secure time synchronization protocols such as Network Time Security (NTS) can be used. If this is technically feasible and supported by the systems, secure protocols SHOULD be implemented. The decision and the result of the check SHOULD be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal, documented evaluation is conducted to determine which systems support NTS or NTP with symmetric keys. For supported systems, a plan for introducing secure time synchronization is created and implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the evaluation documentation. It is checked on a random sample of systems classified as 'capable' whether secure time synchronization is actually configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: NTS or NTP with symmetric keys is used on all capable critical systems. The process for managing the symmetric keys is clearly defined, documented, and secure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An appropriate server infrastructure is operated for NTS. For symmetric authentication, the keys are securely generated, distributed (e.g., via a configuration management tool), and rotated regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the key management process for its security and effectiveness. It is checked whether the key rotation takes place as defined.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: NTS is the standard for all time synchronization in the network. Systems that do not support NTS are operated in dedicated, isolated network segments, and the associated risk is formally accepted. The entire NTS infrastructure (e.g., the Key Establishment Server) is designed redundantly and is monitored for security and availability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All new systems must support NTS to be operated in the main network. The NTS servers are redundant and geographically distributed. Their operational status is continuously monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the implementation of the NTS standard policy. The redundancy and monitoring of the NTS infrastructure are checked. For systems without NTS, the risk acceptance documentation and the effectiveness of the isolation are reviewed.

controls.title: Availability of a sufficient number of accurate time sources

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is only a single internal NTP server, which may get its time from a single source on the internet.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One server in the network is configured as an NTP server and is used by all clients. There is no backup server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the NTP infrastructure represents a single point of failure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are at least two internal NTP servers for redundancy, but they may not be Stratum 1 and may get their time from the same external source.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two servers are configured as NTP servers and both synchronize with `pool.ntp.org`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes the redundancy of the servers but criticizes the lack of diversity in the upstream time sources.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD have at least two Stratum-1 NTP servers in its network. These servers SHOULD be used directly or indirectly as the primary time reference for all internal IT systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two servers in the data center are each equipped with their own GPS receiver and configured as Stratum-1 servers. All other internal NTP servers (Stratum 2) synchronize with these two servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and configuration of the two Stratum-1 servers. It is checked whether they are established as the primary reference in the network. This can be verified by `ntpq -p` on the Stratum-2 servers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution operates several (three or more) Stratum-1 NTP servers. Each of these servers uses a different physical time source (e.g., one GPS, one DCF77, one an external source via NTS) to ensure diversity and resilience against the failure or disruption of a single time system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One server is equipped with a GPS receiver, a second with a DCF77 receiver. A third server synchronizes with a trusted external source such as the PTB via a secure NTS connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the different physical time sources of the Stratum-1 servers. The server configuration is checked to confirm the diversity of the sources.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A geographically distributed cluster of diverse Stratum-1 servers is operated. The health and accuracy of each individual time source is continuously monitored. The system can automatically classify a faulty time source as untrustworthy through cross-comparisons with the other sources and exclude it from the synchronization process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Stratum-1 servers are located in different fire compartments or even at different sites. A central monitoring system permanently analyzes the peer statistics of all Stratum-2 servers and alerts if a Stratum-1 server deviates significantly from the others.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the geographical distribution and the configuration of the monitoring. It is checked whether the process for automatically excluding a faulty source is implemented and has been tested, for example, by a simulated failure of a GPS receiver.

controls.title: Exclusively internal NTP servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Many clients get their time information directly from public NTP servers on the internet, without using the internal servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Standard installations of operating systems that point to public servers are not adjusted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During a random check of client configurations, the auditor finds that many point to external servers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a policy to use internal servers, but it is not strictly enforced, and some systems still point to external servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The internal servers are entered in most configuration templates, but there is no control to prevent divergent manual configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy and determines during the review that there are non-enforced deviations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every IT system in the information network with an NTP service SHOULD obtain time information exclusively from the institution's designated internal NTP servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All system images, installation scripts, and configuration management tools are configured to exclusively register the internal NTP servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configurations of various clients and verifies that they point exclusively to internal NTP servers. This can be done via an automated scan of the configuration files on all systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to client configuration, rules are implemented on the network firewall to block outbound NTP traffic (port 123) from all clients to the internet. This enforces the use of internal servers. Exceptions are documented and tightly controlled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A rule is created on the perimeter firewall that blocks outbound UDP traffic on port 123 from all client VLANs. Only the internal Stratum 1 servers are allowed to send NTP traffic to the internet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rules to confirm the effectiveness of the block. It is checked whether the process for exception rules is being followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy is enforced both by configuration management on the clients and by blocks at the network level. Any attempt by a client to establish outbound NTP traffic is logged and triggers an automated security alert for immediate investigation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The firewall rule for blocking NTP traffic is configured with logging. The logs are sent to a SIEM, which generates an alert upon a hit (a client attempts to reach an external NTP server).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the firewall rule and the SIEM alerting. An attempt is made to reach an external NTP server from a test client to verify that the block and the alerting function as expected.

controls.title: Redundant NTP Servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Critical systems use only one or two NTP servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The client configuration contains only a single `server` entry.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During the review of critical systems, the auditor finds that no redundant NTP servers are configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Critical systems are configured with two or three NTP servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The clients are configured with two servers for simple redundancy, but this is not sufficient for robust fault detection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that redundancy is present, but the number of servers does not meet the best practice for NTP fault detection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT systems for which the accuracy of the system time is of significant importance SHOULD obtain time information from at least four independent NTP servers to enable robust fault tolerance and the detection of outliers (falsetickers).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Four different internal NTP servers are entered in the configuration templates for all systems classified as critical (e.g., domain controllers, database systems).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies the critical systems and checks their NTP configuration for the use of at least four servers. In an automated way, a script can parse the configuration files on the target systems and count the number of `server` entries.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The four (or more) configured servers are a mix of different strata (e.g., two Stratum 2 and two Stratum 3 servers) and are located in different physical locations or network segments to increase resilience against network failures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A critical client is configured to use two NTP servers in the primary data center and two more in the secondary data center.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the NTP topology and the configuration of the critical clients to ensure that the configured servers are in fact independent and resilient (i.e., not all dependent on the same parent server or switch).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration to use at least four independent servers is automatically deployed and verified on all critical systems. The NTP client's peer statistics are continuously monitored to ensure that it is actively communicating with a sufficient number of servers and correctly identifies and discards outliers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitoring system regularly queries the status of the NTP daemon on critical clients (`ntpq -p`, `chronyc sources`). An alert is triggered if the number of reachable and validly marked servers falls below four.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and reports of the monitoring system. It is analyzed how alarms that report an insufficient number of time sources are responded to.

controls.title: NTP servers with authenticated responses

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No authentication is used for NTP communication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All NTP communication takes place unsecured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through configuration review that no authentication mechanisms are configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: NTP authentication (e.g., with symmetric keys) is used for communication between NTP servers (peer-to-peer), but not for communication from servers to clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Stratum 2 servers authenticate each other, but the clients receive unauthenticated time information.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the authenticated communication between the servers, but finds that the clients are communicating unsecured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: NTP servers SHOULD authenticate themselves to clients during communication. This SHOULD also apply to the servers from which the NTP server in turn receives time information. NTP clients SHOULD be configured to only accept authenticated NTP data. For this purpose, e.g., NTP with symmetric keys can be used. A process for managing and distributing the keys is established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A key file (`ntp.keys`) is created and securely distributed to all servers and clients. The configurations (`ntp.conf`) are adapted to use the keys (`key` option in server entries) and to discard non-authenticated packets.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of servers and clients for the correct use of NTP authentication. The process for key distribution and management is evaluated. A packet capture can show whether the NTP packets are authenticated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network Time Security (NTS) is used as the preferred method for authenticated time synchronization, as it provides cryptographic security without the administrative overhead of symmetric keys. The key management process for remaining systems with symmetric keys is automated and secure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Internal servers are configured as NTS-KE (Key Establishment) servers. Clients that support NTS (e.g., chrony) are configured for NTS use. The distribution of symmetric keys for legacy systems is handled by a configuration management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the NTS infrastructure. It is checked whether clients are successfully using NTS. The automated process for managing symmetric keys is evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: NTS is mandatory for all NTP communication. The NTS-KE server infrastructure is redundant and hardened. Any unauthenticated NTP traffic is blocked at the network level and triggers a security alert.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Firewall rules only allow NTP traffic if it runs over NTS (typically via TLS on port 4460 for key establishment). Unencrypted NTP traffic on port 123 is blocked and logged. The NTS servers are designed to be redundant and are monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rules that block unsecured NTP traffic. The redundancy and hardening of the NTS-KE servers are checked. It is verified that blocking attempts are correctly alerted.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Networked IT systems often require synchronous states. The time of day usually serves as a reference. However, the internal clock of IT systems can deviate from the actual time. The Network Time Protocol (NTP) is used to regularly determine a reference time from central timekeepers via network connections and to adjust the internal clock accordingly.

In networks, precise time synchronization allows for information to be provided with uniform timestamps, e.g., to chronologically order data, reconcile data, or limit access rights in time. This is the only way, for example, to correlate temporal sequences from log data of different IT systems. Precise time information is also important in the area of cryptographic protocols. Furthermore, in OT networks it is essential to precisely synchronize all time sources.

NTP clients obtain time information from NTP servers. The NTP servers, in turn, can obtain time information from other NTP servers as NTP clients. This creates a hierarchical time distribution (into so-called "strata"). At the top are NTP servers that receive their time from precise sources (e.g., an atomic clock, a GPS or a DCF77 receiver). These NTP servers are referred to as Stratum-1.

The NTP service uses methods to determine the deviation of the system clock from external time sources, even with differing responses from various time sources. For example, it ignores time data from a time source that suddenly deviates significantly from its own system time.

Control messages allow clients to query status information or to change the behavior of the NTP server, even across the network.

NTP messages are usually transmitted unsecured. However, NTP offers the option of protecting a message with cryptographic keys so that the message cannot be altered without authorization.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to secure NTP servers and clients in such a way that the IT systems in the information network can reliably determine the time and adjust their clocks.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module OPS.1.2.6 NTP Time Synchronization must be applied to every IT system in the information domain that uses NTP.

To create an IT-Grundschutz model for a specific information domain, the entirety of all modules must generally be considered. As a rule, several modules are to be applied to the topic or target object.

This module covers

• the planning for the use of the NTP protocol,

• the operation of NTP servers, and

• the operation of NTP clients.

The following content is also important and is covered elsewhere:

• General requirements for the operation of servers (see SYS.1.1 General Server)

• General requirements for the operation of clients (see SYS.2.1 General Client)

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient planning for the use of NTP
parts.prose:
Inadequate planning can lead to not all IT systems receiving a sufficiently accurate system time.

If it is not properly planned how IT systems can adjust their system time, incorrect time information can arise in applications. In particular, time-critical applications may subsequently exhibit faulty states or fail.

For example, a network can be segmented in such a way that NTP servers and clients can no longer communicate with each other. In addition, inadequate planning of time synchronization can, for example, lead to automated processes being executed at the wrong time.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Missing or incorrect time information
parts.prose:
NTP servers can fail or transmit incorrect time information.

If an IT system can no longer reach its NTP servers because they have failed or are unreachable, it can no longer adjust its system time. This can cause the time of the internal clock to become inaccurate.

If an NTP server transmits incorrect time information to NTP clients, they may adjust their system clock incorrectly. This can lead to incorrect time information being used in applications, for example in log data.

Incorrect time information can also cause certificate-based services or services that use one-time passwords to stop working. As a result, users may no longer be able to log in to IT systems or network services.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Contradictory time information
parts.prose:
Time information from different sources can be contradictory.

If an IT system uses multiple NTP servers to adjust its system clock, the time information from the different NTP servers may vary. As soon as the time information deviates intolerably from each other, the IT system may no longer be able to determine which of the time information is correct. This can lead to the system time being adjusted incorrectly.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Manipulation of NTP communication
parts.prose:
Network packets with time information can be manipulated.

The NTP protocol is vulnerable to various attacks. In an attack, for example, the time information can be manipulated while it is being transmitted, or NTP requests can be redirected to another server. In this way, an attack can manipulate the system time of the NTP clients, for example, to use time-limited access rights even though they have expired.

controls.title: Creation of a strategy for cloud usage (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal strategy for cloud usage does not exist. Decisions are made on an ad hoc, per-project basis, mostly based on cost considerations, without a systematic consideration of risks, opportunities, or legal frameworks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, there are typically no dedicated documents. The 'strategy' can at best be inferred from email threads or meeting minutes of individual projects.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks IT management and project managers whether a formal, written, and approved cloud strategy exists. It is checked whether there is a central document that goes beyond individual projects.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic strategy has been drafted and documented. It names the primary goals (e.g., increasing flexibility, reducing costs) and the preferred cloud services. However, a more in-depth feasibility study or a comprehensive risk analysis is still missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An initial strategy document is created, often as part of IT department planning. Microsoft Word or a wiki system is used to record the basic goals and scope.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the strategy document and checks whether it defines basic goals and the intended services. It is verified that the document is more than just a loose collection of ideas.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A strategy for cloud usage MUST be created. It MUST define the goals, opportunities, and risks that the institution associates with cloud usage. Furthermore, the legal and organizational framework conditions, as well as the technical requirements, MUST be examined. The results of this examination MUST be documented in a feasibility study. It MUST be determined which services in which deployment model are to be procured from cloud service providers in the future.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The strategy is adopted as an official document by the institution's management. A feasibility study is conducted, which includes a cost-benefit analysis, a basic risk analysis, and a review of legal compliance (especially data protection). A template for feasibility studies can be helpful here.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the official cloud strategy and the associated feasibility study. It is checked whether all MUST requirements are met, in particular the definition of goals, opportunities, risks, and the examination of the framework conditions.

parts.name: statement
