parts.prose: A rough individual security analysis SHOULD be carried out for the planned cloud service. This SHOULD be repeated if technical and organizational framework conditions change significantly. For larger cloud projects, a roadmap SHOULD also be developed that specifies when and how a cloud service will be introduced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the strategy, a standardized procedure for security analysis for new cloud services is established. For strategic cloud projects, a roadmap with milestones, a schedule, and responsibilities is created, e.g., using project management software like Jira or MS Project.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and application of security analyses for selected cloud services. For larger projects, the roadmap is reviewed for plausibility and completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The cloud strategy is fully integrated into the overarching corporate and IT security strategy and is regularly (at least annually) reviewed and updated. Security analyses are a fixed, automated component of the onboarding process for new cloud services. The roadmap is supplemented by KPIs for measuring success, and compliance with it is continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cloud strategy is managed in a Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC) tool. The onboarding process for cloud services is automated by a workflow that includes security analysis, legal review, and approval. The progress of the roadmap is visualized via a central dashboard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of the cloud strategy into the overall strategy by inspecting the relevant documents and minutes from the management level. The functionality of the automated onboarding process and the existence of KPIs and monitoring reports for the roadmap are checked.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for cloud usage (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no formal security policy for cloud usage. Security requirements, if any, are communicated only informally and on a project-specific basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Security specifications exist only in the form of verbal agreements or individual emails. There is no central, universally applicable set of rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for a formal, approved security policy for cloud usage. It is checked whether such a document exists and whether employees are aware of it.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A first version of a security policy exists. It contains general security principles, but not yet any concrete specifications for the protection level of data or specific requirements for cloud providers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A general IT security policy is supplemented by a short chapter on cloud usage. The specifications are often kept generic (e.g., 'use secure passwords').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing policy and assesses whether it goes beyond general phrases and contains initial, albeit basic, specifications for cloud usage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the strategy for cloud usage, a security policy for cloud usage MUST be created. It MUST contain concrete security specifications with which cloud services can be implemented within the institution. Furthermore, special security requirements for cloud service providers and the defined protection level for cloud services regarding confidentiality, integrity, and availability MUST be documented therein. If cloud services from international providers are used, the special country-specific requirements and legal provisions MUST be taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated security policy for cloud usage is created and approved by the institution's management. The policy defines protection requirement classes for data and derives concrete requirements from them (e.g., 'data with high protection needs may only be processed by providers based in the EU and with encryption').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the security policy presented to them. It is checked whether concrete specifications, requirements for providers, the protection level of data, and country-specific aspects (if relevant) are documented as required in the requirement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is reviewed regularly, at least annually, and updated as needed. It is supplemented by detailed technical baselines and configuration specifications for the most common cloud platforms (e.g., AWS, Azure, M365).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A review process for the policy is established. Technical guides (hardening guides) are created for the cloud services used in the company and made available to administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the review process based on minutes. Samples of the technical baselines are requested and compared with the configurations of the production systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the security policy and technical baselines is continuously monitored using automated tools (Policy-as-Code, Cloud Security Posture Management - CSPM). Deviations lead to automatic alerts or are, where possible, corrected through self-healing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: CSPM tools such as Microsoft Defender for Cloud or Prisma Cloud are used. Policies are formulated in a machine-readable language (e.g., Open Policy Agent/Rego) and integrated into the CI/CD pipeline to prevent misconfigurations before deployment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration of the CSPM tool and the implemented policies. Based on the dashboard and reports, the continuous monitoring and the response to deviations are tracked. An automated check can be performed via API queries of the CSPM tool.

controls.title: Service definition for cloud services (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no formal definition of the cloud services used. Knowledge of the functional scope is based solely on the provider's general product description.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The description of the services is done ad hoc, often only verbally. There is no central, structured documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for a list and definition of the cloud services used. It is determined whether such documentation goes beyond the mere mention of product names.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic service description exists for the most important cloud services. However, this is not systematically created or kept up-to-date for all services.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a wiki or a simple list, the essential cloud services with their main purpose and key functions are recorded in bullet points.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing list of service descriptions and spot-checks their timeliness and whether they describe the basic functions of the service.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A service definition MUST be developed for each cloud service. In addition, all planned and used cloud services SHOULD be documented. The definition describes the service, its functional scope, and its purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized template for service definitions is created. All cloud services are recorded in a central directory (e.g., a CMDB, a service catalog tool, or a maintained wiki) and described according to this template.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the directory of cloud services and spot-checks whether a service definition according to the requirements exists for each service. It is checked whether the documentation is complete.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The service definition is expanded to include detailed information such as Service Level Objectives (SLOs), dependencies on other services, technical interfaces, and the responsible internal contacts (Service Owner).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The template for service definitions is expanded with fields for SLOs, dependencies, and Service Owner. This information is systematically recorded and maintained for all services.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews selected service definitions and verifies whether the extended information (SLOs, dependencies, etc.) is present, plausible, and up-to-date.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The service definitions are fully integrated into a service catalog tool or a CMDB and linked to the monitoring, incident management, and change management processes. The documentation is automatically updated when changes are made to the configuration or interfaces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Through the use of discovery tools and Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC), dependencies and configurations are automatically captured and the CMDB/service catalog is kept up-to-date. Changes to services require a formal change request that refers to the service definition.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration by tracking a change process for a cloud service and checking whether the service definition is correctly referenced and updated. The configuration of the automation tools is reviewed. An automated check can be done through an API comparison between the IaC repository and the CMDB.

controls.title: Defining areas of responsibility and interfaces (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities are unclear and not documented. There is an assumption that the cloud provider is 'responsible for everything', or conflicts of responsibility arise between internal teams.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are no documents such as RACI matrices or process descriptions. Responsibilities are clarified spontaneously as needed, which leads to delays.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks various stakeholders (e.g., developers, operations, information security) about their responsibilities in connection with a cloud service. Contradictory or uncertain answers indicate this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The basic demarcation of responsibilities is based on the provider's standard model (Shared Responsibility Model), but has not been further detailed or broken down into internal roles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The responsibility matrix of the cloud provider (e.g., for AWS or Azure) is known and used as a reference. A specific adaptation or detailing for the own organization is missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown how the responsibilities are documented. Often, this only refers to the cloud provider's website, without a separate, institution-specific elaboration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the service definition for cloud services, all relevant interfaces and responsibilities for cloud usage MUST be identified and documented. It MUST be clearly recognizable how the areas of responsibility are demarcated between the cloud service provider and the contracting institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) is created for each cloud service. This matrix describes in detail the tasks (e.g., patching the operating system, configuring the firewall, user administration) and assigns the responsibilities to roles at the cloud provider and in the own institution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of responsibilities (e.g., RACI matrix). It is checked whether the demarcation between provider and institution is clearly and unambiguously regulated for all relevant tasks and interfaces.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documented responsibilities and interfaces are reviewed and updated regularly, especially when changes are made to the service. The process descriptions for collaboration (e.g., for security incidents, support requests) are detailed and known to the stakeholders.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RACI matrix is versioned and is part of the annual review cycle for the cloud service. Important cooperation processes are visualized as flowcharts and stored in the process documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the review process for the responsibility documentation. Using an example scenario (e.g., security incident), it is checked whether the process description is clear and feasible and the interfaces are correctly defined.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined responsibilities are technically mapped in the operational tools. Tickets, for example, are automatically routed to the responsible internal or external teams. Compliance with the processes at the interfaces is monitored and evaluated by metrics.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the ITSM tool (e.g., ServiceNow, Jira Service Management), the workflows are configured to correspond to the defined processes and responsibilities. Escalation paths are automated. The performance at the interfaces (e.g., provider's response time) is monitored and considered in the service level reporting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the configuration of the workflows in the ITSM tool demonstrated. Based on sample tickets, it is verified whether the routing and escalation correspond to the documented responsibilities. The existence of metrics and reports on process performance is verified.

controls.title: Planning the secure migration to a cloud service (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration is carried out without a formal concept ('Lift and Shift'). Technical and organizational risks are not assessed in advance, which often leads to failures, data loss, or unexpected costs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The migration is carried out ad hoc by a technical team. There is no written plan, no defined test phases, and no coordination with the business departments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions those responsible about a completed migration and asks for the migration concept. If no such document exists, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic migration plan exists. It focuses primarily on the technical steps (e.g., order of server migration, data transfer). Organizational aspects such as process adjustments or training are only mentioned in passing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A technical procedure plan is created, e.g., in the form of a checklist or a simple project plan. The distribution of tasks is limited to the technical migration team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the migration plan and assesses whether it goes beyond a purely technical checklist and considers at least basic organizational aspects.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before migrating to a cloud service, a migration concept SHOULD be created. For this, organizational regulations and the distribution of tasks SHOULD first be defined. In addition, existing operational processes SHOULD be identified and adapted with regard to cloud use. It SHOULD be ensured that the institution's own IT is sufficiently considered in the migration process. The responsible parties SHOULD also determine whether the institution's employees should receive additional training.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal migration concept is created that includes technical and organizational aspects. It includes an analysis of the systems to be migrated, a plan for adapting ITSM processes (Incident, Change, etc.), a clear distribution of tasks (RACI), and a training plan for affected users and administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the migration concept. It is checked whether all SHOULD aspects mentioned in the requirement (organizational regulations, tasks, process adaptation, consideration of IT, training needs) are addressed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration concept is supplemented by a dedicated risk analysis for the migration phase, a detailed time and resource plan, and an explicit rollback plan. Before the production migration, test migrations and functional tests are carried out in a separate environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The concept is expanded to include chapters on risk analysis, test management, and contingency planning (rollback). A test environment is set up in the cloud to validate the migration and the application's end-to-end functionality before the production move takes place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the expanded migration concept and the logs of the test migrations performed. It is checked whether a documented rollback plan exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration is carried out using specialized, largely automated tools (e.g., cloud-native migration tools, Infrastructure-as-Code). The entire process is closely monitored with automated tools to ensure data integrity and to detect performance bottlenecks or security anomalies in real time. After the migration, an automated verification of the system status is performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools such as AWS Database Migration Service or Azure Migrate are used. The target environment is defined using Terraform or ARM templates (IaC). Monitoring is carried out by cloud monitoring services (e.g., CloudWatch, Azure Monitor) with predefined alarms. Post-migration checks are performed with automated test scripts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the configuration of the automation tools and the IaC scripts demonstrated. The automated migration and verification process is traced using the log files and monitoring dashboards.

controls.title: Planning the secure integration of cloud services (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before a cloud service is used, it SHOULD be carefully planned how it will be integrated into the institution's IT. For this purpose, it SHOULD at least be checked whether adjustments to the interfaces, the network connection, the administration model, and the data management model are necessary. The results SHOULD be documented and updated regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An integration concept is created for each new cloud service. This document analyzes the four mentioned areas (interfaces, network, administration, data management) and describes the necessary changes to the existing IT infrastructure and processes. The documentation is kept in a central knowledge management system (e.g., Confluence).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a cloud service and asks for the corresponding integration concept. It is checked whether the four mentioned areas have been analyzed and the results documented. In addition, it is checked whether a process for regular updates exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integration planning also includes integration into central security components such as Identity and Access Management (IAM), Security Information and Event Management (SIEM), and backup solutions. The configuration of the network connection (e.g., VPN, Direct Connect) is planned in detail and designed with redundancy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The integration concept is expanded with chapters on connecting to the central Azure AD / IAM, forwarding logs to the SIEM (e.g., Splunk or Sentinel), and integrating into the central backup software (e.g., Veeam). A detailed network diagram is created.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the planning of the connection to central security components in the integration concept. The configuration in the IAM and SIEM system is checked to verify the actual implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integration of the cloud service is fully automated using Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) and configuration management tools. Standardized integration patterns (blueprints) for different types of cloud services are predefined and reused to ensure consistent and secure connectivity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Terraform or CloudFormation templates are used for provisioning the infrastructure and Ansible playbooks for the configuration. These blueprints include network integration, IAM roles, logging, and monitoring configuration by default. The blueprints are versioned in a Git repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the IaC templates and blueprints in the Git repository demonstrated. It is traced how a new service is rolled out and whether the standardized and secure integration patterns are applied. An automated check can be performed by static code analysis of the IaC scripts.

controls.title: Creation of a security concept for cloud usage (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the identified security requirements (see OPS.2.2.A2 Creation of a security policy for cloud usage), a security concept for the use of cloud services SHOULD be created.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on the higher-level security policy, a detailed security concept is created for the specific cloud service or cloud project. This document describes the concrete technical and organizational measures to secure the service, e.g., network configuration, identity management, data encryption, and hardening measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security concept for a selected cloud service. It is checked whether the concept is based on the security policy and translates the requirements defined therein into concrete, implementable measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security concept is created for each cloud service and follows a standardized template. It contains a detailed threat modeling and risk analysis tailored specifically to the service and the data to be processed. The measures defined in the concept are specified by technical baselines and configuration guides.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard template for cloud security concepts is established. A threat analysis (e.g., based on the STRIDE model) is performed for each service. The results are incorporated into the definition of security measures. Concrete hardening guides (e.g., based on CIS benchmarks) are attached as an appendix.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the security concept and checks the existence and quality of the threat modeling and risk analysis. It is verified whether the measures are plausibly derived from the risks and supported by technical instructions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security concept is managed as a 'living document' in a code repository (e.g., Git) (Docs-as-Code). The security measures defined therein are directly linked to the Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) scripts that automatically implement the secure configuration. Compliance with the concept is continuously verified through automated compliance checks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security concept is written in Markdown and versioned in a Git repository. The security configurations (e.g., firewall rules, IAM policies) are defined in Terraform or ARM templates. A CSPM tool or Policy-as-Code tools (e.g., OPA) continuously check whether the production environment complies with the specifications defined in the concept and code.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the Git repository with the security concept and the IaC scripts demonstrated. The link between the requirement (concept) and the implementation (code) is traced. The results of the automated compliance checks are reviewed.

controls.title: Careful selection of cloud service providers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the service definition for the cloud service, a detailed requirements profile for cloud service providers SHOULD be created. A service description and a requirements specification SHOULD be created. For the evaluation of cloud service providers, supplementary information sources SHOULD also be used. Likewise, available service descriptions from cloud service providers SHOULD be carefully checked and questioned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal provider selection process is established. This includes the creation of a requirements catalog (requirements specification) that contains functional, technical, security, and legal requirements. For the evaluation, in addition to provider documentation, test reports, analyst ratings (e.g., Gartner), and certifications (e.g., ISO 27001, C5) are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the documentation of the selection process for a selected cloud service shown, including the requirements specification and evaluation matrix. It is checked whether the selection was made systematically and based on the defined requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection process includes a detailed review of the certificates and attestations provided by the provider, including a precise analysis of the scope. A Proof of Concept (PoC) or a trial is conducted to practically verify the guaranteed properties and the suitability of the service.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before signing the contract, the certificates (e.g., ISO 27001) and attestations (e.g., BSI C5, SOC 2) are requested and carefully checked to ensure the relevant service and location are included in the scope. A PoC is conducted with defined test cases and acceptance criteria to validate the functionality and security in practice.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the documentation of the certificate review and the results of the Proof of Concept. It is checked whether the findings from the PoC have comprehensibly substantiated the selection decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution performs continuous vendor management. The performance and security posture of the providers are permanently monitored and regularly (at least annually) assessed as part of a formal review. The results influence the decision on whether to continue or terminate the contractual relationship.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC tool is used to manage and track the risk assessment of providers. Regular service review meetings with the provider are held. The results of audits, new certifications, and public information about the provider's security posture are continuously collected and evaluated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the service review meetings and the documentation of the continuous vendor management. It is checked whether a systematic process for monitoring and re-evaluating providers has been established.

controls.title: Contract design with cloud service providers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The contractual arrangements between the contracting institution and the cloud service providers SHOULD be adapted in type, scope, and level of detail to the protection requirements of the information. It SHOULD be regulated at which location the service is to be provided. In addition, escalation levels and communication channels SHOULD be defined. It SHOULD also be agreed how the data is to be securely deleted. Likewise, termination regulations SHOULD be fixed in writing. The cloud service providers SHOULD disclose all subcontractors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The provider's standard contracts are carefully reviewed and, where possible, supplemented by the institution's own additional agreements (e.g., Data Processing Agreement according to GDPR, individual SLAs). A checklist is used to ensure that all points mentioned in the requirement (location, escalation, deletion, termination, subcontractors) are contractually covered. The legal department is systematically involved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the contracts for a selected cloud service presented. A checklist is used to verify whether all SHOULD aspects mentioned in the requirement are contractually regulated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The contract contains detailed and measurable Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for availability, performance, and support response times. Explicit regulations are agreed upon for audit and control rights, the procedure for security incidents (including reporting deadlines), and support for information requests from data subjects or authorities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SLAs are formulated to be measurable and to include contractual penalties for non-compliance. The audit rights are designed to enable effective review (e.g., right to inspect third-party audit reports). The process for reporting and jointly handling security incidents is described in detail in the contract.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract and checks the existence and quality of the regulations on SLAs, audit rights, and the management of security incidents. It is assessed whether these regulations are sufficiently concrete and enforceable.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The contract design explicitly considers exit scenarios and ensures that data and configurations can be extracted in a standardized, machine-readable format to facilitate a provider change (portability). The contracts are reviewed and renegotiated regularly, at least at each contract renewal, based on accumulated experience and changed legal or technical framework conditions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Detailed clauses on exit support are included in the contract. These specify the data format (e.g., SQL dump, JSON), the deadlines for data provision, and the obligation for secure deletion after handover. A formal process for contract review is established in vendor management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the contractual regulations on contract termination and data portability. It is checked whether a process for regular review and adaptation of the contracts exists and is applied (e.g., by inspecting the negotiation minutes of the last contract renewal).

controls.title: Secure migration to a cloud service (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration to a cloud service SHOULD be carried out based on the created migration concept. During the migration, it SHOULD be checked whether the security concept for cloud use needs to be adapted to potential new requirements. All emergency preparedness measures SHOULD also be complete and up-to-date.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The migration is carried out as a project according to the previously created concept. Milestones are monitored. A 'change freeze' is imposed on the old system before the go-live. It is checked whether the migration creates new risks that require an adaptation of the security concept (e.g., new public interfaces).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the project and migration documentation shown. It is checked whether the migration was carried out according to the concept and whether the security and emergency concepts were reviewed and, if necessary, adapted in the course of the migration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration to a cloud service SHOULD first be checked in a test run. Once the cloud service has gone into productive operation, it SHOULD be checked whether the cloud service providers meet the defined requirements of the institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The migration is completely rehearsed in a test environment (dress rehearsal). After the productive migration, a formal acceptance takes place. A checklist, based on the requirements specification and the contractual agreements, is used to check whether the provider fulfills all guaranteed services and security requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the test run and the final acceptance. It is checked whether the acceptance was carried out systematically based on the previously defined requirements and whether deviations were documented and tracked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration takes place in several, well-planned phases (e.g., pilot operation with a small user group, gradual rollout). The data and configuration reconciliation between the old and new system is automatically monitored during the migration phase. After the migration, the security of the new environment is validated by an automated penetration test or vulnerability analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A phased migration strategy (e.g., 'Canary Release' or 'Blue-Green Deployment') is applied. Automated scripts are used to check the consistency of the data during migration. After go-live, an automated vulnerability scan (e.g., with Tenable or Qualys) is run on the new environment and the results are evaluated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the phased migration plan and the results of the automated consistency checks shown. The reports of the vulnerability scan or penetration test carried out after the migration are inspected and evaluated.

controls.title: Creation of an emergency concept for a cloud service (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An emergency concept SHOULD be created for the cloud services used. It SHOULD contain all necessary information on responsibilities and contact persons. In addition, detailed regulations regarding data backup SHOULD be made. Specifications for redundantly designed management tools and interface systems SHOULD also be recorded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specific emergency concept for the cloud service is created as a supplement to the institution's general emergency manual. It describes scenarios such as service failure, internet connection failure, or loss of access credentials. It contains contact lists, regulates data backup (what, how often, where), and defines which components (e.g., VPN gateway) must be designed redundantly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the emergency concept for the cloud service and checks whether the aspects mentioned in the requirement (responsibilities, contacts, data backup, redundancy) are covered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The emergency concept is extended to include detailed recovery plans for specific failure scenarios. The plans describe the necessary steps, the required time, and the responsible persons. The functionality of the data backup and the recovery plans is tested regularly, at least annually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The emergency concept is supplemented by step-by-step instructions (runbooks) for recovery. Recovery tests are carried out regularly, during which data from the backup is restored in a test environment. The results of the tests are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the recovery plans and the logs of the emergency tests and recovery exercises performed. It is checked whether the tests take place regularly and whether the findings are used to improve the plans.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: High availability is realized through the automated use of multi-region or multi-cloud architectures. The failover to a redundant system is automated and regularly tested as part of 'Chaos Engineering' experiments to proactively check the resilience of the overall system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The service is operated active-active across multiple availability zones or regions of the cloud provider. The failover is automated by load balancers and health checks. Tools like the 'Chaos Monkey' are used to specifically simulate disruptions in the production environment and test the automatic recovery mechanisms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the architecture diagrams and the configuration of the automated failover mechanisms shown. The logs and results of the performed Chaos Engineering tests are inspected to verify the robustness of the system.

controls.title: Maintaining information security in ongoing cloud usage operations (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All documentation and policies created for the cloud services used SHOULD be updated regularly. It SHOULD also be periodically checked whether the contractually guaranteed services are being provided. The cloud service providers and the institution SHOULD also coordinate with each other regularly, if possible. Likewise, how to react to system failures SHOULD be planned and practiced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual review process for all cloud-relevant documents (concepts, policies) is established. Regular service review meetings (e.g., quarterly) are held with the provider to discuss SLA compliance and a-nd overall service quality. Emergency drills are planned and conducted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the minutes of the review meetings and emergency drills. It is checked whether a process for updating the documentation exists and whether it is being followed (e.g., by checking the modification date of the documents).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security of the cloud environment is proactively monitored through regular vulnerability scans and security log monitoring. A defined process for patch and vulnerability management for systems operated in the cloud is established and implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Cloud-native or third-party tools are used for regular vulnerability scans of cloud workloads. Logs from the cloud environment are forwarded to a central SIEM and monitored there using defined correlation rules. A patch management process ensures that security updates are applied promptly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the vulnerability scan reports and the configuration of the log monitoring in the SIEM. The patch management process is verified using examples to check whether patches were applied on time.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security configuration of the cloud environment is continuously and automatically monitored by a Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tool. Deviations from the defined security baseline are reported automatically and, where possible, corrected through self-healing. Threat hunting is proactively conducted to detect attacks early.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CSPM tool is used to permanently compare configurations with industry standards (e.g., CIS Benchmarks) and internal policies. Automated runbooks (e.g., via AWS Lambda or Azure Functions) are used to automatically fix known misconfigurations (e.g., open S3 buckets). A dedicated security team or an external SOC service provider conducts proactive threat hunting in the cloud logs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the dashboard and configuration of the CSPM tool. The reports on detected and corrected deviations are reviewed. The processes and results of the threat hunting are checked. An automated check can be performed by querying the CSPM tool's API.

controls.title: Proof of adequate information security in cloud usage (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD regularly obtain proof from the cloud service providers that the agreed security requirements are being met. The proof SHOULD be based on an internationally recognized framework (e.g., IT-Grundschutz, ISO/IEC 27001, Cloud Computing Compliance Controls Catalogue (C5), Cloud Controls Matrix of the Cloud Security Alliance). If cloud service providers use subcontractors, they SHOULD regularly prove to the institution that the subcontractors are conducting the necessary audits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process is established to annually request and archive the relevant certificates and attestations (e.g., ISO 27001, C5 attestation, SOC 2 report) from the cloud providers and their important subcontractors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the collection of current certificates and attestations of the used cloud providers. It is checked whether these are requested regularly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD carefully review the received proofs (certificates, attestations). It SHOULD be checked whether the scope of the proof covers the used cloud services, locations, and time periods and whether the level of protection described in the proof corresponds to its own protection needs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented review is conducted for each received certificate and attestation. A checklist helps to assess the scope, validity period, and relevance for the services used. Any deviations or deficiencies identified in the attestation are assessed and followed up on.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the certificate and attestation review. It is verified whether a substantive examination of the proofs has taken place and not just a mere filing of the documents.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to reviewing external proofs, the institution conducts its own automated checks of the security configuration on the provider side, as far as technically possible and contractually permissible (e.g., using CSPM tools). The results of the external and internal checks are consolidated in a central GRC tool to enable a holistic risk assessment of the provider.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The results of the provider audits (e.g., from SOC 2 reports) and the own technical checks (e.g., from the CSPM tool) are recorded in the GRC tool. This enables continuous monitoring of provider compliance and risk-based management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the process in the GRC tool. It is verified how external and internal audit results are combined to obtain a comprehensive picture of the provider's security posture and how identified risks are addressed.

controls.title: Orderly termination of a cloud usage relationship (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When the service relationship with the cloud service providers is terminated, it SHOULD be ensured that the institution's business activities or specialized tasks are not impaired. The contracts with the cloud service providers SHOULD regulate how the respective service relationship can be terminated in an orderly manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized offboarding process for cloud services is defined. This process is based on the contractual agreements (see A9) and describes the necessary steps to terminate a service in an orderly manner. This includes planning the data migration to a successor service or back to the own infrastructure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the defined offboarding process. It is checked whether it considers the maintenance of business operations and is based on the contractual regulations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The offboarding process includes a detailed plan for data migration, including checking data completeness and integrity after the transfer. It must be ensured that all data (including backups) is demonstrably and securely deleted from the old provider. The provider must issue a deletion confirmation for this.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The offboarding plan contains a checklist for data migration (e.g., use of hashing for integrity checks) and a template for the deletion confirmation to be requested. The process ensures that all user accounts and access permissions with the old provider are deactivated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In the case of a completed offboarding process, the auditor requests the migration and deletion report, including the provider's deletion confirmation. It is checked whether data integrity has been verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The offboarding process is regularly practiced as part of portability tests (see A15). The data migration and de-provisioning of resources with the old provider are largely automated. Secure deletion is supported by cryptographic methods (crypto-shredding) by destroying the used keys.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Automated scripts are developed to export data and controllably de-provision resources at the cloud provider (VMs, storage, etc.). Where applicable, crypto-shredding is used as part of the deletion strategy. The findings from the portability tests are continuously incorporated into the improvement of the offboarding process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the offboarding drills and is shown the automation scripts for de-provisioning and data migration. The implementation of the crypto-shredding strategy is checked.

controls.title: Ensuring the portability of cloud services (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD define all technical and organizational requirements that make it possible to switch cloud service providers or to bring the cloud service or data back into its own IT infrastructure. The contracts with the cloud service providers SHOULD specify provisions that ensure the necessary portability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document is created that defines the portability requirements. This includes the demand for open standards, documented APIs, and standardized data export formats. These requirements are incorporated into the contract negotiations (see A9).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the document with the portability requirements and checks in the contracts whether these requirements have been legally anchored.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD conduct portability tests regularly, e.g., annually. This involves practicing the export of data and configurations in a standardized, provider-independent format and measuring the time for a full recovery on an alternative platform.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A plan for annual portability tests is created. For a selected service, the data and configurations are exported and an attempt is made to restore the service on an alternative platform (e.g., with another cloud provider or on-premise). The execution and the results are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the plans and logs of the portability tests conducted. It is assessed whether the tests are meaningful and whether the findings are used to reduce vendor lock-in.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Portability is ensured from the outset through an active multi-cloud or hybrid-cloud strategy. Applications and data are primarily managed in container-based architectures or using Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC), which enables a rapid and automated switch between providers. Portability tests are part of the continuous integration and deployment pipeline (CI/CD) and are executed automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Applications are developed in Docker containers and orchestrated via Kubernetes, which can be operated both on-premise and with various cloud providers. The infrastructure is managed with provider-neutral IaC tools like Terraform. CI/CD pipelines regularly deploy the application to different target platforms on a test basis to continuously verify portability.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the architecture (e.g., Kubernetes cluster), the IaC scripts (e.g., Terraform), and the CI/CD pipeline configuration. It is checked whether the architecture and the tools actually enable provider-independent operation and whether portability is tested automatically.

controls.title: Conducting own data backups (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD check whether its own data backups should be created in addition to the contractually agreed data backups of the cloud service providers. This can increase control over the data and protect against provider failures or errors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the risk analysis for the cloud service, it is assessed whether the provider's backup services are sufficient or whether a residual risk (e.g., provider's insolvency, ransomware attack) makes it necessary to create own backups. The decision is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the risk analysis and checks whether the necessity of own backups has been assessed and a comprehensible decision has been made.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If the institution performs its own data backups, it SHOULD create detailed requirements for a backup service. The backups SHOULD be stored in a location independent of the primary cloud provider (e.g., with another provider or on-premise). Restoration from these backups SHOULD be tested regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cloud-to-cloud or cloud-to-on-premise backup solution is implemented. The backup data is stored encrypted in a separate, logically and physically segregated location. Regular restoration tests ensure that the backups are usable in an emergency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the architecture of the own backup solution and the protocols of the restoration tests. It is checked whether the backups are stored in an independent location.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The own data backup includes point-in-time recovery functionality and effectively protects the backups from ransomware attacks through immutability or air-gapping. The entire backup and recovery process is largely automated and continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A backup solution is used that supports immutable storage (e.g., in AWS S3 with Object Lock). This prevents ransomware from encrypting or deleting the backup data. The monitoring of the backup process is integrated into the central monitoring and automatically alerts in case of errors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the configuration of the backup solution and verifies the settings for data immutability. The reliability of the automated backup process is checked using the monitoring logs.

controls.title: Use of encryption in cloud usage (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If data is encrypted by cloud service providers, it SHOULD be contractually specified which encryption mechanisms and which key lengths may be used. The standard encryption functions of the cloud platform are used (encryption at rest and in transit).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Minimum requirements for encryption are defined in the security policy and in the contract (e.g., AES-256 for data at rest, TLS 1.2 or higher for transmission). It is ensured that the corresponding standard options with the cloud provider (e.g., S3 encryption, EBS encryption) are activated for all resources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the contracts for corresponding clauses and randomly checks in the cloud management console whether the standard encryption mechanisms are activated for the services used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If own encryption mechanisms are used, appropriate key management SHOULD be ensured. The institution uses key management systems (KMS) provided by the provider to maintain control over the keys (Customer-Managed Keys). The lifecycle of the keys (creation, rotation, destruction) is actively managed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The native Key Management Service of the cloud provider (e.g., AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) is used. Customer-specific keys (CMK - Customer Master Key) are created and used for the encryption of critical data. Policies for automatic key rotation (e.g., annually) are configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the configuration of the KMS. It is checked whether Customer-Managed Keys are used and whether policies for key rotation are active. The access permissions to the KMS are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the highest confidentiality requirements, a 'Bring Your Own Key' (BYOK) or 'Hold Your Own Key' (HYOK) strategy is implemented. The keys are generated and managed in an own, on-premise operated Hardware Security Module (HSM). In addition, where technically possible, end-to-end encryption or encryption during processing (Confidential Computing) is used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An on-premise HSM is procured and securely operated. The own keys are imported into the cloud KMS via the cloud provider's BYOK function. Alternatively, with HYOK, encryption and decryption are performed client-side. For compute-intensive tasks with sensitive data, confidential computing VMs (e.g., with AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX) are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the architecture and operating documentation of the own HSM. The key import process (BYOK) is verified. The configuration of confidential computing services is checked.

controls.title: Use of federation services (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be checked whether federation services are used in a cloud usage project. The authentication of users is carried out via the institution's central identity management system (Single Sign-On).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cloud service is connected to the central Identity and Access Management (IAM) system, e.g., Microsoft Azure AD or an on-premise ADFS. This is done via standard protocols such as SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the configuration of the federation in the IAM system and in the cloud service. It is checked that users no longer log in to the cloud service with local passwords, but are authenticated via the central IAM.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that only the required information is transmitted to the cloud service provider in a SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) ticket (principle of data minimization). The permissions SHOULD be checked regularly, e.g., as part of recertification campaigns. Access to the cloud service is secured by multi-factor authentication (MFA).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the configuration of the IAM system, the issuance of SAML tokens is configured so that only necessary attributes (e.g., name, email, group memberships) are transmitted to the cloud service. MFA is enforced for all users accessing the service. Annual campaigns are conducted to review access permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the attribute transmission in the SAML ticket. It is checked whether MFA is enforced for the service. The protocols of the last permission recertification campaign are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access is controlled via a 'Conditional Access' framework that dynamically assesses the context of the request (e.g., user, location, device type, device state) to grant or deny access (Zero Trust approach). The provisioning and de-provisioning of user accounts and permissions in the cloud service is automated (e.g., via SCIM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Conditional Access Policies are configured in Azure AD or a comparable system. These require, for example, MFA only for access from outside the corporate network or deny access from non-compliant devices. The 'System for Cross-domain Identity Management' (SCIM) is configured to automatically create or delete users in the cloud service when they join or leave.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the configured Conditional Access Policies and checks their effectiveness using example scenarios. The configuration of the automated user provisioning (SCIM) is checked and it is verified how a new employee receives access.

controls.title: Security screening of employees (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be contractually agreed with external cloud service providers that the provider's personnel who have access to the institution's data are sufficiently qualified and trustworthy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A clause is included in the contract with the cloud provider that obliges the provider to ensure due diligence in the selection, training, and monitoring of its employees. The provider assures that only trustworthy personnel will be used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract with the cloud provider and checks whether it contains a corresponding clause on the reliability and qualification of the provider's personnel.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Criteria for what constitutes qualified and trustworthy personnel SHOULD be jointly defined with the cloud provider. Upon request, the provider SHOULD demonstrate that its employees with administrative rights meet these criteria (e.g., by submitting certificates or confirmation of a background check).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The criteria for the personnel are defined as an appendix to the contract. This may include the requirement for specific technical certifications, regular security training, and, depending on the protection needs, the submission of a police clearance certificate. The process for requesting and reviewing these proofs is defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the contractually agreed criteria. It is randomly verified whether the corresponding proofs for the provider's administrative staff have been requested and checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access by cloud provider employees to the institution's systems is carried out exclusively according to the 'Just-in-Time' (JIT) and 'Least Privilege' principles. Every administrative access is explicitly requested for a limited period, approved, and fully logged. Where possible, access is controlled via 'Customer Lockbox' procedures, which require explicit approval from the institution for each individual access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Cloud-native functions such as 'Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM)' or 'Customer Lockbox' (for Microsoft 365 or Azure) or 'Access Transparency' (for Google Cloud) are used. The process for requesting, approving, and monitoring privileged access is established. All privileged sessions are recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the configuration of the PIM or Lockbox functions. The approval process for a privileged access of the provider support is traced using the audit logs. It is checked whether the sessions are recorded and the logs are kept tamper-proof.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Cloud computing refers to the offering, use, and billing of IT services over a network, dynamically adapted to demand. These services are offered and used exclusively via defined technical interfaces and protocols. The range of services offered within the scope of cloud computing covers the entire spectrum of information technology and includes, among other things, infrastructure (e.g., computing power, storage space), platforms, and software.
Cloud computing offers many advantages: The IT services can be used as needed, are scalable and flexible, and can be billed according to the functional scope, duration of use, and number of users. It is also possible to access the specialized knowledge and resources of cloud service providers, which can free up internal resources for other tasks. In practice, however, it is often the case that the benefits that institutions expect from using the cloud are not fully realized. The reason for this is usually that important critical success factors are not sufficiently considered in the run-up to cloud use. Therefore, cloud services must be strategically planned, and (security) requirements, responsibilities, and interfaces must be carefully defined and agreed upon. Awareness and understanding of the necessarily changed roles, both on the part of IT operations and the users of the client institution, is also an important success factor.
In addition, the topic of governance should also be considered when introducing cloud services (cloud governance). Critical areas include, for example, contract design, implementation of multi-tenancy, ensuring portability of different services, billing of used services, monitoring of service provision, security incident management, and numerous data protection aspects.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module describes requirements for the secure use of cloud services. It is aimed at all institutions that already use such services or plan to use them in the future.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The OPS.2.2 Cloud Usage module must always be applied to a specific cloud service. If an institution uses different cloud service providers, the module must be applied to all cloud service providers. The interface between the cloud service providers is also part of the module and must be considered for all cloud services.
In almost all deployment models, except for the use of a private cloud on-premise, cloud services represent a special form of outsourcing (see module OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing). The threats and requirements described in this module are therefore often also applied in outsourcing. However, with cloud services, there are some special features that are found exclusively in this module. The module OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing is therefore not to be applied to cloud services.
The threats and requirements described in this module generally apply regardless of the service and deployment model used.
Security requirements with which providers can protect their cloud services are not the subject of this module. Threats and specific security requirements that are to be considered relevant due to the connection of a cloud service via corresponding interfaces (API, Application Programming Interface) are also not considered in this module.

Demarcation from classic IT outsourcing
In outsourcing, an institution's work, production, or business processes are outsourced in whole or in part to external service providers. This is an established part of today's organizational strategies. Classic IT outsourcing is usually designed so that the entire rented infrastructure is used exclusively by one customer (single-tenant architecture), even though outsourcing providers usually have multiple customers. In addition, outsourcing contracts are usually concluded for longer terms.
The use of cloud services is similar in many respects to classic outsourcing, but there are some additional differences to consider:

• For economic reasons, multiple users often share a common infrastructure in a cloud.
• Cloud services are dynamic and can therefore be scaled up and down within much shorter periods. This allows cloud-based offerings to be adapted more quickly to the actual needs of the users.
• The cloud services used are usually controlled by the cloud users themselves via a web interface. This allows them to automatically tailor the services used to their needs.
• The technologies used in cloud computing make it possible to dynamically distribute IT performance across multiple locations, which can be geographically widely dispersed both domestically and abroad.
• Users can easily administer the services and their resources via web interfaces or suitable interfaces, with little interaction required with the cloud service providers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Lack of or inadequate strategy for cloud usage
parts.prose: Using cloud services in an institution is a strategic decision. A lack of or an inadequate strategy for cloud usage can, for example, lead to an institution choosing unsuitable cloud services or cloud service providers. The selected cloud services might also be incompatible with the institution's own IT, internal business processes, or protection requirements. This can have negative organizational, technical, or financial impacts on business processes. In general, a lack of or an inadequate strategy for cloud usage can result in the associated goals not being achieved or the security level decreasing significantly.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Dependence on cloud service providers (loss of control)
parts.prose:
If an institution uses external cloud services, it becomes more or less dependent on the cloud service providers. This can lead to the institution no longer being able to fully control the outsourced business processes and the associated information, especially their security. The institution is also, despite possible controls, at some point dependent on the cloud service providers implementing security measures correctly. If they do not, business processes and business-critical information are inadequately protected.
Furthermore, the use of external cloud services can lead to a loss of know-how in information security and technology within the institution. This may mean that the institution can no longer judge whether the protective measures taken by providers are sufficient. A change of cloud service is also very difficult. The cloud service providers could also exploit this dependency, for example, to enforce price increases or reduce the quality of service.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Deficient requirements management in cloud usage
parts.prose: When an institution decides to use a cloud service, many expectations are usually attached to it. For example, employees may hope for higher performance or a greater range of functions from the outsourced services, while the institution's management speculates on lower costs. However, a lack of requirements management before cloud usage can lead to expectations not being met and the service not delivering the desired added value, e.g., in terms of availability.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Violation of legal requirements
parts.prose: Many providers offer their cloud services in an international environment. As a result, they are often subject to different national legislations. Frequently, cloud customers only see the advantages associated with cloud computing (e.g., cost benefits) and misjudge the legal frameworks, such as data protection, information obligations, insolvency law, liability, or information access for third parties. This could lead to violations of applicable guidelines and regulations. The security of the outsourced information could also be compromised.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Lack of multi-tenancy in cloud service providers
parts.prose: In cloud computing, different institutions usually share a common infrastructure, such as IT systems, networks, and applications. If, for example, the resources of the different institutions are not separated from each other with sufficient security, one institution may be able to access the areas of another institution and manipulate or delete information there.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Inadequate contractual agreements with cloud service providers
parts.prose:
Inadequate contractual arrangements with cloud service providers can lead to various and serious security problems. If areas of responsibility, tasks, performance parameters, or efforts have been described insufficiently or ambiguously, it may happen that the cloud service providers unintentionally or due to a lack of resources do not implement security measures or implement them inadequately.
Even if situations arise that are not clearly regulated by contract, disadvantages for the client institution can result. For example, cloud service providers often use the services of third parties for their services. If there are insufficient contractual agreements here or if the dependencies between the service providers and third parties have not been disclosed, this can also have a negative impact on the information security and service performance of the institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Lack of planning for migration to cloud services
parts.prose: The migration to a cloud service is almost always a critical phase. Due to poor planning, errors can occur that affect information security within the institution. For example, if an institution recklessly forgoes a phased migration due to an inadequate planning phase, this can lead to considerable problems in practice. If there are no test phases, pilot users, or a time-limited parallel operation of existing infrastructure and cloud services beforehand, important data can be lost or services can fail completely.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Insufficient integration of cloud services into the own IT
parts.prose: It is necessary that cloud services are appropriately integrated into the institution's IT infrastructure. If the responsible parties implement this inadequately, it may happen that users cannot access the contracted cloud services to their full extent. The cloud services may not deliver the required and agreed-upon performance, or they may not be accessible at all or only to a limited extent. This can slow down business processes or cause them to fail completely. If cloud services are incorrectly integrated into the own IT, serious security vulnerabilities can also arise.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Inadequate regulations for the end of a cloud usage project
parts.prose:
Inadequate regulations for a possible termination of the contractual relationship can have serious consequences for the institution. Experience shows that this is always particularly problematic when a case that is critical from the institution's point of view occurs unexpectedly, such as the insolvency or sale of the cloud service provider or serious security concerns. Without sufficient internal preparation and precise contractual regulations, the institution can only with great difficulty detach itself from the contract concluded for the cloud service. In this case, it is difficult to impossible to transfer the outsourced cloud service to another cloud computing platform in a timely manner or to reintegrate it into the own institution.
Inadequately regulated data deletion after the end of the contract can also lead to unauthorized access to the institution's information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.10. Inadequate administration model for cloud usage
parts.prose: When cloud services are used, the understanding of roles within IT operations often changes on the part of the user institution. For example, administrators often evolve from classic system administration to service administration. If this process is not adequately supported, it can have a negative impact on cloud usage, for instance, if the administrators do not have the necessary understanding of the changes or are not adequately trained for their new tasks. As a result, the cloud services may not be properly administered and thus may only be available to a limited extent or may fail completely.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.11. Inadequate emergency preparedness concept
parts.prose: Inadequate emergency preparedness in cloud usage can quickly have serious consequences. If the cloud service or parts of it fail, shortcomings in the emergency preparedness concepts of the cloud service provider and at the interfaces will always lead to unnecessarily long downtimes with corresponding consequences for the productivity or service of the client institution. In addition, poorly coordinated emergency scenarios between the client institution and the service provider can lead to gaps in emergency preparedness.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.12. Failure of the cloud service provider's IT systems
parts.prose: At cloud service providers, the processes, IT systems, and applications they operate can fail partially or completely, which consequently also affects the cloud customers. If the institutions are inadequately separated from each other, a failed IT system that is not assigned to the institution can also lead to that institution no longer being able to access its contractually guaranteed service. Similar problems arise if the connection between the cloud service provider and the customer fails or if the used cloud computing platform is successfully attacked.

controls.title: Creation of requirement profiles for processes (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Requirement profiles for outsourced processes are created only sporadically or only for the most obviously critical processes. The profiles are often incomplete and disregard important aspects such as dependencies on other processes or a detailed security assessment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, one often relies on the implicit knowledge of the subject matter experts. Documentation, if any, is in the form of simple notes or emails. There is no standardized process or templates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the subject matter experts whether a requirements analysis was carried out before outsourcing. The auditor asks for the created profiles to be submitted and notes that they only exist for some of the outsourced processes and/or are incomplete in content.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic requirement profiles are created for all potentially outsourced processes. These contain a description of the function and the data processed. An assessment of criticality is usually only made in a rough classification (e.g., high, medium, low).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple checklist or a basic template is used to capture fundamental information. The analysis of interfaces and dependencies is still superficial and not systematic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that requirement profiles exist for all processes intended for outsourcing. Upon reviewing the profiles, it is found that while basic aspects are covered, a deep analysis of dependencies and interfaces is missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If no Business Impact Analysis (BIA) is available, requirement profiles in the form of fact sheets MUST be created for the processes that are potentially to be outsourced. These requirement profiles MUST include the function, data processed, interfaces, and an information security assessment. In particular, dependencies between processes and to subordinate sub-processes MUST be considered. The requirement profiles MUST reflect the criticality of the respective process for regular business operations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Standardized fact sheet templates are developed and used for all potential outsourcings. The business owners are trained in the creation of these profiles. The created profiles are centrally collected and versioned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the requirement profiles for a sample of outsourced processes. It is checked whether the profiles contain all required elements: function, data, interfaces, security assessment, dependencies, and criticality. It is verified that these profiles served as the basis for the outsourcing decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for creating requirement profiles is formalized and established throughout the company. The profiles are systematically derived from the results of a Business Impact Analysis (BIA), if one is available. Each profile undergoes a formal review and approval process by the Information Security Officer (ISO).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirement profiles are managed in a central system, e.g., a wiki or a GRC tool. The templates for the profiles are regularly reviewed and improved if necessary. The link to the BIA is explicitly documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies not only the existence and completeness of the profiles but also the formal approval process. It is checked whether the criticality documented in the profile is consistent with the results of the BIA and whether the ISO has demonstrably reviewed and approved the profiles.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The creation and maintenance of requirement profiles is integrated into a central Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) tool. The profiles are dynamically linked to the BIA, the risk register, and the Configuration Management Database (CMDB). The analysis of dependencies includes not only direct, but also indirect and transitive dependencies throughout the entire service chain.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Automated workflows in the GRC tool guide the business owners through the creation process. Changes to dependent systems in the CMDB or a re-evaluation in the BIA automatically trigger a review of the corresponding requirement profile.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses the evaluations from the GRC tool to verify the consistency between requirement profiles, BIA, risk assessment, and CMDB. It is checked whether automated workflows to ensure the profiles are up-to-date have been implemented and are effective. An automated test could check the consistency of data across the various systems: `check-consistency --module-a 'profiles' --module-b 'bia'`.

controls.title: Pursuing a risk-based approach in outsourcing management (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A risk assessment is only carried out informally and undocumented, usually in the form of discussions. Outsourcing is only avoided for processes with obviously very high risk. A regular reassessment does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Decisions are based on the gut feeling of experienced employees. There is no methodology or documented criteria for risk assessment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the risk assessment methodology for outsourcing and finds that no formal methodology exists. Decisions and their justifications are not documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic risk assessment is conducted for all potential outsourcings. This uses a simple scale (e.g., high/medium/low). The results are recorded in a simple list, but there is no structured outsourcing register.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple checklist for risk assessment is used. Reassessment is done ad-hoc, e.g., upon contract renewal, but not at fixed intervals.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of risk assessments. It is checked whether an assessment is available for all outsourcings. The methodology is classified as simple and non-quantitative.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For processes that are potentially to be outsourced, a risk-based assessment MUST be carried out to decide whether they can be outsourced. The requirement profiles SHOULD be used as a basis for this assessment. If the process is outsourced, the result SHOULD be stored in the outsourcing register. To account for changes in processes or the threat landscape, the outsourced processes MUST be re-assessed on a risk basis at regular intervals and on an ad-hoc basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented methodology for the risk assessment of outsourcings is established. An outsourcing register is maintained as a central file (e.g., spreadsheet) and kept up to date. A fixed cycle for reassessment (e.g., annually) is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the risk assessment methodology for appropriateness.
