The outsourcing register is inspected, and it is checked whether the results of the risk assessment are documented there. It is verified that a process for regular and ad-hoc reassessment exists and that evidence of its execution is available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The risk assessment is based on a formal, documented methodology and systematically uses the created requirement profiles. The results are recorded in a structured outsourcing register (e.g., in a database) that contains detailed risk classifications. The process for regular reassessment is scheduled, tracked, and the results are reported to management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The outsourcing register is implemented as an application or database. The regular reviews are controlled via a ticket system or a task management system to ensure timely execution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies compliance with the formal methodology. It is checked whether the outsourcing register is structured and enables the tracking of reassessments. Random checks are performed to see if reassessments were carried out on time and documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The risk assessment for outsourcing is fully integrated into the central company-wide risk management framework. The outsourcing register is a dynamic tool (e.g., part of a GRC tool) that automatically triggers reassessments when underlying parameters change (e.g., new threats, changed criticality). Quantitative risk analyses are performed for particularly critical outsourcings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The GRC tool is linked to other systems such as threat intelligence feeds and the BIA software. Thresholds are defined which, when exceeded, automatically trigger a reassessment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the GRC tool and the linked systems. It is verified that the automation for triggering reassessments is functioning correctly. It is checked whether quantitative risk analyses exist for critical outsourcings and whether they have been incorporated into decision-making processes. An automated test could check if a critical CVE triggers a review process for affected outsourced services: `trigger-test-cve --cve CVE-2024-XXXXX --service ' outsourced-service-A'`.

controls.title: Defining suitability requirements for outsourcing providers (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Internal suitability requirements for potential outsourcing providers MUST be established. These suitability requirements MUST consider the necessary competencies to secure the process from an information security perspective, as well as the reputation for trustworthiness and reliability. It MUST be checked whether potential conflicts of interest exist. Furthermore, outsourcing providers SHOULD be regularly checked against the suitability requirements. If the providers do not meet the requirements, corrective actions SHOULD be taken.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A criteria catalog for provider assessment is created. This includes points such as proven experience, references, certifications (e.g., ISO 27001), financial stability, and reputation. Before signing a contract, each potential provider is assessed against this catalog. A process for the regular reassessment of existing service providers is defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the criteria catalog for provider assessment. For a sample of outsourcing service providers, it is checked whether a documented suitability check took place before the contract was signed. It is verified that a process for regular review has been established and that evidence of its execution is available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The suitability requirements are formally documented, approved by management, and directly derived from the outsourcing strategy. The provider assessment process is standardized, for example, by using a weighted scorecard. Regular reviews are firmly scheduled and documented. A formal process for handling deviations, including a catalog of measures, is established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The scorecard for provider assessment is established as a company-wide standard. The results of the regular reviews are recorded in a central supplier management tool and reported to management. The catalog of measures is linked to a ticket system for tracking.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the suitability requirements are derived from the outsourcing strategy and have been approved. The use of the standardized scorecard is checked. It is checked whether the regular reviews take place as planned and whether deviations and the resulting measures are systematically tracked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The provider assessment process is an integral part of a continuous supply chain risk management. The assessment is comprehensive and includes, in addition to the review of documents, on-site audits, verification of financial stability by external service providers, and technical validation of security claims.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution commissions specialized external auditors for on-site audits at critical service providers. Financial credit checks are regularly carried out via services such as Dun & Bradstreet. Threat intelligence feeds are used to identify risks related to the supply chain and to proactively adapt the suitability requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews audit reports from on-site inspections and the results of credit checks. It is verified that the vendor assessment process is dynamic and reacts to new information (e.g., from threat intelligence sources). It is checked whether the results of the comprehensive assessment process are demonstrably incorporated into contractual decisions and risk management.

controls.title: Basic requirements for contracts with outsourcing providers (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Uniform basic requirements for outsourcing contracts MUST be developed. These basic requirements MUST include aspects of information security, a reservation of consent for onward transfers, as well as a right to inspection, review, and audit. The results of the risk-based consideration and suitability requirements SHOULD be incorporated during development. A non-disclosure agreement SHOULD be concluded with the providers. The basic requirements MUST be implemented uniformly. A uniform contract template SHOULD be created based on the basic requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of mandatory contract clauses for information security, audit rights, and sub-contractor management is created. This list is reviewed by the legal department and the ISO (Information Security Officer). Ideally, a standard contract template or a contract addendum for information security is developed, and its use is sought for all outsourcing arrangements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of basic requirements or the standard contract template. Using a sample of outsourcing contracts, it is checked whether the required clauses (information security, reservation of consent, audit rights) are consistently included. It is verified whether non-disclosure agreements have been concluded.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standardized contract template approved by the legal department is mandatory for all outsourcing projects. This template is regularly reviewed and updated. The specific results of the risk assessment and suitability assessment for the respective case are demonstrably incorporated into the individual adaptation of the contract to establish risk-adequate regulations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The standard contract template is published on the intranet, and its use is enforced by the purchasing or legal department. There is a defined process for how the results of the risk analysis (e.g., higher availability requirements) are translated into specific contract clauses (e.g., stricter SLAs).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a current, approved contract template exists and its use is mandatory. Using a sample, the process of how the results of the risk analysis were incorporated into the final contract is traced. It is checked whether the template is regularly reviewed for necessary updates, e.g., annually.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Contract management is supported by a specialized system. Contract clauses are dynamically assembled from a toolkit of pre-approved clauses based on the risk profile of the outsourced service. The contract includes clauses that trigger automatic responses to specific events, such as an immediate right to audit after a major security incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM) system is used. The clause toolkit is maintained by the legal department and the ISO. The link between the risk profile and the clauses to be used is stored in the system and automates the contract creation process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the CLM system and the clause toolkit. It is checked whether the logic for dynamic contract creation is appropriate for the service's risk profile. The correct application of automation is verified using examples. It is controlled whether event-driven clauses (e.g., after a simulated security incident) apply correctly.

controls.title: Multi-tenancy agreement (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A multi-tenancy agreement with outsourcing providers MUST ensure that data and processing contexts are securely and adequately separated by the outsourcing provider. In this agreement, a tenant separation concept SHOULD be requested from the outsourcing providers. The tenant separation concept SHOULD differentiate between tenant-specific and cross-tenant data and objects and explain the mechanisms used for separation by the outsourcing providers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During contract negotiations, a technical document describing the multi-tenancy architecture is requested from the provider. This document should explain how data, configurations, users, and processes are separated at the logical and, where applicable, physical level.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the requirement for multi-tenancy is stipulated in the contract. It is checked whether a tenant separation concept was requested from the provider and checked for plausibility. The concept is then reviewed to see if it addresses the relevant separation mechanisms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The tenant separation concept submitted by the provider is subjected to a formal and detailed technical review by internal or external experts. The review assesses the robustness of the separation mechanisms against common bypass attempts. The approval of the concept is a prerequisite for a contract conclusion, and the contract explicitly refers to the approved concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A checklist for the technical review of tenant separation concepts is developed. It covers aspects such as database schemas, network segmentation, virtualization technologies, and IAM concepts. The results of the review are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the technical review of the tenant separation concept. It is verified that the review was conducted by qualified personnel and that the results were incorporated into the decision. The auditor checks whether the contract contains a reference to the approved document.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The effectiveness of multi-tenancy separation is not only assessed based on concepts but is also verified through active technical tests. As far as contractually agreed, targeted penetration tests are conducted to verify the separation of tenant environments. Contractual arrangements are made for continuous monitoring for potential data leaks between tenants.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The outsourcing contract enshrines the right to conduct penetration tests (by the institution itself or a commissioned third party). The tests are conducted regularly, e.g., annually. The results are used to demand remediation from the provider.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the reports of the penetration tests conducted for multi-tenancy separation. It is checked whether the tests are conducted regularly and whether the identified vulnerabilities have been demonstrably remediated by the provider. An automated test could check the public interface for known configuration errors related to tenant separation: `nmap --script=http-vuln-tenant-isolation <provider-url>`.

controls.title: Definition of security requirements and creation of a security concept for the outsourcing project (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be contractually agreed with the providers that IT-Grundschutz is implemented or at least the requirements from the relevant modules are adequately met. The users of outsourcing MUST create a security concept for each outsourcing project based on the security requirements resulting from IT-Grundschutz. The user's security concept MUST be coordinated with the providers. Likewise, each provider SHOULD submit an individual security concept. The security concepts SHOULD be merged. The users or independent third parties MUST regularly check whether the security concept is effective.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The using institution creates a security concept that defines its own requirements. This is transmitted to the provider. The provider presents its own concept describing how it implements the requirements. Both documents are reconciled in a joint workshop and merged into an overall security concept. The effectiveness is reviewed through regular audits or by requesting evidence.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the contract requires the implementation of IT-Grundschutz or equivalent requirements. The overall security concept is reviewed to check whether it describes both the requirements of the using institution and the implementation by the provider, and whether it has been coordinated. It is checked whether evidence of the regular review of effectiveness (e.g., audit reports) is available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is contractually agreed that the provider establishes and maintains a certified Information Security Management System (ISMS), e.g., according to ISO 27001. The joint security concept is a formally approved document and an annex to the outsourcing contract. It defines clear responsibilities (RACI matrix) for each security measure. A defined process for joint risk analyses is established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The provider's ISMS certification becomes a mandatory requirement in the selection process. The joint security concept is reviewed annually or upon significant changes and is re-approved by both parties. Joint risk analysis workshops are conducted regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the provider's valid ISMS certificate. It is checked whether the joint security concept exists as a contract annex and contains a RACI matrix. The minutes of the joint risk analyses and the regular reviews of the security concept are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The joint security concept is a living document that is integrated into the ISMS of both parties. The effectiveness of the security measures is not only periodically checked but continuously monitored through shared dashboards and automated compliance checks. The security requirements are dynamically adapted to the current threat landscape.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technical interfaces are created to import telemetry data and compliance status from the provider's environment into the using institution's SIEM or GRC tool. Defined deviations from the security concept's baseline trigger automated alerts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the monitoring tools and dashboards. The effectiveness of the automated compliance checks is verified. It is checked whether the process for dynamically adapting the security concept to new threats works. An automated test could query the provider's dashboard API and compare it with the expected configuration: `check-compliance-api --endpoint 'api.provider.com/status' --expected-config 'config.json'`.

controls.title: Regulations for a planned or unplanned termination of an outsourcing relationship (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Arrangements MUST be made for both planned and unplanned terminations of the outsourcing relationship. It MUST be specified how all information, data, and hardware of the users are to be returned by the provider. Legal requirements for data retention MUST be observed. Furthermore, it SHOULD be verified whether the provider's access rights have been revoked upon termination of the outsourcing relationship.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Detailed exit clauses are included in the outsourcing contract. These describe the data return process (incl. format and deadlines) and the provider's obligation for the verifiable deletion of all remaining data. An offboarding checklist is created, which also includes the deactivation of all accounts and the return of keys and ID cards.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the outsourcing contracts contain appropriate exit clauses. In the event of a recent termination of a relationship, the completion of the offboarding checklist is checked. In particular, it is verified whether the provider has confirmed the deletion of the data in writing and whether all access rights have been verifiably revoked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each outsourcing relationship, a detailed and formally approved exit plan is created as a contract addendum. This plan not only specifies data return but also responsibilities, a detailed schedule, and the criteria for successful termination. The process for blocking all access rights is regularly checked as part of offboarding tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard template for exit plans is developed. The creation of the specific plan is a milestone in the outsourcing project. The verification of access rights after offboarding is a fixed item in the internal control system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and completeness of the exit plans for a sample of outsourcing arrangements. Evidence of the regular execution of offboarding tests (e.g., checking whether a test account of a fictitious, departed provider employee is deactivated) is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The exit plan contains detailed procedures for various scenarios, including an immediate or hostile termination. The data is maintained during operation in such a way (e.g., in standard formats or via data escrow) that a rapid migration to an alternative provider is possible at any time. The revocation of access rights is fully automated and is triggered as part of the formal termination process in the IAM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Data escrow agreements are concluded for critical services. The offboarding process in the IAM system is configured so that all access, keys, and certificates associated with the provider can be revoked with a single click.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the scenarios in the exit plan for completeness and plausibility. The configuration of the automated offboarding workflow in the IAM system is checked. It is verified whether the data escrow agreement is up-to-date and whether the deposited data is regularly verified. An automated test could check the access rights status of a test user after executing the offboarding script: `get-user-access --user 'provider-test-user' | assert-equal 'none'`.

controls.title: Creation of a strategy for outsourcing projects (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A strategy for outsourcing projects SHOULD be created and established. This strategy SHOULD describe the goals, opportunities, and risks of the outsourcing projects. The strategy SHOULD provide the institution with a framework for the requirement profiles, the suitability requirements for providers, and outsourcing management. A multi-sourcing strategy SHOULD be pursued. The users SHOULD retain sufficient skills, competencies, and resources to prevent dependency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A strategy document is approved by the institution's management. It defines which types of processes can generally be outsourced and which must remain in-house (e.g., core business). It sets out the basic objectives (e.g., cost reduction, access to specialist knowledge) and the most important risks to be managed (e.g., dependency, loss of control).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the strategy document for outsourcing and checks whether it has been approved by the management level. It is checked whether the document addresses the required aspects (goals, risks, framework conditions, multi-sourcing, competence retention).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The outsourcing strategy is a formal, management-approved document that is regularly reviewed and updated. It defines explicit criteria for what can and cannot be outsourced. It includes a clear approach to avoiding vendor lock-in and a concrete plan for maintaining and developing necessary internal competencies to manage the service providers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The strategy is reviewed annually as part of strategic corporate planning. A competence management program ensures that the skills required to manage the service providers (e.g., contract management, technical review) are available and developed within the company.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies not only the existence of the strategy, but also the process of its regular review and approval. It is checked whether clear criteria for outsourcing decisions are defined and whether a plan for competence retention exists and is being implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The outsourcing strategy is an integral part of the overall corporate and IT strategy and is reviewed annually. It is supported by dynamic models that assess the risk-reward profile of outsourcing various business functions. It includes a proactive program for managing a diversified portfolio of providers to maximize supply chain resilience.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Sourcing scenarios and business cases are calculated using quantitative models. Provider management is proactive and constantly seeks new, innovative partners to optimize the portfolio and reduce dependencies. The strategy is actively communicated to all relevant stakeholders.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the minutes of the strategy meetings and the quantitative models used. It is checked whether the outsourcing strategy is closely linked to the overall corporate strategy. The implementation of proactive portfolio management for providers is verified.

controls.title: Establishment of a policy for outsourcing (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the strategy for outsourcing projects, a policy for the procurement of outsourcing services SHOULD be created and established within the institution. This SHOULD standardize the general requirements, based on the basic requirements for contracts, as well as other aspects of information security. The testing and approval process for outsourcing projects SHOULD be regulated in this policy. Furthermore, measures SHOULD be considered to manage compliance risks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central policy document is created that covers the entire lifecycle of an outsourcing arrangement. It describes the necessary steps, responsibilities, and templates to be used from the initial idea to termination. The policy is made known to all employees involved in outsourcing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the outsourcing policy. It is checked whether the policy is based on the strategy and covers the required content (standardization of requirements, test and approval procedures, handling of compliance risks). It is verified that the policy is established and known to the relevant employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal, comprehensive policy has been published and verifiably brought to the attention of all relevant employees. It contains clear, detailed procedures for each phase of the outsourcing lifecycle, from the initial assessment to termination. The test and approval process is defined in detail with clear roles and responsibilities (RACI).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is prominently placed on the intranet. Acknowledgment by relevant employees (e.g., project managers, buyers) is documented via a learning management system. The processes described in the policy are linked to clear responsibilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies not only the existence of the policy, but also the proof of acknowledgment by the target group. Based on a specific outsourcing project, it is checked whether the procedural steps and responsibilities defined in the policy have been adhered to.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy is implemented in a workflow management system or GRC tool that actively guides the participants through the outsourcing process. The system ensures that all required steps, checks, and approvals are completed in the correct order. Compliance with the policy is automatically monitored and deviations are escalated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A ticketing system or a GRC tool is configured to map the outsourcing process defined in the policy. Milestones can only be completed once the required documents (e.g., risk analysis, approved contract) have been uploaded and approved by the responsible roles.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the workflow system. It is checked whether the processes mapped in the system correspond to the policy and whether the control mechanisms (e.g., mandatory approvals) are effective. The automated monitoring and escalation reports are reviewed. An automatic test could check the status of a workflow ticket and verify that it cannot be moved to the next phase without the required attachments.

controls.title: Establishment of a responsible person for outsourcing management (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The various outsourcing projects SHOULD be managed by a person responsible for outsourcing management. The responsible person SHOULD be appointed and their powers defined and documented. The responsible person SHOULD be used as an interface in communication between the users and providers. Furthermore, the responsible person SHOULD prepare reports on outsourcing, be involved in contract design, receive an appropriate quota of working days, and be trained and sensitized with regard to information security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A person is officially appointed as outsourcing manager or coordinator. The role and its basic tasks are recorded in a role description. This person is established as the central point of contact for all outsourcing topics.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the letter of appointment and the role description for the responsible person. In discussions with other stakeholders, it is verified that the person is perceived as the central interface. It is checked whether the person has participated in security training.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The role of the outsourcing manager is formally defined with a detailed job description, clearly defined responsibilities, and documented authorities. The person is provided with dedicated resources and regular, specialized training (e.g., on contract law, provider management). They create scheduled reports for management and are a mandatory participant in all contract negotiations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The role is anchored in the organizational chart. The time quotas and training measures budgeted for the role are verifiable. The reports follow a standard template and are presented to a fixed management body (e.g., IT steering committee).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the detailed job description and the evidence of the assigned resources and training. The standardized reports and the minutes of the management meetings in which they were presented are inspected. It is verified whether the person can be proven to have been involved in all relevant contract negotiations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated outsourcing management team (Outsourcing Management Office, OMO) has been established, led by the responsible person. The team uses specialized tools for provider management, performance monitoring, and risk assessment. The role is a key strategic function in the company, actively shaping the sourcing strategy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The OMO is established as a separate organizational unit. Professional Supplier Relationship Management (SRM) and GRC tools are used. The OMO not only creates reports but also proactively develops proposals for optimizing the provider portfolio.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the structure and resources of the OMO. The use of specialized tools is reviewed. Based on strategy papers and minutes, it is verified that the OMO is actively involved in shaping the company-wide sourcing strategy.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
In outsourcing, institutions (outsourcing users) transfer business processes or activities, in whole or in part, to one or more external service companies (outsourcing providers). These so-called outsourcing providers operate the business processes or activities according to specified criteria within the framework of the agreed outsourcing relationship. However, from an information security perspective, the responsibility always remains with the outsourcing institution.
Outsourcing can involve the use and operation of hardware and software, where the service can be provided on the client's premises or at an external operating site of the outsourcing provider. Typical examples of classic "IT outsourcing," which this module refers to, are the operation of a data center, an application, or a website. Outsourcing is a general term that is often specified by other terms, such as hosting, housing, or colocation.
In many cases, an outsourcing relationship involves not only the original user and outsourcing provider but also further sub-service providers downstream from the outsourcing provider. If parts of business processes or activities are further transferred from outsourcing providers to sub-service providers, the business processes or activities outsourced by the user are further fragmented. This affects the complexity of the outsourcing chain, resulting in diminishing transparency for the outsourcing user. The proof that the requirements placed on the outsourcing provider are met extends to both the outsourcing provider and the sub-service providers.
For better understanding, this module uses the term "process" as a substitute for business process, activity, or component that is outsourced.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose:
The goal of this module is to ensure the fundamental values of information security—confidentiality, integrity, and availability—throughout the entire lifecycle of outsourcing by the outsourcing user. Outsourcing here refers to classic "IT outsourcing."
The requirements of module OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing are intended to help identify, prevent, and mitigate potential threats to business operations.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing is to be applied once for each outsourcing provider from the perspective of the outsourcing user.
This module addresses threats and security requirements from the perspective of the users of outsourcing services and is limited to the requirements for the protection of information on the part of the outsourcing institution.
This module does not cover the transmission paths to outsourcing providers.
Likewise, the use of cloud services is not covered in this module; for this, the module OPS.2.2 Cloud Usage must be applied.
Scenarios that deviate from classic "IT outsourcing" (such as the operation of hardware and software, hosting, housing, etc.) may not be fully covered by the module OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing and may require a separate risk analysis.
Special cases such as security services, cleaning staff, maintenance services, and external personnel are exceptions for which the module OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing is not to be applied. These are integrated through the requirements for security services, cleaning staff, maintenance services, and external personnel in the modules ORP.1 Organization and INF.1 General Building.
The counterpart to the module OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing is the module OPS.3.2 Providing Outsourcing, which deals with the outsourcing relationship from the service provider's perspective. Together, the two modules provide a holistic view of the outsourcing relationship and, with their requirements, ensure a fundamentally secure outsourcing project.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Inadequate outsourcing strategy
parts.prose: An inadequate strategy leads to information security not being adequately considered in outsourcing projects. As a result, information security is not properly addressed in the individual phases of the outsourcing lifecycle, and thus a sufficient level of information security is not strived for and implemented in the own institution as well as at outsourcing providers. This can impair or disrupt processes and lead to information leakage to unauthorized third parties.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Risk of outsourcing institution-critical processes
parts.prose: Processes that should remain within the institution due to their criticality or protection needs are outsourced. Consequently, the institution can no longer adequately control and manage the process, which is necessary for proper business operations. If the process fails or is disrupted, proper business operations cannot be ensured. Furthermore, the outsourcing providers gain greater influence. The outsourcing users face a loss of control.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Dependence on outsourcing providers
parts.prose: When an institution decides to outsource, it also becomes dependent on outsourcing providers. This dependency can lead to a loss of knowledge and the outsourced processes can no longer be fully controlled. In addition, the protection needs of the outsourced business processes and information might be assessed differently. This can lead to the implementation of security measures that are inappropriate for the protection needs. Institutions often outsource entire business processes to outsourcing providers. The outsourcing providers can thereby fully control the business processes with sensitive information, resources, and IT systems. At the same time, the knowledge of these areas diminishes for outsourcing users. As a result, it is possible that outsourcing users no longer notice information security deficits. This situation could be exploited by outsourcing providers, e.g., by drastically increasing prices or reducing the quality of services.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Inadequate level of information security in outsourcing
parts.prose: An inadequate level of information security can lead to information security not being adequately considered in outsourcing projects. The consequence is that the outsourcing providers maintain no or only an insufficient standard of information security for the outsourcing process. Consequently, vulnerabilities arise from which IT-based attacks and data losses can originate. In addition, legal consequences with financial implications and reputational damage can arise for the outsourcing users.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Deficient outsourcing management
parts.prose: Non-existent or only partially implemented outsourcing management manifests itself in the inadequate management of ongoing outsourced processes. This reduces or eliminates transparency over the outsourced processes. As a result, outsourcing users can no longer control and adequately steer the outsourcing providers. The outsourcing users can no longer ensure that the outsourcing providers handle information security carefully in the outsourced process.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Inadequate contractual arrangements with outsourcing providers
parts.prose: Inadequate contractual agreements with outsourcing providers can lead to vulnerabilities in information security along the entire outsourcing lifecycle. The contractual agreements define the entire outsourcing process and represent the starting point for claims by the users against the outsourcing providers. Due to inadequate contractual agreements with outsourcing providers, diverse and serious security problems can arise. If tasks, performance parameters, or efforts are insufficiently or ambiguously described, security measures may not be implemented due to ignorance or a lack of resources. This can have many negative consequences, for example, if regulatory requirements and obligations are not met or information duties and laws are not complied with. If the aspect of information security is not considered in the contract design, the processes and data of the outsourcing users may be inadequately secured.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Inappropriate management of entry, access, and access rights
parts.prose: Depending on the outsourcing project, it may be necessary for employees of outsourcing providers to require entry, access, and access rights to IT systems, information, buildings, or rooms of the outsourcing users. These rights can be inappropriately granted, managed, and controlled, which in extreme cases can even lead to the unauthorized granting of rights. Furthermore, the necessary protection of the outsourcing users' information can no longer be guaranteed. For example, it is a serious security risk to grant administrative privileges to employees of outsourcing providers in an uncontrolled manner. They could exploit these privileges and copy or manipulate sensitive information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Loss of control and governance due to onward transfers
parts.prose: Parts of business processes or activities are sometimes passed on in whole or in part to sub-service providers by outsourcing providers. As the outsourcing process becomes more complex due to the additional parties involved, it becomes less transparent for the outsourcing users. Due to this lack of transparency, the outsourcing users can no longer adequately control and govern the outsourced processes. In addition, outsourcing providers may fail to require the minimum level of information security required by outsourcing users from the sub-service provider. One consequence is that the agreed-upon information technology security aspects may not be fully implemented by the sub-service providers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Missing and inadequate instruments for managing outsourcing providers
parts.prose: For an institution to be able to check whether the outsourced processes are being properly implemented by outsourcing providers, it needs not only corresponding agreements but also the instruments to do so. These can be, for example, qualitative and quantitative key performance indicators (KPIs). In order to be able to react to underperformance and poor performance, correspondingly defined key performance indicators are required. Missing and inadequate instruments lead to the fact that the outsourcing providers cannot be adequately controlled and managed. As a result, it can no longer be checked and verified whether the defined security requirements are being met.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.10. Inadequate regulations for a planned and unplanned termination of an outsourcing relationship
parts.prose: An outsourcing relationship can be terminated in an orderly manner or terminated extraordinarily. In this case, inadequate or missing regulations can lead to hardware, data, and access not being handed over or transmitted to the outsourcing users, or not being done so properly.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.11. Insufficient emergency concept
parts.prose: In the event of a disruption, an emergency, or a crisis, insufficient emergency management can lead to the failure of outsourced processes. In particular, insufficient emergency preparedness prepares the institution inadequately for an emergency or crisis situation. Effective emergency response cannot be ensured on this basis. Disruptions, emergencies, and crisis situations cannot be controlled and can lead to direct economic impacts. In this case, not only the own institution is affected, but also all connected institutions that must be considered in emergency preparedness and response. Cascade effects from upstream and downstream service providers lead to considerable impacts on the business operations of the outsourcing users.

controls.title: Compliance with information security objectives through an information security management system

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The information security objectives are only considered for selected customers classified as particularly critical, or only partially (e.g., only availability). Legal or regulatory requirements are only addressed reactively upon explicit request by the customer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this maturity level, the consideration of protection objectives is ad hoc and not anchored in a standardized process. Implementation often focuses on easily achievable aspects, while more complex requirements such as confidentiality or specific regulatory specifications are neglected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through random checks of various customer contracts whether and to what extent protection objectives and regulatory aspects have been taken into account. It is checked whether a pattern is discernible that indicates a systematic neglect of certain protection objectives or customer groups.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The protection requirement categories of confidentiality, integrity, and availability are generally recorded and documented for all customers. However, compliance with the protection objectives is based on informal processes and the individual knowledge of the responsible employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The assessment of protection needs is typically carried out using a simple checklist in the onboarding process. However, there is no formal process to ensure that the identified protection objectives are systematically translated into technical and organizational measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies whether a protection needs assessment is documented for all customers. Subsequently, through interviews with employees and inspection of system configurations, it is checked whether the documented protection objectives have been implemented in a traceable manner, even if the process is informal.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The protection needs for confidentiality, integrity, and availability of outsourcing users MUST be considered in the outsourcing process. It MUST be ensured that the minimum level of information security required by the outsourcing users is maintained. In addition, the applicable regulatory and legal aspects MUST be taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined process is established to systematically record, document, and translate each customer's protection needs into concrete security requirements. This process is repeatable and ensures that all relevant aspects (protection objectives, legal requirements) are treated consistently.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the process documentation for determining and implementing protection needs. Using several customer examples, the correct execution of the process from a requirements survey to the implementation and review of measures is traced. The documentation must be complete and consistent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for ensuring compliance with protection objectives is formalized and reviewed regularly, at least annually, together with the customer and adjusted if necessary. A structured process exists for monitoring regulatory and legal changes, which proactively initiates adjustments to security measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The results of the regular reviews with customers are recorded and fed into the security concepts via a change management system. Specialized feeds or service providers are used to monitor the legal situation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the annual reviews with customers and the evidence from the legal monitoring process. It is verified that identified changes to protection objectives or legal frameworks have demonstrably led to adjustments in security measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire process for managing information security is integrated into a certified ISMS (e.g., according to ISO 27001). The achieved security level is continuously monitored with automated tools (Continuous Controls Monitoring). Customers receive real-time insight into the compliance with their protection objectives and relevant compliance requirements via a portal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool is used to link customers' protection objectives with specific controls and their implementation status. Automated scans and agents permanently check configurations against the defined target values. The customer portal is directly connected to this system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the valid ISMS certificate. The functionality of the GRC tool and the automated monitoring is checked by running test cases (e.g., intentional misconfiguration) and tracing their correct detection and alerting in the system. The correctness of the data displayed in the customer portal is validated on a random basis.

controls.title: Basic requirements for contracts with outsourcing users

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information security requirements are only included in contracts on an ad hoc basis and without a standardized foundation. There is no uniform contract template, and important aspects such as audit rights or regulations on sub-outsourcing are often missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Contracts are drawn up individually by sales or project management. Security clauses are only included if the customer explicitly requests them. There is no central review by a security or legal department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes a selection of customer contracts and finds that no uniform security clauses are used. The absence of essential regulations (e.g., audit rights, subcontractors) is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic checklist or a text block with security requirements, the use of which is recommended in contracts but not enforced. A uniform contract template is not used consistently.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The legal or security department provides a standard information security appendix. However, sales staff decide on a case-by-case basis whether and in what form to use it. SLAs and NDAs are often handled as separate, unrelated documents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares several contracts with the provided checklist or text block and notes deviations and inconsistent application. It is checked whether basic elements such as SLAs and NDAs are systematically missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Uniform basic requirements for outsourcing contracts MUST be developed. These MUST include aspects of information security, user security requirements, handling of sub-outsourcing, and the user's right to inspections, reviews, and audits. These basic requirements MUST be implemented uniformly in agreements and contracts. A non-disclosure agreement, information exchange agreements, and service level agreements SHOULD be agreed upon with the users. Based on the basic requirements, a uniform contract template SHOULD be created and used for all outsourcing projects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized contract template, approved by the legal and security departments, is developed that includes all required clauses as a fixed component. The use of this template is mandatory for all new outsourcing contracts. Deviations require a formal approval process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the official contract template and the process for its application. Subsequently, using a sample of recently concluded contracts, it is verified that the template has been used consistently and contains all required regulations (security, audit rights, subcontractors, SLAs).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The mandatory contract template is reviewed regularly, at least annually, by the legal and security departments for currency and effectiveness and is adapted to new legal or technical framework conditions as needed. The process includes a clear regulation for renegotiating existing contracts in the event of significant changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual review workshop is scheduled with legal, security, and sales to review the contract template. Changes are documented and communicated via a formal change management process. For existing contracts, there is a strategy on how the new standards will be introduced at the next contract renewal.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes and results of the annual contract reviews. It is checked whether identified needs for adjustment (e.g., due to new laws like DORA) were promptly incorporated into the template. The implementation upon contract renewals is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire contract lifecycle is supported by a Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM) system. The standard template and all clauses are stored in the system. Deviations from the norm are automatically detected and trigger an escalation and approval workflow. Compliance with SLAs is automatically monitored and directly compared with the contractual agreements in the CLM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CLM tool is implemented and integrated with the CRM system (for customer data) and the monitoring system (for SLA data). Legal and security approvals are granted directly in the system. The system automatically generates reports on contract compliance and risks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is granted read access to the CLM system. It is checked whether the workflows for contract approval are configured correctly. The correct handling of standard contracts and deviations is traced using the audit logs in the system. The automated SLA monitoring is verified by analyzing the system reports.

controls.title: Passing on of contractually agreed provisions with users of outsourcing to sub-service providers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Contractual obligations are only passed on to sub-service providers who are considered critical. For less critical service providers, a formal transfer of the provisions is waived.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no systematic classification of sub-service providers. The decision on whether to pass on obligations is made by the purchasing or project management department on a case-by-case basis and often without the involvement of the security department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the list of sub-service providers with the contracts concluded with them. It is found that security clauses and other obligations from the customer contracts have been passed on to the sub-service providers inconsistently or not at all.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Obligations from customer contracts are generally passed on to sub-service providers, typically through a standard contract addendum. However, there is no process to verify compliance with these obligations by the sub-service provider.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The purchasing department has a standard document for sub-service provider contracts that regulates the transfer of obligations. However, compliance is not actively monitored; reliance is placed on the sub-service provider's contractual commitment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the contracts with sub-service providers contain the required clauses for passing on obligations. It is then determined by inquiring with the responsible management that no verification mechanisms (e.g., audits, requests for evidence) have been implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If processes are further outsourced by outsourcing providers to sub-service providers, the contractual provisions with the users of outsourcing MUST be passed on to the sub-service providers. This MUST be specified and enforced accordingly in the contracts with the sub-service providers. Upon request from users of outsourcing, these contracts MUST be presented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard process for managing sub-service providers is established. This process ensures that all relevant obligations from the customer contracts are incorporated into the contracts with the sub-service providers. The contracts include a clause that grants the provider the right to check compliance and to grant the end customer insight into the contract upon request (if necessary, in a redacted form).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the sub-service provider management process. Using an example (e.g., a customer with high protection needs and a linked sub-service provider), the chain of contract design is traced. It is checked whether the obligations have been passed on consistently and whether the contracts contain the required clauses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formalized process for verifying compliance with the passed-on provisions at sub-service providers is established. This process includes the regular request for evidence (e.g., certificates, audit reports) and, for critical sub-service providers, the execution of our own audits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual review cycle is defined in the sub-service provider management process. Depending on the criticality of the sub-service provider, specific evidence (e.g., ISO 27001 certificate, SOC 2 report, penetration test results) is requested and evaluated. The results are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the sub-service provider register and the documentation of the reviews performed. Random checks are carried out to see whether current evidence is available for critical sub-service providers and whether it has been plausibly evaluated. The planning and execution of audits is also reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive 'Supply Chain Security Management' program is established, supported by tools. The security posture of sub-service providers is assessed continuously or at short intervals (e.g., through security rating services). The contracts allow for short-term termination or a change if a sub-service provider no longer meets the security requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A security rating service is subscribed to, which continuously assesses the external attack surface of the sub-service providers. The results are incorporated into a dynamic risk assessment. If a service provider falls below a defined threshold, an escalation process is automatically started.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and reports of the security rating service. It is checked whether the defined thresholds are appropriate and whether the escalation process functions as documented when they are breached. The response to a deterioration in a sub-service provider's rating is traced using examples.

controls.title: Creation of a multi-tenancy separation concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multi-tenancy separation is only implemented on one level, e.g., at the network level through VLANs. Separation at the application or database level is missing or insufficient. A comprehensive, written concept does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The separation relies on basic virtualization or network functions. Within an application used by multiple tenants, separation is achieved, for example, only by a simple filter in the database query, which is error-prone.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the system architecture and determines that the multi-tenancy separation is not consistently implemented across all layers (network, system, application, data). The absence of a written concept is documented as a major deficiency.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic multi-tenancy separation is implemented on multiple levels (e.g., network, separate VMs/containers). However, a formal, documented concept that describes all mechanisms in detail and regulates the distinction between tenant-specific and multi-tenant data is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The separation is implemented by the system administrators to the best of their knowledge. The configurations are in place, but their justification and the interaction of the various mechanisms are not documented, which makes verification and maintenance difficult.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies by inspecting the system configurations that basic separation mechanisms exist. However, through interviews, it is determined that there is no comprehensive, written concept that serves as a target specification.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A multi-tenancy separation concept MUST be created and implemented. The concept MUST ensure that data and processing contexts of different users are separated with sufficient security. A distinction MUST be made between tenant-dependent and multi-tenant data and objects. It MUST be stated which mechanisms are used to separate the tenants. The mechanisms MUST be implemented sufficiently. The concept MUST be made available to the users and provide security appropriate to the protection requirements of the data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A written concept is created that describes the architecture of the multi-tenancy separation at all relevant levels (physical, network, virtualization, operating system, database, application). It clearly defines which resources are shared and which are dedicated, and how the logical separation is enforced. This concept is part of the standard documentation provided to customers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the multi-tenancy separation concept for completeness, consistency, and appropriateness for the protection requirements of the customer data. Subsequently, it is checked on a random basis whether the technical and organizational measures described in the concept are correctly and effectively implemented in the production environment. (`show running-config`, database schema analysis).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The effectiveness of the multi-tenancy separation concept and its implementation is verified regularly, at least annually, through targeted technical audits or penetration tests. The concept includes detailed logical separation mechanisms at the application, database, and storage levels.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a year, a specialized penetration test is commissioned with the aim of breaching the tenant boundaries. The results of the test are used to improve the concept and the implementation. All findings are tracked in a ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports of the latest penetration tests on multi-tenancy separation. It is checked whether the tests had an appropriate scope and whether all identified vulnerabilities were demonstrably and promptly remediated. The process for commissioning and evaluating the tests is also assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multi-tenancy separation is enforced wherever possible through cryptographic mechanisms and hardware-based security technologies (e.g., Confidential Computing, HSMs for tenant-specific keys). The correct configuration and effectiveness of the separation is continuously monitored and verified by automated systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Cloud-native technologies like Confidential Containers (e.g., based on AMD SEV or Intel TDX) are used to isolate the runtime environments of the tenants. Each tenant receives their own cryptographic keys in an HSM, so that a mixing of data is excluded even at the storage level. Configuration scanners permanently check compliance with the separation rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the hardware-based separation and the configuration of the cryptographic controls. The functionality of the continuous configuration monitoring is checked. Based on audit logs from the HSM and the confidential computing platform, the strict separation of tenant-specific operations is verified. A `terraform plan` or `ansible --check` can be used to check the declared configuration.

controls.title: Creation of a security concept for the outsourcing service.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is only a very general, high-level security document that does not address the specific services and technologies. Customer-specific security requirements are not systematically recorded in a concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Often it is a marketing document that makes general security statements but does not describe any concrete, verifiable measures. There is no process to capture and document the security requirements of a new customer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the submitted document lacks the character of a security concept because it does not describe detailed technical and organizational measures. The absence of customer-specific concepts is assessed as a deficiency.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general security concept for the service exists and describes the basic measures. Customer-specific requirements are added as informal addendums or notes but are not integrated into a coherent overall system. Reviews of the implementation are carried out on an ad hoc basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a basic document maintained by the technical department. If a customer has special requirements, these are recorded in a separate document. However, there is no guarantee that these two documents are consistent or that the implementation of the measures is regularly reviewed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the general security concept and the customer-specific supplements. Inconsistencies or contradictions are identified. It cannot be proven that the implementation of the concept is checked regularly and systematically.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Outsourcing providers MUST create a security concept for their services. For individual outsourcing projects, specific security concepts MUST also be created based on the security requirements of the users. The provider's security concept and its implementation SHOULD be merged into an overall security concept. Providers and users MUST jointly develop and document security objectives. A common classification for all sensitive information MUST also be created. Furthermore, providers MUST regularly check whether the security concept has been implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A modular structure for security concepts is established: A general concept describes the basic security for all customers. Building on this, customer-specific concepts are created that document the individual requirements and the jointly developed security objectives. A defined process ensures the regular review of the implementation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and structure of the general security concept as well as an exemplary customer-specific one. It is verified whether the documentation of the jointly developed security objectives and the classification of information is available. The logs of the regular implementation reviews are inspected and evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security concept is a living document that is formally reviewed and updated at least annually or in the event of significant changes. The review process involves all relevant stakeholders, including the customer. The implementation of the measures described in the concept is verified through internal audits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Changes to the security concept are controlled via a formal change management system. An annual internal audit plan is created and executed to review the implementation. The results of the audits are reported to management and feed into the continuous improvement process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit plan and the reports of the internal audits on the implementation of the security concept. It is checked whether the audits cover all essential aspects of the concept and whether the identified deficiencies are tracked and remedied. The minutes of the annual reviews of the concept are also checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security concept and the status of its implementation are managed in a GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool. Compliance with the concept is continuously monitored using automated 'Policy as Code' mechanisms. Deviations from the target state trigger automatic alarms and, where possible, self-healing actions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Security requirements are defined as code (e.g. with Open Policy Agent) and integrated into the CI/CD pipeline. This prevents non-compliant configurations from reaching production in the first place. Running systems are permanently checked against these policies. The GRC tool aggregates the results and provides a live dashboard on the compliance status.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the security policies defined in code and their integration into the development pipeline. (`opa test .` or similar). The configuration of the continuous monitoring is checked and it is verified how deviations are displayed and handled in the GRC tool. The effectiveness is verified by a test case (e.g. commit of a non-compliant configuration) which must be correctly blocked by the pipeline.

controls.title: Regulations for a planned and unplanned termination of an outsourcing relationship

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal process for returning customer data at the end of the contract. A guaranteed and documented secure deletion of the remaining data does not take place. The systematic revocation of access rights is neglected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After the end of the contract, an export of the customer data is created and handed over to the customer. The production systems are shut down, but the backups containing customer data are not specifically deleted, but expire with the normal retention period. User accounts are often only deactivated, not deleted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews the responsible employees about the offboarding process and finds that it is not formally documented. No proof of secure data deletion (e.g. deletion log) can be provided. An examination of orphaned accounts in the system shows that access rights have not been consistently revoked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic offboarding checklist that provides for the return of data and the deletion of residual data. However, the process is manual, not consistently documented, and lacks formal verification of successful deletion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator works through a checklist after the contract ends. The deletion of the data on the storage systems is carried out, but no detailed log is created that proves the deletion for each individual resource. The review of the revocation of rights is part of the checklist, but the implementation is not double-checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the offboarding checklist. Based on a recently terminated contract, an attempt is made to trace the processing of the checklist. It is found that the documentation is incomplete and no tamper-proof evidence of secure deletion can be provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Arrangements MUST be made for how to proceed when outsourcing relationships are terminated, whether planned or unplanned. It MUST be specified how all user information, data and hardware are to be returned. Subsequently, the remaining data stocks MUST be securely deleted after the statutory requirements have expired. This MUST be documented by the providers. Furthermore, it SHOULD be checked whether the access rights for users have been revoked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed and formalized offboarding process is defined and documented. This process is contractually anchored and describes the steps for data return, the methods for secure deletion (according to BSI or NIST standards), and the procedure for deactivating and deleting all associated accounts and rights. Each step is documented in an offboarding protocol and countersigned by a second person (four-eyes principle).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the process documentation for offboarding. The correct and complete execution of the process is verified using the offboarding protocols of several terminated contracts. In particular, the existence of evidence of secure deletion and deactivation of access rights is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The exit process is contractually agreed with the customer in detail and includes a precise plan for data migration, timelines, and responsibilities. The secure deletion of the data is proven by a technical procedure (e.g. proof of destruction of cryptographic keys) or confirmed by an independent third party.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each customer, an individual exit plan is created as an annex to the contract at the beginning of the contract. This plan is activated at the end of the contract. For data deletion, cryptographic erasure (crypto-shredding) is used, where only the key needs to be destroyed. The destruction of the key, e.g. in an HSM, is logged and serves as proof.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contractually agreed exit plan and compares it with the process actually carried out. The log of the key destruction from the HSM is checked as proof of secure deletion. Alternatively, the report of the independent third party is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire offboarding process is largely automated. Data is returned via predefined, secure channels. The deletion of data and the revocation of all identities and access rights are triggered by an automated workflow in the IAM system as soon as the contract status is set to 'terminated'. The completion of the process is automatically logged and reported to the customer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script or a runbook in an automation tool (e.g. Ansible, Terraform) is developed that carries out all steps of the offboarding: data export, destruction of the tenant-specific VMs/containers, deletion of the associated keys in the KMS/HSM and removal of the user accounts and groups from the IAM system. The trigger for this run is the status change in the CRM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automation script or runbook and verifies its correctness and completeness. (`ansible-lint`, `terraform validate`). Based on the execution logs of the automation tool and the audit logs of the target systems (IAM, KMS, cloud platform), it is verified that the process for a terminated contract has been completed fully and successfully.

controls.title: Provision of the outsourced service by multiple sub-service providers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The provider is aware of the risk of a critical sub-service provider failing, but has not evaluated or contractually engaged any concrete alternative providers. There is a complete dependency on a single sub-service provider.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the event of a sub-service provider failure, the search for a replacement would have to begin, which would lead to long downtimes for the end customer. This risk is not proactively managed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies the critical sub-service providers in discussion with management and asks about the plans in case of failure. It is determined that no alternative providers or contingency plans exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Alternative sub-service providers for critical processes have been identified and initial contact has been made. However, there are no formal agreements, contracts, or technical plans for a quick switch.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of potential replacement service providers is maintained in purchasing or risk management. However, there is no guarantee that they would be available in an emergency or could meet the technical requirements. A switch would be a lengthy project.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the list of identified alternative providers. Upon inquiry, it is determined that there are no contractual arrangements (e.g. framework agreements) or technical migration plans that would enable an orderly transition.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If processes of outsourcing providers are further transferred to sub-service providers, the outsourcing providers SHOULD have several qualified sub-service providers available in case sub-service providers fail or terminate. This SHOULD be documented jointly with the users of outsourcing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each critical sub-service provider, at least one qualified alternative provider is identified and subjected to a suitability assessment. The existence of this alternative and the basic strategy for a switch-over are recorded in the documentation for the customer (e.g., in the security concept).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the sub-service provider register and the associated risk assessment. For each service provider classified as critical, it is verified whether a qualified alternative provider is documented. The documentation provided to the customer is checked for corresponding entries.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A framework or standby agreement exists with at least one alternative sub-service provider for each critical service. A technical migration plan for the switch-over has been developed and is regularly reviewed for its currency. The essential steps of the plan are run through in a table-top exercise.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A framework agreement ensures that the alternative provider keeps capacities available in an emergency. The migration plan describes the technical steps, data formats, responsibilities, and the timeline for a switch-over. A workshop is held annually to check whether the plan is still aligned with the current systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the framework agreement with the alternative sub-service provider and the technical migration plan. The minutes of the regular reviews or exercises are inspected to assess the currency and plausibility of the plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An active multi-sourcing strategy is established. The service is designed to be technology-agnostic and can be ported with minimal effort between several pre-qualified sub-service providers (e.g., by using containers and standardized APIs). The switch-over process is largely automated and is regularly tested live.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application is run in Docker containers and uses open standards (e.g., S3-compatible storage). The infrastructure is managed as code (Terraform), with a separate provider module for each of the qualified providers. An annual failover test includes the live deployment of the application to one of the alternative providers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the application architecture and the 'Infrastructure as Code' artifacts to verify portability. The logs of the last live failover tests are inspected and analyzed for success, duration, and any issues that occurred. (`terraform validate` for the different provider configurations).

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
In outsourcing, institutions (outsourcing users) transfer business processes or activities in whole or in part to one or more external service companies (outsourcing providers). These so-called outsourcing providers operate the business processes or activities according to specified criteria within the framework of the agreed outsourcing relationship. However, from an information security perspective, the responsibility always remains with the outsourcing institution.
Outsourcing can concern the use and operation of hardware and software, whereby the service can be provided on the premises of the client or at an external operating site of the outsourcing provider. Typical examples of classic "IT outsourcing," to which this module refers, are the operation of a data center, an application, or a website. Outsourcing is an umbrella term that is often specified by other terms, such as hosting, housing, or colocation.
In many cases, an outsourcing relationship involves not only the original outsourcing users and providers but also further sub-service providers downstream from the outsourcing provider. If parts of business processes or activities are further transferred from outsourcing providers to sub-service providers, the business processes or activities outsourced by users are further fragmented. This affects the complexity of the outsourcing chain, resulting in diminishing transparency for the outsourcing users. The proof that the requirements placed on the outsourcing providers are met extends to both the outsourcing providers and the sub-service providers.
For better understanding, this module uses the term "process" to represent the business process, activity, or component that is outsourced.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
