parts.prose: The objective of this module is to ensure the fundamental values of information security—confidentiality, integrity, and availability—are maintained by the outsourcing provider throughout the entire outsourcing lifecycle. The module is intended to help ensure that the outsourcing provider guarantees basic information security to the users of outsourcing. Outsourcing here refers to classic 'IT outsourcing'.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module OPS.3.2 Offering Outsourcing must be applied once from the provider's perspective to each and every user who receives services from the provider.
The module refers to the perspective of the outsourcing provider in the outsourcing relationship. The requirements of the module ensure that fundamental security standards are maintained towards the outsourcing users and help to ensure that the outsourcing users' requirements for information security can be met throughout the entire outsourcing process.
The case of onward transfer is only considered to a limited extent in the module OPS.3.2 Offering Outsourcing, as this represents another outsourcing relationship, and thus the outsourcing providers must model the module OPS.2.3 Using Outsourcing for these sub-service providers.
Scenarios deviating from classic "IT outsourcing" (such as the operation of hardware and software, hosting, housing, etc.) may not be fully covered by the module OPS.3.2 Offering Outsourcing and may require a separate risk analysis.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient information security management at outsourcing providers
parts.prose: A deficient information security management system can lead to the protection goals of information security being inadequately met by the outsourcing providers. Through an outsourcing contract, the outsourcing providers are responsible for maintaining the required level of information security for the outsourcing process. If the outsourcing providers do not fulfill their responsibility, this can lead to a threat for all institutions involved in the outsourcing process.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficient emergency management of outsourcing providers
parts.prose: When disruptions or emergencies occur at outsourcing providers, this can lead to an operational disruption that can also affect the outsourced processes of the outsourcing users and impact their normal business operations. In particular, emergency preparedness is of crucial importance in advance of emergency and crisis situations. In the event of inadequate emergency preparedness, effective emergency response cannot be ensured for the institution. Thus, for the individual institutions, disruptions, emergencies, and crisis situations may be uncontrollable. A cascade effect occurs, which affects not only the outsourcing providers but also all upstream and downstream service providers as well as customers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Inadequate contractual arrangements with outsourcing users
parts.prose: Inadequacies in the contract design can lead to the information security of outsourced processes of the outsourcing users being inadequately protected. Contractual arrangements define the entire outsourcing process and form the legal basis for claims of the outsourcing providers against the outsourcing users. Thus, the inadequacies from the contract design are transferred to the entire outsourcing lifecycle. This is associated with a variety of possible threat scenarios with financial and social impacts for the users as well as the outsourcing providers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Vulnerabilities in the connection of outsourcing users
parts.prose: The technical connection of the outsourcing users to the networks of the outsourcing providers can lead to technical and organizational vulnerabilities at the interfaces. The technical vulnerabilities in the connection can lead to disruptions, data loss, and be the starting point for IT-supported attacks. In contrast, organizational vulnerabilities in the form of unmanned interfaces can lead to communication problems between the outsourcing providers and users. These can pose a threat to the efficiency of risk mitigation measures in emergency and crisis situations.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Dependency on sub-service providers
parts.prose: If activities are further outsourced by outsourcing providers to sub-service providers, there is a risk that the sub-service providers will exploit their positions to enforce demands and disregard the provisions of the agreement. This creates a dependency on third parties to deliver the customer service. If the outsourcing providers are unable to compensate for a disruption or failure of the sub-service providers, a mandatory dependency arises. This puts the sub-service providers in an advantageous position over the outsourcing providers. The sub-service providers may refrain from adhering to the contractually agreed quality and the specified level of information security. This impairs the outsourcing relationship with the outsourcing users and results in legal and financial consequences as well as a loss of reputation for the outsourcing providers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Inappropriate configuration and management of entry, access, and access rights
parts.prose: An inappropriate or insufficient configuration of a central directory service can lead to users receiving rights that potentially enable them to access sensitive or personal data of the outsourcing provider or other customers of the outsourcing provider. Under certain circumstances, outsourcing projects may require outsourcing users to access the information network of the outsourcing provider. This is associated with corresponding entry, access, and access rights, which pose a risk to IT systems, information, and buildings. A consequence is that the integrity and confidentiality of this data are compromised. Ultimately, this can lead to outsourcing users asserting contractual penalties against the outsourcing provider and can result in a loss of reputation for the outsourcing provider and their customers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Insufficient multi-tenancy capability of outsourcing providers
parts.prose: Outsourcing providers typically have different customers who use the same resources such as IT systems, networks, or personnel. If the IT systems and data of outsourcing users are insufficiently separated and secured from each other, there is a risk that users can access the areas of other users and gain unauthorized access to data. This represents a direct violation of the confidentiality of the respective user data. This is particularly problematic for outsourcing users who are in competition with each other. The consequences would be a loss of reputation for the outsourcing providers as well as legal consequences from the affected outsourcing users.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Loss of control and steering in onward transfers to sub-service providers
parts.prose: Outsourced processes may be fully or partially passed on to sub-service providers by outsourcing providers as part of an onward transfer. Insufficient control of the sub-service providers leads to agreed-upon aspects of information security being inadequately adhered to by sub-service providers. This subsequently has consequences for the outsourcing relationship with the outsourcing users, as well as direct financial impacts and reputational damage for the outsourcing providers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Inadequate regulations for a planned or unplanned termination of an outsourcing relationship
parts.prose: Inadequate regulations for the end of an outsourcing relationship can result in hardware and data not being properly handed over or transmitted to the outsourcing users. In addition, existing customer data is not properly deleted after the storage period required by relevant laws and regulations. An outsourcing relationship can be terminated by ordinary notice as well as for extraordinary reasons. An example of this is the insolvency of an outsourcing provider. After the termination of the contract, the outsourcing provider may not adequately protect the existing data of the outsourcing user in accordance with the protection needs of the respective owner. The data can fall into the hands of third parties and, if published, lead to a loss of reputation.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for the detection of security-related events (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are informal or outdated drafts for a detection policy, but they have not been officially adopted or communicated. The requirements are incomplete and are only applied sporadically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In practice, this could mean that an older email from an administrator serves as a de facto instruction on how to react to antivirus alerts, while other event types (e.g., failed logins) are completely ignored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the responsible administrators about existing guidelines for event detection. It is determined that no formal, versioned, and approved documents exist, but only informal notes or emails.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic security policy for detection has been created and brought to the attention of the responsible employees. It describes general requirements but lacks detailed procedural specifications and clear responsibilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document 'Detection Policy' exists and is available on the intranet. It states THAT events are to be detected, but not in detail HOW (e.g., which tools, which thresholds, which escalation paths).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security policy for detection and compares its content with the tasks of the responsible employees. It is checked whether the employees know the policy. It is determined that the policy exists but is not detailed enough to ensure consistent implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the general security policy of the institution, a specific security policy for the detection of security-related events MUST be created. The specific security policy MUST comprehensibly describe requirements and specifications on how the detection of security-related events can be planned, established, and securely operated. The specific security policy MUST be known to all employees responsible for detection and be fundamental to their work. Changes MUST be coordinated with the ISO and documented. It MUST be regularly checked whether the specific security policy is still correctly implemented. The results of the check MUST be documented in a meaningful way.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is managed as a controlled document in the ISMS documentation system. It contains clear sections on scope, responsibilities (RACI matrix), detection sources (e.g., SIEM, EDR, firewall logs), basic use cases (e.g., brute-force attacks), and the process for regular review and updating of the policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the specific security policy and checks it for completeness and comprehensibility. It is verified that the responsible employees know the policy and use it as a basis for their work (e.g., through interviews). The minutes of the last reviews of the policy are inspected to confirm compliance with the review process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy for detection is firmly integrated into the ISMS lifecycle. The review process is supported by the analysis of metrics, such as the Mean Time To Detect (MTTD) or the number of incidents detected by specific rules. The policy is proactively updated based on 'lessons learned' from security incidents and new threat intelligence.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After every major security incident, a post-mortem meeting is held to check whether the policy needs to be adjusted to detect similar incidents more quickly in the future. Changes to the policy lead to automated notifications to the responsible teams.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the minutes of post-mortem meetings and compares them with the versions of the security policy to confirm that a 'lessons learned' process is established. Reports with detection metrics are requested and their influence on the further development of the policy is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is a 'living document' that is dynamically adapted to the threat landscape. Compliance with the policy is continuously and automatically monitored. Policy requirements are directly linked to the configuration of the detection tools ('Policy as Code'), so that a deviation is automatically detected and reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The detection policy is managed as code (e.g., YAML) in a Git repository. A CI/CD pipeline validates changes and automatically rolls them out to the configurations of the SIEM and EDR systems. A compliance scanner checks daily whether the current configuration of the tools corresponds to the policy defined in the repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is granted read access to the 'Policy as Code' repository and the CI/CD pipeline. The history of changes and the automated deployment process are analyzed. The reports from the compliance scanner are inspected to verify continuous compliance with the policy.

controls.title: Compliance with legal conditions in the evaluation of logging data (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general awareness of data protection, but no specific legal review or formal agreement for the evaluation of log data has been carried out. The evaluation takes place in a legal gray area.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators evaluate log data as needed without coordinating with the data protection officer or employee representation. There are no documented rules about what data may be evaluated for how long and for what purpose.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for documentation on the legal admissibility of log data evaluation (e.g., works agreement, data protection impact assessment). It is determined that no such documents exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The legal framework was discussed once with the data protection officer and employee representation. The basic requirements are known, but not laid down in a detailed, binding set of rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a protocol of a meeting with the data protection officer that records the most important points. The employee representation has been informed but has not yet agreed to a formal regulation. The administrators are verbally instructed to handle personal data 'carefully'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing correspondence and minutes with the data protection officer and the employee representation. It is checked whether the administrators are familiar with the basic legal requirements. A lack of formal, binding agreements is identified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When logging data is evaluated, the provisions of the current federal and state data protection laws MUST be complied with. If detection systems are used, the personality rights or co-determination rights of the employee representations MUST be respected. It MUST also be ensured that all other relevant legal provisions are observed, e.g., the Telemedia Act (TMG), the Works Constitution Act, and the Telecommunications Act. This is formally documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a formal works agreement that regulates the purpose, scope, and duration of the evaluation of log data. A data protection concept for the SIEM/detection system has been reviewed and approved by the data protection officer. A role and authorization concept ensures that only authorized persons can access the data (four-eyes principle).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the works agreement and the approved data protection concept. It is checked on a random basis whether the evaluations carried out in practice are in line with the agreements. The access rights to the log data are compared with the authorization concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for complying with legal conditions includes regular, planned reviews with the legal department and the data protection officer to be able to react to changes in the legal situation or case law. All agreements are centrally documented and easily accessible to all parties involved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At least once a year, a review meeting is held with the legal department, data protection, ISO, and employee representation to review the existing regulations. The works agreement is versioned and updated as needed. Training for analysts includes a dedicated module on the data protection-compliant handling of log data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the annual review meetings and checks the currency of the works agreement. Training materials and records of the analysts are inspected to verify awareness of data protection topics.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with legal requirements is technically integrated into the toolchain. The SIEM system has functions for automatic anonymization or pseudonymization of data. Access to unmasked raw data is strictly controlled via a PIM/PAM solution, is only possible on a need-to-know basis after approval, and is logged without gaps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Personal data such as usernames or IP addresses are pseudonymized by default upon ingestion into the SIEM. De-pseudonymization is only possible for a few authorized individuals via a 'break glass' process, which requires a request and approval by a second person. Every such access is logged in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the pseudonymization functions in the SIEM. The logs of the 'break glass' process are analyzed to verify that access to raw data was duly requested, approved, and logged. It is checked whether automated queries (`get_pii_access_logs.sh`) can prove compliance.

controls.title: Definition of reporting channels for security-relevant events (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal point of contact for IT problems, which is also occasionally used for security reports. However, there are no defined processes, response times, or escalation paths for security-relevant events.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees report suspicious emails to the general IT helpdesk. Processing depends on the availability and knowledge of the respective helpdesk employee.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks various employees where they would report a security incident. The answers are inconsistent. It is determined that there is no formal documentation of the reporting channels.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reporting channels for security-relevant events are documented and have been communicated to the relevant persons. The documentation describes who is to be informed and when, but the processes are rarely practiced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document on the intranet lists the phone number of the incident response team and an email address. All employees were informed about this once via email.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the reporting channels and checks awareness of them among a sample of employees. It is found that no evidence of regular tests or drills of the reporting channels exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For security-relevant events, suitable reporting and alerting channels MUST be defined and documented. It MUST be determined which parties are to be informed and when, and how they can be reached. Depending on the urgency, an event MUST be reported via various communication channels. All persons relevant for reporting or alerting MUST be informed of their tasks. The established reporting and alerting channels SHOULD be regularly reviewed, tested, and updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An incident response plan clearly defines the reporting channels, including primary and secondary contacts, means of communication (phone, email, messenger), and escalation matrices based on the incident's criticality. This information is part of the regular security awareness training. At least once a year, a drill (e.g., table-top exercise) is conducted to test the reporting channels.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the incident response plan for completeness of the reporting and alerting channels. The minutes of the latest drills are reviewed to verify regular testing. Sample interviews with key personnel ensure that they know their roles in the reporting process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reporting process is integrated into a central incident management or ticketing system. Reports automatically generate tickets and start predefined workflows. The drills are more complex and test multiple escalation paths and communication channels simultaneously under time pressure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated email address (`incident@`) or a report button on the intranet automatically creates a high-priority ticket in the Jira/ServiceNow system, which is immediately assigned to the on-call team. The annual drill is a simulation exercise that also tests the technical connection to the ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the ticketing system for the automatic creation and assignment of incidents. The logs of the simulation exercises are analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of the integrated reporting process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Alerting is fully automated and integrated into the SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) platform. The system not only creates tickets but also automatically alerts the responsible personnel according to stored on-call schedules (e.g., via PagerDuty, SMS) and escalates in case of non-response according to defined SLAs. The effectiveness of the reporting channels is continuously monitored and improved using metrics (e.g., Time-to-Acknowledge).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A critical SIEM rule triggers a webhook that creates an incident in PagerDuty. PagerDuty alerts the primary analyst. If they do not respond within 15 minutes, the secondary analyst and the team lead are automatically alerted. All steps are logged in the incident ticket.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the SOAR platform and the connected alerting services (e.g., PagerDuty). Reports with metrics such as 'Mean Time to Acknowledge' (MTTA) and 'Mean Time to Resolve' (MTTR) for security incidents are evaluated to verify the efficiency of the process. An automated test (`trigger-test-alert.py --criticality=high`) can check the alerting chain.

controls.title: Employee awareness (B) [Supervisors, Users, Employees]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employee awareness is raised sporadically, e.g., through a one-time mention in a newsletter. There is no structured program.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a year, a short paragraph on IT security is published in the company newsletter, urging employees to be cautious.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the security awareness program. No plan or regular training can be proven, only isolated communication measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Awareness for reporting security incidents is part of the general IT security training that all new employees receive upon hiring.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the onboarding process, a one-hour presentation on IT security is given, which also covers the topic of 'Reporting suspicious events'. There are no regular refreshers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the onboarding documents and confirms that the topic is covered. However, it is noted that no recurring training takes place for existing employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All users MUST be made aware that they should not simply ignore or close event messages from their clients. They MUST forward the messages to the responsible incident management according to the alerting channels. All employees MUST immediately report any security incident they detect to incident management. This is part of a regular, mandatory awareness program.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All employees must complete an annual e-learning module on information security. One chapter is explicitly dedicated to detecting and reporting security incidents. A short quiz is conducted at the end of the chapter. Participation is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the plan for the security awareness program and the training materials. The participation rates and the results of the knowledge tests from the last training wave are reviewed to assess effectiveness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The awareness program is supplemented by practical exercises such as regular, controlled phishing simulations. The reporting behavior of employees is measured and used as a Key Performance Indicator (KPI) for the effectiveness of the program. Employees who correctly report phishing emails receive positive feedback.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Phishing campaigns are conducted quarterly using a specialized tool. The tool measures click rates and reporting rates. The results are analyzed anonymously and reported to management to demonstrate the program's success and identify areas for improvement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the plans and result reports of the last phishing campaigns presented. The development of the reporting rate over time is analyzed. It is checked whether the findings are used to adapt the awareness measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The awareness program is highly individualized and dynamic. Training content is tailored to specific roles (e.g., administrators, developers, financial accounting) and to individual behavior in past simulations. The program's effectiveness is continuously measured using various metrics and adapted based on the current threat landscape.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An awareness platform automatically assigns targeted training modules to employees. For example, a developer receives a module on 'Secure Coding', while an employee who clicked on a phishing email has to complete a short refresher module on 'Recognizing Phishing'. A 'Report Phishing' button in the email client simplifies reporting and gives the user immediate feedback.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the awareness platform and the logic for assigning training. Reports that prove the effectiveness of the role-based and adaptive training are evaluated. The usability and use of the 'Report Phishing' button is checked.

controls.title: Use of built-in system functions for detection (B) [Technical Owners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On some systems, built-in detection functions (e.g., Windows Event Logging) are active with default settings, but the logs are not centrally collected or analyzed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logs remain locally on the respective servers and are only viewed manually in the event of a specific incident analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly checks the logging configuration of some servers and finds that while logging is active, there is no central aggregation or analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Built-in detection functions are intentionally activated on all critical systems. The generated messages are sent to a central location (e.g., an email address) but are not evaluated systematically or in a timely manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrators have a mailbox where alarm emails from various systems are collected. This is reviewed irregularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that detection functions are active on critical systems and are sending messages. A review of the central mailbox shows that although messages arrive, no structured processing procedure exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If deployed IT systems or applications have detection functions, these MUST be activated and used. In the event of a security incident, the notifications from the affected systems MUST be evaluated. Additionally, the logged events of other IT systems MUST be reviewed. It MUST be checked whether additional malware scanners should be installed on central IT systems; if so, they MUST be centrally managed and automatically report their notifications to the responsible personnel. The responsible personnel MUST evaluate and investigate the notifications. The collected notifications SHOULD be checked on a spot-check basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the IT operations concept, the audit policies and logging functions to be activated are defined for each system (e.g., operating system, database, web server). The notifications are forwarded to a central log management system. There is a documented process for how to respond to these notifications. The decision for or against additional scanners (e.g., a second AV scanner on file servers) is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the operational concepts for specifications on the activation of detection functions. It is verified on a spot-check basis whether these are implemented on the systems. In the log management system, it is checked whether the notifications are being received and whether there is evidence of their regular evaluation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The activation and configuration of the system's own detection functions are controlled and enforced centrally and automatically via a configuration management system (e.g., GPO, Ansible, Puppet). This ensures a consistent configuration across the entire system landscape. The spot-checks of the notifications are anchored in a fixed schedule.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Group Policy Object (GPO) in Active Directory enforces the 'Advanced Audit Policy Configuration' on all Windows servers. Ansible playbooks ensure an equivalent, hardened logging configuration on all Linux systems. Any deviation from this configuration is automatically reported.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration in the configuration management tool (e.g., insight into the GPO settings or Ansible playbooks). It is checked whether a compliance reporting exists that shows deviations from the target configuration. A script (`check_audit_policy.ps1`) can compare the local configuration of a system with the central specification.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process is fully automated and integrated into the system lifecycle. A CMDB records which systems have which detection capabilities. A SOAR platform receives notifications from all sources (native and additional), automatically enriches them, and initiates predefined response playbooks. The evaluation of notifications occurs continuously and in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a new server is provisioned via the provisioning tool, the correct logging agents and configurations are automatically rolled out and registered in the SIEM. A malware detection reported by the antivirus system automatically triggers a playbook in the SOAR system that isolates the system, informs the user, and creates a ticket for the helpdesk.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automated provisioning process and the configuration of the SOAR playbooks. Based on a test event, the entire chain from notification to enrichment to automated response is demonstrated and verified live.

controls.title: Continuous monitoring and evaluation of logging data (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Log data is collected centrally but is only evaluated reactively when there is already a concrete suspicion or a reported incident. Proactive monitoring does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SIEM mainly serves as an archive. Analysts only log in to search for traces after a user has reported a problem.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the access logs of the SIEM and finds that logins and searches only occur irregularly and often in temporal connection with known incidents. There is no evidence of regular, proactive reviews.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A team is designated to evaluate the log data. However, monitoring is only carried out on a best-effort basis, e.g., a few hours per week, without a fixed schedule or guaranteed coverage. There are no documented guidelines for active searches.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrators have the task of 'looking into the SIEM from time to time'. What exactly they should look for is not defined and depends on the experience of the individual.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews the responsible team and finds that monitoring is one of many tasks and is performed on an ad-hoc basis. No formal procedures or shift schedules can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All logging data SHOULD be actively monitored and evaluated as permanently as possible. Employees SHOULD be designated who are responsible for this. If the responsible employees have to actively search for security-relevant events, e.g., when they control or test IT systems, then such tasks SHOULD be documented in corresponding procedural instructions. Sufficient personnel resources SHOULD be provided for detection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A team is designated (e.g., SOC team) whose main task is to monitor the SIEM. There is a shift schedule to ensure monitoring during core working hours. There are documented 'Standard Operating Procedures' (SOPs) for investigating the most common alarm types and 'Playbooks' for basic searches for anomalies (e.g., searching for unusual outbound connections).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the shift schedule and personnel planning for the responsible team to assess the resource allocation. The SOPs and playbooks for the evaluation are reviewed. The SIEM logs are checked for evidence of the regular execution of these documented searches.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated SOC team (Security Operations Center) performs continuous monitoring during business hours. Basic, hypothesis-driven threat hunting activities are regularly conducted based on documented procedural instructions. The effectiveness of the monitoring is tracked through metrics such as 'number of analyzed alarms' and 'number of escalated incidents'.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SOC team has weekly 'Hunting Sessions' in their calendar, where they proactively search for specific tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) from the MITRE ATT&CK Framework. The results of each hunt are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the logs of the threat hunting activities and checks whether they take place systematically and regularly. The SOC metrics and reports are analyzed to assess the performance and maturity of the monitoring.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: 24/7 monitoring by a shift team or a Managed Security Service Provider (MSSP) is established. Proactive threat hunting is conducted continuously based on current threat intelligence feeds. The analysis process is supported by advanced tools such as UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) and machine learning to detect complex anomalies and insider threats.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SIEM is coupled with a UEBA solution that automatically creates baselines for the normal behavior of users and systems and reports significant deviations. New indicators from threat intelligence feeds are automatically imported into the SIEM and trigger retroactive searches (retro-hunts) over the log data of the last 30 days.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the Service Level Agreements (SLAs) with the 24/7 MSSP or the internal shift schedules. The configuration of the UEBA solution and the threat intelligence integration is analyzed. The auditor requests examples of incidents discovered through UEBA or threat-intel-based hunting. An automatic check (`check_uebaprofile_status.sh`) could query the status of the behavior profiles.

controls.title: Training of responsible personnel (S) [Supervisors]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The responsible employees learn how to handle detection systems exclusively through 'learning by doing'. There are no formal training sessions or budgets for it.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New team members look over the shoulders of experienced colleagues to learn how to operate the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the team members about their training and qualifications. No certificates or proofs of attendance for relevant training can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The responsible employees receive basic manufacturer training for the tools used (e.g., SIEM basic course). However, there is no overarching training plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a new SIEM is introduced, one or two employees attend the manufacturer's 3-day introductory course and share their knowledge internally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor looks at the certificates of attendance for the product training. However, it is noted that there are no regular refresher courses or further training.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All responsible personnel who check event notifications SHOULD receive further training and qualifications. When new IT components are procured, a budget for training SHOULD be planned. Before the responsible personnel receive training for new IT components, a training concept SHOULD be created.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a formal training concept for the SOC team. The training needs for each team member are determined annually, and a budget is requested. The concept stipulates that when new security technology is procured, the cost of training for administrators and analysts is an integral part of the project budget.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the training concept and the budget planning for training. It is checked on a spot-check basis for procurement projects of the last two years whether training budgets were planned and used. The individual training plans of the employees are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training concept is based on a skills matrix that defines the required skills for each role in the detection team. The annual training plan aims to close gaps in this matrix. The training includes not only tools but also advanced analysis methods, incident response, and current threat landscapes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The skills matrix lists skills such as 'log analysis', 'network forensics', 'malware analysis', and 'knowledge of MITRE ATT&CK'. Each employee is assigned a level (Basic, Advanced, Expert). The training plan includes vendor-neutral courses (e.g., from SANS) and conference attendance in addition to product training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the skills matrix and the individual training plans. It is checked whether the completed training has demonstrably increased the team's competencies, e.g., through internal presentations or improved analysis reports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are actively encouraged and financially supported to obtain and maintain recognized industry certifications (e.g., GIAC certifications like GCIH, GCFA). The organization actively participates in security conferences and workshops and contributes to the community (e.g., through presentations or blog posts). The effectiveness of the training is measured through practical performance assessments, e.g., in cyber range exercises.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The company has a budget for certification attempts and pays bonuses for successfully passed exams. At least two team members attend a major international security conference annually. The team participates in a Capture-The-Flag (CTF) or cyber range exercise quarterly to demonstrate its skills.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the list of certifications held by employees and the evidence of their currency. The reports and results of the cyber range exercises are analyzed. It is checked whether the team gives back knowledge to the community (e.g., through published articles or tools).

controls.title: Use of additional detection systems (S) [Subject matter experts]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single additional detection system, e.g., an Intrusion Detection System (IDS), is placed at the internet gateway. Internal network segments or other important perimeters are not monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An open-source IDS solution like Suricata runs on a machine that mirrors all internet traffic. The signatures are updated irregularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and placement of the IDS. By inspecting the network diagram, it is determined that no other sensors are present for monitoring critical internal segments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Additional detection systems (e.g., NIDS) are deployed at the most important network perimeters defined in the network diagram (e.g., internet, DMZ). The systems are managed decentrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A NIDS appliance is installed at each important perimeter. Administrators log into each appliance individually to manage it and view alarms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the perimeters defined in the network diagram with the locations of the NIDS sensors. It is determined that there is no central management console, which complicates consistent configuration and analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the network diagram, it SHOULD be determined which network segments must be protected by additional detection systems. The information network SHOULD be supplemented with additional detection systems and sensors. Malware detection systems SHOULD be deployed and centrally managed. The perimeters between internal and external networks defined in the network diagram SHOULD also be supplemented with network-based Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on a risk analysis and the network diagram, NIDS sensors are placed not only at the internet gateway but also at perimeters to important internal zones (e.g., server network, development network). All sensors are managed from a central management console that ensures uniform configuration and signature distribution. The alarms are sent to the central SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network diagram and the underlying risk analysis to evaluate the strategic placement of the sensors. The central management console is inspected to verify consistent management. It is checked in the SIEM whether the alarms from all sensors arrive centrally.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The coverage by detection systems is comprehensive and includes the monitoring of critical east-west traffic (server-to-server) within the data center segments. The systems are regularly fine-tuned to reduce false-positive rates. In addition, Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) agents are deployed on critical servers and clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the virtualized server environment, network traffic between VMs is mirrored via a virtual switch and analyzed by a NIDS VM. All endpoints in the company are equipped with an EDR agent that reports suspicious process activities to a central console. The SOC team has a process for continuous rule optimization.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the virtual network TAPs and the deployment rates of the EDR agents. The documentation and the results of the rule tuning process are analyzed. The combination of NIDS and EDR alarms during test attacks is evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A combination of NIDS, EDR, deception technology (honeypots), and other sensor types provides in-depth visibility across the entire network, on endpoints, and in the cloud (XDR approach). The placement of sensors is dynamically reviewed and adjusted based on network changes, new applications, and current threat analytics.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Low-interaction honeypots are placed in each subnet. Any attempt to access a honeypot generates a high-criticality alarm. The alarms from NIDS, EDR, and honeypots are correlated in an XDR platform to create a complete picture of an attack. An automated script checks monthly whether the necessary network TAPs and sensors are active in newly provisioned cloud VPCs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the XDR platform and the integration of the various sensors. The configuration of the deception technology is checked. A controlled access to a honeypot is performed to test the alerting chain. The automation for checking sensor coverage is inspected.

controls.title: Use of TLS/SSL proxies (S) [Subject matter experts]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A TLS/SSL proxy is in use, but a very extensive exception list (e.g., for social media, cloud services, financial sites) means that a large part of the encrypted traffic is not inspected, creating significant blind spots.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The exception list is expanded with every user complaint, without a formal risk assessment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the proxy's configuration and finds that the exception list is very long and contains many popular domains. There is no documentation justifying the exceptions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: At the internet gateway, TLS/SSL proxies are used to inspect general web traffic. The proxies themselves are basically secured against unauthorized access. Detected events are logged but not automatically forwarded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A proxy appliance performs the TLS inspection. The proxy's root certificate is distributed to clients via GPO. Administrative access to the proxy is protected by a password.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the function of the TLS inspection, e.g., by visiting a test malware page via HTTPS. The basic security measures for the proxy are checked. It is noted that the logs remain local.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: At the perimeters to external networks, TLS/SSL proxies SHOULD be used, which intercept the encrypted connection and thus allow the transmitted data to be checked for malware. All TLS/SSL proxies SHOULD be protected from unauthorized access. Security-relevant events SHOULD be automatically detected on the TLS/SSL proxies. An organizational policy SHOULD be created that specifies the data protection conditions under which log data may be manually analyzed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cluster of proxies ensures high availability of TLS inspection. The configuration is hardened. All security-relevant events detected by the proxy (e.g., malware downloads) are automatically sent as syslog to the SIEM. A works agreement governs the handling of the inspected data and defines clear exception categories (e.g., online banking), which are technically implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the proxy cluster and the syslog forwarding to the SIEM. The works agreement is reviewed and compared with the implemented proxy configuration (especially the exception rules). A controlled download of test malware (EICAR) via HTTPS is performed to verify detection and alerting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The TLS inspection is applied not only to incoming, but also to outgoing traffic from servers to detect command-and-control communication. The exception list is reduced to the absolute technically and legally necessary minimum and is regularly (e.g., quarterly) reviewed and re-approved. The proxy automatically blocks connections to known malicious destinations based on threat intelligence feeds.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The proxy is integrated with a threat intelligence service and loads new lists of malicious IPs and domains hourly. The process for reviewing the exception list is documented, and the results of each review are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the process for managing the exception list and reviews the logs of the last reviews. The integration with the threat intelligence feed and the configuration of the automatic blocking rules are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: TLS inspection is fully integrated into the security process. Suspicious, but not clearly malicious, files found in encrypted traffic are automatically forwarded to a sandboxing solution for dynamic analysis. The entire configuration of the proxy cluster is managed as code (Infrastructure as Code), versioned, and rolled out via a CI/CD pipeline.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The proxy forwards all downloaded executable files not from a trusted source to a local or cloud-based sandbox. If the sandbox detects malicious behavior, the file's signature is automatically added to a blocklist and an alarm is triggered in the SIEM. The proxy configuration is stored in a Git repository, and changes require a pull request with approval from a second person.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the integration with the sandbox solution and has the process demonstrated using a suspicious sample file. The 'Infrastructure as Code' repository and the CI/CD pipeline for the proxy configuration are inspected to verify the change management process.

controls.title: Use of a central logging infrastructure for the analysis of security-relevant events (S) [Subject matter experts]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Log data is collected centrally, but analysis is done through manual searches in the raw data, e.g., with command-line tools like 'grep'. There is no dedicated analysis tool.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All syslog messages are written to a large text file on a server. In case of suspicion, an administrator logs in and searches this file.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that a central log collection exists, but no SIEM or log analysis tool is in use. The analysis process is not scalable and is inefficient.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic SIEM or log analysis tool is in use to query the central log data. However, the signatures of the detection systems are updated only irregularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An open-source solution like the ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) is installed. Analysts can perform searches via the Kibana interface. The update processes for signatures and components are manual and performed ad-hoc.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the analysis tool. By querying the version numbers and signature statuses, it is determined that the systems are not consistently kept up-to-date.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Event messages stored on a central logging infrastructure SHOULD be retrievable and analyzable using a tool. The collected event messages SHOULD be regularly checked for anomalies. The signatures of the detection systems SHOULD always be up-to-date and at the same level so that security-relevant events can also be detected retroactively.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A commercial or well-maintained open-source SIEM is used. There is a documented process that ensures that the signatures for all connected detection systems (e.g., NIDS, EDR, AV) are checked for updates and deployed weekly. The SOC team has daily routines to check the dashboards and alarms in the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process for signature management and checks the logs of the last updates. The configuration of the SIEM tool and the corresponding daily checklists of the SOC team are inspected. It is checked whether the signature levels on the various systems are consistent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIEM tool is used to create company-specific correlation rules that are tailored to the organization's specific risks and infrastructure. The process for updating signatures and components is automated and monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the standard rules, the SOC team has developed its own correlation rules, e.g., 'Alert when a user from the finance team has more than 10 failed logins on the ERP system within 5 minutes'. A script checks daily for the availability of new signatures and rolls them out automatically after a short test. An error during the update generates an alarm.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the custom correlation rules implemented in the SIEM and assesses their usefulness in the context of the organization. The automated update process is reviewed and checked for its reliability and error handling.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The analysis is enhanced by a SOAR platform. This automatically enriches alarms from the SIEM with context information from other systems (e.g., CMDB, Threat Intelligence, HR system) and performs initial, automated triage steps to relieve analysts and shorten response times.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When the SIEM generates a 'brute-force attack' alarm, the SOAR platform automatically queries the CMDB to determine the type of system, the HR system to see if the affected user is an administrator, and a threat intel service to check if the source IP address is known to be malicious. All this information is presented to the analyst along with the alarm in the ticket.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown a demonstration of the SOAR playbooks for alarm enrichment. A test alarm is triggered and it is tracked how the SOAR platform collects and displays the information from the various connected systems. The quality and usefulness of the enriched data is assessed.

controls.title: Evaluation of information from external sources (S) [Subject Matter Experts]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security staff informally and irregularly read public security news websites. There is no process to systematically evaluate or use this information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator occasionally reads heise security and informs colleagues in chat if he finds something interesting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the process for using threat intelligence. It is determined that there is no formal process and usage depends on the personal commitment of individual employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organization has subscribed to the free mailing lists of relevant CERTs (e.g., CERT-Bund) and major vendors. The emails are read, but not always systematically evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The warning messages from CERT-Bund go to a team mailbox. A team member is responsible for checking the mailbox daily.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks which mailing lists are subscribed to and who receives the information. Using examples, it is checked whether relevant warnings have been acted upon. It is noted that the evaluation is not always documented in a traceable manner.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To gain new insights into security-relevant events, external sources SHOULD be consulted. Messages from different channels SHOULD also be recognized as relevant by employees and forwarded to the appropriate place. Information from reliable sources SHOULD be evaluated as a matter of principle. All information supplied SHOULD be assessed for its relevance to the organization's own information domain. If this is the case, the information SHOULD be escalated in accordance with security incident handling.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a defined process for 'Threat Intelligence Management'. This specifies which sources (e.g., CERT warnings, vendor advisories, industry ISACs) are used. Incoming information is recorded in a ticketing system, assessed for relevance to the company's own IT landscape (e.g., 'Are we affected by this vulnerability?'), and, if affected, escalated to the responsible teams (e.g., patch management).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the process for threat intelligence management. In the ticketing system, the processing of external warning messages from recent months is traced on a random basis, from recording and assessment to escalation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organization also subscribes to paid, high-quality threat intelligence feeds. There is a formalized process for processing 'Indicators of Compromise' (IoCs), which includes the systematic search for these indicators in its own systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The organization uses a commercial threat intelligence provider. Its portal is evaluated daily by an analyst. New IoCs (IP addresses, hashes, domains) are extracted and used for searches in the SIEM and EDR. The results of these searches are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown access to the threat intelligence portal. The logs of the IoC searches from the last few weeks are reviewed to verify that the information is actively used for threat hunting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Threat intelligence is programmatically fed via an API into the SIEM and other security tools (firewall, proxy, EDR) to enable automated detection and blocking. The organization actively participates in information sharing within its industry (e.g., through membership in an ISAC - Information Sharing and Analysis Center) and shares its own findings with the community.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP) collects feeds from various sources, deduplicates them, and automatically distributes the IoCs to the appropriate security systems. A malicious IP address is thus automatically blocked on the firewall. The SOC team creates anonymized reports after major incidents and shares them with other members via the industry ISAC.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture and configuration of the TIP. The automated distribution of IoCs to a sample system (e.g., firewall) is traced. Evidence of active information sharing with the ISAC (e.g., shared reports, participation in meetings) is reviewed. An automatic check (`check_ioc_feed.py`) can check the timeliness of the feeds.

controls.title: Regular audits of the detection systems (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Audits or reviews of the detection systems only take place if a major failure or a serious security incident has occurred.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After a successful ransomware attack, an investigation is launched to find out why the detection systems failed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for audit reports and finds that they are only created reactively and not as part of a planned program.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An informal review is conducted annually to ensure that the detection systems are still running and functioning correctly. The results are not formally documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a year, an administrator checks whether the SIEM and NIDS services are active and still collecting data. The result is communicated to the supervisor by email.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds evidence of annual reviews (e.g., emails), but notes that there is no systematic review of effectiveness or formal reports with traceable actions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The existing detection systems and measures taken SHOULD be checked in regular audits to see if they are still up-to-date and effective. The metrics that arise, for example, when security-relevant events are recorded, reported, and escalated SHOULD be evaluated. The results of the audits SHOULD be documented in a traceable manner and compared with the target state. Deviations SHOULD be investigated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal audit of the detection capabilities is carried out once a year. The audit plan includes checking configurations, signature levels, log source coverage, and process compliance. Metrics such as 'number of alarms', 'number of false positives', and 'time to alarm processing' are evaluated. The results and identified deviations are recorded in a formal audit report and tracked in the ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the audit plans and reports from recent years. It is checked whether the audits are carried out systematically and at regular intervals. The follow-up of the deficiencies identified in the last audit is checked in the ticketing system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The audit is more comprehensive and includes practical tests such as internal penetration tests or red team exercises to check the actual detection and response capabilities of the systems and the team. The results are used to specifically optimize the systems and rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the internal audit, an external penetration tester is commissioned annually, whose explicit goal is to remain undetected. After the test, the log files and alarms are analyzed to identify detection gaps. Based on this, new SIEM rules are developed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports of the last penetration tests and the measures derived from them to improve detection. It is checked whether a 'Purple Teaming' process has been established in which attackers (Red Team) and defenders (Blue Team) work together to improve the detection rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The audit is a continuous process. 'Breach and Attack Simulation' (BAS) tools are used, which automatically and continuously test the effectiveness of detection controls against the latest attack techniques and tactics (TTPs). Detected gaps are automatically reported and tracked in a GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A BAS platform runs simulated attacks from agents in the internal network daily or weekly. The platform's dashboard shows in real time which attacks were detected and blocked by which controls (e.g., AV, EDR, NIDS) and where detection gaps exist. Each newly discovered gap automatically creates a ticket for the SOC team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is granted read access to the BAS platform and analyzes the dashboards and trend reports. The test coverage against the MITRE ATT&CK framework is evaluated. The integration with the ticketing or GRC system for automated gap tracking is verified. The execution of a test attack (`run_bas_test.sh --ttp=T1059.001`) can be used for live verification.

controls.title: Evaluation of logging data by specialized personnel (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A team has log data monitoring as one of its many responsibilities. However, it is not their primary or sole task, and there is a lack of in-depth specialization.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The general IT operations team is also responsible for reviewing SIEM alerts. This is done in addition to their tasks in patch management, backup, and user support.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the job descriptions and the distribution of tasks in the IT operations team and determines that security monitoring constitutes only a small part of the tasks and that there are no dedicated specialists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees SHOULD be specifically tasked with monitoring all logging data. Monitoring logging data SHOULD be the predominant task of the assigned employees. The assigned employees SHOULD receive specialized advanced training and qualifications. A group of individuals SHOULD be designated who are exclusively responsible for the topic of evaluating logging data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated SOC (Security Operations Center) team with at least two analysts is established. According to their job descriptions, monitoring, analyzing, and responding to security incidents is their main task (> 80% of their working time). They have their own budget for specialized training (e.g., SIEM-Advanced, Incident Handling).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the organizational charts and job descriptions to verify the existence and tasks of the dedicated team. The training plans and records of the team members are reviewed. Interviews confirm that the team focuses primarily on security monitoring.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A multi-level SOC (e.g., L1, L2, L3 analysts) with clearly defined roles, responsibilities, and escalation paths is established. The team has a fixed budget for advanced training and certifications and regularly participates in exercises.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: L1 analysts perform the initial triage of alerts. L2 analysts take over for more in-depth analysis and incident handling. L3 analysts are experts responsible for threat hunting, malware analysis, and developing new detection rules. The handover between levels is clearly regulated by processes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the process documentation of the multi-level SOC. Based on example incidents, the escalation process between the different levels is traced. The qualifications of the employees at the different levels are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The specialized team acts as a recognized expert organization. The employees not only perform monitoring tasks but also actively engage in proactive threat hunting, develop their own analysis tools, perform reverse engineering of malware, and contribute to the security community through publications or presentations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The L3 team develops its own Python scripts to automate analyses and makes them available on the internal Git server. A team member recently gave a presentation at a local security conference about a malware campaign they analyzed. The team has its own lab for malware analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the tools developed by the team and the documentation. Evidence of contributions to the community (e.g., blog posts, conference presentations, CVE reports) is requested. The equipment and use of the analysis lab is checked.

controls.title: Central detection and real-time verification of event notifications (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central SIEM is in use and collects log data from the most important systems. The correlation is limited to the standard rules supplied by the manufacturer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SIEM correlates logins from various sources but has no visibility into application-specific or business process events.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the list of log sources connected to the SIEM and the active correlation rules. It is determined that the coverage is present but not in-depth or tailored to the organization.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Central components and automated analyses using software tools SHOULD be used to detect and evaluate security-relevant events. All events occurring in the system environment SHOULD be recorded and correlated with each other. The security-relevant processes SHOULD be made visible. All delivered data SHOULD be fully viewable and evaluable in the log management. If defined thresholds are exceeded, an alert SHOULD be triggered automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM system is used as a central component. It collects logs from almost all areas of IT (network, servers, clients, security appliances). Both standard rules and company-specific correlation rules with defined thresholds are active (e.g., 'more than 100 outgoing DNS requests per minute from a client'). All raw logs are online searchable for at least 90 days.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the log source coverage in the SIEM and compares it with the system inventory list. The configuration of the threshold-based alarm rules is analyzed. A search for events from 60 days ago is performed to test the complete viewability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system uses advanced correlation and User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) to detect complex, multi-stage attack patterns and behavioral anomalies. Visibility extends beyond the on-premise environment to cloud infrastructures (IaaS, SaaS).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SIEM is equipped with a UEBA engine that reports behavioral anomalies such as 'user logs in from a foreign country for the first time' or 'server starts unusual processes'. Logs from cloud platforms like AWS (CloudTrail) and Microsoft 365 are also centrally collected and correlated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the UEBA models and the connection of the cloud log sources. Examples of anomalies detected by UEBA are requested and their analysis by the SOC team is traced.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully integrated system (e.g., an XDR platform) provides real-time detection, correlation, and visibility across all relevant layers (endpoints, network, cloud, identities, email). The analysis is significantly supported by AI/ML models. All data is kept in a searchable format for long-term analysis (threat hunting, forensics). In the event of an alert, a qualified and needs-based response is initiated immediately.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An XDR platform automatically correlates a NIDS alert, an EDR process alert, and a suspicious cloud login from the same user into a single, high-criticality incident. This triggers an immediate notification to the 24/7 on-call analyst, who initiates the response within minutes. All relevant data is kept in a hot storage data lake for 1 year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the XDR platform. Using a complex attack scenario, it is demonstrated how the platform combines the individual signals into a coherent picture. The SLAs for response time are checked and compared with the logs of past incidents. The availability and performance of the long-term data storage is tested.

controls.title: Use of detection systems according to protection requirement levels (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Standard detection mechanisms are applied equally to all systems, without special consideration for applications with increased protection needs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ERP system with highly critical data is monitored with the same standard logging and antivirus as an unimportant print server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the monitoring configuration of an application with high protection needs with that of a standard system and finds no significant differences.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Applications with increased protection needs SHOULD be protected by additional detection measures. For this purpose, detection systems SHOULD be used, for example, with which the increased protection needs can also be technically ensured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the business-critical web application with customer data, a Web Application Firewall (WAF) is operated in blocking mode in addition to the standard mechanisms. For the central database, detailed audit logs are activated that log every access to critical tables and send them to the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies the applications with high protection needs in the protection needs assessment document. For these applications, it is checked whether additional detection measures appropriate to the protection needs (such as WAF, DAM) have been implemented and are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The additional detection systems for highly sensitive applications are equipped with customized, application-specific rules. This includes, for example, a WAF with a positive security model (whitelist) or a Database Activity Monitoring (DAM) system that detects behavioral anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The WAF in front of the online shop only allows the HTTP requests that are necessary for the operation of the shop; all others are blocked. The DAM system for the patient database has learned what normal queries look like and alerts when an administrator suddenly tries to export large amounts of data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the WAF and DAM systems and assesses the quality and specificity of the rule sets. It is checked whether the systems are operated in learning or blocking mode. The effectiveness is tested through simulated, application-specific attacks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To protect applications with very high protection needs, advanced technologies such as Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) are used. These are directly integrated into the application and can detect and block attacks in real time at the code level. The integrity of the detection systems themselves is protected by Hardware Security Modules (HSM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application server on which the critical application runs is equipped with a RASP agent. This detects and blocks attacks such as SQL injections or cross-site scripting before they reach the application code. The keys for signing the detection rules are securely stored in an HSM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the implementation and configuration of the RASP agent in the application environment. The integration with the HSM is checked. The ability of the RASP system to patch known vulnerabilities in the application without code changes (virtual patching) is demonstrated.

controls.title: Automatic response to security-relevant events (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The detection systems can generate alerts and send notifications. However, all subsequent reactions, such as blocking an IP address, must be carried out manually by an administrator.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NIDS sends an email when it detects an attack. The administrator reads the email and then logs into the firewall to manually block the source IP.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor triggers a test alarm and measures the time until the manual response occurs. It is determined that the process is error-prone and leads to significant delays.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the event of a security-relevant incident, the detection systems in use SHOULD automatically report the event and react with suitable protective measures. Procedures SHOULD be used that automatically detect possible attacks, abuse attempts, or security breaches. It SHOULD be possible to automatically intervene in the data stream to prevent a potential security incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) is used instead of a pure IDS. It is configured to automatically terminate the corresponding connection upon detection of clearly malicious signatures (e.g., known exploits). The EDR system is configured to immediately terminate the process upon detection of known ransomware.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the detection systems are operated in 'Prevention' or 'Block' mode. A controlled attack is carried out with a known, harmless signature to test whether the IPS automatically interrupts the connection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) platform is used to execute predefined but more complex response playbooks. These can coordinate actions across multiple different security tools, such as isolating an endpoint from the network and deactivating the user account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When the EDR system reports a high-criticality alarm for a client, the SOAR platform starts a playbook: It isolates the client from the network via the EDR console, deactivates the associated user account in Active Directory, and adds the C2 domain used by the attacker to the DNS server's blocklist. All steps are documented in an incident ticket.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the playbooks implemented in the SOAR platform and their integration with the various security tools (EDR, AD, DNS). A playbook is manually triggered in a test environment to verify the correct execution of the coordinated actions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The automatic response is dynamic and context-sensitive. AI-supported systems decide on the best possible response based on a real-time risk analysis. The type of attack, the criticality of the affected system, and the potential impact of the countermeasure on business operations are taken into account to ensure a proportionate response.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An AI module analyzes a detected attack. If it is a critical server during main business hours, initially only an alert is triggered and traffic is redirected to a honeypot environment. If it is a non-critical workstation outside of business hours, it is immediately and completely isolated without human interaction and flagged for reinstallation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the decision matrix and the configuration of the AI-supported response system. Various scenarios are run through to test how the system chooses different responses depending on the context. The logs of past automatic responses are evaluated for their proportionality and effectiveness.

controls.title: Performing regular integrity checks (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the detection systems is checked irregularly and manually to ensure that no unintentional changes have been made. The review of permissions is not part of this process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator compares the current configuration of the SIEM with a screenshot of the original configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the integrity check is a manual, error-prone process and that there is no systematic review of user permissions.

parts.name: statement
