parts.prose: All detection systems SHOULD be regularly checked for integrity. User permissions SHOULD also be controlled. Additionally, the sensors SHOULD perform a file integrity check. An automatic alert SHOULD be triggered if values change.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) agent is installed on all critical components of the detection infrastructure (SIEM server, NIDS sensors). This monitors critical system and configuration files. Any change to these files triggers an alert in the SIEM. Administrative permissions on the systems are reviewed quarterly as part of an access review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the FIM system and the list of monitored files. a controlled change is made to a monitored file to test the alerting. The logs of the last access reviews are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity check is automated and centralized. The FIM system is configured to distinguish between expected changes (e.g., from scheduled patches) and unexpected, potentially malicious changes to reduce the number of false positives. The access review process is also partially automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The FIM system is integrated with the change management system. Changes that are part of an approved change request are automatically classified as non-critical. All other changes generate a high-criticality alarm. An Identity and Access Management (IAM) tool automatically generates reports on current permissions and sends them to the system owners for confirmation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the integration between the FIM and change management system. It is tested how the system reacts to an unplanned change compared to a planned change. The automated process for the access review is evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of the detection systems is ensured by hardware-based mechanisms such as Secure Boot and the use of Trusted Platform Modules (TPM) (Root of Trust). Any administrative access to the systems is exclusively via a PIM/PAM (Privileged Access Management) solution with full session recording and just-in-time permission granting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The servers of the detection infrastructure use Secure Boot to ensure that only signed code is loaded. The TPM is used for Measured Boot to cryptographically attest to the system state (Remote Attestation). Administrators have no standing permissions; they must request temporary access via the PAM system, which must be approved. Every one of their actions on the command line is recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the BIOS/UEFI settings for Secure Boot and the configuration of Remote Attestation with the TPM. The process for requesting and approving privileged access in the PAM system is reviewed. The session recordings of an administrative activity are spot-checked. A script (`check_tpm_attestation.sh`) can query the integrity status.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
To be able to protect IT systems, security-relevant events must be detected and handled in a timely manner. To do this, it is necessary for institutions to plan, implement, and regularly practice suitable organizational, personnel, and technical measures in advance. This is because if a predefined and tested procedure can be used, reaction times can be shortened and existing processes can be optimized.
A security-relevant event is defined as an event that affects information security and can impair confidentiality, integrity, or availability. Typical consequences of such events are spied on, manipulated, or destroyed information. The causes for this are varied. Among other things, malware, outdated IT system infrastructures, or insider threats play a role. However, attackers also often exploit zero-day exploits, i.e., security vulnerabilities in programs for which there is no patch yet. Another serious threat are so-called Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs). These are targeted cyber-attacks on selected institutions and facilities, in which attackers gain permanent access to a network and subsequently extend this access to other IT systems. The attacks are characterized by a very high use of resources and considerable technical skills on the part of the attackers and are often difficult to detect.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module shows a systematic way of how information can be collected, correlated, and evaluated in order to detect security-relevant events as completely and promptly as possible. The findings gained from the detection should improve the ability of institutions to recognize security-relevant events and to react to them appropriately.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose: The module DER.1 Detection of security-relevant events must be applied once to the information network.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Disregard of legal regulations and co-determination rights
parts.prose: Programs that detect security-relevant events and evaluate log data often collect a lot of information about the network structure and internal processes of an institution. This may contain protectable information such as personal data, confidential data, or employee workflows. The storage of such data may, however, violate personal rights or co-determination rights. Under certain circumstances, the institution may also violate the respective data protection laws.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficient qualification of employees
parts.prose:
In an institution's daily IT operations, many disruptions and errors can occur, e.g., incoming log data could suddenly increase sharply. If the responsible personnel are not sufficiently aware and trained, it can happen that they do not identify security-relevant events as such and thus attacks remain undetected. And even if the responsible personnel are sufficiently sensitized and trained for the concerns of information security, it still cannot be ruled out that they will not recognize security incidents. Examples include:
• A person who has not been logged into their institution's local network for a long time considers it normal that their notebook has been noticeably slower during internet access for a week. They do not notice that a malware program is active in the background. They have not been trained, or have been insufficiently trained, to inform Incident Management of suspicious anomalies.
• A production manager does not notice that the data in the production systems and also the control display systems have been secretly changed. They do not become suspicious when the SCADA control of the production plant shows strange values, as this only happened for a short time. The incident is not reported because all values correspond to the expected display values again. Thus, no one notices that a malware has manipulated the display values.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Faulty administration of the detection systems used
parts.prose: Faulty configurations can cause the detection systems used to not function properly. If, for example, the alarm is set incorrectly, false alarms can occur more frequently. The responsible persons may then no longer be able to distinguish between a false alarm and a security-relevant event. They may also not notice the messages quickly enough because too many alarms are generated. As a result, attacks may go undetected. The effort required to evaluate the volume of messages also increases significantly.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Lack of information about the information network to be protected
parts.prose: If there is no or insufficient information about the information network to be protected, it can happen that essential areas of the information network are not sufficiently secured by detection systems. This allows attackers to easily penetrate the institution's network and, for example, access protectable information. It also allows them to remain in the system unnoticed for a long time and to have permanent access to the network.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Insufficient use of detection systems
parts.prose: If no detection systems are used and the functions for detecting security-relevant events available in IT systems and applications are not used, attackers can more easily penetrate the institution's network unnoticed. There, they could gain unauthorized access to sensitive information. It is particularly critical if the transitions between network boundaries are inadequately monitored.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Insufficient human resources
parts.prose: If there is not enough staff to evaluate log data, security-relevant events cannot be fully detected. Thus, attacks may remain hidden for a long time or are only discovered after, for example, a great deal of protectable information has already been leaked. Also, if external information sources are not evaluated due to a lack of staff, security vulnerabilities may remain open for too long. They can then be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the institution's IT systems.

controls.title: Definition of a security incident

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only very basic and obvious security incidents, such as a ransomware infection, are recognized as such. A formal, written definition does not exist. The distinction from everyday IT disruptions is made arbitrarily.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, there is no systematic approach. The identification of a security incident depends on the individual knowledge and experience of individual IT staff. There is no central documentation or training on this topic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks various IT staff members what they understand a security incident to be. The answers are expected to be inconsistent. No official documentation with a definition can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic, written definition of a security incident is available and known to the IT team. It distinguishes incidents from disruptions, but does not consider different levels of protection requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The definition is typically part of a general IT handbook or a wiki page. It is introduced to new IT staff during their onboarding, but is not regularly trained or reviewed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the document with the definition of the security incident. It is randomly checked with IT staff to see if they are familiar with the definition and where to find it.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An institution MUST have a clear definition of what a security incident is. A security incident MUST be distinguished as far as possible from disruptions in daily operations. All employees involved in handling security incidents MUST know the definition of a security incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The definition is laid down in a formal policy and is accessible to all relevant employees, including outside of IT. Examples of security incidents and distinctions from disruptions are provided to facilitate understanding. Knowledge of the definition is taught as part of security awareness training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a formally adopted policy with a clear definition. It is checked whether this policy has been made accessible to all relevant groups of people and whether the content is anchored in training materials.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The definition and the thresholds for security incidents are based on the protection requirements of the affected business processes, IT systems, or applications. The definition is reviewed regularly and adjusted as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The definition is supplemented with categories and thresholds based on protection requirements (e.g., normal, high, very high). An incident on a system with high protection requirements is classified differently than an identical incident on a system with normal protection requirements. This logic is stored in the SIEM system for prioritizing alarms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines whether the definition of security incidents is linked to the institution's protection requirements assessment. It is checked whether there is a documented process for regularly reviewing and adapting the definition, e.g., annually or after significant changes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The definition of security incidents is dynamic and is continuously developed based on threat intelligence feeds, results from red team exercises, and past incidents. The definition is directly integrated into automated detection and response mechanisms (SOAR) to enable a context-aware and rapid response.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New attack patterns from threat intelligence sources automatically lead to the creation or adaptation of correlation rules in the SIEM. The definition also includes complex, hard-to-detect scenarios such as Advanced Persistent Threats (APT). The thresholds are fine-grained and are adjusted with machine support.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of threat intelligence feeds into the process for defining and adapting security incidents. Logs and configurations of SIEM and SOAR systems are reviewed to confirm the automated implementation of the dynamic definitions. It is checked whether findings from audits or penetration tests have led to adjustments.

controls.title: Creation of a policy for handling security incidents

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Isolated, informal instructions for incident response exist, for example, in the form of emails or verbal agreements. A coherent, formal policy is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Checklists or instructions for very specific cases (e.g., 'What to do when a virus is found?') may exist, but they are not part of a comprehensive, approved framework.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the security incident handling policy. Only individual, unauthorized documents or email threads can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A draft of a security incident handling policy exists. However, it has not been formally approved by the institution's management, is not known to all employees, or is not regularly updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy was created by IT security management but has not yet completed the approval process. It is known in the IT department but has not been communicated throughout the entire institution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor can view the policy draft but notes that it is not dated, versioned, and signed by management. A survey of employees outside of IT shows that the policy is unknown.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy for handling security incidents MUST be created. It MUST define the purpose and goal of the policy and regulate all aspects of security incident handling. Thus, rules of conduct for the different types of security incidents MUST be described. Additionally, there MUST be target-group-oriented and practically applicable instructions for all employees. The policy MUST be known to all employees, coordinated with IT operations, and approved by the institution's management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is published in the institution's central document management system and is accessible to all employees. It contains clear, understandable instructions, e.g., a short 'What to do in an emergency' guide for regular users and more detailed process descriptions for IT staff. The approval by management is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a formally approved and versioned policy. It is checked whether the publication and notification to all employees is documented. The content is checked for completeness regarding the defined aspects (purpose, goal, rules, instructions).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy is reviewed regularly, at least annually, for currency and effectiveness and updated as needed. Furthermore, the interfaces to other management areas, e.g., to emergency management and data protection, are clearly defined and taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A fixed review cycle for the policy is established. Findings from past security incidents or exercises are incorporated into the update. The policy explicitly references the emergency response manual and data protection impact assessments and defines when a security incident is escalated to an emergency or a reportable data breach.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the revision history of the policy and the minutes of the reviews. It is checked whether the documented interfaces to other processes (e.g., emergency management) are consistent and practicable. It can be checked, for example, whether the policy was adjusted after an exercise.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy is part of an integrated management system (IMS) and is managed in a GRC tool. Changes to the policy are controlled via an automated workflow that also triggers the update of dependent process documents and technical controls (e.g., SOAR playbooks). Compliance with the policy is verified through continuous technical reviews and audits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy has a modular structure. Specific instructions for action are directly linked to automated response plans (playbooks) in the SOAR platform. A change in the playbook can trigger a review of the higher-level policy and vice versa. The effectiveness of the policy and the associated processes is permanently tested by Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS) tools.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is given read access to the GRC tool to understand the lifecycle of the policy and its links to other artifacts (risks, controls, processes). Reports from the BAS tool are evaluated to assess the practical effectiveness of the measures required in the policy. `(e.g., ansible-playbook --check /playbooks/incident-response/containment.yml)`

controls.title: Defining responsibilities and contact persons for security incidents

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities are not formally defined and are assigned ad-hoc in the event of an incident. There is no current or centrally maintained list of contact persons.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the event of an incident, the person considered most competent or currently available is contacted. Contact information is stored in private address books.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for a roles and responsibilities matrix for security incidents. No such document can be provided. Interviews with employees confirm that it is unclear who makes which decision in an emergency.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic responsibilities are mentioned in a general IT role description (e.g., 'The IT manager is responsible for IT security'). A list of contacts for IT problems exists, but it is not specific to security incidents and is not always up-to-date.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The responsibilities are defined too generally and do not describe specific tasks or authorities in the incident process. The contact list is often a simple Excel spreadsheet that is manually maintained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Although the auditor finds general role descriptions, they cannot find any specific assignment of tasks and competencies for the incident handling process. The provided contact list is outdated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be regulated who is responsible for what in case of security incidents. The tasks and competencies for security incidents MUST be defined for all employees. In particular, employees who are supposed to handle security incidents MUST be informed about their tasks and competencies. The contact persons for all types of security incidents MUST be known to the employees. Contact information MUST always be current and easily accessible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) for the incident handling process is created and maintained as an appendix to the policy. Contact information is maintained in a central system (e.g., Intranet, Active Directory) and is easily findable for all employees via a dedicated page.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of responsibilities (e.g., RACI matrix) and compares it with the policy. It is checked whether the contact lists are current and easily accessible (e.g., by accessing the corresponding intranet page). Random interviews with designated persons confirm that they are informed about their role and tasks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is clearly regulated who makes the decision for a forensic investigation, according to which criteria it is carried out, and when it should take place. Deputies are appointed and trained for all key roles in the incident handling process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The authority to commission a potentially expensive and complex forensic analysis is clearly assigned to a role (e.g., CISO, Head of Institution) with defined escalation paths. For each member of the core incident response team, a trained deputy is appointed to ensure operational capability even in their absence.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the process description for the regulation on initiating forensic measures. The appointment and training verification of deputies for key roles are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities and contact information are managed in a central Identity and Access Management (IAM) system and are coupled with the alerting and incident management system (e.g., SOAR). Escalation paths and the assignment of tasks are automated depending on the incident type and severity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a critical security incident is detected on a financial system, the SOAR tool automatically assigns the predefined tasks to the responsible persons from the system owner team, the IT security team, and the legal department, and escalates to their superiors after a defined period without a response. The contact information is pulled directly from the IAM system to ensure it is up-to-date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the SOAR or incident management tool to verify the automated assignment and escalation rules. The integration with the IAM system is checked. As part of a test alert, it is verified that the correct persons are notified automatically. `(e.g., curl -X POST -d '{"incident_type":"critical_financial"}' https://soar.api/trigger)`

controls.title: Notification of affected parties in case of security incidents

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Notifications are made ad-hoc and uncoordinated. Usually, only the directly involved IT staff are informed. Management, data protection, or external bodies are only informed upon request or in cases of obvious damage.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Communication happens through informal channels such as direct calls or chat messages. There are no templates or defined processes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the documentation of past incidents (if any) and finds that no consistent communication and notification strategy is discernible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple checklist for notification exists. It lists internal contacts such as IT management and executive management. The need to inform external parties is decided on a case-by-case basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The checklist is a simple document shared within the team. There are no specifications regarding deadlines or content of the notification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the checklist and assesses its completeness. It is noted that important stakeholders such as the data protection officer or the legal department are not listed by default.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All affected internal and external parties MUST be informed promptly of a security incident. It MUST be checked whether the data protection officer, the works and staff council, and employees from the legal department need to be involved. Likewise, the reporting obligations for authorities and regulated industries MUST be taken into account. Furthermore, it MUST be ensured that affected parties are informed about the necessary measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Notification matrices are created that, depending on the type and severity of the incident, define who must be notified, when, and with what information. This includes a list of relevant authorities (e.g., DPA, BSI) including reporting deadlines and forms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and completeness of the notification matrices. It is verified whether legal and regulatory reporting obligations (e.g., GDPR Art. 33, BSIG §8b) are correctly represented. When analyzing past incidents, it is checked whether the notifications were made according to the matrix.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Communication templates are created in advance for various target groups (e.g., management, users, customers, authorities). The communication channels are clearly defined and the responsibility for external communication (press officer, management) is established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Incident Response Plan includes an appendix with text blocks for emails, internal announcements, or press releases. These templates are reviewed in advance by the legal and communications departments to enable a quick and legally compliant response in an emergency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the communication templates and assesses their quality and completeness. It is checked whether the responsibilities for the approval and execution of communication are clearly regulated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The notification processes are largely automated and integrated into the incident management platform (SOAR). Stakeholder lists are generated dynamically based on the affected systems and data (from CMDB and data classification tools). Compliance with reporting deadlines is monitored automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the event of an incident classified as GDPR-relevant, the SOAR tool automatically starts a timer for the 72-hour reporting deadline, assigns the task of review to the data protection officer, and pre-fills the reporting form with the technical data already known.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the SOAR tool with regard to the automated notification workflows. The integration with the CMDB and other data sources is verified. As part of a simulated incident, the automatic generation of stakeholder lists and the monitoring of reporting deadlines are checked.

controls.title: Remediation of security incidents

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Remediation is reactive and focuses on the quickest possible restoration of operations, often without finding or eliminating the actual root cause. The measures are not documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A typical measure is to restart a system or restore a backup, hoping that the problem will disappear.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In interviews, the auditor determines that there is no systematic root cause analysis. There are no records of the remediation measures taken.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Standard instructions for remediation exist for frequently occurring, simple security incidents (e.g., virus detection). For more complex incidents, remediation is ad-hoc. A list of contact details for external experts is available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The internal wiki has a page 'Instructions for virus removal'. The list of experts is a simple contact collection, without any framework agreements in place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing instructions and assesses their adequacy. It is determined that there are no plans for new or complex attack scenarios.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For a security incident to be successfully remediated, those responsible MUST first contain the problem and find the root cause. Afterwards, the necessary measures to resolve the problem MUST be selected. The head of IT operations MUST grant approval before the measures are implemented. Subsequently, the root cause MUST be eliminated and a secure state MUST be restored. An up-to-date list of internal and external security experts MUST be available and secure communication procedures MUST be established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The remediation process follows a clear scheme: 1. Analysis and root cause investigation, 2. Selection and planning of measures, 3. Approval, 4. Implementation, 5. Verification. Encrypted channels (e.g., PGP-encrypted email, secure data room) are defined for communication with external experts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the documentation of past incidents and checks whether the defined remediation process was followed, including the documented approval. The existence of the expert list and the defined secure communication procedures is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Detailed remediation plans (playbooks) exist for various categories of security incidents. The effectiveness of the remediation measures is systematically verified before the incident is closed. Framework agreements are in place with external security service providers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are playbooks for scenarios such as 'ransomware attack', 'DDoS attack', or 'compromised user account'. After cleaning a system, a verification scan is performed with a different tool to confirm the complete removal of the malware. A retainer contract for incident response is in place with an external service provider, which guarantees response times.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the playbooks for various scenarios and assesses their quality. The existence of the framework agreements is checked. Evidence of the verification of the remediation measures is sought in the incident documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Many remediation measures are automated through the use of a SOAR platform. Root cause analysis is supported by advanced analytical methods and machine learning. Following the remediation of an incident, a proactive search for similar vulnerabilities is conducted throughout the entire infrastructure (threat hunting) to prevent future incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If a compromised account is identified, the SOAR system automatically locks the account, terminates all active sessions, and starts a scan of all systems the account recently accessed. After a malware incident, the indicator set (IOCs) is used to proactively scan the entire network for further, previously undetected infections.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the SOAR playbooks for automated remediation. Reports from threat-hunting activities are reviewed to verify the proactive component. The effectiveness of the automation is tested by a simulated triggering of a playbook.

controls.title: Restoration of the operating environment after security incidents

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Systems are restored from the last available backup without checking if the backup itself is compromised. Important steps like changing passwords are often forgotten.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The restoration focuses exclusively on the functionality of the system, not on its security. It is assumed that a backup is 'clean' per se.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines in interviews and by analyzing tickets (if available) that there is no standardized, security-conscious recovery procedure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple checklist for recovery exists. It specifies to take the affected system offline, secure data, restore the system from a backup, and change passwords.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The checklist ensures that the most basic steps are not forgotten. A deep analysis or hardening of the restored system does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the checklist. It is checked whether all points on the checklist were completed and documented during past restorations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After a security incident, the affected components MUST be taken offline. All necessary data for analysis MUST be secured. The operating system and all applications MUST be checked for changes. The original data MUST be restored from read-only media (e.g., clean installation media), including all security-relevant configurations and patches. If data is restored from backups, it MUST be ensured that they were not affected by the security incident. After an attack, all access credentials on the affected components MUST be changed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of restoring a potentially compromised backup, the system is rebuilt from a trusted medium (golden image). Only the pure application data is taken from the backup after it has been scanned for malware. All passwords, service accounts, and SSH keys stored on the system are changed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the restoration process. It is checked whether 'golden images' or clean installation media are used. It is checked whether a process for checking backups before restoration exists. The forced change of access credentials is tracked using logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The restored components SHOULD undergo a penetration test before being put back into production. The users are involved in the application functional tests. After everything has been restored, the components, including the network gateways, MUST be specifically monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After reinstallation, the system is subjected to an automated vulnerability scan and a short manual test in an isolated network segment. Business users perform an acceptance test. After going live, the network traffic to and from this system is monitored with increased attention in the SIEM for a defined period (e.g., one week).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor looks for evidence of the verification tests performed (scan reports, acceptance protocols) in the documentation. The SIEM configuration is checked for temporary, specific monitoring rules for restored systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The restoration is fully automated using 'Infrastructure as Code' (IaC) and a repository of hardened 'Golden Images'. The entire process, including configuration, patching, testing, and monitoring, is automated and restores a secure and consistent state in the shortest possible time. Threat intelligence is used to scan restored systems for the latest attack indicators.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator triggers the complete reprovisioning of the affected server via a script (e.g., with Ansible or Terraform). The script fetches the latest approved image, configures the application, restores the scanned data, performs automated security and functional tests, and reintegrates the system into production and monitoring. A feed with the latest IOCs is queried and used for verification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the IaC scripts and the CI/CD pipeline processes for creating and maintaining the 'Golden Images'. The automation is demonstrated by a logged execution of the recovery script in a test environment. The configuration of the threat intelligence feed integration is checked. `(e.g. git log -- /path/to/terraform/modules/webserver/)`

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
To limit damage and avoid further damage, detected security incidents must be handled quickly and efficiently. For this, it is necessary to establish a predefined and proven procedure for handling security incidents (Security Incident Handling or Security Incident Response).

A security incident can have a significant impact on an institution and cause major damage. Such incidents include, for example, misconfigurations that lead to the disclosure of confidential information, or criminal acts such as attacks on servers, the theft of confidential information, as well as IT-related sabotage or extortion.

The causes of security incidents are diverse; malware, outdated system infrastructures, and insiders all play a role. However, attackers also often exploit zero-day exploits, which are security vulnerabilities in programs for which no patch is yet available. Another serious threat are so-called Advanced Persistent Threats (APT).

Furthermore, users, IT operations, or external service providers could behave incorrectly, causing security-critical system parameters to be changed or internal policies to be violated. Other conceivable causes include the violation of access rights, modification of software and hardware, or inadequate securing of sensitive rooms and buildings.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to provide a systematic approach to creating a concept for handling security incidents.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module DER.2.1 Handling of Security Incidents must be applied once for the information network.

The focus of this module is on handling security incidents from an information technology perspective. However, before security incidents can be handled, they must be detected. Security requirements for this are contained in module DER.1 Detection of Security-Relevant Events and are a prerequisite for this module. The precautionary measures necessary to enable IT forensic investigations are described in module DER.2.2 Preparation for IT Forensics. The cleanup after an APT incident is the subject of module DER.2.3 Cleanup of Major Security Incidents. A special area of security incident handling is emergency management, which is addressed in module DER.4 Emergency Management and is not further considered here. It should be noted, however, that the decision as to whether or not an emergency exists is made in this module.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Inappropriate handling of security incidents
parts.prose:
In practice, it can never be ruled out that security incidents will occur. This is true even when many security measures have been implemented. However, if acute security incidents are not responded to, or not responded to appropriately, major damage with catastrophic consequences can result. Examples of this are:

• Suspicious entries are found in the log files of a firewall. If it is not investigated promptly whether these are the first signs of a break-in attempt, attackers can overcome the firewall with a successful attack unnoticed and penetrate the institution's internal network.

• Security vulnerabilities in the IT systems or applications in use become known. If the institution does not obtain this information in a timely manner and does not quickly initiate the necessary countermeasures, these security vulnerabilities can be exploited in an attack.

• A burglary at a branch office is mistaken for a case of procurement crime because notebooks and flat screens were stolen. The fact that the notebooks contained confidential information and access data for IT systems in the intranet is not given much importance. The Information Security Officer (ISO) is therefore not informed. The institution is therefore not prepared for the subsequent attacks on the IT systems of other locations and the company headquarters. The data found on the stolen notebooks was used for the attack.

If no suitable procedure for dealing with security incidents is specified, wrong decisions can be made in a hurry and under stress. These can lead, for example, to the press being misinformed. Furthermore, third parties could be harmed by one's own IT systems and claim damages. It is also possible that no contingency or recovery measures are planned, which would significantly increase the damage to the institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Destruction of evidence during security incident handling
parts.prose:
If action is taken carelessly or not according to instructions after a security incident, this can lead to important evidence for clarification or later legal prosecution being unintentionally destroyed or rendered inadmissible in court.

Examples of this are:

• During an attack, malware was placed on a client, whose mode of operation and target can only be analyzed while it is running. For this, information about the active processes and the content of the main memory would have to be secured and evaluated. If the client is now shut down prematurely, the information can no longer be used for an analysis and clarification of the security incident.

• IT operations finds a running process on a server that is causing above-average CPU load. In addition, this process creates temporary files and sends unknown information over the Internet. If the process is terminated prematurely and the temporary files are simply deleted, it cannot be determined whether confidential information was stolen.

• An important server is compromised because IT operations, due to a heavy workload and a lack of a maintenance window, could not install the latest security updates as planned. To avoid possible disciplinary consequences, IT operations installs the missing updates before a security team can analyze the cause of the intrusion and the damage incurred. A poor error culture has thus prevented an analysis of the problem.

controls.title: Review of legal and regulatory frameworks for collection and evaluability (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A legal review is only carried out sporadically and reactively in the event of serious security incidents. There is no systematic recording of the relevant legal frameworks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this maturity level, legal counsel or the data protection officer is typically only consulted when major damage has already occurred. Proactive involvement in process design is completely lacking.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks those responsible whether and when legal reviews have been carried out in the context of IT forensics in the past. It is checked whether there is documented evidence of a systematic approach, which is not expected to be the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The most important legal frameworks, such as the GDPR, are known. The data protection officer is generally informed during IT forensic investigations, but without a formally defined process. Internal regulations or works agreements are not systematically taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple list of known laws is maintained. Communication with the data protection officer is mostly done via email on an ad-hoc basis. The involvement of the works or staff council is decided on a case-by-case basis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of considered legal frameworks and performs random checks on past incidents to see whether the data protection officer was demonstrably informed (e.g., through email correspondence).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If data is collected and analyzed for forensic investigations, all legal and regulatory frameworks MUST be identified and complied with. Furthermore, internal regulations and employee agreements MUST NOT be violated. To this end, the works or staff council and the data protection officer(s) MUST be involved in a defined process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal document is created that describes the process for legal review. This document specifies when and how the data protection officer and the works/staff council are to be involved. A checklist helps to identify all relevant legal, regulatory, and internal requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the process document and the checklist for identifying the framework conditions. Based on the documentation of IT security incidents, it is checked whether the defined process was demonstrably adhered to and whether the involvement of the relevant bodies (data protection officer, works council) was documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for reviewing the legal frameworks is reviewed and updated regularly, at least annually, and whenever the legal situation changes. A clear matrix is maintained that compares data types, IT systems, and the respective applicable legal restrictions. The involvement of external legal counsel for complex cases is formalized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A responsible person is appointed who is in charge of regularly updating the legal requirements and process documents. The matrix is maintained in a wiki or another central system. Templates exist for requests for involvement to the legal department and the data protection officer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the last reviews of the process. They inspect the data-law matrix for currency and completeness. It is verified that for complex cases, the defined process for consulting legal counsel was followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The legal approval process is integrated into the incident response workflows. For various types of security incidents, there are pre-approved, legally vetted procedures (playbooks). Changes in the legal situation lead to automated notifications to the process owners and trigger a formal adjustment process for the playbooks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) tool is used to manage the playbooks. The legal approval for a playbook is stored as a digital stamp in the system. A subscription-based legal information service is used to be automatically informed about relevant changes in legislation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the workflow in the SOAR tool demonstrated. It is checked whether the forensic playbooks have traceable legal approval. A simulated incident is used to verify that the system automatically selects the correct, legally sound playbook. The automatic check can be performed by querying the playbook metadata in the SOAR system, which indicates the status of the legal review.

controls.title: Creation of a guide for initial measures in the event of an IT security incident (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no written instructions for initial measures. The procedure is based on the individual knowledge of individual employees, which leads to inconsistent reactions and potential destruction of evidence.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees who notice an incident act to the best of their knowledge and belief. This often leads to uncoordinated actions such as restarting systems, which destroys volatile evidence.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for documented first-response guides. The absence of such documents confirms this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple, general checklist for initial measures in the event of an IT security incident exists. It contains basic steps such as 'disconnect system from the network' or 'inform IT security', but no system-specific details or warnings about the destruction of evidence.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The checklist is available on the intranet, but its use is not enforced or trained. It is often too generic to be truly helpful in specific situations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the checklist and evaluates its content. They check whether the checklist contains instructions on how to avoid the destruction of evidence, which is not expected to be the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A guide MUST be created that describes for the IT systems in use which initial measures must be carried out in the event of an IT security incident in order to destroy as few traces of evidence as possible. It MUST also describe which actions could potentially destroy evidence and how this can be avoided.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The guide is created as a formal document, versioned, and distributed to the relevant employees. It contains clear instructions (e.g., 'do not restart the system, but create a memory dump') and a 'what-not-to-do' list. The guide is tailored to the primarily used system types (e.g., Windows clients, Linux servers).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the guide and checks its content for the required aspects. In particular, it is verified whether the guide explicitly addresses the risk of evidence destruction and provides concrete examples of actions to be avoided. The availability and awareness of the guide among first responders is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The guide for initial measures is expanded to include system-specific instructions for critical systems (e.g., database servers, domain controllers). It contains illustrated step-by-step instructions and is regularly tested and improved as part of exercises.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate chapter or appendix is created in the guide for each critical system or system group. The instructions are designed so that they can also be carried out safely by non-forensics experts under guidance. The results from security incident exercises are actively incorporated into the revision of the guide.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the guide and checks for the presence of system-specific instructions for systems classified as critical. Logs from exercises or real incidents are reviewed to verify that the guide was applied and its effectiveness was evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The initial measures are implemented in the form of automated or semi-automated playbooks in a SOAR system or a comparable incident response tool. When an incident is reported, the handler is provided with the correct excerpt from the guide or the appropriate playbook in a context-sensitive manner to minimize the error rate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An incident response management system (e.g., TheHive, a SOAR tool) is used. Alarms from the SIEM system automatically trigger the creation of a case and assign the appropriate first-response playbook. This playbook can automatically perform simple actions such as isolating a client on the network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the functionality in the incident response system demonstrated. A test alarm is triggered to check whether the correct playbook for initial measures is automatically assigned and displayed to the analyst. The automated check can be performed via an API query that reads the configuration of the playbook assignment rules.

controls.title: Pre-selection of forensics service providers (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no pre-selection of forensics service providers. In case of need, a suitable provider is reactively searched for via a web search, which leads to significant delays.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In an emergency, a frantic search for potential service providers begins. The selection is made under time pressure without a thorough review of qualifications or contractual conditions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for a list of pre-selected forensics service providers. The absence of such a list or corresponding documentation confirms this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An informal list of potential forensics service providers and their contact details exists. However, no formal qualification check or contractual arrangement has taken place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An employee has created a simple list in a text file or spreadsheet that they would consult in an emergency. The list contains names of companies known from recommendations or conferences.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of potential service providers. They check whether there is any further documentation, such as bid comparisons or audit reports, which is not expected to be the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If an institution does not have its own forensics team, potential suitable forensics service providers MUST be identified in the preparation phase. Which forensics service providers are eligible MUST be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A market analysis is carried out and a shortlist of at least two to three potential service providers is drawn up. For each service provider, the contact details, service portfolio, and initial price indications are documented. This documentation is stored centrally and is known to the relevant persons.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documented pre-selection of forensics service providers. They check whether the documentation makes the identification and basic evaluation of several providers comprehensible and whether it is up to date.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The preselected service providers are evaluated based on a formal catalog of criteria. This includes response times (SLAs), certifications (e.g., BSI-certified IT security service provider), references, and costs. The results of the evaluation are documented, and the selection is approved by management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tender or a formal Request for Information (RFI) is carried out. The responses from the service providers are systematically compared in an evaluation matrix. Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) are concluded with the shortlisted service providers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the criteria catalog, the evaluation matrix, and the final, approved selection decision. It is checked whether the selection is based on a traceable and documented evaluation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A framework agreement or a call-off agreement (retainer) is concluded with at least one prioritized forensics service provider. This contract regulates guaranteed response times, daily rates, the handling of confidential data, and reporting requirements to enable immediate and smooth commissioning in an emergency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The legal department reviews and negotiates the framework agreement. The contract is signed by the institution's management. The contact details and the process for activating the service provider are prominently documented in the emergency plan and the incident response plan. Regular (e.g., annual) coordination meetings with the service provider take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the signed framework agreement or retainer agreement and checks its contents, in particular the regulations on SLAs and confidentiality. It is verified that the activation process is correctly described in the emergency plan. Automated testing can verify the existence of a valid contract date in a contract management system.

controls.title: Definition of interfaces to crisis and emergency management (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Communication between the IT forensics team and crisis management is ad hoc and unstructured. It is not clear who should receive what information and when.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Information is passed on a case-by-case basis by phone or email. This leads to misunderstandings, loss of information, and delays in crisis management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews team members from forensics and crisis management on how communication works in an emergency. The lack of defined processes and responsibilities confirms this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Contact persons in crisis and emergency management are named to whom the forensics team can turn. However, the communication channels and content are not formally defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A contact list with the names and phone numbers of the members of the crisis team exists. However, there are no specifications as to the format or frequency in which status updates are to be delivered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the contact list and checks whether the named persons are aware of their role. Process documents that regulate the flow of information are requested, which are likely to be missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The interfaces between IT forensic investigations and crisis and emergency management SHOULD be defined and documented. For this purpose, it SHOULD be regulated which employees are responsible for which tasks and how they should be communicated with. In addition, it SHOULD be ensured that the responsible contact persons are always reachable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document describes the interface. It specifies who (role) in the forensics team acts as the primary contact for the crisis team. It defines the reporting chain, the communication channels (e.g., dedicated chat room, regular conference calls), and the content of the status reports. Availability is ensured by a 24/7 on-call list, which is known to all participants.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the interface definition document. They check whether responsibilities, communication channels, and reporting content are clearly regulated. The timeliness and availability of the on-call list are verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined interfaces and communication processes are tested regularly, at least once a year, in joint exercises with crisis and emergency management. Templates for forensic interim and final reports are used, which are tailored to the information needs of the crisis team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual exercise plan is created that provides for joint scenarios for forensics and crisis management. After each exercise, a 'lessons learned' workshop takes place, the results of which are used to improve the processes. The report templates are standardized and contain sections for management summary, technical details, and recommendations for action.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the protocols of the last joint exercises as well as the 'lessons learned' documents. They check whether the defined communication processes were applied in the exercise and whether improvement measures were implemented. The report templates used are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Communication and the exchange of situational information between the forensics team and the crisis team take place via a common, integrated situation and collaboration tool. Forensic findings are fed into the crisis team's situational picture in real time as facts to ensure rapid and well-founded decision-making.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated crisis management or incident response tool with a shared dashboard is used. The forensics team updates the status of the investigation and important findings directly in the tool. The crisis team has read access to relevant parts of the forensics case and can submit tasks or information requests directly to the forensics team via the tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the joint collaboration tool demonstrated. It is checked how a forensic indicator (e.g., identified malware) is recorded in the tool and how this information is made available to the crisis team in real time. The automated check can be carried out by a configuration check of the tool, which verifies the permissions and information flows between the teams.

controls.title: Creation of a guide for evidence preservation measures in IT security incidents (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no guide for evidence preservation. It is carried out on an ad hoc basis and is based on the individual knowledge of the people involved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each forensic scientist uses the tools and methods they personally prefer. There is no standardization, which makes it difficult to compare and trace the results.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the evidence preservation guide. The absence of such a document confirms this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic description of the procedure for evidence preservation, for example for creating a hard disk image. However, specific tools, legal aspects, or documentation obligations are not described in detail.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A wiki page or a short document roughly describes how to image a hard drive with a common tool like 'dd' or 'FTK Imager'. Details on securing RAM or the chain of custody are missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the document and assesses its level of detail. It is checked whether aspects such as tools, legal frameworks, and documentation requirements are covered, which will probably be insufficient.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A guide SHOULD be created describing how evidence is to be preserved. It SHOULD list procedures, technical tools, legal frameworks, and documentation requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal, versioned guide to evidence preservation is created. It contains separate sections for: 1. Procedures (e.g., live forensics vs. post-mortem), 2. a list of approved hardware and software tools, 3. a summary of the most important legal aspects (e.g., purpose limitation, private use), and 4. a template for the evidence preservation protocol.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the evidence preservation guide and checks whether all required aspects (procedures, tools, legal, documentation) are included in a structured manner. It is checked whether the guide is known and accessible to the responsible employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The guide is expanded to include specific, detailed instructions (Standard Operating Procedures - SOPs) for securing various system types (e.g., Windows, Linux, macOS, mobile devices, cloud environments) and data sources (RAM, hard drives, logs, network traffic). The SOPs are regularly reviewed and updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed SOP with screenshots and command-line examples is created for each common forensic task. These SOPs are practically tested and refined as part of training (see A6) and exercises (see A15). A review process ensures that the instructions remain up-to-date with the latest technology.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the guide including the specific SOPs. They randomly check an SOP for its clarity, technical correctness, and completeness. Evidence of regular reviews and updates of the documents is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procedures described in the guide are largely automated. Scripts and forensic tools are pre-configured on a dedicated forensics system to ensure fast, consistent, and error-free evidence preservation. The selection of the correct procedure is supported by an expert system or a SOAR playbook.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A forensic workstation or a portable system is equipped with all necessary tools and scripts. For recurring tasks such as creating a RAM image or imaging a hard drive, there are scripts that control the process, automatically log it, and calculate and verify the hashes. A SOAR tool suggests the appropriate script based on the system type.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the forensic workstation and the automated scripts demonstrated. A preservation process (e.g., of a test USB stick) is demonstrated live to verify correct and logged execution. Automated testing can be done through a code analysis of the preservation scripts and their configuration.

controls.title: Training of personnel for the implementation of forensic preservation (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no formal training courses on forensic preservation. Knowledge is passed on informally or must be acquired by the employees themselves.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New team members learn by 'watching' more experienced colleagues. There is no guarantee of a uniform level of knowledge and quality.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for training records or a training plan. The absence of these documents indicates this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: New employees receive a one-time briefing on the basic procedures of evidence preservation. However, there are no recurring or in-depth training sessions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the onboarding process, the evidence preservation guide (if available) is discussed once. Participation in external training is possible, but not systematically planned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the onboarding plans of new employees for a corresponding training item. They ask for a plan for further or regular training, which is unlikely to exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All responsible employees SHOULD know how to correctly secure traces and use forensic tools properly. Appropriate training SHOULD be conducted for this purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A training concept is created that defines the training content, the target group, and the frequency of the training. The training is based on the created guide (A5) and includes both theoretical principles and practical exercises with the approved tools. Participation is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the training concept and the proofs of participation from the last training round. They compare the list of trained employees with the list of employees responsible for forensics.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training program is multi-level and role-based. First responders receive basic training, while the core forensics team participates in advanced, specialized training (e.g., for cloud forensics, malware analysis). Training success is verified through short tests or practical exams.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The training plan provides different curricula for various roles in the incident response process. A budget for external, recognized certifications (e.g., GIAC) is allocated. At the end of an internal training, participants must solve a practical task, e.g., correctly securing a test system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the training plan for its role-based orientation. They request proof of participation in advanced training courses and the results of the success assessments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training program is embedded in a continuous improvement process. Findings from real incidents and regular, challenging exercises (e.g., Red/Blue-Teaming) flow directly into the adaptation of the training content. Employees are encouraged to get involved in the forensics community and actively share their knowledge.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After every major incident or exercise, a 'Lessons Learned' document is created that also addresses training needs. There is a budget for attending professional conferences. The forensics team may maintain an internal blog or wiki to document and disseminate new techniques and findings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews 'Lessons Learned' documents and checks whether resulting adjustments in the training material are verifiable. They interview team members about their participation in conferences or other further education measures that go beyond standard courses.

controls.title: Selection of tools for forensics (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no standardized selection of forensic tools. Employees use freely available tools from the internet without checking their suitability or trustworthiness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If needed, a tool is quickly downloaded and used. This carries the risk that the tools themselves are compromised, alter traces, or deliver unreliable results.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the employees which tools they use and how they are procured. The absence of an approved tool list and a selection process confirms this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal list of common open-source or freeware tools used for forensic tasks. A formal review of the tools or their functionality does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The team has agreed on a set of well-known tools such as 'Autopsy', 'FTK Imager', or 'Volatility'. The tools are downloaded from the official websites, but their integrity is not systematically checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the list of tools used and how it is ensured that they function correctly. The absence of test protocols or integrity checks is an indicator of this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that tools used to forensically secure and analyze traces are suitable for this purpose. Before a tool is used for forensics, it SHOULD also be checked to ensure it functions correctly. It SHOULD also be verified and documented that it has not been manipulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal list of approved forensic tools (both commercial and open source) is created and maintained. Each tool on the list is evaluated on a test system before approval. The integrity of the tools (e.g., through hash checking after download) is verified and documented during installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of approved tools and the corresponding evaluation and integrity check protocols. They check whether such proof exists for all tools used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The forensic tools are maintained and regularly updated on dedicated, hardened systems (forensic workstations). The functionality of the tools is verified by comparing the results of at least two different tools (tool validation). The use of hardware write blockers is mandatory for post-mortem analyses.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Dedicated laptops or desktops are configured as forensic workstations, which are separated from the production network. a process for patch management of the forensic tools is established. For important analysis steps, such as the recovery of deleted files, the results are cross-checked with a second, independent tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the forensic workstation and checks its configuration and up-to-dateness. They ask for documentation of tool validations and check whether the use of write blockers is noted in the evidence collection logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The toolbox is supplemented by a centrally managed and commercially supported forensics suite (e.g., EnCase, X-Ways Forensics, Magnet AXIOM). The integrity of the entire forensic work environment is ensured by Secure Boot and Trusted Execution technologies. All tools are regularly calibrated, and their validation is documented according to standards such as the NIST Computer Forensic Tool Testing (CFTT) Program Reports.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A license for a professional forensics suite is procured and maintained. The forensic workstation is a high-security system with disk encryption, application whitelisting, and activated Secure Boot. The validation documentation is based on external standards and stored in a revision-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the license certificates for the commercial forensics suite. They verify the security configuration of the workstation and request the validation documentation, which is based on external standards. The automated check can be performed by a configuration scan of the forensic workstation that verifies the security settings.

controls.title: Selection and order of evidence to be collected (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of data to be secured is done intuitively and without a clear strategy. Volatile data such as memory is usually ignored, which leads to the loss of crucial traces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The first impulse is often to secure the hard drive of the affected system. This may involve shutting down the system, which causes all information in RAM to be lost.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes logs of past collections (if available) and finds that volatile data was not considered. They question the forensic analysts about their procedure for selecting evidence.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is known that volatile data is important, but there is no formal process for determining the order of collection. The objectives of the investigation are often only vaguely defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The team tries to secure the memory before imaging the hard drive. However, the selection of systems to be secured is based on an initial, superficial assessment and not on a clear definition of objectives.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks evidence collection logs for compliance with the 'Order of Volatility'. They ask how the objectives of an investigation are defined and find that this is not formalized.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A forensic investigation SHOULD always begin by defining the objectives or the work order. The objectives SHOULD be formulated as concretely as possible. After that, all necessary data sources SHOULD be identified. It SHOULD also be determined in which order the data is to be secured and the exact procedure to be followed. The order SHOULD be based on how volatile the data to be secured is. Thus, highly volatile data SHOULD be secured promptly. Only then SHOULD non-volatile data such as fixed storage content and finally backups follow.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each investigation, a formal work order is created that clearly names the questions to be answered (e.g., 'How did the attacker get in?', 'What data was exfiltrated?'). Based on the order, a list of data sources to be secured is created. The collection strictly follows the 'Order of Volatility' (e.g., 1. RAM, 2. running processes, 3. network connections, 4. hard drive, 5. archive logs).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: For a past investigation, the auditor requests the work order, the list of data sources, and the evidence collection logs. They check whether the objectives were clearly defined and whether the collection order in the logs corresponded to the 'Order of Volatility'.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For typical types of security incidents (e.g., ransomware, phishing, web server compromise), predefined checklists for evidence to be collected are created. These checklists consider the specific artifacts of the respective attack type and help to avoid overlooking important traces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Checklists for different scenarios are maintained in the incident response plan or a wiki. In the event of a ransomware incident, for example, the checklist lists the securing of RAM, MFT, event logs, and the ransom note. These checklists are used when defining the work order.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the scenario-based checklists for evidence collection. They compare the checklist for a specific scenario with the data actually collected from a past, matching incident.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection and prioritization of evidence to be collected is supported by a SOAR system. Based on the alarm type, the affected systems, and the information from the CMDB, the system automatically suggests a prioritized list of collection measures, which the forensic analyst can confirm or adjust.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If an alarm for 'possible ransomware activity' is triggered on a database server classified as critical, the SOAR playbook automatically creates a task to secure the RAM of this server with the highest priority, followed by securing the transaction logs and the hard drive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the SOAR system demonstrate how a list of collection measures is automatically generated for a simulated alarm. It is checked whether the prioritization of the measures corresponds to the 'Order of Volatility' and the criticality of the system. The automated check can read and evaluate the configuration logic of the corresponding playbooks.

controls.title: Pre-selection of forensically relevant data (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secondary data such as log data is only kept with standard settings and short retention periods. A conscious decision about which data could be relevant for forensics does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Log files are overwritten after a few days or weeks. Important events such as login attempts or process starts are often not logged at all.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the logging configuration and retention periods on some sample systems and determines that they are insufficient for a retroactive analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Log data from central systems (e.g., firewalls, domain controllers) is collected, but there is no overarching concept of which data sources are relevant for forensic purposes. Retention periods are set on a flat-rate basis, without considering legal requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central syslog server collects some log types. The configuration of which events are logged usually remains at the manufacturer's default. A retention period of e.g. 90 days is set for all logs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for a logging concept. They check whether the retention periods take legal requirements (e.g., from the Telecommunications Act) into account, which is probably not the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be specified which secondary data (e.g., log data or traffic captures) are to be retained, in what way, and for how long within the legal framework for possible forensic evidence preservation measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal logging concept is created. It defines which data sources (e.g., authentication logs, DNS logs, proxy logs, Netflow data) are classified as relevant for forensics. For each data source, a retention period is defined that is based on operational needs and legal requirements and is coordinated with the Data Protection Officer.

parts.name: assessment-method
