parts.prose: The auditor requests the logging concept. They check whether the defined data sources and retention periods are documented and justified. It is verified that the Data Protection Officer was demonstrably involved in the creation of the concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logging concept is extended to include detailed configuration specifications for the most important system types to ensure that forensically valuable events (e.g., process creation, PowerShell commands, registry changes) are actually logged. The integrity of the log data is ensured by forwarding it to a central, read-only SIEM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For Windows and Linux systems, configuration profiles (e.g., GPOs) are created that enable advanced logging. All relevant logs are sent to a SIEM system to which only authorized persons have read access to prevent manipulation. The retention periods are technically implemented in the SIEM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the logging configurations on a client and a server and compares them with the specifications of the concept. They check the configuration of the SIEM system to verify central collection and read-only storage. An automated test could read the logging configuration via a script (e.g., PowerShell) and compare it with a golden image.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection and retention of forensically relevant data is dynamically adapted to the threat landscape. In addition to central logging, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) systems are used on critical endpoints, which enable in-depth, continuous recording of system activities and allow for historical analysis ('Threat Hunting') even without prior log configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An EDR tool is rolled out across all clients and servers. This tool records process starts, network connections, and file and registry access. The data is collected centrally and is available for forensic analysis. In response to new threat intelligence, the logging profile can be adapted centrally and at short notice to capture specific artifacts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the rollout status of the EDR system. They have someone demonstrate a query in the EDR tool that shows historical system activities on a test client. It is checked whether a process for adapting the data collection based on threat intelligence exists and is documented.

controls.title: IT forensic preservation of evidence (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Evidence is not forensically preserved; instead, simple copies of files or folders are created. This process alters metadata, and the integrity of the copy is not proven.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator copies suspicious files to a USB stick via drag-and-drop. This action alters timestamps and makes the copy barely admissible in court.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the data preservation method and finds that no forensic imaging tools are used. There are no hash values or chain of custody documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Forensic imaging tools are used to create 1:1 copies of data carriers. However, the process is not fully documented, and cryptographic checksums for integrity verification are not always created.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A forensic analyst uses FTK Imager to create a copy of a hard drive. However, they forget to record the hash value or save the acquisition log. The acquisition is performed by untrained personnel.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews existing acquisition logs (if any) and identifies gaps, e.g., missing hash values. They check whether the personnel performing the task are verifiably trained (see A6).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data carriers SHOULD be fully forensically duplicated if possible. If this is not possible, e.g., for volatile data in RAM, a method SHOULD be chosen that alters as little data as possible. Cryptographic checksums of the data carriers SHOULD be created and documented in writing. The original data carriers SHOULD be stored sealed. Only trained personnel or a forensic service provider SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each acquisition, a forensic image (e.g., in E01 format) is created that contains metadata and hash values. The hash of the original data carrier and that of the image are calculated and compared in the log. The original data carriers are packaged in sealed, labeled evidence bags. Only personnel who have completed the training according to A6 perform the acquisition.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the evidence acquisition log for a case. They check whether hash values for the original and the image are documented and match. They verify that the person performing the task is on the list of trained employees. They check the process for sealing and storing the originals.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The creation of the cryptographic checksums is witnessed by a second employee (four-eyes principle). The checksums are stored separately from the images and in multiple copies to ensure their integrity. The use of hardware write blockers is mandatory for the acquisition of physical data carriers to prevent any alteration of the original.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The evidence acquisition log is signed by the forensic analyst and a witness. The list of hash values is digitally signed and stored on a separate, secure storage medium. All acquisitions of SATA, IDE, or USB drives are performed using a validated hardware write blocker.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the evidence acquisition log and checks for a witness's signature. They ask about the storage location of the hash lists and check if it is separate from the image storage. They verify the use of hardware write blockers by reviewing the logs or inspecting the equipment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire evidence acquisition process is largely automated and is seamlessly logged by a chain-of-custody tool. The created checksums and logs are timestamped by a trusted timestamping service and stored in an audit-proof archive to maximize admissibility in court and non-repudiation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script or a commercial tool controls the imaging process, automatically calculates and compares hashes (e.g., MD5 and SHA-256), generates the log, and requests signatures. The final log is sent to a qualified timestamping authority (TSA) and the result is stored in an audit-proof manner in a document management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests an evidence acquisition log and checks the digital timestamp from a trusted TSA. They have someone demonstrate the automated acquisition process and verify that all steps are logged seamlessly and in a tamper-proof manner. The automated audit can verify the tool's configuration and the integrity of the audit-proof archive.

controls.title: Documentation of evidence acquisition (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evidence acquisition is not documented at all or only in the form of informal notes. A complete chain of custody cannot be proven.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The forensic analyst takes a few handwritten notes on a piece of paper that is later lost. It is not traceable who did what with the evidence and when.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the documentation of an evidence acquisition. The absence of formal logs confirms this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple log of the acquisition is kept, but it is often incomplete. Important information such as the tools used or exact times are sometimes missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple text template for a log exists, but it is not always filled out consistently. The documentation focuses on the acquisition itself, but not on the transport or storage of the evidence.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews existing logs and identifies gaps and inconsistencies. They check whether the documentation represents a complete chain of custody.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When evidence is forensically acquired, all steps performed SHOULD be documented. The documentation SHOULD provide a complete record of how the original evidence was handled. It SHOULD also be documented which methods were used and why those responsible chose them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized, detailed template for the evidence acquisition log and the chain of custody is used. Every step, from identifying the evidence to acquisition, transport, and storage, is logged with date, time, responsible person, and action performed. The justification for the choice of method is also recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the complete documentation (acquisition log, chain of custody form) for a case. They check the document for completeness and continuity from seizure to analysis. Particular attention is paid to the documentation of the choice of method and its justification.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evidence acquisition documentation is supplemented with photographs. Photos are taken of the system's state before acquisition, of the ports and tools used, and of the sealed evidence. The documentation is proofread and signed off by a second employee.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The forensic analyst uses a camera to visually document the acquisition process. The photos are timestamped and attached to the log as an appendix. The completed log is checked for plausibility and completeness by a colleague before archiving.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation and checks for the presence of supporting photographs. They verify the signature of the reviewer (four-eyes principle) on the document.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Documentation is performed digitally and automatically using a forensic case management or chain-of-custody tool. Every access and every action related to an item of evidence is automatically logged with a user and timestamp. The final reports are digitally signed and archived in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A software solution for forensic case management is used. Evidence items are labeled with barcodes, and every handover is recorded by scanning the barcode and the employee ID card. The software automatically generates complete chain-of-custody reports.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the case management system demonstrated. They track the lifecycle of an evidence item using the automated logs in the system. The automated audit can be performed by querying the system database to verify the completeness of the logging.

controls.title: Secure custody of original data carriers and evidence (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Original data carriers and evidence are stored insecurely, for example on a desk. There is no access control or logging.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A seized hard drive lies unsecured in the office for days, accessible to all employees and cleaning staff. The risk of loss, theft, or tampering is extremely high.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the location and method of storing evidence and determines that no dedicated, secure containers or rooms exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Evidence is stored in a lockable cabinet or room. However, there is no formal regulation as to who has access, and removals are not logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hard drive is placed in a file cabinet in the team office. Several people have a key to this cabinet. No log is kept when someone opens the cabinet or removes something.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the storage location. They ask for an access policy and a removal log, which will likely be missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All seized original data carriers SHOULD be physically stored in such a way that only investigating and specifically named employees can access them. When original data carriers and evidence are stored, it SHOULD be determined how long they are to be kept. After the period has expired, it SHOULD be checked whether the data carriers and evidence still need to be kept. After the retention period, evidence SHOULD be securely erased or destroyed, and original data carriers returned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Evidence is stored in a dedicated, access-controlled evidence cabinet or room. A list of authorized persons is maintained. Every deposit and removal is logged in an evidence log (physical or digital) with date, time, person, and reason. A concept for retention periods and secure destruction is created and implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the evidence room/cabinet and checks the access control mechanisms. They request the list of authorized persons and the evidence log and check it for completeness. They check the concept for storage and deletion.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evidence room is protected by additional security measures such as a burglar alarm system and video surveillance. Access is regulated and automatically logged via an electronic system with two-factor authentication. A certified service provider is commissioned for the destruction of data carriers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room meets enhanced physical security requirements. Access requires, for example, a chip card and a PIN. All access attempts (successful and failed) are logged centrally. For the destruction of hard drives, destruction logs from the service provider are archived.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the additional security measures (alarm, video). They check the logs of the electronic access control system. They request the destruction certificates for disposed evidence. The automated audit can be performed by querying the access logs of the locking system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of evidence is fully integrated into a digital case management system. Evidence items are equipped with barcodes or RFID tags. Every movement is automatically recorded. The system monitors retention periods and automatically generates notifications for the review or destruction of evidence. Regular inventories are carried out with system support.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized evidence management tool is used. When items are checked in and out, the RFID tags of the evidence and the employee ID are scanned. The system warns if an evidence item is not returned on time. An inventory is conducted once a quarter, during which all evidence items managed in the system are physically scanned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the evidence management system demonstrated. They observe the process of checking items in and out with RFID scanners. They request the report of the last system-supported inventory and compare it with the physical stock on a random basis.

controls.title: Framework agreements with external service providers (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Potential service providers have been identified and evaluated (as described in A3), but no firm contractual agreements exist. Commissioning in an emergency requires individual contract negotiation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a shortlist of qualified providers. In case of need, offers must be obtained, compared, and an individual contract must be drawn up, which costs valuable time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that a list of qualified service providers exists, but no framework agreements or retainers have been concluded. They check the process for individual commissioning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Framework agreements have been concluded with one or more forensics service providers, which regulate basic conditions such as hourly rates and confidentiality. However, guaranteed response times (SLAs) are not agreed upon or only on a 'best effort' basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a framework agreement reviewed by the legal department, which allows for a quick call-off of services when needed. However, the service provider gives no guarantee as to how quickly it can provide personnel.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the framework agreement and checks its contents. They determine that essential points are regulated, but binding SLAs for operational readiness are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD conclude call-off agreements or framework contracts (retainers) with forensic service providers so that IT security incidents can be investigated forensically more quickly. These contracts must define guaranteed response times (SLAs), fixed conditions, and clear processes for commissioning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A retainer contract is concluded with a specialized service provider. This guarantees, for example, a telephone response within one hour and the start of the analysis on-site or remotely within 24 hours. The process for activating the retainer is clearly described in the emergency plan and known to several people.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the signed retainer contract and checks the SLAs defined therein. They verify that the activation process is documented in the emergency plan and that the designated contact persons are aware of it. The automated audit can verify the validity of the contract in a contract management system.

controls.title: Definition of standard procedures for evidence collection (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general guide for evidence collection (as described in A5). However, this is not specifically tailored to systems with high protection requirements or widely used configurations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procedure for securing a standard client and a highly critical database server is identical and does not take into account the specific artifacts or requirements of the critical system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes that the general guide does not contain specific instructions for high-security systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For applications and IT systems with high protection requirements, as well as for common system configurations, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) SHOULD be created that allow for the most complete forensic collection of volatile and non-volatile data possible. These procedures are supported by detailed checklists and the provision of the necessary software tools on mobile data carriers and hardware such as write blockers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separate, detailed SOPs for evidence collection are created for the domain controller, the Exchange server, and the standard Windows 10 image. A forensic emergency kit is packed, containing USB sticks with all necessary tools (e.g., KAPE, Volatility) and a hardware write blocker. The processes are tested, but the implementation is still largely manual.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the specific SOPs for high-security systems and checks their level of detail. They inspect the contents of the forensic emergency kit. They check, using logs, whether these SOPs have been applied in exercises or real cases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system-specific standard procedures SHOULD be implemented through tested and, where possible, automated processes. These automated processes are supported by checklists and technical aids, e.g., by pre-configured software tools on mobile data carriers, scripts for the automatic collection of artifacts, and IT forensic hardware such as write blockers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An automation script (e.g., a PowerShell or Python script) is developed for each standard procedure. This script automatically collects the relevant volatile and non-volatile data (e.g., RAM image, important log files, prefetch files) in the correct order. The execution of the script can be done remotely via a management tool or locally from an emergency USB stick and automatically logs all steps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the execution of an automated collection script demonstrated on a test system. They check the source code of the script for correctness and completeness compared to the underlying SOP. They verify that the log generated by the script is complete and correct. The automated audit can perform a static code analysis of the scripts.

controls.title: Conducting evidence collection exercises (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are trained (as described in A6), but the acquired knowledge is not put into practice. Forensic collections are only carried out in an emergency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Theoretical knowledge is available, but there is a lack of practical experience and routine, which can lead to errors in the stress of a real incident. Although the training courses contain practical parts, there are no dedicated, recurring practice sessions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for logs of forensic exercises. The absence of such logs, although training has taken place, indicates this level of maturity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees involved in forensic analyses SHOULD train regularly, at least once a year, in the form of exercises on how to secure evidence in an IT security incident. The exercises include securing evidence on test systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual exercise plan is created. In the exercise, a test PC is prepared with simulated traces. The participants must independently carry out a forensic backup according to the applicable guidelines. The results and the procedure are then discussed and a report is created.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the exercise plan and the reports from the last exercise. They check whether all relevant employees participated and whether the exercise covered the essential steps of evidence preservation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evidence preservation exercises are integrated into complex, realistic scenarios such as Red/Blue Team exercises or Purple Teaming activities. The exercises test not only the technical skills but also the collaboration with other teams (crisis management team, IT operations) and external service providers under time pressure. The findings are directly incorporated into the improvement of processes and tools.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of an annual Red Team exercise, the Blue Team (including the forensic specialists) must uncover the Red Team's activities and perform forensic backups of compromised systems to understand the attack. The exercise is supervised by an external moderator, and the results are presented to management. A 'Lessons Learned' workshop leads to concrete improvement measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the final report and the 'Lessons Learned' documentation from the last Red/Blue Team exercise. They check what role forensics played in the exercise and whether the identified potential for improvement has been demonstrably addressed (e.g., by adapting an SOP or a script).

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
IT forensics is the strictly methodical data analysis on data carriers and in data networks to investigate security incidents in IT systems.

Forensically investigating IT security incidents is always necessary when damages incurred need to be determined, attacks need to be repelled, future attacks need to be prevented, and attackers need to be identified. The decision whether an IT security incident is investigated forensically is made while the incident is being handled. An IT forensic investigation in the sense of this module consists of the following phases:

• Strategic preparation: In this phase, processes are planned and established to ensure that an institution can forensically analyze IT security incidents. It is also necessary even if the institution has no in-house forensic expertise.

• Initialization: After the responsible employees have decided to forensically investigate an IT security incident, the previously planned processes are initiated. Furthermore, the scope of the investigation is defined and initial measures are carried out.

• Evidence preservation: Here, the evidence to be preserved is selected and the data is forensically secured. A distinction is made between live forensics and post-mortem forensics: Live forensics ensures that volatile data, such as network connections or RAM, is secured from a running IT system. In post-mortem forensics, on the other hand, forensic copies of data carriers are created.

• Analysis: The collected data is forensically analyzed. The data is considered both individually and in the overall context.

• Presentation of results: The relevant investigation results are prepared and communicated in a target-group-specific manner.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose:
The module outlines which precautionary measures are necessary to enable IT forensic investigations. It primarily focuses on how evidence preservation can be prepared and carried out.

If forensic service providers carry out evidence preservation in whole or in part, the requirements also apply to the service providers. Contractual agreements and audits can be used to ensure that the service providers also comply with them.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
Module DER.2.2 IT Forensics Preparation must be applied once to the entire information network.

This module deals with precautionary measures that are fundamental for subsequent IT forensic investigations.

Therefore, how the actual forensic analysis is conducted is not the subject of this module. It does not describe requirements to ensure that attacks are detected. These are contained in module DER.1 Detection of Security-Relevant Events and are a prerequisite for this module. Nor does it explain criteria and processes by which those responsible can decide whether or not an IT security incident needs to be forensically investigated. This decision is made while the security incident is being handled (see DER.2.1 Handling of Security Incidents).

Likewise, the module does not refer to IT forensic investigations in the case of criminal offenses.

Finally, the module also does not address how IT infrastructures can be cleaned up after they have been attacked (see DER.2.3 Remediation of Widespread Security Incidents). However, the activities described there can be significantly supported by the results of IT forensic investigations.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Violation of legal frameworks
parts.prose: For IT forensic investigations, all data deemed necessary is often copied, secured, and evaluated. This often includes personal data of employees or external partners. If this data is accessed, for example, without justification and without involving the Data Protection Officer, the institution violates legal regulations, for instance, by disregarding the principle of purpose limitation. It is also possible that the collected data could be used to infer how employees behave, or a connection to them could be established. This creates a risk of violating internal regulations as well.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Loss of evidence due to faulty or incomplete evidence preservation
parts.prose:
If evidence is secured incorrectly or not quickly enough, important data may be lost that cannot be restored later. In the worst-case scenario, this leads to an inconclusive forensic investigation. At the very least, however, the evidential value is diminished.

The risk of losing important evidence increases significantly when employees use forensic tools incorrectly, secure data too slowly, or have insufficient practice. Evidence is also often lost when those responsible fail to recognize and secure volatile data as relevant.

controls.title: Establishment of a steering committee

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After the discovery of a serious incident, a small group of IT staff is informally assembled to coordinate the response. However, this group lacks a formal mandate and overarching authority. Decisions are made ad hoc and reactively, mostly only for the immediately affected systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In practice, this often means that the head of the IT department calls together a few experienced administrators. Communication takes place over existing, potentially compromised channels. There is no formal documentation of decisions or assigned tasks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether there was a designated responsible person or group at all. Through interviews, it is determined whether the group had the necessary authority to act across departments, which is typically not the case at this maturity level. No reports or formal mandates are expected as proof.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A team is designated to be responsible for coordinating the remediation. Although the responsibilities are generally clarified, the authority to issue directives is limited to the IT department. a basic plan for the remediation is created but not formally coordinated with all relevant stakeholders (e.g., management, business departments).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A team leader is appointed. The tasks are distributed within the IT team. A shared folder is created for documents, but there is no structured reporting to a higher authority. Forensic service providers are called in when needed but are not permanently integrated into the committee.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the composition of the response team shown to them. It is checked whether there is a basic understanding of the division of tasks. It is expected that basic planning documents (e.g., a task list) exist, even if they have not been formally approved.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To remediate an APT incident, a steering committee MUST be established to plan, coordinate, and monitor all necessary activities. The committee MUST be granted all the authority necessary for the tasks. If specialized forensic service providers have already been brought in, they SHOULD also be involved in the remediation of the incident. If IT is too heavily compromised, it SHOULD be considered whether a crisis management team should be established. In this case, the steering committee MUST monitor the remediation measures and report to the crisis management team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The steering committee is formally appointed by the management and receives a written mandate. The committee typically includes the IT manager, the information security officer (ISO), and representatives from the most important business departments. If necessary, external experts (forensics, legal, PR) are permanently involved. The reporting lines to a potential crisis management team are clearly defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a formally appointed steering committee by reviewing the appointment document or the management's meeting minutes. The composition of the committee is checked for appropriateness. Interviews and a review of minutes are used to demonstrate that the committee is actively performing its planning, coordination, and monitoring tasks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The steering committee operates based on a predefined and regularly practiced incident response plan. Roles, responsibilities, and escalation paths are clearly documented and known to all members. The committee includes representatives from IT, security, legal, HR, and communications by default. Collaboration with external service providers and authorities is regulated by contracts and processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed 'Major Incident Management Plan' is activated. The committee uses a dedicated and secure communication platform for coordination. Regular status reports are created using a fixed template. The decision-making processes are documented and based on a predefined risk matrix.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the 'Major Incident Management Plan' and the minutes of previous exercises or incidents. It is checked whether the roles defined in the plan are filled and the escalation paths are functional. Interviews are used to verify the members' familiarity with their tasks and the processes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A permanent, highly trained Crisis Response Team (CRT), which constitutes the steering committee, is established. This team has pre-approved emergency budgets and extensive executive powers to act without delay. The effectiveness of the team and processes is continuously measured and improved through complex simulations (e.g., Red Team exercises) and the analysis of past incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CRT uses a dedicated, hardened, and independent infrastructure for management and communication ('dark network'). The decision-making processes are supported by playbooks and automation to minimize response time. Integration with threat intelligence feeds enables proactive planning for likely attack scenarios.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and operational readiness of the independent infrastructure. Evidence is requested for the regular execution and evaluation of complex exercises. The existence of predefined playbooks and evidence of their application in exercises or real incidents are verified. It is checked whether a process for continuous improvement (Lessons Learned) is established and demonstrably implemented.

controls.title: Decision on a remediation strategy

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The remediation is reactive and without an overarching strategy. An attempt is made to remove the found malware on the obviously infected systems with antivirus tools. Backups are restored without prior checking for integrity or compromise.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator runs a virus scan on the affected server. If the scanner finds something, it is deleted. Then the last available backup is restored to recover lost data. The possibility that the attacker is still in the network in other ways is not systematically considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and review of ticket logs that the measures were limited to the mere removal of malware. No strategy document or a record of a decision-making process can be presented. The backup logs show a restore without documented prior forensic examination.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic strategy is established, which typically involves reinstalling the systems that have been identified as certainly compromised. However, a comprehensive forensic analysis to determine the full scope of the attack is only superficially performed. The decision is made by the IT department without formal approval from a steering committee.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT administrators identify the compromised systems based on alarms from the SIEM or antivirus system. These systems are taken offline and reinstalled from a standard image. Backups are subjected to a superficial check (e.g., virus scan) before restoration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the list of reinstalled systems. Through interviews, it is determined on what basis the decision to reinstall was made. It is established that the decision was not based on an in-depth forensic analysis and was not formally approved by an authorized committee.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before an APT incident is actually remediated, the steering committee MUST define a remediation strategy. The basis for these decisions MUST be the results of a previously conducted forensic investigation. In particular, it MUST be decided whether to remove the malware, reinstall IT systems, or replace them, including hardware. All affected IT systems SHOULD be reinstalled. However, before backups are restored, forensic investigations MUST ensure that no manipulated data or programs are transferred. If a reinstallation is waived, the IT systems MUST be specifically monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The steering committee receives a comprehensive report from forensics. On this basis, a strategy paper is created that defines the procedure (e.g., reinstallation of all clients in segment X, replacement of servers Y and Z) and the sequence. Forensic service providers or specialized internal staff are commissioned to check backups. The strategy is formally adopted and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the forensic investigation report and the resulting, formally adopted remediation strategy document. It is checked whether the decisions in the document are plausibly based on the forensic findings. In addition, evidence of the forensic examination of the backups before restoration is requested (e.g., test report from the service provider).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The remediation strategy is developed based on a formal risk analysis of various options (e.g., clean vs. reinstall vs. replace). The decision considers not only technical aspects but also business risks and recovery times. The strategy includes a detailed plan for post-remediation monitoring with specific indicators (IOCs) derived from forensics.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each option, costs, downtime, and residual risks are assessed and documented. The decision is submitted to management for approval. The necessary rules for SIEM, EDR, and network sensors for post-remediation monitoring are developed and tested before operations resume.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the risk analysis and the various assessed courses of action. It is verified that the final decision has been documented and approved by the responsible authority (e.g., management). Furthermore, the existence and quality of the post-remediation monitoring concept are examined.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decision on the remediation strategy is supported by predefined playbooks based on the protection requirements of the affected systems. For highly critical areas, a 'scorched earth' strategy (complete replacement of hardware and software) is planned by default. The impact of various strategies on business operations is simulated in advance to determine the optimal course of action.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Configuration Management Database (CMDB) automatically provides information about system dependencies and criticality. The strategy is selected according to a predefined decision tree anchored in the crisis plan. The systems required for the new installation are procured via a secure, accelerated procurement process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and application of playbooks for the strategy decision. It is checked whether the criticality assessment of the systems from the CMDB has been incorporated into the decision. Evidence of simulations or drills that test these decision-making processes is requested.

controls.title: Isolation of the affected network segments

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Individual systems identified as compromised are manually disconnected from the network by unplugging the network cable. There is no systematic isolation of entire network segments.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator goes to the server room or workstation and physically unplugs the network cable of the affected device. This is done reactively after an alert has occurred. The possibility that the attacker has already moved to other systems in the same subnet is not considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Based on incident tickets and interviews, the auditor determines that the response was limited to disconnecting individual systems. There is no evidence of coordinated, segment-wide isolation. Network diagrams show that the rest of the segment remained online and unprotected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The affected network segments are isolated by manually configuring Access Control Lists (ACLs) on central routers or firewalls. The isolation is done step-by-step and not simultaneously, which potentially gives attackers time to react. Unknown or undocumented internet access points are often overlooked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A network administrator logs into the core firewall and adds rules to block traffic from the affected VLAN to the rest of the network and the internet. This process is then repeated for the next affected VLAN. A complete, up-to-date list of all network egress points does not exist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration changes on firewalls and routers at the time of the incident. Timestamps show that the isolation was sequential and not simultaneous. Interviews and a review of the network documentation reveal that no procedure existed to identify shadow IT internet access points.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network segments affected by an APT incident MUST be completely isolated (cut off), especially from the internet. To effectively lock out the attackers, the network segments MUST be isolated all at once. The scope of the segments to be isolated MUST be determined beforehand by a forensic analysis, whereby all suspicious and even only theoretically infected network segments MUST be included. All local internet connections MUST be identified and taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on the forensics report, a list of segments to be isolated (e.g., VLAN IDs) is created. In a prepared telephone or video conference, the network and firewall administrators coordinate to activate the prepared configuration changes on all relevant switches, routers, and firewalls at the exact same time. An inventory of all known internet gateways is used to verify completeness.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the list of isolated segments with the recommendations from the forensics report. By analyzing configuration backups and log files of the network components, it is verified that the isolation of all affected segments occurred synchronously ('all at once'). Evidence is requested on how the organization ensures it knows and considers all internet access points, including shadow IT.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The isolation of network segments is partially automated through prepared scripts or the use of a Network Access Control (NAC) solution. The network documentation is up-to-date and is used to validate the scope of isolation. At the same time, a secure, isolated 'rescue network' is activated for the response team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central script is executed that logs in via SSH/API to all relevant network devices and applies the isolation rules. Alternatively, in the NAC system, the affected segments are moved to a quarantine policy. A separate, predefined VLAN with filtered internet access is available for analysis and remediation work.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the scripts or the NAC configuration for emergency isolation demonstrated. The existence and test evidence for the 'rescue network' are checked. The quality of the network documentation (e.g., from a CMDB) is assessed, and it is verified that it was used for planning the measure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network isolation can be triggered at the push of a button or even automatically by a Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) system, based on highly-validated threat intelligence. The micro-segmentation of the network allows for very granular and precise isolation down to the workload level. The process is fully automated, regularly tested in drills, and its successful execution is automatically verified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A high-priority alert in the SIEM, indicating APT activity, triggers a SOAR playbook. This playbook identifies the affected systems and segments via the CMDB connection and instructs the firewall management console and the SDN controllers to isolate the corresponding zones in real-time. A subsequent task checks reachability and confirms the successful isolation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the SOAR system and the corresponding playbooks. Logs from automatic isolation procedures (from tests or real incidents) are analyzed. The micro-segmentation architecture is reviewed, and it is checked whether the automation is capable of performing and verifying the isolation completely and correctly.

controls.title: Blocking and changing of access credentials and cryptographic keys

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the passwords of known administrators are changed. Passwords of regular users, service accounts, or system accounts are not considered. Cryptographic keys are not changed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The domain administrators reset their own passwords. There is no systematic approach to identify and reset all privileged accounts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the directory service log files for password changes at the time of the incident. The analysis shows that only a small subset of accounts (typically admins) was affected. No evidence can be provided for the rotation of keys or service account passwords.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All passwords of human users (administrators and standard users) are reset. However, service accounts and hard-coded credentials in applications are largely overlooked. No replacement of TLS certificates or other keys takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In Active Directory, the 'User must change password at next logon' option is set for all user accounts. A manual list of service accounts is gone through, but it is incomplete.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that all human user accounts were forced to reset their passwords. Through interviews and random checks of applications, it is determined that service accounts and other secrets were not systematically changed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All access credentials MUST be changed after the network has been isolated. Centrally managed credentials (e.g., in Active Directory) MUST be reset. If the central authentication server is compromised, all existing access credentials on it MUST be blocked and their passwords changed. If TLS keys or an internal CA were compromised, corresponding keys, certificates, and infrastructures MUST be regenerated, and the compromised artifacts MUST be reliably blocked and revoked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script is prepared that systematically goes through all user and computer accounts in AD and resets the passwords. An inventory list of all service accounts is used to change their passwords manually or in a semi-automated way. If the Domain Controller was compromised, the KRBTGT account is reset twice. A checklist for the replacement and revocation of CA and TLS certificates is processed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests evidence (e.g., scripts, log excerpts, documentation) for the complete change of all credentials, including service and computer accounts. It is checked whether the KRBTGT password was changed correctly (twice) in the event of an AD compromise. The certificate revocation lists (CRLs/OCSP) are checked to verify the successful revocation of compromised certificates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for resetting all credentials is largely automated and includes all types of secrets, including API keys, SSH keys, and passwords stored in configurations. The process is documented and regularly practiced. A dedicated Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is used to efficiently manage the exchange and distribution of new certificates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central secret manager (e.g., HashiCorp Vault) is used to automate the rotation of most credentials. Special emergency scripts are maintained for Active Directory. The replacement of the PKI infrastructure follows a documented emergency plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the automation tools (e.g., secret manager, scripts) demonstrated. The emergency plans for password rotation and PKI replacement are reviewed. Logs from exercises are requested to prove that the process is mastered and complete.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The rotation of all credentials and cryptographic keys across the entire information network is fully automated and can be triggered within minutes. The process is integrated into the SOAR platform. Short-lived, dynamically generated certificates and credentials are used to drastically reduce the window of opportunity for their misuse.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The entire infrastructure (applications, systems, network devices) dynamically retrieves its secrets from a central secret manager. An emergency trigger in the SOAR system initiates an enterprise-wide rotation of all secrets. For authentication, methods that do not rely on long-lived passwords (e.g., FIDO2) are primarily used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the architecture of the dynamic secret management. The capability for enterprise-wide, automated rotation is demonstrated by triggering it in a test environment or by analyzing logs from a real event. The extent to which long-lived passwords are avoided in favor of more modern authentication methods is checked. The automation can be verified by running `terraform plan` or similar tools.

controls.title: Closing the initial point of compromise

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On the system where the initial compromise occurred, the specific vulnerability is remediated, e.g., by installing a single patch. A systemic search for the same vulnerability on other systems is not performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrator identifies that the attack occurred via an outdated Apache version on a web server. He updates Apache on this one server. Other web servers in the organization are not checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor confirms the installation of the patch on the initially compromised system. However, a random check of other, similar systems (or by reviewing vulnerability scan reports) reveals that the same vulnerability still exists elsewhere.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The identified technical vulnerability is remediated on all known systems in the network. If the entry point was a phishing email, a general warning email is sent to all employees to raise their awareness of the issue.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After the vulnerability has been identified, a vulnerability scan is performed across the entire network to find all affected systems. These are then patched. In the case of phishing, an email drafted by the IT department is sent to the 'All Employees' distribution list.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies by reviewing patch management reports or scan results that the vulnerability has been closed throughout the company. The existence of the sent warning email is checked. It is noted that no further procedural or technical measures have been taken.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If a forensic investigation reveals that attackers penetrated through a technical vulnerability, this vulnerability MUST be closed. If the attackers were able to compromise the IT systems through human error, organizational, personnel, and technical measures MUST be taken to prevent similar incidents in the future.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Closing the vulnerability is treated with the highest priority in the patch management process and is tracked. In the case of human error (e.g., successful phishing), a root cause analysis is performed. The resulting measures could include adjusting email filter rules, targeted training for the affected employee group, and revising the corresponding policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the identified point of compromise in the forensics report. Subsequently, evidence of the derived and implemented measures is requested. This can be a report from the patch management system, the changed configuration of the email gateway, training materials, or an updated policy. It is checked whether the measures address the root cause.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive root cause analysis is conducted to identify not only the immediate vulnerability but also the underlying procedural deficiencies. In addition to closing the point of compromise, compensating controls are implemented to make similar attacks more difficult in the future (Defense in Depth).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If the point of compromise was a vulnerability in a web application, it is not only patched, but a Web Application Firewall (WAF) is also configured with virtual patches. If the cause was a weak patch management process, this process is revised and secured with additional controls (e.g., compliance scans). In the case of phishing, targeted phishing simulations are conducted for the affected target group.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the root cause analysis report. It is checked whether the analysis goes beyond the technical cause and also examines organizational aspects. The implementation of the compensating controls (e.g., WAF rules, new process description, results of the phishing simulation) is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The findings from the incident are used to systemically improve the entire security architecture. Instead of just fixing a single class of vulnerabilities, entire technology stacks or architectures are rethought and hardened (e.g., by introducing application whitelisting or browser isolation). The 'Lessons Learned' process is formalized, and the results are demonstrably integrated into strategic security planning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After a phishing incident, not only is the mail filter improved, but a browser isolation technology is introduced that forces the rendering of potentially malicious websites in a secure sandbox. After a compromised server application, a general application control concept is rolled out for all servers. The results are documented in the ISMS and lead to new security goals for the following year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor looks for evidence of a strategic, architectural response to the incident. This can include architectural documents, project plans for the introduction of new security technologies, or adapted security strategies and goals in the ISMS. It is verified that a formal 'Lessons Learned' process exists and that its results are tracked and implemented.

controls.title: Return to production operation

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Systems are brought back online as quickly as possible once they are considered 'clean.' Temporarily installed analysis tools or emergency accounts are often left on the systems. There is no orderly archiving or deletion of evidence.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As soon as a server is reinstalled, it is immediately reconnected to the production network. The EDR software or additional logging scripts installed during the analysis are not removed. Removed hard drives are stored unsorted in a cabinet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During a random check of the recommissioned systems, the auditor finds that non-standard software (analysis tools) and configurations (emergency accounts) are still present. No proof of secure deletion or documented archiving of evidence can be provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The systems are put back into operation according to a simple plan. An attempt is made to remove most of the temporary analysis tools. Decommissioned systems and evidence are collected and stored, but without formal documentation or secure storage.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a checklist for recommissioning. One item on it is 'Remove Tools'. The removed hard drives are labeled and stored in a locked room. The temporary communication channels (e.g., a WhatsApp group) are simply no longer used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the checklist for recommissioning. It is noted that the processes are fundamentally in place but not formalized. The storage of the evidence is inspected and assessed as being present, but not meeting forensic requirements (e.g., chain of custody).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After the network has been successfully cleaned, the IT systems MUST be returned to production operation in an orderly manner. All previously used IT systems and installed programs for analysis MUST be removed or consciously transferred to production operation. The same MUST be done with temporary communication and collaboration systems. Evidence and decommissioned IT systems MUST either be securely deleted or destroyed, or be suitably archived.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The recommissioning follows a detailed restart plan created in advance. For each system, it is checked whether the temporary tools have been removed. Temporary cloud tenants or communication platforms are specifically deleted after a data backup. For evidence, there is a defined process: either they are transferred to an evidence storage with a documented chain of custody, or they are verifiably deleted with certified tools.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the restart plan and randomly checks its implementation. Evidence of the de-provisioning of the temporary systems (e.g., screenshots from the admin portal, cancellation confirmations) is requested. For the evidence, either the chain of custody protocol or the deletion certificate is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The return to production is controlled by a formal 'Return to Service' plan. After recommissioning, the system state is verified against a known good configuration baseline. A formal post-incident review meeting is mandatory to draw lessons from the incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The restart plan contains explicit verification steps where the configuration of the returned systems (e.g., firewall rules, user accounts, installed software) is compared with a predefined target state. The post-incident review is documented, and the resulting measures are tracked in a ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the 'Return to Service' plan and the evidence of the configuration verification (e.g., reports from configuration management tools). The minutes of the post-incident review meeting are requested and it is checked whether the identified improvement measures are subject to a tracking process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The return to production is a fully automated process based on Infrastructure as Code (IaC). Systems are not cleaned, but consistently rebuilt from code ('Immutable Infrastructure'). The archiving and destruction of evidence is carried out by a specialized, audited service provider to fully meet compliance requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The affected environment is decommissioned. A new, identical environment is built in a clean segment by running Terraform or Ansible scripts. The old hard disk images and physical devices are handed over to a certified partner who handles the forensically correct archiving or data protection-compliant destruction and confirms this with a certificate.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the IaC scripts and the deployment pipeline to verify the automated recovery process. The contracts and certificates of the service provider for data destruction and archiving are reviewed. The entire process from decommissioning to recovery can be seamlessly traced using logs from the automation tools.

controls.title: Targeted System Hardening

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After an APT attack, all affected IT systems SHOULD be hardened. This SHOULD be based on the results of the forensic investigations. Additionally, it SHOULD be re-verified whether the affected environment is still secure. Measures that cannot be implemented in the short term SHOULD be included in an action plan and implemented in the medium term. The ISO SHOULD create and review the plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on the attack techniques (TTPs) uncovered in the forensic report, a list of hardening measures is created. Examples include: disabling PowerShell for standard users, tightening macro settings, and implementing LAPS. These measures are documented in a plan with responsibilities and deadlines and are tracked by the ISO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the action plan for system hardening. It is checked whether the measures are plausibly derived from the findings of the forensic report. The implementation status of the plan is verified by inspecting the tracking system (e.g., Jira, Excel list) and by random technical checks of the implemented hardening measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: System hardening is not just reactive but is based on a recognized hardening standard (e.g., CIS Benchmarks, BSI recommendations), which is enriched with specific findings from the incident. The implementation of hardening measures is checked through regular configuration and compliance audits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The existing configuration baselines for servers and clients are compared with the CIS Benchmarks and supplemented with specific measures learned from the incident. These new baselines are distributed via Group Policies (GPOs) or a configuration management tool. A vulnerability scanner is used to regularly check compliance with these baselines.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the hardening baselines and compares them with a recognized standard. Reports from compliance scans are requested to verify the comprehensive implementation and monitoring of the hardening. Deviations from the baseline must be handled in a documented exception procedure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: System hardening is fully managed and enforced via a central configuration management system (e.g., Ansible, Puppet, DSC). Deviations from the desired state are automatically detected and either immediately corrected or trigger a high-priority alarm. The hardening baseline is a 'living' document that is continuously updated based on new threat intelligence and internal tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every system on the network is managed by a configuration management agent. The hardening configuration is declared as code (e.g., in a Git repository). Changes to the hardening policy go through a review and test process before being deployed to production. The system is in 'Enforce' mode, i.e., it automatically corrects configuration drift.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the hardening policies ('Configuration as Code') stored in the configuration management system. The configuration of the system itself is checked to ensure that it is operating in 'Enforce' mode. System logs are analyzed to provide evidence of automatic corrections or alarms in case of deviations. A `git log` for the policy files can demonstrate the process of continuous improvement.

controls.title: Establishment of secure, independent communication channels

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure communication channels SHOULD be established for the management board and the employees tasked with the cleanup. These channels MUST be independent of the potentially compromised corporate network. If third-party communication services are used, care SHOULD also be taken to select a secure communication channel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For crisis communication, a dedicated, newly set up tenant of a trusted cloud collaboration service (e.g., Microsoft Teams, Slack) is used. Access is via private devices or newly acquired laptops connected via a separate internet connection (e.g., mobile hotspots). The choice of service is briefly documented and justified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the concept for emergency communication explained. It is checked whether the chosen channel is logically and physically separated from the compromised network. The security features of the chosen service (e.g., end-to-end encryption) are evaluated, and it is checked whether a conscious selection decision was documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Pre-acquired and prepared emergency devices (laptops, smartphones) with hardened images are kept ready for the crisis team. These devices are configured for use with a predefined, secure, and independent communication channel. The process for activating this emergency communication is documented and regularly practiced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A case with 'crisis laptops' is stored in a fireproof safe. These have a minimal, hardened operating system and are only configured for access to a specific, pre-evaluated, and secured collaboration platform. The internet connection is established exclusively via integrated LTE modules. The crisis plan describes who receives the laptops and how they are put into operation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor physically inspects the emergency devices. The device image is checked for hardening features. The documentation in the crisis plan is analyzed, and logs from exercises in which the commissioning of emergency communication was tested are requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organization operates a permanently available, physically and logically completely separate emergency infrastructure ('dark network') for crisis management. This infrastructure includes dedicated servers, network components, workstations, and communication systems. Access requires strong two-factor authentication with hardware tokens. The functionality of this infrastructure is continuously monitored and regularly tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An autonomous IT environment exists in a separate fire compartment or at another location. This is connected to the internet via a dedicated line that is switched off during normal operation. In a crisis, this line is activated. The crisis members authenticate themselves with their personal smart cards or FIDO2 keys to access the platform.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the emergency infrastructure and has its architecture and functionality demonstrated. The physical and logical separation from the production network is verified. The configuration of the strong authentication is checked. Logs of the continuous monitoring and the latest tests (e.g., starting up the environment) are requested.

controls.title: Hardware replacement of affected IT systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be considered to completely replace the hardware after an APT incident. In particular, if suspicious behavior is still observed on individual IT systems after a cleanup, the affected IT systems SHOULD be replaced. The decision on this is made on a risk basis by the management board.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If a server continues to attempt to establish suspicious connections after being reinstalled, this indicates possible firmware or hardware manipulation. In this case, a decision is made by the management board to physically replace this specific server based on an ad-hoc risk assessment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the minutes of the management board to determine whether the option of hardware replacement was discussed and decided upon in response to persistent anomalies. It is checked whether the decision was comprehensibly justified (e.g., by log files proving the suspicious behavior).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a formal policy that defines the conditions for a mandatory hardware replacement. This applies by default to all systems in zones classified as highly critical or systems that process certain types of data. The process for procuring replacement hardware through a trusted supply chain is defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The incident response policy states that, for example, all domain controllers and PKI servers must be physically replaced after a compromise of the core network. There are framework agreements with 2-3 suppliers that guarantee fast and secure delivery of replacement devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the corresponding policy and checks its scope of application and clarity. The contracts with the hardware suppliers are inspected to verify the regulations on the secure supply chain. In a past incident, it is checked whether the policy was consistently applied.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A 'scorched earth' policy is established by default for all network segments identified as compromised. All hardware (servers, clients, network devices, printers, etc.) in these segments is replaced without further analysis. The newly procured hardware undergoes a hardware-level integrity check (e.g., 'Secure Boot' baseline) before commissioning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The crisis plan contains a 'Scorched Earth' playbook. This is activated and triggers a predefined process for the rapid procurement, delivery, and commissioning of complete segment hardware. The new devices are checked with a tool before being connected to the network, which verifies the firmware signatures and the Secure Boot configuration against a manufacturer baseline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and level of detail of the 'Scorched Earth' playbook. Evidence of the capability for rapid procurement (e.g., warehousing, emergency contracts) is requested. The process and tools for the integrity check of the new hardware are demonstrated and evaluated for their effectiveness.

controls.title: Modifications to make a new attack by the same attackers more difficult

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: So that the same attackers cannot carry out another APT attack, the internal structure of the network environment SHOULD be changed. This can include changes to network segmentation, naming schemes, or the software used. In addition, mechanisms SHOULD be established to quickly detect recurring attackers, e.g., through specific SIEM rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After cleanup, the VLAN structure is revised, the IP address ranges are changed, and the naming convention for servers and administrator accounts is adapted. Based on the indicators from the forensic report, specific correlation rules are created in the SIEM to raise an alarm if the attacker's known tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) reappear.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the network and architecture plans from before and after the incident to identify significant changes. The new SIEM rules are reviewed for their specificity and relevance to the past attack. It is checked whether these rules have been tested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Major architectural changes are made to render the attacker's knowledge of the environment useless. This includes implementing a tiering model (e.g., ESAE for Active Directory) and further micro-segmentation. Additionally, deception technology tailored to the attacker's TTPs is actively used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Active Directory structure is rebuilt according to the 'Enhanced Security Administrative Environment' model to isolate administrative accounts. The network is segmented more granularly, so that, for example, clients can no longer communicate directly with each other. Honeypots and honey tokens (e.g., fake admin accounts, database connection strings) are placed, which immediately trigger a high-priority alarm if touched by an attacker.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is briefed on the new AD and network architecture and checks it for compliance with the mentioned models (ESAE, micro-segmentation). The configuration of the deception technology is reviewed and it is verified that its alarms are correctly received in the SIEM and classified as high-criticality.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire IT architecture is fundamentally redesigned according to Zero Trust principles. Every access is explicitly verified regardless of location ('never trust, always verify'). An internal threat hunting team proactively searches for signs of a new compromise, using hypotheses based on the TTPs of the previous attacker as a foundation. The detection mechanisms are enhanced with user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA) and machine learning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Identity and Access Management (IAM) system combined with a Conditional Access Policy Engine becomes the central control point. Access to an application is only granted if the user, device, location, and context are deemed trustworthy. The threat hunting team continuously analyzes telemetry data from endpoints and the network. A UEBA system learns normal behavior and reports significant deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the Zero Trust architecture and the configuration of the Conditional Access Policies. Reports and playbooks from the threat hunting team are reviewed to verify their proactive approach. The effectiveness of the UEBA system is assessed based on test cases or real alarms. It is checked whether the 'assume breach' principle guides the new security strategy.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) are targeted cyber attacks on selected institutions and facilities. Attackers gain persistent access to a network and extend this access to other IT systems. The attacks are characterized by a very high investment of resources and extensive technical capabilities on the part of the attackers. Attacks of this kind are generally difficult to detect.
After an APT attack is discovered, those responsible in the affected institutions face major challenges. They must carry out a cleanup that goes beyond the usual procedure for handling IT security incidents. It must be assumed that the discovered attackers have had access to the affected IT infrastructure for a considerable time. In addition, they use complex attack tools to bypass standard security mechanisms and establish various backdoors. There is also the risk that the attackers are closely monitoring the infected environment and will react to cleanup attempts by covering their tracks and sabotaging the investigation.
This module assumes a high threat level from a targeted attack by highly motivated individuals with above-average resources. In practice, it is common for (certified) forensic services to be called in for such an incident if the institution itself does not have the appropriate forensic expertise. Forensic service providers are already brought in during the forensic analysis phase. However, the service providers are also involved in the cleanup, at least in an advisory capacity.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module describes how an institution should proceed to clean up the IT systems after an APT attack and restore the information network to its normal, secure operating state.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The DER.2.3 Remediation of Major Security Incidents module should always be applied when IT systems need to be cleaned up after an APT incident in order to restore the normal and secure operating state of an information network. The module should be applied to the information network.
An information network can only be cleaned up if the APT incident has been successfully detected and forensically analyzed beforehand. However, detection and forensics are not the subject of this module. These topics are covered in the DER.1 Detection of Security-Relevant Events and DER.2.2 Preparation for IT Forensics modules, respectively.
This module deals exclusively with the remediation of APT incidents. Other incidents are dealt with in the DER.2.1 Handling of Security Incidents module. The module also does not describe how to derive so-called Indicators of Compromise (IOCs), i.e., traces of a breach, and how they can be used to detect recurring attackers. Likewise, it does not address how to find any backdoors that may have been overlooked during the analysis and remediation.
Only cyber attacks are considered. This means that attacks used to gain physical access to the information network, for example, are not considered. Thus, forms of attack in which data centers are broken into, administrators are bribed, newly acquired hardware is intercepted and manipulated, or electromagnetic radiation is eavesdropped on are not considered in this module.
If forensic service providers clean up the IT systems in whole or in part, the requirements of this module also apply to these service providers. Contractual agreements and audits can be used to ensure that the service providers also adhere to them (see OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing).

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Incomplete cleanup
parts.prose: APT attackers usually want to permanently infiltrate an information network. They have the necessary resources and are able to carry out long-term attack campaigns. To do this, they use tools and methods that are tailored to their attack target. Even if an APT incident is discovered, it cannot be assumed that all of the attackers' access routes have been found, all infections and communication channels of malware have been eliminated, and all backdoors have been removed. In the case of incomplete remediation, however, it is very likely that attackers will regain access to the IT systems at a later point in time, e.g., after a longer period of inactivity, and expand their access again. They can do this, for example, by placing backdoors not only in operating systems and application software, but also by manipulating hardware-related components such as firmware. Such modifications are very difficult to identify and the necessary knowledge to extract and analyze them is not widespread. If those responsible try to clean up the IT components, e.g., by overwriting or updating the firmware, it can still happen that the attackers have also modified the update routines. In this way, they can then regain access to the IT systems.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Destruction of traces
