parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPO configuration for Application Guard on the clients. It is tested whether opening an email attachment starts the Application Guard environment. The policies for data transfer between the container and host are reviewed.

controls.title: Protection against subsequent modification of documents (S) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users are instructed to save and distribute final versions of important documents in PDF format to make unintentional changes more difficult. No other technical protective measures are applied.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This procedure is described as 'best practice' on the intranet or is communicated orally. The creation of PDFs is done with standard settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks users about their procedure for finalizing documents. It is checked whether a corresponding instruction exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Depending on the intended use, documents SHOULD be adequately protected against subsequent modification. Users are trained in the application of the available protection functions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users are trained to use the integrated Office functions according to requirements: 'Mark as Final' for a notification, 'Restrict Editing' with password protection for stronger protection, or saving as a PDF with set security settings (e.g., prohibiting changes). The choice of method is based on documented use cases (e.g., contracts, reports).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the training materials on document protection functions. It is checked on a random basis whether finalized documents (e.g., in the document management system) are provided with appropriate protection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For documents whose integrity and authenticity must be proven, digital signatures are used consistently. The process for finalization and signing is standardized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users who create corresponding documents (e.g., official offers, approvals) are provided with personal or departmental signature certificates. There is a clear instruction on which document types must be digitally signed. The signing process is integrated into the workflows.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the process for issuing and managing signature certificates. It is checked whether the policy for the signature obligation exists and is implemented. Signed documents are checked on a random basis for the validity of the signature and the certificate.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All official documents are stored in a document management system (DMS) or archive system that ensures immutable, revision-proof storage. Each version of a document is logged and cannot be changed unnoticed. Access protection is enforced by the DMS.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A certified DMS for revision-proof archiving is in use. Workflows ensure that finalized documents are automatically transferred to the archive and provided with the appropriate metadata and permissions. Direct access to the file system level of the archive is highly restricted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the certificate and the configuration of the DMS. The workflow for archiving documents is checked. An attempt is made to illicitly modify an archived document to test the effectiveness of the protection.

controls.title: Use of encryption and digital signatures (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For data with increased protection needs, the integrated document encryption of Office products with password protection is used. Users are instructed to use strong passwords and manage them securely.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy specifies which types of information must be encrypted. Users are trained on how to activate password-based encryption in Word, Excel, etc. There are requirements for the complexity of the passwords to be used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy for data classification and encryption. It is checked whether users are trained. Files classified as requiring protection are checked on a random basis to see if they are encrypted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data with high protection needs SHOULD only be stored or transmitted in encrypted form. Before an integrated encryption method is used, its strength SHOULD be checked. Additionally, a procedure for digital signatures for macros and documents SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The strength of the standard Office encryption (e.g., AES-256) is assessed as sufficient and its use is enforced via GPO. A rights management solution (e.g., Azure Information Protection/Microsoft Purview Information Protection) is used for the encryption and protection of documents. This enables certificate-based encryption and fine-grained rights assignment (e.g., 'do not print'), which persists even after the document has been sent. Digital signatures are mandatory for defined document types (e.g., contracts, approvals).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPO settings for encryption strength. The configuration of the rights management solution, especially the protection templates and permissions, is checked. A document classified as requiring protection is examined to see if the protective measures (encryption, rights) are correctly applied. The policies and implementation for digital signatures are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The encryption of documents with high protection needs is performed automatically, based on content analysis and/or manual classification by the user. Key management is centralized, and a secure process exists for data recovery in case of key loss.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The rights management solution is configured to automatically encrypt documents when certain keywords (e.g., 'Social Security Number', 'project codename') or patterns are detected. The classification and its associated protection are enforced when the document is created. A key escrow mechanism is implemented, and the recovery process is documented and regularly tested.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the automatic classification and encryption rules. A test document with sensitive test data is created to verify that the protection is applied automatically. The key recovery process and logs are reviewed and evaluated.

controls.title: Integrity check of documents (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For important documents, hash values (checksums) are manually generated upon finalization and stored in a secure location along with the document. If necessary, the hash value can be recalculated and compared to detect changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented instruction for key users on how to use a provided tool (e.g., 7-Zip, PowerShell command Get-FileHash) to create a SHA-256 hash value of a file and store it in a separate text file in the same directory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the instruction for hash value generation. For important documents, a random check is performed to see if a corresponding hash value file exists and if the value it contains matches the currently calculated hash value of the document.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When data with high protection needs is stored or transmitted, appropriate integrity checking methods SHOULD be used. If data needs to be protected from manipulation, cryptographic methods SHOULD also be used. For documents whose integrity is business-critical, digital signatures are consistently used, as they ensure both integrity and the authenticity of the signer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process for using digital signatures is established. Users who handle critical documents (e.g., financial reports, contracts) are provided with signature certificates from a trusted PKI. It is required by policy that these documents must be digitally signed before distribution or archiving. Office applications are configured to automatically validate signatures and warn the user of invalid signatures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the policy for applying digital signatures. The certificate issuance process is checked. A random sample of critical documents is checked to see if they bear a valid digital signature from an authorized signer. It is tested how the application reacts to a document with a broken signature.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All documents on central file servers are continuously monitored by a File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) system. The FIM system creates a cryptographic baseline of all files and alerts in real-time to any unauthorized or unexpected changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A FIM solution (e.g., Tripwire, Wazuh) is installed and configured on the file servers. It monitors the directories defined as critical. The generated alerts are forwarded to a central SIEM for correlation and analysis. The process for handling FIM alerts is defined and staffed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the FIM solution and the definition of the areas to be monitored. The SIEM rules and the alerts received in the SIEM are checked. The alert handling process is evaluated. As a test, a file in the monitored area is changed to verify the alerting chain.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: The group of office products primarily includes applications used to create, edit, or view documents. These include the free application LibreOffice and the proprietary application Microsoft Office, which are used in many institutions. For most institutions, office products are part of the necessary basic IT equipment. They include, among other things, programs for word processing, spreadsheets, and presentation creation, as well as drawing programs and simple database systems.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to protect the information processed and used by office products. To this end, special requirements are placed on the functionality of the components of office products. The module outlines requirements that should be met to secure office products against specific threats.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module APP.1.1 Office Products is to be applied to every office product that is installed locally and used to view, edit, or create documents, except for e-mail applications.

This module considers the use of office products from the perspective of IT operations and provides guidance for users on how office products should be used. In addition to the requirements of this module, the requirements of the higher-level module APP.6 General Software must be implemented. E-mail applications are not considered in this module; the corresponding requirements can be found in module APP.5.3 General E-mail Client and Server. When using integrated database systems such as Base in LibreOffice or Access in Microsoft Office, the module APP.4.3 Relational Databases must be considered. Also excluded from this module are pure cloud office applications such as Google Workspace with the applications Docs or Sheets. Requirements for cloud applications are specified in the module OPS.2.2 Cloud Usage.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Lack of adaptation of office products to the institution's needs
parts.prose: If office products are procured or adapted without considering the requirements for this software, operations can be significantly disrupted. For example, existing templates and documents may not be compatible, or interoperability with applications of business partners may be lacking. If office products are not adapted to the institution's needs, this can lead to performance losses, disruptions, or errors within business processes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Malicious content in Office documents
parts.prose: Office documents can typically contain various so-called "active content" or macros, which are sometimes used for complex automations. However, active content can also contain malicious code that is executed when the document is opened. Such malicious functions in Office documents can manipulate the affected documents themselves, as well as other data and programs. Furthermore, the malicious code can spread further. All affected business processes of the institution can be disrupted or blocked in their functions. In the worst case, the manipulation remains undetected and leads to security vulnerabilities and the processing of falsified information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Loss of integrity of Office documents
parts.prose: The integrity of Office documents can be compromised if their contents are altered unintentionally or intentionally. Due to careless handling of office products or users' lack of knowledge in handling Office documents, documents can be changed without being noticed. This is particularly problematic when it involves documents used in production. If work continues with documents that have been undetectably falsified, wrong decisions may be made, or the institution's image may be damaged.

controls.title: Use of basic security mechanisms

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only a few basic security mechanisms of the web browser, such as sandboxing, are enabled. Other important mechanisms, such as a Content Security Policy (CSP), are not configured or enforced. The configuration is inconsistent across the organization's various systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, the browser is often operated with its default settings, without a central configuration management ensuring the activation of all necessary security features such as sandboxing, Same-Origin Policy, Subresource Integrity, and CSP. This leads to a patchy and unreliable security posture.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly checks the configuration of web browsers on various endpoints. It is determined whether basic security mechanisms (sandboxing, SOP, SRI) are active and whether a CSP, even a basic one, has been defined. Inconsistencies in the configuration between systems are a clear indicator of this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The basic security mechanisms integrated into the browser, such as sandboxing, Same-Origin Policy (SOP), and Subresource Integrity (SRI), are consistently enabled. However, a Content Security Policy (CSP) is not yet implemented or is only present in a very permissive configuration (e.g., in report-only mode).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The basic mechanisms are often activated via a basic group policy or an MDM profile. The focus is on activating the standard protective functions without implementing application-specific hardening such as a restrictive CSP.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses a central management console or runs test scripts on the clients to check whether sandboxing, SOP, and SRI are active for all users and systems. Additionally, it is checked whether a CSP is implemented. The absence of an effective CSP characterizes this maturity level. Automated tools can scan the browser configurations to verify the activation of the basic mechanisms (`chrome://sandbox`, `about:config` in Firefox).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web browser used MUST ensure that each instance and each processing process can only access its own resources (sandboxing). Web pages MUST be isolated from each other as separate processes or at least as separate threads. Plug-ins and extensions MUST also be run in isolated areas. The web browser used MUST implement the Content Security Policy (CSP). The browser MUST support measures for Same-Origin-Policy and Subresource Integrity. These configurations are documented and consistently rolled out to all systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The implementation is carried out through a central configuration management (e.g., GPO, MDM). A basic but effective CSP is defined and operated in enforce mode. The configurations for sandboxing, SOP, and SRI are checked and, if necessary, hardened. The defined policies are made available to all IT staff.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and implementation of the central configuration policies. It is checked whether sandboxing, thread isolation, SOP, SRI, and a basic CSP are active and enforced on all target systems. Compliance can be checked by evaluating the configuration files or by querying the browser's internal diagnostic pages (e.g., `chrome://policy`). Additionally, the configuration documentation is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Building on the defined configuration, the 'SHOULD' requirement is implemented: The currently highest level of the Content Security Policy (CSP) is met. The CSP policies are restrictive and specifically tailored to the web applications used. The configurations of the security mechanisms are regularly reviewed for improvements and new features.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CSP (e.g., Level 3) is implemented to use protection mechanisms such as `script-src-elem`, `frame-ancestors`, or `trusted-types`. A process for reviewing and adapting the CSP for new and existing applications is established. CSP violations are reported to a central endpoint and actively evaluated to refine the policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the latest version of the CSP specification is being used and whether the policies are restrictive. It is verified that a reporting endpoint for CSP violations is configured and that the incoming reports are analyzed. This can be done by checking the server headers and configuration policies, as well as by reviewing the log analyses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All basic security mechanisms are not only implemented but also maximally hardened. The CSP is strict and dynamically managed. In addition, advanced protective measures such as 'Trusted Types' are enforced to defend against DOM-XSS attacks. The integrity of the browser configuration is continuously and automatically monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system for automated management and distribution of CSPs is in use. CSP violations trigger automated alerts. The sandboxing functions are further strengthened by operating system-level policies (e.g., AppLocker, SELinux). The configurations are permanently monitored by an endpoint security tool, and deviations are automatically corrected or reported.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the effectiveness of the automated monitoring and remediation measures. It is checked whether a tampering attempt on the browser configuration is detected and prevented or reported. The effectiveness of the 'Trusted Types' implementation is verified through targeted penetration tests. Automated compliance checks can be performed by executing a command like `Get-ComputerPolicy -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Google\Chrome'` and comparing it with a golden image.

controls.title: Support for secure communication encryption

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web browser supports TLS, but outdated and insecure protocol versions (SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) are still enabled and can be used for connections. HSTS is not actively used or configured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This state often arises from using the default settings of older browsers or operating systems that retain insecure protocols for compatibility reasons. There is no active management of encryption protocols.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the web browser's configuration on a client system to determine which TLS/SSL protocol versions are enabled. This can be done using online test sites (e.g., from Qualys SSL Labs) or through local configuration checks. The presence of enabled, outdated protocols is an indicator of this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web browser is configured to use secure TLS versions (at least 1.2) by default for communication. Connections to web servers are opportunistically encrypted with TLS if the server offers it. HSTS is supported by the browser but not actively enforced by policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration relies on the default settings of modern browsers, which already provide a secure basic configuration. No central policies are enforced to disable older protocols or manage HSTS.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the browser uses TLS 1.2 or higher by default for connections to modern servers. It is checked whether the browser correctly processes HSTS headers from websites. The absence of a central policy to disable insecure protocols characterizes this state. Automated scans can check the browser's default cipher suites and protocol settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web browser MUST support a secure version of Transport Layer Security (TLS). Connections to web servers MUST be encrypted with TLS if supported by the web server. The web browser MUST support and use the HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) mechanism according to RFC 6797. A policy mandating secure protocol versions and cipher suites is documented and implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Central configuration management (GPO, MDM) is used to ensure that only secure TLS versions (1.2 and higher) and strong cipher suites are used. HSTS is configured for important internal and external domains via policy (e.g., through the 'HSTSPreloadList').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the central configuration policies for web browsers. It is verified that these policies enforce the use of secure TLS versions and cipher suites and that HSTS is correctly configured. Compliance is checked on a sample basis on client systems, e.g., by analyzing the network configuration or the browser's diagnostic pages (`chrome://policy`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The 'SHOULD' requirement is implemented: Insecure versions of TLS (especially 1.0 and 1.1) and weak cipher suites (e.g., those with RC4 or 3DES) are explicitly and verifiably disabled by a central policy. The browser's HSTS preload list is actively used to protect important domains from downgrade attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration policies are tightened to enforce a 'whitelist' of allowed protocols (e.g., only TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3) and cipher suites. The organization's own critical domains are submitted to the official HSTS preload list, and this information is distributed to the organization's browsers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration policies for explicit deactivation or whitelist entries for protocols and cipher suites. It is verified that connection attempts with outdated protocols fail. The HSTS configuration is checked by examining the browser's internal state data (e.g., `chrome://net-internals/#hsts`) and the preload lists. An automated script can attempt to establish a connection with a weak cipher (e.g., `openssl s_client -connect server:443 -tls1_1`), which must fail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A strict policy enforces TLS 1.3 exclusively for all connections, where technically possible. The compliance of the encryption configuration is continuously monitored by endpoint security tools. The browser is configured to enforce Certificate Transparency (CT) for all connections to detect the issuance of malicious certificates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The browser policies are set to the strictest level (`SSLVersionMin` to `tls1.3`). An Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) or a configuration management tool monitors the relevant registry keys or configuration files in real-time and automatically corrects deviations. The policies for enforcing Certificate Transparency (`CertificateTransparencyEnforcementEnabled`) are activated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and alerting rules of the EDR or configuration management tool. A tampering attempt on the TLS configuration is simulated on a test client, which must be detected and corrected by the tool. The CT policy is verified by querying the browser policies (`chrome://policy`) and by analyzing network traffic during connections to test sites.

controls.title: Use of trusted certificates

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web browser performs a basic certificate check, but users can easily ignore warnings for invalid, expired, or self-signed certificates and continue the connection. The browser's or operating system's trust store is not actively managed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This state is typical for unmanaged environments. There are no policies preventing the addition of exceptions for certificate errors. Users are not trained to understand the meaning of certificate warnings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor navigates to a website with an invalid certificate (e.g., expired.badssl.com) and determines how easy it is to bypass the warning and access the site. It is checked whether non-administrator users can add their own root certificates to the trust store.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web browser performs a full check of the certificate's validity (validity period, signature chain). A clear warning is displayed in case of errors. However, the revocation status check is not performed reliably or is not enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Modern browsers perform good validation by default. The problem at this maturity level is often that the online revocation check (OCSP) is implemented as a 'soft-fail' for performance reasons, i.e., if the OCSP responder is unreachable, the certificate is treated as valid.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks if the browser correctly blocks certificates with an expired validity period or a broken chain. Then, a test is performed with a site that has a revoked certificate (e.g., revoked.badssl.com). It is analyzed (e.g., with Wireshark) whether an OCSP query takes place and how the browser reacts when the OCSP responder is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web browser MUST fully check the validity of server certificates, including the revocation status and the entire certificate chain. The trust store (list of trusted root certificates) is managed by IT operations, and users cannot change it. The browser MUST clearly inform the user about the encryption status, terminate the connection for invalid certificates, and may only continue after explicit confirmation by the user. Local certificate revocations are possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The trust store is managed via central policies (GPO, MDM). Unnecessary or untrusted root certificate authorities are removed. The online revocation check is enforced (OCSP Must-Staple is honored). Policies prevent ignoring certificate errors for external sites.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the central policies for managing the trust store. It is verified that users cannot install their own root CAs. The browser's response to various types of invalid certificates (expired, wrong hostname, revoked) is tested. It is checked whether the connection is terminated as required. Automated checking can be done by querying the relevant policies (`EnterpriseRoots`, `BlockUntrustedRoots`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined checks, the 'SHOULD' requirement is implemented: Upon request, the web browser provides the user with an easy way to view the server certificate used and its details. OCSP stapling is preferred and, where offered by the server, used for the revocation check to improve privacy and performance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No special configurations are needed, as modern browsers provide this function. It is more important to train users and the helpdesk to use this function for troubleshooting. On the server-side, it is ensured that important web servers offer OCSP stapling.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the browser's user interface to ensure that certificate details are easily accessible. Using a network sniffer (like Wireshark), a connection to a test server is checked to see if the browser requests OCSP stapling in its TLS handshake request and correctly processes the response provided by the server.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The browser is configured to enforce OCSP Must-Staple whenever required by a certificate. Additionally, the verification of Certificate Transparency (CT) logs is enforced for all public certificates. A minimal, strictly curated set of trusted root CAs is enforced, and all others are actively blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specific browser policies for enforcing Certificate Transparency (`CertificateTransparencyEnforcementEnabled`) and managing root CAs (`EnterpriseRoots`, `BlockUntrustedRoots`) are set to the most restrictive level. This ensures that only certificates from explicitly approved CAs and those properly registered in public logs are accepted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the effectiveness of CT enforcement by connecting to a test site with a certificate that is not included in the CT logs; the connection must fail. The trust store configuration is checked by attempting to connect to a site with a certificate from an untrusted CA. Policy compliance can be read out automatically via script.

controls.title: Password management in the web browser

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web browser's integrated password manager is used to store passwords, but without the use of a master password. The stored passwords are only protected on the system by logging into the operating system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users enable the save function for convenience, without being aware of the risks. There is no organizational guideline for securing the password store.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks on a sample client whether the browser stores passwords and whether they can be accessed without further authentication (i.e. without a master password). This is done by accessing the password management page in the browser (e.g. `chrome://settings/passwords`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of a master password is recommended to users to protect the browser's password store. However, implementation is left up to the users and is not enforced or verified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department communicates a recommendation via email or on the intranet, but there are no technical measures to ensure compliance. Users can continue to use the function without a master password.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews a selection of users to determine if they are aware of and have implemented the recommendation. A technical check on client systems shows inconsistent use of the master password.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If a password manager is used in the web browser, it MUST establish a direct and unique relationship between the website (origin) and the password stored for it. The password store MUST store the passwords in encrypted form. It MUST be ensured that the passwords stored in the password manager can only be accessed after entering a master password. Authentication for access is only valid for the current session. IT operations MUST ensure that users can delete stored passwords.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of the master password is enforced via a policy, if technically possible. Users are trained in the correct use of the password manager, including checking the website origin before entering the master password. The functionality for deleting passwords is ensured and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the browser policies to determine if the use of the master password is enforced. It is verified that the password manager makes phishing attempts more difficult through a strict origin check. The ability to delete individual or all passwords is tested. It is checked that the master password is re-requested after a certain period of inactivity or when the browser is restarted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Saving passwords in the browser is either generally disabled by policy, or the use of a dedicated, organization-approved password manager extension is mandated instead of the integrated function.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The browser's native save function is disabled via a central policy (`PasswordManagerEnabled` set to `false`). An approved and vetted password manager extension is centrally distributed to browsers instead. This often offers better security and management features than the integrated version.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks on the clients whether the integrated password management is disabled and the approved extension is installed. The configuration of the extension is checked to ensure that it complies with the organizational policies (e.g. for the master password). This can be verified by reading the browser policies (`chrome://policy`) and checking the installed extensions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A centrally managed enterprise password manager is in use, integrated as a browser extension. It enforces the organization's password policies, enables secure sharing of credentials in teams, provides detailed audit logs, and proactively warns about compromised or weak passwords by connecting to breach databases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An enterprise solution such as Bitwarden, 1Password or KeePass with central management is implemented. The native browser function is disabled. The solution is configured to perform regular security audits of the passwords stored by users and to generate reports for IT security.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the password manager's central management console. The audit logs, enforced policies, and reporting functions are reviewed. It is verified that a user is warned when they attempt to use a known compromised password.

controls.title: Use of DNS-over-HTTPS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) setting is left to the browser's default settings. This may cause browsers to enable DoH without the IT department's knowledge and use public resolvers, thereby bypassing internal DNS policies and filters.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no conscious decision or configuration regarding DoH. The IT department may not be aware of the feature and its implications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the default settings for DoH in the browser versions used. On a client, the network traffic is analyzed to determine whether DNS queries are sent to the DNS server configured by the operating system or to a public DoH resolver of the browser manufacturer.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A decision on the use of DoH has been made, but it is not technically enforced. IT recommends that users manually disable DoH to ensure the use of the internal DNS resolver, but there is no guarantee of compliance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A guide to disabling DoH is published on the intranet. However, implementation is left to the individual user, which leads to inconsistent configuration throughout the organization.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews users and randomly checks client systems to verify the configuration of the DoH settings. A high rate of deviation from the recommended configuration is found.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST make a documented decision on whether or not the browsers used should use DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH). The browsers MUST be centrally configured according to this decision. If an internal DNS resolver is used, it MUST also be used by the browser (either by disabling DoH or by configuring the browser to use the internal resolver as a DoH endpoint).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision is recorded in a security policy. The configuration is enforced via central management (GPO, MDM). If DoH is disabled, the corresponding policy (`DnsOverHttpsMode` set to `off`) is set. If an internal DoH resolver is used, its URI is entered in the policy (`DnsOverHttpsTemplates`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence of the written policy on DoH use. Subsequently, the configuration in the central management console is verified. On client systems, the browser diagnostic pages (`chrome://policy`) are checked to see if the policy is applied correctly. A network sniffer can confirm that DNS queries are sent to the correct destination (internal DNS or internal DoH resolver).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to central configuration, network controls are implemented to prevent circumvention of the DoH policy. The network gateway (firewall) is configured to block the IP addresses of known public DoH resolvers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of known public DoH providers is maintained and added to the firewall's blacklists. This list is updated regularly. This prevents unmanaged devices or applications from bypassing internal DNS policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the firewall rules. From a test client, an attempt is made to send a DNS query to a blocked public DoH resolver (e.g. using `curl https://chrome.cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query`). This attempt must fail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire DNS infrastructure, including the DoH resolver used, is secured by DNSSEC. Outbound network traffic is actively monitored for DoH requests to unauthorized endpoints (e.g., by analyzing SNI headers in TLS connections). Suspicious activities trigger an alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The internal DNS server (or DoH resolver) is configured to validate DNSSEC signatures. An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) or a Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) is equipped with rules to detect DoH traffic to unapproved destinations. These rules can be based on IP lists, but also on patterns in the TLS handshake.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the DNSSEC configuration of the internal resolver. The rules and alarms in the IDS/NGFW system are reviewed. A test case is carried out in which a client attempts to establish a DoH connection to an unknown, unblocked resolver. This attempt must be detected and reported by the monitoring system.

controls.title: Data minimization in web browsers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users are aware of the privacy settings, but manage them only sporadically and inconsistently. Some settings, such as blocking third-party cookies, may be made, but other privacy-related functions such as browser synchronization or telemetry remain active.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are no organizational guidelines. The level of data protection depends entirely on the initiative and technical understanding of the individual user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A random check of client browsers shows a wide variety of different configurations. Many browsers are in their default state regarding privacy-relevant settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an organizational recommendation for configuring privacy settings. Users are instructed to block third-party cookies and to delete their browser data regularly by hand. However, implementation is not technically enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Guides for improving privacy in the browser are made available to users. The IT department relies on users following these recommendations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews users and checks configurations to determine the extent to which the recommendations have been implemented. A partial but not consistent implementation is found.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic privacy configuration is defined and centrally rolled out. This can include, for example, deactivating the autofill function and browser synchronization with cloud services. Users are trained and instructed to block third-party cookies and are given the opportunity to delete their browser data (cookies, history).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Using GPO or MDM, policies such as `AutoFillEnabled` and `SyncDisabled` are set to `false`. Users receive clear instructions on handling cookies and other browser data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the central configuration policies and compares them with the settings on the client systems. It is checked whether users have the option to delete their data as required. The training materials are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All relevant 'SHOULD' requirements are implemented through a central policy. Third-party cookies SHOULD be blocked. Telemetry functions and the automatic sending of crash reports SHOULD be disabled. Access to peripheral devices (microphone, webcam, location) SHOULD be blocked by default and only allowed after explicit permission per site. The configuration of WebRTC, HSTS, and JavaScript is either made available to the user or is restrictively pre-configured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The corresponding browser policies (`DefaultCookiesSetting`, `SendCrashReports`, `DefaultKameraSetting`, etc.) are centrally set to the most restrictive values. For example, blocking third-party cookies is enforced (`BlockThirdPartyCookies` set to `true`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the comprehensive configuration policies in the central administration console. On a client, it is tested whether access to the webcam is blocked and requires explicit approval. The browser's network communication is monitored to ensure that no telemetry data is sent to the manufacturer. Compliance can be automated with `Get-ComputerPolicy` and by checking the corresponding keys in the registry.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A strict data protection configuration is enforced and cannot be changed by users. This includes blocking all third-party cookies, disabling telemetry and synchronization, and activating advanced tracking protection at the highest level. Additionally, a policy to delete all browser data when closing the browser is enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `ClearBrowsingDataOnExit` policy is activated and configured to include all relevant data (cookies, cache, history). Advanced protection features such as the 'Strict' mode in Firefox's tracking protection are enforced by policy. Any form of speculative preloading of content (`pre-rendering`, `pre-fetching`) is disabled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the strict data protection policies are enforced on the clients and cannot be changed. A test is performed: The user browses several websites, closes the browser, and reopens it. The browser history, cookies, and cache must be empty. The immutability of the settings is checked by attempting to change them in the GUI (the options must be grayed out).

controls.title: Use of an isolated web browser environment

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An isolated browser environment is used only by a few, particularly vulnerable individuals (e.g., administrators) and on a voluntary basis. There is no organizational requirement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Some technically savvy employees may set up a VM with a browser themselves to visit risky websites. However, this is done on an ad-hoc basis and without a standardized procedure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews, the auditor determines that there is no uniform strategy for browser isolation and that only isolated, individual solutions are in use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standardized, virtualized browser instance (e.g., in a simple VM) is made available to high-risk users upon request. The setup is basic and is not centrally managed or hardened.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department provides a simple VM image with a pre-installed browser. Users must manually start and use the VM. Updates for the VM and the browser within it often have to be performed manually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation for the VM deployment. It is noted that there is no process for regular updating or hardening of the VM image and that its use is not enforced.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on a risk analysis, a policy is defined that specifies when an isolated browser environment must be used (e.g., for all access to the internet). A standardized, hardened, and centrally managed virtualized browser instance is provided for all relevant users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 'golden image' for a virtual machine with a hardened operating system and a pre-configured browser is created and maintained. This image is centrally distributed to users. There are clear instructions on which activities this environment should be used for.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the browser isolation policy and the patch and management process for the VM image. Random checks are performed to see if the relevant users are using the isolated environment as required.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD use specially secured, isolated browser environments. A dedicated browser isolation solution (e.g., Remote Browser Isolation - RBI, or a container-based solution like ReCoBS) is implemented. This ensures that web content is executed in a remote, non-persistent environment and only the rendered, secure results are streamed to the client browser.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A commercial or open-source RBI solution is introduced. All internet traffic from the clients is transparently routed through this solution. The policies for isolation (e.g., which content is blocked, which is converted) are centrally managed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the RBI solution and the associated network routes. It is verified on a client system that when visiting a website, no active code (e.g., JavaScript) is executed directly on the endpoint. This can be done by analyzing the DOM and the running processes in the client browser.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The browser isolation solution is fully integrated into the organization's security stack. Traffic from the isolation environment is routed through a central web gateway for content inspection (malware scanning, DLP) before reaching the user. The isolation instances are non-persistent and are guaranteed to be destroyed after each session. The solution itself is hardened and regularly undergoes penetration testing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RBI solution is coupled with the organization's Secure Web Gateway and DLP systems. Policies for data transfer (upload/download, copy/paste) between the isolated environment and the client are enforced. The platform is continuously monitored for security and performance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the entire chain of security controls, from the redirection of traffic to the RBI solution to the content inspection in the web gateway. A test is conducted to see if an attempt to exfiltrate sensitive data from the isolated session is detected and blocked by the DLP controls. The solution's logs are checked for evidence of the correct destruction of session instances.

controls.title: Use of private mode

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users are familiar with the browser's private mode (incognito mode) and occasionally use it at their own discretion, without any organizational requirement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Usage is purely voluntary and depends on the awareness of the individual user. There is no training or policy on this.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By interviewing users, the auditor determines that there is no uniform procedure for using the private mode.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an organizational recommendation to use private mode for browsing on untrusted or sensitive websites. However, compliance is not checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A corresponding recommendation is communicated to the employees. The responsibility for implementation lies entirely with the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the communication channels for the existence of the recommendation. A survey of employees shows that the recommendation is known but not always followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy requires the use of private mode for certain user groups or activities with increased confidentiality needs. The users are trained accordingly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is formally documented and is part of the security training. Although its use is not technically enforced, it is a clear work instruction.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existence of the policy and the training materials. Knowledge of the policy is randomly checked among the affected employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web browser SHOULD be run in so-called private mode for increased confidentiality requirements. The browser SHOULD be configured to delete local content upon exit. This is enforced by a central policy that starts the browser in private mode by default for all users or defined groups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The corresponding browser policy (e.g., `IncognitoModeAvailability` or `BrowserGuestModeEnabled`) is configured via GPO or MDM to force the browser to start in private or an equivalent ephemeral mode. The `ClearBrowsingDataOnExit` policy is also activated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the central configuration policy. On a client system, the browser is started and it is verified that it opens directly in private mode. It is checked that after closing and restarting, no session data (history, cookies) remains. Compliance can be automated by reading the `chrome://policy` policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of private mode is combined with a browser isolation solution (see APP.1.2.A9). The browser sessions take place in a remote, non-persistent instance that is guaranteed to be completely destroyed after each session. This provides a higher level of security than the local private mode.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Remote Browser Isolation (RBI) solution is configured so that a new, clean container or VM instance is started for each user for each session and is irrevocably destroyed after closing the browser tab or window.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the RBI platform. It is verified that the sessions are non-persistent by creating a file in the session or changing a setting. After closing and reopening the session, these changes must have disappeared. The platform's logs are checked for evidence of session destruction.

controls.title: Check for malicious content

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The browser's integrated Safe Browsing function is activated but relies on the default settings. This may involve the transmission of navigation data to third parties (e.g., Google), which can raise data protection concerns.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no active configuration of the function. The organization relies on the protection that the browser offers by default, without evaluating the data protection implications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the Safe Browsing function is active and what data it sends to the provider. It is assessed whether this data transfer is compliant with the organization's data protection policies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The browser's Safe Browsing function is active and, if available, configured in a more privacy-friendly mode (e.g., matching hash prefixes instead of sending full URLs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department has deliberately configured the Safe Browsing feature to maximize protection while preserving privacy. This can be done via browser policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the browser policies for the configuration of the Safe Browsing mode. It is tested whether the browser warns against known phishing or malware sites.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Accessed internet addresses SHOULD be checked for potentially harmful content by the web browser. The web browser SHOULD warn the user, and a connection classified as malicious SHOULD NOT be accessible. The verification method used MUST NOT violate data protection or secrecy regulations. This functionality is enforced by policy and a data protection compliance assessment has been conducted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The 'Safe Browsing' feature is enforced via a central policy (`SafeBrowsingEnabled`). It is documented that the chosen implementation (e.g., the hash-based approach) meets internal data protection requirements. Users cannot easily bypass the warnings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy configuration and the documentation of the data protection assessment. It is tested whether access to a known malicious site is reliably blocked and the user cannot bypass the block, or can only do so with considerable effort (and logging).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to browser-based scanning, all web traffic is routed through a central Secure Web Gateway or a DNS filter. This uses more comprehensive threat intelligence feeds that can be customized for the company to block malicious domains, URLs, and content before they reach the browser.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Secure Web Gateway (SWG) is implemented and all client HTTP/S traffic is routed through it (e.g., via proxy configuration or PAC file). The SWG is fed with multiple threat feeds (commercial, open source, industry-specific) and allows the definition of custom blocklists.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the SWG's configuration, the threat feeds used, and the defined policies. It is tested whether access to a URL that is only present in the SWG's feeds and not in the Safe Browsing list is blocked. The SWG's logs are checked for blocked access attempts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to URL and reputation filtering, the Secure Web Gateway performs real-time content analysis and sandboxing for downloaded files and active content. Unknown or potentially malicious executable files are analyzed in an isolated environment before being delivered to the user. This is combined with a browser isolation solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The sandboxing function of the SWG or an integrated Advanced Threat Protection solution is activated. Policies define which file types or content are sent to the sandbox for analysis. The results of the analysis are used to dynamically update the blocking rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to download a harmless but unknown executable file (or an EICAR test file in an archive) from a test site. The process is monitored to verify that the file is intercepted by the SWG for analysis and the download is only released after a positive analysis result. The sandbox logs are checked for analysis reports.

controls.title: Two-Browser Strategy

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multiple browsers are installed on users' systems because they were bundled with various applications or installed by the users themselves. Their use is uncoordinated and not part of a security strategy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The existence of multiple browsers is coincidental and not the result of a conscious decision for risk mitigation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A software inventory of the client systems shows the presence of multiple browsers. Interviews reveal that there is no policy for their use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An alternative browser is available on the systems as a manual fallback option. However, there is no formal process that defines when or how to switch to this browser.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department installs a second browser by default (e.g., Firefox alongside Chrome) as an alternative for compatibility issues or failures. Its use in a security context is not defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the installation of the second browser. It is determined that no contingency plans or instructions exist that regulate switching to this browser in the event of a serious security vulnerability in the primary browser.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In case of unresolved security issues with the web browser in use, an alternative browser with a different platform (i.e., different rendering engine) SHOULD be installed to serve as a fallback for users. There is a documented process that instructs IT support and users on how and when to make the switch.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the primary browser (e.g., Chromium-based), a second browser with a different engine (e.g., Firefox/Gecko) is centrally installed via software distribution. An emergency plan in the incident response handbook describes the steps to deactivate the primary browser and switch users to the alternative browser.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the installation of both browsers on the clients. The incident response plan is reviewed to verify the process for switching browsers. An exercise can be conducted to test the effectiveness and speed of the switching process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A strict two-browser strategy is actively enforced to separate use cases. A hardened browser is used exclusively for accessing the public, untrusted internet, while a second, differently configured browser is used exclusively for accessing the trusted intranet and internal web applications.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The 'Internet browser' is configured with maximum security settings (blocking plugins, strict script control). The 'Intranet browser' may have less restrictive settings to ensure compatibility with internal applications. Users are trained to use the correct browser for the respective purpose. Shortcuts are named accordingly ('Internet', 'Intranet').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the different configurations of the two browsers. It is checked through observation and interviews whether users consistently adhere to the separation. Proxy logs can be analyzed to determine which browser is used for which destination URLs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The two-browser strategy is technically enforced and combined with browser isolation. All traffic to the internet is automatically and transparently routed to an isolated remote browser (Browser 1). Access to a whitelist of internal, trusted URLs automatically opens in a locally installed, specially configured browser (Browser 2).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A URL filtering agent on the client or at the network gateway routes requests to the correct environment based on the destination URL. For example, a PAC file or an agent forwards all requests that do not end in `*.internal-domain.corp` to the RBI solution, while internal requests are routed directly or via another proxy to the local browser.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the automatic redirection. Accessing an external website (e.g., `www.google.com`) must land in the isolated environment. Accessing an internal website (`intranet.internal-domain.corp`) must open in the local browser. The URL filter configuration is checked to ensure the rule base is correct and complete.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Web browsers are application programs that can retrieve, process, display, output, and store (hypertext) documents, images, video, audio, and other data formats from the Internet on local IT systems. Web browsers can also transmit data to the Internet.

Stationary and mobile clients are unimaginable today without web browsers, because very many private and business applications use corresponding content. At the same time, this content on the Internet is becoming increasingly diverse. Most websites use embedded videos, animated elements, and other active content. Modern web browsers also cover a wide range of additional functions by integrating plug-ins and external libraries. In addition, there are extensions for specific functions, data formats, and content. The complexity of modern web browsers offers a high potential for serious conceptual errors and programming vulnerabilities. It not only increases the potential dangers of attacks from the Internet, but also entails additional risks from programming and operating errors.

The risks to the confidentiality and integrity of data are considerable. The availability of the entire IT system is also threatened by such vulnerabilities. Internet content must therefore be considered fundamentally untrustworthy from the web browser's point of view.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to describe security requirements for web browsers used on clients, i.e., on stationary and mobile IT systems as well as on tablets and smartphones.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module APP.1.2 Web Browser is to be applied once to every web browser.

It contains fundamental security requirements that must be observed and fulfilled during the installation and operation of web browsers for accessing data from the Internet.

Web browsers are one of the most frequently used applications. They access unchecked, potentially harmful data on the Internet and thus represent a gateway for attacks, often with the aim of spreading further to the operating system. To secure the operating systems, the requirements of the modules of the layers SYS.2 Desktop Systems and SYS.3.2 Tablet and Smartphone should therefore be fulfilled.

Web applications used with browsers and the responsible servers are dealt with in the modules APP.3.1 Web Applications and Web Services and APP.3.2 Web Server.

General requirements for the secure use of software are not contained in this module. They can be found in the module APP.6 General Software, which is to be applied in addition to this module.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Execution of malicious code by web browsers
parts.prose:
Web browsers regularly load data from untrusted sources. Such data can contain executable malicious code that can exploit vulnerabilities and infect the user's IT system without their knowledge.

This can be code that can be executed directly by the web browser, such as JavaScript or WebAssembly. It can also be executable code from a plug-in or an extension in the context of the browser, such as Java or components of PDF documents. Finally, it can also be code that is loaded onto the client by the web browser and executed there outside the browser process. If the basic protection mechanisms of modern web browsers are not sufficiently applied, the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information or services of the client or possibly even of the networks connected to it are threatened.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Exploit Kits
parts.prose: Vulnerability lists and so-called exploit kits significantly facilitate the development of individual malware. Cyberattacks can be automated to easily use drive-by downloads or other distribution channels without expert knowledge. Attackers can exploit known vulnerabilities in web browsers, connected resources, or extensions to prepare for subsequent attacks or to load and install code with malicious functionality on clients. Often, the malicious code loaded onto the clients in this way is used to download further malware, which is then executed on the clients with the users' permissions.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Eavesdropping on Internet communication
parts.prose:
The fundamental security of communication on the Internet depends essentially on the authentication method used and on the encryption of data in transit.

Faulty implementations of the corresponding procedures are possible and prevent effective authentication and encryption. Many web services also still offer outdated encryption methods. Thus, in an attack, the authentication of servers can be circumvented or the communication or data is not effectively encrypted. This allows information to be read or altered in transit. In the past, certification authorities have also been compromised. Attackers could thus obtain certificates for third-party websites.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Loss of integrity in web browsers
parts.prose: If web browsers, plug-ins, or extensions are obtained from untrusted sources, malicious functions can be executed unintentionally and unnoticed. For example, attackers can fake browser components like toolbars to lure users to manipulated copies of websites, which are then used to carry out phishing attacks. Malicious extensions can manipulate the content of the viewed websites or spy on data and send it to the attackers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Loss of privacy
parts.prose: If web browsers are configured insecurely, trusted data can be accidentally or maliciously exposed to unauthorized third parties. Passwords can also be unintentionally disclosed. If cookies, passwords, histories, input data, and search queries are stored or unnecessary extensions are activated, data can be more easily read for misuse by third parties or malicious programs.

controls.title: Requirements analysis for the use of apps

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A requirements analysis is only carried out sporadically and on an ad-hoc basis for individual apps that are classified as particularly critical. There is no systematic process or uniform methodology for risk assessment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The analysis is often informal, e.g., through short email exchanges between the IT department and the business department. The results are not centrally documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether a requirements or risk analysis has taken place at all for a randomly selected sample of apps. This can be done by interviewing those responsible and requesting email histories or notes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all new apps, a basic requirements analysis is carried out using a standardized checklist. The analysis focuses on functional requirements and obvious risks, but no in-depth security analysis takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple checklist in Word or Excel format is used. The completed checklists are stored in a central folder but are not systematically evaluated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the completed checklists for a selection of apps and checks whether the analysis was carried out for all apps and the checklist was completed in full. The consistency of the assessments is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A documented and repeatable process for the requirements analysis of mobile apps is established. As part of this process, the risks arising from mobile use MUST be considered in particular. The institution MUST check whether its control and influence options on the mobile device's operating system environment are sufficient to use the app securely. The results are documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The analysis is carried out as an integral part of the app approval process. Catalogs of criteria are used that cover both technical (e.g., required permissions, data storage) and organizational aspects (e.g., support from the manufacturer). The business owners and IT security are involved in the process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation for the requirements analysis. Based on a sample of introduced apps, it is verified whether the process has been followed and the analysis results, including the risk assessment and the review of control options, have been documented completely and comprehensibly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined analysis process is supplemented by formal threat modeling for mobile application scenarios. The risk analysis is directly integrated into the institution's central risk management system. The analysis is repeated not only upon introduction, but also for major updates of an app.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Recognized threat modeling methods such as STRIDE or LINDDUN are used. The results are fed into a central risk management tool, where the risks are assessed and measures are assigned and tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that threat models exist for critical apps and that the identified risks are recorded and addressed in the central risk management tool. It is checked whether the analysis process is repeated for app updates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire requirements and risk analysis process is largely automated. External threat intelligence feeds on mobile vulnerabilities and high-risk apps are automatically included in the assessment. The process is continuously adapted based on new findings and threats.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized tool for 'Mobile Application Vetting' is used. This tool automatically analyzes apps (SAST/DAST), checks permissions, reputation, and known vulnerabilities, and creates a risk score. The results are visualized in a dashboard and directly influence the go/no-go decision of the approval process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the automated analysis tool and its connection to threat intelligence sources. Based on the tool's logs, it is verified that all apps (including updates) go through the process and that the generated risk reports are used as a basis for the approval decision. `grep -i 'risk_score' /var/log/app_vetting_tool.log | awk '$2 > 80' | wc -l` can be used to check the number of rejected high-risk apps.

controls.title: Minimization and control of app permissions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of app permissions is left entirely to individual users. There are no institutional guidelines or controls.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users may receive a one-time awareness training when the device is issued, but are thereafter responsible for configuring the permissions themselves.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects a sample of endpoints and finds that the permissions for the same app are configured inconsistently and often exceed what is necessary.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A written policy exists that establishes the principle of least privilege for app permissions. Users are instructed to implement this policy, but compliance is not technically enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A guide with screenshots is provided on the intranet, explaining how users can restrict permissions on iOS and Android. As part of the app approval process, a list of recommended permissions is communicated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existence and communication of the policy and the guides. During a device inspection, it is checked on a random basis whether users have configured the permissions according to the recommendations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before an app is introduced in an institution, it MUST be ensured that it only receives the minimum necessary app permissions for its function. Permissions that are not strictly necessary MUST be questioned and, if necessary, blocked. Security-relevant permission settings MUST be fixed in such a way that they cannot be changed by people or apps. Where this is not technically possible, the permission settings MUST be checked and reset regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the app approval process, a list of the minimum necessary permissions is defined. This configuration is distributed as a default setting via a Mobile Device Management (MDM) system where possible. If a fixed setting is not possible, a periodic report on the configurations of the endpoints is generated and deviations are tracked manually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the process for defining minimum permissions. They check the MDM configuration for the set permission policies. If a fixed setting is not possible, the reports of the regular checks and the logs of the corrective actions are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An MDM or Mobile Application Management (MAM) system is used to technically enforce permission policies for all managed apps and prevent changes by users. The system generates automated alerts if an app attempts to escalate its permissions, or if an unapproved app with high-risk permissions is installed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The permissions are distributed via configuration profiles of the MDM/MAM system. Compliance rules are configured so that devices that violate the permission policies (e.g., through jailbreaking/rooting) are automatically isolated from the corporate network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the MDM/MAM permission and compliance policies. It is verified that the policies block changes by the user. The system's logs are checked for alerts and automatically executed compliance actions. A test can consist of trying to manually change a permission on a managed device.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM/MAM system implements a zero-trust model for permissions, where all permissions are denied by default. Permissions are granted dynamically and for a limited time only when needed (just-in-time) based on context (e.g., user role, location, device health). A Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) solution monitors app behavior in real-time and automatically revokes permissions if anomalous activities are detected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The dynamic permission granting is integrated into the central Identity and Access Management (IAM) system. The MTD solution analyzes system calls and data flows of the apps to detect suspicious behavior that indicates a misuse of permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the zero-trust policies and the context-based rules in the MDM/MAM and IAM system. The logs of the MTD solution are analyzed to verify the detection of anomalies and the automatic response (revocation of permissions). A simulated attack can be carried out to test the system's responsiveness.

controls.title: Secure storage of local app data

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The responsibility for secure data storage lies solely with the respective app developer or provider. There are no institutional guidelines or reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Developers may use insecure methods such as storing credentials in plaintext in configuration files without it being noticed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the local storage of an app on a test device and finds unencrypted sensitive data (e.g., passwords, tokens, personal data).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general policy that requires sensitive data to be stored encrypted on mobile devices. However, the policy does not specify any specific technical mechanisms or APIs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Developers are advised to use the operating system's encryption features. As part of the app approval process, a random check is performed to see if obviously unencrypted data is being stored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existence of the policy. A manual check of the app data container is performed to verify if sensitive data is encrypted, without assessing the strength of the encryption.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If apps can access internal documents of the institution, it MUST be ensured that the local data storage of the app is adequately secured. In particular, access keys MUST be stored encrypted by using the secure storage APIs of the operating system (e.g., iOS Keychain, Android Keystore). Furthermore, confidential data MUST NOT be cached by the operating system in other locations (e.g., in system caches or backups).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For internally developed apps, coding guidelines are provided that mandate the use of the platform's own secure storage APIs. When procuring external apps, the correct implementation of data storage is defined as a requirement criterion and checked where possible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the coding guidelines. For internal apps, a code review is conducted to verify the correct use of the secure storage APIs. For external apps, the app data container on a test device is examined to ensure that no access keys or confidential data are stored unencrypted outside the designated secure storage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An MDM/MAM solution is used to enforce strict data containerization. All corporate data is stored in an encrypted container on the device, logically separated from personal apps and data. Policies prevent data exchange (e.g., via copy/paste, 'Open in...') between the corporate container and unsecured apps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM/MAM solution is configured to create a work profile (e.g., Android Enterprise Work Profile) or an app container on all managed devices. Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies are activated to control the data flow.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the MDM/MAM system regarding containerization and DLP policies. On a test device, an attempt is made to copy corporate data from a managed app to a personal app. The auditor verifies that this process is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of hardware-backed encryption (e.g., via the Secure Enclave or a StrongBox Keymaster) is mandatory for the storage of all sensitive local data and cryptographic keys. Automated static (SAST) and dynamic (DAST) code analysis are used in the CI/CD pipeline to continuously verify that apps correctly implement the secure storage APIs and do not leak data to insecure areas such as system logs or temporary directories.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CI/CD pipeline is extended with SAST/DAST tools specialized in mobile security vulnerabilities. The build processes fail if violations of the secure storage policies are detected. The procurement of devices is made conditional on them offering strong hardware-backed security features.

parts.name: assessment-method
