parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and rules of the SAST/DAST tools in the CI/CD pipeline. The scan reports are reviewed to verify the effectiveness of the automated controls. It is checked whether the device specifications include the requirement for hardware-backed encryption. `find /data/data/com.example.app -type f -exec strings {} + | grep 'password='` can be used on a rooted test device to detect insecure storage.

controls.title: Prevention of data exfiltration

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no controls to prevent data exfiltration by mobile apps. All network communication from apps is unrestricted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Apps can surreptitiously send data to any server on the internet, including ad trackers, analytics services, or attackers' servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses a network sniffer (e.g., Wireshark, mitmproxy) to capture the traffic of a test device and determines that apps are sending unencrypted or confidential data to unapproved external endpoints.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network traffic of mobile devices is monitored on the central firewall or web proxy. Suspicious traffic indicating data exfiltration is investigated reactively.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The firewall logs are regularly checked for connections to known malicious domains or unusually large amounts of outgoing data from mobile devices. However, this only works when the devices are connected to the internal Wi-Fi.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the firewall rules and logs. It is checked whether a process for investigating suspicious network activities exists and whether it has been applied in the past.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To prevent apps from unintentionally sending sensitive data or creating user profiles from the sent data, app communication MUST be appropriately restricted. As part of the approval process, the app's communication is manually analyzed to identify and evaluate the communication endpoints. A check is performed to see if apps write unwanted logging or auxiliary files that could contain sensitive information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During app testing, network traffic is intercepted and analyzed using an intercepting proxy (e.g., mitmproxy). The identified target domains are checked against a list of approved services. Likewise, the device's file system is searched for suspicious log files.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the testing and approval procedure. For a sample of apps, the analysis logs of the network traffic and the file system scan are inspected to verify the execution and the results.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: App communication SHOULD be analyzed as part of the testing and approval procedure. A Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) or MDM solution is used to actively monitor and control the network traffic of managed apps. Policies are enforced to block connections to known malicious domains or unapproved cloud services. Furthermore, it SHOULD be checked whether an app writes unwanted logging or auxiliary files that might contain sensitive information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MTD solution is integrated with threat intelligence feeds. App-specific firewall rules are distributed via the MDM to allow only necessary communication (whitelisting). Dynamic analysis (sandboxing) of the app is part of the verification process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the MTD/MDM solution, including the network policies and the connection to threat intelligence sources. It is tested whether an app can establish a connection to a non-whitelisted domain. The logs are checked for alerts regarding data exfiltration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All network traffic from managed apps or from the corporate container is routed through a secure institutional gateway (e.g., Always-On VPN, Secure Web Gateway). On this gateway, Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies are applied to analyze the content of the transmitted data for sensitive information and prevent its exfiltration. Anomalous communication patterns trigger an automated response, e.g., blocking the app.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Always-On VPN profile is distributed to the devices via MDM. The VPN endpoint forwards the traffic to a Next-Generation Firewall or a DLP gateway. There, content-based rules are applied that, for example, block the upload of documents with specific keywords or file types to unapproved cloud storage services.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the VPN profile, the gateway, and the DLP policies. A test is conducted in which an attempt is made to upload a file with fictitious but classified-as-sensitive information to an external service via an app. The auditor verifies that the process is blocked and a corresponding alert is triggered.

controls.title: Distribution of sensitive apps

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All apps, including internally developed ones and those that process sensitive data, are distributed manually. There is no central distribution mechanism.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users receive installation files (e.g., .apk for Android) or download links via email or an intranet page. Installation from unknown sources must be enabled on the devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews employees on how they receive corporate apps and confirms the manual distribution method. It is checked whether the 'Allow installation from unknown sources' setting is widespread on Android devices, which poses a significant security risk.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An institutional app store or an MDM solution is available, but its use is only recommended and not mandatory. Some, but not all, sensitive apps are distributed through it.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department maintains a simple app catalog in the MDM. Employees are encouraged to source apps from there but can still install apps from public stores.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the content of the institutional app store and compares it with the list of apps used in the company. It is found that many apps, including those requiring protection, are not distributed through the managed channel.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A documented policy exists that mandates that internal apps and apps processing sensitive information must be distributed via a controlled mechanism. Implementation is achieved by making these apps available in an institutional app store or via an MDM solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An allowlist (whitelist) of approved apps is maintained in the MDM. Apps classified as sensitive are offered for installation exclusively through this channel. For apps with lower protection needs, installation from public stores may still be permitted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the app distribution policy. They compare the list of apps classified as sensitive with the catalog in the MDM/app store and ensure that all these apps are available there and cannot be installed from public sources (if technically enforced).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution's internal apps and apps that process sensitive information SHOULD be distributed via an institutional app store or MDM. The installation of apps from all other sources (sideloading, public app stores) is technically blocked on company-owned devices or within the corporate container on BYOD devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Configuration profiles are distributed via the MDM system that block access to public app stores or enforce an app blacklist that blocks all apps except the approved ones. Only the institutional app store is accessible to users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the MDM configuration that blocks public app stores. An attempt is made on a test device to install an unapproved app from a public store, and it is verified that this fails. A compliance report from the MDM, which shows the app installations on the devices, is checked for unapproved apps. `adb shell pm list packages` can be used to compare installed packages.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM solution enforces the automatic installation (push installation) of all apps required for work and relevant to security. App versions are centrally managed, and security-critical updates are automatically installed on all devices without user interaction. The system performs a continuous inventory and attestation of all apps installed on the devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the MDM, apps are marked as 'mandatory,' which triggers automatic installation. App update policies are configured to distribute updates immediately after they become available in the internal app store. Compliance policies ensure that devices without the required apps are considered non-compliant and their access to corporate resources is blocked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the MDM configuration for mandatory app installation and the update policies. The MDM's compliance reports are analyzed to confirm that all managed devices have the correct apps in the latest versions. It is tested how the system reacts to a device from which a mandatory app has been manually removed.

controls.title: Secure uninstallation of apps

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no process for uninstalling apps or deleting associated data. This is left to the user's responsibility.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When an employee leaves the company, corporate data may remain in apps on their private device. Backend systems continue to contain data that was synchronized by the app.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews former employees or inspects returned devices and finds that corporate apps and data have not been removed. The accounts in the backend systems are still active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The offboarding process includes a manual step that instructs users to delete all corporate apps from their devices. The operating system removes the local app data in the process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An offboarding process checklist includes the item 'Employee has confirmed the deletion of all corporate apps'. There is no process for cleaning up data in backend systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the offboarding checklists and verifies that the item for app deletion is included. However, it is noted that no technical verification of the actual deletion is performed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process is defined to ensure that when an app is uninstalled, its associated local data is also securely removed. The process also includes steps to revoke access to backend systems and, if applicable, to request data deletion from the app providers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Part of the offboarding process is to send a command to wipe the device or remove the corporate profile via the MDM. For apps with backend connectivity, there is a manual procedure to deactivate or delete the user account in the backend.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the offboarding process documentation. Using the MDM logs, it is verified that wipe commands were sent to the devices for departed employees. It is checked on a sample basis whether the associated backend accounts have been deactivated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When apps are uninstalled, data stored on external systems, for example by the app providers, SHOULD also be deleted. An MDM system is used to automatically uninstall all managed apps and securely wipe the corporate data container when a device is decommissioned or an employee leaves. This action triggers automated scripts to deprovision user accounts in the associated backend systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM system is configured to automatically perform a 'Selective Wipe' (deleting the corporate container) or a 'Full Wipe' (factory reset) when a device is removed from management. The MDM and the main backend systems are connected via APIs, so that a wipe command in the MDM also initiates the deactivation of the user in the backend.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the automated wipe procedures in the MDM. The logs of the MDM and the connected backend systems are analyzed for a selected offboarding case to trace the successful execution of the automated process from app uninstallation to backend de-provisioning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire process of app uninstallation and data deletion is fully integrated into the central Identity and Access Management (IAM) system. Any change in user status in the IAM (e.g., departure, role change) automatically and in real-time triggers the complete cleanup process on all associated mobile devices and in all connected backend systems. The process includes verification and audit-proof logging to prove the irrevocable deletion of all data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system acts as the central control instance (Single Source of Truth). Deprovisioning commands are sent to the MDM and all connected SaaS applications via SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) or proprietary APIs. A workflow system orchestrates the entire process and ensures that all steps are successfully completed before the user account is finally archived.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the deprovisioning workflow in the IAM system. Using the audit-proof logs, an offboarding case is tracked from start to finish, verifying the successful command transmission to all systems (MDM, backends) and their positive confirmation of the completed deletion.

controls.title: Support for additional authentication factors in apps

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication to apps is done exclusively via username and password. No additional authentication factors are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Passwords may be stored insecurely on the device to increase user convenience.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies by testing the login function of various apps that no multi-factor authentication (MFA) is offered or enforced. It is checked whether passwords are stored in plain text in the app's local storage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For a few, particularly critical applications, the use of a second factor is offered, but it is not mandatory for users. SMS codes or email links are most commonly used as a second factor.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users can optionally enable MFA in the app's settings. IT recommends its use but does not enforce it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration options of the critical apps and determines that MFA is optional. By inspecting the user accounts on the backend, it is verified how many users have actually enabled MFA.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy requires that a second factor must be used for authentication to apps that access sensitive data. Implementation is done using standard methods such as TOTP (e.g., via an authenticator app). When selecting biometric methods, a documented assessment of their security and resistance to spoofing is carried out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of MFA is enforced server-side for defined user groups or apps. Users are instructed to install and configure an approved authenticator app. The assessment of biometric methods is based on manufacturer documentation and third-party test results.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the MFA policy and the configuration of the backend systems to verify the enforcement of MFA. They request the documentation of the security assessment for the approved biometric methods.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If possible, a second factor SHOULD be used for authentication in apps. MFA is enforced for all corporate apps via a central IAM solution. Phishing-resistant factors such as FIDO2/WebAuthn are preferred over weaker methods such as SMS or TOTP. In this context, it SHOULD be ensured that any required sensors or interfaces are available in all devices used. Additionally, for biometric methods, it SHOULD be considered how resistant the authentication is to potential spoofing attempts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All apps are connected via SAML or OIDC to a central IAM solution that enforces MFA policies. The procurement of devices and security keys is aligned with FIDO2 compatibility. Only biometric methods that exhibit high resistance to attacks (e.g., through liveness detection) are permitted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the central IAM solution and the connection of the apps. They verify that phishing-resistant methods are prioritized. The procurement policies for devices are checked for the requirement of compatible sensors (FIDO2, secure biometrics).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Context- and risk-based adaptive multi-factor authentication is implemented. The required authentication strength (e.g., password, biometrics, FIDO2 key) dynamically adapts to risk signals such as user location, device security status (posture), network, or time of day. Authentication is, wherever possible, bound to the device's hardware (e.g., Secure Enclave, TPM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The central IAM solution collects signals from the MDM/MTD solution (e.g., is the device compromised?), from geolocation services, and behavioral analytics. Based on these signals and a real-time risk assessment, the user is either seamlessly logged in (Single Sign-On), prompted to enter an additional factor (Step-up Authentication), or access is blocked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the adaptive authentication policies in the IAM solution. Various scenarios are tested (e.g., logging in from an unknown network, from a non-compliant device) to verify that the system correctly adjusts the authentication requirements. The logs are analyzed for successful and failed adaptive authentication attempts.

controls.title: Conducting penetration tests for apps

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No penetration tests are conducted for mobile apps. The security of the apps is not systematically reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Security vulnerabilities in apps or their associated backend systems remain undiscovered and can be exploited by attackers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for reports of penetration tests for mobile applications and finds that none are available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automated vulnerability scans are occasionally performed for the most important in-house developed apps. Manual penetration tests do not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An automated scanner (SAST or DAST) is irregularly applied to the code or the running application. The results are passed on to the developers, but remediation is not systematically tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the reports of the vulnerability scans and finds that they are performed irregularly and not for all relevant apps. There is no process for remediating the found vulnerabilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy requires that a manual penetration test be performed for all in-house developed and other apps classified as high-risk before their initial deployment. The test scope is defined and includes the app itself as well as its primary backend interfaces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before a major release, an external service provider is commissioned to conduct a penetration test. The results are recorded in a report, and critical vulnerabilities must be remediated before release.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy for penetration tests. For a selection of high-risk apps, the test reports and the evidence of remediation for the found critical vulnerabilities are requested and reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before an app is approved for use, a penetration test SHOULD be performed. All communication interfaces to backend systems and the local storage of data SHOULD be examined for potential security vulnerabilities. The penetration tests SHOULD be repeated regularly and also for major changes to the app. For procured apps, a current test report from the manufacturer is requested and evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Penetration tests are a fixed milestone (Quality Gate) in the release process for all major app versions. The test scope is explicitly defined to include local data storage, inter-app communication interfaces, and all backend dependencies. The results are recorded in a ticketing system and their remediation is tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that penetration tests are anchored as a fixed component in the documented release process. They check the test reports for completeness of the scope and analyze in the ticketing system whether all critical and high findings were addressed before the release was approved.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A continuous security testing program is established, combining automated static and dynamic analysis (SAST/DAST) in the CI/CD pipeline with regular, in-depth manual penetration tests by an internal or external Red Team. The program is supplemented by a public or private bug bounty program to leverage the knowledge of external security experts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SAST and DAST tools are fully integrated into the development pipelines and block builds with new critical vulnerabilities. A dedicated Red Team regularly conducts unsolicited attack attempts. External researchers are invited via a bug bounty platform to report vulnerabilities for a reward. All findings are tracked centrally in a vulnerability management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the security tools in the CI/CD pipeline. They review the reports of the Red Team and the submissions from the bug bounty program. In the vulnerability management system, the entire lifecycle from discovery to remediation of a vulnerability is tracked to assess the effectiveness of the overall program.

controls.title: Mobile Application Management

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No solution for Mobile Device or Application Management is used. The configuration of apps is done entirely manually by the users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users must manually enter server addresses, usernames, and other settings into each app. This is error-prone and leads to inconsistent configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and examination of devices that no central management solution is in use and all app configurations are done manually.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An MDM solution is used to distribute apps via an internal app store and to enforce device-wide policies (e.g., password complexity). However, the configuration within the apps is still done manually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM is used to push apps to the devices, but the 'Managed App Configuration' features are not used. Users receive instructions on how to configure the apps after installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the MDM configuration and determines that it is used for app distribution, but not for app configuration. The existence of manual configuration guides is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Mobile Application Management (MAM) solution is used to centrally define basic configurations for some important enterprise apps. This typically includes settings such as email server or account names.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For apps that support the 'AppConfig Community' standard or a proprietary configuration method, configuration profiles are created in the MAM system and distributed to the devices. Not all apps and not all settings are managed in this way.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks in the MAM system for which apps configuration profiles exist. On a test device, it is verified that a managed app is automatically configured with the centrally predefined settings after installation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If possible, Mobile Application Management SHOULD be used for the central configuration of corporate apps. The MAM solution is used systematically to centrally distribute all relevant configurations for all managed apps. This eliminates the need for manual setup by users and ensures a consistent and correct configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All procured or developed apps must support central configuration via MAM (e.g., via AppConfig). For each app, a complete configuration profile is maintained in the MAM system and distributed to the corresponding user groups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the procurement policies for apps list support for Managed App Configuration as a mandatory criterion. In the MAM system, they check that configuration profiles exist for all corporate apps and that these cover all necessary settings. The command `adb logcat | grep 'ManagedAppConfig'` can be used on Android devices for troubleshooting the application of configurations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MAM solution is fully integrated into the central Identity and Access Management (IAM) system and other corporate systems. App configurations are dynamically generated and provisioned based on user roles, group memberships, and other attributes from the IAM. The system can remotely update configurations and selectively delete app data (app-wipe) without affecting the rest of the device, enabling secure BYOD scenarios.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MAM system uses variables in the configuration profiles that are populated at runtime with values from the IAM system (e.g., email address, username). Changes to a user's role in the IAM automatically trigger an update of the app configurations on the device. The 'app-wipe' function is integrated into the offboarding process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of dynamic variables and the IAM connection in the MAM system. A test case is conducted where a user role is changed in the IAM, and it is verified that the app configuration on the test device adapts automatically. The successful execution of a selective app-wipe is also tested.

controls.title: Creation of a Security Policy for Directory Services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only informal or incomplete notes on the security aspects of the directory service exist. A formal, binding security policy is completely missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, security decisions are made ad-hoc. There is no central directive, which leads to inconsistent and insecure configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security policy for directory services. It can be determined that no such document exists or that existing notes are fragmentary and not established as an official policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic security policy exists, but it only covers essential aspects such as password complexity and fundamental access rules. It is not aligned with other overarching concepts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A first version of a policy is created and communicated. It serves as basic guidance for administrators but leaves many detailed questions and integration aspects open.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing security policy. It is checked whether the most fundamental security requirements are covered. A comparison with the institution's overarching security concept will reveal a lack of alignment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal security policy for the directory service MUST be created. This policy defines the fundamental security requirements, responsibilities, and rules of use for the directory service.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy is adopted as an official document and communicated to all relevant staff (administrators, users). It forms the binding basis for all configuration and usage decisions regarding the directory service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the adopted security policy for the directory service presented. It is checked whether the document is formally valid and whether it covers the essential regulatory areas (e.g., data structure, access permissions, secure connection).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The created security policy SHOULD be aligned with the overarching security concept of the entire institution. The policy is reviewed regularly, for example annually, and adapted to new circumstances as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy is actively coordinated with the Information Security Officer (ISO) and other relevant bodies to avoid contradictions and create synergies. A process for the regular review and update of the policy is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies by inspecting logs and documents that the security policy is aligned with the overarching security concept. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that a process for the regular review of the policy exists and is being carried out.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is fully integrated into the institution's ISMS. Compliance with essential configuration requirements from the policy is automatically monitored and enforced by technical means (Policy-as-Code). Deviations lead to automated alerts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Configuration management tools or specialized security software are used to continuously reconcile the directory service configuration with the policy's requirements. A formal change management process ensures that all changes are policy-compliant.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the monitoring tools and the generated reports and alerts. It is verified that the automated check covers the critical aspects of the security policy and that deviations are responded to appropriately. This can be checked automatically by executing scripts such as `Get-ADReplicationUpdVector -Target 'domain-controller.example.com' | Test-AgainstPolicy -PolicyFile 'policy.json'`.

controls.title: Planning the Deployment of Directory Services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The directory service is deployed ad-hoc and without structured planning to meet an immediate requirement. Aspects such as a long-term schema, compatibility, or a well-thought-out authorization concept are not considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, the service is installed with default settings. This often leads to an uncontrolled sprawl of objects and attributes, as well as insecure default permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for planning documents, a schema concept, and an authorization concept. It can be determined that none of these documents exist and the deployment was purely reactive.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic planning takes place, primarily focusing on technical commissioning and basic functionality. An initial schema and a simple authorization concept exist but are not tailored in detail to the specific use cases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A plan is created that covers server installation and network integration. The schema is only minimally adapted, and the authorization concept is often based on broad groups like 'all users'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning documents. It is noted that a technical plan exists, but an in-depth analysis of protection needs, data structure, and access requirements is missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The deployment of directory services MUST be carefully planned. This includes defining the specific use, ensuring compatibility with connected applications, developing a concept for the structure of object classes and attribute types, and creating a needs-based authorization concept. When processing personal data, staff representation and data protection officers MUST be involved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal planning document is created. This document describes the 'what' (data used, schema), the 'who' (authorization concept), and the 'how' (compatibility, technical implementation). The involvement of data protection and staff representation is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the planning, schema, and authorization concept presented. It is verified that these documents exist, are aligned with each other, and cover the requirements of the various use cases. In addition, the proof of involvement of data protection and staff representation is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In general, the planned directory service structure SHOULD be fully documented, and the documentation should be kept up-to-date when changes are made. Measures SHOULD be planned and implemented to prevent unauthorized data harvesting from the directory service (e.g., by restricting search queries).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The schema and authorization documentation is maintained in a configuration management system (CMS) or a wiki. In the authorization concept, specific measures such as limiting the number of objects returned per query are implemented to hinder mass exports.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the current state of the directory service with the documentation to assess its up-to-dateness. The directory service configuration is checked for implemented protective measures against data harvesting (e.g., LDAP policies).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process is fully integrated into the institution's IT lifecycle and requirements management. The schema and authorization concept are regularly reviewed for optimization potential and new threats. The planning explicitly considers scenarios for scalability, high availability, and future integrations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Planning is supported by modeling tools. Changes to the schema or authorization concept go through a formal approval process. Regular capacity and security analyses proactively flow into the further development of the service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the IT lifecycle management processes and verifies that the directory service is firmly embedded within them. Logs from regular reviews of the schema and the authorization concept are checked. The existence of documented scalability and emergency concepts is verified.

controls.title: Setting up Access Permissions for Directory Services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no clear separation between the administration of the service (e.g., schema changes) and the management of the data (e.g., creating users). Administrators often have blanket, far-reaching rights for all tasks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Frequently, only the built-in 'Administrator' or 'Domain Admin' account is used for all activities. This violates the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the memberships of the administrative groups in the directory service. It is found that the same accounts can be used for both technical administration tasks and data maintenance.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fundamental separation of administrative tasks is planned, e.g., through separate groups. However, this separation is not consistently enforced technically or regularly reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Different admin groups are set up (e.g., 'Schema Admins', 'User Admins'), but for convenience, the same people are often members of multiple groups, which negates the separation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the definition of administrative roles and compares them with the actual group memberships. Overlaps and unnecessary permissions are identified that contradict the principle of segregation of duties.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The administration of the directory service itself (e.g., configuration, schema) and the actual management of the data it contains (e.g., creating user entries) MUST be separated. In the event of a merger of multiple directory service trees, the resulting effective permissions MUST be controlled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separate administrative roles and groups with different, clearly defined permissions are implemented (Role-Based Access Control). Before merging directory services, a 'what-if' analysis of permissions is performed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the technical implementation of segregation of duties by analyzing the Access Control Lists (ACLs) on the configuration and data partitions of the directory service. In the case of mergers, the planning documents and the results of the permission control are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administrative areas of responsibility and the associated permissions SHOULD be sufficiently documented. The assignment of permissions consistently follows the need-to-know principle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed role and authorization concept is recorded in writing and kept up to date. Each permission assignment is checked for its necessity and justified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the roles documented in the authorization concept with the actual implementation in the directory service. On a random basis, permissions of administrators are checked to see if they correspond to the minimum required scope.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The separation of administrative roles is enforced by technical means, such as Privileged Access Management (PAM) systems. An automated process exists for the regular review and recertification of all administrative permissions. The analysis of effective rights is performed automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM system is used to control, log, and grant administrative access on a temporary basis (Just-in-Time Administration). Tools for analyzing permissions are run regularly to detect configuration errors or privilege escalations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and logs of the PAM system. It is checked whether a regular recertification process for permissions has been established and the results are documented. Automated reports for the analysis of effective rights are inspected.

controls.title: Secure configuration and configuration changes of directory services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The directory service is installed and operated with the default settings. No specific hardening or secure configuration is performed. The configuration of the accessing clients is ignored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This often results in insecure protocols (e.g., unencrypted LDAP) or weak authentication methods remaining enabled and being used by clients.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration of the directory service with common hardening recommendations (e.g., from manufacturers or CIS Benchmarks). Significant deviations and insecure default settings are identified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The directory service server is fundamentally hardened, e.g., by deactivating obviously insecure protocols. However, the configuration of the clients is not systematically included and checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators follow a simple checklist for server hardening. However, it is not ensured that clients are also forced to use the secure configurations (e.g., through group policies).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies a basic hardening of the server but can demonstrate through an analysis of network traffic or client configurations that insecure access methods are still being used by clients.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The directory service MUST be configured securely. For the secure configuration of a directory service infrastructure, not only the server but also the clients (IT systems and applications) MUST be included.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration standard (hardening specification) is defined that applies to both servers and clients. Implementation on the clients is ensured, for example, through central configuration management tools or group policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the configuration standard and randomly checks both servers and clients for compliance. It is verified that the entire communication chain complies with the security requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secure configuration of the directory service and the clients is documented in a configuration management system. If the configuration is changed, users SHOULD be informed in a timely manner about any maintenance work and its effects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All configuration settings are versioned and stored in a CMDB or a Git repository. Changes go through a defined change management process, which also includes communication to users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and currency of the configuration documentation. Using examples from the recent past, the change management process, including user communication, is traced.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the secure configuration (Configuration Baseline) is continuously enforced and monitored on all servers and clients using automated tools (e.g., Security Configuration Management, Policy-as-Code). Deviations (Configuration Drift) are automatically detected and either corrected or reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Ansible, Puppet, Chef, or DSC are used to declaratively describe and enforce the configuration. Specialized security tools regularly scan the systems for conformity with the baseline and create reports.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the automation tools and the reports of the monitoring tools. It is verified that the monitoring is comprehensive and that detected deviations are responded to promptly and according to a defined process. An automated check could be a script that queries the configuration via an API and compares it against a 'golden image' configuration.

controls.title: Secure operation of directory services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security is only considered during the initial setup but is neglected during ongoing operation. Administration tools are not sufficiently protected against access by normal users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once configured, the system runs without regular security checks. File permissions on administration tools are often too lax, so curious users could run them.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to access administrative tools and their configuration files with a normal user account. It is found that this is possible in some places. There is a lack of evidence for regular security reviews.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to administration tools is generally restricted. However, the security of the operation is only checked reactively when problems occur, not proactively.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The basic security mechanisms are active, but there are no planned activities such as patch management reviews or authorization audits to maintain security in the long term.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that direct access to admin tools for normal users is blocked. However, no documents or logs can be presented that prove regular, proactive security maintenance activities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security of the directory service MUST be permanently maintained during operation. Access to all administration tools MUST be prevented for normal users. If the directory service is used to manage credentials, dedicated clients MUST be used for remote maintenance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Regular administrative tasks are defined to ensure security (e.g., monthly patch installation, quarterly permission review). Access to admin tools is prevented by restrictive file system and network permissions. Dedicated, hardened admin workstations or jump servers are used for remote maintenance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the technical measures for restricting access to admin tools. It is verified that a process for regular security maintenance exists and is followed. The existence and use of dedicated clients or jump servers for remote maintenance is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All policies, regulations, and processes concerning the operation of a directory service system SHOULD be comprehensibly documented and kept up to date.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Operating manuals and process descriptions are created for all regular security-relevant activities (e.g., patching, backup, monitoring, user provisioning). These documents are versioned and updated when changes are made.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the operational documentation and compares it with the activities actually performed. The timeliness and completeness of the documentation are assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure operation is supported by automated monitoring tools that detect and report security-relevant events (e.g., changes to admin groups), configuration deviations, and performance anomalies in real time. The entire operation and maintenance process is integrated into the ISMS and is regularly audited internally and externally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM system is connected to the directory service to analyze its logs. Automated configuration audits are performed daily. The results flow into the continuous improvement process (CIP) of the ISMS.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the SIEM system and the defined correlation rules for the directory service. Reports from automated audits and minutes from management reviews dealing with the security of the directory service are inspected.

controls.title: Securing vulnerable credentials

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to attributes containing sensitive credentials is insufficiently restricted. For example, authenticated users or standard administrator accounts can read this information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is often the case when the default permissions of the directory service are not adjusted, which can, for example, allow normal users to read password hashes (e.g., on older systems).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the effective permissions on attributes such as 'unicodePwd' (Active Directory) or 'userPassword'. It is found that accounts that do not require this information have read access.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to sensitive attributes is restricted, but the configuration is not regularly reviewed. It cannot be ruled out that other configuration changes may unintentionally create new vulnerabilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The permissions are initially set correctly, but there is no process to regularly validate this configuration. An ill-considered assignment of a group membership can undermine the protective measure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the permissions are fundamentally restrictive. However, it cannot be proven that this configuration is regularly checked for its effectiveness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For attributes that contain sensitive credentials such as passwords or their hashes, access MUST be strongly restricted. Only explicitly authorized system processes may access these attributes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Very restrictive Access Control Lists (ACLs) are defined on the corresponding attributes in the schema. These typically only allow the 'SYSTEM' account or the directory service process itself to have access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the ACLs on the critical attributes and verifies that no user or normal administrator accounts have read or write permissions on them. This can be checked using special query tools for directory services.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the restrictive ACLs, read and write access to these sensitive attributes is logged (Audit ACLs). The logs are collected centrally and regularly reviewed for unauthorized access attempts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Special System Access Control Lists (SACLs) are configured on the attributes to log success and failure events during access. These logs are forwarded to a central log management system for analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the SACLs and the configuration of the log management system. Samples from the logs are analyzed to ensure that access is correctly recorded and reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to sensitive attributes is not only logged, but also triggers automatic real-time alerts for unauthorized attempts or anomalous access patterns. Wherever possible, passwords are not stored directly, but strong, salted hashing methods are used, and storage is in a dedicated, hardened area of the directory or an external Hardware Security Module (HSM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The access logs are analyzed in real time by a SIEM system that is trained to detect suspicious activities (e.g., a process attempting to read all password hashes). For maximum security, the storage and verification of credentials are outsourced to a connected HSM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the SIEM and the alerting rules. The connection and use of an HSM is checked. As a test, an unauthorized access is attempted to verify the correct triggering of the alarm.

controls.title: Planning of partitioning in the directory service

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Partitioning is used, if at all, only for technical or performance reasons. Security aspects such as damage limitation or separate administration are not taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A large directory is arbitrarily divided to distribute the load across multiple servers, without the partitioning boundaries following a logical or security-related structure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the partitioning structure and finds that it does not follow any discernible security logic. There is no documentation that justifies the partitioning decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Partitioning is in place and roughly follows organizational boundaries. However, the exact effects on administration, delegation of rights, and damage limitation in the event of a failure have not been analyzed or documented in detail.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate partition (e.g., Organizational Unit) is created for each department. However, permissions are not delegated granularly per partition; instead, there are still central administrators for everything.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor recognizes a logical partitioning structure, but can determine by analyzing the permissions that the possibility of delegated administration is not being used and the damage limitation is therefore only minimal.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If partitioning is planned, it SHOULD be based on the protection goals of the directory service and support them appropriately. Partitioning SHOULD be planned in such a way that it limits the impact of security incidents, enables independent administration of different partitions, and follows organizational or security boundaries.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The partitioning strategy is designed as part of the security concept. For example, partitions are created for internal employees, external partners, and technical systems, each with different security policies and their own administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documents for the partitioning. It is analyzed whether the chosen structure demonstrably supports the stated goals (damage limitation, delegated administration, security boundaries). The technical implementation is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The partitioning strategy and the delegated administrative permissions are formally documented and reviewed and adjusted in case of organizational changes. Test scenarios are conducted to verify the effectiveness of damage limitation through partitioning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The partitioning and delegation structure is maintained in the CMDB or a wiki. As part of emergency drills, for example, the failure or compromise of one partition is simulated to test the impact on other partitions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the partitioning strategy and the logs of the emergency tests performed. It is checked whether the test results have led to an improvement of the concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Partitioning is part of a comprehensive security architecture in which different partitions have different security levels and are separated from each other by network segmentation with dedicated firewalls. The administration of the partitions is secured by multi-factor authentication and just-in-time privileges.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Partitions with high protection needs (e.g., for critical infrastructures) are placed in high-security network zones. Administrative access to these partitions requires logging in via a PAM system with MFA, which grants the necessary rights only for the duration of the task.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network architecture, the firewall rules between the segments hosting the partitions, and the configuration of the PAM system. It is verified that the separation is effective at both the directory service level and the network level.

controls.title: Suitable selection of components for directory services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of the directory service software is primarily based on personal preferences, costs, or familiarity, without a formal requirements catalog or a security assessment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The software that 'has always been used' or that is available for free as an open-source product is used, without checking whether it meets the specific security and functionality requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the requirements catalog and the evaluation documentation for the product selection. It can be determined that no such documents exist and the decision is not based on a comprehensible basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a requirements catalog, but it focuses mainly on functional aspects and compatibility with existing systems. Security requirements are only formulated in very general terms (e.g., 'must be secure').

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of features that the software must fulfill is created. Security aspects are only mentioned in passing and are not specified or evaluated in detail.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the requirements catalog and finds that functional requirements are detailed, while security requirements remain non-specific and did not play a decisive role in the selection process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the use of a directory service, suitable components SHOULD be identified. A requirements catalog SHOULD be created, taking into account APP.6 General Software, according to which the components for the directory service are selected and procured. As part of the planning and design of the directory service, security requirements appropriate to the intended use SHOULD be formulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal requirements catalog is created that contains both functional and specific security requirements tailored to the intended use (e.g., 'must support TLS 1.3', 'must allow delegated administration at the attribute level'). The selection is made based on this catalog.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the requirements catalog and the documentation of the selection process. It is verified that specific security requirements were defined and played a significant role in the selection decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In particular, the product selection SHOULD already take into account how further security requirements beyond the basic functions (e.g., connection of an HSM, fine-grained auditing) can be implemented using the respective component. The security assessment of the components also includes an analysis of known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and the manufacturer's update policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of a market analysis, various products are compared. This involves not only evaluating the current range of functions, but also the future viability and support for advanced security functions. The trustworthiness of the manufacturer and its handling of security vulnerabilities are included in the evaluation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the evaluation documents and determines that a structured market analysis was carried out. It is checked whether aspects such as expandability for future security requirements and the manufacturer's security practices were documented and evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The component selection is a formalized process that includes an in-depth security analysis in a test environment, possibly penetration tests of candidate products, and a life cycle analysis (support, end-of-life). The decision is made according to a weighted criteria catalog and is justified in detail.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Promising products are installed in a proof-of-concept (PoC) in the lab and tested for their security and functionality. The results of the PoC flow directly into the weighted criteria catalog, which forms the basis for the final decision.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the selection process, including the criteria catalog, the PoC test plans and results, and the final decision rationale. The thoroughness and traceability of the entire process are evaluated.

controls.title: Setup of access to directory services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The access configuration is inconsistent and deviates from the specifications of the security policy. A directory service exposed to the internet is not protected by a security gateway and is directly accessible from the internet.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access is often configured based on ad-hoc requests, leading to a confusing and inconsistent set of rules. Security risks from direct accessibility from the internet are ignored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a port scan from the internet and finds that the directory service port (e.g., 389, 636) is open. The analysis of the access control lists shows inconsistencies and deviations from the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access is fundamentally configured, but not regularly checked for compliance with the security policy. A security gateway is used for services accessible from the internet, but only with basic settings and without protocol-specific filtering.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The initial access controls are set up. However, there is no process for regular review and adjustment. The security gateway acts as a simple port forwarder without inspecting traffic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes that the access configurations exist, but can find no evidence of regular audits. The security gateway configuration is assessed as insufficient for effective protection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the directory service SHOULD be configured according to the security policy. If the directory service is used as a server on the internet, it SHOULD be protected accordingly by a security gateway (e.g., reverse proxy, application firewall).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The access control lists (ACLs) of the directory service are implemented exactly according to the specifications of the authorization concept and the security policy. A service accessible from the internet is mandatorily placed behind a dedicated and configured security gateway.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the implemented ACLs with the specifications from the security policy. The network architecture is analyzed to ensure that a security gateway is placed in front of internet-accessible services.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security gateway configuration is hardened and filters traffic specifically for the directory service protocol (e.g., LDAP filter). The directory service's own access configurations are audited regularly, e.g., annually, for conformity and necessity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security gateway is configured to only forward valid and permitted requests to the directory service and to block malicious requests. An annual process for reviewing all access permissions is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration details of the security gateway to verify the protocol-specific filtering. Records of the annual authorization audits are reviewed for completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The compliance of the access configuration with the policy is automatically and continuously monitored. The security gateway performs deep protocol inspection to detect and block attacks on the directory service and is integrated into a SIEM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Scripts or tools for Security Configuration Management are used, which trigger an alarm for any deviation from the target configuration of the ACLs. The upstream gateway is a Web Application Firewall (WAF) or a similar system that analyzes LDAP traffic for anomalies and attack patterns.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and reports of the automated monitoring tools. The configuration of the WAF and its connection to the SIEM system are checked. The response to a simulated attack on the directory service is tested.

controls.title: Monitoring of directory services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the basic availability of the directory service server is monitored (e.g., via ping). There is no specific logging of changes in the directory service or to its configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The monitoring system only checks if the server is reachable on the network. Important security-relevant events go unnoticed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the monitoring system and determines that no service-specific checks or log analyses are configured. Auditing is disabled in the directory service logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Although security-relevant changes are logged, the log files are only stored locally on the server and are only analyzed reactively in the event of specific incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Auditing is enabled on the directory service server. However, there is no process for central collection and proactive, regular evaluation of the log data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that auditing is enabled on the server. However, it cannot be proven that the generated logs are regularly backed up and evaluated. Often, the logs are already overwritten after a short time.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Directory services SHOULD be monitored and logged together with the server on which they are operated. In particular, changes within the directory service (e.g., to administrative groups) as well as configuration changes of the directory service SHOULD be logged with priority.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Auditing is configured to capture all security-critical events. This includes changes to permissions, group memberships, the schema, and the service configuration. The log data is sent to a central log management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the audit configuration of the directory service to ensure that all relevant events are logged. It is verified that the logs are collected centrally and in a tamper-proof manner.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The centrally collected log data is regularly (e.g., weekly) checked for anomalies and unauthorized changes. Thresholds are defined for important performance indicators and security-relevant events, and exceeding them triggers a notification to the administrators.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Dashboards and searches are set up in the log management system to visualize the relevant events. Notification rules are configured, e.g., 'Alert when a user is added to an administrator group'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the log management system, especially the dashboards and alerting rules. Records of the regular evaluations and the response to past alarms are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The monitoring is automated and integrated into a central SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system. Predefined correlation rules analyze events from the directory service in the context of other system and network events and automatically trigger alarms or even countermeasures in case of suspicious patterns (e.g., signs of a 'Pass-the-Hash' attack).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized SIEM use cases for directory services are implemented. These detect complex attack chains that span multiple systems. For critical alarms, a affected user account can be automatically locked, for example.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the SIEM correlation rules for the directory service. The effectiveness of the rules is assessed by analyzing past security incidents or by simulated attacks. The integration with SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) platforms is checked.

controls.title: Securing communication with directory services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Encryption of communication is not consistently enforced. Sensitive data, especially login credentials in a simple authentication, can be transmitted in plain text over the network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Older applications or incorrectly configured clients use unencrypted protocols (e.g., LDAP instead of LDAPS). The server is configured to accept these insecure connections.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network traffic to the directory service server with a sniffer (e.g., Wireshark). It is determined that unencrypted requests with sensitive data are being sent. An automated check can be performed by scanning the LDAP port 389.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Although encryption is generally enabled (e.g., LDAPS), insecure protocol versions (e.g., SSLv3, TLS 1.0) or weak encryption algorithms (cipher suites) are permitted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For compatibility reasons with outdated clients, the server configuration is not restricted to modern, secure standards. This makes the encryption vulnerable to known attacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses a security tool (e.g., 'testssl.sh', 'nmap' with SSL scripts) to analyze the protocol versions and cipher suites offered by the server. Outdated and insecure configurations are identified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If confidential information is transmitted, the entire communication with the directory service SHOULD be encrypted using a secure protocol in accordance with the BSI's Technical Guideline TR-02102 (e.g., TLS). The data exchange between the client and the directory service server SHOULD be secured. It SHOULD be defined which data may be accessed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The directory service server is configured to only accept connections with strong, current encryption protocols (e.g., TLS 1.2 or higher) and secure cipher suites. Unencrypted access is disabled. Clients are configured accordingly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the server configuration regarding the allowed TLS versions and cipher suites. It is checked whether unencrypted ports are disabled or no longer accept requests. The client configuration is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Encryption is enforced for all communication, even if no obviously confidential data is transmitted. The server and optionally also the client certificates are managed via an internal, trusted Public Key Infrastructure (PKI).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All clients are configured to mandatorily use TLS for every connection. An internal PKI is set up and used to ensure the authenticity of the communication partners and to avoid warnings about self-signed certificates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that all clients communicate exclusively in encrypted form. The processes and configuration of the internal PKI are audited to ensure their trustworthiness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the encryption policy (e.g., only TLS 1.3 with strong cipher suites) is continuously monitored by automated scans. In addition to transport encryption, sensitive data is encrypted at the application level (e.g., individual attributes) to ensure end-to-end security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Regular automated vulnerability scans check the TLS configuration of all directory service servers. For particularly sensitive data, client-side encryption libraries are used so that the data is already stored encrypted in the directory service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports from the automated configuration scans. The implementation of application-side encryption is verified by analyzing the network traffic and the data stored in the directory.

controls.title: Controlled decommissioning of a directory service

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The directory service is simply shut down. No planned data migration, archiving, or deletion takes place. Dependent systems and users are not informed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This leads to data loss and failures of applications that were still expecting the service. Orphaned data on the servers poses a security risk.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that a service is no longer available, but dependent systems are producing error messages. There is no documentation or communication regarding the decommissioning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic decommissioning plan. However, the deletion of data is not verified and communication to users is incomplete or too late.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The most important data is migrated, but it is not ensured that all data on the old systems is securely deleted. The information about the shutdown does not reach all affected parties.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the decommissioning plan but cannot find any evidence of verified, secure deletion of the old data. Interviews with users show that communication was inadequate.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When decommissioning the directory service, it SHOULD be ensured that required permissions and information remain available to a sufficient extent (e.g., through migration). All other permissions and information SHOULD be deleted. Additionally, users SHOULD be informed. When decommissioning individual partitions, care SHOULD be taken to ensure that other partitions are not affected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed decommissioning plan is created. This includes an analysis of dependencies, a data migration and deletion plan, and a communication plan. The implementation is carefully monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the decommissioning plan and checks its completeness. It is verified that all steps of the plan, especially data migration, deletion, and communication, have been documented and carried out.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decommissioning process is formally documented and includes a checklist for all activities to be performed. The secure deletion of data from the old systems is verifiably verified and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard operating procedure (SOP) for the decommissioning of IT systems is applied. Data deletion is confirmed by a deletion log, which contains, for example, the serial numbers of the data carriers and the deletion method used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the applied SOP and the deletion log. The traceability and completeness of the entire process is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decommissioning is a largely automated process. Tools analyze dependencies on other systems to prevent failures. Data migration is controlled by scripts, and the secure deletion of data is carried out according to cryptographic standards and is certified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Discovery tools are used to identify all connected clients and applications. Data is migrated with tools that perform an integrity check. For the data carriers, a process of cryptographic erasure (crypto-shredding) or physical destruction by a certified service provider is used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports from the discovery tools and the automation scripts for the migration. The certificates for the secure data deletion or destruction of the data carriers are checked.

controls.title: Migration of directory services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration is carried out without a detailed concept ('Lift and Shift'). Problems with permissions, the schema, or local caches on clients are only addressed reactively after the migration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Data is exported and imported into the new system without considering the different structures. This leads to malfunctions and security vulnerabilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the migration concept and finds that none exists. Based on incident tickets after the migration, it can be traced which problems occurred due to the lack of planning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A migration concept exists, but it is incomplete. It focuses on pure data transfer and neglects complex aspects such as the transformation of permission structures or handling of local caches.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A plan for the data transfer is available. The 'soft' factors, such as adapting client configurations or redesigning permission groups, are not adequately planned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the migration concept and identifies gaps related to permissions, schema adjustments, and client handling. It is determined that these aspects have not been systematically addressed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For a planned migration of directory services, a migration concept SHOULD be created in advance. This SHOULD consider whether the permission management of the old and new directory service works analogously. Schema changes SHOULD be analyzed and documented. Far-reaching permissions granted temporarily for the migration SHOULD be revoked afterwards. It SHOULD be considered that IT systems accessing the directory service may have local caches whose update must be initiated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A comprehensive migration concept is created that covers the following points: analysis and mapping of schema and permissions, a plan for handling client caches, a plan for temporary permission granting and their revocation. The migration is carried out according to this plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the migration concept and assesses its completeness. It is checked whether all steps mentioned in the concept, especially the analysis, documentation, and revocation of temporary rights, have been verifiably carried out.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire migration is fully tested in an isolated test environment ('Dry Run') before being carried out in the production system. The migration concept includes a detailed and also tested rollback plan in case of failure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A copy of the production system is restored in a test environment. The migration is carried out there according to the plan to identify unforeseen problems and to estimate the time required. The rollback plan is also tested in the test environment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the test run and the rollback test. It is assessed whether the findings from the test have led to an improvement of the final migration plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration process is largely automated. After the migration, automated test scripts are executed to fully verify data integrity, the correct functioning of permissions, and the connectivity of all dependent systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Data extraction, transformation, and loading (ETL) is automated by scripts. After the 'go-live', a test framework automatically runs a series of checks (e.g., login attempts with test users, queries from applications, verification of permissions).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automation scripts for the migration and the test suites for the verification. The test logs are reviewed to confirm the successful verification of all critical functions after the migration.

controls.title: Planning a replication in the directory service

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Replication is set up without a clear strategy. Often, the entire directory tree is unnecessarily replicated to all instances (full-mesh replication), even if this is not required.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For convenience, all servers are made replication partners, which can lead to high network load and complex error patterns in case of failures.

parts.name: assessment-method
