parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the replication topology and finds that it is not tailored to the actual requirements (e.g., load balancing for a specific application). There is no documentation that justifies the chosen topology.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A replication topology is chosen but not optimally aligned with the defined goal. The impact on network bandwidth is not sufficiently planned, which can lead to replication delays.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A topology (e.g., hub-and-spoke) is chosen, but the bandwidth of the connections, especially to remote offices, is not considered. This leads to changes arriving there only with a long delay.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the chosen topology with regard to the defined goal and the network infrastructure. By analyzing the replication status (e.g., replication latency), bottlenecks and planning deficiencies are uncovered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each replication, the goal (e.g., load balancing, fault tolerance) it pursues MUST be defined. For this purpose, a replication topology and strategy SHOULD be chosen that match the goal or use case. For replications that do not serve the high availability of the service, the replicated content of the directory service MUST be limited to the required objects. Sufficient bandwidth SHOULD be ensured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the planning concept, the goal, topology (e.g., ring, star), strategy (e.g., push, pull), and scope (e.g., only a specific partition) are defined for each replication relationship. The bandwidth requirements are calculated and considered in the network planning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documentation for the replication. It is checked whether the implementation corresponds to the documentation and whether the assumptions made therein (e.g., regarding bandwidth) are plausible and apply in practice.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The replication topology and strategy are formally documented. Replication latency and error rate are actively monitored. There are defined procedures for handling replication conflicts or prolonged replication errors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The monitoring system monitors the status of all replication links and alerts when thresholds are exceeded. The operating manual describes how to resolve manual replication conflicts or repair a faulty replication link.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation and the configuration of the monitoring system. It is checked whether procedures for handling replication problems exist and whether the personnel is trained in their application.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The replication topology is designed to be redundant (e.g., through multiple replication paths) to withstand the failure of individual replication partners or network connections. The integrity of the replicated data is regularly verified by automated consistency checks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A fault-tolerant replication topology is implemented, e.g., through bridgehead servers in each location that are fully meshed with each other. Nightly scripts run that create checksums over partitions and compare them on all replicas to detect silent data corruption.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the replication topology for its fault tolerance. The scripts for consistency checks and their logs are analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of the integrity verification.

controls.title: Handling anonymous access to directory services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Anonymous access is permitted directly on the directory service. There is no distinction between authenticated and anonymous users, which facilitates information gathering.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default setting of many directory services to allow anonymous requests is retained. This poses a significant security risk, as attackers can scout the internal structure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to send an anonymous LDAP request (anonymous bind) to the directory service. If this succeeds, the requirement is not met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Anonymous access is disabled on the directory service itself. Where it is needed, a proxy service is used, but the associated proxy user account has overly broad permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A reverse proxy is placed in front. However, the account used by the proxy for queries is, for example, a normal user account that can see more than would be necessary for the anonymous function.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that direct anonymous access is blocked. Afterwards, the permissions of the proxy user account are analyzed and found not to follow the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If anonymous users are to be granted access to individual sub-areas of the directory tree, a proxy service SHOULD be placed in front of it. This proxy service SHOULD access the actual directory service via a separate account, a so-called proxy user. The access rights for this proxy user SHOULD be assigned sufficiently restrictively. They SHOULD also be completely revoked when the account is no longer needed. To prevent sensitive information from being accidentally disclosed, the search function of the directory service SHOULD be appropriately restricted for the intended purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An LDAP proxy or a reverse proxy is implemented. A dedicated service account ('proxy user') is created, whose rights are minimally restricted to the required objects and attributes. The search function is configured so that, for example, only certain attributes can be searched for and the result set is limited.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture and verifies the use of a proxy service. The permissions of the proxy user account and the configuration of the search function are checked for their restrictiveness. It is checked whether processes for revoking no longer needed accounts exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the proxy service and the permissions of the proxy user are formally documented and regularly reviewed. All access via the proxy is logged and evaluated for suspicious activities (e.g., high query rates).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration is maintained in the CMDB. The logs of the proxy service are sent to the central log management and reports on usage are generated. In case of irregularities, the administrators are notified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration documentation and the logs of access via the proxy. The effectiveness of the log evaluation is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The proxy service is hardened and has advanced protection mechanisms such as rate limiting and query complexity analysis to actively prevent DoS attacks and excessive data collection (scraping). Suspicious activities trigger automatic defense measures, e.g., temporarily blocking the source IP address.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) or a specialized LDAP gateway with security functions is used as a proxy. Rules are configured on it that, for example, block more than 100 requests per minute from one IP address.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the advanced security functions on the proxy service. A simulated scraping attack is used to test whether the protection mechanisms work as expected and the defense measures are triggered.

controls.title: Creation of a contingency plan for the failure of a directory service

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no documented plans or procedures for the event of a failure. The reliance is on administrators improvising in an emergency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In an emergency, uncoordinated actions occur, which prolongs downtime and increases the risk of data loss or misconfigurations during recovery.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the contingency plan for the directory service and finds that no such document exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic contingency plan exists, but it only focuses on the total failure of the service (disaster recovery). Partial failures, data corruption, or the recovery of individual objects are not covered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A plan for restoring the entire service from a backup is available. However, there are no instructions for more frequent, minor disruptions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contingency plan and finds that it only covers a single scenario (total failure) and provides no assistance for other incidents.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of emergency preparedness, there SHOULD be a needs-based contingency plan for directory services. For the failure of important directory service systems, contingency plans SHOULD be in place that define restart procedures and responsibilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Contingency plans are created for various plausible scenarios (e.g., server failure, deletion of an important organizational unit, database corruption). These plans contain step-by-step instructions, contact lists, and defined recovery objectives (RTO/RPO).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the contingency plans for the directory service and assesses whether they cover the relevant scenarios and whether the instructions contained therein are clear and feasible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All emergency procedures for the entire system configuration of the directory service components SHOULD be documented. The contingency plans are tested regularly, e.g., annually, in practical exercises, and the results are used to improve the plans.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The contingency plans are part of a comprehensive operations manual. Emergency drills are scheduled annually, during which recovery is practiced in a test environment. Lessons-learned workshops after the drills lead to concrete adjustments of the plans.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the contingency plans and the logs of the emergency drills performed. It is assessed whether the tests were meaningful and whether the resulting potential for improvement has been implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The contingency plans are fully integrated into the institution's overall Business Continuity Management (BCM). Recovery processes are largely automated to minimize recovery times (RTO). The plans cover a variety of scenarios, including targeted cyberattacks such as ransomware with data manipulation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The recovery of the directory service is part of the orchestrated recovery plans of the entire IT. Automated scripts perform the failover to a redundant system or the recovery from backup. Special plans exist for responding to cyberattacks, which also include forensics and the cleanup of compromised data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the BCM documentation and the automation scripts for recovery. The existence and plausibility of the plans for cyber emergencies are checked. The results of enterprise-wide BCM tests that include the directory service are evaluated.

controls.title: Securing replication

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Replication traffic occurs unencrypted in the internal network. Authentication of the replication partners does not take place or only with weak, shared secrets.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The reliance is on the assumption that the internal network is 'secure'. This allows attackers on the internal network to intercept or manipulate the replication data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network traffic between two replication partners with a sniffer and determines that the data is transmitted unencrypted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The replication traffic is encrypted via the service's own protocol (e.g., LDAPS). However, the authentication of the replication partners is only done with simple, static credentials (username/password).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default encryption function of the directory service is activated. However, the passwords used for replication are weak, are rarely changed, and are potentially the same on multiple systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the activation of transport encryption. However, the security of the authentication method is assessed as insufficient, e.g., by checking the password policies for replication accounts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The replication of confidential content is secured at the transport layer by a strong, compliant protocol such as TLS 1.2 or higher. Strong authentication methods are used for authentication in the context of replication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The directory service is configured to enforce the use of TLS with secure cipher suites for replication. Instead of passwords, stronger methods such as Kerberos or other challenge-response mechanisms are used for partner authentication.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the replication connections and verifies the use of strong encryption and authentication. This can be done by configuration review and analysis of the connection setup in the network.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Replications of confidential content SHOULD be secured by, for example, IPsec at the network layer in addition to encryption at the application or transport layer. For authentication, the strongest possible authentication methods, such as certificate-based authentication, SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the service's TLS encryption, all network traffic between the replication partners is protected by an IPsec tunnel (Defense-in-Depth). The authenticity of the partners is ensured by machine certificates from a trusted PKI.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the IPsec policies on the involved servers. In addition, the configuration of the certificate-based authentication for the replication is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Replication is secured by a combination of IPsec (transport mode) and TLS. The certificates used for authentication are stored on Hardware Security Modules (HSM) or Trusted Platform Modules (TPM) to prevent their compromise. Replication traffic is monitored for anomalies to detect attacks such as manipulation or replay attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The private keys of the machine certificates never leave the TPM/HSM of the servers. An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) on the network monitors the replication traffic for unusual patterns or deviations from the protocol standard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the use of TPM/HSM for key storage by querying the cryptography providers on the systems. The configuration and the alarms of the IDS regarding the replication traffic are analyzed.

controls.title: High availability of the directory service

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are multiple instances of the directory service, but no well-thought-out high availability strategy. This can lead to inconsistencies ('split-brain') or to inconsistent read results during network partitions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Multiple servers are configured as masters without a mechanism for conflict resolution or to ensure consistency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and determines that an unsuitable replication topology has been chosen for high availability. It cannot be proven how the system reacts to the failure of a node or a network connection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic high availability solution (e.g., a simple master-replica configuration) is implemented. However, the behavior in more complex failure scenarios, such as network partitions ('split-brain'), is not fully defined and tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A failover mechanism is in place, but it is purely reactive. There are no precautions to prevent both sides from considering themselves the new master in the event of a network partition.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes the existence of a basic HA solution. However, analysis of the concept reveals gaps in handling network partitioning scenarios.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An appropriate high availability strategy SHOULD be chosen. A decision SHOULD be made as to whether a master-master or master-replica replication is more suitable. The decision is made based on the specific requirements for consistency and availability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the security or operational concept, a deliberate and justified decision is made for a high availability architecture. This is implemented in accordance with manufacturer specifications and best practices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation for the chosen high availability strategy and checks the justification for the decision made. The implementation is checked for conformity with the chosen strategy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The chosen high availability strategy explicitly considers constraints such as distributed locations and the defined behavior in case of data inconsistencies. The functionality of the high availability, especially the failover mechanism, is regularly checked through planned tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The architecture is designed to function robustly even with slow or unstable WAN connections. Regular failover tests are conducted during maintenance windows to verify the automatic switchover and measure the switchover time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the HA concept for its consideration of specific constraints. The logs of the regular failover tests are reviewed and evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A highly available, geographically redundant architecture is implemented (e.g., multi-master replication across multiple data centers with quorum mechanisms). The system has automatic failover mechanisms and mechanisms for automatic inconsistency resolution. The end-to-end availability of the service is continuously monitored through synthetic monitoring.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The directory service servers are distributed across multiple, geographically separate data centers. A quorum witness (e.g., in a third location or in the cloud) ensures that a split-brain scenario does not occur in the event of a network partition between the main locations. Monitoring probes continuously perform login and query transactions to measure the actual availability from a user perspective.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the geographically distributed architecture and the configuration of the quorum mechanisms. The configuration and the results of the synthetic monitoring are checked. The system's reaction to a simulated failure of a complete data center is evaluated as part of a BCM test.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
A directory service provides information about arbitrary objects in a defined manner within a data network. An object can store associated attributes; for example, an identifier can be associated with the user's first and last name, personnel number, and the name of the IT system. This data can then be used equally by various applications. The directory service and its data are typically managed from a central location.
Some typical application areas for directory services are:
• Management of address books, e.g., for telephone numbers, email addresses, and certificates for electronic signatures
• User management, e.g., for managing accounts and permissions
• Provision of a backend service for authentication functions, e.g., for logging into operating systems or applications
Directory services are optimized for read access, as data from the directory service is typically retrieved most of the time. Write access, where entries are created, modified, or deleted, is less frequently required.
When a directory service is used, some administrative tasks within the network, such as account creation, password changes, and assignment of roles and groups, can be performed centrally.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to securely operate general directory services and to adequately protect the information processed with them.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
Module APP.2.1 General Directory Service is to be applied to all directory services in use.
This module considers general security aspects of directory services, regardless of the product used. For product-specific security aspects, there are other modules in the IT-Grundschutz Compendium that must also be applied to the respective directory service. Modules for server operating systems on which directory services are usually run are listed in the SYS.1 Server layer of the IT-Grundschutz Compendium. Basic requirements for software products can be found in APP.6 General Software and are also to be considered.
Directory services should generally be considered within the scope of modules ORP.4 Identity and Access Management, OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management, CON.3 Data Backup Concept, OPS.1.2.2 Archiving, OPS.1.1.5 Logging, OPS.1.2.5 Remote Maintenance, and OPS.1.1.2 Proper IT Administration.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Lack of or insufficient planning for the use of directory services
parts.prose: The security of directory services relies heavily on the security of the base operating system, especially file system security. Directory services can be installed and operated on many operating systems, which can result in a wide variety of security settings to be configured. This diversity increases the planning requirements and presupposes appropriate knowledge of the respective operating system. If the resulting overall solution is very heterogeneous or complex, insufficiently planned deployment of the directory service in live operation can lead to security vulnerabilities.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Incorrect or insufficient planning of partitioning and replication in the directory service
parts.prose: Partitioning allows the directory data of a directory service to be divided into individual sections (partitions). To ensure better load balancing, partitions of the directory service are often replicated to other instances. In addition, the redundant data storage improves fault tolerance and thus increases availability. Suitable planning is therefore of crucial importance here as well, since partition and replication settings can be changed later, but this can cause problems. It can lead to data loss and inconsistencies in data storage, poor availability of the directory service, and overall poor system performance, up to and including failures.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Incorrect administration of access and access rights
parts.prose: Access rights to an IT system and access rights to stored data and IT applications may only be granted to the extent necessary to perform the required tasks. This also applies to the permissions granted to users and groups managed via a directory service, even if these apply to the information in the directory service itself. If these rights are administered incorrectly, on the one hand, operations can be disrupted if necessary rights have not been assigned. On the other hand, security vulnerabilities can arise if rights are granted beyond what is necessary. If the access rights in the directory service are assigned incorrectly or inconsistently, the security of the entire system is significantly endangered. Administrative rights are also a particularly critical point. If these rights are assigned incorrectly, the entire administration concept can be undermined or, in some circumstances, even the administration of the directory system itself can be prevented or unauthorized use can be enabled.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Incorrect configuration of access to directory services
parts.prose: In many cases, other applications such as internet or intranet applications must access the directory service. A misconfiguration can lead to incorrect assignment of access rights. It can also happen that the directory service can be accessed without authorization or that authentication data is transmitted in cleartext. In this case, information can be snooped during transmission.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Failure of directory services
parts.prose: Due to technical failure caused by hardware or software problems, directory services or parts thereof may fail. As a result, the data in the directory is temporarily inaccessible. In extreme cases, data can also be lost or logins to IT systems served by the directory service may no longer be possible. This can hinder business processes and internal workflows. If functional copies of the failed system parts are available, access is still possible, but with limited performance depending on the chosen network topology.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Compromise of directory services through unauthorized access
parts.prose: If attackers succeed in successfully performing or bypassing a necessary authentication against the directory service, they can subsequently gain unauthorized access to a multitude of data. Thus, the entire directory service can potentially be compromised. This could impair or even destroy the entire affected system. The security of a directory service can also be jeopardized if anonymous users are permitted. Since their identity is not verified, anonymous users can initially direct arbitrary queries to the directory service, through which they can obtain at least partial information about its structure and content. Furthermore, if anonymous access is allowed, DoS attacks on the directory service are easier to carry out, as attackers have more access options that are difficult to control.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Incorrect configuration of directory services
parts.prose: Directory services have numerous functions, so the directory service can be used by users with very different needs. Misconfiguration of these numerous functions can lead to unauthorized access to the directory service. For example, if the default configuration is not sufficiently checked and adapted, authentication information can be transmitted in cleartext or inadequately secured and thus be snooped.

controls.title: Planning of Active Directory Domain Services (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is done ad hoc and focuses on the basic functionality of a single domain. A formal authorization concept or documentation does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, AD DS is often set up with the default settings of the installation wizard. There is no conscious decision about functional levels or the structuring of administrative delegations. Schema changes are not documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether a planning document exists at all. It is checked whether the functional level of the domain and the forest corresponds to an outdated standard (older than Windows Server 2016). The existence of undocumented schema changes is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A functional level of at least Windows Server 2016 MUST be selected for the domain(s) and the forest. A needs-based permissions concept for the domain(s) and the forest MUST be designed. It MUST be taken into account that, by product design, there are no security boundaries between the individual domains of a forest. Administrative delegations MUST be equipped with restrictive and needs-based permissions. The planned structure, including any schema changes, MUST be documented in a comprehensible manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning is documented in a concept document. This document defines the domain and forest structure, the functional level to be used (at least Windows Server 2016), the OU design, and the basic delegation model. Administrative tasks are delegated to specific groups instead of directly to user accounts. All schema changes are approved and documented before implementation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the AD DS concept document and compares the planned architecture with the actual implementation. It is checked whether the functional levels of the domains and the forest are set to at least 'Windows Server 2016'. The audit verifies that administrative delegations are assigned to groups and not to individual users and that these permissions are documented. The functional level can be checked automatically with the PowerShell command `(Get-ADForest).ForestMode` and `(Get-ADDomain).DomainMode`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The AD DS planning concept is reviewed regularly, at least annually, and updated as needed. The authorization concept is based on a tiered administration model to make privilege escalation more difficult. Administrative delegations are audited periodically to identify and correct excessive permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal review process for the AD DS concept is established. The tier model (e.g., Tier 0 for domain controllers, Tier 1 for servers, Tier 2 for clients) is defined in the concept. Scripts or specialized tools are used for the audit of delegations to analyze the effective permissions of administrative groups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of logs from the annual concept reviews. It is checked whether a tiered administration model is documented and implemented. The auditor requests the results of the last audits on administrative delegations and checks whether identified deficiencies have been remedied.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The AD DS planning is integrated into a comprehensive IT architecture and security lifecycle. The decision for functional levels and forest designs is made proactively based on security roadmaps and risk assessments. The delegation model is dynamically enforced through technical measures such as Privileged Access Management (PAM) and continuously monitored for deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The AD DS architecture is managed as part of Enterprise Architecture Management (EAM). Changes, including schema extensions, go through a strict Change Advisory Board (CAB) process. A PAM solution is used to grant Just-in-Time permissions. The configuration and permissions are continuously monitored by a Security Posture Management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the AD DS architecture is mapped in the official enterprise architecture documents. It is checked whether a PAM/JIT solution is in use for administrative delegations by inspecting configuration and log data of the solution. The auditor checks the reports of the continuous monitoring tool for configuration deviations and their remediation.

controls.title: Planning of Group Policies on Windows (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Group Policy Objects (GPOs) are created ad hoc to solve specific problems. There is no clear structure, documentation, or naming convention, which leads to unpredictable results and frequent overlaps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: GPOs are often linked directly to the domain root or to large OUs without considering inheritance or the impact on subordinate objects. The default GPOs (Default Domain Policy, Default Domain Controllers Policy) are misused for a variety of settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the GPO structure for the lack of a logical naming convention and a clear hierarchy. It looks for GPOs with a large number of overlapping settings. The auditor checks the default GPOs for non-standard changes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There MUST be a concept for setting up group policies. Multiple overlaps MUST be avoided as much as possible in the group policy concept by creating GPOs with specific, non-overlapping purposes. The documentation of the concept MUST define exception rules and their approval process. All Group Policy Objects MUST be protected by restrictive access rights (e.g., only for GPO administrators). Secure settings (based on security baselines) MUST be defined for the parameters in all GPOs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The concept defines a naming convention, a logical linking strategy (e.g., at the OU level), and the principle of avoiding monolithic GPOs. Instead, GPOs are created for specific functional areas (e.g., 'Windows Firewall Settings', 'User AppLocker Policy'). The permissions on GPO objects are adjusted so that only authorized groups can make changes. Recognized baselines (e.g., from CIS or Microsoft) are used as the basis for secure settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the GPO concept and compares it with the implementation in the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC). It is checked whether a logical structure exists and whether multiple overlaps are minimized. The access rights on a sample of GPOs are checked in the 'Delegation' tab of the GPMC. The command `Get-GPOReport -All -ReportType Html` can be used to generate a report of all GPOs to check the settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal change management process for all GPO changes is established. Changes are validated in a dedicated test environment before being rolled out to production. Compliance with the defined secure settings in the GPOs is regularly audited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools such as Microsoft's Advanced Group Policy Management (AGPM), which is part of MDOP, are used to implement a check-in/check-out process, versioning, and an approval workflow for GPO changes. A separate test OU or domain is used for the validation of GPO changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a change management tool like AGPM is in use and whether the change history is traceable. They check whether a test environment for GPOs exists and is being used. The auditor requests the results of the last GPO audits and checks whether deviations from the baselines have been remediated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management and monitoring of Group Policies is largely automated. Compliance with security baselines is continuously monitored, and deviations trigger automated alerts or remediation actions. The impact of GPO changes is simulated using modeling tools before deployment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: GPO management is supplemented by Desired State Configuration (DSC) or third-party configuration monitoring tools. The 'Group Policy Results' and 'Group Policy Modeling' wizards in the GPMC are used systematically. Log data from GPO processing errors on clients is centrally collected and analyzed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration of the monitoring tool for defined GPO baselines and alerting rules. The ability to simulate GPO changes ('what-if analysis') is demonstrated. The auditor checks the central logs for an effective analysis of GPO errors and the resulting actions.

controls.title: Securing the Domain Controller (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No non-essential services or roles are installed on the domain controller (DC). The password for the Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) account is set and securely documented. The size of the security log is increased from the default value.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During installation, only the 'Active Directory Domain Services' role and its associated features (like DNS) are selected. Other roles such as Web Server (IIS) or File Server are not installed. The DSRM password is set during installation and stored in a secure password safe. The size of the Security Event Log is increased to at least 1 GB via GPO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the installed roles and features in the Server Manager. It is verified that the DSRM password is being managed. The configuration of the Security Event Log is checked on the DC or in the responsible GPO.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A risk assessment for the domain controllers MUST be carried out. Emergency access with the DSRM account MUST be planned and documented as part of emergency management. The size of the security log MUST be sufficiently dimensioned based on the requirements for event detection. On the domain controller, no additional services that are not strictly necessary for AD DS operation MAY be operated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The risk assessment identifies threats to the DCs and defines protective measures. The emergency handbook contains detailed instructions on using the DSRM account for an AD recovery. The log size is set so that security-relevant events can be retained for the defined period (e.g., 90 days). A strict policy is implemented that prohibits the installation of third-party software or additional server roles on DCs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the risk assessment for DCs and the emergency handbook and checks the plausibility of the content regarding DSRM access. The configuration of the event log size is checked and compared with the requirements from the logging concept. The auditor checks the software and roles installed on the DCs for unnecessary components.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Domain controllers are treated as Tier 0 systems and receive the highest level of protection. Physical access to DCs is strictly controlled and limited to a few authorized individuals. The DSRM account password is managed via a LAPS-like solution and rotated automatically on a regular basis. Network traffic to and from the domain controllers is restricted by a firewall to the strictly necessary protocols and sources and is monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: DCs are housed in secure data center areas with access control. Microsoft LAPS or a comparable tool is used to manage the DSRM password. The Windows Defender Firewall on the DCs is configured via GPO to allow only the necessary ports for AD, DNS, etc. from defined IP ranges (e.g., other DCs, management systems). Network flow data is sent to a SIEM for analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the physical security measures for the DCs. The configuration of the LAPS solution for the DSRM account is checked. The host firewall configuration on the DCs is audited. The firewall configuration can be automatically read and analyzed using `Get-NetFirewallRule -PolicyStore ActiveStore`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Domain controllers are run exclusively as Server Core installations to minimize the attack surface. In physically less secure locations such as branch offices, only Read-Only Domain Controllers (RODCs) are used. All administrative access to domain controllers is performed via dedicated, hardened Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All new DC installations are done without a graphical user interface (Server Core). An RODC rollout plan is created and implemented for branch offices. A PAW concept is defined and implemented, which ensures that administrative tools for DCs can only be run from these specially secured devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that all DCs (except possibly for legacy ones) are running as Server Core. This can be checked via PowerShell with `(Get-ComputerInfo).WindowsInstallationType`. The list of DCs is checked for the use of RODCs in branch offices. The auditor examines the login logs of the DCs to ensure that administrative logins only occur from the defined PAW systems.

controls.title: Secure Configuration of Trust Relationships (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All trust relationships (trusts) between domains and between forests MUST be regularly evaluated for their necessity and security configuration. It MUST be checked whether a bidirectional trust is necessary or if a unidirectional one is sufficient. SID filtering on inter-forest trusts MUST NOT be disabled. The default SIDs to be filtered MUST NOT be removed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process for approving, setting up, and regularly reviewing (e.g., annually) trusts is established and documented. When setting up, the trust direction is limited to the bare minimum necessary. SID filtering (quarantine) is retained as the default setting, and its deactivation is strictly prohibited and technically monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the trust management process and the records of the last reviews. The configuration of all existing trusts is read out using the Active Directory Domains and Trusts snap-in or via PowerShell (`Get-ADTrust`) and checked for the necessity of the direction and the activation of SID filtering (`(Get-ADTrust 'trusted.domain.com').SidFilteringEnabled`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all external trust relationships to other forests, 'Selective Authentication' MUST be used to block access from accounts in the trusted forest by default. If a domain does not require a bidirectional trust relationship with other domains in the forest, this domain SHOULD be moved to its own forest.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When configuring forest trusts, the 'Selective Authentication' option is chosen instead of 'Forest-wide Authentication'. Permissions for resources must then be explicitly granted to accounts from the trusted forest on the respective computer object in the trusting forest. The architecture is analyzed to identify domains that should be migrated to a separate forest for security reasons.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of all forest trusts and verifies that 'Selective Authentication' is enabled. This can be checked via PowerShell with `(Get-ADTrust 'trusted.forest.com').SelectiveAuthenticationEnabled`. It is checked whether an analysis for moving domains to their own forests has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of AD DS trusts is architecturally reduced to an absolute minimum. Wherever possible, more modern federation technologies are preferred as an alternative. Authentication traffic over the remaining trusts is actively monitored for anomalies and signs of misuse.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of forest trusts, technologies such as Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) or Azure AD B2B Collaboration are used to enable access to applications without requiring a direct trust relationship at the Kerberos level. The security event logs of the domain controllers are forwarded to a SIEM, where rules for detecting suspicious behavior across trusts (e.g., an unusually high number of authentication requests) are implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture diagrams and determines whether alternatives to trusts have been evaluated and implemented. The configuration of the SIEM is checked to determine whether specific detection rules for trust traffic are present and active. Samples of alarms related to trust activities are analyzed.

controls.title: Implementation of Secure Administration Methods for Active Directory (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that the accounts of service administrators (e.g., Exchange Admins) are managed exclusively by members of a dedicated group of service administrators and not by general Domain Admins. Before accounts are added to predefined, highly privileged AD DS groups (such as Domain Admins), it MUST be checked whether all associated rights are strictly necessary for the task to be performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Tiered Administration Model is defined as a concept. The administration of application servers and their service accounts is delegated to dedicated admin groups (Tier 1), which have no rights on domain controllers (Tier 0). A formal request and approval process for membership in highly privileged groups is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the permissions on service accounts and ensures that they are managed not by Domain Admins, but by dedicated groups. The processes for admitting members to highly privileged groups are checked. The membership list of the 'Domain Admins', 'Enterprise Admins', etc. groups is checked for necessity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the default administrator account, other administrative accounts SHOULD only be temporarily assigned to highly privileged groups such as 'Schema Admins', 'Enterprise Admins', and 'Domain Admins' for the period in which the permissions are actively needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Privileged Access Management (PAM) or Just-in-Time (JIT) solution is introduced. Alternatively, manual or semi-automated processes are implemented where accounts are added to a highly privileged group for a limited period (e.g., 4 hours) upon approval and are automatically removed afterwards. The 'Temporary Group Membership' feature in Windows Server can be used for this purpose.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and use of a PAM/JIT process. The logs of temporary memberships in highly privileged groups are reviewed. It is checked whether there is permanent membership of personalized admin accounts in these groups, which would be an indicator of non-implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administrative access to Active Directory is performed exclusively from dedicated and hardened Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs). The use of privileged accounts is monitored in real-time, and suspicious activities or policy violations automatically trigger high-priority security alarms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAW concept is fully implemented, ensuring that domain admin accounts can never log on to systems with a lower security level (such as normal workstations or servers). Logon events and actions of privileged accounts are sent to a SIEM system, where advanced correlation rules and User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) are used to detect threats.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the technical implementation of the PAW concept by checking GPOs and login logs. The configuration of the SIEM/UEBA system regarding the monitoring of privileged AD accounts is checked. The auditor analyzes sample alarms triggered by administrative activities and the subsequent incident response process.

controls.title: Hardening of AD DS Accounts (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Built-in AD DS accounts MUST be provided with long, complex passwords and used ONLY as emergency accounts. The built-in 'Guest' account MUST be disabled. The permissions of the 'Everyone' group MUST be restricted to a minimum. Privileged accounts MUST be members of the 'Protected Users' group. (Group) Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) MUST be used for service accounts. A process for deactivating and deleting unused accounts MUST exist, taking into account retention periods.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The passwords for accounts like the built-in Administrator are generated and stored in a secure password vault. The Guest account is disabled via GPO. The memberships of the 'Everyone' group are regularly reviewed and reduced to a minimum. All privileged admin accounts are added to the 'Protected Users' group. New services are consistently set up with gMSAs instead of regular user accounts. An account lifecycle process is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the deactivation of the Guest account and the complexity of the passwords for emergency accounts. The membership of the 'Protected Users' group is checked. It is checked on a random basis whether service accounts are configured as gMSAs. The account lifecycle process is reviewed. Membership can be checked with `Get-ADGroupMember 'Protected Users'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the AdminSDHolder object SHOULD be specially protected to prevent unauthorized changes to the permission templates for protected accounts and groups. The SDProp process, which enforces these permissions, is monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The permissions on the AdminSDHolder object in the 'System' container are audited and reset to a secure state. Auditing (SACL) is enabled for this object to log all change attempts. These logs are sent to a central system for evaluation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the Access Control List (ACL) of the AdminSDHolder object. It is checked whether auditing is enabled for this object and whether the corresponding events (Event ID 5136) are recorded and analyzed. This can be checked with `Get-Acl 'AD:CN=AdminSDHolder,CN=System,DC=domain,DC=com' | Format-List`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Kerberos Armoring (Flexible Authentication Secure Tunneling - FAST) is enabled and enforced for the entire domain to increase protection against Kerberoasting attacks. The entire lifecycle of accounts, from creation and permission assignment to deletion, is fully automated and integrated into an Identity and Access Management (IAM) system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: FAST is enabled via the GPO 'Kerberos client support for claims, compound authentication, and Kerberos armoring'. An IAM system is implemented that controls the entire account lifecycle based on HR processes and performs automatic recertification campaigns for permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPO settings for enabling Kerberos Armoring. The configuration and processes of the IAM system are audited. It is checked whether the account lifecycle process (Joiner, Mover, Leaver) is automated and functions without manual intervention.

controls.title: Logon restrictions for highly privileged forest accounts on clients and servers (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logon of highly privileged domain and forest accounts and groups MUST be technically restricted to the minimum necessary IT systems. In particular, the logon of members of the 'Schema Admins', 'Enterprise Admins', and 'Domain Admins' groups MUST be technically restricted to domain controllers. Logon to other IT systems such as clients or member servers MUST be prevented for these groups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is implemented by configuring user rights via Group Policies (GPOs). The GPOs applied to member servers and clients contain the highly privileged groups in the 'Deny log on as a service', 'Deny log on locally', and 'Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services' settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the relevant GPOs for the correct configuration of the user rights assignment. Using the 'Resultant Set of Policy' (rsop.msc) or `gpresult /h report.html` on a sample client and server, it is checked whether the restrictions are applied correctly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A complete Tiered Administration Model is implemented, which technically restricts logons for all administrative accounts to systems of the same or a lower tier. For example, Tier 1 administrators (server admins) are not allowed to log on to Tier 0 systems (DCs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The implementation is carried out through a granular structure of GPOs applied to OUs for the different tiers (Tier 0, Tier 1, Tier 2). Each GPO precisely defines which admin groups are allowed to log on to the systems of the respective tier and which are not.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the OU and GPO structure to verify the correct implementation of the tier model. A random check is performed on systems of all tiers to ensure that the logon restrictions for accounts from other tiers are effective.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: 'Authentication Policy Silos' and the corresponding 'Authentication Policies' are used to create a strong, Kerberos-enforced boundary around highly privileged accounts. This not only restricts where an account can log on, but also from which systems resources can be accessed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Authentication Policy Silo is created for Tier 0 assets (DCs, Tier 0 admins). The corresponding user, computer, and service accounts are assigned to this silo. An authentication policy is configured that restricts the Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) lifetime and enforces logon restrictions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the Authentication Policy Silos and the associated policies using the Active Directory Administrative Center or PowerShell (`Get-ADAuthenticationPolicySilo`). It is verified that all Tier 0 accounts and systems are assigned to the silo.

controls.title: Restricting the addition of new computer objects to the domain (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The default permission that allows all authenticated users to add up to 10 computers to the domain is removed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The 'ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota' attribute in the domain object is set to 0. This prevents non-administrators from adding computers to the domain.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the value of the 'ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota' attribute with ADSI Editor or via PowerShell: `(Get-ADDomain).msDS-MachineAccountQuota`. The value must be 0.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The permission to create new computer objects in the domain MUST be restricted to the minimum necessary administrative accounts or groups. A defined process for adding computers is established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After setting the MachineAccountQuota to 0, the 'Create computer objects' right is specifically delegated to a dedicated group (e.g., 'Helpdesk-Join-Computer') on the OUs where computer objects are to be created. The process of how a technician adds a computer to the domain is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor ensures that the MachineAccountQuota is set to 0. Then, using the 'Delegate Control' wizard or by analyzing the ACLs on the relevant OUs, it is checked which groups have the right to create computer objects. It is verified that these groups only contain the necessary members.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A documented process for pre-staging computer accounts is established and enforced. This ensures that new systems are always created in the correct organizational unit (OU) and immediately receive the correct group policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Helpdesk staff or automated systems create the computer account in the target OU before the physical computer joins the domain. The permission is delegated in such a way that it allows 'joining' to this pre-created account, but not creating new accounts elsewhere.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented process for pre-staging. The configuration of permission delegation on the OUs is checked to ensure that it supports the pre-staging model. The 'Computers' default container is monitored for newly created objects, as this could indicate a circumvention of the pre-staging process.

controls.title: Securing the 'Secure Channel' (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secure channel between domain members and domain controllers MUST be configured so that the transmitted data is always encrypted and signed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is achieved by enabling the following two Group Policy settings for all domain members: 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Digitally sign secure channel data (when possible)'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the GPOs that are applied to all domain members for the correct configuration of these two settings. The effective settings can be checked on a sample client with `gpresult /h report.html`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the configuration for securing the secure channel is regularly monitored on all domain members using a configuration management tool or scheduled scripts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script, which is executed e.g. via GPO as a scheduled task, reads the relevant registry values (`RequireSignOrSeal`, `SealSecureChannel`) and reports deviations to a central log. Alternatively, a configuration management tool such as Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager (MECM) with Compliance Baselines is used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the reports from the monitoring tool or scripts and checks whether deviations are detected and resolved. The configuration of the Compliance Baseline in MECM or the monitoring script is checked for correctness.

controls.title: Protection of authentication when using AD DS (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Kerberos authentication protocol MUST be used consistently throughout the forest, using AES128 or AES256 encryption. The obsolete protocols LM authentication and NTLMv1 MUST be disabled. SMBv1 MUST be disabled and SMB signing MUST be enforced for all SMB traffic. LDAP sessions to domain controllers MUST be signed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: These settings are enforced via GPOs: Support for AES is automatically activated if the domain functional level is sufficiently high. NTLMv1 is set to 'Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM' via the GPO 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level'. SMBv1 is disabled via GPO or PowerShell. SMB signing is enforced via GPO. LDAP signing is enforced server-side on the DCs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the relevant GPO settings for LAN Manager authentication, SMB signing, and the server configuration for LDAP signing and SMBv1. It is checked whether Kerberos tickets use AES encryption by running the `klist` command on a client. Automated tools like PingCastle can be used for a comprehensive review of these settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of NTLMv2 is audited throughout the network to identify remaining dependencies. A plan for complete migration to Kerberos is created and tracked. LDAP Channel Binding is enforced to make Man-in-the-Middle attacks on LDAP sessions more difficult.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Monitoring for NTLM is activated via the GPO 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers' and '...: Restrict NTLM: NTLM authentication in this domain' in audit mode. The resulting events (Event ID 800x, 4624) are centrally collected and analyzed. LDAP Channel Binding is enforced via a registry key on the DCs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that NTLM monitoring is active and the logs are being evaluated. The migration plan for phasing out NTLM is reviewed. The configuration of LDAP Channel Binding on the domain controllers is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: NTLM is completely blocked throughout the domain. All services and applications are verified and use only Kerberos authentication. For Kerberos, encryption with AES256 is enforced as the standard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The GPO setting 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: NTLM authentication in this domain' is set to 'Deny all'. The supported encryption types for Kerberos are configured via GPO to remove RC4-HMAC, leaving only AES128 and AES256.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the GPO settings for the complete deactivation of NTLM. It is checked whether this setting causes application errors, which would indicate an incomplete migration. The GPO for supported Kerberos encryption types is analyzed.

controls.title: Data backup for domain controllers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process for regular, authoritative data backup of the domain controllers is defined and implemented. Access to the backups of the domain controllers MUST be subject to a comparably high level of protection as access to the domain controllers themselves. The backups MUST be kept in a physically and logically separate, secure location.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A backup software that supports AD authoritative restores (e.g., Windows Server Backup) is used. The backups are stored on dedicated, hardened backup servers or on tapes. Access to the backup servers and media is restricted to a small group of backup administrators whose accounts are separate from the domain admin accounts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the data backup concept and checks the backup logs for successful and regular execution. The access permissions to the backup storage locations are checked. It is checked whether the physical security of the backup storage is appropriate.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The backup data of the domain controllers is stored encrypted to ensure the confidentiality of the ntds.dit database contained therein. Regular recovery tests are performed in an isolated environment to validate the integrity of the backups and the functionality of the recovery process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup software is configured to perform backup jobs with strong encryption. An emergency manual documents the recovery process. At least once a year, a full forest recovery exercise is conducted in an isolated test network. The results are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the backup software for active encryption. The logs and result reports of the last recovery tests are requested and checked for completeness and success.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Active Directory Recycle Bin is enabled to allow for the quick recovery of accidentally deleted objects without the need for an authoritative restore from backup. The entire backup and recovery process is largely automated and is continuously monitored for success and integrity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The AD Recycle Bin is enabled via the Active Directory Administrative Center or via PowerShell (`Enable-ADOptionalFeature`). The backup solution is configured to automatically report failing jobs and verify the integrity of the backups. The process for restoring from the Recycle Bin is documented and known to the administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the AD Recycle Bin is enabled. This can be checked with `(Get-ADOptionalFeature -Filter 'name -like "Recycle Bin Feature"').Enabled`. The configuration of the backup monitoring and alerting is checked.

controls.title: Separation of administration into a separate forest (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Tiered Administration Model is defined and documented within the production forest to logically separate administrative accounts and systems and thus reduce the risk of privilege escalation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrative tasks are divided into tiers (e.g., Tier 0 for identity and security infrastructure, Tier 1 for servers, Tier 2 for endpoints). Separate administrator accounts are created for each tier. This is the conceptual basis for a later physical separation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the concept of the Tiered Administration Model and compares it with the implemented account and group structure in Active Directory.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Particularly critical IT systems and the accounts for administering the domains or the forest (Tier 0) MUST be outsourced to a separate, dedicated administrative forest (Enhanced Security Admin Environment - ESAE, also called 'Red Forest'). A one-way trust relationship exists from the production forest to the administrative forest, which allows the administrative accounts to manage the production environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A new, highly hardened forest is built. The privileged accounts for managing the production forest are created in this admin forest. A unidirectional trust relationship is configured so that the admin forest trusts the production forest. All administration of the production forest is done with accounts from the admin forest via PAWs, which are also members of the admin forest.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the separate administrative forest and the correct configuration of the one-way trust relationship. It is checked whether there are still highly privileged accounts in the production forest that do not originate from the admin forest. The login logs are checked to ensure that administrative tasks are performed with accounts from the Red Forest.

controls.title: Operation of virtualized domain controllers (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Virtualized domain controllers (vDCs) are operated on hardened virtualization hosts. The standard security measures for virtual machines, such as separating network traffic and securing the VM files, are applied.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The virtualization hosts on which vDCs run are hardened according to a security baseline. The vDCs use dedicated virtual network adapters connected to a protected network segment. Access to the VM files on the datastore is restricted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the hardening configuration of the virtualization hosts. The network configuration of the vDCs and the access permissions to the VM files are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Virtualized domain controllers are operated on dedicated physical virtualization hosts, which are treated and managed as Tier 0 systems. Virtualization host administrators are considered security-critical equivalent to domain administrators, and their accounts are protected accordingly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cluster of virtualization hosts is reserved exclusively for the operation of vDCs and other Tier 0 systems. These hosts and their management interfaces are isolated from the rest of the server network. The host administrators' accounts are subject to the same strict controls as domain admin accounts (e.g., use of PAWs).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the hosts on which vDCs run do not host any other VMs with lower protection needs. The security measures for the host administrators' accounts are audited.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Virtualized domain controllers SHOULD NOT be operated on the same physical host together with other virtually operated IT systems. The virtualization host, the associated management systems, and the administrator accounts for the virtualization layer SHOULD NOT be members of the forest to which the virtualized domain controller belongs, to prevent a compromise of the host by the guest domain.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The virtualization hosts for the domain controllers are in a separate administrative domain (e.g., the management domain of an ESAE architecture) or in a workgroup and not in the production domain to be protected. Technologies such as 'Shielded VMs' in Hyper-V are used to protect the vDC VMs themselves from compromised host administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the domain membership of the virtualization hosts and their management systems. It is checked whether technologies such as Shielded VMs are configured and in use by checking the configuration of the Host Guardian Service (HGS).

controls.title: Separation of organizational units (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Different organizational units are logically separated within the same domain by a structure of organizational units (OUs) and delegated permissions. This creates administrative boundaries for daily administration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An OU structure is created for each organizational unit. The administration of users, groups, and computers within this OU is delegated to specific admin groups of that organizational unit.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the OU structure and the delegated permissions to verify the logical separation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Separate domains within the same forest are used to create stronger administrative boundaries between organizational units that require greater autonomy (e.g., different password policies).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For organizational units with specific security requirements, a separate domain is created within the existing forest. This allows for separate domain admin control and the application of domain-wide policies, such as Fine-Grained Password Policies (FGPP).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the forest's domain structure and validates the justification for creating separate domains. The trusts and administrative boundaries between the domains are analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Organizational units that require complete independence and a hard security boundary from each other for IT security or other reasons (e.g., legal or regulatory requirements) SHOULD NOT be in the same forest.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Completely separate Active Directory forests are built for these organizational units. If collaboration is required, it is realized through strictly controlled forest trusts with selective authentication or through federation technologies such as AD FS. This ensures that a compromise of Enterprise Admins in one forest cannot spread to the other.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the separate forests for the respective organizational units. The architecture diagrams and the risk assessments that led to this decision are reviewed. The configuration of the connections (trusts, federation) between these forests is audited for security.

controls.title: Configuration of a Tiered Model (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An administrative tiered model (tier model) is documented. All administrative accounts, IT systems, and applications are logically assigned to a tier (e.g., Tier 0, Tier 1, Tier 2).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A concept is created that defines the criteria for assignment to the tiers. Tier 0 includes the identity infrastructure (DCs), Tier 1 the enterprise servers and applications, and Tier 2 the end-user devices. All relevant objects in AD are assigned to a tier (e.g., via their description or OU membership).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the concept of the tiered model. It is checked on a random basis whether accounts and systems are assigned to a tier correctly and comprehensibly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The authorization structure within the forest MUST be designed in tiers and technically enforced. Accounts from a higher tier (e.g., Tier 0 Admins) MUST NOT be allowed to log on to resources of a lower tier (e.g., Tier 2 Clients). Accounts of a lower tier (e.g., Tier 1 Admins) MUST NOT have control over accounts and resources of higher tiers (e.g., Tier 0 DCs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The rules of the tiered model are rigorously enforced technically through Group Policies (User Rights Assignment such as 'Deny log on locally') and 'Authentication Policy Silos'. The delegation models are designed to prevent privilege escalation across tier boundaries (e.g., a server admin cannot manage domain admins).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the technical implementation of the tier boundaries through a detailed analysis of GPOs and the configuration of Authentication Policy Silos. The login logs on systems of different tiers are analyzed to detect violations of the login rules. Tools like BloodHound can be used to identify attack paths that violate tier boundaries.

controls.title: Time-limited permissions for administration (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A manual process is established in which privileged permissions are requested via a ticket system, approved, and manually revoked after the task is completed. Permanent memberships in highly privileged groups are avoided.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process is mapped in the ticket system. An administrator manually adds the requester's account to the required group and removes it again after the ticket is closed. The 'Domain Admins', 'Enterprise Admins', etc. groups are empty during normal operation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the member lists of the highly privileged groups for permanent members. Tickets for administrative tasks are analyzed on a random basis to understand the process of granting and revoking rights.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Accounts used for administration SHOULD only be equipped with the minimum necessary permissions for the administrative task, limited to the required time window, and only when needed (Just-in-Time administration).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution is used. Administrators request access to a specific role or resource for a specific period via the PAM portal. After approval, the system grants the administrator account the necessary permissions, e.g., by adding it to a group. After the time window expires, the permission is automatically revoked. This uses, for example, the 'Temporary Group Membership' feature in Active Directory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration and functionality of the PAM solution. The system's logs are reviewed to check the process of requesting, approving, and automatically revoking permissions. It is checked whether there are alternative, non-PAM-managed ways to obtain administrative rights.

controls.title: Regular analysis of permissions and resulting attack paths (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A regular, manual analysis of the permission structures and potential attack paths in AD DS is performed with specialized tools. In particular, complex permissions that arise from the integration of applications such as Microsoft Exchange are critically reviewed and examined for their necessity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At least quarterly, tools such as BloodHound, PingCastle, or Purple Knight are used to create a snapshot of the AD security configuration. The results, especially the identified attack paths to compromise domain admins, are analyzed, documented, and the identified vulnerabilities are remediated according to a prioritized plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the reports of the latest AD security analyses. It is checked whether the analyses take place regularly and whether the identified risks and attack paths are systematically tracked and remediated. The auditor may request a live execution of such a tool to validate the competence in handling it.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The analysis of permissions and attack paths in AD DS is carried out continuously by automated tools. Possible attack paths via the permissions of AD DS accounts that could lead to the compromise of the domain or forest SHOULD be minimized, and the remaining risks actively monitored. The activities of all accounts identified as critical SHOULD be specially monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated Active Directory Threat Detection and Response (AD-TDR) solution is implemented. This system continuously monitors changes to the AD configuration and permissions in real-time, detects new dangerous attack paths, and generates alerts. The activities of accounts that are part of critical attack paths (e.g., helpdesk staff with high permissions on many systems) are forwarded to a SIEM and monitored for anomalous behavior using UEBA rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and the dashboards of the AD-TDR system. It is verified how the system reacts to newly emerging attack paths (alerting, ticket creation). The auditor analyzes the correlation rules configured in the SIEM for monitoring critical accounts and examines exemplary triggered alerts and the response to them.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Active Directory (AD) is a collective term for various server roles developed by Microsoft for Windows Server. The Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) server role aggregates the functionalities of a directory service, an authentication and authorization service, and a central configuration management for Windows infrastructures.
Active Directory Domain Services is primarily used in networks that are predominantly characterized by Microsoft-based operating systems. An AD DS stores and manages information about network resources (e.g., users, computers, and devices). If necessary, this information can also be extended with application-specific data, as is common in LDAP directory services. It helps users and administrators to organize, provide, and use this information in a hierarchical structure. AD DS structures the objects in namespaces, which are referred to as forests, domains, and organizational units. A forest forms a hierarchical collection of domains, each of which can contain multiple organizational units. The first domain created in a forest, and thus the highest in the hierarchy, inherently takes on the role of the "forest root domain" and contains the administrative groups responsible for forest-wide administrative tasks such as adding more domains or making schema changes. All domains within a forest are implicitly linked by two-way, transitive trusts, making the forest a logical security boundary.
As a standard authentication protocol, AD DS uses Kerberos v5 (in an implementation extended by Microsoft). In addition, the NTLM (New Technology LAN Manager) protocol is still available. NTLM can be more easily exploited by attackers. Windows Servers with the AD DS server role are called domain controllers. For availability reasons, multiple domain controllers are often used in a distributed manner. The AD DS also offers the possibility of a "read-only operation" of a domain controller, which is intended for locations with increased risk to physical security.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to secure Active Directory Domain Services in the regular operations of an institution that uses AD DS for managing Windows systems (client and server) and for central authentication and authorization.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
