The module APP.2.2 Active Directory Domain Services is to be applied to all used directory services based on Microsoft Active Directory Domain Services. It can also be partially used for modeling Active Directory Lightweight Directory Services (AD LDS), which offer a reduced functional scope of AD DS.
This module examines the specific threats and requirements for Active Directory Domain Services. General security recommendations for directory services can be found in the module APP.2.1 General Directory Service. The general requirements described there are specified and supplemented in this module. This module does not repeat the requirements for securing the operating systems of the servers and clients used for the operation and administration of AD DS, such as SYS.1.2.3 Windows Server or SYS.2.2.3 Clients under Windows. This module also does not re-address the requirements of the underlying network infrastructure.
Active Directory Domain Services should not be modeled in isolation from the modules ORP.4 Identity and Access Management, OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management, CON.3 Data Backup Concept, OPS.1.2.2 Archiving, OPS.1.1.5 Logging, as well as OPS.1.1.2 Proper IT Administration, OPS.1.2.5 Remote Maintenance, DER.1 Detection of Security-Relevant Events, DER.2 Security Incident Management, DER.4 Emergency Management, and APP.3.6 DNS Server. It is assumed that the requirements of these modules influence each other.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Inadequate planning of security boundaries
parts.prose: In AD DS, there are different types of boundaries. These boundaries define the forest, the domain, the site topology, and the assignment of rights. An AD DS instance first creates a forest as the highest-level container for all domains of this instance. A forest can contain one or more domain container objects that share a common logical structure, a Global Catalog, a schema, and automatic two-way, transitive trust relationships. This means that between domains within a forest, both trust and access are possible in both directions. The forest therefore represents the security boundary by design, within which information is passed on by default in AD DS. A domain only forms an administrative boundary. If security boundaries are not realized along the forest boundaries, a compromise can cause a higher level of damage than expected, as it can lead to the compromise of all IT systems in the forest. This threat is a peculiarity of AD DS, as the planning of partitioning in the directory service cannot be fully implemented due to product characteristics. A complete compromise of a forest means that attackers have control over all objects belonging to the contained domains, including all accounts and all IT systems. This potentially gives them control over the associated IT systems and services as well.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Too many or negligent trust relationships
parts.prose: Trust relationships between domains and between forests make it possible to grant accounts from another domain or forest access to resources within one's own domain or forest. If trust relationships between forests and between domains are not initially and regularly evaluated to determine whether they are needed and whether the security controls around these trust relationships are sufficient, authorization problems and information leakage can occur. In particular, if the default active SID (Security Identifier) filtering is deactivated, complex configuration errors that are difficult to understand can occur, which can lead to misuse of the trust relationship and far-reaching access rights. The same applies if 'Selective Authentication' is omitted for trust relationships between forests.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Missing security features due to older operating systems and domain and forest functional levels
parts.prose: Up to and including Windows Server 2016, each new generation of the Windows Server operating system brings additional security features and enhancements related to AD DS in the form of domain or forest functional levels. If older operating systems are used as domain controllers or outdated domain or forest functional levels are used, modern security features cannot be used. This increases the risk of insecure default settings. An insecurely configured forest or domain endangers the information processed within it and facilitates attacks by third parties.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Running additional roles and services on domain controllers
parts.prose: If additional services are operated on a domain controller in addition to AD DS, this increases the attack surface of this central component through possible additional vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, in addition to the services already heavily accumulated by AD DS. Such services can be misused consciously or unconsciously, e.g., to copy or modify information without authorization or, in the case of vulnerabilities or misconfigurations that lead to the compromise of the domain controller, to take over the domain or forest.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Insufficient monitoring and documentation of delegated rights
parts.prose: If the creation of company-specific groups and the delegation of rights to these group or to individual user objects is not systematically planned and implemented, the delegation can be difficult to control. It could then, for example, grant far more access than intended, which can be misused by third parties. A lack of regular auditing of the access rights of group and individual user objects can further exacerbate the problem. Even when standard groups are used and their rights are delegated to custom groups, such as when delegating 'Account Operators' to help desk staff, more rights are usually granted than are actually needed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Insecure authentication
parts.prose: So-called 'legacy' (i.e., historical) authentication mechanisms in the AD DS area, such as LAN Manager (LM) and NT LAN Manager (NTLM) v1, are insecure and can be misused in attacks under certain conditions. For example, attackers can obtain and misuse rights without knowing the cleartext passwords and thus compromise parts of the domain, the domain itself, or even the entire forest.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Overly powerful or weakly secured accounts
parts.prose: Application software sometimes requires rights of highly privileged groups (for example, of so-called domain administrators) for service accounts in order to test and deploy products more easily, although significantly fewer rights are necessary for operation. A particular risk exists when these service accounts are secured with weak passwords. Even accounts that are not members of a highly privileged group can be assigned administrative permissions on a large number of servers and clients. They thus possess similarly extensive rights as members of highly privileged groups in AD DS. The far-reaching rights of these accounts can be misused by attackers to move laterally within the domain.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Use of the same local administrator password on multiple IT systems
parts.prose: Even when an IT system is a member of a domain, logging in with local accounts on that IT system is still possible. If the same local login credentials are used on multiple IT systems, a login with these credentials, including with the local built-in Administrator account, can be performed on multiple IT systems. This makes it easier for attackers to move laterally and thus spread throughout the infrastructure. This increases the risk that attackers will find and misuse the credentials of a domain account with higher privileges on one of the IT systems, in order to compromise the domain and potentially the entire forest.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Insecure storage of passwords
parts.prose: Passwords are stored in the central AD DS database (ntds.dit) on the domain controller, among other methods, using the MD4 hash function without a salt, due to product design. This hash function does not meet the requirements of the BSI's Technical Guideline TR-02102-1 'Cryptographic Mechanisms: Recommendations and Key Lengths'. Unauthorized read access to the stored passwords is therefore particularly critical. Due to the widespread use of AD DS, many tools exist to extract the password hashes. The AD DS database can, for example, be decrypted offline using other keys stored on the domain controller, allowing access to the hashes. Furthermore, the weak hash function makes it possible to determine the cleartext passwords.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.10. Insufficient protection of domain controllers
parts.prose: Each (Read-Write) Domain Controller of a domain holds a complete replica of the central AD DS database (ntds.dit), in which the passwords are stored insecurely. In addition to insufficient protection against access by third parties to the domain controllers during operation, an unsuitable backup procedure can also lead to the capture of the central AD DS database and consequently to information leakage and the compromise of the domain and potentially the entire forest. The operation of virtualized domain controllers together with less sensitive virtual machines on a physical virtualization host can also lead to a compromise of AD DS. This also applies if the administrative accounts of the virtualization host, which have full access to AD DS through their administrative activities, are not adequately protected.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.11. Leaving highly privileged credentials on domain member servers and clients
parts.prose: If a login or service usage with highly privileged accounts occurs on a server or client of the domain, the corresponding credentials are cached on it (e.g., in the memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem / LSASS). In case of a compromise, attackers can extract them there. This can lead to the compromise of a single server or client of the domain resulting in the compromise of the entire domain and potentially the entire forest.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.12. Adding untrusted IT systems to the Windows domain
parts.prose: In the default configurations, all users authenticated in AD DS are allowed to add up to ten IT systems to the domain, even if they do not have administrative permissions in AD DS. This allows them to add IT systems to the domain on which they have high privileges. These privileges can be used as a starting point for further attacks. Since adding IT systems to a domain is an administrative task that is typically embedded in an IT process, unpredictable side effects can occur here if IT systems join the domain in an uncontrolled manner without correctly going through this process.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.13. Entanglement of administrative privileges through the integration of additional applications
parts.prose: If applications with AD DS integration (e.g., Microsoft Exchange) are used, the AD DS accounts created by these applications may be assigned administrative permissions in AD DS. As a result, security vulnerabilities in these applications can lead to attackers gaining extensive administrative rights on IT systems within the forest. An example of this is the CVE-2019-0686 (PrivExchange) vulnerability in Microsoft Exchange.

controls.title: Planning and selection of backends and overlays for OpenLDAP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning for the OpenLDAP deployment is rudimentary and focuses only on the basic functionality for a single application. The selection of backends and overlays is done ad-hoc, without considering compatibility or the correct order of overlays.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, the distribution's default backend is used without further adjustments. Overlays, if used at all, are only used for single, obvious requirements such as setting password policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether a planning document exists at all. It is checked whether the configuration of the OpenLDAP server is based on default values and whether the selection of components has been documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic planning for the OpenLDAP deployment is in place. Backends and overlays are deliberately selected, and the compatibility of the database version is ensured. The order of overlays is considered, but without an in-depth analysis of the interactions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple planning document is created that justifies the selection of the backend (e.g., MDB) and the most important overlays (e.g., `ppolicy`, `auditlog`). The compatibility with the primary client applications is checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning document. It is verified that the database version is compatible and that the most important overlays are configured in a logical order. A random check is performed to see if the client applications work.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of OpenLDAP in an institution MUST be carefully planned. If OpenLDAP is to be used with other applications, the planning, configuration, and installation of the applications MUST be coordinated with OpenLDAP. For the database used for data storage, it MUST be ensured that the version used is compatible. Backends and overlays for OpenLDAP MUST be selected restrictively. For this, it MUST be ensured that the OpenLDAP overlays are used in the correct order. The client applications to be selected and supported MUST be considered when planning OpenLDAP.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed concept document is created that describes the architecture, the selected backend (e.g., MDB), all used overlays in their exact order, and their configuration. It contains a list of compatible and supported client applications and their versions. The selection is justified by requirements for security, performance, and functionality.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the live configuration of the OpenLDAP server with the concept document. It is checked whether all MUST requirements are met: coordination with connected applications, compatibility of the database version, restrictive selection of backends/overlays, the correct order of overlays, and consideration of client applications. This can be done by reading the configuration (`cn=config`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process is formalized and reviewed regularly. The selection of backends and overlays is based on performance and scalability tests conducted in a test environment. A catalog of approved client applications and versions is maintained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before introducing new overlays or changing the backend, load tests are performed with tools like `slapd-slapadd` or `slap-bench` to assess the impact on performance. The results are incorporated into the planning documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the performance and compatibility tests performed. It is checked whether a formal process for approving and adding client applications to the catalog exists and is followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire planning and selection process is integrated into the central change management system. Automated tests verify client compatibility and the correct functionality of the overlay chain before each deployment. The selection of backends and overlays is based on a formal risk assessment and continuous performance benchmarks in the production environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CI/CD pipeline is used for the OpenLDAP configuration. Every change to the configuration backend (`cn=config`) triggers a series of automated tests that verify functionality, security, and performance before the change is deployed to production.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the logs of the change management system and the CI/CD pipeline. It is verified that no configuration change has reached production without successful automated tests and formal approval. Compliance with performance SLAs is checked using monitoring data.

controls.title: Secure configuration of OpenLDAP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the slapd server itself is configured with some basic security settings. Configurations of client applications or permissions at the operating system level are ignored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, only the most obvious configuration parameters such as the server name are adjusted. Time and size limits for searches are not set.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly checks the slapd configuration for basic settings. It is determined that no configuration policies exist for clients or the operating system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The slapd server and client applications are configured according to the manufacturer's recommendations (default values). The permissions in the operating system are set, but not checked for the principle of least privilege. The configuration is only checked during initial setup.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration follows the 'install and start' principle. The default values for limits (`sizelimit`, `timelimit`) are retained. The file permissions are left as they were set by the package manager.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration with the manufacturer's documented default values. It is checked whether the operating system permissions correspond to the default settings. It is determined that no regular configuration checks take place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the secure configuration of OpenLDAP, the slapd server MUST be configured correctly. The client applications used MUST also be configured securely. When configuring OpenLDAP, it MUST be ensured that permissions are set correctly in the operating system. The default values of all relevant OpenLDAP configuration directives MUST be checked and adjusted if necessary. The backends and overlays of OpenLDAP MUST be included in the configuration. Appropriate time and size limits MUST be set for searches within OpenLDAP. The configuration on the slapd server MUST be checked after every change.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration policy is created that defines secure values for `sizelimit`, `timelimit`, and other security-relevant directives. The file permissions in the operating system are explicitly set so that only the OpenLDAP service user has read and write access to the database and configuration files. After each change, the configuration is checked for syntactical correctness using `slaptest`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the slapd server (`cn=config`) and compares it with the documented policies. In particular, the values for `olcSizeLimit` and `olcTimeLimit` are checked. The permissions of the database directory are checked with `ls -l`. It is checked whether logs of configuration changes and a subsequent test are available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A documented configuration baseline (hardening standard) for OpenLDAP is created and consistently applied. Configuration changes are managed through a change control process. Automated scripts are used to regularly compare the configuration with the baseline.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible, Puppet) is used to consistently roll out the OpenLDAP configuration to all servers based on a template. A cron job runs a weekly script that reads the current configuration, compares it with the defined baseline, and reports deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the hardening document and the reports from the automated configuration checks. It is checked whether a change management process for configuration changes exists and is followed, e.g., by reviewing the corresponding tickets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration is fully managed and versioned as Configuration-as-Code. Any deviation from the defined state is automatically detected and either reported or corrected. The configuration is continuously monitored, and compliance reports are generated automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The entire OpenLDAP configuration is stored in a Git repository as LDIF files. A CI/CD system automatically applies changes after they have gone through a review and testing process. An Intrusion Detection System or a configuration monitoring tool monitors the configuration (`cn=config`) in real time for unauthorized changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the Git history of the configuration files and the logs of the CI/CD pipeline. It is checked whether the process of automatic correction (self-healing) works by making a manual, unauthorized change and observing its reversal. The automatically generated compliance reports are reviewed.

controls.title: Configuration of the database used by OpenLDAP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The permissions for database files are set during installation but are not specifically restricted to the slapd user. Internal database settings are not adjusted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The database files often have the default permissions specified by the operating system or the installation package, which may lead to broad read permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the file permissions of the OpenLDAP database directory and finds that they do not follow the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The access rights to the database files are restricted to the service account of the slapd server. The default database settings are used without specific adjustments.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Using `chown` and `chmod`, the ownership and access rights of the database directory are correctly set to the `slapd` user (e.g., `ldap:ldap`) and the corresponding permissions (e.g., `700`). The database configuration itself (`olcDbConfig`) remains untouched.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the permissions of the database directory with `ls -ld`. It is checked whether the internal database settings correspond to the default values by reading the `olcDbConfig` attributes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The access rights for newly created database files MUST be restricted to the ID under which the slapd server is running. The default settings of the database used by OpenLDAP MUST be adjusted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The operating system file permissions for the directory containing the MDB database are strictly restricted to the service user. In addition, internal database parameters such as the cache size (`olcDbCacheSize`) and the configuration for lazy commits (`olcDbCheckpoint`) are adjusted to the expected load and hardware to improve performance and stability.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the file permissions of the database directory and ensures that only the `slapd` service user can access it. In addition, the internal database configuration parameters (`olcDb*`) are read and checked for meaningful values that differ from the default values.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The database settings are optimized based on documented best practices for performance and security. The file system permissions are regularly checked for compliance. Automatic and regular integrity checks of the database are performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool ensures that the optimized database parameters (e.g., `olcDbCacheSize`, indexes) and file permissions are consistently applied. A nightly cron job runs `mdb_cv` or a similar tool to check the integrity of the database and reports errors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation on best practices and compares it with the implemented configuration. The logs of the automated integrity checks are reviewed. The configuration of the configuration management tool is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The database is encrypted at rest using file system or database-native encryption. Access to the database files is monitored in real time by a File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) tool. All configuration parameters are managed via a configuration management system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The file system on which the OpenLDAP database resides is encrypted with LUKS. A FIM tool such as AIDE or Wazuh is configured to immediately report any read or write access to the database files that does not originate from the `slapd` process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the status of the file system encryption (e.g., with `cryptsetup status`). The configuration and the alerting logs of the FIM tool are analyzed. It is checked whether an unauthorized access (e.g., with `cat` by root) triggers an alarm.

controls.title: Secure assignment of access rights on the OpenLDAP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only a simple global access control list (ACL) is defined, which often grants broad read access to anonymous or authenticated users. Specific access rights are not implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A typical ACL would be `access to * by * read`, which gives everyone read access to everything.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reads the global `olcAccess` directive and determines that it is too permissive and contains no differentiated rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Both global and database-specific ACLs are used, but they may still be too permissive. The precedence rule (database-specific over global) is known, but is not specifically used to create granular policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a global ACL and an additional ACL for the main database that governs some write access. However, permissions are often granted more broadly than necessary, e.g., write access to the entire own entry instead of only to specific attributes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes both the global (`olcAccess`) and database-specific (`olcDbAccess`) ACLs and identifies overly permissive rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The global and database-specific Access Control Lists (ACLs) maintained in OpenLDAP MUST be correctly considered when using OpenLDAP. Database directives MUST take precedence over global directives.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A default, restrictive global ACL is defined (e.g., only authentication and self-read access). Specific permissions for applications or administrators are granted selectively in the respective database ACLs (`olcDbAccess`). This ensures that specific rules override global ones and the principle of least privilege is implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the global ACLs form a restrictive basis and that specific, required access rights are defined exclusively in the database-specific ACLs. Test queries are used to check whether the ACL hierarchy functions as expected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ACLs are regularly reviewed and audited. A documented access rights policy exists. Complex ACLs that use features like group membership, attribute values, or connection properties are used to enforce fine-grained access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: ACLs use advanced clauses like `group.exact` or `val.exact` to make access rights very specific. For example, a user may only change the `telephoneNumber` attribute, but not the `userPassword`. These policies are recorded in a document and reviewed annually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the access rights policy and compares it with the implemented ACLs. It is checked whether the regular reviews of the ACLs have taken place and are documented. Complex test queries are performed to verify the effectiveness of the granular rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ACLs are managed and versioned as code. Automated tools are used to test the ACLs against a set of predefined security policies. Any change to the ACLs triggers an automated review and approval workflow.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `olcAccess` attributes are stored in LDIF files in a Git repository. A CI/CD pipeline runs a test framework upon each change, which executes a series of LDAP queries and checks whether the access conforms to the expected result (allowed/denied). The change can only be rolled out after successful tests.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the Git history of the ACL files and the logs of the CI/CD pipeline. It is checked whether the test framework provides comprehensive coverage of the security policies. The approval workflow is reviewed for its effectiveness.

controls.title: Secure authentication to OpenLDAP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is required, but communication may occur unencrypted (Simple Bind over cleartext LDAP). Passwords are stored as hashes, but with an outdated algorithm like MD5.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Clients connect via `ldap://` (port 389) and send passwords in cleartext or as part of an unprotected Simple Bind. The `userPassword` attribute contains hashes in `{MD5}` format.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the server configuration for active unencrypted listeners. `ldapsearch` is used to check which password hashing algorithms are used. A network capture would show the unencrypted transmission of credentials.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All authentication communication is encrypted (LDAPS or STARTTLS). A modern hashing algorithm is used, but it may not be the strongest recommended one (e.g., SSHA-1).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The server is configured to accept connections via `ldaps://` (port 636) or via STARTTLS on the standard port. Passwords are stored at least as `{SSHA}` (salted SHA-1).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the server's TLS certificates and protocols. `ldapsearch` is used to check that only modern, salted hashing algorithms are used for passwords.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If the directory service is to distinguish between different users, they MUST authenticate appropriately. Authentication between the slapd server and the communicating parties MUST be encrypted. ONLY the hash values of passwords SHOULD be stored on clients and servers. A suitable hashing algorithm MUST be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The server configuration enforces TLS for all connections that require authentication. A strong hashing algorithm from the SHA-2 family (e.g., `{SSHA256}` or `{SSHA512}`) is configured and used for all new passwords. It is ensured that no cleartext passwords are stored in the directory or in log files.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies by reading the configuration (`olcSecurity`) that encryption is enforced. `ldapsearch` is used to randomly check that all `userPassword` attributes have a hash prefix like `{SSHA256}`. It is checked whether there is a policy that prohibits the storage of cleartext passwords.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of strong, password-based key derivation functions (e.g., Argon2, scrypt, PBKDF2) is enforced as the hashing algorithm. Simple Binds are avoided in favor of SASL mechanisms (e.g., DIGEST-MD5, GSSAPI) whenever possible. Server certificates are properly validated by the clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `argon2` module is loaded in OpenLDAP and configured as the default hashing mechanism. Clients are instructed to authenticate via SASL/GSSAPI (Kerberos) if a corresponding infrastructure is available. The server's TLS configuration is hardened (e.g., only TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the `argon2` or a comparable module is loaded and configured. The `olcAuthzRegexp` directives are checked to determine if they enforce SASL mechanisms. The server's TLS configuration is checked for vulnerabilities using tools like `testssl.sh`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enforced for privileged users. Certificate-based client authentication (SASL EXTERNAL) is used for communication between services. Anonymous binds are completely disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MFA solution is integrated, e.g., via a RADIUS backend or a custom overlay that checks one-time passwords (TOTP). Service accounts receive client certificates with which they authenticate via SASL EXTERNAL. The global ACL is configured to completely prevent anonymous access (`access to * by anonymous auth`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the login process for a privileged account and verifies that a second factor is requested. The configuration for SASL EXTERNAL and the associated ACLs are checked. It is verified that an anonymous `ldapsearch` command fails.

controls.title: Attribute restrictions in OpenLDAP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Restrictions are implemented for only a single, critical attribute, e.g., ensuring that the user ID (`uid`) is unique.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `unique` overlay is configured for the `uid` attribute.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to create a user with an existing `uid` and expects the operation to fail. It is noted that no further restrictions exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The `constraint` overlay is used to enforce the uniqueness and format of values for several important attributes (e.g., `uid`, `mail`). The restrictions apply to all object types.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `constraint` overlay is configured with simple regular expressions for email addresses and rules for the uniqueness of `uid` and `mail`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the `constraint` overlay (`olcConstraintAttribute`). It attempts to create objects with invalid or duplicate attribute values.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Attributes in OpenLDAP SHOULD be restricted using overlays. OpenLDAP SHOULD be adapted so that values in the directory service only match a specific regular expression. In addition, overlays SHOULD be used to ensure that selected values exist only once in the directory tree. Such restrictions SHOULD only be applied to user data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `constraint` overlay is used selectively to ensure data quality. URI-based restrictions (`olcConstraintURI`) are used to apply the rules only to specific parts of the directory tree (e.g., the `ou=people`) and specific object types (`objectClass=inetOrgPerson`). This prevents the restrictions from accidentally affecting service or configuration accounts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the `constraint` overlay and verifies that the `olcConstraintURI` directives are set correctly to limit the scope of the restrictions to user data as required. It is tested whether creating a user with an invalid email address fails, while a service account with a differently formatted attribute can be created.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of attribute restrictions is a standard part of the schema design. Regular expressions for value validation are complex and cover all relevant data formats. A policy specifies which attributes must be unique or conform to specific formats.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each new attribute in the schema, the design process checks whether a restriction (uniqueness, format, value range) is required. These requirements are documented in a central policy and implemented in the `constraint` overlay.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the schema and attribute policy. It randomly checks whether the restrictions defined in the policy are correctly implemented in the `constraint` overlay and are effective.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Attribute restrictions are dynamically enforced and monitored. An automated process regularly validates the entire directory against the restriction policies and reports any violations. The `constraint` overlay is combined with other overlays (e.g., `ppolicy`) for comprehensive enforcement of data quality and security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script runs nightly through the entire LDAP directory and checks each entry against the rules defined in the `constraint` overlay. This serves to find any inconsistent data that may have been created before the rules were introduced. Violations are recorded in a report and assigned to a data owner for correction.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports from the automated validation process. It is checked whether a process exists and is followed for correcting reported inconsistencies. The combination of overlays is checked for logical correctness and completeness.

controls.title: Partitioning and Replication in OpenLDAP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single replica server is set up for basic failover, but the replication mode is not selected based on network or availability requirements. Partitioning is not used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A second OpenLDAP server is set up and configured as a simple consumer (`olcSyncrepl`), often in `refreshOnly` mode.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the second server and its `olcSyncrepl` configuration. It is determined that the configuration is not optimized for high availability and that no partitioning is used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A multi-provider replication is set up for high availability. The replication mode (e.g., sync, refreshAndPersist) is selected, but without an in-depth analysis of its effects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At least two servers are set up as providers in a multi-provider configuration, so that each server can accept write operations. The `refreshAndPersist` mode is used for replication.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration on all replica servers and ensures that multi-provider replication is set up correctly. It is tested whether a change made on one server is correctly replicated to the others.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When partitioning or replicating OpenLDAP, the division SHOULD be selected appropriately for the security objectives. Changes to the data SHOULD be exchanged between servers through replication. A replication mode SHOULD be chosen depending on network connections and availability requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision for a specific replication topology (e.g., multi-provider vs. provider/consumer) and the replication mode (`olcSyncrepl` parameters) is documented and based on failover and write latency requirements. If there are different security requirements for data, separate database backends (partitions) with different replication settings and ACLs are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation on the replication and partitioning strategy. It is checked whether the selected configuration corresponds to the documented objectives. For example, in the case of geographically distributed locations, it is checked whether a mode has been selected that can handle higher network latencies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The replication topology is designed to optimize performance and availability (e.g., geographically distributed replicas). Replication traffic is encrypted and monitored for latency and errors. A documented disaster recovery plan that uses replication exists.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Replication between servers is carried out over TLS-secured connections. Monitoring tools (e.g., Prometheus with an OpenLDAP exporter) monitor the replication status (`contextCSN`) on all replicas and alert in case of excessive deviation (lag). The DR plan describes the steps to restore the service after the failure of an entire data center.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the TLS configuration for replication. The configuration and data of the monitoring system are analyzed. The disaster recovery plan is checked for completeness and plausibility. Ideally, proof of a DR drill is provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully automated failover mechanism is implemented. The system can dynamically adjust the number of replicas to the load. The replication status is continuously monitored, and any delay or inconsistency triggers an automated alert and potentially a corrective action.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A load balancer with health checks automatically redirects requests away from failed servers. In a cloud or containerized environment, an autoscaling mechanism is used to launch additional read-only replicas under high load. A script continuously checks the `contextCSN` of all servers and attempts to reinitialize replication on the affected node in case of inconsistencies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the failover mechanism by deliberately stopping an OpenLDAP server and observing whether the service continues to run without interruption. The configuration of autoscaling and automated corrective actions is checked. The logs of these systems are analyzed for their effectiveness.

controls.title: Secure Updating of OpenLDAP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Updates are applied sporadically without checking for compatibility issues with backends, overlays, or custom scripts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Updates are only performed when a problem occurs or a new feature is needed. The release notes are not read.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that an outdated, potentially vulnerable version of OpenLDAP is running on the system. There is no documentation of performed updates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Updates are applied regularly. A manual check for major compatibility issues (e.g., deprecated overlays) is performed by reading the release notes. The configuration is manually checked after the update.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: OpenLDAP is updated as part of regular patch management. The administrator reads the release notes to determine if used features have been removed. After the update, the service is restarted and a simple test query is performed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies from system logs or the patch management system that updates are applied regularly. It is checked whether a process exists where the release notes are reviewed before an update.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For updates, it SHOULD be checked whether the changes affect used backends or overlays as well as software dependencies. When updating to new releases, it SHOULD be checked whether the used overlays and backends are still available in the new version. If this is not the case, suitable migration paths SHOULD be selected. If administrators use their own scripts, they SHOULD be checked to ensure they work smoothly with the updated version of OpenLDAP. The configuration and access rights SHOULD be carefully checked after an update.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A checklist is worked through before an update. This includes checking the release notes for changes to used backends and overlays, checking the compatibility of connected applications and custom administration scripts. After the update, the configuration is explicitly checked (`slaptest`) and its functionality is verified through a series of defined test cases.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the checklist and the documentation of the latest updates. It is checked whether all points mentioned in the requirement (backends, overlays, scripts, configuration, access rights) have been considered. The results of the post-update tests are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Updates are first tested in a dedicated test environment that mirrors the production environment. A documented rollback plan is created for each update. Custom scripts are checked with an automated test suite.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before rolling out to production, the update is installed on a staging system that contains a current copy of the production database and configuration. An automated test suite that performs typical read and write operations is executed. The rollback plan describes how to restore the old version of the software and the database from a backup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and condition of the test environment. The documentation of the test runs and the rollback plans for the latest updates are reviewed. It is checked whether the automated test suite provides adequate test coverage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire update process is automated. A canary deployment strategy is used to first roll out the update to a subset of the replicas. Automated health and functional tests are run after the update to verify the integrity of the system before the rollout is completed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CI/CD pipeline fetches new OpenLDAP versions, builds a new container image, and first rolls it out to one replica (canary). The load balancer directs only a small portion of the traffic to this replica. Automated end-to-end tests and monitoring of error rates automatically decide whether to extend the update to all other replicas or roll it back.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and the logs of the CI/CD pipeline. The configuration of the canary deployment and the automated tests is checked. The metrics and dashboards of the monitoring system are reviewed to assess the effectiveness of the automated health checks.

controls.title: Restriction of the OpenLDAP runtime environment

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The slapd server runs as a non-privileged user, but no further restrictions are applied to the runtime environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `slapd` process is started as the `ldap` user, but otherwise has full access to the host's file system and network resources as permitted by the user's rights.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies with `ps aux | grep slapd` that the process is running as a non-privileged user. It is determined that no further security mechanisms such as chroot or AppArmor are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The slapd server is run in a simple container or on a dedicated server with standard operating system hardening. Basic restrictions are applied.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: OpenLDAP is run in a standard Docker container or installed on a server where a basic operating system hardening script has been executed. No special profiles are created for the container or the service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the service is containerized or runs on a hardened system. However, it is verified that no specific security profiles (e.g., seccomp, AppArmor) are configured for the OpenLDAP process itself.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The runtime environment of the slapd server SHOULD be restricted to the minimally required files, directories, and functions provided by the operating system, preferably using OS means. If containerization techniques are used for this purpose, they SHOULD be used taking into account SYS.1.6 Containerization. If the slapd server is operated as an exclusive service on a dedicated server, it SHOULD be sufficiently hardened.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specific security profile is created and applied for the slapd process, e.g., using AppArmor or SELinux. This profile restricts file system access to the required directories (`/etc/ldap`, `/var/lib/ldap`) and prohibits the execution of external programs. When using containers, a hardened base image is used and container features are restricted according to the recommendations from SYS.1.6.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the activity and content of the AppArmor/SELinux profile for slapd (e.g., using `aa-status`). It is verified that the profile restricts access to the bare essentials. For containers, the configuration (`docker inspect`) is checked for security settings like `security_opt` or `cap_drop`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A hardened container image is used from which all unnecessary binaries and libraries have been removed. A strict security profile (e.g., AppArmor, seccomp) is enforced, restricting system calls (syscalls) to the absolute necessary minimum. Network access is strictly controlled via firewall rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A custom, minimalist container image is created. A `seccomp` profile is generated (e.g., with `strace`) that only allows the system calls actually used by slapd. Host-based firewall rules (iptables, nftables) only allow incoming connections on the LDAP(S) ports from defined IP address ranges.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the Dockerfile of the used image for its minimality. The `seccomp` profile is checked for completeness and correctness. The firewall rules affecting the slapd process or container are analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The slapd server runs in a minimal, 'distroless' container. All interactions with the host operating system are logged and monitored for anomalies. The integrity of the container is checked at runtime. The entire environment is defined as code and is automatically deployed and audited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The OpenLDAP binary is copied into a 'distroless' or scratch image that contains no shell or other tools. A runtime security tool (e.g., Falco, Sysdig) monitors the container's system calls in real-time and reports suspicious activities. The entire environment definition (container, network, profiles) is managed in a Git repository and deployed via a CI/CD pipeline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the use of a 'distroless' image. The configuration and the alerting rules of the runtime security tool are analyzed. It is checked whether an attempt to start a shell in the container is detected and reported. The CI/CD pipeline and the associated configuration files are audited.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
OpenLDAP is a freely available directory service that provides information about any objects, for example accounts, IT systems or configurations, in a standardized and defined manner within a data network. The information can include simple attributes such as the names or numbers of objects, or complex formats such as photos or certificates for electronic signatures. Typical application areas include address books or account management, but also configurations.
OpenLDAP is a reference implementation of a server service within the framework of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). As open-source software, OpenLDAP can be installed on a variety of operating systems and is considered one of the most widespread directory services. A special feature of OpenLDAP is its overlays. Overlays extend the functional scope of OpenLDAP with numerous features and are also used for basic functions such as logging, replication, and ensuring integrity.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to securely operate OpenLDAP-based directory services and to adequately protect the information processed by them.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
Module APP.2.3 OpenLDAP is to be applied to every OpenLDAP directory.
This module examines the threats and requirements specific to OpenLDAP. It is based on version 2.4 of OpenLDAP. General security recommendations for directory services can be found in module APP.2.1 General Directory Service. These must also be taken into account. The requirements described there are specified and supplemented in this module.
OpenLDAP should generally be considered in the context of the modules ORP.4 Identity and Access Management, OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management, CON.3 Data Backup Concept, OPS.1.2.2 Archiving, OPS.1.1.5 Logging, and OPS.1.1.2 Proper IT Administration.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Missing or insufficient planning of OpenLDAP
parts.prose:
OpenLDAP can be used in conjunction with numerous other applications. These applications can access the directory service's information and usually also change it. If the use of OpenLDAP is not planned or is planned inadequately, the following problems can occur:

• If the backends and the associated directives and parameters are selected incorrectly, they will unintentionally affect the functions that OpenLDAP can offer. For example, if the "back-ldif" backend is used for data storage to avoid installing an additional database, only rudimentary functions of the directory service are available. A large number of users or other objects cannot then be managed appropriately.

• If the use of overlays is poorly planned, unneeded operations can be performed in OpenLDAP or other functions can be impaired. For example, access to the directory service is not logged or is logged incorrectly if the debug function of the slapd server itself and the "auditlog" and "accesslog" overlays are inadequately planned.

• OpenLDAP can be run in an unsuitable system environment. If a distributed file system such as Network File System (NFS) is used to store the OpenLDAP data, file functions of OpenLDAP might not be usable. An example of this is the locking function used by many databases, which makes it possible to lock the directory service's database when multiple users want to access the database with write permissions simultaneously.

• Incompatible versions of one or more applications could access the databases used by OpenLDAP. For example, the specifications of the LDAPv3 protocol are not met by OpenLDAP without additional extensions. In addition, connection problems with the applications can also arise if the wrong version of one or more programs that are not compatible with OpenLDAP is used.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficient separation of offline and online access to OpenLDAP
parts.prose: The data managed by OpenLDAP (objects in the directory service as well as configuration settings) can be accessed in various ways. The offline and online access methods fulfill identical or partially identical functions. With online access, the data is accessed via the LDAP protocol and slapd. With offline access, the database files are accessed directly, or an LDIF export of the directory is edited and then loaded back into the database. If these methods are mixed or the respective mode of action of offline or online access is misinterpreted, numerous errors can occur. As a result, the resulting database for OpenLDAP is inconsistent and can therefore no longer be used without errors.

controls.title: Authentication

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is implemented for only some, but not all, sensitive areas of the web application or web service. There are no, or only very weakly defined, limits for failed login attempts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The developers have only protected the most obvious endpoints such as an admin login, while other, equally sensitive functions (e.g., user profile pages) remain openly accessible. The configuration for login attempts was left at the default values in the web server or framework.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies through manual tests and configuration review whether all sensitive resources enforce authentication. It is checked whether an unlimited number of failed login attempts is possible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All sensitive resources of the web application or web service require client authentication. Simple authentication methods such as username and password are used. Basic limits for failed login attempts are set.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All server-side routes that deliver protected data or execute functions check for a valid user session. A mechanism such as `fail2ban` or an in-application logic is implemented in the configuration, which blocks a user or an IP address for one minute after, for example, 10 failed attempts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor ensures that authentication is enforced for all protected areas. The configuration of the limits for login attempts is reviewed and their basic effectiveness is verified through a test.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations MUST configure web applications and web services so that clients must authenticate themselves to the web application or web service when they want to access protected resources. An appropriate authentication method MUST be selected for this purpose. IT operations MUST set suitable limits for failed login attempts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The choice of authentication method (e.g., form-based, token-based like JWT, or certificate-based) is made based on a risk assessment. The limits for failed login attempts are defined to hinder brute-force attacks but not excessively hinder legitimate users (e.g., 15-minute lockout after 5 failed attempts).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the authentication and the limits for login attempts. It is checked whether the choice of authentication method is appropriate for the protection needs of the application.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is strengthened by the use of multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all user accounts. The selection process for the authentication method SHOULD be documented. The established limits for failed login attempts are actively monitored, and administrators are informed about suspicious activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: MFA is implemented using TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) or push notifications to a mobile app. The selection process is recorded in the application's technical documentation. Login logs are sent to a central log management system, which triggers an alarm if there is a high rate of failed logins from one IP address.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the implementation of MFA and the existence of the documentation for the selection process. The configuration of the log management and the alerting rules are reviewed and tested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is mandatory for all access and by default uses phishing-resistant methods (e.g., FIDO2/WebAuthn). Login attempts and session activities are analyzed in real-time by a SIEM system, which automatically locks accounts, terminates sessions, and generates security incidents in case of anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application is registered as a Relying Party with a FIDO2 server. Users are guided to register a security key or biometric features during registration. The application logs are fed into a SIEM that has playbooks to automatically respond to attacks like credential stuffing or brute-forcing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the FIDO2 implementation and the effectiveness of the automated response mechanisms in the SIEM through simulated attacks. The documentation of the SIEM playbooks and the incident response processes is reviewed.

controls.title: Controlled inclusion of files and content

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The upload function exists, but it only superficially checks the file type (e.g., based on the file extension) or does not enforce size limits. The uploaded files are stored in an insecure location.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The code only checks if the filename ends with `.jpg` or `.pdf`. There is no server-side limit on the file size, which can lead to Denial-of-Service by uploading very large files. The files end up in the same directory as the application scripts and may be directly accessible via a URL.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to upload files with fake extensions (e.g., `shell.php.jpg`), without an extension, or very large files. It is checked whether uploaded files can be executed or downloaded directly via the web server.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The upload function checks the MIME type of the file and enforces a maximum file size. Uploaded files are stored in a separate, dedicated directory, but the file permissions may be too permissive.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `Content-Type` header or magic byte analysis is used server-side to verify the file type. A size limit is set in the web server or application configuration. An `/uploads` directory exists, but its permissions are 777.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the file size and type restriction. Using shell access to the server, the upload directory and its file permissions (`ls -l`) are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If a web application or web service offers a file upload function, this function MUST be restricted by IT operations as much as possible. In particular, the allowed file size, allowed file types, and allowed storage locations MUST be specified. It MUST be specified which clients are allowed to use the function. Access and execution rights MUST also be set restrictively. Furthermore, it MUST be ensured that clients can only save files in the specified allowed storage location.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A whitelist of allowed file types (based on MIME type and file content analysis) and a maximum file size are firmly configured. Upload is only allowed for authenticated users. The files are stored in a directory outside the web root with minimal permissions (e.g., no execute right). Access to the files is via a script that checks the permissions of the requesting user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the whitelist, the size limit, and the storage locations. It is verified that the file permissions are set correctly and that anonymous users cannot upload files. It is tested whether uploaded files can only be accessed after a permission check.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All uploaded files are scanned for malware with an up-to-date virus scanner on the server-side after upload, before they are made available to other users. All upload operations are logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After saving the file, a command-line scanner (e.g., ClamAV) is called. The file is only moved to the final directory or marked as 'available' in the database if the scan is negative. Every upload attempt (successful or not) is written to a log file with user ID, timestamp, filename, and scan result.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to upload a test file with an EICAR signature and verifies that it is blocked or deleted. The log files are checked for completeness of the logged upload operations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The processing of uploaded files (including malware scan and content analysis) takes place in an isolated sandbox environment. The file storage is a dedicated, hardened object storage service that is physically separate from the application server. The filenames are regenerated server-side to prevent path traversal attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application temporarily uploads files to a bucket, which triggers a serverless function (e.g. AWS Lambda). This function performs virus scans and content analysis in a container sandbox and then moves the validated file to a permanent, non-publicly accessible S3 bucket. The application generates signed, short-lived URLs for authorized access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the architecture of the upload processing and verifies the configuration of the sandbox environment and the object storage. It is checked whether the generated filenames contain no user-controlled elements and whether direct access to the storage is blocked.

controls.title: Protection against unauthorized automated use

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No specific protection mechanisms against automated use are implemented. The application is vulnerable to simple brute-force attacks on login forms or resource-intensive queries.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no rate limiting or CAPTCHA functionality. A simple script can call the login form thousands of times per minute without restriction.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester uses an automation tool (e.g., Burp Intruder) to send a high number of requests to a critical function (e.g., login, registration, search) and observes that no countermeasures are triggered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple protection mechanism like a traditional CAPTCHA (e.g., with distorted text) is implemented on the login page. There is a simple, server-wide rate limit.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple CAPTCHA library is integrated into the login form. The web server (e.g., Nginx) is configured to accept no more than 100 requests per second from a single IP address.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester verifies the existence and function of the CAPTCHA. The rate limiting configuration in the web server is checked. It is tested whether the rate limit is effective and whether the CAPTCHA also protects other critical forms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations MUST ensure that web applications and web services are protected against unauthorized automated use. However, it MUST be considered how the protection mechanisms affect the usage options of legitimate clients. If the web application contains RSS feeds or other functions that are explicitly intended for automated use, this MUST also be taken into account when configuring the protection mechanisms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Application-specific rate limits are implemented for sensitive functions (login, password reset, API endpoints). Endpoints for legitimate automated use (such as RSS feeds or APIs for partners) are excluded from the strictest rate limits or receive their own, higher limits. A modern challenge-response system (e.g., hCaptcha) is displayed after several failed attempts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the configuration of the protection mechanisms and verifies that they do not hinder legitimate use (e.g., retrieving an RSS feed). It is tested whether the rate limit is function-specific and whether a challenge is triggered after a certain number of requests.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A modern, user-friendly challenge-response system (e.g., invisible reCAPTCHA) is active by default on all sensitive, unauthenticated endpoints. Temporary blocks are imposed not only per IP address but also per user account. Suspicious automated access attempts are logged and trigger alarms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application integrates a service like Google reCAPTCHA v3, which provides a risk score for each request and only displays a visible challenge for high-risk scores. The application logic tracks failed attempts per account and locks it after too many attempts, regardless of the source IP. These events are sent to a SIEM for monitoring.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester verifies the implementation of the challenge-response system and tests the blocking mechanisms for IP addresses and user accounts. The alerting rules in the SIEM are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated bot management solution is used, which distinguishes between human users, legitimate bots (e.g., search engines), and malicious bots using device fingerprinting, behavioral analysis, and reputation databases. Based on this classification, granular access rules and countermeasures are automatically enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A commercial service (e.g., from Akamai, Cloudflare, Imperva) is placed in front of the application. This analyzes incoming traffic and enriches requests with metadata about the client. The web application or the edge service itself blocks, throttles, or redirects traffic based on the bot classification. For example, search engine crawlers are allowed, while credential stuffing tools are blocked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester reviews the configuration of the bot management solution and the defined policies. Specialized tools are used to simulate various bot identities to verify the correct classification and response of the system.

controls.title: Protection of confidential data

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Credentials are stored hashed, but not salted. Parts of the source code, such as include files or configuration files, may be directly accessible via the web server.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application uses a `sha1($password)` function to store passwords. `.inc` or `.config` files are located in the web root, and the web server is not configured to block direct access to them.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester inspects the source code for password storage. A web scanner or manual requests are used to attempt to directly access known configuration or source code files.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Credentials are stored with a salt and a hash function, but an outdated or weak algorithm (e.g., MD5 or SHA1) is used. The application's source code is generally protected from direct access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application uses a function like `md5($salt . $password)`. The web server is configured to deny access to files with specific extensions (.php, .inc).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester checks the source code and identifies the hashing algorithm used. The web server configuration is checked for rules to protect source code files.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations MUST ensure that credentials for the web application or web service are protected on the server side against unauthorized access using secure cryptographic algorithms. For this, salted hash methods MUST be used. The files with the source code of the web application or web service MUST be protected from unauthorized retrieval.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A modern, recognized as secure, salted hash method (e.g., bcrypt) with an appropriate cost factor is used. The entire application source code is stored in a directory outside the web server's document root, so that only a single `index.php` file is in the public directory (front controller pattern).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester verifies the use of a secure salted hash method in the source code. The directory structure on the server is checked to ensure that the source code is not in the web root.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For storing credentials, a modern, computationally intensive hashing method such as Argon2 or scrypt is used with parameters recommended by security experts. The source code is managed in a secure version control system, and access to it is strictly regulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application uses a standard library that implements Argon2id. The parameters for memory cost, time cost, and parallelism are configured according to current recommendations. The source code is in a Git repository for which branch protection rules and mandatory code reviews for changes apply.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester verifies the configuration of the hashing algorithm and compares the parameters with current best practices. The configuration of the version control system and the access permissions are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hashed credentials are additionally encrypted with an application-specific key, which is securely stored in a Hardware Security Module (HSM) or a dedicated Key Management Service (KMS). The source code is deployed to the production systems via a secure CI/CD pipeline that performs automated security tests (SAST).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application calls a KMS API (e.g., AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) to encrypt and decrypt the hashed passwords. The application's authentication to the KMS is done via short-lived, role-based credentials. The Jenkins or GitLab pipeline includes a step that runs a SAST scan before each deployment and aborts the build if critical findings are detected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the key management architecture and verifies the configuration and access policies of the HSM/KMS. The CI/CD pipeline configuration is checked for the integration and configuration of the SAST tool.

controls.title: System architecture

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The application is developed ad-hoc with a focus on the fastest possible delivery of functions. A documented architecture does not exist, and security aspects are not systematically considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application is monolithic and mixes different responsibilities (e.g., data access, business logic, and presentation) in the same code, which is known as a 'Big Ball of Mud'. There are no clear interfaces.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester determines through interviews with developers and an analysis of the source code that no conscious architectural decision was made and no architectural documentation is available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is basic architectural documentation that describes the main components of the application and their interaction. General security aspects are mentioned but not integrated into the architecture.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a simple diagram showing the web server, the application server, and the database. The documentation contains a general sentence like 'Communication must be secure' without specifying this technically.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester reviews the architectural documentation and compares it with the actual implementation. It is found that security aspects are only treated superficially.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security aspects SHOULD be considered already during the planning of web applications and web services. It SHOULD also be ensured that the architecture of the web application or web service accurately captures and correctly implements the business logic of the institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the planning phase, an architectural decision (e.g., 3-tier architecture, microservices) is made and documented. The architectural design explicitly considers security principles such as separation of concerns and defined interfaces. It is ensured that the architecture correctly maps the business processes to avoid logical errors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester reviews the architectural documentation and verifies that security aspects are part of the design. Through workshops with business departments and developers, it is checked whether the architecture correctly implements the business logic.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A systematic threat modeling (e.g., according to STRIDE) is performed for the planned architecture to identify potential threats. The architecture is designed according to the principles 'Secure by Design' and 'Defense in Depth' and explicitly includes security components (e.g., API Gateway, WAF).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before development begins, a workshop is held to create a data flow diagram and identify threats for each process and data flow using STRIDE. The resulting countermeasures are incorporated into the architecture design. The design is documented in an architecture framework such as the C4 Model.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the threat modeling documentation and the security requirements derived from it. A check is performed to see if the identified countermeasures have been implemented in the final architecture and implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system architecture is based on a zero-trust model, in which no implicit trust relationships exist. Every interaction between components is explicitly authenticated and authorized. The architecture is reviewed and approved by a formal Security Architecture Board and is continuously evolved based on new threat intelligence.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application is implemented as a collection of microservices that communicate via a service mesh (e.g., Istio). The service mesh enforces mutual TLS authentication (mTLS) and fine-grained authorization policies for all internal communication. Architectural changes require the approval of the Architecture Board.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the service mesh and the authorization policies. The minutes of the Security Architecture Board are reviewed. A check is performed to see if the architecture is regularly updated to respond to new threats.

controls.title: Procurement of web applications and web services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the general aspects of software procurement, the institution SHOULD consider at least the following when procuring web applications and web services: secure input validation and output encoding, secure session management, secure cryptographic methods, secure authentication methods, secure methods for server-side storage of credentials, appropriate authorization management, sufficient logging capabilities, regular security updates by the software developer, protection mechanisms against common attacks on web applications and web services, and access to the source code of the web application or web service.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement requirements catalog contains a detailed checklist with the mentioned security properties. Vendors must explicitly address each requirement in their bid and describe its implementation. Fulfillment of these requirements becomes a contractual component.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement documents (tender, requirements catalog) and the received bids. It is checked whether the security requirements are clearly formulated and whether the bids address them. The final contract is reviewed for the binding nature of the security commitments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of the procurement process, vendors must provide evidence of their Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC). The software to be procured undergoes an independent security assessment or a penetration test before purchase. Fixed deadlines for the provision of security patches are contractually agreed upon.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Vendors are asked to provide certifications (e.g., ISO 27001) or reports on their development processes. An external service provider is commissioned to test a trial version of the software.
