The contract stipulates that critical vulnerabilities must be fixed by a manufacturer's patch within 48 hours of being discovered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the evidence provided by the vendor regarding the SSDLC and the report of the independent security assessment. The contract is checked for the clauses on Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for security patches.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Vendors must provide a complete Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for the product. The software undergoes intensive internal and external penetration tests before final acceptance. The contract with the vendor includes strict SLAs for vulnerability remediation and an audit right that allows the institution to review the vendor's development processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SBOM is required in a standard format (e.g., CycloneDX) and is automatically checked for known vulnerabilities in its components. The internal Red Team and an external vendor test the software in parallel. The contract includes a clause that allows for an annual audit of the manufacturer's security practices by a third party commissioned by the institution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the provided SBOM and the results of the internal and external penetration tests. The contract clauses on the audit right and SLAs are checked for their effectiveness and enforceability.

controls.title: Secure connection of backend systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to backend systems, to which functions and data are outsourced, SHOULD only be possible via defined interfaces and from defined IT systems. When communicating across network and site boundaries, the data traffic SHOULD be authenticated and encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web application communicates with backend services (e.g., database, microservices) exclusively via well-defined REST or gRPC APIs. Firewall rules ensure that only the application server can access these services. The communication is encrypted using TLS, and the application authenticates itself to the backend service, e.g., with an API key.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network architecture and the firewall rules. The configuration of the interfaces and the communication is checked for the use of encryption and authentication. An attempt is made to access the backend systems from an unauthorized system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An API gateway is used to serve as the single point of access for all backend systems. The gateway enforces strong authentication (e.g., OAuth 2.0), authorization, rate limiting, and logging for all requests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An API gateway (e.g., Kong, Tyk) is placed in front of the backend services. The web application obtains a short-lived JWT (JSON Web Token) from an Identity Provider and sends it with every request to the API gateway. The gateway validates the token and only forwards the request to the corresponding backend service if the token is valid and has sufficient permissions (scopes).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the API gateway, the Identity Provider, and the token validation. It is tested whether requests with invalid, expired, or insufficiently privileged tokens are correctly rejected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A zero-trust model is applied, where every request between the web application and the backend systems is authenticated and authorized, regardless of its network location. All communication is secured by mutual TLS authentication (mTLS), where both the client and the server identify themselves with certificates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A service mesh (e.g., Istio, Linkerd) is used in the Kubernetes cluster to manage all service-to-service communication. The service mesh enforces mTLS for all connections and applies fine-grained authorization policies that define which service can communicate with which other service. The certificates are automatically rotated by an internal PKI.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the service mesh, the mTLS settings, and the authorization policies. Network sniffing within the cluster is used to verify that all traffic is encrypted. An attempt is made to bypass the authorization policies.

controls.title: Secure Configuration

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Web applications and web services SHOULD be configured so that their resources and functions can only be accessed via the intended, secured communication paths. Access to unneeded resources and functions SHOULD be disabled. If this is not possible, access SHOULD be restricted as much as possible. The following SHOULD be implemented when configuring web applications and web services: Disabling unneeded HTTP methods, configuring character encoding, avoiding security-relevant information in error messages and responses, storing configuration files outside the web root directory, and setting limits for access attempts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web server configuration is manually adjusted to allow only GET, POST, and HEAD requests. Detailed error messages are disabled in the application and generic error pages are displayed. The database credentials are stored in a file outside the `/var/www/html` directory. The character encoding (e.g., UTF-8) is set in the HTTP headers and in the database connection. Limits for access attempts are implemented in the application logic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the web server and the application. The `OPTIONS` HTTP request is used to check which methods are allowed. By provoking errors, it is verified that no sensitive information is disclosed. The directory structure and the configuration of the access limits are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secure configuration of the application and the web server is managed as code (Infrastructure as Code) in a version control system. This ensures a consistent, traceable, and repeatable configuration across all environments (development, testing, production).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Ansible, Puppet, or Terraform are used to create playbooks or configuration files that define all aspects of the secure configuration. These files are stored in a Git repository. Changes to the configuration must go through a pull request process with a review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the IaC scripts in the Git repository and compares them with the security policies. It is checked whether the production configuration corresponds to the state defined in the repository, e.g., by running a `terraform plan` or `ansible --check`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration is continuously monitored for compliance with a defined, hardened baseline. Any deviation from this baseline (configuration drift) triggers an automated alert and/or an automated remediation action. The configuration is subject to regular formal reviews and audits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tool or a configuration management tool in enforcing mode is used. For example, if a firewall rule is changed manually, it is either automatically reset or a high-priority alert is generated in a SIEM. The results of the configuration scans are part of the regular internal and external audits.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the monitoring tool, the defined baselines, and the alerting and remediation workflows. An intentional misconfiguration is made to test the system's reaction. The reports of the regular reviews are inspected.

controls.title: Secure HTTP configuration for web applications

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To protect against clickjacking, cross-site scripting, and other attacks, IT operations SHOULD set appropriate HTTP response headers. At a minimum, the following HTTP headers SHOULD be used: Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Type, X-Content-Type-Options, and Cache-Control. Cookies SHOULD generally be set with the secure, SameSite, and httponly attributes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web server or application is configured to send these headers with every response. The Content-Security-Policy (CSP) is initially relatively open (e.g., allowing scripts from its own domain and known CDNs). HSTS is configured with a short `max-age` time. Cookies have `httponly; secure; SameSite=Lax` set.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester uses the browser's developer tools or a tool like `curl -I` to inspect the application's HTTP headers. They check if the required headers are present and if the cookie attributes are set correctly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the HTTP headers is restrictive and follows the principle of least privilege. The Content-Security-Policy is configured as strictly as possible and avoids unsafe directives such as 'unsafe-inline'. The `max-age` directive of the HSTS header is set to a long period (e.g., one year) and the `preload` directive is included. The `SameSite` attribute of cookies is set to `Strict` wherever possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CSP is configured to use hashes or nonces for allowed scripts instead of whitelisting entire domains. After extensive testing, the domain is entered into the Chrome project's HSTS preload list. Session cookies are set with `SameSite=Strict`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the CSP for weaknesses using an online tool. They check if the HSTS preload directive is set and if the `max-age` is sufficiently high. The application's behavior with different cookie SameSite settings is tested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Content-Security-Policy is operated in 'Enforce' mode and includes a `report-uri` or `report-to` directive. The reported CSP violations are centrally collected, analyzed, and used for continuous improvement of the policy. Additional modern security headers like `Permissions-Policy`, `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` (COOP), and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` (COEP) are implemented to further isolate the application and protect it from cross-site leaks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A service like `report-uri.com` is used to collect and aggregate CSP violations. The security team regularly reviews these reports to detect attack attempts and adjust the CSP if necessary. The COOP/COEP headers are configured to create an isolated context for the application, thus preventing attacks like Spectre.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester verifies the configuration of the CSP's reporting directives and checks if the reports are being received and analyzed. They check if the COOP/COEP headers are correctly implemented and provide the expected isolation, e.g., by checking the `window.opener` object in pop-ups.

controls.title: Penetration Test and Audit

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Web applications and web services SHOULD be regularly checked for security problems. In particular, audits SHOULD be carried out regularly. The results SHOULD be documented in a traceable manner, adequately protected, and treated confidentially. Deviations SHOULD be investigated. The results SHOULD be presented to the ISB (Information Security Board/Officer).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process has been established whereby the application is subjected to an audit or penetration test by an internal team or an external service provider at least once a year and after major changes. The results are summarized in a report, and the identified vulnerabilities are recorded in a ticket system and their remediation is tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports of the last penetration tests and audits. They check whether the tests are carried out regularly and whether a process for tracking and remediating the findings exists. A random sample of the findings is taken to check whether they have been resolved.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The penetration tests are carried out according to an established standard (e.g. OWASP ASVS). The scope of the tests covers the entire application architecture, including the connected backend systems and APIs. The results feed into a formal vulnerability management process that sets clear deadlines for the remediation of vulnerabilities based on their criticality.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The contract with the external penetration tester specifies that the test must cover at least Level 2 of the Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS). SLAs are defined in the vulnerability management process for the remediation of vulnerabilities (e.g. critical vulnerabilities within 7 days, high within 30 days).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the test report with the required standard (e.g. ASVS) and checks if the scope was appropriate. Compliance with the SLAs for the remediation of vulnerabilities is checked using the ticket system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A continuous security testing program is established, which includes automated dynamic application security testing (DAST) in the CI/CD pipeline, regular penetration tests by rotating third-party vendors (to avoid operational blindness), and a public or private bug bounty program to involve the broader security community.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A DAST tool is integrated into the staging phase of the CI/CD pipeline and blocks deployment if new, critical findings are discovered. A different renowned vendor is commissioned for the annual penetration test each year. A bug bounty program on a platform like HackerOne or Bugcrowd motivates external security researchers to continuously test the application.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the DAST tool in the pipeline. The contracts and reports from the various penetration test providers of recent years are reviewed. The processes and results of the bug bounty program are evaluated.

controls.title: Use of Web Application Firewalls

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Institutions SHOULD use Web Application Firewalls (WAF). The configuration of the WAF SHOULD be adapted to the web application or web service to be protected. After each update of the web application or web service, the WAF configuration SHOULD be checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A WAF (e.g. ModSecurity with the OWASP Core Rule Set) is operated in front of the web application in blocking mode. The rule set is adapted to the application to reduce false positives. After each application release, a test plan is executed to ensure that the WAF does not block legitimate functions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the WAF configuration and the applied rule set. They check if the WAF is running in blocking mode. By sending test attacks (e.g. `?id=1' OR '1'='1`), they verify whether the WAF blocks the requests. The processes for adapting the WAF after application updates are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The WAF rule set is carefully tailored to the specific application to minimize false positives and false negatives. The WAF is used for virtual patching to temporarily mitigate known vulnerabilities in the application until an official patch is available. The WAF logs are integrated into a central SIEM and actively monitored for indicators of attack.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For a newly discovered vulnerability (e.g. an SQL injection in a specific parameter), a specific WAF rule is created that blocks requests with malicious patterns in that parameter. This rule remains active until the developers have fixed the vulnerability in the code. WAF block events are sent as alerts to the SIEM and analyzed by the SOC team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the custom WAF rules and assesses their effectiveness. The configuration of log forwarding to the SIEM and the corresponding correlation rules are checked. It is checked whether a process for virtual patching exists and is applied.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The WAF is part of an integrated Web Application and API Protection (WAAP) platform that also includes bot protection, API security, and DDoS mitigation. The platform uses machine learning to learn the normal behavior of the application (positive security model) and automatically adapt to new attack patterns.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cloud-based WAAP service (e.g., from Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva) is used. The service learns the application's API specifications (e.g., from an OpenAPI file) and blocks all requests that deviate from this specification. A dedicated team actively manages and monitors the WAAP platform.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the configuration of the WAAP platform, including the API protection and bot management functions. It is checked how the platform reacts to zero-day attacks and complex attacks that go beyond simple signature detection. The expertise and processes of the responsible team are evaluated.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Web applications offer specific functions and dynamic (changing) content. To do this, web applications use the Internet protocols HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) or HTTPS. With HTTPS, the connection is cryptographically secured by the TLS (Transport Layer Security) protocol. Web applications provide documents and user interfaces, e.g., in the form of input masks, on a server and deliver them on request to corresponding programs on the clients, such as web browsers.
Web services are applications that use the HTTP(S) protocol to provide data for other applications. As a rule, they are not directly accessed by users.
To operate a web application or a web service, several components are usually necessary. Common are web servers to deliver data and application servers to run the actual application or web service. In addition, additional backend systems are needed, which are often connected as data sources via different interfaces, e.g., databases or directory services.
Web applications and web services are used in public data networks as well as in an institution's local networks (intranet) to provide data and applications. As a rule, clients must authenticate to be able to access a web application or a web service.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to securely use web applications and web services, and to protect the information they process.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose: The module is to be applied to every web application and every web service used in the information system.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient logging of security-relevant events
parts.prose: If security-relevant events are insufficiently logged by the web application or web service, it may be difficult to trace them at a later point in time. The causes of an event may then no longer be determinable. For example, critical errors or unauthorized changes in the configuration of the web application may be overlooked.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Disclosure of security-relevant information in web applications and web services
parts.prose: Web pages and data generated and delivered by a web application or web service may contain information about the backend systems, e.g., details about databases or version numbers of frameworks. This information can make it easier to specifically target web applications or web services in attacks.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Abuse of a web application through automated use
parts.prose: If functions of a web application or a web service are used automatically, numerous processes can be executed in a short time. With the help of a repeatedly executed login process, for example, an attempt can be made to guess valid combinations of accounts and passwords (brute force). In addition, a list of valid accounts can be created (enumeration) if the web application or web service returns information about existing accounts. Furthermore, repeated calls of resource-intensive functions such as complex database queries can be misused for denial-of-service attacks at the application level.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Insufficient authentication
parts.prose: Often, special functions of a web application or a web service should be reserved for specific groups only. The corresponding persons then receive, for example, accounts that are exclusively equipped with the necessary access rights. Under these accounts, users authenticate themselves at the beginning of each session in the web application or web service, e.g., with an account name and password. If this authentication is not configured correctly, it may be possible to bypass it. In addition, a web application or web service can be configured in such a way that access data is stored insecurely on the web server. In the event of a successful attack, attackers would then have large amounts of access data that they could also use elsewhere.

controls.title: Secure configuration of a web server (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web server is installed, but only isolated security settings are made, such as deactivating obviously unnecessary modules. The configuration is largely in its default state and the process permissions are not minimal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On a newly installed Apache or Nginx server, only a few modules from the default installation are deactivated. No dedicated, unprivileged user is created for the web server process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether the web server's configuration essentially corresponds to the default installation. Verify if the web server process is running with elevated privileges (e.g., as 'nobody' or 'www-data' without further restrictions).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web server process is generally run under an account with minimal privileges. All obviously unnecessary modules and functions are manually deactivated. Write permissions in the web directory are reduced to the absolute minimum.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated system user with restricted rights is created for the web server. A list of unnecessary modules is manually processed and these are deactivated in the configuration. The permissions in the document root are manually set to read-only for the web server user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verify that the web server process is running under a dedicated, unprivileged user account. Check the list of loaded modules and compare it with the list of required modules. Check the file system permissions for the web content.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There MUST be a documented, secure baseline configuration for the web server that is applied systematically. The web server process MUST be assigned to an account with minimal privileges. All non-essential modules, functions, and write permissions MUST be disabled or revoked. The web server SHOULD be run in a containerized environment or on a dedicated system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A hardening script or a configuration management playbook (e.g., Ansible) is used to roll out a standardized, secure configuration. This includes creating a 'nologin' user, deactivating a whitelist of modules, and setting strict file permissions. The configuration to run the web server in a Docker container (encapsulated environment) is established as a standard procedure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the existence and content of the secure baseline configuration document. Audit the deployed configuration against this document. Verify that the web server is running in an encapsulated environment (e.g., via `docker ps` or `systemd-nspawn --list`) or on a dedicated (virtual) server. This can be checked automatically using a configuration scan against a predefined profile (e.g., with OpenSCAP).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secure configuration is enforced and monitored by a configuration management system. The web server is run in an encapsulated environment (e.g., container or chroot jail) by default. The conformity of the configuration is regularly and automatically checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Puppet, Chef, or Ansible are operated in enforcing mode to automatically correct configuration drifts. The container images for the web server are based on hardened minimal images (e.g., distroless or Alpine Linux). Regular scans with tools like OpenSCAP or lynis check the configuration and report deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration management rules. Review of the reports from the automated compliance scans. Verification that the container images used comply with a defined hardening policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secure configuration is enforced by a fully automated configuration management system. The web servers are run in minimal, read-only containers that are additionally secured by strict Mandatory Access Control (MAC) profiles like SELinux or AppArmor. Any configuration drift leads to an automated alert and, if necessary, to the re-instantiation of the service from a clean image.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Kubernetes cluster with Pod Security Policies or Gatekeeper is used to enforce the execution of containers based on hardened policies. The container file systems are mounted as read-only. Custom SELinux profiles are created and enforced for the web server containers. A SIEM correlates configuration scan results with runtime events.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Audit of the Kubernetes security policies (e.g., Gatekeeper policies). Review of the SELinux/AppArmor profiles for their effectiveness. Verification of the automated response process through targeted, intentional misconfiguration in a test environment.

controls.title: Protection of web server files (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The permissions for the main web content are set, but configuration files, scripts, or log files are partially readable by unauthorized users. Directory listing might still be enabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web files are treated with `chmod -R 755`, which also allows write access for the owner on directories where it is not necessary. The configuration option `Options +Indexes` is still active in the Apache configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check if directory listing is possible by entering a directory URL in the browser. Manually check the permissions of critical configuration files (e.g., `ls -l /etc/nginx/nginx.conf`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The file permissions for all web content, scripts, and configuration files are manually set correctly to prevent unauthorized reading and writing. Directory listing is disabled globally. There is a manual process to regularly check if sensitive files are accidentally placed in the web root.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script is executed periodically to correct file permissions according to a simple policy. The `Options -Indexes` directive is set globally in the Apache configuration. An administrator manually searches the web directories monthly for files with suspicious names like 'backup', '.zip', or 'conf'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the global configuration for disabling directory listing. Perform random checks of file permissions. Obtain evidence of the regular manual checks for sensitive files.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that all files on the web server are protected from unauthorized access. The web server MUST be configured so that web applications can only access the defined WWW root directory and cannot serve files from outside of it. Directory listing features MUST be disabled. A regular process MUST be established to check for mistakenly published sensitive files.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web server configuration uses a `chroot`-like functionality (e.g., `document_root` in PHP-FPM pools) or is run in a container to restrict access to the WWW root directory. File permissions are enforced via a configuration management tool. A documented, quarterly process requires a responsible person to check the web directories for sensitive data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the web server configuration for `chroot` or other encapsulation mechanisms. Test if a directory traversal attack is possible (e.g., `http://example.com/../../etc/passwd`). Request the documentation and logs of the regular checks. The configuration can be automatically checked for directory listing and traversal vulnerabilities using a security scanner like Nikto.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) system is used to promptly detect and report unauthorized changes to configuration and content files. The search for mistakenly published sensitive files is supported by automated scripts that search for specific patterns (e.g., 'private_key', 'password').

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Wazuh, Samhain, or AIDE are used to create a baseline of file system hashes and check for changes daily. A cron job regularly runs a script that uses `grep` or similar tools to search for suspicious patterns in the web directories and create a report.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the configuration and alerting rules of the FIM system. Request and evaluate the reports from the automated file scans. Test by changing a file and checking if a FIM alert is generated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The FIM system is integrated into a central SIEM and triggers automated responses (e.g., alerting the SOC, quarantining the file). Additionally, automated Data Loss Prevention (DLP) tools are used to continuously scan public web content for sensitive information patterns (e.g., credit card numbers, personal data) and immediately alert on discovery.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: FIM agents send their logs in real-time to a SIEM like Splunk or ELK Stack. In the SIEM, correlation rules are defined that immediately create a ticket in a SOAR system in case of critical file changes. A DLP tool, either as a standalone solution or as a cloud service, continuously scans the public website.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the SIEM correlation rules and SOAR playbooks for FIM events. Request and evaluate the DLP scan reports. Conduct a controlled test by uploading a file with a test data pattern (e.g., an EICAR-like test credit card number) to the web server to verify the DLP response.

controls.title: Securing file uploads and downloads (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A maximum file size for uploads is set in the web server configuration. A virus scan of files offered for download is only performed sporadically or on suspicion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `upload_max_filesize` parameter is set in the `php.ini`. There is no formalized procedure for virus scanning files offered for download on the website.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration parameter for the maximum upload size. Ask if and how files are checked for viruses before publication.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All files provided for download are manually scanned with antivirus software before publication. For uploads, a maximum size and sufficient storage quota are configured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An editor is instructed to scan every file with the local virus scanner before uploading it to the server. Limits for the file size and the total size of the upload directory are set in the web server configuration to prevent a DoS through memory exhaustion.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the work instruction for editors. Verify the configuration of the storage and size limits for uploads.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There MUST be a defined process where all uploaded files are scanned for malware on the server side. For all files provided for download, a virus scan MUST also be performed before publication. A maximum size for file uploads MUST be specified and sufficient storage space MUST be reserved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Uploaded files are automatically scanned by a server-side antivirus engine like ClamAV after the upload process. The upload process is only completed if the scan was successful. Uploaded files are stored in a non-executable directory outside the web root. Storage space is limited and monitored by quotas on the file system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the workflow for file uploads, including the connection to the scan engine. Test the upload with an EICAR test file and check if it is rejected. Verify the configured quotas.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to virus scanning, uploaded files are checked for their file type (whitelist approach, checking magic bytes, not just the extension) and analyzed for suspicious behavior in an isolated sandbox environment before they are released.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application checks the first few bytes of a file to determine the real MIME type and compares it against a list of allowed types. For high-risk file types (e.g., PDFs, Office documents), the scan is performed in a Cuckoo Sandbox or a similar system to analyze dynamic behavior.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the source code or configuration of the file type validation. Attempt to upload a file with a wrong extension. Request analysis reports from the sandbox environment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A multi-engine scanning solution is used to maximize the detection rate. Additionally, a Content Disarm and Reconstruction (CDR) technology is used for supported file types. This proactively removes all active content (e.g., macros, scripts) from the files and provides a cleaned, secure version of the file.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A service like OPSWAT MetaDefender is integrated, which scans files with over 30 antivirus engines and performs CDR. The original file is discarded and only the cleaned version is further processed in the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the integration and configuration of the CDR solution. Upload a test file containing harmless macros and check if the resulting file no longer contains these macros, but the content has been preserved.

controls.title: Logging of events (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web server's default logging is enabled, but it only records successful accesses (access log). Error logs are not written or are only written at a very low level. The logs are stored locally and are rarely analyzed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `access_log` directive in Nginx is enabled. The `error_log` directive is left at the default setting 'error', which means less detailed error messages are not logged. Logrotate is configured, but the archived logs are not further analyzed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the web server configuration files for log levels. Viewing the existing log files on the server.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web server is configured to log all required events: successful accesses, failed accesses due to permission errors or non-existent resources, and server errors. The log files are stored locally and rotated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The log level is adjusted so that 4xx and 5xx errors also appear in detail in the error log. The log format may be adjusted to include additional information such as the 'User-Agent'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the log configuration for completeness. Triggering a 404 (Not Found) and a 403 (Forbidden) error and checking if they appear correctly in the logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web server MUST log at least successful accesses, failed accesses (due to lack of permission, non-existent resources, and server errors), and general error messages. The log data SHOULD be analyzed regularly. To protect the logs from manipulation, they are sent to a central log server.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A log shipper like Filebeat or rsyslog is installed on the web server to send all relevant log files to a central ELK stack or Graylog server. There is a documented process where an administrator checks the dashboards in the log management system for anomalies on a weekly basis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configuration of the log shipper. Verifying on the central log server that the web server's logs are arriving. Requesting the protocols of the weekly log reviews.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The centrally collected log data is monitored by automated rules and dashboards. In the event of critical events, such as an accumulation of 403 errors or server-side 5xx errors, alerts are automatically sent to the responsible team. The analysis of the logs is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the central log management system (e.g. Splunk, Graylog), alerts are configured that send an email or a Slack message if there are more than X errors per minute. Dashboards are created that visualize the most important metrics (top errors, traffic sources, etc.).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configured alerting rules in the log management system. Triggering a series of errors and checking whether an alert is generated. Reviewing the log review protocols.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All web server logs are fed in real-time into a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. The SIEM uses advanced correlation rules and machine learning models to detect complex attack patterns (e.g., slow brute-force attacks, web scanning activities) and generate high-fidelity alerts for the Security Operations Center (SOC).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logs are correlated with a Web Application Firewall (WAF) log and other data sources in the SIEM. A User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) component learns normal behavior and detects deviations, e.g., when a user suddenly generates a high number of errors. Alerts are automatically fed into a SOAR system for further processing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the correlation rules and ML models in the SIEM. Performing a simulated attack sequence (e.g. with a web scanner) and checking whether a corresponding, correlated alert is generated in the SIEM.

controls.title: Authentication (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Passwords are stored on the web server, but they are only stored with an outdated or insecure hashing algorithm such as MD5 or SHA1 without a salt.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A legacy application uses a `.htpasswd` file created with the `htpasswd -d` (CRYPT) or `-m` (MD5) algorithm. A function like `md5($password)` is used in the code.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the password storage mechanisms, e.g., by inspecting the relevant source code or the configuration of authentication modules. Checking the format of the password hashes in the database or `.htpasswd` file.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Passwords are stored using a standard hashing algorithm such as SHA-256 with a user-specific salt. The password file is protected from unauthorized reading.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application generates a random salt for each user and stores `hash('sha256', $password . $salt)`. The file in which the hashes are stored is only readable by the web server process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the source code to ensure that a unique salt is used for each user and combined with a strong hash algorithm. Checking the file permissions of the password file.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If clients authenticate to the web server using passwords, these MUST be stored cryptographically secured. For this purpose, a modern, adaptive password hashing function such as Argon2, scrypt, or bcrypt MUST be used. The password hashes MUST be stored protected from unauthorized access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application uses a standard library (e.g., `password_hash()` in PHP with `PASSWORD_ARGON2ID` or `PASSWORD_BCRYPT`) that securely handles salt generation and hashing. The configuration parameters (e.g., cost factor) are set to a current, secure value.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the source code for the use of a recommended, adaptive hashing function. Verifying the used parameters (e.g., cost factor for bcrypt, memory/time costs for Argon2) for appropriateness. A source code scanner can be used to automatically search for outdated hash functions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the secure storage of passwords, server-side mechanisms to protect against brute-force attacks are implemented. These include failed login attempt detection with subsequent account lockout or delay.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like `fail2ban` is used to monitor the log files for failed logins and temporarily block the IP addresses of attackers on the firewall. Alternatively, the application itself implements logic that locks the account or displays a CAPTCHA after several failed attempts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configuration of `fail2ban` or the application-specific protection mechanisms. Performing a test brute-force attack with several incorrect passwords and checking whether the IP address is blocked or the account is locked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication is completely outsourced to a central, hardened Identity and Access Management (IAM) solution that enforces Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) by default. Passwords are no longer processed or stored on the web server itself.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web application is configured as a client (Service Provider) for a central IAM system that supports protocols such as OpenID Connect (OIDC) or SAML 2.0 (e.g., Keycloak, Microsoft Entra ID). All users must authenticate via this central system, which enforces MFA.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configuration of the OIDC/SAML integration. Verifying that a login without MFA is not possible. Ensuring that no local password databases exist on the web server anymore.

controls.title: Legal framework for web services (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic awareness of legal requirements, such as the need for a legal notice. However, implementation is ad-hoc and incomplete. A privacy policy is missing or is an unadapted template.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A legal notice was copied from another site and only partially adapted. Cookies are set without explicit consent.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the website for the presence and completeness of the legal notice and privacy policy. Checking the cookie behavior with the browser's developer tools.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The website has a complete legal notice and a specific privacy policy. Content is checked for obvious copyright infringements before publication. A cookie banner for obtaining consent is available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The texts for the legal notice and data protection were created and adapted by a generator. A standard cookie banner plugin is used. Editors are instructed to use only their own or licensed image material.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the content of the legal notice and privacy policy for plausibility. Functional testing of the cookie banner to ensure that non-essential cookies are only set after consent has been given. Random checks of the image sources.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If content is published for third parties or services are offered via the web server, the relevant legal frameworks MUST be observed. The institution MUST comply with the respective telemedia and data protection laws as well as copyright law. There is a documented process that involves the subject matter experts and compliance officers in the review of new content and services.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A release process for new web content is documented in a wiki. Before publication, a subject matter expert and, for data-processing services, the data protection officer must confirm conformity. A directory of processing activities (DPA) is maintained for the website.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Requesting and reviewing the documented release process. Random checks of recently published content and services for compliance with the process (e.g., by providing proof of the release email or ticket).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for ensuring legal compliance includes regular training for developers and editors. An external legal advisor or the data protection officer formally approves major new functions or changes in data processing. Automated tools are used to check the third-party libraries used for license compliance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Annual mandatory training on data protection and copyright is conducted for all relevant employees. For each new project involving data processing, a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is considered. Tools like FOSSA or Snyk Open Source are integrated into the CI/CD pipeline to scan software licenses.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Requesting training records. Reviewing approval documents for recently introduced features. Inspecting the reports from the license scanning tools.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Legal compliance is firmly anchored in the entire lifecycle of the web service according to the 'Privacy by Design' and 'Security by Design' principles. A dedicated legal or compliance department is actively involved from conception to operation. The effectiveness of the measures is regularly reviewed by independent third parties (e.g., external auditors).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Checklists and requirements catalogs for data protection and legal certainty are an integral part of requirements management and user stories. Regular audits, e.g., according to the IDW PS 980 audit standard (Compliance Management Systems), are carried out.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the evidence of integration of legal requirements into the project management tool (e.g., Jira). Requesting and evaluating external audit reports.

controls.title: Encryption via TLS (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: HTTPS is enabled on the web server, but the configuration is weak. Outdated protocols such as SSLv3 or TLS 1.0/1.1 as well as insecure cipher suites (e.g., those with RC4) are still supported. Mixed content occurs on some pages.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web server's TLS configuration has been left in the operating system's default state, which often means broad compatibility at the expense of security. Content is partially included via `http://` instead of `https://`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Use an online tool like the SSL Labs Server Test to check the TLS configuration. A result worse than 'A' indicates vulnerabilities. Manually check the website for mixed content warnings in the browser console.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web server is configured to offer HTTPS with at least TLS 1.2 and a range of secure cipher suites. Outdated protocols are disabled. A manual process ensures that no mixed content is created on new pages.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the web server configuration, the protocols are explicitly set to `TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3` and a recommended cipher list (e.g., from Mozilla) is adopted. Editors are instructed to always use HTTPS URLs when embedding content.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Re-check with the SSL Labs Server Test to verify the deactivation of old protocols. Randomly check new pages for mixed content.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web server MUST offer secure encryption via TLS (HTTPS) for all connections from untrusted networks and MUST only support strong protocols (TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3) and cipher suites according to current recommendations (e.g., BSI TR-02102-2). When an HTTPS connection is used, all content MUST be delivered via HTTPS; so-called mixed content MUST NOT be used. HTTP requests are automatically redirected to HTTPS.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The TLS configuration is explicitly hardened and is based on the specifications of the BSI or other recognized sources. A Content Security Policy (CSP) with the `block-all-mixed-content` directive is delivered via HTTP header to prevent the loading of mixed content in the browser. A permanent (301) redirect from HTTP to HTTPS is configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the web server configuration for the set protocols and cipher suites. Checking the sent HTTP headers for a correct CSP. Testing whether a request to `http://` is correctly redirected to `https://` with a 301 status code. An SSL Labs test should achieve at least a grade of 'A'.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the strong TLS configuration, the HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) header is used with a long `max-age` and the `includeSubDomains` directive to instruct the browser to communicate exclusively via HTTPS. OCSP Stapling is enabled to improve performance and privacy when retrieving certificate status.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HSTS header `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` is set. The configuration for OCSP Stapling is enabled in the web server and a valid OCSP response is regularly retrieved and delivered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the HTTP headers for the presence and correct syntax of the HSTS header. The SSL Labs Server Test is used to verify the correct implementation of HSTS and OCSP Stapling. An 'A+' rating is the goal.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The HSTS policy is entered into the preload lists of common browsers to ensure maximum protection. In addition, DNS Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records are used to specify which certification authorities are allowed to issue certificates for the domain. Compliance with Certificate Transparency (CT) is actively monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The domain is registered for the preloading list via hstspreload.org. CAA records for the authorized CAs are entered in the DNS. A service like `crt.sh` or commercial CT monitoring services are used to be notified when new certificates are issued for one's own domain.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the HSTS preload status of the domain. Querying the DNS CAA records (e.g., with `dig caa example.com`). Checking the configuration of the CT monitoring service.

controls.title: Planning the use of a web server (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The purpose of the web server is known informally, but there is no written documentation. Responsibilities are not clearly defined and are assigned as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A web server is set up for a new project without creating a formal document about its purpose, content, or target audience. The person who sets up the server is initially responsible for it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Inquiring about planning documents for the web server. Interviewing employees to determine the clarity of responsibilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple document exists that roughly outlines the purpose of the web server and its main content. Those responsible for technical operation and content are known, but not formally and role-based documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A page is created in a project wiki that describes that the web server is for the 'customer portal' and what its main functions are. The names of the responsible persons are noted in the wiki.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the existing documentation and comparison with the actual web presence. Checking whether the named persons are aware of their responsibility.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be planned and documented for what purpose the web server will be used and what content it will provide. The documentation SHOULD also describe the information or services of the web presence and the respective target groups. Appropriate responsible persons SHOULD be designated for the technical operation and the web content.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized operating concept document is created for each web server. This contains dedicated sections for purpose, target group, type of content/services as well as a RACI matrix that clearly assigns the roles and responsibilities for technical operation (IT operations) and content responsibility (business department).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request and review of the operating concept document. Checking whether the defined roles are filled and the named persons know their tasks. Comparison of the documentation with the actual status of the web presence.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning documentation is part of a higher-level service catalog and is reviewed and updated at least annually or in the event of significant changes. The documentation also includes a classification of the processed data (e.g., public, internal, confidential), which forms the basis for the security requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web server is recorded as a service in the organization's CMDB or service catalog. The operating concept contains a chapter on determining the need for protection, which carries out the data classification and from this derives the need for measures such as encryption or increased logging.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the entry in the service catalog and the change history of the operating concept. Verifying whether the security requirements derived in the document have also been technically implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of the web service, from planning through development and operation to decommissioning, is formally managed and documented. The planning documentation is directly linked to the organization's risk management and Business Continuity Management (BCM) processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The operating concept of the web server references the results of the Business Impact Analysis (BIA) and derives the requirements for Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) from it. Risks related to the web server are recorded and managed in the central risk management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the links between the operating concept, BIA, and risk management register. Verifying whether the derived RTO/RPO requirements are technically covered by corresponding backup and failover mechanisms.

controls.title: Defining a security policy for the web server (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no formal policy, but there are some unwritten rules about web server security. The response to security incidents is ad-hoc.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators know from experience which modules they should disable, but this is not written down anywhere. When a website is defaced, it is restored from a backup without a formal incident response process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request for a security policy for web servers. If none exists, interview administrators about their procedures for configuration and incidents.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic document describes the most important security settings for web servers (e.g., 'TLS must be enabled'). It names a person responsible for security, but detailed processes are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A page in the internal wiki titled 'Web Server Hardening' lists some important configuration parameters. The IT operations team leader is named as the contact person for security topics.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the existing document for content and timeliness. Comparison of the specifications with the actual configuration of a web server.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal, approved security policy for web servers SHOULD be created. This names the required measures and responsibilities. It should regulate how information on current security vulnerabilities is obtained, how security measures are implemented, and how to proceed in the event of security incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An official policy document 'RL-Webserver-Security' exists and has been approved by the CISO/ISB. It contains a reference to a technical hardening guideline, defines a patch management process (e.g., 'critical patches within 72 hours'), and outlines an incident response plan for typical web incidents (e.g., defacement, data breach).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request and review of the formal security policy. Checking whether the processes defined therein (patch management, incident response) exist and the responsibilities are clear. Interviewing the responsible persons about the processes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is reviewed annually and updated based on new threats and technologies. The incident response plan is detailed and includes specific playbooks for common types of attacks. The policy is actively communicated to all relevant employees and their acknowledgment is tracked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy has a defined review cycle. The appendix contains detailed step-by-step instructions (playbooks) for incidents. New administrators must verifiably acknowledge the policy as part of their onboarding.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the change history and the review process of the policy. Insight into the incident response playbooks. Checking the evidence of acknowledgment by employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the security policy is continuously monitored by an automated compliance framework. Deviations from the policy are automatically detected and reported. The incident response plan is regularly tested through practical exercises and simulations. The policy is dynamically adapted based on threat intelligence feeds.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Configuration management tools (e.g., Ansible) and security scanners (e.g., OpenSCAP) check the web server configurations daily against the hardening specifications defined in the policy. Table-top exercises or simulated attacks are conducted regularly to test the effectiveness of the playbooks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the automated compliance reports. Requesting the logs and 'lessons learned' from the incident response exercises. Review of the process for incorporating threat intelligence into the security policy.

controls.title: Selection of a suitable web host (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A web host is selected primarily based on cost or ease of use. A formal review of its security practices does not take place. The standard contract is signed without review or negotiation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The marketing team orders a web hosting package from a well-known mass hoster because it is cheap and includes a one-click installer for WordPress.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Inquiry about the selection process and criteria for the web host. Inspection of the contract.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection process includes a basic checklist for security features (e.g., 'Does the host offer backups?', 'Is the server location in the EU?'). The standard contract is reviewed for critical clauses.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before selection, three hosts are compared based on a checklist that also includes items like 'daily backups' and 'DDoS protection'. The Data Processing Agreement (DPA) is signed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Inspection of the comparison checklist and the selection memorandum. Review of the signed DPA.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A documented selection process SHOULD be followed. This includes a thorough review of the host's security measures, e.g., by requesting evidence such as ISO 27001 certificates. A Service Level Agreement (SLA) SHOULD stipulate the security aspects, availability guarantees, and response times for security incidents in writing. The host SHOULD be obliged to implement basic technical and organizational measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal requirements catalog is created. Potential hosts must provide evidence of their security certifications (e.g., ISO 27001, C5). An individual SLA is negotiated, which, among other things, specifies an availability of 99.9% and a maximum response time of 4 hours for critical security incidents. The contract includes an obligation for the host to regularly maintain and patch its systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the documented selection process and the requirements catalog. Inspection of the host's submitted certificates. Review of the negotiated contract and the SLA for the defined security requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution exercises its audit rights or regularly requests independent audit reports from the host (e.g., SOC 2 Type II). The SLA contains specific contractual penalties for non-compliance with security requirements. A clear exit strategy that regulates data export and deletion is contractually agreed upon.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The contract establishes the right to an annual audit or the obligation to submit a current SOC 2 report. The SLA defines penalties, e.g., a credit note for falling below the availability level. An appendix to the contract governs the procedure at the end of the contract, including the formats for data export.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Inspection of the host's requested audit reports. Review of the contract clauses on penalties and the exit strategy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A continuous monitoring program for supply chain security is operated for the web host. This includes active monitoring of its security status, evaluation of its security advisories, and regular strategic reviews of the partnership. The selection is based on a comprehensive risk analysis that also considers geopolitical factors and the long-term stability of the host.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Security rating services like SecurityScorecard or BitSight are used to continuously assess the host's external attack surface. Annual meetings are held with the host's account and security management to discuss the strategic direction and the security roadmap.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Inspection of the reports from the security rating services. Review of the minutes of the strategic meetings with the host. Review of the initial risk analysis for host selection.

controls.title: Appropriate handling of errors and error messages (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The default error pages of the web server or application framework are used. These often output detailed error messages, stack traces, and version information to the user.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In an application's debug mode (e.g., Django, ASP.NET), detailed error pages are displayed, and this mode is accidentally left on the production server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Triggering an error on the website (e.g., by calling a non-existent page or entering invalid data) and analyzing the displayed error page for revealing information.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Custom error pages are configured to prevent the display of stack traces. However, the server version banners in the HTTP header are still sent.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Custom pages for error codes 404 and 500 are configured in the web server (`ErrorDocument` in Apache). However, the `ServerTokens` directive is still set to 'Prod' or 'OS', making the server version visible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the HTTP headers of the server response (e.g., with `curl -I http://example.com`) for the presence of `Server` or `X-Powered-By` headers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Neither the product name nor the version of the web server used SHOULD be apparent from the HTTP information and the displayed error messages. Only general error messages SHOULD be issued that do not contain details about system information. The error message SHOULD contain a unique identifier (e.g., a correlation ID) that allows the IT operations team to trace the error. It SHOULD be ensured that the server does not remain in a vulnerable state after an unexpected error.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The web server configuration is hardened to suppress all version information (e.g., `ServerTokens Prod` and `Header unset X-Powered-By` in Apache). When an error occurs, the application generates a unique ID, displays it to the user on a generic error page ('An error has occurred. Please contact support with the ID: XYZ-123'), and writes the same ID along with the detailed stack trace to the server-side log.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the HTTP headers and error pages for information leaks. Triggering an error and checking if a correlation ID is displayed. Then checking the server-side logs to verify that the error was logged with the same ID and all details.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central error handling framework in the application ensures that all exceptions are correctly caught and that the application process is properly terminated and restarted after a crash. A Web Application Firewall (WAF) is also used to filter outgoing responses and remove any sensitive information that may have slipped through.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A global exception handling module is implemented in the application. A process manager like `systemd` or `pm2` ensures that crashed application processes are automatically restarted. A WAF (e.g., ModSecurity) is configured with rules that prevent the leakage of error signatures (e.g., 'SQL syntax error') in the response body.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Code review of the error handling framework. Review of the WAF rules for protection against information leaks. Simulation of an application crash and verification that the process is automatically restarted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive exception handling framework is established throughout the entire application stack. The system's behavior under various failure conditions (e.g., database unreachable, file system full) is actively tested using chaos engineering principles to ensure resilience and security and to prevent information leaks under all circumstances.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All errors are sent structured (e.g., as JSON) and with correlation IDs to a central log management system. Tools like Chaos Monkey or Gremlin are used in a staging environment to deliberately cause system components to fail and to test how the application reacts and what errors it displays to the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the structured log outputs. Request and evaluation of the logs and results of the chaos engineering tests.

controls.title: Access control for web crawlers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A `robots.txt` file exists but is incomplete or outdated. It may not prohibit access to all administrative or sensitive areas.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A default `robots.txt` file from a CMS was adopted without adapting it to the specific directories of the website. A newly added admin area under `/new-admin` is not listed in the file.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the content of the `robots.txt` file and comparing it with the actual directory structure of the website.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A `robots.txt` file is correctly configured to prohibit the crawling of administrative interfaces and other non-public areas. However, the areas blocked in `robots.txt` are not protected by authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `robots.txt` contains entries like `Disallow: /admin/`. However, the `/admin/` directory itself is accessible without a password (Security by Obscurity).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the `robots.txt` file. Then manually attempting to access one of the URLs blocked there directly in the browser.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access by web crawlers SHOULD be regulated according to the Robots Exclusion Standard (`robots.txt`). Additionally, all content blocked for crawlers SHOULD be protected with effective access control (e.g., authentication) to also protect it from web crawlers that do not adhere to the standard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `robots.txt` is maintained and is part of the deployment. All paths listed in it with `Disallow` are additionally protected on the web server by a configuration that requires authentication (e.g., HTTP Basic Auth, form-based login).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing `robots.txt`. Systematically attempting to access all `Disallow` paths listed there and verifying that each of these paths triggers an authentication prompt.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to `robots.txt` and access control, a Web Application Firewall (WAF) is used to detect and block known malicious or overly aggressive bots and crawlers that ignore the standard, based on their signatures or behavior.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A WAF like ModSecurity is operated with the OWASP Core Rule Set. Rules for detecting scanners and malicious user agents are activated. Additionally, rate limiting is configured for clients identified as crawlers to prevent excessive load.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the WAF configuration and the activated bot protection rules. Attempting to scan the website with a known security scanner tool (e.g., Nikto) with a standard user agent and verifying that the requests are blocked by the WAF.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An advanced bot management solution is in use. It utilizes techniques such as fingerprinting, behavioral analysis, and machine learning to precisely differentiate between legitimate crawlers (e.g., Googlebot), malicious bots, and human users, and to apply granular policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized service (e.g., from Akamai, Cloudflare, Imperva) is placed in front of the web server. This service can allow good bots to pass through unhindered, block malicious bots, challenge suspicious requests with a CAPTCHA, and throttle unknown bots or serve them stale content.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration and policies in the bot management solution. Analysis of the solution's reports and dashboards to evaluate its effectiveness in classifying traffic.

controls.title: Integrity Checks and Malware Protection (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of web files is only checked manually and upon suspicion of a compromise. A virus scan on the server is performed irregularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If a website looks defaced, an administrator manually compares the files with a backup. An antivirus scan is only initiated after a security incident.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing administrators about their processes for integrity checking and malware scanning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A scheduled task runs a virus scanner over the web directory weekly. Configuration files are sporadically checked manually for changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cron job starts a `clamscan` over the `/var/www` directory weekly. An administrator occasionally looks at the Nginx configuration files to see if anything has changed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the configuration of the scheduled virus scan task and viewing the latest scan reports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD regularly check whether the web server's configurations and the files it provides are still intact and have not been altered by attacks. The files intended for publication SHOULD be regularly checked for malware. This is implemented through the use of a File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) tool and regular, scheduled virus scans.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A FIM tool like AIDE or Wazuh is used. A baseline of critical configuration and content files is created and a daily scan is performed, generating a report of all changes. Additionally, a daily, scheduled virus scan runs over the entire web directory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the FIM configuration and the generated reports. Reviewing the configuration and logs of the regular virus scans. Testing by changing a monitored file and verifying that the change appears in the next FIM report.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The FIM tool is configured to send a real-time alert to the security team upon detecting an unauthorized change to critical files. The virus scan is integrated into the CI/CD pipeline, so that content is automatically scanned before deployment to the production environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Wazuh is configured so that FIM alerts are sent directly as an email or Slack message to the responsible team. A step is added to the Jenkins or GitLab CI pipeline script that scans the build artifact with `clamscan` before deployment. A failed scan aborts the deployment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the real-time alerting configuration of the FIM system. Reviewing the CI/CD pipeline configuration to verify the scan step. Testing the deployment of an infected artifact (with EICAR) and verifying that it is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The FIM system is fully integrated into a SIEM and a SOAR system. Critical file changes trigger an automated response, such as reverting the file from version control or automatically isolating the server. In addition to static scans, an Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solution monitors the server for malicious processes and behaviors in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: FIM alerts in the SIEM trigger a SOAR playbook that attempts to automatically restore the changed file from the Git repository. If this fails, the server is removed from the load balancer. An EDR agent (e.g., CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne) is installed on the server and monitors process executions and network connections.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the SIEM/SOAR integration and automation playbooks. Reviewing the EDR configuration and detection logs. Performing a test that simulates suspicious activity (e.g., running a Mimikatz-like tool) and observing the response of the EDR and SOAR systems.

controls.title: Penetration Test and Review (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automated vulnerability scans are occasionally run against the web server. However, the results are not systematically tracked or remediated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator occasionally runs a scan with OpenVAS or Nessus and fixes the simplest 'quick-fix' findings. There is no formal tracking of vulnerabilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Requesting reports from vulnerability scans. Inquiring about the process for remediating the found vulnerabilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authenticated vulnerability scans are performed regularly. Critical and high-severity vulnerabilities are recorded in a ticketing system and their remediation is tracked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monthly, authenticated Nessus scan is set up. A process describes that for all findings with a CVSS score of 7 or higher, a Jira ticket must be created for the responsible team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the configuration of the regular scans and the scan reports. Checking the ticketing system for the recording and processing status of the vulnerabilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Web servers SHOULD be regularly checked for security issues, e.g., through formal reviews and penetration tests, which take place at a fixed interval (e.g., annually). The results SHOULD be documented in a traceable manner, adequately protected, and treated confidentially. Deviations SHOULD be investigated and the results SHOULD be submitted to the ISO.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a contractual agreement with an external service provider for an annual penetration test of the web offering. The test report is transmitted encrypted and stored in a secure directory. All findings are recorded in an action plan, the implementation of which is tracked. The final report and the action plan are brought to the attention of the Information Security Officer (ISO).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Requesting the last penetration test report and the associated action plan. Reviewing the process for secure handling and distribution of the report. Checking the implementation status of the measures. Obtaining confirmation from the ISO that they have received the results.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to planned penetration tests, the institution runs a bug bounty program to leverage the expertise of external security researchers. There is a dedicated process for managing submissions and rewarding researchers. The remediation of reported vulnerabilities is tracked against defined SLAs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A private or public bug bounty program is run through a platform like HackerOne or Bugcrowd. The program's policies define the scope, rewards, and disclosure deadlines. The SLAs for remediation are tiered by criticality (e.g., critical: 7 days, high: 30 days).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the bug bounty program policies and platform statistics. Reviewing the SLAs for remediation and verifying their compliance for recently reported vulnerabilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A continuous, automated security testing program is established, integrating DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) and IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing) tools into the CI/CD pipeline. Additionally, regular red team exercises are conducted to test not only technical vulnerabilities but also the organization's detection and response capabilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: DAST scanners (e.g., OWASP ZAP) are automatically run against the application in the staging environment. IAST agents are integrated into the running application to find vulnerabilities during normal test cycles. An external red team is commissioned annually to simulate a targeted attack on the web offering.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the CI/CD pipeline configuration for the integration of DAST/IAST tools. Requesting the reports of the red team exercises and the resulting improvement measures for the defense.
