parts.prose: The auditor checks `smb.conf` for the configuration of the `idmap config` parameters, especially the defined UID/GID ranges. The local users in `/etc/passwd` are compared with the configured range to rule out collisions. The PAM configuration files are checked for the correct integration of `pam_winbind.so`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A robust and centrally manageable ID mapping configuration such as `idmap_rid` or `idmap_ad` is used to ensure a stable and predictable assignment of UIDs/GIDs. The entire Winbind and ID mapping configuration is documented in detail. The PAM configuration is optimized and includes secure session management, e.g., the automatic creation of home directories.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `idmap_ad` backend is configured to use the `uidNumber` and `gidNumber` attributes stored in the AD user objects, if these are maintained. Alternatively, `idmap_rid` is used for an algorithmic and stable mapping. The PAM module `pam_mkhomedir.so` is added to the `session` stack configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the use of `idmap_ad` or `idmap_rid` in `smb.conf`. The corresponding documentation is checked for completeness and currency. The PAM configuration is examined for advanced security and convenience features such as `pam_mkhomedir.so`. The correct ID mapping is checked on a random basis using `getent passwd <domain_user>` and `id <domain_user>`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of or in addition to Winbind, the System Security Services Daemon (SSSD) is used for connecting to Active Directory. SSSD offers enhanced caching, higher performance, and improved offline capabilities. The entire SSSD configuration and the associated PAM and NSS integration is centrally managed and enforced via a configuration management system. The PAM configuration is hardened and regularly audited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SSSD is configured to connect to Active Directory (`id_provider = ad`). The `sssd.conf` is distributed to all relevant servers using Ansible or Puppet. The PAM and NSS configurations are adapted to use SSSD (`pam_sss.so`) instead of Winbind. Regular audits of the PAM configuration are carried out using automated scripts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that SSSD is running as an identity service and is correctly configured. The configuration in the configuration management system is analyzed. It is checked whether Winbind is deactivated to avoid conflicts. The results of the automated PAM audits are used as evidence. The `sss_debuglevel` command and the analysis of SSSD logs can be used for in-depth inspection.

controls.title: Secure configuration of DNS under Samba (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If Samba is used as a DNS server, the implementation SHOULD be carefully planned and tested beforehand. As Samba supports different AD integration modes, the IT operations SHOULD configure the DNS settings according to the Samba usage scenario.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before promoting to a Domain Controller with a DNS role, a plan is created that describes the DNS scenario (e.g., internal Samba DNS server). The configuration is validated in a test environment. In `smb.conf`, `server services = +dns` is ensured and the server's network configuration (e.g., `/etc/resolv.conf`) is adapted so that it uses itself for the domain's DNS resolution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning and test documentation for the DNS deployment. The `smb.conf` and the server's network configuration are checked for correct settings for DNS operation. The correct resolution of AD-specific SRV records (e.g., `_ldap._tcp.domain.local`) via the Samba server is verified on a random basis using `dig` or `nslookup`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A detailed plan for DNS operation is created and documented. This plan includes the replication topology with other DNS servers (if any), the configuration of zone transfers and forwarders, and a disaster recovery plan for the DNS service. Secure dynamic updates (GSS-TSIG) are configured, permitted, and tested to ensure the integrity of the DNS records.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: `allow dns updates = secure` is configured in `smb.conf`. DNS forwarders to external DNS servers are set up. If other DNS servers exist, zone replication is configured and tested. The disaster recovery plan describes the restoration of the DNS from a backup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the detailed DNS plan and the disaster recovery plan. The Samba configuration is checked for the setting for secure updates. It is verified whether a domain client can successfully register a dynamic DNS entry and whether non-authenticated update attempts are rejected. The configuration of the DNS replication is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Samba DNS service is fully integrated into a company-wide DNS infrastructure. Monitoring tools continuously monitor the state of the DNS service, the replication status, and the response times. For all zones managed by the Samba server, DNSSEC is implemented and enforced to cryptographically ensure the authenticity and integrity of the DNS responses.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitoring system like Nagios or Zabbix is configured with specific checks for the Samba DNS service. DNSSEC is set up with the `samba-tool dns zone-sign` and `samba-tool dns zone-keysign` commands and the keys are managed according to a key management policy. The configuration is enforced via configuration management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the monitoring system and the historical data on DNS performance. The configuration of DNSSEC and the associated keys are checked. Using public tools like `dig` or online DNSSEC validators, it is verified from an external point that the DNSSEC signatures are correct and can be validated.

controls.title: Secure configuration of LDAP under Samba (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If users under Samba are managed with LDAP, the configuration SHOULD be carefully planned and documented by IT operations. The access permissions to the LDAP directory SHOULD be regulated using Access Control Lists (ACLs) to implement the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If Samba uses the internal LDAP server (as an AD DC), the default ACLs are checked and adjusted if necessary. If an external LDAP server is used as a passdb backend, specific ACLs are set up on this server that grant the Samba server only the necessary read and write permissions on the user and group objects. Anonymous access is disabled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning and configuration documentation for the LDAP connection. The ACLs of the LDAP server are analyzed to ensure they follow the principle of least privilege. An attempt is made to access sensitive attributes with an anonymous or unprivileged user to test the effectiveness of the ACLs. Reachability and permissions can be checked automatically using `ldapsearch`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All communication between Samba and the LDAP server, as well as between clients and the LDAP server, is mandatorily encrypted using TLS (LDAPS on port 636 or StartTLS on port 389). The ACLs defined on the LDAP server are fine-grained and regulate access at the attribute level, based on the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Valid TLS certificates from a trusted CA are installed on the LDAP server. Samba and other clients are configured to require the encrypted connection and validate the server certificate. The LDAP ACLs are designed so that, for example, a normal user can change their own password but cannot see the group memberships of others.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of Samba and the LDAP server regarding the enforcement of TLS. Using a network sniffer (e.g., Wireshark), random checks are performed to ensure that no unencrypted LDAP queries are taking place. The fine-grained ACLs are analyzed and their effectiveness is tested through targeted queries with different user accounts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The LDAP schema used in Active Directory is actively managed, and extensions are only carried out after a formal approval process. Any administrative access to the LDAP directory requires multi-factor authentication (MFA). All LDAP queries and changes are logged in detail and monitored by a SIEM system for anomalies (e.g., mass export of data, unusual access times).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A change management process is established for schema changes. MFA is enforced for all administrative accounts in AD. The audit policies on the domain controllers are configured to log detailed LDAP access. Log forwarders send these logs to a central SIEM, where corresponding correlation and alerting rules are implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the change management process for schema changes. It is verified that MFA is enforced for administrative accounts. The configuration of the audit policies on the domain controllers and the rules in the SIEM system are reviewed. As a test, anomalous LDAP queries are performed to verify that they are correctly logged and trigger alerts.

controls.title: Secure configuration of Kerberos under Samba (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For authentication, the Heimdal Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) implemented by Samba SHOULD be used. Care SHOULD be taken to use the Kerberos configuration file (`krb5.conf`) specified by Samba. Only secure encryption methods SHOULD be used for Kerberos tickets. The central time server SHOULD be installed locally on the Samba server, and the NTP service SHOULD be configured so that only authorized clients can query the time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default configuration of the Samba AD DC is used. In `smb.conf`, outdated encryption types are not explicitly allowed by the `krb5_etypes` parameter. The NTP service is installed on the DC and in `ntp.conf`, `restrict` directives are used to limit access to clients from the local network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the `smb.conf` and `/etc/krb5.conf` for security-relevant Kerberos settings, in particular for the absence or explicit deactivation of weak ciphers. The configuration of the NTP service is checked for access restrictions. Using `klist -e` on a client, it is checked which encryption types are used for active tickets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Kerberos configuration is actively hardened by explicitly disabling all known weak encryption types (e.g., RC4-HMAC, DES) in the configuration. NTP access is restricted not only at the application level but also by a host firewall on the server. The NTP configuration and Kerberos hardening are documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In `/etc/krb5.conf` under `[libdefaults]`, the options `default_tgs_enctypes`, `default_tkt_enctypes`, and `permitted_enctypes` are explicitly set to strong algorithms like `aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96`. The firewall (e.g., firewalld, ufw) is configured to allow NTP requests only from defined IP subnets.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the `krb5.conf` for the explicit deactivation of weak ciphers. The firewall rules for the NTP service are checked. The associated documentation is checked for correctness and currency. Tools like nmap can be used automatically to test the reachability of the NTP port from unauthorized networks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated process regularly audits the Kerberos configuration and user account properties (e.g., 'DES encryption for this account') for the use of weak encryption types. The NTP service uses cryptographic authentication (e.g., Network Time Security (NTS) or symmetric keys) to secure the integrity and authenticity of the time sources and prevent man-in-the-middle attacks on time synchronization.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script that runs regularly via cron searches the AD for users or computers with outdated Kerberos settings and reports them. The NTP service is configured for NTS (e.g., with Chrony) or symmetric keys are set up between the NTP server and clients to sign the NTP packets.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and logs of the automated audit script for Kerberos. The NTP service configuration is checked for the use of NTS or symmetric key authentication. The NTP client's configuration is analyzed to ensure that it also performs authenticated time synchronization.

controls.title: Secure use of external programs on a Samba server (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD ensure that Samba only calls external programs that have been checked for malicious functions and are trustworthy. This applies, for example, to scripts that are called via parameters such as `root preexec`.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An informal policy is established stating that only scripts checked and approved by the administrator may be used in the Samba configuration. A list of permitted scripts and programs is maintained in a central location.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor searches the `smb.conf` for all parameters that can call external programs (e.g., `*exec`, `*script`). The called programs are compared with the list of approved programs. The scripts themselves are randomly checked for obviously insecure constructs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a formal, documented approval process for each external program or script to be called by Samba. These scripts are managed in a versioning system (e.g., Git), and changes are subject to a code review process by a second person, with a particular focus on security aspects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated directory (e.g., `/etc/samba/scripts`), whose permissions are highly restricted, is used for all scripts used by Samba. The approval process is mapped in a ticket system. Code reviews are conducted via pull requests in the Git repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the documented approval process. The history in the versioning system is randomly checked to ensure that the code review process is being followed. The file permissions of the script directory are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The execution of external programs is strictly restricted to the approved scripts and programs by technical measures such as application whitelisting and sandboxing (e.g., using AppArmor or SELinux). The SELinux/AppArmor profile for the Samba service (smbd) is hardened to allow only the explicitly required actions. All calls to external programs are logged in detail and monitored for suspicious activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specific AppArmor or SELinux profile is developed or adapted for the `smbd` process. This profile only allows read and execute access to the approved script directory. System auditing rules (e.g., via `auditd`) are created to log every `execve` system call by the `smbd` process and send it to a SIEM system for analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the active AppArmor or SELinux profile for the Samba service. The configuration of the system auditing framework is checked. An attempt is made to call an unapproved script from the Samba configuration to verify that this is prevented and logged by the sandboxing system.

controls.title: Training for the administrators of a Samba server (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The administrators SHOULD be trained in the specific areas of Samba used, such as user authentication, Windows and Unix permission models, but also in NTFS ACLs and NTFS ADS.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: It is ensured that administrators have access to relevant resources such as the official Samba documentation, books, or online courses. If necessary, external training is booked for the responsible administrators on specific topics (e.g., Samba as an AD DC).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts interviews with the Samba administrators to determine their level of knowledge on the relevant topics. Evidence of participation in training courses or access to learning materials is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a formal training plan for all Samba administrators, which is updated regularly. Participation in training is verifiably documented. The training includes hands-on labs for configuration, hardening, and troubleshooting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual training plan is created that provides both basic training for new employees and advanced training for experienced administrators. A separate test environment is available for the practical exercises. Training certificates and certificates of attendance are stored centrally in the personnel file or a training management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the formal training plan and the corresponding evidence (certificates, confirmations of participation) for the administrators. It is checked whether the training content also covers practical security aspects.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The administrators are required to obtain and maintain a relevant, recognized certification (e.g., from a training provider or a Linux certification with a Samba focus). Continuous professional development measures are in place, which also include current security threats, new Samba versions, and best practices. Regular internal workshops are held to share knowledge and solve complex problems together.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The job description for Samba administrators requires a specific certification. The company budgets for the costs of certification exams and recertifications. At least once per quarter, an internal workshop is held in which an administrator presents a special topic or a security problem is analyzed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the presentation of the administrators' valid certificates. The agenda and minutes of the internal workshops are reviewed. It is checked whether a process is in place to keep administrators informed about new security vulnerabilities (e.g., via Samba mailing lists).

controls.title: Regular backup of important system components of a Samba server (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All system components required to restore a Samba server SHOULD be integrated into the institution-wide data backup concept. This includes account information from all backends used (e.g., `passdb.tdb`), all TDB files and, if used for shares, the Samba registry (`registry.tdb`).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to backing up the actual file shares, the backup job is configured to explicitly back up the directories with the Samba databases (e.g., `/var/lib/samba/`, `/var/cache/samba/`, `/etc/samba/`). It is ensured that the backup is consistent during live operation, e.g., by using snapshots or by briefly stopping the services.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the backup software. It is verified that the paths to the critical Samba system files (especially TDB files) are included in the backup job definition. The logs of the last backup runs are checked for successful completion.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The backup process is fully automated. Automated recovery tests are performed regularly, at least semi-annually, to check the integrity and completeness of the backups. These tests include the full recovery of a Samba server (including AD role, if applicable) in an isolated test environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script automates the recovery test: It provisions a new VM, restores the operating system and Samba data from the backup, and runs a series of functional tests (e.g., authentication, file access). The results of the tests are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the logs of the recovery tests performed in the last 12 months. The scripts for the automated tests are reviewed. The documentation of the recovery process is checked for completeness and clarity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The backup and recovery process is documented in a detailed Disaster Recovery Plan. The Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) are defined and regularly checked by the quarterly recovery tests. All backups are strongly encrypted before transfer and at the storage location and are kept in a geographically separate, secure location.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DR plan is reviewed and updated annually. The backup software is configured to use end-to-end encryption. The backups are replicated to a second, physically separate location. The results of the RTO/RPO measurements from the tests are reported to management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the disaster recovery plan and the defined RTO/RPO values. The configuration of the encryption in the backup solution is verified. The logs of the last recovery tests are checked to validate compliance with RTO and RPO. Proof of storage of the backups at an external location is requested.

controls.title: Encryption of data packets under Samba (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The capability for SMBv3 encryption is enabled and available on the server. However, encryption is not enforced globally, but is selectively enabled for individual shares that contain particularly sensitive data. The corresponding policy, which specifies which shares must be encrypted, is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The global setting `smb encrypt` is set to `auto` or `if_required`. For specific shares, e.g., `[Personal_Files]`, the parameter `smb encrypt = required` is set in `smb.conf`. The list of shares to be encrypted is documented in the company's security policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the `smb.conf` for the global and share-specific `smb encrypt` settings. The list of encrypted shares is compared with the company policy. Wireshark is used to verify that access to a sensitive share is encrypted, while access to a non-critical share may be unencrypted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The `smb encrypt = required` setting is applied globally for the entire server or at least for all shares that do not contain exclusively public data. Connection attempts from clients that do not support SMBv3 encryption are actively rejected and logged. Older SMB dialects such as SMBv1 are explicitly disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the global section of `smb.conf`, `smb encrypt = required` and `server min protocol = SMB3` (or a more specific dialect like `SMB3_11`) are set. The Samba logs are monitored for failed connection attempts due to encryption requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the global settings for `smb encrypt` and `server min protocol` in `smb.conf`. An attempt is made to establish a connection with an outdated client (e.g., one that only speaks SMBv1) or without encryption support to check if the connection is correctly rejected. The log files are checked for corresponding entries.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To ensure the security of data packets in transit, the data packets SHOULD be encrypted using the encryption methods integrated from SMB version 3 onwards. This is enforced by a global configuration that requires encryption for all connections. In addition, insecure SMB dialects (SMBv1, SMBv2) are explicitly disabled to prevent downgrade attacks. Network traffic is actively monitored to ensure that no unencrypted SMB traffic occurs to or from the server.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In `smb.conf`, the parameters `server min protocol = SMB3_11` and `smb encrypt = required` are set globally. This configuration is enforced by a configuration management system. An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) in the network is configured with rules that raise an alarm if unencrypted SMB packets (port 445/TCP) are addressed to the Samba server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the Samba configuration in the configuration management system. The rules and alarm logs of the IDS are analyzed. An active scan of the network traffic to the Samba server is performed (e.g., with a SPAN port and Wireshark) to confirm that only encrypted SMB3 communication is taking place.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Samba is a freely available and full-featured Active Directory Domain Controller (ADDC) that can provide authentication, file, and print services, thereby enabling interoperability between the Windows and Unix worlds. Samba brings together many different protocols and technologies. This includes, for example, the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. Samba servers are servers on which Samba is operated. These are typically Unix servers.
If the use of Samba has been correctly designed and suitably configured, Samba interacts with a Windows client or server as if it were a Windows system itself.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to show how Samba can be used securely in institutions and how the information provided by Samba can be protected.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module APP.3.4.Samba is to be applied to every Samba server in the information domain under consideration.
This module considers Samba as an authentication, file, and print service. Since Samba is usually used on Unix servers and provides services known from the Windows server world, the security aspects of the modules SYS.1.1 General Server and SYS.1.3 Server under Linux and Unix must be considered.
A key focus when securing a Samba server is to grant access rights to files only restrictively. In-depth information on identity and access management is not found in this module but in ORP.4 Identity and Access Management.
General security requirements for printers, file servers, or directory services are not part of this module. These are described in the modules SYS.4.1 Printers, Copiers, and Multifunction Devices, APP.3.3 File Servers, and APP.2.1 General Directory Service as well as APP.2.3 OpenLDAP.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Eavesdropping on unprotected communication links of Samba
parts.prose: If unprotected Samba communication links are eavesdropped on, confidential information can be intercepted and misused. When transferring files between Unix servers, Windows servers, and clients, protocols without extensive security features are often used, so that both authentication and usage data are accessible to third parties and could be misused by unauthorized persons. This can lead to sensitive information of the institution falling into the wrong hands.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insecure default settings on Samba servers
parts.prose: To demonstrate some of the Samba server's capabilities and to give administrators a quick start, the configuration file smb.conf is created with default settings during the installation of the Samba server. The Samba server can then be started with the options preset in this file. If this file is used carelessly without further adjustments, it can lead to considerable security gaps. If the example file shares are not commented out, sensitive information can be viewed in these unwanted shares.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unauthorized use or administration of Samba
parts.prose: Unauthorized persons can gain access to confidential information, manipulate it, or cause disruptions by using applications or IT systems. It is possible for them to administer Samba without authorization. It is particularly critical if outdated and no longer updated configuration tools are used, such as the Samba Web Administration Tool (SWAT).

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Incorrect administration of Samba
parts.prose: If administrators are not sufficiently familiar with the extensive components, functions, options, and configuration settings of Samba, this can lead to far-reaching complications. For example, misconfigurations of the DNS or authorization management can lead to unauthorized persons being able to access resources. Furthermore, this can lead to operational interruptions or sensitive information can be disclosed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Data loss in Samba
parts.prose: Data loss has a considerable impact on IT use. If institution-relevant information is destroyed or falsified, business processes and professional tasks can be delayed or no longer be carried out at all. With Samba, for example, it should be noted that the properties of the file systems under Windows and Unix differ considerably from each other. Therefore, it is not always guaranteed that the access rights under Windows are maintained; under certain circumstances, important file properties can be lost. This can also lead to the loss of information on so-called Alternate Data Streams (ADS) and DOS attributes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Loss of integrity of sensitive information in Samba
parts.prose: Samba itself stores important operational data in databases in the Trivial Database (TDB) format. If these databases are not handled with sufficient performance and consistency by the operating system, they can cause problems when Samba services are used.

controls.title: Planning the use of DNS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A rudimentary plan for the use of DNS exists, but it focuses only on basic name resolution for critical external services. Security aspects and internal resolution are not systematically considered. There is no formal documentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Planning is done on an ad-hoc basis and is usually only recorded in the form of notes or emails when a new system that requires external accessibility is put into operation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks through interviews with the administrators whether there is any planning concept for the use of DNS. Any form of documentation (e.g., notes, wiki entries) that justifies the DNS configuration is sought.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic plan for the use of DNS is available and documented. It specifies how the DNS service is fundamentally structured (e.g., which servers serve as primary and secondary servers). The plan covers the most important domains but does not go into detailed security configurations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document (e.g., in the wiki) describes the DNS servers, their IP addresses, and their basic roles (internal resolver, external authoritative server). The zones for the main domains are listed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and timeliness of the DNS planning document. They compare the architecture described in the document with the actual configuration of the DNS servers on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of DNS servers MUST be carefully planned. It MUST first be determined how the DNS network service is to be structured. It MUST be determined which domain information is worthy of protection. It MUST be planned how DNS servers are to be integrated into the network of the information system. The decisions made MUST be appropriately documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DNS plan is a formal document that is part of the network documentation. It clearly defines the separation between internal and external zones, the responsible authoritative servers, the internal resolvers, and basic security policies such as permitted zone transfers. The document is versioned and updated when changes are made to the DNS infrastructure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a detailed and documented DNS plan is in place. It is verified whether the plan covers the distinction of protectable information, the integration of the servers into the network, and the general architecture. The conformity of the actual implementation with the planning document is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNS plan is reviewed regularly, at least annually, and adapted to new threats and requirements as needed. The plan includes detailed security aspects such as DNSSEC deployment strategies, logging requirements, and Response Rate Limiting (RRL). The documentation is stored in a central CMDB.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DNS plan is a living document that is maintained as part of the change management process. It contains explicit policies for configuring DNSSEC, monitoring DNS requests, and defending against DoS attacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the regular reviews of the DNS plan. It is verified that the plan addresses advanced security concepts (DNSSEC, RRL) and that these concepts are implemented in the configuration of the DNS servers. The integration of the documentation into a CMDB is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNS plan is fully integrated into the IT architecture and risk management processes. Changes to the DNS architecture are based on proactive threat modeling. Automated configuration checks ensure that all DNS server deployments and changes are compliant with the plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tools such as Ansible, Puppet, or Terraform are used to automatically manage DNS configurations based on the central planning specification. A system for continuous compliance checking (e.g., with InSpec) reports deviations in real time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the integration of DNS planning into the higher-level management processes. The results of the threat analyses and the resulting changes to the DNS architecture are inspected. The functionality of the automated configuration and compliance checks is verified, e.g., by reviewing the IaC scripts and the logs of the testing tools.

controls.title: Use of redundant DNS servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A secondary advertising DNS server exists only for the institution's main domain, which is classified as absolutely critical. Other important domains are not kept redundantly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A single additional server is configured as a secondary for the www domain. The configuration is done manually and its functionality is rarely checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the NS records for all domains managed by the institution and determines for which domains only a single name server is registered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each primary advertising DNS server, there is a secondary server. However, both servers are located in the same data center or even in the same rack.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A second server is configured as a slave for each zone. Zone transfers are set up but not actively monitored for errors or latency. The servers may share critical infrastructure components (power, network switch).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that at least two NS records exist for all advertising zones. The network topology and the physical location of the servers are checked to identify single points of failure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Advertising DNS servers MUST be designed for redundancy. For each advertising DNS server, there MUST be at least one additional secondary DNS server.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At least two name servers are configured for each authoritative zone. The primary (master) and secondary (slave) servers are located in different fire compartments and are connected to different core switches to increase availability. The configuration is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the DNS configuration and the public NS records for all zones to ensure that at least two servers are defined per zone. The network and infrastructure plans are used to verify that the servers have basic physical redundancy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secondary advertising DNS servers are geographically and topologically separated from the primary server (e.g., in a different data center or with an external provider). Zone transfers are actively monitored, and there are automated alarms for errors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At least one secondary DNS server is operated at a second, geographically separate location. The zones are secured via TSIG. A monitoring system regularly checks the serial number of the zone on all servers and alerts if a secondary server is no longer up-to-date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the IP addresses of the name servers to verify their geographical and topological distribution (e.g., by checking the AS numbers). The configuration and logs of the monitoring system are reviewed to confirm the monitoring of zone transfers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The authoritative DNS services are provided via an Anycast infrastructure with multiple nodes at one or more specialized DNS providers. This ensures highest availability, load balancing, and protection against DDoS attacks. System health is continuously monitored, and traffic is automatically rerouted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A contract is concluded with a managed DNS provider that offers an Anycast-based infrastructure. The primary server (often configured as a 'hidden master') remains under own control and securely replicates the zone data to the provider's Anycast network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contracts and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) with the DNS provider. The configuration of the 'hidden master' and the secure zone transfer to the provider is verified. The effectiveness of the Anycast implementation can be checked by queries from different geographical locations.

controls.title: Use of separate DNS servers for internal and external requests

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single DNS server is used for all tasks (internal caching/resolving and external advertising). An attempt is made to achieve separation through simple Access Control Lists (ACLs), which are however incomplete.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A BIND server is configured to allow recursive queries only for internal IP ranges (`allow-recursion`). However, it is accessible from the internet and also serves as an authoritative server for external zones.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs an external scan to determine whether the public DNS server answers recursive queries (open resolver). The DNS server's configuration file is checked for the mixing of resolver and authoritative functions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On the same hardware, separate DNS server processes or virtual machines are operated for the roles of advertising and resolving. The clients are configured to use the correct process for their requests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two instances of a DNS server (e.g., BIND) run on one server on different IP addresses or ports. One instance is configured as a resolver for the internal network, the other as an authoritative server for the external network. Internal clients receive the IP of the internal resolver via DHCP.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the process list and network configuration of the server to verify the separation of DNS services. The DHCP configuration is checked to ensure that internal clients exclusively use the internal resolver.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Advertising DNS servers and resolving DNS servers MUST be separated on the server side. The resolvers of the internal IT systems MAY ONLY use the internal resolving DNS servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Dedicated IT systems are used for the roles of advertising and resolving. The advertising server is located in a DMZ, while the resolving server is placed in the internal network. Firewall rules ensure that clients from the internal network can only reach the resolving server and not external DNS servers directly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network architecture plans and the firewall rule sets to verify the physical or logical separation of the servers and the enforcement of the communication paths. Random checks on client systems ensure that they are correctly configured to use the internal resolver (`ipconfig /all` or `cat /etc/resolv.conf`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The separation of advertising and resolving functions is further hardened by using different DNS software products for each task (e.g., NSD for advertising, Unbound for resolving). Communication between the internal resolvers and the internet is controlled by a dedicated DNS proxy or a firewall with DNS inspection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the DMZ, an authoritative-only server like NSD or Knot DNS is used. In the internal network, a pure caching/resolving server like Unbound or PowerDNS Recursor is used. This reduces the attack surface, as each software only contains the code necessary for its task.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the installed software on the DNS servers to confirm the functional specialization. The configuration of the firewall or DNS proxy is checked for rules for filtering and logging DNS traffic.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The internal resolving infrastructure is equipped with a DNS firewall (also known as Response Policy Zone, RPZ), which proactively blocks or redirects queries to known malicious, phishing, or command & control domains. The threat intelligence is updated automatically and in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The internal resolving DNS server (e.g., BIND, Unbound, Knot Resolver) is configured to subscribe to one or more RPZ feeds from commercial or open-source threat intelligence providers. The policies are set to block (NXDOMAIN) or redirect requests to listed domains to an internal warning page.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the resolving DNS server for the integration of RPZ zones. The timeliness of the threat intelligence feeds is verified. Test queries to known malicious domains are performed to confirm the correct functioning of the blocking.

controls.title: Secure basic configuration of a DNS server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNS servers are operated with the default settings of the distribution. Critical vulnerabilities such as open recursion are prevented by basic ACLs on the server itself. The software version is not actively hidden.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the configuration file (e.g., `named.conf`), the `allow-recursion` directive is set to restrict queries to the internal network. Other security settings are not configured differently from the default values.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs an external port scan and a DNS query to check whether the server is acting as an open resolver and what version it is disclosing. The configuration file is checked for basic security settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A resolving DNS server MUST be configured to only accept queries from the internal network. When a resolving DNS server sends queries, it MUST use random source ports. If DNS servers are known to provide incorrect domain information, the resolving DNS server MUST be prevented from sending queries to them. An advertising DNS server MUST be configured to always handle queries from the internet iteratively. It MUST be ensured that DNS zone transfers between primary and secondary DNS servers work. Zone transfers MUST be restricted to specific IP addresses. The version of the DNS server product used MUST be hidden.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration of the resolving server is restricted to the internal network by firewall rules and server-side ACLs. Source port randomization is active by default in modern DNS software and is verified. Zone transfers are restricted to the IP addresses of the respective master/slave servers. The version information (e.g., via `version.bind` CHAOS TXT query) is suppressed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the DNS server configurations in detail: restriction of recursion and zone transfers, suppression of the version. It is checked externally whether the version information can be read. The configuration of the source port usage is verified (e.g., `query-source address * port *;`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Additional hardening measures are implemented. Response Rate Limiting (RRL) is activated on authoritative servers to make them harder to use for amplification attacks. On resolvers, DNS cookies are used to improve the authenticity of requests and responses and to make spoofing more difficult.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A `rate-limit` block is defined in the configuration of the authoritative server (e.g., BIND). On the resolver (e.g., Unbound, BIND), DNS cookies (`add-cookie`, `send-cookie`) are activated. Zone transfers are additionally secured by Transaction Signatures (TSIG).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration files for the activation and correct parameterization of RRL and DNS cookies. The security of zone transfers using TSIG is verified by checking the configuration and the key files.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All DNS servers run in a highly restricted environment, e.g., in a minimal container image or with strict Mandatory Access Control (MAC) profiles like AppArmor or SELinux. Outbound traffic from resolvers is routed through a validating DNS proxy (e.g., DNSCrypt-Proxy) that ensures the authenticity and confidentiality of requests. All configurations are managed via an automated system (IaC) and monitored for compliance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: DNS servers are operated as containers with a read-only file system and a narrowly defined SELinux profile. Configuration management is handled via Ansible playbooks, which document every change and are based on a central Git repository. A DNSCrypt proxy is placed upstream to encrypt and authenticate requests to external recursive servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the container definitions and the SELinux/AppArmor profiles. The IaC configurations and the change log in the Git repository are inspected. The network configuration is analyzed to verify the forced traffic routing through the DNSCrypt proxy.

controls.title: Securing dynamic DNS updates

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Dynamic DNS updates are enabled for an internal zone, but security is only provided via an IP-based ACL, which allows updates from the DHCP server, for example. There is no cryptographic authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the DNS server's zone configuration, the `allow-update` directive is used with the IP address of the DHCP server. This allows any process on the DHCP server to change DNS records.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the DNS zone configuration for the `allow-update` directive and verifies whether it is based exclusively on IP addresses. The security of the system authorized as an updater (e.g., the DHCP server) is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that only legitimate IT systems are allowed to change domain information. It MUST be specified which domain information the IT systems are allowed to change.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Dynamic DNS updates (DDNS) are secured using Transaction Signatures (TSIG). A dedicated TSIG key is created for each system or group of systems (e.g., the DHCP server or a group of clients) that is allowed to perform updates. The update policies in the DNS server configuration specify exactly which names (e.g., only its own hostname) may be changed with which key.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the DNS server configuration for the use of TSIG for DDNS. It is verified that the update policies (`update-policy`) are restrictive and follow the principle of least privilege. The secure distribution and storage of TSIG keys on clients is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication for dynamic DNS updates is integrated into a central directory service infrastructure (e.g., GSS-TSIG with Kerberos in an Active Directory environment). Permissions to perform updates are managed via group policies or similar central mechanisms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DNS server is configured to use GSS-TSIG. Windows clients that are joined to the domain automatically use their Kerberos tickets to authenticate with the DNS server and securely update their records. Permissions are configured on the DNS zone in the Active Directory security settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the DNS server and zone configuration for the activation of secure dynamic updates in 'Secure only' mode. The ACLs on the DNS zone objects in Active Directory are checked for correct and restrictive permissions. Secure communication is verified using network analysis tools.

controls.title: Monitoring of DNS servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The basic availability of the DNS servers (reachability via ping) and the state of the DNS service are monitored by a central monitoring system. The log files are saved but not systematically evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitoring tool like Nagios or Zabbix is used to regularly check if the server responds to ICMP requests and if the DNS port (53/UDP/TCP) is open. A simple DNS query is performed to test the function of the service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the monitoring system to verify the established availability checks for the DNS servers. It is checked whether the log files of the DNS servers are centrally collected and stored for a defined period.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: DNS servers MUST be continuously monitored. The load on the DNS servers MUST be monitored in order to adjust the hardware performance capacity in a timely manner. DNS servers MUST be configured to log at least the following security-relevant events: number of DNS requests, number of errors in DNS requests, EDNS errors, expiring zones, and failed zone transfers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DNS server's logging is configured to capture all required events. The log files are sent to a central log management system (e.g., Syslog-NG, Fluentd). The monitoring system records and visualizes performance metrics such as queries per second (QPS), CPU, and memory utilization. Thresholds for alarms are defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the DNS server configuration to ensure that logging is set up correctly and comprehensively. The log management system is checked to verify the central collection of logs. The configuration of the monitoring system is checked for the recording of performance metrics and the definition of alarm thresholds.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logged data is regularly and automatically evaluated to detect anomalies. Dashboards are created to visualize DNS activity and performance. Alarms are triggered in the event of significant deviations from normal behavior, e.g., a sudden increase in NXDOMAIN responses or SERVFAIL errors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM system or a log analysis platform (e.g., ELK stack, Splunk, Graylog) is used to parse, index, and analyze the DNS logs. Correlation rules and dashboards are created that detect and visualize security-relevant patterns. The alarms are forwarded to a central ticket system or a ChatOps channel.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the SIEM or log analysis system. The established dashboards and alerting rules for DNS-specific events are viewed. Samples of past alarms are checked for their correct processing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: DNS monitoring uses machine learning to create baseline profiles of normal DNS traffic and to detect complex, low-level attacks such as DNS tunneling or slow-drip data exfiltration. The analysis is performed in real time and can automatically trigger countermeasures, such as blocking suspicious source IPs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized DNS security solutions or advanced SIEM modules with User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) are used. These systems analyze DNS request patterns, payload sizes, and entropy of domain names to identify suspicious activities that indicate malware communication or data exfiltration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and effectiveness of the specialized DNS analysis tools. Reports and logs from the system are checked for detected anomalies and the resulting responses. The functionality of the automated countermeasures is verified.

controls.title: Management of domain names

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A person from the IT department is designated to be responsible for managing domain names. The renewal of the domains is carried out manually when the notification email arrives from the registrar. There is no central list of all domains.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The access data for the domain registrar is stored with one person. The contact email address for the domains is this employee's personal email address.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the responsible person and has the domain renewal process explained. It is checked which contact email addresses are stored for the most important domains.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that the registrations for all domains used by an institution are renewed regularly and on time. A person MUST be appointed who is responsible for managing the internet domain names. This task can also be performed by the central administration. If service providers are commissioned with domain management, it MUST be ensured that the institution retains control over the domains.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An official role (e.g., 'Domain Administrator'), which can also be filled by the central administration, is designated and documented. A central list of all domains registered by the institution is maintained with their expiration dates. The contact email address at the registrar is a functional email address (e.g., 'domains@institution.com'). Many domains are set to auto-renewal.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence of the role description and the list of managed domains. It is verified that a functional email address is stored as the contact and that the institution is registered as the owner of the domain, even if a service provider performs the management.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All critical domains are protected against unauthorized transfers and changes at the registrar with a transfer lock (Registry Lock). Access to the management account at the registrar is secured by two-factor authentication (2FA). The expiration dates of the domains are monitored by an automated system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the customer portal of the domain registrar, the 'Transfer Lock' option is activated for all important domains. A 2FA application (e.g., TOTP) is made mandatory for login. A calendar or a monitoring system is used to automatically notify 90, 60, and 30 days before a domain expires.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks in the registrar's administration portal (or via screenshots) whether the transfer lock is active and whether 2FA is enforced for the account. The configuration of the automated notification system for expiring domains is checked.

controls.title: Creating a disaster recovery plan for DNS servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general IT disaster recovery plan that mentions the failure of DNS as a possible scenario. However, there are no specific instructions or recovery plans for the DNS service. The configuration files are backed up irregularly as part of system backups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The zone and configuration files of the DNS server are part of a nightly, file-based backup of the entire server. There is no separate process to back up or restore this specific data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the general IT disaster recovery plan for mention of DNS. The configuration of the backup system is reviewed to determine if and how the DNS server data is backed up.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A contingency plan for DNS servers MUST be created. The contingency plan for DNS servers MUST be integrated into the institution's existing contingency plans. The contingency plan for DNS servers MUST describe a data backup concept for the zone and configuration files. The data backup concept for the zone and configuration files MUST be integrated into the institution's existing data backup concept. The contingency plan for DNS servers MUST contain a recovery plan for all DNS servers in the information network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specific chapter or document covering the DNS service is added to the general contingency plan. It describes the steps for restoring a DNS server from backup, including the restoration of the zone and configuration files. The data backup concept provides for a daily backup of these critical files in a separate location.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and content of the DNS-specific contingency plan. It is verified that a data backup and recovery plan for the DNS configurations and zone files is clearly documented and integrated into the higher-level plans. The implementation of the backup concept is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNS contingency plan contains detailed, step-by-step instructions (runbooks) for various failure scenarios (e.g., primary server failure, resolver failure, DNS cache poisoning incident). The configuration and zone files are stored in a versioned repository (e.g., Git), which enables a quick restoration to a known good state.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All DNS configuration files (`.conf`, `.zone`) are managed in a central Git repository. Changes require a commit with a meaningful message. The backup additionally secures the entire Git repository. The runbooks are stored and linked in the IT department's wiki.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and quality of the runbooks for DNS emergencies. The Git repository is checked for completeness, up-to-dateness, and a meaningful commit history. It is verified that the recovery plan describes the restoration from the Git repository.

controls.title: Selection of a suitable DNS server product

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If a DNS server product is procured, care SHOULD be taken to ensure that it has proven itself sufficiently in practice. The DNS server product SHOULD support the current RFC standards. The DNS server product SHOULD assist the responsible personnel in creating syntactically correct master files.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When selecting DNS server software, established open-source (e.g., BIND, Unbound, Knot, PowerDNS) or commercial products are used. It is checked whether the software supports important RFCs (e.g., for DNSSEC, EDNS). The software should provide tools for syntax checking of zone and configuration files (e.g., `named-checkzone`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the product selection documentation. It is verified that the selected product has a broad user base and is actively developed (e.g., by checking the release history and security advisories). Conformance with important RFCs is checked against the product documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When selecting the DNS server product, specific attention is paid to advanced security features. These include a robust implementation of DNSSEC, support for Response Rate Limiting (RRL), DNS-Cookies, and DNS-over-TLS (DoT) or DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH). The selection is documented and justified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal evaluation of different products is carried out, in which the availability and quality of the implementation of security features such as RRL, DoT/DoH, and RPZ (DNS Firewall) are given high priority. A combination of products for different purposes is considered (e.g., NSD for authoritative servers, Unbound for resolvers).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the evaluation documentation and the justification for the product selection. It is verified that the selected products support the mentioned advanced security features and that their use is planned in the operational concept.

controls.title: Sufficient dimensioning of the DNS servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hardware of the DNS server SHOULD be sufficiently dimensioned. The hardware of the DNS server SHOULD be used exclusively for the operation of this DNS server. The network connections of all DNS servers in the information network SHOULD be adequately sized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DNS servers are operated on dedicated (virtual or physical) machines on which no other critical services are running. The dimensioning of CPU, RAM, and network bandwidth is based on the expected number of queries per second (QPS) and the size of the zones, with an appropriate buffer for load peaks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the DNS servers are operated on a dedicated basis. Based on performance data from the monitoring system, it is assessed whether the current load (CPU, RAM, network) is in a non-critical range and whether sufficient reserves are available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The dimensioning of the DNS servers is based on systematic capacity planning. Performance data is analyzed over a longer period to identify growth trends. The servers are dimensioned to handle a moderate DDoS attack (e.g., a DNS amplification attack) without significant performance degradation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A capacity management process is established. At least once a year, QPS trends, memory usage (especially of the cache), and CPU load are analyzed to forecast the demand for the next year. The network card and the connection are designed for 1 Gbit/s or more.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the capacity management process and the analysis reports. It is verified that the hardware and network equipment is capable of handling the forecasted requirements and potential attack scenarios.

controls.title: Restricting the visibility of domain information

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The namespace of an information network SHOULD be divided into a public and an institution-internal area (Split DNS). The public part SHOULD only contain domain information that is needed by services that are intended to be accessible from the outside. IT systems in the internal network SHOULD not receive an externally resolvable DNS name, even if they have a public IP address.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A split-DNS architecture is implemented. The external, authoritative DNS servers provide an 'external view' of the zones, which contains only the public servers (e.g., www, mail, vpn). The internal DNS servers provide an 'internal view,' which contains all internal systems. Internal clients exclusively use the internal servers and thus receive the internal view. Systems that are not intended to be accessible from the outside (e.g., database servers) do not receive an entry in the external zone.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the content of the external zone (by querying an external server, e.g., with `dig @ext-ns axfr domain.tld`) with the content of the internal zone (by querying an internal server). It is checked whether internal hostnames are visible in the external zone.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of internal and external zones is strictly separated by technical means to prevent the accidental publication of internal information. Zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR) from the Internet are blocked on all authoritative servers. Instead, alternative, more secure methods for querying zone content (e.g., DNS Catalog Zones) are used for administrative purposes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The internal and external zone files are managed in separate directories with different access permissions. The configuration of the external authoritative server allows zone transfers only from the IP addresses of the other authoritative servers. Public AXFR requests are explicitly forbidden. DNS Catalog Zones (RFC 9432) are used for automatic provisioning of zones on secondary servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to perform a zone transfer from an external location to verify the blockade. The file system permissions and the DNS server configurations regarding zone management are checked. The use of Catalog Zones is verified.

controls.title: Placement of the nameservers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Primary and Secondary Advertising DNS-Server SHOULD be placed in different network segments.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The primary and secondary authoritative DNS servers are placed in different subnets and ideally behind different firewalls or routers. This increases resilience against network problems or attacks on a specific segment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network plans and the IP configurations of the authoritative DNS servers to verify their placement in different network segments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The authoritative DNS servers are placed not only in different network segments but also in different autonomous systems (AS). At least one secondary server is hosted by an external, specialized DNS provider.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The primary server and a secondary server are operated in the own data center. Another secondary server is procured as a service from an external hoster or a dedicated DNS provider. This achieves a high resilience against failures of the own network or the internet connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the public NS records and the associated IP addresses of the nameservers. With tools like `whois` or BGP looking glass servers, it is verified that the IP addresses belong to different autonomous systems.

controls.title: Evaluation of the log data

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNS server log files SHOULD be reviewed regularly. The DNS server log files SHOULD be evaluated regularly. At a minimum, the following security-relevant events SHOULD be evaluated: number of DNS requests, number of errors in DNS requests, EDNS errors, expiring zones, failed zone transfers, and changes in the ratio of errors to DNS requests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process for the manual review of DNS log data is established and documented. Weekly or monthly, the log files are checked for the mentioned events, and conspicuous occurrences are logged. This can be supported by scripts that extract the relevant log entries.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence of the documented process for log evaluation. The logs of the reviews carried out are inspected to assess the regularity and thoroughness of the evaluation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evaluation of DNS log data is automated by a central log management or SIEM system. Rules and thresholds are defined that automatically trigger alarms in case of significant deviations (e.g., a sudden increase in errors, failed zone transfers). The results are visualized in dashboards.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DNS logs are sent in real-time to a SIEM (e.g., Splunk, ELK-Stack). There they are parsed and indexed. Correlation rules are set up that, for example, alarm when the rate of SERVFAIL responses exceeds 5% of the total queries or when a zone transfer fails multiple times. Dashboards show the history of QPS, error rates, and other KPIs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the alerting rules and dashboards in the SIEM system. The triggered alarms of the last few months and the corresponding processing tickets are inspected to evaluate the effectiveness of the process.

controls.title: Integration of a DNS server into a "P-A-G" structure

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNS servers SHOULD be integrated into a "Packet Filter - Application-Level Gateway - Packet Filter" (P-A-G) structure. The advertising DNS server SHOULD in this case be located in a demilitarized zone (DMZ) of the outer packet filter. The resolving DNS server SHOULD be placed in a DMZ of the inner packet filter.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The network architecture follows the P-A-G model (also known as 'screened subnet'). The externally accessible advertising DNS server is placed in the DMZ, which is located between the outer and the inner packet filter. The internal resolving DNS server is placed in its own secured zone, which is accessible from the internal network but is separated from the general client network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the network architecture plans and the firewall configurations to verify the correct placement of the DNS servers in the corresponding zones (external DMZ, internal server zone) according to the P-A-G structure.

controls.title: Use of DNSSEC

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNS protocol extension DNSSEC SHOULD be activated on both resolving DNS servers and advertising DNS servers. The Key-Signing-Keys (KSK) and Zone-Signing-Keys (ZSK) used in this process SHOULD be changed regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The external, authoritative zones are signed with DNSSEC. The public KSK is stored as a DS record in the parent zone (e.g., the TLD registry). The internal resolvers are configured to validate DNSSEC signatures (`dnssec-validation auto;`). A documented process exists for the regular rollover of the ZSKs (e.g., every 3 months) and the KSKs (e.g., annually).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses external tools (e.g., DNSViz, Verisign DNSSEC Debugger) to check whether the public zones are correctly signed with DNSSEC and the DS records are correctly stored. The configuration of the internal resolvers for DNSSEC validation is checked. The process and the logs for the key rollover are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNSSEC key rollover process is largely automated. DNSSEC validation is enforced on the resolvers. There is active monitoring that alerts in case of validation errors or problems with the signature chain (e.g., expiring signatures).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Modern DNS server software such as BIND 9.11+ or Knot DNS is used to automate the ZSK and KSK rollover via policies in the configuration (`dnssec-policy`). A monitoring plugin continuously checks the validity of the DNSSEC signatures and the reachability of the keys and alerts in case of problems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the automated DNSSEC policies. The logs and alerts from the DNSSEC monitoring are checked for any problems that have occurred and their resolution. The correct functioning of the validation is tested by targeted queries of intentionally incorrectly signed or invalid domains.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The private parts of the DNSSEC keys (especially the KSK) are stored and used in a Hardware Security Module (HSM). This provides the highest possible protection against compromise of the key material. The entire DNSSEC management infrastructure is designed for high availability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One or more network-capable HSMs are integrated into the DNS infrastructure. The DNS server software is configured via a PKCS#11 interface so that the signing operations are performed on the HSM without the private key ever leaving the HSM. The KSK rollover process includes a secure ceremony for generating the new key.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the DNS software for connecting the HSM. The documentation of the HSM setup and the key ceremonies is inspected. The physical and logical security of the HSMs is assessed.

controls.title: Advanced protection of zone transfers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To further secure zone transfers, Transaction Signatures (TSIG) SHOULD also be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to restricting zone transfers to specific IP addresses, a TSIG key is generated. This key is securely transferred to the primary and all secondary servers. The DNS server configuration is adjusted to allow zone transfers only if they are signed with this key.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the DNS server configuration on both sides (master and slave) to verify the configuration of the TSIG keys for the zone transfer. It is ensured that zone transfers without a valid signature are rejected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A separate, unique TSIG key is used for each secondary server. The TSIG keys are changed regularly, at least annually. The key change process is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of a shared key, a separate TSIG key is generated for each master-slave relationship. This limits the damage if a key is compromised. A script or a manual process is established to periodically renew and replace the keys on the servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration for the use of individual TSIG keys per server relationship. The documentation and the logs of the key change process are inspected.

controls.title: Decommissioning of DNS servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The DNS server SHOULD be deleted from both the domain namespace and the network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a DNS server is decommissioned, a defined process is followed: First, the NS records pointing to the server are removed from the zones and from the registry. After the TTL of the removed records has expired, the server is shut down, the software is uninstalled, and the firewall rules for the server are deleted. The process is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented process for decommissioning DNS servers. In the case of a recent decommissioning, the zone configurations, registry entries, and firewall rules are checked to ensure that all references to the old server have been removed.

controls.title: Checking the feasibility of the emergency plan

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The emergency plan for DNS servers is theoretically discussed as part of general IT emergency drills (tabletop exercise). The findings are documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A meeting is held once a year in which the 'failure of the primary DNS server' scenario is run through using the emergency plan. The participants discuss the steps laid out in the plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the tabletop exercises and the resulting findings and improvement measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be regularly checked whether the emergency plan for DNS servers is feasible. This is done through practical exercises in which the failure of a DNS server is simulated and the restart process is actually carried out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A practical emergency drill is carried out at least once a year. For example, a secondary server is shut down in a controlled manner and the restoration from backup on a new virtual machine is tested. The drill is carried out outside of main business hours. The results and the time required are measured and used to improve the plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning and results documentation of the practical emergency drills. It is verified that the drills take place regularly and that the findings from them have led to concrete improvements in the emergency plan and the technical systems.

controls.title: Hidden Master

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The primary advertising DNS server (master) is listed in the public NS records of the zone like the secondary servers and is accessible from the internet.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Both the master server and the slave servers are entered in the NS records of the zone. All servers answer public DNS queries.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the NS records of the zone and determines whether the server configured as the master is publicly listed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To make attacks on the primary advertising DNS server more difficult, a so-called hidden master arrangement SHOULD be made.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The primary DNS server (master), on which the zones are edited, is not accessible from the internet and is not listed in the public NS records of the zone. It is only accessible to the publicly accessible secondary servers (slaves) to allow for zone transfers. The firewall rules allow incoming connections to the master only from the IP addresses of the slaves on the DNS port.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the public NS records and verifies that the IP address of the master server is not listed there. The firewall configuration in front of the master server is checked to ensure that access is restricted to the IP addresses of the slaves. A reachability test of the master from the public internet is performed.

controls.title: Connection of DNS servers via different providers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All externally accessible DNS servers of the institution are connected via the same internet provider.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The company has a framework agreement with a single Internet Service Provider (ISP) through which all external connections, including those for the DNS servers, are routed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses the IP addresses of the public DNS servers and the corresponding AS numbers to determine whether all servers are connected via the same provider.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Externally accessible DNS servers SHOULD be connected via different providers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: To ensure high availability against provider outages or large-scale network disruptions, the secondary DNS servers are placed so that they are connected via at least two different Internet Service Providers (ISPs).
