This can be achieved by renting a server in a data center of another provider or by using a specialized secondary DNS service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the public NS records. Using network tools (e.g., `whois`, BGP looking glass), it is verified that the IP addresses of the name servers belong to different providers (different Autonomous Systems). Contracts with the various providers are inspected.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Domain Name System (DNS) is a network service used to convert hostnames of IT systems into IP addresses. DNS can be compared to a phone book that resolves names not into phone numbers, but into IP addresses. Usually, DNS is used to find the corresponding IP address for a hostname (forward resolution). If, on the other hand, the IP address is known and the hostname is sought, this is referred to as reverse resolution.
Which hostnames belong to which IP addresses is managed in the domain namespace. This is hierarchically structured and is provided by DNS servers. The term DNS server actually stands for the software used, but is usually also used as a synonym for the IT system on which this software is operated.
DNS servers manage the domain namespace on the Internet, but are also frequently used in the internal network of an institution. So-called resolvers are installed by default on the users' IT systems. The requests to DNS servers are made via the resolver. In response, the DNS servers return information about the domain namespace.
DNS servers can be distinguished by their tasks. There are basically two different types: Advertising DNS servers and Resolving DNS servers. Advertising DNS servers are usually responsible for processing requests from the Internet. Resolving DNS servers, on the other hand, process requests from the internal network of an institution.
The failure of a DNS server can have a serious impact on the operation of an IT infrastructure. The problem is not the failed DNS system itself, but the DNS-based services that are consequently restricted. Under certain circumstances, web servers or e-mail servers are no longer reachable or remote maintenance no longer works. Since DNS is required by very many network applications, at least two authoritative DNS servers (Advertising DNS servers) must be operated for each zone according to the specification (RFC 1034).

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module describes the specific threats to a DNS server and the resulting requirements for its secure use.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
Module APP.3.6 DNS Server is to be applied to every DNS server used in the information system.
This module contains fundamental requirements that must be observed and fulfilled when an institution uses DNS servers. The focus is on the availability of DNS servers and the integrity of the transmitted information. It also addresses problems that can occur when DNS servers are used.
General and operating system-specific aspects of a server are not the subject of this module. These are covered in module SYS.1.1 General Server and in the corresponding operating system-specific modules of the SYS IT Systems layer, e.g., SYS.1.3 Server under Linux and Unix or SYS.1.2.3 Windows Server.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. DNS server failure
parts.prose: If a DNS server fails, the entire IT operation can be affected. Since clients and other servers of the institution are then no longer able to resolve internal and external addresses based on hostnames, no more data connections can be established. External IT systems, e.g., from mobile employees, customers, and business partners, also cannot access the institution's servers. As a result, essential business processes are usually disrupted.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficient line capacities
parts.prose: If the line capacities for a DNS server are insufficient, access times to internal and external services can increase. As a result, these services may be available only to a limited extent or not at all. The DNS server can also be more easily overloaded by a Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Missing or insufficient planning of DNS deployment
parts.prose: Planning errors often turn out to be particularly serious, as widespread security vulnerabilities can easily be created. If the DNS deployment is not planned or is planned inadequately, this can lead to problems and security vulnerabilities during operation. For example, if the firewall rules that control DNS traffic are defined too permissively, this could result in an attack. However, if the rules are too restrictive, legitimate clients cannot make requests to the DNS servers and will be affected when using services such as email or FTP.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Incorrect domain information
parts.prose: Even if the DNS deployment has been carefully planned and all security-relevant points have been taken into account, this is not sufficient if semantically and syntactically incorrect domain information is created. This applies, for example, when a wrong IP address is assigned to a hostname, data is missing, non-permitted characters are used, or the forward and reverse resolution are inconsistent. If domain information contains errors, services that use this information will only function to a limited extent due to the misinformation.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Incorrect configuration of a DNS server
parts.prose:
Security-critical default settings, self-configured security-critical settings, or incorrect configurations can cause a DNS server to not function properly. For example, if a resolving DNS server is configured to accept recursive queries without restriction, i.e., from both the internal data network and the internet, the server's availability can be severely impaired due to the increased load. Additionally, this could make it vulnerable to DNS reflection attacks.
Likewise, with incorrectly configured DNS servers, there is a risk that zone transfers are not restricted to authorized DNS servers. This allows any host that can make a request to the DNS servers to read all domain information from these servers. The data obtained in this way can facilitate subsequent attacks.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. DNS manipulation
parts.prose: A DNS cache poisoning attack aims to make the attacked IT system store incorrect mappings of IP addresses and names. This exploits the fact that DNS servers cache received domain information for a certain period. This allows forged data to spread widely. If corresponding requests are then made to the manipulated DNS server, it provides the forged data as a response. The IT system that receives this response caches it, and its cache is thus also "poisoned." The stored data has a defined lifespan (Time-To-Live, TTL). If the resolving DNS server is asked for a manipulated address, it will only query another DNS server again when the lifespan has expired. This allows manipulated DNS information to persist for a long time, even if it has already been corrected on the originally attacked DNS server. If attackers succeed, for example, in taking over the name resolution for a domain by manipulating the entries so that their DNS servers are queried, all subdomains are automatically affected as well. DNS cache poisoning attacks are often carried out with the goal of redirecting requests to malicious servers.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. DNS Hijacking
parts.prose: DNS hijacking is an attack method used to route communication between authoritative DNS servers and resolvers through the attacker's IT system. With this man-in-the-middle attack, it is possible for the attackers to eavesdrop on and record the communication between the servers. However, the far greater danger is that in a successful attack, any data traffic between the two IT systems can be arbitrarily modified. If a client's resolver sends a request to a DNS server after a successful DNS hijacking attack, attackers can, for example, change the association of names and IP addresses. DNS hijacking can also be combined with other attacks, such as phishing.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. DNS-DoS
parts.prose: In a DoS attack on a DNS server, so many requests are sent to it that the network connection to the DNS server or the DNS server itself is overloaded. Typically, the requests are sent via botnets to achieve the necessary data rate. A DNS server overloaded in this way can no longer answer legitimate requests.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. DNS Reflection
parts.prose: A DNS reflection attack is a DoS attack in which the target is not the DNS server to which the requests are sent, but the IT system that receives the responses. It exploits the fact that certain requests generate a relatively large amount of response data. It is possible to achieve an amplification factor of 100 or more. This means that the response, measured in bytes, is at least one hundred times larger than the request. The number and size of the responses overload the network bandwidth or the receiving IT system itself beyond its performance capacity. Thus, any technical IT component can be the target of the attack. DNS reflection attacks are facilitated by open resolvers.

controls.title: Secure configuration of the SAP ABAP stack (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the most important profile parameters, such as for password security, are set. The configuration of system modifiability and clients is done ad-hoc and is not consistently documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration is done manually in transaction RZ10, but focuses only on a small subset of security-relevant parameters. Other aspects such as securing operating system commands are not considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes that only a few profile parameters (e.g., login/*) are set, but no comprehensive configuration policy exists. The configurations of the clients (transaction SCC4) are checked on a random basis and assessed as inconsistent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All profile parameters known to be critical for password security, authentication, and basic encryption are set. The system modifiability and the clients are configured according to SAP recommendations for productive systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administration uses SAP Notes and security guides as a basis for setting the profile parameters. The client configuration in SCC4 is set so that no direct changes are possible in the production system. The IMG customizing is performed manually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies using a checklist that all fundamental security-relevant profile parameters are set. The settings in transactions SCC4 and SE06 are checked for conformity with the operating policies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SAP ABAP stack MUST be configured securely. To do this, the respective profile parameters MUST be set, e.g., for password security, authentication, and encryption. The system modifiability and the clients MUST also be configured, IMG customizing MUST be performed, and the operating system commands MUST be secured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A company-wide configuration document for the ABAP stack is created and implemented. This document defines the values for all relevant profile parameters. The configuration of the clients and system modifiability (transactions SCC4, SE06) is defined for each system type (development, test, production). The operating system commands are secured by maintenance in transaction SM69 and the assignment of corresponding S_ADMI_FCD authorizations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a configuration document for the ABAP stack exists and is up to date. The actual system settings (RZ11, SCC4, SE06, SM69) are compared with the specifications in the document. It is verified that a defined process for IMG customizing exists and is being followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the ABAP stack is regularly checked against a defined baseline using automated scripts. Deviations lead to a notification. All changes to critical configurations, such as system modifiability, are subject to a formal approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Scripts or tools like the SAP Solution Manager (Configuration Validation) are used to monitor compliance with the configuration guidelines. A change management process is established for changes to SCC4 or SE06 settings, which requires a justification and approval by two people.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports of the automated configuration checks. Change tickets for configuration changes are randomly checked to verify compliance with the approval process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire configuration of the ABAP stack is managed as code (Configuration as Code) in a version control system. Changes are deployed exclusively via an automated CI/CD pipeline process that enforces tests and approvals. A File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) system is active for critical configuration files at the operating system level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Ansible or Terraform are used to declaratively manage SAP profile parameters and operating system settings. Jenkins or GitLab CI/CD is used to validate and roll out changes. An FIM tool like Tripwire or OSSEC monitors the SAP profile files for unauthorized changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline and the configuration stored in the version control system. It is checked whether manual changes to the configuration files are detected and reported by the FIM system. The commit history is checked for proper peer reviews and approvals.

controls.title: Secure Configuration of the SAP JAVA Stack (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only a few, known insecure default services are disabled. Access to administration interfaces is not restricted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators manually disable some services in the NetWeaver Administrator (NWA), but do not follow a systematic approach. Default content such as demo applications remains on the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that critical administration interfaces such as the NWA or the System Landscape Directory (SLD) are accessible from the entire network without additional hurdles. A review of the running services shows that many unneeded default services are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All unneeded services are shut down and default content is removed. The protection of HTTP services is ensured by activating TLS. The administrators are familiar with the basic architecture of the JAVA stack.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on SAP security recommendations, a list of unneeded services is created and these are deactivated in the NWA. TLS is configured for all HTTP-based services to encrypt communication.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that all HTTP interfaces use TLS. A list of active services is compared with a list of required services. It is checked whether default users and applications have been removed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SAP JAVA stack MUST be configured securely if it is used. For this, security mechanisms and concepts other than those for the SAP ABAP stack MUST be created. Therefore, administrators MUST know the architecture of the JAVA stack and how it is administered. In addition, unneeded services MUST be shut down, default content removed, HTTP services protected, and access to administration interfaces restricted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate security concept is created for the JAVA stack. This defines which services and applications are allowed to be active. Access to administration interfaces (NWA, Visual Admin, Config Tool) is restricted to a dedicated management network. All HTTP services are protected via TLS and use strong cipher suites.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and implementation of the JAVA stack security concept. It is verified that network ACLs effectively restrict access to administrative ports. The TLS configuration is checked for weaknesses (e.g., outdated protocols, weak ciphers) using common tools.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to administration interfaces requires two-factor authentication. A regular review process for activated services and installed applications is established to identify and remove components that are no longer needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SAP Web Dispatcher or a reverse proxy is placed upstream to filter access to administrative URLs and enforce a second authentication layer (e.g., via SAML or client certificates). A quarterly review of the JAVA components and services is conducted and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests access to administrative interfaces and verifies the effectiveness of the two-factor authentication. The logs of the quarterly reviews are inspected and checked for completeness and traceability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administrative activities on the JAVA stack are forwarded to a central SIEM system for monitoring and alerting. Automated security scans are performed regularly to proactively detect misconfigurations, outdated components, or known vulnerabilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The audit logs of the JAVA stack are sent via syslog or agent to a SIEM (e.g., Splunk, QRadar). Specific correlation rules for suspicious JAVA stack activities are implemented. Tools like the SAP Focused Run Security & Configuration Validation or specialized third-party tools are used for the automated scans.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the SIEM system the arrival and correct processing of the JAVA stack logs. The configuration and reports of the automated security scans are checked. The response to generated alerts is examined on a random basis.

controls.title: Network Security (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To ensure network security, corresponding concepts MUST be created, taking the SAP ERP system into account, and settings MUST be made on the system. Furthermore, the SAP Router and SAP Web Dispatcher SHOULD be used to implement and maintain a secure SAP network. To avoid security gaps due to misinterpretations or misunderstandings, the IT operations, firewall operations, portal operations, and SAP operations departments MUST coordinate with each other.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A network security concept specifically for the SAP landscape is created. This concept defines zones (e.g., DMZ, application zone, database zone) and the allowed communication paths between them. The SAP Router is placed in the DMZ to control external SAP support access. The SAP Web Dispatcher serves as a reverse proxy for all HTTP(S)-based access. Regular coordination meetings between the involved teams (network, SAP Basis, portal) are institutionalized.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the network security concept for completeness and plausibility. The firewall rules, the configuration of the SAP Router (saprouttab), and the SAP Web Dispatcher are compared with the specifications of the concept. Logs of the coordination meetings are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network segmentation is strictly enforced to isolate the different system landscapes (development, QAS, production) from each other. The configurations of SAP Router and Web Dispatcher are optimized according to hardening recommendations and are regularly reviewed. All relevant network traffic is logged and stored for analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separate VLANs or subnets are set up for the different landscapes. The SAP Router is configured to only allow explicitly permitted connections to specific hosts and ports. The Web Dispatcher is hardened, e.g., through URL filtering and modification of HTTP headers. The logs from the firewall, SAP Router, and Web Dispatcher are collected centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts small-scale penetration tests to check the effectiveness of the network segmentation (e.g., attempting to access a production system from a development system). The configuration files of SAP Router and Web Dispatcher are checked for the implementation of hardening measures. The central log collection is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A zero-trust network architecture is implemented. All communication between SAP components is encrypted and authenticated by default, regardless of the network segment. The network traffic is actively monitored for anomalies and attack attempts with a Network Intrusion Detection/Prevention System (NIDS/NIPS).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Secure Network Communication (SNC) or TLS is enforced for all communication between application servers, databases, message server, and frontends. A NIDS/NIPS (e.g., Suricata, Zeek) with SAP-specific rules is used to analyze the network traffic in real time. Alerts are forwarded to the SIEM for correlation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies by means of packet captures that the communication between the system components is encrypted. The configuration and effectiveness of the NIDS/NIPS are tested through simulated attacks. The integration of the NIDS/NIPS alerts into the SIEM and the subsequent incident response process is checked.

controls.title: Securing the delivered SAP standard accounts (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Immediately after the installation of an SAP ERP system, the default passwords of the standard SAP accounts MUST be changed. The configured standard SAP accounts MUST also be secured using appropriate measures. Certain standard SAP accounts MUST NOT be used, e.g., for RFC connections and background jobs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined process as part of the system installation ensures that all default passwords (e.g., for SAP*, DDIC, SAPCPIC) are changed. Accounts that are not required for operation are locked. Strong, random passwords are assigned to required standard accounts. It is documented which standard accounts may (not) be used for which purposes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the password hashes of the standard accounts in the USR02 table to ensure they no longer correspond to the known default values. The list of non-locked standard accounts is compared with the documentation. It is checked whether forbidden accounts (e.g., DDIC) are used in RFC destinations (SM59).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a documented procedure for managing standard accounts, which includes locking unused accounts and assigning strong, unique passwords for required accounts. An automated script regularly checks for standard accounts with default or weak passwords.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ABAP report is developed or a tool like SAP Solution Manager is configured to periodically scan all clients for the use of default passwords for standard accounts. The results are reported to the security team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports from the automated password scans. The documentation of the procedure for managing standard accounts is checked and its implementation is verified on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of standard accounts is logged to a SIEM with high priority. An alert is triggered for every login attempt with a known standard account (e.g., SAP*). Standard accounts are integrated into a privileged access management (PAM) solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SAP Security Audit Log (SM20) is configured to capture all activities of standard accounts and forward them to a SIEM. In the SIEM, correlation rules are created that trigger an immediate alarm for logins or failed login attempts of these accounts. Required standard accounts are managed in a PAM solution (e.g., CyberArk), passwords are rotated regularly, and access is only granted after a check-out process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the alerting rules for standard accounts in the SIEM. It is checked whether the required standard accounts are managed in the PAM solution and whether the access process is followed. A test login with the SAP* account must trigger a traceable alarm.

controls.title: Configuration and Securing of SAP Account Management (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: SAP account management for ABAP systems MUST be administered carefully and securely. Activities such as creating, changing, and deleting accounts, resetting and unlocking passwords, and assigning roles and profiles MUST be part of the account administration tasks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An account administration team is appointed, and its tasks and responsibilities are clearly defined in an operations manual. The authorizations required for these tasks (e.g., via transactions SU01, PFCG) are bundled into dedicated admin roles and assigned exclusively to this team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the operations manual for the definition of the account administration tasks. It is verified that only the named administrators have been assigned the corresponding admin roles. The authorizations within the admin roles are checked for the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a formal, documented process for all account management tasks, including approval workflows. Segregation of duties between those who can create users and those who can assign powerful roles is enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A ticketing system is used to manage all account management requests. Each request requires approval from a supervisor. The admin roles are split, e.g., into a 'User-Creator' role that can only create users and a 'Role-Assigner' role that can only assign roles but not create users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly checks tickets in the ticketing system and compares them with the changes in the SAP system (e.g., via the change documents in SU01). The role definitions of the administrators are checked for the correct implementation of segregation of duties.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Account management is integrated into an Identity and Access Management (IAM) system. The creation, modification, and deletion of users is automated based on events in the HR system (Joiner-Mover-Leaver process). All administrative actions are logged and regularly reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IAM tool (e.g., SAP Identity Management, One Identity) is connected to the HR system and the SAP systems. Business rules in the IAM control the entire lifecycle of SAP user accounts. The Security Audit Log (SM20) is used to capture all administrative activities in SU01 and PFCG, and the logs are sent to a SIEM for analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the business rules in the IAM system. The synchronization between HR, IAM, and SAP systems is verified on a random basis (e.g., by checking a recently departed employee). The logs in the SIEM are checked for complete recording of administrative activities.

controls.title: Creation and implementation of an account and authorization concept (B) [Business Department, Developers]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For SAP ERP systems, an account and authorization concept MUST be developed and implemented. The following points MUST be considered: identity principle, principle of least privilege, position principle, accounting document principle, authorization administration document principle, segregation of duties (SoD) principle, approval principle, standard principle, written form principle, and control principle MUST be taken into account. Procedures for the administration and assignment of roles, as well as naming conventions, MUST be defined. Legal and internal frameworks MUST be considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A comprehensive 'SAP Authorization Concept' document is created, detailing all required principles and procedures. This includes the definition of role types (e.g., single, composite, value roles), the procedure for role creation in the development system and their transport via the TMS, as well as clear naming conventions for roles and users. An SoD rule set is defined. The concept is approved by Information Security and Internal Audit.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the authorization concept for completeness and compliance with BSI requirements and internal/external regulations (e.g., GoB, HGB). The implementation of the concept is verified on a random basis in the system (e.g., adherence to naming conventions, role-based assignment, no transport of roles from the production system).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The concept is reviewed regularly, at least annually, and adapted to new circumstances. Automated tools are used to check for segregation of duties (SoD) conflicts already during role creation and assignment. The default values in transaction SU24 are carefully maintained to reduce administrative effort and increase consistency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual review process for the authorization concept is established. Tools like SAP GRC Access Control or third-party solutions are used for SoD analysis. A dedicated project or an ongoing task is set up to maintain the SU24 values for all relevant transactions, especially for custom developments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the annual concept review. It is checked how SoD conflicts are analyzed and handled, ideally by inspecting the corresponding tool. The maintenance state of SU24 is checked on a random basis for important transactions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The role concept is fully integrated into an IAM solution. Role assignments are automatically provisioned and de-provisioned based on users' job functions (role-based access control, RBAC). Continuous monitoring for SoD violations and critical access with real-time alerting is implemented. The authorization design between all system components (ABAP, HANA, Fiori) is fully synchronized and centrally managed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IAM system is used to maintain a business role catalog that automatically assigns the technical SAP roles. Any deviation from the standard (e.g., manual assignment) triggers a workflow. SAP GRC Process Control and Access Control are used for continuous monitoring and alerting. For S/4HANA, it is ensured that the authorizations in the ABAP backend, the HANA database, and the Fiori gateway are consistent.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the business role catalog in the IAM and its mapping to the technical SAP roles. The configuration of continuous monitoring in SAP GRC is verified. Test cases are performed to check the consistent assignment of authorizations across the different technology stacks.

controls.title: Securing SAP Databases (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to SAP databases MUST be secured. Administrators SHOULD preferably only be able to access the databases with SAP tools. If third-party software is used for this purpose, additional security measures MUST be implemented. In that case, no schema account of the SAP system MAY be used for the connection to the database. Furthermore, default passwords MUST be changed and certain database tables (e.g., USR* tables) must be specially protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Direct access to the database is restricted to a few, dedicated database administrators. The password of the SAP schema user (e.g., SAPSR3) is set to a long, random value and stored only in the SAP application. Direct SQL queries on sensitive tables like USR02 are prevented by database permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies who has permissions at the database level. It is checked whether the password of the SAP schema user is strong and whether access attempts to this account are logged. An attempt is made to access the USR02 table via SQL client, which must fail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All database access, especially direct access bypassing the application layer, is logged and monitored. Encryption of 'Data-at-Rest' (e.g., Transparent Data Encryption, TDE) is enabled for the entire database or at least for sensitive table areas. Communication between the application server and the database is encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Native audit functions of the database are activated to log all administrative access and access to critical tables. TDE is configured at the database level. Secure communication is enforced via the corresponding profile parameters of the SAP system and the database configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the database audit logs for suspicious activities. The configuration of the encryption (TDE and network) is checked. A packet sniffer is used to verify that the traffic between the application server and the database is encrypted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Database Activity Monitoring (DAM) tools are used for real-time analysis of all database queries. Privileged database access requires a Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution with session recording. The database is regularly scanned for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A DAM tool (e.g., Imperva, Guardium) is implemented to monitor all SQL traffic and trigger alerts for suspicious patterns (e.g., mass downloads). Database administrators only gain access via a PAM solution that manages the password and records the session. A database vulnerability scanner is run regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and alerts of the DAM system. It is verified that administrative access is exclusively via the PAM solution and that session recordings are available. The reports of the latest database vulnerability scans are analyzed.

controls.title: Securing the SAP RFC Interface (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To protect the Remote Function Call (RFC) interface, RFC connections, RFC authorizations, and the RFC gateways MUST be securely configured. Uniform management policies MUST be created and implemented for all RFC connections. Unused RFC connections MUST be deleted. All RFC gateways MUST be administered securely, for which suitable profile parameters MUST be set and access control lists (ACLs) such as secinfo and reginfo MUST be defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy for managing RFC connections is created. It requires documentation of all RFC destinations (SM59), the use of dedicated RFC users of type 'System' or 'Communication' with minimal privileges, and the regular deletion of unused connections. Gateway security is hardened with restrictive secinfo and reginfo files that only allow necessary external programs and registrations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the RFC policy and compares it with the configurations in SM59. A random check is performed to see whether the RFC users used have minimal permissions. The secinfo and reginfo files on the gateway server are checked for their restrictiveness. Automated tools such as the `gwmon -a show all` command can be used to check the ACL rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all critical RFC connections, especially those that cross system boundaries or transmit sensitive data, Secure Network Communication (SNC) is used to encrypt and authenticate the data traffic. RFC users are always equipped with specifically adapted roles according to the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SNC is implemented using SAP's own libraries or third-party products. For each RFC connection, a dedicated role is created with only the required function modules (authorization object S_RFC). The use of highly privileged users in RFC destinations is strictly prohibited and technically monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in transaction SM59 that the SNC options are active for critical connections. The roles assigned to the RFC users are analyzed for the presence of unnecessary permissions. It is checked whether connections exist from less secure systems (development) to productive systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All RFC connections throughout the entire SAP system landscape are secured with SNC by default. A central tool is used to manage and monitor all RFC interfaces. Automated scans detect insecure RFC configurations, over-privileged RFC users, or unused connections. The gateway logging is forwarded to a central SIEM for analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of SNC is becoming the company-wide standard. A tool for interface management (e.g., from third-party providers or based on the Solution Manager) is used to ensure a complete overview and control. A periodic job analyzes the RFC statistics (ST03N) and the RFC destination tables to report anomalies. The gateway logs (dev_rd) are integrated into the SIEM to alert on failed ACL checks or suspicious registrations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses the central management tool to get an overall overview of RFC security. The configuration and the results of the automated scans are checked. In the SIEM, it is verified that gateway security events are correctly recorded and correlated.

controls.title: Securing and Monitoring the Message Server (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The message server MUST be secured by appropriate settings in the profile parameters. Among other things, a decision MUST be made as to whether ACLs are still to be set up for the internal message server. The message server MUST be monitored using suitable mechanisms so that, for example, system failures of the message server are quickly detected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The profile parameters of the message server (e.g., rdisp/msserv_internal, rdisp/ms_acl_info, rdisp/ms_acl_logon) are set according to SAP security recommendations to prevent unauthorized access. An Access Control List (ACL) is created and activated via the ms/acl_file parameter to define which hosts are allowed to connect to the message server. The availability of the message server process is monitored by the standard SAP monitoring (e.g., transaction SMMS).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the relevant profile parameters of the message server in the SAP system (e.g., via RZ11). The content of the ACL file on the operating system is checked and compared with the requirements. It is verified that the monitoring of the message server is active in the monitoring infrastructure (e.g., CCMS or Solution Manager). An automated test could be the command `lgtst -H <host> -S <SID>` to test the connection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The ACLs for internal and external ports are strictly configured and regularly reviewed. Any administrative access to the message server is logged. Monitoring includes not only availability, but also performance metrics and security events (e.g., failed login attempts or connections rejected by the ACL).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ACL files are stored in a version control system and changes are subject to an approval process. Monitoring in SMMS is configured to also check the logon groups and server load. The message server trace files (dev_ms) are regularly analyzed for security-relevant entries such as 'permission denied'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the current ACL file with the versioned file in the repository. The configuration of the extended monitoring is checked in the monitoring tools. The trace files are randomly checked for security events.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logs of the message server are integrated into a central SIEM for real-time correlation and alerting on suspicious activities. The communication between the message server and the application servers is secured by encryption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The dev_ms trace file is forwarded to a SIEM system in real time. Correlation rules are implemented there that, for example, trigger an alarm in the event of repeated access attempts from the same IP address that are rejected by the ACL. The ms/ssl_port parameter is configured and the application servers are set to connect to the message server via the secure port.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the alerting rules for the message server in the SIEM. Network analysis is used to ensure that the communication between application servers and the message server is encrypted. A test in which an unauthorized host attempts to connect must trigger a traceable alarm in the SIEM.

controls.title: Secure Installation of an SAP ERP System (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When installing an SAP ERP system, current SAP security guides and documentation SHOULD be taken into account. In addition, the institution's security policies SHOULD be adhered to. It SHOULD also be ensured that the SAP ERP system is installed on a hardened operating system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before installation, the operating system is configured according to a hardening guideline (e.g., CIS Benchmarks). During the installation, the current SAP installation and security guides are used. In particular, secure decisions are made from the outset, e.g., regarding network ports and initial users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the installation log and compares it with the specifications of the SAP guides and the internal policies. The configuration of the operating system is checked against the hardening guideline. It is verified that the basic security measures (e.g., changing default passwords) were carried out immediately after installation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation process is documented in a detailed internal guide that combines SAP recommendations with company-specific policies. After installation, a security checklist is systematically worked through to verify the correct and secure basic configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate, versioned installation guide is maintained in the wiki or document management system. The post-installation checklist includes items such as changing all default passwords, locking unused users, applying current patches, and configuring the Security Audit Log.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the internal installation guide and the completed post-installation checklist. The implementation of the checklist items is randomly verified in the system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire installation process is standardized and made reproducible using automation tools (Infrastructure/Configuration as Code). The automated process includes hardening the operating system, the SAP installation, and the secure basic configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools such as Ansible, Terraform, or SAP Landscape Management (LaMa) are used to fully automate the deployment and installation of SAP systems. The configuration files for the automation are managed in a Git repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration scripts and files in the repository for compliance with the security policies. It is verified that newly installed systems exactly match the defined, hardened baseline.

controls.title: SAP Authorization Development (S) [Business Department, Developers]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Technical authorizations SHOULD be developed based on business requirements. Furthermore, SAP authorizations SHOULD be adapted or newly created in the development system of the SAP landscape. In the case of S/4HANA, this SHOULD also include authorization development on HANA databases. For custom developments, e.g., for transactions or authorization objects, transaction SU24 SHOULD be maintained. The wildcard authorization * or intervals in object values SHOULD be avoided. Authorization development SHOULD be carried out within the framework of change management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process for the request and development of authorization roles is established. Business departments define the required functions, which the SAP authorization administration then implements in technical roles. Development takes place exclusively in the development system, avoiding the use of '*' in authorization objects. For custom developments, the authorization checks (AUTHORITY-CHECK) and the SU24 default values are maintained by the developers. All changes are distributed via the Transport Management System (TMS).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented authorization development process. Spot checks are performed to verify that roles have not been changed in the production system (which should not be the case). The role definitions (PFCG) are analyzed for the use of '*' or overly broad ranges. For a custom development, it is checked whether the SU24 values are maintained. An automatic test can be performed with `find-authorizations` in the Code Inspector transaction `SCI`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal change management process for all role developments is strictly followed. Role development includes peer reviews by a second authorization administrator and automated SoD checks before transport to the production system. The production system is sufficiently protected against direct authorization changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every role change requires an approved change ticket. Before a transport is released, the role is checked by a colleague (four-eyes principle). An SoD tool (e.g., SAP GRC) simulates the effects of the new role and blocks the transport in case of critical conflicts. In the production system, transaction PFCG is only released for display and comparison purposes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews change tickets and the associated transport logs. It is checked whether SoD simulation runs are documented. The authorizations for transaction PFCG in the production system are checked to ensure that no changes are possible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The design and development of roles is supported by specialized tools that suggest optimized authorization values based on usage data (traces). The entire lifecycle (request, design, test, approval, transport) is managed and largely automated in a GRC or IAM tool.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools for role optimization based on evaluations of traces (e.g., STAUTHTRACE) are used to generate precisely fitting roles. The entire workflow, from the request for a new authorization to its assignment to the user, is mapped in the GRC system, including automated tests and approval steps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the workflow for role development configured in the GRC system. It is checked whether the use of trace data for role optimization can be proven. The effectiveness of the process is evaluated based on the quality and minimality of the resulting roles.

controls.title: SAP Password Security (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To ensure secure logon to the SAP ERP system, profile parameters, customizing switches, or security policies SHOULD be set appropriately. The hash algorithms used for the stored hash values of the passwords in an SAP ERP system SHOULD comply with current security standards. Access to tables with hash values SHOULD be restricted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The profile parameters for password security (e.g., login/min_password_lng, login/password_history_size, login/password_expiration_time) are set according to a password policy. The profile parameter login/password_hash_algorithm is set to a strong algorithm (e.g., PBKDF2). Access to the table USR02, which contains the password hashes, is highly restricted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the relevant profile parameters in RZ11 and the password policy in the global security settings. It is verified which hash algorithm is used. The auditor attempts to access the table USR02 (e.g., via SE16), which must fail or be logged.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Different, stricter password policies are enforced for different user groups (e.g., administrators, dialog users). The use of passwords that have been exposed in public data breaches is actively blocked. The parameter `password/downwards_compatibility` is deactivated to prevent insecure password hashes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The transaction SECPOL is used to define and assign separate security policies for highly privileged users. A mechanism (e.g., via a BAdI or a third-party tool) is implemented that checks the new password against a list of compromised passwords (e.g., from 'Have I Been Pwned') during a password change.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the security policies in SECPOL and their assignment to the user groups. The effectiveness of the check for compromised passwords is tested by attempting to set a known bad password.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enforced by default for all dialog users. Password-based logon is completely disabled for highly privileged users and replaced by stronger methods such as smart cards or biometric authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MFA solution is integrated, e.g., via SAP Single Sign-On, which is connected to a RADIUS or SAML-based MFA provider. For administrators, logon via Secure Network Communication (SNC) with client certificates (e.g., from a smart card) is enforced, while password logon is disabled for these users (transaction SU01).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a second factor is requested upon logon for a test dialog user. It is checked whether an administrator configured as an SNC user can still log on with a password (which should not be possible).

controls.title: Identification of critical SAP authorizations (S) [Business Department]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The handling of critical authorizations SHOULD be strictly controlled. It SHOULD be ensured that these authorizations, roles, and profiles are assigned only restrictively. Critical authorizations SHOULD be regularly identified, reviewed, and evaluated. The SAP profiles SAP_ALL and SAP_NEW, as well as the SAP authorization object S_DEVELOP (with change authorizations ACTVT 01 and 02), SHOULD not be assigned in the production system. Emergency accounts SHOULD be excluded from this requirement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of critical authorizations, transactions, and profiles (e.g., SAP_ALL, S_DEVELOP, SE16, PFCG, SU01) is defined and documented. A process for regular review (e.g., monthly) is established to control the assignment of these critical authorizations. Any assignment of SAP_ALL or SAP_NEW in the production system is prohibited.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the list of defined critical authorizations for completeness. Using SAP standard reports (e.g., RSUSR002, RSUSR020) or table queries (AGR_USERS), it is verified that the defined critical authorizations are not assigned to regular users. In particular, it is checked whether SAP_ALL or SAP_NEW are assigned in the production system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated process regularly scans all production systems for the assignment of critical authorizations, profiles, and risky role combinations. The results are sent to the security officers for review. For temporary, necessary critical access, emergency user concepts (Firefighter) are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like SAP GRC Access Control or a custom ABAP report is configured to generate daily reports on the assignment of critical access. A Firefighter concept (e.g., with SAP GRC Emergency Access Management) is implemented, which allows temporary, logged access to highly privileged accounts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports from the automated scans and checks how identified violations are handled. The configuration and usage logs of the Firefighter concept are analyzed to ensure that the process is being followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A GRC system is used for continuous monitoring of critical access. Rule sets for critical authorizations are managed centrally and automatically updated based on threat intelligence. Any assignment of critical access triggers an immediate alert and requires multi-level approval.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SAP GRC Process Control and Access Control are configured for continuous control monitoring. The rule set for critical authorizations is maintained centrally and linked to a workflow for exception approvals. Any assignment of a role with critical authorizations triggers a real-time alert in the SIEM and an approval workflow.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the rule set and the workflows in the GRC system. The effectiveness of the real-time alerting is tested by assigning a critical authorization on a test basis. The auditor verifies the documentation and appropriateness of the approved exceptions.

controls.title: Secure Configuration of the SAP Router (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SAP Router SHOULD regulate access to the network and appropriately supplement the existing firewall architecture. It SHOULD also control access to the SAP ERP system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SAP Router is installed in a DMZ to act as a controlled proxy for connections between the internal network and external networks (e.g., SAP Support). The permission table 'saprouttab' is configured restrictively so that only explicitly defined connections to specific hosts and ports are allowed (whitelist approach).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network topology to verify the correct placement of the SAP Router in the DMZ. The configuration file 'saprouttab' is checked for its restrictiveness. In particular, 'Permit All' entries (P * * *) are searched for, which must not be present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All connections via the SAP Router are encrypted and authenticated using SNC (Secure Network Communication). The SAP Router itself runs with an unprivileged user account on a hardened operating system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SNC is configured for the SAP Router to secure all communication. This requires the generation and distribution of certificates. The router process is started under a dedicated operating system user with minimal privileges.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the SNC configuration of the router and checks the validity of the certificates used. It is checked under which user account the SAP Router process is running. The hardening of the underlying operating system is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SAP Router is part of a cascaded arrangement (router cascade) for maximum security. All activities and connection attempts are forwarded in real time to a SIEM system for monitoring and alerting. The 'saprouttab' configuration is centrally managed, and changes are subject to a strict approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SAP Router in an outer DMZ communicates only with a second SAP Router in an inner DMZ before access to the internal network is granted. The router's log files (dev_rout) are forwarded to a SIEM, where rules check for suspicious activities (e.g., repeated denied connections). The 'saprouttab' is managed in a version control system like Git.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the router cascade. In the SIEM, the correct collection and processing of the router logs is verified. The approval process for changes to the 'saprouttab' is traced using the commit history in the version control system.

controls.title: Implementation of security requirements for the Windows operating system (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SAP ERP system SHOULD NOT be installed on a Windows domain controller. The SAP-specific accounts such as <sid>adm or SAPService<sid> SHOULD be secured. After installation, the <db><sid> account SHOULD be locked. The SAPService<sid> account SHOULD NOT have rights for interactive logon. Regarding these permissions, the system resources belonging to the SAP ERP system, such as files, processes, and shared memory, SHOULD be protected. The specific permissions of the accounts and user groups created by the SAP ERP system SHOULD be secured using appropriate settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SAP systems are installed on dedicated Windows servers that are not domain controllers. The passwords for the <sid>adm and SAPService<sid> accounts are set to strong, random values. The SAPService<sid> account is denied the 'Log on locally' and 'Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services' rights via local security policies (secpol.msc). The NTFS permissions for the SAP directories (e.g., /usr/sap) are set restrictively.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the server does not have the role of a domain controller. The memberships of the SAP-specific accounts and groups are checked. The local security policies regarding the logon rights for the SAPService<sid> account are inspected. The NTFS permissions of the SAP directories are checked on a sample basis.

controls.title: Implementation of security requirements for the Unix operating system (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access permissions SHOULD be set for the SAP ERP system directories under Unix. The passwords for the system-specific accounts <sid>adm and <db><sid> SHOULD also be changed. After installation, the <db><sid> account SHOULD be locked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The file permissions and ownership of the SAP directories (e.g., /usr/sap/<SID>, /sapmnt/<SID>) are set restrictively so that only the <sid>adm user and the sapsys group have write access. The passwords for the <sid>adm and <db><sid> accounts are set to strong values. The <db><sid> account is locked after installation (`passwd -l <db><sid>`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses the `ls -ld` commands to check the permissions and owners of the SAP directories. The status of the <sid>adm and <db><sid> accounts is checked in /etc/shadow to ensure that the passwords are set and the <db><sid> account is locked.

controls.title: Deactivation of insecure communication (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Communication with and between SAP ERP systems SHOULD be secured with SNC. If the database and SAP application server are operated on different systems, the database connection SHOULD be encrypted in an appropriate manner. The internal services of the SAP application server SHOULD ONLY communicate with each other using TLS.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Secure Network Communication (SNC) is configured for communication between SAP GUI and the application server and activated for users. The native network encryption of the database (e.g., Oracle Native Network Encryption, HANA TLS) is activated for the connection between the application server and the database. Internal HTTPS ports are configured for communication between ICM and application servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the SNC configuration in the SAP system (profile parameters) and in the SAP GUI. A network sniffer (e.g., Wireshark) is used to check on a sample basis whether the traffic between the GUI and the server and between the server and the database is encrypted. The configuration of the internal TLS communication is checked.

controls.title: Definition of security policies for accounts (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Specific security policies for passwords and logon restrictions SHOULD be created for the respective accounts and account groups. For example, accounts with critical permissions SHOULD be secured by strong password rules (transaction SECPOL). The security policies SHOULD be correctly assigned to the accounts and reviewed regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At least two security policies are defined in the SECPOL transaction: a standard policy for all dialog users and a stricter policy for administrators and other accounts with critical permissions. The stricter policy enforces, for example, higher password complexity, longer passwords, and a shorter validity period. These policies are assigned to the corresponding users. The assignment is reviewed annually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the defined policies in SECPOL and their parameters. It is checked whether all administrators and critical users are assigned to the stricter policy. The logs of the annual review are inspected.

controls.title: Secure SAP GUI settings (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SAP GUI SHOULD be installed and regularly updated on all clients. SAP GUI ACLs SHOULD also be enabled and appropriate administration rules distributed and enabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A software distribution system is used to ensure that an up-to-date and patched version of the SAP GUI is installed on all clients. The security configuration of the SAP GUI, especially the activation of the security rules (ACL), is centrally specified and distributed. The default rule is 'Deny', and only necessary actions (e.g., file access for specific applications) are explicitly allowed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the version and patch level of the SAP GUI on a sample client. The configuration of the security rules is checked on the client to ensure that the ACL is active and has a restrictive default setting.

controls.title: Protection of the spool in the SAP ERP system (S) [Developers]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that data from sequential data processing such as spool or printing can only be accessed to a limited extent. It SHOULD also be prevented that unauthorized accounts can access the TemSe data storage used by the SAP spool system. The permissions granted for this SHOULD be checked regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The permissions for spool access (object S_SPO_ACT) are assigned restrictively. In particular, the ability to view the spool requests of other users is only granted to administrators. Access to the TemSe data storage is protected via the authorization objects S_ADMI_FCD and S_BTCH_JOB.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the roles that contain the authorization object S_SPO_ACT and checks who has the authorization to view foreign spool requests. It is verified that access to TemSe is restricted to administrative users.

controls.title: Protection of SAP background processing (S) [Developers]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: SAP background processing SHOULD be protected from unauthorized access. For this purpose, different system accounts SHOULD be defined and created for batch jobs according to their functional areas. The user type 'Dialog' SHOULD generally NOT be permitted for this purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For background jobs, only users of type 'System' or 'Service' are used. For different application areas (e.g., HR batch, FI batch), separate, non-personal user accounts with minimal permissions are created. Dialog users may not be entered as executors in job steps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the users entered as job executors in the job overview (SM37). It is verified that these users are not of type 'Dialog' and that their permissions correspond to the principle of least privilege. A search is made for jobs that run under highly privileged accounts such as DDIC or SAP*.

controls.title: Activation and securing of the Internet Communication Framework (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that only necessary ICF services are activated. All ICF services that are under an ICF object SHOULD only be activated individually. ICF permissions SHOULD be assigned restrictively. The communication SHOULD be encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A whitelist of the required services is maintained in the SICF transaction. All other services, especially those under /default_host/sap, are deactivated. Services are not activated at the level of main nodes, but only at the level of the specific service. Access to ICF services is controlled via the authorization object S_ICF. All externally accessible services are configured to require TLS (HTTPS).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses the report RS_ICF_SERV_ADMIN_TASKS to check the active services. It is checked whether entire subtrees are activated. The authorization roles are analyzed for the assignment of S_ICF. A web scanner is used to check whether the services are only accessible via HTTPS.

controls.title: Secure configuration of the SAP Web Dispatcher (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SAP Web Dispatcher SHOULD NOT be the first entry point from the Internet to the SAP ERP system. The SAP Web Dispatcher SHOULD be up to date. It SHOULD be configured securely.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SAP Web Dispatcher is preceded by an upstream reverse proxy (e.g., a Web Application Firewall) in the network architecture. The Web Dispatcher software is regularly updated to the latest patch level. The profile parameters of the Web Dispatcher are hardened according to SAP security recommendations (e.g., through URL filtering, blocking of admin access, configuration of TLS).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network architecture and the configuration of the Web Dispatcher profile. The version of the Web Dispatcher is checked (`sapwebdisp -v`). It is verified that administrative access to the Web Dispatcher via the network is restricted.

controls.title: Protection of self-developed code in the SAP ERP system (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A custom code management process SHOULD be defined so that self-developed code is replaced or removed if it can be replaced by SAP standard code or is no longer used. Furthermore, the requirements from the policy for the development of ABAP programs SHOULD be taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A lifecycle process for custom developments is established. This process includes regular analyses (e.g., with SAP Solution Manager) to identify unused or obsolete code. A secure programming policy (see also APP.4.6) is mandatory for development.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the custom code management process. Reports from the code analysis tools are inspected to verify that the process is being followed. The secure programming guideline is checked for completeness.

controls.title: Audit of the SAP ERP system (S) [Specialist department]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To ensure that all internal and external policies and specifications are complied with, all SAP ERP systems SHOULD be audited regularly. The Security Optimization Service in SAP Solution Manager SHOULD be used for this purpose. The results of the audit SHOULD be evaluated and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual audit plan for the SAP system landscape is created. As part of the audit, automated checks are performed using the Security Optimization Service (SOS) or similar tools (e.g., EarlyWatch Alert Security Checks). The results are analyzed, measures to remediate vulnerabilities are defined, and their implementation is tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit plan and the reports of the last audits, especially the SOS reports. It is checked whether a process for tracking the findings exists and whether the defined measures have been implemented.

controls.title: Creation of an emergency concept (S) [Emergency officer]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An emergency concept SHOULD be created and operated for SAP ERP systems. It SHOULD secure business activities and comply with the specifications from crisis management or business continuity management. The following points SHOULD be described and defined in the emergency concept: detection of and reaction to incidents, data backup and recovery concept, and emergency administration. The emergency concept SHOULD be updated regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specific emergency manual for the SAP systems is created. It describes in detail the procedure for various scenarios (e.g. system failure, data corruption, security incident). It contains the backup and recovery concept, clear instructions for recovery, and the processes for emergency administration (see A29). The concept is reviewed annually and adapted to changes in the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the emergency manual for completeness and up-to-dateness. It is verified that the described concepts (e.g. data backup) correspond to reality. Logs of emergency drills and concept reviews are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The emergency concept is tested regularly, at least once a year, through practical exercises. This includes both recovery tests from backup and the simulation of security incidents. The results of the tests are used to improve the concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A plan for emergency drills is created. The recovery of a test system from the production backup is practiced annually. In addition, tabletop exercises are conducted to train communication and decision-making paths in an emergency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the plans and logs of the emergency drills and recovery tests performed. It is checked whether the improvement measures derived from the tests have been implemented.

controls.title: Setting up emergency accounts (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Emergency accounts SHOULD be created. The created accounts and permissions SHOULD be strongly controlled and precisely documented. Furthermore, all activities performed by emergency accounts SHOULD be logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An emergency user concept (firefighter concept) is implemented. This can be done via SAP GRC Emergency Access Management (EAM) or a manual process. Dedicated, highly privileged emergency accounts are created that are locked by default. The process for requesting, approving, using, and subsequently reviewing the logs of the emergency sessions is clearly defined and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the emergency user concept. It is verified that the emergency accounts are locked during normal operation. The logs of the last emergency sessions are reviewed and checked for compliance with the process (approval, review of activities).

controls.title: Implementation of continuous monitoring of security settings (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be constantly monitored whether all security settings of the SAP ERP system are correct. In addition, it SHOULD be monitored whether all patches and updates have been properly installed. The SAP monitoring SHOULD be integrated into the institution's general system monitoring.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools such as SAP Solution Manager (e.g. System and Application Monitoring, Configuration Validation) are used to continuously monitor critical security parameters, patch status, and system logs. Important alarms from SAP monitoring are integrated into the institution's central monitoring tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the monitoring in SAP Solution Manager or an equivalent tool. It is checked whether the defined thresholds and checks are appropriate. The integration into the central monitoring is verified by triggering a test alarm.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The monitoring is connected to a SIEM system (Security Information and Event Management). Security-relevant logs (e.g. Security Audit Log, Gateway Log, System Log) are sent to the SIEM in real time and automatically evaluated there.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An agent or a syslog forwarder is installed on the SAP servers to send the relevant log files to the SIEM. Specific parsers and correlation rules for SAP events are implemented in the SIEM to detect suspicious activities (e.g. repeated failed logins, use of critical transactions).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the arrival and correct processing of the SAP logs in the SIEM. The effectiveness of the correlation rules is tested by simulating attack or misuse scenarios.

controls.title: Configuration of SAP Single Sign-On (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If multiple SAP ERP systems are present, users SHOULD access the systems using SAP Single Sign-On (SAP SSO). It SHOULD be decided in the planning phase between which SAP ERP systems the SSO mechanism will be used. The SSO SHOULD be securely configured and operated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SAP Single Sign-On is implemented, typically using Kerberos/SPNego for integration into a Windows domain or SAML for web-based scenarios (e.g. Fiori). The configuration is done securely, in particular by using strong encryption algorithms and protecting the cryptographic keys (e.g. in the Secure Storage and Forwarding, SSF).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the SSO configuration in the SAP system (e.g. profile parameters, transaction STRUST). It is verified that users can log in without re-entering their password. The security of the configuration, e.g. the encryption algorithms used, is checked.

controls.title: Real-time detection and alerting of irregular activities (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The most important security recording functions of the SAP ERP systems, such as Security Audit Log or System Log, SHOULD be continuously monitored. In case of suspicious activities, the responsible employees SHOULD be alerted automatically. To be able to analyze SAP-specific security incidents and distinguish false positives from real security incidents, employees SHOULD either be trained or corresponding services from third-party providers SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Security Audit Log (transaction SM19) is configured to record all critical events (e.g. failed logins, transaction starts, system changes). A process is established in which the logs (SM20) are checked daily, either manually or with the help of scripts. In case of critical findings, a manual alert is triggered. The responsible employees receive training on the evaluation of SAP logs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the Security Audit Log filters in SM19. The logs of the daily checks are reviewed. The competence of the employees is checked by asking specific questions about the interpretation of log entries.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security-relevant logs are forwarded to a central Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. Basic correlation rules are implemented there to detect simple attack patterns. The alerting process is formalized and linked to a documented incident response plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SAP logs are sent in real time to a SIEM such as Splunk or QRadar. Rules are configured in the SIEM that trigger an alarm, for example, in the case of 10 failed logins for the same user within a minute or the use of a critical transaction outside of business hours. The alarm is created as a ticket in the incident management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the log collection and correlation rules in the SIEM. The incident response plan is checked. The response to a test alarm is tracked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIEM uses advanced correlation rules and User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) to detect complex and covert attacks. The alarm system is integrated into a SOAR platform (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) to automate initial response measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: UEBA modules in the SIEM create a baseline of normal user behavior and detect deviations (e.g. an accountant who suddenly executes developer transactions). A critical alarm in the SIEM automatically triggers a playbook via the SOAR platform, which, for example, locks the relevant user account in the SAP system and provides the security analyst with all relevant information.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the UEBA module and the SOAR playbooks. Its effectiveness is tested by simulating a complex attack scenario. The auditor verifies that the automatic response (e.g. user lockout) functions correctly and is documented.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Enterprise Resource Planning systems from SAP (SAP ERP systems for short) are used to automate and technically support internal and external business processes. SAP ERP systems therefore typically process confidential information, so all components and data must be appropriately protected.
SAP ERP systems are currently on the market under the product names SAP Business Suite and SAP S/4HANA. An SAP ERP system is composed of various modules that can be used to map the organizational structure of an institution. The modules of an SAP ERP system include accounting, human resources, and logistics, among others. The core components of the SAP ERP system are SAP NetWeaver (application server middleware) and SAP HANA (application server and database). SAP NetWeaver makes it possible to connect SAP ABAP and SAP JAVA applications and to control processes system-wide. SAP HANA can analyze large amounts of data for all business areas in real time.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The module describes which threats to consider for SAP ERP systems and how these systems can be securely installed, configured, and operated. It is aimed at information security officers and administrators who are responsible for planning and implementing SAP ERP systems.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
Module APP.4.2 SAP ERP System is to be applied to every SAP ERP system.
The module is limited to the core installation of an SAP ERP system and focuses on the specific features of the underlying SAP NetWeaver application server.
