Also, not all available SAP products are described in detail in this module. The following descriptions are limited to the configuration of the SAP Basis and do not cover modules or applications.
Requirements for the development of ABAP programs can be found in module APP.4.6 SAP ABAP Programming. Furthermore, no adjacent IT systems, operating systems, or databases are considered in detail. For this, the specific modules such as SYS.1.2.2 Windows Server 2012, SYS.1.3 Server under Linux and Unix, or APP.4.3 Relational Databases must be applied. Likewise, this module does not cover SAP HANA. Current product names are deliberately omitted, as they change frequently.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Failure to consider SAP's security recommendations
parts.prose: If an SAP ERP system is set up without considering SAP's recommended security guides, it can lead to serious security problems in the system. This is the case, for example, if SAP recommendations for account and authorization management are not implemented correctly. Vulnerabilities can also arise if SAP recommendations for protecting communication or interface operations via RFC and web services are ignored. This can make the entire system vulnerable.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Missing or delayed application of patches and SAP Security Notes
parts.prose: SAP ERP systems consist of various modules and components and are complex systems that usually process sensitive data. SAP therefore regularly publishes patches and security notes to fix software bugs and known vulnerabilities. If new patches or SAP security notes are not applied in a timely manner or at all, open vulnerabilities could be exploited by attackers. As a result, attackers could manipulate SAP ERP systems. This could lead to the exfiltration of confidential data, service failures, or a complete standstill of business processes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Lack of planning, implementation, and documentation of an SAP authorization concept
parts.prose:
SAP authorization concepts are functionally and technically complex. Due to these high requirements, they are often poorly planned and implemented, if at all, in many institutions. However, if a well-thought-out authorization concept is missing, accounts are often assigned more authorizations than necessary. These accounts could then intentionally manipulate or accidentally damage the SAP ERP system. This jeopardizes integrity, confidentiality, and availability.
Furthermore, the design of authorizations in S/4HANA systems must be precisely coordinated and synchronized between the integrated components ABAP, HANA, and NetWeaver Gateway (for Fiori applications), as conflicting authorizations could otherwise be granted.
If the SAP authorization concept is not sufficiently documented, granted authorizations can no longer be traced and therefore cannot be maintained. For example, it is possible that employees who have already left the company or been assigned new tasks can still access SAP ERP systems.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Missing SAP documentation and missing emergency concepts
parts.prose: If there is no documentation for the SAP ERP system or it is not maintained, it is no longer possible to trace how the SAP ERP system was set up and with which settings. This delays recovery times in an emergency, for example, and business-critical processes may fail completely. This risk also exists if there are no emergency plans that describe in detail how those responsible should proceed in an emergency.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for database systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are only informal or verbally communicated guidelines for the operation of database systems. These are not documented, not known to all relevant employees, and are not systematically enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, security aspects for databases are only dealt with reactively and on an ad hoc basis. There is no formal basis for decisions or configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with administrators and developers whether there is a common understanding of security requirements. It is checked whether written specifications are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general IT security policy exists and mentions database systems, but a specific, detailed policy that addresses the special features of relational databases is missing. The basic requirements are known, but not sufficiently detailed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The general IT security policy is used as a reference, but the concrete implementation for databases is left to the individual administrators, which can lead to inconsistent configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the general IT security policy and checks whether specific chapters or sections for database systems exist. It is verified whether these are sufficient for consistent implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the institution's general security policy, a specific security policy for database systems MUST be created. It MUST clearly describe requirements and specifications on how database systems are to be operated securely. The policy MUST be known to all employees responsible for database systems and be fundamental to their work. If the policy is changed or if there are deviations from the requirements, this MUST be coordinated with the Information Security Officer (ISO) and documented. It MUST be checked regularly whether the policy is still being implemented correctly. The results MUST be appropriately documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy should contain concrete specifications on topics such as hardening, data backup, authorization management, and logging. It is versioned in a central document management system and made accessible to all responsible employees. Changes to the policy follow a defined approval process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security policy for database systems and checks its content for completeness and comprehensibility. It is verified that the policy is known to the relevant employees (e.g., through interviews or training records). In addition, the logs of regular reviews and documented deviations are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is integrated into the central change management system. The policy review process is formalized, tracked, and the results are used for continuous improvement. The policy also contains specific technical configuration templates and baselines for various types of database systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technical baselines can be provided as scripts or templates for configuration management tools to support the consistent implementation of the policy. The regular review is supplemented by automated compliance scans.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of policy changes into the change management system. It is checked whether technical configuration templates exist and are applied. The results of automated compliance checks are used as proof of the policy's implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the security policy is enforced by technical means, for example, through configuration management tools that automatically detect and report or correct deviations. The policy is dynamically adapted based on threat intelligence feeds and the results of continuous security monitoring.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 'Configuration-as-Code' system is used to translate the policy requirements into executable code. A SIEM system correlates compliance violations with other security events to create a comprehensive situational picture.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the enforcing system (e.g., Ansible, Puppet) and compares the implemented rules with the policy. Real-time compliance dashboards are checked. It is verified that a process for updating the policy based on new threat intelligence exists and is actively used.

controls.title: Basic hardening of the database management system (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardening measures are only carried out ad hoc and on individual database systems classified as particularly critical. There is no documented checklist or repeatable process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, only the most obvious security weaknesses such as default passwords are changed, without a systematic analysis and deactivation of unnecessary functions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a sample of database systems and compares their configurations. Attention is paid to significant inconsistencies and the use of default settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic hardening steps, such as changing default passwords and uninstalling demo databases, are performed on all systems during installation. However, there is no comprehensive, documented checklist that covers all relevant aspects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hardening is based on the individual knowledge of the administrators and not on a standardized procedure, which can lead to different security levels.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies on a sample of systems whether basic hardening measures (e.g., no default accounts) have been implemented. It is checked whether a hardening checklist exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The database management system MUST be hardened. For this purpose, a checklist of the steps to be performed MUST be compiled and processed. Passwords MUST NOT be stored in plain text. The basic hardening MUST be checked regularly and, if necessary, adjusted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The checklist should be based on vendor-specific security recommendations and general best practices. It should cover aspects such as disabling unnecessary services and functions, configuring logging, securing default accounts, and defining secure communication protocols. The regular review can take place as part of internal audits.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the hardening checklist and checks its completeness. It is verified on a random basis on production systems whether the specifications from the checklist have been implemented. The documentation of the regular reviews is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hardening process is supported by the use of automated scripts that ensure consistent application of the checklist. The checklist is based on a recognized standard (e.g., CIS Benchmarks). Deviations from the hardened baseline are automatically detected and reported by regular configuration scans.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: PowerShell, shell scripts, or specialized tools can be used to automate hardening. Tools like OpenSCAP or commercial compliance scanners can be used to check for conformity.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the automation scripts and the configuration of the compliance scanning tools. The scan reports are analyzed to assess the coverage and the handling of identified deviations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A configuration management system (e.g., Ansible, Puppet, Chef) continuously enforces the hardened state of the database management system. Any deviation from the defined baseline is either automatically corrected (self-healing) or triggers a high-priority alarm. The hardening profile also includes security-relevant settings of the underlying operating system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hardening specifications are managed as 'Configuration-as-Code', versioned, and rolled out via a CI/CD pipeline. This ensures that all changes are traceable and tested.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the repository with the 'Configuration-as-Code' and the associated pipelines. The configuration of the configuration management system is checked and it is verified that it actively enforces the desired state. Logs of automatic corrections or alarms are evaluated.

controls.title: Regulated creation of new databases (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrators or developers create new databases as needed, without a formal request or approval process. There is no systematic documentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This often leads to an uncontrolled proliferation of databases ('database sprawl'), where the purpose, owner, or data classification is unclear.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests a list of all databases and randomly questions the administrators about the purpose, owner, and approval process for selected databases. The lack of documentation is taken as an indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal process for requesting new databases, for example, via email to the database administrators. However, the documentation of the newly created databases is incomplete or inconsistent.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Although a request is made, standardized forms are often missing, which means that important information such as the business owner is not always recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the administrators' email inboxes or asks for examples of requests. A list of existing databases is compared with the available documentation to identify gaps.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: New databases MUST be created according to a defined process. When a new database is created, basic information about the database MUST be documented in a comprehensible manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process should include a formal request, approval by the business owner, and technical implementation by IT. The basic information to be documented should at least include the name of the database, its purpose, the business owner, and the IT operations manager. The documentation can be done in a wiki or a simple database.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the process description for creating new databases. The process is traced using the latest requests. It is checked whether documentation with the required basic information is available for all newly created databases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for creating new databases is controlled via a central ticket system. A template is used for the request, which ensures that all necessary information (e.g., owner, purpose, data classification, protection requirements) is recorded. The documentation is done automatically or semi-automatically in a central CMDB.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specific workflow for database requests is configured in the ticket system, which contains the necessary approval steps. After approval, a ticket for the technical implementation is created. A script can update the CMDB with the basic data after the database has been created.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the workflow in the ticket system. The CMDB is inspected and it is checked whether the entries for databases are complete and up-to-date. Ticket histories are randomly compared with the CMDB entries.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire process, from application and approval to the technical provisioning of a new database, is largely automated via a self-service portal. During automatic creation, basic security configurations (e.g., hardening, logging) are applied directly, and the entry in the CMDB is created and updated automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An orchestration engine (e.g., Ansible Tower, Rundeck) is used to execute the provisioning scripts after approval has been granted in the self-service portal. The configurations are derived from templates based on the requested data classification and protection requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the self-service process. The configuration of the orchestration engine and the provisioning templates are analyzed. It is checked whether a newly provisioned database automatically appears correctly in the CMDB and has the security baselines corresponding to the protection requirements.

controls.title: Data backup of a database system (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data backups are performed only irregularly or only for some selected databases. Transaction logs are not backed up, and recovery tests are not performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Backups are often initiated manually by administrators when they remember to do so, leading to inconsistent and unreliable backups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the backup logs for regularity and completeness. A list of all databases is compared with the list of backed-up databases to identify gaps.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Full data backups are performed regularly (e.g., nightly) for all databases. However, transaction logs are not backed up, which prevents point-in-time recovery. Recovery tests are not performed regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Standard DBMS maintenance plans are used for nightly full backups. The maximum data loss is up to 24 hours.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the backup jobs and the logs. They check if transaction log backup is configured and if there is evidence of performed recovery tests.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: System backups of the DBMS and data MUST be performed regularly. The database system MUST also be backed up before a new database is created. Data backups are carried out according to a defined plan, which is documented in the data backup concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A data backup plan is created that defines backup intervals and retention periods. Backups should be performed using the designated DBMS utilities. The execution of recovery tests should also be planned and documented, even if they do not yet take place regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the data backup concept and compares its specifications with the configuration of the backup jobs. The completeness and success of the backups are checked using the logs. Documentation of recovery tests is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All transactions SHOULD be backed up in such a way that they can be restored at any time (point-in-time recovery). This is achieved through a combination of regular full/incremental backups and backing up transaction logs. Recovery tests are planned and performed at regular intervals to verify the functionality of the backups. The backup strategy is adapted to the data's protection requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For databases with high protection requirements, transaction logs are backed up more frequently (e.g., every 15 minutes) than for less critical systems. Recovery tests can be performed on a separate test system to avoid disrupting production operations. The test results are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the backup jobs for data and transaction logs. The logs of the performed recovery tests are requested and checked for regularity and success. It is compared whether the backup frequency corresponds to the RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defined in the protection requirement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire process of data backup and recovery is fully automated. Recovery tests are also automated and performed at short intervals (e.g., daily), with the integrity of the restored data being automatically verified. The backup solution is integrated into an overall disaster recovery plan and includes the replication of backups to an external, geographically separate location.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized backup software or cloud services are used to automate the process. Scripts automatically perform a restore on a dedicated server, run test queries, and compare checksums to confirm integrity before the test is reported as successful.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and logs of the automated backup and testing system. The reports of the automated recovery tests are reviewed. The configuration of the offsite replication is checked and compared with the specifications of the disaster recovery plan.

controls.title: Sufficient hardware sizing (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The sizing of hardware for database systems is based on rough estimates or minimum manufacturer recommendations, without an analysis of the specific application load.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This often leads to under-provisioning and thus to performance problems in productive operation, which are only addressed reactively.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the administrators about the hardware procurement process and asks about the basis for the sizing decisions. The lack of load analysis or capacity planning is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hardware is sized based on current requirements and loads. However, future growth is not systematically considered in the planning, which leads to regular bottlenecks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The initial performance is sufficient, but as soon as the amount of data or the number of users grows, the hardware has to be upgraded at short notice and unplanned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the hardware order history for database systems for frequent, unplanned upgrades. They check whether growth assumptions were documented in the original planning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Database management systems SHOULD be installed on sufficiently sized hardware. The hardware SHOULD have enough reserves to meet potentially increasing demands. When sizing the hardware, the expected growth for the planned period of use SHOULD be taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before procurement, a capacity planning is carried out, which considers the current load (e.g., number of transactions, users) and a forecast for growth (e.g., +20% per year) for the planned hardware lifecycle (e.g., 3-5 years). This planning is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the capacity planning documentation for recently procured database systems. They check whether the planning contains both current loads and realistic growth assumptions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal capacity management process is established. The performance of the database systems (CPU, RAM, I/O, storage) is continuously monitored. A trend analysis is used to proactively identify future resource requirements. A defined process exists for scaling resources when predefined thresholds are exceeded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Monitoring tools (e.g., Prometheus, Zabbix) collect performance data. Regular reports show utilization trends and predict when an expansion will be necessary. Thresholds are set so that there is enough time for the procurement and implementation process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process description for capacity management. The trend analysis reports and the configuration of the monitoring system (esp. thresholds and alarms) are checked. It is traced how past resource bottlenecks were responded to.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The database system is implemented on an elastic infrastructure (e.g., a private or public cloud or a highly virtualized environment). This infrastructure can automatically scale the allocated resources (CPU, RAM) based on real-time load without service interruption to ensure optimal performance and cost-efficiency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technologies such as VMware vSphere, Kubernetes, or cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, GCP) are used. Autoscaling rules are configured to react to specific database performance indicators and adjust resources within predefined limits.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the virtualization or cloud platform. The autoscaling rules and metrics are checked. The performance logs are evaluated to verify that scaling worked as expected during load peaks.

controls.title: Uniform configuration standard of database management systems (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Each database server is configured individually and to the best of the respective administrator's knowledge. There is no standard, which leads to widely diverging and inconsistent configurations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This significantly complicates administration, troubleshooting, and the systematic securing of the database landscape.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configurations of several database servers of the same type and documents significant deviations in critical parameters (e.g., logging, memory allocation, security settings).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are unwritten rules or informal instructions for configuring database servers. However, there is no formal, documented, and versioned configuration standard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New administrators have to rely on the knowledge of colleagues. Although the configurations are more similar than at Level 1, they are still not guaranteed to be consistent.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions several administrators about their configuration procedure and asks for written specifications. The lack of an official document is noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A uniform configuration standard SHOULD be defined for all database management systems used. All database management systems SHOULD be configured and operated uniformly according to this standard. If it is necessary to deviate from the configuration standard for an installation, all steps SHOULD be approved by the ISB and documented in a traceable manner. The configuration standard SHOULD be reviewed regularly and, if necessary, adapted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The standard is maintained and versioned as a document in a management system (e.g., Wiki, SharePoint). It contains specific values or recommendations for the most important configuration parameters. A process for exceptions (exception handling) is defined and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the configuration standard. The configuration of productive systems is compared with the standard on a random basis. The documentation and approval for any deviations are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration standard is implemented and maintained using automation scripts or configuration management tools. Regular, automated checks are performed to detect and report deviations from the standard (configuration drift).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Installation and configuration scripts ensure that all new systems are set up in compliance with the standard. Tools such as OpenSCAP or commercial compliance scanners regularly check the conformity of existing systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automation scripts and the reports from the compliance scanners. They check how the reported deviations are handled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration standard is managed as 'Configuration as Code'. All changes to the standard and to the configurations are versioned (e.g., in Git), peer-reviewed, and tested and rolled out via an automated CI/CD pipeline. The system actively prevents or automatically corrects any configuration drift.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Ansible, Puppet, or Chef are operated in enforcing mode. Configuration changes are only possible via the defined code review and pipeline process. Direct manual changes to the system are prevented or immediately reverted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the 'Configuration as Code' process, including the Git repository, the pull request and review processes, and the CI/CD pipeline. It is verified that the system actively prevents or corrects configuration drift, e.g., through a test change that must be reverted.

controls.title: Restrictive handling of database links (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Database links are used by developers and administrators without restrictions or oversight. The use of PUBLIC database links is common. There is no documentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This creates uncontrolled and often unnoticed dependencies between systems and poses a significant security risk, as permissions can be exploited across system boundaries.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests a list of all database links on multiple systems (e.g., via `SELECT * FROM DBA_DB_LINKS;`) and notes the lack of documentation and the frequent use of PUBLIC links.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an awareness of the risks of database links, but there is no formal process for their approval, documentation, or review. Private DB links are preferred, but not consistently enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators are verbally instructed to be cautious with DB links, but the procedural and technical controls to ensure this are lacking.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the existing DB links with any available documentation (e.g., in wikis or ticket systems) and determines that it is incomplete and that no formal approval process exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that only authorized personnel are permitted to create database links (DB links). If such links are created, so-called Private DB links MUST be created in preference to Public DB links. All DB links created by authorized personnel SHOULD be documented and regularly reviewed. Furthermore, DB links SHOULD be taken into account when the database system is backed up.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `CREATE DATABASE LINK` permission is granted restrictively. A list of all approved DB links is maintained with justification, owner, and target system. The necessity of each DB link is confirmed as part of an annual review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks who has the permission to create DB links. The maintained list of approved DB links is compared with a technically extracted list of a<U+00AD>ctual links. The logs of the regular reviews are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The creation of DB links is strictly controlled by technical permissions. A regular, semi-automated audit process is performed to identify all existing DB links and compare them with the list of approved links. Unused or undocumented links are marked for removal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script is run regularly (e.g., monthly) that reads all DB links from the data dictionaries and generates a report. This report is compared with the central CMDB to find discrepancies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the audit script and the reports from the last few months. It is checked how identified discrepancies (undocumented or unused links) were handled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of database links is minimized by default and is only permitted after a formal risk analysis and approval. An automated system continuously monitors the creation of new or unauthorized DB links in real time and immediately triggers an alarm in the SIEM. The necessity of each existing link is recertified annually by the business owner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Database auditing or a DAM (Database Activity Monitoring) tool is configured to react to `CREATE DATABASE LINK` events and send a warning to the security team. The recertification process is managed via a workflow tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the monitoring system (DB auditing, DAM, SIEM). It is checked whether test alarms function as expected. The logs of the annual recertification process are inspected.

controls.title: Encryption of the database connection (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only connections from selected, particularly sensitive client applications to the database server are encrypted. All internal communication between servers or from admin workstations is unencrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Encryption is configured on an application-specific basis in the connection string, rather than being enforced server-side.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the database server's configuration to determine if encryption is enforced. Additionally, connection strings in application configurations are checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Connection encryption is generally enabled on the database server, but it uses insecure default settings such as self-signed certificates or outdated protocols and ciphers. Certificate validation on the client may not be enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The focus is on getting encryption to work 'somehow' without evaluating its cryptographic strength. Clients are often configured to accept any certificate to avoid connectivity issues.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the encryption configuration on the server (TLS version, cipher suites) and analyzes the certificate used (issuer, validity). It is checked whether clients are forced to validate the server certificate.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The database management system SHOULD be configured so that database connections are always encrypted. The cryptographic methods and protocols used for this SHOULD comply with the institution's internal policies (see CON.1 Crypto Concept).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On the database server, encryption is enforced for all incoming connections (e.g., `ssl=on` and `ssl_ca_file` in PostgreSQL). The configuration is based on a central crypto concept that specifies permitted TLS versions and cipher suites. Certificates from a trusted internal or external CA are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the crypto concept and compares its specifications with the live configuration of the database server. Tools like `nmap` or `openssl s_client` are used to check the configuration from the outside. It is ensured that unencrypted connections are rejected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only strong, current cryptographic protocols (e.g., TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3) and cipher suites are enforced according to the institution's crypto concept. Certificate management (issuance, renewal, revocation) is centralized and semi-automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central certificate server (e.g., with ACME protocol) is used to manage the lifecycles of the certificates. Configuration management tools are used to keep the cryptographic settings on all database servers consistent.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a scan of the TLS configuration with a specialized tool (e.g., SSLScan, TestSSL.sh) and evaluates the results against current best practices. The certificate management process is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Mutual authentication (mTLS) is enforced for all database connections, where both the client and the server must present valid, trusted certificates. Connection attempts with weak protocols or ciphers are actively blocked and logged for security analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The database server is configured to require client certificates and verify them against a specific CA (`clientcert=verify-full` in PostgreSQL). The distribution and management of client certificates is integrated into the onboarding process for new applications or users. An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) or a database firewall can be used to block unwanted connection attempts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the mTLS configuration on the server and client side. An attempt is made to establish a connection without a valid client certificate, which must fail. The logs of the server and the blocking systems are analyzed for corresponding events.

controls.title: Data takeover or migration (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data is imported using ad-hoc scripts or manual copy processes, without any verification of completeness or integrity after the import.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This poses a high risk of data loss or corruption, which is often only noticed much later during application operation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions those responsible about the migration process and asks for the submission of migration scripts and verification logs. The absence of these artifacts is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After the data takeover, a simple check is performed, e.g., comparing the number of rows in the source and target tables. However, no content-based integrity checks (e.g., using checksums) are carried out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple `SELECT COUNT(*)` is executed on the most important tables. Subtle data corruption is not detected this way.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the verification process described to them and checks its documentation. It is assessed whether the checks performed are sufficient to ensure data integrity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be defined in advance how data is to be initially or regularly imported into a database. After data has been imported, it SHOULD be checked whether it is complete and unchanged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A migration plan is created that describes the procedure. After the migration, a log is created that records the results of the verification (e.g., row counts, comparison of samples). This process is repeated for each data import.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the migration plan and the verification logs for a recent data import. It is checked whether the defined process was followed and the checks are documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration process is fully scripted and repeatable. Automated pre- and post-migration checks are implemented that, in addition to row counts, also compare checksums or hashes over key data fields to ensure integrity. A detailed log of the entire migration run is generated automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) tools or custom scripts are used. The scripts calculate hashes for each row or for aggregated data before migration and compare them after migration. The result is recorded in a log file.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the migration scripts, especially the implementation of the integrity checks. The automatically generated logs are inspected for completeness and errors.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data migration process includes a mandatory 'dry run' (test run) in a production-like test environment. A detailed rollback plan is created for the production migration and is also tested. The entire process is automated to such an extent that it requires minimal manual interaction. After the migration, an automated data quality and integrity report is generated for the business owners.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The migration process is integrated into a CI/CD pipeline for databases. Tools like Flyway or Liquibase can be used to manage schema- and data-based migrations. The rollback plan uses database snapshots or logical restore points.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the test run and the rollback plan. It is checked whether these plans have been tested. The configuration of the automation tools is analyzed. A sample of the automatically generated quality report for business owners is reviewed.

controls.title: Monitoring of the Database Management System (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Monitoring is limited to basic server reachability tests (e.g., via ping). There is no monitoring of database-specific services or performance parameters.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Problems such as a full hard drive, a crashed database instance, or massive performance degradation are only noticed when users complain.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the monitoring system demonstrated and checks which metrics are collected for database servers. The absence of database-specific checks is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic operating system metrics (CPU, RAM, disk space) of the database servers are monitored. However, monitoring of internal database parameters, as well as defined thresholds and an alerting process, are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators only look at the utilization graphs reactively when a problem is reported. There is no proactive notification of impending bottlenecks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configured checks in the monitoring system and determines whether thresholds and notification rules are defined for critical metrics.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The parameters, events, and operational states of the database management system that are critical for secure operation SHOULD be defined. These SHOULD be monitored using a monitoring system. Thresholds SHOULD be set for all critical parameters, events, and operational states. If these values are exceeded, an appropriate response MUST be taken. The responsible employees SHOULD be alerted in this case.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of critical parameters is defined, e.g., availability of the database instance, free space in the tablespace, number of active connections. In the monitoring tool, thresholds (e.g., 'Warning' at 80% full, 'Critical' at 90%) and alerting rules (e.g., email to DB admins) are configured for these parameters.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of defined critical parameters and compares it with the configuration in the monitoring system. It is checked whether the thresholds and alerting rules are reasonably defined and active. It is verified whether past alarms have been responded to.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The monitoring includes detailed, database-specific performance indicators such as average query times, index usage statistics, cache hit rates, and wait events (lock waits). The thresholds are dynamically adjusted based on historical performance data. The alerting is integrated into a central ticketing system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Special plugins or exporters for the monitoring system are used to collect the database-specific metrics. The alerting automatically creates a ticket in the ticketing system, which is assigned to the database team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the metrics collected in the monitoring system for their depth and relevance. The integration with the ticketing system is checked by triggering a test alarm or by tracing a past alarm-to-ticket case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A specialized tool for database performance analysis (Database Performance Analyzer, DPA) or an APM tool (Application Performance Monitoring) is used. This provides deep insights, performs root cause analysis for performance problems, and uses machine learning to predict potential bottlenecks. The dashboards are tailored to the needs of different roles (administrators, developers, management).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like SolarWinds DPA, pgAnalyze, or commercial APM suites are used. These tools can, for example, identify inefficient SQL queries and provide direct feedback to developers. Anomaly detection algorithms warn of unusual behavior before it leads to an outage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the functionality of the DPA or APM tool demonstrated. It is checked how the results of the tool are used for proactive problem solving and optimization. The role-based dashboards are reviewed.

controls.title: Protection against malicious database scripts (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Database scripts are written by developers or administrators and executed directly in the production environment without any tests, quality controls, or reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This leads to a high risk of errors, data loss, and security vulnerabilities, as faulty `UPDATE` or `DELETE` statements without a `WHERE` clause, for example, can have devastating effects.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions those responsible about the process of script creation and execution. The absence of test and review processes is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Database scripts are informally reviewed by a colleague before execution (four-eyes principle). However, they are not systematically tested in a dedicated test environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The review helps to find obvious errors, but without testing in a realistic environment, unexpected side effects or performance problems cannot be detected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a review process is established (e.g., through comments in tickets). It is asked whether dedicated test environments for databases exist and are used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When database scripts are developed, mandatory quality criteria SHOULD be defined for them (see CON.8 Software Development). Database scripts SHOULD undergo extensive functional tests on separate test systems before being used in production. The results SHOULD be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The quality criteria can include, for example, programming guidelines, the necessity of transaction blocks, and error handling. For each change, a test plan is created and its execution in the test environment is logged. The release to production only occurs after a successful test.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the defined quality criteria and programming guidelines. For a recent change, the test plan and the test log are reviewed. It is checked whether the release was documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The development of database scripts follows the institution's formal software development process. This includes managing the scripts in a version control system (e.g., Git), performing static code analysis to detect potential security vulnerabilities (e.g., SQL injection patterns), and mandatory deployment in a staging environment that is an exact copy of production.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools for static analysis (SAST) are integrated into the development process. Changes are managed via pull requests, which require a review. Before production deployment, acceptance is carried out on the staging system by the business department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the development process mapped in the version control system (branches, pull requests, reviews). It is checked whether and how static code analysis tools are used and how their results are handled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A full CI/CD pipeline is implemented for database scripts and schema changes. Changes are automatically scanned for security vulnerabilities and undergo automated tests (unit tests, integration tests). Deployment to production is also automated and requires formal approval. A 'least privilege' model is enforced for executing the scripts in production, i.e., the scripts run only with the minimum necessary permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Jenkins, GitLab CI, Flyway, or Liquibase are used to implement the pipeline. For execution, dedicated, temporary technical users with minimal rights are used, instead of running the scripts as a highly privileged administrator.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the entire CI/CD pipeline, from the code change to the production deployment. The configuration of the automated tests and security scans is checked. It is verified how the permissions for executing the scripts in the production environment are managed and restricted.

controls.title: Regular Audits (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Audits or reviews of the database systems only take place reactively, for example, after a security incident or in case of obvious problems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no planned, proactive process for reviewing the security configurations. Security vulnerabilities or misconfigurations remain undetected for a long time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for audit plans and reports from the last 1-2 years. The absence of such documents indicates a purely reactive approach.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Informal reviews of the database systems are carried out occasionally. However, they are not systematic, not comprehensive, and the results are not consistently documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, an administrator manually checks the permissions when there is time, but without a fixed checklist or schedule.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions administrators about their review routines and asks for evidence (e.g., emails, short notes). The lack of system and documentation is noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All components of the database system SHOULD be regularly checked to ensure that all defined security measures have been implemented and are correctly configured. It SHOULD be checked whether the documented state corresponds to the actual state and whether the configuration corresponds to the documented standard configuration. In addition, the log files SHOULD be examined. The audit results SHOULD be documented in a traceable manner and compared with the target state. Deviations SHOULD be investigated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual audit plan for database systems is created. The audit is conducted using a checklist that includes configuration, permissions, and the analysis of log files. The audit report documents the findings, and measures to correct deviations are assigned and tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the audit plan, the checklists used, and the audit reports from the last audits. It is checked whether the audits took place as planned and whether the identified deficiencies are being tracked (e.g., in a ticketing system).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The audits are supported by the use of automated compliance scanning tools that check the configurations against internal standards and external benchmarks (e.g., CIS). The audit process is formalized with a defined scope, schedule, and a standardized report template. The findings are centrally tracked in a GRC tool or ticketing system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like OpenSCAP, Nessus (with compliance checks), or specialized database scanners are used regularly. The results of these scans form the basis for the manual part of the audit. The entire process is described in the organization's QM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the compliance scanning tools and their reports. The audit process description is reviewed and it is verified that the results are systematically managed in a tracking system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Continuous, automated auditing is implemented. A central dashboard displays the real-time compliance status of the database landscape. Deviations from the security baseline trigger automatic alarms or even corrective actions. The audit logs of the databases are centrally collected in a SIEM system and correlated with other security events to detect complex attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool in non-enforcing mode or a CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management) tool is used for continuous auditing. The SIEM correlation rules are specifically designed to detect suspicious database activities (e.g., multiple failed logins followed by a successful one, access to sensitive tables outside of business hours).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the real-time compliance dashboard. The configuration of the SIEM correlation rules for databases is checked. It is verified that alarms from the continuous audit process are handled appropriately and in a timely manner.

controls.title: Use of Database Security Tools (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A database security tool is installed, but it is mainly operated with the default settings and only in monitoring or logging mode. There is no active blocking of attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The tool is used as a 'log collector', but the alarms are not systematically evaluated or the configuration to actively prevent attacks is missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the security tool and determines whether it is operated in pure monitoring mode. It is checked whether and how the generated alarms are processed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information security products for databases SHOULD be used. The products used SHOULD provide the following functions: creation of an overview of all database systems, advanced configuration options and rights management, detection of possible attacks (e.g. brute force, SQL injection) and audit functions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized tool (e.g., a database firewall or a Database Activity Monitoring tool) is implemented. It is configured to analyze network traffic to the database and to detect and alert on known attack patterns. It is also used for regular audits of user permissions and configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the tool demonstrated to them. The configuration of the detection rules and audit scans is reviewed. The reports and alarms generated in recent weeks are analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security tool is fine-tuned to the specific application environment to minimize the number of false positives. For attacks with high detection certainty (e.g., known SQL injection signatures), the tool is switched to active blocking mode. The tool's alarms are integrated into the central SIEM/SOAR platform to enable correlation with other events and automated response.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A whitelisting approach is implemented where the tool learns the normal, legitimate SQL queries of the application and only reports deviations. The integration into the SIEM is done via Syslog or an API. A SOAR rule could, for example, block the source IP address on the network firewall in the event of a brute-force attack.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the tool, in particular the active blocking rules and the whitelisting profiles. The SIEM/SOAR integration is verified by analyzing the corresponding correlation rules and playbooks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The tool uses machine learning to create a baseline of normal database activities (Database Activity Monitoring - DAM) and detects and blocks anomalous behavior in real time, even if it does not match any known signatures. Additionally, the tool offers a virtual patching function to mitigate known vulnerabilities in the database that have not yet been patched by the manufacturer. The collected data is actively used for threat hunting activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DAM system is fully integrated and continuously learns normal behavior. Virtual patching rules are activated based on CVE notifications until the official patch can be applied. Security experts use the detailed activity logs to proactively search for signs of compromised accounts or insider threats.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the machine learning and anomaly detection functions. It is verified which virtual patches are active and what the process for their activation looks like. Examples of threat hunting analyses that have been carried out are requested.

controls.title: Emergency Preparedness (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic recovery plan that essentially describes restoration from the last backup. However, the plan does not cover aspects such as communication channels, distribution of roles, emergency operation with limited functionality, or dependencies on other systems. The plan has never been tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The plan is often a short document that lists the technical steps for recovery but completely ignores the organizational aspects of an emergency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the recovery plan and assesses its completeness with regard to organizational aspects. Evidence of tests that have been carried out is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An emergency plan SHOULD be created for the database management system, which specifies how emergency operation can be realized. The resources required for the emergency plan SHOULD be determined. In addition, the emergency plan SHOULD define how normal operation can be restored from emergency operation. The emergency plan SHOULD specify the necessary reporting channels, response channels, resources, and response times of the responsible personnel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The emergency plan is a detailed document that describes various scenarios (e.g., hardware failure, data corruption). It contains contact lists, clear responsibilities, and step-by-step instructions. It is part of the overarching IT emergency manual.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the emergency plan for the database system and checks it for completeness in accordance with the requirement (resources, reporting channels, recovery, etc.). It is checked whether the plan is known to the relevant persons.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The emergency plan is regularly reviewed and improved (e.g., annually) through emergency exercises, such as tabletop exercises or technical tests. The plan is fully integrated into the organization's overarching Business Continuity Plan (BCP). Dependencies on and from other IT systems are clearly mapped out in a recovery plan and taken into account when defining the Recovery Time Objectives (RTO).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The results of the exercises are documented and used to improve the plan. The recovery sequence of the systems is coordinated to ensure that dependent systems are started in the correct sequence.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the logs of the last emergency exercises and checks whether the resulting suggestions for improvement have been implemented. The recovery plan is checked for the correct mapping of dependencies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A technical high-availability or failover solution (e.g., database cluster, replication to a hot standby system) is implemented that enables a recovery time of a few minutes or seconds (near-zero downtime). The failover process is automated and regularly tested. The emergency plan also covers disaster scenarios that involve a complete failure of the primary data center by falling back on a geographically separate backup data center.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technologies such as Oracle RAC, SQL Server Always On Availability Groups, or Patroni for PostgreSQL are used. The automated failover is tested through regular, scheduled switchovers. Data is continuously replicated to the backup site.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture and configuration of the high-availability solution. Logs of the automated failover tests are requested. The disaster recovery plan for the data center failure is reviewed and checked for plausibility and completeness.

controls.title: Archiving (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Old data is offloaded to inexpensive offline storage (e.g., tapes, external hard drives) to relieve the production system. However, there is no concept for the retrievability, indexing, or ensuring the long-term readability of this data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Archiving is a 'write-only' process. If data from the archive is needed, the effort for searching and restoring is very high and the success is uncertain.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the responsible persons about the archiving process. A concept for searching and restoring archived data is requested and the lack of one is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If it is necessary to archive data from a database system, an appropriate archiving concept SHOULD be created. It SHOULD be ensured that the data can be made fully and consistently available again at a later date. The archiving concept SHOULD define both the archiving intervals and the retention periods for the archived data. Additionally, it SHOULD be documented which technology was used to archive the databases. Restoration tests SHOULD be carried out regularly with the archived data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The concept defines which data is archived and when, based on legal and business retention periods. Archiving is done in a defined format. A process for restoration tests is defined and the results are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the archiving concept and checks its completeness. The documentation of the restoration tests carried out is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The archiving process is automated. The archived data is stored in a structured, searchable format on a dedicated archive system that ensures the integrity of the data (e.g., through WORM storage - Write Once, Read Many). Restoration tests are planned and carried out at regular intervals to verify the accessibility and integrity of the data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script or an ETL process extracts the data to be archived, transforms it into an open format (e.g., XML, CSV), and loads it into the archive system. The archive system provides search functions and ensures the immutability of the data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automated archiving process. The properties of the archive system (e.g., WORM capability) are checked. The logs of the regular restoration tests are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The archiving solution is fully integrated into the data lifecycle management processes. Data is automatically classified and moved to the archive based on business rules. The archive system supports e-discovery requests and can place data on legal hold. The integrity of the archived data is continuously verified using cryptographic checksums.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Information Lifecycle Management (ILM) tool is used. It is connected to the database system and the archive system and controls the entire lifecycle of the data from its creation to its final deletion after the retention period expires. The integrity check runs as a periodic background job.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the ILM system and the rules. The implementation of the e-discovery and legal hold functions is tested. The logs of the continuous integrity checks are reviewed.

controls.title: Data encryption in the database (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire database is encrypted using Transparent Data Encryption (TDE). However, key management is weak, e.g., the key is stored unprotected on the same server, rendering the encryption ineffective if the server is compromised. An impact analysis was only conducted superficially.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: TDE is enabled, but the master key is stored in the default wallet on the local file system without additional protective measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that TDE is active. Then, the storage location and protection of the master key are examined. The absence of external or hardware-based key storage is noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data in the databases SHOULD be encrypted. The following factors, among others, SHOULD be considered beforehand: impact on performance, key management processes and procedures, including separate key storage and backup, impact on backup-recovery concepts, and functional effects on the database, such as sorting capabilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented analysis is performed to select the appropriate encryption method (e.g., TDE, column-level encryption). A process for the secure handling of cryptographic keys is defined, which provides for separate storage from the database system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the analysis and the concept for database encryption. It is checked whether the mentioned factors have been considered and whether the key management process is defined and implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A hybrid encryption approach is used: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) protects all data at-rest, while the most sensitive data is also encrypted on a column-level basis. A dedicated Hardware Security Module (HSM) or a Key Management Service (KMS) is used for the secure storage and management of cryptographic keys.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DBMS is integrated with the HSM or KMS. This ensures that the keys are never in plaintext on the database server and that access to the keys is strictly controlled and logged. Column-level encryption is used for fields such as credit card numbers or social security numbers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the TDE and the column-level encryption. The integration with the HSM/KMS is checked, and the access logs of the key management system are analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Advanced encryption technologies such as Format-Preserving Encryption (FPE) or tokenization are used. These allow data processing (e.g., searching, sorting) in encrypted form and minimize the risk of disclosure. The key management processes, including regular key rotation, are fully automated. Access to unencrypted keys is restricted to an absolute minimum and is strictly audited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized cryptography gateways or libraries are used for FPE or tokenization. An automated system rotates the encryption keys according to the policy (e.g., annually) without interrupting ongoing operations. Access to the keys in the HSM/KMS requires multi-factor authentication and follows the four-eyes principle.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the implemented FPE/tokenization solution. The configuration and logs of the automated key rotation process are checked. The access control policies on the HSM/KMS are audited to ensure that the 'least privilege' principle is enforced.

controls.title: Security audits of database systems (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Ad-hoc manual reviews of the database configuration are performed using a public checklist (e.g., from CIS). However, this is not done regularly or systematically for all systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator performs such a review when a new system is commissioned, but there are no planned, recurring reviews for existing systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the reports and logs of the security audits performed and finds that they are only available irregularly and not for all systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Database systems SHOULD be regularly checked using security audits. The security audits SHOULD consider the systemic and specific aspects of the manufacturer of the database infrastructure used (e.g., directory services) as well as the database management system used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual plan for security audits is created. These audits include a review of the DBMS configuration, patch levels, user permissions, and interaction with dependent systems such as Active Directory. The results are documented in a report.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the plan for security audits and the reports of the last audits. It is assessed whether the scope of the audits meets the requirements and whether the identified deficiencies have been remediated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automated security assessments are performed regularly (e.g., quarterly) with a specialized tool for database security. The checks include detailed configuration analyses, patch level checks, and permission audits. The results are formally recorded in a vulnerability tracking system, and their remediation is monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Nessus (with database plugins) or specialized Database Assessment Tools are used to perform the scans. The results are imported and assigned to the system administrators for remediation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the scanning tool and the reports. The process for handling the identified vulnerabilities in the tracking system is traced.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to automated assessments, regular penetration tests specifically targeting the database systems are conducted by specialized external service providers. Security checks are also integrated as a fixed component in the CI/CD pipeline (DevSecOps) to identify configuration errors and vulnerabilities before they reach production.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Penetration tests for databases are commissioned annually. In the CI/CD pipeline, container scanners and configuration scanners are used to check the database images and configuration scripts before deployment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the reports of the last penetration tests and checks the remediation of the deficiencies identified there. The configuration of the CI/CD pipeline is analyzed to verify the integration of the security scans.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: Database systems (DBS) are a commonly used tool to digitally organize, create, modify, and manage large data collections. A DBS consists of the so-called database management system (DBMS) and one or more databases. A database is a collection of data along with its description (metadata), which is permanently stored in the database system. Since database systems often play a central role in an IT infrastructure, they are subject to significant security requirements. Often, an institution's core processes depend on the information from the databases. This results in corresponding availability requirements. In addition, there are often high requirements for the confidentiality and integrity of the information stored in the databases.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is to be able to securely operate relational database systems and to adequately protect the information processed and stored in databases. To this end, requirements are described that allow database systems to be securely planned, implemented, and operated, and by which threats can be reduced.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose: The module APP.4.3 Relational Databases is to be applied once to each relational database system. This module describes requirements for relational database systems. Security requirements for non-relational database systems are not the subject of this module. To consistently protect the information in the databases, security requirements for the structure of the database tables and access to the database should already be considered during application development. However, requirements on these topics are not listed in this module. Likewise, the module does not address threats and requirements concerning the operating system and hardware on which the database system is installed. Aspects of this can be found in the corresponding operating system-specific modules of the SYS IT Systems layer, e.g., SYS.1.3 Servers under Linux and Unix or SYS.1.2.3 Windows Server. Relational database systems should generally be considered within the scope of the modules OPR.4 Identity and Authorization Management, OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management, CON.3 Data Backup Concept, OPS.1.2.2 Archiving, OPS.1.1.5 Logging, and OPS.1.1.2 Orderly IT Administration.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient dimensioning of system resources
parts.prose: If the hardware of a database system does not have sufficient system resources, the database may fail completely or operate incorrectly. This can, for example, prevent data from being saved. Resources can also be heavily utilized during peak times. This can degrade performance. This, in turn, can cause applications to fail to run or to run with errors.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Activated default accounts
parts.prose: During the initial installation or in the delivery state of a database management system, default accounts (user and administrator accounts) are often not secured or are secured only with publicly known passwords. This can lead to these accounts being misused. For example, attackers can log into the database management system as users or even as administrators using the publicly known login credentials. They can then read, manipulate, or delete the configuration or the stored data.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Unencrypted database connection
parts.prose: In the default configuration, many database management systems connect to applications without encryption. If communication between applications and the database management system is unencrypted, transmitted data and access information can be read or manipulated in transit.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Data loss in the database
parts.prose: Due to hardware or software errors, as well as human error, data in the database can be lost. Since databases usually store important information for applications, services may fail or entire production processes may come to a standstill.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Loss of integrity of stored data
parts.prose: Due to misconfigured databases, software errors, or manipulated data, the integrity of the information in the database can be violated. If this is not noticed or is noticed late, the core processes of the institution can be severely affected. For example, if the integrity relationships (referential integrity) between the tables are not defined correctly, this can lead to the data in the database being faulty. If this error is only noticed during production operation or not at all, not only do the inconsistent data have to be laboriously cleaned up and reconstructed, but great damage may also have been caused over time, for example if it involves critical data, such as tax-relevant data, invoice data, or even control data for entire production systems.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. SQL Injections
parts.prose: A common attack method on database systems are SQL injections. When an application accesses the data of an SQL database, commands in the form of SQL statements are transmitted to the DBMS. If input data within the application is insufficiently validated, attackers can inject their own SQL commands into the application, which are then processed with the permissions of the application's service account. Attackers can thus read, manipulate, delete data, add new data, or even call system commands. Although SQL injections primarily affect the applications in the frontend, they also have a significant impact on the database system itself and the associated infrastructure.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Insecure configuration of the database management system
parts.prose: Often, in the default configuration of the database management system, unneeded functions are activated that make it easier to read or manipulate information from the database in a potential attack. For example, due to an unchanged default installation, attackers can connect to a programming interface not used by the institution to administer the DBMS without having to authenticate. This allows them to gain unauthorized access to the institution's databases.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Malware and insecure database scripts
parts.prose: With many database management systems, it is possible to automate certain actions via scripts that are executed in the context of the database, e.g., using Procedural Language/Structured Query Language (PL/SQL). This also includes so-called database triggers. However, if these are used unchecked by the responsible parties, the database scripts might not meet the institution's software development requirements. Core functions of a database, such as Data Dictionary Tables, can also be manipulated during attacks, for example, using malicious programs or database scripts. This type of attack is very difficult to detect. Quality defects in these scripts and malware can jeopardize the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the data stored in the databases.

controls.title: Planning the separation of applications

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a rudimentary, undocumented plan for separating applications, which mainly focuses on separating production and test environments on different clusters, without detailed regulations at the network, CPU, or storage level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The separation is often only done through manual conventions, e.g., naming prefixes for pods. Technical separation mechanisms like Kubernetes namespaces are not used consistently.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing administrators about the separation procedure. Manually checking some pods to determine if a logical separation is recognizable.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic, documented plan for separating applications into production and test environments. Each environment is operated in its own namespace, but without differentiated resource quotas.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All production applications run in the `prod` namespace, all test applications in the `test` namespace. No `ResourceQuotas` or `LimitRanges` are defined, which can lead to resource conflicts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the planning documents. Checking if all pods are correctly assigned to the intended namespaces (`prod`, `test`) using `kubectl get pods -A`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before commissioning, it MUST be planned how the applications operated in the pods and their different test and production operating environments are to be separated.
