parts.prose: The ATC check variant is configured to identify all `OPEN/DELETE DATASET` statements and to verify whether a preceding S_DATASET check is performed and whether the used variables are populated in a secure manner (e.g., from the FILE configuration) and not directly from user input.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the ATC configuration for specific checks for path traversal and insecure file access. Analysis of transport logs to verify the effectiveness of the blocking rule.

controls.title: Authorization check in remote-enabled function modules (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that all remote-enabled function modules explicitly check in the program code whether the caller is authorized to execute the associated business logic.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each function module marked as 'remote-enabled' (RFC) contains one or more `AUTHORITY-CHECK` statements at the beginning of its source code. These check whether the user in whose context the RFC is executed has the necessary authorizations for the actions performed in the module. Alternatively, the authorization is checked via the S_RFC object.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: All customer-specific, remote-enabled function modules are identified (table TFDIR, where FMODE = 'R'). The source code of each of these modules is then checked to see if an appropriate authorization check (e.g., on S_RFC or on specific application objects) is implemented at the beginning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The authorization object S_RFC is used for access to remote-enabled function modules. Function modules are grouped into authorization groups (transaction RFC_GROUP) to enable granular rights assignment. This is checked in code reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All custom RFCs are assigned to logical function groups. The authorization check within the RFC is then performed centrally on the S_RFC object with the fields RFC_TYPE='FUNC', RFC_NAME='FUGR', and the name of the corresponding function group. This is mandated in the development guidelines.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether customer-specific RFCs are organized in function groups. Review of the source code for the correct check of S_RFC. Analysis of the assigned roles to ensure that access to RFCs is controlled granularly via these groups.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic code analysis tool checks all remote-enabled function modules upon transport release. If an authorization check (e.g., on S_RFC or another suitable object) is missing, the transport is blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant contains a specific check that identifies all objects of type 'FUGR' with remote-enabled modules and verifies that each of these modules contains an `AUTHORITY-CHECK` statement. Missing checks are reported as a critical error.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration and transport logs to verify that insecure RFC function modules cannot be transported to production systems.

controls.title: Prevention of operating system command execution (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every call to a permitted operating system command SHOULD be preceded by a corresponding authorization check (authorization object S_LOG_COM). User inputs SHOULD NOT be part of a command. Therefore, operating system calls SHOULD be executed exclusively via dedicated standard SAP function modules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The execution of external operating system commands is performed exclusively via the function module `SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE`. Before it is called, an authorization check is performed on the S_LOG_COM object. The parameters used in the command must not contain unvalidated user input. User input is validated using `CL_ABAP_DYN_PRG=>CHECK_COMMAND_INJECTION`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code is scanned for the use of operating system commands. It is checked whether the standard function module `SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE` is used and whether it is preceded by an authorization check on S_LOG_COM. It is also analyzed whether user input can become part of the command and whether it is sufficiently validated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of operating system commands is restricted to an explicitly approved whitelist of commands in transaction SM69. Direct calls via obsolete mechanisms such as `CALL 'SYSTEM'` are prohibited and are checked in code reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All required external commands are defined and approved by the system administration in SM69. ABAP programs only reference these predefined commands. The development guideline prohibits the `CALL 'SYSTEM'` statement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the commands defined in SM69 for their necessity and security. Analysis of the source code for the use of `CALL 'SYSTEM'` or other insecure methods for executing OS commands.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic code analysis tool detects any form of operating system command execution. Only the use of the standard function module `SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE` with a preceding authorization check and without direct user input in the command is permitted. Any deviation blocks the transport.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant is configured to report the `CALL 'SYSTEM'` statement and similar constructs as a critical error. It also checks whether the call to `SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE` is preceded by an S_LOG_COM check and whether the parameters contain potentially dangerous user input.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration and transport logs to verify that insecure calls of operating system commands are detected and blocked.

controls.title: Prevention of injected malicious code (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The ABAP commands INSERT REPORT and GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL SHOULD NOT be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The development guidelines prohibit the use of the `INSERT REPORT` and `GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL` statements, as they enable the dynamic generation and execution of code, which poses a significant security risk.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The entire customer-specific source code is searched for the strings `INSERT REPORT` and `GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL`. Every finding is rated as a critical security vulnerability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The prohibition of `INSERT REPORT` and `GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL` is enshrined in the development guidelines and is checked through regular, manual code reviews using the four-eyes principle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Code review checklists contain an explicit item for checking for prohibited, dynamic code generation statements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Inspection of the code review protocols to verify compliance with the requirement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic code analysis tool is configured to detect the use of `INSERT REPORT` and `GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL` and to automatically block the transport release if they are found.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant classifies the use of these statements as a critical priority 1 error, which leads to a halt in the transport process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the ATC configuration and transport logs to ensure that code with these statements cannot be transported.

controls.title: Avoidance of generic module execution (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Transactions, programs, function modules, and methods SHOULD NOT be generically executable. If there are important reasons for generic execution, it SHOULD be documented in detail where and why this occurs. Additionally, an allowlist containing all permitted modules SHOULD be defined. Before a module is called, user input SHOULD be checked against the allowlist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Generic execution of code units (e.g., `CALL FUNCTION l_funcname`, `SUBMIT (l_progname)`) is avoided. If unavoidable, the module name passed by the user (`l_funcname`, `l_progname`) is checked against a list of permitted modules (allowlist) defined fixed in the code or in a customizing table before the call.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code is scanned for generic calls such as `CALL FUNCTION variable`, `SUBMIT (variable)`, `CALL METHOD (variable)=>...`. If such constructs are found, it is checked whether a robust allowlist validation of the variable takes place immediately before the call.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of generic calls is highly restricted in the development guidelines and must be explicitly approved and documented. The maintenance of the allowlists is subject to a controlled process (e.g., four-eyes principle).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Any necessity for a generic call must be justified in a design document and approved by an architect. The corresponding allowlist is maintained in a customizing table, whose changes are logged in a revision-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the design documents and approval processes for generic calls. Check of the change documents for the allowlist customizing table.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic code analysis tool detects generic module executions and checks whether a validated allowlist check is implemented. Calls without such a check block the transport release.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ATC check is configured to find all forms of dynamic/generic calls. It analyzes the data flow to determine if the variable containing the module to be called originates from user input and if it is validated against an allowlist. Missing validations are reported as critical.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration and transport logs to verify that insecure generic calls are detected and blocked.

controls.title: Avoidance of generic access to table contents (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Table contents SHOULD NOT be read generically. If there are important reasons to do so, it SHOULD be documented in detail where and why this happens. Furthermore, it SHOULD then be ensured that the dynamic table name is restricted to a controllable list of values.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Generic read access to tables (e.g., `SELECT * FROM (l_tabname) ...`) is avoided. If unavoidable, the table name passed in `l_tabname` is checked against a permanently defined allowlist of permitted table names before the SQL statement is executed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code is scanned for generic SQL statements (e.g., `FROM (variable)`). If found, it is checked whether a robust allowlist validation of the table name takes place before execution.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of generic table access is subject to approval and must be documented. The allowlists of permitted tables are centrally managed and their changes are subject to a four-eyes principle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The necessity of generic table access is justified and approved in the technical concept. The allowlist is maintained in a customizing table that is protected against changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the technical concepts and approval processes. Check of the change documents of the allowlist table.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic code analysis tool detects generic table access and blocks the transport if no validated allowlist check for the table name is implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant is configured to identify dynamic FROM clauses in SQL statements and to check whether the table name used is checked against an allowlist before execution. Missing checks lead to a transport stop.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration and transport logs to verify the effectiveness of the rule.

controls.title: Avoidance of Native SQL Statements (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The ABAP Database Connectivity (ADBC) interface SHOULD NOT be used. User input SHOULD NOT be part of ADBC commands.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The development guidelines mandate the exclusive use of Open SQL for database access. The use of Native SQL (`EXEC SQL`) and ADBC classes (CL_SQL_*) is to be avoided. If unavoidable, user input must under no circumstances enter the SQL statement unescaped. Instead, escaping functions such as `CL_ABAP_DYN_PRG=>ESCAPE_QUOTES` are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code is searched for `EXEC SQL` and the use of ADBC classes. For each finding, it is checked whether it is absolutely necessary and whether all variable inputs are correctly handled (escaped) to prevent SQL injection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of Native SQL or ADBC is strictly regulated, must be approved by a database architect, and is subject to particularly intensive scrutiny during code reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal approval process is required for any use of Native SQL/ADBC. The code review checklist includes a dedicated section for checking for SQL injection vulnerabilities in these code parts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the approval documents and code review logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic code analysis tool detects the use of Native SQL and ADBC. It checks whether variable inputs are used and whether they are correctly handled with the designated escaping methods. Unsafe uses block the transport.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant is configured to find `EXEC SQL` and ADBC calls and performs a data flow analysis to detect whether user input flows into the SQL statement. If this is the case, it checks whether an escaping function was applied to the input.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration and transport logs to verify the effectiveness of the check.

controls.title: Prevention of Data Leaks (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A sufficiently secure authorization check SHOULD be performed before business-critical data is displayed, transmitted, or exported. Intended export options SHOULD be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In programs that process or export sensitive data, explicit and granular authorization checks are implemented before display or export. These go beyond the mere start authorization and check, for example, for authorizations for specific company codes or organizational units. Intended export functions are documented in the application's technical concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code of reports and interfaces that process sensitive data is checked to ensure that adequate authorization checks take place before data access and output. The technical documentation is checked for the description of export functions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Export functions for critical data are additionally protected by an authorization check for a specific export activity (e.g., in the authorization object). Each export action is logged in the application log (SLG1) with user, timestamp, and scope of the exported data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Customer-specific authorization objects are extended by a field for the activity (e.g., 'DISPLAY', 'EXPORT'). The export function in the program explicitly checks for the export activity. The export process is logged using the function module `BAL_LOG_CREATE`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the source code for the implementation of the export activity check and logging. Regular evaluation of the application logs for unusual export activities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Data Loss Prevention (DLP) system or a comparable monitoring solution is integrated to monitor and, if necessary, block the export of critical data. Automatic code analysis tools detect data selections from critical tables and check for the presence of adequate authorization and logging functions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant contains a list of critical tables (e.g., HR, financial data). If a program accesses these tables, the ATC checks whether a granular authorization check and a logging function are present in the code. Missing controls lead to a transport stop.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of the DLP solution and the ATC check variant. Analysis of the alerts and logs of these systems.

controls.title: Avoidance of system-dependent function execution (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ABAP programs SHOULD NOT be programmed to be system-dependent so that they can only be executed on a specific SAP system. However, if this is absolutely necessary, it SHOULD be documented in detail. In addition, the code SHOULD then be manually reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of system-dependent logic (e.g., `IF sy-sysid = 'PRD'.`) is avoided. If such a check is unavoidable (e.g., for interfaces that may only be active in the production system), the necessity is explained in detail in the technical concept. The code section is conspicuously commented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code is searched for queries on `sy-sysid` or other system-dependent fields. For each finding, the associated documentation is checked to understand the necessity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: System-dependent behavior is not hard-wired into the code, but controlled via a customizing table that is maintained differently for each system (development, test, production). Any system-dependent logic requires approval.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of `IF sy-sysid ...`, the value is read from a customizing table that contains the mode (e.g., 'TEST', 'PROD') for the respective system. Maintaining this table is an administrative act and not part of development.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check of the source code for the use of the central customizing table instead of hard-coded system IDs. Check of the maintenance authorization for this table.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic code analysis tool detects hard-coded system-dependent logic (check for `sy-sysid`) and blocks the transport. Only the use of the approved customizing table is permitted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant is configured to report any `IF sy-sysid...` query as a critical error and stop the transport.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration and transport logs to verify the effectiveness of the rule.

controls.title: Avoidance of client-dependent function execution (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ABAP programs SHOULD NOT be programmed to be client-dependent so that they can only be executed from a specific client. However, if this is absolutely necessary, it SHOULD be documented in detail. In addition, additional security measures SHOULD then be taken, such as a manual code review or quality assurance on the respective client.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of client-dependent logic (e.g., `IF sy-mandt = '100'.`) is avoided. If such a check is unavoidable, the necessity is explained in detail in the technical concept and the code section is specially checked in the code review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code is searched for queries on `sy-mandt`. For each finding, the associated documentation and the review logs are checked to understand the necessity and the additional security measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Client-dependent behavior is not hard-wired into the code, but controlled via a client-dependent customizing table. Any client-dependent logic requires approval.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of `IF sy-mandt ...`, the value is read from a client-dependent customizing table that controls the behavior for the respective client. Maintaining this table is an administrative act.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check of the source code for the use of the central customizing table instead of hard-coded client numbers. Check of the maintenance authorization for this table.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic code analysis tool detects hard-coded client-dependent logic (check for `sy-mandt`) and blocks the transport. Only the use of the approved customizing table is permitted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant is configured to report any `IF sy-mandt...` query as a critical error and stop the transport.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration and transport logs to verify the effectiveness of the rule.

controls.title: Avoidance of Open SQL Injection Vulnerabilities (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Dynamic Open SQL SHOULD NOT be used. If database access with dynamic SQL conditions is necessary, NO user input SHOULD be transferred in the respective query. If this is nevertheless the case, the user input MUST be checked (Output Encoding).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of dynamic WHERE, FROM, or other clauses in Open SQL statements is avoided. If unavoidable, user input that becomes part of a dynamic condition is treated with the `CL_ABAP_DYN_PRG=>QUOTE` method or similar escaping mechanisms before use to prevent SQL injection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code is examined for the use of dynamic clauses in Open SQL (e.g., `WHERE (condition)`). It is analyzed whether the `condition` variable is influenced by user input. If so, it is checked whether a correct escaping function is applied to the input before it becomes part of the condition.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of dynamic Open SQL is highly restricted, requires approval, and is intensively checked for SQL injection risks in code reviews. Instead, parameterized approaches such as the use of `FOR ALL ENTRIES` are preferred.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Development guidelines recommend replacing dynamic WHERE clauses with static SQL statements with `FOR ALL ENTRIES` or `RANGE` tables. Any remaining use of dynamic SQL must be justified and approved in the technical concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the code review logs for the explicit check of dynamic SQL. Analysis of whether alternative, safer programming patterns could have been used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic code analysis tool detects dynamic Open SQL and performs a data flow analysis to determine whether user input enters the statement unescaped. Such findings are classified as a critical security vulnerability and block the transport.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant is configured to find all dynamic SQL statements and, by means of taint analysis, trace the path of user input into the SQL statement. If an unsecured use is detected, this leads to a transport stop.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration to check the SQL injection checks. Review of the transport logs to ensure that insecure code has been blocked.

controls.title: Protection against Cross-Site Scripting (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Self-developed HTML in Business Server Pages (BSP) applications or HTTP handlers SHOULD be avoided as much as possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When developing web applications with BSP or ICF handlers, standard UI libraries (e.g., SAPUI5) that offer inherent XSS protection mechanisms are preferred. If raw HTML has to be written, all dynamic outputs that could originate from users are encoded with `cl_abap_utility=>escape_html` or corresponding functions of the BSP runtime environment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code of BSPs and HTTP handlers is checked to see if user input or data read from the database is written directly to the HTML output. It is verified that appropriate HTML encoding (escaping) takes place before output.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All web outputs are context-sensitively encoded (e.g., different encoding for HTML body, JavaScript variables, URL parameters). The development guidelines prescribe the exact escaping procedures for each context. Compliance is checked in code reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Developers use a library of escaping functions that are optimized for different contexts (HTML, JavaScript, CSS, URL). The development guideline contains clear examples of which function to use in which context.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the code review protocols for the explicit check of XSS vulnerabilities. Manual check of the source code for the correct application of context-sensitive encoding.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated code analysis tool analyzes web applications for XSS vulnerabilities. It performs a taint analysis to trace the flow of user input to the output and reports missing or incorrect escaping. Such findings block the transport.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant is configured with specific checks for XSS. These detect insecure outputs in BSPs and ICF handlers and classify them as critical errors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration and transport logs to verify that code with potential XSS vulnerabilities is blocked.

controls.title: No access to another tenant's data (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The automatic tenant separation SHOULD NOT be bypassed. Data from other tenants SHOULD NOT be accessed using EXEC SQL or the Open SQL option CLIENT SPECIFIED.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The development guidelines prohibit the use of the `CLIENT SPECIFIED` addition in Open SQL statements and of `EXEC SQL`, as these can bypass the database's automatic tenant filtering.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The source code is searched for the use of `CLIENT SPECIFIED` and `EXEC SQL`. Each finding is assessed as a potential security vulnerability and reviewed for its necessity and correct, secure implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of `CLIENT SPECIFIED` requires approval and must be justified in detail in the technical concept. Compliance with the prohibition is explicitly checked in code reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the rare but necessary use of `CLIENT SPECIFIED` (e.g., in central base components), a formal approval process exists. The approval is recorded in the code review protocol.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the approval documents and code review protocols for exceptional cases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated code analysis tool detects the use of `CLIENT SPECIFIED` and `EXEC SQL` and automatically blocks the transport release, unless there is an explicitly approved exception (e.g., via a pragma statement in the code).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC check variant is configured to report `CLIENT SPECIFIED` and `EXEC SQL` as critical errors. Approved exceptions must be marked in the source code with a special pragma (`##CLIENT_SPECIFIED_OK`), which is recognized and ignored by the ATC.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the ATC configuration and review of the process for approving exceptions via pragmas.

controls.title: Prohibition of hidden ABAP source code (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The source code of a self-created ABAP program SHOULD always be readable. Techniques that prevent this (obfuscation) SHOULD NOT be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Developers are instructed not to use code cloaking or obfuscation techniques. The program status 'Generated only' is not used for custom developments; the source code must always be available and readable.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: It is checked whether the source code for all customer-specific programs (Z* and Y* namespace) is present and readable in the system. The program attributes are checked to ensure that the status is not set to 'Generated only'.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated tool regularly checks all customer-specific development objects and raises an alarm if programs without readable source code are found. The creation of such programs is technically prevented where possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A periodically running job executes a program like `RSINVALI` or a customer-specific equivalent to identify inconsistent or unreadable programs in the customer namespace and report them to the responsible administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration and logs of the periodic check job.

controls.title: Use of ABAP code analysis tools (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standardized ABAP code analysis tool is available to all developers. Its use is recommended but not mandatory, and the results are primarily used for information, without enforcing the correction of any defects found.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SAP ABAP Test Cockpit (ATC) is set up system-wide and is usable by all developers. There is a standard check variant. However, regular training on its use does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the system-wide availability of the code analysis tool. Checking whether developers are informed about its availability. The review of the scan results will likely show inconsistent use and bug fixing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An ABAP code analysis tool SHOULD be used for the automated review of ABAP code for security-relevant programming errors, functional and technical errors, as well as for quality weaknesses.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ABAP code analysis tool (e.g., SAP ABAP Test Cockpit - ATC) is configured with a company-specific check variant that includes security-relevant checks. Developers are instructed to manually check their developments with this tool before releasing the transport.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking whether a code analysis tool is licensed and installed. Checking the configuration of the check variant for the activation of security tests. Reviewing the result logs of completed scans.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of an ABAP code analysis tool is established as a fixed quality assurance step before the release of transports. Critical and severe security vulnerabilities found by the tool must be fixed before transport. The results are documented and checked using the four-eyes principle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ATC is configured to run automatically when transport requests are released. A transport is stopped for priority 1 and 2 errors. The results are transmitted to the change management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configuration of the Transport Management System (TMS) and the ATC. It is verified that the scans are automatically triggered upon transport release. Checking transport logs for transports rejected due to code quality issues.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An ABAP code analysis tool is fully integrated into an automated CI/CD pipeline. Every commit triggers a scan. Found vulnerabilities not only block the build/transport but also automatically lead to the creation of correction tickets in the issue tracking system. The scanner's rule set is continuously adapted to new threats and internal company policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use of tools like gCTS (Git-enabled Change and Transport System) in conjunction with Jenkins/GitLab-CI to run ATC scans on every push to the main branch. The integration with Jira or another ticketing system ensures the automatic assignment of tasks for bug fixing. There is a dedicated process for reviewing and updating the ATC check variants.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the CI/CD pipeline configuration and logs. Verifying the integration with the issue tracking system by inspecting automatically created tickets. Reviewing the process documentation for the maintenance and further development of the check variants. Automated check: Evaluation of the CI pipeline logs to confirm that builds fail due to ATC results and that tickets are generated automatically.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Custom developments are frequently programmed in SAP systems. The reasons for this are varied; for example, business processes or reporting requirements can be individually adapted to the institution with the help of custom developments. It is also possible to create special functions that are not available in the standard delivery.

Custom developments are programmed by developers from the institution or by contracted developers. In the SAP environment, ABAP (Advanced Business Application Programming) is often used for this purpose.

ABAP is a proprietary, platform-independent programming language from the company SAP. It was developed for programming commercial applications in the SAP environment and its basic structure is remotely similar to the COBOL language. Important features are:

• Integration of an authentication, role, and authorization concept,
• Use of a proprietary, database-independent SQL derivative (Open SQL),
• Support for communication between different SAP systems, and
• Integration of audit options.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose:
The module shows ABAP developers and security testers relevant technical risks that can arise from custom ABAP developments. It also defines requirements that show how ABAP programs can be developed and deployed securely.

The module assumes a basic knowledge of ABAP and familiarity with ABAP development tools.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module APP.4.6 SAP ABAP Programming is to be applied once to each SAP system if custom developments are created in the ABAP programming language.

This module extends the modules CON.8 Software Development, APP.6 General Software and APP.7 Development of Custom Software with specific aspects for the development of ABAP programs.

The module does not represent a complete guide to developing ABAP programs, but describes the general risks of the ABAP programming language. The module defines requirements that should be met from a security perspective when developing ABAP programs.

Since web applications make up only a very small proportion of all ABAP applications in SAP implementations, web vulnerabilities are not the focus of this document.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Missing authorization checks
parts.prose: In SAP, authorizations are only checked if a corresponding authorization check has been implemented in the program by developers. Without such a check in the program code, it is not tested whether users are actually authorized to perform an action. In custom-developed program code, however, authorization checks are often forgotten. Thus, the entire authorization concept often fails to apply and unauthorized persons can access the data stored in the SAP system. This can also lead to violations of compliance requirements. This can have serious consequences, especially during financial audits.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Loss of confidentiality or integrity of critical data
parts.prose: SAP systems contain a lot of information that is critical to the institution. The SAP standard provides various mechanisms to protect this data. However, faulty custom ABAP developments could allow unauthorized access to institution-critical information. Employees or attackers could then transfer the data to an environment that is no longer controllable. Likewise, critical data could be manipulated with the help of ABAP programs by bypassing the security mechanisms of the SAP standard.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Injection vulnerabilities
parts.prose:
Injection vulnerabilities arise when attackers inject control characters or commands into an application via the input field. A successful attack can disrupt the planned program flow with unexpected commands.

Injection vulnerabilities represent the greatest security risk for custom developments. Flawed code in an ABAP application can sometimes allow attackers to gain complete control of an SAP system. Since such attacks are very complex and there are many variants of them, they are difficult to detect and fix without special training.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Bypassing existing SAP security mechanisms
parts.prose: The SAP standard provides various protection mechanisms for data. These include client separation, identity management, and roles and authorizations. However, these security mechanisms can be deliberately bypassed or unintentionally omitted in the code.

controls.title: Planning the use of Exchange and Outlook

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning for the use of Exchange and Outlook is only done on an ad-hoc basis for individual projects or departments. There is no institution-wide plan, and important aspects such as the selection of protocols or the integration of clients are not systematically considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning is often limited to a simple list of servers to be installed, without an analysis of dependencies or future requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews whether a planning document exists. It is checked whether the planning only applies to a limited part of the organization and whether fundamental aspects of the e-mail infrastructure are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic plan for the use of Exchange and Outlook exists. It covers the essential components such as servers and clients, but may not be formally documented or consider long-term aspects such as functional extensions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An informal document or a meeting note outlines the structure of the e-mail infrastructure. The planning focuses on the initial installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documents, even if they are informal. It is assessed whether the four core points (infrastructure, clients/servers, extensions, protocols) have been considered at least in outline.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before deploying Exchange and Outlook, the institution MUST plan their use carefully. It MUST consider at least the following points: structure of the e-mail infrastructure, clients or servers to be integrated, use of functional extensions, and the protocols to be used. The planning process is documented and repeatable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal planning document is created that serves as the basis for the selection of the infrastructure (APP.5.2.A2). This document records and justifies the decisions on the four points mentioned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning document for the use of Exchange and Outlook. It is verified that all four required aspects (infrastructure, clients/servers, extensions, protocols) are covered and the decisions are documented in a comprehensible manner.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of the Exchange deployment is formally documented, regularly reviewed, and integrated into the overall IT strategy. It includes a detailed analysis of the security implications of the chosen protocols and contains a roadmap for future functional and security-related extensions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning includes capacity planning, a risk assessment for different operating models (e.g., on-premises vs. cloud), and a timeline for implementation. The results are approved by management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies not only the existence of the plan but also its integration into strategic processes. Minutes of reviews and updates to the plan, as well as approval records, are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process is dynamic and uses a formal risk management framework to evaluate architectural decisions. The plan is continuously updated based on threat intelligence and changing business requirements. Alternative architectures are modeled and simulated before a decision is made.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools for modeling the IT architecture are used. Planning is a continuous process within the framework of IT Service Continuity Management and Enterprise Architecture Management. The effects of changes are assessed automatically.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the planning process for its dynamics and risk orientation. Evidence for the use of threat intelligence feeds, the execution of simulations, and the connection to a risk management tool is examined.

controls.title: Selection of a suitable Exchange infrastructure

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Exchange infrastructure is selected arbitrarily, based on existing hardware or personal preferences. A structured decision between cloud and on-premises solutions does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The solution that is most quickly available is implemented, without an evaluation of alternatives or consideration of the planning phase.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews that no formal or informal basis for the decision on the chosen infrastructure exists. It is checked whether the selection was made without reference to a deployment plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic decision about the Exchange infrastructure (e.g., on-premises) is made. However, this decision is not formally documented and is not based on a comprehensive analysis of various criteria.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision is often made verbally within the IT team and focuses primarily on the server component, while application components or the hierarchical structure are neglected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews the IT staff about the decision-making process. It is checked whether a conscious decision was made, even if the documentation and the basis for the decision are rudimentary.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the Exchange deployment plan, IT operations MUST decide which IT systems and application components will be used to implement the Exchange infrastructure and in what hierarchical structure. As part of the selection, a decision MUST also be made as to whether the Exchange systems should be operated as a cloud or on-premises service. The decision must be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision is recorded in a document that builds on the planning document from APP.5.2.A1. The choice between on-premises and cloud, as well as the basic system architecture (e.g., central vs. decentralized servers), is explicitly defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the infrastructure selection document. It is verified that the decision was made based on the deployment plan and that the choice of operating model (cloud/on-premises) and architecture is explicitly documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The infrastructure selection process is formally documented and includes a structured comparison of on-premises with various cloud offerings (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS). The decision is based on an analysis of criteria such as total cost of ownership (TCO), security, compliance, and scalability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A utility analysis or a scoring sheet is used to objectively compare the different options. The final decision is approved by management or an architecture committee.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the selection process, including the comparative analysis and the scoring sheets. It is checked whether the decision is comprehensible and criteria-based and whether a formal approval was given.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The choice of infrastructure is validated by a proof of concept (PoC) or a pilot implementation of the favored solution. The decision is made using a formal, weighted scoring matrix. The choice made is validated annually as part of the strategy review.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the final decision, a test environment is set up to verify the technical feasibility, performance, and security of the chosen solution. The results of the PoC are incorporated into the final decision.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests evidence of the execution of a PoC or pilot, including test logs and result reports. It is checked whether the infrastructure decision is regularly reviewed and adapted to current conditions.

controls.title: Authorization management and access rights

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access rights for Exchange are granted ad-hoc and without a specific concept. The default NTFS permissions are used, which often grant excessively broad access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators grant permissions on request, without following a central policy or the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs spot checks of the NTFS permissions in the Exchange directory and compares them with the default settings. It is determined that no documentation for an authorization concept exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic but undocumented concept for Exchange permissions exists. The default NTFS permissions are manually adjusted to close obvious security gaps. Server-side profiles are used for most users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators follow unwritten rules for granting rights. The adjustments to NTFS permissions are not consistent across all systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews the administrators about their procedure for granting rights. Spot checks of NTFS permissions and the use of server-side profiles are carried out to verify the basic implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the general authorization concept, the institution MUST create, appropriately document, and apply a specific authorization concept for the Exchange infrastructure. IT operations MUST use server-side user profiles for machine-independent access. They MUST adjust the default NTFS permissions for the Exchange directory so that only authorized administrators and system accounts can access the data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document is created that describes the Exchange authorization concept. This concept is technically implemented by restrictively configuring the NTFS permissions on the file system of the Exchange servers and setting up server-side profiles for all users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documented Exchange authorization concept. It is verified via script or manual review that the NTFS permissions on the Exchange directory correspond to the concept and grant access only to authorized accounts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The authorization concept is consistently based on the principle of least privilege and is regularly audited (e.g., annually). Administrative tasks are delegated granularly to different administrator groups using Exchange's role-based access control (RBAC) model.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specific RBAC roles are defined in Exchange (e.g., for helpdesk, user management, compliance management). The results of the regular permission audits are documented and lead to corrective actions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the Exchange RBAC model and compares the assigned roles with the defined tasks of the administrators. Logs of the last permission audits are requested and reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The granting and revocation of access rights are fully integrated into an Identity and Access Management (IAM) system and automated. Regular access reviews are performed automatically and reports are generated. Privileged administrative access is managed and monitored via a Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IAM tool controls membership in Exchange RBAC roles based on the employee's job function. A PAM system enforces just-in-time access and session recording for administrative activities. SIEM rules detect and alert on anomalous access patterns.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of Exchange into the IAM and PAM system. Log data from the PAM and SIEM is analyzed to confirm the effectiveness of the monitoring and automation. An automated comparison of permissions can be done, for example, using `Get-ManagementRoleAssignment -RoleAssignee <user> | fl` and comparing it with the IAM data.

controls.title: Data backup of Exchange

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data backups are performed irregularly and not before every configuration change. Only simple file backups of the servers are made, which are not application-consistent for Exchange databases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, only the server's operating system is backed up, but no special backup software is used that can back up the Exchange databases during operation and truncate transaction logs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the backup logs and the configuration of the backup software. It is checked whether the backups are performed sporadically and whether an application-consistent backup method for Exchange is configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Regular, scheduled backups of the Exchange databases are performed with suitable software. However, recovery tests are not conducted. Deleted objects are immediately and permanently removed from the database.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A backup software with an Exchange agent is used to create daily backups of the databases. The default settings for the retention of deleted items are not adjusted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of regular, successful backup jobs for the Exchange databases. Documentation for recovery tests is requested. The configuration of the retention periods for deleted items is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Exchange servers MUST be backed up before installations and configuration changes, as well as at cyclical intervals. In particular, the Exchange server databases MUST be backed up in an application-consistent manner. A defined process for the backup is in place and is followed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented backup plan that specifies when and how the Exchange databases are backed up. Ad-hoc backups before significant changes are part of this plan. A backup solution that supports VSS (Volume Shadow Copy Service) for Exchange is used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the backup plan and compares its specifications with the logs of the backup software. Evidence of backups before major changes (e.g., installation of a cumulative update) is requested on a spot-check basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data backups are regularly checked for their restorability. Deleted Exchange objects SHOULD only be permanently removed from the database after a defined retention period (e.g., 30 days) to allow for easy recovery. The recovery procedures are documented and tested periodically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The retention period for deleted items and mailboxes is configured in the database settings. At least once a year, a full recovery of a test database is performed in a separate environment and logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the configuration of the retention periods for deleted items shown to them (e.g., with `Get-MailboxDatabase | fl *DeletedItemRetention*`). The logs of the last recovery tests are requested and checked for completeness and success.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The backup and recovery process is largely automated. Point-in-time recovery of the databases is possible. Regular, automated disaster recovery tests verify compliance with RTO/RPO requirements. The backup data is encrypted and stored in a geographically separate, secure location (e.g., off-site or another cloud region).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Exchange Database Availability Group (DAG) is used for high availability. The backup solution supports point-in-time recovery. The recovery tests are automated by scripts and the results are reported to a monitoring system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the DAG and the backup solution. Evidence of automated DR tests and the encrypted, external storage of backups is requested. The possibility of a point-in-time recovery is demonstrated by a test recovery.

controls.title: Migration of Exchange systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A migration to a new Exchange version is carried out without significant planning or testing. This often leads to unforeseen outages and compatibility problems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The migration is attempted as an 'in-place upgrade', even though this is not supported, or work is done directly on the production system without prior testing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and analysis of incident tickets that past migrations were unplanned and associated with significant problems. There are no migration plans or test reports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple plan is created before a migration, which mainly focuses on moving mailboxes. Other aspects such as security policies or the connection of third-party systems are barely considered. Superficial tests are carried out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A checklist for the migration is used, but it does not cover all dependencies. A short functional test is performed after the migration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing migration checklist and interviews the team about their testing procedure. It is assessed whether essential aspects (objects, policies, connections) are missing from the plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A defined, documented plan is created for an Exchange migration. This plan considers the most important elements to be migrated, such as mailboxes and basic Active Directory concepts. The new system is tested for its basic functions in a test environment before production deployment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A migration plan is created that includes the individual steps, responsibilities, and a timeline. A separate test environment is set up to test the basic coexistence and mailbox migration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the migration plan and the test reports. It is verified that a structured plan exists and that basic tests were carried out in a separate environment before the production migration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD thoroughly plan and document all migration steps. It SHOULD consider mailboxes, objects, security policies, Active Directory concepts, and the connection to other email systems. Functional differences between the versions SHOULD be taken into account. The new system SHOULD be tested in a separate test network before installation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed migration manual is created. The test environment mirrors the production environment as closely as possible to perform compatibility tests with all connected systems (e.g., archive, CRM). The differences in functionality and in the PowerShell cmdlets are analyzed and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the migration manual for completeness and level of detail. It is checked whether the test reports prove a comprehensive verification of all relevant functions and interfaces. The documentation on the functional differences is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The migration is carried out in clearly defined phases with pilot user groups. Automated scripts are used for the migration and the subsequent verification of the configuration and data integrity. A detailed and tested rollback plan is in place. End users are proactively informed via a communication plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: PowerShell scripts are developed to automate and validate migration steps. The rollback plan is practically tested in the test environment. A communication plan specifies when which user group is informed about the upcoming changes and any new functions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the migration scripts, the rollback plan including test report, and the communication plan. It is checked whether a phased rollout with feedback loops from pilot groups has taken place.

controls.title: Secure configuration of Exchange servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Exchange servers are installed with the default settings. No specific security configuration or hardening takes place. Unnecessary services remain enabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installation follows the 'Next, Next, Finish' principle, without adapting the configuration to security requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration of an Exchange server with the Microsoft default values. It is checked whether hardening measures, such as disabling unnecessary protocols or services, have been omitted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic hardening measures are carried out manually after installation, e.g., disabling known insecure protocols. Connectors are configured to be functional, but not necessarily secure. Logging is enabled but not regularly reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators follow a simple checklist for basic hardening. The log files are only reviewed in case of acute problems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the implementation of basic hardening steps (e.g., disabling TLS 1.0/1.1). It is checked whether logging is enabled and what the configuration of the connectors looks like.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Exchange servers are installed and configured according to a defined security policy. This configuration includes the secure setting of connectors and the activation of basic logging for a-uditability of events.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document exists that describes the basic configuration for Exchange servers. This is applied to every new installation. Logging is configured to record security-relevant events.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation for the basic configuration and compares it with the actual configuration of a server on a random basis. It is checked whether the logging is activated as defined.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD install and configure Exchange servers according to the specifications from the security policy. Connectors SHOULD be configured securely. The logging of the Exchange system SHOULD be activated. A concept SHOULD be created for user-specific customizations. When using functional extensions, it SHOULD be ensured that the protection goals are still met.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration is based on a recognized hardening standard (e.g., CIS Benchmarks). Logging is extended (e.g., message tracking logs) and regularly reviewed. A security assessment is performed before the introduction of add-ins or extensions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration with the specifications of the security policy and, if applicable, a hardening standard. The configuration of the logging and the process for approving extensions are checked. An automated tool such as the Microsoft Exchange Health Checker can be used for verification: `.\HealthChecker.ps1`

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the Exchange servers is automatically enforced and monitored by a Desired State Configuration tool (e.g., PowerShell DSC). Deviations from the hardened target state are automatically corrected or trigger an alarm. All relevant logs are centrally collected in a SIEM and analyzed in real time for anomalies and attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: DSC scripts define the hardened state of the Exchange servers. The Exchange logs (e.g., OWA, ECP, Message Tracking) are forwarded to a SIEM collector, where specific correlation rules for Exchange attack patterns are implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the DSC configuration scripts and the monitoring reports. In the SIEM, the configuration of the Exchange data sources and the specific alerting rules are checked. An automatic configuration audit can be performed via a script that checks DSC compliance.

controls.title: Secure configuration of Outlook

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users configure their Outlook clients themselves without any guidelines or support. This leads to inconsistent and potentially insecure settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are no policies or templates for Outlook configuration. Each user sets up their profile at their own discretion.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly inspects the configuration of Outlook on various client computers and finds significant deviations and potentially insecure settings (e.g., automatic download of external content).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a recommended standard configuration for Outlook, but compliance is not enforced. Users are not actively informed about the risks of information leakage.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instructions for the recommended configuration are made available on the intranet. However, implementation is left to the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the instructions for the standard configuration and compares them on a random basis with the settings on client computers to assess the degree of implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A defined Outlook profile with basic settings is created for each user. The configuration is made in such a way that unnecessary information leakage, such as the automatic sending of read receipts to external addresses, is prevented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The basic security settings are set by IT support or by a simple script when the Outlook profile is set up. Users are informed about the most important settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a documented process for setting up Outlook profiles exists. It is randomly checked whether the basic settings for preventing information leakage (e.g., read receipts) are set correctly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD create a separate Outlook profile for each user and configure Outlook so that only necessary information is transmitted. Users SHOULD be informed about what information is transmitted automatically. Read receipts and information that could reveal the internal structure SHOULD NOT be transmitted to external parties.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration of Outlook is centrally controlled via Group Policies (GPOs) or a comparable management tool (e.g., Intune). Users receive specific information on data protection-relevant Outlook functions as part of security training or via the intranet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configured Group Policies for Outlook. It is checked whether the policies effectively prevent the transmission of read receipts to external parties and other potentially sensitive information. Evidence of user information is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Outlook configuration is strictly and verifiably enforced via GPOs or MDM policies. The policies include blocking dangerous file types, disabling macros from external sources, and enforcing email encryption (e.g., S/MIME) for defined communication scenarios. Regular awareness campaigns train users in the secure use of Outlook.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrative Templates (ADMX) for Office are imported and used to achieve granular control of all security-relevant settings. S/MIME certificates are automatically distributed to users. Phishing simulations related to Outlook functions are conducted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts an audit of the GPO/MDM settings and verifies their application on the clients. It is checked whether policies for macro security and encryption are active. The implementation and results of the awareness measures are evaluated.

controls.title: Securing communication between Exchange systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only some communication channels are encrypted, e.g., HTTPS is used for Outlook on the Web (OWA), but internal client-server communication (MAPI) is unencrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Encryption is only activated where it is suggested by default by the wizard. Internal server-to-server communication is considered 'trusted' and is not encrypted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses a network sniffer (e.g., Wireshark) to analyze the traffic between a client and the server, as well as between two servers, to identify unencrypted protocols.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The default encryption settings are used for most communication paths. However, it is possible that outdated, insecure protocols such as SSLv3 or TLS 1.0 are still enabled. Administrative interfaces are not considered separately.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Encryption is enabled for client access and server communication, but the configuration of cipher suites and protocol versions is not hardened.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses a tool like `nmap` or `testssl.sh` to scan the TLS/SSL protocols and cipher suites enabled on the Exchange services and check for outdated versions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A documented decision is made on how to secure the essential communication paths (client-server and server-server). As a rule, encryption using TLS is mandated and implemented for these channels.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy stipulates that MAPI-over-HTTP, Outlook Anywhere, and SMTP communication between servers must be TLS-encrypted. The corresponding configurations are made on the servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the security policy and checks the Exchange configuration (e.g., Receive/Send Connectors, MAPI Virtual Directory) to ensure that TLS encryption is configured as required.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD make a traceable decision on which protection mechanisms are used to secure communication. In particular, it SHOULD be specified how administrative interfaces, client-server, server-server communication, WebDAV interfaces, and the underlying PKI are to be secured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed concept for communication security is created. It defines the required protective measures for each interface. For SMTP, for example, STARTTLS is enforced. The PKI used for the TLS certificates is documented and securely managed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the communication security concept. The configuration of all mentioned interfaces is checked. The validity and trustworthiness of the TLS certificates used are verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All communication is encrypted using strong, up-to-date TLS configurations (e.g., TLS 1.2/1.3 with Forward Secrecy). Certificate management is automated. Server-to-server communication is additionally protected by network segmentation. DANE and MTA-STS are used for SMTP communication with external partners.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The TLS configuration of the servers is centrally hardened and monitored via GPO or script. An internal certificate authority with an automated enrollment process (SCEP/ACME) is used. The Exchange servers are located in their own network segment protected by firewalls. DNS records for DANE and MTA-STS are configured and policies are enforced.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the hardened TLS configuration using external and internal scans. The firewall rules for the Exchange segment are analyzed. The DNS configuration for DANE/MTA-STS is checked. Automated scripts can check the conformity of the TLS settings on all servers.

controls.title: Use of Outlook Anywhere, MAPI over HTTP and Outlook on the Web

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: External access methods such as Outlook on the Web (OWA) are enabled with default settings for all users, without additional security controls or access restrictions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After the Exchange installation, the external access services are accessible to the entire internal network and potentially also from the internet, without this having been consciously configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the accessibility of the OWA/MAPI endpoints from an external and internal network. It is checked whether access is possible for any user account.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The external access services are configured in a basic way. Access from the internet is restricted by a firewall to the necessary ports, but there is no further restriction to specific user groups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A rule is created on the firewall that forwards port 443 to the Exchange server. Within Exchange, access is not further restricted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rules for Exchange access. It is checked whether access restrictions for OWA or MAPI over HTTP are configured in Exchange itself.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A defined configuration for Outlook Anywhere, MAPI over HTTP, and Outlook on the Web is implemented. Access to these services is restricted to a clearly defined group of users who need this access for their work.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Active Directory group for 'remote access authorized users' is created. Using client access rules or similar mechanisms, access to external services is restricted to members of this group.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the concept for granting remote access authorizations. The technical implementation of the access restriction in Exchange is checked. An attempt is made to access with an unauthorized account as a test.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD configure Outlook Anywhere, MAPI over HTTP, and Outlook on the Web according to the institution's security requirements. Access to Exchange over the internet SHOULD be restricted to the necessary users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration is based on a documented security policy for remote access. This policy defines not only the authorized persons but also security requirements for the end devices. The virtual directories in IIS are hardened (e.g., removing unnecessary HTTP headers).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration of the services with the security policy. The configuration of the virtual directories in IIS is checked for hardening measures (e.g., with the command `Get-OwaVirtualDirectory | fl`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All external access to Exchange requires multi-factor authentication (MFA). The services are published via a hardened application proxy or a Web Application Firewall (WAF). Strict security policies such as session timeouts are enforced. Access is further restricted via Conditional Access policies (e.g., based on device status, location).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Azure AD Application Proxy or a third-party WAF is placed in front of the Exchange server. Azure AD Conditional Access or a comparable solution is used to enforce MFA and block access from non-compliant devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the application proxy/WAF and the Conditional Access policies. It is practically tested whether access without MFA or from a non-permitted location/device is successfully blocked.

controls.title: Encryption of Exchange database files

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Encryption of database or PST files does not take place or is only carried out sporadically by individual users for their own PST files without a central directive.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The server hard drives are unencrypted. There is no policy or instruction to encrypt local data files.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the status of drive encryption on the Exchange servers. It is checked whether a policy for encrypting PST files exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The drives of the Exchange servers are encrypted with BitLocker, but key management is weak (e.g., key stored on the same system). The encryption of PST files is recommended to users, but not enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: BitLocker is enabled on the servers, but the recovery key is not stored centrally and securely in Active Directory or another solution. A guide to PST encryption exists.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that BitLocker is active (`manage-bde -status`). It is checked whether and how the recovery keys are managed. The guide for PST encryption is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic concept for encrypting Exchange databases on the servers (data-at-rest) exists and is implemented. Typically, the operating system's drive encryption (e.g., BitLocker) is used for this purpose. Users are informed about the options for encrypting local PST files.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: BitLocker is enabled on all drives with Exchange databases and log files. The recovery keys are centrally backed up in Active Directory. A written guide for manually encrypting PST files is made available to users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the activation of BitLocker on the relevant server drives. It is verified that the recovery keys are stored in AD. The existence and distribution of the guide for PST encryption is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD create a concept for encrypting PST files and information store files. The institution SHOULD inform users about the functionality and protection mechanisms. Aspects such as encryption functions, levels, and securing the PST file SHOULD be considered. Mechanisms such as EFS or BitLocker SHOULD be used for protection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal encryption concept is written and approved. BitLocker is used on all Exchange servers. In addition, it is specified via group policy that newly created PST files must be encrypted by default. Awareness measures are taken to inform users about the importance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the encryption concept. The group policies regarding PST files are analyzed. Evidence of the implementation of user awareness measures (e.g., emails, intranet articles) is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Drive encryption (BitLocker) is enforced on all Exchange servers with secure key protection (e.g., TPM+PIN or storage in a dedicated HSM). The use of PST files is technically prevented or severely restricted; online archives are used instead. Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies prevent the export of sensitive data to unencrypted files.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: BitLocker keys are managed in a Hardware Security Module (HSM). The creation of new PST files is blocked via GPO (`DisablePST`). Exchange DLP policies are configured to monitor and block, for example, the sending of files containing personal data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the BitLocker configuration, including the key protection. The GPO settings for blocking PSTs are checked. The configuration and effectiveness of the DLP policies in Exchange are analyzed and tested.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Microsoft Exchange Server (hereinafter "Exchange") is a groupware solution for medium to large institutions. It allows for the electronic transmission of messages and has other services to support workflows. Messages, such as emails, can be centrally managed, delivered, filtered, and sent with Exchange. Likewise, typical groupware applications such as notes, contact lists, calendars, and task lists can be offered and managed. To use Exchange's functions, additional client software or a web browser is necessary in addition to the server service.
Microsoft Outlook (hereinafter "Outlook") is a client for Exchange that is made available directly through the installation of the Microsoft Office suite or by integration into the operating systems of mobile devices. Furthermore, the web application "Outlook on the web" (formerly "Outlook Web App") allows access to emails, contacts, and the calendar, for example, via the browser. This function is already included in Exchange.
The combination of Exchange servers and Outlook clients is referred to as an Exchange system in this module.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to inform about typical threats to Exchange and Outlook and to show how Exchange and Outlook can be used securely in institutions.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module is to be applied to all Exchange systems in the information network.
General requirements for the security of email systems can be found in module APP.5.3 General E-Mail Client and Server. It must also be applied to any email system based on Exchange or Outlook.
The module contains specific threats and requirements for Exchange systems. Specific requirements for server platforms and operating systems are not part of this module. These can be found in modules SYS.1.1 General Server and SYS.2.1 General Client and in the respective operating system-specific modules.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Missing or inadequate regulations for Exchange and Outlook
parts.prose: Overarching regulations and specifications for Exchange and Outlook are necessary to ensure the security of the information processed with Exchange and Outlook. For example, data can be lost, unintentionally altered, or deleted if Exchange is incorrectly and unregulatedly integrated into Active Directory. The same applies if mailbox databases are unregulatedly unpublished and Exchange is inadequately considered in the security policy. The same is true if Outlook clients can access the Exchange servers in an unregulated manner.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Faulty migration of Exchange
parts.prose:
In practice, Exchange systems are more often migrated than newly installed. To migrate to a new version of Exchange Server, the operating system must in some cases be updated to a newer version.
