New versions of operating systems often in turn place demands on the existing domain concept and the existing directory services.
If the migration is not carefully planned and carried out, internal communication via Exchange in the institution can be massively disrupted, which could in turn reduce productivity. During the migration, configuration problems can occur, for example, because the configuration settings for the different versions or the options for connecting to directory services have changed. Furthermore, incorrect protocol settings can lead to irregularities in information transmission, authentication, and encryption.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Unauthorized browser access to Exchange
parts.prose:
With Exchange, users can access their own e-mail account via a browser. This is done using Internet Information Services (IIS), which are part of the Windows operating system. If this function is improperly planned and incorrectly configured, it may be possible to access the internal network from the outside in an uncontrolled manner.
If e-mails are to be accessed via the internet with a browser, this poses a major potential risk. Without direct access to the institution's network, attackers could access the e-mails and, among other things, spy on e-mail addresses and content, misuse e-mail functions, send spam e-mails and gain access to internal company information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Unauthorized connection of other systems to Exchange
parts.prose:
Exchange systems are closely intertwined with the Windows operating system and work together with third-party systems through so-called connectors. With the help of connectors, it is possible for other email systems to retrieve emails from Exchange servers via certain protocols (e.g., POP3).
If the connectors are not taken into account during the installation or migration of Exchange, the existing connectors may be incompatible with the migrated Exchange version. This can result in emails being lost or unintentionally modified.
Outside of the homogeneous Microsoft environment, security settings that relate to the Exchange system are invalid.
If different subsystems are administered separately, inconsistencies can always occur. Improperly connected third-party systems can also result in data being lost or the Exchange system being blocked.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Incorrect administration of access rights and permissions under Exchange and Outlook
parts.prose: If access rights to an Outlook client or to data stored within Exchange and Outlook are incorrectly created and administered, security vulnerabilities can arise. This is the case, for example, if additional rights are granted beyond the necessary rights and unauthorized persons can thereby access confidential information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Incorrect configuration of Exchange
parts.prose: A common cause of successful attacks on services such as Exchange is incorrectly configured Exchange systems. Since an Exchange system is very complex, numerous security problems can arise from various configuration settings and the parameters that influence each other. The possible misconfigurations range from the installation and operation of Exchange components on unsuitable IT systems, to a lack of encryption and insufficient access restrictions on Exchange servers, to the incorrect allocation of rights when creating or initializing an Exchange database.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Incorrect configuration of Outlook
parts.prose: The Outlook e-mail client is an important part of the Exchange system. For the overall security of the Exchange system, it is important that the clients are configured correctly. The selected communication protocol alone can lead to special security problems. Likewise, private keys used to encrypt and sign e-mails could be compromised. If encryption is used at the network level, e.g. via IPSec or TLS, this encryption mechanism can become ineffective if a client is incorrectly configured. Misconfiguration can lead to security problems, e.g. loss of confidentiality through unauthorized access.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Malfunctions and misuse of self-developed macros and programming interfaces in Outlook
parts.prose: Many software manufacturers provide programming interfaces, so-called Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), in their tools and applications. These make it possible to use certain functions from other programs or to extend the functional scope of the application. Such functions in Outlook can be misused to spread malware. The malware variants include, for example, malicious tools and macros that directly exploit Outlook and the associated e-mail functions to retrieve, change or delete information. Macros, in turn, can be used to forward or move messages, appointments or tasks. Errors in macros can pose an increased risk. Index errors within macros can lead to incorrect results and possibly uneconomical decisions in the institution. Specific consequences can be unnecessary costs or an automated data leak.

controls.title: Secure configuration of email clients (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic configuration for email clients is only implemented for individual users or systems classified as critical. There is no uniform standard for the entire institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, manual configuration instructions are sent via email to a few employees. No verification of implementation takes place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through random checks that only a small proportion of email clients have any form of security configuration. No configuration document can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standardized basic configuration is rolled out to all email clients. However, this configuration can be easily changed by users. Attachment scanning for malware is enabled, but further protective measures such as disabling active content are not consistently implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration is often done via the default settings of the email client installer or a simple script. There are no mechanisms to prevent users from changing the settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a configuration exists on all clients. However, a random check reveals that users have independently changed security-relevant settings (e.g., HTML display).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST specify a documented, secure configuration for email clients and provide it pre-configured. File attachments MUST be scanned for malware before opening. Email clients MUST be configured not to automatically interpret HTML code and other active content. Email filter rules and automatic forwarding MUST be restricted to necessary use cases. Secure transport encryption MUST be used for communication with email servers over untrusted networks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The secure configuration is centrally distributed and enforced via a client management system (e.g., GPOs in Active Directory). The configuration explicitly includes disabling automatic HTML display and configuring the preview function so that no files are automatically interpreted. Attachment scanning is performed by local antivirus software or a server-side solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration document for email clients and checks the settings in the central management tool. Test clients are used to verify that active content is blocked and that transport encryption (e.g., TLS) is enforced for server communication.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD ensure that security-relevant parts of the configuration cannot be changed by users. If this is not technically feasible, the institution MUST explicitly and verifiably inform users that the configuration must not be changed. Preview functions for file attachments are configured in such a way that they do not automatically interpret or execute files under any circumstances.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration settings are locked by technical means (e.g., client management software). Users are given read-only rights to the relevant configuration files or registry entries. Regular scans check the conformity of the clients.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts, as a normal user, to change security-relevant settings such as disabling HTML display or transport encryption. It is verified that these attempts fail. Alternatively, the configuration of the client management system for locking the settings is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the email clients is not only enforced by a central management system, but also continuously monitored. Any deviation from the defined security baseline leads to an automated alert and, if possible, to an immediate automatic correction of the configuration. The security policies for email clients are integrated into the general endpoint security concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) or Mobile Device Management (MDM) solution is used to monitor the configuration in real time. Configuration baselines are defined and versioned as code (Configuration as Code). All security-relevant events of the email client are forwarded to a central SIEM system and correlated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the EDR/MDM system for conformity checks and automatic correction measures. A test case is carried out in which a configuration is manually changed (with administrative rights) to validate the response time and success of the automatic correction. The integration into the SIEM is verified using test events.

controls.title: Secure operation of email servers (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The email server is installed with the default settings. There is no specific hardening or configuration to prevent it from being an open relay or to defend against DoS attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The server was set up according to a simple guide from the internet. Security aspects such as transport encryption or access restrictions were not considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: An external test shows that the server can be abused as an open relay. A port scan analysis shows unencrypted email protocols such as SMTP (Port 25) without STARTTLS.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The email server offers secure transport encryption (TLS) but does not enforce it. Unencrypted connections are still possible. The server is basically configured so that it does not function as an open relay.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A valid TLS certificate is installed on the server. However, the configuration allows both encrypted (e.g., SMTPS Port 465, IMAPS Port 993) and unencrypted connections.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that an encrypted connection can be established to the server. However, a subsequent test shows that an unencrypted connection is also accepted. The open relay test is negative.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For receiving emails over untrusted networks, the email server MUST offer secure transport encryption. IT operations MUST configure the server so that email clients can only access mailboxes via secure transport encryption. IT operations MUST configure the server so that it cannot be abused as a spam relay. A suitable size limit for mailboxes MUST be set up and documented, and IT operations MUST take protective measures against DoS attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The server configuration enforces TLS for client connections (e.g., via SMTPS, IMAPS, POP3S, or STARTTLS with mandatory encryption). The receipt of unencrypted emails from other servers is still tolerated but logged. As DoS protection, rate limiting for connections and messages per unit of time are configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the server configuration to ensure that unencrypted client logins are disabled. The documentation for mailbox sizes and DoS protection measures is reviewed. A test client cannot connect without TLS.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Receiving emails over unencrypted connections SHOULD be disabled. When sending emails to other servers, secure transport encryption SHOULD be used, and sending over insecure connections SHOULD be disabled (opportunistic TLS with enforced encryption where possible).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The email server is configured to enforce TLS when communicating with other servers (e.g., via `smtp_tls_security_level = encrypt` in Postfix). For important communication partners that do not offer TLS, exception rules are defined and documented. The unencrypted receipt of emails is completely rejected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the server configuration files for TLS policies for outgoing and incoming server-to-server traffic. Email headers of test messages are analyzed to confirm the use of TLS. It is checked whether an email from a test server that does not offer TLS is rejected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Email communication is comprehensively secured through the use of DANE and MTA-STS. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks by downgrading encryption. Only current and strong encryption protocols and cipher suites are permitted. The server configuration is regularly and automatically checked for compliance with the security policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: DNSSEC is enabled for the institution's domains. TLSA records for DANE are published in the DNS. An MTA-STS policy is provided via HTTPS and the corresponding DNS entries are set. The server configuration is regularly checked using specialized tools (e.g., `testssl.sh`, Qualys SSL Labs) and the results are used for improvements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the correct configuration of DNSSEC, DANE (TLSA records), and MTA-STS (HTTPS policy and DNS records) with publicly available online tools. The server configuration is checked for the exclusive use of strong cipher suites and protocols (e.g., TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3). Automated configuration audit reports are reviewed.

controls.title: Data backup and archiving of emails (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations MUST regularly back up the data of the email servers and clients. For this, the institution MUST regulate how the sent and received emails of the email clients as well as the emails on the servers are backed up.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented data backup concept that explicitly includes the email servers. The backup of the server data is automated and regular (e.g., daily). For emails stored locally on clients (e.g., in PST files), there is a clear instruction for users to move them to network drives that are also backed up.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the data backup concept and the backup logs of the email server. The policy for backing up client-side emails is reviewed. The successful execution of the server backups is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD consider during archiving that emails may only be stored locally on clients. The data backup concept is extended by an archiving concept that takes into account legal and regulatory retention periods. Recovery tests are performed regularly to verify the integrity of the backups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated email archiving solution is used, which stores all incoming and outgoing emails in an audit-proof manner. This reduces the need to back up client-side archives. The backup concept is supplemented by annual, logged recovery tests for the email system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the email archiving concept and checks its compliance with the relevant retention obligations. The logs of the performed recovery tests are inspected. It is checked whether the archiving solution is functioning correctly (e.g., by searching for a test email in the archive).

controls.title: Spam and virus protection on the email server (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations MUST ensure that incoming and outgoing emails on email servers, especially their attachments, are checked for spam characteristics and malicious content. The introduction and use of email filtering programs MUST be coordinated with the data protection officers and the staff council. The institution MUST define how to handle encrypted emails if they cannot be decrypted by the antivirus program.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central email security gateway or software installed on the mail server scans all incoming and outgoing email traffic. There is a documented policy, created in consultation with the data protection officer, that describes, for example, the procedure for encrypted attachments (e.g., quarantine and manual release).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration of the spam and virus protection. The documented coordination with the data protection officer and the staff council is reviewed. The policy for handling encrypted, non-scannable emails is checked. A test email with a (harmless) test virus (e.g., EICAR) is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Spam and virus protection is enhanced with advanced features such as sandboxing and URL rewriting. Attachments with unknown or potentially dangerous content are executed and analyzed in an isolated environment before being delivered. Links in emails are checked for maliciousness at the time of click.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The email security solution used has a licensed Advanced Threat Protection (ATP) module. This module is activated for all incoming emails. Users are informed that links in emails may look different because they are rewritten by the protection service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the ATP module. A test email with a link to a known malware test site is sent, and it is verified that clicking the link is blocked. Another test email with a harmless but unknown executable attachment is moved to the sandbox quarantine.

controls.title: Definition of substitution rules for email use (S) [Supervisors]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD establish substitution rules for processing emails, taking data protection aspects into account. If emails are forwarded, the persons being represented SHOULD be informed. The institution SHOULD establish rules for the secure use of auto-reply functions, in particular that no internal information is disclosed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a written policy or company agreement that describes the process for setting up a substitution (e.g., for vacation or illness). This regulation requires the consent of the employee concerned and is implemented by the IT department. For out-of-office messages, there are approved text templates that do not contain sensitive internal details.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy on substitution rules and the templates for out-of-office messages. It is randomly checked whether the necessary documentation (e.g., employee consent) is available for established substitutions. Active out-of-office messages are checked for compliance with the requirements.

controls.title: Definition of a security policy for email (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD create and regularly update a security policy for the use of email. The policy SHOULD regulate aspects such as access rights, handling of spoofed senders, information security, private use, handling of attachments, and the use of webmail. All users and administrators SHOULD be informed about the policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A comprehensive email security policy is written down, approved by management, and made accessible to all employees (e.g., on the intranet). The policy is handed out to new employees upon hiring. Changes are actively communicated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the current email security policy and checks its content for completeness according to the requirement. It is verified that the policy is accessible to all employees and that a process for regular review and updating exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the email security policy is regularly checked. The policy is extended to include specific requirements for administrators, defining setting options for email applications and permitted access points to servers. The handling of newsgroups and mailing lists is also regulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The email policy contains a detailed appendix for administrators with specific configuration requirements. Compliance with the policy by users is checked on a random basis as part of internal audits or by technical means (e.g., DLP systems that monitor the sending of sensitive data).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the specific policies for administrators and compares them with the actual configuration of the email system. Reports from internal audits or DLP systems that document the verification of policy compliance are reviewed.

controls.title: Training on security mechanisms of email clients for users (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD educate staff as part of general training and awareness on the risks of using email and how to handle it securely. This SHOULD include the dangers of attachments and how to recognize spoofed senders.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Email security is an integral part of the annual, mandatory security awareness training for all employees. The training content includes concrete examples of phishing emails and instructions on how to handle suspicious messages securely.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the training materials of the security awareness campaign and checks whether email security topics are adequately covered. The attendance lists of the training sessions are inspected to verify staff coverage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to general training, phishing simulations are regularly conducted to test and improve employee awareness and responsiveness. Employees who fall for the simulations receive targeted follow-up training.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized tool or an external service provider is used to conduct realistic but harmless phishing campaigns quarterly. The anonymized results are evaluated to adapt training content and identify problem areas.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the planning, execution, and anonymized result reports of the phishing simulations. It is checked whether a process for follow-up training exists and how the findings from the campaigns are used to improve general training.

controls.title: Handling of spam by users (S) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In principle, users SHOULD ignore and delete all spam emails. They SHOULD not reply to unsolicited emails or follow links in them. If a central spam management system exists, users SHOULD forward spam emails to it.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users are instructed by the email policy and training on how to handle spam. There is a dedicated email address (e.g., spam@institution.de) to which suspicious emails can be forwarded to train the filters. Email clients may offer a plugin to do this with one click.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the email policy and training materials for clear instructions on handling spam. It is verified whether a process for reporting spam exists and is known to the users.

controls.title: Extended security measures on the email server (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution's email servers SHOULD check incoming emails using Sender Policy Framework (SPF) and DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM). The institution SHOULD use DKIM and SPF itself to authenticate emails it sends. The SPF record SHOULD only use the softfail parameter (~all) for testing purposes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The email server is configured to perform SPF and DKIM checks for incoming emails and to note the results in the email header. For its own domain, an SPF record with all authorized sending servers and a softfail entry (~all) is published in the DNS. A DKIM key is generated and the public part is stored in the DNS; the server signs outgoing emails.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the DNS records (SPF, DKIM) of the domain with public tools. By sending a test email from and to the institution, it is verified in the headers that outgoing emails are signed and incoming emails are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SPF record SHOULD contain the "-all" (Hardfail) parameter. The institution SHOULD use DMARC. DMARC records SHOULD specify that emails are rejected in case of failure (`p=reject`). DMARC reports SHOULD be evaluated regularly. Email communication SHOULD be secured via MTA-STS.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SPF record is tightened to `-all`. A DMARC record is published in the DNS, first with `p=none`, then `p=quarantine`, and finally `p=reject`. DMARC analysis tools are used to evaluate the incoming reports. An MTA-STS policy is provided on a web server and anchored in the DNS.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the DNS records for SPF (`-all`) and DMARC (`p=reject`). The processes and tools for evaluating DMARC reports are checked. The correct configuration of MTA-STS is validated with online tools.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and MTA-STS, the institution SHOULD also secure email communication via DANE to validate the authenticity of the target server's TLS certificate. The evaluation of DMARC reports is automated to detect and respond to spoofing attacks in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A prerequisite for DANE is the use of DNSSEC for the institution's domain. Corresponding TLSA records are published in the DNS. The mail server is configured to validate DANE records for outgoing connections. The DMARC reports flow into a SIEM system, which triggers alarms in case of anomalies (e.g., high volume of failed authentications).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the correct implementation of DNSSEC and the associated TLSA records for DANE using public test tools. The mail server configuration for DANE validation is checked. In the SIEM system, the correct processing and alerting for DMARC anomalies are monitored.

controls.title: End-to-End Encryption and Signature (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For exchanging emails with particularly high protection requirements, end-to-end encryption (E2EE) and digital signatures are used on an individual basis. Users are trained to use the appropriate tools (e.g., S/MIME, PGP) when necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a policy that defines when E2EE should be used. Individual users or departments receive the necessary certificates or keys and are trained in their use. Usage is voluntary or event-driven.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the E2EE policy. It is verified through interviews with key personnel whether and how E2EE is used in practice for sensitive communication.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD use end-to-end encryption and digital signatures for emails. Only protocols (e.g., S/MIME, OpenPGP) that are state-of-the-art SHOULD be used. Key and certificate management SHOULD be centralized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central gateway or a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is used for managing keys and certificates for S/MIME or OpenPGP. The E2EE functionality is integrated and pre-configured in the email clients of all relevant employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the central key management. It is verified that the protocols and algorithms used are state-of-the-art (e.g., no outdated hash or encryption algorithms). The correct configuration of the clients is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of end-to-end encryption and digital signatures is automatically enforced based on content or recipient policies. Emails that meet certain criteria (e.g., sent to external partners, contain keywords) are automatically signed and encrypted without user intervention.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An email gateway with policy-based encryption is used. This gateway manages the keys and applies the encryption transparently. Alternatively, client plugins that enforce policy-based encryption are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the encryption policies on the gateway. Test emails that meet the defined criteria are sent to validate that the automatic encryption and signature are applied correctly.

controls.title: Use of redundant email servers (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution has a secondary mail exchanger (MX) with a lower priority at an external provider. This accepts emails if the primary server is unreachable and delivers them later.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two MX records with different priorities are entered in the DNS. The second MX record points to a backup MX service. This only ensures the redundancy of email reception, not of sending or mailbox access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the domain's MX records. It is tested (e.g., by temporarily blocking the primary server in a firewall) whether the secondary MX accepts emails correctly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD operate redundant email servers. The redundant email servers SHOULD be stored with the appropriate priority in the MX records of the affected domains. It SHOULD be specified how emails are synchronized between the email servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At least two full-fledged email servers are operated in a cluster setup (e.g., active/passive or active/active), ideally at separate locations. The mailbox databases and configurations are replicated between the servers in short intervals or in real-time. A load balancer or DNS failover is used for client access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the cluster concept and the replication settings. A planned failover test is performed to verify that the second server takes over seamlessly and the data is up-to-date.

controls.title: Monitoring of public block lists (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In case of problems with email delivery, IT operations manually checks whether the email server IP addresses are listed on common public block lists (RBLs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: IT administrators use web-based tools (e.g., MXToolbox) as needed to check the reputation of their own IP addresses.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the administrators about their procedure when users report undeliverable emails. There is no proactive monitoring.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD regularly check whether the institution's email servers are listed on public spam or block lists.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An automated monitoring system or an external service is used to check the IP addresses of the mail servers daily against a curated list of important block lists. In case of a positive entry, a notification is sent to the IT department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the monitoring tool and the notification logs of the last few months. It is checked whether a defined process exists for the case of a listing (root cause analysis, delisting request).

controls.title: TLS Reporting (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD use TLS reporting to receive reports on successful or failed TLS encryption during email delivery. It SHOULD be determined whether TLS reports are sent to other institutions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A DNS record for TLS-RPT is published that points to an endpoint that receives the reports. A service (internal or external) is used to aggregate and evaluate the incoming JSON reports. This helps to proactively identify problems with transport encryption.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the TLS-RPT record in the DNS. The collected reports and the measures derived from them are reviewed. The mail server configuration for sending its own TLS reports is checked.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Email is one of the most frequently used and oldest internet applications. Emails are used to send texts and attached files. This requires an email address.

To use email, email servers are needed that receive and send electronic messages. Typically, email clients, which are used to access email services, retrieve messages intended for them from the email server using the POP3 or IMAP protocols and use the SMTP protocol to send messages themselves to the email server, which then forwards them to another email server if necessary.

Since email is widespread, especially in companies and public authorities, email servers are often the target of attacks.

Email clients are also the focus of attacks. They are attacked, for example, by sending malware via email. In addition, emails are also often used as a tool for social engineering attacks.

For these reasons, the secure operation and use of email applications is of particular importance.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to protect the information that is processed with e-mail clients or on e-mail servers.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
Module APP.5.3 General Email Client and Server is to be applied to every email client and server in the information system.

The module contains requirements for general email clients and servers. Requirements for server platforms, operating systems, and clients are not part of the module. These can be found in modules SYS.1.1 General Server and SYS.2.1 General Client and in the respective operating system-specific modules.

Module APP.5.3 General Email Client and Server is usually used in an information system in conjunction with another specific module from the APP.5 Email/Groupware/Communication layer. These must also be implemented separately. These modules include, among others, APP.5.2 Microsoft Exchange and Outlook.

Requirements for logging and data backup can be found in modules OPS.1.1.5 Logging and CON.3 Data Backup Concept.

Not covered in this module are groupware functions that, in addition to email, also offer other functions such as managing contact data and calendars. Likewise, pure cloud solutions, such as those found as part of Microsoft 365 or Google G Suite, are not covered. General requirements for this can be found in module OPS.2.2 Cloud Usage. Also not considered are web browsers, which are used to access webmail services via websites. Requirements for web browsers can be found in module APP.1.2 Web Browser.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Inadequate planning of e-mail use
parts.prose:
E-mail applications cannot be used securely in the institution without appropriately documented regulations and a defined security procedure. If the procedural, organizational, and technical regulations are neglected in the planning of e-mail systems, this could result in internal as well as external attacks.

For example, an undersized e-mail server can fail due to a large number of incoming e-mails. If sufficient security measures are not planned, it is also possible that the e-mail clients are more vulnerable to e-mails containing malware.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Incorrect setting of e-mail clients and servers
parts.prose:
Because an email infrastructure can be very complex, numerous security problems can arise from the many possible settings and the mutually influencing parameters.

For example, an email server may reject legitimate emails from other servers due to incorrect configuration. Additionally, it would be possible for essential settings to be ignored or disregarded, e.g., the transport encryption of emails.

Furthermore, incorrect configuration in email clients can lead to them executing malicious code in emails. These security vulnerabilities can lead to a significant loss of availability, integrity, and confidentiality of information.

Many institutions do not use security mechanisms that allow other email servers to verify whether an email actually originates from the specified sender address. In addition, a misconfigured email server can be misused to send spam emails.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Unreliability of e-mail
parts.prose: E-mail applications allow data to be exchanged quickly and conveniently. However, this is not always reliable. For example, messages can be lost due to faulty e-mail servers or disrupted transmission paths. Causes for this are, for example, spam filters that filter out and discard legitimate messages. E-mails can also be lost if the destination address was not specified correctly. In the worst case, confidential information may have been sent to incorrect destination addresses.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Malware in e-mails
parts.prose:
There are various ways in which malware can be spread via email during an attack. On the one hand, malicious code can be contained directly in an email. If the email client is not configured correctly, the code is executed when the email is opened.

Anotner possibility is that files with malware are sent as email attachments. If such emails are not filtered out by spam or virus filters and the attachments are opened, the malware is executed. This can lead to extensive damage to other IT systems as well, for example, if ransomware (often called an "extortion Trojan") is executed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Social Engineering
parts.prose:
Emails are often used in attacks to obtain confidential information or to entice personnel into other malicious behavior. For example, in an attack, an email can be sent that supposedly comes from superiors and contains instructions that harm the institution (so-called CEO fraud). This often involves instructions to transfer money to accounts abroad.

It is also possible that a forged email from a supposedly trustworthy source asks for credentials to be entered on a website (phishing). The credentials obtained in this way can then be used for further actions in an attack.

The danger of social engineering is increased if the institution does not regularly provide training and raise awareness about these threats.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Eavesdropping on and manipulating e-mails
parts.prose: E-mails are usually sent unencrypted and without a digital signature. Therefore, in the event of an attack, e-mails can be read and even arbitrarily modified. This can lead to the disclosure of confidential information or the distribution of false information. It is also possible for malware to be introduced this way.

controls.title: Planning of UCC (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Planning for UCC services exists only for individual aspects, for example, for replacing classic telephony. Cross-functional features such as collaboration, chat, or video conferencing are introduced on an ad hoc basis and without strategic planning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning is limited to a list of requirements for a telephony client. There is no analysis of dependencies on the network infrastructure or other applications. Organizational rules for use are not created.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing planning documents. It is checked whether the planning only covers isolated UCC services and whether essential aspects such as functional requirements for the entirety, security, or organizational regulations are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic plan has been created that describes the main use cases and functional requirements for the UCC services. However, the plan does not sufficiently consider the interactions between the services or the integration into the existing IT infrastructure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document lists the desired UCC services and their main functions. However, a detailed analysis of the network requirements or the necessary interfaces is missing. The selection of products is based primarily on the list of functions, not on security or integration requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the plan with the requirements from the building block. It is determined whether the plan describes the basic services, but aspects such as 'analysis of communication and dependencies' or 'integration into the IT infrastructure' are treated only superficially or not at all.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be planned comprehensively and in detail how and for what purpose UCC is to be used. The planning MUST in particular take into account the interactions of the UCC services and include at least the following aspects: use cases, functional requirements, security requirements, definition of transferable information, analysis of dependencies, product selection, and organizational regulations. The planning MUST consider how UCC will be integrated into the IT infrastructure, including network segmentation and interfaces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed UCC concept is created that covers all points mentioned in the requirement. This concept is reviewed and approved by the relevant stakeholders (IT operations, information security, data protection) before implementation. The product selection is based on a defined catalog of requirements, which also includes security criteria.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the UCC planning document or concept. It is verified that all aspects mentioned in the requirement (use cases, functional and security requirements, data flows, dependencies, product selection, regulations, integration) are treated and documented in detail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: UCC planning is a recurring process that is reviewed and updated regularly, at least annually, and with every significant change to the services or infrastructure. The planning includes a detailed risk analysis for the selected UCC services and defines concrete measures for risk mitigation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: UCC planning is part of the IT service catalog and is managed via a formal change management process. The risk analysis is carried out based on threat scenarios from the IT-Grundschutz-Kompendium (e.g., threats from this building block). The results flow directly into the configuration specifications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the regular reviews of the UCC concept. It is checked whether a documented risk analysis exists and whether its results have been traceably incorporated into the planning and security requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The UCC planning is fully integrated into the organization's overarching ISMS and IT strategy. It is based on a continuous improvement process that collects and evaluates key performance indicators (KPIs) for the security, availability, and use of the services. Threat modeling is used to proactively define security requirements for future UCC use cases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UCC planning is managed by a dedicated committee that meets regularly. Dashboards visualize the defined KPIs. Automated tools support the analysis of dependencies. Threat modeling workshops are held to identify potential vulnerabilities in the planned architecture at an early stage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of UCC planning into the ISMS, e.g., by reviewing management reviews. It is checked whether defined KPIs for UCC services exist, whether they are measured, and whether the results demonstrably lead to adjustments in the UCC concept. The existence of threat modeling reports is checked on a random basis.

controls.title: Consideration of UCC in network planning (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When planning the network, only the roughly estimated additional bandwidth for UCC is taken into account. Specific performance parameters such as packet loss, jitter, and latency are ignored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The network capacity is increased by a flat percentage without a detailed analysis of the requirements for real-time communication such as voice or video. Quality of Service (QoS) is not configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network planning documentation. It is determined that no specific requirements for UCC services regarding latency, jitter, or packet loss were defined and taken into account.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before the introduction of UCC services, a basic check of bandwidth and latency in the network is carried out. However, the check is not systematic and does not cover all usage scenarios (e.g., large video conferences). Aspects such as PoE and WLAN availability are not proactively planned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Manual tests are performed with tools like `ping` and `iperf` to get a rough estimate of network performance. There are no dedicated QoS classes for UCC traffic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the results of the network audit. It is found that the tests only cover simple scenarios and no comprehensive analysis of the performance parameters under load has taken place. The documentation is incomplete.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before UCC services are introduced, it MUST be verified whether the network meets the UCC-specific performance parameters. If not, a way of handling this MUST be defined. As part of general network planning, the following aspects in particular SHOULD be considered: fulfillment of parameters such as packet loss, jitter, and latency; sufficient network capacity (bandwidth) for the planned usage; consideration of Power over Ethernet (PoE) and the availability of WLAN for mobile devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of network planning, the threshold values for packet loss, jitter, and latency recommended by the UCC manufacturer are defined as requirements. The network capacity is calculated based on the expected number of concurrent voice and video streams. The PoE budgets of the switches are checked and the WLAN coverage for mobile UCC usage is verified. If the requirements are not met, either the network is upgraded or the UCC services are restricted (e.g., no HD video telephony).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network planning documents. It is verified that the specific performance parameters for UCC (packet loss, jitter, latency, bandwidth) are documented and that a check against these values has taken place. Switch configurations are spot-checked for PoE settings and WLAN controller configurations for coverage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network planning includes dedicated Quality of Service (QoS) policies that prioritize UCC traffic (especially voice and video). These aspects are re-evaluated with each expansion of UCC services. The network is actively monitored for compliance with the defined performance parameters.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: QoS configurations (e.g., based on DSCP markings) are implemented in all relevant network components (routers, switches, firewalls) to prioritize real-time traffic. A network monitoring system continuously monitors jitter, latency, and packet loss on critical paths and alerts when thresholds are exceeded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of routers and switches for the existence and correct implementation of QoS policies. The data from the network monitoring system is reviewed to verify that the UCC-specific performance parameters are being monitored.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network planning uses simulation tools to model the impact of UCC traffic under various load scenarios and to proactively identify capacity bottlenecks. Quality of Service is managed dynamically. Redundant and fault-tolerant network paths are planned and implemented for critical UCC services.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Simulations are carried out with tools such as OPNET or GNS3 before major rollouts. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) is used to control QoS policies centrally and dynamically. Critical UCC servers and gateways are connected via separate switches and routers to ensure high fault tolerance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests reports from the network simulations. The configuration of the SDN controller is checked for dynamic QoS policies. The redundant connection of critical UCC components is verified using network diagrams and configurations.

controls.title: Initial and regular testing of UCC services (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only informal functional tests are carried out by IT staff before a new UCC service goes live. Interactions with other applications or tests by end users do not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator tests whether they can log in to the new client and make a call. The tests are not documented and there are no defined test cases.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for test protocols for the introduction of UCC services. It is determined that no formal test documents or user acceptance tests exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before introduction, initial functional tests of the UCC components are carried out among themselves. However, tests are not repeated after changes or extensions. User tests are informal and not systematically evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A small group of IT-savvy users is asked to 'give the new features a try'. The feedback is collected verbally. There are no formal test plans or acceptance criteria.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for a description of the testing process. It becomes clear that while tests are initially conducted, there is no process for regression testing when changes are made. The results of user tests are not documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the UCC services, tests MUST be carried out initially to verify that the UCC components function without interference with each other and with other UCC services. Tests MUST also be carried out with selected users to check for interactions with other applications in particular. These tests SHOULD be repeated when the UCC services are expanded or changed. In addition, the configuration of the UCC services SHOULD be checked for plausibility and conformity for the defined purposes at regular intervals.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A test plan is created that includes technical tests (e.g., parallel use of telephony and video conferencing) and User Acceptance Tests (UAT). A representative group of users from different departments is involved in the UAT. The test results are documented and approved before go-live. The change management process specifies that relevant test cases must be repeated for UCC changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews test plans and test protocols for the introduction and for recent changes to the UCC services. It is verified that both technical interference tests and documented user tests have been carried out. It is checked whether a process for regular configuration review exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a dedicated test environment that largely replicates the production environment. Comprehensive regression tests are carried out there before the introduction of new versions or major changes. The regular review of the configuration is partially automated by scripts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A staging environment is operated with a copy of the production configuration. Test cases are documented in a test management tool. Configuration checks are implemented, e.g., with PowerShell or Python scripts, and executed periodically. The results are collected centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and current state of the test environment. Insight is gained into the test management tool to check the coverage of the test cases. The scripts for configuration review and their execution logs are checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Test processes are largely automated and integrated into the CI/CD pipeline for UCC management. Automated test suites run regression tests, performance tests, and load tests after every configuration change. The conformity check of the configuration is carried out continuously, and deviations automatically trigger an alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Selenium or Cypress are used for automating client tests. Load testing tools like JMeter are used to simulate behavior under high load. A configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible) continuously checks and enforces the desired state of the UCC configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline and the automated testing tools. Reports from the automated test runs (function, load, performance) are checked. The configuration of the configuration management tool is checked for the rules for reviewing the UCC services.

controls.title: Deactivation of unneeded functions and services (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The UCC services are operated with the manufacturer's default configuration. Only obviously insecure or problematic functions are manually deactivated if necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, the administrator deactivates the 'send files to external parties' function after an incident has occurred. A systematic review and reduction of the range of functions does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the active configuration with a list of potentially risky functions. It is found that many unneeded functions (e.g., public team areas, storage of log data) are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on a general checklist, some unneeded functions are deactivated. However, this is done without a detailed analysis of the specific use cases and without considering interactions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During initial setup, a generic hardening guide is followed that recommends disabling certain functions. It is not checked whether these functions would actually be useful for the organization or whether other functions not on the list pose a risk.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the checklist or hardening guide used. It is checked whether it is tailored to the specific use cases defined in the UCC planning. A discrepancy is often found.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: UCC services MAY ONLY be operated with the minimum necessary set of features. The available functions and services MUST be selected according to the defined use cases. Interactions MUST be taken into account. In particular, the necessity of the following services and functions MUST be reviewed and, if necessary, they MUST be deactivated: storage of personal data, access to and processing of this data, usability of functions by external parties, sending of data to external parties. Conversation-related log data MAY ONLY be stored minimally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on the UCC concept (see A1), a configuration policy is created that precisely defines which functions may be activated for which user groups (Principle of Least Functionality). This policy is applied when setting up all UCC components. For example, the chat function for external guests is deactivated by default.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the configuration policy and the UCC plan. The configuration of UCC servers and clients is checked on a random basis to verify that the policy specifications are implemented and that unneeded functions (especially those mentioned in the requirement) are actually deactivated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A 'default-deny' policy for UCC functions is implemented. All functions are disabled by default and must be explicitly enabled for specific roles or user groups based on a documented need. Compliance with this configuration is regularly reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A hardening script is used during deployment, which initially deactivates all optional functions. Subsequently, functions are selectively enabled according to the role and authorization concept. Regular configuration audits verify the implementation of this policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and application of the 'default-deny' policy. The approval processes for new functions are checked. The results of the regular configuration audits are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the functional scope is automatically enforced and monitored by a configuration management tool. Any deviation from the defined, hardened baseline is automatically corrected or triggers a security alert. Functions are enabled dynamically based on user context (e.g., device, location, role).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like Ansible or Puppet is used to define and enforce the desired state of the UCC configuration. A SIEM system correlates configuration change logs with the specifications and alerts on unauthorized changes. Conditional Access Policies are used to control functions based on context.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration in the configuration management tool ('Infrastructure as Code'). The rule base in the SIEM for monitoring the UCC configuration is checked. Alerts for configuration deviations are traced on a random basis.

controls.title: Role and Authorization Concept for UCC (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no specific role definition for UCC services. A distinction is only made between normal users and administrators. External users receive the same rights as internal standard users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All users are assigned to the standard user group during setup. There are no differentiated rights, e.g., who can record conferences or invite external participants.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the user and group management of the UCC platform. It is determined that no differentiated roles exist and the permissions are largely identical for all users.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic role concept with a few roles (e.g., 'Moderator', 'Guest') is documented. However, the assignment and review of roles are performed manually and irregularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A wiki document describes 2-3 roles. Administrators assign these roles manually during user setup. There is no process for a regular review of the assigned permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the documented roles with the actual permissions in the UCC platform. It is checked whether a process for regular access reviews exists, which is typically not the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The role and authorization concept MUST be supplemented with UCC-specific definitions of roles and permissions. This MUST apply to both internal and external users. Permissions MUST be defined for targeted use, for adjusting conversation configurations, and for special functions such as recording. Permissions MUST be reduced to the necessary minimum. The definitions MUST be documented, reviewed, and updated regularly and on an ad-hoc basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The existing company-wide role concept is extended with a chapter on UCC. It details specific roles (e.g., 'Standard User', 'Team Lead', 'External Guest') and their permissions (e.g., 'can record', 'can invite externals', 'can only participate in chats'). Implementation is done by configuring user groups in the UCC platform. A review of the role definitions and the most important assigned permissions takes place at least once a year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the extended role and authorization concept. It is verified that UCC-specific roles are defined for internal and external users. The configuration of user groups in the UCC platform is checked on a random basis. Logs of the regular reviews are requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The role and authorization concept is fine-grained and distinguishes between different conversation types and functions. Only explicitly authorized users SHOULD be able to access data such as recordings or file repositories. Role assignment is linked to the employee lifecycle (Joiner, Mover, Leaver). Semi-annual access reviews for critical permissions are conducted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UCC role concept is linked to the HR process, so that new employees automatically receive the standard role, and rights are adjusted or revoked upon a change of department or departure. A separate permission group is used for accessing conference recordings. An identity management tool supports the execution of access reviews.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the connection of the UCC permission management to the HR processes. The configuration of permissions for accessing recordings is checked. The logs and results of the semi-annual access reviews are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The permission management for UCC is fully integrated into a central Identity and Access Management (IAM) system. An Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) approach is used, where permissions are based not only on static roles but also on dynamic attributes (e.g., project affiliation, device type, location). The access reviews are fully automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central IAM system provisions and de-provisions users and their permissions in the UCC platform via an API (e.g., SCIM). The ABAC policy specifies, for example, that only employees from the legal department may access team areas marked as 'legally confidential' from a device classified as secure. The IAM tool automatically generates recertification tasks for supervisors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the IAM system and the ABAC policies for the UCC platform. The automated process for access reviews is verified by inspecting the workflows and logs of the IAM tool. It is checked how dynamic attribute changes lead to permission adjustments.

controls.title: Encryption of UCC Data (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Encryption is only used where it is enabled by default by the manufacturer. There is no uniform policy or review of the encryption settings. Stored data (at rest) is generally not encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Web traffic to the UCC portal is encrypted via HTTPS because the web server is configured this way by default. However, SIP signaling or media data are transmitted unencrypted, as this would have had to be activated manually. Files shared in chats are stored unencrypted on the file server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs network sniffing to check the encryption of signaling and media data. It is checked on the storage system whether stored UCC files are unencrypted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All communication over insufficiently trusted networks (e.g., the internet) is consistently transport-encrypted. Encryption of data at rest or end-to-end encryption does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For all external connections, TLS is configured for signaling (e.g., SIPS) and SRTP for media data. However, internal communication takes place unencrypted. Conference recordings are stored unencrypted on a network drive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the UCC servers and gateways to ensure that TLS and SRTP are enforced for external communication. It is verified that internal communication and stored data are unencrypted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All communication over insufficiently trusted networks MUST be encrypted using secure methods. File repositories containing persistent personal or confidential data MUST be secured using secure encryption mechanisms. This applies to both internal and externally connected file repositories. Users MUST be informed about the encryption status within conversations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An encryption policy for UCC is defined. It mandates transport encryption (TLS, SRTP) for all connections (internal and external). For file repositories, server-side encryption (Encryption at Rest) is activated on the storage systems. The UCC clients indicate the encryption status, e.g., with a lock icon.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the encryption policy. The configuration of the UCC components is checked for the consistent enforcement of transport encryption. The configuration of the storage systems is checked for the activation of Encryption at Rest. It is verified in the client whether the encryption status is displayed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The encryption methods, algorithms, and key lengths used comply with the current recommendations of the BSI (e.g., TR-02102). Where technically possible and reasonable, end-to-end encryption is used for chats and 1:1 calls. A central system for certificate management is used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration of the UCC systems is specifically checked for compliance with BSI TR-02102 (e.g., deactivation of old TLS versions and insecure cipher suites). The E2EE function of the UCC client is activated for all users. Certificates are managed via an internal PKI or a professional certificate management service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration of the encryption settings (TLS versions, cipher suites) with the specifications of BSI TR-02102. It is checked whether E2EE is active for chats. The certificate management process is audited.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure end-to-end encryption is consistently enforced for all forms of communication, including multi-person conferences (signaling and media). Critical keys for server-side encryption are protected in Hardware Security Modules (HSM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UCC solution is used that supports protocols like MLS (Messaging Layer Security) or a comparably secure method for E2EE in group conferences. This function is enforced for all users. The storage systems are connected to an HSM to protect the keys for encrypting data at rest.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the technical documentation of the UCC solution and the configuration to verify the implementation of E2EE for groups. The connection of the storage systems to the HSM is checked and the HSM's configuration is audited.

controls.title: Regulations for the secure use of UCC services (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no specific regulations or training courses on the secure use of UCC services. Users are encouraged to act on their own responsibility.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A general IT user policy states that 'Confidential information must be handled with care'. There are no concrete instructions on how to secure a video conference with external partners, for example.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for usage policies and training materials for UCC services. It is determined that no specific documents or measures exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A document exists with basic rules for the secure use of UCC (e.g., 'do not share passwords in chat'). However, acknowledgement of the document is not verified and no active training takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 'Guide to UCC' is published on the intranet. Users are notified of it by email upon introduction. There is no awareness-raising for specific risks such as social engineering via chat or accidental screen content sharing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the guide and checks its content for completeness. By interviewing employees, it is determined that the policy is largely unknown and its contents have not been internalized.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Conversations conducted using UCC MUST be secured. The following aspects MUST be considered: selection of participants, additional security (PIN/password), assignment of moderation rights, regulations for recordings and for the use of shared endpoints. Users MUST be informed about the security functions and made aware of secure usage (esp. external chats, video conferences).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A mandatory usage policy for UCC is created and communicated to all users. It contains clear instructions on the points mentioned in the requirement. As part of an introductory event or e-learning, users are familiarized with the functions and rules. Particular attention is paid to the risks of dealing with external communication partners and screen sharing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the usage policy as well as the training and awareness materials. It is verified that all aspects mentioned in the requirement are covered. By interviewing users, a random check is performed to see if the contents are known.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Awareness measures take place regularly, at least annually, and are mandatory for all users. The use of security mechanisms such as passwords for external conferences is enforced where technically possible through configuration templates or policies. There are clear guidelines for the classification of conferences and the associated security requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All employees must complete an annual security awareness training that includes a dedicated module on UCC security. In the UCC platform, meeting templates ('Internal', 'External-Confidential') are provided that automatically activate corresponding security settings (e.g., waiting room, mandatory password). The classification policy is documented and communicated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the attendance lists of the mandatory awareness training. The configuration of the meeting templates in the UCC platform is checked. It is checked whether the classification policy exists and is known to the users.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The success of the awareness measures is checked through regular, targeted phishing simulations (e.g., via prepared chat invitations). Technical controls (DLP - Data Loss Prevention) are integrated into the UCC platform to detect and prevent the sharing of sensitive information. User actions that violate the security policy are logged and evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An awareness platform is used that conducts phishing simulations via email and chat and provides targeted feedback to employees. A DLP system scans chat messages and shared files for predefined patterns (e.g., credit card numbers) and blocks them. The SIEM system receives audit logs from the UCC platform and has rules to detect policy violations (e.g., recording a conference classified as 'strictly confidential').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the reports from the phishing simulations. The configuration and effectiveness of the DLP system are checked (e.g., by a test upload of a sensitive file). In the SIEM, the rules for monitoring the UCC platform and the alarms based on them are analyzed.

controls.title: Use of a Session Border Controller at the provider gateway (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No Session Border Controller (SBC) is used. The connection to the SIP provider is made directly through the firewall, on which the necessary ports are opened. No application-specific security is in place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On the perimeter firewall, a port forwarding for SIP (port 5060/5061) and RTP (a large port range) to the internal UCC system is set up. This exposes the system directly to attacks from the Internet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the perimeter firewall and the network diagram. It is determined that there is no SBC in the signal path to the provider and the UCC system is directly accessible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An SBC is used, but mainly to solve network problems such as NAT traversal. It is operated with a basic default configuration that only offers minimal security functions such as topology hiding.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SBC is configured to hide the internal network topology and to perform address translation correctly. Advanced filter functions, encryption termination, or validation of SIP messages are not used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the configuration of the SBC. It is determined that although an SBC is present, its security functions (e.g., filter rules, DoS protection) are not activated or are only activated in the default setting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For UCC communication over partially trusted networks, a Session Border Controller (SBC) SHOULD be used at the network gateway to the SIP provider, at least for voice services. The SBC SHOULD act as an encryption endpoint, terminating the signaling and media streams. The SBC SHOULD support filter functions for signaling and media streams to provide additional security for the respective conversations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SBC is installed at the gateway to the SIP provider. It is configured to act as a B2BUA (Back-to-Back User Agent), terminating and rebuilding the SIP and RTP streams. It terminates the encrypted connection to the provider (TLS/SRTP) and establishes a separate connection to the internal system. Basic filter rules are configured to block invalid SIP methods or known attack patterns.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the positioning and function of the SBC as a B2BUA based on the network diagram and the SBC's configuration. It is checked whether the SBC terminates the encryption and whether basic filter rules for securing the communication are implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SBC's filter rules are adapted in detail to the organization's communication policies. The SBC performs deep packet inspection (DPI) of SIP messages to detect anomalies and attack attempts. It has mechanisms to protect against Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks. Its log data is forwarded to a central SIEM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specific rules are implemented on the SBC that, for example, prevent calls to expensive premium-rate numbers or limit the number of calls per second from a source IP (rate limiting). The logging function is configured to send all relevant events to the SIEM server, where corresponding correlation rules exist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the detailed filter and security rules of the SBC and compares them with the requirements of the security policy. The configuration of the DoS protection and the log forwarding to the SIEM is checked. The processing of the SBC logs in the SIEM is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SBC is operated as a high-availability cluster. It enforces dynamic policies based, for example, on external threat intelligence feeds to proactively block attacks from known malicious IP addresses. The SBC is able to transcode media data if necessary to ensure interoperability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two or more SBCs are configured in a failover cluster to ensure uninterrupted operation. The SBC automatically obtains IP blacklists and applies them to incoming traffic. The transcoding functions are configured for connecting partners with different codec requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the SBC cluster and tests the failover mechanism. The connection to the threat intelligence feeds and the implementation of the resulting rules are checked. The configuration of the transcoding rules is analyzed.

controls.title: Secure configuration of UCC (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The UCC systems are configured with the manufacturer's default settings. Only the most obvious security settings, such as changing the default administrator password, are made.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During installation, the password for the 'admin' user is changed. All other settings, such as encryption parameters, open services, or logging level, remain in their default state.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a configuration scan of the UCC system and compares the result with known hardening recommendations. A high number of deviations and the use of default settings are identified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic hardening of the UCC systems is carried out using a generic checklist. However, the configuration is not adapted to the specific context of the organization or the defined protection needs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrator works through a general hardening guide from the internet. It is not assessed whether all points are useful for their own environment or whether other, unmentioned settings would be relevant.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the hardening checklist used and compares it with the specific requirements of the organization. It is checked whether the configuration takes into account risks beyond the checklist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To configure UCC securely, at least the following aspects SHOULD be considered: encryption of signaling and media data, including on trusted transmission paths; protection of stored data, in particular defining access rights to recordings; restriction of services to internal users only; restriction of the transmission of availability information. Stored data SHOULD be encrypted. Users SHOULD only be able to access stored data after prior authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A mandatory configuration and hardening policy for the UCC systems is created. This policy mandates encryption, including on the internal network, defines who can access recordings, and restricts the visibility of presence information to defined groups. The implementation of the policy is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
