parts.prose: The auditor requests the hardening policy. The configuration of the UCC systems is spot-checked for the implementation of the mentioned points (internal encryption, access rights to recordings, etc.).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure configuration baselines are defined, documented, and versioned for all UCC components. Malware protection SHOULD be enabled for text-based conversations. The implementation of the configuration SHOULD be regularly and on an ad-hoc basis checked for compliance with the specifications and adjusted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hardening policies are developed as detailed configuration baselines (e.g., according to CIS Benchmarks) and published on the intranet. A virus scanner with a connection to the UCC platform checks uploaded files in chats. Regular internal audits check compliance with the baselines.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the defined configuration baselines. The configuration of the malware protection is checked. The logs and results of the internal configuration audits are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration baselines are managed and enforced using automation tools (Infrastructure as Code). Any deviation from the defined target state is automatically detected and either corrected or an alarm is triggered. The security configuration is continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Ansible playbooks or Puppet manifests define the hardened state of all UCC components. These are run regularly to ensure compliance. A Security Configuration Management (SCM) tool monitors the systems in real time and reports deviations to the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the code of the automation scripts (e.g., Ansible playbooks) to verify the implementation of the hardening policy. The configuration of the SCM tool and the handling of alarms for configuration deviations are checked.

controls.title: Securing and restricting content analysis (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Functions for the automatic analysis of conversation content (e.g., transcription, translation, summarization) are used without prior review, policy, or obtaining consent from the data subjects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users activate live transcription in meetings to avoid taking notes. The generated transcripts are stored unprotected, and it is unclear which third-party provider performs the analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews users and administrators about their use of analysis functions. It is determined that such functions are actively used without a data protection or security assessment having taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a policy that recommends users refrain from the automatic analysis of content. However, no technical controls are implemented to disable these functions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UCC usage policy states that transcription services may only be used after consulting the data protection officer. However, the function is available to all users in the client and can be easily activated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy and then checks in the UCC platform whether the corresponding functions are technically blocked. A discrepancy between the policy and the technical reality is identified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The nature of a (automatic) analysis of conversation content SHOULD be carefully examined in advance and its benefits weighed against the need for protection. It SHOULD be possible to disable corresponding functions either completely or per conversation. If content is analyzed beyond the purpose of the conversation, consent MUST also be obtained from the persons participating in the conversation. If persistent data is generated during the analysis, appropriate protective measures SHOULD be implemented for it.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before activating analysis functions, a protection requirement assessment and, if necessary, a data protection impact assessment are carried out. Functions that perform analysis via external online services (especially AI functions) are disabled by default. If they are to be used, the moderator must obtain the consent of all participants at the beginning of the meeting. Generated data (e.g., transcripts) are classified as requiring protection and stored in secured locations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation for the review of analysis functions (e.g., DPIA). The configuration of the UCC platform is checked to determine whether critical analysis functions are disabled by default. It is checked whether regulations for handling the generated data exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Analysis functions are disabled by default at a technical level for all users. Activation can only be requested and granted for specific, authorized user roles. Users are actively informed through technical notices or pop-ups when an analysis is taking place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Functions such as transcription or translation are globally disabled via a central policy in the UCC admin console. An activation process is defined in the ticket system. If a function is used exceptionally, the client displays a permanent banner to all participants, indicating the active analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the global deactivation of the analysis functions in the central administration interface. The defined activation process is audited. It is tested whether the visual cues for all participants appear during an active analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Data Loss Prevention (DLP) system is integrated, which monitors communication for sensitive content and prevents violations, independent of the analysis functions. Every use of an analysis function is centrally logged in an audit-proof manner and is subject to regular reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A DLP system is connected to the UCC platform via API. For example, it blocks the posting of document names classified as 'internal' in chats with external participants. All events related to analysis functions (activation, deactivation, access to results) are sent to the SIEM and evaluated there.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and the rule sets of the DLP system. In the SIEM, the audit logs for the use of analysis functions are analyzed, and it is checked whether regular reports are created and evaluated.

controls.title: Ensuring the availability of communication services (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The availability of the UCC services depends on single, non-redundant components. There are no specific measures to ensure availability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The entire UCC platform runs on a single physical or virtual server. If it fails, all services are unavailable. Monitoring is limited to a ping check of the server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the UCC environment and identifies Single Points of Failure (SPoFs).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic hardware redundancies such as redundant power supplies or hard disk RAIDs are available for the central servers. However, there is no redundancy at the service level. Service availability is monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UCC server is equipped with two power supplies and uses a RAID system. However, if the UCC application itself fails, there is no failover. A monitoring system checks if the UCC service is running on the server and alerts in case of a failure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the hardware specifications of the servers and the monitoring configuration. It is verified that no application or site redundancy is implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The availability of UCC services is ensured through planned measures. This includes a redundant design of central servers and the use of Call Admission Control (CAC) for quality assurance. Availability is monitored by a monitoring system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Critical central servers are configured as an active/passive cluster. CAC is set so that no new video calls are allowed in case of network congestion to ensure the quality of existing calls. The monitoring not only checks reachability but also specific UCC quality parameters.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the server cluster. The configuration of the Call Admission Control is analyzed. The configuration and data of the monitoring system are inspected to verify the monitoring of availability and quality.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The availability of UCC services SHOULD be ensured in particular by the following technical measures: redundant design of central servers and services, use of Call Admission Control (CAC), and, as far as possible, self-sufficient UCC services. For cloud-based services, the cloud provider and the internet provider SHOULD be connected in a fail-safe manner. A high-availability SIP provider SHOULD also be connected in a fail-safe manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Central servers are operated as an active/active cluster. For cloud services, redundant internet connections via different providers are used. The SIP trunk is also implemented redundantly via two different providers or locations. Care is taken to ensure that the UCC solution is designed in such a way that the failure of one component (e.g., chat server) does not affect the core functionality (telephony).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the architecture plans and configurations to verify the redundant design of servers, internet connections, and SIP providers. The design of the UCC services is checked for their self-sufficiency in the event of a failure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All critical UCC components are distributed across multiple geographic locations in a fully redundant high-availability architecture (geo-redundancy). The failover process is fully automated and regularly tested. Comprehensive monitoring of the Quality of Experience proactively provides indications of impending problems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UCC platform is operated in two separate data centers in an active/active configuration. In the event of a data center failure, the systems in the other location seamlessly take over operation. Regular, automated failover tests are part of operations. Dedicated monitoring probes simulate user behavior and measure the perceived quality of calls and conferences.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the geo-redundancy architecture. The logs of the automated failover tests are reviewed. The configuration and reports of the Quality of Experience monitoring are checked.

controls.title: Integration of UCC into emergency planning (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: UCC services are not explicitly considered in the organization's emergency planning. It is assumed that they will not be available in an emergency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The emergency manual contains no instructions on how to handle or restore UCC services. Alternative communication channels are not defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the emergency manual and determines that UCC services are not mentioned.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The emergency plan acknowledges the dependency on UCC services but does not contain specific recovery procedures or alternative solutions. The availability of emergency calls is assumed but not explicitly planned or tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the Business Impact Analysis (BIA), 'Communication' is listed as a critical process, but the associated plans contain no technical details for restoring the UCC platform. It is assumed that emergency calls will work somehow.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the BIA and the emergency plans. It is determined that the plans for UCC are too general and do not contain actionable restart plans. The planning for emergency calls is assessed as insufficient.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on a Business Impact Analysis, it SHOULD be verified which UCC services are considered in the emergency planning. In emergency situations, alternative applications SHOULD be provided for individual UCC services. In particular, the availability of important services such as emergency calls SHOULD be guaranteed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The BIA identifies the maximum tolerable downtime for telephony, chat, and video conferencing. Based on this, an emergency plan is created which provides, for example, for switching to a cloud-based video conferencing solution in the event of a total failure. The emergency call functionality is designed to work even if the central system fails (e.g., via local gateways).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the BIA and the emergency plan for UCC based on it. It is checked whether alternative applications have been defined and their use prepared. The technical design for guaranteeing emergency calls is analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An emergency plan SHOULD be created for the UCC services that addresses necessary configurations and routing adjustments (also with the provider). Likewise, the restart of the UCC components and services SHOULD be defined, taking into account the interdependencies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The emergency manual contains detailed step-by-step instructions for the recovery of UCC services, including the necessary commands for configuration changes. There is a defined plan for redirecting phone numbers with the SIP provider. The restart plan specifies a precise sequence (e.g., 'first database, then application server, then clients') to avoid dependency issues.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the level of detail and feasibility of the UCC emergency manual. It is checked whether the restart plan correctly considers the dependencies. The agreements with the SIP provider for emergencies are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The emergency plan for UCC is regularly tested through practical exercises, at least once a year. The switch to alternative systems or recovery from backups is largely automated. The UCC emergency plan is fully integrated into the organization's overall Business Continuity Management System (BCMS).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Emergency drills are held regularly, during which, for example, the failure of the primary UCC system is simulated and the administrators have to perform the recovery on a test system. Recovery scripts automate the process. The results of the drills are used to improve the emergency plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the plans, protocols, and lessons-learned documents from the emergency drills. The automation scripts for recovery are analyzed. The integration into the BCMS is verified by inspecting the corresponding documents and processes.

controls.title: Secure administration of SIP trunks (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Any administrator with access to the UCC platform can change all settings of the SIP trunk unilaterally and without review.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A single administrator changes a routing configuration to fix a problem, but in doing so, unintentionally makes it impossible to make international calls. There is no control body.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the permissions for the administration of the SIP trunk settings and finds that several people have unrestricted write access. There is no documented or enforced approval process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an organizational rule that critical changes to SIP trunks should be reviewed by a second person. However, compliance with this rule is not technically enforced or systematically monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the team, it is agreed that one 'briefly informs' before changing something in the routing. This is done informally via chat. A formal approval or documentation does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews the administrators about the change process. It becomes clear that the process is informal and there are no technical means to prevent a unilateral change.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For critical changes to the configuration of SIP trunks, a four-eyes principle is applied as part of the change management process. All changes are documented in a change request ticket and must be approved before implementation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator creates a ticket in the change management system that describes the planned change (e.g., to the routing configuration). A second, designated administrator or the team leader reviews and approves the ticket. Only then is the change implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the change management logs for recent changes to SIP trunks. It is verified that for all critical changes, documented requests and approvals according to the four-eyes principle exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When administering SIP trunks, a four-eyes principle SHOULD be applied for the following activities: changes to routing configurations, to Call Admission Control parameters, to encryption, and to the local storage of connection data. Where technically possible, the four-eyes principle is enforced through separate roles and permissions in the administration interface.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two admin roles are configured in the UCC platform: 'Change Preparer' and 'Change Approver'. A Preparer can prepare a change for the areas mentioned in the requirement, but cannot activate it. Only an Approver can review and activate the prepared change. All actions are logged in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of administrative roles and permissions in the UCC platform. It is verified that a technical separation between preparation and activation of a change exists for the critical areas. The audit logs are checked for the correct application of the principle.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The administration of SIP trunks is carried out exclusively via a Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution. Changes are handled via an automated workflow with a four-eyes principle. Configuration changes are managed as code (Infrastructure as Code) and changes go through a peer review and an automated testing process before being submitted for approval.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators no longer have direct access to the UCC platform. They check in configuration changes to a Git repository. A pull request triggers automated syntax and security tests. A second administrator must review and approve the code. Only then does a CI/CD pipeline deploy the change to the production system via the PAM solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the PAM solution and the CI/CD pipeline. The Git repository is checked for the history of changes, reviews, and approvals. It is verified that no direct administrative access to the SIP trunk configuration is possible.

controls.title: End-to-end encryption (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only transport encryption is used. End-to-end encryption (E2EE) is not considered a requirement or used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The communication is encrypted on the transport path (e.g., between client and server), but the server operator can view the entire communication in plain text. This is the typical configuration for TLS/SRTP termination on the server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture and determines that the encryption is terminated at the server and therefore there is no end-to-end encryption.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: End-to-end encryption is used for simple communication forms such as 1-to-1 text chats, provided the UCC platform offers this by default. It is not used for calls, video conferences, or group chats.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The chat function of the UCC client is E2E encrypted. However, as soon as a call is started or another person is added to the chat, the communication falls back to transport encryption.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that E2EE is active for 1:1 chats, but tests and confirms that it is not active for other communication forms (groups, calls).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy has been created that requires the use of end-to-end encryption (E2EE) for communications with high protection needs. A UCC solution is used that supports E2EE for 1-to-1 calls and chats, and this feature is enabled for all users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy defines that, for example, conversations of the management or with the legal department must be E2E-encrypted. The UCC solution used is configured so that all direct calls and chats use E2EE by default. For group conferences, the use of transport encryption is pointed out.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy and checks the configuration of the UCC platform to ensure that E2EE is enforced for the defined 1-to-1 scenarios for all users.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure end-to-end encryption SHOULD be used for UCC communication. The E2EE SHOULD extend to both the signaling and the media data of audio and video communication with two or more participants. In conversations between UCC services from different manufacturers, the transmitted information SHOULD be restricted if E2EE is not possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UCC solution is used that also supports E2EE for group conferences (e.g., using MLS or a comparable protocol). This function is enabled by default for all internal conferences. Users are trained to refrain from transmitting sensitive information in mixed conferences with external participants whose clients do not support E2EE.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the technical documentation and configuration of the UCC solution to verify the implementation of E2EE for group conferences. It is checked how users are informed about the E2EE status in mixed conferences.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The end-to-end encryption used is technically enforced for all forms of communication. The implementation uses modern cryptographic properties such as Forward Secrecy and Post-Quantum Cryptography algorithms. The identity of the communication participants is strongly verified before the key exchange (e.g., by comparing security numbers or certificate pinning).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UCC solution is used whose cryptographic implementation is publicly documented and ideally independently audited. The configuration enforces E2EE and does not allow unencrypted or transport-encrypted-only fallbacks. The organization trains users in the verification of security numbers for particularly sensitive conversations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the independent audit reports of the E2EE implementation of the UCC solution. The configuration is checked for strict enforcement of E2EE. The identity verification process is analyzed and the corresponding training materials are reviewed.

controls.title: Restriction of AI functions (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AI functions of the UCC platform (e.g., transcription, summarization, background filters) are used by users without any review or policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users activate the AI-powered summarization feature for meetings without knowing that the conversation data is sent to an external cloud service in an insecure third country for this purpose.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews users and determines that AI functions are being used. An analysis of network traffic shows communication with external AI services.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an organizational policy that advises caution when using AI functions, especially when processing confidential data. However, there are no technical means to prevent their use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An email to the staff points out that AI functions can pose a data protection risk. However, the functions are still available and can be activated in the UCC client for all users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy and compares it with the technical configuration of the UCC platform. It is determined that the policy is not technically enforced.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of AI functions is analyzed as part of a risk assessment. All AI functions that require data processing by external or untrusted services are disabled by default at a technical level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the data protection impact assessment for the UCC platform, each AI function is evaluated. The administrator globally disables all cloud-based AI functions in the admin console. Locally executed functions such as simple background blur remain permitted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the risk assessment or DPIA. In the admin console of the UCC platform, it is verified that the AI functions classified as risky are globally disabled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of AI functions SHOULD be disabled or reduced to a minimum. If a permanent deactivation is not possible or desired, it SHOULD be specified that users of the UCC services purposefully deactivate AI functions at the beginning of a conversation, if this is possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All AI functions are disabled by default. There is a defined process to enable AI functions for specific use cases or user groups after a risk assessment. Users are trained on how to check the status of AI functions at the beginning of each conference and disable them if necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the default configuration (AI disabled) and the enablement process. The training materials for manual deactivation by users are reviewed. The behavior of users is checked through random sampling in conferences.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of AI functions is strictly controlled by technical policies. Only those AI functions are permitted that are demonstrably running 'on-premise' or in a trusted, contractually secured cloud environment without data usage for training purposes. Every activation of an AI function is centrally and audit-proof logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UCC solution that can operate AI functions on its own servers is preferred. For cloud services, contracts are concluded (incl. DPA/SCCs) that exclude any non-purposed use of the data. The activation of AI functions is only possible for specific user roles and is logged and evaluated in the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contracts with the cloud providers and the architecture plans to verify the location of data processing. The configuration of permissions for AI functions and the corresponding audit logs in the SIEM are checked.

controls.title: Use of an SBC at other network perimeters (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no internal network segmentation. All UCC components and clients are in the same, flat network. An SBC is used, if at all, only at the perimeter to the internet.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The internal network is a large, unsegmented LAN. An attacker who compromises a client PC can access the central UCC servers without hindrance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network plan and the configuration of the network components and determines the lack of internal segmentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network is divided into basic segments such as 'clients' and 'servers'. The segmentation is realized by a firewall with simple port forwarding, which does not allow application-specific control of UCC traffic.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal firewall separates the server VLAN from the client VLAN. For UCC, the necessary SIP and RTP ports are opened between the segments. However, the firewall cannot analyze or secure the SIP traffic at the protocol level.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the rules of the internal firewall and determines that they operate purely at the port level and do not perform application layer inspection for UCC protocols.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of the network design, the use of SBCs or application-specific firewalls at transitions between internal network segments with different protection needs is evaluated and planned. In particular, the protection of the server network from the client networks is considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The network concept provides for securing the transition from the client network to the data center network, where the UCC servers are located, with an application-layer firewall or an internal SBC. The implementation is planned for the next renewal of the network infrastructure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network architecture concept and verifies that the use of SBCs or comparable technologies at internal segment boundaries is planned.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to an SBC at the network perimeter to the provider, further SBCs SHOULD be used at internal network perimeters. In this context, network perimeters between network segments with different protection needs SHOULD be particularly considered. The SBC SHOULD ensure that the encryption mechanisms at the secured network segment perimeters are implemented in accordance with requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal SBC is placed between the general client network and the highly protected server network. This SBC enforces that internal communication between clients and servers is also encrypted (TLS/SRTP) and filters SIP traffic for anomalies. Another SBC could secure the transition to a less trusted production network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and function of the internal SBCs based on the network plan and configuration. It is checked whether they control the communication between the segments and enforce encryption.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A zero-trust architecture is implemented in which all UCC communication, even within the same network segment, is routed through a policy enforcement point (such as an SBC or a micro-segmentation gateway). Each communication relationship is explicitly authenticated and authorized before it is permitted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: With the help of micro-segmentation, network access for each UCC server is restricted to the absolutely necessary ports and communication partners. Each connection, e.g., from the client to the server, is checked and approved by a central policy controller. Direct network access between the components is no longer possible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the micro-segmentation solution and the policy controller. It is verified that a 'default-deny' rule applies to network traffic and that every UCC communication must be explicitly permitted by a policy.

controls.title: Restriction of the use of UCC services (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no restrictions on the use of UCC services. All functions are equally available to all users, both internal and external.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every user can use all functions, invite external guests, record conferences, and access all team areas. Multi-factor authentication is not used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests access to various functions with a standard user account and finds that there are no significant restrictions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic restrictions are implemented for external users, e.g., they cannot start conferences. Multi-factor authentication is enabled for administrators, but not for normal users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the admin console, the guest role is configured to have restricted rights. However, the MFA setting for standard users remains disabled so as not to affect usability.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the guest role and the MFA settings for the different user groups.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of UCC services is restricted based on the protection needs of the information being transmitted. The use of multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all internal and external users is planned as a standard. Functions for external users are reduced to the necessary minimum.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy defines which UCC functions may be used for the transmission of data classified as 'confidential'. MFA is rolled out and enforced for all user accounts. The default guest role is configured so that they can only participate in conferences, but cannot share content or use chats.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy on data classification-based usage. The configuration for enforcing MFA for all users is checked. The permissions of the guest role are analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The following aspects SHOULD be considered at a minimum to further secure the UCC services: restriction of services according to protection needs, use of MFA, deactivation of functions for external users, deactivation of metadata storage, restriction of visibility of communication data for admins. In addition, technical and organizational measures SHOULD be taken to secure conversations beyond the allocation of PINs/passwords.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All points mentioned in the requirement are implemented. In particular, the storage of metadata (e.g., call lists) is reduced to the legally necessary minimum. Administrative roles are restricted so that they cannot view content or metadata of user communication. Technical measures such as waiting rooms or the mandatory explicit admission of each participant by a moderator are enforced for external conferences.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a comprehensive configuration review covering all points mentioned in the requirement. In particular, the settings for metadata storage and administrative permissions are audited. The enforced security settings for conferences are tested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The restriction of use is enforced dynamically and automatically by a Conditional Access and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) system. Access to UCC services and functions depends on the user, the end device, the location, and the protection requirements of the data. Every administrative activity requires just-in-time approval via a Privileged Access Management (PAM) system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, a Conditional Access policy requires MFA and a company-managed device for access to UCC. A DLP system blocks the sharing of documents marked as 'confidential' in chats with external participants. An administrator must submit a justified request in the PAM system to receive administrative rights on the UCC platform for a limited time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the Conditional Access policies, the DLP rule set, and the PAM workflows. The complete logging and the effectiveness of these automated controls are verified.

controls.title: Integration of UCC into security monitoring (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The log files of the UCC components are stored locally on the systems with the default settings, but are not centrally collected or evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the event of an error, an administrator logs into the respective UCC server and examines the local log files. There is no proactive or central monitoring of security-relevant events.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that no central log collection for UCC components exists and no integration into a SIEM system has been carried out.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The log files of critical UCC components such as SBCs and central servers are centrally collected and archived. However, there are no specific rules or use cases for the automated evaluation of this data for security incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A log management system collects the syslog messages from the UCC servers. The data is retained for later forensic analysis. Only generic alarms (e.g., 'Server not reachable') are generated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the log management system that the UCC logs are being received. However, it is determined that no specific parsing or correlation rules for UCC security events are implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The central UCC components are integrated into security monitoring. Basic use cases for the detection of security incidents are defined and implemented in the SIEM system, e.g., the detection of a large number of failed login attempts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logs from the UCC servers and SBCs are sent to the SIEM. There are rules that trigger an alarm if there are more than 10 failed logins from the same IP address within one minute. The SOC (Security Operations Center) has an instruction on how to respond to this alarm.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the SIEM system and verifies the implementation of basic detection rules for UCC systems. It is checked whether action instructions (playbooks) exist in the SOC for the resulting alarms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The central UCC components SHOULD be monitored by a security monitoring system. This SHOULD be implemented at least for components that realize encryption endpoints (e.g., MCUs) or are positioned at trust boundaries (e.g., SBCs). If a central detection system (SIEM) is used, the central UCC components SHOULD be integrated into it. Specific detection rules for UCC attacks are implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All SBCs, MCUs, Call Managers, and connected databases send their logs to the SIEM. Specific correlation rules are implemented there to detect, for example, fraud attempts (Toll Fraud), registration hijacking, or attacks on encryption. The rules are based on known attack patterns for the UCC solution in use.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the data sources in the SIEM and ensures that all critical UCC components are covered. The implementation of specific UCC attack detection rules is examined in detail. The effectiveness may be tested by a simulated attack.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security monitoring for UCC uses behavior analytics (User and Entity Behavior Analytics, UEBA) to detect anomalies in communication behavior. The monitoring is integrated into a SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) platform to respond to detected threats automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UEBA module in the SIEM learns the normal call behavior of users and raises an alarm if an account suddenly starts making hundreds of calls to high-risk countries. In case of such an alarm, the SIEM triggers a webhook to the SOAR platform. This platform executes an automated playbook that blocks the suspicious IP address on the SBC and temporarily suspends the user account.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the UEBA module for the UCC data. The SOAR playbooks for UCC security incidents are analyzed. The functionality of the automated response is verified by a test alarm.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Unified Communications refers to a service that combines various communication services in one application and usually also one soft client. This reduces the proportion of traditional telephony in personal digital communication. The possible communication channels are expanded to include additional services such as video, various forms of chat, and presence indicators.
A communication relationship between two or more participants is referred to as a conversation, regardless of the service used.
The collaboration often mentioned in Unified Communications and Collaboration (UCC) goes one step further. While in the past this often only referred to services such as screen sharing and (digital) whiteboarding, UCC services now provide many other functions. Especially in team collaboration, a number of applications have been established that are often used as a cloud service and, in addition to telephony, presence indicators, classic chats, video calls, and conferences, also include team chat areas and shared file storage. There are also (open) interfaces, through which additional applications can be integrated, so that the overall service can become very extensive in terms of functionality.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to establish information security as an integral part of the extended communication spectrum of UCC services, to create awareness of the potential threat situation for these applications, and to offer approaches for avoiding threats.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module APP.5.4 Unified Communications and Collaboration (UCC) is to be applied to all IT systems and communication networks as well as applications with which UCC services are operated.
Since UCC is operated via data networks, the requirements of the modules NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design and NET.3.2 Firewall must also be considered in addition to this module.
As the scope of communication services is increasingly expanding through UCC, there is a particularly large number of overlaps with other modules.
This module covers the following content:
•
the UCC services as well as interaction and interdependencies of different services
•
the (soft) clients that are provided to use these services and their functional scope
•
the associated infrastructure components, unless they are already covered by other modules
•
topics that arise from the seamless transition (from the user's perspective) between the UCC environment and other applications
The following content is also important and is covered elsewhere:
•
If telephony is conducted via a dedicated PBX system, the module NET.4.1 PBX Systems must be applied.
•
For Voice over IP (VoIP) as an elementary service in UCC services, the module NET.4.2 VoIP must be applied.
•
For the central servers as well as various end devices and clients, the modules SYS.1.1 General Server and SYS.2.1 General Client, and if applicable, specific modules must be applied.
•
For the underlying networks, the module NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design must be applied.
•
If UCC services are provided from the cloud, the module OPS.2.2 Cloud Usage must be applied.
•
To secure file storage provided as part of the UCC services, the modules APP.3.3 File Server and SYS.1.8 Storage Solutions are particularly relevant.
This module does not cover the following content:
•
The email service is generally not part of the UCC services. Here, the module APP.5.3 General Email Client and Server must be applied.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Limited availability of UCC services
parts.prose:
UCC services are often subject to increased availability requirements, and at the same time, the functionality of UCC services depends on other IT systems and applications.
If the data networks used by UCC services are not fully functional, this can impair the availability of the UCC services. For example, disruptions in the data network or the internet connection can limit the quality of communication, which can cause delayed speech comprehension, artifacts in the video image, or a dropped connection.
Dependencies between critical IT systems can also hinder the functionality of other services or organizational units. For example, if UCC is absolutely necessary as a communication platform to rebuild the network, but the network is needed for the UCC services to function, then both are blocked and cannot be restored.
UCC services are often used as a cloud service or operated by a service provider, which means that disruptions in external networks or at the service provider can lead to limited availability of the UCC services. The same applies to the authentication service through which users log on to the UCC services. If the authentication service fails, the UCC services can often no longer be used.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Inadequate planning of UCC
parts.prose:
If UCC is not planned according to its intended actual use, this can impact the functionality of all UCC services. If UCC components are modified or used more intensively, e.g., due to an increased number of users, an initially suitable plan can become inadequate.
Depending on the deployment model and the services used, the network requirements for UCC components can vary greatly. For example, a UCC component focused on voice communication on the internal network may have different requirements for internet and WAN connections than a cloud service intended for mobile use. If networks are not planned to accommodate UCC services, the UCC services will not be sufficiently usable.
Similar threats exist for the endpoint devices that need to be considered. Video communication and its associated functions, in particular, place very high demands on clients. This can lead to problems, especially with thin clients, as UCC services are often executed wholly or partly on the endpoint device to optimize communication data streams. Clients with insufficient processing power can cause dropouts or artifacts in video communication, for example.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Incorrect configuration of UCC
parts.prose:
A large number of functions and services often means a multitude of configuration options. This can lead to misconfigurations.
Users may be able or required to configure their UCC clients themselves. The vast number of configuration options can overwhelm users and lead to incorrect configurations. For example, if different headsets are used in the office and at home, the configuration may need to be adjusted. Misconfigurations can result in users not being heard or seen in meetings, or not hearing any sound themselves. Furthermore, information can be unintentionally disclosed if room systems are configured to automatically accept incoming communication requests.
Similarly, an inadequate identity and access management concept can lead to errors when configuring UCC services. Administrators who also change central routing settings when setting up new accounts can cause a serious misconfiguration. This can lead to data loss or the failure of the UCC service.
Misconfigurations due to an inadequate identity and access management concept also include insufficiently restricted permissions for external participants. If they can, for example, access conversation content without authorization, information can be leaked or manipulated.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Unauthorized or abusive use of the administration rights of a UCC service
parts.prose:
Assigned administrative rights allow administrators to make potentially profound changes to UCC services. If administrative rights are used without authorization or abused, this can have far-reaching consequences. For example, administrative rights can be used to make a private area, such as a chat or a file repository, which was originally accessible only to a limited group of people, available to all users of the UCC service. This can allow sensitive information to be viewed and possibly modified by unauthorized persons.
Furthermore, intentionally altered routing configurations can make UCC services unavailable or only partially available. For example, if all outgoing calls are blocked by central IT systems, the telephony service can no longer be used.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Disclosure of sensitive information
parts.prose:
Modern UCC clients have a wide range of functions and are therefore complex for many users. This encourages user errors that can lead to information being shared in a non-compliant manner. If the wrong contact is accidentally selected, they may receive sensitive information via chat unintentionally. Another scenario is unintentionally disclosing information during a screen share, for example, by accidentally sharing the email client instead of the intended presentation.
Many users are not aware that UCC services store data, for example, data sent in private chats, in a cloud. This can lead to unintentional violations of the institution's data retention policies. The same applies to files in which conversations have been recorded.
Although team spaces usually have a defined circle of users and corresponding access restrictions, many users are not aware that access rights and memberships can be modified later. This allows additional people to access all files previously stored there. Furthermore, public team spaces are often created, which other people can join without explicit permission. This may allow data to be viewed by unauthorized persons. For example, a project's team space may consist exclusively of internal users. Participants then upload internal documents because all team members are internal. If external individuals are invited to the space later in the project, they can access all previous documents.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Disclosure of personal information
parts.prose:
UCC services collect data in many places that is also displayed to other users. This can lead to the unintentional disclosure of personal information.
Among other things, the availability of users can be visible. Timestamps on chat posts, and even extensive analytics on conversations, activities, or content for individual users can be part of a UCC component. UCC services can even create user profiles. People without extended permissions often gain access to these analytics. This allows them to draw conclusions about the working hours, work content, and personal relationships of others and use this for performance monitoring, for example.
When using virtual conferences for remote work, private information can be unintentionally transmitted to conference participants. This includes, for example, people walking through the video frame, personal objects in the background of a video feed, or noises and voices from the private environment.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Interactions in UCC services
parts.prose:
UCC services can have interactions with each other that restrict functionality.
To improve the user experience, different services are often linked in a single user interface. However, this can lead to dependencies between the services. For example, if the video conferencing service is integrated into a team collaboration interface, the video service can no longer be used if the interface fails.
UCC services often use shared resources. This can lead to conflicts that impair functionality. For example, if headsets are used by a telephony and a video conferencing application at the same time, the headsets can be blocked by one application and then no longer be available for the other.
Some applications have very high resource requirements. If multiple UCC services are running on an IT system at the same time, this can cause the client to become overloaded and the IT system to fail or crash. For example, if several video conferencing applications are running in parallel in the background, the resulting memory load can severely impact the client.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Access to applications or resources by sharing control
parts.prose:
When desktop or screen content is displayed to participants in a conversation, the presenter can transfer control to other users. However, this can lead to the presenter losing control over further actions.
Since the feature is often available but generally rarely used, many users are not familiar with its operation, accept the control request, and then lose control of their client. For example, users may grant control of their mouse without knowing how to end the sharing session. This could potentially allow conversation participants to access other applications on the client.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Impersonation of false identities
parts.prose:
The introduction of new UCC services and new ways for external parties to make contact create new avenues for attackers who want to impersonate trusted communication partners to obtain confidential information.
The complexity of UCC services increases the likelihood of user error or unintentional violations of security policies by users. For example, hyperlinks to malicious content may be opened because UCC services are perceived as an internal platform with a higher level of trust.
Often, users are not aware that they can also be contacted by unknown external parties. This makes them more susceptible to social engineering, for example, via a chat or a conversation invitation.
Furthermore, attackers can manipulate their displayed names, their voice, or their appearance. For example, an external person can impersonate a manager on the supposedly internal communication platform to obtain confidential information or documents directly via chat.

controls.title: Planning of software use (B) [Functional Owners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of software use is only sporadic and not documented. Decisions are made ad-hoc for individual software acquisitions. Often, only the primary purpose of the software is considered, while aspects such as resource requirements, integration, or vendor dependencies are overlooked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, there is no formal process. Planning is often limited to informal emails or brief meetings where basic functionality is discussed. There are no templates or checklists.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks through spot checks of recently introduced software whether a planning phase has taken place at all. This is done by interviewing the responsible employees and reviewing project communication (e.g., emails).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic but informal checklist for software planning exists, covering key points such as purpose and resource requirements. User involvement is minimal and responsibilities are assigned only informally. The process is applied to most new software products but is not formally documented or approved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple checklist in a text document or on a wiki page is used as a guideline. However, the results are not systematically stored or versioned. Security aspects are mentioned in general terms but not considered in detail.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the checklist used for software introduction and compares it across several projects. It is checked whether the basic planning points were consistently considered, even if formal documentation is missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before an institution introduces (new) software, it MUST decide what the software will be used for, how users will be involved, how integration will take place, what resources are needed, and whether a vendor dependency will arise. Security aspects MUST already be considered here. In addition, the institution MUST clarify, define, and document the responsibilities for functional support, approval, and operational administration in advance. The responsibilities MUST be updated as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The results of the planning phase are recorded in a standardized document that serves as the basis for the next steps. This document is created by the functional owners and coordinated with IT operations. Responsibilities are recorded in a RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) matrix.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and completeness of the planning documents for newly introduced software. It is verified that all points mentioned in the requirement (purpose, users, integration, resources, dependency, security) have been addressed. In addition, the documentation of responsibilities is checked for clarity and completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process is integrated into a higher-level IT portfolio management. A formal template for software planning is used, which includes a detailed risk assessment regarding vendor dependency and data processing. The documentation is stored in a central repository, and user feedback is systematically collected and considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Planning is carried out via a standardized form on the intranet or in a ticket system. The risk assessment for vendor dependency includes an analysis of the vendor's financial stability and the availability of alternative products. User feedback is collected through structured surveys.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the planning process is formalized and integrated into higher-level processes. The use of formal templates and the performance of the detailed risk assessment are verified. The storage of documents in the central repository and the systematic collection of user feedback are also checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire process of software planning and introduction is managed and monitored by a dedicated tool (e.g., an IT Service Management suite). The strategic alignment with business goals is formally assessed. Vendor dependencies are continuously monitored, and for all critical software products, exit strategies are defined and regularly reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IT portfolio management tool is used to manage the software lifecycle from idea to decommissioning. The exit strategies define technical and organizational steps for a switch to an alternative product, including data migration and retraining.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and the process mapping in the management tool. The existence and quality of the exit strategies for critical applications are verified. Automated reports from the tool are used to check the continuous monitoring of vendor dependencies.

controls.title: Creation of a requirements catalog for software (B) [Functional Owners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Requirements for software are collected informally, often just as a list of desired features in an email. Security and legal requirements are not systematically considered or are completely overlooked. There is no formal requirements catalog.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Requirements are exchanged ad-hoc in meetings or via email. There is no central collection or structuring of the requirements. The focus is exclusively on user-visible functions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews the project stakeholders and checks the available communication (e.g., emails, meeting notes) to determine if and in what form requirements were captured. The absence of a structured document is noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic template for a requirements catalog is used, but it mainly focuses on functional aspects. Security requirements are mentioned but are formulated generically (e.g., 'must be secure') and are not specific. The catalog is created but not formally approved by all stakeholders.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple Word or Excel template is used to record the requirements. The requirements of the business department are recorded, but those of IT operations or security are only covered superficially. A formal coordination does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the created requirements catalogs for the use of a template. It is assessed whether, in addition to functional requirements, non-functional requirements (especially security) are at least fundamentally recorded. The absence of a formal coordination process is noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the results of the planning, the requirements for the software MUST be collected in a requirements catalog. The requirements catalog MUST include the basic functional and non-functional requirements, especially the security requirements. The requirements of the business owners, IT operations, and legal requirements MUST be taken into account. The completed requirements catalog SHOULD be coordinated with all affected departments.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirements catalog is created as a structured document that clearly separates functional, non-functional, security, and legal requirements. Workshops with business owners, IT operations, the data protection officer, and the information security officer are conducted for the collection process. Coordination is carried out via a documented review process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the requirements catalogs for completeness with regard to the mentioned types of requirements (functional, non-functional, security, legal). It is verified that the requirements of various stakeholders (business department, IT operations) have been incorporated. The evidence of coordination with the affected departments is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements catalog is a formal, versioned document. It uses a standardized structure that distinguishes between mandatory and desirable requirements (e.g., according to MoSCoW). Security requirements are specific and traceable to the institution's security policies. The coordination process is formally documented and requires the signature of all department heads.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The catalog is managed in a document management system with versioning. Each requirement has a unique ID and a priority (e.g., Must-have, Should-have, Could-have, Won't-have). Security requirements are derived from a central security requirements catalog. Approval is given digitally via a workflow.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the versioning and the formal structure of the requirements catalog. The traceability of security requirements to the higher-level policies is checked on a random basis. The formal approval records (e.g., digital signatures) are verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire requirements process is managed in a specialized tool for requirements management. The requirements are traceable from their source (e.g., business requirement, legal regulation) to implementation and testing. The process includes automated checks against a central library of standard security and data protection requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like Jira with specific plug-ins or a dedicated requirements engineering tool is used. Each requirement is created as a separate object with attributes such as source, status, and test case link. An automated process checks newly created requirements against predefined rules and security templates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process mapping in the requirements management tool. Using examples, the end-to-end traceability of a requirement from its creation to the acceptance test is verified. The configuration of the automated checks against the requirements library is inspected.

controls.title: Secure Procurement of Software (B) [Procurement Office]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Software is occasionally downloaded from unofficial sources or via personal accounts. Integrity checks are not performed. Maintenance contracts are not considered during procurement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees download software from third-party download portals or use private licenses. There is no process for verifying the origin or integrity of the software.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks, by interviewing employees and analyzing installed software, whether there are cases of procurement from non-official sources. The absence of processes for integrity checks and for concluding maintenance contracts is noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Software is generally procured from official manufacturer websites or well-known distributors. Integrity checks (e.g., hash values) are performed if they are easily available, but not systematically enforced. Maintenance is considered, but may not cover the entire lifecycle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement office has an informal list of preferred distributors. The IT staff checks hash values if they are prominently displayed on the download page. There is no clear instruction on what to do if hash values are missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the source of supply for several procurement processes. It is checked on a random basis whether available hash values were used for integrity checks. The existing maintenance contracts are checked for their term and basic content.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When software is procured, a suitable software MUST be selected based on the requirements catalog. The selected software MUST be procured from trusted sources. The trusted source SHOULD provide a way to check the software for integrity. In addition, the software SHOULD be procured with a suitable maintenance contract that specifically guarantees that emerging security vulnerabilities will be fixed in a timely manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement office selects software only from manufacturers or certified distributors. IT operations is instructed to verify the integrity of every downloaded software using hash values or digital signatures and to document the result. Standardized requirements for maintenance contracts (e.g., response times for security incidents) are negotiated during procurement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the software selection is based on the requirements catalog. It is verified that the software comes from trusted sources and that the integrity check has been documented. The concluded maintenance contracts are checked for the required guarantees for fixing security vulnerabilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A list of approved, trusted software sources is maintained. Integrity checking (hash values, digital signatures) is mandatory for all procured software and is logged. Maintenance contracts are formally reviewed by the legal and IT security departments before conclusion to ensure they meet defined SLAs for vulnerability response.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement office maintains a whitelist of suppliers in its system. The integrity check process is integrated into a script or checklist for software deployment. For maintenance contracts, there is a standard template with the required security SLAs, which serves as a basis for negotiation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence, maintenance, and application of the whitelist for software sources. The logs of the performed integrity checks are inspected. It is verified that the maintenance contracts have gone through the formal review process and contain the defined SLAs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement process is integrated into a supplier risk management system. The trustworthiness of the sources is continuously reassessed. The integrity check of the software is automated as part of the software onboarding process. Maintenance contracts include financial penalties for non-compliance with patching SLAs. A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is requested from the manufacturer by default.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An automated script fetches new software versions from the manufacturer's source, automatically checks the digital signature and hash value, and, if successful, uploads the software to an internal, trusted repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the automated software onboarding process and the logs of the automatic integrity checks. The integration with supplier risk management is verified. It is checked on a random basis whether SBOMs are available for newly procured software and whether the contracts contain corresponding clauses (SLAs, penalties).

controls.title: Regulation for the installation and configuration of software (B) [Business Owners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Installations are performed manually by various people with default settings ('click-through'). There are no formal rules for configuration, which leads to inconsistent and often insecure setups. Patches, if any, are only applied after commissioning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each administrator installs software to the best of their knowledge and belief. The manufacturer's default configuration is adopted without modification. Configuration is not documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the same software on multiple systems and identifies inconsistencies. The absence of installation and configuration policies is confirmed by interviewing the administrators.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are informal guidelines for installation. Minimal functionality and least privilege are aimed for, but not consistently enforced or documented. The integrity of installation files is sporadically checked. A 'standard' configuration exists as a mental model, but is not formally documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The team wiki contains a simple checklist for new installations, which includes points like 'disable unnecessary features'. The implementation is at the discretion of the individual administrator.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks for the existence of informal guidelines (e.g., wiki pages). It is checked on a random basis whether basic hardening measures have been implemented. The absence of a formal, documented standard configuration is noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation and configuration of the software MUST be regulated by IT operations in such a way that it is only executed with the least necessary scope of functions, with the least possible permissions, and with data-minimizing settings. All relevant security patches MUST be installed before production use. Dependent components MUST also be considered. IT operations MUST create installation instructions if a manual installation is required. IT operations MUST regulate how the integrity of the installation files is checked. If digital signatures or checksums are available for an installation package, they MUST be used to check the integrity. If necessary, IT operations SHOULD define and document a secure standard configuration of the software.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration and hardening guide is created for each standard software and stored in the central knowledge management system. This guide describes the standard configuration and the steps for verifying integrity. A detailed step-by-step guide is available for manual installations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and quality of the regulations and instructions for installation and configuration. It is verified that a documented standard configuration exists and that the process for integrity checking is defined. Random checks are performed on production systems to see if the configuration complies with the documented standard.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All software installations are carried out centrally by IT operations, ideally using automated distribution tools. The secure standard configuration is implemented as a script or configuration template. Deviations from the standard configuration require formal approval. Integrity checks are mandatory and are logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A software distribution solution (e.g., Microsoft SCCM, Matrix42 Empirum) is used to distribute software packages automatically. The hardening settings are applied via Group Policies (GPOs) or the distribution solution itself. Deviations are requested and approved via a change management process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the software distribution solution. It is verified that the standard configurations are stored as automated templates or scripts. The logs of the installations and integrity checks, as well as the documentation of the approved deviations, are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully automated system for 'Infrastructure as Code' (IaC) or configuration management (e.g., Ansible, Puppet) is used for all installations and configurations. The secure standard configurations are stored in a version control system and are automatically applied and enforced. A system continuously monitors for configuration deviations and either corrects them automatically or triggers an alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Ansible playbooks or Puppet manifests define the desired state of a system, including the installed software and its exact configuration. These configuration files are managed in a Git repository. A monitoring tool such as Ansible check mode or specialized compliance tools periodically check the system state against the definitions in the repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the IaC scripts and configuration definitions in the version control system. The configuration of the automation and monitoring system is verified. Reports from the monitoring tool are analyzed to assess the effectiveness of the automatic enforcement and correction of configurations.

controls.title: Secure installation of software (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users occasionally install unapproved software or versions other than the specified ones. Deviations from the (informal) specifications are not tracked or documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees with local administrator rights install software at their own discretion. There are no technical controls to prevent this.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a random check of the software installed on the client systems and compares it with a list of approved standard software. Deviations are documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Installations generally follow the rules, but there is no active enforcement. Unmodified versions are used, but this is based on trust rather than verification. Approvals for deviations are informal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a company policy that prohibits the installation of unapproved software. However, compliance is not technically enforced or regularly checked. Deviations are approved by email to the supervisor.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence of the policy. The informal approval process for deviations is understood by interviewing employees and supervisors.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Software MUST be installed on the IT systems in accordance with the regulation for installation. In doing so, only unmodified versions of the released software MUST be used. If these instructions are deviated from, this MUST be approved by supervisors and IT operations and documented accordingly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installation is carried out by IT operations, who follow the instructions from the configuration and hardening guide. The use of unmodified versions is ensured by the previously performed integrity check. Approvals for deviations are requested, approved, and documented via a ticket system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the installations carried out comply with the documented regulations. It is verified that only released software versions have been installed. For any deviations found, proof of approval and documentation in the ticket system is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Technical controls (e.g., application whitelisting) are implemented to prevent the installation of unauthorized software. The installation process automatically logs which version was installed on which system. The approval process for deviations is managed via a formal change management system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technologies such as AppLocker or other application control solutions are used to block the execution of unapproved installation files. The software distribution solution automatically creates logs of all installations performed. Changes to the whitelist require an approved change request.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the application whitelisting solution. The logs of the software distribution are inspected and checked for completeness. The process for approving deviations is traced in the change management system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of the system is continuously monitored to detect any unauthorized changes to installed software. The deployment pipeline automatically ensures that only approved, unmodified, and digitally signed software packages from a trusted internal repository can be installed. Any attempt at a deviation is automatically blocked and triggers a security alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) solution is active on all systems. The CI/CD pipeline for software distribution includes a step that verifies the digital signature of each package against a trust store with the keys of the approved manufacturers and the internal signing key. Failed installations due to signature errors are reported to the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and reports of the FIM solution. The configuration of the deployment pipeline, in particular the signature verification step, is analyzed. The rules in the SIEM for alerting on blocked installation attempts are verified.

controls.title: Consideration of recommended security requirements (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security requirements are treated as an afterthought in software selection. If a security feature like logging happens to be present, it may be used, but there is no proactive requirement for it during selection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection of software is based almost exclusively on functional criteria and costs. Security features are only considered if they solve an immediate problem.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the requirements catalogs (if any) for the systematic query of security functions. The absence of such requirements is noted.
