parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements catalog contains basic security requirements such as 'must support authentication'. However, more advanced topics such as hardening functions, secure protocols, or certificate management are not explicitly specified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirements catalog has a 'Security' section, but it only contains general, non-specific points. The evaluation is limited to the presence, but not the quality or configurability of the security features.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the requirements catalogs contain a security section. The specificity of the requirements is assessed, and it is determined that only basic functions are queried.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD consider the following security requirements in the requirements catalog for the software: The software SHOULD include general security functions such as logging and authentication that are required in the application context. It SHOULD make it possible to use the hardening functions of the deployment environment. If data is transmitted over public networks, the software SHOULD use secure encryption functions and check data integrity. If the software uses certificates, it SHOULD enable their transparent display and management. These functions SHOULD also be used in operation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirements catalog contains a detailed checklist for security requirements covering the points mentioned (logging, authentication, hardening, encryption, certificate management). During the evaluation, it is checked whether the software not only offers these functions, but also allows their configuration in accordance with internal security policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the requirements catalogs for the systematic consideration of the mentioned security aspects. It is verified that the evaluation documentation contains a check of these functions. A random check is carried out on installed software to see whether the required and existing security functions are actually configured and activated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security requirements are specific and detailed (e.g., 'must support MFA via OIDC', 'must log all authentication attempts to the central SIEM', 'must use TLS 1.3'). The ability to integrate into the central security infrastructure (such as SIEM or Identity Provider) is a key selection criterion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security department provides a catalog of specific, measurable security requirements that must be incorporated into the general requirements catalog for software. The integration with the central IdP and SIEM is technically tested as part of a Proof-of-Concept (PoC).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the security requirements in the requirements catalog are specific and measurable. The PoC documentation is reviewed to verify the successful testing of the integration capability. The configuration of the connection to the central security infrastructure is checked in the production system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution maintains a comprehensive, mandatory library of security requirements (a 'secure baseline profile'). Every new software must be evaluated against this profile. The requirements include advanced topics such as support for Hardware Security Modules (HSMs), detailed cryptographic agility, and the provision of a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM). Compliance with these requirements is verified by automated tests before the software is approved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal 'Security Requirements Profile' is documented and versioned. Part of the software onboarding process is an automated scan or a test suite that checks the software candidates against this profile. The requirement of an SBOM and its analysis for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) is a mandatory step before release.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the 'Security Requirements Profile' for timeliness and completeness. The configuration and the results of the automated test suite are analyzed. It is checked on a random basis whether SBOMs are available and have been analyzed for newly introduced critical software.

controls.title: Selection and evaluation of potential software (S) [Subject matter experts, Procurement department]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the requirements catalog, the products available on the market SHOULD be reviewed. They SHOULD be compared with each other using a rating scale. Afterwards, it SHOULD be examined whether the shortlisted products meet the institution's requirements. If there are several alternatives, user acceptance and the additional effort (e.g., for training) SHOULD also be considered. Subject matter experts, together with IT operations, SHOULD select a suitable software product based on the evaluations and test results.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A market analysis is conducted and the results are summarized in a comparison table. The rating scale contains criteria that are directly derived from the requirements catalog. For the top 2-3 candidates, test environments are set up or demo versions are evaluated. The final selection is justified in a report.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the market analysis documentation and the evaluation table. It is verified that the evaluation criteria are consistent with the requirements catalog. The documentation of the test results and the report of the final selection decision are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evaluation process uses a formal, weighted scoring matrix. A proof-of-concept (PoC) is conducted for the top candidates to test them in a lab environment. A formal report documenting the evaluation process, scores, and PoC results is created to justify the final decision.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The criteria in the scoring matrix are weighted to reflect priorities (e.g., security, cost, functionality). The PoC takes place in a test environment that mirrors the production environment and is conducted by a test team with predefined test cases. The final report is signed by the project manager and the information security officer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the weighted scoring matrix and the definition of the weights. The test plans and logs from the PoC are analyzed. The formal final report and the corresponding approvals are verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The evaluation process is integrated into a supplier risk management program. For critical software, third-party security certifications (e.g., Common Criteria) or independent penetration tests are required. The PoC includes rigorous security tests and integration tests with the existing security infrastructure (SIEM, IdP). The final decision is formally approved by a cross-functional committee (including security, legal, data protection, and the business department).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the PoC, a risk assessment of the manufacturer is carried out. The results of external penetration tests or certifications are directly incorporated into the weighted scoring matrix. The final decision is made and documented in a meeting of the IT steering committee.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the integration of the process into the supplier risk management. The requirement and evaluation of external security evidence (certificates, test reports) is verified. The minutes of the decision-making committee are inspected to confirm the formal and multidisciplinary approval.

controls.title: Regulation on the availability of installation files (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD ensure the availability of the installation files to be able to reproduce the installation. For this purpose, IT operations SHOULD back up the installation files appropriately or ensure their availability through the source. In addition, it SHOULD be ensured that software can be configured in a reproducible manner. For this, the configuration files SHOULD be backed up, or it SHOULD be documented how the software is configured. This regulation SHOULD be integrated into the institution's data backup concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central, secure network share is set up as a software library. For each software, the installation files and a document with the configuration settings are stored there. This library is backed up as part of the regular backup process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and organization of the software library. It is checked on a random basis whether the corresponding installation and configuration files/documentation are available for installed software. The integration of the library into the data backup concept and the backup logs are verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a central, versioned software repository (e.g., Artifactory, Nexus) for all approved installation files and their dependencies. All configuration files are managed as 'Configuration as Code' in a version control system (e.g., Git), enabling fully reproducible deployments. The backup and restore process for this repository is tested regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central repository (e.g., Artifactory) is used for binary files. The configuration instructions (e.g., Ansible playbooks, PowerShell DSC scripts) are stored in a Git repository. Every change to the configuration can be tracked as a commit. Restore tests are performed semi-annually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the software and configuration repositories. The commit history in the Git repository is checked on a random basis for traceability. The logs of the performed restore tests are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The software and configuration repository is geographically replicated for high availability. The process for retrieving, verifying, storing, and deploying software is fully automated. The system automatically manages the installers for the current version (N) and the previous version (N-1) to enable quick rollbacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Artifactory repository is operated in a high-availability cluster distributed across two data centers. The CI/CD pipeline automatically fetches, checks, and stores new software versions. The system retains the last two versions of each software marked as stable.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the architecture and configuration of the high-availability repository solution. The CI/CD pipeline definition is analyzed to verify the degree of automation. It is checked whether the repository holds versions N and N-1 for critical applications as intended.

controls.title: Inventory of software (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Software SHOULD be inventoried. An inventory SHOULD document on which systems the software is used and under which license. If necessary, the security-relevant settings SHOULD also be recorded. Software SHOULD only be used with licenses that correspond to the purpose and contractual provisions. The inventory SHOULD be updated on an ad-hoc basis and be structured in such a way that a quick overall overview is possible in the event of security incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central Excel spreadsheet or a simple database is maintained as a software inventory. After each installation or uninstallation, this list is manually updated by IT operations. The inventory contains columns for software name, version, license type, number of licenses, and the systems/servers on which it is installed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the software inventory and checks it for completeness and timeliness by comparing it with data from the asset inventory and random checks on real systems. It is checked whether license information is available and whether the process for updating the inventory is defined.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated discovery tool is used to scan the network and endpoints to create and maintain the software inventory. The inventory is linked to the asset inventory and the CMDB. The system generates warnings for unlicensed software or non-compliant installations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An inventory solution (e.g., Lansweeper, SCCM inventory) regularly scans all systems and automatically updates the CMDB with the discovered software installations. The solution's license management module is used to monitor compliance and generate reports on under- or over-licensing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the automated discovery tool and the frequency of the scans. The linking of the data with the CMDB is verified. The reports and warnings from the license management system are inspected to assess the effectiveness of the monitoring.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The software inventory is a dynamic real-time system that not only lists installed software but also generates a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for each application. This inventory is integrated with a vulnerability scanner and a threat intelligence feed to proactively identify systems with vulnerable software components. In the event of an incident, the system can immediately identify all affected assets.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An advanced asset management tool is used that extracts SBOMs from the software packages during inventorying or imports them from the manufacturers. The SBOM data is continuously compared with CVE databases and threat intelligence sources. The result is a dashboard that displays the risk from vulnerable components in real time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the inventory tool and the process for generating and importing SBOMs. The integration with the vulnerability and threat intelligence data sources is verified. Using a current CVE, it is checked whether the system is able to correctly and promptly identify all affected software instances and assets.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for the use of software (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD summarize the regulations that define how the software is used and operated in a security policy. The policy SHOULD be known to all relevant managers and employees. In terms of content, the policy SHOULD also include a user manual. It SHOULD be regularly checked whether the employees are adhering to the policy. The policy SHOULD be updated regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate policy document is created for each important software or software category. This document describes the permitted use, the configuration of security options, and the responsibilities. It is published on the intranet and communicated during training sessions. It is updated annually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence, availability, and timeliness of the security policies for software. By interviewing employees, their knowledge of the policies is checked on a random basis. The logs of the regular reviews and updates are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a dedicated, role-based security policy for software usage (e.g., different rules for users, administrators, developers). The policy is published on the intranet, and employees must formally confirm that they have read and understood it. Spot checks and audits are conducted regularly, and the results are formally tracked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy framework has a modular structure and is assigned to the roles in the identity management system. As part of the onboarding process, new employees must read the policies relevant to their role and confirm this with a click. The results of audits are recorded as tickets in a system for tracking measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the role-based structure of the policies. The system for tracking read receipts is verified. The audit reports and the associated measure tracking tickets are inspected to confirm consistent review and remediation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is a living document integrated into the ISMS. Policy content is provided to users in context (e.g., as in-app tips). Compliance is monitored through technical controls and analysis of user behavior where appropriate and permissible. Policy updates are automatically triggered by changes in the risk landscape or the introduction of new technologies and are managed through a formal change control process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool is used to manage the policy framework. This tool is linked to the SIEM and other monitoring tools to technically detect policy violations. When new software is introduced, a workflow is automatically started to review and adapt the relevant policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and processes in the GRC tool. The technical implementation of monitoring for policy violations is analyzed. The change management process for policy changes is reviewed using examples (e.g., after the introduction of a new cloud application).

controls.title: Use of plug-ins and extensions (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only strictly necessary plug-ins and extensions SHOULD be installed. If extensions are used, the software SHOULD provide the ability to configure and disable extensions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the initial configuration of a software, all plug-ins and extensions not required by default are disabled or uninstalled. This configuration is part of the documented standard installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the standard configuration documentation to see if it contains instructions for disabling unnecessary plug-ins. Spot checks on installed systems verify whether these instructions have been implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal whitelisting process for plug-ins is established. Only approved plug-ins from the whitelist can be installed. This is enforced by technical controls (e.g., GPOs, MDM policies). A regular review is conducted to remove unused but approved plug-ins.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For common applications such as browsers or office suites, the permitted plug-ins are managed centrally via group policies or an MDM solution. Users cannot install unlisted plug-ins themselves. The whitelist is reviewed once a year, and plug-ins that are no longer needed are removed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the GPO/MDM policies for plug-in management. The whitelist and the process for its approval are inspected. The logs of the annual review are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security of all whitelisted plug-ins is continuously monitored (e.g., through code scans, supplier assessments). Plug-ins are centrally deployed and managed via an automated system. The system enforces the principle of least functionality by default by disabling all plug-ins unless they are explicitly enabled by a role-based policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before a plug-in is added to the whitelist, it undergoes a security assessment. Distribution is handled via central software distribution. The configurations enforce a 'default-deny' principle for plug-ins, and necessary plug-ins are specifically enabled only for certain user groups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the security assessments for plug-ins. The configuration of the software distribution and the role-based activation is analyzed. It is verified that for a standard user, no or only the absolutely necessary plug-ins are active by default.

controls.title: Regulated decommissioning of software (S) [Business Owners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When software is decommissioned, IT operations SHOULD coordinate with the business owners on how this is to be carried out in detail. It SHOULD also be determined how the users are to be informed about this. It SHOULD be clarified whether the functional requirements persist (e.g., for processing archive data). If this is the case, then it SHOULD be determined how the required functions will remain available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a checklist for decommissioning software. This includes items such as 'inform users,' 'archive data,' 'uninstall system.' If data is in a proprietary format, it is checked whether a read-only license or a conversion tool is needed to meet retention periods.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: For recently decommissioned software, the auditor checks whether the decommissioning checklist was used. It is checked whether the users were informed and whether a solution was found for accessing archive data. The documentation of the process is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a formal decommissioning procedure. It includes a data migration plan, an archiving strategy for required data, and a communication plan for all stakeholders. The process is tracked as a formal project. Legal retention obligations are explicitly considered and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decommissioning process is created and tracked as a change request in the change management system. The plan includes technical steps (data export, conversion), organizational steps (communication to users, works council), and legal steps (review of retention obligations by the legal department).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the formal decommissioning plan in the change management system. It is verified that all aspects (data migration, archiving, communication, legal review) are covered. The documentation of the successfully completed data migration and archiving is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire application lifecycle, including decommissioning, is managed in an IT portfolio management system. The decommissioning plan includes the destruction of cryptographic keys associated with the application's data, formal sign-off by the data owners, and a post-decommissioning review to ensure no remnants are left on the systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the IT portfolio management tool, the application's status is set to 'decommissioned,' which triggers an automated workflow. This workflow includes the secure deletion of data and keys, the deactivation of associated service accounts, and the removal of firewall rules. A final audit script scans the systems to confirm complete removal.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the decommissioning process mapped in the IT portfolio management tool. The documentation on key destruction and the formal approvals by the data owners are inspected. The results of the final audit scan are used to confirm complete removal.

controls.title: Uninstallation of software (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When software is uninstalled, all created and no longer needed files SHOULD be removed. All entries made in system files for the product that are no longer needed SHOULD be reverted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Part of the decommissioning checklist is an item that requires manual checking and deletion of remaining program folders (e.g., in 'Program Files', 'ProgramData', '%APPDATA%') and known configuration files after automatic uninstallation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: On a system from which software was recently uninstalled, the auditor checks whether known locations for application data still contain remnants of the software. The uninstallation checklist is checked for instructions on manual cleanup.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standardized uninstallation script is used that not only runs the official uninstaller but also actively searches for and removes common remaining files, directories, and configuration entries. After uninstallation, a check is performed to verify a clean removal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For standard applications, PowerShell or batch scripts are created that encapsulate the uninstallation process. After calling the uninstaller, the script specifically deletes known remnants. The script logs its actions in a log file.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the uninstallation scripts for completeness and correctness. The log files of the performed un-installations are randomly inspected to confirm the successful cleanup.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The uninstallation process is fully automated via a configuration management system. The system uses a snapshot or a manifest created during installation to ensure that every file, registry key, and configuration change is perfectly reverted. For critical systems, the application may have been run in a container, and decommissioning simply consists of destroying the container image and its persistent volumes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The software distribution solution creates a manifest of the created files and registry entries during each installation. This manifest is used during uninstallation to perform a complete cleanup. Alternatively, the application is deployed via Docker or a similar container technology, where uninstallation is equivalent to deleting the container.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the ability of the software distribution solution to create and use installation manifests. For containerized applications, the decommissioning procedure is reviewed. It is verified that the chosen method ensures the complete removal of application artifacts.

controls.title: Use of certified software (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When procuring software for use in high protection requirement scenarios, it SHOULD be determined whether vendor assurances regarding implemented security functions are recognized as sufficiently trustworthy. If this is not the case, a certification of the application, e.g., according to Common Criteria, SHOULD be used as a decision criterion. If several products are available, security certificates SHOULD be considered, especially if the evaluated scope of functions covers the minimum functionality and the strength of the mechanism corresponds to the protection requirement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the selection process for software with high protection requirements, an explicit risk decision is made as to whether certification is required. If so, the existence of a relevant certificate (e.g., Common Criteria) becomes a knock-out criterion. It is checked whether the certificate (Security Target) covers the functions that are actually required.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks during procurement processes for high protection requirements whether the requirement for certified software has been evaluated. If certification was required, it is checked whether the selected product's certificate is valid and its scope (Security Target) matches the institution's requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is a mandatory policy that for all software processing highly sensitive data, either a recognized security certification (such as CC EAL4+ or FIPS 140-2) is required, or an independent third-party source code review and penetration test must be conducted. The results are formally analyzed by the security team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT security policy includes a section that mandates the requirement for certifications or external tests for software in the 'high' protection requirement category. The procurement department is instructed to request corresponding proof from the manufacturer. The analysis reports of the security tests are archived.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the IT security policy for the mandatory requirement of certificates or tests. It is verified that for procured high-protection-requirement software, corresponding certificates or test reports are available and that they have been evaluated by the security team.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution defines specific Protection Profiles (PPs) for its critical use cases. Software is only procured if it has been certified against these specific PPs or a comparable international standard. The institution actively collaborates with vendors to encourage them to pursue relevant certifications for their products. For critically in-house developed software, a formal certification is sought.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In collaboration with the BSI or other bodies, the company's own protection profiles for key applications (e.g., 'Secure Document Management System') are developed and published. These PPs are the mandatory basis for tenders. For in-house developments, the requirements of the Common Criteria are already considered in the design phase.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and application of the company's own protection profiles in tender and procurement documents. Communication with vendors regarding certification requirements is analyzed. For in-house developments, the consideration of certification requirements in the development documents is checked.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
This module groups all software under the term General Software, regardless of whether it is a word processor, an operating system, a mobile communication app, custom-developed software, or a distributed content management system.
As a rule, all software goes through a lifecycle that includes planning, requirements gathering, procurement, software testing including approval, installation in the production environment, training, operation, updates and change management, as well as decommissioning including deinstallation. This lifecycle can vary depending on the application context, so that individual applications may have additional individual intermediate steps and the scope of the individual steps also varies.
However, recurring aspects of information security arise in the listed intermediate steps that can be applied to any type of software.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The module shows which security requirements must be met so that general software can be used securely throughout its entire lifecycle. The primary goal is to protect the software and the information processed with it.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The APP.6 General Software module is generally to be applied to any software used in the information domain. Excluded from this are operating systems that run on closed systems such as IoT devices, routers, printers, or embedded systems. Software is often delivered in bundles (e.g., office suites or operating systems with extensively integrated on-board tools) or extended with plug-ins, add-ons, or comparable extensions. In such cases, the module can be applied once to the entire software bundle.
This module only deals with standardized and generic procedures in the software lifecycle. No specific recommendations are described on how to configure software in detail and how it should be secured by individual protection mechanisms on the IT systems used. For this, the specific modules of the APP layer must be applied.
The intermediate steps of approval (including software tests) and patch and change management are not covered in this module, but in the modules OPS.1.1.6 Software Tests and Approvals and OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management.
If software requirements cannot be met by a finished software product, e.g., by adjusting the configuration, but an individually developed product is needed, then the APP.7 Development of Custom Software module must be modeled in addition.
Software and its associated data must often be available even in emergencies. The module DER.4 Emergency Management presents initial considerations on this.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Unsuitable selection of software
parts.prose:
For many purposes and applications, a wide variety of software solutions are offered on the market. If unsuitable software is selected that does not meet the institution's requirements, operations can be significantly disrupted. For example, file formats might not be compatible with programs already in use, or new products might have too limited a range of functions. This can lead to performance losses, disruptions, or errors within business processes.
Especially if the software does not meet the institution's security requirements, the data processed with the software could be disclosed or manipulated, e.g., if login functions of applications have not been designed for the planned operating environment in an open data network.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Disclosure of sensitive information through faulty configuration
parts.prose:
If a software is configured incorrectly, sensitive information can be unintentionally disclosed, e.g., if unneeded functions are still activated, such as cloud backup functions that unintentionally synchronize data to a cloud. This could allow sensitive data to be viewed and disclosed by unauthorized third parties.
This can lead to financial losses or damage the reputation of an institution. In addition, the institution could also violate applicable law, e.g., if personal data is disclosed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Obtaining software from an unreliable source
parts.prose: If software is obtained from unreliable sources, it is not guaranteed that an unmodified original version of the software is being used. Instead, a defective or compromised version of the software might have been obtained. This also applies to extensions such as plug-ins or add-ons. If compromised software is installed, malicious code can be distributed within the institution. It is also possible that the software will not function as intended. Furthermore, the integrity and availability of IT systems can be compromised.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Security vulnerabilities due to inadequate maintenance
parts.prose:
Security gaps and software vulnerabilities can in principle occur throughout the entire period of use of software. This can lead to the information security of the data processed with the software being compromised, for example, by bypassing login functions or breaking encryption.
Security gaps and vulnerabilities can especially not be remediated in a timely manner if no suitable maintenance contract has been concluded with the manufacturing or providing company, or if the software is simply used beyond its maintenance period. Violations of license terms can also lead to mechanisms such as (auto-)updates being deactivated, resulting in the software no longer being maintained.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Data loss due to incorrect use of software
parts.prose: By using software incorrectly, employees can accidentally delete data or modify it in such a way that it becomes unusable. This can block entire business processes. Even if encryption functions are used incorrectly, the data might still exist but can no longer be decrypted. In this case, the data can no longer be restored, or only with increased effort.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Insufficient resources for software execution
parts.prose: If IT systems have insufficient resources to run the software, this can significantly increase the processing and response time for users. In the worst case, the software cannot be run on such a system at all. This can significantly disrupt business processes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Disregarding user requirements
parts.prose: Regardless of whether software meets the functional requirements, it may not be accepted by users if it is, for example, cumbersome and complicated to operate. This, in turn, can lead to users resorting to alternative forms of processing and misusing other IT systems or software for this purpose. For example, private IT systems could be used without coordination with IT operations. These alternative forms of processing are rarely created with information security in mind and thus represent an increased risk.

controls.title: Extending software deployment planning to include aspects of custom software

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the development of custom software, only a technical contact person is designated. There are no formalized responsibilities or a defined process model.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In practice, this often means that communication and control of the development are handled ad hoc and informally through a single developer or project manager, without being anchored in an organizational framework.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether a contact person for software development has been designated at all. It is checked whether any documentation on roles and responsibilities is missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A responsible body has been designated for the control and coordination of software development. A basic but informal project management model (e.g., a simple list of tasks and milestones) is used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A person or a department is officially declared responsible. Project planning is often done in standard office documents and is not systematically tracked or updated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of an official designation of the responsible body. It is checked whether basic, albeit informal, project planning exists (e.g., task lists, email correspondence).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of software deployment MUST be extended to include aspects of custom software by defining who is responsible for controlling and coordinating the software development or the contractor, as well as the organizational framework within which the software is to be developed (project management model).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Responsibilities are documented in a Roles and Responsibilities Matrix (RACI). An established project management model such as Scrum, Kanban, or a classic waterfall model is selected, and its application is made mandatory for the project.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of responsibilities and the chosen project management model. It is verified that these documents apply to the specific development project and are known to the stakeholders.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Custom software SHOULD be developed within the scope of a development project. The development project should be roughly scheduled using a timeline. The chosen project management model is linked to the institution's overarching security policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal project charter is created. A rough schedule with the most important phases (concept, development, testing, commissioning) and milestones is recorded in a project management tool and regularly updated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a formal development project has been set up and whether a schedule exists. It is checked whether the plan is realistic and whether progress is tracked against the plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The project management model is fully integrated into the institution's risk management and security governance processes. The defined roles include specific security responsibilities. The planning is supported by dedicated tools that enable continuous monitoring of project progress and adherence to security milestones.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Jira or Azure DevOps are used to manage not only functional requirements but also security requirements (Security Stories). The project's risk management is directly linked to the organization's central risk register. Compliance is monitored through automated reports and dashboards.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the project management tools to verify the integration of security processes. Spot checks are used to determine whether security risks in the project are systematically identified, assessed, and transferred to the central risk management. An automated retrieval of compliance reports from the tool can be part of the audit.

controls.title: Defining security requirements for the software development process

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the general expectation that the software should be developed 'securely' is expressed. No specific requirements for the development process or the development environment are formulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This often corresponds to a contract based purely on functional requirements, where security aspects are left to the developer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By inspecting the tender and contract documents, the auditor determines that no specific security requirements for the development process are documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: General security policies of the institution are handed over to the software developer. However, there are no specific instructions on how to implement them in the development process or what technical measures are required in the development environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, the company's general IT security policy is provided to the developer without any specific derivations for the project.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that general security documents were transmitted to the developer but also notes that no project-specific requirements for the development process were derived and defined.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST define clear requirements for the software development process. The requirements MUST specify the environment in which the software may be developed and which technical and organizational measures must be implemented by the contracted software developers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is implemented through a document that includes specifications for secure coding guidelines (e.g., OWASP Secure Coding Practices), securing the development environment (e.g., access controls on repositories), and conducting code reviews.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the document with the requirements for the development process. It is checked whether it contains clear and actionable specifications for the development environment and the required measures by the developer.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements for the development process include measurable security metrics. This includes specifications for minimum test coverage by security tests, the mandatory use of static code analysis (SAST) tools, and a cap on the number of permissible critical vulnerabilities upon delivery.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, the contract stipulates that the code must pass a SAST scan with no critical or high findings before a release is accepted. The results of the scans must be submitted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the contractual agreements for measurable security requirements. Reports from security tests and SAST scans are requested on a spot-check basis and compared with the specifications.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the security requirements for the development process is automatically enforced by a secure CI/CD pipeline (DevSecOps). The pipeline integrates SAST, DAST, and SCA (Software Composition Analysis) tools and prevents deployment if predefined security gates are not met.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the Jenkins, GitLab, or Azure DevOps pipeline, security scans are configured as mandatory steps. A build fails and cannot be delivered if, for example, new critical vulnerabilities are found in the code or in used libraries.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline (e.g., `gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`). It is verified that security gates are correctly implemented and cannot be bypassed. An automated test could consist of submitting code with a known vulnerability and checking if the build is blocked as expected.

controls.title: Defining security functions for system integration

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the general purpose of the software is described, without specific requirements for the technical platform, resources, or interfaces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, the requirement is 'We need a system to manage customer data,' without details about the database, operating system, or connection to other systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Based on the requirements documents, the auditor determines that no technical specifications have been defined for the operating environment or interfaces.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The target platform (e.g., 'Windows Server with IIS') is roughly specified. However, resource constraints and detailed interface requirements are only described in general terms and not formally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: It is specified that the application must run on the existing server infrastructure, but without precise details on available RAM, CPU, or the exact versions of the software stacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the target platform is named, but notes that detailed, quantifiable requirements for resources and interfaces are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations and the responsible subject matter experts MUST create requirements for the technical operating environment of the planned custom software and coordinate them with software development. The requirements MUST clearly state: on what kind of hardware platform, on what kind of software platform (including the entire software stack), with what available resources (e.g., CPU cluster or memory), and with which interfaces to other IT systems or applications the application is to be deployed, as well as the resulting security functions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A technical target document is created that specifies the exact versions of the operating system and database, the assigned vCPU cores and RAM, the required network ports, and the formats of the data interfaces (e.g., REST endpoints with sample data).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the requirements document for the operating environment. It is checked whether all aspects (hardware, software stack, resources, interfaces) are clearly and unambiguously defined and whether the resulting security functions (e.g., the need for authentication at an interface) have been derived.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Interfaces with other IT systems SHOULD be modeled and defined in standardized technical formats. This includes the definition of data models and endpoints.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An OpenAPI specification (version 3.x) is created for REST APIs. A WSDL file is provided for web services. These specifications are versioned and managed as part of the requirements documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the interface specifications (e.g., OpenAPI/Swagger file). It is checked whether these specifications are complete, compliant with standards, and up-to-date. It can be checked whether code generators can process these specifications without errors.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All platform and interface requirements are defined as 'Infrastructure as Code' (e.g., with Terraform, Ansible) and 'Policy as Code' (e.g., with Open Policy Agent). This ensures automated validation and consistent deployment of the operating environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Terraform scripts define the target VM including network configuration. Ansible playbooks install and harden the software stack. OPA rules define the permissible communication between the systems. These artifacts are co-managed in the application's code repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the 'Infrastructure as Code' and 'Policy as Code' scripts in the repository. It is checked whether the production environment was demonstrably created from these scripts and whether the scripts correctly implement the defined security requirements. An automated audit can compare the configuration of the cloud environment with the state defined in the repository.

controls.title: Commissioning according to requirements

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The development is commissioned based on an informal request or a brief description of the desired result. Formal requirements documents are not used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A typical example is commissioning by email with the content 'Please create a tool for recording working hours'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the development order was not based on any of the formal requirements documents (requirements catalog, process requirements, integration requirements).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The commission is based on a functional requirements catalog. However, security requirements for the process or system integration are not part of the commissioning basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The developer is given a specification sheet with user stories, but none of the security documents created in A2 and A3.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the commissioning documents with the existing requirements documents and determines that the functional requirements catalog was used, but the specific security documents were not.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If custom software is developed by the own institution or commissioned externally, then in addition to the existing legal and organizational requirements, the requirements catalog, the security requirements for the software development process, and the security functions for system integration MUST be used as the basis for software development.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All relevant requirements documents (functional catalog from APP.6, process requirements from APP.7.A2, integration requirements from APP.7.A3) are made an integral part of the tender documents or the internal project order.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the complete tender documents or the internal project order. It is verified that all three mentioned requirements documents are explicitly listed and attached as a basis for the development.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement process includes a formal verification step in which the offers of potential contractors are checked to ensure that all specified security requirements have been adequately addressed and understood.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An evaluation matrix is used in which it is checked for each security requirement how the bidder plans to implement it. Bids that ignore or inadequately describe security requirements are excluded from the further procedure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the minutes of the award procedure and the evaluation documents. It is checked whether a systematic evaluation of the security aspects in the bids has taken place and how the result influenced the award decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The contract with the contractor includes conventional penalties for non-compliance with essential security requirements. The contractor is contractually obliged to prove compliance with verifiable evidence (e.g., third-party audit reports, penetration test results, SAST/DAST logs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, the contract states: 'If a critical vulnerability according to OWASP Top 10 is found during acceptance, a contractual penalty of X will be due. The contractor must submit an unsolicited SAST report before each delivery.'

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the final contract and verifies the existence of clauses on contractual penalties and obligations to provide evidence regarding security. Random checks are carried out to see whether the agreed evidence (e.g., test reports) was actually requested and checked.

controls.title: Appropriate control of application development

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The development is managed ad-hoc through informal status updates. There is no structured process or project management model.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Management is carried out through occasional phone calls or emails between the client and the developer, without fixed dates or a structured agenda.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By interviewing the participants and reviewing the project communication, the auditor determines that no systematic management model is used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A project management model such as Scrum or Kanban is used, but it focuses purely on the implementation of functional requirements. Aspects such as risk management or formal quality objectives are not explicitly integrated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are regular sprint meetings and a product backlog. However, security requirements are treated like normal functional requirements and are not separately prioritized or tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the project's approach (e.g., by participating in a sprint review). It is determined that an agile model is being used, but explicit artifacts for risk management or the control of quality objectives are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When developing custom software, a suitable control and project management model SHOULD be used. The selected model SHOULD be coordinated with the contractor. The control SHOULD take into account that the required personnel is sufficiently qualified. All relevant phases SHOULD be covered during the software's life cycle. Furthermore, it SHOULD contain a suitable development model, risk management, and quality objectives.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the project begins, it is decided together with the developer whether to proceed according to Scrum or a V-Modell XT, for example. A risk register is created for the project. Quality objectives, such as response time behavior or code quality, are explicitly defined and documented. The qualification of the personnel is ensured by checking resumes or certificates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the project charter or similar founding documents to verify the agreed model. It is checked whether a risk register and a list of quality objectives exist and whether these artifacts are maintained during the project. The qualification certificates of the personnel involved are checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The control process includes regular, formal reviews of security milestones and risk assessments. The results of these reviews are documented and demonstrably flow into the further development process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Security Review Meeting is held at regular intervals (e.g., once a month) to discuss the status of security requirements and the risk register. The decisions and new tasks are recorded and entered into the project management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the minutes of the Security Review Meetings from the last few months. It is checked whether the identified measures and risks have been tracked and implemented in the project management system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The control is supported by a project management tool that automatically tracks security-relevant tasks, risks, and quality metrics. It provides stakeholders with real-time dashboards on the project's security status.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In Jira or Azure DevOps, special ticket types are used for security requirements and security risks. Dashboards are configured to visualize the number of open security tickets per criticality, the results of security scans from the CI/CD pipeline, and the status of the risk register.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is granted read access to the project management tool. The configuration of the dashboards and automated reports is analyzed. It is checked whether the displayed data is correct and up-to-date and whether it is actively used for project management. The audit can be performed automatically by querying the tool's API to verify the conformity of the processes.

controls.title: Documentation of requirements for the custom software

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Requirements only exist in an unstructured form, for example as a collection of emails, tickets, or user stories in a backlog. There is no consolidated, versioned requirements document.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All requirements are recorded in a Jira project, but there is no higher-level specification or documentation that describes the overall context.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that there is no summary and versioned requirements documentation that was made available to the developers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements are summarized in a document and made available to the developers. However, this document is updated informally and not via a controlled process when changes are made.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a Word document "Requirements_v1.docx". Changes are discussed orally and the document is only updated sporadically and distributed in new versions via email.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies the requirements document but finds that there is no formal change management process and that different, inconsistent versions may be in circulation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements from the requirements catalog, the security requirements for the software development process, and the security functions for system integration SHOULD be comprehensively documented. The documentation, including the security profile, SHOULD be made available to the developers for software development. The documentation SHOULD be updated when changes are made to the custom software and for functional updates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All requirements documents are maintained in a central, versioned repository (e.g., Confluence, SharePoint, Git). There is a defined process for change requests that ensures the documentation is updated with every relevant change. An initial security profile is created as part of the documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and completeness of the central, versioned documentation. It is checked whether a change management process is defined and followed. A recent functional change is selected on a random basis and checked to see if the corresponding documentation has been updated accordingly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In particular, a security profile for the application SHOULD be created. This SHOULD document the protection requirements of the data and functions to be processed. The security profile is versioned and subject to a formal approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated document "Security Profile" is created. It contains a protection needs assessment for the application and the data categories processed. Each new version of the profile must be formally approved by the Information Security Officer (ISO) and the business owner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security profile and checks its content, in particular the protection needs assessment. The version history and approval notes are used to check whether the formal approval process is being followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire requirements documentation is managed in a central repository as "Documentation as Code" and is directly linked to the source code, tests, and deployment configurations. Changes to requirements trigger automated workflows for review, testing, and deployment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Requirements are stored in a format like Markdown or AsciiDoc in a Git repository next to the application code. Pull requests that change the documentation require approval. The link to user stories in Jira and to test cases in a test management tool is included directly in the documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the Git repository and the configuration of the CI/CD pipeline. It is verified whether the documentation is managed as code and whether the review workflows (e.g., via pull requests) are established. The traceability from requirement to code to test is checked on a random basis.

controls.title: Secure procurement of custom software

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The contractor for the software development is selected primarily on the basis of the lowest cost. An assessment of the contractor's security competence does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision is made in favor of the cheapest provider, without checking their references or certifications in the field of secure software development.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the award documents and determines that security competence was not a criterion in the evaluation and decision-making process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement process assesses the general capabilities of the contractor. However, their security expertise is not a primary or decisive selection criterion. Public tenders may disclose high-level architectural decisions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the tender, general company information and references are requested, but no specific evidence of secure development. The performance description in the public tender may contain details about the planned technology.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that security plays only a subordinate role in the tender's criteria catalog. It is checked whether the public tender unnecessarily contained sensitive information.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The development project SHOULD be commissioned within the framework of the most suitable project management model for this purpose. Security aspects SHOULD be considered as early as the tendering and awarding stage, so that on the one hand only suitable contractors are commissioned, and on the other hand, no far-reaching conclusions can be drawn about the security architecture from the publicly available information. The institution SHOULD have defined processes and designated contact persons to ensure that the respective framework conditions are taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The tender contains suitability criteria regarding the provider's security competence. The performance description is deliberately kept abstract in order not to disclose details of the security architecture. A defined process ensures that the procurement office cooperates with the information security officer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the tender documents for suitability criteria regarding security and the wording of the performance description. It is checked whether the defined coordination process between procurement and information security has demonstrably taken place (e.g., through minutes, emails).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement process requires potential contractors to provide explicit proof of their security expertise. This can be certifications (e.g., ISO 27001) or detailed references for comparable projects on secure software development.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As a suitability criterion in the tender, it is required: "The bidder must provide evidence of a valid ISO 27001 certification for the scope of software development OR name at least two reference projects with a comparable protection level from the last three years."

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the suitability criteria in the tender require corresponding proof and whether the proof submitted by the successful bidder was checked and assessed as valid.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A multi-stage procurement procedure (e.g., competitive procedure with negotiation) is used. Detailed information on the security architecture is only passed on to a shortlist of bidders after a suitability check and signing of a non-disclosure agreement (NDA). The final contract contains specific service level agreements (SLAs) on information security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the first stage, only general information is published and the suitability of the applicants is checked. In the second stage, the qualified bidders receive the detailed performance description after signing an NDA. The contract contains SLAs such as "The time to fix critical vulnerabilities is a maximum of 48 hours."

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the entire course of the award procedure and checks the documentation of both stages. The contract is checked for the existence of security SLAs and it is checked on a random basis whether their compliance is monitored during operation.

controls.title: Early involvement of business owners in development-accompanying software tests

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The business owners are only involved immediately before commissioning through a demonstration of the finished product. No tests are carried out by the business owners.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A presentation of the software is held one week before go-live. Although feedback is received, it can usually no longer be implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by interviewing the business owners that their only involvement was a final presentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The business owners are involved in formal user acceptance tests (UAT) at the end of the development cycle. There is no involvement during development.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After the developer reports the software as "finished", the business owners receive a test version and a list of test cases to check the software before final acceptance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the UAT protocols and verifies the involvement of the business owners. At the same time, it is determined that there was no earlier involvement in the development process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Business owners SHOULD be involved in development-accompanying tests by the software developers at an early stage, even before final acceptance. This SHOULD be taken into account in the project schedule in coordination with the contractor from the outset.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Fixed dates for interim reviews or tests by the business owners are scheduled in the project plan (e.g., at the end of each development phase or after reaching important milestones). The business owners are given access to test versions of the software.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the initial project schedule for planned, early test activities with the business owners. It is verified, using protocols or test reports, that these tests have actually taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The business owners are continuously involved in the agile development process, for example by participating in sprint reviews. They have permanent access to a staging environment to test new functions as soon as they are developed. Their feedback is formally recorded and scheduled in subsequent sprints.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At the end of each sprint, the developers present the new increments to the business owners. The feedback is directly converted into user stories or bugs for the backlog. A dedicated test environment is automatically updated after each successful build.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor participates in a sprint review or reviews the minutes of several such meetings. It is checked in the backlog management tool how the feedback from the business owners is recorded and taken into account in the planning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automated acceptance tests are developed in collaboration with business owners using a framework such as Behavior-Driven Development (BDD). These tests run automatically in the CI/CD pipeline and provide immediate feedback on whether new code meets the business requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Business owners write or validate test cases in a simple language (e.g., Gherkin: "Given-When-Then"). These specifications are used by developers to implement automated tests (e.g., with Cucumber or SpecFlow). The execution of these tests is a mandatory part of the build pipeline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the code repository for BDD feature files and their corresponding test implementations. In the CI/CD pipeline, it is checked whether the execution of these acceptance tests is mandatory. It is verified that a build fails if an acceptance test is not successful.

controls.title: Escrow deposit

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The risk of software vendor failure is recognized as existing, but no measures such as a source code escrow are taken.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a risk assessment, the vendor risk is noted but classified as accepted or with low priority, without initiating contracts or processes for an escrow deposit.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies the risk in the risk documentation but finds no evidence of an implemented or planned escrow measure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A contractual clause for source code escrow exists. However, the scope of the materials to be deposited is not specified in detail, and the conditions for release are vaguely formulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The contract contains a standard clause such as "The source code is to be deposited with a trustee". A detailed list of what else is needed besides the code (build scripts, documentation, etc.) and what exactly constitutes a "failure" of the vendor is missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract and finds the escrow clause but determines that the specifications and release conditions are insufficient to ensure successful use in an emergency.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For institution-critical applications, it SHOULD be checked whether they are secured against the failure of the manufacturing company. For this purpose, materials and information not included in the application's scope of delivery SHOULD be placed in escrow, for example with an escrow agency. Documented code, design plans, keys, or passwords SHOULD be included. The obligations of the escrow agency for deposit and release SHOULD be contractually regulated. It SHOULD be clarified when and to whom the deposited material may be released.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal escrow agreement is concluded with a specialized service provider. The contract explicitly lists all artifacts to be deposited (e.g., Git repository, Dockerfiles, CI/CD pipeline configuration, documentation, private keys). The release conditions (e.g., insolvency, non-fulfillment of maintenance obligations) are unambiguously defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the escrow agreement presented and checks it for the completeness of the deposited artifacts and the clarity of the release conditions. A confirmation from the escrow agent about the initial deposit is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The escrow agreement includes a process for the regular updating of the deposited materials to keep them in sync with new software versions. The agreement also provides for a verification process in which an independent third party periodically checks whether the deposited materials are complete and compilable/usable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The contract stipulates that an update of the deposit must occur after each major release. Once a year, a technical expert is commissioned to confirm that the runnable application can be built from the deposited materials.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the contractually agreed updates and verifications have taken place. For this purpose, the update confirmations from the escrow agent and the inspection reports from the technical expert of recent years are requested and reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The deposit of the source code, build scripts, and all other artifacts with the escrow agent is integrated as an automated step into the CI/CD release pipeline. The release conditions are linked to automated monitoring of the vendor's operational or financial status.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script in the release pipeline packages all relevant artifacts after a successful build and uploads them via an API of the escrow service provider. In parallel, a service monitors public registers for insolvency notices or other contractually defined trigger events.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the release pipeline to verify the automated deposit step. The configuration of the monitoring service for the trigger events is reviewed. A test of the API connection can be performed by manually triggering the deposit script, and the successful transfer to the escrow agent can be verified.

controls.title: Commissioning certified software development companies

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The development company is selected without its security certifications or proven experience in security-critical projects playing a role.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection is based on criteria such as price, availability, or existing business relationships; the security of the company's development processes is not assessed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines from the procurement files that security certifications or corresponding evidence were not a requirement or evaluation criterion.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Companies are required to demonstrate experience with security-critical projects, but a formal certification is not mandatory.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Reference projects are requested as part of the tender. Whether the development processes in these projects followed a certified standard is not checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that references were obtained but finds that no formal certification was required of the company.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If particularly security-critical applications are developed, certified software development companies SHOULD be commissioned for this purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For projects with high or very high protection requirements, a relevant certification is required as a suitability criterion in the tender, e.g., an ISO 27001 certification that covers the area of software development.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the commissioning of a certified company for projects with high protection requirements is anchored as a requirement in the procurement guidelines. It is checked whether the certificate of the selected company is valid and covers the relevant area.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The required certification must cover specific and relevant aspects of software development. The certification SHOULD include security aspects for relevant aspects of software development, for example, a certification according to Common Criteria or an ISO 27001 certification with the explicit scope of "Secure software development according to BSI-Grundschutz".

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of a general ISO 27001 certification of the company, a more specific requirement is formulated that ensures the development processes themselves were the focus of the certification. Another option is to require a product certification for a comparable software from the company.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes not only the existence but also the exact scope of the presented certificate. It is checked whether this scope explicitly includes the secure development practices relevant to the contract.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Beyond a general company certification, it is required that the developers and architects assigned to the project hold recognized, personal security certifications (e.g. CISSP, CSSLP). The contract also mandates verifiable compliance with a specific standard for secure development (e.g. OWASP ASVS Level 3).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The contract stipulates that the lead architect must have a CISSP certification and at least 50% of the developers must have a recognized certification for secure programming. Compliance with the ASVS is verified by an external penetration test before final acceptance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the contractual agreements and requests the certificates of the involved persons as well as the final report of the external penetration test. It is checked whether the results of the test confirm the conformity with the required standard.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Many institutions are facing challenges that they can no longer adequately solve with non-customized software. The tasks associated with these challenges often require software solutions that are tailored to the individual needs of the institutions. In the following, these software solutions are referred to as custom software. For this purpose, base solutions consisting of a basic set of typical functions can be used and individualized. The basic functions are adapted for the individual purpose of the institution and expanded with individually required functions. Common examples of this are IT applications such as ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning), CMS (Content Management Systems), or IDM systems (Identity Management). Custom software can also be developed completely new by the institution itself or by third parties. This includes applications for business process management or individually adapted specialized applications, such as personnel management software, procedures for managing social data, or registration data.

It is of essential importance here that the required security functions are considered as early as the planning and design phase of the custom software and that information security is taken into account throughout the entire lifecycle of the custom software. Errors in planning or missing security functions cannot be compensated for during operation, or only with high additional effort.
