parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration of the failover cluster. They check the validity and appropriateness of the maintenance contracts. They have the logs of the last planned failover test shown to them or attend such a test.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: High-availability architectures are distributed across multiple geographically separate locations or availability zones (in the cloud) to absorb the failure of an entire data center. The failover between locations is automatic and supported by Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB). The functionality of the cross-location redundancy is regularly verified through controlled 'Chaos Engineering' experiments.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A database cluster is spanned synchronously across two data centers. A GSLB system distributes user requests to both locations. If one data center fails completely, the GSLB automatically redirects all traffic to the remaining location. The failure of a location is simulated regularly to test the switching mechanisms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the architecture of the cross-location redundancy, including the network configuration and the GSLB setup. They analyze the logs of the cross-location failover tests and the chaos engineering experiments to assess the resilience of the overall solution.

controls.title: One Service per Server (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Functionally unrelated services are run on separate servers. For example, database servers and web servers are separated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a typical three-tier architecture, at least one dedicated (physical or virtual) server is used for each of the web tier, the application tier, and the database tier.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the server inventory and architecture diagrams to verify that the basic separation of services (e.g., web, app, DB) is implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Depending on the threat level and the protection requirements of the services, only one service SHOULD be operated on each server. This applies in particular to servers that are accessible from the internet.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated virtual machine or container is provided for each individual service (e.g., per web application, per database instance). Servers are no longer shared. This allows for tailored hardening and resource allocation per service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks servers on a random basis and verifies that only the processes and open ports belonging to a single main service are present on each server. They check, for example, that no database processes are running on a web server.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The 'one service per server' principle is taken to the extreme through the use of microservices architectures and containers. Each server (container) runs only a single process. The servers are short-lived (immutable/ephemeral) and are rebuilt on every change instead of being modified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A complex application is broken down into dozens of microservices, each running in its own minimal container. Deployment is done via a Kubernetes platform. To update the application, new container images are created and the old instances are terminated and replaced with new ones.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the microservices architecture and the configuration of the container orchestration. They check whether the container images follow the 'single process' principle and whether the infrastructure is configured to enforce 'immutable' deployments.

controls.title: Use of Execution Control (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic form of execution control is implemented on servers by blocking the execution of programs from temporary directories or user profiles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Using Software Restriction Policies (SRP) or GPOs, rules are created that prohibit the execution of EXE files from the `%TEMP%` and `%USERPROFILE%` directories.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configured SRP/GPO rules. They try to start a harmless executable file from a blocked directory and verify that the execution is prevented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Execution control SHOULD be used to ensure that only explicitly permitted programs and scripts can be executed. The rules SHOULD be as narrow as possible. If paths and hashes cannot be explicitly specified, certificate-based or path rules SHOULD be used as an alternative.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Using an application whitelisting solution (e.g., AppLocker), a 'default deny' approach is implemented. Only programs in protected directories (such as `C:\Program Files\`) and programs that are digitally signed by trusted publishers are allowed to run. PowerShell is configured in 'Constrained Language Mode'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the AppLocker rules. They try to launch an unsigned, unauthorized application from any location and check if this is blocked. They analyze the event logs for messages about blocked execution attempts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Execution control is fully automated and dynamic. For each server, a whitelist is automatically generated based on the installed and required software. Any attempted execution of a non-listed program is blocked and triggers a security alarm. The management of the whitelists is integrated into the software deployment process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A modern application control solution is operated in 'enforcement' mode. When new software is installed via the central software distribution system, the hash of the new executable files is automatically added to the server's whitelist. If an attacker tries to upload and execute their own malware on the server, this is blocked and the EDR system alerts the SOC team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the process for automatically generating and updating the whitelists. They analyze the alarms generated by blocked execution attempts and assess the security team's response.

controls.title: Active Management of Root Certificates (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The root certificates installed on the servers are checked regularly. Obviously untrustworthy or expired certificates are manually removed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator checks the list of trusted root certification authorities in the operating system's certificate store semi-annually and manually removes certificates from unknown or known compromised CAs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor exports the list of root certificates from a server and compares it with the list of CAs classified as trustworthy by Microsoft or other relevant bodies. They look for anomalies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During the procurement and installation of the server, it SHOULD be documented which root certificates are necessary for the operation of the server. Only the root certificates necessary for operation and documented in advance SHOULD be on the server. It SHOULD be regularly checked whether the existing root certificates still comply with the institution's specifications. All certificate stores on the IT system SHOULD be included in the check.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution maintains a central whitelist of permitted and required root certification authorities. Group policies or a script are used to ensure that only the certificates from this whitelist are present in the trusted root certificate store on all servers. All other certificates supplied by the operating system are removed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the list of root certificates installed on a server with the institution's central whitelist. They check the configuration of the GPO or the script that performs the certificate management. Automated check: `Get-ChildItem cert:\LocalMachine\Root | ForEach-Object { $_.Thumbprint }` is executed and compared with the whitelist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of root certificates is fully automated and continuously monitored. Any deviation from the defined whitelist is immediately detected and automatically corrected or an alarm is raised. The check also extends to the certificate stores of applications such as Java (cacerts) or browsers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool (e.g., Puppet) manages the content of all relevant certificate stores on the servers, including the Java Keystore. A security scanner checks the integrity of the certificate stores daily and reports any deviation from the centrally defined 'Policy as Code' to the SIEM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the code of the configuration management tool for certificate management. They try to manually import an unauthorized root certificate and verify that it is automatically removed or a critical alarm is triggered. They check the scans of the application certificate stores.

controls.title: Hard Disk Encryption (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For servers with particularly sensitive data, the data carriers are encrypted. The recovery keys are kept in a secure location.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The database server containing personal data is encrypted with BitLocker (Windows) or LUKS (Linux). The recovery key is printed out and stored in the IT department's safe.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the encryption status on the server. They have the process for secure storage and use of the recovery keys shown to them and check the access rights to the safe.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For higher protection requirements, the server's data carriers SHOULD be encrypted with a product or procedure considered secure. This SHOULD also apply to virtual machines with production data. A TPM SHOULD NOT be the sole key protection. The recovery password SHOULD be stored in a suitable secure location. For very high requirements, e.g., for confidentiality, Full Volume or Full Disk Encryption SHOULD be performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All servers, both physical and virtual, are operated with disk encryption by default. The recovery keys are stored centrally and automatically in a secure database or a directory service (e.g., Active Directory for BitLocker keys). Access to the keys is strictly regulated and logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the encryption status of the entire server fleet using a script or the central management console. They audit the access permissions and access logs for the central key repository. Automated check: `(Get-BitLockerVolume -MountPoint C:).KeyProtector` is checked to ensure that a recovery password is on file.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Disk encryption is managed by a central Key Management System (KMS) that is FIPS 140-2/3 certified. Hardware-based encryption solutions (Self-Encrypting Drives, SEDs) are preferred. Unlocking the drives during the boot process requires a network connection to a 'Pre-Boot-Authentication' server, which provides additional protection against theft.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All servers are equipped with TCG Opal 2.0 compliant SEDs. Key management is handled by a central KMS. On startup, the server must perform a network authentication with the KMS before the drive is released (Network-based Unlock). Without this authentication, the data remains encrypted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the architecture and configuration of the KMS and the Pre-Boot-Authentication system. They check the certification of the KMS. They disconnect a test server from the network and verify that it does not boot and that the encrypted data cannot be accessed.

controls.title: Securing the boot process (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On all servers, the UEFI feature 'Secure Boot' is enabled with the manufacturer's default keys. A BIOS/UEFI password is set to prevent unauthorized changes to the boot configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During the initial setup of the server, 'Secure Boot' is activated in the UEFI setup and a strong administrator password is set for the setup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor restarts a server, enters the UEFI setup, and verifies that it is password-protected and that Secure Boot is enabled. Automated check: In Windows, the status can be checked with `Confirm-SecureBootUEFI`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Bootloader and operating system kernel SHOULD be signed with self-controlled key material and verified in a trusted chain at system startup (Secure Boot). Unnecessary key material SHOULD be removed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to enabling Secure Boot, the default Microsoft keys are replaced in the UEFI with the company's own controlled keys (Custom Secure Boot Keys). Only bootloaders and operating system kernels signed with the company's own key can be started. This prevents the booting of unauthorized operating systems, even if they are signed by Microsoft.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the UEFI configuration and verifies that the installed keys correspond to the company's own keys. They audit the process for signing the company's own operating system image and for securely managing the custom keys.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire boot chain is verified by a hardware-based 'Root of Trust' (e.g., TPM) (Measured Boot / Trusted Boot). The measurements of the boot components (firmware, bootloader, kernel, drivers) are cryptographically sealed and can be verified by an external service (Remote Attestation). Servers whose boot integrity is compromised are denied access to the network or to sensitive keys.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Secure Boot is combined with TPM-based Measured Boot. A Remote Attestation server queries the state of the TPM at startup. Only if the measurements of the boot chain correspond to a known, 'good' configuration does the Attestation Server issue a health certificate that grants the server access to the network (via 802.1X) and to the keys for disk decryption.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration of the Remote Attestation server and the 'Golden Measurements' stored there. They intentionally manipulate a boot component on a test server (e.g., a driver) and verify that the server does not receive a network connection on the next boot and that the attestation error is reported in the central log.

controls.title: Hardening the host system using a read-only file system (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The server's system partition is put into read-only mode after installation and configuration. Write access is only possible to explicitly defined partitions for variable data (e.g., logs, database files). Changes to the system require a reboot into a special maintenance mode.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For Linux servers, the operating system is installed on a partition that is mounted with the 'ro' (read-only) option. Variable data is moved to separate partitions. To patch the server, it must be booted into a maintenance mode where the system partition is mounted as writable.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor logs into the server and checks the mount options of the system partition (`mount | grep 'on / '`). They try to create or modify a file in the system directory (`/bin` or `C:\Windows`) and verify that write access is denied.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of the host system SHOULD be ensured by a read-only file system (Immutable OS). The operating system is loaded from an immutable image. Any changes to the running system are not persistent and are discarded upon reboot. Updates are performed by replacing the entire system image.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized, immutable operating system such as Fedora CoreOS, Flatcar Container Linux, or a custom image based on 'overlayfs' is used. The server boots from a read-only base image. Runtime changes and application data are stored in a writable overlay layer that can be deleted if necessary. An update consists of downloading a new base image and booting the server from this new image.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the architecture of the Immutable OS. They create a file on the system partition, restart the server, and verify that the file is gone. They audit the process for the 'Atomic Update' of the system image and the rollback capabilities.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: A "General Server" refers to IT systems with any operating system that provide services to users and other IT systems. These services can be basic services for the local or external network, or they can enable email exchange or offer database and printer services. Server IT systems are of central importance for information technology and thus for the functioning of an institution's workflows. Servers often perform tasks in the background without users interacting directly with them. On the other hand, there are server services that interact directly with users and are not perceived as a server service at first glance. A well-known example is X servers under Unix.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to protect information that is processed, offered, or transmitted on or via servers, as well as to protect the related services.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.1.1 General Server is to be applied to all server IT systems with any operating system.
As a rule, servers are operated with operating systems that each have specific security requirements to consider. The IT-Grundschutz Compendium contains specific modules for common server operating systems, which build on this module. The module SYS.1.1 General Server forms the basis for the modules of specific server operating systems. If a specific module exists for an IT system under consideration, it must be applied in addition to module SYS.1.1 General Server. If no specific module exists for the server operating systems in use, the requirements of this module must be appropriately specified for the target object and a supplementary risk analysis must be performed.
The specific services offered by the server are not part of this module. For these server services, other modules must be implemented in addition to this one, according to the results of the modeling according to IT-Grundschutz.
The provision of user sessions by terminal servers is also to be considered a service. For terminal servers, the module SYS.1.9 Terminal Server should be modeled accordingly.
In principle, the requirements for the role and authorization concept from module ORP.4 Identity and Access Management must be taken into account. Also to be considered are requirements from module DER.4 Contingency Management.
Servers should generally be included in the concept for protection against malicious software. Requirements for this can be found in module OPS.1.1.4 Protection against Malware.
For servers, there are special requirements for administration as well as for handling patches and changes. Therefore, the requirements of modules OPS.1.1.2 Orderly IT Administration and OPS1.1.3 Patch and Change Management must be observed.
Servers often offer services to a large number of clients, often also over the internet. For this reason, they must be particularly separated from the rest of the institution's network. Requirements for this can be found in module NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Inadequate planning
parts.prose: Servers are complex IT systems with a large number of functions and configuration options. Even if modern server operating systems come with good default settings in many areas, the basic configuration is still not the most secure in every case. In case of inadequate planning, this can lead to a variety of vulnerabilities and weaknesses through misconfiguration, which can be easily exploited by unauthorized third parties. Furthermore, if central decisions are not made before installation, servers are often run in an insecure and undefined state that can hardly be corrected afterwards.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Flawed administration of servers
parts.prose:
New versions of server operating systems are regularly enhanced with new functions compared to their predecessors. For existing features, sub-functions, parameters, or default configurations can also change in new versions. If the institution's IT operations staff is not adequately trained in the specifics of the operating systems, there is a risk of configuration errors and human error, which can impair not only the functionality but also the security of the IT system.
A particular danger is posed by inconsistent server security settings (e.g., for SMB, RPC, or LDAP). If the configuration is not systematically and centrally planned, documented, reviewed, and tracked, there is a risk of so-called "configuration drift." The more the actual configurations of functionally similar systems diverge without reason and documentation, the more difficult it becomes to maintain an overview of the status quo and to uphold security holistically and consistently.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Unauthorized Acquisition or Misuse of Administrative Privileges
parts.prose: Regular work with administrative privileges, such as performing tasks and activities on a client system that are generally intended and possible with standard permissions, poses a security risk on a server. If separate administrative accounts are not restricted to the minimum necessary rights to perform administrative tasks (principle of least privilege), a takeover of such accounts can lead to obtaining extensive rights on the server or other IT systems and causing significant damage. Misuse of privileges by legitimate administrators is also a relevant damage scenario. Since the roles are often very powerful, the impact is usually considerable, for example, with so-called domain administrators. Even without guessing or cracking passwords, suitable credentials can be extracted and misused, for example, through so-called pass-the-hash techniques, to move laterally within the network.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Data loss
parts.prose:
Data loss, especially on servers, can have significant impacts on business processes and specialized tasks, and thus on the entire institution. A great many IT systems, such as clients or other servers, are typically dependent on the data stored centrally there always being available.
If institution-relevant information of any kind is destroyed or falsified, this can delay business processes and specialized tasks or even prevent their execution. Overall, the loss of stored data, in addition to the outage and the costs of data recovery, can lead above all to long-term consequences such as a loss of trust in business relationships, to legal repercussions, and to a negative public image. In many institutions, there are rules that no data may be stored on local clients, but that central repositories on the servers must be used instead. A loss of this centrally stored data has serious consequences in such a case. The direct and indirect damages caused can even threaten the very existence of an institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Denial-of-Service-Attacks
parts.prose: An attack on the availability of data assets, called a Denial of Service, aims to prevent needed and normally available functions or devices from being used. This attack is often related to distributed resources. By heavily taxing these resources during attacks, they can no longer be accessed regularly. Typically, IT systems are also highly interdependent. Thus, the scarcity of a server's resources quickly affects other servers. For example, CPU time, storage space, or bandwidth can be artificially made scarce. This can lead to services or resources being completely unusable.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Provision of unnecessary applications and services
parts.prose:
During the installation of the server operating system, it is already possible to install bundled applications and services, some of which may not be used at all. Also during later operation, software is often installed for a quick test but is no longer needed afterward. It is often not even known that these unused applications and services exist. In this way, numerous applications and services are present on the servers that are not used and thus place an unnecessary load on them.
Furthermore, these unused applications and services can contain vulnerabilities, for instance, if they are no longer updated. If the installed applications and services are unknown, the institution is not even aware that they also need to be updated. In this way, they can easily become an entry point for attacks.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Server overload
parts.prose:
If servers are not sufficiently sized, a point is eventually reached where they no longer meet the institution's requirements. Depending on the type of IT systems affected, this can have a variety of negative consequences. For example, the servers or services may be temporarily unavailable, or data loss may occur. In complex IT landscapes, the overload of a single server can also lead to problems or failures on other servers.
Triggers for the overload of IT systems can be that
• installed services or applications are misconfigured and thus consume an unnecessary amount of memory,
• existing storage capacities are exceeded,
• numerous requests at the same time overwhelm an IT system,
• too much processing power is consumed by the services, or
• a too large number of messages are sent at the same time.

controls.title: Planning for Windows Server 2012

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning for the use of Windows Server 2012 is ad-hoc and incomplete. Typically, it only focuses on individual aspects such as hardware procurement, while important decisions on the server edition, Active Directory integration, or the use of cloud services are not made.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, a server is often simply ordered without a formal analysis of the software requirements. The decisions are made by individual administrators without formal documentation or coordination.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether any planning documents exist at all. Through interviews with the administrators, it is determined whether the decision-making process for the server deployment was systematic or spontaneous.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic planning for the use of Windows Server 2012 is carried out. The hardware requirements and the server edition are determined. However, the planning process is not formally documented and aspects such as cloud integration or specific security configurations are not considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple planning document or a checklist is used. The specification of the purpose and the integration into Active Directory are considered, but not worked out in detail or formally approved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the basic planning documents and checks whether the essential aspects (hardware, edition) are covered. It is checked whether the decisions are traceable, even if there is no formal approval.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of Windows Server 2012 MUST be carefully planned before installation. The hardware requirements MUST be checked before procurement. A reasoned and documented decision MUST be made for a suitable edition of Windows Server 2012. The purpose of the server and its integration into Active Directory MUST be specified. The use of cloud services integrated into the operating system MUST be fundamentally weighed and planned. If not needed, the creation of Microsoft accounts on the server MUST be blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A template is used for planning that covers all points mentioned in the requirement. The decision for or against cloud services is documented in a concept. The blocking of Microsoft accounts can be implemented via a Group Policy (GPO).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documentation. It is verified that the hardware check, the edition decision, the specification of the purpose, and the planning of the AD integration are documented. It is checked whether a documented consideration of cloud services exists and whether the blocking of Microsoft accounts (if applicable) has been technically implemented, e.g., by checking the corresponding GPO setting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process is formalized, documented, reviewed, and approved. The plan contains specific requirements for the basic configuration and hardening of the system. The decision on the use of cloud services is based on a documented risk analysis. The entire process is versioned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning process is integrated into the IT service management system. Templates for server plans are maintained centrally. The results of the planning, including the configuration baselines, are stored in a configuration management system (CMS).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the formal planning and approval documents. It is checked whether the planning includes a risk analysis for cloud services and whether the planned configurations represent a traceable security baseline. The versioning of the planning documents is also checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process is fully integrated into an overarching enterprise architecture management and change management framework. The planning considers lifecycle, disaster recovery, and business continuity aspects. The planning documents are living documents that are dynamically adapted to changes in the system landscape.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized tools for enterprise architecture management are used for planning and visualizing the server landscape. Capacity planning and performance analysis are integral parts of the planning process. The planning is regularly audited and improved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of the planning process into the higher-level management frameworks. It is checked whether disaster recovery plans exist and are consistent with the server planning. By analyzing change requests, it is verified whether the planning processes are adhered to during changes to the IT infrastructure and whether the documents are updated.

controls.title: Secure Installation of Windows Server 2012

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation of Windows Server 2012 is performed without observing the principle of least privilege. Typically, the full GUI version is installed with numerous unneeded roles and features. Patching during installation does not occur.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installation is performed manually via the installation medium, largely accepting the default settings. The selection of components to be installed is made without prior analysis of actual needs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects a selection of servers and compares the list of installed roles and features with the server's actual purpose. The patch level is checked to determine if patches were applied promptly after installation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During installation, care is taken to install only the required server roles and features. However, patching is only performed as a separate step after the installation is complete. The decision between Server Core and the GUI version is not formally justified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators use a checklist to ensure that only necessary roles and features are selected during manual installation. The system is connected to the central patch management system after installation and before being put into production.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the installed roles and features for their necessity. Logs or tickets are used to determine how quickly the system was patched after installation. Interviews are conducted to ask for the reasoning behind the choice of installation variant (Core/GUI).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: NO server roles and features or functions other than those required MUST be installed. If the feature set is sufficient, the Server Core variant MUST be installed. Otherwise, a justification MUST be provided as to why the Server Core variant is not sufficient. The server MUST be brought to an up-to-date patch level during the installation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: To apply patches during installation (offline servicing), the installation media are regularly updated with the latest updates, for example, using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management). The decision for or against Server Core is documented in a concept for each server role.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the list of installed roles and features on multiple systems. The documentation justifying the use of the GUI variant is reviewed. It is checked whether the process for updating the installation media is established and regularly performed, e.g., by checking the timestamps of the installation images.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation process is automated using answer files (unattend.xml) or deployment scripts to ensure consistency. The decision for Server Core is the documented default, from which deviations are only made with a justified exception. An initial security configuration (hardening) is applied during the installation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools such as Windows Deployment Services (WDS) or the Microsoft Deployment Toolkit (MDT) are used. PowerShell scripts are used to automatically apply hardening settings after the base installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the answer files or deployment scripts used and checks them for correctness and completeness. It is verified whether the Server Core variant is the de-facto standard. The auditor compares the configuration of a newly installed server with the defined hardening baseline.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully automated 'Golden Image' pipeline is used for deployment. These images are pre-hardened, contain all current patches and minimal roles, and are automatically scanned for vulnerabilities before release. The use of Server Core is mandatory where technically possible, and deviations require a formal approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CI/CD pipeline (e.g., with Jenkins, Azure DevOps, or Packer) is used to automatically create, patch, test, and distribute the golden images. The images are versioned and managed in a central artifact registry. The configuration is enforced using Desired State Configuration (DSC).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the CI/CD pipeline and the associated scripts. It is verified that automated security scans are part of the pipeline and that their results are tracked. The approval process for deviations from the Server Core policy is checked for its effectiveness.

controls.title: Secure Administration of Windows Server 2012

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only individual administrators are trained in the security-relevant aspects of Windows Server 2012. The rule of not surfing the web on servers is known but not actively enforced or monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Training sessions are held irregularly, often only at the initiative of individual employees. There is no policy prohibiting surfing on servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions several administrators about their level of knowledge and randomly checks the browser history on a server or looks for installed, non-administrative browsers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administrators have received basic training in secure administration. Surfing the web on servers is actively prohibited and documented in a policy, but it is not prevented by technical means.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A one-time training is conducted for all new administrators. A written IT usage policy contains a clause prohibiting surfing on server systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the training records for all administrators. The IT usage policy is checked for the corresponding clause. It is verified that no technical controls for browser usage exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administrators responsible for the server system MUST be trained in the security-relevant aspects of administering Windows Server 2012. Web browsers on the server MUST NOT be used for surfing the web.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A training concept is created that defines the relevant content and the group of people to be trained. The training sessions are documented. The use of web browsers is restricted, for example, by not placing browser shortcuts on the desktop or in the start menu for administrative users and by setting the homepage to a blank page (about:blank).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the training concept and the training records. On a representative server, it is checked in the context of an administrator account whether the web browser is easily accessible and whether attempts have been made to prevent its use for general surfing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security training for administrators is repeated regularly and participation is tracked. The use of the web browser is severely restricted by technical means, such as group policies or AppLocker, so that only access to explicitly approved, administrative websites is possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The training sessions are repeated annually. The restriction of the web browser is implemented via the 'Internet Explorer Enhanced Security Configuration' in combination with whitelists for trusted sites in the group policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the records of the repeated training sessions. The corresponding Group Policy Objects (GPOs) that restrict browser usage are analyzed. On a server, it is practically tested whether access to an unapproved website is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The administration of the servers is carried out exclusively from dedicated, hardened Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs). The training for administrators is role-based and includes practical exercises as well as regular knowledge checks. All administrative activities are centrally logged and regularly reviewed. The use of a web browser on the server is completely blocked or encapsulated in a secure sandbox.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAW concept is implemented. Just-In-Time (JIT) and Just-Enough-Administration (JEA) principles are enforced with PowerShell. Administrative actions are channeled and recorded through a Privileged Access Management (PAM) system. AppLocker or WDAC are used to completely prevent the execution of browsers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the PAW concept and its implementation. It is checked whether administrative access is only possible from these systems. The configuration of the PAM system and the logs of the administrative sessions are randomly checked. It is technically verified that a browser cannot be started on a server.

controls.title: Secure Configuration of Windows Server 2012

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardening of the server systems only occurs sporadically and on an ad-hoc basis on particularly critical systems. There are no consistent security baselines or templates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Individual administrators manually change some security settings they are aware of, without this being based on a documented standard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configurations of several servers and finds significant inconsistencies in the security settings. No documentation on a hardening policy can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic hardening checklist or a simple script is used. However, it is not consistently applied to all servers or regularly updated, which leads to configuration drift.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A basic security template (e.g., from the Security Compliance Manager) is applied during initial setup, but subsequent changes to the template are not rolled out to existing systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the hardening checklist or script. It is then checked on several older and newer servers whether the configuration matches the template to detect configuration drift.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before commissioning, the system must be fundamentally hardened. For this purpose, function-specific and institution-wide security templates must be created, maintained, and rolled out to the servers. This process must be repeatable and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Security templates are created as Group Policy Objects (GPOs) and assigned to the corresponding servers via Organizational Units (OUs) in Active Directory. There is a base GPO for all servers and specific GPOs for different server roles (e.g., web servers, database servers).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the GPO structure and the security templates defined therein. Using tools like `gpresult`, it is checked on a representative server whether the correct policies are being applied. The documentation of the templates is checked for currency and completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Essential functions and roles are distributed across different servers to reduce the attack surface. Internet Explorer is only used in 'Enhanced Security Configuration' and 'Enhanced Protected Mode'. The application of security templates is automated and regularly checked for compliance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, a dedicated server is used only for the web server role and not simultaneously as a database server. The IE settings are enforced via GPO. Compliance is monitored using Security Compliance Manager (SCM) or configuration items in System Center Configuration Manager (SCCM).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the server architecture for a meaningful separation of roles. The GPOs for IE hardening are inspected. Reports from the monitoring tool (SCM/SCCM) are requested to verify the compliance rate of the server fleet.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The server configuration is managed and enforced by a Desired State Configuration (DSC) tool. Any deviation from the hardened baseline is automatically detected and either reported or immediately corrected. The configuration baseline is based on internationally recognized benchmarks (e.g. CIS Benchmarks) and is continuously audited and improved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: PowerShell DSC or a third-party tool like Ansible, Puppet, or Chef is used. The DSC configurations are versioned in a Git repository (Infrastructure as Code). A central DSC pull server or an equivalent system is used for distributing and monitoring the configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the DSC configuration scripts and their management in the repository. The dashboard of the configuration management tool is viewed to check the compliance status of the entire server fleet. A test is performed to see if a manual, unauthorized configuration change on a server is detected and corrected. The automatic check can be performed using `Test-DscConfiguration -Detailed` on a target node.

controls.title: Malware protection on Windows Server 2012

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An antivirus program is installed on only some servers, but not on all. Scans are performed manually and irregularly, and there is no central alerting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Often, stand-alone installations of antivirus software are used that are not centrally managed. Updates and scans are left to the responsibility of the local administrator.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a sample of servers and manually checks on each system whether an antivirus software is installed and active. The log files are checked for recently performed scans.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An antivirus program is installed on all servers, but it is operated with default settings. Regular, scheduled scans are configured, but alerts are not centrally collected or evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A centrally managed antivirus solution is used to ensure installation and signature updates on all servers. The configuration of scan schedules is done via the central console, but alerting is only configured via email to a general address.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks in the central management console of the antivirus solution whether all servers are registered and have current signatures. The configuration of the scheduled scans is checked. Inquiries are made as to how alerts are responded to.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An antivirus program must be installed before the first connection to the network or removable media. A malware protection concept must provide for regular full scans of all hard drives. Alerts for virus findings must be configured to be forwarded to a responsible body. This does not apply to stand-alone devices without a network connection and removable media.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The antivirus client is part of the standard server image to ensure installation before the first network contact. The concept defines the scan frequency (e.g. weekly) and the responsible body (e.g. IT security team) for alerts. Alerting is configured via the central console to inform a ticketing system or a dedicated email group.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the malware protection concept. It is checked whether the installation process ensures that AV software is present from the beginning. In the management console, the configuration of the full scans and the alert forwarding is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The antivirus solution is centrally managed and the policies are tailored to the respective server roles (e.g. specific exceptions for database or Exchange servers to avoid performance issues). Alerts are forwarded to a central Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. The solution includes not only signature-based but also behavior-based detection mechanisms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separate antivirus policies are created for different server OUs in Active Directory. The manufacturer's recommended exclusions (e.g. Microsoft for Exchange) are implemented and documented. The antivirus console is configured to send Syslog messages to the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the various antivirus policies and checks the role-specific exceptions for their plausibility. In the SIEM, it is checked whether the alerts from the antivirus solution arrive and are processed correctly. The product documentation is checked to confirm the existence of behavior-based detection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of a traditional antivirus solution, a modern Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solution is used. This offers deep system visibility, threat-hunting capabilities and is integrated with other security tools (e.g. network firewall, SIEM) for a coordinated, automated response (SOAR). The configuration is regularly audited for its effectiveness against current threats.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An EDR solution such as Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is implemented. Playbooks in a SOAR platform are created to automatically trigger actions for specific EDR alerts, such as the network isolation of a server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the EDR solution and the defined SOAR playbooks. The threat hunting capability is demonstrated by searching for indicators of compromise (IOCs) on the servers. The effectiveness is tested through simulated attacks (e.g. with the Atomic Red Team Framework). An automated test could query `(Get-MpComputerStatus).AMEngineVersion` to ensure that the EDR component is active.

controls.title: Secure authentication and authorization in Windows Server 2012

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only standard authentication mechanisms are used without additional hardening measures. Privileged accounts are not specially protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Authentication is done only via username and password. There are no measures to protect credentials in memory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes that none of the advanced security features such as LSA Protection or the 'Protected Users' group are configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: LSA (Local Security Authority) protection is enabled on the most critical servers, such as domain controllers, but is not universally enforced on all servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa` with the value `RunAsPPL` is set manually or via a special GPO on domain controllers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the mentioned registry key on domain controllers and compares this with the configuration on regular member servers to determine the inconsistent application.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: PPL (Protected Process Light) protection for the Local Credential Store (LSA) must be enabled on all servers to make it harder to read credentials from memory.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: LSA protection is enabled via a Group Policy for all servers in the domain. This is done by setting the registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa` to `RunAsPPL` = 1.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the relevant Group Policies to ensure that the setting is enforced globally. The registry key is checked on a representative server. This can be checked automatically using PowerShell: `(Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' -Name 'RunAsPPL').RunAsPPL -eq 1`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to LSA protection, on Windows Server 2012 R2, all user accounts with elevated privileges are made members of the 'Protected Users' security group. For service accounts, 'Managed Service Accounts' (MSAs) or 'group Managed Service Accounts' (gMSAs) are used where possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process is established to add all administrative accounts (e.g. Domain Admins) to the 'Protected Users' group. Existing services that run with standard user accounts are identified and converted to use MSAs/gMSAs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the memberships of the 'Protected Users' group and compares them with the list of administrators. The configuration of services on servers is checked on a sample basis to verify the use of MSAs/gMSAs. `Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Protected Users'` can be used for automated checking.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All controls of the previous levels are implemented and automated. In addition, authentication for all administrative access is strengthened by multi-factor authentication (MFA). For authorization on file servers, Dynamic Access Control (DAC) is used for fine-grained, attribute-based access rights management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MFA solution (e.g. smart cards, Windows Hello for Business, or a third-party solution) is enforced for RDP and PowerShell Remoting access. DAC is configured by defining central access rules and policies and distributing them via Group Policies based on user and device claims.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the MFA configuration and tests an administrative login attempt to verify the MFA requirement. The DAC configuration, including the defined claims and central access rules, is analyzed. It is practically tested on a file server whether access is correctly granted or denied according to the DAC policies.

controls.title: Protection of system integrity

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AppLocker is only used in 'audit-only' mode on a few systems or is only used to block a small list of known malicious applications (blacklisting).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: AppLocker policies are manually configured on individual servers to gain initial experience, but there is no comprehensive rollout plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the AppLocker event logs and finds that rules are only present in audit mode. The configured rules are checked for their blacklisting approach.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AppLocker is enabled on all servers, but with very permissive rules that, for example, allow the execution of all programs in the default 'Program Files' and 'Windows' directories. This provides only limited protection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default AppLocker rules are enabled and distributed via Group Policy without further customization to the specific requirements of the server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the AppLocker GPO and determines that only the default path rules are used. A check is performed to see if an unauthorized program can be executed if it is copied to an allowed directory such as C:\Windows\Temp.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AppLocker must be enabled to prevent the execution of unauthorized applications. Basic rules must be defined and enforced based on the principle of whitelisting (deny by default).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: AppLocker policies are distributed centrally via GPO. Rules are created based on paths for native applications and on publisher certificates for installed third-party software. The policies are operated in 'Enforce rules' mode.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the AppLocker GPO and verifies that the enforcement mode is active. An attempt is made to launch an unauthorized, portable application from a user directory, which must fail. The status of the AppIDSvc service (`Get-Service AppIDSvc`) and the configuration in the GPO can be checked automatically.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The AppLocker rules are strictly configured according to the 'Deny-by-Default' (whitelisting) principle. The rules are primarily based on secure attributes such as publisher certificates and file hashes for unsigned applications, rather than on insecure path rules. PowerShell is operated in 'Constrained Language Mode' to complicate script-based attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A systematic process for collecting the software inventory is used to create the whitelists. File hash rules are created for all critical applications without a valid signature. The 'Constrained Language Mode' is enforced for normal users through AppLocker policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the AppLocker rules and verifies the primary use of publisher and hash rules. It is checked whether PowerShell starts in 'Constrained Language Mode' for a non-administrator, which can be verified by querying the `$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode` variable.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AppLocker policies are centrally managed and dynamically updated, ideally integrated with a Software Asset Management system. Where possible, the hardware-assisted and more robust Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) is used. All AppLocker events (especially blockages) are forwarded to a SIEM for correlation, analysis, and alerting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process for approving new software is coupled with the process for updating the AppLocker/WDAC policies. Event Forwarding is configured to send the relevant AppLocker event IDs (e.g., 8004 for blockages) to the central log collector.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the software release process and its coupling with the update of the application control policies. In the SIEM, it is checked whether AppLocker block events arrive and trigger corresponding alerts. The configuration of the event forwarding is reviewed.

controls.title: Attack Detection on Windows Server 2012

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging on the servers is enabled with the default settings. The event logs are only stored locally on the machines and are only reactively analyzed manually after a security incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No advanced audit policies are configured. The size of the local event logs is often too small, which causes important information to be overwritten quickly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the audit policies (`auditpol /get /category:*`) and the size of the event logs on a server and finds that only the basic settings are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Important security-related events are collected centrally, for example, in a log aggregator. However, there is no established process for active and regular analysis or alerting based on this data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) or a log agent is used to send the security event logs to a central server. The collected data is primarily kept for archival and forensic analysis purposes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the log forwarding configuration. The central log server is checked to see if logs are arriving from the servers. Through interviews, it is determined that no proactive evaluation of the logs takes place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security-relevant events must be enabled on the server and forwarded to a central log management system for collection and evaluation. Encrypted partitions (e.g., with BitLocker) must be configured to lock after a defined number of failed unlock attempts to hinder brute-force attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Advanced audit policies are configured and enabled via GPO. The logs are sent to a SIEM system. The BitLocker lockout after failed attempts is also configured via GPO ('Standard user lockout').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the GPOs for the audit policies. It is checked whether logs from the servers arrive in the SIEM. The BitLocker-related GPO settings for lockout are verified. The audit policies can be read automatically with `auditpol`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logs collected in the central SIEM are actively and automatically analyzed using predefined correlation rules to detect suspicious activities and attack patterns. In case of high-priority events, alerts are automatically generated to the security team. Logging is hardened, e.g., by enabling PowerShell Script Block Logging.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Rules are implemented in the SIEM that check for things like failed login attempts from multiple sources, the creation of new administrative accounts, or the clearing of event logs. PowerShell Script Block Logging is enabled via GPO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the correlation rules in the SIEM and their thresholds. The configuration of the alerting is checked. It is verified that PowerShell Script Block Logging is active and that the corresponding events (ID 4104) are generated and forwarded.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIEM uses advanced analytics and machine learning (User and Entity Behavior Analytics - UEBA) to detect anomalies and complex attacks. The attack detection is integrated with a Security Orchestration, Automation and Response (SOAR) system to contain threats automatically and in near real-time (e.g., by network isolating a compromised server). The security team regularly conducts proactive threat hunting based on the collected log data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM with a UEBA module is used. SOAR playbooks are developed to respond to specific alarms, e.g., by executing scripts on firewalls or on the affected endpoint. For threat hunting, hypotheses are formed based on threat intelligence and systematically checked against the available data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration of the UEBA module and the SOAR playbooks. A simulated attack is carried out to verify that the automated response works as expected. The documentation and results of the conducted threat hunting activities are reviewed.

controls.title: Redundancy and High Availability on Windows Server 2012

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Redundancy is considered exclusively at the hardware level, e.g., through redundant power supplies or hard disks (RAID). There are no measures for high availability at the operating system or application level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When purchasing servers, attention is paid to redundant components, but the high availability features provided by the operating system are not used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the hardware specifications of the servers. It is found that no OS-level HA technologies such as Failover Clustering or NLB are configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Simple redundancy functions such as NIC Teaming (LBFO) to increase network availability are implemented. However, more complex high availability technologies such as Failover Clustering are not used even where they would be necessary to meet availability requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: NIC Teaming is configured as standard on all servers with multiple network adapters. An analysis of whether a Failover Cluster is required for certain services does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the NIC Teaming configuration on the servers. Critical, non-redundant services for which no high availability solution has been implemented are identified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A documented analysis must be performed to determine which native Windows Server high availability features (e.g., Failover Clustering, Network Load Balancing, DFS, NIC Teaming) are suitable for meeting the defined availability requirements. The functions selected based on the analysis must be basically configured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Service Level Agreement (SLA) regarding availability is defined for each critical service. Based on this, a concept determines which HA technology (e.g., Failover Cluster for an SQL database) will be used. The installation and basic configuration of this technology is performed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the analysis and concept documents and compares them with the defined SLAs. It is checked whether the selected HA technologies are installed on the corresponding systems and are fundamentally functional, e.g., by querying the cluster status (`Get-Cluster`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Failover Clustering and/or Network Load Balancing are consistently implemented and optimized for critical services based on the analysis. For cross-site scenarios, Distributed File System (DFS) is used for resilient file access. For branch offices, BranchCache is enabled to improve availability and performance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Cluster quorum settings are optimized and cluster validation tests are performed regularly. DFS Namespaces and Replication are set up for important file shares. BranchCache is enabled via GPO for the corresponding servers and clients in the branch offices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration of the Failover Clusters, including the quorum settings. The DFS topology is reviewed. The GPOs for configuring BranchCache are analyzed and it is spot-checked whether the service is running on the target systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive high availability and disaster recovery solution is implemented, potentially spanning multiple data centers (e.g., a multi-site cluster or stretch cluster). The functionality of the solution is regularly verified through planned, automated failover tests. The integrity of the cluster and the replicated data is continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A stretch failover cluster is set up with synchronous or asynchronous replication (e.g., via Storage Replica or third-party solutions). Automated test scripts are developed to simulate a failover at regular intervals and check the service's availability. Monitoring tools permanently monitor the cluster state and replication latency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the architecture of the multi-site solution. The logs and results of the automated failover tests are requested and evaluated. The monitoring dashboard is viewed to verify the current state of the cluster and replication.

controls.title: Shutting down encrypted servers and virtual machines

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Servers are only shut down manually and irregularly when they are explicitly no longer needed. There is no formal policy that mandates this.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Shutting down systems is at the discretion of individual administrators. Servers that are only needed periodically (e.g., test systems) often run continuously.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies servers with periodic usage and determines from their uptime that they run continuously for long periods. No policy for shutting down systems can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy exists that requires shutting down unneeded servers. However, implementation is purely organizational and relies on administrators following the policy manually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IT operations policy includes a clause on resource-saving operation that requires shutting down servers outside of usage hours.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the policy. By checking the uptime of servers, it is determined to what extent the policy is implemented in practice, with deviations often being found.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There must be a policy that requires unneeded servers with encrypted data (including virtual machines) to be shut down. Data decryption upon restart must require an interactive step (e.g., PIN entry for BitLocker) or at least be traceably logged in the security log.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy defines clear usage times for specific server groups. For decryption, BitLocker is configured with the TPM+PIN protection method, which requires manual entry at startup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the policy. The BitLocker configuration on the servers is checked to ensure that an interactive decryption method is active. This can be checked with the command `manage-bde -status`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process of shutting down servers outside of defined usage times is automated through scheduled tasks or scripts. A monitoring system is used to send alerts if servers that should be turned off are running unexpectedly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Windows Task Scheduler or PowerShell scripts are used to shut down servers at specific times. A monitoring tool regularly checks the status of the servers and sends a notification if a server is online outside of its scheduled operating hours.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configured scheduled tasks or scripts. The configuration and alerts of the monitoring system are reviewed to assess the effectiveness of the control.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The start and stop process is fully integrated into an infrastructure automation and orchestration platform. Systems are only started automatically when needed (e.g., by a user request or a scheduled job) and shut down again immediately afterward. The requirement for interactive decryption (e.g., TPM+PIN) is technically enforced; any form of automated decryption (e.g., via BitLocker Network Unlock) is specially secured and intensively monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like System Center Orchestrator or Ansible Tower are used to control the lifecycle of the VMs. BitLocker Network Unlock is only operated in a dedicated, high-security network segment with WDS and DHCP servers that are themselves heavily hardened and monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration of the automation platform and the associated workflows. The security architecture of the BitLocker Network Unlock infrastructure is thoroughly examined. It is verified that all decryption events (both interactive and automatic) are centrally logged and monitored for anomalies.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
With Windows Server 2012 in September 2012, Microsoft launched a server operating system that brought various security improvements over previous Windows versions, especially over its predecessor Windows Server 2008 R2. Technically, it is not based on Windows Server 2008 R2, but on the codebase of the client operating system Windows 8. With the release of Windows Server 2012 R2 in October 2013, the operating system was updated and expanded again to make it the server equivalent of Windows 8.1 on the client side.
This module deals with securing Windows Server 2012 and Windows Server 2012 R2 equally. When both versions are meant, the uniform notation "Windows Server 2012" is used. Differences in the R2 version are mentioned separately. The expiry date for mainstream support and extended support ("End-of-Life", EOL) for both operating systems is October 9, 2018 and October 10, 2023, respectively.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to protect information and processes that are processed or controlled by server systems based on Windows Server 2012 in regular operation.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.1.2.2 Windows Server 2012 is to be applied to all server systems on which the Microsoft Windows Server 2012 operating system is used. For newer versions of Windows Server, there is the module SYS.1.2.3 Windows Server.
This module specifies and supplements the aspects dealt with in the module SYS.1.1 General Server to include the specifics of Windows Server 2012. Accordingly, the two modules must always be applied together.
Within the scope of this module, a standard integration into an Active Directory domain is assumed, as is common in institutions. Specifics of stand-alone systems are only mentioned selectively where the differences seem particularly relevant. Requirements for Active Directory are part of the module APP.2.2 Active Directory Domain Services.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Inadequate planning of Windows Server 2012
parts.prose: Windows Server 2012 is a complex operating system with a large number of features and configuration options. There is a great deal of leeway when integrating it into the domain and networking it with other IT systems and services. Even though modern Windows versions come with good default settings in many areas, the basic configuration is not always the most secure. With insufficient planning, this can lead to a variety of attack vectors that can be easily exploited by unauthorized third parties. Furthermore, if central decisions are not made before installation, Windows Server 2012 will be run in an insecure and undefined state that can hardly be rectified afterwards.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Inconsiderate cloud usage
parts.prose: Windows Server 2012 offers the possibility to use cloud services in various places without having to install third-party software. These include, for example, Microsoft Azure Online Backup or the online storage of BitLocker recovery keys. While cloud services can offer fundamental advantages, for example in terms of availability, careless use poses risks to confidentiality and creates additional dependency. For example, data can fall into the hands of unauthorized persons via cloud services. These can be both criminal and state actors. If a cloud service is discontinued, this can have a significant impact on one's own business processes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Incorrect administration of Windows servers
parts.prose:
Compared to previous versions, Windows Server 2012 and Windows Server 2012 R2 have gained many new security-relevant functions. For other (known) features, sub-functions, parameters or standard configurations have changed. If IT operations are not sufficiently trained in the specifics of the systems, there is a risk of configuration errors and human misconduct that can affect the functionality as well as the security of the system.
A particular danger is posed by inconsistent Windows Server security settings (e.g. for SMB, RPC or LDAP). If the configuration is not systematically and centrally planned, documented, checked and maintained, there is a risk of so-called configuration drift. The more the concrete configurations of functionally similar systems diverge without reason and without documentation, the more difficult it becomes to maintain an overview of the status quo and to maintain security holistically and consistently.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Improper use of Group Policies (GPOs)
parts.prose: Group Policy Objects (GPOs) are a useful and powerful way to configure many (security) aspects of Windows Server 2012, especially in a domain. With the large number of possible settings, it is easy to accidentally set contradictory or incompatible settings or to forget areas. In a non-systematic approach, this leads at least to operational disruptions that are sometimes difficult to resolve, and at worst to serious vulnerabilities on the server or on connected clients. In particular, misunderstood inheritance rules and filters can lead to GPOs not being applied to a system at all.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Loss of integrity of sensitive information or processes
parts.prose: Windows Server 2012 has a variety of functions to protect the integrity of information processed by the operating system. Each of these functions can be flawed with vulnerabilities. In addition, there is often a lack of consistent configuration, not least for reasons of convenience. Information and processes can thus be falsified by unauthorized persons and often even the tracks can be covered. Malware is also frequently used to manipulate information remotely.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Unauthorized acquisition or misuse of administrative privileges
parts.prose: Regular work under standard permissions is now common practice. However, since administrators still need to elevate their rights at certain points, attackers can potentially gain privileged rights there. Misuse of rights by legitimate administrators is also a relevant damage scenario. Since the roles are often very powerful, the impact here is usually considerable, especially for so-called domain administrators. Even without guessing or cracking passwords, suitable credentials can be read and misused, e.g., through so-called pass-the-hash methods, to move laterally in the network.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Compromise of remote access
parts.prose: Since Windows Server 2012 has a variety of ways to be managed remotely, these can in principle also be misused. Remote access such as RDP sessions can be made accessible to third parties through insecure or insecurely used protocols, weak authentication (e.g. weak passwords) or incorrect configuration. This can largely compromise the server and the information stored there. Often, other IT systems connected to the server can also be compromised in this way.

controls.title: Planning for Windows Server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Planning for the deployment of Windows Server is only done sporadically and is undocumented. Decisions about the edition, purpose, or use of cloud services are made ad-hoc. The blocking of Microsoft accounts is not consistently implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, planning is often carried out by individual administrators without a central process. Decisions may not be documented, leading to inconsistent server configurations throughout the company.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through spot checks that there are no documented decisions for the choice of Windows Server editions. It is checked whether Microsoft accounts can be created on servers where they are not needed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic but not formalized planning process. The server edition is usually chosen deliberately, but the reasoning and purpose are not consistently documented. The blocking of Microsoft accounts is configured during installation but not regularly checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators follow unwritten rules or team conventions for server planning. The configuration to block Microsoft accounts is typically set via a base installation image, but its effectiveness is not verified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions administrators about the planning process and finds that it is informal. By checking the configuration of several servers, it is determined that while the blocking of Microsoft accounts is mostly present, it is not enforced by a central policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A reasoned and documented decision MUST be made for a suitable edition of Windows Server. The server's purpose and its integration into Active Directory MUST be specified. The use of bundled cloud services in the operating system MUST be fundamentally considered and thoroughly planned. If not needed, the creation of Microsoft accounts on the server MUST be blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each new server, a planning document is created or an entry is made in a central system (e.g., Wiki or CMDB). This document contains the chosen edition, the reasoning, the planned roles, and an assessment of cloud services. The blocking of Microsoft accounts is configured via a Group Policy Object (GPO).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documentation for a selection of servers. It is verified that the documentation contains the decision for the edition, the purpose, and the assessment of cloud usage. A GPO analysis is used to check whether the policy to block Microsoft accounts is configured and applied to the relevant servers. The application of the GPO can be automatically checked on the target systems with `gpresult /r`.

parts.name: statement
