parts.prose: The planning process is formalized and integrated into a central Configuration Management Database (CMDB). The decision-making includes an analysis of the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) and performance. The policy to block Microsoft accounts is centrally managed and enforced through regular, automated compliance checks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process is controlled by a ticketing system. The CMDB is automatically updated with the planning data. For compliance checks, scripts (e.g., PowerShell DSC or specialized audit tools) are used to report deviations from the defined policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the formalized planning process by reviewing the ticketing system and the CMDB. The reports from the automated compliance checks are reviewed to assess the effectiveness of policy enforcement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire server lifecycle, from planning to decommissioning, is largely automated. The choice of edition is based on automated profiling and business requirements. The assessment of cloud services is a continuous process with automated monitoring for policy deviations. The blocking of Microsoft accounts is enforced by a technical solution that prevents and reports circumvention.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) tools like Terraform or Ansible are used for server provisioning, with planning parameters mapped as code. A Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) or similar tools monitor the use of cloud services. AppLocker or similar technologies are used to prevent the creation of Microsoft accounts at a deep system level.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the IaC configuration files and the logs of the automation pipeline. The configuration of the monitoring tools (e.g., CASB) is checked and it is verified that alerts are generated for policy violations. An attempt is made to bypass the account creation protection mechanisms to demonstrate their effectiveness.

controls.title: Secure Installation of Windows Server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Server Core variant is used only rarely and usually only upon explicit request. A formal check to see if Server Core would be sufficient does not take place for most installations with a graphical user interface (GUI).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators install the GUI version by default out of habit or because they shy away from command-line administration. No process exists that promotes or mandates the use of Server Core.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies, through a system inventory, servers that are installed with a GUI but only run roles that would also run under Server Core (e.g., a dedicated DNS or DHCP server). It is determined that there is no justification for choosing the GUI version.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Server Core variant is considered as an option during installation. However, the decision against Server Core is often made verbally and not formally justified or documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The type of installation is discussed in team meetings, but the final decision rests with the installing administrator and is not traceably recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions administrators about the decision criteria for or against Server Core. It is found that while there is an awareness of the option, no traceable justifications for GUI installations exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If the feature set is sufficient, the Server Core variant MUST be installed. Otherwise, it MUST be justified why the Server Core variant is not sufficient. This justification is to be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision and justification are recorded as part of the planning process (see SYS.1.2.3.A1) in a designated document or system (e.g., CMDB, Wiki). A Server Core image is used as the standard for installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the corresponding justification for a selection of servers with a GUI installation. A check is performed to see if the justification is plausible and documented. The installation type of all servers can be queried automatically via a PowerShell script (`Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsInstallationType`) and compared with the documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal policy exists that specifies which server roles require the full GUI version. All other installations use Server Core by default. Deviations from this standard require a formal exception request with approval. The installation images are hardened.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is published in the QM system. The exception process is handled via a ticketing system. The installation images (WIM) are pre-hardened using DISM and Security Baselines (e.g., from Microsoft).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existence and content of the policy. The approved exception requests for GUI installations are inspected. The configuration of the hardening measures in the base image is analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation process is fully automated. The system automatically selects the Server Core or GUI variant based on the requested server role profile. Any attempt to install a GUI version where it is not permitted according to the role profile is automatically blocked and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The deployment is carried out via an automation platform (e.g., System Center VMM, Ansible, Terraform). The logic for selecting the installation type is embedded in the automation code. The block can be implemented through validation hooks in the pipeline or by downstream configuration management tools.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the code of the automation pipeline to verify the logic for selecting the installation type. An attempt is made to initiate a non-compliant GUI installation to check the effectiveness of the block and the logging. The logs are checked for corresponding alerts.

controls.title: Telemetry and usage data on Windows Server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The telemetry level is manually set to 'Security' on some servers, but this is not done consistently across all systems. There are no additional network controls to prevent data transmission.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Individual administrators change the setting after installation, but there is no company-wide process, which leads to patchy implementation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor spot-checks the telemetry settings on several servers and finds inconsistencies. It is also checked whether network traffic to known Microsoft telemetry endpoints is possible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The 'Security' telemetry level is configured as the default setting during installation or by a script after installation. However, there is no regular check to ensure the setting is effective and has not been changed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The setting is typically set in a base image or a post-installation script. A mechanism for continuous monitoring and enforcement of the setting is missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the default installation routine sets the setting correctly. However, by checking active servers, it is determined that there is no guarantee that the setting will be maintained.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To significantly reduce the transmission of diagnostic and usage data to Microsoft, the telemetry level MUST be configured to 0 (Security) on the Windows Server. If this setting is not effectively implemented, then it MUST be ensured through appropriate measures, for example at the network level, that the data is not transmitted to the manufacturer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The setting is centrally set via a Group Policy Object (GPO): 'Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Data Collection and Preview Builds > Allow Telemetry' to 'Enabled' with option '0 - Security'. Additionally, the known telemetry endpoints from Microsoft are blocked on the corporate firewall.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the corresponding GPO and checks its link to the server OUs. The firewall rules are checked for the blocking of Microsoft telemetry domains. The effective registry key (`HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DataCollection\AllowTelemetry`) can be read automatically on the servers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The telemetry setting is centrally enforced via GPO. In addition to blocking on the perimeter firewall, regular, automated configuration audits are performed on all servers to detect and report deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool (e.g., PowerShell DSC, Ansible) is used to continuously monitor the state of the telemetry setting and automatically correct it or trigger an alarm in case of deviation. The audit results are centrally collected and evaluated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and reports of the configuration management tool. The configuration of the alerting for deviations is checked. An attempt is made to change the setting manually to verify the automatic correction.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to GPO enforcement and firewall blocking, a Network Traffic Analysis (NTA) solution is in use. This actively monitors all outbound traffic and alerts on any connection attempts to known or new, unknown telemetry endpoints. These alerts are integrated into the SIEM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An NTA appliance or an EDR tool with network monitoring functionality is used. The signatures for telemetry traffic are constantly updated. Correlation rules are defined in the SIEM that generate a security-relevant incident in case of telemetry attempts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the NTA solution and the associated SIEM rules. Test connections to telemetry endpoints are initiated to check the detection and alerting live. The recorded network logs are analyzed for undetected telemetry connections.

controls.title: Protection against exploitation of vulnerabilities in applications

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Exploit protection measures SHOULD be enabled for all programs and services that support Windows Exploit Protection (e.g., Windows Defender Exploit Guard). The configuration is deliberately applied and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The system-wide exploit protection settings (like DEP, ASLR) are enabled. Additionally, application-specific settings for common software (e.g., Office, browsers, PDF readers) are configured via Windows Security or PowerShell cmdlets (`Set-ProcessMitigation`) and documented in a configuration policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the exploit protection policy. On selected systems, the configuration is verified using `Get-ProcessMitigation -System` and `Get-ProcessMitigation -Name <Application.exe>` and compared with the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Exploit protection is centrally managed and rolled out via Group Policies (GPO) or a comparable configuration management tool. The settings are optimized specifically for critical applications based on manufacturer recommendations and internal tests. Detections in pure audit mode are regularly reviewed to refine the policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An XML configuration file for exploit protection is created and distributed via GPO. For new applications, compatibility with the exploit protection measures is tested in a test environment before production deployment. The audit logs are centrally collected (e.g., in the Event Log) and regularly evaluated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the GPO configuration for exploit protection. The audit event logs and the documentation of the policy refinement process are reviewed. It is checked whether a process for compatibility testing of new applications exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Exploit protection is fully integrated into the Security Operations Center (SOC) workflows. All relevant protection functions are activated in block mode. Any blocking events are automatically transmitted to a SIEM system and trigger alarms and predefined incident response processes there.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Windows Defender for Endpoint (or a comparable EDR system) is used to manage and correlate Exploit Guard events. In the SIEM, playbooks (e.g., in a SOAR platform) are implemented that automatically initiate initial containment measures, such as isolating the affected server, in the event of an exploit attempt.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the EDR system and the SIEM/SOAR integration. Using simulated attacks (e.g., with the Atomic Red Team Framework), the entire chain from detection and blocking to alerting and automated response is tested.

controls.title: Secure authentication and authorization in Windows Server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In Windows Server, all user accounts SHOULD be members of the "Protected Users" security group. Service and computer accounts SHOULD NOT be members of "Protected Users". Service accounts SHOULD be configured as "Managed Service Account" (MSA or gMSA) where technically possible. These procedures are defined in a policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented procedure to add new user accounts to the 'Protected Users' group. When setting up new services, the use of gMSAs is checked and implemented. The policy is brought to the attention of the administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the memberships of the 'Protected Users' group and compares them with the list of active user accounts. It is checked whether service or computer accounts are mistakenly members. It is spot-checked whether services run with gMSAs or regular user accounts. The membership can be checked automatically via PowerShell (`Get-AdGroupMember 'Protected Users'`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Membership in the 'Protected Users' group is automatically managed based on user roles defined in an Identity Management (IdM) system. A regular, automated audit process reports deviations, such as user accounts outside the group or service accounts within the group. The use of gMSAs is enforced for all new services.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IdM system is configured to synchronize group membership in Active Directory. PowerShell scripts run on a scheduled basis to check for compliance and send reports to the security team. An onboarding process for new applications mandates the use of gMSAs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the IdM system and the synchronization rules. The reports from the automated audit scripts are reviewed. The onboarding process for new applications is checked for the requirement to use gMSAs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of the 'Protected Users' group and the use of gMSAs are fully automated and technically enforced. Any attempt to create a service account that is not a gMSA is blocked. Privileged Access Management (PAM) solutions are used in conjunction with 'Protected Users' to enforce just-in-time access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A provisioning workflow enforces the correct account configuration. Technical controls, e.g., via Service Connection Points or configuration scripts, prevent the creation of non-gMSA service accounts. A PAM solution such as Microsoft Privileged Access Management or a third-party product is integrated to further enhance login security.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the automation and PAM workflows. An attempt is made to create a non-compliant service account to test the effectiveness of the block. The logs of the PAM solution are checked for correct just-in-time privilege assignment.

controls.title: Security for remote access via RDP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: RDP access is restricted to a dedicated group of authorized users. In more complex environments, an RDP Gateway is used. Mechanisms such as Remote Credential Guard or RestrictedAdmin are evaluated and deployed if necessary. The use of convenience features such as clipboard or drive sharing is deliberately reviewed and configured according to security requirements. The cryptography protocols used comply with internal guidelines. RDP is disabled on servers that do not require remote access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The group of RDP users is assigned via GPO under 'Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment > Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services'. The configuration of convenience features and cryptography (e.g., TLS requirements) is also done via GPO. Deactivation is ensured by a separate GPO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the GPOs for RDP configuration. The membership of the authorized group is checked. The effective configuration of convenience features and deactivation is verified on selected servers. The configuration of user rights and RDP settings can be automatically read and validated via PowerShell.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All RDP traffic MUST run through an RDP Gateway that is additionally secured with multi-factor authentication (MFA). Remote Credential Guard and RestrictedAdmin mode are enforced via GPO. All convenience features (clipboard, drive mapping, etc.) are disabled by default and are only enabled in exceptional cases with justification. RDP session activities are logged to a central SIEM.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RDP Gateway is coupled with a RADIUS server or a cloud MFA solution. GPOs enforce the use of the gateway and the Credential Guard modes. A restrictive GPO disables all redirections. The relevant event IDs for RDP logons and logoffs (e.g., 4624, 4634, 4647) are sent to the SIEM via Windows Event Forwarding (WEF).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the RDP Gateway and the MFA integration. The corresponding GPOs are checked. RDP events are searched for in the SIEM and the completeness of the logging is assessed. An attempt is made to establish a direct RDP connection without a gateway to test the block.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the measures from Level 4, just-in-time (JIT) access is implemented, where RDP access is granted only on request and for a limited time. All RDP sessions are recorded (video and keystroke logging) for audit and incident response purposes. Network Level Authentication (NLA) is strictly enforced for all connections.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution is used to control JIT access and for session recording. The PAM solution acts as a central, controlled jump server and replaces the standard RDP Gateway. The GPO for NLA is configured to the highest level.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the PAM solution, including the JIT workflows and recording policies. A JIT access is requested to verify the process. Samples of session recordings are reviewed. An attempt is made to establish a connection without NLA to test the enforcement.

controls.title: Use of Windows PowerShell

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a defined policy for the use of PowerShell. PowerShell execution (Module Logging, Script Block Logging, Transcription) is centrally logged to a SIEM system. The execution policy for scripts is set to 'AllSigned', which requires a digital signature for all scripts. Older PowerShell versions (especially v2) are disabled. The use of Constrained Language Mode and Just Enough Administration (JEA) is evaluated and the decision is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Logging and deactivation of PowerShell v2 are configured via GPOs. Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) forwards the relevant logs to the SIEM. An internal code-signing infrastructure (e.g., based on AD CS) is used to sign administrative scripts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the GPOs for PowerShell configuration. The arrival and content of the PowerShell logs are checked in the SIEM. An attempt is made to run an unsigned script to test the effectiveness of the 'AllSigned' policy. The documentation on the evaluation of JEA and Constrained Language Mode is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to Level 3, Just Enough Administration (JEA) is implemented for all administrative roles to restrict administrators to the commands they need for their tasks. PowerShell Constrained Language Mode is enforced for all interactive sessions of non-administrators. The PowerShell logs in the SIEM are actively monitored with alert rules for suspicious activities (e.g., obfuscated commands).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: JEA role configuration files (.psrc) and session configuration files (.pssc) are created and registered on the target servers. Administrators connect via `Enter-PSSession -ConfigurationName <JEA-Endpoint>`. In the SIEM, correlation rules are implemented that check for known patterns of malicious PowerShell code (e.g., from lolbas-project.com).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the JEA configuration files for correct and minimal privilege assignment. An attempt is made to execute an unauthorized command as an administrator via a JEA endpoint. The alert rules in the SIEM are checked for their effectiveness and logic.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: JEA is fully implemented company-wide. All administrative scripts are stored in a secure, versioned repository (e.g., Git) and signed by an automated CI/CD pipeline. PowerShell logs are analyzed in real-time by an AI/ML-driven security analytics platform to detect novel threats. Any attempt to disable logging or bypass JEA is immediately blocked and triggers a high-priority security incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CI/CD pipeline (e.g., Azure DevOps, Jenkins) fetches scripts from Git, performs static code analysis (e.g., with PSScriptAnalyzer), signs them, and distributes them. EDR tools and advanced SIEM solutions with User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) are used to analyze the logs. AppLocker or similar technologies are used to additionally secure the PowerShell processes and block bypass attempts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the CI/CD pipeline, the configuration of the UEBA platform, and the AppLocker rules. Advanced bypass techniques are simulated to test the resilience of the protective measures. The response to triggered alarms is checked in the SOC.

controls.title: Use of Virtual Secure Mode (VSM)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When using Virtual Secure Mode (VSM), it SHOULD be considered that forensic investigations, e.g., for security incident response, are restricted or made more difficult. This risk assessment (increased protection of credentials vs. limited forensic visibility) is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision to activate VSM features like Credential Guard is made as part of a risk assessment for the respective system. A note is added to the Incident Response Plan that points out the limitations in analyzing memory dumps on VSM-protected systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the risk assessment for VSM-protected systems and checks whether the forensic limitations have been taken into account. The Incident Response Plan is checked for corresponding notes and adjustments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Incident Response Plan is actively updated with alternative procedures and tools to collect evidence from VSM-enabled systems. The security team receives training on these alternative forensic techniques (e.g., in-depth analysis of event logs, network traffic, and live system artifacts) to compensate for the lack of memory dumps for protected processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The incident response playbooks contain specific sections for VSM systems. Live forensics tools are procured and analysts are trained in their use. Logging on the endpoints (e.g., PowerShell Logging, process creation events) is intensified to create alternative data sources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the Incident Response Playbooks for specific instructions for VSM systems. Training records for the security team are reviewed. A simulated incident is conducted on a VSM system to evaluate the application of alternative forensic techniques.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated system checks the VSM activation status and correlates it with the asset information in the CMDB. The incident response playbook automatically provides investigators with specific instructions depending on whether VSM is active on a compromised host. The organization invests in advanced EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) solutions that provide insight into system behavior without relying on traditional memory forensics for VSM-protected areas.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool or an EDR agent reports the VSM status to the CMDB. A SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) platform automatically enriches incident data with the VSM status and selects the appropriate playbook. The deployed EDR solution uses kernel-level sensors to also monitor activities of VSM-protected processes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the automated workflow from VSM status detection to the adjustment of the response playbook in the SOAR platform. The EDR solution's capabilities to monitor VSM-protected processes are verified through targeted tests (e.g., running Mimikatz on a system with Credential Guard).

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: With Windows Server, Microsoft offers an operating system for servers. The main versions 2016, 2019 and 2022 of Windows Server are so-called long-term versions (Long-Term Servicing Channel, LTSC), each based on the code base of the client operating system Windows 10. As with Windows 10, Microsoft is also increasingly supplying cloud-based functions and applications as well as interfaces to the Microsoft Azure cloud platform with Windows Server.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to protect information that is processed, stored and transmitted by server systems based on Windows Server 2016, 2019 and 2022 in regular operation.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.1.2.3 Windows Server is to be applied to all server systems on which the Microsoft Windows Server operating system in versions 2016, 2019 or 2022 is used. For Windows Server 2012, the module SYS.1.2.2 Windows Server 2012 should be modelled instead.

This module specifies and supplements the platform-independent security aspects for servers, which are dealt with in the module SYS.1.1 General Server, to include the specifics of Windows Server in the versions mentioned. Accordingly, the two modules must always be applied together.

This module deals with basic protection at the operating system level with on-board tools, regardless of the server's purpose. Security requirements for possible server roles and functions such as file server (APP.3.3 File Server) or web server (APP.3.2 Web Server) are the subject of separate modules, as is the topic of virtualisation (SYS.1.5 Virtualisation).

In addition, some operating system variants also have other applications pre-installed, such as the Microsoft Internet Explorer browser. The corresponding modules must be modelled for these applications.

Within the scope of this module, it is assumed that the server is included as a "Member Server" in an Active Directory domain, as is common in institutions. Specifics of stand-alone systems are only mentioned selectively where the differences seem particularly relevant. Requirements for Active Directory are part of the module APP.2.2 Active Directory Domain Services. For the use of the sometimes included functions and applications of cloud services as well as interfaces between the Microsoft Azure cloud platform and Windows Server, the module OPS.2.2 Cloud Usage must be applied, which also deals with threats and general requirements for cloud use.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Inconsiderate Cloud Usage
parts.prose: Windows Server offers the possibility to use cloud services in various places without having to install third-party software. These include, for example, Microsoft Azure Online Backup or the online storage of BitLocker recovery keys. While cloud services can offer possible advantages, for example in terms of availability, there are risks to confidentiality and a dependency on service providers in the case of ill-considered use. For example, data can fall into the hands of unauthorized third parties via cloud services. These can be both criminals and state actors. If a cloud service is terminated by the provider, this can have a considerable impact on one's own business processes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Compromise of Remote Access
parts.prose: Since Windows Server has a variety of ways to be managed remotely, these can in principle also be misused. Remote access such as RDP or WinRM sessions can be made accessible to third parties through insecure or insecurely used protocols, weak authentication methods (e.g. weak passwords) or incorrect configuration. This can largely compromise the server and the information stored there. Often, other IT systems connected to the server can also be compromised in this way.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Telemetry of Windows Server
parts.prose: By default, Windows Server sends so-called diagnostic data to the manufacturer Microsoft. In addition, Microsoft can use the telemetry service integrated in Windows Server to specifically query information from a server. Depending on the telemetry level, this includes, for example, access to crash dumps of the memory (so-called 'crash dumps') as well as access to operating system events on the server. There is a risk that the diagnostic and telemetry data contain sensitive information that can reach third parties in this way.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Limited Forensics when using the Virtual Secure Mode (VSM)
parts.prose: The use of Virtual Secure Mode (VSM) limits or complicates forensic investigations, e.g. for security incident handling. Processes protected by the Secure Kernel or the Isolated User Mode (IUM) are no longer accessible. For example, memory dumps of these processes cannot be evaluated due to cryptographic measures.

controls.title: Careful assignment of IDs (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The assignment of login names, UIDs, and GIDs is largely manual and without a fixed process. Although attempts are made to avoid duplicates, this is not systematically checked, which occasionally leads to conflicts, especially on individual systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: IDs are entered 'by hand' into the /etc/passwd and /etc/group files as needed. There is no central documentation or management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Manual spot check of the /etc/passwd file on a single server for obvious duplicates. It is not expected that all inconsistencies will be found.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The uniqueness of login names, UIDs, and GIDs is ensured on each individual system. There is a fundamental rule that every GID in /etc/passwd must also exist in /etc/group. However, consistency across system boundaries is not actively managed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators use basic shell commands (grep, sort, uniq) to search for duplicates before assigning new IDs. Management is done on a per-system basis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Systematic check of local configuration files (/etc/passwd, /etc/group) on each server for internal consistency and duplicates. No cross-system comparison takes place. Automated: Run `awk -F: 'seen_name[$1]++ {print "Duplicate name: " $1}; seen_uid[$3]++ {print "Duplicate UID: " $3}' /etc/passwd` and `awk -F: 'seen_gname[$1]++ {print "Duplicate group name: " $1}; seen_gid[$3]++ {print "Duplicate GID: " $3}' /etc/group` on each system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every login name, user ID (UID), and group ID (GID) is uniquely assigned according to a defined schema. It is ensured that every user account is a member of at least one group. All GIDs referenced in /etc/passwd are defined in /etc/group. Group memberships are limited to the necessary minimum. In networked environments, the consistent assignment of names and IDs for users and groups is actively ensured to avoid conflicts during cross-system access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The assignment of IDs is supported by documented processes and checklists. In networked environments, a central list or a simple script is used to check for consistency across multiple systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the files /etc/passwd, /etc/group for duplicate names, UIDs, and GIDs. Check if every GID in /etc/passwd is defined in /etc/group. Interview administrators about the ID assignment process. In networked systems: Compare the ID databases or configuration files on multiple systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central identity management system (e.g., LDAP, FreeIPA) is used for managing users, groups, and IDs to ensure system-wide consistency. Regular, automated scripts check the configuration files on all connected systems for deviations from the central database and report them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use of tools like SSSD or nslcd to connect the Unix servers to a central directory (e.g., FreeIPA, Active Directory). A cron job runs a check script daily, which sends the results to a central logging or monitoring system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the configuration of the identity management system and the connection of the clients. Analyze the reports of the automated check scripts from the last month. Randomly check the local ID consistency on clients to verify correct synchronization.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ID management is fully automated and integrated into the provisioning process for users and systems. Any manual changes to local ID configuration files are actively prevented by a configuration management system (e.g., Ansible, Puppet) and immediately reverted. Cross-system access is secured by mechanisms such as Kerberos, which build on the consistent ID base.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Integration of Identity Management (IdM) with the HR system for the user lifecycle. Use of Ansible to enforce the SSSD configuration on all servers and to clean up and lock the local passwd/group files (except for system users). Regular audits are performed automatically and the results are correlated in a SIEM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the automated provisioning workflow. Analysis of the configuration management rules that manage the local ID files. Verification that alarms are generated in the SIEM for manual change attempts. Automated: Run a configuration management tool in 'check mode' (e.g., `ansible --check`) to confirm compliance.

controls.title: No automatic mounting of removable drives (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automatic mounting of removable drives is disabled on some, but not all, systems. There is no uniform policy or configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The deactivation may have only been carried out manually on systems considered critical, while others have retained the distribution's default settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Random check of various servers by plugging in a USB stick to see if it is automatically mounted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On all servers, the automatic mounting of removable drives such as USB sticks or CDs/DVDs is prevented by system-wide configuration settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is typically achieved by blacklisting kernel modules (e.g., `usb-storage`) or by adjusting udev rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the relevant configuration files (e.g., in `/etc/modprobe.d/`, `/etc/udev/rules.d/`) on all server types to verify the deactivation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Removable media such as USB sticks or CDs/DVDs must not be mounted automatically. A defined process is established that describes how authorized users can manually mount a drive if necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Disabling automount services (e.g., via `systemctl disable udisks2.service`) is standard. Administrators are aware of and have documented the `mount` command for these purposes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verification that no automount services are active. Review of the documentation for the manual mount process. Automated check: `systemctl is-enabled udisks2.service` should return 'disabled'.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Disabling the automatic mounting of removable drives is enforced and regularly checked by a configuration management system (e.g., Ansible, Puppet). Every manual mount operation (`mount`) is centrally logged and monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Ansible playbook ensures that the udev rules are correct. Auditd rules are used to monitor the `mount` system call and send it to a SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the configuration management rules. Analyze the audit logs for `mount` events and check if they were authorized.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Physical ports (e.g., USB) on servers in the data center are disabled by default via BIOS/UEFI and additionally at the operating system level. Any attempt to detect or mount a device triggers a high-priority security alarm in the SIEM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The BIOS/UEFI settings are centrally managed and enforced. At the operating system level, kernel modules are removed or a strict whitelist of allowed devices (which can be empty) is enforced by `usbguard`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the BIOS/UEFI configurations. Review of the `usbguard` rules. Performing a penetration test that attempts to connect an unauthorized USB device and verifies that an alarm is triggered.

controls.title: Protection against exploitation of vulnerabilities in applications (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is ensured that the distribution's default protection mechanisms, such as ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization), are enabled in the kernel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The setting `/proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space` is checked during system installation and set to the default value (typically 2).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the value of `/proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space`. It should not be 0. Automated: `cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To make it more difficult to exploit vulnerabilities in applications, ASLR and DEP/NX must be enabled in the kernel and used by the applications. Security features of the kernel and the standard libraries, such as heap and stack protection, must not be disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The activation of these features is standard in modern Linux distributions. It is actively ensured that these settings are not disabled by outdated instructions or incorrect configurations. The use is ensured by the presence of the `nx` flag in `/proc/cpuinfo` and the ASLR kernel parameter.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check if the `nx` flag is present in the output of `cat /proc/cpuinfo`. Check if `/proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space` is set to 2. Check binary files with `checksec` or a similar tool to ensure they were compiled with Stack Canary, NX, etc.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is actively monitored and enforced by configuration management that ASLR and DEP/NX are active system-wide. Applications and especially exposed services are specifically compiled as Position Independent Executable (PIE) to fully exploit the effectiveness of ASLR.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible) sets the `sysctl` parameters for ASLR. The compiler flags `-fPIE` and `-pie` are used when compiling custom software. A `checksec` script runs regularly on critical binaries and reports deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the configuration management rules for kernel parameters. Review of the build scripts for custom developments for PIE flags. Evaluation of the reports from the `checksec` monitoring script.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All applications are run in restrictive environments (such as containers with seccomp filters and AppArmor/SELinux) that go beyond ASLR/DEP. The kernel is compiled and deployed with additional, non-standard hardening flags (e.g., from the GRSecurity/PaX project or by `CONFIG_INIT_ON_ALLOC_DEFAULT_ON=y`) to provide maximum protection against memory corruption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use of a self-compiled hardened kernel or one obtained from a specialized provider. All services run in containers whose seccomp profiles restrict the allowed system calls to a minimum. The kernel configuration is versioned and audited.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the kernel build configuration for hardening options. Analysis of the seccomp and AppArmor/SELinux profiles for critical applications. Attempting to make disallowed system calls from a service to test the effectiveness of the filters.

controls.title: Secure installation of software packages (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an instruction not to compile software from source code as a privileged user (root). The installation is done after compiling, e.g., with `make install`.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators create a temporary user or use their own unprivileged account for the `configure` and `make` process. Only the last step, `make install`, is executed with `sudo`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interview administrators about their procedure for compiling software. Check the `history` files for tell-tale command chains.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If software to be installed is to be compiled from source code, it may only be unpacked, configured, and translated under an unprivileged account. Subsequently, the software to be installed must not be installed uncontrolled into the root file system of the operating system. The selected parameters and installation steps are documented to be able to compile the software in a traceable and reproducible manner at any time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of using `make install`, tools like `checkinstall` or `fpm` are used to create a temporary software package (.deb, .rpm). This package is then installed with the system's package manager. The build steps are recorded in a wiki or a readme document.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the documentation for self-compiled software. Spot-checking of manually installed software to determine if it is tracked by the package manager (e.g., using `dpkg -S /usr/local/bin/some-app`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated build system is used to create reproducible native packages (.deb, .rpm) from the source code. These packages are cryptographically signed before installation and made available for distribution in an internal, trusted package repository.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use of the Open Build Service (OBS) or a Jenkins pipeline with `fpm` for automated package building. The packages are signed with a GPG key and uploaded to a dedicated `apt` or `yum` repository. The clients are configured to only accept packages from this repository and to verify the signatures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configuration of the build system and the package repository. Verifying the package manager configuration on the clients to ensure they use the internal repository and check signatures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire build process takes place in isolated, clean, and ephemeral containers (CI/CD pipeline). Each dependency is scanned for known vulnerabilities (Software Bill of Materials, SBOM). The resulting artifact is signed, and only signed packages whose SBOM shows no critical vulnerabilities can be released for installation via the configuration management system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GitLab CI/CD pipeline starts a new Docker container for each build. Tools like `Trivy` or `Grype` scan the source code and dependencies. After a successful scan and build, the package is signed with `cosign` or GPG and stored in Artifactory. Ansible or Puppet only retrieve the packages from there and verify the signature before installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the CI/CD pipeline configuration, including the scan and signing steps. Inspection of the SBOMs and scan reports for recently built packages. Verification of the configuration management rules that enforce secure package installation.

controls.title: Managing users and groups (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an instruction to use the operating system's standard tools for managing users and groups and not to edit the configuration files directly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators are taught to use `useradd`, `usermod`, `groupadd`, etc. For sudo configuration, `visudo` is used to avoid syntax errors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing administrators about their working methods. Spot-checking the shell history for the use of editors for configuration files like `/etc/passwd`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The appropriate management tools should be used for managing users and groups. Direct editing of the configuration files /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group, and /etc/sudoers should be avoided.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of standard management tools (`useradd`, `usermod`, `groupadd`, `visudo`) is specified in the work instructions for administrators. This ensures that all necessary files are updated consistently and that locking mechanisms are effective.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the work instructions. Reviewing the system logs for the execution of the corresponding management tools. It is verified that no direct write access to the configuration files by administrators takes place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of management tools is encapsulated in standardized scripts to ensure consistent and error-free execution. Changes to the `sudoers` configuration are distributed exclusively via a configuration management system that automatically checks the syntax before rollout.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Shell scripts (e.g., `create_user.sh`) bundle the necessary commands and query parameters. The `/etc/sudoers` file or configurations in `/etc/sudoers.d/` are managed via Ansible or Puppet modules that use `visudo -c` for validation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the administration scripts. Review of the configuration management rules and the validation steps for the `sudoers` configuration contained therein.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: User, group, and sudo rights management is fully integrated into a central identity management system with an approval workflow. Direct changes on the target systems are technically prevented and are only carried out via the central platform according to the four-eyes principle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use of FreeIPA or a commercial IdM solution that centrally manages users, groups, and sudo rules. Changes are requested via a web interface and approved by a second person before being rolled out to the systems. Local management tools are blocked for administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration and approval process in the IdM system. Verification that administrators do not have permissions to override the configurations locally. Audit logs of the IdM are checked for changes made and their approvals.

controls.title: Encrypted access via Secure Shell (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: SSH is the established standard for remote access. Insecure protocols such as Telnet, rsh, and rlogin are disabled on all systems. However, password authentication is still permitted system-wide.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The services for Telnet, etc., are uninstalled or disabled via systemd. The SSH configuration still allows `PasswordAuthentication yes`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check if Telnet or rsh services are running (`ss -tlpn`). Check the SSH configuration file `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` for the `PasswordAuthentication` setting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To establish an encrypted and authenticated, interactive connection between two IT systems, only Secure Shell (SSH) should be used. All other protocols whose functionality is covered by Secure Shell should be completely disabled. For authentication, certificates or key pairs should be used primarily instead of a password.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All systems are configured so that Telnet, rlogin, etc. are disabled. The `sshd_config` is set so that `PubkeyAuthentication yes` applies. The use of key pairs is recommended and established for administrative access, even if password authentication may still exist as a fallback for normal users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verification that no insecure remote access services are running. Review of the `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` for the preferred use of key authentication. Interviewing administrators about the established practice of authentication.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SSH server configuration (`sshd_config`) is hardened. This includes disabling direct root login, disabling password authentication, using strong ciphers, MACs, and KEX algorithms, and restricting access to specific users or groups. Keys must have a minimum strength (e.g., RSA 3072 bit, ED25519).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `sshd_config` is distributed via configuration management (e.g., Ansible) and contains `PermitRootLogin no`, `PasswordAuthentication no`, and explicit lists for `Ciphers`, `MACs`, `KexAlgorithms`. Old or known weak keys in `authorized_keys` files are regularly searched for and removed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the `sshd_config` with a scanning tool like `ssh-audit` or by manual comparison with a hardening guideline (e.g., from Mozilla). Checking the public keys in `authorized_keys` files for their length and type.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: SSH access is only possible via a hardened bastion host (jump host) that enforces two-factor authentication. Instead of long-lived static keys, short-lived SSH certificates issued by an internal Certificate Authority (CA) are used. All SSH sessions are centrally and immutably recorded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SSH CA server (e.g., with `step-ca` or HashiCorp Vault) issues certificates with a validity of a few hours after successful 2FA login. The `sshd_config` on all servers is configured to only accept certificates from this CA (`TrustedUserCAKeys`). Session recording is done using tools like `tlog` or commercial PAM-based solutions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of the SSH CA, the bastion host, and the target servers. Verification that a login without a valid certificate fails. Inspection of the recorded SSH sessions.

controls.title: Preventing lateral movement when exploiting vulnerabilities (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Mandatory Access Control (MAC) systems such as SELinux or AppArmor are installed on the systems and active in enforcing mode. However, only the default profiles supplied by the distributor are used without any further customizations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During system installation, care is taken to ensure that SELinux or AppArmor is not deactivated. The status is checked with `sestatus` or `aa-status`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Run `sestatus` (for SELinux) or `aa-status` (for AppArmor) to check if the system is running in enforcing/protect mode and profiles are loaded.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Services and applications should be protected with an individual security architecture (e.g., with AppArmor or SELinux). Chroot environments as well as LXC or Docker containers should also be considered. It should be ensured that supplied standard profiles or rules are activated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On all systems, either SELinux or AppArmor is active in enforcing mode. For container environments like Docker, it is ensured that the default security profiles (AppArmor/SELinux) are not deactivated. For simple services, a `chroot` environment can also serve as an isolation measure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the MAC system status (`sestatus`, `aa-status`). Checking the configuration of container runtimes (`dockerd`) to ensure that security options are not disabled (`--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` or `--security-opt apparmor=unconfined`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The default profiles of SELinux/AppArmor are actively adapted to the respective application and its legitimate needs in order to implement the principle of least privilege. Unnecessary permissions (e.g., write access in certain directories) are removed. All policy violations are centrally logged and regularly evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Using tools like `audit2allow` (SELinux) or `aa-logprof` (AppArmor), the log files are analyzed to refine the profiles. The customized profiles are distributed via a configuration management system. Logs are sent to a central SIEM and monitored for anomalies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the custom SELinux/AppArmor policies for their specificity. Review of the logs in the SIEM for MAC violations and the subsequent reactions. Comparison of the active profiles with the default profiles to identify customizations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all critical and exposed services, custom, highly restrictive SELinux/AppArmor profiles are developed from scratch. In addition, `seccomp-bpf` filters are used to drastically reduce the allowed system calls per application to an explicit whitelist, thus making attacks at the kernel level more difficult.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The development of minimal profiles is part of the deployment process for every new application. `seccomp` filters are loaded either directly by the application (e.g., in Go programs) or by the runtime environment (e.g., `systemd`, Docker, Kubernetes). Any attempt to perform a non-permitted action is blocked and triggers an alarm.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Code review of the custom MAC profiles and `seccomp` filters. Performing penetration tests that specifically attempt to break out of the application. Verifying that the blocks and alarms function as expected.

controls.title: Prevention of information snooping about the system and users (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The output of information about the operating system and access to log and configuration files should be restricted to the necessary minimum for users. Furthermore, no confidential information should be passed as parameters in command calls.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The file permissions on configuration files in `/etc` and log files in `/var/log` are adjusted so that normal users cannot read them. In scripts, care is taken not to pass passwords on the command line, but to read them from files or via environment variables.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of file permissions in the `/etc` and `/var/log` directories. Manual code review of administration scripts for passing passwords as command line arguments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A systematic review and hardening of file permissions is enforced. The use of commands that reveal information about other users (e.g., `who`, `finger`, `w`) is prohibited for normal users. The process list is restricted to the user's own processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: File permissions are enforced via configuration management. The mentioned information commands are removed or their permissions are changed so that they cannot be executed by normal users. The `/proc` filesystem is mounted with the `hidepid=2` option to hide process information.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration management rules for file permissions. Verification of the `hidepid` mount option in `/etc/fstab`. Attempting to execute the information commands or view processes of other users as a normal user.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A hardened kernel and strict MAC rules (SELinux) prevent information leakage between processes and access to system information that goes beyond what is absolutely necessary for the process's function. The transfer of confidential information to processes occurs exclusively via dedicated and secure mechanisms such as the kernel keyring or a secret management service.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SELinux policies are designed to restrict information flow even via covert channels (e.g., file locks). Applications are rewritten to obtain their secrets from HashiCorp Vault or via the Linux kernel keyring, instead of from configuration files or environment variables.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the SELinux policies for their strictness regarding information flows. Review of the application code or configuration to verify how secrets are handled. Verification that no secrets are visible in the process environment or on the command line (`cat /proc/[pid]/cmdline` or `/proc/[pid]/environ`).

controls.title: Additional prevention of lateral movement when exploiting vulnerabilities (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of system calls for exposed services and applications is restricted to the absolute necessary minimum by activating standard profiles from, for example, SELinux or AppArmor.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: It is ensured that the SELinux or AppArmor profiles supplied by the distributor for exposed services such as web servers or mail servers are active in enforcing mode.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check via `sestatus` or `aa-status` whether the corresponding profiles for the services are loaded and running in enforcing mode.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The standard profiles or rules of, for example, SELinux, AppArmor are manually reviewed and, if necessary, adapted to the own security policies. If required, new rules or profiles are created to further restrict permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The audit logs of the MAC system are analyzed (`audit2allow`, `aa-logprof`) to identify and remove unused permissions in the standard profiles. The adapted, more restrictive profiles are distributed via configuration management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Comparison of the active profiles with the distributor standard profiles to identify the implemented tightenings. Analysis of the audit logs to ensure that no unnecessary 'allow' rules are still present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For exposed services, new, minimal SELinux/AppArmor profiles are developed from scratch, which only allow the actions strictly necessary for operation. In addition, the allowed system calls are restricted to a minimal whitelist using `seccomp-bpf`.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The development process for new applications includes the creation of a minimal AppArmor/SELinux profile and a `seccomp` filter. Tools like `strace` are used to determine the required system calls. The filters are applied by `systemd` (via `SystemCallFilter=`) or the container runtime.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Manual review of the created MAC profiles and seccomp filters for completeness and minimality. Performing tests that attempt to trigger non-allowed system calls and verifying that they are correctly blocked and logged.

controls.title: Additional protection of the kernel (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Appropriate protective measures such as memory protection or file system security are implemented to prevent the exploitation of vulnerabilities and spread within the operating system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Important file systems are mounted with security-relevant mount options such as `noexec`, `nodev`, `nosuid`. This particularly affects `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and `/home`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking `/etc/fstab` and the output of the `mount` command for the correct application of the security-relevant mount options.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Specially hardened kernels (e.g., with GRSecurity/PaX patches) are used, or the standard kernel is operated with additional hardening options and kernel modules such as the Linux Kernel Runtime Guard (LKRG) to protect the integrity of the kernel at runtime.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A self-compiled kernel with activated hardening options (e.g., `CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM`) is used. The LKRG kernel module is loaded and active to detect and block the exploitation of kernel exploits.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the kernel boot parameters and the loaded modules (`lsmod`). Checking the kernel logs (`dmesg`) for messages from LKRG or other hardening mechanisms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Commercially supported, hardened kernels (e.g., from GRSecurity) are used. In addition, immutable system partitions (Immutable Root Filesystem) are used to protect the integrity of the kernel and system files at runtime and prevent tampering.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The server boots from a read-only root filesystem (e.g., using `overlayfs` or specific features of btrfs/ZFS). Changes to the system configuration require a restart and a special maintenance mode. The kernel is sourced from a provider with a security support contract.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the immutable root setup configuration. Attempting to modify a system file during operation and verifying that this fails. Checking the kernel version and support contracts.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
The Linux or Unix operating systems are often used on server systems. Examples of classic Unix systems are the BSD series (FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD), Solaris and AIX. Linux, on the other hand, is not a classic Unix, but a functional Unix system. This means that the Linux kernel is not based on the original source code from which the various Unix derivatives were developed. This module considers all operating systems of the Unix family, including Linux as a functional Unix system. Since the configuration and operation of Linux and Unix servers are similar, this module refers to Linux and Unix as "Unix servers" or "Unix-like".
Linux is free software developed by the open source community. This means that it can be used, copied, distributed and modified by anyone. There are also companies that combine and maintain the various software components into a distribution and offer other services. The distributions Debian, Red Hat Enterprise Linux / CentOS, SUSE Linux Enterprise / openSUSE or Ubuntu Server are often used for Linux servers. In addition, there are Linux distributions tailored to special applications and devices, such as OpenWRT for routers.
The services offered on a Unix server are often central and therefore particularly exposed. For this reason, Unix servers are not only critical for business processes or specialized tasks, but also frequently become the focus of attacks. Therefore, the availability and security of Unix servers are of particular importance.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is to protect information provided and processed by Unix servers. The requirements of the module apply primarily to Linux servers, but can generally be adapted for Unix servers. Requirements are formulated on how the operating system should be configured and operated, regardless of the server's purpose.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.1.3 Server under Linux and Unix must be applied to all servers on which Linux or Unix-based operating systems are used.
The module contains fundamental requirements for the setup and operation of Unix servers. It specifies and supplements the aspects dealt with in module SYS.1.1 General Server with the particularities of Unix systems. Accordingly, the two modules must always be applied together.
Security requirements for possible server functions such as web servers (see APP.3.2 Web Server) or e-mail servers (see APP.5.3 General E-Mail Client and Server) are not considered in this module, but are the subject of their own modules. An exception is the Unix-specific server service SSH, which is also dealt with in this module. The topic of virtualization is also not covered in this module, but in module SYS.1.5 Virtualization.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Snooping for information about the system and about users
parts.prose:
Using various Unix programs, it is possible to query data that the IT system stores about its users. This also affects data that can provide information about the performance profile of users. This information includes information about other logged-in users as well as technical information about the operating system installation and configuration.
For example, with a simple program that evaluates the information provided by the "who" command at a specific time interval, any user can create a detailed usage profile for an account. In this way, the absence times of system administrators can be determined in order to use these times for unauthorized actions. Furthermore, it can be determined which terminals are permitted for privileged access. Other programs with similar possibilities for data misuse are "finger" or "ruser".

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Exploitability of the scripting environment
parts.prose: Scripting languages are often used in Unix operating systems. Scripts are a list of individual commands that are stored in a text file and can be called, for example, from the command line. Due to the large functional scope of the scripting environment, attackers can extensively abuse scripts for their purposes. Furthermore, activated scripting languages are very difficult to contain.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Dynamic loading of shared libraries
parts.prose: With the command line option LD_PRELOAD, a dynamic library is loaded before all other standard libraries required in an application. This makes it possible to overwrite individual functions of the standard libraries with your own. For example, attackers could manipulate the operating system in such a way that malicious functions are also executed when certain applications are used.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Software from third-party sources
parts.prose: On Unix-like IT systems, it is common for users to download and compile software source code themselves instead of installing ready-made software packages. If ready-made software packages are used, they are in some cases also installed from third-party sources without further checks, instead of exclusively from the vendor's existing package repositories. Each of these alternative ways of software installation carries additional risks, as it can lead to the installation of faulty or incompatible software as well as malware.

controls.title: Secure use of virtual IT systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access rights for administrators are restricted only for a few virtual systems considered particularly critical. There is no systematic monitoring of performance; it is only carried out reactively when problems occur.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The reduction of rights is done manually and irregularly. Performance metrics are only read from the management console when needed. There is no concept for isolation or encapsulation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During a spot check of administrators, the auditor finds that most have extensive default permissions. No evidence of regular performance monitoring can be provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access rights for all administrators are reduced to a basic level sufficient for most daily tasks. The performance of the virtual systems is checked regularly, but manually. Basic network connectivity is ensured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard admin role with restricted rights is defined in the virtualization platform and assigned to all administrators. Once a week, the most important performance indicators (CPU, RAM) are manually checked and recorded in a list.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that all administrators are assigned to the defined standard role. The manually kept lists of performance checks are reviewed. Automated check: A script queries the assigned roles of the administrators via the platform's API.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every person who administers virtual IT systems MUST know how virtualization affects them. Access rights for administrators to virtual IT systems MUST be reduced to the level actually required. It MUST be ensured that the necessary network connections are available and that the requirements for isolation and encapsulation are met. During operation, the performance of the virtual IT systems MUST be monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A role concept with different permission levels is implemented. Performance is continuously recorded by the virtualization platform. The network configuration (e.g., assignment to VLANs) is deliberately made and documented when creating a VM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews administrators about their understanding of the virtualization impacts and checks the assigned rights in the management system. The configuration of the performance monitoring and the network configuration of VMs are checked on a random basis. Automated check: A script checks whether administrators only correspond to their assigned, minimal roles and whether performance monitoring is active for all productive VMs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The performance of the virtual IT systems is monitored by an automated system that proactively alerts when thresholds are exceeded. Access rights are reviewed and recertified regularly, at least once a year.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitoring tool like Zabbix or Prometheus is used to collect performance metrics and trigger alarms. A formal process for the annual review of administrator permissions is established and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the monitoring system and the alarms triggered in recent months. The logs of the annual rights recertification are reviewed. Automated check: A script queries the API of the monitoring system to validate the configured thresholds and alerts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Performance monitoring is coupled with an automated resource allocation system (e.g., VMware DRS) that independently balances load peaks. Isolation between virtual systems is enforced through hardware-assisted security functions and micro-segmentation based on a zero-trust architecture.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Functions like VMware Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS) are operated in fully automated mode. Technologies like NSX or similar are used for micro-segmentation. Access rights are granted just-in-time (JIT) for specific tasks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and logs of the automated resource system. The configuration of micro-segmentation and JIT access rights allocation is reviewed. Automated audit: A script validates the DRS configuration and the micro-segmentation firewall rules directly via the platform's APIs.

controls.title: Secure Configuration of Virtual IT Systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Direct access from guest systems to host interfaces is not explicitly prevented. Virtual systems are configured on an ad-hoc basis without uniform security policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators use the default settings of the virtualization platform, which may allow access to devices such as USB ports. There are no templates or checklists for system configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds in a random sample of VMs that they have direct access to host devices. The configurations of the VMs are inconsistent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access from guest systems to host devices and interfaces is disabled by default. Access is granted when needed, but without a formal approval process or time limit.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: By default, no host devices are passed through in the VM templates. Requests for exceptions are made via email and implemented by an administrator.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that new VMs do not have access to host devices by default. For systems with shared devices, the request and implementation process is checked, with an informal process being expected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Guest systems MUST NOT access devices and interfaces of the virtualization server. However, if such a connection is necessary, it MUST be allocated exclusively and MUST only exist for the required duration. Binding regulations MUST be defined for this purpose. Virtual IT systems SHOULD be configured and protected according to the institution's security policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented process for the request, approval, and time-limited allocation of host devices. The configuration of VMs is based on documented security policies and standardized templates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the regulation process for device access and inspects the applications and approvals. The configuration of VMs is randomly checked against the applicable security policies. Automated audit: A script reads the configuration of all VMs and reports which VMs have access to host interfaces in order to compare this with the approved exceptions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Any exclusive access of a guest system to a host interface is centrally logged and regularly reviewed. The configuration of virtual systems is enforced by configuration management tools and monitored for deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Changes to the VM configuration, especially the allocation of devices, generate log entries in a central SIEM. Tools like Ansible or Puppet are used to manage and harden the configuration of the VMs according to the security policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the log entries regarding device access in the SIEM. The playbooks or manifests of the configuration management tool are checked for correct implementation of the security policies. Automated audit: The configuration management server is queried to determine the compliance status of the managed VMs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware mechanisms such as IOMMU (Input/Output Memory Management Unit) are used to strictly enforce isolation between devices and guest systems at the hardware level. Any configuration change to virtual systems is made exclusively through a reviewed and approved Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) pipeline.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On the virtualization servers, it is ensured that Intel VT-d or AMD-Vi is enabled and correctly configured. All VM definitions are managed in a Git repository and rolled out via a CI/CD pipeline (e.g., with Terraform) that includes automated security tests.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the BIOS/UEFI settings of the host systems as well as the hypervisor configuration regarding IOMMU. The configuration and the approval workflows of the IaC pipeline are analyzed. Automated audit: A script checks on the host systems whether IOMMU is active (`dmesg | grep -e DMAR -e IOMMU`).

controls.title: Secure configuration of a network for virtual infrastructures (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Virtual systems are mostly operated in a single, large virtual network. The risk of bypassing physical security mechanisms is known but not systematically addressed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New VMs are connected to the primary virtual switch by default. There is no separation of, for example, development and production systems at the network level.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that almost all VMs, regardless of their protection goal, can communicate in the same network segment and that no virtual firewalls or segmentation are used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic virtual networks (vSwitches/VLANs) are used to separate environments such as production, development, and management. Unwanted network connections through VMs with multiple network cards are avoided to the best of one's knowledge, but not technically prevented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate VLAN and a corresponding port group/vSwitch on the hypervisor are set up for each environment (Prod, Dev, Test, Mgmt). Administrators are instructed not to connect VMs to multiple networks simultaneously.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and correct assignment of VMs to the basic network segments. It is randomly checked whether VMs with multiple network cards exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that existing security mechanisms (e.g., firewalls) and monitoring systems cannot be bypassed via virtual networks. It MUST also be ruled out that unwanted network connections can be established via virtual IT systems connected to multiple networks. Network connections between virtual and physical IT systems as well as for virtual firewalls SHOULD be configured according to the security policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The virtual network architecture is documented and designed so that all relevant data traffic is routed through physical or virtual firewalls. A policy prohibits the creation of multi-homed VMs, and compliance is checked during VM creation. Virtual firewalls are configured to the same standards as physical firewalls.

parts.name: assessment-method
