parts.prose: The auditor compares the documented virtual network architecture with the actual implementation. It is checked whether there is a policy on multi-homed VMs and how it is implemented. Firewall rule sets of virtual firewalls are randomly checked. Automated audit: A script runs through all VMs and reports systems with more than one active network interface in different security zones.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The virtual network infrastructure is actively monitored for unauthorized configuration changes and the emergence of unwanted multi-homed systems. Granular network segments are set up per application or service (application segmentation).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) or a specialized Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tool monitors the network configuration in real time. For each major application, a separate VLAN/VXLAN segment is set up with a dedicated virtual firewall in front of it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and alerts of the monitoring tool. The effectiveness of the application segmentation is verified through penetration tests or simulated attacks. Automated audit: The API of the monitoring tool is queried to generate compliance reports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive micro-segmentation with a "default-deny" policy is implemented, where each individual VM or even each process may only communicate with explicitly allowed counterparts. The entire network configuration is managed as code (Network as Code) and is subject to a strict review and approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technologies such as VMware NSX, Cilium, or other CNI plugins are used to enforce Layer 7 firewall rules directly at the virtual network card level. The network and firewall policies are defined in a Git repository and automatically rolled out via a CI/CD pipeline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the "default-deny" policy and the explicit approvals in the configuration database of the micro-segmentation solution. The Git history and the pipeline logs are checked for compliance with the four-eyes principle and successful tests. Automated audit: A tool exports the effective firewall rules for a sample of VMs and validates them against an expected positive list of communication relationships.

controls.title: Protection of the administration interfaces (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The administration interfaces are accessible from the entire internal network and are only protected by a password. Insecure protocols such as HTTP or Telnet are still partially active.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are no network firewall rules that restrict access to the management IPs. Administrators access the web interface via HTTP because the SSL certificate has expired or is displayed as invalid.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor can establish a connection to the management port of the virtualization platform from any client in the internal network. A port scan shows open, unencrypted management services.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administration interfaces are configured to use secure protocols (HTTPS, SSHv2). Access is restricted to a specific subnet for administrators.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Insecure protocols are disabled on the management interfaces. An Access Control List (ACL) on a switch or firewall restricts access to the IPs of the administrators' workstations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the deactivation of insecure protocols and checks the firewall or ACL configuration. An attempt is made to access the interfaces from an unauthorized network, which must fail. Automated audit: An authorized port scanner checks the open ports and the protocol versions used on the management IPs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administration and management access MUST be restricted. It MUST be ensured that administration interfaces cannot be accessed from untrusted networks. Protocols considered secure SHOULD be used. If insecure protocols are used nevertheless, a separate administration network MUST be used for administration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated management network (management VLAN) is set up, separate from the rest of the traffic. Access to the administration interfaces of the virtualization environment is only permitted from this network. The use of secure, encrypted protocols is mandatory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network architecture to confirm the separation of the management network. It is checked whether the firewall rules permit access exclusively from this network. The protocol configuration is verified on the end devices. Automated check: A script checks the firewall rules applied to the management IPs to ensure that the only permitted source is the management network.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Two-factor authentication (2FA) is enforced for all access to administrative interfaces. All administrative sessions are logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The virtualization platform is connected to a central RADIUS or Identity Provider (e.g., ADFS, Okta) that enforces 2FA. The platform's audit logs are forwarded to a central SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the login process to verify the 2FA requirement. The log forwarding configuration and the incoming logs in the SIEM are checked. Automated check: A script attempts to log in to the API with password-only credentials, which must fail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative access is permitted exclusively from dedicated, hardened Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs). All administrative sessions are recorded (session recording) and analyzed for anomalous behavior.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Special, highly secure laptops or virtual desktops are provided for administrative tasks. A bastion host / jump host solution with session recording functionality is placed in front of all administrative access. The recordings are archived and reviewed randomly or by automated analysis tools.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the PAW concept and its technical implementation (e.g., hardening, software restrictions). The configuration of the session recording solution and the stored recordings are checked. Automated check: The firewall rules for the management network are checked to ensure that only the PAWs and the jump host are allowed as sources.

controls.title: Logging in the virtual infrastructure (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging is left at the default settings of the virtualization platform. The logs are stored locally on the host systems and are only viewed manually by an administrator in case of acute problems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no central log collection. The log files are not regularly backed up or archived and are subject to the systems' standard log rotation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that there is no central log management solution and that the log configuration on the hosts is inconsistent. Historical log data is not available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All relevant logs from the virtual infrastructure (system status, errors, administrative access) are sent to a central log server. A regular, manual review of the summarized reports takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A syslog server is set up to collect the logs from all virtualization servers and management components. A report is generated weekly and reviewed by an administrator for conspicuous events.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the log forwarding configuration on the source systems and the incoming data on the central log server. The weekly reports and the documentation of the reviews are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Operating status, utilization, and network connections of the virtual infrastructure MUST be continuously logged. If capacity limits are reached, virtual machines SHOULD be moved. It MUST also be monitored whether the virtual networks are correctly assigned to the respective virtual IT systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM or a dedicated monitoring system is used to log performance and configuration data. Thresholds are defined for CPU, RAM, storage, and network utilization. When thresholds are reached, a ticket is created for IT operations to react manually (e.g., move VM).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the logging and monitoring system, especially the defined thresholds. The generated tickets or notifications from recent months are analyzed to assess the response to capacity bottlenecks. Automated check: A script queries the monitoring API to validate the threshold configuration and the recording of network assignments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logging and monitoring system proactively generates alarms when utilization approaches a critical threshold. The response to capacity bottlenecks is partially automated, e.g., through scripts that initiate a live migration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Trend analyses and forecasts are configured in the monitoring system to detect bottlenecks early. Automation workflows (e.g., with vRealize Orchestrator or Ansible) are created to respond to specific alarms and move VMs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the predictive alerting and the automation workflows. The logs of the automated actions are checked for successful execution and correct functioning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Resource allocation and load balancing in the virtual infrastructure are fully automated by the virtualization platform itself. The system reacts autonomously to load changes to ensure optimal performance and utilization at all times, without requiring manual intervention.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Features like VMware Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS) or similar equivalents are operated in fully automated mode with aggressive load balancing settings. Logging is used to monitor the automatic actions and for long-term capacity planning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the automatic load balancing (e.g., DRS settings). The history of automatic VM migrations is analyzed to assess the system's effectiveness. Automated check: The DRS configuration and recommendations are read and validated via the platform's API.

controls.title: Time synchronization in virtual IT systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Time synchronization is only set up for individual virtual IT systems classified as critical. There is no organization-wide approach, and many systems run with the virtualization server's time, the correctness of which is not ensured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration is done manually on the respective systems. Often, the operating system's default time server is simply used without further customization.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a sample of virtual IT systems and checks their time configuration. It is expected that the configuration will be inconsistent and missing on many systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All virtual IT systems are configured to synchronize their time, typically using the integrated guest tools that get the time from the host system. The correctness of the host systems' time is ensured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Time synchronization is activated for all VMs via the virtualization platform (e.g., VMware Tools, Hyper-V Integration Services). It is ensured that the host systems themselves obtain a correct time from a reliable NTP server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the management console of the virtualization environment that time synchronization is enabled for all virtual machines. It is checked whether the host systems themselves are correctly synchronized.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system time of all virtual IT systems used in production MUST always be synchronized. This is ensured by configuring a dedicated and reliable Network Time Protocol (NTP) service directly in the guest operating systems to avoid dependency on the host time and to ensure higher accuracy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One or more central NTP servers are operated in the internal network. All production virtual machines are configured via configuration management (e.g., Ansible, Puppet) to use these internal servers as a time source. Host time synchronization is disabled in the guest systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the NTP service configuration on a representative selection of production virtual systems. It is checked whether the configured NTP servers correspond to the internal, specified sources. An automated check could run `ntpq -p` or `chronyc sources` on the guests and compare the result with a list of allowed servers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The status of time synchronization is actively monitored, and automated alerts are generated if a system's time deviation exceeds a defined threshold. At least two redundant, internal NTP servers are used to ensure the service's reliability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitoring system (e.g., Nagios, Zabbix) is used to monitor the NTP offset of each virtual system. The NTP configuration on the guests includes multiple servers to be able to fail over to another server if one fails.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the monitoring system and the historical alerting data regarding time deviations. The NTP configuration of the guests is checked for redundancy. Automated check: A script queries the monitoring system's API to validate the configuration and status of the NTP checks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Time synchronization between NTP clients and servers is secured by cryptographic mechanisms (e.g., Network Time Security - NTS, or NTP with symmetric keys) to prevent manipulation of time information during transmission.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NTP software used (e.g., chrony) is operated in authenticated mode. Key material is securely distributed and managed via a configuration management tool. If available, the Network Time Security (NTS) protocol according to RFC 8915 is used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration files of the NTP service on the clients and servers to verify the activation of authentication mechanisms. The management and rotation of the key material is checked. Automated check: A configuration scanner checks the NTP configuration files (e.g., `/etc/chrony.conf`) for the presence of `keyfile` and `authselectmode` directives.

controls.title: Planning a virtual infrastructure (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The setup of the virtual infrastructure SHOULD be planned in detail. The applicable regulations and guidelines for the operation of IT systems, applications, and networks SHOULD be taken into account. If multiple virtual IT systems are operated on one virtualization server, there SHOULD be NO conflicts regarding the protection requirements of the IT systems. Furthermore, the tasks of the individual groups SHOULD be defined and clearly delineated from one another, as well as the responsibilities for operation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the introduction or expansion of the virtualization environment, a planning document is created. This document addresses the system architecture, network integration, storage connection, a concept for avoiding protection requirement conflicts (e.g., through dedicated clusters), and a RACI matrix for administrative tasks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning document for the virtual infrastructure and compares its contents with the requirements. It is checked whether the roles and responsibilities have been clearly defined and communicated to the corresponding teams. The implementation of the concept for the separation of protection requirement classes is audited.

controls.title: Network Planning for Virtual Infrastructures (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network design for virtual infrastructures SHOULD be planned in detail. It SHOULD be determined whether a separate network is necessary for functions such as live migration. It SHOULD be planned which network segments (management network, storage network) are to be set up and how they will be securely separated from each other. The availability requirements for the network SHOULD be met.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed network plan is created as part of the overall planning. This plan defines all necessary VLANs or VXLANs, IP address ranges, and dedicated networks for management, vMotion/live migration, and storage (iSCSI/NFS). Separation is implemented through firewall rules and physically or logically separate switches. Redundant network paths are planned for critical connections.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network plan and compares it with the actual configuration of the switches, firewalls, and the virtualization platform. It is checked whether the network separation is effective and whether availability measures (e.g., link aggregation, redundant switches) have been implemented.

controls.title: Introduction of Administration Processes for Virtual IT Systems (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For virtualization servers and virtual IT systems, processes for commissioning, inventorying, operation, and decommissioning SHOULD be defined and established. The processes SHOULD be documented and regularly updated. It SHOULD be specified which virtualization functions may be used. Test and development environments SHOULD NOT be operated on the same virtualization server as productive virtual IT systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Workflows are defined in a ticket system or process management tool for the entire lifecycle of a VM. Inventory is carried out by connecting the virtualization platform to a central CMDB. A policy is created that governs the use of functions such as snapshots. Physically separate clusters are set up for production and test/development.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented processes and compares them with the actions performed (e.g., based on ticket histories). The CMDB is checked for completeness and correctness of the VM data. It is verified that test and production workloads are running on separate physical systems.

controls.title: Administration of the Virtualization Infrastructure via a Separate Management Network (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The virtualization infrastructure SHOULD be administered exclusively via a separate management network. The available security mechanisms of the management protocols used for authentication, integrity protection, and encryption SHOULD be activated. All insecure management protocols SHOULD be deactivated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated management VLAN is used for all management interfaces (hypervisor, vCenter, storage). Access to this VLAN is strictly controlled. On all components, insecure services such as Telnet or unencrypted HTTP are deactivated and replaced by their secure counterparts (SSH, HTTPS). Strong encryption algorithms and protocol versions are configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network configuration to confirm the existence and correct use of the management network. A port scan of the management interfaces is performed to check for insecure, open ports. The service configuration is checked for the use of strong cryptography. Automated check: A compliance scanning tool (e.g., Nessus) is run against the management interfaces to identify insecure protocols and weak encryption.

controls.title: Rights and Roles Concept for the Administration of a Virtual Infrastructure (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A rights and roles concept SHOULD be created and implemented. All components SHOULD be integrated into a central identity and access management system. Administrators of virtual machines and administrators of the virtualization environment SHOULD be distinguished and equipped with different access rights. The management environment SHOULD allow the grouping of VMs for assigning rights.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A role concept is documented that distinguishes at least between platform admins (who manage the hypervisor) and VM admins (who only manage their own VMs). The virtualization platform is connected to a central directory (e.g., Active Directory). VMs are grouped in folders or with tags, and permissions are assigned to these groups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented role concept and compares it with the implementation in the virtualization platform. It is checked whether the connection to the central directory works and whether permissions are assigned granularly to groups and not to individual users. Automated check: A script exports the permissions from the virtualization platform and compares them with the specifications of the concept.

controls.title: Selection of Suitable Hardware for Virtualization Environments (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hardware used SHOULD be compatible with the virtualization solution being used. It SHOULD be ensured that the manufacturer of the virtualization solution also offers support for the hardware in operation for the planned period of use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before purchasing new hardware, the official Hardware Compatibility List (HCL) of the virtualization software manufacturer is checked. It is ensured that the server models, as well as individual components such as network cards and HBAs, are certified for the planned software version. A support contract is concluded with the hardware manufacturer that covers the planned operating period.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the inventory list of the hardware used (server models, components) with the HCL of the virtualization software. The validity of the support contracts is checked. Automated check: A script collects the hardware information from the host systems and automatically compares it with a downloaded version of the HCL.

controls.title: Uniform Configuration Standards for Virtual IT Systems (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Uniform configuration standards SHOULD be defined for the virtual IT systems used. The virtual IT systems SHOULD be configured according to these standards. The configuration standards SHOULD be reviewed regularly and, if necessary, adjusted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: VM templates are created that contain all standard configurations (e.g., hardware version, deactivated unnecessary devices, network configuration). These templates are documented and used for the creation of all new VMs. The standards and templates are reviewed at least annually and updated if necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the configuration standards and the configured VM templates. It is checked on a random basis whether productive VMs were created based on these templates and comply with the standards. Automated check: A script compares the configuration of all VMs with the parameters defined in the standard template and reports deviations.

controls.title: Operation of Guest Operating Systems with Different Protection Requirements (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If virtual IT systems with different protection requirements are operated together on one virtualization server, it SHOULD be ensured that the virtual IT systems are sufficiently encapsulated and isolated from each other. The network separation in the virtualization solution used SHOULD also be sufficiently secure. If this is not the case, further security measures SHOULD be identified and implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A risk assessment is performed before systems with high protection requirements are operated on a shared infrastructure. As a rule, dedicated clusters are set up for different protection requirement classes (e.g., a cluster for DMZ systems, a cluster for internal systems). If a mix is unavoidable, strict network ACLs and hardened VM configurations are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the risk assessment and the concept for separating the protection requirement classes. The configuration of the clusters and the network segmentation is checked to validate the effectiveness of the separation. It is checked whether VMs with high protection requirements are actually running on the dedicated, secured clusters intended for them.

controls.title: Encapsulation of Virtual Machines (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The "Copy" and "Paste" functions for information between virtual machines and the administration client SHOULD be deactivated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the configuration of the virtualization platform (e.g., via global settings or VM configuration files), clipboard synchronization (Copy/Paste) is deactivated. This can be done, for example, by setting `isolation.tools.copy.disable = true` and `isolation.tools.paste.disable = true` in the VMX file of a VMware VM. This setting is included in the standard VM templates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor actively tries to copy text between their client and a test VM via the virtualization platform's console. The configuration of VM templates and, on a random basis, of productive VMs is checked for the correct deactivation of the function. Automated check: A script reads the configuration files of all VMs and checks whether the corresponding isolation parameters are set.

controls.title: Monitoring the Operating Status and Configuration of the Virtual Infrastructure (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The operating state of the virtual infrastructure SHOULD be monitored, especially the availability of resources and possible conflicts. The configuration files of the virtual IT systems SHOULD be regularly checked for unauthorized changes. Planned configuration changes SHOULD be checked and tested before they are implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitoring system is used to monitor the availability of CPU, RAM, and storage space on the hosts and datastores. A File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) system is set up for the VM configuration files (e.g., VMX files). All configuration changes are controlled via a change management process that includes a test in a separate environment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the monitoring system and the historical data on resource availability. The configuration and alarms of the FIM system are checked. The logs of the change management process are checked on a random basis for compliance with the testing procedure.

controls.title: Regular Audits of the Virtualization Infrastructure (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be regularly audited whether the actual state of the virtual infrastructure corresponds to the state defined in the planning and whether the configuration complies with the specified standard configuration. The audit results SHOULD be documented in a comprehensible manner and deviations SHOULD be corrected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal audit of the virtualization environment is conducted at least once a year. Checklists based on the planning documents and configuration standards are used for this. The results are recorded in an audit report, and a ticket is created and tracked for each identified deviation to be remedied.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the audit reports from the last few years. The completeness of the audits, the quality of the documentation, and the follow-up on identified deficiencies are checked. Automated testing: A compliance tool (e.g., a CSPM or a custom script framework) is used to support the audit process and automate a large part of the configuration checks.

controls.title: Use of high-availability architectures (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The virtual infrastructure SHOULD be designed for high availability. All virtualization servers SHOULD be grouped into clusters.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The virtualization servers are operated in a cluster with a high-availability feature enabled (e.g., VMware HA, Hyper-V Failover Clustering). This ensures that if a physical server fails, the virtual machines running on it are automatically restarted on another server in the cluster. It is ensured that there are enough free resources in the cluster to compensate for the failure of at least one host (N+1 redundancy).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the high-availability cluster in the management console. The admission control settings are checked to ensure that sufficient failover capacity is reserved. A planned HA test (e.g., by simulating a host failure in a test environment) should be conducted and documented regularly.

controls.title: Secure configuration of virtual IT systems with increased protection requirements (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Resource over-commitment functions SHOULD be deactivated for virtual IT systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For critical virtual machines with high protection requirements, CPU and memory resources are fully reserved. This ensures that the committed performance is available under all circumstances and performance fluctuations due to other VMs (noisy neighbor problem) are excluded. Memory overcommitment is disabled on the host systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration settings of the critical virtual machines to verify the full reservation of CPU and RAM. The host configuration is checked for disabled memory overcommitment. Automated testing: A script reads the configuration of all VMs and reports systems where the reservation is not 100% of the allocated resources.

controls.title: Hardening of the virtualization server (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The virtualization server SHOULD be hardened. To additionally isolate and encapsulate virtual IT systems from each other and from the virtualization server, Mandatory Access Controls (MACs) SHOULD be used. Likewise, the IT system on which the management software is installed SHOULD be hardened.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hypervisor installation is configured according to the manufacturer's hardening recommendations (e.g., VMware vSphere Security Configuration Guide). This includes disabling unnecessary services and configuring secure protocols. If the hypervisor supports it (e.g., on KVM-based systems), a MAC framework such as SELinux or AppArmor is configured for further isolation of the VM processes. The management server (e.g., vCenter Server) is also installed and configured according to hardening guides.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration of the host systems and the management server with the official hardening guides. The configuration of the MAC framework is checked. Automated testing: A compliance scan tool that uses the hardening guides as a policy template is run against the systems to identify deviations.

controls.title: Rights restriction of virtual machines (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All interfaces and communication channels that allow a virtual IT system to read and query information about the host system SHOULD be disabled or blocked. Virtual IT systems SHOULD NOT share memory pages.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specific advanced hypervisor configuration settings are set to prevent information leaks from the host to the guest. Memory optimization features based on sharing identical memory pages between VMs (e.g., Transparent Page Sharing - TPS) are disabled system-wide to prevent potential side-channel attacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the global configuration settings of the hypervisor as well as the individual settings of the VMs for the correct deactivation of the mentioned functions. It is checked whether TPS or similar functions are deactivated. Automated testing: A script queries the advanced settings of the host systems via the API and validates that the corresponding isolation and memory settings are set correctly.

controls.title: Deactivation of snapshots of virtual IT systems (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The snapshot function SHOULD be deactivated for all virtual IT systems with increased protection requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The permission to create and manage snapshots is revoked from administrators for the corresponding VMs or clusters. Alternatively, snapshots can be technically blocked per VM via advanced configuration settings (`snapshot.maxSnapshots = 0`). For data backups, backup solutions based on agents or storage APIs are used instead.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the permissions in the virtualization platform's rights system to ensure that snapshot rights are revoked. The VM configuration is checked for technical blocks for snapshots. It is verified that an alternative backup strategy is implemented. Automated testing: A script checks the permissions for all relevant users and groups and scans the VM configurations for snapshot locks.

controls.title: Minimal use of console access to virtual IT systems (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Direct access to the emulated consoles of virtual IT systems SHOULD be reduced to a minimum. The virtual IT systems SHOULD preferably be controlled over the network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The standard method for administration is access via the network (e.g., SSH for Linux, RDP for Windows). Access to the virtual console (e.g., via the vSphere Client or Hyper-V Manager) is declared as emergency access. The right to use the console is granted only to a small group of administrators, and its use is logged and monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the role concept to verify the restriction of console access. The audit logs of the virtualization platform are evaluated for the use of console accesses. It is checked whether each console access can be justified (e.g., by an associated ticket).

controls.title: Use of a PKI (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) SHOULD be used for communication between the components of the IT infrastructure that is protected by certificates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal, trusted Certificate Authority (CA) is operated. All components of the virtualization infrastructure (e.g., vCenter Server, ESXi hosts) are equipped with certificates from this CA to replace the default self-signed certificates. This ensures that administrators can unequivocally verify the identity of the components and that no certificate warnings occur.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the certificates installed on the management components and verifies that they were issued by the trusted internal CA and are valid. The CA configuration is checked for secure operation. Automated testing: A script connects to the management interfaces and validates the certificate chain.

controls.title: Use of certified virtualization software (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Certified virtualization software of level EAL 4 or higher SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When selecting virtualization software, care is taken to ensure that the manufacturer can provide a certification according to Common Criteria (CC) Evaluation Assurance Level (EAL) 4 or higher. This provides an independent confirmation that the software has been methodically designed, tested, and verified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests proof of certification (e.g., the certificate or a reference to the official CC website) for the product version used. It is ensured that the version used corresponds exactly to the certified version.

controls.title: Encryption of virtual IT systems (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All virtual IT systems with a high protection requirement SHOULD be encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The virtualization platform's own encryption functions (e.g., VMware vSphere VM Encryption) are used to encrypt the virtual hard disks (VMDKs) of the critical VMs. Key management is handled by an external, hardened Key Management Server (KMS) that is integrated into the virtualization platform.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks in the management console whether encryption is activated for the defined critical VMs. The configuration and secure operation of the KMS are checked. Automated testing: A script queries the encryption status of all VMs and compares it with the list of systems to be protected.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
When virtualizing IT systems, one or more virtual IT systems are run on a physical IT system. Such a physical IT system is called a "virtualization server". Several virtualization servers can be combined to form a virtual infrastructure. In it, the virtualization servers themselves and the virtual IT systems running on them can be managed jointly.
The virtualization of IT systems offers many advantages for IT operations in an information domain. For example, costs for hardware procurement, electricity and air conditioning can be saved if the resources of the physical IT systems are used more efficiently. However, virtualization is also a challenge for the operation of the information domain. Since different areas and fields of work in the information domain are affected by the virtualization technology used, knowledge and experience from these areas must be brought together. In addition, problems on one virtualization server can also affect all other virtual IT systems running on the same virtualization server. Likewise, virtual IT systems can interfere with each other's operation.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to show how virtualization servers can be securely introduced and operated in the information domain.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The SYS.1.5 Virtualization module must be applied to every virtualization server.
In addition to this module, the relevant server or client modules of the SYS IT Systems layer must also be applied to each virtualization server. In addition to the operating system-specific modules, the SYS.1.1 General Server and SYS.2.1 General Client modules must also be applied, as these modules summarize the platform-independent security aspects for servers and clients.
This module only deals with the virtualization of complete IT systems. Other techniques that are also sometimes associated with the word "virtualization" (e.g. application virtualization using terminal servers, storage virtualization and containers) are not the subject of this module.
In the area of software development, the terms "virtual machine" and "virtual machine monitor" are also used for runtime environments, e.g. when Java or Microsoft .NET are used. Such runtime environments are also not considered in this module.
Virtual infrastructures are usually managed with special management systems. Since these IT systems can be used to access the virtualization infrastructure comprehensively, it is important to secure them sufficiently. This applies to both the physical or virtual server on which the management software is executed and the product itself.
Virtualization environments are usually used together with storage networks (NAS or SAN). The connection and security of these systems are also not considered in this module (see module SYS.1.8 Storage Solutions for this).
Virtualization requires the institution's networks to be structured differently. This topic is not covered comprehensively in this module. For this, the requirements of the NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design module must be met. Network virtualization is also not covered in the necessary depth in this module.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Flawed planning of virtualization
parts.prose: A virtualization server enables the operation of virtual IT systems, integrates the IT systems into the data center and controls their connection to other infrastructure elements, e.g. networks (including storage networks). If there is no plan for how the virtualization servers are to be technically and organizationally integrated into the existing infrastructure, this can lead to the responsibilities for different areas, e.g. for applications, operating systems and network components, possibly not being clearly defined. Furthermore, the responsibilities of different areas may overlap or there is no suitable permission structure to separate administrative access for the different areas.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Incorrect configuration of virtualization
parts.prose: Virtualization changes the way servers are provisioned. Resources such as CPU, RAM, network connection and storage are usually configured centrally via a management system and are no longer dictated by hardware and cabling. This can quickly lead to configuration errors. For example, if a virtual IT system with high protection requirements is mistakenly placed in an external Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), it is consequently accessible from the Internet and thus exposed to an increased risk.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Insufficient resources for virtual IT systems
parts.prose:
Virtualization servers require storage space to operate the virtual IT systems, which is provided either locally in the virtualization server itself or in a storage network. If the storage capacities required for this are not planned to be sufficiently large, there are extensive risks to the availability of the virtual IT systems and the integrity of the information processed in them. This is especially true when special virtualization functions, such as snapshots or the over-provisioning of storage space, are used.
Bottlenecks can affect not only the storage space on hard disks or in storage networks, but also the processor performance, the main memory (RAM), or the network connection. In addition, insufficient resources on the virtualization server could cause the virtual machines to interfere with each other's operation and ultimately no longer work correctly or fail completely.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Information leakage or resource bottleneck due to snapshots
parts.prose:
A snapshot can be used to freeze and save the state of a virtual machine. If such a snapshot is restored at a later point in time, all changes made in the meantime are lost. This can also re-open security vulnerabilities that have already been patched. Furthermore, inconsistent data can arise from open files, file transfers, or database transactions at the time of the snapshot.
In addition, snapshots can be misused in attacks to gain unauthorized access to the data of a virtual IT system. This is because if the snapshot was created during live operation, the content of the main memory has also been saved to the hard disk and can be restored and analyzed in a virtual environment outside the original IT infrastructure. Likewise, snapshots can become very large, which can lead to a shortage of available storage capacity.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Failure of the management server for virtualization systems
parts.prose: Since all functions of a virtual infrastructure are controlled and administered via the management server, a failure of this management system means that no configuration changes can be made to the virtual infrastructure. During this time, IT operations cannot react to emerging problems such as resource bottlenecks or the failure of individual virtualization servers and cannot integrate new virtualization servers into the infrastructure or create new virtual IT systems. Live migration and thus the dynamic allocation of resources for individual guest systems is also not possible without a management server.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Malicious use of guest tools
parts.prose: Guest tools often run with very high privileges in the virtual machines. This allows them to be misused, for example, for denial-of-service attacks or for attackers to take over the entire virtualization server with them.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Compromise of the virtualization software
parts.prose: The virtualization software (also known as "hypervisor") is the central component of a virtualization server. It controls all virtual machines running on this server and allocates processor and memory resources to them. If this component is successfully attacked, it also means that all virtual IT systems running on the virtualization server are compromised.

controls.title: Planning of container use

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of containers is done on an ad-hoc basis for individual projects or use cases. A formal, overarching plan or definition of objectives does not exist. Security aspects are only considered reactively and not from the beginning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Developer teams use containers independently to simplify local development environments, without this being anchored in a central IT strategy. There is no documentation about the container technologies used or their purpose.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask various IT teams if and how they use containers. Check if there is a documented deployment strategy or plan. It is expected that no or only fragmentary, project-specific documents exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic plan that defines the goal of container use (e.g., scaling). This plan covers the essential phases such as installation and operation, but often neglects aspects such as secure decommissioning or a detailed consideration of operational effort.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple document describes the general goals of container use and the intended platform. However, the plan is not detailed enough to cover all security-relevant aspects and is rarely updated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the planning documentation for container use. Check if the basic goals are defined. Compare the documentation with the requirements from SYS.1.6.A1 and identify gaps, especially regarding decommissioning and consideration of operational efforts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before containers are used, the objective of the container deployment (e.g. scaling, availability, disposable containers for security, or CI/CD) MUST first be defined so that all security-relevant aspects of installation, operation, and decommissioning can be planned. The planning MUST be adequately documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A planning document is created and maintained that describes the strategic goals of the container deployment, the selected technology, the architecture, and the processes for the entire lifecycle (installation, operation, maintenance, decommissioning). This document serves as the basis for all container implementations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the planning documentation for the container deployment presented to you. Check whether the goals are clearly defined and whether all lifecycle phases, including security-relevant aspects, are covered. Verify that the documentation is up-to-date and available to the responsible employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of the container deployment is supplemented by a detailed analysis of the operational effort and the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). The plan is reviewed regularly, e.g. annually or in the event of significant changes to the architecture, and adapted if necessary. Planning templates are used to ensure consistency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During planning, not only the technical goals but also the personnel and financial effort for licensing, operation, training, and maintenance are assessed. This analysis is documented and influences the decision for or against a container deployment in new projects. The planning documents are version-controlled and stored in a document management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the planning documents for the consideration and analysis of the operational effort. Verify that a process for regular review and updating of the plan exists and is being carried out. Check the use of planning templates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The container deployment planning is fully integrated into the organization's strategic IT planning process and risk management. The decision for or against containers is based on a formalized, risk-based assessment model. The planning is supported by automated tools that analyze dependencies, capacity requirements, and security risks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An application onboarding process uses an automated system to assess the suitability and requirements of an application for container operation. Results feed directly into a dynamically generated, application-specific deployment plan. The risk management tool continuously assesses the risks of the container platform.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the integrated planning and risk management process demonstrated. Check the criteria of the assessment model and the automation tools used. Verify that the results of the automated analysis verifiably influence the planning decisions.

controls.title: Planning the management of containers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Containers are managed manually via command-line commands (e.g. `docker run`, `docker stop`). There is no uniform management software or planned procedure. Management is reactive and dependent on individuals.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators or developers manage containers directly on the hosts via SSH. There is no central overview or control over the running containers. Updates are performed manually by deleting and recreating the containers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask the administrators how they start, stop, and monitor containers. Check whether a central management software is used. It is expected that management is decentralized and based on individual scripts or manual commands.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic plan for the management of containers exists and names a uniform management software. The plan focuses on commissioning and basic monitoring (start/stop). Processes for updates and decommissioning are not formally defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple management software such as Docker Compose or a central management UI (e.g. Portainer) is used to start and stop containers. The plan exists as a simple document that mandates these tools.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether planning documentation for container management exists. Verify that a uniform management software is named and in use. Determine whether the plan covers the entire lifecycle, particularly updates and decommissioning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of containers MAY ONLY be carried out according to a suitable plan. This plan MUST cover the entire lifecycle from commissioning to decommissioning, including operation and updates. It MUST be taken into account that creators of a container are to be treated as administrators. Start, stop, and monitoring of the containers MUST be carried out via the deployed management software.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented planning policy specifies the management software to be used (e.g. a container orchestration platform such as Kubernetes or Nomad), the processes for the entire lifecycle, and the distribution of roles. It is clearly defined what permissions developers (creators) have and how their actions are monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the planning documentation for container management. Check whether the entire lifecycle is covered and management is carried out via the defined software. Verify that the special role of the container creators and the associated risks are addressed and regulated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning documentation for container management is version-controlled and subject to a formal approval process. The administrative activities of the container creators are restricted to the necessary level by technical measures (e.g. role-based access control - RBAC) and all administrative actions are logged centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Container management is carried out via an orchestration platform whose RBAC functions are used to give developers only the permissions they need for their namespaces. All API calls to the management software are audited and stored in a central log system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the approval process for the planning documentation. Verify the configuration of the RBAC policies in the management software. Review the audit logs for logged administrative actions and ensure that they are traceable.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire container management is fully automated through a GitOps approach. Changes to the container configuration (e.g. deployments, services) are made exclusively via commits in a Git repository, which go through an automated test, approval, and rollout pipeline. Manual administrative access is restricted to absolute emergencies and highly regulated (break-glass process).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Argo CD or FluxCD are used to reconcile the state of the cluster with the state defined in a Git repository. Direct administrative access (e.g. `kubectl exec`) is blocked by admission controllers or reduced to a minimum. A documented break-glass process with temporary, audited permissions exists for emergencies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the GitOps tools and the associated CI/CD pipeline. Verify that configuration changes are traceable through the defined Git workflow. Have the break-glass process demonstrated and check the logging of its application.

controls.title: Secure use of containerized IT systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: With containerized IT systems, it MUST be considered how containerization affects the operated IT systems and applications. Based on the protection requirements of the applications, it MUST be checked whether the requirements for isolation and encapsulation of the containerized IT systems and the virtual networks, as well as the operated applications, are sufficiently met. The deployed containerized IT systems MUST meet the requirements for availability and data throughput.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before migrating an application into a container, a documented review is performed. This review assesses whether the application's security requirements (e.g. separation from other applications) are met by the container isolation and the network configuration. Performance tests ensure that the application in the container meets the required throughput and response time targets.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: For a selection of containerized applications, request the documentation of the protection requirement analysis and the suitability check. Check if aspects of isolation, encapsulation, availability, and performance were assessed. Compare the results with the actual performance data and the configuration of the container environment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The check of isolation SHOULD include a detailed consideration of the native operating system mechanisms (e.g. namespaces, cgroups) and their configuration SHOULD be assessed. During operation, the performance and state of the containerized IT systems SHOULD be proactively monitored (so-called health checks).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The protection requirement analysis includes a detailed examination of the kernel namespaces and cgroups that are used for isolation. For each application, health check endpoints (e.g. HTTP endpoints) are implemented, which are regularly queried by the orchestration platform to monitor the application's state and automatically initiate a restart in case of failure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the protection requirement analysis for a detailed examination of the kernel's isolation mechanisms. Verify in the container orchestration configuration (e.g. liveness and readiness probes in Kubernetes) that health checks are configured and active for the applications.

controls.title: Planning the provisioning and distribution of images

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for provisioning and distributing images MUST be planned and adequately documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document exists that describes the entire workflow: where base images are sourced from, how application images are built (e.g. using a Dockerfile), where the images are stored (e.g. in an internal registry), and how they are rolled out to the production environment. The responsibilities in this process are clearly defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the process documentation for image provisioning and distribution presented. Trace the lifecycle of an image using the documentation and compare it with the actual procedure. Check if the documentation is up-to-date and if the defined responsibilities are being followed.

controls.title: Separation of administration and access networks for containers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The networks for host administration, container administration, and their access networks MUST be separated appropriately according to the protection requirements. Only communication relationships necessary for operation SHOULD be permitted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The network infrastructure is segmented (e.g., through VLANs or separate physical networks) such that administrative access to the container hosts (e.g., via SSH) occurs from a dedicated admin network. Access to the container platform's management API is also restricted to this network. The application containers communicate in one or more of their own networks, which are separate from the admin networks. Firewall rules implement the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the network architecture documentation and the configuration of network components (switches, firewalls). Verify that separate networks exist for host administration, container administration, and application traffic. Conduct reachability tests (e.g., using `ping` or `nmap` from an application container to the host management interface) to confirm the effectiveness of the separation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basically, at least the administration of the host SHOULD only be possible from the administration network. In addition, communication between the application containers themselves is restricted to the bare essentials by network policies (zero-trust networking).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to physical or VLAN-based separation, container-native network policies (e.g., Kubernetes NetworkPolicies or Calico Policies) are used. These policies explicitly define which container may communicate with which other container or external service and on which ports. By default, any communication that is not explicitly allowed is prohibited.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the container network policies (e.g., with `kubectl get networkpolicies -A -o yaml`). Verify that a 'Default-Deny' policy exists and that all allowed communication paths are explicitly and restrictively defined. Conduct tests to confirm the blocking of unauthorized communication attempts between containers.

controls.title: Use of secure images

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that all images used originate only from trusted sources. The source MUST be selected based on its practice of regularly checking for and fixing security problems. It MUST be clearly identifiable who created the image. The version of base images used MUST NOT be deprecated. If an image with a newer version number is available, it MUST be checked as part of patch and change management whether and how it can be rolled out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy is defined that specifies which public registries (e.g., Docker Hub, Red Hat Quay) and which specific organizations/repositories within them are considered trustworthy. Internally, a private registry is used in which only verified images are stored. The patch management process includes regularly scanning base images for outdated versions and planning their updates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the policy for trusted image sources shown to you. Check the configuration of the container hosts to ensure they can only access the permitted registries. Review the patch management process and randomly verify with running containers that no deprecated base images are being used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All images intended for use in the production environment are automatically scanned for known vulnerabilities (CVEs). Images that have vulnerabilities above a defined threshold (e.g., 'Critical' or 'High') are automatically prevented from being deployed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An image scanner (e.g., Trivy, Clair, Snyk) is integrated into the CI/CD pipeline and/or the container registry. The scan is triggered with every new push of an image. An admission controller (e.g., OPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno) in the container platform checks the scan result before each deployment and blocks the start of insecure images.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the image scanner and the CI/CD pipeline. Verify the configuration of the admission controller and its policies. Try to deploy a known vulnerable image (in a test environment) and ensure that the process is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is created and managed for each image. All images must be digitally signed, and the container platform is configured to only run images whose signature comes from a trusted party. The lifecycle of the images, including the updating of base images, is fully automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Syft or Tern are used in the CI pipeline to generate an SBOM in SPDX or CycloneDX format. The images are signed with Cosign or Notary V2. An admission controller (e.g., Kyverno) checks the signature of each image before launch. An automation tool (e.g., Renovate Bot or Dependabot) monitors the base images in the Dockerfiles, automatically creates pull requests for updates, which then go through the CI/CD pipeline with scans and tests.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the CI pipeline for SBOM generation. Verify the image signing process and the configuration of the admission controller that checks the signatures. Have the automated update process for base images demonstrated and track a pull request from its creation to successful deployment.

controls.title: Persistence of container logging data

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logging data of the containers MUST be stored outside the container, at least on the container host.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The container engine (e.g., Docker) is configured to use a logging driver (e.g., `json-file` or `journald`) that captures the standard output (stdout/stderr) of the container processes and writes it to a file or the system journal on the host system. This ensures that the logs are preserved even after a container restart.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the container engine (e.g., in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`). Start a test container that produces output, then stop and delete it. Afterwards, verify on the host system that the container's log data is still present (e.g., using `journalctl` or in the log directories under `/var/lib/docker/containers`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All logging data from the container hosts is forwarded to a central log management system. The log data is enriched with metadata (e.g., container name, image, host) to facilitate analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A log forwarding agent (e.g., Fluentd, Fluent Bit, Promtail) runs on each container host, collecting the container logs and sending them to a central system (e.g., ELK Stack, Graylog, Loki). The agent is configured to automatically retrieve metadata from the container engine API and add it to the log messages.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the log forwarding agent on the container hosts. In the central log management system, search for the logs of a specific container and verify that they are present and enriched with the correct metadata. Ensure that the logs arrive in the central system promptly after their creation.

controls.title: Secure storage of credentials for containers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Credentials MUST be stored and managed in such a way that only authorized persons and containers can access them. In particular, it MUST be ensured that credentials are only located in specially protected places and not in the images. Passwords, API keys, and private keys MUST be stored securely.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Credentials are not checked into Dockerfiles or source code. Instead, they are passed to the containers at runtime via the mechanisms provided by the management software. These can be, for example, Docker Secrets, Kubernetes Secrets, or environment variables loaded from a secure backend.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Randomly check Dockerfiles and source code repositories for hard-coded credentials. Check the configuration of running containers and verify that credentials are provided via the intended secret management mechanisms. Run `docker history [image_name]` or similar commands to ensure that no secrets are contained in any of the image layers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of storing credentials directly in the native secret management mechanisms of the container platform, an external, dedicated secret management system (like HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager) is used. The platform's native secrets are encrypted at rest.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The container platform is configured to use the 'Encryption at Rest' feature for its secret objects. Applications in the container authenticate at runtime with an external Vault system (e.g., via a sidecar injector) to dynamically and just-in-time retrieve their required secrets. This means the secrets are never permanently stored on the cluster.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the container platform to verify the activation of 'Encryption at Rest' for secrets. Review the configuration of the integration with the external secret management system. Trace the process of how an application retrieves its secrets and ensure that no unencrypted secrets remain on the host's hard drive or in the etcd storage.

controls.title: Suitability for container operation

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The application or service to be operated in the container SHOULD be suitable for container operation. It SHOULD be taken into account that containers can be terminated unexpectedly more often for the application running in them. The results of the check according to SYS.1.6.A3 SHOULD be documented in a comprehensible manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the onboarding process for a new application, it is checked whether it follows the best practices for containerized applications (e.g., the principles of a 12-Factor App). In particular, it is assessed whether the application is stateless or manages its state externally, whether it can be configured via environment variables, and whether it supports 'graceful shutdown' upon receiving SIGTERM signals. The result is documented in a checklist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: For a selection of containerized applications, request the documentation on the check of container suitability. Check whether the mentioned criteria (statelessness, configurability, graceful shutdown) have been evaluated. Simulate an unexpected termination (e.g., `docker kill`) and check whether the application is correctly restored afterwards.

controls.title: Policy for images and container operation

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy SHOULD be created and applied that defines the requirements for the operation of the containers and the permitted images. The policy SHOULD also include requirements for the operation and provision of the images.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central document ('Container Security Policy') is created and communicated to all relevant employees. This policy bindingly defines: which base images may be used, how Dockerfiles must be structured (e.g., use of unprivileged users), which ports may be exposed, which labels must be set, and what the process for image creation and release looks like.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Obtain the policy for image and container operations. Randomly inspect Dockerfiles and the configuration of running containers to ensure they comply with the policy. Verify that all developers and administrators are aware of the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the policy for images and container operation is checked by automated tools. Violations of the policy are detected early in the CI/CD pipeline and block the build or deployment process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Static analysis tools (linters) like `hadolint` for Dockerfiles or `conftest` for configuration files are integrated into the CI pipeline. An admission controller (e.g., Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper) in the container platform enforces runtime policies, such as prohibiting privileged containers or requiring specific labels.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the linter tools in the CI pipeline and the policies of the admission controller. Attempt (in a test environment) to introduce a Dockerfile or a container configuration that violates the policy, and verify that the process is blocked and a meaningful error is reported.

controls.title: Only one service per container

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Each container SHOULD provide only one service.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The application architecture is designed according to the 'Single Concern Principle'. Instead of running a container with a database, a web server, and an application, three separate containers are created that communicate with each other over the network. This simplifies scaling, updating, and error analysis for each individual service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the process list (`ps aux`) within a sample of running containers. Ensure that ideally only one main process (plus any helper processes) is running in each application container. Check Dockerfiles to see if they start multiple services via a start-up script.

controls.title: Distribution of secure images

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be appropriately documented which sources for images have been classified as trustworthy and why. Additionally, the process of how images or the software components contained in the image are obtained from trustworthy sources and finally made available for productive use SHOULD be appropriately documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented whitelist of base image sources (e.g., `docker.io/library/alpine`, `registry.access.redhat.com/ubi8`). The process describes how a developer can have a new base image added to the whitelist (including a security check). The entire build and promotion process for images (e.g., from a development registry to a test and then to a production registry) is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the documentation for the trusted sources and the image promotion process shown to you. Compare the Dockerfiles of production applications with the whitelist of base images. Check the configuration of the registry(s) and the build processes to ensure they correspond to the documented process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The images used SHOULD have metadata that makes the function and history of the image traceable. Digital signatures SHOULD secure every image against modification.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CI/CD pipeline is configured to add standardized labels (metadata) to every built image, e.g., the Git commit hash, the build number, the author, and a link to the documentation. After a successful build and scan, the image is automatically digitally signed with a tool like Cosign or Notary V2. An admission controller checks the signature before deployment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Run `docker inspect [image_name]` for production images and check for the existence and correctness of the metadata labels. Check the configuration of the CI pipeline for automatic signing. Verify the configuration of the admission controller that enforces signature verification.

controls.title: Release of images

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All images for production use SHOULD undergo a testing and release process like software products, in accordance with module OPS.1.1.6 Software Testing and Release.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before an image tag is marked as 'production-ready' and moved to the production registry, it must go through a defined process. This typically includes automated unit and integration tests, a vulnerability scan, and manual approval by a QA team or the product owner in a staging environment. The release is documented in a ticket system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the documented testing and release process for container images shown to you. Trace a recently rolled-out image back through the process and check the corresponding test protocols, scan results, and the documented release (e.g., in the ticket system or CI/CD system).

controls.title: Updating images

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When creating the concept for patch and change management, it SHOULD be decided when and how the updates of the images or the operated software or service will be rolled out. For persistent containers, it SHOULD be checked whether, in exceptional cases, an update of the respective container is more suitable than completely re-provisioning the container.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The patch management concept stipulates that updating containerized applications is fundamentally done by rolling out a new, updated image (Immutable Infrastructure). The process describes how new images (e.g., with patched base images or application versions) are built, tested, and deployed to production using a rolling update strategy. For a few, defined exceptional cases (e.g., large database containers), a documented in-place update process is provided.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the patch and change management concept for the specific regulations for containers. Verify that the standard process is based on rolling out new images. Check the documentation and justification for all defined exceptional cases in which in-place updates are permitted.

controls.title: Limitation of resources per container

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each container, resources on the host system, such as CPU, volatile and persistent storage, and network bandwidth, SHOULD be appropriately reserved and limited. It SHOULD be defined and documented how the system reacts in case these limits are exceeded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each containerized application, resource requests (reserved resources) and limits (maximum resources) for CPU and memory are defined in the configuration (e.g., in the Kubernetes Deployment Manifest). These values are based on load tests and empirical data. The documentation describes that if the memory limit is exceeded, the container is terminated by the kernel (OOMKilled) and that this is monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration files of production containers (e.g., with `kubectl get deployment [name] -o yaml`). Verify that `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` for CPU and memory are set for all containers. Check the documentation on behavior when resource limits are exceeded.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The assignment of resource limits and requests is enforced by a policy. Standard resource profiles (e.g., 'small', 'medium', 'large') are defined to simplify configuration and ensure consistency. Resource usage is continuously monitored to validate the set limits and adjust them if necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An admission controller (e.g., Kyverno) enforces that no container can be started without defined resource requests and limits. Standard profiles for resources are defined in a central wiki, which developers can reference in their deployments. Monitoring tools (e.g., Prometheus/Grafana) visualize resource usage compared to the set limits and alert when an application consistently operates at its limit.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the admission controller that enforces the resource limits. Verify the existence and application of the standard resource profiles. Have the monitoring dashboards for resource utilization shown to you and check if there is a process for adjusting the limits based on the monitoring data.

controls.title: Administrative remote access to containers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative access from a container to the container host and vice versa SHOULD be treated in principle like administrative remote access. There SHOULD be NO administrative remote access from a container to the container host. Application containers SHOULD NOT contain remote maintenance access points. Administrative access to application containers SHOULD always be done via the container runtime.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A strict policy is implemented that prohibits mounting the Docker socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) into application containers. No SSH servers are operated in application containers. Administrative access for debugging purposes is exclusively done via the commands provided by the container platform (e.g., `docker exec`, `kubectl exec`), the use of which is restricted to authorized personnel and logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of running containers for mounting of the Docker socket or other sensitive host paths. Check Dockerfiles and running processes in containers for the presence of SSH servers.
