Check the RBAC policies of the container platform to determine who has permission for `exec` commands and check the audit logs for their usage.

controls.title: Execution of containers without privileges

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The container runtime and all instantiated containers SHOULD only be run by a non-privileged system account. Exceptions SHOULD be appropriately documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the Dockerfiles, a non-privileged user is explicitly created and activated using the `USER` instruction, under which the application process runs in the container. Privileged containers (`--privileged`) are generally prohibited. Exceptions for system containers that require extended rights are documented and approved in a document with justification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check Dockerfiles for the use of the `USER` instruction. Run `docker exec -u 0 -it [container_id] whoami` or `kubectl exec [pod_id] -- whoami` to check which user the process in the container is running as. Check the list of documented exceptions and compare it with the configuration of the running containers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The container runtime SHOULD be encapsulated by additional measures, such as using the virtualization extensions of CPUs. If containers are exceptionally required to perform host system tasks, the privileges on the host system SHOULD be limited to the required minimum.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Container runtimes based on micro-VMs are used (e.g., Kata Containers, gVisor) to achieve stronger isolation through hardware virtualization. If a container requires extended rights, specific Linux capabilities (e.g., `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`) are specifically added instead of running the container fully privileged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the container platform configuration to determine which runtimes are being used. Review the configuration of containers with elevated privileges (e.g., in the `securityContext` in Kubernetes) and verify that only the absolutely necessary capabilities are granted and that this is documented.

controls.title: Application Service Accounts

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system accounts inside a container SHOULD NOT have permissions on the host system. Where this permission is necessary for operational reasons, it SHOULD only apply to absolutely necessary data and system access. The account in the container required for this data exchange SHOULD be known on the host system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Using user namespaces ensures that the user ID inside the container (e.g., `root` with UID 0) is mapped to an unprivileged user ID on the host. If a container needs to access a host directory (via volume mount), the file system permissions on the host are set so that only the specific, mapped host UID has the necessary rights (e.g., read-only access).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the container engine configuration for the activation of user namespaces (`userns-remap`). Check the permissions of directories on the host that are mounted into containers and ensure they follow the principle of least privilege.

controls.title: Mounting data stores in containers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Containers SHOULD ONLY be able to access the storage and directories necessary for their operation. Permissions SHOULD only be granted explicitly when needed. If the container runtime mounts local storage for a container, file system access rights SHOULD be restricted to the container's service account. If network storage is used, permissions SHOULD be set on the network storage itself.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of mounting entire host directories into containers, named Docker volumes or Kubernetes PersistentVolumes are used. Access to these volumes is restricted to the containers that need it. If a volume can be used read-only, it is explicitly mounted as `readonly`. When using network storage (e.g., NFS, iSCSI), the export or LUN masking policies are configured so that only the container nodes can access it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of running containers (Mounts section in `docker inspect` or `volumes` in Kubernetes manifests). Verify that named volumes are primarily used instead of host path mounts. Check if the `readonly` mode is used where appropriate. Review the network storage configuration for restrictive access controls.

controls.title: Securing configuration data

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The description of the container configuration data SHOULD be versioned. Changes SHOULD be documented in a traceable manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All configuration files for containers, such as Dockerfiles, Docker-Compose files, or Kubernetes manifests, are managed in a Git repository. Every change to the configuration requires a commit that includes a description of the change. This makes the entire history of the configuration traceable.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request access to the Git repository containing the configuration data for a production application. Check the commit history for traceable change messages. Compare the configuration defined in the repository with the actual running configuration in the production environment to ensure that no unversioned changes have been made.

controls.title: Advanced security policies

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Advanced security policies such as Mandatory Access Control (MAC) are used to restrict container permissions. The default profiles provided by the container platform (e.g., AppArmor or SELinux) are enabled for all containers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The container platform is configured to apply the `docker-default` AppArmor or SELinux profile (or an equivalent) to all started containers by default. This provides basic protection against container breakouts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the container engine and of running containers (`docker inspect` or `kubectl describe pod`) to verify that a MAC security profile (e.g., under `AppArmorProfile` or `seLinuxOptions`) is active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Advanced policies SHOULD restrict container permissions. Mandatory Access Control (MAC) or a comparable technique SHOULD enforce these policies. The policies SHOULD at least restrict network connections, file system access, and kernel requests (syscalls). Violations are logged centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A customized, restrictive security profile for AppArmor/SELinux and Seccomp is created for each application. The Seccomp profile limits the allowed system calls to the absolute minimum necessary for the application. The MAC profiles restrict file access and network capabilities. Violations of these profiles are logged by the kernel (audit log) and forwarded to a central SIEM for evaluation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the application-specific AppArmor/SELinux and Seccomp profiles. Compare the allowed actions with the actual requirements of the application. Check the configuration of the audit system and the SIEM to ensure that violations are reported and evaluated.

controls.title: Provision for investigations

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To have containers available for later investigation if necessary, an image of their state SHOULD be created according to defined rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the event of a security incident, a process is defined and documented on how to create a forensic image of a container believed to be compromised. This is done using `docker commit` or `docker export` to save the state of the file system. The resulting image or archive is stored securely and with a documented chain of custody.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the documented process for the forensic backup of a container shown to you. Carry out the process in a test environment to check its functionality and the correctness of the documentation. Check the provisions for the secure storage of the images.

controls.title: Immutability of containers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Containers SHOULD NOT be able to change their file system during runtime. File systems SHOULD NOT be mounted with write permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All containers are started by default with the `--read-only` option (or the equivalent `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` in Kubernetes). If the application needs to write temporary data, a dedicated, empty directory (`tmpfs` mount) is provided, the content of which is discarded when the container terminates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of running containers (e.g., in the `HostConfig` of `docker inspect` or in the `securityContext` of Kubernetes pods). Verify that the root file system is configured as 'read-only'. Check if temporary `tmpfs` mounts are used for necessary write operations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy for container immutability is technically enforced. Any attempt to start a container with a writable root file system is blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An admission controller (e.g., Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper) is installed on the container platform and configured with a policy that prevents containers from starting where `readOnlyRootFilesystem` is not set to `true`. Exceptions to this rule must be explicitly defined and approved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the admission controller and its policies. Attempt to start a container without the `readOnlyRootFilesystem` setting (in a test environment) and verify that the start is blocked and a corresponding error message appears.

controls.title: Host-based intrusion detection

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The behavior of the containers and the applications and services operated within them SHOULD be monitored. The behavior to be monitored SHOULD include at least network connections, created processes, file system access, and kernel requests (syscalls). Deviations from normal behavior SHOULD be detected and reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A runtime security monitoring tool such as Falco, Sysdig Secure, or Aqua Security is installed on all container hosts. It is configured with a basic set of rules that detect suspicious activities, e.g., starting a shell in a container, writing to sensitive directories, or unexpected outgoing network connections. Alerts are sent to a central SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check if a runtime security tool is installed and active on the container hosts. Have the configured rules shown to you. Simulate a suspicious activity (e.g., with `docker exec [container_id] bash`) and verify that an alert is generated and received in the SIEM.

controls.title: High availability of containerized applications

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For high availability requirements of containerized applications, a decision SHOULD be made at which level the availability is to be realized (e.g., redundantly at the host level).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The high availability concept specifies how the application is made resilient. Typically, this is achieved by running multiple instances (replicas) of the container on different host systems (nodes). A load balancer distributes the traffic to the available instances. If a container or an entire host fails, the orchestration platform automatically handles the recovery by restarting the container on another host.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the high availability concept. Check the configuration of the containerized application (e.g., `replicas` in a Kubernetes Deployment). Verify that the container instances are running on different physical hosts. Simulate the failure of a container or a node and ensure that the application remains accessible and the failed container is automatically restarted.

controls.title: Advanced isolation and encapsulation of containers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If further isolation and encapsulation of containers is required, measures such as a fixed assignment of containers to container hosts SHOULD be considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For applications with particularly high protection requirements or specific licensing requirements, the orchestration platform is configured (e.g., using node affinity rules or taints/tolerations in Kubernetes) so that their containers are only allowed to run on a dedicated group of host systems. These hosts can be additionally hardened.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the container orchestration for highly sensitive applications. Verify the effectiveness of the node affinity or taint configurations by checking on which nodes the containers are running. Ensure that the assignment is documented and justified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To achieve even stronger isolation, the individual containers and/or the container hosts SHOULD be run with hypervisors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Container runtimes are used that are based on micro-VMs (e.g., Kata Containers, gVisor). These use hardware virtualization technologies (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) to provide each container or pod with its own, highly isolated kernel. This offers significantly stronger protection against container breakouts and kernel exploits compared to pure namespace isolation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the container platform to determine which runtimes (e.g., via Kubernetes RuntimeClasses) are used for which applications. Verify on the host system that for containers that use a virtualized runtime, separate virtual machines (e.g., QEMU processes) are actually started.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
The term containerization refers to a concept in which an operating system's resources are partitioned to create execution environments for processes. Depending on the operating system used, different techniques can be employed, which differ in their functional scope and security properties. This is often referred to as "operating system virtualization." However, a complete operating system is not virtualized; instead, only certain resources are made available through a shared kernel. The term container is generally used to describe the resulting construct.
Before complex container environments are hastily built and used, it should first be thoroughly considered whether the effort for creating and operating container environments is in a suitable proportion to the actual benefit. The proper operation of container environments is very complex, and many requirements must be observed. Containers can be used as an additional separation mechanism to achieve a hardening of the environment, provided that the type of container technology and the configuration are appropriate and suitable for this purpose.
A distinction is made between application containers (e.g., according to the specification of the Open Container Initiative / OCI) and system containers. System containers are the oldest type of containers, such as FreeBSD Jails, Solaris Zones, OpenVZ, LXC, and LXD. They provide an environment that behaves similarly to an independent operating system, can offer corresponding services, and run multiple applications. Application containers, on the other hand, are specifically designed to run a single application. They follow the lifecycle of the application but do not offer operating system-specific services within the container. From a technical point of view, however, both types rely on the same mechanism for separation, namely process isolation by the kernel.
In the example of Linux containers (LXC), the mechanisms of namespaces and cgroups are mainly used to supplement process isolation.
Namespaces control which resources a process can see. There are seven different namespaces: Mount (mnt), Process ID (pid), Network (net), Inter-Process Communication (ipc), UTS (uts), User ID (user), and Control Group (cgroup).
Cgroups control which resources, or which share of a resource, a process can use. Resources include in particular Memory, CPU, BLKIO, or PIDS.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to protect information that is processed in, by, or with containers, offered by them, or transmitted via them. The module deals with how containers can be secured in principle. A distinction is made between the services for operating the containers, i.e., the software responsible for configuring and managing the containers, and the applications and services that are executed within the containers.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The SYS.1.6 Containerization module must always be applied as soon as services or applications are operated in containers.
This module considers containers independently of specific products. The requirements are based on the capabilities of implementations currently available on the market. For product selection, the APP.6 General Software module must be considered.
The module supplements the aspects treated in the SYS.1.1 General Server and SYS.1.3 Server under Linux and Unix modules with specifics of containerization. The requirements of these modules should be met by the host system, regardless of whether it is run on physical servers or is virtualized. Furthermore, the requirements of these modules also apply to each of the userspace environments created as part of containerization. This regularly requires consideration of other modules such as CON.8 Software Development or the modules of the OPS.1.1 Core IT Operations sub-layer. This is especially true for the creation of images.
Typically, containers communicate with each other through virtual networks on the host system. The modules of the NET.1 Networks and NET.3 Network Components sub-layers must be considered accordingly.
Security requirements of possible services, such as web servers (APP.3.2 Web Server) or web applications (APP.3.1 Web Applications and Web Services), are the subject of their own modules, which must be applied additionally. If the host system is virtualized, the SYS.1.5 Virtualization module must be modeled.
If the containers and the underlying infrastructure are not operated and used entirely by oneself, but parts thereof are provided by or used by third parties, additional requirements of the OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing and OPS.2.2 Cloud Use as well as OPS.3.2 Offering of Outsourcing modules must be considered.
The module contains basic requirements for the setup and operation of containerization. The other services common in this subject area, such as orchestration of containers, storage systems, virtual networks, automation for CI/CD pipelines, or the operation of image registries, are not considered here. Likewise, this module makes no statements about requirements that apply to the building of images. For requirements on the orchestration of containers with Kubernetes, the APP.4.4 Kubernetes module is to be considered.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Vulnerabilities or malware in images
parts.prose:
Containers are primarily created based on prefabricated images, which can be self-created but are also often obtained from the internet. Furthermore, software is increasingly being delivered in the form of images. IT operations can also use these images to create their own images by adding, changing, or removing software or configurations.
The software contained in the images could be vulnerable, and the containers started from the image could therefore be attackable. Such vulnerabilities may often be unknown to IT operations, as the software contained in the images is often not recorded in their own software management. IT operations must fundamentally rely on updates being made available through the image creation process. From the outside, it is often difficult to determine which software packages are present in these images.
In addition, images could contain intentionally integrated malware, such as ransomware or cryptominers. Since a single image is often deployed in a large number of containers, the resulting damage can be immense.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Unsecured administrative access
parts.prose: To manage container services on a host, administrative access is required. This access is often implemented as services that can be addressed either locally or over the network. Mechanisms for authentication and encryption of administrative access are often available, but not enabled by default in all products.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Resource conflicts on the host
parts.prose: Individual containers can overload the host and thus endanger the availability of all other containers on the host or even the operation of the host system itself.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Unauthorized communication
parts.prose:
All containers on a host are fundamentally able to communicate with each other, with the host, and with any other hosts. If this communication is not restricted, it can be exploited to, for example, attack other containers or hosts.
Furthermore, there is a risk that containers can be reached from the outside, even if this is not desired. This could allow an attack from the outside against services that should actually only be accessible internally. This threat is increased by the lower attention often paid to such internal services. For example, if a vulnerability in a service used only internally is tolerated and this service is also accessible from the outside, this can significantly jeopardize the entire operation.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Escaping from the container to the host system
parts.prose:
If it is possible to execute custom code within the container, an attack may be able to overcome the container's isolation from other containers or the host, and access other containers, the host system, or the infrastructure. This is also referred to as a 'container escape.' This attack can occur, for example, through vulnerabilities in processors, in the operating system kernel, or in locally offered infrastructure services such as DNS or SSH.
Thus, an attack could lead to taking control of the host system or other systems in the infrastructure. This threatens the loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all containers running on this host, as well as on the host itself if elevated privileges can also be obtained there.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Data loss due to container management
parts.prose: As part of container management, containers can be shut down without giving the software currently running inside them the opportunity to complete tasks, such as current write processes (improper shutdown). If data is being processed by the container at these times, all this data is lost. Data stored persistently in the container can also be permanently lost in this way.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Loss of confidentiality of credentials
parts.prose:
The principles of building and creating images for containers presuppose that credentials, e.g., for databases, are available within the container. Through the images themselves, the scripts for creating the images, or the version control of the scripts, such credentials can fall into unauthorized hands.
Often, credentials are also made available as environment variables at the time of container creation. Here too, there is a threat of loss of confidentiality for this data.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Uncontrolled deployment and distribution of images
parts.prose: In contrast to classic installations by IT operations, where control over the deployed applications, components, and services lies entirely with IT operations itself, this control is lost, for example, with automation through CI/CD in container environments. Instead, IT operations merely provides a platform into which developers can directly introduce their applications, including all dependencies, and modify them at any time.

controls.title: Use of restrictive z/OS identifiers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only a few highly-privileged RACF attributes, such as SPECIAL, are restricted. The IBMUSER identifier is not in productive use, but is not formally locked. An emergency user concept does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The implementation focuses on the most obvious risks. Group attributes and user ID 0 under USS are often overlooked. Locking IBMUSER is considered optional.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether, in addition to SPECIAL, OPERATIONS, AUDITOR and UID 0 are also assigned without restriction. Check whether the IBMUSER identifier is still active or can be reactivated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All of the mentioned highly-privileged RACF attributes (SPECIAL, OPERATIONS, AUDITOR, UID 0) are handled restrictively. The IBMUSER identifier is locked. An emergency user exists, but the process for its use is informal and the traceability of its assignment is done through manual log reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The basic requirements are met. The RACF commands to lock IBMUSER (e.g., `ALTUSER IBMUSER REVOKE`) are executed once. Traceability is ensured by retaining SMF logs, which are manually evaluated when needed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verify that all highly-privileged attributes are only assigned to defined roles. Check that the IBMUSER account has the status REVOKED. Question the administrators about the emergency process and inspect the corresponding log files.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Permissions with high authorization (especially the RACF attributes SPECIAL, OPERATIONS, AUDITOR and the corresponding GROUP attributes as well as user ID 0 under USS) MUST ONLY be granted to users who require these rights for their activities. The granting and use MUST be traceable. The IBMUSER identifier MAY ONLY be used during a new installation and MUST be permanently locked afterwards. An emergency user procedure MUST be established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A roles and permissions concept defines which person receives which privileges. Traceability is ensured through documentation in the change management system. The emergency user process is documented and describes who is allowed to approve its use and how it is logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the permissions concept. Random check of the assigned attributes against the documented roles. Verification of the lock status of IBMUSER. Review of the documentation and effectiveness of the emergency user procedure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined processes, a regular, semi-automated review process is carried out for all highly-privileged permissions. The use of the emergency user triggers automatic notifications to the security team. The granting of high privileges requires two-factor approval.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Scripts or tools like zSecure Audit are used to create reports on the granting of SPECIAL, OPERATIONS, etc. and to compare them with the target specifications. Notifications are implemented via email or a ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the reports from the last review cycles and the handling of any identified deviations. Test the alerting mechanism for the emergency user. Check the implemented two-factor approval in the change management process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Privileged Access Management (PAM) system is used for granting all highly-privileged permissions. Access is granted only temporarily and Just-in-Time (JIT). All actions with these permissions are monitored in real time and analyzed by a SIEM. The emergency user process is fully automated and requires multi-level approval via the PAM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM solution (e.g., from CyberArk, Broadcom) is integrated, which automates RACF commands for temporary rights assignment (`ALTUSER ... RESUME`) and revocation (`... REVOKE`). SIEM correlation rules are specifically configured for z/OS privilege abuse.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of the PAM system and the JIT policies. Analysis of the SIEM logs for the monitoring of privileged sessions. Performing a test of the automated emergency user process to verify compliance with the approval chain.

controls.title: Securing security-critical z/OS utilities

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the best-known security-critical programs are protected by RACF profiles. Alias names are often not taken into account. The installation of (third-party) programs is not systematically controlled and is often done manually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: RACF profiles are created for programs like `ICKDSF` or `AMASPZAP`, but aliases or lesser-known tools remain unprotected. SMP/E is not consistently used for all software installations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether their aliases are also protected for known security-critical programs. Search for software in system libraries that is not managed via SMP/E.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All known security-critical programs and their aliases are protected by RACF profiles. Programs are installed by default via SMP/E, but the origin of the installation packages is not systematically verified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of critical programs and their aliases is maintained and implemented in RACF. SMP/E is established as the standard tool for software distribution. The sources of the software (e.g., from IBM or third-party providers) are assumed to be trustworthy, but are not cryptographically checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the RACF profiles for the list of critical programs and aliases. Verification that new software has been installed via SMP/E. Questioning the administrators about the source verification process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security-critical (utility) programs and commands as well as their alias names MUST be protected with permissions on corresponding RACF profiles so that they can only be used by the designated and authorized persons. It MUST be ensured that (third-party) programs cannot be installed without authorization. In addition, programs MAY ONLY be installed from secure sources and via traceable methods (e.g. SMP/E).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A comprehensive list of security-critical programs and their aliases is maintained. Access is controlled via the `PROGRAM` class in RACF. All program installations and updates must be done via SMP/E and documented in the change management system. Secure sources are defined, trusted repositories.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the RACF configuration for the `PROGRAM` class. Random check of installations for compliance with the SMP/E process and documentation in change management. Review of the definition and security of the software sources.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined protection, an integrity monitoring system is used that regularly checks critical system libraries (e.g. `SYS1.LPALIB`, `SYS1.LINKLIB`) for unauthorized changes. The SMP/E process is firmly integrated into the change management system and requires formal approval for each installation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Tripwire or zSecure Alert/Audit are configured to monitor the integrity of critical datasets and to alert on changes. The SMP/E process is controlled by a workflow tool that documents the approval.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration and logs of the integrity monitoring system. Analysis of change tickets to verify compliance with the approval workflow for SMP/E activities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All security-critical libraries are protected by cryptographic signatures. The system automatically prevents the execution of programs that are unauthorized or whose signature is invalid. Program installation is fully automated via a CI/CD pipeline that integrates security tests (e.g. code scanning) and automatic signing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Functions such as program control with digital signatures are used. The CI/CD pipeline (e.g., with Jenkins or GitLab) is configured to automatically sign the software packages after successful tests and roll them out in a controlled manner using SMP/E.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of program control and signature verification. Audit of the CI/CD pipeline configuration to verify the correct implementation of the security gates and the signing process.

controls.title: Maintenance of Z systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Patches and updates are applied reactively, typically only after a problem or error has occurred. There is no formal maintenance plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrators rely on manufacturer notifications or system errors that have occurred as a trigger for maintenance activities. Integration into change management is not provided.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the patch level of the system and compare it with the currently recommended levels. Question the administrators about the patch installation process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic maintenance plan that provides for regular maintenance windows. Updates are applied, but the process for controlling manufacturer updates (especially remote) is not formalized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Maintenance windows are entered in the calendar. Patches are installed in these windows. Remote access by the manufacturer is permitted, but not actively monitored or explicitly approved per session.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the maintenance plan and comparison with the activities carried out. Questioning about the handling of remote maintenance access by the manufacturer.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Z hardware and firmware, the operating system, and the various programs MUST be maintained regularly and as needed. The necessary maintenance activities MUST be planned and integrated into the change management. In particular, updates by the manufacturing company MAY ONLY be carried out under the control of the operators, locally via SE/HMC or remotely via the RSF.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed maintenance plan is created and maintained. Each maintenance activity is recorded as a change request in the ITSM tool, approved, and documented. Remote access by the manufacturer is explicitly initiated and monitored by the operators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the change management logs for maintenance activities. Verification that for remote maintenance by the manufacturer, explicit approval and control by the staff has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The maintenance plan is proactive and based on manufacturer announcements and subscribed vulnerability feeds. All significant updates are validated in a dedicated test environment before productive use. Remote maintenance sessions are logged and randomly checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A test LPAR is maintained that is as close as possible to the production environment. Before installing patches (PTFs), they are tested for compatibility and functionality in the test LPAR. Remote sessions (e.g., via RSF) are recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verification of the existence and use of the test environment. Analysis of test logs before the production rollout of patches. Review of logs from remote maintenance sessions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The patch and maintenance process is highly automated. The system automatically scans for available and necessary updates, tests them in a sandbox environment, and automatically applies them according to a risk-based policy. All maintenance activities are centrally logged and correlated with system behavior to detect anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Modern software management tools (e.g., z/OSMF) are used to automate the entire patch lifecycle. Automated test scenarios validate functionality after patching. The logs are fed into a SIEM, which monitors for deviations during or after maintenance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration and workflows of the automated patch management system. Analysis of SIEM rules and dashboards for monitoring maintenance activities. Verification of automated test coverage.

controls.title: Training of z/OS operating personnel

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Training is informal and takes place mainly 'on-the-job'. Only a few key individuals occasionally receive external training.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New personnel learn by watching and imitating experienced colleagues. There are no formal training materials or a training plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing employees about their level of training and how they were onboarded. Looking for evidence of formal training measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic induction or basic training is offered for new personnel. However, there are no regular refresher courses or specialized training for complex functions such as RACF.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are standard introductory training courses that all new team members go through. Specialized knowledge continues to be passed on informally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the documents for the basic training courses. Interviewing specialized administrators (e.g., for RACF) for specific training certificates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrators, operators, and auditors in the z/OS area MUST be trained according to their tasks. In particular, RACF administrators MUST be familiar with the security system itself and, if applicable, with other functions relevant to them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A training concept is created that defines specific training requirements for each role (e.g., operator, system programmer, RACF admin, auditor). Participation in the training is documented and tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the training concept. Spot-checking of employee training records against the requirements in the concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A continuous training program is established, which includes regular refresher courses and updates on new threats and system functions. Training success is assessed through practical exercises or tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to basic training, annual z/OS-related security awareness training and advanced courses are offered. Effectiveness is checked, for example, through small quizzes or simulated tasks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the plan for continuous training and attendance records. Inspection of the results of the success assessments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training program includes advanced topics such as mainframe forensics and incident response. Personnel regularly participate in realistic cyber-range exercises simulating attacks on z/OS. Training is personalized based on individual performance and role development.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Contracts are concluded with specialized providers for cyber-range training on the Z platform. Participation is mandatory for the security team and key administrators. The results are incorporated into personal development planning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of participation in and results of cyber-range exercises. Review of individual development plans for adjustments based on the exercise results.

controls.title: Use and security of system-related z/OS terminals

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only physical access to the consoles (HMC, SE) is restricted. Logical security measures such as changing default passwords are not consistently implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The consoles are located in a locked data center, but the default logins (e.g., on the HMC) are still active.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Attempting to log in to the consoles with known default passwords. Checking the configuration for active default user accounts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Physical access is protected and all default passwords on the consoles have been changed. However, unneeded services are not disabled and encryption for remote access is not consistently enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After installation, the passwords are changed. However, the configuration of the services (e.g., web server on the HMC) remains in the delivery state.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Port scan of the HMC and SE interfaces to identify active services. Review of the configuration of the remote access services for the use of encryption.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: System-related z/OS terminals (Support Elements, HMC, MCS, SMCS consoles, etc.) MUST be physically protected against unauthorized entry and logically protected against unauthorized access. Preset passwords MUST be changed. Access via web servers and other remote access MUST be protected by encryption. Unneeded web servers and remote access MUST be disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A hardening concept for HMC and SE is created and implemented. This includes password policies, disabling unneeded services, and configuring TLS for all web-based access. Physical protection is ensured by data center access control.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the HMC and SE configuration files against the hardening concept. Verification of the password policies. Checking whether remote access uses TLS and whether unneeded ports are closed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enforced for all console access, especially for remote access. All access is logged and actively monitored for suspicious activity. The management network is isolated from the rest of the network through network segmentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HMC is integrated with a RADIUS or LDAP server to enable MFA. The HMC's syslogs are sent to a central SIEM where they are monitored. Firewall rules separate the HMC network from other network segments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the MFA configuration. Analysis of SIEM logs for console access. Review of firewall rules for the management network.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A 'Zero Trust' access model is applied to all consoles. Access is only possible from dedicated, hardened administrative workstations (PAWs). All sessions are recorded and subject to real-time analysis. Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) are used to protect the cryptographic keys on the HMC.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: HMC access is controlled via a bastion host or a PAM system, which restricts the source IP addresses to PAWs and performs session recording. The HMC is configured with an enterprise HSM for key storage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the bastion host/PAM system configuration and the PAW policies. Verification of the integration and use of the HSM. Spot-checking of session recordings.

controls.title: Use and security of the Remote Support Facility

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Remote Support Facility (RSF) is used, but access is not explicitly enabled and disabled for each session, but remains permanently open.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The firewall rules for RSF are permanently active so as not to delay support when needed. There is no explicit activation process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the firewall configuration and HMC settings for RSF to determine if the connection is permanently open.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The RSF access is explicitly enabled for each maintenance session and disabled afterwards. However, the communication does not run via a dedicated proxy server and the security of the connection is not actively checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrators manually enable and disable the RSF connection on the HMC for each maintenance case. It is assumed that the connection is secure by default from the manufacturer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing the administrators about the process of enabling and disabling. Checking the network configuration for the absence of a proxy for the RSF connection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A decision MUST be made as to whether and how RSF is used. The use MUST be provided for in the maintenance contract. The RSF configuration may only be changed by authorized persons. Maintenance access by the manufacturer MUST be explicitly enabled by operators and disabled again after completion. The RSF communication MUST take place via proxy servers and additionally via secured connections (such as TLS).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision on RSF usage is documented. The process for enabling/disabling is defined in the operating manual. A dedicated, outbound proxy is configured for the RSF connection. The authorization to change the RSF configuration on the HMC is restricted to a small group of people.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the contract documents and internal documentation on RSF usage. Review of the proxy configuration in the network and on the HMC. Verification of the permissions for configuration changes on the HMC.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All RSF sessions are logged in detail (e.g., executed commands). A local operator monitors the remote session in real time. Access outside of the planned maintenance windows automatically triggers an alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The monitoring functions of the HMC are used to mirror the remote session. The logs from the proxy and the HMC are forwarded to a SIEM, which monitors access times and suspicious activity.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the session monitoring configuration. Analysis of SIEM logs and alarms related to RSF activities. Interviewing the operators on the execution of real-time monitoring.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: RSF access is only possible via a bastion host/jump server that enforces MFA and full session recording. The allowed commands for the remote manufacturer are restricted by a command-filtering proxy. All session logs are automatically fed into a SIEM for analysis and correlation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM system is implemented as a gateway for RSF access. A whitelist of allowed commands for IBM support is defined and enforced in the proxy. The video recordings of the sessions are archived in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of the PAM system and the command-filtering proxy. Verification of the MFA and recording function. Spot-checking of the archived session recordings.

controls.title: Restrictive authorization under z/OS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The principle of least privilege (PoLP) is only applied to user datasets. System resources such as APF-authorized libraries or Parmlib members are not granularly protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators focus on protecting application and user data, while system datasets often remain broadly accessible, e.g., via `UACC(READ)`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the RACF profiles of critical system libraries (e.g., `SYS1.PARMLIB`, `SYS1.PROCLIB`) for overly permissive authorizations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The PoLP principle is generally applied, but role definitions are coarse, leading to users having more permissions than necessary. Regular permission reviews do not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: RACF groups are used for assigning rights, but the groups are defined very broadly (e.g., 'All Developers', 'All Operators').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the RACF group structure and the permissions bundled within it. Inquiry as to whether and how often permissions are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of the basic configuration, the authorization mechanisms MUST be configured so that all individuals (defined user IDs in groups according to role) only receive the access rights they need for their respective activities. For this purpose, APF authorizations, SVCs, z/OS operating system resources, IPL parameters, Parmlib definitions, Started Tasks, and JES2/3 definitions MUST be taken into account in particular.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed role and authorization concept is created. Access to all critical system resources is controlled via RACF profiles. APF lists, SVC tables, and Parmlib members are treated as critical resources, and their write protection is enforced by RACF.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the role and authorization concept. Verification of the RACF profiles for APF libraries, Parmlib, Proclib, and other system resources. Check whether access to SVCs and Started Tasks follows the PoLP principle.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal role-based access control (RBAC) model is defined and implemented. Access rights are reviewed semi-automatically on a regular basis (e.g., quarterly). A formalized process for requesting and approving exceptions is established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The roles are documented in a matrix. Tools like zSecure are used to generate regular reports for permission reviews. Exception requests are handled via an ITSM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the RBAC documentation. Analysis of the reports from the last permission reviews and the implemented corrections. Review of tickets for exception requests.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated Identity and Access Management (IAM) system manages the entire lifecycle of roles and permissions. Permission reviews are automated and require regular re-certification by supervisors. Anomaly detection is used to identify privilege escalations or unusual access patterns.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IAM tool (e.g., from Broadcom, IBM) is integrated with RACF. The IAM tool controls the workflow for requests, approvals, and recertifications. SIEM or UEBA tools analyze SMF data to detect anomalies such as access to rarely used but critical resources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the IAM system configuration and recertification workflows. Analysis of reports and alerts from the anomaly detection system. Verification that recertifications are carried out on time.

controls.title: Use of the z/OS security system RACF

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: RACF is active, but many settings are default. Password rules are weak (e.g., short length, no complexity). Not all critical datasets are protected. User accounts are not automatically locked after inactivity or failed attempts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: RACF is operated with the default `SETROPTS` settings. The focus is on protecting login and application data; system datasets are neglected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Display the active RACF options with `SETROPTS LIST`. Review the password rules. Randomly check the protection of system datasets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: RACF is configured with customized rules for passwords and the account lifecycle. Critical datasets are protected. Advanced features like KDFAES for passwords or the Enhanced PassTicket Algorithm are not enabled. RACF exits are used without proper documentation or monitoring.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `SETROPTS` are adjusted to enforce password length and history. There is a process for account locking. The use of RACF exits is accepted as a given but not actively managed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the `SETROPTS` settings. Verify if KDFAES is active (`PASSWORD(ALGORITHM(KDFAES))`). Search for active RACF exits and check their corresponding documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of RACF for z/OS MUST be carefully planned. This includes selecting the character set, defining rules for user ID and password, activating KDFAES encryption and the Enhanced PassTicket Algorithm (if PassTickets are used). Default passwords MUST be changed. The use of RACF exits MUST be justified, documented, and regularly monitored. Procedures for creating, locking, unlocking, and deleting IDs MUST be defined. An ID MUST be locked after a specified number of failed attempts (exception: emergency users). User IDs MUST be locked after prolonged inactivity. Files, Started Tasks, and programs MUST be protected by RACF profiles according to the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A RACF configuration document specifies all `SETROPTS` parameters and the policies for the account lifecycle. There is a documented list of the RACF exits used with justification and review date. The protection profiles for critical resources are part of the authorization concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the active RACF configuration (`SETROPTS LIST`) against the configuration document. Verification that KDFAES and the Enhanced PassTicket Algorithm are active. Check of the exit documentation. Random check of user accounts for compliance with inactivity and locking rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All relevant RACF functions are active, and the configuration is hardened based on security best practices (e.g., DISA STIGs). All administrative RACF actions (e.g., `ALTUSER`, `CONNECT`) are logged and regularly reviewed. A regular audit of the RACF database for misconfigurations is performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RACF configuration is checked and adjusted against a hardening guide. Tools like zSecure Audit are used to regularly generate reports that show administrative activities and potential configuration weaknesses. These reports are reviewed by the security team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the RACF configuration against an external benchmark (e.g., STIG). Analysis of the reports from the last RACF audits and the processing of findings. Review of the logs of administrative actions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The RACF configuration is managed and versioned as code (Infrastructure as Code). Changes are automatically tested against a security policy before deployment. RACF event logs (SMF Type 80) are integrated into a SIEM in real-time, and automated responses to critical security events are configured. MFA is integrated for all user logins in RACF.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: RACF commands are maintained in scripts (e.g., REXX) and managed via a version control system like Git. A CI/CD pipeline runs tests before the commands are executed on the system. A SIEM connector forwards SMF data; SOAR playbooks respond to alarms (e.g., locking a user during a brute-force attack).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the Infrastructure-as-Code process and test coverage. Review of the SIEM correlation rules and SOAR playbooks for RACF events. Verification of the end-to-end MFA implementation.

controls.title: Multi-tenancy under z/OS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The separation of tenants is mainly based on naming conventions and organizational rules. A strict technical separation through RACF is not consistently implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Datasets are named with a tenant abbreviation as a prefix (e.g., `MANDANT1.PROD.DATA`), but there are no RACF profiles that actively prevent access by other tenants.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Attempt to access another tenant's data as a user of one tenant. Review of RACF profiles for missing tenant-specific restrictions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: RACF profiles are used to separate tenants. However, high system privileges (SPECIAL, OPERATIONS) are not strictly limited to the central operator, so tenant administrators have some system-wide rights. Maintenance windows are announced but not actively coordinated with tenants.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Generic RACF profiles (`MANDANT1.**`) protect the data. However, some tenant admins receive the OPERATIONS attribute, for example, to manage their own jobs. Maintenance windows are announced via email.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the assignment of system privileges to tenant-specific users. Interviewing tenants about the coordination of maintenance windows.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If a z/OS system is used by tenants, a RACF concept for tenant separation MUST be created. The data and applications of the tenants MUST be separated by RACF profiles. High privileges (SPECIAL, OPERATIONS, AUDITOR) and changing access to files of the z/OS operating system MAY ONLY be granted to employees of the operator. The maintenance windows MUST be coordinated with all tenants.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A multi-tenancy concept is created that describes the separation at the level of datasets, jobs, Started Tasks, and other resources using RACF profiles and groups. The assignment of system privileges is strictly limited to operator personnel. Maintenance windows are planned in coordination with the tenants via a shared ticket system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the multi-tenancy concept. Review of the RACF database for the correct implementation of the separation. Verification that no tenant users have system privileges. Inspection of the planning logs for the maintenance windows.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logical partitions (LPARs) are used for stronger isolation between tenants. Network traffic between tenant LPARs is controlled by a mainframe firewall. Regular audits are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the separation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each tenant or tenant group is given its own LPAR. A software firewall on z/OS (e.g., as part of z/OS Communications Server) or an external firewall is configured to filter traffic between the LPARs. Audits are conducted by internal or external auditors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the LPAR configuration and network firewall rules. Analysis of the reports from the last tenant separation audits.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Each tenant runs in a completely separate LPAR or, if security requirements demand it, on separate physical hardware (in different Central Processor Complexes). All potential covert channels between the tenant environments are identified and mitigated. The separation mechanisms are certified by an independent third party.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Dedicated machines are provided for high-security tenants. A covert channel analysis is performed, e.g., regarding shared resources in the processor cache or I/O subsystem. A certification report (e.g., according to Common Criteria) is available.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the physical or logical system architecture. Analysis of the study on covert channels. Inspection of the external certificate for tenant separation.

controls.title: Protection of session data

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Encryption for terminal sessions is available but not enforced. Administrators and users often use unencrypted protocols such as standard TN3270 for convenience or due to lack of awareness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The TN3270 server is configured to accept both encrypted and unencrypted connections. There is no policy mandating the use of encryption.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the TN3270 server configuration. Performing network sniffing to identify unencrypted traffic.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Session data for RACF administrators is encrypted using TN3270E (TLS). However, other users' sessions remain unencrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separate ports or policies are configured for administrators and regular users, with encryption only being enforced for administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the TN3270 server configuration for port-based or user-based encryption rules. Verification that administrators cannot log in without encryption.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Session data for RACF administrator connections MUST be transmitted encrypted. For the connections of other employees, this SHOULD also be implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy defines which connection types must be encrypted. Encryption for administrative connections is enforced using TN3270E or an upstream TLS proxy. Encryption for regular users is recommended and configured, but not strictly enforced by blocking.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the policy for protecting session data. Review of the technical configuration (e.g., TN3270 server) to verify the implementation of the policy, especially for administrative access.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All interactive user sessions (both from administrators and regular users) with the mainframe are encrypted using modern, strong TLS protocols and cipher suites. A central policy enforces encryption for all connections, and non-compliant connection attempts are blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The z/OS Communications Server configuration enforces TLS for all TN3270 ports. Weak protocols (e.g., SSLv3, early TLS) and cipher suites are disabled. This is centrally managed via the AT-TLS functionality.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the AT-TLS policies for enforced use of strong TLS (e.g., TLS 1.2 or higher) and the absence of weak ciphers. An attempt to establish an unencrypted or weakly encrypted connection must fail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All data transfers, including interactive sessions, batch jobs (e.g., FTP), and system-to-system communication, are transparently encrypted by AT-TLS (Application Transparent TLS). The policy is centrally managed and automatically deployed. An intrusion detection system monitors for attempts to downgrade or bypass encryption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Comprehensive AT-TLS rules are defined for all relevant applications and protocols (TN3270, FTP, CICS Web Services, etc.). A Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) is configured with rules for TLS downgrade attacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the AT-TLS policies for completeness and correct application to all communication paths. Review of NIDS logs for alerts related to encryption attacks.

controls.title: Reporting for the secure operation of z/OS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security-relevant log data (SMF) is collected, but it is analyzed infrequently and usually only reactively after a security incident. There is no regular reporting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SMF data is archived on tape or in datasets, but there are no tools or processes for proactive analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing administrators about their handling of SMF data. Looking for evidence of regular analysis or reporting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Predefined reports are created with a security tool (e.g., zSecure, RACF-Report-Writer), but there is no formal process for their review or for addressing identified deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A batch job generates weekly standard reports (e.g., about all users with the SPECIAL attribute), but the reports are not systematically reviewed or followed up on.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Requesting the generated reports. Asking who reviews the reports and what happens when anomalies are found.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process SHOULD be established to monitor all security-relevant activities on z/OS. This process SHOULD define which security reports are created regularly, which tools and data sources are used (e.g., System Management Facility), and how deviations from the requirements are handled. The security reports SHOULD be used as information during audits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented process specifies who (e.g., the security team) creates and reviews which reports (e.g., failed logins, changes to critical datasets, new privileged users) at what interval (e.g., weekly). Deviations are recorded as tickets and tracked. The reports are kept for internal and external audits.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the established reporting process. Inspection of the reports from recent months and the corresponding tickets for deviations. Verification that the reports were used in the last internal or external audit.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reporting process is semi-automated. A Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system collects and correlates SMF and other log data from z/OS. Dashboards provide a near real-time overview of the security status. Defined deviations trigger automatic alerts to the security team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SMF feed is integrated into the central SIEM (e.g., Splunk, QRadar). Specific correlation rules and dashboards for z/OS security events are created in the SIEM. Thresholds for alerts (e.g., more than 10 failed logins per minute for a user) are defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the SIEM configuration for the z/OS data source. Analysis of the dashboards and correlation rules. Review of the alerting logs and the response to alerts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIEM uses User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) to proactively identify threats and anomalies in the z/OS environment. The reporting process is fully integrated into the Security Operations Center (SOC) workflow, with automated incident response playbooks for z/OS-specific incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SIEM's UEBA module is trained with z/OS data to learn normal behavior and detect deviations (e.g., a user accessing data they have never worked with before). For critical alerts, SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) playbooks are executed, which, for example, automatically suspend a user in RACF.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration and effectiveness of the UEBA module for z/OS. Analysis of the SOAR playbooks and their execution logs. Simulation of an attack to test the automated detection and response.

controls.title: Monitoring of z/OS systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Monitoring is limited to observing the master console for critical WTOR (Write To Operator with Reply) messages. Other data sources such as SYSLOG or SMF are not actively monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The operations team is responsible for keeping an eye on the console. There is no automation or filtering of messages.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing the operators on how they detect system problems. Checking if there are processes for analyzing SYSLOG or other log data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automation product is used to filter console messages but handles only a few basic events. Thresholds for capacity and utilization are not defined or monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A product such as NetView or another automation tool is used to reduce the flood of messages on the console and to automatically answer known, recurring messages. Performance and capacity monitoring does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the automation product's configuration. Asking how performance bottlenecks or capacity issues are detected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During operation, the z/OS system SHOULD be monitored for important messages, events, and compliance with thresholds. In particular, error messages on the HMC console, WTOR and important WTO messages, system tasks, security violations, capacity limits, and system load SHOULD be considered. For monitoring, at least the MCS console, the System Management Facility, SYSLOG, and the relevant application log data SHOULD also be used. It SHOULD be ensured that all important messages are detected promptly and responded to if necessary. System messages SHOULD be filtered so that only important messages are displayed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central monitoring tool (e.g., an automation product) is configured to monitor all mentioned data sources. Thresholds for CPU utilization, memory consumption, and DASD space are defined. Important messages are highlighted or trigger a notification to the operations team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the monitoring tool's configuration. Verification of the defined thresholds. Analysis of the tool's logs to understand the detection of and response to events.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Monitoring is centralized and automated. A dedicated monitoring solution provides dashboards for all important metrics. Thresholds are dynamically adjusted based on workload patterns. The system automatically opens tickets in an ITSM system for certain events.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized performance monitoring tool (e.g., from BMC, Broadcom) is used. An integration with the ticketing system (e.g., ServiceNow) is established, so that, for example, a `D SN,DASD,V,-,GT,90` (dataset occupancy over 90%) automatically creates an incident ticket for the storage management team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the monitoring dashboards. Analysis of the dynamic threshold configuration. Review of the integration with the ITSM system and the generated tickets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Predictive analytics are used to foresee potential problems (e.g., capacity bottlenecks, performance degradation) before they affect the service. The monitoring system is capable of performing automated remediation for common problems (e.g., extending a dataset, restarting a failed task).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: AIOps (AI for IT Operations) tools are used to analyze historical performance data and predict future bottlenecks. Automation playbooks are implemented that respond to specific alarms with corrective actions without requiring human intervention.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration and models of the AIOps tool. Analysis of the automation playbooks and their execution logs. Verification that the predictive warnings lead to proactive measures.

controls.title: Synchronization of z/OS passwords and RACF commands

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A synchronization mechanism is used, but it also synchronizes the locking of IDs after incorrect entries. This causes a user to be locked out on all systems simultaneously, which can lead to denial-of-service issues.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default configuration of the synchronization tool is used without enabling the option to suppress the `REVOKE` status synchronization.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the synchronization tool's configuration. Testing the behavior by deliberately entering a password incorrectly on one system and checking the user's status on the other systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The synchronization is correctly configured to not synchronize lockouts. However, the involved z/OS systems are not standardized, which leads to occasional synchronization errors. The administrative function of the tool is not adequately protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The systems have different RACF settings or exit routines that interfere with command synchronization. Access to the sync tool's admin interface is not restricted to a few administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Comparing the system configurations for relevant differences. Reviewing the permissions for the synchronization tool's administrative interface.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If z/OS passwords or RACF commands are to be automatically synchronized across multiple z/OS systems, the respective systems SHOULD be standardized as much as possible. The revocation of IDs due to incorrect password entries SHOULD NOT be synchronized. The risk of synchronizing security-critical RACF commands SHOULD be taken into account. The administrative function of the synchronization program SHOULD only be available to authorized employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system standardization concept is implemented. The synchronization tool is configured so that the `REVOKE` status is not propagated on password errors. A risk analysis assesses which RACF commands (e.g., `DELUSER`, `DELGROUP`) may not be synchronized or only after manual confirmation. Access to the tool's admin functions is protected via RACF profiles.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the synchronization tool's configuration and the system standardization documentation. Reviewing the risk analysis for critical commands. Verifying the RACF profiles for protecting the admin function.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The synchronization process is logged and monitored. A 'dry run' mode is used to test the effects of synchronizing critical commands before actual execution. A central, highly available system is responsible for synchronization to avoid split-brain scenarios.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The synchronization tool's logs are sent to a SIEM and monitored for errors. Before synchronizing a critical command, a simulation is executed, the result of which must be reviewed by an administrator. The tool runs on a highly available LPAR.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the synchronization process logs and alerts in the SIEM. Review of the process for the 'dry run' mode. Verification of the high-availability configuration of the synchronization system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of command synchronization, a Parallel Sysplex with a shared RACF database is used. This provides a consistent and highly available security domain across all systems in the Sysplex and eliminates the risks associated with command forwarding and synchronization delays.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Parallel Sysplex is implemented. The RACF database is held in a Coupling Facility or configured as shared DASD, so that all LPARs in the Sysplex use the same physical database. Command synchronization is turned off.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the Sysplex configuration. Verifying that all systems in the Sysplex access the same RACF database and that the synchronization of RACF database copies (if any) works correctly.

controls.title: Role concept for z/OS systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Roles exist only informally and are not documented or technically implemented in RACF (e.g., through groups). Permissions are granted individually per user.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access rights are based on verbal agreements or shout-outs. There are no RACF groups that represent functional roles.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing employees about their roles and tasks. Checking the RACF database for the absence of a group structure and the presence of many user-specific permissions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A role concept is documented and RACF groups are used. However, the separation of duties for the SPECIAL, OPERATIONS, and AUDITOR attributes is not implemented; one person can hold several of these powerful attributes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a document that describes roles like 'System Programmer' or 'Operator'. Corresponding RACF groups exist. However, the separation of top privileges is not enforced due to staff shortages or convenience.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Comparing the RACF database with the role concept. Checking if there are users who simultaneously have SPECIAL and AUDITOR or other critical combinations of attributes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: At least for the system administration of z/OS systems, a role concept SHOULD be introduced. For all important system administration roles, deputy arrangements SHOULD also be in place. The RACF attributes SPECIAL, OPERATIONS, and AUDITOR SHOULD be assigned to different people (separation of roles).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal role concept for administration is created and implemented in RACF using groups. The documentation names at least one deputy for each important role. It is ensured that the attributes SPECIAL, OPERATIONS, and AUDITOR are assigned to different people.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the role concept and the documentation of the deputy rules. Checking the RACF database to ensure that SPECIAL, OPERATIONS, and AUDITOR are assigned to different user IDs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The role concept includes not only administrators, but also application developers and end users. The access rights for each role are documented in a role matrix. A regular recertification process ensures that the assigned roles are still appropriate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The role concept is extended to all users of the system. A matrix (e.g., in a table) lists all roles and their permissions. Annually, supervisors must review and confirm the role assignments of their employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the completeness of the role matrix. Analysis of the logs from the last recertification campaign and the resulting adjustments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The role-based access control (RBAC) model is managed by a central IAM solution. The role definitions are fine-grained and strictly adhere to the principle of least privilege. The system can automatically detect and report toxic permission combinations that violate separation of duties policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IAM tool manages the roles and their assignment to users and synchronizes this with RACF. An SoD (Segregation of Duties) matrix is stored in the IAM tool, which is automatically checked when assigning roles.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the configuration of the IAM tool and the SoD matrix. Analysis of the reports on detected SoD conflicts. Testing the assignment of a conflicting role to verify the correct functioning of the detection.

controls.title: Securing z/OS transaction monitors

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Subsystems like CICS or IMS use their own, internal security function (e.g., CICS internal transaction security). This is not integrated with RACF, which leads to separate and inconsistent user management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security settings in CICS (`SEC=YES`) are active, but the system interface to an external security manager (`XTRAN`) is not configured for RACF. Users and permissions are maintained directly in CICS tables.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the system initialization parameters of CICS or IMS. Comparing the user lists in CICS/IMS with those in RACF for inconsistencies.

parts.name: statement
