parts.prose: The subsystem is secured by RACF, but the permissions are granted very broadly (e.g., all users in a department get access to the same CICS transactions), without following the principle of least privilege (PoLP).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The subsystems are connected to RACF. RACF groups are used to control access to transactions, but these groups are very coarse-grained and not task-specific.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the RACF profiles and groups that control access to CICS, IMS, or Db2 resources. Interviewing application owners to determine if the permissions comply with PoLP.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If transaction monitors or databases (e.g., IMS, CICS, Db2) are used under z/OS, they SHOULD be secured using RACF. This also applies to the associated system commands and files. Internal security mechanisms of the transaction monitors and databases SHOULD, however, only be used where corresponding RACF functions are not available. Users and administrators SHOULD only receive the access rights they need for their respective tasks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All relevant resource classes of the subsystems (e.g., `TCICSTRN` for CICS transactions, `DBSUB` for Db2 commands) are activated in RACF and protected with profiles. The authorization concept defines task-specific roles and assigns them the necessary access rights in RACF. The use of internal security functions is reduced to a minimum.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the active RACF classes (`SETROPTS LIST`). Verifying that the relevant subsystem resources are protected by RACF. Spot-checking the permissions of users against the authorization concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to transactions and data within the subsystem is controlled by fine-grained RACF profiles. Security exits in the subsystems are used to enforce additional, application-specific security logic. Their use is documented and controlled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of generic profiles, specific profiles for individual transactions or tables are used. A CICS security exit, for example, is implemented to perform a context-dependent check (e.g., a transaction may only be executed at certain times of the day). The source code of the exits is version-controlled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the granularity of the RACF profiles. Review of the documentation and source code of the security exits in use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All security-relevant events from the subsystems (e.g., transaction execution, database queries, failed accesses) are logged in SMF and integrated into a SIEM for real-time monitoring and threat detection. Database Activity Monitoring (DAM) tools are used to analyze access to sensitive data in Db2.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The audit options in CICS, IMS, and Db2 are configured so that all relevant events write SMF records. These are sent to the SIEM in real-time. A DAM tool (e.g., IBM Guardium) monitors the SQL traffic to Db2.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the audit configuration of the subsystems. Verifying the data flow from SMF to the SIEM. Analyzing the rules and reports configured in the SIEM and DAM tool for subsystem monitoring.

controls.title: Decommissioning of z/OS systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system is shut down, but references from other systems (e.g., in Sysplex definitions or network configurations) are not removed, which leads to errors in ongoing operations. The data storage media are not securely wiped.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The focus is only on shutting down the one system. The effects on the remaining landscape are not analyzed. Hard drives are removed and stored without erasing their content.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configurations of remaining systems for orphaned references. Inquiry about the data carrier disposal process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system is properly removed from the cluster. The data carriers are erased using standard software utilities (e.g., `ICKDSF`). There is no contractual agreement regarding the destruction of data carriers that are replaced by the manufacturer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before shutting down, the definitions in the other systems are adjusted. An `ICKDSF` job is run to initialize the disks, which overwrites the data. Defective disks are returned to the manufacturer without any further conditions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of system definitions for orphaned entries. Checking the job logs of the data carrier erasure. Inspection of maintenance contracts regarding the handling of defective media.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When decommissioning z/OS systems, other z/OS systems, clusters, and management systems SHOULD be adapted so that they no longer reference the decommissioned system. Impacts on licenses SHOULD be considered. Data carriers with confidential data SHOULD be erased in such a way that their content can no longer be reproduced. For defective data carriers that are exchanged by the manufacturer, it SHOULD be contractually agreed that they will be securely destroyed or erased.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A decommissioning process is defined. It includes technical decoupling, a review of the license situation, and secure data erasure. A standard procedure (e.g., multiple overwriting) is established for data erasure. A clause for certified erasure or destruction of replaced data carriers is included in maintenance contracts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the documented decommissioning process. Verification of the executed erasure logs. Review of the maintenance contracts for corresponding clauses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal decommissioning checklist is used. Data erasure follows a recognized standard (e.g., NIST SP 800-88). A destruction or erasure certificate is obtained for all disposed or replaced data carriers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The checklist ensures that all aspects (technology, licenses, data, disposal) are considered. Tools are used that perform erasure according to NIST standards and issue a certificate. Certificates are also requested from service providers or the manufacturer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the completed checklists for past decommissionings. Inspection of the collected erasure and destruction certificates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire decommissioning process is automated where possible. For the highest security requirements, data carriers are physically destroyed on-site before disposal (e.g., shredded or degaussed). The process is documented with a complete audit trail that includes the serial numbers of the destroyed media.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated degausser or shredder for hard drives is operated on-site. The entire process from identifying the disk to its destruction is logged in a database, including photos and witnesses.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the audit trail of the data carrier destruction. Observation of a physical destruction on-site. Verification that the serial numbers in the log match the removed devices.

controls.title: Securing the boot process of z/OS systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system can be started, but the necessary parameters are not documented and are based on the knowledge of individual employees. A checklist for post-startup (IPL) verification does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The startup process (IPL) is performed manually, with operators entering the necessary responses from memory. Whether the system runs correctly afterward is only checked superficially.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Questioning the operators about the IPL process. Searching for documentation such as an operations manual or IPL instructions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The startup process is documented, but there is no defined fallback configuration with which the system can be safely started after a faulty change. Post-IPL checks are informal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a written guide for the IPL. After the IPL, operators check if the most important applications (e.g., CICS) have started, but there is no structured checklist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the IPL documentation. Inquiry about the procedure if the system no longer starts after a change.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The parameters necessary for the startup process (IPL) of a z/OS system SHOULD be documented and known to the operating personnel. The required hardware configurations (IOCDS, LPARs) SHOULD be available. A z/OS master console and a backup console SHOULD be defined. After the startup process, a checklist SHOULD be used to verify that the system status complies with the target specifications. Furthermore, a fallback configuration with which the system was successfully started before the last change SHOULD be maintained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An operations manual documents all IPL parameters (e.g., in `IEASYSxx`) and the associated hardware profiles. A written checklist is completed after each IPL. Before any major change, the current runnable configuration (e.g., Parmlib members) is backed up to serve as a fallback.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the operations manual and IPL documentation. Inspection of the completed checklists from the last IPLs. Review of the process for backing up and restoring the fallback configuration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The startup parameters (e.g., Parmlib members) are subject to version control. The post-IPL check is automated, with a script verifying the most important system settings and services. The process for activating the fallback configuration is documented and regularly tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All Parmlib members are managed in a version control system like Git or Endevor. After the IPL, a REXX or Ansible script is automatically run, which checks the status of subsystems, the availability of resources, and critical system settings, and generates a report. Fallback tests are conducted semi-annually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the version control system and the change history of the Parmlib. Analysis of the automated check script and its result logs. Review of the logs from the last fallback tests.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system uses the Secure Boot capabilities of the Z hardware to cryptographically ensure the integrity of the IPL code and important operating system components. Any deviation from the 'Golden Image' boot configuration triggers an alarm and prevents the system from transitioning to a productive state.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The 'IBM Z Trusted Key Entry (TKE)' function is used to manage the keys for Secure Boot. The system firmware is configured to only load signed code during the IPL process. The integrity of the Parmlib members is also cryptographically checked before use.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the Secure Boot configuration in the system firmware and the HMC. Verification of the key management process with TKE. Attempting to load an unsigned or manipulated component must fail and be logged.

controls.title: Securing the operational functions of z/OS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Dynamic changes are often made directly to the production system without a formal change request. Access to SDSF is not granularly controlled, so many users have extensive permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Changes are made 'through informal channels'. The protection of SDSF functions via RACF is not used; instead, the default settings are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Comparison of system logs with change management tickets for undocumented changes. Review of SDSF-related RACF profiles in the `ISFPARMS` class for missing restrictions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A change management process is used, but emergency changes often bypass this process without subsequent documentation. Operator commands are protected, but not with fine-grained controls.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tickets are created for planned changes. In case of disruptions, commands are issued directly to resolve the problem quickly. Access to operator commands is protected via RACF, but the permissions are broadly defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of emergency changes and their documentation. Review of RACF profiles for operator commands for overly broad permissions (e.g., use of wildcards).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All maintenance work affecting production, as well as dynamic and other changes, SHOULD only be carried out within the framework of change management. SDSF and similar functions, as well as priority control for jobs, SHOULD be protected against unauthorized access using RACF. z/OS system commands and particularly security-relevant commands for dynamic changes SHOULD be protected via RACF. When dynamically defining hardware, it SHOULD be ensured that a resource in productive operation is not assigned to multiple individual systems outside of a Parallel Sysplex.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every change that affects production requires an approved change ticket. Access to SDSF panels and commands is granularly controlled via RACF profiles in the `SDSF` and `ISFPARMS` classes. Critical operator commands are protected via the `OPERCMDS` class. Processes for dynamic hardware configuration (Dynamic I/O) are documented and controlled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the change management logs. Review of the RACF configuration for SDSF and OPERCMDS. Verification of the processes for dynamic hardware changes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All operator commands are logged. An automation tool is used to restrict the parameters that can be used with powerful commands. The change management process includes automated pre-deployment checks to validate the change against system policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Command logging is activated in RACF. An automation product (e.g., NetView) intercepts commands and checks their parameters before they are executed. Before a change is implemented, a script is run that checks the configuration for compliance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the logs of executed operator commands. Review of the configuration of the automation tool for command filtering. Examination of the pre-deployment check scripts and their results.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A 'Least Privilege' model is applied to operator commands, where operators can only execute commands that are whitelisted for their specific role. All dynamic configuration changes are performed via automated, tested, and audited scripts instead of manual commands. Hardware configuration changes are validated against a central Configuration Management Database (CMDB).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RACF class `OPERCMDS` is used to control access to commands very granularly (whitelisting). Changes are rolled out via Ansible playbooks or REXX scripts that are versioned and tested. The CMDB (e.g., in ServiceNow) is used as the 'source of truth' for the hardware configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of `OPERCMDS` profiles for the implementation of the whitelisting principle. Audit of automation scripts for configuration changes. Verification of consistency between the actual system configuration and the data in the CMDB.

controls.title: Securing z/VM

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: z/VM is used and default passwords are changed. However, security administration is performed via the internal mechanisms of z/VM (CP commands) and not via an external security manager like RACF. Virtual machines are not strictly separated from each other.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default passwords of the service machines are changed after installation. User rights are administered using `CP DEFINE` and `CP SET` commands. There is no strict separation of virtual switches or other resources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether z/VM is connected to an external security manager. Analyze the User Directory for permissions and resource sharing between virtual machines.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If z/VM is used, the product SHOULD be integrated into patch management and default passwords SHOULD be changed. The z/VM system administrator role SHOULD be assigned restrictively. Security administration SHOULD be performed via RACF for z/VM. Passwords of real and guest users SHOULD be encrypted using RACF. Security-critical z/VM system commands SHOULD be protected via RACF. Virtual machines SHOULD only receive the necessary resources and be strictly separated from each other. Only required services SHOULD be started. During reviews, the z/VM journaling function and RACF audit functions SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: z/VM is integrated with RACF/VM (or the z/VM RACF Security Server). A patch and service process for z/VM is established. A permissions concept defines the z/VM admin role and protects critical CP and diagnostic commands via RACF. Virtual machines are defined in the User Directory to use separate resources (memory, CPU, network via VSWITCH). The journaling and audit data are regularly evaluated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the integration of z/VM with RACF. Reviewing the z/VM User Directory for compliance with PoLP and resource separation. Analyzing the RACF profiles for z/VM commands. Reviewing the journaling and audit logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, the separation of virtual machines is enforced by dedicated VSWITCHes with VLAN tagging. The integrity of the z/VM system itself is ensured by regular checks of critical system files. All security-relevant logs are forwarded to a central SIEM and monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separate virtual switches with IEEE 802.1Q VLAN support are configured for different security zones to separate network traffic. A tool like zSecure Audit for z/VM is used for integrity checking. A SIEM agent or Syslog forwarder is installed on a service machine to export audit data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the VSWITCH and VLAN configuration. Analysis of the integrity check reports. Verification of the data flow from z/VM to the SIEM and the correlation rules there.

controls.title: Defining standards for z/OS system definitions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Informal naming conventions exist, but they are not documented or enforced. This leads to inconsistencies in the naming of datasets, jobs, and other objects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Teams agree on certain prefixes, but new employees or other teams do not always adhere to them. There is no written policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Searching the system catalog for objects with inconsistent names. Interviewing employees about the current naming conventions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Standards and naming conventions for z/OS system definitions SHOULD be defined and documented. The documentation SHOULD be available to administrators. Compliance with the standards SHOULD be checked regularly. Standards SHOULD be defined in particular for file, database, job, and volume names, as well as for application, system, and user IDs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 'z/OS Naming and Definition Standards' document is created and published on the intranet. It defines the structure for dataset names (e.g., `<HLQ>.<APPL>.<TYPE>.<NAME>`), job names, user ID formats, etc. Compliance is checked as part of code reviews or manual audits.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the standard document for completeness and clarity. Spot-checking objects in the system (datasets, jobs, user IDs) for conformity with the standards.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the naming and definition standards is enforced by automated checks. For example, system exits or pre-submission checks prevent the creation of objects or the starting of jobs with non-compliant names.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A RACF exit (`ICHRDX01`) is implemented to validate the names of new datasets or user IDs. A JES exit is used to check job names before execution. Violations are rejected and logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the source code and configuration of the system exits. Attempting to create an object with a non-compliant name must fail.

controls.title: Separation of test and production systems under z/OS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Test and production environments run on the same physical system, separated by naming conventions. There is no strict technical separation, so test applications could potentially access production data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Production datasets are named `PROD.**` and test datasets `TEST.**`. However, RACF rules for separation are incomplete or missing, so a developer with their permissions can accidentally or intentionally access `PROD.**`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the RACF profiles to see if they enforce a strict separation between test and production datasets. Attempting to access production resources from a test user ID.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Technical measures SHOULD be taken to separate development and test systems from production systems under z/OS. Possible access via shared hard disks and the Parallel Sysplex SHOULD be considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The separation is achieved through separate logical partitions (LPARs) for test and production. The RACF databases for test and production are separate. It is ensured that no DASD volumes are used by both environments in write mode simultaneously (except for explicit data transfer processes). In the Parallel Sysplex, care is taken to ensure that test and production LPARs do not access the same application resources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the LPAR configuration and system configuration (e.g., `GRS` for resource serialization) to verify the separation. Analyzing the RACF settings to ensure that test user IDs do not have access to production resources and vice versa.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to LPAR separation, network traffic between test and production LPARs is strictly controlled by a firewall. Data transfers from production to test are only possible through a controlled, documented, and approved process, where sensitive data is anonymized or pseudonymized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A mainframe firewall or VLANs are used to restrict communication between the LPARs to the bare essentials. A formal process for the 'Prod-to-Test-Refresh' is established, which uses data masking tools before the data is loaded into the test environment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the firewall rules between the LPARs. Analyzing the process documentation and logs for the data transfer from production to test. Checking test databases for the presence of unmasked production data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Test and production environments run on completely separate physical hardware (different Central Processor Complexes). Any connection between the environments is only possible through a strictly controlled and monitored Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate mainframe machine is operated for development and testing. Data transfers between the machines are carried out exclusively via dedicated, secured FTP servers in a DMZ. Direct channel-to-channel or network connections do not exist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the physical hardware inventory and network diagrams to verify complete physical separation. Auditing the configuration and logs of the DMZ components that control data exchange.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: 'IBM Z' type systems belong to the server systems commonly referred to as mainframes. Mainframes have evolved from classic single systems with batch processing to modern client-server systems. The Z-Architecture is the successor to the S/360 architecture introduced in 1964 and is frequently used in today's mainframe installations.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to protect information that is processed, offered on, or transmitted via Z systems.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.1.7 IBM Z is to be applied to any server based on IBM's Z-Architecture.

The module SYS.1.1 General Server forms the basis for securing servers. For Z systems, both the general requirements listed there and the specific requirements in this module must be met.

Various operating systems are available for the Z hardware (e.g., z/OS, z/VM, KVM, or Linux on Z). The choice is usually made based on parameters such as machine size and purpose. The recommendations of this module are essentially limited to the z/OS operating system. Selected security aspects of z/VM are also addressed. For the Linux on Z operating system, reference is made to module SYS.1.3 Server under Linux and Unix.

Other requirements particularly relevant to IBM Z can be found in module ORP.4 Identity and Access Management and in OPS.1.2.5 Remote Maintenance.

A key component of the security concept for Z systems at a technical level is the security system used, for example, TopSecret, ACF2 (Access Control Facility), or RACF (Resource Access Control Facility). To simplify the presentation, the following will only refer to RACF. The recommendations should be adapted accordingly if a different security system is used.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient or incorrect configuration of the hardware or the z/OS operating system
parts.prose: The configuration of a z/OS operating system is very complex and requires intervention by system administrators in many places. Incorrect or insufficient configuration can create vulnerabilities that can lead to corresponding security problems. Supervisor Calls (SVCs), for example, are calls to special z/OS utility programs that run in the highly authorized kernel mode. Insecure SVC programs can potentially be used to bypass z/OS security mechanisms.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Incorrect configuration of the z/OS security system RACF
parts.prose: In a z/OS operating system, a special security system is responsible for user authentication and their authorization to access resources. RACF is often used for this purpose. The default configuration of RACF usually does not meet the security requirements of the respective operational scenario. Resources and z/OS system commands, for example, are protected by special classes in RACF. Insufficiently defined classes may allow users to issue system commands that could potentially impair stable system operation.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Maloperation of z/OS system functions
parts.prose: Due to the complexity of a z/OS operating system and its components, operational errors cannot be completely ruled out. Depending on the type of error, individual components or the entire system may subsequently fail. For example, if resources mutually lock each other (contention), certain functions may be unavailable until the lock is released. Often, a series of system queries (displays) and considerable operational experience are necessary to resolve mutual locks using the correct z/OS commands.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Manipulation of z/OS system control
parts.prose: z/OS systems can be influenced through a variety of interfaces, for example, via the Hardware Management Console, local and remote MCS consoles, automation procedures, and remote maintenance access points. If, for instance, the physical or logical access to remote MCS consoles is inadequately protected, z/OS systems could potentially be manipulated from there without authorization.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Attacks on z/OS systems via TCP/IP
parts.prose: To attack a z/OS system via its network connection, special knowledge of the network architecture or of z/OS is often not required. Due to the TCP/IP connection to (potentially public) networks and the Unix System Services, many z/OS systems are accessible for internal or external attacks via standard protocols and services, such as HTTP or FTP. In the case of external attacks, the TCP/IP connection to public networks could potentially be used to carry out Denial-of-Service attacks against the offered services or to read or manipulate transmitted data without authorization. Internal attackers can try to escalate their privileges via the TCP/IP connection to internal networks, for example, by spying on the username and password of users with SPECIAL privileges.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Incorrect character set conversion when using z/OS
parts.prose: EBCDIC, ASCII, and Unicode are character sets that define how letters, digits, and other characters are represented using bits. z/OS systems work with EBCDIC code. Only HFS and zFS file systems, which are used under Unix System Services (USS), allow both ASCII and EBCDIC storage. When exchanging data between z/OS systems and IT systems that work with ASCII or Unicode (e.g., also from USS to z/OS), there is a risk that information will be corrupted if incorrect translation tables (Code Page Translation) are used. The translation of special characters is particularly often affected by this.

controls.title: Suitable installation of storage systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the core components of the storage solution, such as the storage controllers, are housed in a locked room. Peripheral components such as SAN switches may be located in generally accessible areas. There are no formal regulations for access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, physical protection is implemented ad-hoc and only for the systems perceived as most critical. Often, a simple office room or a cabinet is used that is lockable but has no other security features.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the location of the storage components. It is checked whether at least the central storage systems are behind a locked door. It is checked on a random basis whether peripheral components such as switches are unsecured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All IT components of the storage solution are located in locked rooms. Access is restricted to a predefined group of people, but is not actively logged. Basic power supply and air conditioning are available, but do not necessarily meet the manufacturer's recommendations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implementation is done by using standard server or technical rooms. Key or card access is managed through general company processes. The environmental conditions are maintained passively but not actively monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that all components of the storage solution (controllers, drive bays, switches) are housed in locked rooms. The list of authorized persons is checked, but it is not expected that detailed access logs exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The IT components of storage solutions MUST be set up in locked rooms. ONLY authorized personnel MAY have access to these rooms. Furthermore, a secure power supply MUST be ensured. The manufacturer's specifications for recommended ambient temperature and humidity MUST be adhered to.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirement is met by installation in a dedicated server room with controlled access. A list of authorized persons is maintained and must be kept up-to-date. The power supply is secured by an uninterruptible power supply (UPS). Compliance with the environmental specifications is ensured by appropriate air conditioning and checked periodically.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the site to ensure that the components are in a locked room. He checks the access control regulations and the list of authorized persons. Evidence of the secure power supply (e.g., maintenance logs of the UPS) and compliance with the environmental conditions (e.g., climate logs) is requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, access to the rooms is electronically logged and the logs are regularly reviewed. The power supply is designed redundantly (e.g., two separate power circuits). Environmental conditions (temperature, humidity) are continuously monitored and alarms are automatically triggered in case of deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An electronic locking system with a logging function is used. The logs are analyzed at least quarterly. The storage components are connected to A and B power rails, which are fed by separate UPSs. Sensors for environmental monitoring are installed and connected to a central monitoring system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the electronic access logs and the analysis reports. They check the concept of the redundant power supply and the physical cabling. In addition, the configuration of the monitoring system and exemplary alarm messages for environmental conditions are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The server room housing the storage solution meets the requirements of a high-availability data center (e.g., according to EN 50600 or equivalent). Access is secured by a multi-level procedure (e.g., mantrap with biometric authentication). Power supply and air conditioning are fully redundant (N+1 or 2N) and undergo predictive maintenance. Video surveillance is installed at all relevant entrances and exits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The operation takes place in a certified data center. Access control is integrated into the central physical security management system. Predictive maintenance systems are used for the infrastructure components. The video recordings are archived in an audit-proof manner and evaluated in the event of an incident.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the valid certificates for the data center. The functionality of the multi-level access control is demonstrated live. The topology and maintenance plans for the redundant power and climate control systems are checked. The configuration and operation of the video surveillance system are verified. Automatic check: `check-datacenter-certification --tier 3`

controls.title: Secure basic configuration of storage solutions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The storage solution is put into operation with the factory settings. Only the default passwords are changed. Firmware updates and the deactivation of unused services are only performed sporadically when a specific problem occurs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration is done manually and without documented specifications. The focus is on the quick commissioning of the basic functionality. Security aspects are only treated reactively.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the running configuration with the manufacturer's known factory settings. It is checked whether default passwords are still active and whether the firmware version is severely outdated. A list of active services is checked for obviously unnecessary protocols (e.g., Telnet).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before productive commissioning, the firmware is brought up to date. A basic hardening is carried out, which includes changing default passwords and deactivating known insecure services. Unused physical interfaces are deactivated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple checklist is used for commissioning. The configuration is applied manually to each system. A backup of the configuration is created after the initial setup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the checklist for commissioning. The current firmware version is compared with the manufacturer's recommendations. The configuration is checked for the deactivation of insecure services (e.g., insecure SNMP versions) and open ports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before a storage solution is used in production, it MUST be ensured that all software components and the firmware are up to date. Afterwards, a secure basic configuration MUST be established. Unused interfaces of the storage system MUST be deactivated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented standard for the basic configuration (hardening guide) for each type of storage solution. This process is followed for every new installation. The deactivation of interfaces includes both physical ports and logical services and protocols. The initial configuration is saved and stored securely after setup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the hardening guide and compares it with the configuration of one or more production systems. It is checked whether the process for updating the firmware is documented and whether the versions are current. The list of active interfaces and services is compared with the specifications.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined basic configuration, the configuration files (default, applied basic configuration, current configuration) are stored redundantly and protected. The hardening guide is reviewed regularly (e.g., annually) and adapted to new threats and manufacturer recommendations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration files are versioned and stored in a central, access-protected repository (e.g., a dedicated file share with restrictive permissions). There is a defined process for reviewing and updating the hardening guides, which is approved by the Information Security Officer (ISO).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and protection measures of the repository for configuration files. The logs of the last reviews and the change history of the hardening guide are inspected. It is checked whether current security recommendations (e.g., from the manufacturer or CERTs) have been incorporated into the guide.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The creation and application of the secure basic configuration is fully automated. The configuration is managed as code (Infrastructure as Code) in a versioning system. Any deviation of the running configuration from the defined target state is automatically detected and alerted or corrected (Desired State Configuration).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Ansible, Puppet, or Terraform are used in conjunction with Git for configuration management. A compliance scanner continuously checks all storage systems against the baseline configuration defined in Git. Changes to the baseline configuration require a peer review and approval process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automation scripts and the configuration templates. They check the configuration and logs of the compliance scanner as well as the alerting for deviations. The process documentation for configuration changes, including the approval workflows in Git, is reviewed. Automatic check: `ansible-playbook --check a_compliance_playbook.yml`

controls.title: Protection of the administration interfaces

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative access to the storage systems is only protected by a password. Access is possible from the general production network. Both secure and insecure protocols are used for administration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administration is carried out via the system's standard IP interface, which is also used for data traffic. There is no network segmentation that restricts administrative access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to establish a connection to the administration interfaces (web GUI, SSH, Telnet) of the storage system from a standard client in the production network. A port scan of the system from the production network identifies open administrative services.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative access is restricted to the use of secure protocols (e.g., SSH, HTTPS). Access is restricted to a small group of administrators. However, access is still from the production network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Insecure protocols such as Telnet and HTTP are deactivated in the storage system's configuration. Access control is handled via local user accounts on the storage system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the storage system's configuration that insecure protocols are deactivated. The list of local administrator accounts is checked for necessity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administration and management access to the storage systems MUST be restricted. It MUST be ensured that the administration interfaces cannot be accessed from untrusted networks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrative access is restricted by network firewall rules so that it is only possible from dedicated management subnets or jump hosts. Untrusted networks include the general client network, the internet, and other external networks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rules that govern access to the management IP addresses of the storage systems. Penetration tests from various network segments are used to attempt to reach the administration interfaces. Automatic check: `nmap -p 22,443 --script firewall-bypass <storage-mgmt-ip> -e <interface_in_untrusted_net>`

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Protocols considered secure SHOULD be used. If insecure protocols are nevertheless used, a separate administration network (see NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design) MUST be used for administration. Access to the administration network is protected by two-factor authentication (2FA).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A physically or logically (VLAN) separate management network is used for all administrative access. Access to this network is via a hardened jump host on which 2FA is enforced for login. If insecure protocols are absolutely necessary (e.g., for legacy systems), they are routed through an encrypted tunnel (e.g., IPsec or SSH tunneling).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network architecture plans and the VLAN configuration to verify the separation of the administration network. The configuration of the jump host and the 2FA system is checked. The process for administrative access is run through to confirm the 2FA requirement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative access is only possible via dedicated, physically separate management consoles (Privileged Access Workstations, PAWs) that are used exclusively for administrative tasks. All administrative sessions are recorded (Session Recording) and the logs are archived in an audit-proof manner and regularly analyzed for suspicious activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Hardened PAWs are used that have no internet access and no standard office applications. A Privileged Access Management (PAM) system is implemented to control access, manage passwords, and record sessions. The analysis of session recordings and logs is supported by a SIEM system with specific use cases for storage system administration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects a PAW and its configuration. They check the architecture and configuration of the PAM system. Random samples of session recordings are viewed. The SIEM rules and dashboards for monitoring administrative activities on storage systems are analyzed.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for storage solutions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no specific documented security requirements for storage solutions. Administration is based on the unwritten knowledge and individual experience of the administrators.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Security-related decisions are made on a case-by-case basis and are often reactive. There is no consistent approach.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the submission of policies or concepts for storage security. The absence of such documents and interviews with administrators that reveal inconsistent procedures substantiate this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are basic, informal guidelines or checklists for the configuration and operation of storage solutions. However, these have not been adopted as a formal policy and are not regularly updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The guidelines are often part of commissioning documentation or internal wiki articles created by the technical teams.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing checklists and technical documentation. It is checked whether these documents have an official status (e.g., approval by a responsible body) and how up-to-date they are.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the institution's general security policy, a specific security policy for storage solutions SHOULD be created. It SHOULD comprehensibly describe specifications on how storage solutions can be securely planned, administered, installed, configured, and operated. The policy SHOULD be known to all administrators responsible for storage solutions and be fundamental to their work.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal security policy is created that covers topics such as data classification, access control, encryption, segmentation, backup, and disaster recovery for storage solutions. The policy is approved by the ISO and management and made available to all relevant employees (e.g., via the intranet). Training sessions are held to communicate the content.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security policy for storage solutions. It is checked whether it covers the essential security aspects, whether it has been officially approved, and whether it is known to the responsible employees (e.g., through interviews or training records).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is reviewed regularly, at least annually, for its timeliness and effectiveness and adjusted if necessary. If the policy is changed or if there are deviations from the specifications, this SHOULD be coordinated with the ISO and documented. The results of the reviews SHOULD be appropriately documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal review process for the policy is established that involves all stakeholders. Deviations from the policy must be requested, evaluated, and approved through a documented exception process (exception handling). The results of the reviews and the approved exceptions are documented centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the policy reviews from recent years. They check the process for exception approvals and request sample applications and approvals. The documentation of the results is checked for completeness and traceability.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the security policy for storage solutions is continuously monitored through automated technical checks. The results of these checks feed directly into the policy's review process. The policy is stored in a management system (e.g., GRC tool) and linked to the specific technical controls and their audit results.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A compliance scanning tool is used to automatically check the configuration of the storage systems against the policy's specifications. The results are visualized in a dashboard. A GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool is used to manage the entire lifecycle of the policy, from creation and reviews to monitoring implementation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the compliance scanning tool and the generated reports. In the GRC tool, they check the link between the policy specifications and the technical controls and the current compliance status. The process of how the automated audit results influence the policy review is traced.

controls.title: Planning of storage solutions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before storage solutions are deployed in an institution, a requirements analysis SHOULD be conducted. In the requirements analysis, topics such as performance and capacity, among others, SHOULD be considered. Based on the determined requirements, a detailed plan for storage solutions SHOULD then be created. The following points SHOULD be considered in it: selection of manufacturers and suppliers, decision for or against central management systems, planning of the network connection, planning of the infrastructure, and integration into existing processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before procuring a new storage solution, a formal requirements catalog is created. This contains quantitative data on IOPS, throughput, latency, and required capacity (including growth forecast). The planning documentation describes the chosen architecture (e.g., SAN/NAS), the network connection (ports, bandwidth), the necessary infrastructure (rack space, power, cooling), and the migration plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: For a recently procured storage solution, the auditor requests the requirements analysis and the planning documentation. They check whether the mentioned points (performance, capacity, network, infrastructure, etc.) have been addressed and whether the documentation is comprehensible.

controls.title: Selection of a suitable storage solution

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The technical fundamentals of different storage solutions SHOULD be examined in detail. The effects of these technical fundamentals on the possible use in the institution SHOULD be checked. The possibilities and limits of the different types of storage systems SHOULD be presented transparently to those responsible at the institution. The decision criteria for a storage solution SHOULD be documented in a comprehensible manner. Likewise, the decision for the selection of a storage solution SHOULD be documented in a comprehensible manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the selection process, a market analysis is conducted that compares different technologies (e.g., block, file, object storage) and products. An evaluation matrix with clearly defined criteria (technical, economic, security) is created. The final decision is made based on this matrix and justified in writing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the selection process. This includes the market analysis, the evaluation matrix with the criteria, and the final decision justification. It is checked whether security aspects were given appropriate weight in the evaluation.

controls.title: Selection of suppliers for a storage solution

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the specified requirements for a storage solution, suitable suppliers SHOULD be selected. The selection criteria and the decision SHOULD be documented in a comprehensible manner. Furthermore, aspects of maintenance and servicing SHOULD be recorded in writing in so-called Service Level Agreements (SLAs). The SLAs SHOULD be clear and quantifiable. It SHOULD be precisely regulated when the contract with the suppliers ends.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection of the supplier is based on transparent criteria such as references, support quality, and economic stability. The maintenance contract (SLA) defines clear response and recovery times, the availability of spare parts, and the duration of support. The contract terms are legally reviewed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation for supplier selection. They check the concluded maintenance contract (SLA) for clarity, measurability, and completeness of the regulations. It is compared whether the services agreed in the SLA cover the institution's requirements.

controls.title: Creation and maintenance of an operations manual

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An operations manual SHOULD be created. It SHOULD document all regulations, requirements, and settings that are necessary to operate storage solutions. The operations manual SHOULD be updated regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An operations manual is created and maintained for each storage solution. It contains information on the architecture, configuration, administrative interfaces, standard operating procedures (e.g., creating LUNs, changing permissions), monitoring, and troubleshooting. The manual is updated with every relevant configuration change.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the operations manual for one or more storage solutions. They check its completeness based on the mentioned points. It is checked on a random basis whether the configuration documented in the manual matches the live configuration of the system. The date of the last update is checked.

controls.title: Secure operation of a storage solution

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The storage system SHOULD be monitored with regard to the availability of internal applications, system load, and critical events. Furthermore, fixed maintenance windows SHOULD be defined for storage solutions, during which changes can be carried out. In particular, firmware or operating system updates of storage systems or the network components of a storage solution SHOULD only be carried out within such a maintenance window.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitoring system is used to monitor important parameters such as CPU/memory utilization, free capacity, latency times, and the status of hardware components. Critical events trigger alarms. A change management process is established that prescribes the planning and approval of updates in defined maintenance windows. These maintenance windows are communicated to the users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the monitoring system and the dashboards for the storage solution. They review the process documentation for change management and inspect change tickets for recently performed updates. It is checked whether the updates were carried out within the communicated maintenance windows.

controls.title: Monitoring and management of storage solutions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Storage solutions SHOULD be monitored. All collected data (messages) SHOULD be primarily checked to ensure that the specifications of the operations manual are being met. The essential messages SHOULD be filtered out with message filters. Individual components of the storage solution and the overall system SHOULD be managed centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The log data and performance metrics of the storage systems are collected centrally (e.g., in a SIEM or a log management solution). Rules and filters are defined to identify and alert on relevant events (e.g., failed logins, configuration changes, hardware errors). If possible, a central management console is used for administration, providing an overview of all systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the central log management and the alerting rules for storage solutions based on it. Sample alert messages are checked. They review the central management console and check whether all relevant storage systems are integrated there.

controls.title: Securing a SAN through segmentation

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A SAN SHOULD be segmented. A concept SHOULD be developed that assigns the SAN resources to the respective servers. For this purpose, a decision SHOULD be made based on the security requirements and the administrative effort as to which segmentation should be used in which implementation (e.g., FC SANs or iSCSI storage networks). The current resource allocation SHOULD be easily and clearly recognizable using management tools. Furthermore, the current zoning configuration SHOULD be documented. The documentation SHOULD also be available in emergencies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the Fibre Channel SAN, a zoning concept is created, typically based on "Single Initiator, Single Target" or "Single Initiator, Multiple Targets" zones (Soft-Zoning). The configuration is documented and versioned in a central file or a wiki. The documentation is stored in a fault-tolerant location.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the zoning concept and the current configuration documentation. They compare the documentation with the live configuration of the SAN switches on a sample basis. A check is performed to see if the documentation is available in an emergency (e.g., on a separate system).

controls.title: Secure separation of tenants in storage solutions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be defined and comprehensibly documented what requirements the institution places on the multi-tenancy capability of a storage solution. The storage solutions used SHOULD meet these documented requirements. In the block storage environment, LUN masking SHOULD be used to separate tenants from each other. In file service environments, it SHOULD be possible to operate with virtual file servers. Each tenant SHOULD be assigned their own file service. When using IP or iSCSI, tenants SHOULD be separated from each other by segmentation in the network. If Fibre Channel is used, separation SHOULD be achieved using VSANs and soft-zoning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A concept for tenant separation is created. Technically, this is implemented through: LUN masking on the storage controllers to ensure that a server only sees its assigned LUNs. Use of virtual servers (e.g., V-Servers or SVMs) on NAS systems to separate administrative and network domains. VLANs for iSCSI networks. VSANs (Virtual SANs) on Fibre Channel switches to create logically separate fabrics, combined with soft-zoning within the VSANs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the concept for tenant separation. They perform spot checks on the configuration of LUN masking, virtual file servers, VLANs, and VSANs/Zoning to ensure that the separation is effective according to the concept. An attempt is made to access resources of another tenant from a server of one tenant.

controls.title: Secure deletion in SAN environments

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In multi-tenant storage systems, it SHOULD be ensured that Logical Unit Numbers (LUNs) assigned to a specific tenant are deleted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a LUN is no longer needed, a defined deletion process is applied. This process includes at least overwriting the LUN with zeros or random data (one pass) using the storage system's functionality, before the LUN structure itself is removed from the system. The execution is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the process documentation for the secure deletion of LUNs. They check the logs of recently performed deletion operations. If possible, an attempt is made to recover data blocks from the physical storage after a deletion operation to test its effectiveness.

controls.title: Documentation of storage system settings

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All system settings of storage systems SHOULD be documented. The documentation SHOULD contain the technical and organizational specifications as well as all specific configurations of the institution's storage systems. If the documentation of the system settings contains confidential information, it SHOULD be protected from unauthorized access. The documentation SHOULD be reviewed regularly. It SHOULD always be up-to-date.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The documentation is maintained as part of the operations manual. It includes network settings, admin accounts, storage configuration (RAID level, pools), LUN mappings, zoning information, and backup jobs. The documentation is stored on an access-protected server and updated with every configuration change. A formal review takes place at least once a year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the system settings. They check the access permissions for the documentation. Documented settings (e.g., IP address, LUN ID) are compared with the live configuration of the system on a spot-check basis. The logs of the regular reviews are inspected.

controls.title: Security audits and reporting for storage systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All storage systems in use SHOULD be audited regularly. An appropriate process SHOULD be established for this purpose. It SHOULD be regulated which security reports with which contents are to be created regularly. In addition, it SHOULD also be regulated how deviations from specifications are to be handled and how often and in what depth audits are to be carried out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An audit plan for storage systems is created, which provides for annual audits. The audits include checking configurations against the hardening policy, checking access permissions, and analyzing security-relevant log data. The results are recorded in an audit report. A process for tracking findings (action tracking) is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the audit plan, the audit reports from recent years, and the corresponding action plans. They check whether the audits took place as planned and whether the identified deficiencies were tracked and rectified.

controls.title: Decommissioning of storage solutions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If entire storage solutions or individual components of a storage solution are no longer needed, all existing data on them SHOULD be transferred to other storage solutions. A transition phase SHOULD be planned for this. Subsequently, all user data and configuration data SHOULD be securely deleted. All references to the decommissioned storage solution SHOULD be removed from all relevant documents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented process for decommissioning IT systems, which also applies to storage solutions. The process includes planning data migration, performing the migration, verifying data integrity on the new system, and then securely erasing the data on the old system according to recognized standards (e.g., through multiple overwrites or physical destruction). The execution is logged. Subsequently, the systems are removed from the CMDB, monitoring, and documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the process documentation for decommissioning. For a recently decommissioned system, they request the migration plans and the erasure logs. It is checked whether the system has been removed from the CMDB and other management systems.

controls.title: Emergency preparedness and incident response for storage solutions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An emergency plan SHOULD be created for the storage solution in use. The emergency plan SHOULD describe exactly how to proceed in certain emergency situations. It SHOULD also contain instructions in the form of measures and commands that support fault analysis and fault correction. Appropriate tools SHOULD be used to fix errors. Regular drills and tests SHOULD be carried out based on the emergency plan. After the drills and tests, as well as after an actual emergency, the data generated in the process SHOULD be securely deleted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specific recovery plan is created as part of the operations manual. It describes scenarios such as the failure of a controller, a power supply, or a total failure. The plan contains step-by-step instructions and the necessary commands. An emergency drill (e.g., failover test) is conducted at least once a year, the results of which are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the emergency plan and checks it for completeness and clarity. They review the logs of the last emergency drills and check whether improvement measures derived from them have been implemented.

controls.title: Use of storage pools for tenant separation

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Tenants are assigned to logically separate storage pools. LUNs generated from a pool are assigned to only a single tenant. However, there is no strict physical separation of the storage media per pool.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Within the storage system, logical pools (Storage Pools) are defined, each assigned to a tenant. All LUNs for this tenant are created exclusively from its dedicated pool. However, the pools can share physical hard drives (in a RAID array).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the storage pools and their assignment to the tenants. They perform spot checks on the configuration of LUNs and verify that they originate from the correct, tenant-specific pool.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Tenants SHOULD be assigned storage resources from different so-called storage pools. In this process, a storage medium SHOULD always be assigned to only a single pool. The logical disks (LUNs) generated from such a pool SHOULD only be assigned to a single tenant.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each tenant (or each security zone), a dedicated storage pool is created, which consists of an exclusive group of physical hard drives (e.g., its own RAID group). There is no sharing of physical storage media between the pools of different tenants. This creates a strong physical separation at the disk level.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the physical configuration of the storage system. Using the system documentation and the configuration, they verify that the hard drives that form a storage pool are exclusively assigned to this pool and are not shared by other pools. The assignment of pools to tenants is checked.

controls.title: Use of a high-availability SAN solution

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The storage solution is designed to be internally redundant. This includes redundant controllers, power supplies, and multipath connections for the servers. However, there is no replication to a second site.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Storage systems with a dual-controller architecture are used. Servers are connected via at least two paths (through separate SAN switches). Multipathing software on the servers manages the paths.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the hardware equipment and the configuration of the redundancy features (controller status, multipath configuration). A planned failover test of a controller or path is performed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A high-availability SAN solution SHOULD be used. The replication mechanisms used SHOULD correspond to the institution's availability requirements for the storage solution. The configuration of the storage solution SHOULD also meet the availability requirements. In addition, a test and consolidation system SHOULD be available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A fully redundant SAN architecture across two sites (e.g., metro cluster) is implemented. This includes redundant SAN fabrics and storage systems at both sites. Data is replicated synchronously or asynchronously (depending on RPO/RTO requirements) between the sites. An identical test system is available to validate changes and updates before production deployment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture plans of the cross-site SAN solution. They check the replication configuration and the failover mechanisms. The existence and use of the test system are verified. The logs of regular disaster recovery tests are reviewed.

controls.title: Use of encryption for storage solutions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For storage solutions containing data classified as highly sensitive, data-at-rest encryption is implemented. It is defined which data must be encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The encryption is realized through the native functions of the storage system, e.g., through controller-based encryption or the use of Self-Encrypting Drives (SEDs). Key management is handled by the storage system itself (Local Key Management).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies, based on the data classification and system configuration, whether all data classified as highly sensitive is encrypted. The encryption configuration on the storage system is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All data stored in storage solutions SHOULD be encrypted. It SHOULD be specified at which levels (data-in-motion and data-at-rest) encryption is applied. It SHOULD be noted that transport encryption is also relevant for replication and backup traffic.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Both data-at-rest and data-in-motion are encrypted by default. For data-at-rest, an external Key Management System (KMS), ideally connected to a Hardware Security Module (HSM), is used. For data-in-motion, protocols such as IPsec for iSCSI or FC-SP for Fibre Channel are used. Encryption is also enforced for all replication and backup traffic between sites.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the encryption concept. They check the configuration of the data-at-rest encryption, the external KMS, and the data-in-motion encryption (e.g., switch configuration, IPsec policies). The configuration of the replication and backup jobs is checked for the activation of transport encryption. Automated check: `check-storage-encryption --all-luns --transport --kms-status`

controls.title: Ensuring the integrity of the SAN fabric

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the management interfaces of the SAN switches is restricted by strong passwords and access control lists (ACLs). Changes to the configuration are logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Dedicated admin accounts with secure, non-default passwords are used on the SAN switches. Management access is restricted to dedicated admin workstations via ACL. The switches are configured to send all configuration changes to a central syslog server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the user accounts and ACLs on the SAN switches. They check the syslog configuration and review the log entries for configuration changes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To ensure the integrity of the SAN fabric, protocols with additional security features SHOULD be used. For the following protocols, their security properties SHOULD be considered and corresponding configurations SHOULD be used: Diffie Hellman Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (DH-CHAP), Fibre Channel Authentication Protocol (FCAP), and Fibre Channel Password Authentication Protocol (FCPAP).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The mentioned authentication protocols are activated on the SAN switches to secure communication between switches (E-Port authentication) and between switch and end device (F-Port authentication). DH-CHAP is configured for switch-to-switch authentication. FCAP or FCPAP is used to ensure that only authorized devices (HBAs) can connect to the fabric. The configuration is managed centrally via a SAN management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the SAN switches for the activation and correct parameterization of DH-CHAP and FCAP/FCPAP. They check whether authentication is enforced for all relevant ports. The list of authorized devices and their credentials is checked.

controls.title: Multiple overwriting of the data of a LUN

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When a LUN with highly sensitive data is decommissioned, the associated storage segments are overwritten once with zeros or random data before the LUN is deleted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process for decommissioning LUNs requires using the storage system's 'LUN Shredding' or 'Secure Erase' function, which performs a single overwrite. The successful execution is documented in the change ticket.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation and the change tickets for deleted LUNs. They check the logs of the deletion processes generated by the storage system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In SAN environments, data SHOULD be deleted by overwriting the associated storage segments of a LUN multiple times.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The defined process for deleting LUNs with highly sensitive data is extended to include multiple overwrites according to a recognized standard (e.g., DoD 5220.22-M or BSI VSITR). This process is realized by the storage system or by special software tools. A non-repudiable certificate of destruction is created for the process and archived in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the process documentation and the certificates of destruction for recently decommissioned LUNs. They check whether the applied standard meets the requirements. If possible, forensic tools are used to verify on a random basis that no data remnants have remained on the physical media.

controls.title: Securing a SAN through hard zoning

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To segment the SAN, soft zoning based on the World Wide Names (WWN) of the end devices is used throughout.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The segmentation is done by configuring zones on the SAN switches that contain the WWNs of the allowed communication partners (initiator and target). This is the standard method for SAN segmentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the zoning configuration on the SAN switches and compares it with the documentation. It is checked whether the zones follow the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To segment SANs, hard zoning SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to or instead of soft zoning, hard zoning is used. The segmentation is enforced based on the physical switch ports. This prevents a compromised server from accessing LUNs intended for other servers on other ports through WWN spoofing. Hard zoning is activated in the configuration of the SAN switches for all security-critical connections.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the SAN switches to verify that hard zoning (port zoning) is active. They check which ports belong to which zones and whether this assignment is documented and meets the security requirements. An attempt is made to test the effectiveness through a simulated WWN spoofing attack.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for the use of terminal servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are isolated, informal agreements about which applications may be used on the terminal server. However, a formal, documented security policy is either completely missing or very incomplete.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, decisions about the use of the terminal server are made ad hoc. There may be an email or a wiki entry that outlines a few rules, but there is no formal approval or review process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews administrators and users to determine if there are unwritten rules for use. The auditor notes the absence of a formal, comprehensive, and approved security policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic security policy for the use of terminal servers is available and documented. It covers essential points such as allowed applications and user groups, but leaves out more detailed aspects such as network requirements or encryption standards.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document is created that defines the basic operating rules. This document is made available to the administrators, but may not be known to all users or regularly updated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security policy for terminal servers and reviews its content. It is checked whether the basic aspects (e.g. allowed applications) are covered, and at the same time it is determined which of the points required in the requirement are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal security policy MUST be created for the use of terminal servers. When creating the security policy, all of the following points MUST be considered: allowed applications (individually and in combination), security requirements for clients, physical environment of the clients, allowed source and destination networks, allowed communication protocols, encryption and authentication methods, allowed data transfer paths, and connected peripheral devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy is created as an official, versioned document, approved by management, and made available to all relevant stakeholders (administrators, users). The policy serves as the basis for the configuration and operation of the terminal servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the valid security policy for terminal servers and verifies that all aspects mentioned in the requirement (applications, clients, networks, protocols, encryption, data transfer, peripherals) are covered. It is also checked whether the policy has been approved and published.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is reviewed and updated regularly, at least annually, and in the event of significant changes to the infrastructure or threat landscape. The policy contains specific, technically verifiable requirements (e.g., a list of allowed cipher suites) instead of general formulations. Compliance with the policy is audited periodically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal review process for the policy is established, involving IT operations, information security, and, if necessary, business departments. Changes are documented and communicated. Technical configuration requirements are derived directly from the policy and stored in configuration management tools.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the revision history of the security policy and the minutes of the review meetings. It is checked whether the policy contains specific, measurable configuration requirements and whether evidence of regular internal audits to ensure compliance with the policy exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The rules defined in the security policy are enforced and monitored automatically wherever technically possible. Deviations from the policy (e.g., attempting to use a non-permitted protocol or connect an unauthorized peripheral device) are detected in real time, automatically blocked, and trigger a security alert.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The terminal server configuration is managed using an Infrastructure-as-Code tool (e.g., Ansible, Puppet), which ensures compliance with the policy. A SIEM or Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) system is used to monitor policy compliance in real time and implement automated responses.
