parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the automation tools (e.g., IaC playbooks, SIEM correlation rules). Test cases are used to verify that policy violations are automatically detected and blocked. The auditor checks whether corresponding alerting processes are established. A possible automated test would be `Test-TerminalServerPolicyCompliance -Policy 'Policy-File.json'`.

controls.title: Planning the deployment of terminal servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server is commissioned based on a rough estimate of the number of users and without a formal survey of application requirements. Functionality and performance tests are not carried out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator sets up a server because 'some users need a specific application'. The hardware is selected from the available stock without a specific performance analysis. Problems are only discovered during live operation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for planning documents for the terminal server. It is determined that no requirement profiles, performance forecasts, or test reports exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before commissioning, the basic functional requirements of the applications to be provided are recorded. The number of concurrent users is estimated to perform basic hardware sizing. A simple functional test is carried out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of applications and an estimate of the number of users is created. The hardware is sized based on the manufacturer's general recommendations. Before go-live, some users test whether the application starts and is operable.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning documents and verifies that a list of applications and a user forecast exist. The auditor checks whether a basic test has taken place, even if load tests or detailed license checks are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the applications to be provided, the functional requirements (requirement profile) MUST be determined and documented. The total number of users and the number of potentially concurrent users MUST be forecasted. Based on this, the performance requirements (CPU, memory) MUST be determined and the server sized accordingly. It MUST be tested whether the applications function correctly on the terminal server. The applications' licensing scheme MUST be checked for suitability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal planning document is created. It contains the requirement profile, a detailed forecast of user numbers (e.g., based on department sizes and working hours), and the resulting hardware sizing. The compatibility of each application is checked in a test environment. The license conditions are clarified with the legal or purchasing department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documentation and checks its completeness: requirement profile, user forecast, performance requirement, test results, and license check. It is verified that the server sizing is based on this planning data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning includes detailed load and performance tests with simulated user workloads to validate the determined performance requirements and identify bottlenecks. A formal capacity management process is established to continuously monitor utilization and plan for future requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized tools (e.g., Login VSI, RAMP) are used to simulate realistic user sessions and measure system performance under load. The results are incorporated into a capacity planning document that is updated regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the load test reports and compares the results with the performance requirements. The existence and currency of a capacity management plan are checked. The current CPU and RAM utilization can be read automatically with `Get-Counter` (Windows) or `vmstat` (Linux) and compared with the planned values.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire planning and deployment process is largely automated. The capacity of the terminal server farm is dynamically and automatically adjusted to the actual load (autoscaling). Performance and user experience are monitored in real time, and predictive analytics are used to forecast future capacity needs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The terminal servers are operated in a virtualized environment or cloud platform that offers autoscaling features. An Application Performance Monitoring (APM) tool is used to measure not only server metrics but also end-to-end response times for the user. Machine learning models analyze historical data to predict future peak loads.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the autoscaling rules in the virtualization or cloud platform. The dashboards and reports of the APM tool and the predictive analytics tools are inspected. It is checked whether scaling works as expected during an artificially generated load increase.

controls.title: Defining roles and permissions for the terminal server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Permissions are granted on an ad hoc, per-user basis. There is no defined role concept. Shared accounts are often used for user groups to reduce administrative overhead.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a new user needs access, the administrator copies the permissions of an existing user. There is no systematic check to see if these permissions comply with the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the permission structure on the terminal server and notes the lack of a documented role concept. Spot checks are used to determine whether users have excessive privileges and whether shared accounts are being used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are basic roles such as 'User' and 'Administrator'. All regular users receive the same, often overly broad, permissions. The use of shared accounts is avoided but not explicitly prohibited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In Active Directory, groups like 'TS-Users' and 'TS-Admins' are created and used for assigning logon rights and basic file system permissions. There is no fine-grained control per application or function.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the memberships and permissions of the created groups. It is verified that no shared accounts are actively used, but it is noted that the permissions within the 'TS-Users' group are not differentiated according to the need-to-know principle.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A role and permission concept based on the principle of least privilege MUST be created. The permissions for the following activities MUST be defined as a minimum: running applications in a foreign context (e.g., 'root'), accessing operating system-specific functions, accessing the server's and client's file system, accessing downstream services, as well as file and object transfer and connecting peripheral devices. Shared accounts MAY NOT be used if it violates internal regulations or license conditions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed permission concept is documented that defines various user roles (e.g., 'Finance Clerk', 'Controller', 'Administrator'). For each role, the required access to applications, file systems, and devices is precisely defined. Implementation is carried out using granular security groups and policies (e.g., GPOs).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the role and permission concept and compares it with the technical implementation on the terminal server. For various roles, it is checked on a random basis whether the permissions correspond to the documented concept and the principle of least privilege. It is verified that no unauthorized shared accounts exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The roles and permissions are reviewed regularly, at least semi-annually, as part of a re-certification process. The technical separation between the sessions of different users is ensured by additional hardening measures to prevent unauthorized communication or access between sessions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An identity management system is used to implement automated workflows for access reviews, where supervisors must confirm their employees' access. Specific operating system hardening settings are applied to strengthen session isolation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the last access review campaigns. The configuration of the operating system hardening for session isolation is checked. A test could consist of user A trying to access processes or file system objects of user B.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Role and permission management is fully integrated into a central IAM (Identity and Access Management) solution. Privileged access is controlled via a PAM (Privileged Access Management) solution, which enables just-in-time permissions and records all privileged sessions. Any attempts of unauthorized access between sessions are detected and blocked in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IAM solution like Azure AD, Okta, or Keycloak manages the entire lifecycle of identities and their access. A PAM solution like CyberArk or Thycotic brokers administrative connections, hides the passwords, and records the sessions as a video. An EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) agent on the server monitors process interactions and blocks unauthorized access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the IAM and PAM systems. The session recordings of privileged accesses are spot-checked. It is verified that administrative logins are only possible via the PAM system. It could be automatically checked whether the EDR agent is active and its protection functions are enabled: `Get-Service -Name EDRService | Select-Object -Property Status`.

controls.title: Secure configuration of the terminal server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server is installed with the default settings. Only the most obvious insecure configurations are adjusted manually, without following a documented hardening guide.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator installs the server and may change the administrator password and enable the Windows Firewall with default rules. No systematic hardening takes place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the server's configuration with a recognized hardening standard (e.g., CIS Benchmarks) and finds numerous deviations and the use of default settings. The lack of an internal configuration policy is noted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Documented specifications for the secure configuration (hardening) of terminal servers MUST be created. Manufacturer recommendations MUST be taken into account. The specifications MUST be fully implemented and the implementation documented. The configuration specifications and their implementation MUST be reviewed regularly. At a minimum, roles and permissions, the scope of protocol encryption, authentication functions, and the ability to view other users' sessions must be considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal hardening guide is created based on manufacturer documentation and best practices (e.g., CIS, BSI). This guide is used as a checklist for every server installation. Implementation is ensured via Group Policies (GPOs) or configuration scripts. The configuration is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the hardening guide and compares it with the configuration of a terminal server on a random basis. They check whether the configuration is documented and whether there is a process for regular review. An automated check could read the applied GPOs: `gpresult /r`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the hardening specifications is checked regularly and automatically with a configuration scanner. The hardening guide is updated at least annually and whenever new vulnerabilities or attack techniques become known.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool such as the Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit or OpenSCAP is used to automatically check the server configuration against the defined baseline. Deviations are recorded in a report and assigned to IT operations for remediation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports from the configuration scanner and the tickets created to fix deviations. The revision history of the hardening guide is checked to verify its currency.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secure configuration is continuously enforced by a Desired State Configuration management system. Any manual or unauthorized change that deviates from the hardening baseline is automatically detected and reverted in real time (self-healing).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like PowerShell DSC, Ansible, or Puppet are used to define and continuously enforce the desired configuration state of the server. An agent on the server monitors the state and immediately corrects deviations. All corrective actions are logged centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration definitions (e.g., Ansible Playbooks, DSC configurations). To test the self-healing capability, a configuration change is made manually in a test environment (e.g., activating an insecure service) and it is verified that this change is automatically reverted within a short time. The logs of the configuration management system are checked for corresponding entries.

controls.title: Planning of the clients and terminal client software used

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are recommendations for the terminal client software to be used and its version. The use of thin clients or fat clients is not explicitly regulated, and there are no specifications for the operating system or hardware configuration of the clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT team provides a link to download the recommended client software. There are no technical controls that prevent the use of other software or older versions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the specifications for client systems and finds that only recommendations for the software exist. A random check of client systems reveals that a heterogeneous landscape of software versions and operating systems is in use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be defined and documented which terminal client software is permitted to access the terminal server. It MUST be specified on which clients (thin/fat clients, hardware configuration, operating system) this software may be run. Furthermore, it MUST be specified what additional software is permitted on the clients and whether a client may access different terminal servers in parallel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A client standard is defined that specifies the permitted hardware models, operating system versions, and the exact version of the terminal client software. These standards are documented in a policy. Images are created for the standard clients that contain the permitted software configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the policy for client systems and verifies that all points mentioned in the requirement (software, client type, hardware, OS, additional software, parallel access) are regulated. Random checks are used to verify whether the clients in use comply with the policy. An automated check can be performed with an inventory tool that uses `Get-WmiObject Win32_Product` or `Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\\Software\\...`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with client standards is enforced by a central client management system (Unified Endpoint Management). Only authorized software can be installed, and the configuration of the terminal client software is centrally managed and specified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system such as Microsoft Intune, VMware Workspace ONE, or Matrix42 is used to control software distribution, configuration management, and patch management for all clients. The configuration of the terminal client (e.g., server addresses, security settings) is distributed via the UEM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration profiles and application policies in the client management system. Reports from the system are analyzed to determine the compliance rate of the clients.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the terminal server is made conditional on the client fully meeting the defined standards (Device Posture Check) by a technical control (e.g., Network Access Control or a function of the connection gateway). Clients that are not compliant (e.g., outdated OS, missing virus scanner, unauthorized software) are denied access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A NAC solution (e.g., Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass) or the Conditional Access Policies of a terminal gateway (e.g., Citrix Gateway, Azure AD Application Proxy) are configured to check the state of the client before the connection is established. The check includes patch level, antivirus status, disk encryption, and running processes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the device posture checks in the NAC or gateway solution. A test is performed with a non-compliant client to verify that access is blocked. The system's logs are analyzed for blocked access attempts.

controls.title: Planning of the networks used

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During planning, a rough estimate of the total required bandwidth is made based on the number of users. Detailed requirements for latency, jitter, or packet loss are not considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The network administrator is asked if the 'line is sufficient for 50 more users'. The answer is based on experience and the current overall network load, not on specific measurements for the terminal server protocol.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the network capacity planning and finds that only a rough bandwidth estimate exists. There are no documented requirements for Quality of Service parameters.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The networks MUST be planned based on the requirements of the applications. At a minimum, the expected number of concurrent sessions, the required transmission capacity, as well as the maximum acceptable packet loss, jitter, and the maximum tolerable latency MUST be considered and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on the manufacturer's specifications for the terminal server protocol and the type of applications (e.g., CAD vs. Office), specific requirements for network quality are defined (e.g., latency < 150ms, jitter < 30ms). These requirements are documented and given to the network team as a basis for planning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the document with the network requirements and verifies that all required parameters (capacity, latency, jitter, packet loss) are defined based on the number of sessions. They check if the network planning is based on these requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network infrastructure is configured with Quality of Service (QoS) to prioritize terminal server traffic and ensure compliance with the defined requirements for latency, jitter, and packet loss. Network performance is continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: QoS policies (e.g., using DSCP markings) are implemented on the switches and routers to assign a high priority to the terminal server protocol packets. A network monitoring tool (e.g., PRTG, Zabbix) is used to permanently measure latency and jitter on the relevant routes and to alert on threshold breaches.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the QoS configuration on the network components. The graphs and reports of the network monitoring tool are viewed to verify compliance with the defined service levels. An automated check can be performed with `ping -t` or specialized tools like `iperf` to measure latency and jitter.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Software-Defined Networking (SDN) or SD-WAN solution is used to dynamically control network resources. Based on the application and real-time conditions, traffic is intelligently routed over the best route and bandwidth is dynamically allocated to ensure an optimal user experience.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SD-WAN solution is implemented that offers application recognition for the terminal server protocol. The solution continuously measures the quality of multiple WAN paths (MPLS, Internet, LTE) and dynamically routes terminal server sessions over the path that best meets the defined latency and jitter requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the application routing policies and the Service Level Agreement (SLA) profiles in the SD-WAN management console. It is analyzed how the solution reacts to a simulated deterioration of a WAN path and whether the traffic is rerouted as expected.

controls.title: Secure access to the terminal server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the terminal server is restricted to the internal network. The default encryption of the terminal server protocol is enabled, but no additional security measures such as VPN encapsulation or strict mutual authentication are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The firewall allows access from the entire LAN. The encryption setting in the terminal server service is left at a default value such as 'Client Compatible'. Users authenticate with a password, but the client does not necessarily check the server's identity.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the firewall rules and the encryption settings of the terminal server service. A network sniffer (e.g., Wireshark) is used to perform random checks to see if the communication is encrypted, even if the strength of the encryption may not be optimal.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be specified which networks are permitted to access the terminal server. It MUST be specified how the communication is secured, including encryption with the terminal server protocol. If the protocol encryption is insufficient, the communication MUST be additionally secured (e.g., via VPN). When accessing from insufficiently trusted networks, both the users and the terminal server MUST authenticate themselves.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Firewall rules are configured to allow access only from defined, trusted client networks. The terminal server is configured to enforce a high level of encryption. The server is assigned a certificate from a trusted PKI so that clients can verify its identity (server authentication).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the firewall rules for access to the terminal server. The configuration of the terminal server service regarding encryption and authentication is examined. It is verified that the server uses a valid certificate and that clients are configured to check this certificate.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All access to the terminal server is routed through a dedicated and hardened gateway (e.g., RDP Gateway, Citrix ADC). This gateway enforces strong user authentication (e.g., with two-factor authentication) and client compliance checks before allowing access to the actual terminal server.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Microsoft RDP Gateway or a comparable product is installed in a DMZ. It is integrated with a RADIUS server for multi-factor authentication (MFA). Policies (Connection Authorization Policies, Resource Authorization Policies) are defined on the gateway that specify exactly which user is allowed to access which server from where.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the gateway, including the connection to the MFA solution and the defined access policies. It is tested whether access without a second factor or from an unauthorized client is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access is managed according to a Zero Trust model. Each individual access request is individually authenticated and authorized based on the user's identity, the state of the endpoint, and the context. The network connection is established dynamically only after successful verification and only for the specific session (Just-in-Time Access).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) solution is implemented. Instead of letting clients into a network, the client's ZTNA connector establishes an outgoing, encrypted tunnel to the nearest ZTNA PoP. After strong authentication and device security checks, the ZTNA service establishes a direct, secure connection to the requested application on the terminal server without granting the client broad network access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the Zero Trust access policies in the ZTNA management console. It is verified that a user can only access the applications approved for them and that no other network access is possible. The logs are analyzed for access decisions based on user, device, and context risk.

controls.title: Secure assignment of the terminal server to network segments

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server is placed in a general server network. There is no specific segmentation that takes into account its special role as a client-like system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The server is placed in the same VLAN as most other application servers. The firewall rules between the servers are often very permissive, which potentially gives the terminal server far-reaching access to backend systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network plan and the firewall configuration and determines that the terminal server is in the same segment as critical backend servers and that communication between them is barely restricted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server MUST be positioned in a dedicated network segment or in a client network segment. An existing network separation (e.g., between client and server networks) MUST NOT be circumvented via a terminal server. This must be ensured by appropriate firewall rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate VLAN (e.g., 'Terminal Server Zone') is set up for the terminal servers. Rules are created on the firewall that control the communication of this segment. In particular, access from the terminal server segment to critical server segments (e.g., database or storage networks) is restricted to the absolutely necessary ports and protocols.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network plan and the firewall configuration to ensure that the terminal server is in an appropriate segment. The firewall rules governing the outgoing traffic from the terminal server segment are analyzed to verify that no circumvention of the security zones is possible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server is placed in a dedicated DMZ-like zone. All traffic to and from this server, both from clients and to backend systems, is controlled and logged in detail by a firewall with strict 'default-deny' rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The terminal server zone is configured as a separate interface on the firewall. Every required connection (e.g., to a specific application server on port TCP/1234) must be explicitly approved by a dedicated firewall rule. All other connections are blocked and logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a detailed review of the firewall rule sets for the terminal server zone. It is checked whether an 'Any-Any-Allow' rule is missing and whether all rules were created according to the principle of least privilege. The firewall logs are analyzed for blocked connection attempts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Micro-segmentation is used to isolate each terminal server and potentially even individual applications on it from each other. Communication policies are enforced at the workload level, regardless of their network address or location, and follow a pure whitelist approach.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A micro-segmentation solution (e.g., VMware NSX, Illumio) is implemented. Policies are defined based on metadata (labels) such as 'Application: SAP', 'Environment: Production'. The policy 'SAP app servers may only communicate with SAP DB servers via port X' is enforced on the virtual network cards of the involved VMs, even if they are in the same subnet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the defined micro-segmentation policies and their application to the terminal server workloads. The visualization of allowed and blocked traffic in the management console is checked. A port scan from a terminal server is used to verify that only the explicitly allowed ports on backend systems are reachable.

controls.title: User awareness training

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users receive a short written guide on logging in and basic operation. Security-relevant aspects such as handling data or the importance of session disconnections are not covered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A one-page PDF document ('Quick Start Guide') is published on the intranet or sent to new users by email.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the user guides and notes that important security topics are missing. By interviewing users, it is verified that their knowledge is limited to basic operation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All users MUST be made aware of the secure use of terminal servers. At a minimum, the following content MUST be conveyed: basic functionality and effects of latency/bandwidth, allowed storage locations for data, exchange options (e.g., clipboard), effects of one's own resource consumption, configured roles and permissions, authentication procedures, and the importance of maximum session duration and automatic logoff procedures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A mandatory training course or reading a detailed user manual is required for all new users. The content covers all required points. Existing users are regularly informed about the most important rules, e.g., through newsletters.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the training materials or manuals and checks them for completeness regarding the required content. It is proven that all users have access to this information and that their acknowledgment (e.g., through a test or signature) is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The awareness training is conducted through an interactive Computer-Based Training (CBT), the successful completion of which is mandatory for all users and is tracked. The training is repeated annually or updated in case of significant changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An e-learning platform is used to provide the training module. The module contains short videos, texts, and a final test. The system logs which user completed the training, when, and with what result. Human resources is informed about incomplete training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the e-learning module and checks the reports from the learning platform to verify participation and success rates. The process for the annual repetition of the training is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Awareness training is part of a continuous security culture campaign. Risky user behavior in handling the terminal server (e.g., repeated attempts to copy data to local drives when this is prohibited) is technically detected and triggers an automated, context-related just-in-time awareness measure (e.g., a pop-up window with a brief explanation of the corresponding rule).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM system or an EDR agent on the terminal server is configured to detect certain risky user actions. These events trigger a targeted micro-training for the respective user via an API connection to a security awareness tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the detection rules in the SIEM/EDR and the associated automation workflows. The logs are analyzed to determine how often and for which users such just-in-time warnings were triggered. It is tested whether a simulated risky action triggers the expected reaction.

controls.title: Use of a central identity and access management for terminal servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For logging into the terminal server, local user accounts are managed on the server itself. There is no central management of identities and passwords.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators create an account for each user directly in the computer management of the terminal server. Passwords must be changed separately on each server, and the enforcement of password policies is inconsistent.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor opens the local user management (lusrmgr.msc) on the terminal server and notes the existence of local user accounts. The lack of connection to a central directory is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the use of terminal servers, a central system for identity and access management SHOULD be used. All user accounts and groups are managed centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The terminal server is added as a member server to an existing Active Directory domain. Authentication is performed exclusively via domain accounts. Permissions are assigned via domain groups that are managed centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the domain membership of the terminal server. It is checked whether login permissions and other important permissions (e.g., file system) are tied to domain groups and not to local accounts or individual domain users. The domain membership can be checked automatically with `(Get-WmiObject Win32_ComputerSystem).Domain`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated Identity and Access Management (IAM) system is used that goes beyond the functions of a pure directory service. It offers functions such as Single Sign-On (SSO) to the terminal server applications and automated workflows for requesting and approving access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The terminal server is connected to a cloud IAM solution (e.g., Azure AD) via a federation service (e.g., ADFS) or an application proxy. Users authenticate to the IAM system, which then issues a ticket or token that the user uses to log on to the terminal server without having to re-enter a password.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the IAM system and the federation service. The workflow for requesting and approving permissions is reviewed. It is tested whether the SSO process works correctly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The connection to the central IAM system enforces multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users. Access for administrative accounts is additionally controlled via a Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution, which hides passwords and records sessions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the IAM system, Conditional Access policies are configured that always require MFA for access to the terminal server. Administrators can no longer log on to the server directly, but must establish their connection via a PAM solution (e.g., CyberArk), which automatically inserts the credentials and logs the session.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the MFA policies in the IAM system. It is tested whether a login without a second factor fails. The configuration of the PAM solution is analyzed, and it is checked whether all administrative accounts are managed via this solution and direct login is blocked.

controls.title: Secure configuration of profiles

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Server-stored profiles (roaming profiles) are used so that users have the same settings on different servers. However, there are no specific security configurations or quotas for these profiles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In Active Directory, a profile path to a file share is entered for each user. The default settings for profiles are retained, which can lead to large profiles ('bloated profiles') and long logon times.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the user properties in Active Directory for the use of server-stored profiles. The configuration of the group policies for profiles is checked and it is determined that no hardening measures or quotas are defined.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users SHOULD NOT be allowed to change their specific settings (user profiles) in a way that compromises information security or restricts the use of the terminal server. An appropriate maximum size SHOULD be set for user profiles. When terminal server farms are used, user profiles SHOULD be stored centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Settings for user profiles are enforced using Group Policy Objects (GPOs). In particular, changes to security-relevant system areas (e.g., parts of the registry, Control Panel items) are blocked for normal users. Quotas are set up on the file share for profiles to limit the maximum profile size.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the group policies applied to the terminal servers and users and looks for the corresponding policies for hardening user profiles. The configuration of the quotas on the file server is checked. The GPO settings can be read out automatically with `Get-GPOReport`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A solution for user environment virtualization is used. Instead of classic roaming profiles, only the user's specific settings are dynamically loaded and saved at logon and logoff, which significantly shortens logon times and improves stability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Products such as Microsoft UE-V, Citrix Profile Management or Ivanti User Workspace Manager are implemented. It is precisely configured which application settings and registry keys are to be stored in the user's profile, while the rest of the profile is discarded on logoff.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the UEV solution. It is analyzed which application settings and paths are configured for synchronization. The logon times are measured on a random basis and compared with those of classic roaming profiles.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Container-based profile solutions are used to encapsulate the entire user profile in a VHD(X) file that is dynamically mounted at logon. This provides the best performance and compatibility. Changes to profiles that could affect security are monitored and logged in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Microsoft FSLogix Profile Container is implemented and configured. The profile containers are stored on a highly available and high-performance file share. Monitoring rules in the SIEM are created to detect suspicious changes within the mounted profile containers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the FSLogix configuration via GPOs. It is verified that the file share for the containers is highly available. The SIEM rules for monitoring profile changes are analyzed. It is checked whether the profile container is mounted correctly when a user logs on.

controls.title: Automatic termination of inactive sessions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Inactive sessions are automatically disconnected after a certain time, but not logged off. The user's applications continue to run on the server.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Only the timeout for disconnecting inactive sessions is configured via group policies. This protects against unauthorized access to an unlocked client, but allows potentially resource-intensive processes to continue running on the server and carries the risk of session hijacking.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the GPOs for session timeouts and determines that only the 'disconnect' timeout is set. A session is started, waits until it is disconnected, and then it is checked on the server (e.g., with the Task Manager) whether the user's processes are still running.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Inactive sessions SHOULD be terminated (logged off) after a predefined period. The period SHOULD be set depending on the user group. Users SHOULD be notified of the impending automatic termination. The user SHOULD be automatically logged off by the operating system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two timeouts are configured via group policies: a shorter one for disconnecting the session (e.g., 30 minutes of inactivity) and a longer one for completely logging off the disconnected session (e.g., 60 minutes after disconnection). The standard Windows notification is used to warn the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the GPO settings for session timeouts (for both 'disconnect' and 'logoff'). It is verified that the logoff actually occurs after the defined period. The relevant registry keys set by the GPOs can be read out automatically (`HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Different timeout policies are applied for different user groups based on their role and the sensitivity of the data used. Privileged users or users who access critical data have significantly shorter inactivity timeouts. The notification is customizable and gives the user sufficient time to react.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Multiple GPOs with different timeout settings are created and applied to the respective user groups via security group filtering. For example, the 'Admins' group gets a timeout of 15 minutes, while the 'Standard Users' group has a timeout of 60 minutes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the different GPOs and their links to the user groups. It is tested on a random basis for users from different groups whether the correct timeout is applied.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The timeout values are dynamic and context-dependent. The system considers factors such as the client's network location (internal vs. external), the device's security status, or the time of day to assess the risk and adjust the timeout accordingly. All logoff events are centrally logged and monitored for anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script triggered by the Task Scheduler or an advanced function of a terminal server gateway is used to monitor the sessions. Based on the session parameters (e.g., client IP address), the appropriate timeout for logging off is set dynamically. The logoff events are sent to a SIEM, which checks for unusual patterns (e.g., hundreds of logoffs in a short time).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the script or the configuration of the gateway policies for the dynamic timeouts. It is tested whether a session from a location classified as 'unsafe' receives a shorter timeout than a session from the internal network. The SIEM rules for monitoring the logoff events are checked.

controls.title: Logging on terminal servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging on the terminal server is enabled with the operating system's default settings. The logs are stored locally on the server and are not centrally collected or regularly evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Windows Event Viewer contains the default logs. These are only viewed reactively by an administrator in the event of acute problems. Proactive monitoring does not take place. The logs are overwritten after a short time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor opens the Event Viewer on the terminal server and checks the configuration of the log size and retention policies. It is determined that no central log collection is configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be decided which events are to be transmitted to a central logging infrastructure. At a minimum, the following specific events SHOULD be logged: connection of peripheral devices of the clients, actions on the server by clients that require extended rights, and configuration changes to the terminal server service.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The audit policies on the terminal server are configured via GPOs so that the required events (e.g., by activating 'Audit PNP Activity' and advanced process monitoring) are generated. An agent (e.g., Winlogbeat, NXLog) is installed on the server, which forwards these events to a central log management system (e.g., Graylog, ELK stack).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the audit policies on the terminal server. It is verified that a log forwarding agent is installed and correctly configured. The central log management system is searched for the required event types on a spot-check basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The centrally collected logs are monitored using automated rules and dashboards. For critical events (e.g., a configuration change to the terminal server service), alerts are automatically generated to inform IT operations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specific dashboards for terminal server monitoring are created in the central log management system or SIEM. Correlation rules are defined that trigger an alarm, for example, if a normal user attempts to perform an administrative action or if a non-whitelisted USB device is connected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the dashboards and alerting rules in the log management system. It is checked whether the rules cover the required events and whether there is a defined process for handling the alerts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The log data is enriched and correlated in a SIEM system with User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) functions. The system automatically detects anomalous behavior that could indicate an attack (e.g., a user logging in at unusual times, accessing atypical data, or starting suspicious processes) and can trigger automated responses.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The terminal server logs are sent to a SIEM with a UEBA module (e.g., Splunk UBA, Microsoft Sentinel). The system learns the normal behavior of each user and entity and alerts on significant deviations. Critical alerts can trigger an automated response via SOAR playbooks, e.g., immediate disconnection of the suspicious session.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the UEBA module and the learned behavioral baselines. The risk scores generated by the system for users and the triggered anomaly alerts are analyzed. It is checked whether SOAR playbooks are configured for automated response.

controls.title: Monitoring of the terminal server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server is monitored for basic availability (e.g., via a ping check). Detailed monitoring of performance parameters does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple monitoring tool checks every five minutes if the server responds to a ping. If not, an email is sent to the administrator. CPU, RAM, or network utilization are not recorded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the monitoring tool and finds that only the server's reachability is monitored, but no performance parameters.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server SHOULD be monitored centrally. For this purpose, at least the utilization of server resources, the utilization of network interfaces, and the available bandwidth and latency at the connected clients SHOULD be monitored. For monitoring, thresholds (baselining) SHOULD be determined in advance and reviewed regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central monitoring system (e.g., Nagios, Zabbix, PRTG) is used to continuously record the defined parameters (CPU, RAM, network I/O, latency). In an initial baselining phase, the normal operating values are determined. Based on this, thresholds are defined for warnings (e.g., CPU utilization > 80%) and critical alerts (e.g., CPU > 95%).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the monitoring checks in the monitoring system. It is checked whether all required parameters are monitored and whether meaningful thresholds based on baselining are defined. The alerting configuration is also checked. The current values can be read out automatically with `Get-Counter` or `vmstat`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The monitoring also records specific metrics of the terminal server service, such as the number of active and disconnected sessions, the latency per session, and the CPU load caused by individual processes. The alerts are automatically recorded in a ticketing system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specific performance counters for Remote Desktop Services are integrated into the monitoring system. The alerts are forwarded to the central IT service management tool (e.g., Jira, ServiceNow) via an API interface to ensure traceable processing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the terminal server-specific metrics are recorded in the monitoring system. The integration with the ticketing system is verified by triggering a test alert and checking whether a corresponding ticket is created.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An Application Performance Monitoring (APM) tool is used, which provides an end-to-end view of the user experience. It measures not only server performance but also the actual response times in the application as perceived by the user. The system uses machine learning to proactively detect anomalous performance values and emerging problems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An APM solution like Dynatrace or AppDynamics is implemented. It monitors the entire service chain from the user action on the client, through the terminal server, to the backend databases. Using AI algorithms, dynamic baselines are created for thousands of metrics and deviations are automatically reported as problems with root cause analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the service flow maps and the user experience dashboards in the APM tool. The automatically detected problems and their root cause analyses are reviewed. The system's ability for predictive warning of capacity bottlenecks is analyzed.

controls.title: Hardening of the terminal server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some obviously unneeded applications and services are manually uninstalled or deactivated. There is no systematic review or restriction of access to peripheral devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator removes some default apps like 'Games' or 'Mail' after installing the operating system. Peripheral devices like USB sticks or printers work without restrictions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the list of installed programs and running services and finds that many unneeded components are still present. It is tested whether access to local client drives or USB sticks is possible without restrictions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unneeded applications on the terminal server SHOULD be removed or their execution prevented. Access from a session to peripheral devices SHOULD be restricted to the required devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the server build process, a script is run that removes all Windows features and applications not required for terminal server operation. Group Policies are used to control the redirection of peripheral devices. For example, the redirection of drives and USB ports is disabled, while the redirection of printers and the clipboard remains permitted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the hardening script and the GPO settings for device redirection. It is checked on the server which applications and services are active. In a test session, it is verified that access to the blocked peripheral devices is actually blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An application whitelisting solution is operated in audit mode to identify the applications that are actually used. Access to peripheral devices is controlled granularly, so that, for example, only specific, approved USB devices (based on their serial number) can be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker is configured to log the execution of all programs. This creates a baseline for later enforcement. A third-party device control software is used to enable fine-grained control of the USB port.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the application whitelisting solution and the collected logs. The policies of the device control software are analyzed. It is tested whether an unapproved USB stick is blocked while an approved one works.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Application whitelisting is operated in enforcement mode. Only explicitly approved and signed applications can be executed. Any attempt to run other software is blocked and an alert is raised. The state of hardening is continuously monitored, and deviations are automatically corrected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The AppLocker or WDAC policies are active in 'Enforce' mode. The list of allowed applications is strictly managed and is part of the change management process. A Desired State Configuration Management (as in A4) ensures that the hardening settings (e.g., deactivated services) are permanently maintained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the application whitelisting policies are in enforcement mode. An attempt is made to run an unauthorized portable application, and it is checked whether this is blocked. The logs of the DSC system are analyzed for compliance checks and corrections.

controls.title: Optimization of compression

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The compression settings of the terminal server protocol are left at their default values. No application-specific optimization takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The same manufacturer-predefined compression algorithms and quality settings are used for both graphics-intensive and text-based applications. This can lead to poor image quality in graphics applications or unnecessarily high bandwidth consumption in office applications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the policies for configuring the remote protocol (e.g., RDP settings in GPOs) and finds that no specific settings for compression or image quality have been made.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The degree of compression SHOULD be optimized according to the respective application's requirements for graphical quality. The requirements for accuracy of graphical elements, color fidelity, and the required frame rate SHOULD be taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The compression settings are adjusted via policies. For user groups that mainly work with office applications, a stronger, lossy compression for images and a lower frame rate are chosen. For user groups working with CAD or image editing software, lossless compression or very high quality and a higher frame rate are configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the policies (e.g., GPOs) that control the protocol settings and verifies that different settings are defined for different use cases or user groups. The documentation of the application requirements, on which the settings were based, is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The optimization considers not only the application but also the available bandwidth and latency of the client. Policies are created that automatically apply stronger compression for connections over slow networks to maintain usability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Modern terminal server protocols often offer the ability to adjust quality settings based on the detected network connection. These functions are specifically configured. For example, a high quality is selected for connections from the LAN and a setting optimized for low bandwidth is chosen for connections over WAN or VPN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the network-dependent protocol settings. A connection is established over a simulated slow network (e.g., with a WAN emulator) and it is checked whether the compression is adjusted as expected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server system dynamically selects the optimal codec in real-time for different areas of the screen. Text is transmitted and compressed with a text codec, videos with a video codec (e.g., H.264/AVC), and static images with an image codec. This ensures the best possible quality with minimal bandwidth consumption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The latest versions of protocols such as RDP (with RemoteFX/AVC444) or Citrix HDX are used and configured to use 'Adaptive Display' or 'Optimize for the entire screen' mode. This enables dynamic codec selection per screen content.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the protocol version and configuration used support dynamic codec selection and that it is enabled. The manufacturer's special analysis tools are used to monitor session performance and check which codecs are actually used for different content (e.g., playing a video in the session).

controls.title: Encryption of the transmission

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All communication between the client and the terminal server SHOULD be appropriately encrypted. Secure protocols according to BSI TR-02102 SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The terminal server is configured to accept only connections with a high encryption level (e.g., 128-bit TLS). Outdated or insecure protocols and cipher suites are disabled. The configuration is based on the current recommendations of BSI TR-02102 'Cryptographic Mechanisms: Recommendations and Key Lengths'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the terminal server's configuration (e.g., via GPOs or local policies) regarding the enforced encryption level and the activated protocols (e.g., TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3) and cipher suites. An automated test can be performed with tools like `testssl.sh` or Qualys SSL Labs against the connection gateway to verify the configuration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The encryption configuration is automated and regularly checked for compliance with the requirements of BSI TR-02102. Deviations are reported. For server authentication, only certificates from a trusted, internal PKI are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration scanner (as in A4) is equipped with a profile that maps the specifications of TR-02102 and performs weekly scans. The terminal servers receive their certificates automatically via an auto-enrollment function from an internal Microsoft CA.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports from the configuration scanner. The configuration of the internal PKI and auto-enrollment is checked. It is verified that the certificates used on the servers comply with the internal policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The private keys of the terminal servers used for encryption are protected in a Hardware Security Module (HSM). Compliance with encryption policies is monitored in real-time, and attempts to establish an insecure connection are immediately blocked and treated as a security incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The terminal servers are configured to use a network-based or local HSM Key Storage Provider for all TLS operations. An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) in the network analyzes the TLS handshake of connection attempts and blocks those that use outdated protocols or weak cipher suites.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the Key Storage Provider on the terminal server and the integration of the HSM. The signatures and rules of the IPS for detecting weak cryptography are checked. A test is performed with a client intentionally configured to use a weak protocol (e.g., SSLv3) to see if the connection is blocked.

controls.title: Use of Thin Clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Physical thin clients SHOULD be used. ONLY thin clients that the company that produces the terminal client software has designated as compatible SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For workstations with high protection requirements, a standard thin client model is defined that is on the terminal server manufacturer's compatibility list (e.g., Citrix Ready, VMware Ready). These devices are centrally procured and configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of client models used and compares it with the manufacturer's official compatibility list. It is checked on a random basis whether the standardized thin clients are actually used at the corresponding workstations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All thin clients are managed via a central management console. Firmware updates, configuration changes, and security settings are centrally distributed and enforced. The operating system of the thin clients is read-only.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The management software provided by the thin client manufacturer (e.g., HP Device Manager, IGEL Universal Management Suite) is implemented. The devices are configured to retrieve their configuration from the management server at startup. The operating system's 'Write Filter' is activated to prevent changes to the local system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration profiles and policies in the thin client management console. It is checked whether all devices are managed and have current firmware versions installed. A test device is used to attempt a permanent change to the system to verify the function of the write filter.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of the thin client operating system is checked at startup by a secure boot process with a root of trust anchored in the hardware memory (TPM). Any unauthorized modification of the firmware or operating system results in the device not starting or not being able to connect to the terminal server.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Thin clients with Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and support for Secure Boot are used. The Secure Boot chain is configured so that only manufacturer-signed firmware and operating system images can be loaded. The connection gateway or a NAC solution performs a remote attestation check to validate the client's integrity before establishing a connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the BIOS/UEFI settings of the thin clients for the activation of Secure Boot and TPM. The configuration of the remote attestation policies is checked in the gateway or the NAC solution. It is analyzed whether a device with manipulated firmware (in a test environment) is prevented from establishing a connection.

controls.title: Advanced monitoring of the terminal server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server is continuously monitored for the occurrence of the security-relevant events described in SYS.1.9.A13. The server is regularly scanned for vulnerabilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logs defined in A13 are sent to a central log management system. Simple alerts are configured there, e.g., for the connection of a peripheral device. An authenticated vulnerability scan is performed against the terminal server once a month.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the alerting rules in the log management system. The reports of the last vulnerability scans are requested and checked for critical, open vulnerabilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server is integrated into a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. The monitored events are analyzed in the SIEM for anomalies and simple attack patterns. Vulnerability scans are performed weekly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Correlation rules are created in the SIEM that link security-relevant events from the terminal server with other data sources (e.g., firewall logs). For example, an alert is triggered if a user account attempts to log in from many different IP addresses within a short period of time. The results of the weekly scans are tracked in a vulnerability management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the correlation rules and dashboards in the SIEM that are relevant to the terminal server. The process for remediating the vulnerabilities found in the weekly scans is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIEM automatically analyzes the monitored events for complex anomalies and attack patterns, ideally using Machine Learning (UEBA). The results of the regular vulnerability scans are automatically enriched with threat intelligence and prioritized. An Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) agent is active on the server.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SIEM uses a UEBA module to detect deviations from normal user behavior (e.g., execution of rare commands, access to unusual resources). An EDR agent (e.g., Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) monitors the system for suspicious process activities and tactics not detected by scanners and can automatically terminate suspicious processes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and alerts of the UEBA and EDR system. It is analyzed how the system reacts to simulated attacks (e.g., execution of a Mimikatz-like tool). It is checked whether a process for handling high-priority alerts has been established.

controls.title: Different terminal servers for different groups of users or business processes

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Terminal server users SHOULD be grouped based on similar permissions and required applications. A terminal server SHOULD NOT be made available to multiple groups of users. If this is not possible, dedicated terminal servers SHOULD be used per business process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separate terminal server farms (silos) are set up for different user groups or security zones. For example, there is one farm for internal administration, one for the development department, and another for external partners. The separation is achieved through separate server VMs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the terminal server environment and verifies that separate servers or farms exist for the defined groups. It is checked which user groups are allowed to access which farm.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The separation between the different terminal server farms is enforced at the network level. Firewall rules prevent any direct communication between the servers of the different silos. Each silo is located in its own dedicated network segment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each terminal server farm is placed in its own VLAN. Rules are configured on the central firewall that block any traffic between these VLANs (deny inter-VLAN routing), unless there is an explicitly approved and documented exception.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network topology and the firewall rules between the terminal server segments. A port scanner is used to try to reach a server in Silo B from a server in Silo A to check the effectiveness of the separation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For user groups with particularly high protection needs or conflicting security requirements (e.g., administrators of security systems vs. external developers), physically separate terminal server environments with their own infrastructure (e.g., dedicated domain controllers, dedicated gateways) are operated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the administration of Tier-0 systems, a dedicated 'Privileged Access Workstation (PAW)' environment is set up. This is completely isolated from the standard IT infrastructure and has no connection to the internet. External developers access a separate, hardened environment in a DMZ that has no connection whatsoever to internal production systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture documentation of the various separate environments. The physical or logical separation of the network and administration infrastructure is verified. It is checked whether there are routing paths or common components that could undermine the separation.

controls.title: Use of highly available IT systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server SHOULD be operated in a highly available manner. For this purpose, the terminal server and its network connection SHOULD be designed to be redundant. The terminal servers used SHOULD be operated in a cluster. Spare devices SHOULD be kept available for the accessing clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At least two terminal servers are combined in a farm and operated via a load balancer or a connection broker. Each server is connected to two different switches with two network cards (NIC teaming). Some pre-configured spare clients are kept in storage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the connection broker and the server farm. The network configuration of the servers is checked for redundancy. The inventory of spare clients is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All central components of the terminal server infrastructure, including the connection brokers, license servers, and gateways, are designed to be redundant and have an automatic failover function. The servers in the farm are distributed across different physical host systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The connection brokers are operated in high-availability mode, which uses an SQL database to synchronize the state. The gateway appliances are configured as an HA pair. Anti-affinity rules are created in the virtualization environment to ensure that the VMs of the terminal server farm do not run on the same physical host.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the HA configuration of the brokers, gateways, and the virtualization platform. A failover test is performed by shutting down an active component (e.g., a server or gateway) and checking whether the sessions are switched to the redundant component without interruption.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The terminal server infrastructure is distributed across two geographically separate data centers (Geo-Cluster). In the event of a total failure of one site, operations can be fully taken over by the second site. The failover process is automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Active/Active or Active/Passive architecture is implemented across two data centers. A Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB) system directs user requests to the available data center. User profile data and other central configurations are replicated between the sites.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the cross-site architecture and the configuration of the GSLB and data replication. The disaster recovery manuals and the logs of the last disaster recovery tests are checked. It is verified that a failover between the sites complies with the defined RTO and RPO targets.

controls.title: Preventing the transfer of application data between client and terminal server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The transfer of application data between the client and the terminal server SHOULD be disabled. The transfer of the clipboard SHOULD also be disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The 'Client Drive Redirection' and 'Clipboard Redirection' functions are disabled for all sessions via group policies or connection gateway policies. This prevents users from moving files between their local device and the terminal server session via copy-paste or mapped drives.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the relevant policies (GPOs, etc.) and verifies that the redirection of drives and the clipboard is disabled. In a test session, an attempt is made to copy a file from the local desktop to the session to verify the effectiveness of the measure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policies are applied granularly. The clipboard redirection can be configured to allow only text, but not files or images. Any attempts to use blocked transfer functions are centrally logged and evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The terminal server protocol policies are refined so that the clipboard only works in one direction (e.g., from server to client) or only for certain data formats (e.g., CF_TEXT). The corresponding audit settings are activated to log failed redirection attempts in the event log and forward them to a SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the granular configuration of the clipboard policies. It is tested whether text can be copied while copying a file is blocked. The logs in the SIEM are analyzed for corresponding audit events.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solution is integrated that monitors the content of data flow across all permitted channels (e.g., permitted clipboard, printing). Attempts to transfer sensitive information (e.g., credit card numbers, patient data) are detected and blocked. In addition, visible watermarks are displayed in the sessions to discourage and attribute screenshots.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A host-based DLP solution is installed on the terminal server or a network-based DLP solution inspects the gateway's data traffic. DLP policies are defined that search for sensitive data patterns using regular expressions and keywords. The watermark function of the terminal server protocol is activated and configured to display the username, IP address, and timestamp.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the DLP policies and watermarks. It is tested whether the attempt to copy or print a file with fictitious sensitive data is blocked by the DLP solution. A screenshot of a session is taken and checked to see if the watermark is visible and correct.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
A terminal server is a server on which client applications (applications for short) are executed directly and which only forwards their graphical user interface (GUI) to the clients. Terminal server software is used for this purpose. The terminal server is then the underlying IT system on which this software is executed. The inputs on the client, e.g., via keyboard and mouse, are transmitted to the terminal server software, which then passes these inputs to the terminal server. In the application provided on the terminal server, the actions that may be triggered by the inputs are then executed, and the terminal server determines the new (possibly changed) user interface. This user interface is then transmitted from the terminal server software to the client.
In a terminal server-based environment, clients typically connect to the terminal server software on the terminal server using corresponding terminal client software. This communication uses terminal server protocols, over which the inputs and outputs are transmitted. Examples include the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), Independent Computing Architecture (ICA), PC-over-IP (PCoIP), or Virtual Network Computing (VNC).
The type of applications provided in this way is generally not restricted and can include, for example, productive applications such as web browsers, office applications, or financial software, as well as administration tools such as SSH clients or management tools.
In a typical deployment scenario, a terminal server centrally provides applications to multiple clients that should not or cannot be run locally on these clients for organizational or technical reasons. An example of this is administration tools that should not be run directly on the administrators' clients. Another example is software with special technical requirements for the underlying hardware of the clients, such as specific graphics cards that are not present on all clients.
In a terminal server-based environment, the clients can be so-called fat clients or thin clients. Fat clients are equipped with a full-fledged client operating system. Thin clients, on the other hand, can only be used to connect to and operate the terminal server.
On a terminal server, multiple people can work simultaneously on the same operating system and use the same or several different applications in parallel.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is to protect information that is stored, processed, and transmitted when using terminal servers. To this end, special requirements are placed on the involved applications, IT systems, and networks.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The SYS.1.9 Terminal Server module is to be applied to the terminal server itself as well as to the accessing fat clients and thin clients with terminal client software. For both servers and clients, both the software and hardware components must be considered.
To create an IT-Grundschutz model for a specific information domain, the entirety of all modules must generally be considered. As a rule, several modules are applicable to the topic or target object.
This module covers the following content:
• A terminal server within the meaning of this module is any IT system on which applications are made available centrally in the manner described above. The connection must be initiated directly from the client.
• The SYS.1.9 Terminal Server module is to be applied if only user inputs are transmitted to the terminal server by a terminal client software.
• This module contains specific requirements for the networks used to secure communication between clients and the terminal server.
The following content is also important and is dealt with elsewhere:
• For the terminal server and the clients, the modules SYS.1.1 General Server and SYS.2.1 General Client, as well as any specific modules for the server or client operating systems, must be applied.
• The module APP.6 General Application, as well as any other relevant modules from the APP Applications layer, must be applied to the terminal server software.
• For the applications provided via the terminal server, the module APP.6 General Application, as well as any corresponding specific modules from the APP Applications layer, must also be applied.
• The NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design module must be applied to secure the networks used for communication between clients and the terminal server.
This module does not cover the following content:
