• Remote maintenance tools are not terminal servers within the meaning of this module. To secure these tools, the OPS.1.2.5 Remote Maintenance module must be implemented.
• If an IT system to be administered is accessed via terminal server protocols, this does not constitute use of the terminal server within the meaning of this module.
• This module does not address the case where clients directly access other clients via terminal server protocols or collaboration tools.
• If the terminal server service is provided via additional security components such as Application Delivery Controllers (ADC, see Chapter 4 Further Information), these additional components must be considered separately.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Loss of quality in application delivery
parts.prose:
An application provided by the terminal server is used in real time. Since the user interface is prepared on the terminal server and transmitted to the clients, work can only be done smoothly if the terminal server's response to an input arrives at the clients without noticeable delay and is clearly recognizable. If the clients receive the terminal server's responses with a time delay, usability may be so limited that it is equivalent to a service failure. Both a consistently high delay and frequently occurring, unpredictable peaks can cause this effect.
A delay that is too high can be caused by excessive latency of the transmission paths or network components. If communication is secured via additional security components such as VPN gateways, which may be inadequately dimensioned, the delay can be further increased. This can lead to the application being usable only to a limited extent.
If the terminal server is heavily loaded, it can only respond with a delay. For example, if the CPU or main memory is insufficiently dimensioned, the terminal server can quickly become overloaded and ultimately respond only with a delay. The same applies if the terminal server is used by too many people simultaneously.
If the screen content is not clearly recognizable, it is no longer possible to work efficiently with the terminal server. For example, text or the mouse pointer may be difficult to recognize due to compression artifacts if there is not enough line capacity available.
All of this can result in users being unable to use the terminal server at all or only to a very limited extent.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Failure of application delivery
parts.prose:
In a terminal server-based environment, applications are executed centrally and their output is transmitted to the corresponding clients. If the terminal server is unavailable, no more inputs can be processed and the applications provided by the terminal server immediately fail to provide their service. If the clients receive their entire user interface from the terminal server, the IT system completely fails from the users' perspective.
If the client fails, the applications provided by the terminal server cannot be accessed via it, even if they are available there. The same applies if the connection between the client and the terminal server is disrupted.
Failures of the network or the terminal server generally affect not just individual clients. In many cases, numerous or even all clients of an institution depend on the terminal server. If the terminal server fails, a large number of clients are affected simultaneously in this case.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Insufficient network separation for terminal servers
parts.prose:
Terminal servers usually provide applications that act as clients. This makes a terminal server more similar to a client than a server in terms of trustworthiness.
If this is not adequately considered in the network separation, it may be possible to gain unauthorized access to other server applications via the terminal server, for example, through a web browser. This can allow the terminal server to be misused as a starting point for attacks on other IT systems and applications.
A high degree of interaction with the terminal server is to be expected due to the inputs on the client. This makes it easier to exploit potential vulnerabilities. This is particularly relevant when a terminal server provides applications for user groups that are assigned to different network segments. In this case, it could be possible to gain unauthorized access to other applications in these network segments from the terminal server.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Insufficient protection of sessions on the terminal server
parts.prose:
Terminal servers can provide different clients with dedicated application instances running on the same operating system. The applications share common resources such as shared libraries, the kernel, and the required resources of the terminal server (e.g., CPU or RAM).
Due to misconfigurations or software vulnerabilities, individual application instances may be able to communicate with each other, even if this was not originally intended. For example, if sessions on terminal servers are run with overly broad permissions, it may be possible to access any part of the file system from within an application. This can be exploited, for example, through program dialogs for saving or opening files, which can be used to write to or read from unintended areas of the hard disk.
Another example is so-called RDP Session Hijacking, which is based on the sessions of the terminal server itself. If users remain logged in after their sessions on the terminal server have ended, this can lead to problems. If attackers are equipped with appropriate rights, which they may have previously obtained through insufficient rights management or by exploiting software vulnerabilities, they may be able to take over an existing session from another session. In this case, attackers can continue the session in the context of the user(s).
If the operating system is shared by multiple applications or application instances, sessions of other users may be influenced via CPU or RAM. This requires corresponding security vulnerabilities in the respective applications through which the necessary malware can be executed. For example, special malware can then read passwords from RAM. Even without software vulnerabilities, attackers can read any sensitive data from other sessions through hardware vulnerabilities (e.g., Meltdown).

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Insufficient security of the terminal server protocol
parts.prose:
Many terminal server protocols offer the option of authenticated and encrypted communication. However, this option is not always sufficient to secure the communication. If the terminal server protocol uses outdated and vulnerable mechanisms or if important security functions are disabled due to misconfigurations, the communication between clients and the terminal server can be eavesdropped on. Information that is transferred between the terminal server and the clients and that can potentially be intercepted or modified includes, in particular:
• Authentication information and user input sent from the clients to the terminal servers,
• Screen information displayed on the clients,
• Clipboard data,
• File transfers between the client's local drives and the server, and
• Information from redirected client devices (e.g., audio devices, serial or parallel ports, USB devices, and printers).
However, even if the protocol mechanisms provide fundamentally strong security for the communication, the implementation of the protocol within a terminal server or terminal client software may contain vulnerabilities. This can lead to the terminal server becoming directly vulnerable without the need for communication to be spied on.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Unauthorized use of shared accounts
parts.prose:
If multiple people want to use an application on a terminal server at different times, shared accounts are often set up. However, this may contradict internal regulations or the license terms of the software provided via the terminal server.
Using shared accounts also prevents actions performed on the terminal server from being attributed to specific individuals. This makes it impossible to trace who did what. This can pose a significant legal risk, especially if there are legal requirements for traceability, e.g., if personal data is processed on the terminal server.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Inappropriate restriction of user access rights
parts.prose:
A terminal server can simultaneously function as both a server and, in relation to the applications running on it, as a client. This can lead to errors in the assignment of access rights.
Secure configurations of IT systems and applications usually provide for the most restrictive assignment of rights possible. This also applies in particular to terminal servers. However, if the permissions for using a terminal server are restricted too much, users can only use the provided applications with severe limitations. This can result from either an overly strict policy or a misconfiguration.
If work is made too difficult by such restrictions, for example by completely prohibiting write access to local drives, this can have undesirable consequences. For instance, users might resort to unintended workarounds and process data in inappropriate places, e.g., via data exchange platforms after an export.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Unsuitable applications for use on terminal servers
parts.prose:
Not all applications can be deployed on any terminal server. For example, if necessary functions of the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) are not supported in the emulated graphics unit, 3D applications cannot be used or can only be used with limitations via a terminal server. The same applies if input from application-specific or industry-specific peripheral devices is not supported by the terminal server, the terminal client software, or the terminal server protocol.
If individual application functions or the connection of peripheral devices are not tested or are tested inadequately before procurement, these limitations may only be discovered during live operation. This can severely restrict the availability of the application, and the terminal server may not be usable as intended. It may even need to be replaced completely.

controls.title: Secure authentication of users

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication via password is only required for individual users or systems. There are no company-wide requirements to activate the screen lock.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is often the case in environments where security settings are left to individual users. The configuration is done ad-hoc and is not documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Random check of several clients. It is found that many systems do not have a password requirement and the screen lock is not configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All users must authenticate to the client with a password. Users are instructed to manually lock the screen when they are away. An automatic lock is not configured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The password requirement is implemented via basic operating system functions or group policies. The instruction for manual locking is given via email or notice.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the system configuration on all clients to verify the password requirement. Interviewing employees to see if they are aware of the instruction for manual screen locking.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To use the client, users MUST authenticate themselves to the IT system. Users MUST use a screen lock if they operate the client unattended. The screen lock MAY ONLY be deactivated by a successful authentication. This process is defined for all clients and is implemented in a repeatable manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration is done centrally via management tools such as GPOs or MDM. The settings enforce authentication and ensure that the screen lock can only be unlocked after re-authentication. Users are informed about the need for the screen lock.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the central configuration policies (e.g., GPO settings) for correct settings for authentication and screen lock. Observation of user behavior when leaving the workplace.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, the screen lock SHOULD be activated automatically if no action is taken by the user for a specified, short period of time (e.g., 5-15 minutes). Users SHOULD also be required to actively log off from the IT system after completing their tasks. Compliance with these requirements is monitored technically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The automatic screen lock is configured via a central policy (GPO/MDM) with a fixed timeout and cannot be changed by the users. The obligation to log off is stipulated in the security policy and users are regularly reminded of it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the central policies for the configuration of the automatic screen lock with an appropriate timeout. Evaluation of system logs to determine whether clients remain logged in overnight.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication on the client is consistently carried out using multi-factor authentication (MFA). The automatic screen lock is supplemented by dynamic mechanisms such as presence detection (e.g., Bluetooth pairing with a smartphone) to lock the client immediately upon absence.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: MFA solutions such as smart cards, FIDO2 tokens, or authenticator apps are used. Tools such as `Dynamic Lock` under Windows are used for the dynamic lock. These configurations are centrally specified and actively monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verification of the MFA implementation for all user accounts. Testing the dynamic lock function by simulating the removal of the paired device. Checking the configuration and monitoring logs of the central management system.

controls.title: Activating autoupdate mechanisms

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation of updates is the responsibility of individual users. There are no central specifications or mechanisms, and the autoupdate function is disabled on many systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This situation often arises in unregulated environments where users have local administrator rights and can change system configurations at will.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking patch levels on randomly selected clients. A widely diverging and outdated patch level is found on most systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The operating system's own autoupdate mechanisms are activated on all clients with their default settings. There is no central monitoring or control.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Activation typically occurs during the initial system installation. The interval for a new update search is often set to the manufacturer's specification (e.g., weekly).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configuration of the autoupdate services on the clients. It is verified that the service is active on all systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automatic update mechanisms (autoupdate) MUST be enabled, unless other mechanisms such as regular manual maintenance or a central software distribution system are used for updates. This process is defined and implemented consistently for all clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The activation and configuration of autoupdates are centrally controlled via policies (GPO/MDM) to ensure they are active on all clients and cannot be disabled by users. Alternatively, a central patch management system (e.g., WSUS) is used as a defined mechanism.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the central policies for the autoupdate configuration. If a central system is used, its configuration and client assignments are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If a time interval can be specified for autoupdate mechanisms, it SHOULD automatically check for and install updates at least daily. The success of the update installation is centrally monitored and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The check interval is set to 24 hours or less in the central policies. The reporting functions of the central patch management system are used to identify and track failed installations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the update interval configuration in the central administration. Insight into the monitoring logs to assess the success rate of update installations and how errors are handled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central software distribution system is the exclusive source for all updates. Updates are tested for compatibility and stability in a reference environment before rollout. The rollout is done in staggered rings to minimize risk. Critical security updates are distributed on an accelerated basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An advanced management system such as SCCM/MECM, Ivanti, or a cloud-based equivalent (e.g., Intune) is used. Test and pilot groups are defined. Clear SLAs exist for the distribution of patches according to their criticality.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the patch management process documentation, including test protocols and rollout plans. Verification of the rollout ring configuration in the management system. Analysis of the time span between release and installation of critical patches.

controls.title: Use of protection programs against malicious software

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An antivirus program is installed on some, but not all, clients. The configuration and updating is the responsibility of the respective user.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is often the case in environments with heterogeneous client hardware and without central IT management. Free antivirus solutions are often used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Random check of clients. It is found that on many systems no protection program is active or the virus signatures are severely outdated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standardized antivirus program with basic configuration is installed on all clients. It performs regular scans and updates its signatures automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installation of the protection program is part of the standard setup process for new clients. The configuration is usually the manufacturer's default configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check on all clients whether the standardized protection program is installed, active, and has current signatures. A shell command to check the status of the AV service can be executed via script: `sc query windefend` on Windows or `systemctl status clamav-freshclam` for ClamAV on Linux.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Malware protection programs MUST be configured so that users cannot make security-relevant changes to the settings or disable the protection programs. The protection program MUST scan for malware when files are exchanged or transferred (on-access scan). The entire data stock of a client MUST be regularly scanned for malware (on-demand scan).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central management console for the antivirus solution is used to roll out a uniform, tamper-proof configuration to all clients. This configuration enforces real-time protection and schedules weekly full system scans.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check of the policies in the central management console of the protection program. It is verified that the configuration is locked. An attempt is made to disable the protection program on a client, which must fail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to signature-based protection, behavior-based protection mechanisms (HIPS) and ransomware protection are activated. If a client is reported as infected, a forensic investigation MUST be conducted in offline mode. The status of all clients is centrally monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Advanced protection modules such as 'Host Intrusion Prevention System' and 'Ransomware Protection' are activated in the central configuration. A documented incident response process exists for the event of an infection, which includes disconnecting from the network and conducting an investigation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the activated protection modules in the central policy. Insight into the incident response plans. Check of the management console's dashboard for current client statuses and unhandled warning messages.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solution is used. It integrates antivirus, HIPS, application whitelisting, and forensic analysis functions. All events and alerts are forwarded to a central Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system and are correlated and analyzed there by a Security Operations Center (SOC).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A modern EDR platform (e.g., from CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) is rolled out on all clients. The integration with the SIEM is done via defined data connectors. The SOC team uses the EDR data for proactive threat hunting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the EDR agent installation and connectivity on the endpoints. Verification of the data flow from the EDR to the SIEM. Analysis of sample alarms in the SIEM to understand the analysis and response process of the SOC team.

controls.title: Securing the boot process

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A BIOS/UEFI password is set on a few devices classified as particularly critical (e.g., laptops of executives).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The setup is done manually and on request. There is no standardized process or overall policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Random check of devices by restarting and attempting to enter the BIOS/UEFI setup. It is found that most devices are unprotected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A BIOS/UEFI password is set on all clients to prevent unauthorized changes to the hardware configuration. The boot order is set to primarily boot from the internal hard drive.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Setting the password and configuring the boot order are part of the standard manual setup process for each new client.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Physical inspection of a representative sample of clients to verify the presence of the BIOS/UEFI password and the correct boot order.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The boot process MUST be secured against manipulation. It MUST be specified from which media booting is allowed. It MUST be ensured that only administrators can boot the clients from a drive other than the preset ones or from external storage media. The configuration settings of the boot process MAY ONLY be changed by administrators. All unnecessary functions in the firmware (e.g., Wake-on-LAN, if not used) MUST be disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: These settings are centrally managed and rolled out to all devices via a manufacturer tool (e.g., Dell Command | Configure, HP BIOS Configuration Utility). Booting from external media (USB, PXE) is disabled by default for normal users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check of the central configuration files for the BIOS/UEFI management tool. Verification on a client that booting from a USB stick is prevented for a normal user. An automated test could read the configuration via script, e.g., `Get-WmiObject -Namespace root/hp/instrumentedbios -Class HP_BIOSSetting`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be decided whether and how the boot process should be cryptographically protected. UEFI Secure Boot is activated to ensure that only signed bootloaders and operating system kernels are loaded. The manufacturer's default keys are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: UEFI Secure Boot is activated as part of the central BIOS/UEFI configuration for all compatible devices. This protects against bootkit malware.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the Secure Boot setting in the central configuration policies. On a client, the status can be checked, e.g., on Windows with the PowerShell cmdlet `Confirm-SecureBootUEFI` or on Linux with `mokutil --sb-state`. This can be automated on all devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: UEFI Secure Boot is operated with company-owned, self-managed keys (Custom Keys). Additionally, the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is used for a 'Measured Boot'. The integrity of the boot chain is measured at every start and can be verified by a remote attestation instance before the client receives full network access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is set up to manage the own Secure Boot keys. A Remote Attestation Service, e.g., as part of Microsoft Device Health Attestation, is implemented. Network Access Controls (NAC) are integrated with the Attestation Service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the PKI documentation for the Secure Boot keys. Inspection of the Remote Attestation Service configuration. Testing a non-compliant client to verify that it is denied network access. Check of the TPM and attestation logs.

controls.title: Use of cloud and online functions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users can use all cloud and online functions of the operating system without restrictions. There are no organizational policies or technical controls.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This state is typical when operating systems are installed with default settings and no further hardening takes place. Examples are the default integration of OneDrive, Cortana, or the synchronization of settings with an online account.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Random check of clients. It is found that various online functions are active and data is being exchanged with external servers without central approval.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic policy that prohibits the use of certain, particularly critical online functions. The implementation is left to the users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An instruction via email or on the intranet asks employees to disable, for example, the synchronization of browser data or the use of non-business cloud storage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Employees are surveyed on whether they know and have implemented the policy. A technical review of compliance does not take place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ONLY strictly necessary cloud and online functions of the operating system MAY be used. The corresponding settings of the operating system MUST be checked for compliance with the organizational data protection and security requirements and be configured restrictively or the functions deactivated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the client hardening process, a defined list of unneeded online functions and telemetry services is deactivated via central policies (GPO/MDM). The decision as to which functions are necessary is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the central configuration policies for the deactivation of unwanted functions. Comparison of the configured settings with the list of functions defined as necessary. An automated test can read the relevant registry keys or configuration files on the clients.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The necessary cloud and online functions SHOULD be documented. The configuration is implemented as restrictively as possible ('default-deny' approach), so that only explicitly permitted functions are active. Compliance with the configuration is checked regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An allowlist of permitted functions is created and implemented in the central configuration. All other functions are blocked. The configuration of the clients is regularly (e.g., monthly) checked for deviations using configuration management tools.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the documentation of the permitted functions (allowlist). Analysis of the reports from the configuration management tool to determine the compliance rate and to trace deviations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All client network traffic to external cloud and online services is routed through a central, logging web proxy or a Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) solution. Unknown or unauthorized connections are blocked and reported as a security incident. The client configuration is continuously monitored, and deviations are automatically corrected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CASB solution is implemented to control the use of cloud applications in detail. The client configuration is managed via an MDM system in Desired State Configuration (DSC) mode, which performs corrections independently.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the proxy/CASB logs for blocked connection attempts. Review of the DSC mechanism's configuration. Tentative change of a locked setting on a client to observe the automatic correction.

controls.title: Defining a security policy for clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the institution's general security policy, the requirements for general clients SHOULD be specified in a specific policy. The policy SHOULD be known to all users and all persons involved in the procurement and operation of the clients and should form the basis of their work. The results of the implementation SHOULD be documented in a comprehensible manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal document 'Security Policy for Clients' is created, adopted, and published on the intranet. The document covers topics such as password usage, data storage, software installation, and handling of mobile devices. New employees are required to acknowledge it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check of the existence, content, and approval status of the client security policy. Interviewing employees to determine if the policy is known and where it can be found.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The implementation of the content required in the policy SHOULD be checked regularly. The policy is reviewed and updated annually or in the event of significant changes. Users are actively informed about changes and must confirm their acknowledgement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual review process for the policy is established in the ISMS. The implementation is checked through internal audits, where technical configurations are verified against the policy requirements. E-learning tools are used to confirm acknowledgement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Insight into the review process logs and the version history of the policy. Review of the internal audit reports. Analysis of the confirmation rates in the e-learning tool.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements of the client security policy are directly translated into technical controls and automated configuration baselines. Compliance with the policy is continuously and automatically monitored by compliance scanning tools. Deviations lead to automatic notifications to the security team and, depending on their criticality, can lead to the automatic quarantine of the client.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy requirements are transferred to configuration profiles for the MDM/GPO system. A compliance module in the central management system or a dedicated tool (e.g., based on SCAP) permanently checks the clients. The integration with a NAC solution enables automatic network quarantine.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the mapping documentation from policy points to technical controls. Analysis of the compliance dashboard for historical and current data. Triggering a test alarm by deliberately misconfiguring a test client to verify the response chain.

controls.title: Planning the use of clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be planned in advance where and how clients are to be used. The planning SHOULD not only consider aspects of IT security, but also operational aspects. All decisions made in the planning phase SHOULD be documented in such a way that they can be traced at a later date.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A planning document is created for each major rollout or the introduction of a new client type. This document describes the purpose, user groups, required software, and basic security requirements. The documents are centrally archived.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request and review of the planning documents for recent client rollouts. Comparison of the documentation with the actual use of the clients.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process is standardized and uses templates that ensure all relevant aspects (data protection, license management, support, disposal) are considered. The planning is reviewed and approved by the Information Security Officer (ISO) and the Data Protection Officer (DPO).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a formal template for 'Client Deployment Planning'. The process is integrated into the IT Service Management System (ITSM) and requires explicit approval steps by relevant roles such as ISO and DPO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Insight into the defined planning process in the ITSM system. Review of the planning documents for completeness according to the template and for visible approvals by ISO and DPO.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Client deployment planning is part of an overarching enterprise architecture strategy. Based on the defined user roles and workplace types, standardized client models (hardware, operating system, software packages) are maintained. Planning for new requirements is checked against these standards to avoid uncontrolled growth and to maximize efficiency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Enterprise Architecture Management (EAM) tool is used to model the client landscape and its dependencies. A 'Service Catalog' for clients defines the available standard configurations that can be ordered by the departments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the EAM model and the service catalog. Analysis of the order and approval processes for new clients to verify compliance with the standard models.

controls.title: Procurement of clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before clients are procured, a list of requirements SHOULD be created, against which the products available on the market are evaluated. The respective manufacturing companies SHOULD provide patches for vulnerabilities in a timely manner for the entire planned period of use. Operating systems with a rolling-release model SHOULD be avoided.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized checklist containing functional and security requirements is used for each procurement. One criterion is the manufacturer's commitment to a defined patch support lifecycle. Devices are ordered exclusively from established business suppliers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the procurement documents from recent months. It is verified whether requirement lists were used and how the selection of the supplier and product was documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The systems to be procured SHOULD have a firmware configuration interface for UEFI SecureBoot and, if available, for the TPM (version 2.0), which ensures control by the institution. Supplier relationships are formalized and suppliers are regularly evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirements list for procurement mandatory includes the items 'TPM 2.0' and 'UEFI Secure Boot capable'. Framework agreements are concluded with a few selected suppliers who are regularly reviewed for their reliability and security practices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the technical data sheets of the procured models for the required security features. Insight into the supplier contracts and the documentation of the supplier evaluations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Procurement takes into account the entire supply chain (Supply Chain Security). Measures are taken to minimize manipulation of the hardware or firmware before delivery. This can include direct manufacturer relationships, sealed deliveries, or the verification of hardware signatures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Only manufacturers who can demonstrate robust supply chain security measures (e.g., through certifications) are selected. The devices are ordered with a manufacturer-specific configuration (custom imaging) to minimize the attack surface from the outset. The integrity of the delivered devices is randomly checked upon receipt.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the contracts with manufacturers for clauses on supply chain security. Inspection of the goods receipt process and the logs of the integrity checks.

controls.title: Access to execution environments with unobservable code execution

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to execution environments with unobservable code execution (e.g., specially secured memory areas, firmware areas) SHOULD only be possible with administrative privileges. The corresponding settings in the BIOS or UEFI firmware SHOULD be protected by a password against unauthorized changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrative password for the BIOS/UEFI is set on all clients and securely managed. Standard users do not have permissions that would allow direct access to such hardware-level functions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether a standard user on a client can access BIOS/UEFI settings or special system tools. This must fail. Review of the process for managing the BIOS/UEFI passwords.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If control over hardware-level functions is delegated to the operating system (e.g., Virtualization-based Security, VBS), access to these functions SHOULD also only be permitted with administrative privileges. These settings are centrally managed and monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Functions such as Windows Defender Credential Guard are activated and configured via central policies (GPO/MDM). The configuration cannot be changed by users. The activation status of these functions is centrally monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of GPO/MDM policies for configuring VBS features. Querying the status of Credential Guard on clients using the 'Device Guard and Credential Guard hardware readiness tool' or via WMI/PowerShell. Automation is possible: `(Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard).SecurityServicesRunning`

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to secure execution environments (enclaves like Intel SGX or AMD SEV) is governed by strict code signing and attestation policies. Only explicitly approved and signed code is allowed to run in these environments. Every access attempt is logged and monitored for anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An in-house code signing infrastructure is used. The configuration of the enclaves and the allow policies are distributed via central, secure channels. The logs are sent to a SIEM system for analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the code signing policies and processes. Analysis of the configuration and log data in the SIEM to verify the correct application of the policies and the monitoring of access.

controls.title: Secure installation and configuration of clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be specified which components of the operating system, which business applications, and which other tools are to be installed. The installation and configuration of the IT systems SHOULD only be carried out by authorized persons according to a defined process. After the installation and configuration are complete, the basic settings SHOULD be checked. All installation and configuration steps SHOULD be documented in such a way that they can be understood by knowledgeable third parties.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized operating system image containing the basic software is used. The installation is carried out by trained IT staff in a controlled environment. After installation, a manual checklist is used to check and document the configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the installation process documentation and the completed checklists. Comparison of the configuration of a newly installed client with the specifications of the checklist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation and configuration of clients is largely automated. Hardened standard images are centrally maintained and rolled out via a software distribution system. The basic settings are checked by automated scripts after installation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like the Microsoft Deployment Toolkit (MDT) or SCCM are used to automate the installation process. The image is regularly updated (patch slipstreaming) and already contains basic hardening settings. A PowerShell script checks important security settings after deployment and logs the result.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the configuration of the deployment system and the task sequences used. Review of the logs of the automated configuration checks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire client configuration is managed as code (Infrastructure as Code) in a version control system. Deployment is carried out via a fully automated 'Zero-Touch' process. The configuration is continuously monitored in Desired State Configuration (DSC) mode and automatically corrected in case of deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Modern management frameworks such as Microsoft Intune with Windows Autopilot, JAMF Pro, or Ansible are used. Configuration files (e.g., YAML, JSON) are managed in a Git repository and tested and rolled out via a CI/CD pipeline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the Git repository, the CI/CD pipeline, and the configuration of the management framework. Evaluation of the DSC compliance reports. Testing the self-healing function by a manual misconfiguration on a test device.

controls.title: Deactivation and uninstallation of unneeded components and accounts

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After installation, it SHOULD be checked which firmware and operating system components and which applications and other tools are installed and activated on the clients. Unneeded modules, programs, services, tasks, firmware functions, runtime environments, accounts, and interfaces SHOULD be deactivated or uninstalled. The decisions made SHOULD be documented in a comprehensible manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the manual setup process, a system hardening checklist is completed. This list includes items for uninstalling default apps (bloatware), deactivating unnecessary services (e.g., Telnet client), and deleting default user accounts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the hardening checklist and the documentation for a newly set up client. Comparison of the client state (installed software, running services) with the specifications of the checklist. Manual check e.g. with `Get-Service` or `Get-AppxPackage` in PowerShell.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The deactivation and uninstallation of unneeded components is an automated part of the image creation or deployment process. It SHOULD be prevented that these components can be reactivated. This is enforced by central policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Hardening scripts, which are executed during automated deployment (e.g., via MDT/SCCM), remove unnecessary components. Central policies (GPO/MDM) set the configuration for services and interfaces to 'disabled' and prevent changes by the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analysis of the hardening scripts and the central policies. Verification on a client whether a deactivated service can be started manually (should fail). Automated check of the configuration via scripting across all clients is possible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of a reactive removal, a proactive 'allow-listing' approach is taken. Only software, services, and drivers explicitly approved and defined in a baseline are allowed to run on the client. The integrity of this baseline is continuously monitored, and deviations are automatically blocked and reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technologies such as Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker are used in 'Enforce' mode. The baseline is centrally managed. Any new software must go through an approval process before it is added to the allow-list.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration and rules of the application control solution. Analysis of the event logs for blocked execution attempts. Test by trying to run an unapproved portable application, which must be blocked.

controls.title: Encryption of clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Encryption is only performed for individual, particularly sensitive files or folders by the users themselves using native operating system functions (e.g., EFS) or additional tools.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users are instructed to encrypt sensitive data, but there is no technical requirement or control. The management of the keys is the responsibility of the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Surveying users on whether and how they encrypt data. A comprehensive statement on the encryption status cannot be made.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All laptops are manually equipped with disk encryption (e.g., BitLocker) during setup. The recovery keys are stored in a central location (e.g., in a password-protected document on a network drive).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Activating encryption is part of the manual checklist for laptop setup. The process for storing recovery keys is informal.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Spot check of laptops to see if encryption is active. Checking the central storage location for the existence and completeness of the recovery keys.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If confidential information is stored on the clients, at least the sensitive files and selected file system areas, or better yet the entire data carriers, SHOULD be encrypted. A dedicated concept SHOULD be created for this, which regulates authentication, the storage of recovery information, and write permissions on unencrypted data carriers. Access to the key material used MUST be adequately protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a formal concept for client encryption. Encryption (e.g., BitLocker) is enforced for all mobile and optionally for stationary clients via central policy (GPO/MDM). The recovery keys are automatically and securely stored in a central database (e.g., Active Directory, Intune/Azure AD).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the encryption concept. Review of the central policies for enforcing encryption. Verification in the central database that recovery keys exist for the clients. The encryption status can be queried automatically: `manage-bde -status` or `(Get-BitLockerVolume).ProtectionStatus` in PowerShell.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The details of the configuration are documented with particular care. The chosen encryption algorithms and key lengths comply with current recommendations (e.g., BSI TR-02102). The process for data recovery is formalized, tested, and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A strong encryption algorithm such as XTS-AES 256 is explicitly configured in the central policy. There is a documented work instruction for the helpdesk in case of a key recovery, which requires an identity check of the requester. Each recovery process is recorded in a ticket system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of the encryption algorithm in the central policies. Review of the work instruction and the logs of the recovery processes in the ticket system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The disk encryption is secured by using a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) in 'TPM and PIN' mode, so that pre-boot authentication (entering a PIN before the operating system starts) is required. This protects the keys from offline attacks. The compliance status of the encryption is continuously monitored, and automatic warnings are triggered in case of deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The BitLocker policy is configured to require a TPM protector in combination with a PIN protector. The compliance status is permanently monitored via the central management system (e.g., Intune Compliance Policies).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the BitLocker policy for the configuration of the 'TPM and PIN' mode. Restart of a client to verify the pre-boot authentication prompt. Analysis of the compliance dashboard in the management system for historical and current encryption statuses.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: A "General Client" refers to an IT system with any operating system that allows for the separation of users and is not intended to provide server services. A client should at least allow for the setup of separate environments for administration and use. The IT system typically has drives and connection options for external or removable storage media, other interfaces for data exchange, and other peripheral devices. Such an IT system is typically integrated into a client-server network. The IT system can be, for example, a PC with or without a hard drive, a mobile or stationary device, but also a Linux workstation or an Apple Mac.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to protect information that is created, read, edited, stored, or sent on any type of client, regardless of the operating system used.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.2.1 General Client is to be applied to all clients, regardless of the specific operating system.

As a rule, clients run on an operating system that requires its own security measures. For common client operating systems, specific modules are available in the SYS.2 Desktop Systems layer, which build on this module and must also be applied. If no specific module exists for the clients in use, the requirements of this module must be suitably specified for the target object, and a supplementary risk assessment must be carried out.

Security recommendations for mobile devices with a fixed operating system, such as smartphones or tablets, can be found in the SYS.3 Mobile Devices layer. If a client has additional interfaces for data exchange, such as USB, Bluetooth, LAN, or WLAN, these must be secured according to the institution's security policies as described in the corresponding modules. Requirements for this can be found, for example, in SYS.4.5 Removable Media or NET.2.2 WLAN Usage.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Malware
parts.prose:
Malware is developed with the aim of executing unwanted and malicious functions on IT systems. It usually becomes active "secretly," i.e., without the user's knowledge or consent. Depending on its design, it can offer extensive communication and control capabilities with many different functions during an attack. Among other things, it could specifically read passwords, remotely control IT systems, deactivate protection software, spy on, or encrypt data.

Clients are particularly vulnerable to malware. They are operated directly by users and are therefore often the gateway for malicious content of all kinds. If users visit malicious websites, open emails with malicious content from private accounts, or copy malware onto the client via local storage media, the malware can spread through the clients into the institution's network. Central protection mechanisms, such as antivirus protection on the file or email server, can often be bypassed in this way.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Data loss due to local data storage
parts.prose:
Despite regular recommendations to the contrary, important data is often stored exclusively locally. For example, data is frequently stored in local directories instead of on a central file server. Emails are also often archived only locally. This means data can easily be lost in the event of hardware defects. If data important to the institution is destroyed or corrupted, business processes and specialized tasks can be delayed or even completely prevented. Overall, the loss of stored data, in addition to work stoppage and replacement costs, can also lead to long-term consequences such as a loss of trust in business relationships and a negative public image. In extreme cases, the direct and indirect damages caused by data loss can threaten the very existence of an institution.

If important data is kept exclusively locally, other people also cannot access it, for example, in the case of substitution during vacation or illness.

Even if basic guidelines for central storage are followed, local copies of centrally stored data are often created in addition. This not only frequently leads to inconsistent version statuses but also to data being deleted either prematurely or not as required.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Hardware defects in client systems
parts.prose: Unlike central IT systems such as servers, users work directly on or with the client endpoint device. This means they could intentionally or unintentionally damage the client. For example, they could kick IT systems standing on the floor, trip over cables and thus damage interfaces, or spill liquids on devices. If no quick replacement is available, the IT system cannot be used as intended until the repair is completed. If a mobile device such as a laptop fails on the go, work can often only be resumed after returning to the institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unauthorized use of clients
parts.prose: The identification and authentication of persons is intended to prevent a client from being used without authorization. However, even IT systems where users must identify and authenticate themselves via IDs and passwords can be used without authorization if attackers succeed in spying out or guessing the access credentials. If no screen lock is activated, the client can also be used without authorization during brief absences.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Installation of unnecessary operating system components and applications
parts.prose: When installing an operating system, it is usually possible to install optional software. Software is also regularly installed and tested during ongoing operations. With each additional application, not only do the computing and storage load of a client increase, but also the probability of hidden vulnerabilities within it. Furthermore, unneeded software is often not subject to regular patch management, meaning that even known security gaps are not closed in a timely manner. As a result, such vulnerabilities can be exploited for attacks.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Eavesdropping on rooms using microphone and camera
parts.prose: Many clients have a microphone and a camera. In principle, these can be activated and used by anyone with the appropriate access rights, including external parties in the case of networked systems. If these rights are not carefully assigned, unauthorized persons can misuse the microphone or camera to eavesdrop on rooms over the internet or to secretly record meetings. This also includes Intelligent Personal Assistants (IPAs) or voice assistants, which permanently listen to the environment and, after an activation word specific to the device is spoken, perform certain functions such as playing music, calling contacts, controlling lighting, or changing the room climate. If conversations are transmitted to third parties, e.g. by IPAs, they could potentially be overheard by unauthorized persons. The recorded conversations could also be stored and processed long-term by the manufacturing companies of IPAs.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Incorrect administration or use of devices and systems
parts.prose:
Modern client operating systems are very complex. Therefore, misconfigurations of components in particular can impair security, so that the IT system functions incorrectly or can be compromised. In principle, every interface on an IT system not only offers the possibility of legitimately using certain services of the IT system, but also carries the risk of unauthorized persons accessing the IT system. For example, if identifiers and associated passwords can be spied on due to misconfiguration of the authentication mechanisms, unauthorized use of the applications or IT systems protected by them is conceivable.

Incorrect or improper use of devices, systems, and applications can also impair security, especially if existing security measures are disregarded or bypassed. For example, overly permissive rights, easy-to-guess passwords, insufficiently protected data carriers with backup copies, or workstations that are not locked during temporary absence can lead to security incidents. Another consequence of incorrect operation of IT systems or applications can be the accidental deletion or modification of data. It is also possible for confidential information to fall into the hands of third parties, for example if access rights are set incorrectly.

controls.title: Planning the use of cloud services under Windows

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of cloud services integrated into Windows is only regulated sporadically and on an ad-hoc basis. There is no central strategy or policy, which means that individual departments or users activate and use cloud services at their own discretion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, there are typically no technical controls. The use of Microsoft accounts and services like OneDrive is uncontrolled. There is a lack of awareness of the associated risks regarding data protection and information security.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through random checks on clients and interviews with employees that no uniform policy for the use of cloud services exists. It is checked whether Microsoft accounts are used for login and whether data is stored on the public OneDrive.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic, informal guideline regarding which cloud services (e.g., OneDrive) may not be used for business data. However, this guideline is not formulated in detail or technically implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The guideline is communicated via email, for example. There are no specific configurations via Group Policy to prevent its use. Compliance is based on the goodwill of the users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the presentation of communication measures (e.g., emails) regarding the regulation of cloud usage. A review of client configurations reveals that no technical enforcement measures exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Since Windows-based devices are tightly integrated with the manufacturer Microsoft's cloud services, it MUST be strategically determined before their use which included cloud services should or may be used and to what extent. This determination is documented and communicated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy is created that clearly defines which cloud services (e.g., Microsoft account login, OneDrive, Store connection) are permitted and which are prohibited. This policy is implemented via standard management tools such as Group Policies (GPOs) or MDM profiles to control usage accordingly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the strategic policy for the use of cloud services. It is checked whether this policy considers the protection requirements of the data. Furthermore, the technical implementation of the policy is verified by analyzing the relevant GPO or MDM settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The strategic determination for the use of cloud services is underpinned by a formal risk assessment for each individual service. The policy is regularly reviewed and adapted to new Windows features. Compliance with the policy is technically monitored on a random basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the configuration via GPO/MDM, network firewall rules are implemented to block access to unwanted Microsoft cloud services. The effectiveness of the blockade is verified by analyzing network logs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies not only the policy and its technical implementation, but also the documentation of the risk assessment for the cloud services. In addition, the configuration of the network firewall and the log data for monitoring compliance are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy on the use of cloud services is fully integrated into the ISMS. The configuration is automatically enforced by a configuration management system and continuously checked for deviations (compliance monitoring). All access to cloud services is logged and automatically analyzed for anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) or a comparable technology is used to gain granular control over the use of cloud services and to enforce data loss prevention policies. The policies are automatically adjusted based on the status of the endpoint and the user role.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the integration of the process into the ISMS. The configuration and reports of the configuration management system and the CASB are analyzed. The automated alerting and response processes for policy violations are verified. Automatic check: `Invoke-ComplianceCheck -Rule 'CloudServicePolicy' -Target 'AllClients'`.

controls.title: Selection and procurement of a suitable Windows version

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of the Windows version is unsystematic, often based on the licenses supplied with the hardware (e.g., Windows Home or Pro). There is no consideration of different protection requirements or management needs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The organization has a mix of different Windows editions (Home, Pro, Enterprise) and service branches, which makes uniform security management difficult or impossible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through an inventory of the deployed clients, the auditor determines that different and in some cases unsuitable Windows editions (e.g., Home editions) are being used in the corporate environment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organization has agreed on a standard Windows version, typically Windows Pro, for all clients. However, the selection does not yet explicitly consider the protection requirements or the need for specific Enterprise features.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the procurement process, the Pro edition of Windows is requested by default. Special requirements such as LTSC for production facilities are not systematically considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the procurement process that a standard edition of Windows is defined. It is checked whether there was an analysis to determine if this edition is sufficient for all purposes and protection requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The functional scope and the provision of functional changes of a Windows version MUST be selected considering the determined protection requirements and the purpose of use. The feasibility of the required security measures MUST be considered during the selection. Based on the result of the review, the established procurement process MUST be extended to include the selection of the corresponding license model and "Service Branches" (CB, CBB, or LTSC).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A matrix is created that maps the protection requirements of system groups (e.g., standard office, management, critical infrastructure) to the appropriate Windows editions (Pro, Enterprise) and service branches (CBB, LTSC). This matrix is part of the official procurement process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation for the selection of Windows versions and service branches. It is checked whether the selection is based on a traceable protection requirement analysis and is anchored in the procurement process. A sample of the system landscape is checked for conformity with the selection policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection and procurement process for Windows versions is formally documented and is regularly reviewed and updated, especially when new Windows versions or features are announced. The decision for a specific edition and branch is justified and documented for each system class.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection criteria are stored in the asset management system. When a new client is procured, the requirement is automatically checked against the stored policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks not only the process but also the documentation of the regular reviews and the justifications for the selection decisions made. The configuration of the asset management system to support the process is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of Windows versions, from selection and procurement to distribution, maintenance, and decommissioning, is controlled by an automated process. The version selection is fully integrated into the automatic client provisioning and is dynamically determined based on the user's and system's role.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system management tool such as Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager (MECM) or Intune is used to automate the entire process. A service catalog allows users to request pre-configured systems based on protection requirements and role, with the correct Windows version automatically assigned and installed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration and the process flows in the system management tool. An end-to-end test of the provisioning process is performed to ensure that the selection rules are applied correctly and automatically. Automatic check: `Get-AssetPolicy | Test-Compliance -Rule 'WindowsVersionSelection'`.

controls.title: Telemetry and privacy settings in Windows

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The telemetry settings on the clients are left in the default configuration. There is no awareness or action to reduce the diagnostic data sent to Microsoft.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During the installation of Windows, the express settings are used, which include comprehensive data transmission. No Group Policies or MDM profiles are configured to control telemetry.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By checking the configuration of several clients, the auditor determines that the telemetry level is set to 'Full' or 'Optional' (default). This can be verified by running `Get-PrivacySetting -Setting 'TelemetryLevel'` on a client.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic configuration to reduce telemetry data. Typically, the 'Required' (formerly 'Basic') setting is set via a Group Policy, but no further measures are taken.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Group Policy is applied to the clients that sets the 'Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Windows Components -> Data Collection and Preview Builds -> Allow Telemetry' setting to '1 - Required'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the corresponding Group Policy. It is checked on a random basis on clients whether the policy is effective by analyzing the Resultant Set of Policy (RSOP).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To greatly reduce the transmission of diagnostic and usage data to Microsoft, the telemetry level 0 (Security) MUST be configured in the Enterprise edition of Windows. If this setting is not effectively implemented or cannot be implemented on other Windows editions, then appropriate measures, such as at the network level, MUST be taken to ensure that the data is not transmitted to the manufacturer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For Windows Enterprise/Education, the GPO setting 'Allow Telemetry' is set to '0 - Security'. For other editions or as an additional measure, the known telemetry endpoints of Microsoft are blocked on the central firewall or proxy server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPO setting for Enterprise clients. In addition, the configuration rules of the firewall or proxy are checked to ensure that the telemetry endpoints are blocked. It is checked whether a list of endpoints to be blocked is maintained.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of telemetry settings and the network-level blockade are regularly checked for effectiveness. Outgoing network traffic is actively monitored to see if data is being sent to known telemetry servers despite the measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The list of blocked telemetry endpoints is updated regularly (e.g., quarterly) based on official Microsoft documentation and community resources. The firewall logs are analyzed to document blocked connection attempts and to identify new, unknown endpoints.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the process documentation for updating the endpoint list and the reports from the log analysis. The timeliness of the blocked endpoints in the firewall configuration is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Telemetry settings are enforced by a central configuration management tool that continuously monitors the compliance of each client and automatically corrects or alerts in case of deviations. The network blockade is implemented by a next-generation firewall with application recognition, which can detect and block telemetry traffic even without knowing the exact IP addresses.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Microsoft Intune or MECM is used to configure and monitor the 'Diagnostic Data' setting. A Palo Alto, Fortinet, or similar firewall is configured with App-ID signatures for Microsoft telemetry to block the traffic. All blocked attempts are sent to a SIEM system for correlation and analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the compliance reports in the configuration management tool. The configuration of the application recognition on the firewall and the alerting rules in the SIEM are verified. Automatic check: `Get-EndpointCompliance -Policy 'TelemetryControl' | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne 'Compliant' }`.

controls.title: Protection against malware on Windows

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Protection against malware is handled inconsistently. Some clients use the built-in Windows Defender, others may have free antivirus software installed, and on some systems, active protection is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no central management or monitoring of the antivirus status. Virus signature updates depend on the configuration of the individual client and the user's behavior.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through a random check of clients that there is no uniform and consistently active malware protection. The status in the Windows Security Center is checked on several devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An antivirus solution (e.g., the default Windows Defender) is active on all clients. However, there is no central management to control configurations, updates, and alerts uniformly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The organization relies on Windows Defender being active by default and updating itself via Windows Update. There is no central console to check the status or respond to findings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies on a sample of clients that an antivirus solution is active and has up-to-date signatures. It is noted that no central management console is in use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unless equivalent or higher-value measures, such as execution control, have been taken to protect the IT system from malware infection, a specialized component for malware protection MUST be used on Windows clients. This component is centrally managed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A centrally managed antivirus solution is rolled out on all clients. This can be Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (Plan 1) or a comparable third-party solution. Policies (e.g., for regular scans, real-time protection) are distributed, signature update status is monitored, and alerts are collected centrally via a central console.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests access to the central management console of the antivirus solution. The configuration of policies, client coverage, and update status are checked. The alerting and reporting functions are verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The deployed malware protection solution includes behavior-based detection mechanisms and exploit protection in addition to signature-based ones. The configuration is hardened, e.g., by activating 'Attack Surface Reduction' (ASR) rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Endpoint Protection Platform (EPP) is used. In Microsoft Defender, ASR rules are activated via Group Policy or Intune to block typical attack vectors (e.g., macros in Office, scripts). Alerts are analyzed centrally, and there is a defined process for response.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the activation of advanced protection features such as ASR rules in the management console or the GPO/Intune settings. The process for handling alerts is reviewed, and it is checked whether it is practiced regularly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solution is in use, enabling in-depth monitoring, analysis, and response to threats. This is supplemented by strict execution control (Application Whitelisting), which only allows the execution of explicitly approved software.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (Plan 2) or a comparable EDR solution is used. The EDR telemetry data is actively monitored by a Security Operations Center (SOC). In addition, Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker is operated in 'Enforce' mode to enforce an allowlist of applications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the EDR and application whitelisting solution. The SOC team's processes for threat hunting and responding to EDR alerts are reviewed. Automatic check: `Get-WDACPolicy -Effective` and `Get-AdvancedThreatProtectionStatus`.

controls.title: Integration of online accounts into the operating system

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users can log in to the operating system with private Microsoft accounts without restriction. There is no policy or technical control to prevent this.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is the default state for non-domain-joined clients. Data such as settings, BitLocker keys, and documents can be uncontrollably synchronized with the user's private cloud.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by checking the user accounts on a client that logins with Microsoft accounts are possible and are being used. Command for checking: `wmic useraccount get name,domain`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal instruction to users not to use Microsoft accounts for logging in. However, technical controls to enforce this instruction are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users are asked during orientation or via email to use only their domain accounts or local accounts. Compliance is not checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the communication measures shown to them and determines through a technical check that the GPO setting to block Microsoft accounts is not configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Login to the system and the domain SHOULD only be possible with an account from a self-operated directory service. Logins with local accounts SHOULD be reserved for administrators. Online accounts for login, such as a Microsoft account or accounts from other identity management systems, MUST NOT be used, as this transmits personal data to third-party systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Group Policy 'Accounts: Block Microsoft accounts' ('Computer Configuration -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options') is enabled to prevent logging in with or adding Microsoft accounts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the mentioned Group Policy is applied to all relevant clients. An attempt is made to add a Microsoft account on a test client to confirm the effectiveness of the block. Automatic check: `Get-GPO -Name 'Client-Haertung' | Get-GPRegistryValue -Key 'Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System' -ValueName 'NoConnectedUser'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy for blocking online accounts is checked for compliance through regular audits. There is a documented process for exceptions if they are absolutely necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the GPO, configuration verification scripts (e.g., via the configuration management system) are used to regularly check the status of the setting and report deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports from the configuration verification. The process for approving and documenting exceptions is reviewed and assessed for its adequacy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The blocking of online accounts is implemented using a defense-in-depth approach, combining client hardening (GPO) and network controls (firewall). Any deviation from the policy leads to an automatic correction or a security alert.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the GPO, Microsoft's authentication endpoints (e.g., login.live.com) are blocked on the corporate firewall for client networks. A configuration management tool enforces the GPO setting and reports violations to the SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies both the GPO setting and the firewall rules. The configuration of the configuration management tool and the alert rules in the SIEM are checked. A test is performed to confirm that both the client and network controls are effective.

controls.title: Secure central authentication in Windows networks

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The authentication protocols are left in the default Windows configuration. This allows the use of NTLMv1 and LAN Manager hashes, especially when communicating with older systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No specific group policies are configured to harden the authentication protocols. Security depends on the default settings of the respective Windows versions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by analyzing the effective security settings on a client that the 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' is not explicitly set to a secure level.

parts.name: statement
