parts.prose: The use of LAN Manager (LM) and NTLMv1 is prevented by a basic policy. NTLMv2 is used as the default, but no active effort is made to reduce the use of NTLM in favor of Kerberos.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Group Policy 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' is set to 'Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM' (Level 5).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the GPO for the LAN Manager authentication level. It is checked whether the policy is rolled out comprehensively.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For central authentication, Kerberos SHOULD be used exclusively. A group policy SHOULD prevent the use of older protocols. If this is not possible, NTLMv2 MUST be used as an alternative. Authentication using LAN-Manager and NTLMv1 MUST NOT be permitted within the institution and in a production operating environment. The cryptographic mechanisms used SHOULD be configured and documented according to the determined protection requirement and based on internal policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to enforcing NTLMv2 (Level 5), measures are taken to promote the use of Kerberos, e.g., by correctly configuring Service Principal Names (SPNs). The encryption algorithms used for Kerberos (e.g., AES-256) are defined via GPO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPOs for setting the authentication level and Kerberos encryption types. It is checked whether documentation of the configuration and a justification for deviations exist. Misconfigured SPNs are searched for using tools like `setspn -X`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of NTLM authentication is actively monitored and logged on the network. There is a plan to gradually reduce the remaining NTLM usage by correcting the underlying applications or configurations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Auditing for NTLM authentication events (Event IDs 8001-8004) is enabled on the domain controllers. The logs are centrally collected and analyzed to identify the sources of NTLM usage and create a migration plan to Kerberos.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the activation of NTLM auditing. The logs and the plan to reduce NTLM are reviewed. The progress of the plan's implementation is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of NTLM authentication is technically disabled throughout the network. Authentication is performed exclusively via Kerberos with strong encryption algorithms. For highly privileged accounts, additional protective measures such as 'Authentication Policy Silos' are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The GPO 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: NTLM authentication in this domain' is set to 'Deny all'. 'Authentication Policies' and 'Silos' are configured in Active Directory to restrict the logon rights of administrative accounts to secure systems and to reduce the Kerberos TGT lifetime.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPOs for disabling NTLM and the configuration of the 'Authentication Policy Silos' in Active Directory. It is checked whether there are processes to test new systems and applications for Kerberos compatibility before they are put into operation.

controls.title: File and share permissions in Windows

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: File permissions are barely managed. Users often work with local administrator rights, which gives them unrestricted write access to the entire file system. The 'Everyone' group with full access is often used on shares.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No permission concept exists. The default Windows settings are used or even weakened to bypass application compatibility issues.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that users have excessive rights by checking local groups and share permissions. Tools like `AccessChk` from Sysinternals can be used for quick analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic permission concept that assigns standard user rights to users. Users do not have write access to system folders such as C:\Windows. Authenticated user groups are used on shares instead of 'Everyone'.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users are not members of the local administrators group. Shares are configured with basic permission groups (e.g., 'Department X'), but often with overly broad rights (Modify instead of just Read).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that user accounts do not have local administrator rights. The permissions on important shares are checked to determine whether the principle of least privilege is applied.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to files and folders on the local system and on network shares SHOULD be configured according to a permission and access concept. The default administrative shares on the system SHOULD also be taken into account. Write permissions for users SHOULD be restricted to a defined area of the file system. In particular, users SHOULD not be granted write permissions to operating system or installed application folders.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented permission concept based on the principle of least privilege is implemented. Users only have write access to their profile folders and defined data areas. Administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$) are disabled on client systems via GPO or script. The AGDLP principle (Accounts -> Global Groups -> Domain Local Groups -> Permissions) is applied for access to network shares.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the permission concept and compares it with the actual implementation on a sample of clients and file servers. It is checked whether administrative shares are disabled on clients. The memberships in the permission groups are analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The permission concept is reviewed regularly, e.g., annually, and the assigned permissions are recertified. Access to particularly sensitive files and folders is monitored (auditing).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A permission recertification process is established in which data owners must regularly confirm the access rights for their data. The System Access Control List (SACL) is configured on critical folders to log read and write access. These logs are collected centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the evidence of performed permission recertifications. The configuration of auditing at the file system level and the collection of audit logs are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management and monitoring of permissions is largely automated. Windows Dynamic Access Control (DAC) is used to dynamically control access rights not only based on groups, but also on file classifications and user attributes. Changes to permissions and access attempts are monitored in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: DAC is configured in Active Directory to automatically classify data (e.g., based on content) and to centrally define access policies. A Data-Centric Audit and Protection (DCAP) tool is used to analyze and optimize permissions and to monitor and alert on access in real time.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of DAC in Active Directory and on the file servers. The functionality of the automatic classification and the dynamic access policies is tested. The configuration and reports of the DCAP tool are analyzed.

controls.title: Use of the SmartScreen feature

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SmartScreen feature is active on all systems in the default setting. There are no measures to disable it for data protection reasons.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default configuration of Windows is retained, which means that information about downloaded files and visited websites is sent to Microsoft for verification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the feature is active by accessing the SmartScreen settings (Windows Security -> App & browser control).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SmartScreen feature, which scans files downloaded from the internet and web content for possible malware and may transfer personal data to Microsoft for this purpose, SHOULD be disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SmartScreen feature is disabled centrally via Group Policies. This affects the settings for the Microsoft Edge browser, File Explorer, and for Microsoft Store apps. The relevant GPOs are located under 'Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Windows Components' in the respective subfolders.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the relevant Group Policies for disabling SmartScreen. On a test client, the effectiveness of the policies is checked using RSOP (Resultant Set of Policy) analysis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The disabling of the SmartScreen feature is regularly checked for its effectiveness. In addition, alternative protective mechanisms are strengthened to compensate for the potential loss of protection from disabling SmartScreen.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the GPO configuration, the configurations are regularly checked via script. The protection at the web gateway (proxy with content filtering) and the client-side antivirus protection are strengthened and explicitly documented as compensating measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports of the configuration review. The configuration of the compensating protective measures (e.g., proxy filter rules) is reviewed and assessed for its effectiveness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The disabling of SmartScreen is enforced by client policies and underpinned by a network firewall as a second line of defense, which blocks access to Microsoft's SmartScreen services.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the GPO configuration, the DNS names of the SmartScreen endpoints (e.g., smartscreen.microsoft.com) are blocked on the corporate firewall or the DNS filter. The compliance of the client settings is continuously monitored by a configuration management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies both the client policies and the network firewall configuration. The compliance reports from the management tool are checked. A test is conducted to confirm the network blockade.

controls.title: Use of the voice assistant Cortana

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cortana is active on the systems because it is the default setting. There is no policy restricting its use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users can use Cortana as they wish, which can lead to voice data and other information being sent to Microsoft servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by checking the taskbar and Windows settings on a client that Cortana is active and functional.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cortana SHOULD be disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The deactivation of Cortana is enforced centrally via the Group Policy 'Allow Cortana' ('Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Windows Components -> Search').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the Group Policy for disabling Cortana. On a test client, it is checked whether Cortana can no longer be started.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The disabling of Cortana is enforced by client policies and supplemented by network controls that block access to Cortana's backend services. The compliance of the setting is continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the GPO, the DNS names of the Cortana services are blocked on the firewall. A configuration management tool monitors the setting and automatically corrects deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the client policy, the firewall rules, and the reports from the configuration management tool. It is checked whether an alarm is triggered if the setting is changed manually.

controls.title: Use of synchronization mechanisms in Windows

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The synchronization of user settings and data with the Microsoft Cloud is possible without restriction, especially when users are logged in with Microsoft accounts. Wi-Fi passwords may also be synchronized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default settings for synchronization in the Windows settings remain unchanged. There are no central policies to control these features.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines in the Windows settings under 'Accounts -> Sync your settings' that synchronization is active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The synchronization of user data with Microsoft Cloud services and the sharing of Wi-Fi passwords SHOULD be completely disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Synchronization is disabled via Group Policies. Relevant settings are 'Do not sync' ('Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Windows Components -> Sync your settings') and 'Allow Windows to automatically connect to suggested open hotspots, to networks shared by contacts, and to hotspots offering paid services' ('Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> WLAN Service -> WLAN Settings').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the corresponding Group Policies. On a client, RSOP is used to check whether the settings are effective.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The disabling of synchronization mechanisms is enforced by client policies and supplemented by network controls that block access to the synchronization endpoints as a defense-in-depth measure. Compliance is continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the GPO, the DNS names of the synchronization services (e.g., onesettings-win.data.microsoft.com) are blocked on the firewall. A configuration management tool ensures compliance with the GPO settings and alerts in case of deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the client policies, the firewall configuration, and the reports from the configuration management tool. The reliability of the alerting for configuration changes is checked.

controls.title: Connecting Windows to the Microsoft Store

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of the Microsoft Store SHOULD be reviewed and assessed for compatibility with the institution's data protection and security requirements. The general installation of apps on Windows does not depend on the connection to the Microsoft Store; therefore, it SHOULD be disabled if it is not needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented assessment is carried out to determine whether the Microsoft Store should be used. If the decision is negative, access to the Store is blocked via the Group Policy 'Turn off the Store application' ('Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Windows Components -> Store').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the assessment documentation. If the Store is supposed to be disabled, the configuration of the corresponding Group Policy and its effectiveness on a client are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If the Microsoft Store is used, a 'Microsoft Store for Business' is set up. This allows for the central curation of apps available to users and offers only approved applications for installation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The 'Microsoft Store for Business' is configured and linked to the clients via a Group Policy so that only the private store is displayed. Apps undergo a security check before being approved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the 'Microsoft Store for Business' and the associated GPO. The process for approving and releasing apps is checked for its appropriateness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The deactivation or restriction of the Microsoft Store is enforced by client policies and supplemented by network controls that block access to the Store endpoints. The installation of apps is only possible through a central, approval-based software distribution process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the GPO, the Store endpoints are blocked on the firewall. App installation is completely controlled by a software distribution system (e.g., Intune, MECM), which also allows the installation of Store apps (offline licensed) without direct user access to the Store.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPOs, the firewall rules, and the configuration of the software distribution system. It is checked whether a user is able to bypass the controls and install an unapproved app.

controls.title: No storage of data for automatic logon

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users can freely store credentials (passwords, certificates) in browsers and other applications to log on automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are no policies that restrict saving passwords in the browser or using the Windows Credential Manager for websites.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By inspecting the browser settings and the Windows Credential Manager, the auditor determines that credentials for various services are stored.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The storage of passwords, certificates, and other information for automatic logon to websites and IT systems SHOULD NOT be permitted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The storage of passwords in common web browsers (Edge, Chrome, Firefox) is prevented via central Group Policies. Users are recommended or required to use a centrally managed password manager as a secure alternative.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the Group Policies for the common browsers. On a test client, it is checked whether the prompt to save passwords is suppressed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy to prohibit password storage is actively monitored. The use of the Windows Credential Manager is restricted via GPOs to prevent the storage of credentials for network and web services.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Group Policy 'Network access: Do not allow storage of passwords and credentials for network authentication' is enabled. The compliance of browser settings is regularly checked via script.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPO setting for the Credential Manager and the configuration review reports. The policies and the use of the recommended password manager are checked.

controls.title: Use of Windows Remote Assistance

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Windows Remote Assistance is enabled, but its use is not further hardened. Invitations can be created without a password and have a long validity period.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default settings for Remote Assistance are used. IT support staff use this function as needed, without a formal process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By checking the GPO settings, the auditor determines that no configurations have been made to harden Remote Assistance.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The effects on the local firewall configuration SHOULD be considered when planning Windows Remote Assistance. Remote assistance SHOULD only be provided after an explicit invitation. When saving an invitation to a file, it SHOULD have a password. A session SHOULD always be explicitly approved before being established. The maximum validity of the invitation SHOULD be appropriate. If Windows Remote Assistance is not used, it SHOULD be completely disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Remote Assistance is configured via Group Policies ('Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> System -> Remote Assistance'). The 'Offer Remote Assistance' option is enabled and configured so that the user retains control ('Do not allow help seekers to be controlled', 'Ticket validity' set to e.g. 1 hour). If the function is not needed, it is completely disabled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the GPOs for Remote Assistance. It is checked whether the settings follow the principle that the user retains control and must explicitly approve the session. If the function is not used, it is checked whether it is disabled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All Remote Assistance sessions are centrally logged to track who accessed which system and when. Usage is restricted to a defined group of support staff.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The 'Offer Remote Assistance' GPO setting is configured so that only members of a specific security group (e.g., 'IT-Support') can offer help. Event logging for Remote Assistance is enabled, and the logs are sent to a central SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPO setting for restricting the helper group and the logging configuration. It is checked in the SIEM whether the Remote Assistance events are correctly recorded.

controls.title: Security for remote access via RDP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: RDP is enabled on the clients and the group of authorized users is restricted to 'Remote Desktop Users'. However, no further hardening measures are taken for the protocol or the convenience features.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default settings for RDP are used. Convenience features such as clipboard, printer, and drive redirection are fully active.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By checking the system settings and GPOs, the auditor determines that RDP is enabled, but no specific hardening policies (e.g., for encryption or for disabling redirections) are configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The group of authorized RDP users SHOULD be defined. The use of convenience features (clipboard, printer, drive redirection, smart cards) SHOULD be reviewed and configured in accordance with the protection requirements of the target system. The cryptographic protocols and algorithms used SHOULD be secure. If RDP is not intended to be used, it SHOULD be completely disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: RDP is hardened via Group Policies ('Computer Configuration -> Admin. Templates -> Windows Components -> Remote Desktop Services -> Remote Desktop Session Host'). This includes enforcing Network Level Authentication (NLA), configuring a high encryption level, and specifically disabling unneeded client redirections (e.g., clipboard, drives).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the GPOs for hardening RDP. It is checked whether a documented decision on the use of convenience features exists and whether it has been technically implemented. If RDP is not used, it is checked whether the service is disabled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Direct RDP access to clients is blocked on the network. Access must instead be through a central Remote Desktop Gateway, which serves as a control and logging point.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An RD Gateway server is set up. The Windows Firewall on the clients is configured to accept RDP connections only from the RD Gateway server. Connection and resource authorization policies are defined on the RD Gateway to control access in a granular manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the RD Gateway and the firewall rules on the clients. The policies on the gateway are checked for correctness and adherence to the least privilege principle.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For administrative RDP access, the 'Restricted Admin' mode is enforced to prevent the transmission of credentials to the target system. All RDP sessions are logged, and suspicious activities, such as logins at unusual times, are automatically reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The GPO 'Delegate credentials from the client to the remote server' is configured accordingly for administrative access to use the 'Restricted Admin' mode. RDP login events (Success and Failure) are sent to a SIEM and correlated there with abnormal behavior patterns.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPOs for the 'Restricted Admin' mode. The configuration of the log forwarding and the alerting rules in the SIEM are checked. A test is performed to see if an abnormal RDP login triggers an alarm.

controls.title: Use of User Account Control (UAC) for privileged accounts

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: User Account Control (UAC) is disabled on many systems, especially for administrators, to not restrict usability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The GPO 'User Account Control: Run all administrators in Admin Approval Mode' is disabled or the UAC level is set to 0 via the registry.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By checking the effective GPO settings, the auditor determines that UAC is disabled. This leads to a significant security risk, as all processes in the administrator context run with full privileges.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The User Account Control (UAC) configuration parameters SHOULD be applied to privileged accounts with a balance between usability and security level. The decisions for the configuration parameters to be used SHOULD be documented. Furthermore, the documentation SHOULD include all accounts with administrative rights and be regularly reviewed to determine whether it is necessary to be able to elevate rights.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: UAC is enabled via Group Policy for all accounts, especially administrator accounts. For administrators, the most secure setting 'Prompt on the secure desktop' is selected. The configuration decisions made are justified in a hardening document. A list of all administrator accounts is maintained and regularly recertified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the UAC configurations in the GPOs. The document with the configuration decisions and the list of administrator accounts are requested and checked for currency and completeness. The process for recertifying admin rights is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The principle of 'Least Privilege' is consistently implemented by ensuring that standard users are not local administrators. Administrative tasks are performed with dedicated admin accounts, which elevate their rights only when needed via UAC.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All users, including technical staff, work with standard user accounts in their daily routine. For administrative tasks, they use a separate administrator account. The use of 'Run as administrator' is the standard way to obtain elevated rights.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor ensures that standard user accounts do not have administrative rights by analyzing group memberships. It is verified whether dedicated administrator accounts exist for technical staff and are being used.

controls.title: Use of the Encrypting File System (EFS)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Individual users use EFS to encrypt files, but there is no central management, no recovery agent, and no backup of the keys. This poses a high risk of data loss.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users manually enable EFS via the file properties. No recovery agent is assigned via GPO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor searches for EFS-encrypted files on clients (e.g., with `cipher /s:C:\`) and determines that no recovery policy is configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Since EFS protects keys with the account's password, a strong password SHOULD be used. The recovery agent SHOULD be a dedicated account. Its private key SHOULD be backed up and removed from the system. Backups SHOULD be made of all private keys. When using EFS with local accounts, the password stores SHOULD be encrypted using Syskey. Users SHOULD be trained in the correct use of EFS.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A data recovery agent is configured for the domain via GPO. The agent's certificate and private key are securely exported and stored offline in a protected location (e.g., a safe). The key is deleted from the issuing system. There is a policy that mandates strong passwords. Users are informed about the functionality and risks of EFS.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the EFS recovery policy in the GPO. The process for securely storing the recovery key is reviewed. The training materials for users are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data recovery process using the recovery agent is documented and tested regularly. Instead of the outdated Syskey, Windows Defender Credential Guard is used to protect credentials.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A playbook for EFS data recovery is created. An exercise is conducted at least once a year, in which an encrypted file is decrypted with the recovery agent. Credential Guard is enabled on compatible hardware via GPO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the recovery playbook and the evidence of the tests performed. The configuration of Credential Guard is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of EFS, a centrally manageable disk encryption solution like BitLocker is used. The recovery keys are securely stored in Active Directory or a dedicated key management solution to simplify management and minimize the risk of data loss from individual encrypted files.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: BitLocker is enforced on all clients via GPO or Intune. The policy requires backing up the recovery key in AD DS. Access to the recovery keys in AD is restricted to a small, authorized group and is logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the BitLocker policies and checks the encryption status of the clients via the management console. The process for recovering a BitLocker-locked drive is reviewed. The access permissions to the recovery keys in AD are analyzed.

controls.title: Use of Windows PowerShell

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The execution of PowerShell scripts is set to the default 'Restricted' or 'AllSigned' setting. However, there is no restriction on who can use PowerShell interactively, and there is no central logging.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The PowerShell Execution Policy is set to 'AllSigned' via GPO to prevent the execution of unsigned scripts. However, standard users can still open the PowerShell console and execute commands.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPO for the Execution Policy with `Get-ExecutionPolicy`. It is checked whether a standard user can use PowerShell interactively.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: PowerShell and WPS files SHOULD ONLY be executable by administrators. The PowerShell execution itself SHOULD be centrally logged and the logs monitored. The execution of PowerShell scripts SHOULD be restricted with the command Set-ExecutionPolicy AllSigned to prevent unsigned scripts from being accidentally executed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Execution Policy is set to 'AllSigned'. PowerShell logging (Module Logging, Script Block Logging, Transcription) is enabled via Group Policies. The generated logs are forwarded to a central SIEM. The interactive use of PowerShell for standard users is prevented using AppLocker or WDAC.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPOs for the Execution Policy and PowerShell logging. The AppLocker/WDAC rule for restricting PowerShell usage is checked. In the SIEM, it is verified whether PowerShell logs are received and analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: PowerShell's 'Constrained Language Mode' is enforced for all non-administrators. This severely restricts access to sensitive commands and .NET types, preventing many attack techniques, but still allows the execution of simple scripts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An AppLocker or WDAC policy is configured to enforce 'Constrained Language Mode' by only allowing Microsoft-signed scripts in Full Language Mode. All other scripts and interactive use run in restricted mode.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the AppLocker/WDAC policy. On a test client, it is checked as a standard user whether the command `$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode` returns the value 'ConstrainedLanguage'.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All PowerShell activities are not only logged, but also analyzed in real time by an EDR solution. Suspicious command chains or the use of techniques like 'Reflection' lead to an immediate security alert. All scripts required for operation are signed via a central, trusted code signing infrastructure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: PowerShell logging is integrated with an EDR solution (e.g., Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) that has special analysis and detection rules for PowerShell-based attacks. An internal PKI is used to issue a code-signing certificate with which all internally developed PowerShell scripts are signed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and detection rules in the EDR console. The process for signing scripts and the secure management of the code-signing certificate are reviewed. A test with a known 'Living off the Land' script is performed to verify detection.

controls.title: Enhanced protection of credentials under Windows

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On UEFI-based systems, Secure Boot is enabled, as it is often the manufacturer's default setting. However, there is no active monitoring or enforcement of this setting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The organization relies on the hardware's factory settings. There are no GPOs to manage or monitor security-relevant firmware settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether Secure Boot is active by running `msinfo32` or `Confirm-SecureBootUEFI` on a sample of clients. It is checked whether central controls exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On UEFI-based systems, SecureBoot SHOULD be used and the status of the protected mode for the Local Credential Store LSA SHOULD be monitored at system startup. If remote maintenance of clients via RDP is planned, the 'restrictedAdmin' option for RDP SHOULD be used when using Windows in a domain with a functional level of 2012 R2 or higher.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Secure Boot is enabled on all compatible devices. The GPO 'Configure LSA for additional protection' is enabled to harden the LSA process. For administrative RDP connections, the `/restrictedadmin` parameter is used or enforced via GPO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the activation of Secure Boot and the GPO settings for LSA protection and RDP Restricted Admin Mode. It is checked whether the use of Restricted Admin Mode is documented in the work instructions for administrators.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Windows Defender Credential Guard is enabled on all compatible systems to isolate credentials in a hardware-assisted manner using virtualization-based security (VBS). The status of Secure Boot, Credential Guard, and other VBS functions is monitored centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Credential Guard is enabled via Group Policy or Intune. A management tool like Microsoft Endpoint Manager is used to centrally monitor the security status of devices (including Secure Boot and Credential Guard) and identify non-compliant devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the GPOs for activating Credential Guard. The compliance reports in Endpoint Manager are analyzed. On a client, `msinfo32` is used to check whether 'Virtualization-based security' and 'Credential Guard' are running.

controls.title: Activation of the last access timestamp

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The last access timestamp is disabled on all systems, which is the default Windows setting to improve performance. The forensic disadvantages are accepted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No changes are made to the default configuration. The registry key `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem\NtfsDisableLastAccessUpdate` is at its default value (1 or not present).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by checking the aforementioned registry key that the last access timestamp is disabled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be checked whether the last access timestamp can be activated in the file system to facilitate the analysis of system misuse. The check SHOULD take into account possible effects of this setting, such as performance aspects or resulting restrictions for incremental backups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented assessment is performed that weighs the forensic benefits against the performance disadvantages. If the decision is positive, the timestamp is activated by setting the registry key `NtfsDisableLastAccessUpdate` to 0 via GPO. The effects on the backup system are checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the assessment documentation. If the timestamp is to be activated, the configuration of the GPO and the registry key on the clients is checked.

controls.title: Handling of remote access functions of the "Connected User Experience and Telemetry"

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be taken into account that the "Connected User Experience and Telemetry" (CUET) component allows Microsoft remote access to the local system. Such remote access to the Windows client SHOULD be logged on the network side and blocked if necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This requirement is addressed as part of the risk assessment. The network firewall is configured to log connections to known Microsoft endpoints used for diagnostics and remote maintenance (e.g., the telemetry endpoints identified as part of A4). Based on the risk assessment, these connections can also be blocked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the risk documentation that this risk has been addressed. The configuration of the firewall rules for logging and, if applicable, blocking the corresponding endpoints is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The outgoing network traffic from the clients is actively monitored to detect connection attempts by the CUET service. All detected connections are compared with a regularly updated list of known diagnostic endpoints.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Network logs are collected centrally and analyzed automatically to identify connections to Microsoft diagnostic IP ranges. A process for regularly updating these IP lists is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the log analysis reports and the process for updating the IP lists. It is checked whether alarms are generated for new, unknown connections.

controls.title: Use of Virtual Secure Mode (VSM)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When using Virtual Secure Mode (VSM), it SHOULD be considered that forensic investigations, e.g., for security incident response, are restricted or made more difficult.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When VSM-based functions such as Credential Guard are activated, this restriction is noted in the risk documentation. The Incident Response Team is informed about the forensic challenges (e.g., impossibility of creating memory dumps of LSASS).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the decision to activate VSM/Credential Guard was preceded by a risk assessment that considers the forensic limitations. It is checked whether the Incident Response Team has been informed accordingly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The incident response playbooks are adapted to include alternative investigation methods for systems on which VSM is activated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The playbooks are supplemented with sections describing which alternative data sources (e.g., EDR telemetry, extended logging) must be used when traditional methods such as memory analysis are not applicable on VSM-protected systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the Incident Response Playbooks and ensures that they contain specific instructions for VSM-protected environments. It is checked whether the IR team is trained in these adapted procedures.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
With Windows 10, Microsoft adapted its client operating system Windows to a new corporate strategy. In particular, the fundamental philosophy has also changed, away from the previous principle of the “local operating system” towards a service (“Windows as a Service”). This means that, in addition to the previous functions, the operating system also contains further, especially cloud-based, applications and is therefore dependent on a close connection to Microsoft's server infrastructure. Important new aspects compared to previous Windows versions are, above all, the deeply embedded and sometimes uncontrollable data exchange between the clients and the manufacturer's infrastructure, as well as the increasing outsourcing of security-critical core components of a Windows infrastructure (e.g. authentication) to the cloud.
With Windows 11, a successor version was released in October 2021. It contains new functions, has a revised user interface and, compared to Windows 10, significantly increased system requirements. In particular, Windows 11 officially requires a 64-bit capable CPU, UEFI SecureBoot, and a TPM 2.0. However, despite the version jump, Windows 11 is not a complete new development, but is based on Windows 10. This module is therefore applicable to both Windows 10 and Windows 11.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is the protection of information that is processed by and on Windows clients with Windows 10 or 11.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.2.2.3 Clients under Windows is to be applied to all clients on which the Microsoft Windows 10 or 11 operating system is used.
This module contains specific requirements that must be observed and fulfilled for the secure operation of clients under the Windows operating system in addition to the requirements from the module SYS.2.1 General Client. For application programs used on the Windows clients, the requirements of the corresponding modules must be fulfilled, for example APP.1.1 Office Products or APP.1.2 Web Browser. When used in a Windows domain, the requirements of the corresponding modules such as APP.2.2 Active Directory Domain Services must be fulfilled.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Malware on Windows clients
parts.prose: Due to the high prevalence of Windows operating systems and the backward compatibility that often exists between system generations to older versions, the threat from malware and unauthorized intrusion into IT systems is comparatively high for Windows.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Integrated cloud functions
parts.prose: Windows includes numerous functions with which data can be stored and synchronized using Microsoft's services (“cloud services”). This creates the risk of using them unconsciously, or at least thoughtlessly, for potentially institution-critical or personal data. In addition, users can violate data protection laws if data is stored with third parties, usually abroad. If a person logs on to a new device with an already activated Microsoft account, the Microsoft cloud services they use are automatically set up. In this way, the institution's data can be unintentionally synchronized to the employees' private devices. As a further example, Windows offers as a default setting the option of backing up the BitLocker recovery key directly via the Microsoft account in the cloud, thus placing sensitive cryptographic secrets in the hands of third parties.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Impairment of software functions due to compatibility problems
parts.prose: Software that could be successfully operated on predecessor versions of an operating system does not necessarily have to work with the current version of Windows. Possible causes are new security features or operating system properties, as well as the discontinuation of functions or services. As a result, the software cannot be used or can only be used to a limited extent. Examples of activated security features that can be the cause of possible compatibility problems with new Windows versions are User Account Control (UAC) or, for 64-bit versions of the operating system, Kernel Patch Guard. In addition, signed drivers could be necessary, which may no longer be available for older devices.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Telemetry functions of Windows
parts.prose: By default, Windows sends so-called diagnostic data to the manufacturer Microsoft. In addition, Microsoft can use the telemetry service integrated in Windows to specifically query information from a client. At the telemetry level “Full”, which is the default level in the Windows Home and Pro editions, this includes, for example, access to the client's registry and the execution of certain diagnostic tools on the client. There is a risk that the diagnostic or telemetry data contains sensitive information that can be passed on to third parties in this way.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Limited forensics when using Virtual Secure Mode (VSM)
parts.prose: The use of Virtual Secure Mode (VSM) limits or complicates forensic investigations, e.g. for security incident response. Processes protected by the Secure Kernel or Isolated User Mode (IUM) are no longer accessible. For example, memory dumps of these processes cannot be analyzed due to cryptographic measures.

controls.title: Authentication of administrators and users (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Direct login as "root" is prevented on some, but not all, clients. The use of "sudo" is not uniformly configured or enforced for all administrative tasks. The prevention of simultaneous logins by multiple users is not enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, the `/etc/shadow` file for the root account is typically edited manually (`passwd -l root`), but there is no central configuration. Sudo rules exist only sporadically and are often too broad (`ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check on a random sample of several clients whether a direct SSH login as root is possible. Check the `/etc/sudoers` file for consistency and restrictive design. Test whether multiple users can log in interactively at the same time.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Direct login as "root" is disabled system-wide on all clients. "sudo" is used for administrative tasks, but with a basic configuration. Simultaneous logins by multiple users are prevented, but the logging of sudo usage is only active with default settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SSH configuration (`/etc/ssh/sshd_config`) is adjusted on all systems to set `PermitRootLogin no`. A standard `sudoers` configuration is rolled out that gives an admin group extended rights. The maximum number of user sessions is configured, e.g., via PAM (`pam_limits.so`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the `sshd_config` on all clients for the `PermitRootLogin no` setting. Verify that a defined group for administration via `sudo` exists and is used. Check the configuration in `/etc/security/limits.conf` or equivalent files for limiting user sessions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Persons with administrative rights MUST NOT log in as "root" during normal operation. For system administration tasks, "sudo" or a suitable alternative with appropriate logging is used. It is technically prevented that multiple users can log in to a client at the same time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a clear policy that prohibits direct root login and requires the use of `sudo`. The `sudoers` file is defined and assigns granular permissions. Logging of `sudo` activities is enabled and the logs are collected. PAM modules are used to limit the number of simultaneous logins per user to one.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ensure that the policy to prohibit root login and to use `sudo` is documented. Check the `sudoers` configuration for correctness and that logging is enabled. Check the PAM configuration (`/etc/pam.d/`) to see if it effectively implements the restriction to a single user session.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The `sudo` policy is very granular and designed according to the principle of least privilege. `sudo` logs are sent to a central log management system and regularly evaluated there. Alternatives such as `Polkit` are evaluated and used for specific use cases. The prevention of multiple logins is enforced by a central configuration management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `sudoers` configuration is managed centrally (e.g., via Ansible, Puppet, or LDAP). The `sudo` logs are forwarded to a SIEM server via `syslog`. Rules for detecting anomalous `sudo` usage are implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the central `sudo` configuration management. Inspection of the central log management system to verify the collection and analysis of `sudo` logs. Checking the `Polkit` rules for correctness and security.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of `sudo` or its alternatives requires two-factor authentication (2FA). All `sudo` sessions are fully recorded (I/O logging) to ensure complete traceability. Automated systems provide real-time alerts for suspicious command executions or policy violations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM module for 2FA (e.g., `pam_google_authenticator`, `pam_u2f`) is enabled for the `sudo` service. The `sudo` plugin for I/O recording (`sudo-io`) is configured and the logs are securely archived. SIEM rules are configured to detect complex attack patterns based on `sudo` logs and I/O recordings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Testing the 2FA requirement for `sudo` commands. Checking the configuration of the `sudo-io` plugin and sampling session recordings. Verifying the SIEM alerting rules for `sudo`-related security incidents.

controls.title: Selection of a suitable distribution (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of the Linux/Unix distribution is made ad-hoc and without a formal process. The decision does not systematically consider the support period or the availability of required software in the official package repositories. Software from third-party sources is frequently installed without review.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Different teams or individuals choose different distributions based on personal preferences, leading to a heterogeneous and difficult-to-maintain landscape. There is no policy for software procurement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Inventory of the operating system distributions and versions in use. Interviewing those responsible about the selection process. Checking the installation sources of software on several clients.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An established standard distribution (e.g., Debian, Ubuntu LTS, RHEL) is selected. The selection basically considers Long-Term Support (LTS). Most applications come from the official package repositories of the distribution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An informal decision is made to use a specific LTS distribution as the standard for new clients to improve maintainability. The use of third-party sources is avoided but not formally prohibited.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether a standard distribution is predominantly in use and whether these are versions with Long-Term Support. Analysis of the package source configuration (`/etc/apt/sources.list` or `/etc/yum.repos.d/`) for the use of third-party sources.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the security requirements and the intended use, a suitable Unix derivative or Linux distribution MUST be selected. Support MUST be available for the planned operational life of the operating system. All required application programs should be directly available as part of the distribution. Distributions where the operating system itself is compiled are not permitted for productive use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented process for selecting distributions, which specifies criteria such as security, support period, and application availability. A list of approved distributions and versions is maintained. A policy explicitly prohibits the use of source-based distributions such as Gentoo in production environments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the documented selection process and the list of approved distributions. Verification that the clients in use comply with these specifications. Ensuring that no source-based distributions are used in production environments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection process is expanded to include an assessment of the distribution's security history and the vendor's response time to security vulnerabilities. A policy governs the rare exceptions for the use of software from third-party sources and requires a formal risk assessment and approval in these cases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before releasing a new distribution version, an analysis of known CVEs and the average patching time is performed. A documented exception handling process for third-party software is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the documentation on the security assessment of distributions. Audit of the exception handling process and the associated risk assessments for installed third-party software.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selected distribution is a specially hardened enterprise version or a security-focused distribution, if suitable for the use case. The selection process is regularly reviewed and updated. A central software inventory tracks all installed packages and their sources to ensure policy compliance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Distributions such as RHEL with CIS hardening or Qubes OS for high-security workstations are used. An automated inventory tool (e.g., based on osquery) continuously records all installed packages and checks the sources against a positive list.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the justification for selecting the hardened distribution. Inspection of the data from the central software inventory and review of the compliance reports regarding package sources.

controls.title: Kernel updates on Unix-like systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Kernel updates are installed, but system reboots are performed irregularly or with long delays. This leaves the systems vulnerable for extended periods, even though the patch is already installed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The responsibility for rebooting lies solely with the user, who ignores the system prompts. There is no monitoring to track the reboot status.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: On a client, compare the installed kernel version (`dpkg -l | grep linux-image` or `rpm -qa | grep kernel`) with the running kernel version (`uname -r`). A significant discrepancy indicates a pending reboot.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a manual process to reboot clients after kernel updates. The process relies on instructions to users or administrators to perform reboots promptly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After rolling out kernel updates, an email is sent to all users requesting them to restart their computers. Compliance is not systematically checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing users and administrators about the process for reboots after kernel updates. Spot-checking clients for pending reboots.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The client MUST be rebooted promptly after the operating system's kernel has been updated. If this is not possible, kernel live patching MUST be enabled as an alternative.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy requires that clients must be rebooted within a defined time window (e.g., 48 hours) after a kernel update. This process is monitored (e.g., by scripts that check the reboot status). For critical systems where a reboot is not possible, a live patching solution like KernelCare or Ksplice is implemented and configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the reboot policy. Examination of the monitoring reports on the reboot status of clients. For systems without reboot: review of the configuration and status of the live patching service (e.g., `kcare-uname -r` or `uptrack-uname -r`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reboot process is automated. Users are automatically informed about a pending reboot and given a grace period, after which the reboot is forced. The status of kernel versions and pending reboots is centrally recorded and monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible) or a script on the clients checks daily for pending reboots. If necessary, the user is informed via a pop-up window. After a deadline expires, the reboot is triggered automatically. A central dashboard shows the patch and reboot status of the entire client fleet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of the automated reboot management. Inspection of the central dashboard for monitoring the reboot status. Verification of the notification and enforcement process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully automated patch management system manages the entire lifecycle of kernel updates, including the subsequent reboot, for the entire client fleet. Live patching is systematically used for all critical systems to minimize downtime, and the effectiveness of live patches is regularly reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated patch management tool such as Foreman/Katello, Uyuni, or a commercial product is used. This tool controls the distribution of updates, live patching, and orchestrated reboots. Regular scans ensure that all systems have the desired patch level and all live patches have been applied correctly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of the central patch management system. Inspection of the system's compliance reports, which document the patch level, live patch status, and reboot status of the clients. Review of the process documentation for patch management.

controls.title: Secure installation of software packages (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Software from source code is occasionally compiled directly with root privileges. The installation is done by a direct call to `make install`, which leads to an uncontrolled distribution of files on the system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Developers or administrators download source code and run `configure && make && sudo make install` directly in the home directory or in `/tmp`. There is no documentation about the installed files.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the process history (`history`) of administrators for the use of `sudo make install`. Searching for manually installed files in directories like `/usr/local/bin`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrators are instructed to always compile software as a non-privileged user. The installation is still done via `sudo make install`, but the compilation process itself runs without elevated privileges.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an internal instruction or a wiki that describes the process `tar xf software.tar.gz && cd software && ./configure && make && sudo make install` to ensure compilation as a normal user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing administrators about the compilation process. Checking file permissions in the build directory to ensure they do not belong to root.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If software to be installed is to be compiled from source code, it MUST ONLY be unpacked, configured, and translated under an unprivileged account. Subsequently, the software to be installed MUST NOT be installed uncontrolled into the operating system's root filesystem. The selected parameters and installation steps are documented appropriately.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a strict policy that requires compiling as an unprivileged user. Instead of `sudo make install`, a staging directory is used (e.g., `make DESTDIR=/tmp/staging install`). From this directory, a native system package (e.g., `.deb` or `.rpm`) is created using tools like `fpm` or `checkinstall`. This package is then installed via the package manager. The build scripts and selected options are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the policy for software installation from source code. Verification that no software is installed outside of the package management (e.g., `dpkg -S /usr/local/bin/somefile` should return no match). Checking the documentation of the build processes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for creating a system package from source code is standardized and supported by templates. All compilation parameters and installation steps are fully documented to ensure exact reproducibility. The created packages are stored in an internal repository.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Templates for `debian/rules` or `.spec` files are provided. The created packages are stored and signed in an internal package repository (e.g., with `reprepro` for Debian or `createrepo` for RPM-based).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the templates and the process documentation for package creation. Checking the internal repository and the packages and their signatures contained therein.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated, automated build system (e.g., a private PPA, Jenkins pipeline, or Open Build Service) is used to compile software from source code and generate signed packages. It is ensured that no software is ever compiled directly on a production client. All installations are done exclusively via the package manager from trusted, internal repositories.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Open Build Service (OBS) or a Jenkins CI/CD pipeline is set up, which automatically checks out the source code upon a code commit, builds it in a clean environment, creates a package, signs it, and uploads it to the internal repository. The package sources on the clients are configured to use only these internal repositories.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of the automated build system. Tracking a software build from source code to the finished package in the repository. Review of the package source configuration on the clients to ensure that only authorized repositories are used.

controls.title: No automatic mounting of removable drives (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On some systems, automatic mounting of removable drives (automount) is disabled, but this is not implemented across the board. The `noexec` mount option is not used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Individual users or administrators manually disable automount in their desktop environment settings, but there is no central policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Plugging a USB drive into various clients and observing whether it is mounted automatically. Checking the mount options (`mount | grep /media`) after manual mounting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automatic mounting of removable drives is disabled system-wide. Users must mount drives manually. However, the `noexec` option is not enforced by default.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The automount function of the desktop environment is centrally disabled, e.g., via GSettings for GNOME or a corresponding configuration file. Users must use the file manager or the command line to explicitly mount a drive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the central configuration for disabling automount (e.g., using `gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.media-handling automount`). Plugging in a USB drive to confirm the deactivation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Removable drives are NOT automatically mounted. The mounting of removable drives is configured so that all files are marked as non-executable (mount option "noexec").

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Automount is disabled. Additionally, a `udev` rule is created that ensures that any removable drive manually mounted by a user is mounted by default with the `noexec` option. This is often achieved via UDisks2 configurations in `/etc/udisks2/mount_options.conf`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verification that automount is disabled. Manually mounting a removable drive and then checking the active mount options with `mount | grep <device>` for the presence of `noexec`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the `noexec` option, the mount options `nodev` (do not interpret character or block special devices) and `nosuid` (ignore SUID/SGID bits) are enforced for all removable drives. This configuration is centrally managed and enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration file (`/etc/udisks2/mount_options.conf` or `udev` rules) is extended to enforce `noexec,nosuid,nodev`. This configuration file is distributed to all clients via a configuration management tool (Ansible, Puppet) and its integrity is monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the mount options after mounting a removable drive for the presence of `noexec`, `nosuid`, and `nodev`. Checking the configuration management software for the correct distribution of the configuration file.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware-level controls such as `usbguard` are used to generally prevent the use of removable drives. Only explicitly approved and encrypted devices may be used. When these authorized devices are mounted, all relevant security options (`noexec`, `nosuid`, `nodev`) are enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: `usbguard` is configured with a `Deny` default rule. A whitelist contains the hardware IDs of the allowed USB devices. This configuration is centrally managed. Attempts to connect unauthorized devices are logged and trigger an alarm.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the `usbguard` configuration and rules. Attempting to connect an unauthorized USB device and verifying that access is blocked and a log entry or alarm is generated. Connecting an authorized device and checking the mount options.

controls.title: Restrictive permission assignment on files and directories (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The sticky bit is set on `/tmp`, but the file permissions for services and applications are often left at their default settings. Services sometimes run under shared or overly privileged accounts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Most distributions set the sticky bit on `/tmp` by default. However, when installing new services, no attention is paid to whether they run with their own, unprivileged user or whether their data directories have correct permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check with `ls -ld /tmp` if the sticky bit (t) is set. Check with `ps aux` the user accounts under which various services are running. Random check of directory permissions in `/var/lib`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The sticky bit is checked and set on all globally writable directories such as `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`. When installing services, it is ensured that they run under their own user account. The file permissions are set correctly during installation but are not continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A basic installation script or a checklist ensures that `chmod 1777` is applied to `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`. When a package is installed, it is verified that a specific user is created (e.g., `useradd -r -s /bin/false <service>`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the permissions of `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and `/dev/shm`. For important services, verify that they run under a dedicated, unprivileged user and that their data directories belong to this user.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is ensured that services and applications may only create, modify, or delete the files assigned to them. On directories where all accounts have write permissions (e.g., “/tmp”), the sticky bit is set.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy for file system permissions based on the principle of least privilege is defined and implemented. Each service runs with its own user account and can only write in the directories assigned to it. The sticky bit is set on all relevant directories and this configuration is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the permission assignment policy. Checking the implementation of this policy on a reference client. This includes checking service users, file ownership and permissions in `/etc`, `/var` and `/run` as well as the sticky bit on `/tmp` & co.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A configuration baseline for file permissions and ownership is established. This baseline is periodically checked by scripts or auditing tools. Deviations from the baseline are reported and corrected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool (Ansible, Puppet) is used to define file permissions and regularly check for deviations in `--check` mode. Alternatively, a shell script is run as a cron job, which checks the permissions of critical files and directories and creates a report.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configuration of the auditing tool or script. Reviewing the audit reports and checking how reported deviations were handled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) system such as AIDE or Tripwire is used to continuously and automatically monitor critical system files, directories, and service-specific files for unauthorized changes to permissions, ownership, or content. Deviations trigger an alarm immediately.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: AIDE is configured to create an initial database of the file system. A daily cron job runs `aide --check` and sends the report to a central management system. Any change (except for expected log rotations, etc.) is forwarded to the SIEM system for alerting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the AIDE configuration (`/etc/aide/aide.conf`) for completeness of the monitored areas. Checking the cron job configuration. Test-wise changing a monitored file and checking whether the FIM check detects the change and an alarm is triggered.

controls.title: Use of techniques to restrict application permissions (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AppArmor or SELinux is installed, but runs in permissive mode (Complain/Permissive) for most services. Only a few profiles, activated by default by the system, are in enforcing mode (Enforce).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrator has not disabled SELinux, but has set it to `permissive` to avoid application problems. Log entries about violations are ignored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the global status of the MAC system. For SELinux: `getenforce`. For AppArmor: `aa-status`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AppArmor or SELinux is active and running in enforcing mode. The default policies provided by the distribution for important system services are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SELinux is operated in `enforcing` mode with the `targeted` policy. For AppArmor, the profiles supplied with the distribution are loaded and activated. No custom profiles are created.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check if the MAC system is running in enforcing mode (`getenforce` or `aa-status`). Check which profiles/domains are active and whether they cover the critical services.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AppArmor or SELinux is used to restrict application access to files, devices, and networks. The solutions best supported by the respective Unix derivative or Linux distribution are used. Rights are fundamentally withdrawn according to the deny-by-default principle and explicitly granted where necessary via whitelists. The access restriction runs in enforcing mode.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MAC system intended for the distribution (e.g., AppArmor for Debian/Ubuntu, SELinux for RHEL/Fedora) is consistently operated in enforcing mode. The policies are designed to deny everything by default and only allow explicitly necessary access. This applies to all network-exposed services.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verify that the MAC system is in enforcing mode. Randomly check policies for important services (e.g., web server, DNS server) to ensure they follow the whitelist principle and are not overly permissive. Check the audit logs (`/var/log/audit/audit.log` or `dmesg`) for violations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For internally developed or third-party applications that are delivered without their own policy, custom AppArmor or SELinux profiles are actively developed. Logs of policy violations are sent to a central server and regularly evaluated there.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like `aa-genprof` (AppArmor) or `audit2allow` (SELinux) are used to create base profiles for new applications. These are then manually reviewed and hardened. Audit logs are forwarded to a central SIEM via `auditd` or `rsyslog`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of self-created MAC profiles for their quality and restrictiveness. Inspection of the central log system to verify the collection and evaluation of MAC violations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: MAC policies are very granular and are managed and distributed via a central configuration management system. An automated system analyzes logs, suggests policy improvements, and provides real-time alerts for significant or repeated violations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SELinux policy modules or AppArmor profiles are managed as part of Ansible/Puppet roles. A SIEM system correlates MAC violation logs with other events and uses machine learning to detect anomalous behavior that could indicate an attack despite an active MAC policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the process for managing and distributing MAC policies in the configuration management. Verification of the SIEM rules and dashboards for analyzing MAC events. Simulation of a policy violation and checking the entire alerting chain.

controls.title: Secure use of passwords on the command line (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users and administrators occasionally pass passwords as command-line parameters, especially in quickly created scripts. This causes passwords to appear in plain text in process lists and shell histories.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A typical example is `mysql -u user -pMyPassword` in a cron job script. There is no awareness of the associated risk.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Search the shell histories of users (`.bash_history`) and the system cron files (`/etc/crontab`, `/etc/cron.*`) for commands that contain passwords as arguments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal policy or recommendation for developers and administrators to avoid passing passwords on the command line.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In an internal wiki or during introductions, it is pointed out that passwords should not be used on the command line. Instead, alternatives such as interactive prompts or configuration files are recommended.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviewing administrators and developers about their handling of passwords in scripts. Random checking of new or recently changed scripts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Passwords are NOT passed as parameters to programs. There is a strict policy that prohibits this. Secure alternatives such as interactive password prompts, the use of password files with restrictive permissions, or (to be used with caution) environment variables are prescribed and documented as replacements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is known to all relevant employees. For services like MySQL, configuration files (`~/.my.cnf`) with the access data and restrictive permissions (`chmod 600`) are used. In scripts, `read -s` or similar constructs are used for interactive prompts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the corresponding policy. Checking scripts executed by services or cron jobs for compliance with the policy. Checking the permissions of configuration files containing passwords.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Scripts and applications are regularly audited for violations of the password policy. Static code analysis tools are used to detect passwords in scripts and configuration files. Secure credential management systems are recommended and integrated where possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like `gitleaks` or `truffleHog` are integrated into CI/CD pipelines to scan code repositories for hard-coded secrets. It is recommended to manage credentials using systems like HashiCorp Vault or KeePass.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration and results of the static analysis tools. Checking the extent to which recommendations for the use of credential management systems are implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A system-wide process monitoring is configured to actively scan process lists (`ps`) for arguments that look like passwords and triggers an alarm if one is found. All credentials used by applications and scripts are managed exclusively via a central, secure credential store (e.g., HashiCorp Vault) and retrieved at runtime.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An audit daemon (`auditd`) is configured with rules that monitor system calls like `execve` and log the arguments. These logs are analyzed in real time. Applications are rewritten to retrieve their secrets from a vault server via an API instead of storing them in configuration files.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Reviewing the configuration of the audit daemon and the analysis rules. Verifying that critical applications retrieve their secrets from the central credential store. Attempting to pass a password on the command line and checking if an alarm is triggered.

controls.title: Preventing local disk overload (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system uses a single large partition for the root directory (`/`). No quotas or other mechanisms are in place to limit disk space consumption. A single user or a faulty process can fill up the entire disk and bring the system to a halt.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During installation, the default option "Guided partitioning - use entire disk" is selected without further adjustments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Run the `df -h` command to check the partitioning structure. The presence of only one `/` partition indicates this state.

parts.name: statement
