parts.prose: Separate partitions are used for important directories such as `/home`, `/var`, and `/tmp`. This provides basic protection against a user or a log file filling up the root file system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During system installation, manual partitioning is performed to create separate partitions for the specified directories. This isolates the growth of user data and log files from the operating system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check with `df -h` or `lsblk` whether separate partitions exist for `/home`, `/var`, and `/tmp`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Quotas are set up for accounts or services, leaving sufficient free space for the operating system. Generally, different partitions are used for the operating system and data. Alternatively, mechanisms of the file system in use are utilized, which grant write permissions only to the "root" account once a suitable fill level is reached.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to separate partitioning, file system quotas (user/group quotas) are enabled for `/home` to limit storage consumption per user. Alternatively, the amount of space reserved for root on file systems like ext4 (`tune2fs -m`) is set to a reasonable value to ensure that the system remains administrable even with a full partition.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check if quotas are enabled (`/etc/fstab` for `usrquota`, `grpquota` and run `repquota -a`). Alternatively, check the percentage of space reserved for root with `tune2fs -l <device>`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Quotas are actively monitored. Automated notifications are sent to users and administrators when storage consumption reaches defined thresholds (soft limits).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cron job regularly runs `quotacheck` and `warnquota`. `warnquota` is configured to send emails to users who have exceeded their soft limits. Administrators receive reports on the quota status.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Checking the configuration of the quota warning system (e.g., `/etc/warnquota.conf`) and the associated cron jobs. Checking the log files to determine if notifications are being sent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive solution for disk space management is implemented. This includes granular quotas, automated monitoring and alerting, as well as automated cleanup routines for temporary directories. Logical Volume Management (LVM) is used to enable flexible, on-demand resizing of partitions during operation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The entire system is built on LVM. A monitoring system (e.g., Prometheus with Node Exporter) monitors the fill level of the logical volumes and quotas in real time and alerts proactively. Scripts that run via `systemd-tmpfiles` or cron jobs regularly clean up old files in `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check with `lsblk` and `vgs`/`lvs` if LVM is used. Review the configuration of the monitoring system (e.g., Prometheus alerting rules). Check the configuration of the automated cleanup services (`/etc/tmpfiles.d/`).

controls.title: Secure use of appliances (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Appliances are put into operation with their default configurations and without a formal security assessment. Default passwords may not be changed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A new network appliance is unpacked, connected to the network, and configured with the default credentials found in the manual.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Inventory of the deployed appliances. Attempt to log in to the appliances with known default credentials. Review of the configuration for insecure default settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before commissioning an appliance, a basic security check is carried out. This involves changing default passwords and deactivating obviously unnecessary services.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a simple commissioning checklist for appliances that includes items like "Change password" and "Deactivate SNMP with public/private community."

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the commissioning checklist. Random checks of appliances to see if the points on the checklist (e.g., changed passwords) have been implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is ensured that appliances meet a similar level of security as clients on standard IT systems. It is documented how corresponding security requirements are met with a deployed appliance. If the requirements cannot be met without a doubt, a declaration of conformity is requested from the manufacturing company.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before procurement, the appliance is evaluated against internal security policies for clients. A configuration matrix (or a similar document) is created that maps each security requirement to a specific appliance setting. In case of ambiguities, the manufacturer is contacted to request written confirmation (e.g., a Common Criteria certification or a CAIQ document).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the evaluation documentation and the configuration matrix for a deployed appliance. Review of the declarations of conformity requested from the manufacturer. Comparison of the documented configuration with the actual configuration of the appliance.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal procurement process includes a mandatory security assessment of each appliance. The manufacturer must provide detailed security documentation, such as a hardening guide and information on its vulnerability management process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security department is an integral part of the procurement process for IT products. Manufacturers must complete a standardized security questionnaire. The availability of a hardening guide and a transparent process for publishing security advisories are knock-out criteria.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the process documentation for procurement. Review of the completed security questionnaires and the manufacturer documentation provided for recently procured appliances.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Appliances are subjected to an independent penetration test before being deployed in critical environments. They are fully integrated into central security monitoring, logging, and patch management, just like any standard client.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The appliance is placed in a test network and tested for vulnerabilities by internal or external testers. The appliance's syslog and SNMP outputs are sent to the central SIEM system. The appliance is added to the central patch management system to ensure the firmware is up to date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the penetration test reports. Review of the configuration in the SIEM system and in the patch management system to verify the complete integration of the appliance.

controls.title: Protection against the use of unauthorized peripheral devices (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unneeded kernel modules for common but unwanted device classes (e.g., Firewire, Bluetooth, Thunderbolt) are prevented from loading via a blacklist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration file is created in `/etc/modprobe.d/` containing entries like `blacklist firewire_core` or `blacklist bluetooth` to prevent these modules from loading automatically.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the files in `/etc/modprobe.d/` for corresponding blacklist entries. Try to connect a device of the blocked class and check with `lsmod` if the module was loaded.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Peripheral devices can only be used if they are explicitly approved. Kernel modules for peripheral devices are only loaded and activated if the device is approved. This is implemented by a device control tool with a default-deny policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like `usbguard` is installed and configured to block all new USB devices by default (`default-deny`). A whitelist (`rules.conf`) is maintained that explicitly authorizes the allowed devices (e.g., based on hardware ID).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the `usbguard` service configuration and the `rules.conf` file. Try to connect an unauthorized USB device and verify that it is blocked. Connect an authorized device and verify that it works.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The device control policies are centrally managed and distributed to all clients. The policies are granular and can restrict the approval of certain devices to specific users or groups. Attempts to connect unauthorized devices are centrally logged and trigger an alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `usbguard` rule files are managed via a configuration management tool (Ansible, Puppet). The `usbguard` logs are sent to a central SIEM system where alerting rules for `block` events are configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration in the central management tool. Inspection of the central logs and SIEM rules. Simulation of a violation and verification of the alerting chain.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to device control at the USB level, the loading of kernel modules is further restricted. A kernel lockdown mechanism or the signing of kernel modules is used to prevent an unauthorized kernel module from being loaded. This provides robust protection against physical and software-based attacks on the kernel space.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Secure Boot is enabled and the kernel is operated in lockdown mode (`integrity` or `confidentiality`). Alternatively, only kernel modules signed with a trusted key are permitted. Any required third-party module must be manually signed and added to the UEFI key store.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check if lockdown mode is active with `cat /sys/kernel/security/lockdown`. Check the kernel configuration for `CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE=y`. Try to load an unsigned kernel module (`insmod`) and verify that this fails.

controls.title: Additional protection against the execution of unwanted files (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The partition on which the `/tmp` directory is located is mounted with the `noexec` mount option to prevent the execution of files from this directory.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In `/etc/fstab`, the entry for the `/tmp` partition is supplemented with the `noexec` option.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the active mount options for the `/tmp` partition with `mount | grep /tmp`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Partitions and directories where users have write permissions are mounted in such a way that no files can be executed (mount option 'noexec'). This includes `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and all user home directories.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In `/etc/fstab`, the `noexec` mount option is set for the partitions containing `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and `/home`. If `/home` is not on its own partition, this measure can be more difficult to implement for home directories.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the `/etc/fstab` and the output of `mount` for all relevant partitions (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/home` or `/dev/shm`) for the `noexec` option.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The `fstab` configuration, which enforces `noexec` on user-writable partitions, is centrally managed and monitored by a configuration management system to prevent tampering. In addition to `noexec`, the `nosuid` and `nodev` options are also applied to these partitions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool like Ansible ensures that `/etc/fstab` on all clients contains the correct entries (`defaults,noexec,nosuid,nodev`) and reports deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration management code for `fstab` management. Manual check of the `mount` output on a client to verify the implementation of all three options (`noexec`, `nosuid`, `nodev`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the mount options, an allow-listing solution for application control is implemented. This prevents the execution of any binaries not on an explicit allow list, regardless of their location or permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system based on `fanotify` or `fs-verity` is used. Alternatively, a commercial application whitelisting solution can be used. An allow list of all permitted executable files (including their hashes) is created and enforced on the systems. Any attempt to execute a non-listed file is blocked and reported.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the configuration of the allow-listing solution and its corresponding allow list. Attempt to execute an unauthorized program (e.g., a self-compiled 'Hello World') from the home directory and verify that the execution is blocked.

controls.title: Additional prevention of lateral movement when exploiting vulnerabilities (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The default profiles supplied with AppArmor or SELinux for exposed services are reviewed to ensure they are sufficiently restrictive and are operated in enforcing mode.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before commissioning a service with network exposure (e.g., a web server), the associated MAC profile (e.g., `/etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.apache2`) is manually reviewed to identify and remove superfluous permissions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Inspection of the MAC profiles of network-exposed services and comparison with the actually required functionality. Review of the audit logs for violations that indicate overly restrictive or incorrect rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of system calls is restricted to the absolute minimum necessary, especially for exposed services and applications, by using `seccomp-bpf` filters. Existing MAC profiles are manually reviewed and adapted to the company's own security policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: `seccomp` filters are enabled for critical services such as web browsers, container runtimes, or exposed daemons. This is often done via the service's own configuration (e.g., in `systemd` unit files with `SystemCallFilter=`). Existing AppArmor/SELinux profiles are actively hardened by commenting out or removing unneeded rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the `systemd` unit files or the application configuration for the activation of `seccomp` filters. Comparison of the active MAC profiles with the distribution standards to identify any hardening that has been carried out. Review of the audit logs for `seccomp` violations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A systematic process is established for developing and maintaining highly restrictive `seccomp` filters and MAC profiles for all exposed services. Tools are used to automatically create base profiles by analyzing application behavior in a test environment, which are then manually reviewed and hardened before deployment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like `strace` are used to log the system calls used by an application. A `seccomp` allow list is generated from this. For AppArmor/SELinux, learning tools (`aa-genprof`, `audit2allow`) are used in a dedicated test environment to create the tightest possible profile. This process is part of the deployment workflow for new application versions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the process documentation for profile creation. Inspection of the generated and manually hardened `seccomp` and MAC profiles. Verification that this process is applied during application updates.

controls.title: Additional protection of the kernel (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Standard kernel hardening options available in the distribution's default kernel are enabled via `sysctl` settings. This includes basic protection against information leaks and unauthorized access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration file in `/etc/sysctl.d/` is created that sets hardened settings, such as `kernel.kptr_restrict=1`, `kernel.dmesg_restrict=1`, `net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1`, and `vm.mmap_rnd_bits=32`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration files in `/etc/sysctl.d/`. Run `sysctl -a` and compare the active values with the defined hardening settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A specially hardened kernel provided by the distribution (e.g., `linux-hardened`) or a self-compiled kernel is used. This enables advanced security features such as stronger Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), protection against control-flow manipulation, and other compile-time hardenings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of the standard kernel, a hardened kernel package from the distribution's repositories is installed (if available). Alternatively, the kernel itself is compiled with security-relevant options such as `CONFIG_GCC_PLUGIN_STACKLEAK` or `CONFIG_SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED`.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check which kernel is being used with `uname -a` and compare this with the available hardened versions. Check the kernel configuration file (`/boot/config-<version>`) for the presence of specific hardening options.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A kernel with advanced proactive protection mechanisms such as `grsecurity`/`PaX` is used. This implements comprehensive protection measures against memory corruption, file system manipulation, and unauthorized access through role-based access control (RBAC) at the kernel level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A commercial `grsecurity` kernel is licensed and installed on the clients. The extensive configuration options of `grsecurity` (e.g., RBAC rules) are carefully adapted to the client's use case to ensure maximum security while maintaining functionality.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check with `uname -a` or specific tools from `grsecurity` whether the hardened kernel is active. Perform a review of the `grsecurity` policies to assess their restrictiveness and correctness. Attempt to run typical memory corruption exploits in a test environment to demonstrate the effectiveness of the protection.

controls.title: Hard disk or file encryption (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users' home directories are encrypted with a standard mechanism such as `ecryptfs` or `fscrypt`. This protects user data at rest as long as the user is not logged in.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When creating a user, the option to encrypt the home directory is enabled. This is a standard feature of many Linux distributions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check if an encrypted directory (e.g., `~/.ecryptfs` or `~/.Private`) exists. Run `mount` to see if an ecryptfs or fscrypt file system is mounted for the home directory.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Full Disk Encryption (FDE) with LUKS/dm-crypt is implemented for the entire system, including the operating system and all user data. The decryption passphrase is not stored on the hard drive and must be entered at system startup.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During system installation, the option for full disk encryption with LUKS is selected. This creates an encrypted LVM group in which all system partitions are located.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check with `lsblk -f` if the partitions have the file system type `crypto_LUKS`. Restart the system and verify that a passphrase is required before the operating system boots.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Disk encryption is implemented using an AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) scheme such as AES-GCM. The decryption key is protected by a hardware security module (TPM). The TPM only releases the key if the integrity of the boot process (via Secure Boot) has been verified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: LUKS2 is configured with an AEAD cipher. The key is stored in a TPM-secured key slot. The `systemd-cryptenroll` command is used to bind the volume to the system's TPM. Secure Boot is enabled in the UEFI.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the used algorithms and cipher modes with `cryptsetup luksDump <device>`. Check the binding to the TPM with `systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=list`. Verify in the UEFI that Secure Boot is active. The system should boot without a passphrase prompt as long as the boot chain is intact.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to FDE with AEAD ciphers and TPM integration, `dm-verity` is used on read-only partitions like `/usr`. This prevents offline manipulation of system files. Keys are managed centrally, e.g., through Network Bound Disk Encryption (NBDE), to enable automatic unlocking in trusted networks, while a passphrase is still required for offline access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An NBDE system like Clevis/Tang is set up. The LUKS container is configured to unlock automatically when the Tang server is reachable on the network. The `/usr` partition is set up as a read-only `dm-verity` volume whose hash tree is verified at every boot.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verification of the Clevis/Tang configuration on the client and server. Testing the boot behavior inside and outside the trusted network. Checking the `dm-verity` configuration with `dmsetup table` and `veritysetup status`.

controls.title: Disabling critical SysRq functions (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SysRq functionality is completely disabled if it is not absolutely necessary for operation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a `sysctl` configuration file (`/etc/sysctl.d/`), the value `kernel.sysrq = 0` is set.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the active value with `sysctl kernel.sysrq` or `cat /proc/sys/kernel/sysrq`. The value should be `0`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is defined which SysRq functions may be executed by users. In general, no critical SysRq functions can be triggered by users. The kernel is configured to allow only a limited, non-critical set of SysRq functions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy defines the permitted SysRq functions. The value of `kernel.sysrq` is set to a bitmask that only allows non-critical actions such as `sync` (16), `unmount` (32), and `reboot` (128). A value of `176` (128+32+16) would be an example. Critical functions like `SAK` (2) or `crash` (4) are disabled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the SysRq policy. Checking the value of `kernel.sysrq` and comparing it with the defined bitmask. Ensuring that the enabled functions can be classified as non-critical.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of permitted SysRq functions is centrally managed via a configuration management tool and enforced on all clients to ensure a consistent and tamper-proof setting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool like Ansible or Puppet is used to distribute the `sysctl` configuration file with the correct `kernel.sysrq` value to all systems and to regularly check for compliance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the code in the configuration management tool that sets the `kernel.sysrq` value. Checking the tool's compliance reports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the physical or virtual console, through which SysRq commands could be issued, is strictly controlled and audited. The kernel is configured to send all invoked SysRq events to a central log server for security monitoring.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Physical access to the clients is secured. Access to virtual consoles (e.g., for VMs) is restricted to a few administrators and is logged. `rsyslog` is configured to forward kernel messages (including SysRq calls) to a central SIEM, where corresponding analysis and alerting rules exist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of physical and logical access controls for the system console. Inspection of the `rsyslog` configuration and the rules in the SIEM. Triggering an allowed SysRq function and verifying that the event is logged centrally.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
In addition to Windows, Linux-based or, less frequently, Unix-based operating systems are being installed on more and more clients. Examples of classic Unix systems are the BSD series (FreeBSD, OpenBSD, and NetBSD), Solaris, and AIX. Linux, on the other hand, does not refer to a classic, but a functional Unix system, as the Linux kernel is not based on the original source code from which the various Unix derivatives were developed. Since the configuration and operation of Linux and Unix clients are similar, this module linguistically groups Linux and Unix together as "Unix client" or "Unix-like".
Linux is free software developed by the open-source community. This means that it can be freely used, copied, distributed, and modified. There are also companies that bundle and maintain the Linux kernel and the various software components into a distribution and offer other services. Derivatives of the Debian, Fedora / Red Hat Enterprise Linux, or openSUSE / SUSE Linux Enterprise distributions are frequently used. In addition, there are Linux distributions tailored for special purposes and devices. These include, for example, Qubes OS, which attempts to achieve a high level of security through virtualization, LibreElec for use on a Home Theater PC (HTPC), or Kali Linux, a distribution specializing in security, computer forensics, and penetration testing. Clients can also boot live distributions without changing the operating system installed on the client. The market share of the Linux operating system on clients has increased in recent years. In special operating environments, "classic" Unix systems in various derivatives continue to be used. Typically, such an IT system is networked and operated as a client in a client-server network.
The number of pre-selected software packages in a standard installation of common Linux distributions or Unix derivatives increases the attack surface. At the same time, however, Unix-like operating systems also offer extensive protection mechanisms.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is to protect information that is created, edited, stored, or sent on Linux and Unix clients. The requirements of the module apply primarily to Linux clients, but can generally be adapted for Unix clients.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.2.3 Clients under Linux and Unix must be applied to all clients on which Linux or Unix-based operating systems are used.
This module contains fundamental requirements for the operation of Unix-like clients. It specifies and supplements the aspects covered in module SYS.2.1 General Client with the special features of Unix systems. Accordingly, the two modules must always be applied together.
Although Apple's macOS is a Unix-like operating system, this operating system is not covered in this module. Recommendations for this can be found in module SYS.2.4 Clients under macOS.
The module only covers the actual operating system that is usually installed during a basic installation of a distribution. Software built on top of it, such as email clients or office software, is not considered in this module. Requirements for this can be found, for example, in the modules of the APP.1 Client Applications layer of the IT-Grundschutz Compendium.
This client module assumes that, in addition to administrators, only one unchanged person is permanently active with an interactive account. Clients that are used by multiple people sequentially or simultaneously require additional measures that are not covered in this module.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Software from third-party sources
parts.prose: On Unix-like IT systems, it is common for users to download and compile software source code themselves instead of installing ready-made software packages. If ready-made software packages are used, they are in some cases also installed from third-party sources without further checks, instead of exclusively from the vendor's existing package repositories. Each of these alternative ways of software installation carries additional risks, as it can lead to the installation of faulty or incompatible software as well as malware.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Exploitability of the scripting environment
parts.prose: Scripting languages are often used in Unix-like operating systems. Scripts are a list of individual commands that are stored in a text file and, for example, called up in the command line. Due to the large functional scope of scripting environments, attackers can extensively misuse scripts for their purposes. In addition, activated scripting languages are very difficult to contain.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Dynamic loading of shared libraries
parts.prose: With the command line option LD_PRELOAD, a dynamic library is loaded before all other standard libraries required in an application. This makes it possible to overwrite individual functions of the standard libraries with your own. For example, attackers could manipulate the operating system in such a way that malicious functions are also executed when certain applications are used.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Incorrect configuration
parts.prose:
Even in a standard installation, numerous applications are installed on Unix-like operating systems that must be configured separately. Post-installed applications must also be configured separately, so that countless configuration files are eventually located on the operating system.
Since many applications are configured independently of each other, the configuration options can contradict each other without this being apparent from the individual settings. For example, a remote administration service could be listening on a port that is blocked by packet filter rules. In this way, the applications can provide additional functions that are not desired, or not offer important functions. This can lead to certain tasks on the client being made more difficult or not being fulfilled at all.

controls.title: Planning the secure deployment of macOS (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The introduction of macOS clients is done ad hoc, without a comprehensive plan. Decisions about data storage, backups, or necessary applications are made on a case-by-case basis and are inconsistent.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In practice, this means that individual employees or departments procure and set up Macs at their own discretion. There is no central directive on whether data should be stored locally, on a network drive, or in a cloud.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by interviewing IT staff and sampling macOS users that no planning documents for the deployment of macOS exist. The configurations of the clients vary considerably.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic, informal checklist exists for the introduction of macOS clients. It covers the most important points such as data storage, backup, and update procedures, but is not formally documented or enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IT administrator uses a personal checklist to ensure that the same basic steps are performed for every new Mac installation. However, this checklist is not part of an official process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews, the auditor identifies a recurring procedure for setting up macOS clients. However, no formal planning documents or policies can be presented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The introduction of macOS MUST be carefully planned. It MUST be decided where and how data is stored. It MUST be planned how data backup can be integrated into the institution-wide data backup concept. It MUST be planned how security and other updates for macOS and applications can be installed systematically. It MUST be determined which applications are needed when switching platforms to macOS. If the Mac is operated in a data network, it MUST also be considered which network protocols are to be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A planning document is created that serves as a guide for every macOS deployment. This document specifies that user data must be stored on a central, secure file server and that Time Machine backups are stored on a dedicated network drive. A list of approved applications and permitted network protocols (e.g., SMB instead of AFP) is maintained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning document for the deployment of macOS and compares its specifications with the configuration of several clients. It is checked whether the data storage, backup solution, and installed applications comply with the documented specifications.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The plan for macOS deployment is reviewed and updated annually or for major macOS releases. It contains specific configuration requirements for different user groups (e.g., standard, developers, management). The selection of network protocols is based on a documented security assessment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The deployment plan is implemented as a configuration profile in a Mobile Device Management (MDM) system. New devices are automatically configured with the profile appropriate for their user group. Changes to the configuration are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and revision status of the deployment plan. It is checked whether the configuration profiles stored in the MDM comply with the plan's specifications and whether the assigned profiles correspond to the users' roles.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of a macOS client, from procurement through operation to decommissioning, is planned and integrated into the central ISMS. Compliance with configuration specifications is monitored automatically. Application and protocol whitelists are technically enforced by a central management system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM system, coupled with an endpoint security tool, ensures policy enforcement. Any deviation from the target configuration (e.g., installation of unauthorized software) leads to an automatic alert and, if necessary, to the network quarantine of the device. The planning is part of the annual management review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports from the MDM and endpoint security system to verify the continuous compliance of the macOS clients. It is checked whether deviations are automatically detected and handled according to a defined process. A script can be run on a test device to check if the installation of unauthorized software is blocked: `curl -O http://unauthorized-app.com/app.dmg && hdiutil attach app.dmg && cp -R /Volumes/app/app.app /Applications/` – the command must fail.

controls.title: Using the integrated security features of macOS (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some security features like System Integrity Protection (SIP) are active by default, but there is no verification of their activity. Users can disable these features. The Gatekeeper settings are set to the least secure level, allowing the execution of applications from any source.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users with administrator rights can disable SIP with the `csrutil disable` command in Recovery Mode. Gatekeeper is disabled system-wide with `sudo spctl --master-disable` to bypass compatibility issues with old software.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor runs the commands `csrutil status` and `spctl --status` on several clients. The output shows that SIP is disabled on some devices and Gatekeeper is turned off system-wide.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On all macOS clients, it is manually checked whether the integrated security features System Integrity Protection (SIP), XProtect, and Gatekeeper are active with their default settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During the initial setup of a Mac, an IT staff member manually ensures that SIP is active and Gatekeeper is configured to allow apps from the App Store and verified developers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor runs the commands `csrutil status` and `spctl --status` on a sample of clients to check the activation of SIP and Gatekeeper. It is verified that the systems are using the default settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The protection mechanisms integrated in macOS, 'System Integrity Protection' (SIP), 'XProtect', and 'Gatekeeper', MUST be enabled. Gatekeeper MAY ONLY allow the execution of signed programs, unless unsigned programs are absolutely necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented instruction that SIP (`csrutil status`) and Gatekeeper (`spctl --status`) must be enabled on all Macs. Gatekeeper is configured to only allow apps from the App Store and verified developers. If an unsigned app is needed, there is a documented exception process where the app is manually authorized via a right-click and 'Open'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the status of SIP and Gatekeeper on a sample of clients via the command line (`csrutil status`, `spctl --status`). Additionally, the list of exceptions for Gatekeeper is checked (`spctl --list --type execute`) and compared with the list of approved unsigned applications.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The activation and configuration of SIP, XProtect, and Gatekeeper are enforced by a central policy, e.g., via an MDM. Any attempt to change these settings is logged and triggers an alert. The use of unsigned programs is controlled by a strict approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration profile in the MDM system enforces the Gatekeeper policy and prevents changes by the user. The MDM logs are regularly checked for manipulation attempts. A request for an unsigned app must be formally approved before it is whitelisted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration profiles for security settings stored in the MDM system. It is verified that these profiles are active on all managed clients. The logs are analyzed for warning messages related to these settings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of SIP, XProtect, and Gatekeeper is continuously monitored in real time. Only applications from the Mac App Store and from pre-vetted, identified developers are permitted. Any attempt to run an unsigned or unauthorized application is blocked and immediately reported to a SIEM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An endpoint security agent monitors the integrity of macOS security features. The app whitelist is managed via the MDM system and is extremely restrictive. Integration scripts forward the blocking and alerting events directly to the SIEM, where correlation rules trigger downstream actions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the SIEM dashboards and alarms related to macOS client security. A penetration test is performed, attempting to launch an unauthorized application. The system must demonstrably block this and generate an alarm. Compliance can be automatically checked via `system_profiler SPApplicationsDataType | grep 'Obtained from: Not Signed'`; the output must be empty or contain only approved exceptions.

controls.title: Use of appropriate accounts (B) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users often work with the administrator account created during initial setup for their daily tasks. The guest account is enabled on many devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For convenience, the first account set up, which has administrator rights by default, is used for everything from surfing the internet to word processing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor runs the command `dscl . -read /Users/$(whoami) PrimaryGroupID` on a client. A result of `80` (admin group) indicates that the user is working with an administrator account. Additionally, it is checked in the system settings whether the guest account is enabled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standard user account is created for daily work, but the original administrator account is also occasionally used for non-admin tasks. The guest account is disabled on all systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: IT staff set up a separate standard account for the user, but the user knows the admin account's password and, for convenience, does not always switch back.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a standard account exists for the main user. Through questioning, it is determined whether the admin account is also used for regular activities. It is checked whether the guest account is disabled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The account created during the initial configuration of macOS has administrative rights and MUST ONLY be used for administrative purposes. For normal use of the Mac, an account with standard permissions MUST be created. If the Mac is used by multiple users, a separate account MUST be created for each user. The guest account MUST be deactivated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A written policy and a setup guide for IT staff are created. This prescribes creating an admin account (e.g., 'it-admin') with a strong password and creating a separate standard account for the user's daily use. The guest account is disabled during setup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the user accounts on a client in the system settings or with `dscl . -list /Users`. It is verified that the main user uses a standard account and a separate administrator account exists. It is checked whether the guest account is disabled. An automated check can be performed via `defaults read /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow GuestEnabled`, which must return `0`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The creation of standard user accounts and the deactivation of the guest account are enforced via a configuration profile. The password for the administrator account is complex and stored securely in a password vault. All administrative actions require authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM system distributes a profile that prevents the creation of local admin accounts by standard users and deactivates the guest account. A separate, local admin account is created during enrollment, whose password is rotated (LAPS principle).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration profiles in the MDM system. It is checked whether the password policy for the admin account is documented and implemented. A random attempt is made to perform an administrative action without a password, which must fail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Just-in-Time (JIT) privilege elevation is used for administrative tasks instead of a permanent admin account. User account creation and role assignment are fully automated and integrated into a central Identity and Access Management (IAM) system. All account and rights-related activities are logged and centrally monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Privilege Access Management (PAM) tools are used to grant standard users temporary and task-specific elevated rights. User accounts are provisioned on clients via the IAM system (e.g., via SCIM). All sudo activities are forwarded to a SIEM system for monitoring.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the PAM and IAM system. It is checked that no permanent local admin accounts (except for a break-glass account) exist on the clients. The SIEM logs are examined for the correct recording of privilege elevations.

controls.title: Use of disk encryption (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only a few Macs, especially those of executives, have FileVault disk encryption enabled. Recovery keys are stored inconsistently, sometimes on a piece of paper attached to the device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: FileVault is only activated on request. There is no standardized process for storing recovery keys.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor runs the command `fdesetup status` on several clients and finds that encryption is disabled on many devices. No proof of secure storage of the existing keys can be provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: FileVault is enabled on all mobile Macs (MacBooks). However, users are allowed to store the recovery key in their iCloud account. Personal recovery keys are stored locally in a file on the user's desktop.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When setting up a MacBook, the user is guided to enable FileVault. The default option to store the key with Apple/iCloud is retained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies with `fdesetup status` that FileVault is active on MacBooks. A survey of users reveals that most have stored the key with iCloud and have no knowledge of alternative secure storage methods.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Disks SHOULD be encrypted, especially on mobile Macs (e.g., MacBooks). If the built-in macOS function FileVault is used for this, the key material MUST NOT be stored online with Apple. The recovery key generated by FileVault MUST be stored in a secure location. It SHOULD be considered whether an institutional recovery key for FileVault should be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy requires the activation of FileVault for all laptops. When activating, the option to store the key with Apple is explicitly deselected. The user is instructed to print out the personal recovery key and deposit it in a secure physical location (e.g., a safe). The IT department is evaluating the introduction of an institutional key.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the activation of FileVault on a sample of MacBooks with `fdesetup status`. The existence of the key storage policy is checked. Through questioning, the implementation of secure storage of personal keys is verified. An automated check via `fdesetup hasinstitutionalrecoverykey` can be used to check for the use of an institutional key.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: FileVault is enforced via a central policy on ALL Macs (not just mobile ones). An institutional recovery key is implemented and stored in a secure key management system (Key Escrow). Regular audits check whether encryption is enabled on all clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM system distributes a configuration profile that enforces FileVault and deposits the institutional recovery key. The key is stored in a dedicated, secure system such as HashiCorp Vault or a specialized Key Escrow service. The MDM inventory is checked weekly for encryption compliance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the MDM profile for encryption and its assignment. The process for depositing and retrieving the institutional key from the Key Escrow system is checked. The MDM inventory reports are analyzed to verify complete encryption coverage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: FileVault encryption is enforced at the time of device enrollment via an MDM solution. Both an institutional and a personal recovery key are required. The institutional key is stored in a Hardware Security Module (HSM). The encryption status is continuously monitored, and any deviation triggers an automatic device lock.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The enrollment process in the MDM (e.g., via Apple Business Manager) includes a mandatory step to activate FileVault. An endpoint security agent on the client reports the encryption status in real-time to a central console. If the status 'disabled' is reported, the MDM automatically sends a remote lock command.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the automated enrollment process. The configuration of the real-time monitoring and the automatic locking response is checked. A test case is conducted in which an attempt is made to disable encryption, which must lead to the immediate locking of the device. The secure storage of the institutional key in the HSM is verified by inspecting the HSM management console and logs.

controls.title: Deactivation of security-critical functions of macOS (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The location services integrated into macOS SHOULD be disabled. Downloaded data SHOULD NOT be opened automatically. Content from optical and other media SHOULD NOT be executed automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy exists that instructs users to disable location services in the system settings. Likewise, the 'Open safe files after downloading' option in Safari's settings is disabled. The automatic launching of programs from CDs/DVDs or USB drives is to be prevented in the system settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs random checks on clients for the corresponding settings in System Settings (Privacy & Security -> Location Services) and in Safari settings. Automated check: `defaults read /System/Library/CoreServices/SystemVersion.plist ProductVersion` returns the macOS version. For Safari, `defaults read com.apple.Safari AutoOpenSafeDownloads` (must be `0`) can be checked, and for Location Services, `defaults read /var/db/locationd/clients.plist` (should be empty or controlled) can be checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: These security-critical settings (disabling of location services, auto-open, auto-run) are enforced via a configuration profile from a central management system. Any change by the user is automatically reverted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM system distributes a configuration profile ('Restrictions Payload') that deactivates location services and prohibits the user from changing this setting. Another profile or script ensures that the Safari setting for automatic opening remains deactivated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration and assignment of the corresponding profiles in the MDM system. On a test client, an attempt is made to change the settings, which must be prevented by the profile. The MDM's compliance reports are checked for deviations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A strict application control policy prevents any automatic execution of downloaded content, regardless of the browser setting. Location services are disabled at the firmware level where possible, and any application request for location data is logged and reported centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An endpoint security tool with application control functions is used to enforce a whitelist of executable processes. Any request to the CoreLocation API is intercepted by an agent, logged, and sent to a SIEM. Selected MDM commands can further restrict certain hardware functions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the endpoint security tool and the whitelist rules. A test is performed in which a file is downloaded and an attempt is made to have it executed automatically, which must be blocked. The SIEM logs are reviewed for location requests.

controls.title: Use of current Mac hardware (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When new Macs are procured, current models SHOULD be selected. If existing Macs are used, it SHOULD be checked regularly whether they and the operating system installed on them are still receiving security updates from Apple. If the Macs are no longer supported by Apple, they SHOULD no longer be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement department is instructed to order only models from Apple's current product line for new orders. An inventory list (e.g., in a spreadsheet) is maintained, recording the model and purchase date of each Mac. This list is compared semi-annually with Apple's published list of vintage and obsolete products.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement policies and the inventory list. It is checked on a random basis whether the models in the list still receive security updates from Apple. A device can be identified via `system_profiler SPHardwareDataType | grep 'Model Identifier'` and compared with Apple's support list.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal policy for the hardware lifecycle of Macs is established. It defines a maximum operating age (e.g., 5 years) and mandates replacement before the end of support announced by Apple. The hardware inventory is managed automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM or asset management system automatically records all Macs on the network, including model identifier and serial number. The lifecycle policy is documented and part of the annual budget planning process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the hardware lifecycle policy. The data in the asset management system is checked for completeness and correctness. It is verified that a process exists to proactively identify and replace devices approaching their end of support.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hardware lifecycle policy is integrated into the procurement and asset management systems. The system automatically reports devices approaching their end of support and initiates a replacement process. Unsupported devices are automatically isolated from the network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A workflow in the asset management system automatically creates a ticket for a device's replacement 6 months before its end of support. A Network Access Control (NAC) system receives information about the support status of devices and automatically moves devices whose support has expired into a quarantine network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the automated workflow in the asset management and ticketing system. The configuration of the NAC system is checked to ensure that the isolation rule is implemented correctly. A test case is performed with a device marked as 'obsolete', which must be demonstrably isolated upon network connection.

controls.title: Two-factor authentication for Apple ID (S) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Two-factor authentication for using the Apple ID account SHOULD be enabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented policy and a guide for users that requires two-factor authentication (2FA) to be enabled for every Apple ID used on company devices. Compliance is checked randomly during initial setup and for support requests.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy and the user guide. Implementation is verified on a random basis by interviewing users and inspecting the device settings (System Settings > Apple ID > Password & Security).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If Managed Apple IDs are used, two-factor authentication is enforced centrally. For private Apple IDs, compliance is audited regularly, and users without 2FA are followed up until activation is complete.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In Apple Business Manager, 2FA is configured as mandatory for all Managed Apple IDs. For private IDs, a script or MDM query is used to check the 2FA status (as far as technically possible). A report lists all non-compliant users, who are then contacted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the settings in Apple Business Manager. The process for auditing and following up on private Apple IDs is reviewed for its effectiveness. The reports from the last audits are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of services requiring an Apple ID is only possible via Managed Apple IDs, where two-factor authentication with strong authenticators (e.g., hardware security keys) is enforced. Every login attempt to a critical service is monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of private Apple IDs is blocked on the devices via an MDM profile. All users receive a Managed Apple ID. Logging into iCloud via a browser on unmanaged devices is blocked by a Conditional Access Proxy. The login logs from Apple Business Manager are integrated into a SIEM and monitored for anomalies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the MDM configuration that blocks private Apple IDs. It is checked whether the use of hardware security keys as a second factor is enforced. The SIEM rules for monitoring logins are analyzed.

controls.title: No use of iCloud for sensitive data (S) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be prevented that sensitive data is synchronized between multiple devices via iCloud services. Instead, data SHOULD only be synchronized via self-operated services. Sensitive data SHOULD NOT be stored in iCloud. Drafts, for example of e-mails or documents, SHOULD NOT be automatically saved in iCloud.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A user policy explicitly prohibits the storage of data classified as 'confidential' or 'internal' on iCloud Drive, in iCloud Photos, or other iCloud services. Users are provided with and trained on alternative, in-house solutions (e.g., a Nextcloud or SharePoint server) for data synchronization.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the data classification and user policies. By interviewing and randomly, consensually checking the iCloud directories on users' devices, compliance with the policy is monitored. It is checked whether functioning and accepted alternatives are provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Technical controls via an MDM system are used to restrict iCloud functionality. For example, iCloud Drive, iCloud Mail, and the synchronization of photos and contacts are disabled. Users are provided with a sanctioned, equally user-friendly alternative for file synchronization.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM configuration profile ('Restrictions Payload') is distributed to all devices, which prevents the use of specific iCloud services. Only non-critical functions like 'Find My Mac' may remain enabled. The provided alternative is pre-installed on the clients and configured as the default storage location.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration and assignment of the MDM profile. On a test client, an attempt is made to access blocked iCloud services, which must fail. The user acceptance of the alternative solution is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solutions are deployed on the endpoints to detect and block the transfer of data classified as sensitive to iCloud or other unapproved cloud storage services in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A DLP agent is installed on all Macs. It analyzes outgoing data traffic and file operations. Rules are configured so that files marked as 'confidential' or containing specific patterns (e.g., credit card numbers) cannot be uploaded to iCloud Drive or via browser upload to iCloud. The attempt is blocked and reported to a central security console.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and rules of the DLP system. A test is conducted in which an attempt is made to save a document marked as confidential to iCloud Drive. The process must be blocked and a corresponding alert triggered. The reports in the DLP console are analyzed for effectiveness and false-positive rates.

controls.title: Use of additional protection programs under macOS (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If necessary, for example, if Macs are operated in a heterogeneous network, third-party antivirus solutions SHOULD be used in addition to the integrated protection mechanisms of macOS.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented risk assessment is carried out to determine the need for additional antivirus software. Since the Macs are operated in a network with many Windows clients and could serve as potential carriers of Windows malware, it is decided to install a third-party antivirus solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the risk assessment and checks its conclusions. It is verified on a random basis on the clients whether the selected antivirus software is installed and running.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A centrally managed, company-wide Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) or antivirus solution is deployed on all Macs. Its signature files and engine are kept up-to-date automatically, and its status is monitored from a central console.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An EDR solution (e.g., from CrowdStrike, SentinelOne) is rolled out to all Macs via the MDM system. The configuration is centrally managed to ensure that real-time protection and regular scans are enabled. The central dashboard is checked daily by the IT security team for alerts or non-compliant devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration in the central management console of the EDR tool. It is verified that all known Macs are registered in the system and have up-to-date signatures. The alerting and reporting functions are checked for their effectiveness. A test with an EICAR test file must be successfully detected and reported: `curl -O https://secure.eicar.org/eicar.com.txt`

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An advanced EDR solution is deployed that is fully integrated into a central SIEM. It offers behavioral analysis, proactive threat hunting capabilities, and automated response measures (e.g., isolating an infected client from the network).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The EDR solution sends all collected telemetry data and alerts to the SIEM system (e.g., Splunk). There, correlation rules trigger automated actions via the EDR tool's API (SOAR principle). IT security analysts actively use the EDR data to search for signs of advanced threats.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the data integration between EDR and SIEM. The SOAR playbooks for automated responses are analyzed. A simulated attack is carried out to test whether the detection, alerting, and automatic isolation function as configured. The reports on completed threat hunting activities are reviewed.

controls.title: Activation of the Personal Firewall on macOS (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The personal firewall integrated in macOS SHOULD be enabled and appropriately configured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an instruction for IT staff and users to enable the Personal Firewall in the System Settings. The configuration allows connections for signed software by default.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the status of the firewall on a client in the System Settings or via the command line with `sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate`. An active status is expected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The firewall is enabled and configured via a central policy (MDM). It is configured with a restrictive rule set that only allows specific applications and services required for work. Stealth mode is enabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM system distributes a firewall configuration profile to all Macs. This profile enables the firewall, stealth mode, and blocks all incoming connections except for those explicitly allowed for approved applications (e.g., video conferencing tools).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the firewall profile in the MDM system. A port scanner is used from another computer to try to scan the Mac, which should be prevented by stealth mode. The list of allowed applications is checked for necessity. Automated check: `sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getstealthmode` should return `enabled`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A more advanced, host-based third-party firewall is used, which allows for granular, context-aware rules (e.g., different rule sets for trusted vs. untrusted networks). All firewall logs are forwarded to a central SIEM for analysis and correlation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A solution like Little Snitch or LuLu is centrally deployed and configured. It has location-aware profiles: more connections are allowed on the office network than on a public Wi-Fi. The firewall logs are sent to the SIEM using a log shipper.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the third-party firewall and its location-aware profiles. The integration with the SIEM is verified by creating a blocked connection on the client and searching for the corresponding log entry in the SIEM. The SIEM rules for evaluating the firewall logs are analyzed.

controls.title: Decommissioning of Macs (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When decommissioning a Mac, the non-volatile random-access memory (NVRAM) and the System Management Controller (SMC) SHOULD be reset.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a checklist for device decommissioning. This includes instructions for resetting the NVRAM (hold down `Cmd+Option+P+R` on startup) and the SMC (different key combinations depending on the model). Afterwards, the system is reinstalled via Recovery Mode, and the hard drive is erased in the process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the decommissioning checklist. The process for a device to be decommissioned is observed to verify the correct execution of the steps.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A documented, repeatable procedure for decommissioning Macs is followed. This includes resetting NVRAM/SMC, performing a cryptographic erase by destroying the FileVault keys, and then reformatting the drive. A decommissioning record is created.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decommissioning procedure is stored in the asset management system. The technician follows the steps, which also include sending a remote wipe command from the MDM system, which performs the cryptographic erase. Afterwards, the device is started from Recovery Mode and the hard drive is formatted. The execution is logged in a ticket.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented decommissioning procedure and the logs (e.g., closed tickets) of recently decommissioned devices to verify compliance with the process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decommissioning process is managed via an asset management system. All steps are tracked in a checklist. For devices that contained highly sensitive data, in addition to cryptographic erasure, the physical destruction of the storage media is performed and certified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a device is marked as 'to be decommissioned' in the asset management system, a workflow with a mandatory checklist is initiated. Depending on the device's data classification, at the end of the workflow, either a ticket for storage is created or an order for certified physical destruction is placed with a specialized service provider. The certificate of destruction is stored in the asset management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the workflow in the asset management system. The checklists and destruction certificates for a sample of highly sensitive devices are checked. The data classification process for the devices is also evaluated.

controls.title: Firmware Password and Boot Protection on Macs (H) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On older Macs, a secure firmware password prompt SHOULD be enabled in so-called "Command Mode" to prevent unauthorized booting of the Mac from another startup disk. On Macs with a T2 security chip or Apple Silicon, a firmware password SHOULD be set via the Startup Security Utility. The "Secure Boot: Full Security" option SHOULD be enabled. The "Disallow booting from external media" option SHOULD be enabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a documented instruction that requires setting a firmware password depending on the Mac model. On newer Macs, the Startup Security Utility is opened in Recovery Mode, and the most secure options (Full Security, no external booting) are selected and protected with a password.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the process demonstrated on a test device. It is checked whether holding down the Option key (Intel) or the Power button (Apple Silicon) on startup displays a password prompt as expected before the boot menu is shown.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The firmware password and secure boot settings are centrally enforced, as far as technically supported by the MDM system. The firmware password itself is complex and is securely stored in an institutional password vault. Regular audits verify compliance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM system is used to set and manage the firmware password during device enrollment. The password is generated per device and stored in the MDM. The MDM system performs regular queries to ensure that the settings have not been tampered with.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration in the MDM system for setting the firmware password. The process for secure storage and retrieval of the password is checked. The MDM's compliance reports are analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The deployment and management of firmware passwords and secure boot settings is fully automated. Any attempt to tamper with the boot process or firmware settings is logged and triggers an immediate warning and potentially a remote lock or wipe of the device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The entire process is handled via Apple Business Manager and an MDM system. An endpoint agent monitors the integrity of the boot configuration. Tampering attempts (e.g., multiple incorrect firmware password entries) are detected and reported to a SIEM/SOAR system, which automatically sends a 'Remote Lock' command to the MDM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the fully automated process from registration to configuration. The SIEM/SOAR rules for responding to tampering attempts are analyzed. A test case is conducted in which tampering is simulated to verify the automatic lockdown.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: macOS is a client operating system from Apple. macOS is based on Darwin, Apple's freely available Unix operating system, which in turn is based on the open-source operating system FreeBSD. macOS essentially consists of Darwin as well as the proprietary graphical user interface "Aqua" and other applications and services. According to Apple's license terms, macOS may only be installed on IT systems ("Macs") from Apple. For this reason, the peculiarities of these systems are also part of this module.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is to protect information that is processed on or transmitted with IT systems under macOS. To this end, IT systems under macOS must be adequately secured.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.2.4 Clients under macOS is to be applied to all client systems on which the Apple macOS operating system is used.
The focus of this module is on securing a Mac with macOS that is operated as a stand-alone system or as a client in a client-server network. This module thus supplements the general aspects from the additionally applicable module SYS.2.1 General Client. A possible use of macOS as a server operating system is not considered in the module. In professional use, the so-called Profile Manager and Mobile Device Management provide the option of centrally managing the Macs used. These solutions offer extended configuration and management functions, but are not considered in this module. Corresponding security aspects are dealt with in module SYS.3.2.2 Mobile Device Management (MDM). It should also be noted that the two Apple operating systems macOS (for Macs) and iOS (for iPhones) or iPadOS (for iPads) are closely intertwined. Therefore, module SYS.3.2.3 iOS (for Enterprise) should also be considered if devices with iOS or iPadOS are used in addition to macOS.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Uncontrolled access to offloaded data
parts.prose: macOS offers a range of functions that are executed on central servers operated by Apple. For example, Apple's iCloud can be used for storing and synchronizing data between different macOS and iOS devices. Since data is temporarily stored on third-party servers and is therefore no longer under one's own control, unauthorized persons could in principle also access these servers and view the data stored or transmitted there and misuse it for their own purposes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Misuse of the Apple ID as central access information for Apple services
parts.prose: To use some macOS functions, a unique Apple ID is required as access information. With the Apple ID, various Apple services, such as iCloud, iMessage, and the App Store, can be accessed centrally. If unauthorized persons gain access to the Apple ID access information, they may be able to use these services under a false identity and access information in iCloud.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Attacks on wireless interfaces
parts.prose: A Mac usually has wireless interfaces such as WLAN or Bluetooth, which are also used by many services and are activated accordingly. For example, files can be exchanged directly between Apple devices (AirDrop). Furthermore, the WLAN and Bluetooth function can be used to synchronize macOS and iOS devices (Continuity). With AirPlay, it is possible to send video and audio data to compatible playback devices. Attackers could try to misuse these radio interfaces for attacks in order to intercept confidential information between Mac, iPhone, iPad and other devices or to compromise the devices.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Attacks on applications with preview function
parts.prose: Some of the applications integrated in macOS support a preview function for certain file formats (e.g. image files). These include the Finder, the "Safari" browser, and the email program integrated in macOS. The preview function automatically displays an excerpt of an email attachment, for example, if the file format is known. An attacker could thus try to hide malicious code in the attachment of an email. The preview function would display the email attachment and possibly execute the malicious code, which in turn could compromise the Mac.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Insecure protocols in macOS or macOS applications
parts.prose: macOS and its applications support various, partly Apple-proprietary protocols (e.g. AFP) for communication with central servers or other end devices. If these communication protocols do not have sufficient security mechanisms or are configured insecurely, the data transmitted via them could be read without authorization, falsified or otherwise misused.

controls.title: Planning the use of virtual clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a rough idea of which applications are to be used on virtual clients. However, there is no detailed analysis of performance requirements or systematic collection of usage profiles. Resource allocation is based on estimates, not on concrete measurements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, a standard configuration is often used for all virtual clients, regardless of actual usage. For example, a configuration with 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM is set for all users, without checking if this is suitable for all use cases (e.g., simple office applications vs. CAD software).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests planning documents. It is checked whether there is merely a simple list of applications without further specification of the requirements. In interviews with the planning managers, it is determined that no systematic requirements analysis has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic plan for which applications will be used. The basic requirements for CPU and memory are recorded and documented for the most common use cases. Special requirements such as the need for graphics cards are only considered for obvious cases (e.g., CAD workstations).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A few templates are created for different user groups, e.g., 'Office User' and 'Developer'. Resource allocation is based on documented basic requirements but does not account for peak loads or parallel application usage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning documents and compares them with the created VM templates. It is checked whether the basic requirements for CPU and RAM are documented and implemented in the templates. However, it is also noted that no detailed performance analyses or load tests were part of the planning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be defined which applications are to be used on the virtual clients. The tasks to be solved with these applications MUST be defined. For these applications, it MUST be checked and documented what requirements are placed on the virtualization infrastructure and any additional hardware (e.g., graphics cards). The virtualization server used MUST provide the necessary resources in terms of CPU, RAM, and data storage.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process for requirements gathering is established. For each major application group, a standardized form is used to document CPU, RAM, storage, and graphics requirements. Based on these documented requirements, specific VM templates and resource pools are configured in the virtualization platform.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly checks whether a documented requirements analysis exists for various user groups (e.g., administration, development, design). It is verified that the configuration of the corresponding virtual clients (e.g., number of vCPUs, RAM size, assigned GPU) matches the documented requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process is enhanced with performance baselining and load testing for critical applications. Resource allocation is done dynamically within defined policy limits to guarantee performance for different user groups. The planning process is reviewed regularly, at least annually, and adapted to new requirements as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before a new application or a major update is introduced, automated load tests are carried out in a test environment to determine the exact resource requirements. The virtualization platform is configured to dynamically adjust resource allocation (e.g., via VMware DRS or similar technologies) within the defined minima and maxima per user group.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the results of load tests for recently introduced applications. The configuration of the dynamic resource allocation in the virtualization platform is checked. In addition, logs from planning reviews are inspected to verify the regularity of the process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire planning and deployment process is automated. A central system continuously analyzes the performance requirements of applications, user roles, and the current infrastructure load to automatically provision optimally sized virtual clients or adjust their configuration.
