Capacity management is proactive and uses trend analysis to predict future demand.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cloud management portal or a comparable automation platform is used. This platform is integrated with monitoring tools and Active Directory. Based on predefined rules and machine learning algorithms, the system adjusts VM configurations or provides proactive recommendations for expanding the infrastructure before bottlenecks occur.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and logs of the automation platform. It is verified that configuration adjustments are performed automatically and traceably. In addition, the system's capacity forecasts are compared with the actual development over the past few months to assess the accuracy of the prediction model. An automated test can run `kubectl get hpa` or equivalent commands on the virtualization platform to check the existence and effectiveness of automatic scaling policies.

controls.title: Planning of the networks used for virtual clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The networks for the connection between accessing clients and virtual clients, as well as the networks for connecting downstream services to the virtual clients (e.g., directory service, email, or internet access), MUST be designed to be sufficiently powerful. It MUST be planned which network segments are to be used for the virtual clients. The network segments for virtual clients MUST be separate from network segments for servers. An existing network separation MUST NOT be bypassed using a virtual client or a virtualization server. For virtual clients, it MUST be defined whether and to what extent communication to untrusted networks should be restricted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of a network concept, dedicated VLANs are defined for the VDI environment. At least one VLAN is provided for the virtual clients themselves and another for the VDI infrastructure components (brokers, gateways). The firewall rules between the VDI client VLAN, the server VLAN, and the internet are explicitly defined and implemented. The bandwidth requirements are calculated based on the number of users and the applications used (e.g., video conferencing) and provided in the network backbone.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network concept and the firewall rule sets. It is checked whether dedicated network segments for virtual clients, separate from server networks, are documented and implemented. A port scan from a test client in the VDI network is used to verify that no unauthorized access to the server network is possible. The utilization statistics of the relevant switch ports and firewall interfaces are checked to verify sufficient dimensioning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network planning includes Quality of Service (QoS) policies to prioritize VDI traffic (especially the display protocol like RDP, PCoIP, or HDX) over less critical traffic. Micro-segmentation is planned to isolate different groups of virtual clients (e.g., by department or protection level) from each other. Network performance is actively and regularly monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: QoS rules are configured on the network switches to prioritize packets with the corresponding DSCP markings of the VDI protocol. Micro-segmentation is implemented using a distributed firewall (e.g., VMware NSX or Cisco ACI) that filters traffic between the virtual NICs of the VMs. A monitoring tool continuously checks latency, jitter, and packet loss for VDI traffic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the network switches for active QoS policies for VDI traffic. The configuration of the distributed firewall is checked for the implementation of micro-segmentation. The dashboards and alarms of the network monitoring tool are viewed to verify the continuous monitoring of the quality of service.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network planning and configuration is fully integrated into an Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) process. Network segmentation and security policies, including micro-segmentation, are automatically provisioned and enforced based on the virtual client's profile (defined by role and protection requirement). All network traffic is continuously analyzed for anomalies and potential threats.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Terraform or Ansible scripts are used to automatically create the associated VLANs, subnets, firewall rules, and micro-segmentation policies when a new VDI pool is provisioned. A Network Detection and Response (NDR) system analyzes all VDI network traffic (e.g., via a SPAN port) and uses behavioral analysis to detect threats such as lateral movement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the IaC scripts (e.g., in the Git repository) and compares them with the actually deployed network configuration to ensure consistency. The logs and alarms of the NDR system are analyzed to prove its functionality. An automated test can check the network connectivity between two VMs in the same segment but with different security profiles to verify the dynamic application of micro-segmentation rules.

controls.title: Protection against malware on the virtual clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standard antivirus client is installed on all virtual clients. Management is centralized but not specifically optimized for a virtualized environment. This can lead to performance issues, e.g., through simultaneous scans ('scan storms') on many VMs on the same host.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A conventional endpoint protection agent is integrated into the master image (template) of the virtual clients. Signature updates are distributed to the running VMs via a central management console. No VDI-specific optimizations such as randomization of scan times or the use of a security virtual appliance are made.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies via the central management console that all active virtual clients have reported an antivirus agent and have current signatures. The configuration is checked for the absence of VDI-specific optimizations. Performance logs of the virtualization hosts can be examined for CPU and I/O peaks that correlate with scheduled scan times.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the virtual clients, malware protection MUST be implemented in accordance with modules OPS.1.1.4 Protection against malicious programs and SYS.2.1 General Client, as well as considering the operating system-specific modules. If an antivirus program is used, it MUST be defined and documented whether this protection is implemented centrally in the virtualization infrastructure, decentrally on the virtual clients, or in a hybrid form. If the virtual clients are to be protected with central components, these central components MUST have sufficient performance. If an antivirus program is run on the virtual clients, it MUST be ensured that the performance of the virtualization infrastructure is sufficient.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A conscious and documented decision is made for a malware protection architecture. This can be a conventional agent where scan times are randomized to avoid 'scan storms'. Alternatively, a VDI-optimized solution with a central Security Virtual Appliance (SVA) per host can be chosen, which offloads the scan load from the individual VMs. The chosen solution must be sufficiently dimensioned to support the maximum number of VMs per host.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the malware protection concept and the document that justifies the decision for the chosen architecture. The configuration of the antivirus program is checked to ensure that it corresponds to the documentation (e.g., configuration of the SVA or randomization of scan times). Performance data of the VDI infrastructure is analyzed during scan times to rule out an overload.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An antivirus solution specially developed for VDI is used, which offloads scans to a dedicated Security Virtual Appliance (SVA) to optimize performance and avoid resource conflicts. The solution includes not only signature-based detection but also behavioral analysis to detect zero-day exploits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SVA from the security solution vendor is deployed on each virtualization host. Only a very lightweight agent is installed on the virtual client images, which redirects file and process access to the SVA. In the central console, in addition to signature-based detection, the modules for behavioral analysis and exploit protection are activated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and operational status of the Security Virtual Appliances on the hosts on the virtualization platform. The management console of the security solution is checked to see if the behavioral analysis modules are active. Test malware (e.g., EICAR test file) is placed on a test client to verify the detection function.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An integrated Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solution, specifically designed for VDI environments, is used. It provides deep insight into processes and network connections, automates threat hunting and response measures, and is fully integrated with the virtualization platform and a central SIEM.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The EDR solution collects telemetry data from all virtual clients and correlates it in a central analysis engine. When a complex threat is detected (e.g., fileless malware in memory), the system can react automatically by isolating the affected VM from the network (via API calls to the virtualization platform) and creating forensic snapshots. All alarms and actions are forwarded to the SIEM for further correlation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the EDR platform and the integration with the virtualization environment and the SIEM. A simulated attack (e.g., using Atomic Red Team) is carried out to verify that the EDR solution detects the suspicious activities, triggers an alarm, and correctly executes the defined automated response (e.g., network isolation). This can be verified by running `Get-NetIPAddress` or `ip a` on the isolated VM to confirm the loss of network connectivity.

controls.title: Use of a dedicated virtualization infrastructure for the virtual clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Virtual clients SHOULD be operated on a dedicated virtualization infrastructure. Virtual servers SHOULD NOT be run on the same virtualization infrastructure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separate virtualization clusters are set up for server workloads and for VDI workloads. Although they may be managed by the same central management instance (e.g., vCenter Server), the clusters consist of different physical hosts. This ensures that resource-intensive VDI operations (e.g., login storms) do not affect the performance of the enterprise servers and vice versa.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the virtualization platform. It is verified that at least two clusters are defined: one for servers and one for VDI. The host lists of the two clusters are compared to ensure that there are no overlaps. An automated test can use scripts (e.g., PowerCLI for VMware: `Get-Cluster`) to retrieve and compare the cluster definitions and host assignments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Virtual clients are operated on a completely separate virtualization cluster that includes its own management instance, dedicated hosts, and potentially also dedicated storage, to ensure strict resource and security isolation from the server infrastructure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate vCenter instance (or an equivalent from another vendor) is installed exclusively for the VDI environment. The hosts of the VDI cluster are connected to their own storage system (e.g., a dedicated SAN or an HCI solution) that is not used by the server workloads. This prevents 'noisy neighbor' problems at both the CPU/RAM and storage levels.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a separate management instance for the VDI environment. The network configuration and storage configuration of the VDI hosts are checked to ensure that they access dedicated resources that are separate from the server environment. It is checked whether the administrative access for the VDI and server platforms are separate.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to a dedicated cluster, the VDI environment uses a physically separate network infrastructure (switches, firewalls) and storage systems. For use cases with high protection needs, this creates an environment that is logically and physically largely separate from the rest of the production landscape.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VDI hosts are connected to dedicated top-of-rack switches, which in turn are connected to their own firewall instance for north-south and east-west traffic control. The entire VDI infrastructure is located in a separate rack or even its own area in the data center to maximize physical separation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the data center documentation, including rack plans and network diagrams, to verify the physical separation of the VDI infrastructure. A physical inspection of the cabling can be carried out. It is checked whether the VDI infrastructure has its own power supply units (PDUs). An automated test is difficult here, but network traceroutes to and from the VDI systems can help to trace the data path through dedicated network components.

controls.title: Additional network segmentation for virtual clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The following criteria SHOULD be considered for additional network separation of virtual clients: usage scenario for the virtual clients and group membership of the users, user permissions derived from group membership, applications installed on the virtual clients and made available to the users, protection requirements of the information processed on the virtual clients, trustworthiness of the virtual clients, and network connections necessary for the functionality of the virtual clients. Based on these criteria, segmentation is implemented using VLANs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on an analysis of user groups, several VLANs are created for virtual clients. For example, standard office users get one VLAN, developers get a separate VLAN with access to test systems, and external service providers get a third, highly restricted VLAN. Communication between these VLANs is regulated by a central firewall.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation on network segmentation and compares the defined groups with the configured VLANs and firewall rules. The VLAN membership of virtual clients from different user groups is checked on a random basis. A ping or port scan test is performed from a client in VLAN A to a client in VLAN B to verify the effectiveness of the firewall separation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Micro-segmentation is implemented using the capabilities of the virtualization platform or a dedicated solution. Firewall rules are applied at the virtual network interface (vNIC) level to restrict traffic between individual virtual clients, even within the same VLAN, according to the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A distributed firewall solution (e.g., VMware NSX Distributed Firewall) is used. Security groups are created based on VM names, tags, or operating systems. The firewall rules are applied to these groups, so that, for example, web server VMs can only communicate with database VMs on port 443, even if they are in the same subnet. By default, communication between VMs is blocked if no explicit rule exists.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the distributed firewall and the definition of the security groups and policies. It is verified that a 'default deny' rule is active. An attempt is made from a test VM to access another VM in the same subnet on a disallowed port to confirm the blocking. An automated test can query the API of the micro-segmentation solution to list the applied rules for a specific VM.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Micro-segmentation policies are dynamically generated and applied based on the user's identity, the state of the endpoint device, and the application being accessed. The system uses a zero-trust model, where all traffic is prohibited by default and only explicitly allowed connections are permitted. All traffic between segments is logged and analyzed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The micro-segmentation solution is integrated with Active Directory and a Network Access Control (NAC) solution. When a user from the finance department logs in from a device classified as compliant, their VM is automatically added to the 'Finance-Trusted' security group and receives the corresponding firewall exceptions. If the same user tries to log in from an unknown device, their VM is placed in the quarantine group with highly restricted access. All rule applications and traffic flows are sent to a SIEM for analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor simulates various login scenarios (e.g., users from different departments, login from trusted and untrusted endpoints) and verifies that the virtual machine is dynamically assigned to the correct security group and receives or loses the appropriate network access rights. The SIEM logs are checked for the correct logging of these events.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Client virtualization refers to the virtualized provisioning of clients. Clients can be virtualized both locally on a physical client and by means of a (central) virtualization infrastructure. Virtualization infrastructures can be used to operate virtual clients from a remote workstation.
This module deals with the secure use of client virtualization by means of a virtualization infrastructure. A virtualization infrastructure comprises one or more physical virtualization servers in accordance with the SYS.1.5 Virtualization module. The individual virtual clients are executed on the respective virtualization servers and are composed of the virtual hardware resources defined for this purpose, such as CPU, main memory, and the corresponding hard disk image. These images are usually created using templates.
Users interact via physical clients that connect to the virtual clients using terminal server technologies and protocols. Thus, the virtual client is also a terminal server in the sense of the SYS.1.9 Terminal Server module.
Virtual clients that are executed on a virtualization infrastructure are generally easier to administer than physical clients that are geographically distributed throughout the institution. Furthermore, virtual clients can be provisioned more easily than physical clients using templates. In addition, virtual clients can be updated more easily via snapshots or cloned virtual machines. Another typical use case is virtual clients that are created to test specific applications and are therefore only needed for a short period of time.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to protect information that is processed and transmitted during client virtualization. To this end, special requirements are placed on the virtual clients and the underlying virtualization infrastructure, as well as on the networks used.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.2.5 Client Virtualization is to be applied to the virtualization infrastructure and all virtual clients, provided they are centrally provisioned as described above.
To create an IT baseline protection model for a specific information network, the entirety of all modules must always be considered. As a rule, several modules must be applied to the topic or target object.
This module covers the following content:
• The module SYS.2.5 Client Virtualization addresses those parts of client virtualization that are specific to the provisioning and use of virtual clients.
• This module contains specific requirements for the networks used to secure the communication between the accessing client and the virtualization infrastructure.
The following content is also important and is dealt with elsewhere:
• Accessing and virtual clients communicate via terminal server software running on the virtual clients. Therefore, module SYS.1.9 Terminal Server must be applied to both the virtual clients and the accessing clients.
• To address the general aspects of virtual clients, module SYS.2.1 General Client must be applied. Furthermore, the operating system-specific modules of the SYS layer may also need to be applied.
• The general aspects of virtualization, for example, isolation via the virtualization server, are addressed in module SYS.1.5 Virtualization.
• The module NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design must be applied to secure the networks used for communication between the accessing client and the virtualization infrastructure.
This module does not cover the following content:
• The local provisioning of virtual clients on physical clients.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient dimensioning of the network connection of virtual clients
parts.prose: If the performance requirements for the network connection of virtual clients are not taken into account or are inadequately considered during planning, the virtual clients may not function correctly. For example, if the network connection to downstream services (e.g., video conferencing solutions or file storage) is not powerful enough, the virtual clients may only be able to access information to a limited extent, e.g., for latency-critical applications. The same applies if the virtual clients are not connected to the accessing clients with sufficient network capacity.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficient performance of the virtual clients due to resource scarcity
parts.prose:
To be able to work as smoothly as possible on virtual clients, it is important that they are powerful. If a virtual client is allocated insufficient resources (e.g., CPU, main memory, or graphics performance), the availability of the applications installed on the virtual client may be impaired. For example, certain graphically demanding programs cannot be executed on the virtual client without dedicated graphics processors. A processor clock speed that is too low also leads to slow processing speed.
If the virtual clients behave differently, this can lead to a scarcity of resources. For example, if users run many applications permanently and in parallel, the virtual clients may no longer be able to provide the required performance.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Mutual interference of the virtual clients
parts.prose:
The dimensioning of the underlying virtualization infrastructure is decisive for the actually available performance of several parallel virtual clients. If many other virtual IT systems are executed simultaneously on a virtualization server in addition to a virtual client, the virtualization server might no longer be able to cover the resource demand. This in turn can lead to the actual performance of the virtual client being limited and no longer predictable. Processor performance and main memory play the biggest role here if they are dynamically allocated. If too many different people demand performance at the same time, they compete for it.
Especially if virtual clients are used improperly and the provided resources are heavily utilized, other virtual clients can be affected. In an extreme case, the underlying virtualization server can terminate a virtual IT system due to a lack of resources or even fail completely itself.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Insufficient separation of the virtual clients at the network level
parts.prose:
Virtual clients are clients in the sense of the SYS.2.1 General Client module, which may have different protection needs. If these clients are operated on a common virtualization infrastructure, an existing separation at the port level could be canceled by the virtualization server used (at the level of the virtual switches).
If the virtual clients are not assigned to the intended network segments, e.g., due to configuration errors at the level of the virtual switches, VLANs, or physical interfaces, they could access protected networks and the information located there for which they are not authorized.
Virtualization servers are usually operated in central IT operating areas (data centers), where other central servers are also located. If virtual clients and central servers are not located in network segments that are separated from each other, virtual clients can access servers without authorization or unintentionally. If these network segments contain virtual clients that are allowed to access the Internet, this increases the attack surface.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Loss of virtual clients and data stored on them
parts.prose: In client virtualization, the images of the virtual clients are stored and managed centrally. Incorrect administration or mishandling of virtual clients can damage or delete them. The loss of virtual clients during operation can also lead to the deletion of information stored on these virtual clients. In addition, the loss of virtual clients means that information processed on these virtual clients is no longer available.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Unavailability of virtual clients and data stored on them
parts.prose:
As a rule, virtual clients cannot be switched on by the users themselves, but only by the IT operations team that also administers the virtualization infrastructure. During updates or general maintenance work on the virtualization infrastructure, it is common for virtual clients to be switched off. If someone forgets to switch them back on afterwards, they remain switched off and are therefore unreachable.
Likewise, a failure of the underlying virtualization server can lead to virtual clients being temporarily unreachable. In this case, users can no longer access the respective virtual client and the data stored on it.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Software vulnerabilities on the virtual clients
parts.prose:
Virtual clients are composed of the specified virtual hardware resources such as CPU and main memory and the corresponding hard disk image. These images are usually created from templates. When these templates are created, they are usually on an up-to-date software version without known vulnerabilities.
However, without regular updating of these templates, it is possible that a newly created virtual client has vulnerabilities that became known after the template was created. If other IT systems can access this virtual client, the known vulnerability can possibly be exploited and the virtual client can thus be compromised.
It may also be necessary to provision virtual clients with known vulnerabilities, e.g., for compatibility tests or for required software that only runs on outdated operating systems. These vulnerabilities can occur predictably and thus be more easily exploited.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Bypassing the isolation between a virtual client and other virtualized IT systems
parts.prose:
Virtual IT systems are often used on a shared virtualization infrastructure to use resources more efficiently and provide them more flexibly. As a result, the various virtualized IT systems can influence each other. Unlike virtual servers, virtual clients can be compromised more easily because the applications running on them are more diverse and interactive.
A compromised virtual client can endanger the shared virtualization infrastructure, as not only network-accessible IT systems but also other virtual IT systems on the virtualization server can be attacked. Because the physical IT system is shared, side-channel attacks such as Spectre or Meltdown can be carried out, or it is possible to break out of the virtual machine to subsequently compromise the underlying hypervisor or operating system. In this case, virtual IT systems can be taken out of service, or the data processed in them can be read or modified.

controls.title: Planning the use of a VDI

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning for the VDI deployment is done ad-hoc and focuses only on an immediate, limited use case, such as a pilot project. A long-term strategy or the requirements of the entire user base are not considered. Performance requirements are only roughly estimated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, often only the number of initial users and the required standard applications are recorded. The planning is typically recorded in a simple document or spreadsheet, without formal analysis of growth rates or support lifecycles.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether any planning documents exist at all. It is checked whether the planning goes beyond a simple list of users and software and whether basic aspects such as server dimensioning have been considered, even if only superficially.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic planning for VDI deployment exists. The number of virtual clients to be supplied and their general performance requirements (e.g., for office workstations) have been identified. However, the planning is not detailed and only marginally considers aspects such as future growth or the solution's support lifecycle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning includes initial sizing for servers, storage, and network based on current user numbers. There is basic coordination between the VDI components and the virtualization platform, mostly based on the manufacturer's standard recommendations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a planning document that defines the number of clients and the basic performance requirements. It is checked whether an initial sizing of the VDI components has been carried out and whether the planned support period is mentioned.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The performance requirements and number of required virtual clients, as well as the resulting requirements for the sizing of the VDI MUST be identified. The VDI components MUST be planned according to these sizing requirements. The VDI components and the used virtualization infrastructure MUST be planned in a coordinated manner. The support for the entire planned deployment period of the VDI solution MUST be considered during planning. The number of virtual clients and their required performance per virtualization server MUST be determined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal capacity planning document is created. This document lists the different user profiles (e.g., Office, Power User, Developer) and their specific requirements for CPU, RAM, GPU, and storage. The planning also considers the requirements for the network infrastructure, such as bandwidth and latency. The support contracts for hardware and software are reviewed and aligned with the planned deployment period.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the planning document for completeness. It is verified whether the performance requirements for different client types are defined, whether the VDI components are sized accordingly, and whether a valid support contract exists for the planned deployment period. A random check is performed to see if the determination of the maximum number of clients per server is based on traceable criteria.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning includes detailed capacity management that incorporates forecasts for user growth and changing application requirements over the entire lifecycle of the VDI solution. A formal capacity plan is created and periodically (e.g., annually) reviewed and adjusted to ensure that resources will be sufficient in the future.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Capacity planning is based not only on estimates, but also on the results of pilot phases or measurements of existing systems. The planning also considers peak loads and defines clear thresholds that trigger an expansion of the infrastructure when reached. The plan is approved in the Configuration Management Board (CMB).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a formal and approved capacity plan. It is checked whether the plan contains forecasts for future growth and whether there is a defined process for regular review and adjustment of the plan. Minutes of reviews are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: VDI planning is fully integrated into strategic IT planning and financial controlling. Automated tools are used for capacity forecasting, based on real-time usage data and trend analyses. The planning process includes the simulation of "what-if" scenarios to proactively assess the impact of major business changes (e.g., company acquisitions).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized monitoring tools continuously collect performance and usage data from the VDI environment. This data is fed into a forecasting tool that uses machine learning to predict future resource requirements. The results are visualized in a management dashboard and serve as a basis for investment decisions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the integration of the VDI planning process into the overarching corporate processes. The use of automated forecasting tools is verified, and it is checked whether the results of scenario simulations are documented and considered in strategic decisions. An auditor can request the execution of an automated capacity forecast report: `Show-VDIUsageForecast -Period 12Months`.

controls.title: Secure installation and configuration of VDI components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation of the VDI components is done with the manufacturer's default settings ("Next, Next, Finish"). Security aspects are considered minimally or not at all. Documentation of the configuration is incomplete or non-existent.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators often install the software under time pressure and without reading the manufacturer's security guides. Standard service accounts with excessive permissions are used, and communication between components is unencrypted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether the configuration of the VDI components deviates from the insecure default settings. It is checked whether documentation of the settings made exists, even if it is incomplete.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation of the VDI components follows the manufacturer's basic installation instructions. Some obvious security settings, such as changing default passwords, are made. However, the configuration is not systematically hardened or restricted to what is necessary. Basic documentation of the installation is available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During the installation, the most important security recommendations from the manufacturer's quick start guide are implemented. Clients are assigned to users, but the securing of communication channels may not yet be consistently implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies whether the manufacturer's basic security recommendations (e.g., from the "Getting Started Guide") have been implemented. It is checked whether the configuration is documented and whether default passwords have been changed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When the VDI components are installed and configured, it MUST at least be considered how to restrict them to operationally and technically necessary functions, how to secure the communication between VDI components, and how to securely assign virtual clients to users or groups thereof. Recommendations from the VDI solution's manufacturer for secure configuration MUST be considered. The configurations of the VDI components MUST be suitably documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An installation checklist based on the manufacturer's hardening recommendations is used. Unnecessary services and API endpoints of the VDI components are disabled. Communication between the components is enforced by TLS. The assignment rules for virtual clients are carefully configured and documented. The documentation is done in a central system such as a wiki or a CMDB.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the VDI components against the manufacturer's hardening guides and the internal documentation. It is checked whether the communication is encrypted, whether the range of functions has been restricted, and whether the assignment rules are implemented correctly. The quality and timeliness of the documentation are assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal hardening guide for the VDI components has been developed that goes beyond the manufacturer's recommendations and is based on established benchmarks (e.g., CIS). The configurations are centrally managed and versioned in a configuration management system (e.g., Ansible, Puppet). Automated scripts are used to ensure the consistent application of security settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration of the VDI components is treated as code (Infrastructure as Code). Every change to the configuration requires a review and approval process. The automation scripts are run regularly to check the configuration and correct configuration drift.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the internal hardening guide and compares it with the implemented configuration. The code repositories for the configuration automation are inspected. It is checked whether a change management process for configuration changes is established. An auditor can request the execution of a compliance check script: `Test-VDIComponentHardening -Profile 'CIS_Level_1'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire installation and configuration process is fully automated (Zero-Touch-Provisioning). Security configurations are continuously monitored and enforced with Policy-as-Code tools. Any deviation from the defined security baseline immediately triggers an alarm and an automated restoration of the desired state.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like HashiCorp Terraform is used for deploying the infrastructure and a tool like Open Policy Agent (OPA) for the continuous validation of the configuration. The security policies are also defined and versioned as code. The results of the compliance checks are displayed in real-time on a security dashboard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the automation and Policy-as-Code infrastructure. It is verified that the process from deployment to monitoring is seamless. The auditor performs an unauthorized configuration change as a test to observe whether it is automatically detected and corrected and whether a corresponding alarm is triggered.

controls.title: Secure installation and configuration of virtual clients using VDI

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Although the VDI solution is used to deploy some virtual clients, many clients are still created and configured manually directly in the hypervisor. This leads to inconsistent configurations and security vulnerabilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Manual VMs are often created for 'urgent' or 'special' requirements because the process via the VDI solution is perceived as too slow or too restrictive. These 'shadow VMs' are often not hardened and are not managed centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the list of VMs in the hypervisor with the list of managed clients in the VDI console. Discrepancies indicate manually created VMs. It is checked whether there are policies that regulate the creation of VMs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VDI solution is the preferred tool for installing and configuring virtual clients. However, there are no technical controls that prevent administrators from creating VMs directly in the hypervisor or manually importing them into the VDI solution when needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an organizational directive to use the VDI solution. However, implementation is not technically enforced, which leads to exceptions and inconsistencies, especially when it comes to the configuration of imported VMs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the permissions on the virtualization infrastructure. It is examined whether administrators who manage VDI also have the permission to create VMs directly. Hypervisor logs are checked for manual VM creation or import operations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VDI solution SHOULD be used to install and configure the virtual clients. Virtual clients SHOULD NOT be manually integrated into the VDI solution. In the virtualization infrastructure used for VDI, virtual clients SHOULD NOT be created independently of the VDI.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The provisioning and configuration of virtual clients is carried out exclusively via the management console or the automation interfaces of the VDI solution. Manually created VMs are not supported and are not integrated into the VDI environment. This is ensured by corresponding process specifications and organizational policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the documented process for provisioning virtual clients. It is checked whether the process mandates the exclusive use of the VDI solution. The inventory lists of the VDI solution and the hypervisor are compared to identify unmanaged VMs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Technical controls are implemented that strictly prevent administrators from creating or modifying VDI-managed virtual clients outside of the VDI management console. This is enforced by a granular role-based access control (RBAC) at the hypervisor level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On the virtualization platform (e.g., vSphere, Hyper-V), dedicated roles are created for VDI administrators. These roles only grant the permissions required for the VDI solution (e.g., Power-On/Off) but revoke the permission to create, clone, or directly modify their configuration (vCPU, RAM). These actions are only permitted for the VDI service account.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the RBAC configuration on the virtualization platform. It is verified that the permissions of the VDI administrators are configured according to the principle of least privilege and that the creation of VMs outside the VDI solution is technically prevented. An auditor can try to manually create a VM as a VDI admin: `New-VM -Name 'Test-VM'` should fail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: API access to the virtualization platform is restricted to the dedicated service account of the VDI solution. The entire lifecycle management of virtual clients is fully automated and is seamlessly audited via the logs of the VDI solution, which are fed into a SIEM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Network ACLs or a firewall on the hypervisor's management interface restrict API access to the IP addresses of the VDI management servers. All administrative activities are performed exclusively via the VDI console. The audit logs of the VDI solution are sent to a SIEM in real time, where correlation rules check for suspicious activities (e.g., creation of a VM outside of business hours).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the network controls that restrict API access to the hypervisors. The configuration of log forwarding from the VDI solution to the SIEM is checked. In the SIEM, it is checked whether alerts for anomalous VM lifecycle events are configured and whether they are functioning.

controls.title: Network segmentation of VDI components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All VDI components (management, broker, gateways) and the virtual clients are located in a single, large network segment. There is no internal segmentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a quick or initial deployment, all systems are often placed in an existing server VLAN to minimize network configuration complexity. This allows unrestricted communication between all components.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the IP configuration of the VDI components and some sample clients. It is determined whether all systems are in the same subnet and whether there are firewall rules between them.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic separation is in place by separating the VDI management network from the general user network. However, the virtual clients themselves are not further segmented from each other and are located in a common network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate VLAN is set up for the management interfaces of the VDI servers. The virtual clients are placed in one or more larger VLANs that are separate from the management components but have no further subdivision by risk level or user group.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the network architecture documentation. It is checked whether separate VLANs exist for management and virtual clients. Network scans are used to check whether clients from different user groups can reach each other on the network.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VDI components, including the virtual clients, SHOULD be considered separately in network segmentation. Networks SHOULD be separated at least with the help of the virtualization infrastructure. Dedicated network segments SHOULD be set up at least for the VDI components' administration network and for the networks for internal communication between VDI components.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The network architecture provides for separate virtual switches or port groups for different zones: an administration network for access to the management consoles, an internal communication network for data exchange between the VDI components (e.g., database access), and one or more networks for the virtual clients. The data traffic between these segments is controlled by a firewall.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the virtual network infrastructure in the hypervisor. It is verified whether dedicated network segments exist for administration, internal communication, and client traffic. The firewall rules between these segments are checked for correctness and the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Micro-segmentation is used to separate different groups of virtual clients into their own network zones based on their security profile or user group (e.g., HR, development, external partners). The firewall rules between these zones strictly follow the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technologies like VMware NSX or Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security are used to dynamically create security groups for virtual clients. The rules, for example, only allow communication from developer clients to the development servers and block any direct contact with HR department clients.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the micro-segmentation solution. It is checked whether the segmentation is based on logical groups and whether the firewall rules correspond to the defined communication relationships. As a test, an attempt is made to establish an unauthorized connection between clients of different segments. An auditor can query the effective firewall rules for a random VM: `Get-VMNetworkPolicy -VMName 'HR-Client-01'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Zero Trust network architecture is implemented. All network traffic between VDI components as well as between virtual clients and to the target applications is blocked, authenticated, and encrypted by default. Network policies are dynamically applied based on the user's identity, the device's state, and the context of the access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Zero Trust platform (e.g., Zscaler Private Access, Appgate SDP) is used. Every connection request from a virtual client is terminated at the gateway and checked against a policy that considers user identity (via IdP), device compliance (via EDR), and the requested application. Only after successful verification is a short-lived, encrypted 1:1 connection established to the target.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration of the Zero Trust platform. The policy definition is checked and it is verified whether the default rule set is 'Deny All'. The integration with the Identity Provider and the endpoint security solution is controlled. It is checked whether all data traffic is encrypted and whether the logging enables complete tracking of all connection attempts.

controls.title: Standardized access to virtual clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The mechanisms and services of the VDI solution SHOULD be used to control and secure access to the virtual clients. If additional software is used for this access on the accessing clients, this software SHOULD be standardized and provided centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access to the virtual desktops is exclusively via the gateway provided by the VDI manufacturer and the corresponding client software. The client software is distributed to the users' end devices via a central software distribution system. Direct RDP or SSH connections to the virtual clients are blocked at the network level.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that access to the VDI environment is via a defined access point (gateway). It is checked whether the client software is centrally deployed and managed. Firewall rules are checked to ensure that direct connections to the virtual clients are prevented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of the standardized VDI client is mandatory and technically enforced. Its configuration is centrally managed via group policies or an endpoint management solution to ensure consistent security settings (e.g., disabling the clipboard, no drive or USB redirection) on all end devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Group policies (GPOs) or policies in a UEM (Unified Endpoint Management) solution like Intune or Workspace ONE are used to dictate the configuration of the VDI client software. Users cannot change these security-relevant settings. Different policies can be applied depending on the user group (e.g., developers may use the clipboard, clerks may not).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configured group policies or UEM policies for the VDI client. On a sample client, it is verified that the settings have been applied correctly and cannot be changed by the user. It is checked whether the policies are documented and designed according to the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access is controlled via a secure gateway that enforces multi-factor authentication (MFA) and a device posture check before establishing a connection. The VDI client software itself runs in a containerized or hardened, read-only environment on the end device to prevent attacks on the client.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VDI gateway is integrated with an Identity Provider (e.g., Azure AD, Okta) for MFA and an endpoint security solution (e.g., CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) for posture checks. Access is only granted if the user provides MFA AND the end device is reported as compliant (e.g., antivirus up-to-date, disk encryption active). The client software is deployed as an App-V package or in a Docker container on the end device.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the VDI gateway and its integration with the IdP and the endpoint security solution. A test connection is attempted with a non-compliant device or without MFA. The isolation of the VDI client software on the endpoints is checked.

controls.title: Use of a dedicated infrastructure for virtual VDI components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If the VDI components are operated in a virtualized environment, they SHOULD be run on a dedicated virtualization infrastructure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The virtual machines running the VDI management components (e.g., Connection Broker, database, license server) are operated on a separate cluster of hypervisor hosts. This management cluster is not used to run regular virtual clients or other server workloads to avoid resource conflicts and security risks from the compromise of other systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the management console of the virtualization platform that a dedicated cluster exists for the VDI management components. It is checked whether only the intended management VMs and no other workloads are running on the hosts of this cluster.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Not only the hypervisors, but also the underlying storage and network infrastructure for the VDI management components are physically or logically strictly separated from the infrastructure that serves the virtual clients and other applications.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VDI management cluster uses dedicated storage LUNs or volumes and is connected to separate switch ports. The network traffic of the management cluster is routed via dedicated VLANs that are separate from the VLANs of the virtual client workloads. This prevents performance bottlenecks ('noisy neighbor' problem) and improves security.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration of the storage and network infrastructure. It is verified whether dedicated resources (LUNs, VLANs, switch ports) are allocated to the VDI management cluster. The network and storage architecture diagrams are checked for correct separation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VDI management plane is operated in a dedicated high-security zone, ideally on dedicated physical hardware, with strict physical and logical access controls and intensive monitoring. It is treated as critical infrastructure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The servers for the VDI management components are housed in a separate, access-protected rack in the data center. Administrative access to these systems is restricted to a few specialized administrators and requires multi-factor authentication and a Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution. All activity on these systems is logged and analyzed without gaps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the physical security measures for the VDI management hardware. The configuration of the PAM solution and the access permissions are checked. The logs are checked for completeness and for analysis by a SIEM system.

controls.title: Hardening of the virtualized clients through the VDI solution

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The capabilities of the VDI solution SHOULD be used for hardening the virtual clients according to the requirements of module SYS.2.5 Client Virtualization. The operating systems of the clients SHOULD be configured exclusively via the management component of the VDI solution. Individual configuration of existing virtual clients via the virtualization infrastructure SHOULD be prevented by technical means.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Hardening policies are defined centrally in the VDI management console and applied to the client pools. This includes, for example, disabling USB ports, restricting system settings, or configuring the Windows Firewall. Direct access to the console of the virtual machines via the hypervisor client is restricted for administrators to prevent manual changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the hardening policies defined in the VDI solution. A random check is performed on a virtual client to see if these policies are applied correctly. The permissions on the virtualization platform are verified to ensure that manual configuration changes to the VMs are prevented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hardening policies within the VDI solution are comprehensive, based on recognized benchmarks (e.g., CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs), and are versioned. Regular, automated audits are conducted to check the compliance of the virtual clients with these policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The master images are hardened with scripts based on CIS benchmarks. In addition, VDI policies are used to enforce dynamic settings. A compliance scanning tool regularly checks all running virtual clients for deviations from the baseline. The results are displayed in a dashboard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the implemented hardening policies with the chosen external benchmark. The results of the automated compliance audits are reviewed and checked for unaddressed deviations. An auditor can request the execution of a compliance scan for a random VM: `Invoke-VMComplianceScan -VMName 'Finance-Client-05' -Benchmark 'CIS_Windows11_v1.0'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Desired State Configuration (DSC) management system is used. The hardening of the virtual clients is continuously enforced. Any unauthorized change to the configuration of a virtual client is automatically detected, logged, and immediately reset to the defined target state.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technologies such as PowerShell DSC, Ansible, or Puppet are used to define the desired configuration state. An agent on each virtual client ensures that this state is permanently maintained. Any attempt at a manual change (e.g., enabling a service) is automatically corrected within minutes. The correction attempts are reported to a central logging system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration of the DSC management system. A configuration change is attempted on a virtual client to verify that it is automatically reset. The logs are checked to determine if the correction process was reported correctly.

controls.title: Hardening of the VDI solution

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automatic login to the VDI SHOULD not be possible. Authentication SHOULD only occur after the user has interacted with the VDI.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Features such as 'pass-through authentication' from the endpoint or saving credentials in the VDI client are disabled. The user must actively enter their credentials (e.g., username and password) for each new connection to the VDI gateway.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the VDI gateway and the VDI client policies. It is verified that options for automatic login or saving passwords are disabled. A session is started on a trial basis to confirm that manual interaction is required for authentication.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VDI solution is configured to require re-authentication for each new session, even if the user is already logged into their endpoint and has a valid Single Sign-On session. Single Sign-On is only configured to pre-fill the username, but the password or a second factor must be actively entered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VDI gateway's policies enforce the re-authentication requirement. The lifetime of authentication tokens for the VDI session is limited to a short period, so that a new login is required even after a short period of inactivity.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the authentication policies of the VDI system. It is tested whether a new entry of credentials is required after logging out and immediately logging in again. The token lifetime configuration is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enforced for every login attempt to the VDI gateway. The system is also hardened against attacks such as session hijacking and replay attacks, for example, by using cryptographically bound tokens.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VDI gateway is integrated with a modern identity provider (e.g., Azure AD Conditional Access, Okta) that enforces adaptive MFA. Protocols such as OpenID Connect with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) are used for session management to prevent replay attacks. The session tokens are bound to the client's IP address.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the MFA configuration in the identity provider and its connection to the VDI gateway. It is checked whether MFA is enforced for all user groups. The configuration of the session management is checked for the use of modern, secure protocols and mechanisms such as token binding.

controls.title: Integration of the virtual clients into patch and change management

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The virtual clients SHOULD, if possible, be managed centrally via the management components of the VDI solution. The virtual clients SHOULD also be patched when they are turned off, if this is supported by the VDI solution. The templates from which virtual clients are created SHOULD be updated regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined process for patch management of VDI clients is established. This process includes the regular (e.g., monthly) updating of the master images/templates. For persistent clients, a conventional patch management tool is used. If the VDI solution supports patching of powered-off VMs, this feature is used to ensure that even rarely used clients remain up-to-date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the patch management process for VDI clients. The date of the last update of the master templates is verified. The patch status of running and powered-off virtual clients is checked on a random basis. It is checked whether the feature for patching in the powered-off state is configured, if available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The patch process is largely automated. The release of new security patches by vendors triggers an automated workflow that updates the master template, creates a test VM for validation, and, after a successful test, performs a staged rollout of the updated image to the virtual client pools.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Automation scripts (e.g., PowerShell, Ansible) monitor patch sources. When new patches are available, the master image is automatically started, patched, shut down, and a new snapshot is created. A test group of clients is then updated with the new image. If no problems occur, the image is rolled out to all users in stages (e.g., first IT, then pilot groups, then everyone).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the automated patch workflow. The configuration of the automation scripts and the definition of the rollout groups are checked. The workflow logs are reviewed to verify the successful execution of the last patch cycles.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For non-persistent desktops, a regular (e.g., daily) user logoff is enforced to ensure that they receive a fresh, fully patched client from the latest template upon their next login. For persistent desktops, patch compliance is continuously monitored, and non-compliant systems are automatically isolated from the production network (quarantined) until they are patched.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Session timeouts in the VDI solution enforce a daily re-login. The patch management solution is integrated with the Network Access Control (NAC) system. If a client reports an outdated patch level, it is automatically moved to a quarantine VLAN by the NAC system, where it can only reach the patch server. After a successful update, access is restored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the session timeouts. The integration between the patch management and NAC system is checked. As a test, a client with an outdated patch level is simulated to observe whether the quarantine function is triggered correctly. An auditor can query the status of a client: `Get-ClientComplianceState -ClientName 'Sales-Client-02'`.

controls.title: Monitoring of VDI availability and utilization

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The state of the VDI components SHOULD be centrally monitored. At a minimum, the following parameters SHOULD be monitored for each VDI component: reachability of the required network interfaces, availability of the services provided by the VDI component, and utilization of the CPU and memory.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central monitoring system (e.g., Nagios, Zabbix, Prometheus) is used to monitor the defined parameters. For each VDI component (broker, gateway, database, etc.), checks are set up to regularly query network reachability (ping), the availability of specific services (e.g., port check on the broker port), and the basic utilization of CPU and RAM. Basic threshold values are defined, which trigger a notification to the administrators when exceeded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the monitoring system. It is verified whether all VDI components are recorded in the monitoring and whether the required parameters (network, services, CPU, RAM) are being monitored. It is checked whether alerting rules are configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The monitoring includes application-specific health checks for the VDI services. Detailed thresholds for performance indicators (e.g., login duration, protocol latency) are defined, which automatically trigger alarms when exceeded. A central dashboard provides a real-time overview of the health of the entire VDI environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Special management packs or plugins for the VDI solution are used in the monitoring system. These perform more in-depth checks, e.g., querying database connection pools or measuring the license server response time. The dashboard (e.g., in Grafana) visualizes the most important metrics and the overall status of the environment at a glance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the monitoring dashboard and the configuration of the application-specific checks. It is checked whether the thresholds for performance indicators are reasonable and documented. The alerting history is checked for relevant events and their processing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Predictive monitoring is used. The system analyzes trends in resource utilization to predict potential bottlenecks before they affect users. Synthetic user logins are continuously performed from various locations to proactively monitor end-to-end performance and availability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitoring solution with AIOps (AI for IT Operations) capabilities is used. It analyzes historical data to learn normal behavior patterns and detect anomalies. Dedicated probes (e.g., LoginVSI, eG Innovations) simulate user logins and application launches around the clock and measure performance. In case of deviations, a ticket is proactively created in the ITSM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the predictive analysis and synthetic monitoring tools. It is checked whether the trend analyses and the results of the synthetic tests are used for capacity planning and proactive troubleshooting. The logs of the last simulated logins are reviewed.

controls.title: Monitoring of security-relevant events of the VDI

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the VDI components, at least the following events SHOULD be forwarded to a central monitoring system: successful and failed login attempts, configuration changes to VDI components or virtual clients, successful and failed updates to VDI components, failed updates to virtual clients. The VDI components SHOULD be regularly checked for vulnerabilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Audit logging on all VDI components is enabled to capture the required events. A log forwarding agent (e.g., Winlogbeat, Syslog-ng) is installed on the components to send these events to a central log management server (e.g., ELK stack, Graylog). Regular, authenticated vulnerability scans are performed against the VDI components.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the logging configuration of the VDI components and the log forwarding agent. In the central log management system, random checks are performed to see if the required events are arriving. The configuration and the reports of the last vulnerability scans are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The collected log data is correlated in a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system with other data sources (e.g., firewall logs, Active Directory logs). Basic alerting rules are configured to indicate suspicious events (e.g., excessive failed logins from one IP address, configuration change outside of a maintenance window).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the SIEM (e.g., Splunk, QRadar), special parsers for the VDI logs are developed or imported. Correlation rules are created to detect simple attack patterns, e.g., 'Brute-force attack: 10 failed logins for one user within 5 minutes' or 'Suspicious configuration change: Administrator changes a policy outside of business hours'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration of the SIEM, especially the parsers and correlation rules for the VDI environment. The alerting history is checked for relevant security events and their investigation by the security team. It is verified that the rules are documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) are applied to the VDI log data to detect anomalous activities that are not caught by rule-based systems. The results of vulnerability scans are automatically fed into a ticketing system to track and escalate remediation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UEBA module in the SIEM or a standalone tool learns the normal behavior of users and systems (e.g., usual login times, applications used, data access patterns). It raises an alarm in case of deviations, such as an administrator logging in at night from an unusual location and downloading large amounts of data. The integration of the vulnerability scanner with the ITSM tool (e.g., Jira, ServiceNow) automatically creates tickets for found vulnerabilities and assigns them to the responsible teams.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration and functionality of the UEBA system. Sample alerts for anomalous behavior are analyzed. The integration between the vulnerability scanner and the ticketing system is checked by tracking the lifecycle of a ticket from the discovery of a vulnerability to its remediation.

controls.title: Distribution of virtual clients on virtualization servers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The maximum performance that each virtualization server is allowed to provide for virtual clients SHOULD be defined. These limits SHOULD be used in the VDI management component to distribute the virtual clients across different virtualization servers in case of high load.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the VDI management console, maximum values for the number of VMs, CPU, or memory utilization are set for each host or cluster. These thresholds are based on capacity planning and prevent excessive overbooking of resources. The VDI solution uses these limits to place new VMs on the least loaded host, thus ensuring a basic load distribution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks in the VDI management console whether limits for host utilization or the number of VMs per host are defined. It is checked whether these values are consistent with capacity planning and whether the load balancing function is enabled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The load balancing mechanism is fine-tuned based on historical performance data. For placement decisions, not only CPU and RAM but also other metrics such as storage I/O and network bandwidth are considered to achieve a more balanced distribution and better performance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VDI solution or an integrated tool of the virtualization platform (e.g., VMware DRS) is configured to also consider the utilization of datastores and network adapters in its decisions. The weighting of the various metrics is adjusted to match the specific requirements of the workloads (e.g., higher weighting of I/O for database-intensive applications).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the advanced configuration of the load balancing mechanism. It is verified that metrics beyond CPU/RAM (such as storage I/O and network) are included in the decision-making. The configuration is checked for plausibility and documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully automated, policy-driven resource scheduler is used. This dynamically migrates virtual clients between hosts in real time to optimize performance and ensure service quality for all users according to predefined Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An advanced resource management tool (e.g., VMware vRealize Operations, Turbonomic) is integrated with the VDI and virtualization platform. It continuously analyzes utilization and predicts bottlenecks. Based on defined SLAs (e.g., 'Financial applications must have a latency of <5ms'), it proactively performs live migrations of VMs to prevent performance degradation before it occurs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the automated resource scheduler. It is checked whether SLAs for different application categories are defined. The tool's logs are reviewed to understand the optimization actions performed (e.g., live migrations) and their justification.

controls.title: Use of separate VDI solutions for different user groups

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be checked whether there are user groups that differ so much in their permissions that the use of a common VDI solution is not feasible. In this case, a separate VDI solution SHOULD be used for each user group.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A risk analysis identifies user groups with highly divergent security requirements, e.g., standard office users, privileged administrators, and external developers. Based on this analysis, the decision is made to build separate VDI environments (i.e., separate sets of brokers, gateways, databases) for these groups to ensure logical separation and minimize the risk of compromise propagation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the risk analysis and checks whether user groups with different protection needs have been identified. It is verified whether the documented architecture provides for separate VDI instances for these groups. The configuration is checked to ensure that users are correctly assigned to the respective VDI solutions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The separate VDI environments are deployed in completely isolated network segments and managed by different administrator teams to enforce a strict Separation of Duties.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each VDI instance has its own dedicated VLANs for management, internal communication, and client access. Network traffic between the VDI instances is completely blocked. The administrative tasks for the high-security VDI environment (e.g., for administrators) are performed by a different team than that for the standard VDI environment, which is implemented through different permissions in Active Directory and on the systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the network architecture and firewall rules to verify the complete isolation of the VDI instances. The administrative permissions are checked to confirm the implementation of the Separation of Duties. It is verified whether different administrator accounts are used for managing the different environments.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The separate VDI solutions are physically separated (Air-Gapped) or use hardware-enforced separation mechanisms (e.g. separate hypervisor clusters, storage systems and network hardware) to provide the highest possible security guarantee.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VDI environment for highly privileged users runs on a completely separate set of physical servers located in a separate, high-security area of the data center. There are no shared infrastructure components (no shared hypervisor, no shared storage array, no shared network core switch) with the standard VDI environment. Access is provided via a separate, dedicated access solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the physical separation of the hardware by inspecting the data center documentation and rack plans. The hardware inventory lists are checked to ensure that no components are shared between the environments. Network diagrams are analyzed to confirm the physical separation of the communication paths.

controls.title: Use of non-persistent virtual clients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After being used or at a defined point in time, the virtual clients SHOULD be reset to their basic state, i.e. to the underlying template, or be re-provisioned if necessary. These time windows SHOULD be documented and communicated to those affected. Non-reset virtual clients SHOULD NOT be used by multiple different users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For use cases that do not require persistent data on the client (e.g. call centers, training rooms), non-persistent desktop pools are set up. The VDI solution is configured so that the virtual machines are automatically reset or deleted and recreated from the master template after the user logs off. Users are informed that all data stored on the desktop will be lost.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the desktop pools in the VDI management console. It is verified whether the option to reset/delete after logoff is activated for the corresponding pools. The communication documents for the users are checked for corresponding notices. It is checked whether it is ensured that subsequent users receive a clean VM.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The clients are automatically reset after each logoff. Robust mechanisms for redirecting user profiles and data (e.g., to network storage) are implemented to ensure a seamless user experience while maintaining the statelessness of the client operating system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Technologies such as FSLogix Profile Containers or VMware Dynamic Environment Manager are used to offload the user profile and user-specific data to a virtual hard disk file (VHDX) on a fast file server. When logging in, this file is mounted into the otherwise stateless client, so the user finds their personalized environment. After logging off, the machine is nevertheless reset.
