parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the profile management solution. It is checked whether the reset policy for the clients is consistently set to 'on logoff'. As a test, a file is saved on the desktop, a logoff and new logon is performed, and it is checked whether the file is present again in the new client (which proves profile persistence) and the client itself has been reset.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire user session, including the applications, is containerized. After logging off, the container is completely destroyed, leaving no traces of the session on the virtual client. This is combined with an enforced daily new logon to ensure that each user starts each day with a clean, newly provisioned environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Application virtualization or layering technologies (e.g. VMware App Volumes, Citrix App Layering) are used to dynamically attach applications to a base client at runtime without installing them. After logging off, these application layers are removed again and the base VM is reset. Session time limits in the VDI policy enforce the daily logoff.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration of the application layering solution and the assignment rules. It is verified that the base VMs do not contain any installed applications. The configuration of the session time limits is checked. It is checked whether the logs confirm the destruction and recreation of the session containers after each logoff.

controls.title: Highly available deployment of VDI components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VDI components SHOULD be designed redundantly. Each component SHOULD also be redundantly connected to the relevant networks. If the VDI components are operated on physical IT systems, these IT systems SHOULD have redundant power supply and data storage. If the VDI components are operated virtualized, mechanisms of the virtualization infrastructure SHOULD be used for high availability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Critical VDI components such as Connection Brokers and Gateways are operated as a cluster with at least two nodes. These are operated either in an active/active mode behind a load balancer or in an active/passive cluster with automatic failover. For virtualized components, the high availability function of the virtualization platform (e.g. VMware HA, Hyper-V Failover Clustering) is used to automatically restart the VMs on another host in the event of a host failure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the architecture of the VDI environment and verifies that critical components are designed redundantly. The configuration of the load balancer or the failover cluster is checked. In virtualized environments, the configuration of the hypervisor's high availability function is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VDI solution is distributed across two physically separate data centers in a stretched cluster configuration, providing site-level resiliency. The failover process is tested regularly (e.g., semi-annually) as part of a formal disaster recovery plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VDI infrastructure extends across two sites with synchronous storage mirroring and a resilient network. In the event of a complete site failure, the VDI solution can continue to operate at the remaining site. The DR tests include a controlled failover and failback of the entire environment and are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the disaster recovery plan and reviews the logs of the last DR tests. The configuration of the cross-site clusters and the storage mirroring is analyzed. It is checked whether the tests were successful and what lessons were learned from them.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A cross-site active-active architecture with Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB) is implemented. Users are automatically and transparently routed to the nearest or best-performing data center. The system can withstand the total failure of one site without data loss and with minimal or no service interruption for users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A complete, active VDI environment runs at both sites. A GSLB service (e.g. F5 GTM, Cloudflare Load Balancing) distributes incoming user requests to the two sites based on geographical proximity, latency, and system health. The user data is kept up-to-date between the sites using asynchronous replication or a global file system technology.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the GSLB service and the routing policies. The architecture is checked for true active-active capability. A simulated site failure is performed (e.g., by deactivating the GSLB endpoint for one site) to observe whether traffic is automatically and seamlessly redirected to the remaining site.

controls.title: Integration of the VDI into a SIEM

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system is used, the VDI components SHOULD be integrated into it. In the SIEM, the monitored events SHOULD be automatically analyzed for anomalies, including attack patterns.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All relevant VDI components (brokers, gateways, web servers) are configured to send their security-relevant logs to the central SIEM system. In the SIEM, basic parsers for these logs are configured and there are initial correlation rules to detect known, simple attack patterns or policy violations (e.g. brute-force login attempts).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the log forwarding on the VDI components. In the SIEM, it is checked whether the logs are arriving and being parsed correctly. The existence and functionality of basic correlation rules for VDI-specific events is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIEM has a dedicated VDI dashboard and a set of fine-tuned correlation rules to detect complex attack patterns specific to VDI environments. This includes, for example, 'impossible travel', session hijacking attempts, or data exfiltration via the clipboard or redirected drives.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A VDI-specific content pack or app is installed in the SIEM. Correlation rules are developed that combine VDI logs with Geo-IP data, Active Directory group memberships, and data from endpoint security solutions. A dashboard visualizes suspicious activities, such as logins by the same user from different countries within a short period or unusually high data transfers over the VDI connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the VDI dashboard in the SIEM and analyzes the logic of the complex correlation rules. It is checked whether these rules are regularly reviewed and adapted to new threats. The handling of alarms triggered by these rules is tracked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIEM integration is bidirectional. The SIEM can trigger automated responses in the VDI environment via a SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) platform. Examples include automatically isolating a suspicious virtual client from the network, forcing a user logoff, or blocking an IP address at the VDI gateway.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SIEM is integrated with a SOAR platform (e.g., Splunk SOAR, Palo Alto Cortex XSOAR). Playbooks are developed that automatically trigger actions in response to specific SIEM alarms. Example: A UEBA alarm for anomalous behavior leads to the SOAR playbook terminating the affected user's session via the VDI API and temporarily suspending the user account until the incident is investigated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration of the SOAR platform and the defined playbooks for the VDI environment. The integration between SIEM, SOAR, and the VDI API is checked. A test alarm is triggered to verify that the corresponding playbook is executed correctly and that the intended response occurs in the VDI environment.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
A Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) controls and manages standardized virtual clients. This allows individual applications (e.g., Office programs) or entire desktops to be provided centrally. Virtual clients are virtualized IT systems that can be accessed via terminal server protocols. The virtual clients run on virtualization servers, which are combined with a management system to form a virtualization infrastructure (see modules SYS.1.5 Virtualization and SYS.2.5 Client Virtualization).
Depending on the product used, a VDI typically consists of access, control, and management components that are operated on one or more distributed IT systems. These central VDI components manage the virtualization infrastructure, among other things, and establish the connections between accessing and virtual clients. Therefore, the virtualization infrastructure, the connected storage systems, and the virtual and accessing clients are also an implicit part of the VDI. However, in this module, "VDI components" always refers to the following three central components of a VDI:
• The VDI access components authenticate the users and, based on their permissions, decide whether access is permitted or not and for which type of virtual client the users are authorized.
• The VDI control components select the appropriate virtual clients for the permitted access and establish the connection between the accessing and virtual client.
• The VDI management components manage the rules (e.g., the assignment of users to client types) and settings (e.g., the protocols to be used). They also manage the virtual clients (according to SYS.2.5 Client Virtualization). This also includes the assigned resources and their provisioning, as well as the terminal server-specific settings of the virtual clients.
In addition, it may be necessary to connect other infrastructure services that are not part of the VDI solution itself (e.g., directory services, name resolution, or IP address management).

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to protect information that is stored, processed, and transmitted when using a VDI. For this purpose, special requirements are placed on the VDI components described in the introduction.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The SYS.2.6 Virtual Desktop Infrastructure module is to be applied to every IT system that is used as part of a VDI solution.
This module covers the following content:
The SYS.2.6 Virtual Desktop Infrastructure module deals with the secure use of a VDI. The focus is on the three central components of a VDI.
This module contains specific requirements for the networks used in order to secure the communication between the accessing client and the virtualization infrastructure.
The following content is also important and is covered elsewhere:
• The basic functionality of communication between an accessing and a virtual client in a VDI solution is fulfilled using terminal server techniques. Therefore, the SYS.1.9 Terminal Server module must also be applied to the VDI solution, where the individual virtual clients are the actual terminal servers.
• Likewise, the SYS.2.5 Client Virtualization and SYS.1.5 Virtualization modules are to be applied for the individual virtual clients and the virtualization infrastructure, respectively, especially for the isolation of the virtual clients via the virtualization server.
• Basic requirements for the individual server components as well as the accessing and virtual clients can be found in the SYS.1.1 General Server and SYS.2.1 General Client modules, respectively. In addition, operating system-specific modules may need to be applied.
• The NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design module must be applied to secure the networks used for the VDI.
This module does not cover
• those IT systems that are used in the context of the VDI in addition to the VDI components described above (e.g., storage systems) and
• the techniques used for virtualization or for communication between accessing and virtual clients.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Loss of quality in the provisioning of virtual clients
parts.prose:
In many cases, a VDI is used to optimize resources. However, if many virtual clients are placed on individual virtualization servers, the available resources can be overbooked. Resources can also be overbooked if the planned number of users was estimated incorrectly.
This can cause virtual clients in the VDI to compete heavily for resources, and performance can drop unpredictably. This can lead to the virtual clients becoming temporarily unavailable.
The performance drops are usually non-transparent to the users, so that data is lost or unintentionally changed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Incorrect assignment of virtual clients to users
parts.prose:
Virtual clients and their resources are assigned to users centrally by the VDI based on profiles. If such an assignment is incorrect, this can result in
• high costs if high-performance virtual clients are assigned to users with low resource requirements,
• low-performance virtual clients being assigned to users with high resource requirements or special hardware requirements, e.g., for CAD tasks,
• users gaining unauthorized access to IT systems and information, or
• external USB devices being connected and information being transferred to virtual clients not intended for it.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Insufficient network separation due to misconfiguration in the VDI
parts.prose:
Typically, different virtual clients are operated in a VDI solution, which differ greatly in their application areas and can accordingly be assigned to different networks. The VDI management component manages all these clients. If the VDI management component is configured incorrectly, a necessary network separation can be lifted. Under certain circumstances, this can allow virtual clients to communicate with each other without authorization.
This situation arises, for example, if the virtual clients are assigned to the users based on properties such as group memberships and are assigned incorrectly. In this case, a network separation that should actually exist between clients of different groups can be bypassed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Loss of virtual clients due to misconfiguration in the VDI
parts.prose:
A strength of VDI is that many different virtual clients can be easily managed via a few templates. This allows new desktops to be provisioned quickly and faulty desktops to be repaired or replaced.
However, this centralized management can lead to the loss of virtual clients due to deleted or corrupted templates. If certain user data is stored exclusively on the virtual clients' storage, the loss of a virtual client also leads to a loss of this data.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Failure of VDI components
parts.prose:
A VDI typically consists of several components that are dependent on each other. If even one of these components fails, for example due to hardware or software errors or due to misconfigurations, this can impair the availability of the entire VDI solution and thus the ability of the users to work.
A failure of one or more components can have very different effects. For example, in the event of a failure of the VDI management component, normal operation is in principle possible, but no adjustments can be made. This can lead, among other things, to the fact that
• new virtual clients cannot be provisioned,
• virtual clients cannot be reset to a functional base state after errors,
• troubleshooting is made more difficult because the collected information of the management functions is not available, or
• the resources of a virtual client cannot be adjusted if they are insufficient for individuals.
The access or control components of some VDI products do not offer their full range of functions without the management component.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Unauthorized access to virtual clients
parts.prose:
A VDI management component manages all associated clients. If the VDI management component is compromised (for example, due to exploited vulnerabilities or misconfiguration), the virtual clients can be accessed from there. In this case, the availability, confidentiality, or integrity of the virtual clients can be compromised.
Some VDI solutions come with agent software that is used within the virtual clients and is required for certain VDI functions (e.g., connection setup, 3D acceleration, optimization of memory consumption). If a misconfiguration affects this agent software, the virtual clients can be endangered.
The agent software and the management component of the VDI control many clients, depending on the size of the environment. In these cases, many different virtual clients can be accessed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Use of templates with software vulnerabilities
parts.prose:
In a VDI, virtual clients can be created quickly and centrally from a defined set of templates. When these templates are created, they are usually on an up-to-date software version without known vulnerabilities.
However, without regular updating of these templates, it is possible that a newly created virtual client has vulnerabilities that became known after the template was created. If other IT systems can access this virtual client, the known vulnerability can be exploited and the virtual client can thus be compromised.

controls.title: Regulations for the mobile use of laptops

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no formal, written regulations for the mobile use of laptops. At best, individual employees are given verbal, ad-hoc instructions on general conduct. A large proportion of users are unaware of specific risks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, the organization relies entirely on the individual sense of responsibility of its employees, without supporting this with clear guidelines. This often happens in very small organizations or during phases of rapid, unstructured growth.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with various employees whether they have received instructions on mobile use. It is checked whether there are any documented regulations. If these are missing, maturity level 1 is reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic, written regulation on mobile use, but it is very general. It is part of the general IT usage policy and is made available to employees upon hiring. Specific instructions for different scenarios (e.g., international travel) are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard template for an IT usage policy is supplemented with a short section on mobile device usage. Communication occurs once during onboarding. There are no regular reminders or training sessions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the IT usage policy and checks whether a section on the mobile use of laptops exists. Random checks with employees are used to verify whether they are aware of the existence of the regulation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be clearly regulated what employees must consider when using laptops on the go. In particular, it MUST be specified which laptops may be used on the go, who is allowed to take them, and what basic security measures must be observed. Users MUST be informed of the regulations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate document (policy) on the mobile use of laptops is created. This document is published on the intranet and is accessible to all employees. Security briefings explicitly refer to this policy and its contents. The regulations cover at least how to handle the device in public, in transport, and in hotels, as well as requirements for secure storage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the dedicated regulation for mobile use presented to them. It is checked whether the contents cover the required aspects (who, what, which measures). In addition, it is checked whether and how employees are verifiably informed about these regulations (e.g., through minutes of briefings or references on the intranet).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regulations for mobile use are detailed and differentiate according to the protection needs of the processed data and the travel scenario (e.g., stricter rules for travel to high-risk countries). Compliance with the regulations is ensured through mandatory annual security training with a final test. Participation is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is supplemented with a chapter on travel to countries with special risks. A mandatory briefing takes place before such trips. The security training is implemented via an e-learning platform, which automates tracking.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the policy for its level of detail and differentiation. Evidence of the annual training sessions and their successful completion by employees is requested (e.g., excerpts from the learning management system).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regulations are fully integrated into the ISMS and are supported by technical measures. For example, context-aware security reminders are displayed on the laptop when it connects to a public Wi-Fi network. The policies are reviewed annually or on an ad-hoc basis (e.g., after a relevant security incident) and optimized based on threat analyses and incident statistics.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An endpoint management tool is used to enforce location-dependent policies. A script detects insecure networks and displays a warning with the most important rules of conduct. The review of the policy is a fixed component of the annual management review of the ISMS.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the technical implementation of the context-aware notices, e.g., through a demonstration. Minutes of the annual review of the policy and evidence that the findings from incidents and threat analyses have been incorporated into the update are requested.

controls.title: Use of personal firewalls

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On some laptops, the personal firewall included in the operating system by default is active. There is no central management or review of the configuration. Users can disable the firewall at will.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This situation often arises when there are no central configuration specifications for operating systems and the setup is left to the end users or the standard installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines a sample of laptops and determines whether the personal firewall is active. In addition, it is checked whether the user has the permission to disable the firewall. If the firewall is inactive on a significant portion of the devices or can be disabled by the user, this is maturity level 1.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On all laptops, the personal firewall is enabled by default. However, the configuration is limited to the operating system's default settings, which are often very permissive (e.g., 'allow all outgoing connections'). There is no regular review or adjustment of the rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple group policy or a basic script ensures that the firewall service is running on all clients. However, no effort is invested in creating a restrictive rule set.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies on a sample of laptops that the firewall is active. The configuration is then checked. If only standard rules are active and no specific, restrictive rules for the organization have been defined, this corresponds to maturity level 2.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A personal firewall MUST be active on laptops when they are used outside of the institution's networks. The firewall's filter rules MUST be as restrictive as possible. The filter rules MUST be tested regularly. The personal firewall MUST be configured so that users are not bothered by warning messages they cannot interpret.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined, restrictive rule set for the personal firewall is created. This is distributed centrally (e.g., via GPOs or an MDM system) to all laptops. Outgoing connections are restricted to the bare essentials. There is a documented process for the regular (e.g., semi-annual) review and adjustment of the rules. The configuration suppresses unspecific 'Do you want to allow app XYZ?' requests to the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the defined firewall rule set and the documentation of the test process presented to them. On a test laptop, the configuration is read out and checked for its restrictiveness and central manageability. It is verified that end users cannot easily change the configuration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The personal firewall is managed centrally via an endpoint management system. Different firewall profiles (e.g., 'Internal', 'Home Office', 'Public Network') are used, which are automatically activated depending on the network environment. The profile for public networks is particularly restrictive. Firewall logs (especially blocked connections) are collected centrally and regularly checked for anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The functionality of the MDM or UEM system is used to define and distribute location- or network-dependent profiles. Log collection is realized by configuring an endpoint agent that forwards the logs to a central SIEM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the configuration of the different firewall profiles in the management system demonstrated to them. It is demonstrated how a profile change works when moving to a different network. The auditor requests insight into the centrally collected firewall logs and the evaluation processes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The personal firewall is part of a comprehensive Endpoint Protection Platform (EPP/EDR). It works together with a Host-based Intrusion Prevention System (HIPS) component that acts not only at the port/IP level, but also at the application and behavioral level. Suspicious outgoing connections from unknown processes are automatically blocked, even if they use allowed ports. The rules are dynamically updated based on threat intelligence feeds.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A modern EDR solution is used. The firewall component is configured to enforce application whitelisting for network connections. Rules for blocking anomalies (e.g., an Office program starts a Powershell that establishes a connection to the internet) are defined and activated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the configuration of the EDR platform demonstrated to them. The HIPS rules and the integration of threat intelligence are analyzed. Through a simulated attack (e.g., executing a prepared macro), the system's ability to automatically block anomalous network connections is practically tested.

controls.title: Secure remote access with laptops

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some internal network services are directly accessible from the internet to enable remote access. A VPN solution exists, but its use is not mandatory or technically enforced for all access scenarios.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Port forwarding on the central firewall gateway is used to make services such as RDP or file sharing directly accessible from the internet. This is often implemented as a supposedly simple solution for remote access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a port scan on the organization's public IP address and analyzes the firewall configuration for port forwarding rules that point to internal systems. Interviews with users and administrators clarify whether VPN use is optional.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standard VPN service is provided for remote access to the internal network, and its use is mandatory for all employees. Authentication to the VPN is done exclusively via username and password.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A VPN server (e.g., based on OpenVPN or the firewall manufacturer's VPN service) is set up. User authentication is configured against a central directory (e.g., Active Directory).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the VPN configuration and verifies that all traffic to the internal network is routed through the VPN. The configuration of the authentication methods is checked to ensure that no stronger methods than username/password are in use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: From publicly accessible networks, the institution's internal network MUST ONLY be accessed via a secure communication channel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access to the institution's internal network is consistently restricted to the VPN service on the perimeter firewall. A VPN system is used that employs current and securely rated cryptographic protocols (e.g., IKEv2/IPsec or TLS). The use of the VPN is technically enforced for all remote access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the perimeter firewall and verifies that no incoming connections to internal services other than the VPN access are allowed. The configuration of the VPN server is checked for the use of secure protocols and cipher suites.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Remote access via VPN is secured by multi-factor authentication (MFA). In addition, the identity of the accessing device is verified using a device certificate. The VPN configuration prevents split-tunneling to stop threats from being introduced from insecure networks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VPN service is coupled with an MFA provider (e.g., via RADIUS). A Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is used to roll out unique device certificates and to check their validity during connection setup. The client configuration of the VPN enforces that all traffic is routed through the tunnel (split-tunneling disabled).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown a demonstration of the configuration of the MFA integration and certificate authentication. The VPN client configuration is checked to see if split-tunneling is effectively prevented. A test login is performed to verify the MFA requirement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of a traditional VPN, a Zero-Trust Network Access (ZTNA) solution is used. Before granting access to a specific application, the security state of the laptop (Device Health/Posture) is checked (e.g., patch level, active EDR solution). Access is granted based on the principle of least privilege only to the required application and not to the entire network. All access attempts are logged in detail and analyzed for anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A ZTNA or SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) solution is implemented. Policies for 'Conditional Access' are defined, which query the device status from the endpoint management system. Each internal application is individually connected via the ZTNA broker and provided with specific access rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture and configuration policies of the ZTNA solution. It is demonstrated how a non-compliant laptop is denied access to an application. The access logs are examined for their level of detail and the effectiveness of the analysis processes.

controls.title: Security policies for laptops

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no specific security policies for laptops. The only requirements are unwritten rules or verbal instructions that are only known to some of the employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This situation is typical for organizations without formalized security management. Security depends solely on the individual judgment of the users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews employees and administrators about the existence of security policies for laptops. If no documented policies can be presented, this level of maturity is reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general IT usage policy exists and contains a short, non-specific section on laptop use. The policy is handed to employees during onboarding, but there is no further awareness training on the specific dangers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard template for IT policies is used and minimally adapted. It is distributed passively, e.g., as an attachment to the employment contract or as a document on a network drive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the IT usage policy and assesses the level of detail of the section on laptops. It is checked whether the policy only covers basic aspects and whether active user awareness training takes place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A security policy SHOULD be created for laptops, which regulates how the devices may be used. Users SHOULD be made aware of the protection requirements for laptops and the data stored on them. They SHOULD also be made aware of the specific threats and the corresponding requirements for use. They SHOULD also be informed about what type of information they are allowed to process on laptops.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated security policy for laptops is created, approved, and demonstrably communicated to all relevant employees (e.g., via the intranet or by email). The policy clearly defines permitted use, user responsibilities, and the most important security measures (e.g., screen lock, password handling, incident reporting). It also contains a clear statement on which data categories (e.g., 'public', 'internal', 'confidential') may be stored and processed on laptops.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the dedicated security policy for laptops and checks its content for completeness according to the requirement. Proof is requested that the policy has been communicated to the target group (e.g., distribution list, intranet news, minutes of a training session).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is supplemented by regular, mandatory awareness training sessions whose content is aligned with the policy. Employees must formally confirm their acknowledgment of the policy (e.g., with a digital signature). The policy is reviewed annually for currency and updated as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual e-learning training on information security is introduced, which includes a specific module on secure laptop use. A policy management system is used to document and track employee acknowledgment of the policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests evidence of the training sessions and the confirmation of policy acknowledgment by the employees. The minutes of the annual review of the policy are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the security policy is enforced through technical controls and verified through regular, automated compliance checks. The effectiveness of the policy and its associated measures is measured using key performance indicators (e.g., number of reported incidents, results of phishing simulations) and optimized as part of a continuous improvement process (CIP).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An endpoint management tool is used to enforce configurations according to the policy (e.g., password complexity, automatic screen lock). A script regularly checks for compliance and reports deviations to a central dashboard. The effectiveness metrics are part of the regular ISMS reporting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration of the technical controls in the management tool. The reports from the automated compliance checks and the defined key performance indicators for measuring effectiveness are analyzed. It is checked whether the findings from the measurements have demonstrably led to improvements.

controls.title: Regulated handover and return of a laptop

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Pool laptops are passed informally from employee to employee. There is no process to delete remaining data or to check the device for malware.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This often happens when laptops are shared for business trips or temporary projects without central administration and without a clear sense of responsibility for device cleanliness.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks users of pool laptops how the handover takes place. A laptop that has been handed over on loan is examined to determine whether data from the previous user or a traceable history is present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a verbal or informal instruction that users should delete their personal data before returning or passing on a pool laptop. There is no verification or enforced process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT support asks users upon return to 'please delete your data'. There is no technical support or control of this process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks if there is a documented instruction for data erasure. During the inspection of a returned laptop, it is randomly checked whether user profiles and data are still present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If laptops are used alternately by different people, it SHOULD be regulated how they can be handed over securely. Before handing over a laptop, any sensitive data present SHOULD be securely deleted. If the laptop is not re-imaged before being handed over, it SHOULD be ensured that there is no malware on it. A leaflet with instructions for the safe handling of the device SHOULD be handed out with a laptop.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process for issuing and returning pool laptops is established. This process is the responsibility of the IT operations team. Before each new issue, the previous user's profile is deleted and a virus scan is performed. When issued, the user is given a short leaflet with the most important security rules. The handover and return are documented in a list or a simple ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documented process for handover and return. The documentation (e.g., issue list) and the handed-out leaflet are checked. A laptop prepared for issue is inspected to ensure that no data from the previous user remains and that a virus scan has been performed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before any laptop is handed over, it is mandatorily reimaged by IT operations with a clean, standardized software image. The entire process of handover and return, including the reinstallation, is logged completely in an asset management system to be able to trace the 'Chain of Custody'.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard image for pool laptops is created and maintained. Imaging tools (e.g., Clonezilla, Microsoft Deployment Toolkit) are used for reinstallation to speed up the process. Each checkout and return generates an entry in the asset management system, which is linked to the device record and the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the re-imaging process demonstrated. Excerpts from the asset management system are requested to verify the complete logging of the handover processes. It is checked whether a laptop ready for issue actually corresponds to a freshly installed system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for borrowing and returning pool laptops is fully automated. Employees request devices via a self-service portal and can retrieve them from a smart dispensing station (Smart Locker). After being returned to the station, the laptop is automatically connected to a re-imaging infrastructure that erases, reinstalls, and scans the device for viruses without manual intervention before it is released for borrowing again.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Physical laptop dispensing cabinets are procured that are networked with the IT infrastructure. The control of the cabinets and the lending process are implemented via a self-service portal in the intranet. The backend automation for re-imaging is implemented via PXE boot and scripts (e.g., using Ansible or PowerShell).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the entire system demonstrated, from the request in the portal and retrieval from the cabinet to the automated reinstallation after return. The configuration of the automation and the system's logs are reviewed to assess the reliability and security of the process.

controls.title: Secure connection of laptops to data networks

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no restrictions on connecting devices to the internal data network. Any laptop, including private or third-party devices, can be connected to a free network socket and receives full access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Network switches are not configured to restrict access. This is a state of 'plug-and-play' without any security considerations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor connects an unauthorized test laptop to a free network socket. If the device receives an IP address and can access internal resources, this maturity level is confirmed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a policy stating that only company-owned, approved laptops may be connected to the internal network. However, compliance with this policy is not technically enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The rule is part of the general IT usage policy. It relies on employees adhering to this requirement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the policy and then performs the same technical test as for maturity level 1. If a third-party device can establish a connection despite the policy, maturity level 2 is achieved.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be regulated how laptops are securely connected to own or third-party data networks and to the internet. Only approved laptops SHOULD be able to log on to the institution's internal network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A basic Network Access Control (NAC) is implemented, e.g., via a MAC address filter on the network switches. Only laptops with a pre-registered MAC address are granted access to the internal network. For connection to external networks, users are instructed to always activate the personal firewall and not to enter any confidential data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the MAC address filters on the switches and the list of registered addresses. An attempt is made to connect a device with an unregistered MAC address to test the effectiveness of the block.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A port-based Network Access Control (NAC) solution according to IEEE 802.1X is used. A laptop must authenticate itself to the network with a unique device certificate before the port is enabled. Unauthenticated devices are automatically moved to a quarantine or guest VLAN that has no access to internal resources.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A RADIUS server is set up and connected to an internal PKI for issuing device certificates. The network switches are configured as RADIUS clients and 802.1X is enabled on all access ports. The laptops are configured to perform certificate authentication automatically.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the RADIUS server, the switch ports, and a client device. It is tested what happens when a device without a valid certificate is connected. It is verified that this device ends up in the quarantine VLAN.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The NAC solution is fully integrated with the endpoint management and the EDR solution. Before and during the connection, the security posture of the laptop is continuously checked (e.g., patch status, up-to-date AV signatures, no critical vulnerabilities). If a laptop is no longer compliant, its network access is automatically revoked or restricted in real-time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NAC solution is configured to query the compliance status from the UEM system or the EDR agent. 'Posture Policies' are defined that specify the minimum requirements for network access. Automated actions (e.g., 'Move to quarantine VLAN', 'Block port') are configured for cases of non-compliance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the configuration of the 'Posture Policies' in the NAC solution demonstrated. A test is performed in which a compliant laptop is intentionally put into a non-compliant state (e.g., by disabling the antivirus software). It is checked whether network access is automatically and promptly revoked as defined.

controls.title: Reconciliation of laptop data inventories

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees manually copy data between their laptop and network drives as needed. There is no automated process and no central solution, which often leads to version conflicts and data loss.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, data consistency is left entirely to the discipline of individual employees. No tools are provided for support.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews employees about their data synchronization procedures. Samples of files on a laptop and the corresponding network drive are compared to identify version conflicts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central filesync solution (e.g., Nextcloud, OneDrive) is provided. However, the configuration and responsibility for correct synchronization and conflict resolution lie entirely with the user. There are no instructions or guidelines.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A cloud storage or on-premise solution is licensed and made available to users. The installation and setup of the sync client on the laptop is the user's responsibility.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a sync solution is in place. By interviewing users and reviewing the client configuration, it is determined that there are no central guidelines or assistance.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be regulated how data from laptops is transferred to the institution's information network. If a synchronization tool is used, it SHOULD be ensured that synchronization conflicts can be resolved. The synchronization process SHOULD be logged. Furthermore, users SHOULD be instructed to check the synchronization logs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An official synchronization solution is selected and defined as the standard. A written guide is created for users that explains how to use the tool, how to recognize and handle synchronization conflicts, and where to find the logs. Users are informed of their duty to check the synchronization during training sessions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the regulation or user guide. It is checked whether the guide covers the required points (conflict resolution, log review). Through interviews with users, it is checked on a random basis whether they know the instruction and how to view the logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the synchronization tool is centrally managed and distributed to the laptops. Policies are enforced that define which folders are allowed to be synchronized (e.g., to prevent the synchronization of system folders). The synchronization status (e.g., 'Successful', 'Error', 'Conflicts') of the clients is centrally monitored by IT to proactively intervene in case of problems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The synchronization tool is configured and distributed via an endpoint management system. Most tools with an enterprise license offer a central dashboard through which the status of all clients can be viewed. IT checks this dashboard regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the central configuration of the sync tool and the central monitoring dashboard. It is checked whether there is a defined process for how IT reacts to reported synchronization errors.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data synchronization is integrated with a Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solution. Based on content analysis and classification labels, the system automatically prevents unauthorized or highly sensitive data from being synchronized to laptops. The synchronization process is so robust and transparent that it works reliably in the background even with changing network conditions, without user intervention.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A DLP agent on the laptop scans files before they are synchronized. If a file is classified as 'Strictly Confidential', for example, and the policy prohibits the synchronization of such data to laptops, the process is blocked and both the user and IT security are notified. The synchronization solution uses advanced techniques to handle connection drops and low bandwidth.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the DLP policies for data synchronization demonstrated. A test is performed in which an attempt is made to synchronize a file classified as sensitive. It is checked whether the synchronization is blocked as expected and a notification is issued.

controls.title: Ensuring the power supply of laptops

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No precautions or instructions are given regarding the power supply of laptops. Each user is responsible for themselves.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The organization assumes that users know how to charge and carry their devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews that there are no instructions or provided accessories for mobile power supply.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of the general IT briefing, employees are reminded to take their power adapter with them when traveling. Spare batteries or power banks are not provided as standard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This point is part of a general checklist for business trips, which is communicated orally or in a short memo.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the instruction documents or information sheets and finds that they only contain a reference to the power supply unit.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All users SHOULD be informed on how to optimally ensure the power supply for laptops in mobile use. Existing spare batteries SHOULD be stored and transported in suitable cases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A short guide is created that contains tips for maximizing battery life (e.g., reducing screen brightness) and for the safe handling of spare batteries. This guide is made available to users of mobile devices. If spare batteries are issued, they are provided in special, fire-resistant protective cases.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the information materials on power supply. If spare batteries are in use, it is checked whether they are stored and transported in the prescribed protective cases.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organization provides employees who frequently work remotely with standard accessories to ensure power supply. This includes certified high-capacity power banks or a second original spare battery. There are clear guidelines for the safe storage, transport, and maintenance of these components to maximize their lifespan and safety.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the procurement process for laptops, suitable accessories such as power banks are also evaluated and included in the equipment catalog. The battery care guidelines are part of the general laptop security policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the equipment catalog and verifies through spot checks on mobile employees that they are equipped with the appropriate accessories. The existence and content of the battery care guidelines are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The battery status of all laptops is centrally monitored via the endpoint management system (e.g., remaining charge capacity, number of charge cycles). Laptops with severely degraded batteries are proactively identified and the batteries are replaced before failures occur. Uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) are provided for the home office workplace for employees in critical functions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Scripts or the native functionality of the UEM system are used to regularly read the battery statistics of the laptops and aggregate them in a central dashboard. Thresholds for proactive replacement are defined. UPSs are procured and managed as standard equipment for defined roles.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the battery monitoring dashboard and checks the defined thresholds and the process for proactive replacement. It is verified that employees in critical roles are actually equipped with UPSs.

controls.title: Laptop Loss Report

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no formalized process for reporting lost or stolen laptops. Employees may report a loss to their supervisor, but it is unclear how the information reaches IT security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, incidents are handled reactively and often with considerable delay, which allows the window of opportunity for countermeasures such as a remote wipe to pass unused.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions employees and IT staff about the process for loss reports. If no clear process known to all exists, this maturity level is reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are instructed to report a loss or theft to the general IT helpdesk. However, there is no specialized incident response procedure for this type of incident on the IT side.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The report is recorded as a normal IT problem in the ticketing system. The response to it depends on the availability and knowledge of the respective helpdesk employee.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the reporting channel via the helpdesk has been communicated. Then, the downstream process in the IT team is examined. If no standardized playbook for handling exists, maturity level 2 is applicable.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users SHOULD promptly report if a laptop is lost or stolen. For this purpose, there SHOULD be clear reporting channels in the institution. If lost laptops reappear, it SHOULD be investigated whether they have been tampered with. The software installed on them, including the operating system, SHOULD be completely reinstalled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Clear reporting channels (e.g., a dedicated email address and phone number) for loss reports are defined and made known to all employees. A documented procedure (Incident Response Plan) exists that specifies which steps to take after a report (e.g., locking the user account). The procedure also requires that recovered devices be security-checked and mandatorily reinstalled before further use.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the reporting channels and the Incident Response Plan. It is checked whether the employees are aware of the reporting channels. The plan is analyzed to see if it prescribes the investigation and reinstallation of recovered devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated, 24/7 accessible reporting channel (e.g., a 24/7 hotline or a portal) is established. Reporting a loss immediately and automatically triggers the initial measures defined in the Incident Response Plan, such as remote locking or wiping of the device via the MDM/UEM system and deactivating the associated user account. The entire incident is seamlessly documented in a ticketing system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Incident Response Plan is developed into a detailed playbook. The technical requirements for remote wipe are implemented and tested. The playbook is anchored in the ISMS and the responsible employees are trained on it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the Incident Response Playbook and verifies the existence and accessibility of the 24/7 reporting channel. The technical capability for remote wipe is demonstrated. The documentation in the ticketing system is checked using a (possibly fictitious) incident.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reporting and response process is highly automated. A report by the user in a self-service portal triggers an automated workflow chain (SOAR - Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) that locks/wipes the device, locks the user account in Active Directory, terminates all active user sessions in cloud applications, and creates a ticket for the security team without manual intervention. The effectiveness of the process is regularly checked through unannounced drills.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SOAR platform or corresponding scripting solutions are used to control the APIs of the various systems (MDM, Active Directory, Cloud Identity Provider) and to orchestrate the process. A plan for regular loss and theft simulations is created and implemented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration of the automation workflows in the SOAR platform. Logs of past drills and the resulting improvement measures are reviewed. The seamless automation from reporting to response is verified.

controls.title: Encryption of Laptops

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Disk encryption is not systematically enabled on the laptops. Its use is left to the individual users, which leads to patchy or no implementation at all.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This state arises when there are no policies or technical specifications for encryption.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines a sample of laptops and checks the status of disk encryption. If a significant proportion of the devices are unencrypted, this maturity level is confirmed. A command-line command such as `manage-bde -status` (Windows) or `diskutil apfs list` (macOS) can be used for verification.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The native disk encryption (e.g., BitLocker, FileVault) is enabled on all laptops. However, the recovery keys are not managed centrally. They are either kept by the user or not backed up at all, which leads to a total loss of data in case of a password loss.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The encryption is activated during the operating system installation or by a simple script. However, no process for the secure storage of the recovery keys is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the disks are encrypted. Then, the key recovery process is queried. If no central, secure process for managing the recovery keys exists, this is maturity level 2.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data carriers such as hard drives or SSDs installed in laptops SHOULD be encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy is issued that mandates the full encryption of all laptop hard drives. The encryption is implemented using native operating system tools (BitLocker, FileVault). A defined and secure process is established to store the recovery keys centrally (e.g., in Active Directory for BitLocker or in a secure password safe).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the encryption policy and the process for managing the recovery keys. It is checked on a sample basis whether the laptops are encrypted and whether a recovery key is stored centrally for them. The security of the storage location for the keys is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Disk encryption and the management of recovery keys are centrally enforced and monitored via an endpoint management system. The encryption policy requires strong pre-boot authentication that goes beyond the mere login password (e.g., a separate PIN or smart card) to increase protection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: BitLocker is configured via GPOs or a UEM system to require a PIN at system startup ('TPM and PIN' protector). The UEM system continuously monitors the encryption status of all devices and reports deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration policies in the UEM system that enforce encryption and pre-boot authentication. The dashboard for monitoring the encryption status is viewed. The boot process is observed on a test device to verify the PIN prompt.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware-based encryption is used through self-encrypting drives (SEDs, e.g., according to the Opal 2.0 standard), which is managed via a central tool. The integrity of the boot process is ensured by Secure Boot and a TPM-based measurement of the boot components. Decrypting the hard drive is only possible if the system integrity has been verified. The disk encryption is supplemented by a Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solution that controls the data outflow to external media.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During procurement, only laptops with Opal 2.0-capable SSDs are selected. Software for central management of SEDs is used. Secure Boot is enabled in the UEFI/BIOS. The DLP solution is configured to prevent the copying of data classified as confidential to unencrypted USB sticks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests a demonstration of the specifications of the laptops in use and the configuration of the SED management software. The UEFI/BIOS settings regarding Secure Boot and TPM are checked. The effectiveness of the DLP control is tested by attempting to copy classified data to an unencrypted USB drive.

controls.title: Appropriate storage of laptops

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no instructions for storing laptops. They are often left openly on desks overnight or visibly in parked vehicles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The physical security of the devices is not considered an essential topic. People rely on the general security of the building or on luck.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts a walk-through after office hours ('Clean Desk Audit') and documents the number of laptops left in the open. Interviews with employees confirm the lack of instructions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The general IT usage policy contains a sentence that asks employees to 'handle their laptop with care and protect it from theft'. There are no specific instructions on how to do this.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This general advice serves more for formal compliance than for practical security improvement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the policy and notes the general nature of the wording. A walk-through shows that the behavior in practice does not differ from maturity level 1.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All users SHOULD be instructed on how to securely store laptops outside the institution. Depending on the protection requirements of the data stored on them, laptops SHOULD also be secured against theft or kept locked away within the institution's premises outside of usage hours.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A clear instruction is formulated as part of the laptop security policy. It states that laptops must never be left visible in a car outside the office and must be stored in a safe in a hotel room. Within the institution, laptops must be stored in a lockable cabinet or mobile pedestal after work. Employees are verifiably informed of these rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the corresponding policy or instruction and checks its content and the verifiable communication to the employees. A walk-through after office hours is used to randomly check compliance with the 'Clean Desk' and locking rules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The rules for secure storage are mandatory and are supported by the provision of appropriate resources. Every employee with a laptop receives a high-quality laptop lock (security cable). The use of this lock is mandatory at workstations in non-exclusive areas (e.g., co-working spaces, shared offices). Compliance with the 'Clean Desk' policy is regularly checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: High-quality laptop locks are procured and issued to employees as standard accessories. The 'Clean Desk' checks are announced and conducted by security officers or managers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that laptop locks have been issued to employees. Records of the 'Clean Desk' checks are requested to see if and how compliance is monitored.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the storage policies is regularly monitored through unannounced 'Clean Desk Audits'. For the transport of laptops with very high protection needs, tamper-evident laptop bags or cases are mandatory. The laptops are equipped with a tracking technology (configured in compliance with data protection laws) that can be activated in the event of theft.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The 'Clean Desk Audits' are part of the internal audit program of the ISMS. Tamper-evident bags are procured for specific projects or roles. A tracking function, which is integrated into the BIOS/UEFI or managed via the UEM system, is activated and its use is anchored in the incident response plan for theft.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit plan and the reports of the unannounced 'Clean Desk Audits'. It is checked whether tamper-evident bags are available for defined high-risk groups. The configuration and functionality of the tracking technology is demonstrated, including the data protection assessment.

controls.title: Suitable selection of laptops

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Laptops are procured without a formal process. The selection is mainly based on price, availability, or the wishes of individual users. Security aspects play no role.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Procurement is decentralized and ad-hoc, often by individual departments or people without coordination with IT.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the latest procurement processes for laptops. If no requirement documents or evaluation matrices exist and a high variety of non-standardized models are in use, this maturity level is confirmed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are a few standard models for laptops. However, the selection of these models is primarily based on functional requirements (performance, weight) and price. Specific security features are not systematically evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department defines a small selection of 'standard laptops' to reduce support overhead. The criteria for selection are mainly economic and practical.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for an explanation of the process for defining the standard models. If the decision criteria do not include explicit security requirements (e.g., TPM version), this maturity level is reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before laptops are procured, a requirements analysis SHOULD be conducted. Based on the results, all eligible devices SHOULD be evaluated. The procurement decision SHOULD be coordinated with IT operations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process for laptop procurement is established. This begins with a documented requirements analysis that includes both functional and basic security requirements (e.g., compatibility with the encryption software). Different models are evaluated based on these requirements. The final decision is made in coordination between procurement, IT operations, and, if applicable, the information security officer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the documentation of the procurement process. For a recent procurement, the requirements analysis and the evaluation documents are requested. It is checked whether IT operations were verifiably involved in the decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements analysis for laptop procurement is mandatory and includes a detailed catalog of security criteria (e.g., support for TPM 2.0, UEFI Secure Boot, BIOS/UEFI passwords, Intel vPro). A limited hardware catalog of approved models is maintained, all of which have been extensively tested and approved by IT operations and IT security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized requirements catalog for IT hardware is created and anchored in the ISMS. New models undergo a standardized testing and approval process before being added to the official hardware catalog.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the requirements catalog with the security criteria and the official hardware catalog. For a model from the catalog, the records of the testing and approval process are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement process is fully integrated into Supply Chain Risk Management. The manufacturer's security practices (e.g., secure software development lifecycle, vulnerability management) are assessed and factored into the selection decision. Devices are specifically chosen that offer advanced hardware-level security features, such as protection against physical attacks, hardware-based memory protection, and self-healing firmware.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of supplier management, security questionnaires are sent to the hardware manufacturers or publicly available information (e.g., certifications, vulnerability reports) is analyzed. The selection is focused on models from manufacturers who are considered leaders in device security and, for example, offer features such as Microsoft Secured-Core PCs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the supply chain risk management for hardware manufacturers. The assessment documents for selected manufacturers are analyzed. It is checked whether the procured devices actually have the advertised advanced security features.

controls.title: Central administration and management of laptops

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Laptops are not centrally managed. Each device is configured individually and manually as needed, e.g., when an employee reports a problem.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This situation is typical for very small environments or those without professional IT operations. There are no tools for central management.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with administrators and by examining several laptops that no central management solution is in use and that the device configurations vary greatly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic tool is used for central management, but its functionality is limited. Typically, it is only used for software distribution or for a simple hardware inventory. Central configuration or policy management does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, a simple script for software installation or an open-source inventory solution is used. Windows devices may be in an Active Directory domain, but group policies are used minimally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for a demonstration of the management tool used and assesses its scope of functions and degree of use. If the tool is used primarily reactively or for individual tasks, but not for proactive configuration and security management, maturity level 2 is reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A suitable regulation SHOULD be defined on how to centrally administer and manage laptops. A tool for central laptop management SHOULD support all operating systems in use if possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy for the central management of endpoints is created. A suitable Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) or Mobile Device Management (MDM) solution is selected that supports the operating systems in the company (e.g., Windows, macOS). This tool is used to centrally distribute basic security policies (e.g., password complexity, screen lock) and configurations. The process for enrolling new devices into management is defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the management policy and the configuration of the UEM/MDM tool. It is checked whether all types of operating systems used are covered by the management solution and whether basic security policies are distributed via the tool. The process for onboarding new devices is analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The UEM/MDM solution is used extensively to enforce security configurations, automatically distribute software and patches, and monitor device compliance. The system enables remote lock and wipe of laptops, and this function is ready for use in the event of loss or theft. The compliance status of each device is displayed on a central dashboard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Detailed compliance policies are defined in the UEM system (e.g., 'disk encryption must be active', 'antivirus must be running'). Automated patch management cycles are configured for operating systems and standard applications. The remote wipe process is documented and tested.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the compliance policies and the patch management configuration in the UEM system shown to them. The dashboard for monitoring the compliance status is reviewed. The remote wipe capability is demonstrated (on a test device).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The central management solution is fully integrated with other security systems such as Network Access Control (NAC), SIEM, and the Identity Provider (IdP). The compliance status of a device, determined in the UEM/MDM, is used as a condition for accessing corporate resources (Conditional Access). The system can automatically correct non-compliant configurations (Self-Remediation). Administrative tasks are largely automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UEM/MDM platform is connected via API to the IdP (e.g., Azure AD, Okta) and the NAC solution. In the IdP, conditional access policies are created that query the device status as a criterion ('Grant access only from compliant devices'). Automation workflows are created, e.g., to automatically reactivate a disabled firewall.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the integrations between UEM, IdP, and NAC. A conditional access policy is analyzed and its functionality is demonstrated by putting a device into a non-compliant state and denying access. The configuration of a self-remediation workflow is checked.

controls.title: Collective storage of laptops

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unused laptops (e.g., pool devices, inventory) are stored in an unsecured location, for example, on an open shelf in the IT office.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no awareness of the theft risk for stored devices. Storage is based on practical, not security-related, considerations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to be shown the storage location for unused laptops. If this location is not lockable and is freely accessible, this maturity level is confirmed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unused laptops are stored in a lockable office cabinet or a simple storage room. However, there is no formal access control to this room or cabinet.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple metal cabinet or a basement room secured with a standard lock is used for storage. The key is accessible to many employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the storage location. It is checked whether it is lockable, but also who has access to the key and whether access is logged. If there is no formal access control, this is maturity level 2.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unused laptops SHOULD be kept in a suitably secured room. The room used for this purpose SHOULD meet the requirements from the module INF.5 Room and Cabinet for Technical Infrastructure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated room is designated for the storage of IT equipment. This room is permanently locked, and access is restricted to a small, defined group of IT staff. Inside the room, the laptops are stored in lockable cabinets. The requirements from INF.5 and INF.6 (e.g., for stability, lock quality) are taken into account.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the storage room and the cabinets within it. The access control to the room and the key management are checked. The physical condition of the room and the cabinets is compared with the basic requirements of the INF.5 and INF.6 modules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The laptop storage room is secured by an electronic access control system that logs all entries. Inside the room, the laptops are kept in high-quality, certified security cabinets. An up-to-date inventory list of the stored devices is maintained and regularly verified (e.g., quarterly) by a physical stocktake.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An electronic locking system with a card reader or PIN code is installed at the storage room. Access rights are granted restrictively. Security cabinets with a certified resistance class are procured. The inventory list is maintained in the asset management software.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the access control system and the inventory list. The certificates of the security cabinets are inspected. The logs of the last physical inventory count are requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The storage room has enhanced physical security, including video surveillance (CCTV) and a burglar alarm system (EMA) connected to a central monitoring station. Access requires two-factor authentication (e.g., card and PIN). Storage is in smart lockers that log the removal and return of each individual device and grant access only to authorized persons for specific devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room is classified as a security area and equipped accordingly. The video recordings and EMA alarms are monitored by the security service or an external emergency call and service control center. Networked laptop dispensing cabinets are procured and integrated into the asset management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the video surveillance and EMA installations and checks their connection to the central station. The configuration of the two-factor access system is analyzed. The functionality and logging of the smart locker system are demonstrated.

controls.title: Use of anti-theft devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No anti-theft devices such as laptop locks are provided, nor is their use mandated. Individual employees may procure them on their own initiative.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The physical security of the individual device is not seen as a responsibility of the organization.

parts.name: assessment-method
