parts.prose: The auditor determines by interviewing IT and employees that no anti-theft devices are centrally procured or recommended.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Standard laptop locks (e.g., simple Kensington locks) are issued to employees on request. There is no regulation on when and where they are to be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Some simple cable locks are kept in stock and issued when needed. Their use is at the discretion of the employee.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that locks are available, but finds through interviews that there are no clear rules for their use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be regulated which anti-theft devices are to be used for laptops. For mechanical locks, special attention SHOULD be paid to a good lock.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A regulation is issued that mandates the use of laptop locks in certain locations (e.g., in public areas, at trade fairs, in co-working spaces). A specific model or a quality standard is defined for the locks to be procured to ensure that no inferior products are used. These locks are made available to all relevant employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the regulation on the use of anti-theft devices and the specification for the procured locks. It is checked on a random basis whether the relevant employees are equipped with the corresponding locks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of high-quality, standardized laptop locks is mandatory for all laptops when left unattended at workstations (including in one's own office). Compliance with this requirement is checked through regular, random checks ('Clean Desk Audits'). For laptops at publicly accessible presentation stations, special, more robust locks or alarm-secured brackets are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The obligation to use laptop locks is enshrined in the security policy. The checks are carried out and documented by security officers or managers. Special solutions are procured for trade fair laptops.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the checks. A walk-through is conducted to check compliance with the locking obligation. The locks at public presentation stations are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to high-quality mechanical locks, laptops used in high-risk scenarios are equipped with hardware-based tracking and recovery technologies. These enable location and remote locking even without an internet connection for the operating system. At critical locations, docking stations are used that secure the laptop both mechanically and electronically and trigger an alarm if an unauthorized removal is attempted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Laptops with integrated tracking modules (e.g., in the BIOS/UEFI) or special retrofit solutions are procured. Their management is integrated into the incident response process. Alarm-secured docking stations are procured for fixed workstations in insecure environments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown a demonstration of the configuration of the tracking technology and the alarm-secured docking stations. The corresponding section in the Incident Response Plan, which describes the use of these technologies in an emergency, is reviewed.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
A laptop (also called a notebook) is a PC that can be used portably. It has a compact design, integrates peripherals such as a keyboard and screen, can operate temporarily without an external power supply via batteries, and often consists of hardware components specifically designed for mobile use. Laptops are common in most institutions and frequently replace the traditional desktop PC.
Laptops are typically run on common desktop operating systems like Microsoft Windows, Apple macOS, or Linux. The lines between laptops, tablets, and similar devices are blurred nowadays. For example, there are tablets with desktop operating systems like Windows 10, as well as keyboard accessories for mobile devices like iPads with iPadOS, allowing them to be used as laptops.
Since laptops are often used on the go, they are frequently not permanently connected to the institution's LAN. Instead, they can usually connect to the institution's network via a Virtual Private Network (VPN), for example, over the internet. Furthermore, the infrastructure of a classic office environment, which offers controllable environmental conditions, a stable power supply, or access-protected areas, cannot be assumed when using laptops portably.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to enable institutions to use laptops securely and to raise awareness of the specific threats associated with this class of device.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.3.1 Laptops is to be applied to all laptops, whether used portably or stationary.
As with all IT systems, the operating system and software components of laptops must be carefully selected and installed. The requirements to be met here depend on the laptop's operating system and are therefore described in the client-specific modules, for example, SYS.2.2.3 Clients under Windows, SYS 2.3 Clients under Linux and Unix, or SYS.2.4 Clients under macOS. Likewise, requirements that apply to all types of clients are not part of this module. These can be found in module SYS.2.1 General Client.
This module also does not cover how to set up data transmission, such as WLAN configuration (see NET.2.2 WLAN Usage) or a VPN connection (see NET.3.3 VPN).
Since laptops are often used outside an institution for extended periods, they require special consideration for data backup. Further requirements can be found in module CON.3 Data Backup Concept.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Impairment due to changing operating environment
parts.prose: Laptops are used in very different environments and are therefore exposed to many threats. These include, for example, damaging environmental influences such as excessively high or low temperatures, as well as dust or moisture. With laptops, there is also always the risk of transport damage. In addition, laptops often communicate with unknown IT systems or networks, especially when on the move, which always carries a potential threat to the own device. For example, malware can be transmitted or sensitive information can be copied in the process.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Theft and loss of laptops
parts.prose: Employees often use their laptops outside the institution as well. The devices are transported in private vehicles or on public transport, left behind in other offices during breaks, or placed unattended in hotel rooms. Thus, laptops are exposed to a higher risk of theft and can also be easily forgotten or lost. If a laptop is lost, costs and effort are incurred for its replacement. Unsecured data is also lost. Likewise, unauthorized persons could access sensitive data, which could lead to further damage. In many cases, this damage is significantly more severe than the purely material loss of the laptop.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Unregulated transfer of laptops
parts.prose: If employees only need mobile IT systems in exceptional cases, such as for infrequent business trips, it is often more practical to keep only a few laptops centrally available. These can then be passed on to one another. However, if the laptop is simply handed over to the next employee, there is a risk that sensitive data still on the device will be passed on. It is also possible that the laptop is infected with malware. Without a suitable regulation, it can be difficult to track who used the laptop and when, or who is currently using it.

controls.title: Establishing a policy for the use of smartphones and tablets (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no formal, written policies for the use of smartphones and tablets. At most, verbal or informal instructions are passed on to individual employees. The use of the devices is largely unregulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this maturity level, there is no systematic implementation. Responsibility is often fully delegated to individual users, which leads to inconsistent and insecure operation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with IT managers and spot checks with users that no formal policy exists and is known. It is checked whether there are any instructions at all for regulating the use of devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic usage policy for mobile devices exists. However, it is general in nature and does not cover all specific aspects, such as access to certain classes of information or detailed control measures. The policy is made available to employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is usually created as part of the general IT usage regulations and distributed to employees, for example, via the intranet. However, compliance is not systematically checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the basic policy. Through questioning of employees, it is checked on a random basis whether the policy is known. The completeness of the policy is compared with the basic requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before an institution provides, operates, or uses smartphones or tablets, a general policy for the use and control of the devices MUST be established. This MUST specify, among other things, who is allowed to access which information of the institution with smartphones. The policy is documented, approved, and communicated to all relevant employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is drafted as a standalone document that clearly defines the permitted use cases, the data categories to be protected, and the responsibilities of the users. It is communicated to new employees as part of the onboarding process and is available at any time on the intranet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the official, approved policy. It is checked whether the content meets the MUST criteria of the requirement (esp. regulation on information access). Documentation (e.g., training materials, intranet page) is used to verify that the policy has been made available to users.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy for the use of mobile devices is reviewed regularly, at least once a year, and updated as needed. It is integrated into the institution's general security policies and contains concrete examples of permitted and prohibited actions. Compliance with the policy is supported by technical controls wherever possible and promoted through regular awareness measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is technically underpinned by an MDM (Mobile Device Management) system, which, for example, restricts access to certain apps or data based on the user's role. Users must periodically confirm their acknowledgement of the policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the process for the regular review of the policy (e.g., based on minutes). It is checked whether the policy is enforced by technical measures (e.g., MDM configurations). The implementation of related awareness campaigns is proven with examples.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy is dynamic and adapts to new threats and technologies. Its compliance is fully and automatically enforced by a UEM/MDM system. Deviations from the policy (e.g., installation of unauthorized profiles) are detected in real time and lead to automated countermeasures, such as quarantining the device. The effectiveness of the policy and technical controls is audited regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UEM (Unified Endpoint Management) system is used to enforce granular, context-based access rules. For example, access to highly sensitive data can only occur from devices located in a trusted location and that pass all compliance checks. Policy compliance is a prerequisite for network access (Conditional Access).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the UEM system and the defined automation rules. The effectiveness of the automated detection and response to policy violations is checked using log data and test cases. The integration into the Conditional Access mechanism is verified.

controls.title: Defining a strategy for cloud usage (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no strategy or regulation for the use of cloud services with mobile devices. Employees use private or business cloud services at their own discretion, which can lead to an uncontrolled leakage of company data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This situation often arises from a lack of awareness of the risks of cloud usage. There are no technical or organizational controls governing the use of cloud services.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and analysis of network traffic (if possible) that uncontrolled use of various cloud services is taking place. It is confirmed that no corresponding strategy or policy exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic regulation that prescribes the use of certain cloud services provided by the institution (e.g., "Only the official company storage may be used"). However, the regulation regarding private use on company devices is unclear or missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The regulation is communicated to the employees but not technically enforced. It relies on the cooperation of the employees to refrain from using other cloud services.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the basic regulation. Spot checks of device configurations and interviews with users show the extent to which the regulation is known and followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST define a general strategy for cloud usage as well as for the protection and control of information in connection with smartphones and tablets. The permitted use of cloud services for the institution's information MUST be clarified and defined. It MUST be specified whether and to what extent cloud services are permitted for private use of the devices. Users MUST be regularly made aware of the use of such cloud services.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cloud strategy is drafted as a separate document or as part of the IT security policy. It lists approved cloud services and classifies which types of data may be stored in which services. Regular awareness measures, e.g., via newsletters or short training sessions, are carried out.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the cloud usage strategy and checks its completeness according to the requirement. It is verified that the strategy is implemented (e.g., through configuration of apps) and that user awareness is raised (e.g., through training materials).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The cloud strategy is enforced by technical measures. An MDM system configures the devices so that only approved cloud services and accounts can be used. Data exchange between managed apps and unapproved cloud apps is prevented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Configuration profiles are distributed via MDM that restrict the 'Open In' function so that corporate data can only be opened in other managed apps. Access to unapproved cloud services can also be blocked via a web filter or proxy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM configuration profiles and verifies that the technical controls for enforcing the cloud strategy are effective. Test cases are conducted to confirm that data exchange with unapproved services is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of cloud services is monitored and controlled by a Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB). Access is dynamically regulated based on user, device, location, and device state (compliance). Automated Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies prevent the upload of sensitive data to unapproved or private cloud storage in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All cloud traffic from mobile devices is routed through a CASB solution (e.g., via VPN or proxy configuration). The CASB policies are tightly integrated with the MDM (for device state) and the Identity Provider (for user context) to realize a comprehensive Zero Trust approach.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and policies of the CASB. The effectiveness of the real-time controls and DLP policies is checked using log data and simulated attacks (e.g., attempting to upload sensitive data from a non-compliant device).

controls.title: Secure baseline configuration for mobile devices (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Mobile devices are put into operation without any adjustments to the security configuration (out-of-the-box). Users are responsible for all settings themselves. There are no guidelines or support.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This situation is typical for environments without central device management and without security awareness. It poses a high risk, as the default settings are often not secure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects several devices on a random basis and finds that insecure default settings are active and there is no uniform configuration. Interviews confirm the lack of configuration guidelines.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic guide or checklist for the basic configuration of mobile devices. However, the implementation is carried out manually by the IT department or the users themselves and is not centrally checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple checklist is provided when the device is issued. This contains basic steps such as setting a password or installing a company app. The consistency of the configuration across all devices is not guaranteed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the checklist or guide. The consistency of the manual implementation is assessed by checking several devices, and deviations from the specification are documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All mobile devices MUST be configured to adequately meet the required level of protection. For this purpose, a suitable baseline configuration of security mechanisms and settings MUST be compiled and documented. The activation of communication interfaces MUST be regulated and reduced to the extent necessary for official duties.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented standard configuration (baseline) is created for each supported device type. This baseline is applied to the devices during initial setup. It contains settings for passwords, screen lock, restrictions, and the configuration of necessary interfaces. Unnecessary functions and interfaces are deactivated in the baseline according to the SHOULD recommendation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documented baseline configuration and compares it with the requirements. It is checked on a random basis on devices whether the documented configuration has been implemented correctly. It is checked whether the regulations for the use of interfaces have been implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secure baseline configuration is centrally managed, distributed, and its compliance monitored via an MDM system. All SHOULD recommendations of the requirement, such as deactivating unneeded functions and interfaces, are technically enforced. Changes to the configuration are logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM profile containing the hardening guidelines is automatically rolled out to all registered devices. The MDM performs regular compliance checks and reports devices that deviate from the baseline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration profiles and compliance policies stored in the MDM system. The reports from the MDM system are evaluated to assess the compliance of the device fleet. It is checked whether deviations lead to alerts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The baseline configuration is based on recognized hardening standards (e.g., CIS Benchmarks) and is enforced automatically. The MDM/UEM system automatically corrects configuration deviations (auto-remediation). The state of the device configuration is a criterion for Conditional Access to corporate resources. Any manipulation of the configuration leads to the immediate quarantine of the device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration baseline is managed and versioned in an IaC (Infrastructure as Code) approach. The UEM system is integrated with the Identity Provider and an MTD (Mobile Threat Defense) solution to ensure continuous monitoring and dynamic adjustment of security policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration-as-code definitions. The effectiveness of the auto-remediation and Conditional Access rules is verified through test cases in which a device is intentionally made non-compliant. The logs of the UEM and IAM systems are analyzed to confirm the correct functioning of the chain.

controls.title: Use of Access Protection (B) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of access protection (PIN, password, etc.) is optional for users. There are no requirements regarding complexity or the activation of the automatic screen lock.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, many devices are operated without protection, which poses an extremely high risk to the data stored on them in the event of loss or theft.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects a sample of devices and determines that a significant portion has no access protection configured or that it is trivial. Interviews confirm the absence of corresponding policies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an instruction that all devices MUST be equipped with access protection. However, the complexity (e.g., a simple 4-digit PIN) and the time for the automatic lock are not strictly regulated and are left to the default settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department or supervisors instruct users to set a PIN when issuing the device. There is no technical verification to check if this is implemented and maintained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the instruction. A device inspection reveals that while most devices have a lock, the complexity and lock times vary greatly and are often weak.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Smartphones and tablets MUST be protected with an appropriately complex device lock code. The screen lock MUST be used. The display of confidential information on the lock screen MUST be disabled. All mobile devices MUST automatically activate the screen lock after an appropriately short period of time. This time period MUST correspond to the intended level of protection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy defines the minimum complexity of the lock code (e.g., 6-digit PIN or alphanumeric password), the maximum time until automatic lock (e.g., 5 minutes), and the prohibition of notifications on the lock screen. These settings are ideally implemented through a baseline configuration (e.g., via an ActiveSync policy).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the access protection policy. Using configuration screenshots or a direct device inspection, it is verified on a random basis whether the MUST requirements (complex code, auto-lock, no sensitive notifications) are implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All aspects of access protection are centrally enforced and monitored via an MDM system. This includes the implementation of SHOULD requirements: The waiting time after failed login attempts is increased, a password history is enforced, and the device is automatically reset to factory settings (wiped) after a defined number of failed attempts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM profile enforces high password complexity (e.g., 8-character alphanumeric), a short lock time (e.g., 1 minute), a password history (e.g., the last 5 passwords cannot be reused), and an automatic wipe after 10 failed attempts. Users cannot change these settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the corresponding MDM configuration profile and compares it with all MUST and SHOULD requirements. The MDM compliance reports are reviewed to confirm widespread implementation. The wipe function can be verified in a test environment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The access protection is supplemented by multi-factor authentication (MFA) at the device level, wherever technically possible and secure (e.g., strong biometric feature plus PIN). Compliance with the access protection policy is a mandatory prerequisite for accessing any corporate data. The deletion process used for a wipe is cryptographically secured and certified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM system is configured to enforce the use of secure biometrics (e.g., Face ID, but not simple 2D facial recognition) in combination with a strong password. Integration with a Conditional Access system ensures that a device whose access protection has been compromised or disabled immediately loses access to resources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the MFA configuration in the MDM and the Conditional Access rules in the Identity Provider. A test case (with an intentionally outdated test device) is used to verify the automatic quarantine. The manufacturer's documentation regarding secure deletion is reviewed.

controls.title: Updates of operating system and apps (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no process for managing updates or the lifecycle of devices and apps. Users are fully responsible for installing updates themselves. Outdated and unsupported devices and apps remain in use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, the institution's attack surface grows continuously as known vulnerabilities are not patched. Patch management for mobile devices does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By inspecting a sample of devices, the auditor determines that many devices have outdated operating system and app versions. Interviews with the IT department confirm the lack of an update and lifecycle management process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users are regularly instructed to keep their devices and apps up to date. There is an informal process to retire very old devices, but no proactive monitoring or firm criteria.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Regular emails remind users to install updates. The IT department replaces devices when they are obviously no longer functioning or are extremely outdated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the communication measures for prompting updates. A device sample shows a mixed picture, with some up-to-date and some outdated devices. It is noted that no systematic decommissioning process exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When selecting mobile devices to be procured, the institution MUST ensure that the manufacturing institution specifies the planned period of use during which security updates will be provided for the devices. Older devices for which updates are no longer provided MUST be decommissioned and replaced by devices supported by the manufacturing institution. Apps SHOULD also NO longer be used if they are no longer supported by the manufacturing institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented process for the lifecycle management of mobile devices and apps is established. This process includes criteria for procurement (commitment to security updates), an inventory list with the support status, and a defined process for decommissioning end-of-life devices and apps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the procurement policies for the criterion of update support. The existence and maintenance of the lifecycle management process and the associated inventory list are verified. It is checked on a random basis whether end-of-life devices have been decommissioned according to the process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An MDM system is used to enforce the installation of operating system and app updates. Policies are defined that specify a maximum delay for the installation of updates. The MDM monitors the versions of all devices and apps and reports outdated or unsupported software.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy is configured in the MDM that, for example, requires OS updates to be installed no later than 14 days after release. The MDM inventory is used to proactively identify devices and apps that are nearing their end of support in order to plan their replacement in a timely manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the update policies in the MDM. The MDM's compliance reports are evaluated to assess the patch level of the device fleet. The process for responding to alerts about outdated software is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire update process is automated. Critical security updates are rolled out immediately and without user interaction. Devices that do not reach the required patch level within a short period of time are automatically isolated from the network (Conditional Access). The selection of devices and apps is based on a strict assessment of the manufacturer's security and support model.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UEM system is integrated with the Identity Provider. A Conditional Access Policy denies access to devices whose OS version does not meet the minimum requirements. Procurement favors manufacturers who participate in the Android Enterprise Recommended program or provide comparable guarantees for updates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the automated update distribution and the Conditional Access Policies. The automatic quarantine is demonstrated through a test case (with an intentionally outdated test device). Procurement documents are checked for consideration of the manufacturer support models.

controls.title: Privacy settings and permissions (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no guidelines or controls for app permissions. Users grant permissions at their own discretion, often without understanding the consequences. Apps have extensive access to sensitive data such as contacts, location, and microphone.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This state leads to a significant risk of data leakage and privacy violations, as many apps request more permissions than are necessary for their function.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects devices on a random basis and finds that apps have excessive permissions. Interviews confirm the lack of policies or technical controls.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users are advised in a general policy or training to grant app permissions restrictively. However, there are no specific requirements or technical controls to enforce this.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The topic of app permissions is covered as part of security awareness. However, implementation is entirely the responsibility of the individual user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the training or policy documents. A review of devices shows whether user awareness has led to a more restrictive granting of permissions, although the results are likely to be inconsistent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access by apps and the operating system to data and interfaces MUST be appropriately restricted. The privacy settings MUST be configured to be as restrictive as possible. In particular, access to the camera, microphone, and location and health or fitness data MUST be checked for conformity with the organization's internal data protection and security policies. Security-relevant permission settings MUST be set so that they cannot be changed by users or apps, where technically possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy defines which apps are allowed to receive which permissions. Where technically possible (e.g., via MDM), certain permissions are disabled globally or set to a default setting (e.g., 'Ask every time'). For whitelisted apps, a default set of permissions is defined. Where a technical restriction is not possible, a process for regular review of the settings is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the app permissions policy. The configuration in the MDM is analyzed to verify the technical implementation of the restrictions. For settings that require manual review, the audit process and its documentation are assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Permissions for all apps installed on the device are managed centrally via an MDM system. A 'default-deny' approach is followed, where apps receive no permissions by default. Necessary permissions are explicitly granted per app on an allowlist based on a risk assessment. Users cannot change these centrally mandated permissions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each app in the corporate app store, a permission profile is stored in the MDM. This profile is automatically applied when the app is installed. The MDM prevents users from overwriting these settings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the permission profiles in the MDM for a sample of apps. It is verified that the 'default-deny' principle is implemented and that users cannot change the settings (e.g., by testing on the device).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) solution continuously monitors the behavior of apps and their access to data and permissions. Any suspicious activity or the request for an inappropriate permission by an app leads to an immediate alert and automated countermeasures, such as revoking the permission or uninstalling the app.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MTD solution is installed on all devices and integrated into the UEM system. Behavioral analysis and anomaly detection are used to identify risks that are not detected by static permission analysis (e.g., a flashlight app trying to access contacts).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and detection rules of the MTD solution. Using test cases (e.g., installing an app with known risky behavior in a test environment), the effectiveness of the automated detection and response is verified. The log files are examined for relevant events.

controls.title: Rules of conduct for security incidents (B) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no formal rules of conduct or a defined reporting process for security incidents related to mobile devices. Users do not know what to do in the event of device loss or suspicious behavior.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This situation leads to incidents being reported late or not at all, causing valuable time to be lost for countermeasures such as the remote wiping of data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews with users and the IT department, the auditor determines that no established and known reporting process for mobile security incidents exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users are instructed to report the loss of a device to the IT helpdesk. However, the process is informal and there are no clear guidelines for other types of incidents (e.g., a suspicious app).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The instruction to report a loss is part of the general IT policies. There is no special training or reminders on this topic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the instruction in the general policies. By interviewing users, it is determined whether the reporting channel for device loss is known and whether other incidents would also be reported.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If devices are lost or unauthorized changes to the device and software are detected, users MUST immediately inform the responsible persons. A clearly defined and documented reporting process, including the responsible contact points, is established and known to all users.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The rules of conduct and the reporting process are part of the mobile usage policy. Contact information (phone number, email) for reporting incidents is easily accessible, e.g., as a sticker on the device or on a card in the wallet. The topic is covered in security training sessions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the documented reporting process. It is checked whether it covers the required incident types and whether the contact points are clearly named. Random interviews with users verify that the process is known.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reporting process is integrated into the institution's central incident response plan. Users are provided with a simple reporting method, e.g., a self-service portal where they can report a device as lost. A report immediately triggers a predefined process, which includes, for example, the immediate locking or wiping of the device via MDM.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A self-service portal for users is set up. When a user reports their device as lost there, the command to lock and display a message is automatically triggered via an API connection to the MDM system. The incident response plan describes the further escalation levels.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the incident response plan for the integration of mobile incidents. The functionality of the self-service portal and the associated automation are verified in a test environment. The logs of past incidents are evaluated to check compliance with the process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to user-initiated reports, security incidents are proactively detected by a Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) solution. The MTD solution automatically reports compromises (e.g., jailbreak, installation of malware) to the SIEM and incident response team and can initiate predefined, automated countermeasures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MTD app installed on the devices detects threats and reports them to a central console. The console is integrated with the organization's UEM/MDM and SIEM system. Critical events, such as a detected compromise of the operating system, automatically lead to the blocking of device access via Conditional Access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the MTD solution and its integration with other security systems (SIEM, UEM). Using test cases, the automatic detection and reporting of threats is verified. The effectiveness of the automated response is checked by analyzing the corresponding log files.

controls.title: App Installation (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users can install any apps from any sources. There are no restrictions on third-party app stores or sideloading. App installation is completely unregulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This situation is extremely risky, as apps from untrusted sources are one of the main sources of infection for malware on mobile devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies on a test device that the installation of apps from unknown sources (sideloading) is possible. Interviews with users confirm the lack of any regulations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an organizational directive to install apps only from the official app stores (Google Play, Apple App Store). However, this directive is not technically enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The instruction is part of the IT usage policy. Users are advised not to activate the operating system setting that allows installation from unknown sources.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence of the instruction in the policies. On a sample of devices, it is checked whether the setting to block unknown sources is active. It is checked whether users could change this setting themselves.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST regulate if, how, and which apps users are allowed to install on their devices. The institution MUST specify from which sources apps may be installed. It MUST be prevented that apps can be installed from unapproved sources. It is recommended (SHOULD) that users may only install approved apps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy specifies that only the official app stores are permissible as an installation source. Installation from unknown sources is technically blocked (e.g., via MDM). In addition, a list of recommended and vetted apps is maintained, the installation of which is supported by IT.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the policy for app installation. It is technically verified (e.g., by analyzing the MDM configuration or on the device) that installation from unknown sources is blocked. The existence and maintenance of the list of approved apps is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation of apps is controlled via a corporate app store or an allowlist in the MDM system. Users can only install apps that have been previously reviewed and approved by the institution. Direct access to public app stores can be restricted or monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Enterprise App Store is set up in the MDM. Only the apps listed there can be installed by the user. All other installations are blocked. For each app in the store, there is a documented approval process that considers security and data protection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the Enterprise App Store or the app allowlist in the MDM. It is tested on the device whether the installation of a non-approved app is blocked. The process for approving new apps is checked for its traceability and thoroughness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All apps necessary for work are installed on the devices by the IT department via a push method through the MDM system ('Silent Install'). Users have no way to install apps themselves. The MDM system continuously monitors the device app inventory and automatically uninstalls any unauthorized app (e.g., from a previous configuration or a compromise).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The devices are operated in 'Kiosk Mode' or in a highly restricted mode that only allows access to the apps provided by IT. The MDM system performs daily scans of the app inventory and compares it with the central allowlist. Any deviation triggers an automatic uninstallation and a notification to IT security.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the Kiosk Mode in the MDM. The configuration of the automatic app inventorying and the remediation measures are checked. Based on log files, the effectiveness of the detection and removal of unauthorized apps is demonstrated.

controls.title: Restrictive use of functional extensions (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Functional extensions (like widgets or third-party keyboards) SHOULD only be used restrictively. There is a policy that regulates the handling of such extensions and points out that they must not have automatic access to sensitive information and must not bypass the basic configuration. It is recommended (SHOULD) to refrain from such extensions if possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT security policy contains a section on functional extensions. Users are made aware of the risks that can arise from extensions, especially from keyboards that could log keystrokes, as part of security training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the policy for corresponding regulations. A random sample of users is asked whether they are informed about the risks of extensions. The extensions installed on devices are checked for plausibility.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of functional extensions is restricted by technical controls via an MDM system. For example, the installation of third-party keyboards is generally blocked. The use of widgets on the lock screen is prevented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM configuration profile containing the corresponding restrictions is distributed. These settings cannot be changed by the user. Permitted extensions are explicitly maintained on an allowlist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM configuration profile and verifies that the technical restrictions for extensions are active and cannot be bypassed. This is confirmed by a test on the device.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of any functional extensions is blocked by default. Exceptions are granted only after a thorough security review and approval for specific use cases. An MTD solution monitors the communication and behavior of extensions to detect malicious activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM profile implements a 'default-deny' policy for all extensions. The process for requesting and reviewing an exception is formalized. The MTD solution analyzes data traffic to and from extensions to detect data leaks or communication with command-and-control servers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the 'default-deny' configuration in the MDM. The approval process for exceptions is checked for its thoroughness. The configuration and detection capabilities of the MTD solution with regard to extensions are analyzed.

controls.title: Policy for employees on the use of mobile devices (S) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A mandatory policy for employees on the use of mobile devices SHOULD be created. It SHOULD define how mobile devices are to be used and maintained. The topics of safekeeping and loss reporting SHOULD be covered. Furthermore, it SHOULD be forbidden to uninstall management software, root the device, or change security-relevant configurations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed 'Acceptable Use Policy' (AUP) for mobile devices is created. It is verifiably brought to the attention of all users (e.g., via signature or digital confirmation). The AUP explicitly covers all points mentioned in the requirement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the AUP presented to them and checks it for completeness regarding the SHOULD requirements. It is proven that the users have acknowledged the policy (e.g., through a list with confirmations).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the policy is supported by technical controls. An MDM system is used to detect rooting or jailbreaking of devices. It also prevents users from removing the management software (MDM client) or changing security-relevant configurations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM system performs regular compliance checks that explicitly check for signs of rooting/jailbreaking. The MDM profile is configured so that it cannot be removed by the user. Policy compliance is also promoted through regular awareness training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM configuration regarding root/jailbreak detection and the protection of the MDM profile. The effectiveness of the detection is verified using compliance reports. Training materials for awareness measures are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The detection of policy violations such as rooting/jailbreaking or the manipulation of security software is automated and leads to immediate, also automated, countermeasures. A compromised or manipulated device is instantly excluded from access to corporate resources and networks (quarantine).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) solution is deployed that provides reliable and continuous detection of compromises. In the event of a positive finding, the MTD solution reports the status to the UEM/MDM and the Identity Provider, which leads to the immediate blocking of the device via a Conditional Access Policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the entire automated response chain. This is done by analyzing the configurations of MTD, UEM, and Conditional Access, as well as by a practical test with a (simulated) compromised device in a test environment. The log files are evaluated to prove correct functionality.

controls.title: Storage Encryption (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The non-volatile storage of the mobile device SHOULD be encrypted. Data worthy of protection on additionally used storage media, such as SD cards, SHOULD be encrypted. There is a policy that requires encryption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On modern operating systems (iOS, newer Android versions), the encryption of the internal storage is active by default as soon as a device passcode is set. The policy ensures that this applies to all devices. For SD cards, the use of the encryption feature offered by the operating system (if available) is mandatory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence of the corresponding policy. A sample of devices is used to verify that encryption is active for the internal storage. It is checked how the requirement for encryption of SD cards is implemented and controlled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The encryption of internal storage and external storage media (SD cards) is technically enforced and monitored via an MDM system. Devices on which encryption is not active are marked as non-compliant.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM compliance policy is created that checks whether device encryption is active. The use of unencrypted SD cards can either be blocked by the MDM or their encryption can be enforced.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM policy for enforcing encryption. The MDM's compliance reports are evaluated to confirm the complete encryption of the device fleet.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only devices that use hardware-backed encryption (e.g., via Secure Enclave) are used. Encryption status is a mandatory prerequisite for access to corporate resources (Conditional Access). An unencrypted device has no access whatsoever.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement policy mandates devices with specific hardware security features. The Conditional Access Policy in the Identity Provider is configured to use the encryption status reported by the MDM as a criterion for access. A device reported as 'unencrypted' is automatically blocked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement policies and the technical specifications of the device models in use. The configuration of the Conditional Access Policy is analyzed and its effectiveness is verified through a test case (simulated 'unencrypted' message).

controls.title: Use of non-personalized device names (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The device name SHOULD not contain any information about the institution or the users. There is a policy that prescribes a neutral naming of devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT use policy contains the instruction for users to change the device name to a neutral scheme, e.g., 'Mobile Device'. This is pointed out during device issuance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the policy. For a sample of devices (e.g., in the WLAN device list or in the MDM), it is checked whether the device names contain personalized information.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standardized, non-identifiable naming convention is automatically set via the MDM system during device enrollment. The system monitors the device names and corrects deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM is configured to automatically assign a name to each new device based on a neutral convention, e.g., 'CORP-MD' followed by a random number. A compliance rule regularly checks whether the device name matches this pattern.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM configuration for automatic naming and the corresponding compliance rule. The list of device names in the MDM is checked for conformity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to standardized naming, other identifying characteristics that could be revealed via network interfaces (e.g., hostname in DHCP) are also set to neutral or randomized values. The device name is changed automatically at regular intervals to make tracking more difficult.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Where supported by the operating system, MAC address randomization is enforced. Scripts in the MDM system are used to periodically change the device name (e.g., every 30 days) to a new, random value within the convention.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM scripts for name rotation and the configuration for MAC address randomization. Network scans are performed in a test environment to verify that the devices do not reveal static, identifiable characteristics.

controls.title: Regulations for screen sharing and casting (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be decided whether and how functions for transmitting screen content, audio, or video (screen sharing or casting) are to be used. The functions SHOULD be regulated organizationally or technically. An corresponding agreement SHOULD be made with the users for this purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy defines under which circumstances screen sharing is permitted (e.g., only in internal meetings, not in public areas). Users are made aware of the risks of accidentally disclosing confidential information. The agreement becomes part of the AUP.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and content of the regulation on screen sharing in the policy. It is checked whether the users have been made aware accordingly (e.g., through training materials).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of screen sharing and casting functions is technically restricted via an MDM system. For example, casting is only allowed to a whitelist of company-owned devices (e.g., specific Apple TVs or conference room systems).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM configuration profile (e.g., for AirPlay) is distributed that contains a list of allowed destination devices. All other casting attempts are blocked by the operating system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the corresponding MDM configuration profile. A practical test verifies that casting is only possible to the whitelisted devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All screen sharing and casting is blocked by default. It can only be used within managed apps that enforce Data Loss Prevention features, such as displaying a watermark with user and time information on the shared content to deter screenshots and photographs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM profile blocks the system-wide casting function. Only certain apps approved for collaboration (e.g., a secure conference app) are allowed to use the function. The app itself is configured to display a dynamic watermark with every transmission.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the blocking of the system-wide function in the MDM. The configuration of the exception app is checked, and during a test transmission, the correct display of the watermark is verified.

controls.title: Deactivation of unused communication interfaces (S) [Users]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Communication interfaces such as Bluetooth or NFC SHOULD only be activated when needed and only in suitable environments. A policy instructs users to deactivate unused interfaces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The AUP for mobile devices includes a clause instructing users to turn off Bluetooth and NFC by default and only turn them on during active use. This is explained as part of security awareness training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the policy for the corresponding instruction. A random device check is used to verify whether users are following this instruction. User awareness of this regulation is surveyed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of communication interfaces is controlled centrally via an MDM system. The MDM system can completely disable certain interfaces (e.g., NFC) or restrict their configuration (e.g., allow Bluetooth but disable discoverable mode).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM profile that restricts the use of interfaces according to the security policy is created and distributed. For example, NFC is disabled for all devices as it is not needed for business purposes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM profile that contains the interface restrictions. On a test device, it is verified that the blocked interfaces cannot be activated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM system uses context-based policies to manage interfaces dynamically. For example, Bluetooth is only activated automatically when the device is at a trusted location (geofencing) or when a connection to an approved peripheral is to be established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UEM/MDM solution is configured with location-based services and a list of trusted Bluetooth devices (e.g., company-owned headsets). Outside of the defined contexts, the interfaces remain disabled by default and cannot be activated manually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the context-based policies in the UEM/MDM. The functionality is checked through practical tests at different locations and with different peripheral devices to confirm correct dynamic activation and deactivation.

controls.title: Use of biometric authentication (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If biometric methods are to be used for authentication, it SHOULD be verified whether they can provide a similar or higher level of protection compared to a device password. In case of doubt or if the protection is weaker, biometric methods SHOULD NOT be used. Users SHOULD be made aware of the spoofability of biometric features.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A risk assessment is conducted to evaluate the security of the biometric methods available on the devices. A policy defines which biometric methods (e.g., fingerprint, 3D facial recognition) are considered secure enough and are permitted. Users are informed about the risks (e.g., circumvention by third parties).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the risk assessment and the resulting policy on the use of biometrics. Training materials are checked to verify user awareness. It is checked whether insecure biometric methods (e.g., simple 2D facial recognition) are explicitly prohibited.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of biometrics is technically regulated via an MDM system. Only the biometric methods that have been assessed as secure and explicitly permitted can be activated. The use of biometrics requires the mandatory presence of a strong device password as a fallback.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM profile is distributed that prevents the use of insecure biometric methods (e.g., via the MDM's allow/block list). At the same time, the MDM enforces a high level of complexity for the device password that serves as a fallback.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM profile and verifies that only permitted biometric methods can be used and that a strong password is enforced as a fallback. This is checked on the test device.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Biometric authentication is only permitted on devices where the biometric data is processed and stored in a secure hardware element (e.g., Secure Enclave, Titan M). For access to highly sensitive applications or data, multi-factor authentication that combines biometrics and a password is enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement policy only allows devices that have verifiably secure hardware elements for biometrics processing. Per-app VPN or app protection policies are configured so that starting certain apps requires re-authentication with multiple factors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the technical specifications of the procured devices. The configuration of the app protection policies to enforce MFA is analyzed in the MDM/UEM and tested on the device.

controls.title: Use of voice assistants (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Voice assistants SHOULD only be used when strictly necessary; otherwise, they SHOULD be disabled. In general, a voice assistant SHOULD not be usable when the device is locked. A corresponding policy is issued.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The AUP for mobile devices contains an instruction to disable voice assistants, especially their use from the lock screen. Users are informed about the data privacy risks arising from the processing of voice data by third-party providers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the policy. In a sample of devices, it is checked whether the voice assistant is disabled on the lock screen. User awareness of the risks is surveyed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of voice assistants, especially from the lock screen, is technically prevented via an MDM system. Users cannot change this setting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM profile is distributed that disables the 'voice assistant on lock screen' feature. Depending on the operating system and MDM capabilities, the voice assistant can also be completely disabled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the corresponding MDM configuration profile. On the test device, it is verified that the voice assistant cannot be invoked when the screen is locked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All voice assistants are disabled on the devices by default and cannot be changed. Exceptions for specific business requirements are only possible after a detailed risk assessment and approval, and are implemented in a way that ensures no company data is sent to the providers' servers (on-device processing, if available).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM profile completely disables all known voice assistants. The process for requesting an exception is formalized. If an exception is approved, technical controls (e.g., app configurations, network filters) are implemented to minimize data transmission.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the complete deactivation in the MDM profile. The exception approval process is checked. In the case of an approved exception, the effectiveness of the implemented controls for data minimization is reviewed (e.g., by analyzing network traffic).

controls.title: Integration of mobile devices into the internal infrastructure via VPN (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Mobile devices SHOULD only be integrated into the institution's infrastructure using a VPN. A suitable method SHOULD be selected and used for this purpose. Instead of passwords, the devices SHOULD authenticate to the internal infrastructure using certificates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A VPN solution is implemented for remote access. Authentication at the VPN gateway is performed using client-side certificates installed on the devices. The certificates are issued via an internal PKI or a trusted service.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the VPN gateway and the VPN clients. It is verified that authentication is certificate-based and not based on passwords. The process for issuing and distributing the certificates is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VPN profile is managed centrally via an MDM system and distributed to the devices. An 'Always-On VPN' or 'Per-App VPN' is configured to ensure that all relevant data traffic is automatically routed through the VPN tunnel without user interaction. The user cannot disable the VPN connection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A VPN profile containing the certificates and the configuration for an 'Always-On VPN' is created in the MDM. For 'Per-App VPN', it is defined which business apps must automatically route their traffic via the VPN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the VPN profile in the MDM. On the test device, it is verified that the VPN connection is established automatically and cannot be terminated by the user. In the case of a Per-App VPN, it is checked whether the traffic of the defined apps is correctly tunneled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of a traditional VPN, a Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) solution is used. Access to internal applications is granted on a per-session basis, based on a continuous verification of device compliance, user identity, and other context factors. Network traffic is micro-segmented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A ZTNA agent is installed on the devices and managed via the UEM system. The ZTNA solution is integrated with the Identity Provider and the UEM/MTD solution to perform a dynamic trust assessment. Each app communicates only via a dedicated, encrypted tunnel with the backend service approved for it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture and policies of the ZTNA solution. It is tested how the system reacts to changes in the device context (e.g., deactivating encryption leads to immediate revocation of access). Network connectivity is checked to confirm micro-segmentation.

controls.title: Use of the filter option for websites (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For web browsers, filter options based on allowlists or blocklists or third-party content filters SHOULD be used. If the institution already uses a reputation service or a corresponding proxy server, this SHOULD be set as the global HTTP proxy for all installed browsers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A DNS-based content filter is configured on the devices, which blocks access to known malicious domains (malware, phishing). Alternatively, the data traffic is routed through the organization's central web proxy when the devices are connected via VPN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the DNS filter or the proxy settings on the devices. It is tested whether access to a known malicious test page is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The web filter (e.g., via a global proxy or a local app) is enforced via an MDM system and cannot be bypassed or disabled by the user. The filtering is permanently active, even when there is no VPN connection. In addition to malicious sites, unwanted content categories (e.g., gambling, adult content) are also filtered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM profile configures a global HTTP proxy or a local web content filter that cannot be bypassed. The policies for the content categories are defined centrally in the filter solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM profile for enforcing the web filter. It is tested whether the filter is active even without a VPN and whether the configured content categories are correctly blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) solution provides advanced, on-device protection against phishing and malicious web content. The solution analyzes URLs and website content in real-time and blocks threats before the user can access them. The filtering works in all apps, not just in the browser.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MTD app is installed on all devices via MDM. It integrates at the operating system level to monitor and filter all network traffic. Detected threats are reported to a central console for analysis and reporting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the MTD solution. The effectiveness of the phishing protection is verified by accessing test pages (e.g., from the Anti-Phishing Working Group). It is checked whether the filtering also works in other apps (e.g., email client).

controls.title: Regulation on Mobile Payment (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be regulated whether mobile payment is permitted with company smartphones and tablets. A corresponding decision is to be recorded in a policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT usage policy contains a clear clause that either explicitly prohibits the use of mobile payment services (such as Apple Pay, Google Pay) on company devices or permits it under certain conditions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the policy contains a clear regulation on mobile payment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If mobile payment is not permitted, the use of the corresponding functions is technically blocked via an MDM system. Users cannot add credit cards or bank accounts to the wallet apps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM configuration profile is distributed that prohibits the modification of wallet settings or the use of Apple/Google Pay. This setting cannot be changed by the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM profile and verifies on the test device that adding a card to the wallet app is not possible.

controls.title: MDM Usage (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Smartphones and tablets SHOULD be managed by an MDM system. An MDM system is used to enforce basic security policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM system is procured and implemented. All company-owned devices are registered in it. It is used to distribute basic settings such as password policies and Wi-Fi profiles.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and operation of the MDM system. Based on the device list in the MDM, it is checked whether all known company devices are managed. The configured basic policies are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM system is used comprehensively to manage the entire lifecycle of the devices. This includes automated registration (zero-touch enrollment), distribution of configurations and apps, monitoring of compliance, and secure decommissioning of devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Programs such as Apple Business Manager or Android Zero-Touch are used to automate device registration. The MDM enforces a wide range of security policies and compliance rules. The remote wipe function is tested regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the entire device lifecycle process mapped in the MDM. The configuration of automated registration, compliance policies, and decommissioning processes is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM system is part of a comprehensive Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) platform. It is tightly integrated with other security systems such as the Identity Provider (for Conditional Access) and a Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) solution (for threat detection and response).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UEM system shares the compliance status and threat level of each device in real-time with the Identity Provider. A Conditional Access Policy uses this information to dynamically control access to corporate resources. A threat detected by the MTD thus leads to the automatic blocking of the device by the UEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the integration configurations between UEM, MTD, and the Identity Provider. The entire chain of dynamic access control is verified from start to finish through test cases (e.g., simulating a threat).

controls.title: Selection and installation of security apps (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All mobile devices SHOULD be protected from malicious programs. If possible, security apps suitable for the device SHOULD be selected. A market analysis and evaluation is carried out to identify a suitable security app (e.g., Mobile Threat Defense).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process for evaluating and selecting an MTD solution is carried out. Criteria include detection rate, performance impact, and management capabilities. The result is a well-founded product selection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the selection process for the security app, including the evaluation criteria and the result.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selected security app SHOULD be installed automatically, for example, through an MDM. The installation is enforced for all managed devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM system is configured to automatically install the MTD app as a 'Managed App' on all devices during device enrollment. Users cannot uninstall the app.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM configuration for automatic app distribution. Based on the inventory and compliance reports of the MDM, it is verified that the security app is installed on the entire device fleet.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security app is deeply integrated into the management and security infrastructure. Activation and configuration of the app is a mandatory prerequisite for access to corporate resources. Threats detected by the app lead to automated responses in the UEM and the Identity Provider.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An app configuration is distributed via MDM that ensures the MTD app is configured with the correct server settings. A Conditional Access Policy checks not only the presence of the app, but also its state (e.g., 'no threats detected') before granting access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the app's configuration and the Conditional Access Policies. By simulating a threat on a test device, the entire response chain, from detection by the MTD app to the blocking of access, is verified.

controls.title: Configuration of the DNS server used (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Default gateway entries, such as DNS servers from the manufacturing or developing institutions, SHOULD be replaced by those of the provider or by own ones. A policy is issued that prescribes the use of trusted DNS servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the Wi-Fi or VPN configuration, the company's own DNS servers or a trusted external DNS service (e.g., one with integrated malware protection) are distributed to the devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the DNS configuration in the distributed network profiles (WLAN, VPN). On the device, it is checked which DNS server is actually used for name resolution.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the DNS server is enforced via an MDM system and cannot be changed by the user. If the DNS provider used offers DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) or DNS-over-TLS (DoT), this SHOULD be used to encrypt the DNS queries.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MDM profile for a global HTTP proxy or a DNS profile is used to configure the DNS settings system-wide and in a non-bypassable way. If DoH/DoT is supported, the corresponding profile is configured and distributed in the MDM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM profile for the DNS configuration. By means of a network analysis (packet capture) on a test device, it is verified that the DNS queries are sent encrypted via DoH/DoT to the correct server.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of the prescribed, encrypted DNS service is ensured by a non-bypassable configuration (e.g., Always-On VPN that tunnels all traffic). Attempts by apps to bypass the DNS configuration (e.g., by hardcoding DNS servers or using DoH bypassing system settings) are detected and blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MTD solution or an advanced firewall on the device is used to monitor all outgoing network traffic. Outgoing connections on port 53 to DNS servers other than the permitted ones are blocked. Known third-party DoH resolvers are placed on a network blocklist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the firewall or MTD solution. Tests are performed to verify that attempts to contact alternative DNS servers (both unencrypted and via DoH) are successfully blocked.

controls.title: Use of separate work environments (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If employees are allowed to use company devices for private purposes, solutions for separate work environments on the device SHOULD be used. Company data SHOULD remain exclusively in the company environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Operating system-native container solutions such as Android Enterprise Work Profile or iOS User Enrollment are implemented. Business apps and data are installed in a separate, managed container, while the rest of the device is available for private use.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the separate work container on a test device. It is checked whether business apps are correctly installed in the container.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The separation between the work environment and the private area is technically enforced by strict Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies. It is prevented that data can be copied from the work container to the private area or opened there. If possible, only certified products (e.g., according to Common Criteria) SHOULD be procured for this purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: DLP policies are configured in the MDM that, for example, block copying and pasting of content between the work and private profile, sharing of data, or screenshots of the work container. When selecting the container solution, attention is paid to recognized certifications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the DLP configuration in the MDM. On a test device, an attempt is made to copy data from a business app to a private app to verify the effectiveness of the block. The certification evidence of the solution used is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The work environment (container) is protected by its own authentication, independent of the device password and stronger. The state of the private environment is monitored, and a compromise in the private area (e.g., installation of a malicious app) leads to the locking or deletion of the work container.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM enforces a separate, complex password for the work container. An MTD solution is configured to monitor the entire device (private and business) for threats. If a threat is detected in the private area, this triggers an automated action for the business container via the MDM.

parts.name: assessment-method
