parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the separate authentication for the container. The integration between MTD and MDM is analyzed. By (simulated) installation of an app classified as malicious in the private area, the automatic response in the work container is tested.

controls.title: Use of PIM containers (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information on mobile devices SHOULD be encapsulated, for example in a PIM container. A secure container app for email, calendar, and contacts (PIM) is used to separate this data from other apps on the device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Instead of the native mail, calendar, and contacts apps, a special, secure PIM app (e.g., from Microsoft, BlackBerry) is used. All business accounts are configured exclusively in this app.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the native PIM synchronization is disabled and that the specified secure PIM app is used for all business accounts instead. This is checked by inspecting the MDM configuration and by device spot checks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Additionally, the data SHOULD be secured by separate authentication and by data and transport encryption that is independent of the operating system. The PIM container requires its own PIN or biometric authentication upon launch. The data within the container is additionally encrypted by the app itself.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The PIM app is configured via MDM to require re-authentication upon launch or after a short period of inactivity. The app configuration ensures that the in-app encryption, which is independent of device encryption, is enabled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the PIM app distributed via MDM. On the test device, it is verified that the app requires separate authentication. The app's documentation is reviewed to understand how the independent encryption works.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The PIM container app uses a per-app VPN to route all its communication through a secure tunnel. Strict DLP policies enforced by the app prevent any data leakage, including exporting contacts or copying content from emails.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The PIM app is configured via MDM to use a specific per-app VPN configuration. The app protection policies are set to be maximally restrictive to prevent any data exchange with unmanaged apps or the operating system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the per-app VPN and the DLP policies in the MDM. Practical tests are conducted to try to export contacts or copy content to confirm the effectiveness of the controls. A network analysis shows that all app traffic is tunneled through the VPN.

controls.title: Use of highly secured devices (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process is established to decide, based on protection needs, whether highly secured mobile devices must be used for specific use cases or user groups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of risk management, scenarios are identified (e.g., processing of classified information, use in high-security areas) that preclude the use of standard smartphones. This leads to a requirement for specially hardened devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the risk management documentation to determine whether the need for highly secured devices has been assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Depending on the protection needs, institutions SHOULD use highly secured mobile devices that are certified for processing information according to legal information protection classifications. For the identified high-protection-need cases, devices are procured that have a recognized security certification (e.g., BSI certification, Common Criteria EAL).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement department receives a directive to exclusively procure devices for certain user groups that are on a list of certified products. The corresponding certificates are requested from the manufacturer and archived.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement policies and records. It is verified that the devices used for high-protection-need cases actually have the required certifications by inspecting the certificates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to certification, the highly secured devices are operated with a minimal, hardened operating system and managed in a completely separate, high-security management infrastructure. Any non-essential hardware and software components are disabled or removed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated, physically or logically separated MDM instance is operated for these devices. The operating system image is a 'thin image' containing only the absolutely necessary services and apps. Interfaces such as camera, microphone, or USB data transfer are disabled at the hardware level if not needed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the separate management infrastructure. The device's operating system image is examined for its minimization and hardening. The deactivation of hardware and software components is verified through physical inspection and software analysis.

controls.title: Use of an institution-specific APN (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be checked whether an institution-specific access point to the cellular network (APN, Access Point Name) can be used to limit the pool of allowed devices. The possibility of using a private APN with the mobile network operator is evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department holds talks with the mobile network operator to clarify the technical possibilities, conditions, and costs for setting up a private APN. The result of the evaluation is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the APN evaluation, including the communication with the mobile network operator and the final decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A private APN is set up with the mobile network operator. All company devices are configured to exclusively use this APN. All data traffic via this APN is routed directly to the corporate network. For authentication, a complex password SHOULD be agreed upon with the mobile provider and the CHAP protocol SHOULD be implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The private APN is provisioned. An APN profile is distributed to all devices via MDM, which prevents the use of the public APN. The data traffic is filtered at the institution's central internet gateway. Authentication at the APN is done using CHAP and a secure password.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the APN profile in the MDM. The network configuration with the mobile network operator is checked. A network analysis is used to verify that a device's traffic is routed to the corporate network via the private APN and that authentication is performed correctly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Authentication at the private APN is not only done via a password but is strengthened by a RADIUS connection to the company's internal directory. This ensures that only active and authorized user and device accounts can use the APN. The private APN is combined with an Always-On VPN to ensure end-to-end encryption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The mobile network operator sets up a connection to the institution's RADIUS servers. The RADIUS server checks the validity of the device certificate and the user account in Active Directory upon each connection attempt. The MDM profile enforces an Always-On VPN connection in addition to the APN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the RADIUS connection and the corresponding policies on the RADIUS server. It is tested whether a blocked account is denied access. The combination with the Always-On VPN is verified by analyzing the MDM profiles and network traffic.

controls.title: Restriction of app installation using an allowlist (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For high protection needs, an organizational policy is issued stating that only approved and vetted apps may be installed on mobile devices. Such an allowlist is created and maintained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process for the security review and approval of apps is defined. The result is a documented list of approved apps that is made available to users. Compliance is enforced organizationally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the app approval process and the resulting allowlist. Compliance with the organizational requirement is assessed through user interviews and random device checks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For high protection needs, only approved and vetted apps SHOULD be allowed to be installed on mobile devices. If an MDM is used, it SHOULD prevent other apps from being installed. The app allowlist is technically enforced via the MDM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An app allowlist is configured in the MDM. The devices are denied the installation of any apps that are not on this list. The allowlist is provided via a corporate app store.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the app allowlist in the MDM. On a test device, an attempt is made to install an app not on the list to verify the effectiveness of the block.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM system not only enforces the allowlist but SHOULD also immediately remove any unauthorized installed apps. The system continuously monitors the app inventory of the devices and automatically uninstalls any app that is not on the allowlist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A compliance policy is configured in the MDM that regularly compares the app inventory of each device with the central allowlist. In case of a deviation, the non-compliant app is uninstalled as an automatic remediation measure and an alert is sent to the security department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the compliance policy and the automatic remediation measure. The effectiveness is tested by removing a (previously allowed) app from the allowlist; it is checked whether the app is then automatically uninstalled from the test device.

controls.title: Use of a firewall (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A firewall SHOULD be installed and activated on smartphones and tablets. The firewall integrated into the operating system is activated and configured with a 'default-deny' rule for incoming connections.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The activation of the OS-native firewall is included in the standard configuration guide for the devices. The users or the IT department ensure that it is activated during setup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies on a sample of devices whether the native system firewall is active and whether incoming connections are blocked by default.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The firewall configuration is centrally managed via an MDM system and cannot be changed by the user. Rules for outgoing traffic are also defined to restrict app communication to the bare essentials.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A firewall app or an MDM profile is used to define granular rules. For example, a weather app is only allowed to communicate with the weather service's server, but not with ad networks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rules configured in the MDM (for both incoming and outgoing traffic). On a test device, a network sniffer is used to verify whether the rules for outgoing traffic are effective.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The firewall is part of an MTD solution and dynamically adjusts its rules based on the detected threat level or the network environment. For example, the rules in a public, unsecured Wi-Fi network are automatically more restrictive than in the secure corporate Wi-Fi.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MTD solution is configured to recognize different trust levels for networks. When switching to an untrusted network, a more restrictive firewall profile is automatically activated, which, for example, blocks all connections except to the VPN gateway.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the dynamic firewall rules in the MTD solution. The correct switching of profiles is tested by connecting the test device to various WLANs (trusted, external) and analyzing the respective active firewall rules.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: Smartphones are IT systems designed for mobile use with an adapted interface that can be operated with a large, usually touch-sensitive screen (touch display). In addition to telephony, smartphones combine, for example, a media player, personal information manager, and digital camera in one device and also offer users many other applications and functions, such as a web browser, email client, or location services (e.g., via GPS). They are also equipped with mobile radio, WLAN, Bluetooth, and NFC interfaces. Tablets are, simply put, smartphones with a large form factor, which usually cannot be used for phone calls over the mobile network.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to provide those responsible for security management and IT operations with information on the typical threats to smartphones and tablets, as well as to convey requirements on how these can be avoided or eliminated. In addition, it aims to show those responsible how to create configuration profiles that are appropriate for the protection needs. These configuration profiles can be distributed and managed via a central infrastructure with a Mobile Device Management (MDM). However, given the variety of different mobile operating systems, it cannot generally be assumed that the devices can be integrated into such an MDM.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
Module SYS.3.2.1 General Smartphones and Tablets is to be applied to all smartphones and tablets used for business purposes.
This module does not address how to secure specific operating systems of smartphones and tablets, as this is described in detail in the modules for the respective systems, e.g., in SYS.3.2.3 iOS (for Enterprise) or SYS.3.2.4 Android. Security requirements for the operation of an MDM are described in SYS.3.2.2 Mobile Device Management (MDM). These modules are to be applied additionally when smartphones and tablets are used in institutions.
Smartphones, like ordinary clients, are threatened by malware. They must be considered in the concept for protection against malicious software. Requirements for protection against malware can be found in module OPS.1.1.4 Protection against Malicious Programs.
Smartphones and tablets usually offer the possibility to install mobile applications (apps). To ensure that no unnecessary security risks arise from this, the requirements of module APP.1.4 Mobile Applications (Apps) must be taken into account. In addition, other modules from the APP Applications layer, such as APP.1.2 Web Browser, may also be relevant.
Since smartphones usually have mobile phone functions, the relevant requirements of module SYS.3.3 Mobile Phone must be taken into account.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Missing operating system updates
parts.prose: New versions and updates of mobile operating systems are released regularly. For devices that have specific extensions of the operating system from the manufacturing institution, these must first be integrated into their version and then distributed. Updates are usually provided for the latest device generation and for a number of older device generations. However, not all previous operating system versions are supplied with (security) updates to the same extent. In some cases, operating systems are also no longer developed for economic reasons. Subsequently discovered vulnerabilities in the operating system of a device generation that has already been discontinued can then no longer be closed by updates and can be exploited particularly easily in an attack.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Software vulnerabilities in pre-installed applications (apps)
parts.prose: Even pre-installed apps can contain vulnerabilities that can be exploited for local attacks or attacks over network connections. In addition, many apps from third-party developers are no longer maintained after some time. Consequently, detected security flaws can then no longer be fixed by corresponding updates.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Manipulation of smartphones and tablets
parts.prose: In an attack, access to smartphones or tablets can be gained to specifically manipulate data. For example, the configuration could be changed, additional services started, or malware installed. This can, for example, lead to communication connections being intercepted on the manipulated system (unwanted data leakage) or security settings being changed (e.g., allowing access from the internet to the end device).

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Malware for smartphones and tablets
parts.prose: Like any device connected to the internet, mobile devices are also threatened by malware. The risk of infection is still lower compared to client operating systems like Microsoft Windows, but attackers are increasingly focusing on mobile devices. Especially when apps are obtained from untrusted sources or no updates are available for known vulnerabilities, there is a risk of infection. If a device is infected, data can be read, modified, or deleted, internal IT resources of the institution can be accessed, or actions can be taken in the name of the institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Web-based attacks on mobile browsers
parts.prose: Mobile browsers, but also many other apps, can display web pages and web content. As a result, the devices can be affected by phishing attacks, drive-by exploits, and other web-based attack forms.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Misuse of health, fitness, and location data
parts.prose:
The operating system of many smartphones and tablets usually contains special functions to manage health, fitness, and location data. This personal data represents an attractive target for attacks and is particularly worthy of protection, especially when collected and stored over a longer period. The prerequisite is that these functions have been activated.
For example, the location of the device can be identified through an attack on the device itself or on associated cloud services. In addition to the data protection implications, this can also lead to further attacks under certain circumstances. For example, burglaries of employees who are on a trip according to their location are conceivable.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Misuse of sensitive data on the lock screen
parts.prose:
Many mobile operating systems have a feature that allows notifications from enabled widgets and push notifications to be displayed on the lock screen. This can expose confidential information to unauthorized third parties, who can then exploit it. Furthermore, voice assistants often allow access to phone functions and contact data even when the device is locked. This can also lead to unauthorized third parties gaining access to confidential information.
Additionally, it is often possible to configure interfaces such as WLAN or Bluetooth from the lock screen. For example, this allows an additional attack vector to be activated if the Bluetooth interface is switched on by an attacker with physical access.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Risks of private use of business smartphones and tablets
parts.prose: When employees use company-owned smartphones and tablets for private purposes, several problems arise for the institution's information security. For example, users could independently install apps containing malicious functions or visit a website that infects the device with malware. Likewise, many privately installed apps pose a risk to the institution's information stored on the device, as they can, for instance, read address books and transfer them to unknown servers or potentially access emails or documents. This could lead to data leakage or, conversely, an uncontrolled inflow of data into the institution. Typical examples of apps with such risks are social media and messenger apps.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Risks from Bring Your Own Device (BYOD)
parts.prose:
Using private devices for work purposes creates various potential threats. For example, legal problems can arise regarding software licenses. If company data must be deleted from the device via MDM in an emergency, this can also affect private data on the device.
Furthermore, IT staff cannot check every single private device to see if it meets company requirements. This can lead to the use of devices that cause users to violate data protection and security requirements. Additionally, users are often responsible for maintaining and repairing their own devices. During such a repair, company data could be accessed without authorization. The same risk exists if there are no regulations on what should happen to the data on the device when employees leave the institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.10. Privilege escalation through vulnerabilities
parts.prose:
Vulnerabilities are repeatedly discovered in the operating systems of smartphones and tablets that make it possible to bypass the security concepts established by the manufacturing institutions and thus access system processes and protected memory areas. As a result, programs can obtain unintended permissions with which they can perform unauthorized actions. For example, the programs could access data from the operating system and other apps.
So-called jailbreaks exploit these vulnerabilities, for example, to be able to use alternative app stores or other extensions. In the event of an attack, jailbreak techniques can be used to install malware or carry out other malicious manipulations on the device.
Malware can also exploit vulnerabilities to install itself on a device or manipulate it. This allows the operating system to be used differently than intended and important security functions can be bypassed.
Data stored by the mobile operating system in protected areas is particularly affected, as an app with superuser rights may be able to read it.
Similar threat scenarios can arise from intentional privilege escalation ("rooting") if access to the privileged rights is not protected.

controls.title: Defining a strategy for Mobile Device Management (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no uniform or written strategy for Mobile Device Management. Decisions about the use and integration of mobile devices are made on an ad hoc and decentralized basis. At most, there are isolated, uncoordinated regulations for specific teams or use cases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In practice, this means that individual department heads give verbal instructions on the use of smartphones, but these are not applicable or documented institution-wide. There is no central document that serves as a reference.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts interviews with various IT managers and department heads to determine the existence of strategic guidelines. It is found that no consistent, documented strategy exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic strategy document for MDM, but it is incomplete and does not cover all aspects required in the module. The strategy may not have been formally approved by the ISO(s) and is not known to all relevant employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A first draft of an MDM strategy exists as a text document on a network drive. Important points such as the regulations for private devices (BYOD) or the integration of cloud services are still missing. Formal approval is still pending.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing strategy document and compares its contents with the list of aspects that must be covered at a minimum. The lack of formal approval by the ISO is documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A strategy MUST be developed that defines how employees may use mobile devices and how the devices are integrated into the institution's IT structures. The basis for this MUST be the protection requirement of the information to be processed. The strategy MUST cover at least the following aspects: operating model (cloud/on-prem), app deployment, infrastructural integration, support services, compliance requirements, supported devices/operating systems, multi-tenancy capability, integration of cloud and document management systems as well as peripheral devices, and the regulation for different ownership models (BYOD, COPE, etc.). The strategy MUST be laid down in writing and approved by the ISO.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM strategy is stored as an official, versioned document in the institution's document management system. The process for creation and approval involves IT operations, IT management, and the ISO. The document is made available to all relevant stakeholders.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the currently valid, approved version of the MDM strategy. They check whether the document covers all required aspects and whether there is an approval note from the ISO (e.g., a signature or a digital signature). The existence of the document in the official document management system is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The defined MDM strategy is reviewed regularly, at least annually, and whenever there are significant changes in the framework conditions (e.g. new technologies, changed business processes), and adjusted if necessary. The review and its results are documented. The strategy contains measurable goals (KPIs) to verify its effectiveness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A recurring task for the annual review of the MDM strategy is set up in the ITSM system. The KPIs, such as the number of non-compliant devices or the average time to implement new policies, are visualized in a dashboard and feed into the review process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs and change requests from the last review cycles of the MDM strategy. It is verified that the review takes place on time and is documented. The existence and use of KPIs for performance measurement is proven by means of reports or dashboard excerpts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM strategy is fully integrated into the overarching ISMS and Enterprise Risk Management. It is dynamically adapted based on threat intelligence feeds, automated compliance evaluations from the MDM system, and changed business requirements. The adaptation process is largely automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool is used to manage the MDM strategy. The tool automatically receives feeds from threat intelligence providers and compliance data from the MDM. In the event of deviations or new relevant threats, a workflow for reviewing and adapting the strategy is automatically initiated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the GRC tool and the associated workflows. It is checked on a random basis whether a new, relevant security vulnerability (e.g., for iOS) has automatically led to a notification and a review process for the MDM strategy. The seamless integration and automation is verified.

controls.title: Specification of permitted mobile devices (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There MUST be a documented list of permitted mobile devices (models) and operating system versions. All permitted devices and operating systems MUST meet the requirements of the MDM strategy and fully comply with the institution's technical security requirements. The MDM MUST be configured so that only approved devices can access the institution's information. Only mobile devices approved by the institution MAY be procured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A positive list (allow list) of permitted device models and minimum operating system versions is stored in the MDM system. The purchasing department receives this list as a requirement for procurement. The MDM is configured to block access for unlisted or outdated devices (compliance rule).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of approved devices and operating systems. In the MDM system, it is checked whether a corresponding compliance rule to enforce this requirement is active. A test in which an attempt is made to register an unapproved device can verify the effectiveness of the rule. The auditor can also view the procurement policies to ensure that only approved devices are procured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The list of permitted devices and operating systems is reviewed regularly, at least every six months, and adapted to the manufacturers' lifecycle. Outdated devices or operating system versions that no longer receive security updates are proactively removed from the list. Users are informed about upcoming changes and necessary updates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT operations team subscribes to the end-of-life notifications of the relevant manufacturers (e.g., Apple, Samsung). A process is defined in the ITSM system that initiates the regular review of the list and includes a workflow for communicating necessary changes to users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the change history of the list of permitted devices. They check whether the list is up-to-date and whether devices whose manufacturer support has expired have been removed. In addition, the communication measures to the users (e.g. e-mail distribution lists, intranet news) are checked for their existence and appropriateness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for managing permitted devices and operating systems is automated. The MDM system continuously checks against external data sources (e.g. CVE databases, manufacturer APIs) whether the approved configurations are still secure. If a critical vulnerability for a device model or an operating system version is discovered that cannot be fixed in a timely manner, the model is automatically moved to a quarantine group and access is restricted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script or an integrated tool compares the device list stored in the MDM daily with public CVE databases and manufacturer security bulletins. If a match is found for an approved model, a compliance rule in the MDM is automatically adjusted to isolate the affected devices, and a ticket is created for IT support for further processing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automation solution. The configuration of the scripts and the connection to the external data sources are checked. The auditor can simulate a test case (e.g., by manually adding a known vulnerability for a test device) and verify whether the automated isolation and notification process is triggered correctly.

controls.title: Selection of an MDM product (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If a suitable MDM software is to be procured, it MUST be ensured that it can fulfill all requirements set out in the MDM strategy. It MUST also be able to implement all technical and organizational security measures and support all approved mobile devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before procurement, a detailed requirements catalog based on the MDM strategy is created. This catalog is used as the basis for a market survey or a formal tender. Potential products are evaluated against the requirements in a test environment (Proof of Concept).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement documents for the MDM software. They check the requirements catalog and the documentation of the product evaluation (e.g., evaluation matrix, test reports). It is verified that the decision for a product is based on a traceable consideration of the fulfillment of strategic and security requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When selecting the MDM product, its security certifications (e.g., according to Common Criteria) and the trustworthiness of the manufacturer are also taken into account. It is checked whether the product has a future-proof roadmap and whether the manufacturer guarantees timely support for new operating system versions (zero-day support).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the tender, proof of recognized security certifications is included as an evaluation criterion. The manufacturer must contractually guarantee (SLA) to fully support new major operating system versions within a defined period (e.g., 30 days).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the evaluation matrix of the product selection and checks whether criteria such as certifications and manufacturer roadmap were taken into account. They check the contract with the MDM manufacturer for the existence of Service Level Agreements (SLAs) regarding support for new operating system versions.

controls.title: Distribution of the basic configuration to mobile devices (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All mobile endpoints MUST be integrated into the MDM (enrollment) before they are deployed. When the devices receive their basic configuration, they MUST be in a factory state. The connection from mobile endpoints to the MDM MUST be adequately secured. For previously used devices, all institution-related data MUST be deleted beforehand. A device not configured via MDM MUST NOT be able to access the institution's information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized process is used for commissioning new devices, e.g., via the Apple Device Enrollment Program (DEP) or Android Zero-Touch Enrollment. These methods ensure that devices are automatically enrolled into the MDM upon initial startup, without any possibility for user intervention. For previously used devices, a factory reset is enforced before enrollment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the enrollment process. They check the MDM system's configuration regarding the use of automated enrollment programs (DEP, Zero-Touch). The status of newly added devices is spot-checked in the MDM to ensure they have been correctly registered and configured. It is verified whether access rules (e.g., for email) require an MDM profile.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The enrollment process is designed to require as little user interaction as possible (zero-touch principle). After enrollment, the device status is automatically checked and compliance with the basic configuration is verified. Deviations lead to an automatic notification to IT support and the user.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After successful enrollment, the MDM automatically performs an initial compliance check. This checks whether all profiles have been applied correctly and no unwanted apps or configurations are present. The result is logged. Users receive a welcome email with the most important rules of conduct.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the logs of the MDM system for recently performed enrollments. It is verified that a compliance check takes place immediately after enrollment and its results are logged. The configuration of automatic notifications is checked.

controls.title: Installation of the MDM client (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When mobile endpoints are handed over to employees, the MDM client MUST be installed and configured on them, unless already provided by the operating system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In most modern MDM implementations (e.g., with Apple DEP or Android Zero-Touch), a separate 'client' in the sense of an app is no longer necessary, as the MDM functionality is deeply integrated into the operating system. The requirement is met by an enforced enrollment process that installs and activates the MDM profile on the device. If a client (agent app) is required, its installation is enforced by the MDM and cannot be removed by the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks on a representative, managed endpoint whether the MDM profile is active and correctly configured. They check if the profile can be removed by the user (this should not be possible). If an agent app is used, it is checked whether it is installed and cannot be uninstalled.

controls.title: Regular review of the MDM (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security settings MUST be reviewed regularly. With new operating system versions of the mobile endpoints, it MUST be checked in advance whether the MDM fully supports them and whether the configuration profiles and security settings are still effective and sufficient. Deviations MUST be corrected. The assigned permissions for users and administrators MUST be regularly checked to see if they are still appropriate (principle of least privilege).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual review process is established for all MDM configurations and permissions. Before a new major operating system version (e.g., iOS 18) is released, it is tested in a test environment with the MDM for compatibility and effectiveness of the security profiles. The results of these tests are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the last MDM configuration and permission reviews. They inspect the test reports for the compatibility check of new operating system versions. The permissions of some users and administrators in the MDM are spot-checked for compliance with the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The review of MDM configurations and permissions is conducted semi-annually. The MDM system is configured to automatically generate reports on deviations from the defined security baselines. Tests of new operating system versions are conducted in a dedicated and isolated test environment before they are released to a pilot group.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM generates weekly compliance reports that are sent to IT operations. For testing new OS versions, dedicated test devices and a formalized test plan exist. After successful testing, a phased rollout is carried out (pilot group, then all users).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automatically generated compliance reports from recent months. They review the formal test plan for new operating system versions and the documentation of the phased rollout process (e.g., communication plans for the pilot group).

controls.title: Logging of device status (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The lifecycle, including the configuration history of a mobile endpoint, SHOULD be adequately logged and centrally accessible. If necessary, IT operations SHOULD be able to determine the current status of the managed endpoints (Device Audit).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM system is configured to log important events in a device's lifecycle. This includes: enrollment, installation/uninstallation of profiles and apps, compliance status changes, and unenrollment. This log data is retained for a defined period (e.g., 90 days) and is searchable by authorized administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly selects some devices and has the log data from the MDM system shown. It is checked whether the essential lifecycle events (e.g., the last update of a configuration profile) are traceable. The configuration of the log retention periods is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The log data from the MDM system is forwarded to a central SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system. In the SIEM, correlation rules are defined to detect suspicious activities, e.g., repeated failed compliance checks or attempts to remove the MDM profile.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM is configured as a log source in the SIEM system. Specific use cases and the corresponding correlation rules have been defined, e.g., 'trigger an alarm if a device is reported as non-compliant more than 10 times within 24 hours'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks in the SIEM system whether the MDM logs are arriving and being parsed correctly. They review the configured correlation rules and have their functionality explained. A test case can be triggered to verify that a corresponding alarm is generated.

controls.title: Installation of apps (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Apps SHOULD be installed, uninstalled, and updated via the MDM according to the requirements of the planned deployment scenario. The MDM SHOULD enforce installation, uninstallation, and updates as soon as a connection to the mobile endpoint is established. Apps installed via the MDM SHOULD NOT be able to be uninstalled by users. The MDM SHOULD enable a block or allow list for the installation of apps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal app catalog (Enterprise App Store) is provided via the MDM. This contains all apps approved for business use. The installation of apps from the public app stores is prevented (block list). Updates for the apps distributed via the MDM are applied automatically and enforced.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of app management in the MDM. They check the list of approved apps in the internal catalog as well as the configuration of the block list. On a test device, it is verified that only apps from the internal catalog can be installed and that apps installed by the MDM cannot be removed by the user.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal process is defined for approving new apps. Each new app undergoes a security check before being added to the internal app catalog. This involves analyzing the required permissions and the app's data transmission behavior in particular. For company-owned apps, a secure configuration is distributed via Managed App Configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the approval of new apps, an approval workflow is used in the ITSM system, which includes a review by IT security and the data protection officer. Specialized tools (e.g., mobile app scanners) or service providers are used for the analysis. For in-house apps, configuration parameters (e.g., server URL, username) are passed to the app via MDM, so the user does not have to enter them manually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the documented app approval process shown. The documentation of the security check for some recently approved apps is requested on a random basis. The configuration of Managed App Configurations in the MDM is checked for a relevant app (e.g., email client).

controls.title: Securing the MDM operating environment (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM itself SHOULD be secured by technical measures to meet the protection requirements of the stored or processed information. The underlying operating system SHOULD be hardened.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If the MDM is operated on-premise, the server is configured according to the hardening recommendations of the manufacturer and the institution. This includes disabling unnecessary services, applying security patches, and configuring a host-firewall. Access to the management console is restricted to a minimum of authorized persons and requires two-factor authentication.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation on the hardening of the MDM server. They spot-check the server configuration for the implementation of the hardening measures. The configuration of access permissions and two-factor authentication for the management console is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM environment is continuously monitored for vulnerabilities and configuration errors. Administrative access to the MDM console is logged in detail and forwarded to a SIEM system for analysis. There is a separate, isolated management network for accessing the MDM management console.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A vulnerability scanner regularly checks the MDM server. The logging configuration is adjusted so that all administrative actions (who changed what when) are recorded and sent to the SIEM. Access to the web console is only possible from a specially secured VLAN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the vulnerability scanner reports for the MDM server. In the SIEM, it is checked whether the administrative logs are arriving and whether alarms for critical actions are configured. The network architecture and the firewall rules for the management net are checked.

controls.title: Management of certificates (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Certificates for the use of services on the mobile device SHOULD be installed, uninstalled, and updated centrally via the MDM. The installation of untrusted and non-verifiable (root) certificates by users SHOULD be prevented by the MDM. The MDM SHOULD support mechanisms to check the validity of certificates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM is integrated with the internal PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) or a certificate service. Required certificates (e.g., for WLAN authentication or VPN) are automatically distributed to the devices via a configuration profile. A restriction in the MDM profile prohibits the user from manually installing their own trust certificates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the MDM configuration for certificate distribution. They check whether the certificate profiles are configured correctly and whether the restriction to prevent the installation of root certificates is active. On a test device, it is verified that the certificates have been installed correctly and that the attempt to install a foreign root certificate fails.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM uses protocols such as SCEP (Simple Certificate Enrollment Protocol) or CMP (Certificate Management Protocol) for automated and secure distribution of device-specific certificates. The certificate lifecycle (renewal, revocation) is also managed automatically via the MDM. The MDM checks revocation lists (CRL) or uses OCSP to verify the validity of certificates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SCEP server is set up and connected to the PKI and the MDM. The MDM profiles are configured so that each device requests a unique device certificate upon registration. The validity check profiles (OCSP/CRL) are also configured on the devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the SCEP configuration in the MDM and on the SCEP server. They check on several devices whether they have individual, valid certificates. It is verified that the configuration for certificate validity checking is active on the devices.

controls.title: Remote wipe and decommissioning of devices (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The MDM SHOULD ensure that all official data on the mobile device can be deleted remotely (remote wipe with an existing data connection). The process for decommissioning the mobile device (unenrollment) SHOULD ensure that no sensitive data remains on the mobile device or connected storage media. If external storage is used, it SHOULD be checked whether it is also deleted during a remote wipe.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented process is defined for the event of device loss, which provides for immediate notification to IT support and the triggering of the remote wipe command by an administrator. For regular decommissioning (e.g., when changing devices), a full factory reset is triggered via the MDM before the device is removed from management. Encryption of the device storage is mandatory to ensure the effectiveness of the deletion process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation for device loss and decommissioning. They have someone show them in the MDM system how a remote wipe command is triggered. Based on the logs, a random check is performed to see whether a wipe command was successfully executed on recently decommissioned devices before the device was removed from the MDM.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The remote wipe process is designed so that it can also be triggered by a helpdesk employee following a clearly defined procedure or by the user themselves via a self-service portal to shorten the response time. The MDM confirms the success of the wipe command. If a device has not connected to the MDM for a defined period of time (e.g., 30 days), it is automatically marked as 'lost' and the wipe command is queued to be executed immediately upon the next connection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A self-service portal is set up for users where they can see their registered devices and trigger a remote wipe themselves in case of loss. A compliance rule is configured in the MDM that automatically locks devices after 30 days of inactivity and marks them for deletion.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the functionality of the self-service portal for remote wipe. They check the configuration of the compliance rule for inactive devices. The logs are searched for an example of a successful wipe process confirmed by the MDM.

controls.title: Use of external reputation services for apps (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If users are allowed to install apps on their devices independently, a so-called reputation service SHOULD be used. The MDM SHOULD then use this information from the reputation service to at least restrict the installation of apps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) system that offers app reputation services is integrated into the MDM. A rule is configured in the MDM that blocks the installation of apps that are classified by the MTD system as malicious or risky (e.g., due to excessive permissions or data leaks).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the integration between MDM and MTD. They check the rules configured in the MDM that are based on the information from the reputation service. It is tested whether the attempt to install a known malicious app is prevented by the system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reputation service is used not only to block known bad apps, but also for risk assessment. Apps are divided into different risk classes based on their reputation score. Depending on the risk class, different measures are taken, e.g., warning the user, blocking access to company data, or forcing uninstallation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Different risk levels (e.g., 'Low', 'Medium', 'High') are defined in the MTD/MDM based on the reputation score. An automated response chain is configured for each level. Example: At 'Medium', the user receives a request to uninstall; at 'High', the corporate container on the device is immediately locked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configured risk levels and the associated automated actions in the MTD/MDM. Test cases for the different risk levels are run through to verify that the defined measures are implemented correctly and in a timely manner.

controls.title: Control of the use of mobile devices (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Appropriate criteria SHOULD be defined on the basis of which the devices are to be monitored without violating legal or internal regulations. In particular, so-called jailbreaks or so-called rooting SHOULD be detected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A compliance rule is activated in the MDM that regularly checks whether a device has a jailbreak (iOS) or root access (Android). If such a state is detected, the device is automatically marked as 'non-compliant' and access to corporate resources is revoked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the compliance rules in the MDM and checks the configuration for detecting jailbreaks/root. They have someone show them the automated actions that are triggered upon detection. If possible, a jailbreak is performed on a test device to verify the effectiveness of the detection and response.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to jailbreak/root detection, a Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) system is used, which can also detect advanced attacks. This includes the detection of malicious profiles, man-in-the-middle attacks in the network, and operating system anomalies. Upon detection, a multi-stage response is automatically triggered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An MTD client is installed on all devices and integrated into the MDM. The MTD reports detected threats to the MDM, which then carries out compliance actions based on them. Example: If an insecure WLAN is detected, the VPN connection is automatically forced.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the MTD system and its integration with the MDM. They review the configured threat detection rules and the associated response plans. Various attack scenarios (e.g., connecting to a manipulated WLAN hotspot) are simulated to test the detection and response capabilities.

controls.title: Use of geofencing (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: By implementing a geofencing policy, it SHOULD be ensured that devices with sensitive information cannot be used outside a predefined geographical area. If the geographical area is left, appropriately classified information or the entire device SHOULD be deleted. The areas where these additional security measures are necessary SHOULD be identified. The measures must be implemented in compliance with legal and internal regulations. Before the device is deleted, the responsible administrators, security management, and users SHOULD be informed with a reasonable time delay.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For a small group of devices with highly sensitive data (e.g., prototypes in the development department), a geofencing policy is defined in the MDM that is restricted to the company premises. If a device leaves this area, an email notification is sent to IT support and the device owner. After a delay of 30 minutes, a command to selectively wipe the business container on the device is automatically triggered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the definition of the geofencing policy in the MDM, including the defined area and the assigned devices. They check the configuration of the notification and wipe workflow, especially the adherence to the time delay. It is checked whether the affected users have been transparently informed about this measure (e.g., through a supplementary agreement).

controls.title: Enforcement of compliance requirements (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Violations of the institution's regulations or even manipulation of the operating system SHOULD be detected with a suitable solution. In case of a suspected violation, an alarm SHOULD be sent to the responsible administrators and security management. Functions SHOULD be provided to execute actions such as locking the device or deleting confidential information in case of violations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Compliance policies are configured in the MDM that detect basic violations (e.g., outdated operating system, disabled encryption, jailbreak). In the event of a violation, access to corporate resources (email, intranet) is automatically blocked and a notification is sent to IT support and the user. The violation must be remedied manually by support or the user.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configured compliance policies and the associated actions (blocking, notifying). A compliance violation is provoked on a test device (e.g., removing the passcode, if possible) to verify that the block and notification work as configured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A tiered and automated response chain for compliance violations is implemented. Different measures are taken depending on the severity of the violation. The user is provided with instructions via the system for self-remediation of the problem.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Example workflow: For a minor violation (e.g., outdated app version), the user receives a push notification with a link to update. For a medium violation (e.g., disabled passcode), access is blocked, and the user receives instructions for reactivation. For a severe violation (e.g., jailbreak), the device is immediately wiped completely.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configured, multi-level compliance workflows in the MDM. They review the content of the self-remediation instructions. Test cases for different severity levels of violations are simulated to verify the correct execution of the respective response chain.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
For many employees, smartphones, tablets, and phablets have become an indispensable part of their work. However, IT operations must provide an increasing number of such devices in many different versions while ensuring adequate security. Additionally, mobile devices are exposed to special risks, and their administration differs from other IT systems in fundamental ways.
Therefore, Mobile Device Management (MDM) is essential for the orderly and secure operation of these devices, especially in institutions with a large number of smartphones, tablets, and phablets. With appropriate MDM software, the devices can be managed centrally, security rules can be enforced, and emergency actions can be triggered. An MDM thus ensures an identical or at least comparable security standard on all devices.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to show how mobile devices can be used securely by institutions with an MDM. It also provides guidance on operating an MDM.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.3.2.2 Mobile Device Management (MDM) is to be used for the information network if mobile devices are managed with a Mobile Device Management (MDM).
Mobile devices in the context of this module are smartphones, tablets, and phablets on which mobile operating systems such as Android or iOS are installed. The security requirements for smartphones, tablets, notebooks, and tablets with desktop operating systems are described in other modules of the SYS IT Systems layer. The requirements from SYS.3.2.1 General Smartphones and Tablets must also be taken into account when an MDM is used. How smartphones, tablets, and phablets are specifically secured is also described in detail in the modules for the respective operating systems, e.g., in SYS.3.2.3 iOS (for Enterprise) or SYS.3.2.4 Android.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient synchronization with the MDM
parts.prose: For the MDM to enforce the policies defined by the administrators on the mobile devices, the devices must be synchronized with the MDM regularly. If a device is not connected to the MDM for an extended period, new or updated policies cannot be applied, for example. Also, if there is no connection to a lost device, the data can no longer be remotely wiped.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Incorrect administration of the MDM
parts.prose: MDM solutions are complex applications with typically several hundred different rules. Not all rules are compatible with each other, and conversely, many rules are interdependent. Errors in administration can expose both the MDM and the devices to various threats that directly or indirectly affect the confidentiality, availability, or integrity of data and applications.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Inadequate rights management in the MDM
parts.prose: The MDM's rights management determines which users can make which settings on the mobile devices and who can access which data. If users are assigned the wrong role, there is a risk that they will be granted excessive rights. For example, they could view data without authorization or change device settings. It would also be possible for them to install and use apps that are not approved in the institution, such as those for using cloud storage services. This can lead to the leakage of sensitive data from the institution or a violation of legal data protection regulations.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Unauthorized creation of movement profiles by the MDM
parts.prose: Most MDM products can determine a device's current location, and data or apps can be enabled or blocked based on location (so-called "geofencing"). This creates detailed movement profiles of the devices and thus of the users. If this data is collected without properly informing the users, those responsible may be violating data protection regulations. There is also a risk that this data could fall into unauthorized hands in the event of an attack. Likewise, geofencing can be misused to improperly monitor employees.

controls.title: Strategy for iOS Usage

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic strategy for iOS usage exists but focuses mainly on device selection. Regulations for app usage and the prevention of jailbreaks are only partially implemented or only for individual device groups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The strategy is often only informally documented in emails or short memos. There is no central, binding policy for everyone. Implementation is the responsibility of individual departments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks various department heads if they are aware of an iOS strategy. A random check is performed to see if unapproved apps or signs of a jailbreak are present on devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic strategy for iOS usage is available and documented. It covers device selection, data backup, and app usage. Management via an MDM is implemented, but the configurations are not yet fully tailored to all usage scenarios. Jailbreaks are organizationally prohibited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A basic policy is published on the intranet. All devices are enrolled in an MDM but receive a uniform standard profile. The prohibition of jailbreaks is communicated in the user agreement but not actively technically prevented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the iOS usage strategy and compares it with the MDM basic configuration. It is checked whether all active iOS devices are registered in the MDM.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There MUST be a strategy for iOS usage that defines aspects such as the selection of end devices or strategies for data backups. It MUST be regulated whether additional apps from third-party providers should or may be used. Furthermore, jailbreaks MUST be organizationally prohibited and, if possible, technically prevented. If iOS-based devices are managed via an MDM, they MUST be configured through it.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal, approved policy for iOS usage exists and is enforced. All devices are mandatorily managed via an MDM. The MDM profile contains a configuration that prevents the installation of unauthorized apps and activates jailbreak detection functions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and content of the iOS usage strategy. The MDM configuration is checked, particularly the settings for app control and the activation of jailbreak detection mechanisms. A compliance report from the MDM is used for verification.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The iOS usage strategy is regularly reviewed and adapted to new threats and technological developments. The MDM configurations are differentiated according to user groups and security levels. The technical prevention of jailbreaks is actively monitored through specialized MDM functions or additional security software.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The review process for the strategy is documented and takes place annually. Different profiles for different roles (e.g., standard user, management, IT admin) are implemented in the MDM. The MDM performs regular compliance scans to detect jailbreaks and other policy violations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the strategy reviews. The different MDM profiles are checked for their appropriateness for the respective user group. The configuration and the reports of the jailbreak monitoring are analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The iOS usage strategy is fully integrated into the ISMS process and is continuously monitored through automated compliance checks via the MDM system. Any deviation (e.g., a detected jailbreak attempt) triggers automatic reactions, such as the immediate blocking of the device or disconnection from the corporate network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The iOS strategy is part of the central security concept. The MDM is coupled with a Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) solution and the SIEM system. Automated playbooks (e.g., in a SOAR tool) react to compliance violations in real-time without manual intervention.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the integration of iOS management into the ISMS and the configuration of the automated response rules in the MDM/SOAR. A simulated attack (e.g., installation of a suspicious app) is carried out to test the automatic detection and response.

controls.title: Planning the Use of Cloud Services

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a verbal or informal regulation that generally restricts the use of cloud services like iCloud, but it does not contain specific details or technical controls.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The regulation is communicated verbally when the device is issued. There is no written policy or technical implementation that prevents users from activating iCloud services.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews employees and IT staff about the regulations for cloud usage. On sample devices, it is checked which iCloud services are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a documented policy that generally specifies which cloud services are permitted or prohibited. However, it is not yet systematically checked whether Apple Business Manager can be used for device registration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A general policy on cloud usage is in place, which also mentions Apple services. Implementation is organizational, but not technically enforced via MDM. Device registration is often still done manually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the cloud usage policy. It is checked whether a process for reviewing the Apple Business Manager has been established, even if it is not yet consistently used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before iOS-based devices are used, it MUST be determined which cloud services are to be used and to what extent. This determination must take into account the close integration of iOS with Apple services such as iCloud and must be made before the devices are first used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A binding policy exists that regulates the use of iCloud and other cloud services in detail. This policy is technically implemented via an MDM profile by selectively disabling or allowing specific services (e.g., iCloud Backup, iCloud Drive).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and content of the policy for cloud services. The MDM configuration is used to check whether the policy's requirements are technically implemented. This includes checking which iCloud functions are blocked for users.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy for cloud services is implemented through technical configurations in the MDM that actively prevent the use of unwanted services. Apple Business Manager is used by default for device registration to ensure a separation of private and corporate Apple IDs and to enforce the configuration during initial setup.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of Apple Business Manager is the standard process for procuring and registering all new iOS devices. This ensures that the devices are in supervised mode and that the cloud policies cannot be circumvented. Managed Apple IDs are used exclusively for corporate purposes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the device registration process and verifies that it runs through Apple Business Manager. It is checked whether managed Apple IDs are used on the devices instead of private ones. A compliance report from the MDM is used to verify the configurations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of cloud services is not only configured via the MDM, but also continuously monitored. Any data flows to unapproved cloud services are detected and blocked by a Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) solution or a Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB). The use of Apple Business Manager is mandatory and fully automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM is integrated with a CASB that analyzes the data traffic of the mobile devices. Policies in the CASB prevent the upload of corporate data to private or unapproved cloud storage. The process from ordering the device to delivering it to the user with the correct configuration is fully automated (Zero-Touch-Deployment).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the CASB configuration and the logs of blocked access attempts. The Zero-Touch-Deployment process is checked by registering a new device and verifying the automatic application of the cloud policies. A pen test can attempt to exfiltrate data to an unapproved cloud service.

controls.title: Prevention of unauthorized deletion of configuration profiles

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Configuration profiles are deployed to the devices, but there is no technical measure that prevents users from deleting them. It is relied upon that users will not remove the profiles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The devices are operated without 'supervised mode'. The MDM profiles can therefore be removed by the user in the settings. This is treated as an accepted risk.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a sample device and attempts to remove the MDM configuration profile in the settings. If this is successful without administrator rights, the control is not effectively implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For new devices, supervised mode is manually activated via the Apple Configurator, which prevents the user from deleting profiles. However, this process does not scale for a large number of devices and is not consistently implemented on existing devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IT employee connects each new device to a Mac with Apple Configurator to put it into supervised mode before it is enrolled in the MDM. This is time-consuming and error-prone.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the process for commissioning new devices. It is checked in the MDM how many devices are marked as 'supervised' and whether there are any discrepancies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To prevent configuration profiles from being deleted without authorization, appropriate technical measures MUST be taken and implemented. This is achieved through the 'Supervised Mode', which prevents the user from removing MDM profiles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All company-owned devices are put into supervised mode either via the Apple Configurator or the Apple Business Manager. This marks the MDM profile as non-removable.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies via the MDM console that all managed devices have the 'supervised' status. On a test device, it is checked whether the option to remove the profile in the settings is grayed out or not present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All company-owned devices are mandatorily registered via Apple Business Manager and are thus automatically placed in supervised mode upon first activation (Zero-Touch Deployment). Additionally, users are made aware of the purpose and necessity of the security measures and profiles.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process is designed so that devices can be sent directly from the reseller to the user. Upon first startup, the device connects to Apple's servers, is recognized as company-owned, and is automatically registered and configured in the MDM. Awareness is raised through regular training or notices on the intranet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the Apple Business Manager and its link to the MDM. The existence of training materials or communication measures to raise user awareness is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity of the configuration profiles is continuously monitored by the MDM. Any attempt or successful deletion of a profile (if possible due to a new security vulnerability) is immediately detected and triggers an automatic alert and the immediate blocking of the device or revocation of network access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MDM performs compliance checks at short intervals. A rule is configured so that the absence of the expected configuration profile is considered a critical violation. This rule triggers an automated response that is implemented in the MDM or a connected NAC (Network Access Control) system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the compliance rules and the associated automated actions in the MDM. If possible in a test environment, it is simulated that a device is no longer compliant to test the automated response. The logs of the MDM and the NAC system are checked for corresponding events.

controls.title: Use of Apple IDs

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a recommendation not to use private Apple IDs for business purposes, but no technical enforcement. Users can still set up their private accounts on the devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When devices are issued, a fact sheet with recommendations is provided. There is no MDM configuration that prevents the use of a private Apple ID.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the device issuance documents. On sample devices, it is checked whether private Apple IDs have been set up.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of private Apple IDs is organizationally prohibited. Instead, anonymized, company-owned Apple IDs are created and managed manually, but Apple Business Manager is not yet used for managed IDs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department creates generic Apple IDs (e.g., 'department-x@company.com') and assigns them to users. This process is manual and not scalable.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the process for creating and managing the company-owned Apple IDs described to them and checks the documentation (e.g., a list of assigned IDs).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Instead of a user's personal Apple ID, an anonymized Apple ID SHOULD be used. A clear policy is implemented that prohibits the use of personal Apple IDs for business purposes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An official policy prohibits private Apple IDs on company devices. A process is established to either create anonymized, company-owned IDs or, preferably, to use Managed Apple IDs via Apple Business Manager.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the policy. It is checked which type of Apple ID (anonymized or managed) is in use on the devices. The MDM configuration is checked to see if it restricts the use of unwanted accounts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of Managed Apple IDs via Apple Business Manager is standard. In addition, Apple Business Manager is used for Volume Purchasing (formerly VPP) to procure apps centrally and assign them to the Managed IDs or devices, so that users do not have to make their own purchases.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Apple Business Manager is fully implemented. All users receive a Managed Apple ID. All required apps are purchased through the Volume Purchase Program and distributed via MDM. Access to the public App Store is blocked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the Apple Business Manager, especially the list of Managed Apple IDs and the purchased app licenses. In the MDM, it is verified that app distribution is done this way.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of Managed Apple IDs is automated and integrated into the organization's central Identity and Access Management (IAM). The creation, modification, and deletion of Managed Apple IDs occurs automatically based on the user's status in the IAM system (e.g., upon joining or leaving).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The Apple Business Manager is connected to the organization's Azure AD / Entra ID or another IdP via a SCIM interface or federated authentication. User accounts and Managed Apple IDs are synchronized automatically. When an employee leaves the company, their Managed Apple ID is automatically blocked or deleted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the federated authentication or the SCIM connection between the IAM/IdP and the Apple Business Manager. The process for a new employee and a departing employee is run through to test the automatic provisioning and de-provisioning.

controls.title: Use of the 'Restrictions' configuration option in iOS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only a few, particularly critical functions (e.g., installing apps from the App Store) are disabled via the restrictions. A comprehensive review and deactivation of all non-essential functions does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the MDM profile, only the setting 'Allow App Installation' is set to 'No'. Other functions like Siri, AirDrop, or the camera remain unconfigured and thus activated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the MDM configuration profile and determines that only a minimal number of restrictions are configured. On a test device, it is checked which potentially risky functions are still available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a standard configuration profile that deactivates a basic selection of functions via a 'Restrictions' payload. This profile is applied equally to all devices, without differentiation based on purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 'one-size-fits-all' profile is used, which represents a compromise between security and usability. It deactivates common risky functions but is not tailored to specific protection needs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the standard configuration profile for the configured restrictions. It is assessed whether this profile is appropriate for the different user groups in the organization.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All unnecessary or disallowed iOS functions or services SHOULD be disabled.
