Since such protocols are only output after a fax has been sent or a transmission error has occurred, they could also remain in the device for a longer period of time or not be collected at all. As a result, confidential information may be left unattended in the output tray and, in the worst case, be stolen.
In addition, uncollected documents are eventually disposed of. This is often done by randomly throwing the printouts into nearby wastebaskets instead of securely destroying printouts with information worthy of protection. As a result, this information can get into the public waste disposal and thus into the hands of third parties.
Many teleworking places are also equipped with their own printer or multifunction device. This can also expose information worthy of protection.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Visibility of metadata
parts.prose:
Metadata, such as user ID, date, time, and print job name, is sent with a print job. This data is displayed on the control panel and web server of many printers and multifunction devices. The print job name is often derived from the name of the digital document. If the printer has an integrated web server, confidential operations can often be viewed via a browser. The metadata is also visible in clear text on the print servers unless it is anonymized. This allows third parties to gain access to confidential information. Many devices also allow print jobs to be stored for later printing after authentication via a PIN. In this case as well, the names of all existing documents are displayed on the control panel of an output device.
Certain printers and copiers print so-called "Yellow Dots" (also "Machine Identification Code", "Tracking Dots", "Secret Dots") on the paper. These often undocumented watermarks can contain the date, time, and the printer's serial number and are barely visible to the naked eye. This allows a printout to be directly assigned to an institution or a specific person and thus traced back to the person who authored the text. In addition to data protection implications, this could lead to information unintentionally leaving the institution.
Fax logs can also be printed on many multifunction devices without access protection. Even if only the phone number, date, time, and page number are listed, conclusions can already be drawn about personal data or business processes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficient protection of stored information
parts.prose:
Printers, copiers, and multifunction devices are often equipped with non-volatile memory where information is stored temporarily or for longer periods. For example, address books, documents, fax files, and print jobs are stored there. If this information is inadequately protected, third parties can access and read it. Under certain circumstances, even already deleted information can be reconstructed if insecure deletion methods were used.
Data can be stored and read on the device via network protocols. Printers and multifunction devices with data carriers, if not secured, can often be used as unauthorized file servers. In this way, information can be stored decentrally in an uncontrolled manner and is not considered in the data backup concept.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unencrypted communication
parts.prose:
Print and scan data are often transmitted unencrypted over the network. This allows the sent documents to be intercepted and read. Similarly, temporarily stored print files on print servers can be read. This also applies to central scanning and document processing systems.
Further sources of danger are unencrypted communication interfaces for the administration of the devices. If, for example, printers are accessed via HTTP, SNMPv2, or Telnet, the information is transported unprotected. This jeopardizes the access information, including device passwords.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unauthorized sending of information
parts.prose:
Many multifunction devices can send digitized paper documents via email and fax. Without special protective measures, information can intentionally or accidentally be sent to unauthorized recipients. For example, users could enter addresses or phone numbers incorrectly. As a result, potentially sensitive data may be unintentionally sent to the wrong recipients. In addition, the email or fax function can be used to quickly leak confidential documents.
Many networked printers can be configured to receive print jobs from the internet via email and send scanned documents as email attachments. The free entry of the sender's address can be misused to send emails under a false name to internal and external individuals.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Uncontrolled data exchange via storage interfaces on printers, copiers, and multifunction devices
parts.prose:
Paper documents can be quickly copied using multifunction devices. With existing USB or SD ports, it is also possible to digitize even large quantities of paper documents directly and without any control and save them to USB sticks or SD cards. Documents stored on these media can also be printed directly via the storage interfaces.
If the printers, copiers, and multifunction devices are connected to a data network or directly to clients, IT systems can often also directly access the storage media connected to the printers, copiers, and multifunction devices. Even if the integration of storage media into IT systems is technically prevented, information can be copied uncontrollably via the storage interfaces through this detour.
In this way, on the one hand, (mal)ware can get from the storage interfaces via the multifunction devices to the connected clients or into the institution's data network. On the other hand, confidential (paper) documents can be digitized unnoticed and stolen untraceably.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficiently secured network access of printers, copiers, and multifunction devices
parts.prose: Firewalls between the LAN and the internet are often configured to allow entire subnets to access the internet. In addition, printers, copiers, and multifunction devices are often assigned to the same subnet as the clients. As a result, network printers, for example, can also access information on the internet. Even if the institution's IT systems only access the internet via a proxy, printers, copiers, and multifunction devices can also use it. If connections from and to the printers from the internet are not rejected by the firewall, sensitive information may undesirably leave the own data network. Conversely, a network-capable device could undesirably receive and further distribute data from the internet. A network printer can thus, for example, become a gateway for attacks from the internet.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Inadequate access protection for device administration
parts.prose:
Networked printers, copiers, and multifunction devices can be managed via the control panel and the built-in web server. When the devices are delivered, they usually have no password or only a default password. If the password is not set or not changed, the devices can be accessed very easily.
In many institutions, uniform passwords are also used for all printers and multifunction devices, which are rarely changed. As a result, they are often known to many internal and external persons, and unauthorized third parties can thus easily access the devices.
Furthermore, printers and multifunction devices can be reset to factory settings via boot menus. This also affects the security settings. For example, the device password is often no longer present after the printer or multifunction device has been reset to factory settings. Unsecured boot menus facilitate administration but at the same time reduce security.
Printers, copiers, and multifunction devices are equipped with numerous network protocols. On delivery, most protocols are activated. This could allow attackers to access the device settings and change them in such a way that sensitive information flows out of the network.
Many devices can transmit their control panel to support over the network. However, this also allows confidential user inputs on the device's control panel to be read.
In larger institutions, there are usually very many printers, copiers, and multifunction devices. To be able to manage and monitor them efficiently, device management software is often used. However, many institutions do not adequately protect this software from unauthorized access, as it is perceived as a less critical system. This allows individual or all devices to be changed unintentionally or deliberately.

controls.title: Regulations for handling embedded systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An inventory exists for only a portion of the embedded systems. Regulations for handling them, if they exist, are informal and not known to all relevant personnel. No secure pre-configuration or integrity tests are performed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, regulations are only passed on orally for systems considered particularly critical. A central record or documentation is completely missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly questions various employees to see if they are aware of regulations for handling embedded systems. The auditor asks for an inventory list and finds that it is incomplete or non-existent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All embedded systems and their interfaces are inventoried. Basic rules of conduct and reporting channels exist and have been communicated to the responsible employees. A standardized, secure pre-configuration is performed, but not consistently documented or tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple list of all systems is maintained in a spreadsheet. The rules are communicated once during onboarding.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the inventory list and compares it with the actually existing systems. They check whether basic rules of conduct are documented and accessible to all users and administrators.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All users and administrators MUST be informed about rules of conduct and reporting channels for failures, malfunctions, or suspected security incidents. All embedded systems, including interfaces, MUST be inventoried. The embedded systems MUST be securely pre-configured. The configuration performed SHOULD be documented. Furthermore, regulations SHOULD be established to test the integrity and functionality of the embedded systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central inventory database (e.g., a CMDB) is used. The rules of conduct are part of the security policies and are regularly trained. The configuration is carried out using standardized templates and documented in a configuration management tool. There is a defined process for regular, manual integrity tests.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and completeness of the inventory list. They check whether the rules of conduct and reporting channels are documented and known to all relevant personnel. They request the documentation of the configuration and the logs of the integrity tests for a sample of systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The recording, configuration, and documentation of the systems are part of a formalized configuration management process. The documentation is versioned and regularly reviewed. Integrity tests are partially automated where technically possible, and the results are collected centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Configuration Management System (CMS) is used to manage the systems and their configurations. Automated scripts are used to check the configuration and perform periodic integrity tests (e.g., checking file hashes).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the processes of the configuration management. They check the configuration of the automated test scripts and the centrally collected results for plausibility and completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of embedded systems is fully integrated into a central Configuration Management Database (CMDB) and an automated configuration management system. Configuration policies are automatically enforced. Integrity tests run continuously and fully automated, and deviations lead to automated alarms to the security team.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Ansible, Puppet, or SaltStack are used for automated configuration management and enforcement. File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) systems continuously monitor system integrity. The results flow directly into a SIEM system for correlation and alarming.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the CMDB and the automation tool. They check the rules in the SIEM system that react to integrity violations. They can trigger a test integrity violation to check the correct functioning of the automated alerting chain.

controls.title: Deactivating unused interfaces and services on embedded systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unused interfaces or services are only deactivated sporadically and reactively, for example, when a problem occurs. A systematic approach to hardening is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator manually disables a port after a suspicious network scan is noticed. There is no policy to do this proactively.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor scans a sample of systems and typically finds several open but unused ports (e.g., Telnet, FTP).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic hardening procedure is applied, where known insecure or unnecessary services and interfaces are deactivated on all systems according to a checklist. Authentication on application interfaces uses standard mechanisms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During initial setup, a list of services is processed and they are manually deactivated. A simple, local password is used for access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the hardening checklist and checks on a sample of devices whether the steps have been implemented. They check the configuration of the authentication.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that only required interfaces can be accessed. All other interfaces MUST be disabled. In addition, ONLY required services MAY be enabled. Access to application interfaces MUST be protected by secure authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each system type, a 'golden image' or a base configuration is created in which all unneeded interfaces (e.g., JTAG, serial ports) and network services are disabled. Access to administration web interfaces is secured by strong, individual passwords and HTTPS.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the base configuration (golden image) for a system type and compares it with the list of actually needed functions. They perform a port scan on a production system to verify that no unauthorized services are running. They check the configuration and effectiveness of the authentication mechanisms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for hardening the systems is automated through configuration management tools. Regular, automated scans are performed to detect and report deviations from the hardened base configuration. Authentication is done via a central directory (e.g., LDAP/RADIUS).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A script or a tool like Ansible is used to apply the hardening policies to all new and existing systems. A vulnerability scanner periodically checks the configuration of the systems and reports open ports or active, unapproved services.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the automation tool. They review the reports of the configuration and vulnerability scans for anomalies and for the follow-up of findings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A 'deny-by-default' policy is enforced on all systems by a central configuration management system. Any deviation from the approved state leads to an automated alert and, if possible, automatic remediation. Physical interfaces are sealed by hardware measures (e.g., potting with epoxy resin) when not needed. Access is secured by multi-factor authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration is continuously monitored by a tool that enforces compliance with the security policy. Deviations are corrected immediately. Unused USB or Ethernet ports are physically blocked or sealed. Login requires a password and a certificate or token.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the physical devices for sealed ports. They check the configuration of the central management tool and the logs of the automatic remediation measures. They attempt to activate an unauthorized service to test the automatic remediation.

controls.title: Logging of security-relevant events in embedded systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging is enabled on the systems, but left in the default configuration. The logs are only stored locally, not checked regularly, and are quickly overwritten. Organizational regulations for reporting incidents are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The manufacturer's default log settings are retained. In case of an error, an attempt is made to access the local logs, but they are often no longer available or not meaningful.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the log configuration on a sample of devices and finds that no adjustments have been made and the log rotation is very aggressive.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security-relevant events are logged locally on the devices. An organizational directive exists on how to proceed in case of security breaches, but it is not consistently implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Logging for security-relevant events (e.g., failed logins) is explicitly enabled on the devices. A written instruction for reporting incidents exists.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the local log configuration. He asks employees if they know the reporting channels for security breaches.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security breaches MUST be logged. If electronic logging is not feasible or only very limited, alternative, organizational regulations SHOULD be created and implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Wherever technically possible, the logs of the embedded systems are sent to a central syslog server. For systems without this capability, there is a defined process for manually entering critical events into an operations logbook. This process is documented and the responsible employees are trained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the log forwarding to the central server. For systems without this function, he asks to be shown the organizational process and the operations logbook. He checks whether the documented processes are known to the employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All electronically available logs are collected centrally in a log management system. The logs are regularly checked manually or by simple scripts for suspicious patterns. The organizational regulations are formalized and part of the incident response process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central log management tool (e.g., Graylog, ELK stack) is used. There are weekly or daily reviews of the most important log events. Simple correlation rules (e.g., 'more than 10 failed logins in one minute') are set up.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the log management system and the reports of the log reviews. He checks the formalized organizational procedures and their integration into the incident response plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All logs are forwarded to a central Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. Complex correlation rules are used to automatically detect and alert on security incidents. The entire process, from logging to response, is integrated into a formal and regularly practiced incident response plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SIEM system is used for real-time analysis of log data. Application-specific parsing and correlation rules are implemented that can detect complex attack patterns. An alarm in the SIEM automatically triggers a ticket in the incident response system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the correlation rules in the SIEM for their effectiveness. He asks to see the logs of past security incidents and traces the process from detection to resolution of the incident to check the functionality of the entire chain.

controls.title: Creation of procurement criteria for embedded systems (S) [Procurement office]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement of embedded systems is primarily based on functional requirements and price. Security aspects are, if at all, only considered marginally and unsystematically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection is based on the manufacturer's information on functions and costs. A formal catalog of criteria does not exist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the procurement documents of recent years and finds that security requirements did not play a role in the selection decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple checklist with basic security requirements is used for procurement. However, it does not cover all relevant aspects and is not used consistently in all procurements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A short list of yes/no questions on security topics (e.g., 'Supports encrypted communication?') is used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the checklist and compares it with the requirements of the building block. He checks whether the checklist was filled out for the last procurements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before embedded systems are procured, a list of requirements SHOULD be created, against which the systems or components in question are evaluated. The list of requirements SHOULD at least cover the following security-relevant aspects: aspects of physical security, requirements for the security properties of the hardware and software, support for a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) by the operating system, security aspects of the development environment, and organizational security aspects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized requirements catalog is used for each procurement, which queries the mentioned points in detail. The manufacturers' answers are documented and included in the purchase decision. For example, it is explicitly asked about the availability of a TPM 2.0 and its OS integration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the requirements lists for recently procured systems. He checks whether all aspects mentioned in the building block are covered and how the manufacturers' answers were considered in the procurement decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security requirements catalog is a formal and mandatory part of the procurement process. It contains detailed and measurable criteria. Manufacturers must provide evidence for their claims (e.g., through technical data sheets, test reports, or manufacturer's declarations).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirements are specifically formulated, e.g., 'The system must support Secure Boot according to the UEFI standard' instead of just 'secure boot process'. The procurement office actively requests supporting documents and evaluates their validity.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor not only checks the requirements lists, but also the supporting documents submitted by the manufacturers. He assesses whether the criteria are measurable and whether the evaluation of the evidence is comprehensible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement process requires independent security certifications or third-party attestations (e.g., Common Criteria, FIPS) from manufacturers for their products. The fulfillment of security requirements is heavily weighted in the award process. The institution may conduct its own tests on sample devices to verify the manufacturer's claims.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The tender explicitly requires a certification according to a specific protection profile. Alternatively, the offered products are tested for compliance with the most important security criteria in a test laboratory before the final decision.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the tender documents for the requirement for certificates. He reviews the submitted certificates for their validity and applicability. If internal tests were carried out, he checks the test concepts and protocols.

controls.title: Protection against harmful environmental influences for embedded systems (S) [Developers, Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the most obvious environmental risks, such as rain for outdoor devices, are considered. A systematic analysis of the location and the associated risks does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An outdoor sensor is installed in a simple plastic housing that is not explicitly specified for outdoor use.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly inspects the physical installation of devices and finds that the protective measures are inadequate for the respective location.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Standard industrial enclosures or other protective measures are used, but without a specific analysis of the exact environmental conditions at the location. The compatibility of the protective measures with the overall system is not explicitly checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The same housing type is used for all systems in production halls, regardless of whether a system is next to a furnace (heat) or a washing facility (wetness).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the specifications of the protective measures used with the real conditions at some locations and identifies potential discrepancies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that embedded systems are adequately protected against harmful environmental influences according to their intended use and location. The requirements for this SHOULD already be analyzed during the planning phase. Furthermore, it SHOULD be ensured that the precautions to protect individual components from dust, heat, moisture, and contamination do not cause problems with the requirements of the parent system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: As part of the planning, an analysis of the environmental conditions (temperature range, humidity, dust exposure, vibrations, etc.) at the planned location is carried out. Based on this analysis, suitable protective housings and measures (e.g., fans, seals) are selected. It is checked whether, for example, a completely encapsulated housing could lead to overheating problems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the planning documents and the analysis of the environmental influences. He checks whether the selected protective measures correspond to the determined requirements and whether possible negative interactions with the overall system have been considered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The protection against environmental influences is based on formal standards such as the IP protection classes (Ingress Protection) or NEMA ratings. The selection is documented. The compatibility of the protective measures with the parent system is formally tested and recorded in the test protocol.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For use in a humid environment, a housing with protection class IP67 is specified and procured. As part of a system test, it is checked whether the heat dissipation of the system in the IP67 housing is sufficient even under full load.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning documentation for the specification of protection classes. They examine the test protocols to understand the verification of compatibility and the protective effect.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, humidity) inside the protective enclosure are actively monitored by sensors. Exceeding defined thresholds triggers an alarm or leads to automatic countermeasures (e.g., activating a fan). The system design is explicitly engineered for resilience against the specified environmental hazards.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A temperature sensor inside the enclosure reports data to a central monitoring system. If the temperature exceeds 60°C, a warning is sent to operations. At 70°C, the system is shut down in a controlled manner to prevent damage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration of the monitoring system and the alarm thresholds. They request to see the logs of the environmental sensors. If possible, a limit value test is performed to verify the alarm chain.

controls.title: Preventing debugging capabilities in embedded systems (S) [Developers]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the final software version, only debugging symbols are removed. Hardware debugging interfaces like JTAG or SWD remain accessible and active on the circuit board.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The compiler is called with the 'strip symbols' option. The JTAG header on the board remains unpopulated, but the connection pads are still functional.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the hardware and identifies accessible debug ports. Using a suitable debug probe (e.g., J-Link), they attempt to establish a connection to the microcontroller.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Common debugging interfaces are disabled in the final software configuration. However, no physical measures are taken to prevent access to the interfaces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The microcontroller's fuse bits are programmed to disable the JTAG/SWD interface. However, the physical connections on the circuit board remain.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reads the microcontroller's fuse bit configuration to verify that the debug interface has been disabled. They note that the physical connections are still present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Any debugging capabilities SHOULD be removed from embedded systems as completely as possible. If on-chip debugging is used, it MUST be ensured that debugging functions cannot be used or activated without authorization. Furthermore, it SHOULD be ensured that no input interfaces for test signals and measurement points for connecting analyzers are activated and usable by unauthorized persons. Additionally, all hardware debugging interfaces SHOULD be disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the final build process, all debug functions are removed or disabled on the software side. The microcontroller's fuse bits are set to permanently disable the hardware debug interfaces. Test points and connection pads for debug interfaces are removed in the final version of the board layout.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the build script for instructions on disabling debug functions. They read out the controller's fuse bits to confirm the deactivation of the debug ports. They inspect the board layout and the physical board for the absence of debug connections.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware debugging interfaces are not only disabled but also made physically inaccessible, e.g., by removing components in the signal chain or potting with epoxy resin. A secure process exists to make the interfaces accessible again for authorized maintenance cases (if required).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The JTAG connectors on the board are sealed with epoxy resin. Alternatively, a resistor in the JTAG signal line, which was required for production, is not populated in the final assembly, thereby interrupting the signal chain.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a physical inspection of the board and verifies the implementation of the physical protection measures. They have the process for authorized maintenance interventions described to them and check it for plausibility.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system design avoids standardized debug interfaces from the outset and instead relies on a proprietary, authenticated diagnostic interface. The device is able to actively detect and respond to attempts to attach debug probes (e.g., by deleting keys).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access to diagnostic functions requires challenge-response authentication with a device key provisioned at the factory. The device has tamper protection that also detects attempts at invasive debugging.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the design of the diagnostic interface for its security. They check the documentation of the active anti-debugging measures. If possible, a penetration test is carried out to attempt to bypass the protective measures.

controls.title: Hardware realization of functions of embedded systems (S) [Developers, Planners, Procurement Body]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When embedded systems are developed in-house, security aspects SHOULD be considered in the design decision for hardware and software implementation. Security aspects SHOULD also be considered when deciding to implement a specific hardware technology.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the design phase, a deliberate trade-off is made as to whether a security-critical function (e.g., an encryption routine) is implemented in software or as dedicated hardware logic (e.g., in an FPGA). Aspects such as attack surface, tamper resistance, and performance are evaluated. The decision is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the design documentation and checks whether a comprehensible trade-off between hardware and software implementation for security-critical functions has taken place. They question the developers about the decisions made.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal trade-off analysis is conducted and documented for security-critical functions. This analysis provides a detailed assessment of the attack surface, robustness against physical attacks, and the updatability of hardware and software options.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized evaluation form is used to systematically compare the pros and cons of the implementation alternatives. Criteria include, for example, 'resistance to side-channel attacks', 'patchability', and 'complexity of verification'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the formal trade-off analyses and the associated documentation. They check whether the methodology of the analysis is sound and the conclusions are logical.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The design uses dedicated Hardware Security Modules (HSM), Secure Elements (SE), or Physically Unclonable Functions (PUFs) for the most critical security functions such as storing master keys, performing cryptographic operations, and device identity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A certified Secure Element is used to store private keys and perform signature operations. The main processor never has direct access to these keys. The device identity is derived from a PUF, which makes cloning the device more difficult.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the use of HSMs, SEs, or PUFs based on the hardware design (schematic, bill of materials) and software documentation. They check whether these are correctly integrated into the security architecture and whether their security functions are used as intended.

controls.title: Use of a secure operating system for embedded systems (S) [Developers, Planners, Procurement Body]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The operating system used and the configuration of the embedded system SHOULD be suitable for the intended operation. For example, the operating system SHOULD have sufficient security mechanisms for the intended task. The required services and functions SHOULD be enabled. The operating system SHOULD support the use of a Trusted Platform Module (TPM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An operating system designed for embedded use (e.g., Yocto Linux, FreeRTOS) is selected. The operating system configuration is adapted to include only the services and drivers absolutely necessary for the device's function. If a TPM is present, support for it is enabled in the operating system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the justification for the operating system selection. They analyze the configuration files of the operating system build to determine which components are included. They check whether TPM support is enabled in the kernel and system tools.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A real-time operating system (RTOS) or a formally hardened embedded operating system is used. The configuration is reduced to a minimalist image. The TPM functions are actively used for integrity measurements during the boot process and for sealing secrets.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An OS like QNX or a Linux with PREEMPT_RT patch and security extensions like SELinux in enforcing mode is used. The TPM is used to measure the state of the boot components (Measured Boot) and to bind disk encryption keys to the state of the system (Sealing).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the SELinux policy. They check the configuration of the Measured Boot process and the key sealing functions. They have the values of the Platform Configuration Registers (PCR) of the TPM displayed to verify the correct measurement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An operating system certified according to a recognized standard (e.g., Common Criteria) is used. The entire toolchain used to create the operating system image is secured and its integrity is verified. The configuration used corresponds to the certified configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An operating system such as PikeOS or VxWorks Cert Edition, which has a certification for safety-critical environments, is used. The build server for the OS image is hardened and the build process is reproducible, i.e., a new build produces a bit-identical image.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and validity of the operating system certificate. They check whether the version and configuration of the operating system used are covered by the certification. They check the security measures of the build system and the procedures for reproducible builds.

controls.title: Use of cryptographic processors or coprocessors in embedded systems (S) [Developers, Planners, Procurement Body]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If an additional microcontroller is used for cryptographic calculations, its communication with the system microcontroller SHOULD be sufficiently secured. The necessary roots of trust SHOULD be implemented for the embedded system. A chain of trust SHOULD also be implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The communication between the main processor and the crypto coprocessor (e.g., via I2C or SPI) is protected by at least simple encryption. An immutable code in the main processor (boot ROM) serves as a root of trust and verifies the signature of the next boot stage, thus establishing a simple chain of trust.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the communication protocol between the processors for security flaws. They review the implementation of the trust anchor and the signature verification in the boot process through code review and analysis of the boot logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Communication between the main processor and the crypto-processor is protected by a session-based authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) protocol, ensuring both confidentiality and integrity. The chain of trust extends from a hardware trust anchor (e.g., Boot-ROM) through multiple stages to the crypto-processor's firmware.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For communication, a protocol such as TLS over the internal bus or a custom protocol with AES-GCM is used. Each firmware component in the boot process is cryptographically signed and verified by the previous stage before it is executed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the implementation of the AEAD protocol. They verify the entire chain of trust by verifying the signature checks at each stage and ensuring that the public keys used are securely anchored in the device.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A certified Hardware Security Module (HSM) or Secure Element (SE) is used as the crypto-processor. This is physically tamper-proof. Its firmware is securely loaded and verified by the main processor as part of a Measured Boot process before the crypto-processor accepts commands.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An HSM with FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certification is used. The main processor measures the hash of the HSM firmware into a TPM PCR register before releasing the HSM from reset. Communication is additionally secured by the key material anchored in the HSM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the HSM's certificate. They check the implementation of the Measured Boot process for the HSM firmware and the correct use of the TPM registers. They ensure through analysis that critical keys never leave the HSM.

controls.title: Recovery of embedded systems (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Embedded systems SHOULD have rollback capabilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The system implements a mechanism that allows a manual return to the previous, working version after a failed firmware update. This can be done, for example, through a special bootloader mode or a physical switch. The process is documented for administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for a demonstration of the rollback mechanism and the corresponding documentation. If possible, a faulty update is applied in a test environment to practically test the rollback process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system has an A/B partitioning scheme for atomic updates. After an update that leads to a non-bootable state, the system automatically switches to the previously working partition and reports the error.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The flash memory is divided into two identical partitions (A and B) for the operating system and the application. An update is always written to the inactive partition. After the update, the bootloader attempts to start from the new partition. If this fails (e.g., due to a watchdog timeout), the active partition pointer is reset and the system starts from the old, working partition.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the partitioning layout and the bootloader configuration. They check the logic for the automatic switchover. A test could involve flashing a corrupt image to the inactive partition and then restarting to observe the automatic rollback.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system initiates an automatic rollback to a secure, known state not only after a failed update, but also upon detection of a critical integrity failure during operation (e.g., by a File Integrity Monitoring System). The incident is reported in detail to a central management system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A runtime integrity monitor (e.g., IMA/EVM in Linux) detects an unauthorized change to a critical system file. This triggers an immediate, controlled reboot into the clean A/B partition. In parallel, a detailed forensic report is sent to the central server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the runtime integrity monitor and the associated automatic actions. In a test environment, they modify a monitored file and verify that the automatic rollback and the report are triggered correctly.

controls.title: Secure decommissioning of an embedded system (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before embedded systems are decommissioned, all data on the system SHOULD be securely erased. If this is not possible, the system SHOULD be destroyed. The erasure or destruction SHOULD be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a defined process for decommissioning. This involves executing a 'factory reset' function. If the device contained sensitive data and the effectiveness of the reset is unclear, the device is physically destroyed (e.g., by shredding). The process is logged in a list with the serial number and date of destruction.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the decommissioning process described to them and reviews the logs of the last destruction actions. They check whether the documentation is complete.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For data erasure, secure methods according to recognized standards (e.g., NIST SP 800-88) are used that go beyond a simple factory reset. The physical destruction is carried out by a certified service provider who issues a certificate of destruction.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The device's firmware includes a secure erase function that overwrites the flash memory multiple times. Alternatively, a certified disposal company is commissioned. The certificate of destruction is stored in the asset management system for the respective device.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the documentation of the implemented erasure methods for compliance with the mentioned standards. They review the certificates of destruction and check the qualifications of the service provider.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle, including decommissioning, is tracked seamlessly in an asset management system. Secure erasure (crypto-erase or overwriting) can be triggered remotely before the device is physically uninstalled. High-security devices are designed to self-destruct or at least irretrievably delete all keys in case of tampering attempts during the decommissioning process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before dismantling a device, an administrator sends a 'decommission' command from the central management system. The device then erases its key storage and overwrites the configuration before shutting down. The asset management system records the device as 'decommissioned'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tracks the decommissioning process of a device in the asset management system. They review the technical specifications of the remote erase function and the tamper-response mechanisms for high-security devices.

controls.title: Selection of a trustworthy supply and logistics chain and qualified manufacturing institutions for embedded systems (H) [Procurement office]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Effective controls SHOULD be implemented in the supply chain to ensure that embedded systems do not contain manipulated, counterfeit, or substituted components, that systems comply with the specification, and that no hidden functions have been implemented. Unauthorized parties SHOULD not be able to access confidential information about the system. The participating companies SHOULD be demonstrably qualified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Components are only sourced from known and reputable manufacturers and distributors. Upon delivery, the components are randomly checked for external signs of tampering or counterfeiting. Manufacturers must provide proof of qualification, e.g., an ISO 9001 certification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the list of approved suppliers and the criteria for their selection. They ask to be shown the procedures for incoming goods inspection and check the manufacturers' proof of qualification.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organization requires manufacturers and distributors to provide evidence of their supply chain security practices (e.g., ISO 27001 certification). Tamper-evident packaging is used for all deliveries of critical systems. A significant proportion of components are systematically tested for authenticity and tampering upon delivery.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Suppliers must complete a questionnaire on the security of their logistics processes. The devices are delivered in sealed boxes with tamper-evident stickers. Upon delivery, the firmware is read out and compared with the reference firmware provided by the manufacturer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the evidence requested from suppliers (certificates, questionnaires). They check the instructions for checking the tamper-evident packaging and the logs of the component tests in the incoming goods inspection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A complete Software and Hardware Bill of Materials (SBOM/HBOM) is required from the manufacturer. The entire supply chain is mapped and audited as far as possible. High-security delivery mechanisms, such as trusted couriers, are used. All critical components are forensically analyzed for counterfeits and hardware Trojans upon receipt.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Procurement requires an SBOM in CycloneDX format. For critical deliveries, a secure transport with an unbroken chain of custody is commissioned. In incoming goods inspection, samples of microchips are X-rayed and decapsulated to compare them with reference designs and rule out manipulation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the received SBOMs for completeness and plausibility. They check the contracts and logs of the secure transports. They review the reports of the forensic hardware analyses.

controls.title: Use of a certified operating system (H) [Developers, Planners, Procurement office]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The operating system SHOULD be evaluated against a recognized standard at an appropriate level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When selecting the operating system, the availability of security certifications is considered a positive criterion. It is checked whether manufacturers offer an evaluation according to standards such as Common Criteria (CC).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the documentation on operating system selection and checks whether the existence of certifications was listed and evaluated as a decision criterion.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An operating system is used that has been evaluated against a recognized standard at a basic assurance level (e.g., Common Criteria EAL2). The deployed configuration is based on the evaluated configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An operating system is deliberately selected for which a CC certificate at level EAL2 or higher is available. The system is configured to comply with the specifications from the Security Target of the certification process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the certificate and checks the associated Security Target. They compare the actual configuration of the deployed system with the specifications from the certification documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An operating system is used that is certified according to a recognized standard at a high level of trustworthiness (e.g., Common Criteria EAL4+ or according to a specific protection profile). The configuration used MUST exactly match the certified configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A high-security operating system (e.g., PikeOS, INTEGRITY-178) is specifically selected for the system, which has a certification suitable for the intended use (e.g., according to an avionics or automotive protection profile). Any deviation from the certified configuration is not permitted or requires recertification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester checks the certificate and the corresponding protection profile for applicability to the intended use. They perform a detailed check of the system configuration and compare it bit-for-bit (where possible) with the certified reference configuration.

controls.title: Secured and authenticated boot process for embedded systems (H) [Developers, Planners, Procurement Office]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic secure boot mechanism is implemented. The bootloader checks the integrity of the operating system (e.g., using a hash) before starting it.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The bootloader (e.g., U-Boot) is configured to calculate the SHA-256 hash of the kernel image to be loaded and compare it with a known hash stored in the bootloader image. The kernel is only started if they match.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the bootloader configuration and the boot log to verify the execution of the hash check. They determine that the bootloader itself is not protected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The boot process of an embedded system SHOULD be secured by the bootloader verifying the integrity of the operating system and only loading it if it is classified as correct. Conversely, the operating system SHOULD also check the integrity of the bootloader. A multi-stage boot concept with cryptographically secure verification of the individual steps SHOULD be implemented. Secure hardware roots of trust SHOULD be used. For an ARM-based system, ARM Secure Boot SHOULD be used, and for UEFI, Secure Boot SHOULD be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A complete chain of trust is implemented. An immutable code in the processor's boot ROM (hardware root of trust) checks the digital signature of the bootloader. The bootloader checks the signature of the operating system kernel. The kernel checks the signature of the drivers and applications to be loaded. The necessary public keys are securely stored in the device (e.g., in OTP fuses).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the entire boot chain. They check the configuration of each stage, the implementation of the signature check, and the secure anchoring of the public keys. They attempt to load an unsigned component in a test environment to verify its correct rejection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to Secure Boot, a full Measured Boot process is implemented. A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) or a comparable hardware function records cryptographic hashes of all loaded boot components. These measurements (in the Platform Configuration Registers, PCRs) are used for Remote Attestation to prove the correct boot state of the device to a verification server before it receives full network access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each stage of the boot chain (firmware, bootloader, kernel, etc.) measures the hash of the next stage into the TPM's PCRs before executing it. Before the device is allowed to access critical network resources, a Network Access Control (NAC) system requests a 'quote' from the TPM, which contains the signed PCR values. The NAC server compares the values with a 'Golden Measurement' list and grants or denies access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the configuration of the Measured Boot at the system level and the configuration of the Remote Attestation process on the verification server. They boot a test device, read out the PCR values, and compare them with the expected values. They check whether a device with deviating PCR values is correctly isolated from the network.

controls.title: Memory protection in embedded systems (H) [Developers, Planners, Procurement Office]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Memory protection mechanisms SHOULD already be considered in the design of embedded systems. The type of memory protection as well as the number and size of protected areas SHOULD be appropriate for the intended use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Memory Protection Unit (MPU) of the microcontroller is used to define basic protection areas, e.g., to separate the memory area of the operating system kernel from the applications and to mark the code memory as non-writable (read-only).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the MPU configuration in the system's start-up code. They check whether the defined memory regions and their attributes (read, write, execute) meet the requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An MPU or Memory Management Unit (MMU) is used to implement strict process isolation that separates critical processes (e.g., cryptography) from less critical ones (e.g., user interface). Additionally, software-based protection measures such as Stack Canaries, Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), and Data Execution Prevention (DEP/W^X) are used to make memory attacks more difficult.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The operating system is configured so that each process runs in its own virtual address space. The compiler and linker flags are set to enable Stack Canaries, ASLR, and DEP for the generated binaries.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the operating system and MMU configuration. They check the build scripts and analyze the generated binaries with tools like `checksec` to verify the activation of the software-based protection measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware-enforced memory protection such as ARM TrustZone or Intel SGX is used to create isolated, secure enclaves for the most sensitive code and most critical data. These are protected even from a compromised operating system kernel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Cryptographic keys and the associated operations are completely offloaded to the ARM TrustZone Secure World. The Normal World (with the normal operating system) can only call these operations via a strictly defined, secure API and never has direct access to the key material.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester conducts a detailed review of the TrustZone architecture. They analyze the code of the Secure World and the interface (Secure Monitor Call API) to the Normal World for potential vulnerabilities to ensure that the isolation is effective.

controls.title: Tamper protection for embedded systems (H) [Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A tamper protection concept SHOULD be developed for embedded systems. Appropriate mechanisms SHOULD be established to detect, record, and prevent tamper attacks. Finally, appropriate guidelines SHOULD be established on how to respond to a tamper attack.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tamper-proof seals or stickers are placed on the housing. Opening the housing is detected by a simple mechanical switch and saved as an event in the log. In the event of detected tampering, the operating manual describes a procedure for reporting and decommissioning the device.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester requests the tamper protection concept. They inspect the physical devices for seals and switches. They check the log entries and the documented procedure for the case of tampering.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Active mechanisms for tamper detection are used, such as light sensors in the housing or a mesh of conductive traces on the circuit board. Detected tampering attempts are securely logged and trigger an immediate alarm to a central system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The inside of the housing is coated with a conductive paint that is part of a circuit. Any attempt to drill through or open the housing interrupts this circuit, which triggers a non-resettable alarm and reports it to the central management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the design of the active tamper protection. They check the configuration of the alarm chain. If possible, a tampering attempt is simulated in a test environment to verify the correct triggering and reporting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system has an active tamper response mechanism. Upon detection of a physical intrusion, all sensitive data and cryptographic keys are irretrievably deleted (Zeroization) and the device is put into a non-functional state. The system is certified to a standard such as FIPS 140-2/3 Level 3 or 4.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The device contains a dedicated security controller that monitors the tamper sensors. When triggered, it disconnects the power supply to the flash memory where the keys are stored and triggers an internal short-circuit that physically destroys the memory chip. The system is certified to FIPS 140-3 Level 3.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester verifies the device's FIPS certificate and checks the associated Security Policy. They analyze the hardware design to understand the implementation of the Zeroization function. Physical tests are usually destructive in this case and are replaced by design reviews and certificate checks.

controls.title: Automatic monitoring of component function (H) [Planners, Procurement Office]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All components of an embedded system with increased requirements SHOULD have built-in self-test (BIST) facilities. Tests SHOULD check the integrity of the system during the power-on process and at appropriate time intervals during operation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each component performs a basic functional check during power-on (Power-On Self-Test, POST). In addition, a watchdog timer runs, which resets the system if the main application no longer responds. The results of the POST are logged in the boot log.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester analyzes the design documentation for the specification of the BIST functions. They check the boot logs for POST entries and verify the configuration of the watchdog timer.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As far as possible, the self-test functions SHOULD also check the security functions and security properties of the component. The integrity of the memory and I/O components SHOULD be checked regularly as part of the BIST. Existing BIST functions SHOULD be supplemented with the required functions, if possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The POST includes a test of the cryptographic accelerators by calculating and verifying a test vector. During operation, a periodic CRC check of the program memory (flash) and a test of the working memory (RAM) are performed. The results are logged centrally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The tester conducts a code review of the BIST module to verify the coverage of security functions and the correctness of the memory checks. They check the central logs for regular and successful BIST runs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system employs continuous, out-of-band monitoring of all critical hardware components through a dedicated management controller. Any detected anomaly or a BIST failure triggers an immediate, automatic response, such as isolating the faulty component or switching to a redundant system, in addition to alerting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) monitors voltages, temperatures, and the status of the main CPU. If a BIST of the main CPU fails, the BMC can restart it or, in a redundant system, initiate a failover to a second CPU card. The incident is reported via a separate network interface.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the monitoring system and the configuration of the management controller. They check the logic for the automatic fault response. In a test environment, a fault is simulated (e.g., by unplugging a fan) to verify the correct system response.

controls.title: Resilience of embedded systems against side-channel attacks (H) [Developers, Procurement office]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Appropriate precautions SHOULD be taken against non-invasive and (semi-)invasive side-channel attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Basic countermeasures are implemented in the software, e.g., when implementing cryptographic algorithms, care is taken to avoid code with data-dependent branches or memory accesses (constant-time programming).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a code review of the critical cryptographic routines and looks for known vulnerabilities that could lead to side-channel leaks, such as the use of non-constant-time comparison operations on secret data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Both software and hardware countermeasures are implemented. These include blinding techniques in asymmetric cryptography, random execution orders, and adding noise to the power supply to obscure power analysis attacks. The design is actively tested for its resilience against common side-channel attacks (e.g., DPA, EMA).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For RSA or ECC operations, the operands are 'blinded' with a random value before computation, and the result is subsequently 'unblinded'. The circuit board contains a noise generator that obscures the processor's power consumption profile. In the laboratory, test attacks are conducted using an oscilloscope and special software.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the implementation of the blinding techniques and the design of the noise generator. They review the logs of the conducted side-channel tests and evaluate their results and methodology.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system uses cryptographic cores specifically designed and hardened against a wide range of side-channel attacks. The design may include hardware masking, dual-rail logic, or other advanced countermeasures. The resilience is validated through an independent evaluation and certification (e.g., as part of a FIPS or Common Criteria certification).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A microcontroller or crypto co-processor is used whose manufacturer explicitly advertises resistance to DPA/SPA attacks and can prove this with a certificate from an independent testing body (e.g., Riscure, BSI).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the manufacturer's certificate regarding side-channel resistance. They check whether the use of the component complies with the specifications from the certification to avoid undermining its protective effect.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Embedded systems are information-processing systems that are integrated into a larger system or product. They perform control, regulation, and data processing tasks and are often not directly perceived by users. Embedded systems are found in high-tech fields such as aerospace, medical technology, telecommunications, and automotive engineering, as well as in the consumer and household appliance sector.

An embedded system forms a functional unit of software and hardware that performs only a defined task. The software of embedded systems is called firmware and is usually stored in a flash memory, an EPROM, EEPROM, or ROM and cannot be replaced by users, or only with special means or functions. It essentially consists of the bootloader, the operating system, and the application. Specialized systems can also do without an operating system. Although embedded systems are specialized devices, they are universal computers, unlike pure hardware implementations (ASIC). Various CPU architectures or flexible, highly integrated Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) modules are used as platforms.

Embedded systems either have no user interface or use special peripherals such as functional keys, rotary switches, and displays designed for the respective application purpose. The spectrum of output units ranges from a simple signal lamp to LCDs to complex cockpit displays. Embedded systems often communicate via data buses, which are heterogeneously networked in complex systems. In addition, peripheral components such as sensors and actuators can also be connected via several different and multi-channel input/output ports. Some types of embedded systems also have a web interface through which they can be configured via a browser.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to provide information on typical threats to embedded systems and to show how these systems can be used securely in institutions.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module SYS.4.3 Embedded Systems must be applied once to each embedded system in the information network.

This module deals with embedded systems in general. It is applicable to a wide range of different embedded systems. Dedicated security properties, such as those of operating and display systems or specific hardware and software architectures, are not discussed in detail. Likewise, security aspects of embedded systems used in industrial control are not specifically addressed. For this purpose, the modules of the IND Industrial IT layer must also be consulted. Specific security aspects of IoT devices are also not the subject of this module. As networked devices or objects with additional smart functions, IoT devices, unlike embedded systems, are not integrated into a larger system or product. Due to their wireless connection to data networks, different security requirements apply here. They are covered in SYS.4.4 General IoT Device.

A special application of an embedded system is a smart card. These cards typically have a processor, memory, and I/O interfaces. For smart cards, too, although basic security aspects are addressed in this module, no specific aspects are considered.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficient security requirements in the development of embedded systems
parts.prose: For cost reasons, information security often plays a less important role in the development of embedded systems than, for example, performance or reliability. However, if security requirements are not sufficiently considered in one or more development phases, the embedded systems can have serious vulnerabilities.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unsecured input and output interfaces on embedded systems
parts.prose:
The interfaces of embedded systems are potential points of attack. This applies to interfaces at all levels of the OSI layer model and all transmission media used. If access via the interfaces is not controlled or if the control mechanisms are too weak, an attacker could penetrate the system, read and manipulate data without authorization, and initiate follow-up attacks. For example, espionage or sabotage devices, such as miniaturized controllers or data loggers, could be connected unnoticed.

At the microcontroller level, signals could be fed into the I/O registers via the I/O lines when the systems are connected to the I/O ports, or output signals could be recorded.

If a reset input is present, attackers could trigger it and temporarily put the system out of operation.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficient physical security for embedded systems
parts.prose: If embedded systems are easily physically accessible, attackers could destroy or damage the systems, e.g., through mechanical force, short circuits, or overvoltages. They could also access the electronic components, e.g., IC pins or contacts, and thus unnoticedly record the electrical signals with appropriate measurement and analysis tools, as well as inject signals themselves. If they get possession of an embedded system, they can use physical methods to read and manipulate data or access data that has not been securely deleted. This can then lead to a violation of the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the information stored on the embedded system.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Hardware failure and hardware errors in embedded systems
parts.prose: Environmental influences such as electromagnetic interference, temperature fluctuations, an unstable power supply, material defects due to manufacturing, and production variance can cause embedded systems to fail. Normal or premature wear and tear, which can be caused, for example, by harsh environmental influences such as dust, sand, or dirt, can also result in system failure. This could also severely impact the surrounding systems.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Installing (flashing) manipulated software updates on embedded systems
parts.prose: Many embedded systems store their software on flash memories and EEPROMs and offer the ability to update their firmware with a programming device connected via a data interface or a network connection. However, attackers can also use this to install manipulated software updates and thus modify the system's function. As a result, the original tasks of the system can be interrupted or manipulated.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Side-channel attacks on embedded cryptosystems
parts.prose: Attackers could use a side-channel attack to break encryptions or signatures by exploiting observable properties of the physical implementation of a cryptosystem. For example, they could draw conclusions about executed operations and keys from the power consumption of a microprocessor during cryptographic calculations. They could also carry out timing attacks, microarchitectural attacks, or (semi-)invasive attacks. For instance, in the past, researchers were able to determine the secret key of a TLS/SSL server that used the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) with Elliptic Curve Cryptography. The attack was based on the fact that the time required for a multiplication allows conclusions to be drawn about its operands.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Intrusion and manipulation via the communication interface of embedded systems
parts.prose:
Embedded systems are often limited in terms of code size, timing behavior, power consumption, cost, as well as size and weight. Therefore, they are often not equipped with sufficient security functions, such as strong cryptography. Modern embedded systems are increasingly networked using widespread techniques and protocols and are therefore potentially vulnerable.

In an attack, an attempt could be made to manipulate data or software on an embedded system by trying to misuse the standard communication interfaces and protocols for one's own purposes. For example, if IP communication or Ethernet, WLAN, Bluetooth, and mobile or digital radio interfaces are not sufficiently secured, attackers can take over connections, forge messages, or penetrate a system and carry out follow-up attacks. Furthermore, attempts can also be made to penetrate the system using other available communication interfaces, e.g., USB ports.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Use of counterfeit components
parts.prose: In the production process or when components are replaced during service, it can happen that counterfeit components are installed in embedded systems. Since counterfeits of many components are in circulation, this can also happen unintentionally. Counterfeit components often work less reliably than the original components. This could cause functions to fail or work incorrectly. Attackers can also specifically develop a device or component that looks exactly like the original but whose function is manipulated. Such a component could, for example, be used to install backdoors, manipulate individual functions, or restrict availability.

controls.title: Deployment criteria for IoT devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic deployment criteria, such as the presence of an update function, are only checked for individual IoT devices classified as particularly critical. A systematic process for all devices is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The check is performed ad-hoc by an administrator, usually just by looking at the manufacturer's datasheet. There is no formalized checklist or documentation of the results.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that no uniform procurement policies for IoT devices exist. Spot checks show that for most devices, no security features were assessed before deployment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all new IoT devices to be procured, a simple checklist is used to manually check for the presence of update functions, the possibility of authentication, and the absence of hard-coded credentials. The check is based on manufacturer specifications.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement department uses a simple Excel checklist to query the basic criteria. The completed list is added to the respective procurement file.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement files of recent IoT devices and verifies the existence and completeness of the filled-out checklists. It is checked on a random basis whether the manufacturer's information is plausible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is ensured that IoT devices have update functions and that the manufacturing companies offer an update process. The devices MUST allow for appropriate authentication. NO hard-coded or derivable credentials may be included in the devices. These criteria are part of a documented procurement process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal requirements list (catalog of criteria) for the procurement of IoT devices is established. Each potential product is evaluated against this catalog. The evaluation is a prerequisite for the purchasing decision and is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and application of the formal catalog of criteria in the procurement process. It is checked whether a documented evaluation based on the criteria is available for recently procured IoT devices. This can be done by reviewing procurement documents and ticket systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement process requires manufacturers to provide formal confirmation of security functions, for example, through certificates (e.g., BSI's IT Security Label) or test reports. The deployment criteria are regularly reviewed and expanded based on new threat intelligence.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The criteria list for procurement is updated annually by the ISO. Manufacturers must complete a standardized security questionnaire and provide evidence such as a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) or external audit reports.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether current procurement processes include manufacturer certificates or completed security questionnaires. Additionally, it is checked whether the catalog of criteria is up-to-date and whether a process for its update exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An allowlist of approved IoT devices is maintained, which have undergone rigorous internal security testing in a lab environment. Procurement is strictly limited to devices from this list. The testing includes practical tests for hard-coded credentials and analysis of the update process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated team conducts penetration tests and analyses on sample devices in a test lab before they are added to the approval list. The results are documented in detail. A Network Access Control (NAC) system actively blocks the integration of unapproved devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
