parts.prose: The auditor requests the test reports for several devices on the allowlist and evaluates their depth and quality. It is verified through network scans and checking the NAC configuration that only approved device types are active on the network.

controls.title: Authentication

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Default passwords are only changed on some IoT devices considered critical. Integration into a central identity management system does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators change the passwords manually after installation if they deem it necessary. The new passwords are often stored locally and insecurely.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a network scan to find IoT devices with known default passwords. Spot checks on various devices confirm the inconsistent handling.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all IoT devices, the default credentials are changed after installation and replaced with individual, but not necessarily complex, passwords. The passwords are managed in a central list.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an instruction that all default passwords must be changed. The new passwords are documented in a password-protected Excel sheet or a simple password safe.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the central password list and compares it with the inventory list of IoT devices. During spot checks, attempts are made to log in with default passwords.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Appropriate authentication MUST be enabled. IoT devices MUST be integrated into the institution's identity and access management system. This ensures that individual and strong credentials are used for all devices and that management is centralized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For authentication, strong, unique passwords are assigned according to the institution's password policy. Where technically possible (e.g., via LDAP, RADIUS, or SAML), the devices are connected to the central Active Directory / IAM system. The process is documented in the installation guide for IoT devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of randomly selected IoT devices. It is checked whether authentication is active and no default or weak passwords are used. Additionally, the configuration of the connection to the central IAM system (if available) is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all administrative access to IoT devices, two-factor authentication (2FA) is enforced wherever technically supported. The integration with the IAM system is automated to the extent that user accounts are automatically provisioned and de-provisioned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The connection to the IAM is established via a RADIUS proxy that enforces 2FA. User management for IoT systems is integrated into the central user lifecycle management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the administrative login process on critical IoT systems and verifies the enforcement of 2FA. The IAM system is checked to ensure that accounts for IoT systems are correctly linked to the HR process (onboarding/offboarding).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For device and user authentication, certificate-based authentication (e.g., according to IEEE 802.1X) is consistently used. This eliminates passwords for device-to-device communication and administrative access and links the device identity to a central PKI.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) issues device certificates via an automated protocol such as SCEP or EST. A Network Access Control (NAC) system enforces certificate-based authentication for all devices in the IoT network segment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the PKI and the NAC system. It is verified that devices without a valid certificate do not receive network access. The certificate renewal and revocation process is also checked. An automatic scan can check the conformity of TLS certificates: `nmap --script ssl-cert,ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 <device-ip>`

controls.title: Restriction of Network Access

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Some IoT devices are placed in a separate guest VLAN, but the firewall rules between the networks are very permissive. UPnP is disabled on some, but not all, routers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Segmentation is performed opportunistically in the existing guest network. There are no specific firewall rules for IoT traffic. The UPnP setting is not systematically checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies IoT devices in various network segments and determines that no uniform segmentation strategy exists. A port scan from an IoT device reveals extensive access to internal systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All IoT devices are placed in a dedicated VLAN. Simple firewall rules prevent direct access from IoT devices to critical servers (e.g., Domain Controllers). UPnP is disabled on the central internet router.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A new VLAN for IoT is set up on the core switches. A firewall rule blocks traffic from the IoT VLAN to the server VLAN but allows internet access. The UPnP deactivation is done manually on the edge router.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the IoT VLAN and the assignment of the devices. The firewall rules are checked for basic segmentation. The configuration of the edge router is checked for a disabled UPnP function.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network access for IoT devices MUST be restricted to the required minimum. This includes operation in a separate network segment, the definition of restrictive firewall rules (ACLs) for inbound and outbound connections, restrictive routing configurations, and the deactivation of the UPnP function on all routers. This SHOULD be checked regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate network segment (VLAN) is set up for IoT devices with a whitelist-based firewall policy that only allows explicitly permitted communication to management servers or cloud services. If possible, no default route is configured on the devices themselves. A configuration standard for routers mandates the deactivation of UPnP.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rule sets for the IoT segment and verifies that they follow a default-deny principle. The routing tables of sample devices are checked. The configuration of all relevant routers is examined for a disabled UPnP function. An automated test could run a UPnP discovery command in the IoT network to find active UPnP services.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IoT devices are operated in a separate segment that is only allowed to communicate with a dedicated management network. The communication between these two networks is additionally tunneled through a restrictively configured VPN to ensure confidentiality and integrity. The firewall rules are reviewed quarterly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A site-to-site VPN is established between the gateway of the IoT network and the gateway of the management network. The firewall only allows the VPN tunnel traffic. The rule review is a fixed part of the network team's calendar.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the VPN configuration for strong encryption and correct endpoints. The log of the last firewall rule reviews is inspected. A packet capture is used to verify that no unencrypted traffic leaves the IoT segment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A zero-trust architecture is implemented through micro-segmentation, where each IoT device or small groups of devices form their own logical zone. Communication is permitted based on a unique device identity (e.g., certificate) and only to explicitly allowed destinations. All data traffic is monitored by an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) for anomalies and attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A micro-segmentation platform (e.g., VMware NSX, Illumio) is used to enforce dynamic firewall rules based on metadata and device identity. An IPS sensor is integrated at the switch port of the IoT gateway or virtually in the hypervisor.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the policy definitions in the micro-segmentation platform and verifies that the rules follow the least privilege principle at the device level. The IPS logs are checked for detected and blocked attacks in the IoT segment. A penetration test attempts to break out laterally into the network from a compromised IoT device.

controls.title: Inclusion of IoT devices in the institution's security policy

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements for IoT devices SHOULD be specified in the general security policy of the institution. The policy SHOULD be known to all persons who procure and operate IoT devices and should be the basis for their work. The implementation of the content required in the policy SHOULD be regularly reviewed and the results appropriately documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated chapter or a separate guideline for 'Internet of Things (IoT)' is created as part of the overarching information security policy framework. This policy defines clear requirements, roles (e.g., device owner), and processes for the entire lifecycle of IoT devices. The policy is published on the intranet and mentioned during the training of new employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security policy and verifies the existence, completeness, and timeliness of the section on IoT devices. Through interviews with employees from procurement and IT operations, random checks are carried out to determine whether the policy is known and serves as a basis for work. The documentation of the last review of the policy implementation is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The overarching IoT security policy is supplemented by detailed technical specifications and hardening guidelines for specific classes of IoT devices (e.g., IP cameras, climate sensors, smart speakers). Compliance with the policy is an integral part of the internal audit program.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each major category of IoT devices, there is a standardized configuration document ('Golden Image' description) that is based on the overarching policy. These documents are available to administrators in a central knowledge base.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the configuration of several production IoT devices with the corresponding technical specifications and hardening guidelines. In addition, the last internal audit report is reviewed to check whether compliance with the IoT policy was audited and what findings were made.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The IoT security policy and the associated technical specifications are dynamically adapted based on threat intelligence feeds and the results of continuous monitoring. Compliance with the policy is enforced and continuously monitored through automated technical controls (e.g., configuration compliance scanners, NAC).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A security compliance tool automatically checks the configuration of all reachable IoT devices against the defined hardening specifications on a daily basis. Deviations automatically lead to the creation of a ticket in the ITSM system and, if necessary, to the network quarantine of the device by the NAC system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the compliance tool and the defined policies. The tool's reports are evaluated to assess the effectiveness of the automated review and the response times to deviations. A test case is conducted in which a device is intentionally misconfigured to verify the automatic detection and response.

controls.title: Planning the deployment of IoT devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To ensure the secure operation of IoT devices, it SHOULD be planned in advance where and how they will be used. The planning SHOULD not only concern aspects that are traditionally associated with the term information security, but also normal, operational aspects that entail security requirements. All decisions made during the planning phase SHOULD be appropriately documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before introducing a new type of IoT device, a formal deployment concept is created. This document describes the purpose, the physical locations, the requirements for the network infrastructure (incl. segmentation), the authorization concept, and the responsibilities. The concept is reviewed and approved by the Information Security Officer (ISO) and the works council (if required).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the corresponding deployment concepts for recently introduced IoT systems. It is checked whether these concepts cover all relevant aspects (physical, network, permissions) and whether the necessary approvals have been granted. The actual implementation is compared with the concept on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process for the deployment of IoT devices includes a formal risk assessment. This considers specific threats to the device type and the planned locations, including data protection risks and potential impacts on operational safety. The planning documents are managed in a central CMDB.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized risk assessment template is used as part of the planning. The results, including the identified risks and the planned measures, are recorded in the deployment concept. The planned configuration elements are created as CIs (Configuration Items) in the CMDB.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects an IoT system and checks whether a documented risk assessment is available. The appropriateness of the assessment and the derived measures are evaluated. A comparison with the CMDB ensures that the planned systems are correctly recorded.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each new IoT ecosystem, a detailed threat modeling (e.g., based on the STRIDE model) is carried out in the planning phase. The results flow directly into the definition of specific, tailor-made security controls, hardening measures, and rules for the monitoring systems, even before the first device is implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A security specialist conducts a threat modeling workshop together with the project team. The identified threats, attack vectors, and protective measures are recorded in a separate document and form the basis for creating the technical security concept and the SIEM use cases.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the threat modeling documentation for a complex IoT system. It is assessed whether the process was carried out systematically and whether the derived security measures adequately address the identified threats. It is checked whether the derived SIEM rules are actually implemented in the monitoring system.

controls.title: Procurement criteria for IoT devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Information Security Officer (ISO) SHOULD be involved in all procurements of IoT devices. Before IoT devices are procured, it SHOULD be determined which security requirements they must meet. When procuring IoT devices, aspects of physical security as well as requirements for the security features of the software SHOULD be given sufficient consideration. A list of requirements SHOULD be created, against which the products available on the market are evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement process requires mandatory approval by the Information Security Officer (ISO) for all IoT devices. The ISO maintains a standard requirements list (checklist) that covers aspects such as update provision, configurability, authentication, encryption, and data protection. This list is made available to the specialist departments and serves as the basis for product selection and tenders.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the ticketing system or process management tool that the Information Security Officer (ISO) was demonstrably involved in the latest IoT procurements. The existence, level of detail, and currency of the requirements list are checked. For a specific procurement, it is traced how the products were evaluated based on the list.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement process requires binding evidence from suppliers regarding security properties. This includes demanding a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) as well as recognized security certificates or declarations of conformity (e.g., to the ETSI EN 303 645 standard).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirements list for procurement is supplemented with mandatory items that require the delivery of an SBOM and valid certificates. Bids without this evidence are rated lower in the selection process or are excluded. The received SBOMs are analyzed for known vulnerabilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the tender documents and contracts of current IoT procurements and checks whether the requirement for SBOM and certificates is included. It is checked whether the documents received have been reviewed for plausibility and for known vulnerabilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before a product can be procured, a sample device is subjected to an independent penetration test and an in-depth security analysis in a laboratory environment. Only products that pass this test are placed on an approved product list, from which the departments may choose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated security testing team (internal or externally commissioned) performs a standardized test procedure that includes firmware analysis, network sniffing, and active attack attempts. The detailed test reports are archived and form the basis for inclusion in the Approved Product List, which is published on the intranet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the test reports for several products on the Approved Product List and assesses their quality and scope. It is checked whether a clearly defined process for adding products to the list exists and is being followed. It is also ensured that recently procured devices actually come from this list.

controls.title: Regulation of the use of IoT devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each IoT device, a person responsible for its operation SHOULD be designated. The responsible persons SHOULD be sufficiently informed about the handling of the IoT device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the asset management database or CMDB, a 'device owner' is named as the responsible person for each IoT device (or group of devices). This person receives instruction on the operation and security-relevant aspects of the device during commissioning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests an excerpt from the asset management database and checks whether a responsible person is registered for all IoT devices. Random checks are conducted by interviewing the named individuals to see if they are aware of their responsibility and have received appropriate instruction.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The roles and responsibilities for the operation of IoT devices are formally documented in a roles and permissions concept. Regular (e.g., annual) refresher training on security topics is offered to the device owners, and their participation is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution's general role concept is expanded to include the role of 'IoT Device Owner' with clearly defined tasks and duties. The institution's training program includes a short e-learning module on 'Secure Handling of IoT,' which is mandatory for all owners.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the role concept and verifies the definition of IoT responsibilities. The training materials and attendance lists from the last training sessions are inspected to check the implementation of the awareness measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Automated workflows in the ITSM system directly notify the responsible device owners about relevant security warnings, necessary maintenance, or upcoming audits for their devices. The competence of the owners is regularly assessed, e.g., through short online tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The SIEM system is coupled with the CMDB and the ticketing system. If a security-relevant anomaly is detected on an IoT device, a ticket is automatically created and assigned to the device owner stored in the CMDB. Annually, the owners must complete a short test on the IoT security policies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor triggers a test security alarm for an IoT device and follows the automated notification workflow. It is checked whether the correct ticket is assigned to the correct person. The results of the competency tests are reviewed.

controls.title: Secure installation and configuration of IoT devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be defined under which framework conditions IoT devices are installed and configured. IoT devices SHOULD only be installed and configured by authorized persons according to a defined process. All steps SHOULD be documented in a traceable manner. Default settings SHOULD be checked and adjusted. If possible, IoT devices SHOULD only be connected to data networks after the configuration is complete.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each class of IoT devices, a standardized installation and configuration guide (checklist) exists. This specifies which default settings (e.g., passwords, open services) must be changed. The installation takes place in a staging network without a connection to the production network. The completion of the configuration is documented in the asset management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the installation guides for various IoT devices and checks them for completeness and compliance with the security policies. The commissioning process is traced to ensure that the configuration is completed before network connection. The documentation in the asset management system is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the most common IoT device classes, standardized configuration templates and hardening scripts are used to ensure a consistent and secure baseline configuration. The application of these templates and the successful execution of the scripts are verified and logged before commissioning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For IP cameras, sensors, etc., 'Golden Configuration' templates exist. Part of the commissioning is the execution of a PowerShell or Python script that configures the device via its API and sets the security-relevant settings (e.g., deactivating Telnet, configuring NTP, Syslog). The script generates a log that is archived.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration templates and hardening scripts and assesses their quality. For a newly installed device, the script's execution log is requested and compared with the device's actual configuration. A command like `Get-Content C:\scripts\hardening_log.txt` could provide the evidence.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire installation and configuration process is fully automated by a central configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible, Puppet). After commissioning, the device's configuration is continuously checked against the defined desired state (security baseline). Deviations trigger an automatic reconfiguration attempt or a security alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Ansible Playbooks are used to fully automatically configure IoT devices from unboxing to production deployment. A daily Ansible run in '--check' mode verifies the configuration of all devices in the inventory. Changes that were not made via the management tool are detected and reported.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the Ansible Playbooks and the security baselines defined therein. The reports of the daily configuration check are evaluated. To test the process, a security-relevant setting on a device is manually changed and it is observed whether the deviation is correctly detected and reported/corrected. A command like `ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini --check site.yml --limit <test-device>` could demonstrate this.

controls.title: Use of encrypted data transmission

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IoT devices SHOULD only transmit data in encrypted form. The device configuration must ensure that current and strong encryption protocols (e.g., TLS 1.2 or higher) are used for all communication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hardening guidelines for IoT devices require that all management interfaces (e.g., web UI) and data transmissions (e.g., to a cloud backend) enforce the use of TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites. Insecure protocols like Telnet, FTP, or HTTP are disabled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of IoT devices on a random basis to ensure that encryption is enabled and insecure protocols are disabled. A network scan with tools like `nmap` or `testssl.sh` is used to check the TLS configuration of the device interfaces: `testssl.sh <device-ip>:<port>`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The encryption configuration is standardized and enforced. Additionally, a network monitoring solution actively monitors the data traffic in the IoT segment and alerts when unencrypted communication (e.g., via HTTP, Telnet, FTP) is detected from or to an IoT device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) like Suricata or Zeek is used to monitor IoT network traffic. Specific rules are activated that trigger an alarm in the SIEM system when cleartext protocols are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the IDS and the corresponding alerting rules. The SIEM logs from the past few weeks are checked for alarms related to unencrypted protocols in the IoT network. A test can be conducted by attempting to establish an unencrypted connection to a test device to verify the alarm trigger.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Mutual TLS (mTLS) with centrally managed certificates is used throughout. This ensures that not only the server but also the IoT device (client) must authenticate cryptographically, and all communication is strongly encrypted. The conformity of the cryptographic configuration is continuously checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All IoT devices and the associated management servers or cloud endpoints are equipped with certificates from an internal PKI. The server configurations are set to require client certificates for authentication (mTLS). A compliance scanner daily checks the TLS configurations of all systems for compliance with internal specifications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the server services and the PKI to verify the enforcement of mTLS. An attempt is made to establish a connection without a valid client certificate, which must fail. The reports of the compliance scanner are reviewed. An automated test could check the successful mTLS connection using `curl --key client.key --cert client.crt https://<server>`.

controls.title: Deactivation and deinstallation of unneeded components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After installation, it SHOULD be checked which protocols, applications, and other tools are installed and activated on the IoT devices. Unnecessary protocols, services, login credentials, and interfaces SHOULD be deactivated or completely uninstalled. If this is not possible on the device itself, unneeded services SHOULD be restricted via the firewall. The decisions made SHOULD be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Part of the standardized installation guide is a hardening checklist. This lists known, often insecure or unnecessary services (e.g., Telnet, FTP, SNMPv1/v2, UPnP) and interfaces (e.g., USB ports, JTAG) that must be deactivated. The execution is checked off and documented for each device. Services that cannot be deactivated are blocked by a firewall rule on the switch port or the network gateway.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a port scan (`nmap -sV <device-ip>`) on an installed IoT device and compares the open ports with the list of approved services. The device's configuration is inspected to verify the deactivation of features. The firewall rules for the device are also checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each device class, a security baseline is defined that specifies the minimum required set of services and protocols. An automated script is run during commissioning to deactivate all services not included in the baseline and to check the correct configuration. Physical interfaces, if not needed, are sealed with port blockers or epoxy resin.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security baseline is stored as a configuration file (e.g., YAML). An Ansible playbook or a PowerShell script reads this baseline and implements the corresponding configuration on the device. The script generates a compliance report.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the security baseline definition and the associated automation script. The compliance report for a newly set up device is requested and checked. A physical inspection of the device verifies the sealing of unused ports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only IoT devices that allow a minimal firmware installation without unnecessary components are procured. The configuration is locked (read-only) after commissioning, and a File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) system monitors the operating system and configuration files for any changes. Any unauthorized change triggers an immediate alert and network isolation of the device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A lightweight FIM agent (e.g., OSSEC, Wazuh) is installed on the IoT devices, if possible. Alternatively, a network-based FIM is used, which periodically logs in and checks the hash values of critical files. The FIM alarms are sent to the central SIEM, which initiates network isolation via the NAC system through a SOAR integration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the FIM system and the monitored files. A test change is made to a configuration file on a test device to verify the entire alerting and response chain (FIM -> SIEM -> SOAR -> NAC).

controls.title: Restrictive assignment of rights

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access permissions to IoT devices SHOULD be granted as restrictively as possible. The Principle of Least Privilege is applied to ensure that user and system accounts only have the permissions they absolutely need for their tasks. If this is not possible via the IoT devices themselves, it SHOULD be considered to regulate this on the network side.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each IoT system, at least two roles are defined: an administrator account with full rights and a user or service account with highly restricted, mostly read-only rights. Wherever possible, granular permissions are used. If this is not possible, access to administrative functions (e.g., a specific web path or port) is restricted to administrative subnets on the network firewall.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the user and rights structure of an IoT system demonstrated. It is checked whether dedicated, restricted accounts exist for normal operation. The permissions of the accounts are checked for plausibility regarding their necessity. The corresponding firewall rules are also checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal role-based access control (RBAC) model is defined for the entire IoT ecosystem and is technically implemented, usually by connecting to a central IAM system. The assigned permissions are recertified in a regular (e.g., semi-annual) access review process by the supervisors or system owners.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAM system manages the roles (e.g., 'Camera Administrator', 'Sensor Viewer') and assigns them to users. The IoT systems authenticate users via the IAM (e.g., via RADIUS or SAML) and receive the role information to enforce the permissions. An automated workflow starts the access review process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the documented RBAC model and its implementation in the IAM system. The logs of the last access review process are inspected to check whether the recertification has taken place and whether superfluous rights have been revoked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administrative access to IoT devices is handled through a central Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution. This enforces the use of temporary, Just-in-Time (JIT) permissions for administrative tasks. All privileged sessions are recorded and can be audited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators do not have direct passwords to the IoT devices. They authenticate to the PAM solution, request access to a device, and the PAM establishes a temporary, logged connection (e.g., via an SSH or RDP proxy). Direct access is blocked on the firewall.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the PAM solution, including the JIT policies and logging. Random samples of recorded sessions are reviewed. It is tested whether direct administrative access to an IoT device bypassing the PAM is possible, which must fail.

controls.title: Removal of malicious programs on IoT devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: IT operations SHOULD regularly check whether the deployed IoT devices could be infected with malicious programs and how infections can be removed. Malicious programs SHOULD be removed immediately. If the cause of the infection cannot be resolved or reinfection cannot be effectively prevented, the affected IoT devices SHOULD no longer be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT operations subscribes to relevant security feeds and manufacturer information. There is a documented incident response plan that describes how to deal with infected IoT devices. The standard response is to disconnect from the network, reset to factory settings, and reconfigure securely. If a known, unpatchable vulnerability was exploited, the device is decommissioned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the incident response plan and checks whether it covers the 'infected IoT device' case. They inquire about which information sources are used for IoT-specific threats. If there has been an incident in the past, the associated tickets and logs are reviewed to verify compliance with the plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) are used to monitor the data traffic of IoT segments for signs of malicious program activity. This includes signatures for known malware communication (C2 traffic) and suspicious scan activities. An alarm automatically triggers the incident response process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IDS like Suricata is connected to the mirror port of the IoT network segment. Current rule sets (e.g., ET Pro) specialized for IoT-specific threats are used. The IDS alarms are forwarded to the SIEM, where they are correlated and prioritized.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the IDS, the currency of the rule sets, and the connection to the SIEM. As a test, an attempt is made to send harmless but signature-recognizable traffic (e.g., EICAR test string via HTTP) through the segment to verify detection and alerting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Wherever technically possible, Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) agents are deployed on the IoT devices themselves. Upon detection of a threat, the affected device is automatically isolated from the network. A forensic analysis of the device is performed to understand the attack vector and prevent future compromise.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For IoT devices based on a standard operating system (e.g., Linux), an EDR agent is rolled out. The EDR system is integrated with a SOAR platform, which automatically instructs the NAC system to block the device's switch port in the event of a high-criticality alarm. An image of the device's memory is saved for later analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the coverage of IoT devices with EDR agents. The configuration of the automatic isolation rules in the EDR/SOAR system is checked. A simulated attack on a test device is performed to test the entire chain of detection, isolation, and forensic acquisition.

controls.title: Monitoring of network traffic from IoT devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be monitored whether the IoT devices or sensor systems only communicate with IT systems that are necessary for the operation of the IoT devices. This is ensured by regularly checking network logs against a list of allowed communication relationships.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each IoT device class, it is documented with which internal servers or external cloud services it must communicate. Weekly, the firewall logs for the IoT network segment are exported and checked against this list of allowed destinations with a script. Unexpected connections are reported to the IT security team for analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the allowed communication relationships. The logs of the last log analyses are reviewed. The configuration of the firewall log collection is checked to ensure that all connection attempts (allowed and blocked) are logged.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated system (e.g., SIEM) monitors network traffic from and to IoT devices in near real-time. Correlation rules are implemented that trigger an immediate alarm for any communication to or from a destination that is not explicitly approved.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Network flow data (e.g., NetFlow, sFlow) from the IoT segment is sent to the SIEM. In the SIEM, a whitelist of allowed destination IPs and ports is stored for each IoT device group. A correlation rule checks each flow against this whitelist and generates an alarm in case of a deviation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the whitelist rules in the SIEM and compares them with the documentation. A test connection to a non-allowed destination is initiated from a test IoT device to verify the alarm triggering. An automated test could run `Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <forbidden_destination> -Port 443` from a computer in the IoT VLAN and check the SIEM alarms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Network Behavior Anomaly Detection (NBAD) system is used to learn the normal communication behavior of each individual IoT device (or each homogeneous group) and create a dynamic baseline. Any significant deviation from this baseline, such as unexpected protocols, changed data volumes, or new communication partners, triggers an alarm, even if the destination itself would be permitted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized NBAD tool analyzes the mirrored traffic of the IoT segment. After a learning phase, the system is switched to monitoring mode. The anomaly alarms it generates are sent to the SIEM and correlated with other security events to better assess the threat landscape.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor evaluates the configuration and the learned baselines in the NBAD system. It is checked how the system reacts to simulated anomalies (e.g., an IoT device that suddenly starts uploading large amounts of data). The quality of the alarms and the rate of false positives are assessed.

controls.title: Logging of security-relevant events for IoT devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security-relevant events SHOULD be logged automatically. If this is not possible through the IoT devices themselves, routers or logging mechanisms of other IT systems SHOULD be used for this purpose. The logs SHOULD be appropriately evaluated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: IoT devices are configured to send their logs (e.g., login attempts, configuration changes) via Syslog to a central log server. If a device does not support this, the logs of the network firewall that filters the device's traffic are used for analysis. The logs are checked weekly for suspicious patterns.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly checks the configuration of IoT devices for correct Syslog forwarding. On the central log server, it is verified whether the device logs are arriving. The logs of the last log evaluations are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All security-relevant logs from IoT devices and the associated network components are forwarded to a central Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. There, the events are analyzed in near real-time and examined for suspicious activities or attack patterns using correlation rules. The logs are archived according to the retention policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A log profile is defined for each IoT device class, specifying which events must be sent to the SIEM. Specific use cases are implemented in the SIEM, e.g., 'Alarm on multiple failed login attempts on an IoT device' or 'Alarm on configuration change outside the maintenance window'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the SIEM configuration, including the data sources and correlation rules for IoT. A test event (e.g., a failed login) is generated to verify that it is correctly received, processed, and displayed as an alarm. The log archiving configuration is also checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The scope of logging is comprehensive and includes detailed application-level events. The SIEM also uses User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) to proactively identify threats by analyzing behavioral anomalies based on log data, without relying on static rules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Logging on the devices is set to the highest possible level of detail. The UEBA module of the SIEM is trained with the IoT log data to create a baseline of normal behavior for users and devices. Anomalies, such as a login at an unusual time or from an unusual location, lead to an increase in the risk score and, if necessary, to an alarm.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor evaluates the configuration of the UEBA module and the learned behavioral models. The alarms generated by the UEBA system in the past are checked for their relevance and accuracy. A scenario is played out (e.g., access from a new administrator account) to test the system's reaction.

controls.title: Protection of the administration interfaces

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the administration interfaces of IoT devices SHOULD be restricted. Network-based administration interfaces SHOULD be limited to authorized IT systems or network segments. Local administration interfaces on the IoT device or via local networks SHOULD be used preferentially. The methods used SHOULD be defined in the security policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access to administrative ports (e.g., SSH, HTTPS, manufacturer software ports) is restricted on the network firewall so that it is only possible from a dedicated administrative VLAN (Admin network). If physical administration is possible, network access to the administrative interface is completely disabled.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rules that govern access to the administration interfaces of the IoT devices. A port scan from a normal client network is attempted to reach the administrative interfaces, which must fail. A successful scan must be performed from a computer in the admin network.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative access is only permitted from dedicated, hardened Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs). Access is not direct but via a central Bastion Host (Jump Server) located in a demilitarized zone (DMZ).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators use a special, hardened VM or laptop (PAW) for all administrative tasks. From there, they connect to the Bastion Host via SSH or RDP. Only from this host is access to the administrative interfaces of the IoT devices permitted, which is enforced by firewall rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the hardening configuration of the PAWs and the Bastion Host. The firewall rules are analyzed to ensure that only the Bastion Host can administratively access the IoT devices. The logs of the Bastion Host are checked for unauthorized access attempts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every administrative access is mediated through a Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution. The solution enforces multi-factor authentication, establishes connections without revealing the password to the administrator (credential vaulting), records the entire session on video, and can filter potentially dangerous commands. Direct access is technically impossible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM solution like CyberArk or Thycotic is used. The passwords of the IoT devices are stored in the PAM system and are automatically rotated regularly. Administrators authenticate to the PAM portal, which then builds a proxy-based session to the target device. Direct routes from admin workstations to the IoT devices are blocked on the firewall.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the PAM solution, including MFA enforcement, password rotation, and session recording. Randomly selected recorded sessions are checked. It is verified that direct access bypassing the PAM solution is effectively prevented by network rules.

controls.title: Regulated decommissioning of IoT devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There SHOULD be an overview of what data is stored where on IoT devices. A checklist SHOULD be created that can be worked through when decommissioning IoT devices. This checklist SHOULD include at least aspects of data backup for data that is still needed and the subsequent secure deletion of all data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized checklist for the decommissioning process exists in the ITSM tool. This includes steps such as: 1. Backup of configuration/data (if necessary), 2. Removing the device from monitoring and management systems, 3. Resetting to factory settings, 4. Securely erasing all remaining data by multiple overwrites or a 'Secure Erase' function, 5. Updating the asset management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the checklist for decommissioning and assesses its completeness. For recently decommissioned devices, the completed checklists and the associated tickets are reviewed to verify compliance with the process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire decommissioning process is tracked in the asset management system. After securely erasing the data, a formal certificate of deletion is created and archived for each device. Devices that have processed sensitive data are handed over to a certified disposal service provider for physical destruction.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process is supported by a workflow in the asset management system. The deletion certificate is automatically generated and contains details about the device, the deletion method, and the executing employee. Contracts exist with service providers for data protection-compliant disposal and destruction of data carriers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the archived deletion certificates and the destruction records from the disposal service provider. The workflow in the asset management system is analyzed to ensure that all steps are properly mapped and documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure data deletion is performed, wherever supported, using cryptographic erasure (Crypto Erase) by deleting the cryptographic key. If it cannot be guaranteed that all data (e.g., on wear-leveling storage) has been securely removed, the device is fundamentally physically destroyed (e.g., by shredding). The process is fully integrated into asset and configuration management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Internal policies fundamentally require the physical destruction of IoT devices with fixed storage during disposal, unless the manufacturer can prove the effectiveness of Crypto Erase. An internal shredder for small electronic devices is kept on hand.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policies for data deletion and destruction for their stringency. The logbook of the internal shredder is inspected. The technical documentation of devices where Crypto Erase is used is checked to assess the reliability of the method.

controls.title: Operating environment and power supply

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is clarified whether IoT devices may be operated in the intended operating environment (protection needs of other IT systems, data protection). IoT devices SHOULD be protected against theft, destruction, and tampering in the operating environment. Requirements for the physical environment (e.g., temperature, power supply) are taken into account. For battery-powered devices, there is a regulated process for functional tests and replacement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The physical protection of the device is defined in the deployment concept (e.g., installation in lockable housings, out of reach). The manufacturer's environmental requirements are checked. A recurring task in the ticket system serves as a reminder for the quarterly battery test and replacement for critical sensors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts an on-site inspection of critical IoT devices and assesses their physical protection. The deployment concept is reviewed for consideration of environmental factors. The ticket history for battery replacements is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Critical IoT devices are connected to an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) to maintain operation during power outages. Environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity are actively monitored on-site by dedicated sensors, and an alarm is triggered in case of deviations from the defined thresholds.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: IoT gateways and important sensors are connected to UPS systems, which are also linked to the monitoring system. Environmental sensors are installed in technical rooms with IoT devices, and their data is collected in the central monitoring system, which triggers alarms if thresholds are exceeded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs an on-site check of the connection of devices to UPSs. The configuration of the monitoring system for UPS and environmental sensors is analyzed. A UPS test (power outage simulation) is conducted to verify its functionality.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The physical housings of highly critical IoT devices are tamper-resistant and equipped with tamper switches. Any attempt to open the housing triggers an immediate physical and logical alarm. The power supply has a redundant design (e.g., via two separate power circuits or Power over Ethernet plus a local battery).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Special security enclosures with tamper contacts are used. The contact is connected to an alarm input of the IoT device or a separate alarm system. The alarms are reported to the SIEM and the physical security control center. Critical switches provide redundant PoE power supply.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the security enclosures and tests the function of the tamper contact by controlled opening of a test enclosure. The entire alarm chain is observed in the process. The design of the redundant power supply is checked using circuit diagrams and the switch configuration.

controls.title: System Monitoring

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The IoT devices SHOULD be integrated into a suitable system monitoring or monitoring concept. The system status and functionality of the IoT devices SHOULD be continuously monitored. Error states and the exceeding of defined limit values SHOULD be reported to the operating personnel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All IoT devices are recorded in the central monitoring system (e.g., Nagios, Zabbix). At a minimum, a ping check is configured for reachability testing. Wherever possible (e.g., via SNMP), basic system values such as CPU utilization and memory consumption are also monitored with defined thresholds for warnings and alarms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests an excerpt from the monitoring system and compares the list of monitored IoT devices with the asset list. The configuration of the monitoring (thresholds, notifications) for individual devices is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The monitoring also includes application-specific function and health checks (e.g., 'Is the camera providing an image?', 'Is the sensor value plausible?'). The monitoring system is integrated into the ITSM tool and can automatically create incident tickets for critical errors. For high-availability systems, clusters or standby devices are procured and their status is also monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Custom scripts are developed to check the state of the application on the IoT device and report the results to the monitoring system. An API integration between the monitoring and ITSM system ensures automatic ticket creation. High-availability clusters are mapped as one service in the monitoring.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the custom monitoring scripts for their effectiveness. A failure is simulated (e.g., stopping a service on a test device) to verify the automatic ticket creation. The configuration and the test of the failover mechanism of clusters are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Predictive monitoring using machine learning algorithms is used to predict potential failures of IoT devices before they occur. An automatic failover to standby systems is implemented without manual intervention and is tested regularly. The overall availability of the IoT services is measured and reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The monitoring system collects long-term time-series data from the IoT devices and uses an AIOps module to detect anomalies and trends that indicate an impending failure (e.g., slowly increasing memory consumption). Automated runbooks in the SOAR tool or the automation platform carry out the failover process in the event of a failure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor evaluates the configuration and models of the predictive monitoring system. The logs of the regular, automated failover tests are reviewed. The availability reports of the last few months are analyzed. A failure of a primary cluster node is simulated to test the automatic failover live.

controls.title: Auditing of IoT Devices

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All deployed IoT devices SHOULD be audited regularly. This is done as part of a planned audit program that checks compliance with security policies and configuration specifications.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The annual internal audit plan includes a dedicated audit point for 'IoT security'. As part of this audit, various IoT systems are selected on a random basis and their configuration is manually checked against the internal hardening guidelines. The audit report is presented to the management level.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The external auditor reviews the internal audit plan and the audit reports from recent years on the subject of IoT. The methodology and depth of the internal audit are assessed. The follow-up of the deficiencies identified in the internal audit is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The audits are conducted by an independent body (e.g., internal audit or external auditors). To support the audit, automated configuration compliance scanners are used to achieve broader and deeper coverage.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The internal audit department plans and conducts the IoT audits. It uses specialized tools (e.g., Nessus with compliance checks, OpenSCAP) to automatically check the device configurations against recognized standards (e.g., CIS Benchmarks) and internal requirements. The results are used for manual verification and reporting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The external auditor requests the reports from the compliance scanner and evaluates the scan configuration. The independence of the auditing body (internal audit) is assessed. The results of the automated scan are compared with manual spot checks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Continuous, automated auditing is implemented. The system permanently monitors the configuration of IoT devices against a 'golden image' baseline and the defined security policies. Any deviation is immediately reported and, where possible, automatically corrected (self-healing). In addition, penetration tests are regularly conducted against the IoT systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible) or a security compliance tool runs in continuous enforcement mode. It constantly checks the configuration and automatically corrects deviations. An external service provider is commissioned annually to conduct a penetration test specifically for the IoT ecosystem.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and reports of the continuous compliance system. A misconfiguration is intentionally created on a test device to observe the automatic detection and correction. The reports of the latest penetration tests are requested and the remediation of the identified vulnerabilities is tracked.

controls.title: Secure configuration and use of an embedded web server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Web servers integrated into IoT devices SHOULD be configured as restrictively as possible. This includes disabling unused modules, configuring strong TLS protocols and cipher suites, and setting security-relevant HTTP headers. The web server SHOULD, where possible, NOT be run under a privileged account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hardening guideline for IoT devices contains a specific section on web server configuration. It requires HTTPS-only, TLS 1.2+, Forward Secrecy, and setting headers such as HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, and X-Frame-Options. It is checked whether the web server process runs with minimal privileges (e.g., as user 'www-data').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor uses a web security scanner (e.g., `testssl.sh`, OWASP ZAP, or the browser's developer tools) to check the web server's TLS configuration and HTTP security headers. Via SSH login on the device, it is checked under which user account the web server process is running (`ps aux | grep httpd`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) is placed in front of the web interfaces of critical IoT systems to protect them from common web attacks (e.g., SQL Injection, Cross-Site Scripting). The web server configuration is regularly checked for known vulnerabilities using vulnerability scanners.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A reverse proxy with WAF functionality (e.g., Nginx with ModSecurity, Cloudflare) is placed in front of the IoT web servers. The WAF runs with an up-to-date rule set (e.g., OWASP Core Rule Set). Weekly, authenticated vulnerability scans with tools like Nessus or OpenVAS check the web servers for known vulnerabilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the WAF configuration and its rule sets. The reports from the latest vulnerability scans are reviewed and checked for critical, unpatched findings. An attempt is made to carry out a simple test attack (e.g., `.../?id=<script>alert(1)</script>`) to see if the WAF blocks it.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The embedded web server is completely disabled. Administration is carried out exclusively via a more secure alternative, such as a hardened command-line interface (CLI) via SSH or a dedicated management API. Access to these interfaces is additionally protected by Mutual TLS (mTLS) and a PAM solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hardening guideline specifies the deactivation of the web server as the default. Administration is performed via Ansible playbooks that log in to the device via SSH with key authentication. The SSH access itself is mediated through a PAM solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a port scan on the device to verify that no web ports (80, 443) are open. The administrative process via the alternative interface (e.g., SSH via PAM) is traced and its security is assessed.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Unlike classic endpoint devices, devices with functions from the Internet of Things (IoT) domain are networked devices or objects that have additional "smart" functions. IoT devices are usually connected wirelessly to data networks. Most devices can access information on the internet and be reached through it. This allows them to have an impact on the information security of the entire information network.
IoT devices, such as smartwatches or other wearables, can enter institutions by being worn by employees or external parties. However, many institutions also procure and operate IoT devices, including fire, gas, and other warning detectors, coffee machines, or building control elements like cameras and HVAC (Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning).
A general distinction can be made between directly addressable IoT devices and IoT devices that require a central control unit. Directly addressable devices are typically connected to the LAN with their own IP address or have their own direct network connection, e.g., via mobile communication, and can operate autonomously or be managed by a central control unit. In addition, there are IoT devices that communicate exclusively and directly with control units, e.g., via wireless networks like Bluetooth or ZigBee, and are thus not directly connected to existing data networks.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to secure IoT devices in such a way that they do not compromise the information security of the own institution or that of third parties. Therefore, both unauthorized data leakage and device manipulation should be prevented, especially with regard to attacks by third parties.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The SYS.4.4 General IoT Device module should be applied to any device with functionalities from the Internet of Things (IoT) domain.
This module deals with IoT devices in general and is intended to be applicable to a wide range of different IoT devices. It does not go into detail on dedicated security features, such as those of operating and display systems or specific hardware and software architectures.
Depending on the characteristics of the IoT devices, the transitions to industrial control systems (ICS systems) or embedded systems are fluid. Requirements for devices used in production and manufacturing can be found in the modules of the IND Industrial IT layer.
Embedded systems, on the other hand, are information-processing systems that are integrated into a larger system or product, where they perform control, regulation, and data processing tasks and are often not directly perceived by the users. For these systems, the SYS.4.3 Embedded Systems module must be implemented.
Requirements for the radio links frequently used in connection with IoT devices can be found in the modules of the NET.2 Radio Networks layer.
The IoT devices used in the information network under consideration must be taken into account in identity and access management. For this, the ORP.4 Identity and Access Management module must be implemented.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Espionage via IoT devices
parts.prose:
In the development of IoT devices, the aspect of information security is typically not considered or is given only secondary importance. In the past, this has led to IoT devices being repeatedly misused to collect information about users or the area of application. For example, there have been repeated incidents with networked or IP-based surveillance cameras:

• In 2021, surveillance cameras were hacked by re-registering the camera ID. This made it possible to take over control.
• In 2022, video streams from baby monitors were redirected in an attack on other servers due to a lack of authentication. Due to the lack of authentication, it was even possible to take over control.

At the end of September 2016, it became known that some models of surveillance cameras and room sensors were equipped with backdoors that enable espionage. This particularly affected surveillance cameras used in data centers and server rooms. The backdoors apparently made it possible to access the image and video data of the cameras and to copy this data to servers on the internet. In this way, for example, user or administrator passwords could be compromised or device configurations, infrastructure details, and other confidential information could be made accessible to third parties. This facilitated further attacks by exploiting the habits of employees.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Use of UPnP
parts.prose: IoT devices integrated into LANs often independently establish a connection to the internet by configuring routers in the network via UPnP (Universal Plug and Play) to create a port forwarding. The devices can then not only communicate within the local network but are also visible and reachable from outside the LAN. If a vulnerability in the IoT device is then exploited by an attacker, this device could become part of a botnet. Furthermore, additional malware could be introduced into the information network. This security vulnerability can also be exploited for further malicious activities at a later time.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Takeover into a botnet
parts.prose:
If IoT devices are not patched regularly, known vulnerabilities remain open and can be exploited for extensive attacks. One goal of an attack could be to integrate the IoT devices into a botnet. In this case, they could be misused, for example, to carry out Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks and restrict the availability of services.
Botnets are often used for this purpose, which largely consist of IoT devices. With the "Mirai" malware, which has existed since 2016, for example, webcams, cameras, digital video recorders, routers, and printers are integrated into a botnet. They then independently scan the internet for other devices to infect them with malware and add them to the botnet. In addition, there are also other variants of such malware such as "Mozi" or "BotenaGo", which used a similar approach in 2019 and 2021.

controls.title: Awareness training for the secure handling of removable media

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employee awareness training on the secure handling of removable media is only carried out sporadically, for example after a security incident, but does not reach all relevant persons.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A one-time email circular or a notice on the bulletin board are typical examples of only partially implemented awareness training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through spot checks on employees that regular and comprehensive awareness training is not taking place and that knowledge of correct handling is incomplete.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees are fundamentally informed about handling removable media as part of their hiring process. The information covers the most important prohibitions, such as connecting third-party USB drives.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Awareness training is an integral part of the onboarding documents for new employees, but it is not repeated or reinforced later.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies on the basis of the hiring documentation that basic awareness training is provided for all new employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All users MUST be made aware of the secure handling of removable media. The institution MUST specifically point out how users should handle removable media to prevent loss or theft and ensure a long service life. The institution MUST inform users that they are not allowed to connect removable media from unknown sources to their IT systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Awareness is implemented through regular, documented training (e.g., annually) or through targeted information campaigns. The content is based on the current policy for removable media.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the training materials and the attendance lists of the awareness measures. Interviews with employees are used to check on a random basis whether the key messages have been understood.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The awareness measures are designed to be target group-specific. Employees who frequently transport sensitive data on removable media receive in-depth training. The effectiveness of the training is checked by knowledge tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to general training, special modules are offered for specific roles (e.g., administrators, field sales staff) that address their specific risks. The results of the knowledge tests are used to improve the training content.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the differentiation of the training content by target group and checks the results of the knowledge tests carried out and the improvement measures derived from them.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The awareness training is integrated into a continuous security awareness program, which is supplemented by regular, realistic phishing tests with specially prepared USB sticks (USB dropping). The results are analyzed and lead to automated, individual follow-up training.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A security awareness platform is used to control, conduct, and evaluate the campaigns. Employees who connect a test USB stick immediately receive an explanatory message and are automatically booked for a short e-learning module.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the conception, implementation, and detailed evaluations of the USB dropping campaigns. It is verified that the results demonstrably lead to an improvement in security awareness and an adjustment of the training strategy.

controls.title: Loss and tampering notification

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users MUST immediately report if a removable storage device has been stolen, lost, or if there is a suspicion of tampering. When reporting, users MUST specify what information is stored on the removable storage device. For this purpose, the institution MUST have clear reporting channels and responsibilities. The institution MUST define how removable storage devices that are found after being lost should be handled. Found removable storage devices MUST NOT be used without prior inspection for tampering and malware.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A clearly defined reporting process is established, e.g., via a ticket system or a dedicated email address for IT support. A standard procedure for handling recovered storage media is documented, which includes a forensic examination on an isolated workstation before the media is released for use again.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and awareness of the reporting channel by reviewing the documentation and interviewing employees. Using examples (test cases or past incidents), the auditor checks whether the process for handling recovered storage media is being followed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reporting process for lost or tampered removable media is integrated into the central incident response management. Reports are classified according to the criticality of the potentially compromised data to ensure prioritized processing. There is a documented process that also provides for the initiation of measures such as remote locking or wiping, if technically possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Reports are recorded via a central incident management tool. A playbook for the loss of removable media defines clear escalation paths and response measures, depending on the data classification. The inventory list of removable media is used to assess the potential damage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the incident response plans and playbooks regarding the loss of removable media. Based on the logs of past incidents, the correct classification, escalation, and processing of the reports are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process of reporting loss and tampering is largely automated. A user's report automatically triggers workflows that, for example, block the access of the associated storage medium to IT systems, inform the data protection officer, and, depending on the criticality, start a predefined incident response process. Recovered media are automatically analyzed for tampering and malware in a secure forensic environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The report is made via a self-service portal that is linked to the asset management and the SIEM system. Automated SOAR playbooks (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) execute the initial response steps. The analysis of recovered media is carried out in a sandbox environment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the automated workflows in the incident management or SOAR tool. A test case is used to verify that a report triggers the correct automatic responses and that the forensic analysis environment meets the defined standards.

controls.title: Data carrier encryption

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Encryption of removable media is only used for individual, particularly critical projects or on a voluntary basis by technically savvy users. A company-wide requirement or control is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Individual users use portable encryption software for their USB sticks, but there is no uniform standard or policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by interviewing users and checking samples of removable media that there is no consistent encryption.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general recommendation to encrypt removable media that leaves the company. However, the implementation is done manually by the users, often with simple passwords and without a central specification of the encryption software or algorithms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users are instructed to use their operating system's on-board encryption (e.g., BitLocker), but password complexity is not enforced and there is no central management of recovery keys.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the recommendation and checks on a random basis whether users encrypt their storage media, but finds that the quality of the encryption (e.g., password strength) is not guaranteed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If removable media are used or transported outside a secure area and contain sensitive data, the data MUST be encrypted using a secure, documented procedure. It is specified which encryption software and algorithms are considered secure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy requires the use of specific software (e.g., BitLocker To Go, VeraCrypt) with defined minimum standards for algorithms (e.g., AES-256) and passwords. Users are trained in the use of this software.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the encryption policy and verifies the configuration on client systems. The correct encryption of removable media in circulation is verified on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The encryption of removable media is technically enforced. IT systems are configured to block write access to unencrypted removable media. There is a central, secure process for managing recovery keys.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Group Policies (GPO) or Mobile Device Management (MDM) are used to enforce the encryption requirement for removable media on all end devices. The recovery keys are stored centrally in Active Directory or a dedicated key management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the GPOs or MDM policies that enforce encryption. The process for securely recovering data using a recovery key is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only certified removable media with hardware encryption are used. Access to the encrypted data is linked to the user's identity (e.g., via smart card or biometric feature). All access attempts are logged centrally and monitored for anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Only FIPS 140-2/3 or BSI-certified USB sticks with an integrated crypto-processor are procured and issued. The sticks are managed via a central management console that enforces policies and sends audit logs to a SIEM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies on the basis of the procurement documents and the technical specifications that only certified hardware-encrypted storage media are used. The configuration of the central management console and the log analysis in the SIEM are checked.

controls.title: Protection against malware

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST ensure that only data that has been checked for malware is transferred to removable media. Before data from removable media is processed, it MUST be checked for malware.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A virus protection program with a real-time scanner is installed on all client systems, which automatically scans removable media when connected ('on-access scan'). The virus signatures are updated centrally and regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the antivirus software on a representative sample of clients. It is verified that the on-access scan for removable media is enabled and the signature updates are current. A test with an EICAR test virus on a USB stick can verify the function.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the client-side scan, a dedicated scan station (data sluice) is used for all removable media from external or untrusted sources. This station is isolated from the production network. The autorun/autoplay functionality for removable media is disabled system-wide on all clients.

parts.name: guidance
