parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation. Based on current vulnerability reports, it is tracked whether the process is consistently followed from identification through assessment to the decision on treatment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to reports from manufacturers and CERTs, regular organizational and technical audits are conducted for vulnerability analysis. The implementation of patches or mitigating measures is tracked and monitored via a ticket system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Regular, but cautiously configured vulnerability scans are performed in the OT environment, often during maintenance windows. The results are imported into the vulnerability management tool. For each vulnerability to be addressed, a ticket is created in the change management system, which contains clear deadlines for remediation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the vulnerability scan reports and the scanner configuration. It is verified in the ticket system that the identified vulnerabilities are systematically processed and that compliance with the deadlines is monitored.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The vulnerability management process is largely automated. This includes the automated correlation of vulnerability information with the asset inventory, risk assessment including system criticality, and the generation of tickets. Patches are tested in a test environment for their impact on the stability of the plant before rollout.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized vulnerability management platform is used, which is integrated with the CMDB and the ticket system. Patches for critical OT systems are first applied to a 'digital twin' or in a test lab to ensure they do not affect the plant control. The rollout is then controlled via a central patch management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the integration of the various systems (scanner, CMDB, ticket system). The logs of the patch tests in the test lab are reviewed. The effectiveness of the process is assessed by analyzing KPIs such as 'Time to Patch' or 'Number of open critical vulnerabilities'.

controls.title: System documentation

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The standard manufacturer documentation for the ICS components is available and stored centrally. There is no extended, institution-specific documentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: PDF manuals from the manufacturers are collected on a network drive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the manufacturer documentation for the systems in use is available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An extended system documentation SHOULD be created. It SHOULD record special features in operation and the options for system administration. Furthermore, it SHOULD be documented when ICS components are modified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the manufacturer's documentation, an operating manual is created for each important ICS system. This document describes the specific configuration, administrative access, start and stop procedures, and the history of changes made. The operating manual is versioned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and level of detail of the operating manuals. Using the change log, it is verified whether the documentation corresponds to the actual system state.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system documentation is integrated into a central knowledge base or CMDB. It contains detailed information on dependencies on other systems, configuration baselines, and recovery procedures. The documentation is regularly reviewed for currency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The operating manuals are transferred to a wiki system that allows for easy linking and searching. The restart plans from the documentation are regularly checked and updated as part of tests. An annual review process ensures the documentation is up-to-date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the structure and content of the knowledge base. It is verified that the review process for the documentation is demonstrably carried out, e.g., by checking review protocols or approval notes.

controls.title: Documentation of communication relationships

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The basic communication relationships are roughly depicted in the network plan. Detailed documentation at the protocol or data level does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the network plan, lines are drawn between systems that communicate with each other, without specifying the type of communication in more detail.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that the network plan only provides a superficial overview, which is not sufficient for a detailed security analysis (e.g., creating firewall rules).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be documented with which systems an ICS component exchanges which data. In addition, the communication links of newly integrated ICS components SHOULD be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each important communication relationship, a communication matrix (e.g., in a table) is created. This matrix lists the source, destination, protocol used, port, and the purpose of the communication. This documentation is the basis for creating firewall rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the communication matrix for completeness. It is randomly checked whether the relationships documented in the matrix match the rules implemented on the firewalls.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documentation of the communication relationships is supplemented by a baseline of the normal network traffic. Deviations from this baseline are monitored. The documentation is so detailed that it enables a 'least privilege' implementation at the network level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A network monitoring tool is used to capture the actual data traffic and compare it with the documented communication matrix. Firewall rules are formulated as specifically as possible (e.g., allowing only certain function codes of an OT protocol).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports of the network monitoring tool and checks whether detected deviations have been investigated and either the documentation has been adapted or the unwanted communication has been blocked. The specificity of the firewall rules is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The communication relationships are captured and visualized in real time by an OT-specific monitoring system. The system learns the normal behavior and automatically detects and reports new or anomalous communication attempts that violate the defined security policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A passive OT security platform is implemented that continuously analyzes network traffic. It creates and maintains a dynamic map of the assets and their communication relationships. Policies are defined that, for example, prohibit a PLC from communicating directly with the internet. A violation triggers an alarm.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and the learned baselines of the OT security platform. Through a simulated attack or a targeted misconfiguration, it is tested whether the system detects and reports anomalous communication as expected.

controls.title: Central system logging and monitoring

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Log data from ICS components is archived manually and at irregular intervals on a central file server. Automatic alerting does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators copy log files from the OT systems to a network drive to protect them from being overwritten. Analysis only takes place on an as-needed basis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the central repository for completeness and timeliness of the log files and determines that the process is incomplete and not timely.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Log data from ICS components SHOULD be stored centrally. In the event of security-critical events, an automatic alert SHOULD be triggered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central log server (e.g., based on Syslog-ng or a SIEM) is set up. All relevant ICS components are configured to send their logs to this server. In the log management system, simple rules are defined that trigger an email notification for specific keywords (e.g., 'failed login', 'error').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the logs from the critical systems are arriving centrally. The configuration of the alerting rules is checked and a critical event is simulated to test whether the alerting works.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The central logging is integrated into a SIEM system that performs correlations between events from different systems. The alarms are prioritized according to criticality and forwarded to the responsible team for processing via a ticket system. The integrity and availability of the log data is ensured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: More sophisticated correlation rules are created in the SIEM (e.g., 'multiple failed logins from the same IP address on different systems within a short period'). The SIEM is integrated with the ticketing system to ensure traceable processing of alarms. The log server has a redundant design, and the logs are digitally signed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the effectiveness of the correlation rules in the SIEM. The workflow from alarm creation to ticket closure is tracked. The measures to ensure log integrity and availability are verified.

controls.title: Decommissioning of ICS components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Decommissioned ICS components are physically disposed of. However, there is no systematic deletion of data and configurations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Old controllers or computers are sent to electronic scrap without securely erasing the hard drives or flash memory.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews that there is no process for secure data deletion during decommissioning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When old or defective ICS components are decommissioned, all sensitive data SHOULD be securely erased. In particular, it SHOULD be ensured that all access credentials have been permanently removed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented process for the decommissioning of IT systems is also applied to OT components. It stipulates that all data carriers (hard disks, flash memory, etc.) must be securely erased using a certified method or physically destroyed (shredded) before disposal. Special attention is paid to removing configuration files containing passwords or IP addresses.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation. Proof of secure erasure or destruction of the data carriers from recently decommissioned devices is requested (e.g., erasure logs, certificate from the disposal service provider).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decommissioning process is integrated into the asset management lifecycle. The decommissioning of a device is documented in the asset inventory (CMDB) and the status is changed accordingly. All licenses and maintenance contracts associated with the device are terminated or reallocated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decommissioning process is controlled via the asset management system. The erasure log is attached to the asset in the CMDB as proof. The process automatically triggers a notification to license management and purchasing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies in the CMDB that decommissioned devices are correctly marked and that the corresponding evidence (e.g., erasure log) is linked. It is checked whether the downstream processes (license management) have been initiated.

controls.title: Emergency planning for OT

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic emergency plans exist for the failure of the most important OT systems. A backup procedure for the failure of remote administration is documented but not regularly tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Recovery plans describe the steps for restoration after a total failure. For remote administration, an alternative dial-in option (e.g., via ISDN or LTE router) is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and level of detail of the emergency plans and the backup procedure. It is noted that no test logs are available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Emergency plans for the failure and compromise of each zone SHOULD be defined, documented, tested after every major change, and regularly practiced. In addition, an effective backup procedure for the failure of the (remote) administration capability SHOULD be defined, documented, and tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each zone defined in the zone concept, specific emergency plans are created that cover both technical failures and cyberattacks (compromise). These plans are reviewed at least once a year in tabletop exercises. The alternative remote maintenance procedure is also tested annually. The results of the tests and exercises are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the zone-specific emergency plans and the logs of the exercises and tests performed. It is verified that the lessons learned from the tests have led to an improvement of the plans.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The OT emergency planning is fully integrated into the institution's Business Continuity Management (BCM). The emergency plans are practiced in comprehensive, realistic simulations involving IT, OT, corporate communications, and management. The Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) defined for the emergency are reviewed and optimized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The OT emergency plans are part of the overarching BCM framework. Large-scale crisis exercises are held regularly, for example, simulating a plant-wide ransomware attack. The entire reporting and response chain, up to and including crisis communication, is practiced. The results are used to optimize technical and organizational resilience.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the integration of OT emergency management into the BCM. The planning, execution, and follow-up of the crisis exercises are analyzed. It is verified that the measured recovery times meet the requirements defined in the Business Impact Analysis (BIA).

controls.title: Strong authentication on OT components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Personalized accounts with complex passwords that must be changed regularly are used for authentication on OT components. The use of group or default accounts is reduced to a minimum.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A password policy that prescribes minimum length, complexity, and a maximum age for passwords is enforced for the OT environment. Default passwords are changed during commissioning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the password policy and its technical implementation on the OT systems. It is verified that no insecure default passwords are still in use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the secure authentication of privileged users in control systems, a central directory service SHOULD be established. Authentication SHOULD be additionally secured by using multiple factors such as knowledge, possession, or biometrics. It SHOULD be ensured that authentication of operationally required technical accounts can also be performed in emergencies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central directory service (e.g., Active Directory) is established for authentication in the OT environment. All privileged access (e.g., to engineering workstations, servers) is secured with a second factor (e.g., smart card, OTP token). For emergencies, secure 'break-glass' accounts exist, whose passwords are kept in a sealed envelope or a digital password safe.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the connection of the OT systems to the central directory service and the configuration of the multi-factor authentication (MFA). The process for using the 'break-glass' accounts is checked for security and traceability. It is tested whether access to privileged accounts is possible without MFA.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multi-factor authentication is enforced for all user access (not just privileged) to all OT systems, where technically feasible. The dependencies arising from the use of a central directory service have been analyzed and minimized through redundant, hardened authentication servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: MFA is also enforced for operators at HMI terminals. The domain controllers for the OT environment are physically separated from the office IT, hardened, and redundantly located in different fire compartments to ensure high availability of the authentication services. A failure of the connection to the office network does not affect authentication within the OT.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the comprehensive implementation of MFA. The architecture and the hardening measures of the authentication infrastructure are analyzed. A simulated failure of the connection to the office IT is used to test whether authentication in the OT environment continues to function.

controls.title: Monitoring of far-reaching permissions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A list of all users with administrative or far-reaching permissions on critical OT systems is maintained. This list is reviewed annually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Excel spreadsheet lists all administrator accounts and their owners. The system owner checks once a year whether all permissions are still necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the list and compares it with the accounts actually configured on the systems. It is checked whether the annual review has taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution SHOULD maintain an inventory that contains all assigned entry, access, and access rights to critical systems. The inventory SHOULD include which rights a specific user effectively has and who has which rights on a specific system. All critical administrative activities SHOULD be logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A CMDB or an IAM system is used to centrally manage and document all permissions. Reports can be generated that show 'who has access to what' and 'what rights exist on system X'. All administrative actions are centrally logged and the logs are regularly reviewed (e.g., weekly) for suspicious activities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the completeness and correctness of the permissions directory. The logs of the administrative activities are inspected and checked for plausibility. It is verified that the regular review of the logs takes place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The monitoring of permissions and administrative activities is automated. A Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution monitors and records all privileged sessions in real time. Deletion or manipulation of the logs by IT operations is technically prevented. Automated analytics detect suspicious behavior of privileged accounts.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM solution with session recording and command filtering is used. The log data is sent to a SIEM system that has a UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) module to detect anomalous behavior of administrator accounts (e.g., logging in at unusual times, executing rare commands). The log files are archived on WORM storage to prevent tampering.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the PAM solution and the UEBA module. The protection of the log data against tampering is verified by a technical inspection. It is tested whether a suspicious administrative action triggers an alert as expected.

controls.title: Stronger zone segregation

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The zones in the OT network are separated from each other by firewalls or Layer 3 switches with Access Control Lists (ACLs). The rules are based on IP addresses and ports.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Firewalls are placed between the VLANs that represent the zones. The rules allow the necessary communication, e.g., 'allow RDP from the engineering workstation to server X'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the firewall rules for correctness and ensures that there are no 'any-any-allow' rules. The effectiveness of the separation is tested by network scans from one zone to another.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For ICS environments that require high protection or are difficult to secure, interface systems with security inspection functions SHOULD be used as a preventive measure. End-to-end external connections SHOULD be terminated by implementing one or more connectivity zones (DMZ) in a P-A-P structure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For communication between the office and OT network, a demilitarized zone (DMZ) is set up according to the Production-Access-Production (P-A-P) pattern. Systems such as terminal servers or data servers are placed in the DMZ to avoid direct connections. Data traffic is filtered by application-level gateways or reverse proxies. The security inspections are designed in such a way that no adjustments to the ICS system itself are necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the architecture of the DMZ and the configuration of the firewalls and the systems placed within it. It is verified that all communication between the office and OT is terminated and inspected in the DMZ and that no direct connections are possible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Zone separation is enforced at the highest level through the use of data diodes for unidirectional communication or Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) firewalls that understand and validate OT protocols. All cross-zone traffic is inspected at the application level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: To securely transfer data from the OT network to the office network (e.g., for monitoring), a data diode is used that physically guarantees communication without a return channel. For necessary bidirectional communication (e.g., control system commands), an OT-capable Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) is used, which, for example, only allows permitted Modbus function codes and blocks all others.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the data diode and the OT-NGFW. Targeted test attacks with manipulated OT protocol packets are used to verify that the firewall's DPI function works as expected and blocks the attacks.

controls.title: Regular security review

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security configurations of OT components are checked after initial commissioning and after major changes. There are no regular, scheduled reviews.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Checklists for secure configuration are worked through during commissioning and after important changes. The review is part of the change management process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the completed checklists and compares them with the actual configuration on a random basis to assess the diligence of the review.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security configuration of OT components SHOULD be reviewed regularly and as needed in the event of suddenly occurring new, previously unknown threats. The security review SHOULD at least cover the exposed systems with external interfaces or user interaction. The implemented security concept SHOULD also be reviewed regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual audit plan for OT security is created. It provides for regular internal reviews (e.g., configuration reviews, firewall rule audits) of the most critical systems. In the event of new, critical threat situations (e.g., Log4Shell), ad-hoc reviews are carried out to assess the impact and the effectiveness of countermeasures. The results of the reviews are documented and their measures are tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit plan and the corresponding reports. It is verified that the deficiencies identified in the reports are systematically remediated. The response to a recently disclosed threat situation is analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security review SHOULD be carried out as a configuration audit or through automated compliance checks. Regular, comprehensive penetration tests and red teaming exercises, specifically tailored to the OT environment, are carried out by external specialists.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool for automated monitoring of configuration compliance (Security Content Automation Protocol - SCAP or similar) is used. It continuously checks the OT systems against defined hardening baselines. Every two years, an external penetration test is commissioned to attempt to penetrate the most critical parts of the plant. The results are reported at the management level and feed directly into the security strategy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and reports of the automated compliance tool. The reports from the external penetration tests are reviewed and it is tracked how the organization has dealt with the most serious findings. The effectiveness of the improvement process is assessed.

controls.title: Communication in case of an incident

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an emergency contact list with the telephone numbers of the relevant personnel. The primary communication in case of an incident is via the normal telephone network and e-mail.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list with the private mobile phone numbers of the on-call team is maintained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the currency of the contact list.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Alternative and independent communication options SHOULD be established and operated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to the normal telephone network, alternative means of communication are provided that are not dependent on the primary IT infrastructure. These can be satellite phones, a dedicated radio network (e.g., TETRA), or a separate LTE-based solution. The functionality of these means is tested regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence of the alternative means of communication. Based on test records, it is verified that they are regularly checked for functionality. The independence from the primary IT is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A comprehensive crisis communication plan is established that regulates the use of the various communication channels (primary and alternative). The alternative means of communication are designed with redundancy and are actively used in regular crisis drills to ensure staff familiarity with the systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The crisis communication plan specifies when to switch to which alternative channels. For example, in the event of a cyberattack that could also potentially affect the telephone system, there is an immediate switch to satellite phones. During the annual crisis drill, the use of normal means of communication is prohibited to enforce the use of the alternatives.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the crisis communication plan. Based on the logs of the crisis drills, it is verified that the alternative means of communication were used successfully and that communication worked as planned. The redundancy of the alternative systems is checked.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Process control and automation technology (Operational Technology, OT) is hardware and software that monitors and controls physical devices, processes, and events in the institution.
In industry, which also includes critical infrastructures, this particularly includes industrial control systems (ICS) and automation solutions that perform all kinds of control and regulation functions there. Other examples are laboratory equipment, e.g., automated microscopes or analysis tools, logistics systems, such as barcode scanners with small computers, or building management technology.
The physical separation of OT from other IT systems and data networks in office applications, which was common in the past, is now only applicable in exceptional cases with increased protection requirements due to increasing integration demands. Multi-stage production steps and their overarching control, as well as regulatory requirements, make it increasingly necessary to open up OT even across organizational boundaries. This development is further accelerated by the trend towards optimizing manufacturing processes, especially in the context of Industry 4.0.
Since OT increasingly uses IT components from office IT, it is now similarly endangered. At the same time, however, OT has significant differences from classic IT, which make it difficult to apply established security procedures there. For example, there may be restrictions due to manufacturer specifications or legal requirements that prevent or complicate changes to components, such as installing security updates or subsequent hardening measures. OT is also subject to significantly longer life cycles, even beyond the support of the manufacturing companies, so that security updates are not consistently available.
A significant difference for OT also arises from the often high availability and integrity requirements. In comparison, availability is often of secondary importance in office IT. Malfunctions of OT systems, on the other hand, can lead to dangers to life, limb, and the environment and are usually not to be remedied by a restart.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of this module is to identify suitable requirements for the information security of OT. It contains cross-component, conceptual, and architectural security requirements.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The IND.1 Process Control and Automation Technology module must be applied at least once to every IT system with process control and automation technology within the information network.
The module should be implemented comprehensively. If there are different security requirements for information security in the individual areas with process control and automation technology, the module should be applied separately to each IT system.
The design of OT can vary greatly depending on the purpose, industry, the IT systems and technology used, as well as due to the long deployment period, even in comparable use cases. When selecting security measures based on the requirements from this module, these special features must be taken into account. They can have a significant influence on the design of the security concept. For this reason, risk analysis can also be of great importance when creating a security concept for normal protection needs.
Operating personnel should be trained and sensitized with regard to relevant threats and dangers. For this purpose, the ORP.3 Awareness and Training for Information Security module must be implemented.
In addition to this module, the surrounding infrastructure of the OT, i.e., locations, facilities, buildings, or rooms, should be modeled using the most specific modules possible in order to supplement the protective effect of this module.
For suitable logging in the area of process control and automation technology, the OPS.1.1.5 Logging module must be implemented.
ICS systems should generally be taken into account when implementing the ORP.4 Identity and Access Management module.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Impairment by harmful environmental influences
parts.prose: In industrial environments, ICS components are often exposed to special conditions that can impair safe operation. These include extreme heat, cold, humidity, dust, vibration, or even caustic or corrosive environments. Often, several factors occur simultaneously. Due to such harmful influences, ICS components can wear out faster and fail earlier.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Inappropriate integration of OT into the security organization
parts.prose: Due to different framework conditions, knowledge, and procedures in the areas of Office IT and OT, problems can arise in the implementation of overarching security specifications. Security specifications from the Office IT area may not be implementable due to technical or procedural peculiarities of ICS systems. On the other hand, it could be that ICS-specific information security and safety aspects, i.e., aspects of functional safety, are not known to the information security officer of the Office IT. This can lead to friction in communication and implementation. Furthermore, risks might not be recognized or could be inadequately addressed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Unsuitable integration of OT into operational processes
parts.prose:
Even though OT and IT are increasingly converging, there are special features that make it difficult to transfer established operational processes. Operational interventions within the framework of change and incident management for secure configuration, troubleshooting, or installing security updates may, for example, require renewed official approval or result in the loss of support. Unauthorized changes can affect the function of a component and thus potentially also have an impact on its safety function.
OT is used to monitor, control, and automate technical processes. Malfunctions of these systems can lead to production downtimes, technical or personal damage, and environmental damage. These potential impacts must be taken into account during operational interventions.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Insufficient access protection
parts.prose:
Industrial control systems are increasingly rarely operated in complete isolation from the outside world. Modern manufacturing and production processes require an exchange of information with upstream and downstream production steps and are often connected to an institution's central production planning and control systems. To exchange information electronically, production facilities must also be connected to third-party networks, such as office IT or the networks of partners and service providers. Interactive access from office or mobile workstations and operationally required electronic data exchange, for example for the provision of software and updates, mean further networking with the outside world. The setup of remote access for on-call duty or for service providers can also enable access from the outside.
If the required communication channels are defined too broadly or are inadequately secured, third parties can exploit these access routes to access and compromise them. On the one hand, industrial control systems can be affected by targeted malware attacks. On the other hand, they can also be compromised by malicious programs that are actually aimed at manipulating office IT. Malware can get onto the systems due to a lack of segmentation or control of data traffic.
However, the use of antivirus software can also pose a risk to OT. For example, if there is no approval from the manufacturing company for the environment or if false positives and active system interventions jeopardize operation. A comparable potential for disruption can also arise from the operation of network-based intrusion prevention systems (IPS), as connections can be interrupted.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Insecure project planning/application development process
parts.prose:
Adjustments and further developments of IT systems, applications, and control programs can represent a critical intervention in the control system. Malfunctions can arise from functional errors due to insufficient testing and validation steps, incorrect or manipulated project data, or vulnerabilities in the software. For example, when important security functions such as input/output or authorization checks are inadequately implemented.
Further dangers can arise from insecure development environments, the unsuitable storage of program code, documentation or project data, as well as from the data transfer interfaces.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Insecure administration concept and remote administration
parts.prose: The administration of industrial control systems is in certain cases carried out via network access. Various public and private networks are used for this, such as telephone networks, radio networks, mobile networks, and increasingly the internet. If this access is inadequately planned, insecurely configured, or not monitored, third parties may be able to gain unauthorized access to individual OT components or the infrastructure. This allows them, for example, to bypass security mechanisms at the perimeter.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Insufficient monitoring and detection methods
parts.prose:
An essential function of industrial control systems is to monitor the operation of an automated process. For example, a corresponding warning is issued if fill levels fall below a certain point or if temperatures or valve positions deviate. The supporting IT infrastructure, on the other hand, is often not sufficiently monitored.
If unusual or security-relevant events in such operating environments are not controlled or are controlled inadequately, attack attempts, network bottlenecks, or foreseeable failures cannot be detected early. Furthermore, a poor evaluation or a confusing presentation of the events can also lead to warnings and errors being detected late.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Insufficient test concept
parts.prose:
Industrial control systems are often subject to high availability requirements. This is because malfunctions or technical failures can potentially cause serious damage and high consequential costs. For this reason, OT systems are often designed to be fail-safe.
If changes to such an environment are not carefully planned, coordinated, and tested in a realistic environment, there is a risk that logical or software-technical errors will be overlooked and malfunctions will occur in the system. Even updates approved by the manufacturing company can cause malfunctions in the system when modifying or adjusting parameters.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Lack of life cycle concepts
parts.prose:
In addition to specific ICS components, components and software from office IT are increasingly being used. Due to the very long life cycles in OT, these components are usually operated for much longer than is common in office IT, sometimes even beyond the support cycles of the manufacturing companies.
As a result, after the manufacturing companies' support expires, no more updates are provided to fix vulnerabilities. In contrast, there are often publicly documented vulnerabilities and tools that exploit these vulnerabilities. This also allows non-expert attackers to successfully penetrate the OT systems. This also applies if updates are not installed or are installed with a very long delay.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.10. Insufficient security requirements in procurement
parts.prose: Due to insufficient security requirements and for cost reasons, information security is often not taken into account during procurement. As a result, ICS components can sometimes contain serious vulnerabilities, e.g., in hardware or software, which can later only be rectified with great effort.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.11. Use of insecure protocols
parts.prose:
ICS components communicate with each other via various network protocols and standards. In addition to protocols and standards from office IT such as Ethernet, TCP/IP, WLAN or GSM, OT-specific protocols are used. These were not always developed with information security in mind and therefore sometimes offer no or only limited security mechanisms. Information is often transmitted in plain text and without integrity protection or authentication.
Attackers with access to the network could read or change the content of the communication and in this way influence the processes, for example by faking sensor data or falsifying control commands. This is particularly true for protocols that are used for communication over freely accessible areas, for example with radio protocols or in the context of site networking.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.12. Insecure configurations of ICS components
parts.prose:
In the default configuration of ICS components, security measures are not always activated. This allows unauthorized persons to gain access easily. The operation of insecurely configured components can also threaten the security of other components in the environment, for example if access data to them can be read or if they are in a trusted relationship with other systems.
For example, default passwords could be used, plain text protocols for system administration could be used, unnecessary services could be operated, unsecured interfaces such as USB or Firewire ports could be used, or security functions could be deactivated.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.13. Dependencies of OT on IT networks
parts.prose:
OT is now being operated less and less in complete isolation. If there are dependencies on other systems, networks, or services, failures or security incidents in the IT network also affect the OT.
In particular, if these systems and networks are not under the direct control of the operator, the availability of the OT and its processes can be severely impaired. In addition, an incident or error can usually only be rectified with external support.
Examples of dependencies on other systems and networks are internet connections, shared infrastructure components, operation and monitoring by service providers, or the use of cloud services.

controls.title: Restriction of access to configuration and maintenance interfaces (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the most obvious default passwords (e.g., "admin/admin") are changed during commissioning. Access to maintenance interfaces is not formally regulated and is based on implicit trust in the employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This situation often occurs when there are no clear security policies for commissioning ICS components and the technicians are working under time pressure. The password changes are made ad hoc and are not documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The inspector asks the technicians if and which passwords are changed. A spot check of critical systems shows that many default passwords are still active. There is no documentation of password changes or access permissions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All known default passwords are changed during commissioning. There is a list of authorized persons for access to configuration and maintenance interfaces, but this is not technically enforced. The new passwords are managed in a simple list or file.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple Excel list is used to document the changed passwords and the authorized employees. The list is stored on a network drive with general access permissions. The configuration changes are not systematically approved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The inspector asks to see the password list and the list of authorized persons. A review of the systems confirms that the default passwords have been changed. However, the inspector notes that password security (e.g., secure storage) is low and there is no approval process for changes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Default passwords or passwords set by the manufacturer MUST be changed. The change MUST be documented. The passwords MUST be stored securely. It MUST be ensured that only authorized employees can access configuration and maintenance interfaces of ICS components. The configuration of ICS components MAY ONLY be changed after approval by the responsible person or after authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A password manager is used for the secure storage of passwords. Access to configuration interfaces is regulated via separate user accounts on the components. Changes to the configuration require formal approval, which is documented by e-mail or via a simple ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The inspector verifies, based on the documentation (e.g., commissioning records, password manager logs), that all default passwords have been changed and stored securely. They check the user accounts on the ICS components and compare them with the list of authorized employees. On a random basis, configuration changes from recent months and the corresponding approval documents are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to configuration and maintenance interfaces is controlled by a role-based access control (RBAC) concept. All access attempts and configuration changes are logged centrally. The approval process for changes is formalized and technically supported, for example, by a change management system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Authentication is performed via a central directory service (e.g., LDAP or Active Directory), which manages the roles. Log data from the ICS components is sent to a central syslog server. The change management process is mapped in an ITSM tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the central directory service and the RBAC. They analyze the central log files for unauthorized access attempts. They examine the change management process mapped in the ITSM tool and compare implemented changes with the approved tickets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to configuration and maintenance interfaces is secured by multi-factor authentication (MFA). All configuration activities are logged and actively monitored in a central, tamper-proof system. Automated alerts are triggered for unauthorized access attempts or unapproved changes. Access is time-limited to the necessary maintenance window.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Privileged Access Management (PAM) system is used to control access, enforce MFA, and record all sessions. Log data is sent to a SIEM system, which checks for anomalies and rule violations and generates alerts. The configuration of the PAM system can be checked automatically via an API (`pam-cli session create --user auditor --target plc123 --duration 2h`).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the PAM and SIEM systems. They verify the MFA requirements and the alerting rules. They request session recordings for recently performed configuration changes and check whether the changes match the approved change tickets. The audit can be supported automatically by querying the PAM API (`pam-cli audit trail --since 24h`).

controls.title: Use of secure transmission protocols for configuration and maintenance (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure protocols are only used for a few configuration tasks that are classified as particularly critical. Older, insecure protocols such as Telnet or unencrypted HTTP are still active and used for most maintenance work.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of secure protocols is limited to the web interface of a central management station (HTTPS), while the direct configuration of PLCs is still done via Telnet. There are no network policies that prevent insecure data traffic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a network scan to identify open ports for insecure services such as Telnet (port 23) or FTP (port 21). A brief capture of network traffic during a simulated maintenance session reveals unencrypted credentials.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure protocols (e.g., SSH, HTTPS) are set as the standard for all new configurations. A policy exists that mandates their use, but compliance is not technically enforced. Insecure protocols are still active on many systems for compatibility reasons.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The work instructions for technicians state that SSH should be used instead of Telnet. The configuration of the secure protocols uses default settings, which may allow weak encryption algorithms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the relevant policies and work instructions. A review of the configurations on the end devices shows that both secure and insecure services are running in parallel. An automated check with a tool like `ssh-audit` would reveal weak configurations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure protocols MUST be used for the configuration and maintenance of ICS components. The information MUST be transmitted securely.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of secure protocols such as SSHv2, SFTP, or HTTPS with TLS 1.2 or higher is mandatory for all maintenance access. Wherever possible, insecure protocols are disabled on the ICS components. Compliance is ensured through regular configuration checks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies from the configuration files of the ICS components that insecure services are disabled. They check the configuration of the secure protocols used for compliance with internal requirements. A network scan (`nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 <host>`) can be used to check the TLS configuration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of secure protocols is enforced by central network policies (e.g., firewall rules) that block insecure ports. The configuration of the secure protocols is hardened by allowing only strong cipher suites and current protocol versions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Explicit rules are implemented on the firewalls between the OT zones that block ports like 21 (FTP) and 23 (Telnet) and only allow 22 (SSH) and 443 (HTTPS) to the management interfaces. The configurations of SSH and web servers are managed via central configuration management tools to ensure uniformly strong cryptography.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rule set to verify the blocking of insecure protocols. They check the central configuration templates (e.g., in Ansible or Puppet) for the correct configuration of the cipher suites. Compliance can be automatically checked with a script that connects to the services and verifies the negotiated algorithms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity and authenticity of the communication endpoints are ensured by means of a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) and certificate-based authentication. All maintenance communication is centrally logged and monitored for anomalies. The use of unauthorized protocols is detected and blocked by an Intrusion Detection System (IDS).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal PKI is used to issue client and server certificates for all maintenance access. Instead of passwords, certificate-based SSH authentication is enforced. All network traffic to the maintenance interfaces is routed through a central gateway that records the traffic and forwards it to an IDS for analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the PKI and checks the certificate issuance policies. They check the SSH server configuration to ensure that only certificate-based authentication is allowed (`ssh -o PasswordAuthentication=no <host>`). The IDS rules and alarms are checked for their effectiveness in detecting insecure protocols.

controls.title: Deactivation or uninstallation of unused services, functions, and interfaces (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only obviously unnecessary services, such as a web server on a PLC, are deactivated on some critical components on an ad-hoc basis. A systematic approach to system hardening does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The deactivation is done manually by a technician who happens to come across an unnecessary service. There is no documentation or checklist for this process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a port scan on a sample of devices and finds numerous open, but unused ports (e.g., for FTP, Telnet, or SNMP) on most systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During commissioning, a manual check of the running services and open ports is carried out. Unneeded services are deactivated based on a general checklist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A technician goes through a simple checklist and deactivates services manually via the device's configuration interface. This process is ticked off in the commissioning protocol.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the system hardening checklist. They compare the results of a port scan with the services marked as deactivated in the checklist and find broad agreement, but note that the process is not tracked over time.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All unused services, functions, and interfaces of the ICS components MUST be deactivated or uninstalled. This process is a fixed, documented part of the standard procedure for commissioning and hardening of components.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each component type, there is a specific hardening guide that specifies exactly which services, protocols, and physical ports (e.g., USB) are to be deactivated. The implementation is documented in the commissioning protocol.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the hardening guides and compares them with the configuration of a live component. The audit can be supported by a script that reads the device's configuration and compares it with the specification, or by a validated port scan (`nmap -p- <host>`) and comparison of the open ports with an allowlist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each type of ICS component, a hardened "Golden Image" or a baseline configuration is created and managed, which contains only the absolutely necessary services and functions. Regular automated configuration checks are performed to detect deviations from this baseline.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The baseline configurations are versioned in a central repository (e.g., Git). A configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible) is used to check the compliance of the systems with the baseline and to report deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the baseline configurations stored in the repository. They review the reports of the configuration management tool for reported deviations. The effectiveness can be verified by running a compliance scan (`ansible-playbook --check hardening.yml`) during the audit.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: System hardening is fully automated. An application whitelisting solution prevents the execution of any unauthorized software or services. The integrity of the system configuration is continuously monitored in real time, and any deviation from the secure baseline automatically triggers an alarm and, if necessary, initiates a corrective action.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like AppLocker or a specialized industrial endpoint security product is operated in enforcement mode. A File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) system monitors critical configuration files. A Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) playbook reacts to FIM alarms by reverting the unauthorized change or isolating the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and rules of the application whitelisting and FIM solutions. They try to launch an unauthorized application or change a configuration file to test the system's reaction. The review of the automation rules in the SOAR system verifies the response mechanism.

controls.title: Network segmentation (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single firewall separates the entire OT network from the office IT network as a whole. Within the OT network, there is no further segmentation; all ICS components are in a single, flat network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple firewall with a rule like `allow from OT-subnet to any` and `deny from IT-subnet to OT-subnet` is implemented. Internal communication in the OT network is unrestricted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network topology and the ruleset of the central firewall. A ping scan from one ICS component to another in a different plant section confirms the lack of internal segmentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ICS components are located in a separate VLAN or physical network, which is segregated from the office IT. Basic firewall rules exist, but they are often too permissive (e.g., "allow established connections" in both directions).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separation is achieved via VLANs on the switches. The firewall rules between the VLANs are kept simple and have not been adjusted since the initial setup. The documentation of the allowed communication relationships is incomplete.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the switch configurations to verify the VLAN separation. They analyze the firewall ruleset for excessively permissive rules. They compare the allowed rules with the actually required communication paths and uncover unnecessary permissions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ICS components MUST be separated from office IT. If ICS components depend on other services in the network, this SHOULD be sufficiently documented. ICS components SHOULD communicate with other ICS components as little as possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The separation between IT and OT is achieved through a demilitarized zone (DMZ) according to the Purdue Model. Communication between ICS components is reduced to the technologically and procedurally necessary minimum. Necessary communication relationships (e.g., to a Historian in the DMZ) are documented in a network diagram.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the network diagram and the firewall rules with the actual network topology. They check whether the documentation of the communication relationships is complete and up-to-date. Using a network monitoring tool or by analyzing Netflow data, it is verified that only the documented communication paths are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The OT network is consistently segmented into zones and conduits (data flows) according to the Purdue Model. Strict firewall rules based on the "deny-by-default" principle are enforced between the zones. All allowed communication relationships are documented in detail, justified, and regularly reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Internal segmentation firewalls or Layer 3 switches with Access Control Lists (ACLs) separate the process control level (Level 1) from the supervisory level (Level 2). The firewall rules only allow the specific protocols and ports necessary for the process (e.g., allow Modbus/TCP from HMI to PLC).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a detailed review of the zone-based firewall ruleset. They verify that a documented justification exists for each rule. Automated firewall ruleset analysis tools can be used to identify inconsistent or risky rules (`fw-policy-validator --policy policies.yml`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Micro-segmentation is implemented to isolate individual or small groups of ICS components from each other. Communication policies are enforced directly on the endpoints or on intelligent switches. All network traffic is continuously monitored for policy violations and suspicious activities, and anomalies are automatically blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Network Access Control (NAC) solution or a host-based firewall on the ICS components (if supported) is used to enforce micro-segmentation. An industrial Intrusion Detection/Prevention System (IDS/IPS) monitors east-west traffic within the zones and actively blocks attack attempts or unauthorized communication patterns.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the micro-segmentation solution and the host-based firewall rules. They attempt to establish an unauthorized connection between two segmented devices to test the effectiveness of the block. The logs and alerts of the IDS/IPS are analyzed to verify its detection and response capabilities.

controls.title: Creation of data backups (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data backups are created occasionally and on an ad-hoc basis, but not systematically before every system change. The process is manual and depends on the individual technician.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A technician manually copies the configuration file to their laptop before a major update. There is no central directory or uniform naming convention for backups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions several technicians about their backup practices and receives inconsistent answers. A review of recent system changes shows that for most of them, no backups exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a documented instruction to create a backup before every change. However, this is not technically enforced or verified. The backups are stored locally or on a general network drive.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the change management form, there is a checkbox for "Backup created". The backups are stored in a central folder, but without a strict naming convention or version control.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the change management documents and the associated backup files. They find that although backups are created, their completeness and recoverability are not checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Backups MUST be created before every system change on an ICS component. This is a formal, required step in the change management process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Creating the backup is a fixed item on the checklist for system changes. The backup files are stored in a dedicated, secure location with a clear versioning and naming convention. The successful creation of the backup is noted in the change ticket.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly selects several completed changes and verifies that a corresponding, correctly named backup exists in the central repository for each one. They check if the process was followed consistently for all changes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The backup process is partially automated. Backups are stored in a central, secured, and versioned location. Regular tests are performed to ensure that the backups can be successfully restored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central backup system compatible with ICS components (e.g., Auvesy-MDT AutoSave or Versiondog) is used to schedule and manage backups. At least once per quarter, a restore test is performed and logged for a selection of critical systems in a test environment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and logs of the central backup system. They request the logs of the latest restore tests. Recoverability can be automatically checked by comparing the hash of the restored backup with the original.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire backup and recovery process is fully automated and integrated into the change management workflow. A system change can only proceed in the workflow after a successful and verified backup has been confirmed. The integrity of the backups is checked regularly and automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The change management tool (e.g., ServiceNow) is integrated with the backup system via an API. When a change for an ICS component is approved, the tool automatically triggers a backup. The backup system reports the success and the integrity hash back to the change ticket, which unlocks the next step in the workflow.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automated workflow in the change management tool and the API integration with the backup system. They check if a change ticket is actually blocked when the backup fails. The system's audit trail (`backup-cli show-log --target plc456 --since 30d`) provides a complete record of all performed backups.

controls.title: Protection against malware (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Antivirus software is installed on some engineering workstations connected to the ICS network. The ICS components themselves are unprotected. Signatures are updated irregularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The company's standard antivirus software is installed on the Windows-based maintenance laptops. There are no special configurations or exceptions for ICS software, which occasionally leads to performance issues.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks a sample of maintenance laptops and verifies the installation and update status of the antivirus software. They find that the ICS endpoints, such as PLCs and HMIs, have no protection of their own.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Antivirus software is used on ICS components where technically possible and approved by the manufacturer. Signature updates are distributed manually and at irregular intervals, often via USB sticks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A technician downloads the latest virus scanner signatures, checks them on a separate system, and then distributes them to the ICS HMIs during scheduled maintenance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the manufacturer's approval list for antivirus software. They check the signature status on several systems and find that it is often several weeks or months old.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ICS components SHOULD be protected from malware by suitable mechanisms. If an antivirus program is used for this purpose, the program and the virus signatures SHOULD always be up-to-date after approval by the manufacturer. If resources on the ICS component are insufficient or real-time requirements could be jeopardized, alternative measures such as isolating the ICS component or the production network SHOULD be taken.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For Windows-based HMIs, a manufacturer-approved antivirus solution with central management is used. Signature updates are tested for compatibility with the ICS software in a test environment before distribution. For low-resource devices like PLCs, endpoint protection is omitted; instead, network segmentation is strengthened as a compensating measure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the anti-malware policy, which differentiates between various component types. They check the configuration of the central antivirus management and the update logs. They verify the network configuration to confirm the isolation of the unprotected components.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Application whitelisting is used as the primary protective measure on ICS endpoints, as it is better suited for static environments than signature-based antivirus software. All removable media are scanned for malware in a kiosk system before use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An application whitelisting solution is introduced in audit mode to create a baseline of all legitimate applications. After a test phase, it is switched to enforcement mode. A dedicated computer in the DMZ serves as a gateway for USB sticks, formatting them and scanning for viruses before data can be copied onto them.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and rules of the application whitelisting system. They attempt to run an unauthorized portable application from a USB stick and verify that it is blocked. They check the process and the technical controls at the kiosk system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A multi-layered defense-in-depth approach is pursued, combining network-based intrusion detection, application whitelisting on endpoints, and file integrity monitoring. Security events from the OT environment are correlated and analyzed in a central SIEM.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An industrial IDS monitors network traffic for known exploits and anomalous behavior. Application whitelisting and FIM are active on all endpoints with an operating system. Logs from all security components (firewall, IDS, endpoints) are sent to a SIEM that uses ICS-specific correlation rules to detect complex attacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the overall system. They check the configuration and the rules of all involved security components. By simulating an attack (e.g., with an ICS-specific exploit framework in a test environment), the entire detection and alerting chain from the endpoint via the network to the SIEM is verified.

controls.title: Maintenance of ICS Components (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security updates are applied reactively and without structure, often only after a vulnerability has become known or an audit has resulted in a finding. Pre-installation testing does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a technician learns about an important patch, they download it and install it directly in the production system, often with the risk of compatibility issues.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the installed patch levels on several systems with the list of security patches released by the manufacturer and finds a significant and inconsistent backlog.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process exists for tracking manufacturer-released patches. The patches are applied during planned maintenance windows, but pre-testing is minimal or limited to basic functional tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: One person is responsible for subscribing to the manufacturers' security advisories. The installation of patches is tracked in an Excel spreadsheet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the list of tracked and installed patches. They determine that a basic process exists, but the risk assessment and testing depth are insufficient.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When maintaining an ICS component, the current and approved security updates SHOULD always be applied. Updates for the operating system SHOULD only be installed after approval by the ICS component manufacturer. Alternatively, the update SHOULD be tested in a test environment before being deployed on a production ICS component. For critical security updates, maintenance SHOULD be carried out at short notice.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a dedicated test environment that is representative of the most critical production systems. All patches are tested here for functionality and stability before being released for production. The release process is documented. Critical patches go through an accelerated emergency change process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the patch management process, including the test and release procedures. They request test logs for recently rolled-out patches. They verify the process for emergency patches.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated, representative test environment exists to validate all patches before production deployment. A central patch management system is used to monitor the status of all systems and distribute updates in a controlled manner. A risk-based approach is used to prioritize the urgency of patch installation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like WSUS (for Windows) or a specialized OT Patch Management System is used to get an overview of the patch status and to control distribution. Vulnerabilities are assessed with a CVSS score to objectify prioritization.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the patch management system and the reports on the patch status of the facilities. They analyze the process for risk assessment and prioritization of patches. Compliance can be checked by an automated scan (`Get-HotFix` on Windows systems) and comparison with the approved baseline.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for validating and distributing patches is largely automated. Virtual patching is used via an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) to immediately protect vulnerable systems until a permanent patch can be safely installed. A complete, automatically maintained inventory of software and patch levels is kept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A SOAR playbook automates the patch management process: New manufacturer advisories are automatically imported, the asset inventory is checked for affected systems, a ticket is created, and the patch is automatically rolled out in the test environment. An industrial IPS is updated with specific rules for known vulnerabilities to block attack attempts (virtual patching).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the SOAR playbook for patch management. They review the configuration and effectiveness of the virtual patches in the IPS by running a (harmless) test exploit against a protected system. Comparing the automatically maintained software inventory with manufacturer advisories provides insight into the completeness of the process.

controls.title: Proper commissioning of ICS components (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: New components are occasionally checked for updates, but there is no formal baseline or defined target state. Integration into management processes such as monitoring or backup occurs late and manually, if at all.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A technician connects a new device and commissions it to get the plant running. The configuration and securing are supposed to be done 'later', which is often forgotten.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the software version of a recently commissioned component with the manufacturer's current version and finds that outdated versions are in use. The component is not recorded in either the asset inventory or the backup system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During commissioning, a manual checklist is used to ensure that components are updated to the latest version and basically configured. Integration into management processes is a separate, manual step.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a commissioning checklist that includes items like 'Update firmware' and 'Change default password'. After the device is running, an email is sent to the responsible departments to include it in monitoring and backup.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks to see the completed checklists for new components. They find that the basic steps are performed, but the integration into downstream processes is error-prone and often delayed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before ICS components are commissioned, they SHOULD comply with the current, internally approved firmware, software, and patch level. New ICS components SHOULD be integrated into the existing operational, monitoring, and information security management processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The commissioning process is formalized. A device is only considered ready for operation once it has been verified to comply with the internal baseline and has been successfully registered in all relevant systems (asset inventory, backup, monitoring, patch management). This process is documented and approved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the protocol of the commissioning process. They verify on a random basis in the respective management systems (e.g., backup server, monitoring console) whether the new component has been correctly recorded and is being actively managed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Commissioning is a formal, gated process. A component can only be switched to production once its compliance with the security baseline has been technically verified and the successful integration into all relevant management systems has been confirmed. This process is supported by a workflow system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A change management ticket for commissioning goes through several phases (e.g., 'physical installation', 'basic configuration', 'security scan', 'integration tests'), each of which must be approved. A compliance scan automatically checks adherence to hardening guidelines.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the commissioning process mapped in the workflow system. They check the results of the compliance scan and the approval steps in the ticket. The automation can be verified by running the compliance scan script (`./check_compliance.sh --host <new_device>`) during the audit.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The commissioning process is fully automated. A new device connected to the network is isolated in a quarantine network by a Network Access Control (NAC) solution. There, it is automatically scanned, patched to the correct baseline, configured, and only moved to the production network after successful verification.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NAC solution detects new devices based on their MAC address and assigns them to the quarantine VLAN. An automation server (e.g., Ansible Tower) runs playbooks to inventory, harden, and configure the device. After successful completion of all steps, the NAC solution assigns the correct production VLAN to the device.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the automated process demonstrated live by connecting a new device. They review the configuration of the NAC solution, the quarantine network, and the automation playbooks. The system logs (`cat /var/log/nac.log | grep <mac_address>`) provide a complete record of the entire process.

controls.title: Protection of external interfaces (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Physical ports such as USB on the control cabinets are freely accessible. Only the external network connection is filtered by a general firewall.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are no policies regarding the handling of physical interfaces. Technicians regularly use private USB sticks to transfer data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts a site inspection and finds that all USB and serial ports on the devices are freely accessible and active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unused physical ports are disabled in the device's BIOS/UEFI where possible. There is an organizational directive not to use private removable media.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During commissioning, the use of USB ports is disabled in the BIOS. Compliance with the ban on private USB sticks is not technically enforced.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly checks the BIOS/UEFI settings of some devices. They find that the implementation is inconsistent and that there are no technical controls for the use of removable media.

parts.name: statement
