parts.prose: Externally accessible interfaces SHOULD be protected against misuse. This includes both physical (e.g., USB, serial) and network interfaces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a clear policy on which interfaces are necessary for operation. All others are systematically disabled, either in the BIOS/UEFI or at the operating system level. The use of removable media is only permitted for authorized and tested devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to be shown the policy for the protection of interfaces. They check the configuration on multiple devices to verify the systematic deactivation of unnecessary ports. This can be done by physical inspection and checking the operating system configuration (`lsusb`, `dmesg`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Technical controls are used to enforce port security, for example, through a central device control solution that only allows authorized USB devices. Network access from external interfaces (e.g., remote maintenance access) is strictly controlled via a dedicated, hardened access gateway.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An endpoint security solution with a device control module is used to enforce a whitelist of allowed USB devices (e.g., by serial number). Remote maintenance access is handled exclusively via a bastion host in a DMZ.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the device control solution. They attempt to connect an unauthorized USB device and verify that access is blocked. They analyze the network architecture and the configuration of the remote maintenance gateway.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For any required data transfer to or from an external network, a dedicated security solution such as a data diode is used. All activities on external interfaces are logged and actively monitored for anomalies. Physical access to ports requires two-person control or explicit, time-limited authorization.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A data diode ensures that data can only flow in one direction (e.g., out of the OT network). A PAM system is used to control access to physical ports: A technician must request access to a USB port via the PAM system, which is then granted for a limited time. All connection attempts are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the implementation of the data diode. They check the configuration and logs of the PAM system for port control. They verify the authorization process and the subsequent automatic locking of the port after the time expires.

controls.title: Use of secure protocols for the transmission of measurement and control data (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure protocols are only used for data transmission leaving the OT network towards the IT network. Within the OT network, unsecured, cleartext-based industrial protocols such as Modbus/TCP or S7 protocol are the norm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An OPC server collects data via insecure protocols and makes it available to a historian in the IT network via a secure interface (e.g., HTTPS). The communication between the PLCs and the OPC server is unprotected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network traffic in the process network (east-west traffic) and finds that control commands and measurement values are transmitted unencrypted. This can be demonstrated with a tool like Wireshark and a corresponding protocol dissector.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For new installations, secure industrial protocols (e.g., OPC UA with Security, PROFINET with Security) are preferred. As a compensating measure for the unavoidable use of insecure protocols in the existing network, network segmentation is used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a new plant section, OPC UA with activated encryption and authentication is used throughout. In the old plant section, which continues to use Modbus/TCP, a strict firewall rule is implemented that restricts Modbus traffic to the absolute necessary endpoints.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the OPC UA communication in the new plant section. They check the firewall rules that isolate the insecure traffic in the old plant section. They determine that a mixed operation is taking place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Measurement or control data SHOULD be protected from unauthorized access or modification during transmission. For applications with real-time requirements, it SHOULD be checked whether this is feasible. If measurement or control data is transmitted over public networks, it SHOULD be adequately protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A risk analysis is performed to determine which data streams need to be encrypted. For critical control data, OPC UA with Security or a VPN tunnel (e.g., IPsec) is used between the components. Feasibility is verified by performance tests under load to ensure compliance with real-time requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the risk analysis and the protective measures derived from it. They check the configuration of the secure protocols or VPN connections. They request to be shown the results of the performance tests.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Secure protocols are implemented and enforced throughout the entire OT network. A Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is used to manage certificates for device authentication and encryption. The network is monitored for the use of insecure protocols.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal PKI issues certificates for all communicating ICS components. OPC UA is consistently operated with certificate-based authentication. A network monitoring tool issues an alert if traffic is detected on ports of insecure protocols such as Modbus (502).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the PKI configuration and the certificates on the end devices. They check the alerting rules in the network monitoring system. A network capture (`tcpdump -i any port 502`) should no longer show any traffic and can verify compliance.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All process data communication is encrypted and authenticated with strong, modern cryptography. The integrity of the data is continuously verified. The security layer is hardware-accelerated if necessary to meet real-time requirements without performance degradation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Protocols such as CIP-Security or TSN (Time-Sensitive Networking) with integrated security mechanisms are used. Special network cards or FPGAs in the ICS components handle the encryption and decryption to offload the CPU. Integrity is ensured by Message Authentication Codes (MACs) in each packet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the high-level architecture and the specifications of the secure protocols used. They check the configuration of the hardware-accelerated security modules. Integrity can be tested by deliberately inserting a manipulated packet in a test environment to verify that the system detects and discards it.

controls.title: Communication in case of an incident (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The responsible employees have each other's private mobile phone numbers, but there is no formal plan or alternative technical means.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the event of a failure of the main communication system (VoIP, email), employees are expected to call each other on their private mobile phones.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the emergency communication plan and learns that none exists. The effectiveness depends on chance (battery charged, phone available, number known).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a documented out-of-band communication plan, for example, based on a phone tree via the public telephone network. No dedicated alternative devices have been procured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A printed list with the phone numbers of the crisis management team and a defined call sequence is available in the control room.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to be shown the emergency communication plan and the phone list. They note that the plan has not been practiced and its effectiveness is not guaranteed in the event of a public telephone network failure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There SHOULD be alternative and independent communication options that can be used in the event of an incident in order to remain capable of acting. This requirement is considered a defined state for the increased protection need.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Several satellite phones or a dedicated radio network (e.g., DMR or TETRA) are procured for the crisis management team. The handling of these devices is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests a demonstration of the alternative communication devices. They check the documentation and instructions for the employees. They verify that the devices are functional (e.g., charged batteries, valid SIM cards).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The alternative communication system (e.g., satellite phones, radio network) is regularly tested as part of emergency drills. The responsible employees are trained in its use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An emergency drill is held at least twice a year, during which all communication must be handled exclusively via the alternative system. The participation and results of the drill are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to be shown the logs and the 'lessons learned' from the last emergency drills. They question some members of the crisis management team about the handling of the devices to check the success of the training.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Several redundant and technologically diverse communication channels are available (e.g., satellite, private radio network, and mobile). The availability and functionality of these systems are continuously and automatically monitored. The activation of emergency communication is part of an automated emergency plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central system monitors the status of the primary communication channels. In the event of a failure, an alert conference is automatically convened via the alternative system (e.g., a mass notification app that uses multiple channels in parallel). The satellite phones are kept in docking stations with trickle charging and automatic functional testing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the redundant communication systems and the configuration of the monitoring system. They request a live demonstration of the automatic alerting chain by simulating a failure. Checking the system logs (`cat /var/log/comm_monitor.log`) verifies the continuous monitoring.

controls.title: Security Tests (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Vulnerability scans are performed occasionally, but not on a fixed schedule and without a formal process for remediating the found vulnerabilities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IT administrator performs a network scan once a year with a freely available tool. The report is sent by email, but the follow-up of the results is not regulated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the results of security tests and receives an outdated scan report. A comparison of the found vulnerabilities with the current system state shows that most have not been remediated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Regular, automated vulnerability scans are performed. There is a process for reviewing the results, but it is not always consistently followed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a quarter, an authenticated vulnerability scan is performed on the Windows-based systems in the OT network. The results are discussed in a meeting, and tickets are created for critical findings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the scan reports from the last few quarters and the associated meeting minutes and tickets. They find that although a process exists, the remediation deadlines are often exceeded and medium-priority findings are ignored.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be checked with regular security tests whether the technical security measures are still effectively implemented. The security tests SHOULD not be carried out during ongoing plant operation. The tests SHOULD be scheduled for maintenance periods. The results SHOULD be documented. Identified risks SHOULD be assessed and treated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an annual plan for security tests, which includes vulnerability scans and configuration reviews. These tests are performed during planned maintenance windows to avoid disrupting operations. For each finding, a risk assessment process is carried out, and a measure is recorded in the risk treatment plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the annual plan for security tests and the reports of the last tests performed. They check whether the results are fully documented and whether the identified risks are assessed according to a defined process and tracked in the risk treatment plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to vulnerability scans, penetration tests are regularly conducted by specialized external third parties. The test scope includes network, application, and physical security aspects of the ICS environment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every two years, a white-box penetration test for the entire OT network is commissioned. The results are presented to management, and the remediation of findings is tracked in a dedicated project.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the scope of work, the final report, and the action plan of the last penetration test. They verify the implementation status of the derived measures. The check can be automated by executing a check from the pentest report to verify remediation, e.g., `curl -k -X POST https://vulnerable-app/api/endpoint`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A continuous security validation program is established, which uses techniques like Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS) to constantly test defensive measures against the latest attacker tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). A "Purple Team" approach is followed, where attack (Red) and defense (Blue) teams collaborate to improve the security posture in real-time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A BAS platform executes daily automated, yet safe, attack sequences against the OT environment to uncover gaps in detection and response. In regular purple team exercises, the Red Team simulates a specific attack path while the Blue Team attempts to detect and stop it. The results are directly used to improve rules and configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and reports of the BAS platform. They request the logs and results of the last purple team exercise. They verify that the identified gaps have been demonstrably closed by reviewing the corresponding configuration changes (e.g., new SIEM rule, hardened firewall policy).

controls.title: Trusted Code (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Technicians are instructed to download updates only from the manufacturer's official website. However, there is no technical verification of the downloaded files.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The source of the firmware is not systematically checked. There is a risk that tampered files from phishing emails or unofficial forums may be used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews technicians about the firmware download process and determines that no integrity checks are performed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a manual process to compare the cryptographic hash value (e.g., SHA-256) of downloaded files with the value published by the manufacturer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A technician copies the hash value from the manufacturer's website and manually compares it with the hash value of the downloaded file, which is calculated using a tool like `certutil` or `sha256sum`. This step is ticked off on a checklist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the checklist for software updates. They ask a technician to demonstrate the hash comparison process. The auditor notes that the process is error-prone and depends on the diligence of the individual employee.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Firmware updates or new control programs SHOULD ONLY be installed if their integrity has been verified beforehand. They SHOULD only originate from trusted sources.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process is defined: Software may only be obtained from official manufacturer portals. Before each installation, the provided hash value (preferably SHA-256 or better) of the file must be checked. The successful comparison is documented in the change ticket.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the change management logs and verifies that for each installed update, there is documented proof of the integrity check. The verification can be automated by a script that calculates the hashes of the firmware files in the repository (`sha256sum firmware.bin`) and compares them with the documented values.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All software and firmware is digitally signed by the manufacturer. The ICS component itself or the programming device automatically verifies this signature before the installation is permitted. Unsigned code is rejected by default.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Only components and programming tools that support the verification of digital signatures are procured. The manufacturers' public keys are securely managed within the company. The installation process fails if the signature check yields a negative result.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the signature verification process demonstrated by attempting to install unsigned firmware or firmware signed with an incorrect key. They verify that the process fails and an appropriate error message is generated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A secure supply chain is established. All software is obtained from a private, trusted repository where its integrity and signature have been independently verified beforehand. The ICS hardware itself supports a secure boot process, which ensures that only signed and trusted firmware and operating systems can be loaded at startup.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All updates are procured centrally, analyzed for malware in a sandbox, signature-checked, and only then transferred to the internal repository. The ICS components are configured (e.g., in the BIOS/UEFI) so that Secure Boot is enabled and only works with the company's own keys or the trusted manufacturer keys.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the software procurement and verification process for the internal repository. They check the Secure Boot configuration on the end devices. They attempt to start the device with an unsigned boot medium to verify that the boot process is aborted.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
An ICS component is an electronic component that controls or regulates a machine or plant. It is therefore part of an Industrial Control System (ICS) or, more generally, Operational Technology (OT). These components can be Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs), sensors, actuators, a machine, or other parts of an ICS.
Due to the high availability requirements typical in the OT environment and the often extreme environmental conditions such as heat or cold, dust, vibration, or corrosion, ICS components have always been designed as robust devices with high reliability and a long service life.
ICS components are normally configured or programmed using special software from the respective manufacturing company. This is done either via so-called programming devices, e.g., as an application under Windows or Linux, or via an engineering station, which loads the application programs into the programmable logic controllers.
The role of the information security officer for the field of industrial automation is named differently depending on the type and orientation of the institution. Another designation besides ICS Information Security Officer (ICS-ISB) is also Industrial Security Officer.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is to secure all types of ICS components, regardless of manufacturer, design, purpose, and location. It can be used for a single device or a modular device composed of multiple components.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module IND.2.1 General ICS Component is to be applied to every ICS component used in the information network.
The requirements have been developed for a general ICS component. For more specific ICS components, e.g., sensors and actuators or machines, additional modules such as IND.2.3 Sensors and Actuators and IND.2.4 Machine are available. They describe requirements that go beyond the general requirements of this module and must also be implemented.
The module contains no organizational requirements for securing an ICS component. For this, the requirements of the module IND.1 Process Control and Automation Technology must be implemented.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insecure system configuration
parts.prose:
The default configuration of ICS components is often designed to ensure that the components function correctly and are easy to commission. Security mechanisms often play a subordinate role. For example, in the default setting, all services, protocols, and ports are often switched on and remain active even if they are not used. Similarly, preset permissions often remain unchanged.
It is easy for attackers to take over and manipulate these ICS components. It is also possible that in an attack, the insecure system configuration is exploited to use the ICS component as a starting point for further attacks. As a result, institution-critical information can be leaked or the entire operation of the institution can be impaired.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficient user and authorization management
parts.prose: Some ICS components have their own user and authorization management. If this is inadequately designed, it can happen that employees share accounts or that authorizations of former employees or service providers are not deleted. Overall, this can allow unauthorized persons to access ICS components.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Insufficient logging
parts.prose: With ICS components, logging is often limited to process-relevant events. Data relevant to information security is often not recorded. This makes it difficult to detect security incidents and impossible to reconstruct them afterwards.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Manipulation and sabotage of an ICS component
parts.prose:
The diverse interfaces of ICS components lead to an increased risk of manipulation for IT systems, software, and transmitted information. Depending on the motivation and knowledge of the attackers, this can have local but also cross-site effects. In addition, status and alarm messages or other measured values can be suppressed or altered.
Manipulated measured values can lead to incorrect decisions by ICS components or the operating personnel. Manipulated systems can be used to attack other systems or sites or to cover up an ongoing manipulation.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Use of insecure protocols
parts.prose: The protocols used in the industrial control systems environment sometimes offer no or only limited security mechanisms. Technical information such as measurement and control values are often transmitted in plain text and without integrity protection or authentication. Third parties with access to the transmission medium can then read and change the contents of the communication or inject control commands. In this way, actions can be provoked or operations can be directly influenced. An attack at the protocol level is also possible if the ICS component is otherwise securely configured and has no vulnerabilities itself.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks
parts.prose: Attackers can impair the operation of ICS components through DoS attacks. In processes that run under real-time conditions, even a shorter disruption can lead to a loss of information or control.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Malware
parts.prose: The threat from malware is also becoming increasingly severe for industrial control systems. Infection opportunities arise from interfaces to office IT (vertical integration) and to the outside world. But mobile devices such as service notebooks or removable media used for programming and maintaining ICS components also pose a threat. The latter can also be used to introduce malware into isolated environments.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Spying on information
parts.prose:
ICS components often contain detailed information about the regulated or monitored process or procedure. This information can also be partially reconstructed from other transmitted values such as measurement or control data. The same applies to control programs or parameters.
Third parties could obtain trade secrets here in the context of industrial espionage, e.g., recipes, procedures, or other intellectual property. They can also obtain information about the functioning of an ICS component and its security mechanisms, which they can use for further attacks.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Manipulated firmware
parts.prose: In ICS components, in addition to the application program, the operating system (firmware) can also be changed. This can allow manipulated software to enter the system. The internal memories could be altered by attackers via a compromised programming device, a local data interface (e.g. USB), or another existing network connection. A software update could also have been manipulated on its way from the manufacturing company to the operator. Finally, an ICS component could arrive at the operator with already compromised firmware, for example, in the case of a manipulated supply chain or a purchase from insecure sources. This gives attackers the opportunity to change or falsify processes and procedures.

controls.title: Advanced System Documentation for Programmable Logic Controllers (S) [OT Operations (Operational Technology, OT)]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Backups of PLC configurations and control programs are made only irregularly and often only after a change. Documentation of changes is only done for systems considered critical and is often incomplete.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Backups are stored manually on local disks or network drives without a uniform naming convention or structure. Documentation is often limited to handwritten notes or comments in the code.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the administrators about the procedure for changes. They check whether any backups exist for a randomly selected PLC and whether the last change is traceable. Significant gaps in the backup history and documentation will likely be found.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Regular backups of configurations and control programs are created for all PLC systems. Basic documentation of changes exists, but it is not standardized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a fixed schedule for creating backups (e.g., monthly). Changes are recorded in a simple logbook or a table, noting the date and type of change.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of regular backups for all PLC systems. They check whether a change log is maintained and whether the entries can be matched to the actual changes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Control programs and configurations are systematically backed up before changes are made. All changes to the configuration or replacement of PLC components are documented in a standardized and traceable manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central repository (e.g., a version control system like Git or a specialized PLC management tool) is used to store configurations and control programs. Each change is recorded with a timestamp, the person responsible, and the reason for the change. The documentation includes configuration parameters, network addresses, and the physical location of the components.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the change log of the PLC systems. They check on a sample basis whether for recent changes (e.g., within the last 6 months), corresponding backups exist from before the change and complete documentation is available after the change. It is verified whether the procedure for backup and documentation is known to all relevant employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for backing up and documenting PLC configurations is integrated into a change management system. Before each change, a backup is automatically created and versioned. The documentation is managed centrally and is accessible to all relevant stakeholders.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized system for configuration management of industrial plants is used. Every change requires a ticket in the change management system, which documents the approval process. The documentation is automatically updated when new components are added or configurations are changed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the change management process demonstrated. They check whether a corresponding backup and version history exists in the repository for a selected change and whether the linked documentation is consistent. Automated check: A script could query the management tool's API and compare the timestamps of the last configuration changes with the timestamps of the last backups.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of PLC configurations is automated, from backup and versioning to deployment. The integrity of the backed-up configurations and control programs is regularly checked automatically. Regular restoration tests from backups are conducted to ensure their functionality.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The integrity check is performed by automatically comparing checksums of the running configuration with the version stored in the repository. Deviations trigger an alarm. The restoration tests are carried out in a test environment or using digital twins to avoid impacting production operations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the automatic integrity checks and the results of the restoration tests. They verify that the system correctly raises an alarm in case of an unexpected configuration change (baseline deviation). Automated check: A script verifies the monitoring system's configuration for active integrity checks and inspects the log files for successful restoration test runs.

controls.title: Time Synchronization (S) [OT Operations (Operational Technology, OT)]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system time on PLC systems is only set manually as needed. There is no central time source, which leads to significant time discrepancies between different systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators set the time manually during commissioning or after a power outage, often based on an inaccurate reference such as a wristwatch. No time synchronization protocol like NTP is configured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor queries the system time on multiple PLC systems and compares them with each other and with a reference time. Significant deviations are expected. It is checked whether time synchronization services are configured and active, which is not expected to be the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A time synchronization service is enabled on most PLC systems. However, there is no uniform, central time source, or the sources used are not classified as trustworthy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Some PLCs are configured to use an internal server (e.g., a domain controller) as a time source, while others use public NTP servers on the internet. The configuration is not uniform and the accessibility of the time sources is not monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the time configuration on a sample of PLC systems. It is found that different or unauthorized time sources are configured. It is checked whether a process for monitoring time accuracy exists, which is not expected to be the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system time of all Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) is automatically synchronized via a central and trusted time source. A defined process for configuring and monitoring time synchronization is in place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central NTP (Network Time Protocol) server is operated in the OT network, which serves as the sole time source for all PLC systems. This NTP server, in turn, synchronizes with a secure, external time source (e.g., DCF77 or GPS-based). The PLC systems are configured to exclusively use this internal NTP server as their time source.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of a sample of PLC systems to ensure they point to the central NTP server. The configuration of the NTP server itself is checked for its synchronization source and security settings. Log files are reviewed to confirm successful synchronization.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The time synchronization of the PLC systems is carried out via a redundant pair of central, internal NTP servers. The accuracy of the system time and the state of the synchronization service on each PLC are actively monitored, and an alarm is triggered in case of significant deviations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two or more internal NTP servers are operated in a redundant configuration (e.g., stratum hierarchy). A monitoring system regularly queries the time offset and the status of the NTP client on the PLCs. Thresholds for maximum deviations are defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the redundant configuration of the NTP infrastructure. The configuration of the monitoring system and the alarm thresholds are checked. A test case can be simulated (e.g., stopping an NTP server) to verify the correct functioning of redundancy and alarming. Automated check: A script queries the NTP status (e.g., with `ntpq -p` or equivalent commands) on the PLCs and compares the offset with the defined thresholds.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Time synchronization is carried out using a secure protocol (e.g., NTS - Network Time Security or NTP with symmetric keys) to prevent manipulation of the time data. The central time sources are physically secured and use high-precision reference sources such as GPS with secured antennas.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: NTP authentication is configured between the central servers and the PLC clients to prevent spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks. For particularly time-critical processes, protocols such as PTP (Precision Time Protocol) are used. The GPS receivers for the time reference are protected against interference signals (jamming/spoofing).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of NTP authentication on the servers and clients by inspecting the configuration files and keys. The physical security of the time sources (e.g., GPS receivers) is inspected. It is checked whether the protocols meet the time accuracy requirements of the controlled processes.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
A Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) is an ICS component. It performs control and regulation tasks in Operational Technology (OT). The boundaries between different device classes and designs are fluid; for example, a Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) can also take on the functions of a PLC, or a Programmable Automation Controller (PAC) can attempt to combine the advantages of a PLC and an industrial PC. However, the PLC is still the classic automation device, so in this module the terms PLC, RTU, and PAC are used synonymously.

A PLC has digital inputs and outputs, a real-time operating system (firmware), and other interfaces for Ethernet or fieldbuses. The connection to sensors and actuators is made via the analog or digital inputs or outputs or via a fieldbus. Communication with process control systems usually takes place via the Ethernet interface and IP-based networks.

The possible implementations are diverse; a programmable logic controller can be used as an assembly, a single device, a PC plug-in card (slot PLC), or as a software emulation (soft PLC). The most common are modular programmable logic controllers, which are assembled from various functional plug-in modules. Increasingly, other functions such as visualization, alarming, and logging are also being taken over by the PLC.

Due to the high availability requirements typical in the OT environment and the often extreme environmental conditions such as heat or cold, dust, vibration, or corrosion, ICS components have always been designed as robust devices with high reliability and a long service life.

A PLC is normally configured or programmed using special software from the respective manufacturing company. This is done either via so-called programming devices, e.g., as an application under Windows or Linux, or via an engineering station, which distributes the data over a network.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is to secure all types of programmable logic controllers, regardless of manufacturer, design, purpose, and location.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module IND.2.2 Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) is to be applied once to each PLC component.

This module is to be applied to secure all types of programmable logic controllers and devices with similar functions. It supplements the module IND.2.1 General ICS Component. This must also be taken into account during application.

The module contains no organizational requirements for securing an ICS component. For this, the requirements of the module IND.1 Process Control and Automation Technology must be implemented. Likewise, the area of functional safety is not covered. For this, the module IND.2.7 Safety Instrumented Systems must be applied.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Incomplete documentation
parts.prose: Programmable logic controllers are often incompletely documented, so not all product functions are known. The information about the services, protocols, and communication ports used, as well as about authorization management, is often particularly incomplete. However, this makes the threat analysis more difficult, because interfaces, functions, and security-relevant mechanisms are overlooked. Potential threats cannot then be taken into account. In addition, it is not possible or only to a limited extent to react to new vulnerabilities if they are not recorded.

controls.title: Installation of sensors (B) [Operational Technology (OT) Operations, Maintenance Personnel]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only critical sensors are specifically installed to be robust, while for others, the specific environmental conditions are not systematically considered. There is no uniform installation process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installation is carried out ad-hoc by the on-site personnel. Protective housings or special fastenings are only used where failures have occurred in the past. For most sensors, the standard mounting materials are used without further inspection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly selects several sensors not classified as critical and checks their installation for suitability for the local environment (e.g., protection against moisture, vibration). It is checked whether a documented installation standard exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All sensors are installed according to a basic, general installation instruction that requires a baseline robustness. However, there is no specific adaptation to special environmental conditions such as strong corrosion or extreme temperatures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard installation kit is used for all sensors of one type. The manufacturer's instructions are followed, but no additional hardening for the specific operating environment is carried out. The installation is marked as complete when the sensor provides a signal.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies whether the basic installation instructions have been followed for all installed sensors. It is checked whether there are areas with special environmental requirements and whether the sensors installed there can withstand them, even if no specific adaptation has been made.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Sensors MUST be installed in a suitable manner. Sensors MUST be sufficiently robust. They MUST be able to measure reliably under the existing environmental conditions such as high heat, cold, dust, vibration, or corrosion. The installation procedure is defined and is applied in a repeatable manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before installation, an assessment of the environmental conditions at the installation site is carried out. Based on this, sensors with a suitable IP protection rating and temperature range are selected. The installation follows a documented checklist, which also includes correct alignment and fastening.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation for the assessment of environmental conditions and the installation checklists. At several locations, random checks are carried out to verify whether the installed sensors meet the documented requirements and whether the installation was carried out according to the checklist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The installation of the sensors is carried out according to a documented, site-specific concept that takes into account the respective environmental conditions in detail. After installation, the functionality is verified and logged under real conditions. The robustness of the installation and the condition of the sensors are regularly checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The environmental conditions are not only assessed once, but are periodically monitored to detect changes. The acceptance protocols of the installation are centrally archived. Regular maintenance plans include a visual inspection of the sensor installations for corrosion, contamination, or damage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and implementation of the site-specific installation concept. The acceptance protocols and the evidence of regular checks of the sensor installations are reviewed for plausibility and completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire lifecycle of the sensor installation, from selection and assembly to decommissioning, is managed by an automated system. Sensor data (e.g., internal temperature, voltage) is continuously correlated with environmental parameters to predictively identify deviations and potential wear (Predictive Maintenance). The assembly is supported by special, calibrated tools and automatically verified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An asset management system for OT components manages all information about the sensor installation, including environmental conditions and maintenance history. Analysis software monitors the measured values and internal status parameters of the sensors and automatically generates maintenance tickets for anomalies. Digital torque wrenches are used for assembly, and their values are logged directly in the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown a demonstration of the predictive maintenance process in the analysis tool used. It is checked whether the asset management system is up-to-date and whether the automated verification steps of the assembly are completely documented. It is proven that alarms about anomalies lead to concrete measures.

controls.title: Calibration of sensors (S) [Maintenance Personnel]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Calibrations are only performed in case of obvious measurement errors or sporadically upon request. Documentation is largely missing and access to the calibration functions is not explicitly protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Calibration is performed reactively when a process error occurs. The maintenance personnel often use the manufacturer's default passwords to access the calibration menus. The results, if any, are recorded in local notebooks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the sensor calibration process. It is checked on a random basis whether access to calibration functions (e.g., on a device on site) is open. Calibration protocols for critical sensors are requested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All sensors deemed necessary are calibrated, but not necessarily at fixed, defined intervals, but at the discretion of the maintenance personnel. Access to calibration is generally protected (e.g., by a password), but the documentation of the calibrations is incomplete or not standardized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a general instruction to calibrate critical sensors 'regularly'. The maintenance team uses a shared password to access the calibration functions. The results are recorded in a simple list or table, which is not always consistently maintained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the password protection for the calibration function demonstrated on a sample sensor. The maintained lists for calibration are inspected and checked for completeness and traceability for a specific period.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a defined process that specifies which sensors must be calibrated, when, and how. The performed calibrations are documented in a traceable manner. Access to the calibration of a sensor MUST be protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For critical sensors, fixed calibration intervals are set in a maintenance plan. The documentation is done in a standardized form that includes the sensor, date, results (before/after), and the performing technician. Access to calibration functions requires an individual, non-trivial password or a physical safeguard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the maintenance plan and the standardized calibration protocols for several sensors. It is checked whether the intervals are being adhered to. The protection of access to the calibration is verified on a random basis on one device.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If necessary, sensors SHOULD be calibrated regularly. The calibrations SHOULD be documented appropriately. Sensor calibration is performed according to established industry standards and at centrally planned intervals. The results are recorded and analyzed in a central system to detect trends or deviations (drift). Access to calibration functions is secured at multiple levels and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central calibration management system is used to manage planning, execution, and documentation. The calibration tools themselves are certified regularly. Access to calibration requires personalized authentication, and all changes are logged in the system with a timestamp and user account.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the functionality of the calibration management system demonstrated, in particular the trend analysis and access logging. It is checked whether the calibration tools have valid certificates. The access audit logs are examined for unauthorized attempts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Sensors with self-calibration or self-monitoring functions are preferentially used. The calibration process is largely automated, and the results are automatically compared with the process control systems. Any manual access to calibration functions triggers a security alarm and requires two-factor authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When purchasing, preference is given to sensors that have an internal reference for continuous self-monitoring. Where possible, calibration is initiated remotely and automatically via the management system. A SIEM system correlates manual calibration access with maintenance tickets; access without a ticket is treated as a security incident.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the process of automated calibration and self-monitoring in the system. It is demonstrated that a manual calibration access that is not legitimized by a ticket triggers an alarm in the SIEM. It is checked whether self-calibration criteria are considered during procurement.

controls.title: Wireless Communication (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only for sensors classified as highly critical are unused wireless interfaces such as WLAN or Bluetooth manually deactivated on occasion. There is no company-wide policy or systematic review.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Deactivation is done on an ad-hoc basis by technicians when they are aware of the interface. Often, wireless interfaces remain active because they are enabled in the factory state and their existence is not known. No checks are carried out.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a critical sensor and checks its configuration for active, unused wireless interfaces. It is asked whether there is an instruction or a process for deactivating interfaces.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general instruction to deactivate all unused communication interfaces on sensors. However, implementation is not systematically controlled or documented. Wireless interfaces are often left in their factory state if they are not actively used for configuration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When commissioning sensors, the checklist includes an item 'deactivate unnecessary interfaces'. This is often checked off as a matter of course without explicitly checking the wireless interfaces. Bluetooth or NFC are frequently overlooked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the manufacturer's documentation of an installed sensor with its live configuration to identify active but unused interfaces. The commissioning checklists are checked for plausibility.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A binding policy exists that mandates the deactivation of all communication interfaces on sensors that are not essential for operation. Deactivation is systematically checked during commissioning. All unused communication interfaces, especially wireless management interfaces, SHOULD be deactivated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A configuration policy (hardening guideline) for sensors is maintained, which explicitly requires the deactivation of WLAN, Bluetooth, NFC, and other unused ports (e.g., USB). Compliance with this policy is checked and documented using a protocol during commissioning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the hardening guideline for sensors. The documented implementation is checked using the acceptance protocols. It is verified on a random basis on some sensors whether the configuration complies with the policy. An automated test could use `nmap` or similar tools on known IPs to check for open ports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Wireless management interfaces such as Bluetooth, WLAN, or NFC SHOULD NOT be used. The configuration of the sensors, including the deactivation of unused interfaces, is managed by configuration management tools and regularly checked automatically. Any deviation from the target configuration (e.g., an activated WLAN interface) is reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central configuration management or OT asset management system is used to distribute configuration baselines for sensor types and to scan their compliance regularly. An alert is generated when a scan detects an unexpectedly active interface.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration baseline in the management tool. The history of the compliance scans and the response to generated alarms are checked. An automated test could query the API of the management tool and evaluate the compliance reports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If not absolutely necessary for operation, wireless interfaces are physically removed or permanently deactivated at the hardware level (e.g., by removing the module or potting the port). In addition, continuous monitoring of the frequency spectrum is used to actively detect unauthorized activated or introduced wireless interfaces.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During procurement, care is taken to ensure that sensors without unnecessary wireless interfaces are available. If modules are present, they are removed before installation. In security-critical areas, Wireless Intrusion Detection Systems (WIDS) are used, which monitor permitted wireless traffic and sound an alarm for new or unknown transmitters (e.g., an activated Bluetooth adapter).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement policies for criteria for minimizing interfaces. It is physically checked on a random basis on sensors whether modules have been removed. The configuration and alarm history of the WIDS are inspected to assess its effectiveness.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Sensors are transducers designed as electronic components with a microprocessor and software, which convert a physical quantity into an electrical output value. This value is provided as a standardized unit signal (often 4 to 20mA, 0 to 10V) at a serial interface or as digital information transmitted via a fieldbus or Ethernet protocols. In addition to the measured values, transducers often provide interfaces for diagnostics and parameterization. Thus, a sensor can have other interfaces besides an electronic output value, e.g., WLAN, Bluetooth, or WirelessHART interfaces for parameterization and diagnostics.
There are many different sensors on the market, for example, to measure physical quantities. The functional scope and performance of a sensor vary greatly depending on the task. The spectrum ranges from sensors that only provide measured values and do not need to be configured, to those that enable calibration, configuration, or data preprocessing up to complete signal processing (intelligent sensors, smart sensors).

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of this module is to secure all types of sensors, regardless of manufacturer, design, purpose, and location. It can be applied to a single sensor or a related sensor assembly.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module IND.2.3 Sensors and Actuators is to be applied once to sensors and actuators.
This module is to be applied to secure sensors. It supplements the higher-level module IND.2.1 General ICS Component and presupposes it.
Simple sensors without configuration interfaces or more complex processing logic are not covered by the module. This is because for these, the possible protective measures are limited to securing access to the sensor and monitoring whether it is active.
The module also does not address the protection of complex wireless sensor networks. It only describes how individual sensors can be secured. Furthermore, no security requirements for process control and automation technology are described. For this, the module IND.1 Process Control and Automation Technology must be implemented.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficient security requirements in procurement
parts.prose:
Sensors for ICS components in industrial environments are often exposed to special conditions that can impair safe operation. Examples include extreme heat, cold, humidity, dust, vibration, or caustic or corrosive atmospheres. Often, several factors occur simultaneously. Such harmful environmental influences can cause the sensors of ICS components to wear out faster and fail earlier or measure incorrect values.
Due to a lack of awareness of the risks and for cost reasons, information security is often not considered during procurement and installation. As a result, sensors can sometimes contain serious vulnerabilities that are very costly to fix later.

controls.title: Remote maintenance by machine and plant manufacturers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Remote maintenance is carried out on an ad-hoc basis and without central guidelines. Agreements with service providers exist only in isolated cases and the monitoring of remote maintenance activities takes place only sporadically, if at all.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, individual departments or technicians use remote maintenance access at their own discretion. There are no uniform tools or security protocols. Often, standard access provided by the manufacturer is used without further security measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews with various technicians and department heads, the auditor determines that no uniform regulation for remote maintenance exists. A sample of remote maintenance access points shows different and often insecure configurations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an initial draft of a policy for remote maintenance that prescribes basic security requirements such as the use of VPNs. There are simple contractual agreements for all service providers. However, the implementation of the policy is not systematically checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A basic requirement to use VPN connections for every remote maintenance is communicated. However, the configuration of the VPNs and the monitoring of activities are left to the individual teams and are not standardized.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a basic remote maintenance policy. By examining the network configurations and contracts, it is determined that the basic requirements (e.g., mandatory VPN) formally exist, but their uniform and correct implementation is not ensured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There MUST be a central policy for the remote maintenance of a machine. It MUST regulate how the respective remote maintenance solutions are to be used. The policy MUST also specify how communication links are to be protected. Furthermore, it MUST also describe which activities are to be monitored during remote maintenance. It MUST be agreed with service providers how they may use the information stored in the machine.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The defined policy is communicated to all relevant employees and service providers. The implementation includes the standardization of VPN clients and profiles, the setup of logging for remote maintenance sessions, and the inclusion of corresponding clauses in all new and existing service provider contracts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence, content, and approval status of the central remote maintenance policy. On a sample basis, it is verified that the communication links are protected according to the policy (e.g., by checking the VPN configuration), that the monitoring logs exist, and that the contracts with service providers contain the required agreements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined processes, technical measures are implemented to ensure that other IT systems or machines of the institution CANNOT be accessed via the remote maintenance of a machine. The monitoring of remote maintenance activities is automated and proactively generates alarms for suspicious patterns.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Remote maintenance access is routed through a dedicated jump host or gateway. Strict firewall rules and network segmentation isolate the maintained machine from the rest of the production and office network. SIEM rules are used for automated analysis of the monitoring logs and for alerting on anomalies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the network architecture and firewall rules to confirm the effective isolation of remote maintenance access. It is checked whether a dedicated jump host exists. In addition, the configuration of the SIEM system and the generated alarms are analyzed to assess the effectiveness of the automated monitoring.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All remote maintenance access is exclusively via a central, hardened gateway with multi-factor authentication (MFA). Every session is fully recorded (video and keystroke logging). Access rights are granted according to the just-in-time (JIT) principle only for the duration of the required work and are automatically revoked afterwards. Any data access by the service provider is logged in detail and automatically examined for signs of data exfiltration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution is used to control, monitor, and record all remote maintenance access. The PAM solution is integrated with the Identity and Access Management (IAM) system for MFA and with the SIEM for advanced threat analysis. JIT access is requested and approved via automated workflows.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the PAM solution, including MFA integration and JIT policies. Session recordings are checked on a random basis. The automated data access analysis reports are evaluated. It is checked whether an automated process exists to verify the implementation, e.g., `check-pam-config --policy company-remote-access`.

controls.title: Operation after end of warranty

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The issue of post-warranty operation is only addressed reactively in case of failures or problems with individual, particularly critical machines. There is no systematic planning or contractual provision.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If a machine fails outside of its warranty period, ad-hoc support is sought from the manufacturer or third-party providers. This often leads to longer downtimes and incalculable costs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews and analysis of maintenance tickets that no proactive process exists. Random checks of machines whose warranty has expired show that for most of them, no support contracts are in place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an awareness of the need for post-warranty support. Shortly before the warranty expires, attempts are made on a case-by-case basis to arrange support services with suppliers. The process is reactive and not embedded in an overall strategy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list of machine warranty expiration dates is maintained manually. Based on this list, suppliers are contacted as needed to inquire about support options.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the list of warranty expiration dates. It is noted that while efforts are made to conclude follow-up contracts, this is not done systematically and often occurs too late.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A process MUST be established to ensure that the machine can continue to be operated securely beyond the warranty period. For this purpose, further support services MUST be contractually agreed upon with the suppliers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal lifecycle management process for machines is introduced. This process is stored in the asset management system and automatically triggers a notification, e.g., six months before the warranty expires. Subsequently, a decision on continued operation is made by default and a follow-up contract is concluded if necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and documentation of the established process. Using the asset management system, random checks are performed to see if the process was initiated in a timely manner for machines with expiring warranties and whether corresponding support contracts exist or a documented decommissioning decision is available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The established process is extended to include a regular reassessment of the machine's security status and the quality of supplier support. The process also defines alternative strategies if the original supplier can no longer offer support, e.g., a third-party support evaluation or planning for in-house maintenance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The lifecycle process is supplemented with regular (e.g., annual) review dates for all machines out of warranty. For critical machines, alternative support providers are evaluated in advance, and their contact information is stored in a database.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the process documentation for the existence of alternative strategies. The records of regular reassessments and the database of alternative support providers are reviewed to verify proactive planning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The lifecycle process is fully integrated into the organization's asset and risk management. Decisions on continued operation are based on a formal risk assessment. The organization maintains a knowledge base with maintenance instructions and has a contingency plan for each critical machine, which includes, for example, stocking critical spare parts or alternative production methods to ensure business continuity even in the event of a complete failure of supplier support.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The asset management system is linked to the GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool. Risk assessments are initiated automatically. A detailed Business Continuity Plan (BCP) exists for every machine of the highest criticality level. Spare parts inventories are digitally managed and automatically trigger orders when minimum stock levels are breached.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of the systems (Asset Management, GRC, BCM). It is checked whether formal risk assessments and associated BCPs are available for a selection of critical machines. The effectiveness of the contingency plan is validated by checking spare parts inventories and the documentation of alternative procedures. An automated check could be: `check-asset-bcp --criticality=high`.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
A machine is a technical device that performs automated tasks. A typical example is a machine tool that processes workpieces in a predefined way. It is controlled by an IT system that specifies the corresponding work instructions and steps. Such machines are also referred to as automated machines or automata.
Machines are usually designed by mechanical engineers and equipped with specific predefined functions. However, the machine operator can also determine the parameters according to which it should work. For example, shapes to be milled or calibrations for certain materials can be set. To enable operators to change the parameters, machines have various interfaces, e.g., for removable media, specialized programming devices, or network access.
Mechanical engineers often also offer remote maintenance services to detect early wear and tear or to be able to react quickly in problem situations.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module describes how electronically controlled, semi- or fully-automatic machines (e.g., CNC machines) can be secured, regardless of manufacturer, design, specific purpose, and location.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module IND.2.4 Machine is to be applied once to each machine.
This module supplements the higher-level module IND.2.1 General ICS Component and requires its implementation. Furthermore, requirements are only defined for machines whose internal structures an institution cannot access.
No security requirements for process control and automation technology are described either. For this, the module IND.1 Process Control and Automation Technology must be implemented. Likewise, the area of functional safety is not covered. More details can be found in the module IND.2.7 Safety Instrumented Systems.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Failure or malfunction due to insufficient maintenance
parts.prose: If machines are not maintained regularly, they may stop functioning correctly or fail completely at an early stage. Malfunctions can, for example, endanger employees or significantly impair production.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Targeted manipulations
parts.prose: If the interfaces of a machine are inadequately protected, the machine can be manipulated, e.g., via local programming devices or network services. This can damage workpieces or cause entire product series to be faulty. An attack could also damage the machine itself, resulting in economic loss.

controls.title: Inventory and Documentation

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic inventory list of all hardware and software components belonging to the SIS is maintained. However, the documentation may be incomplete regarding connections, roles, and detailed configuration information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Inventory is typically managed in spreadsheets or simple lists. The lists are maintained manually and on an as-needed basis, but without a formalized review and update process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks for the existence of the inventory lists. Through random checks, the correctness of the recorded components (e.g., type, manufacturer) is verified, but it is not expected that all connections or responsibilities are documented without gaps.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All hardware and software components belonging to the SIS, relevant information, connections, as well as roles and responsibilities MUST be separately recorded and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The documentation is maintained in a dedicated system, e.g., a Configuration Management Database (CMDB) or a specialized asset management tool for OT. A defined process exists for recording and updating, which is followed for every change to the SIS.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the completeness and currency of the SIS documentation. It is verified that the hardware and software versions, the network connections (including ports and protocols), and the assigned roles (administrator, operator) are documented for all components. This can be done by comparing with the actual system and reviewing change requests.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The SIS documentation is maintained in a central, versioned system and is regularly checked for correctness. Dependencies between the components and to external systems are clearly depicted. The documentation is formally audited at least annually.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The CMDB is linked with a passive network scanning tool to automatically compare the recorded data with the actual state. Deviations trigger a notification to the responsible staff. The documentation also includes lifecycle data such as installation date and end-of-life date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the version history of the documentation and the logs of the regular checks. It is verified that a process for automated deviation detection is implemented and that detected deviations are tracked. The depiction of dependencies is checked for plausibility.

controls.title: Purpose-bound use of hardware and software components

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A written policy exists that prohibits the non-intended use of SIS components. Compliance with this policy is communicated to staff and relies on employee discipline.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is part of the general security training for personnel working with the SIS. However, there are no technical controls to enforce compliance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the policy and randomly asks employees if they are aware of the rule regarding purpose-bound use. Compliance itself is difficult to audit.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hardware and software components that belong to or are used in connection with the SIS MUST NOT be used for unintended purposes. This is ensured through organizational regulations and basic technical measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On engineering stations and other operator devices, unnecessary programs are uninstalled and ports (e.g., USB) are disabled if they are not required for operation. Internet access from these systems is blocked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly inspects SIS components such as engineering stations to check if unauthorized software is installed or unnecessary interfaces are active. Firewall or proxy configuration files are reviewed to verify that internet access is blocked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The purpose-bound use of SIS components is enforced through technical controls such as application whitelisting. Deviations from the defined baseline configuration are detected and reported.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An application whitelisting solution is implemented on engineering stations and HMI systems, which only allows the execution of explicitly approved applications. The system configuration is hardened and monitored using File Integrity Monitoring (FIM).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the application whitelisting solution and the list of approved applications. It is verified that an FIM system is active and that alarms are generated and processed for configuration changes. A test could involve attempting to run an unapproved application.

controls.title: Changing the application program on the logic system

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A list of individuals authorized to make changes to the logic system's application program exists. Changes require informal approval, e.g., via email.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access to the engineering station is protected by a password known among the authorized individuals. A key switch on the logic system must be physically operated to enable program changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks for the existence of the list of authorized persons. It is verified whether the physical protection mechanism (key switch) is present on the logic system and if its use is regulated in an operating instruction.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Existing protection mechanisms on the logic system MUST be activated. If this is not possible, alternative measures MUST be taken. Application programs on the logic systems MAY ONLY be changed or released for transfer by authorized persons.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access to programming functions is protected by individual user accounts and passwords. Changes require documented approval as part of a change management process. The physical key switch on the controller is kept in the 'protected' position by default.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether individual accounts have been set up for all authorized persons. Using random samples from the change management system, it is verified that changes to the application program have followed the defined approval process. The state of the physical key switch is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Changes to the application program require formal approval according to the four-eyes principle. All activated protection mechanisms on the logic system are documented and their effectiveness is regularly reviewed. Every change is automatically logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A change management tool is used to enforce the approval process. The engineering software or the logic system itself creates an audit log of all program changes, including user, timestamp, and type of change. This log is stored centrally and in a tamper-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the change management tool and the audit logs for completeness and tamper resistance. It is verified that the logs are regularly analyzed to detect unauthorized changes.

controls.title: Anchoring Information Security in Functional Safety Management

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All processes and responsibilities regarding the information security of SIS SHOULD be clearly defined. In Functional Safety Management (FSM), these SHOULD be described and named specifically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The FSM manual is supplemented with a chapter on information security (cybersecurity). It describes the roles (e.g., ICS-ISB), responsibilities, and the security processes relevant to the SIS (e.g., patch management, user administration). The interfaces between safety and security processes are defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the FSM manual and related process documentation. It is verified that responsibilities for information security are clearly assigned and that the security processes consider the specific requirements of SIS.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Information security is an integral part of all phases of the FSM lifecycle, from specification to decommissioning. Regular, institutionalized meetings between safety and security managers ensure coordination.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Checklists for safety assessments are expanded to include specific cybersecurity aspects. Every requirement change in the FSM undergoes a mandatory security assessment. The minutes of the coordination meetings between the teams are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether a security assessment has demonstrably taken place for safety assessments and change requests. The minutes of the coordination meetings are reviewed to verify the actual collaboration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Functional Safety Management and the Information Security Management System (ISMS) are fully integrated and supported by common tools. A change in one area automatically triggers a predefined workflow in the other area.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An integrated GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool is used to manage both safety and security requirements. For example, identifying a new cyber threat automatically triggers a reassessment of the associated safety instrumented function (SIF) in the FSM process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and workflows in the GRC tool. Using examples, it is traced how changes in one management system (e.g., ISMS) automatically and demonstrably lead to activities in the other system (FSM).

controls.title: Emergency Management of SIS

parts.name: statement
