parts.prose: The remote maintenance solution is built as a redundant cluster (firewalls, VPN concentrators, jump servers) to ensure high availability. The systems are housed in their own rack in an OT data center. The power supply and network connections are also separate from the office IT.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the complete physical separation of the infrastructure. The high-availability configuration is checked, e.g., by a simulated failure of a component. The documentation of the emergency concept for the remote maintenance solution is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The OT has a completely air-gapped or physically separate remote maintenance infrastructure, including its own, dedicated, and redundant internet connection. All hardware components are specially designed for this purpose and are tamper-proof. All software is minimal, hardened, and its integrity is continuously verified by boot-time and run-time measurements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Hardware Security Modules (HSM) are used to secure keys and Trusted Platform Modules (TPM) in the servers are used to ensure a 'Trusted Boot' process. Each component of the solution monitors the integrity of the other components. Any unauthorized change leads to the immediate shutdown of the service and an alarm.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the hardware-based security functions (TPM, HSM). The 'Measured Boot' process is analyzed. An attempt is made to make an unauthorized change to a system component to test the effectiveness of the integrity monitoring and the automatic response.

controls.title: Logging of the contents of remote access sessions in the OT (H) [Planners, Data Protection Officers]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic system event logs (e.g., Windows Event Logs) are collected on the target systems. However, they are not centrally aggregated or correlated with the remote maintenance session, which makes subsequent analysis difficult.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Standard logging is enabled on the target systems. In the event of an incident, the logs must be collected manually from many different systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor selects a past remote maintenance ticket and asks to trace the associated activities in the logs. This reveals the high manual effort and the difficulty of correlation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the remote maintenance of OT applications or systems, logging SHOULD be extended so that all activities can be traced completely and promptly. For this purpose, in addition to the logging of events and session data, the contents of remote maintenance access SHOULD also be logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A session recording solution is implemented. This records the user's entire screen interaction during the remote maintenance session as a video. The recordings are centrally archived in a tamper-proof manner and linked to the session's metadata (user, time, target system).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the architecture of the session recording solution. They randomly select some past sessions and view the corresponding video recordings to assess their completeness and quality. It is checked whether the storage location of the recordings is sufficiently protected against manipulation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to video recording, all commands entered in command-line interfaces (CLI) are logged as text. The recordings are securely stored, timestamped, and linked to the corresponding access request ticket. They are regularly checked on a random basis by security personnel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The PAM or session recording solution used is configured not only to create a video but also a searchable text file of all input and output on the shell (Keystroke Logging). A process for the regular, random review of these logs is defined and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the keystroke logging. They search the logs for specific commands that were executed during a past session. They review the documentation of the random checks by the security team.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to video and text recording, detailed logging of GUI interactions (e.g., opened windows, clicked buttons, changed values in form fields) is also implemented. All logs are sent in real-time to a central SIEM system, where they are analyzed for policy violations and anomalous behavior.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An advanced PAM solution that supports 'Process- and Application-Level' logging is deployed. The logs are sent to the SIEM in CEF or LEEF format. In the SIEM, correlation rules are created that, for example, trigger an alarm if a user attempts to change a critical system setting or if unexpectedly large amounts of data are transferred.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the detailed GUI logging. They have the correlation rules in the SIEM that are applied to the remote maintenance logs shown to them. A test session is conducted in which a rule violation is provoked to verify the alerting in the SIEM.

controls.title: Technical control of remote maintenance sessions (H) [Planners, Data Protection Officers]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic Intrusion Detection System (IDS) monitors network traffic for known malicious signatures. However, it lacks specific context of the remote maintenance session or the allowed commands and can therefore hardly distinguish legitimate from malicious maintenance activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A network IDS sensor is placed at the gateway to the OT zone. It generates many general alarms that are often difficult for OT personnel to interpret.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the IDS alarms during a known maintenance window and finds that the alarms are too generic to allow for specific control of the session.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: OT remote maintenance sessions SHOULD be continuously regulated by a technical solution in addition to observation (IND.3.2.A10). Activities at the command level (manual and automated commands) SHOULD be technically monitored and, if necessary, automatically blocked. Additionally, sessions SHOULD be monitored across components, and an alarm SHOULD be triggered in case of anomalies in user behavior (e.g., a sudden increase in communication volume).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Privileged Session Management (PSM) solution or a host-based IDS is used. Blacklists of known dangerous commands (e.g., 'shutdown', 'format') are defined, which are blocked upon entry or require additional confirmation. Basic behavioral rules are configured in the SIEM, which, for example, trigger an alarm in case of unusually high network traffic from a maintenance session.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the command blacklists. In a test session, an attempt is made to execute a blocked command. The configuration of the behavior analysis rules in the SIEM is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Privileged Session Management (PSM) solution acts as a proxy that actively filters the data stream. It can filter commands not only based on blacklists but also on more complex rules. It can detect and report anomalous behavior, e.g., access to unauthorized file paths or unusual login times.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The PSM solution is configured to block not only individual commands but also command chains or commands with specific parameters. Profiles for normal user behavior are created (e.g., 'User A normally only accesses database X'). If user A accesses another system, an alarm is triggered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the advanced filter rules in the PSM solution. A test scenario is carried out that triggers a behavioral anomaly (e.g., access to a forbidden configuration file) to test the alerting.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The PSM solution enforces a whitelisting approach for commands and processes. Only explicitly allowed commands and actions are permitted; all others are blocked by default. The system uses machine learning to create a baseline of normal user behavior for each role and triggers highly reliable alarms for any deviation. The cross-component session monitoring correlates activities on the jump server with events on the target system and network sensors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each role (e.g., 'PLC programmer', 'database admin'), a profile with the exactly allowed commands is created. The PSM system learns the normal behavior over a period of time and then flags deviations. Logs from the PSM, the target system (via agent), and network TAPs are correlated in the SIEM to detect complex attack patterns (e.g., an allowed command on the jump server triggers an unexpected network scan from the target system).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the command whitelists. An attempt is made to execute a harmless command that is not on the whitelist to verify the block. The quality of the machine learning baseline is assessed. A complex test scenario is run through to check the correlation in the SIEM.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
The operational technology (OT) of an institution often has a decentralized infrastructure. Different areas of OT can be geographically distant from each other. In addition, Industrial Control Systems (ICS) usually consist of a multitude of products from different manufacturers, i.e., different ICS components and IT systems for OT applications. Therefore, an institution's OT typically requires numerous remote maintenance access points.
These remote maintenance access points are often individual solutions in the form of individually assembled hardware and software components. Consequently, a variety of different techniques are used for OT remote maintenance. The lifecycles of the remote maintenance solutions usually correspond to those of the products being accessed, i.e., remote maintenance solutions for OT may be used for a much longer period than is common in IT. A wide variety of access points, services, and interfaces exist in parallel. The interfaces communicate using a wide variety of protocols.
Some plant components in OT are also implemented as a closed unit by the manufacturers (so-called package units). These plant components often contain several decentralized access points for remote maintenance, which the manufacturers have integrated ready for operation for their own access from the outset.
Remote maintenance access in an industrial environment is generally used by OT operations and maintenance personnel to configure, control, maintain, and repair OT components. Only in exceptional cases, e.g., in the event of malfunctions, do other employees use OT remote maintenance access points.
OT components are accessed via remote maintenance from various institutions. Not only the operator's internal personnel, but also external personnel from manufacturers, integrators, and service providers use remote maintenance access points.
Basically, remote maintenance access takes place in the security segment of an OT network in which the remote maintenance service is provided. The remote maintenance service then communicates from this segment with the target system to be maintained, e.g., with an ICS component.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to ensure the information security of remote maintenance in the industrial environment.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module IND.3.2 Remote Maintenance in the Industrial Environment must be applied once to the entire OT of an institution as soon as it contains remote maintenance capabilities. Whether further requirements for remote maintenance in the industrial environment must be defined, which cannot be listed in this module in a generally applicable manner, depends on the respective areas of application of the ICS. Depending on the area of application, the measures that should be implemented to meet the requirements may also differ.
To create an IT-Grundschutz model for a specific information domain, the entirety of all modules must always be considered. As a rule, several modules must be applied to the topic or target object.
This module covers
• the specific aspects of OT remote maintenance that go beyond the general administration of network components and IT systems via remote maintenance, and
• the specific aspects of OT remote maintenance that deviate from the general administration of network components and IT systems via remote maintenance.
The following contents are also important and are dealt with elsewhere:
• the general administration of network components and IT systems via remote maintenance by IT operations in office and building IT (see OPS.1.2.5 Remote Maintenance) (The requirements in this regard must also be fulfilled in OT in principle.)
• the general aspects of network architecture and design, as well as segmentation (see NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design)
• the individual aspects of the hardware and software components that make up the respective remote maintenance solution, e.g., network components, server and client systems, OT applications (The relevant modules must be modeled here.)
• the general aspects of logging (see OPS.1.1.5 Logging)
• the general aspects of outsourcing (see OPS.2.3 Use of Outsourcing)
• the general aspects of cloud-based remote maintenance solutions (see OPS.2.2 Cloud Use)
• the general aspects of web-based remote maintenance solutions (see APP.3.1 Web Applications and Web Services)
• the general aspects of securing ICS at the control level (see IND.1 Process Control and Automation Technology and IND.2.7 Safety Instrumented Systems)
This module does not cover
• the observation and operation of ICS at the process level, or
• controlling access via remote maintenance to ICS, e.g., starting or stopping plants. Such access can fundamentally cause personal injury and property damage on site!

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Incompletely documented remote maintenance access points in the OT
parts.prose:
Remote maintenance access points in an institution's OT are typically numerous and diverse. Furthermore, a large number of internal and external individuals access them. The management of remote maintenance access in an industrial environment is therefore inherently confusing and prone to errors. There is a greater risk than in office and building IT that the various access points are inadequately recorded and documented, i.e., they are not verifiable.
If unknown, open OT remote maintenance access points are not documented, operators cannot prevent access. As a result, unauthorized users can directly influence the physical processes of an ICS, which can lead to malfunctions of individual components, the shutdown of an entire production plant, and even dangers to the life and limb of on-site employees. If, for example, plants including decentralized components for remote maintenance are implemented as a complete system (package unit) by the manufacturing company, they are initially not subject to sufficient control by the operators. The operators must record each OT remote maintenance component individually and often actively reconfigure it.
If some OT remote maintenance access points are, for example, only recorded and documented decentrally, there is also the risk that necessary changes to individual access points will not be made or that changes that are made will not be traceable.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficient availability due to dependencies on office and building IT
parts.prose:
ICS are partially dependent on a completely uninterrupted flow of information. This applies in particular to all real-time data streams. Even very short interruptions in data availability, which can be tolerated in office and building IT, can be critical in an ICS. Furthermore, security vulnerabilities can arise from dependencies on networks, services, or IT systems. This is often overlooked during planning when an institution's OT and office and building IT communicate with each other.
If dependencies between OT and office and building IT are disregarded and security vulnerabilities are consequently not closed, security incidents can quickly spread to the entire OT.
If central components and services of the office and building IT are used for remote maintenance of the OT (cross-functional administration), coordination errors can also occur between the office and building IT and the OT. As a result, the remediation of critical errors in the OT's ICS can be delayed. An example is a central VPN gateway for remote access that is provided by an organizational unit outside the OT and is not operated in a coordinated manner, so that it is not available quickly enough when needed. The downtime of a plant can then be significantly extended.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Inadequate regulations for the use of OT remote maintenance access
parts.prose:
OT remote maintenance access points have a very large potential user base outside the operating institution. At the same time, the seamless availability of real-time data in an ICS is essential, while the availability of data in office and building IT is generally somewhat less time-critical. General regulations on how remote maintenance access is used for office and building IT are often unsuitable for OT or leave too much leeway.
If the use of OT remote maintenance access is inadequately regulated by contract, there is a lack of clear specifications on how to restrict the user group for each individual access point. The operators can then not control who uses their OT remote maintenance access. For example, access credentials can be passed on by integrators, manufacturers, and maintenance service providers to users who are unknown to the operators. This is not tolerable for an ICS.
If restrictive usage regulations specifically for OT are missing, operators also cannot adequately control how OT remote maintenance access is used. In the event of a (security) incident, for example, the (forensic) analysis is made more difficult because causes cannot be identified quickly enough. This can prolong costly production downtimes.
If OT remote maintenance access is provided and operated jointly with or by the office and building IT and this shared use of the access hardware or software is not clearly regulated, inconsistent configurations can occur. These then only meet the security requirements of the office and building IT, but not the different or additional security requirements of the OT.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Insufficient human control over OT remote maintenance sessions
parts.prose:
The data and configuration settings within an ICS, as well as on-site personnel, property, and production processes, can be endangered by any access from other zones that is not or is only inadequately controlled by internal on-site staff. In particular, the personnel of external maintenance service providers, integrators, and manufacturing companies have the necessary specialized knowledge of the plant, machine, or component to be maintained, but do not know what harmful effects the specific remote maintenance session can have on the overall system.
If the progress and content of OT remote maintenance sessions cannot be adequately controlled by the operators, then configuration errors with high risk potential, as well as unintentional or intentional misconduct by maintenance personnel, cannot be detected and traced quickly enough. This can lead to failures or manipulation of real-time data streams, or malware can spread unnoticed throughout the entire OT. The consequences can be harm to the life and limb of on-site operating personnel, or high financial damages from production downtimes up to the destruction of entire plants. Disclosure of trade secrets is also possible. In addition, the integrity of the manufactured products can be compromised, e.g., through manipulation of recipes, resulting in the production of scrap that may be difficult to detect. If defective products are not recognized as such, this can damage the institution's reputation.
An example is decentralized OT remote maintenance components within plants that are implemented as a complete system by manufacturing companies (package units). These remote access points are often designed in such a way that the manufacturing companies can access the plant at any time. If this happens without coordination with the operator's personnel, hazardous situations can arise in the current production process, for example.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Direct IP-based access to ICS from insecure zones
parts.prose:
The data within an ICS, as well as on-site personnel, property, and production processes, are fundamentally endangered by direct IP-based access options from other zones and networks. This is true, for example, due to the special patch cycles in OT, which can be significantly longer than in office IT. At the same time, remote maintenance access to an ICS is usually carried out from only partially trusted networks. Such networks include not only private networks of other institutions, but also other zones of the own network. Partially trusted zones within the own institution include, for example, those of the internal office and building IT or other zones of the OT network (e.g., for operations and production management with MES, ERP).
Direct access from other zones and networks to an ICS, e.g., via a local connection or VPN, can introduce malware and facilitate targeted attacks. As a result, there can be dangers to life and limb in the OT zones to be protected, the threat of high financial damages due to downtime, or the leakage of confidential information such as trade secrets.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Insecure alternative OT remote maintenance access for faults
parts.prose:
Especially in the event of disruptions, OT remote maintenance access points must be more reliable and powerful than those in office and building IT. In the industrial environment, alternative remote maintenance access points are therefore set up specifically for fast access. These ensure the operational capability of the ICS even if the respective primary access fails or is not performant enough to, for example, resolve critical error states on remote plants quickly enough. However, such alternative remote maintenance access points can be particularly vulnerable to an attack.
If a fast alternative remote maintenance access, e.g., via cellular network, is created, but it does not fully meet the institution's security requirements, then attackers can more easily penetrate the OT network.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Insecure design of OT remote maintenance access
parts.prose:
An ICS often has a decentralized infrastructure with numerous OT remote maintenance access points from different manufacturing companies. Both the confusingly wide distribution of the access points and the diverse proprietary remote maintenance solutions make it difficult for operators to adequately secure all OT remote maintenance access points centrally.
If OT remote maintenance access points are located in openly accessible areas, attackers can easily penetrate OT networks and carry out manipulations via these access points.
Even if OT remote maintenance access points are only protected by security components provided by the manufacturer and these do not meet the institution's security requirements, attackers can easily penetrate OT networks and carry out manipulations via these access points.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Outdated technical design of OT remote maintenance access
parts.prose:
Due to the long lifecycles in the industrial environment, it is not uncommon for there to be OT remote maintenance solutions that have been in use for ten years or longer and have security vulnerabilities due to their age. In addition, there are often historically grown special environmental conditions, such as the installation of remote maintenance access points in openly accessible areas.
If OT remote maintenance access points are not adequately secured due to long lifecycles, this facilitates unauthorized access to an ICS and also to other networks and systems inside and outside the OT. This makes manipulations possible that can lead to dangers to life and limb.
Furthermore, integrated remote maintenance access points in plants may have been unknown for many years. As a result of increasing dependencies on other networks and systems due to more recent technical changes, unauthorized access with critical consequences can then become increasingly likely.

controls.title: Network Security Policy (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the institution's general security policy, a specific security policy for the network MUST be created. It MUST describe comprehensible requirements and specifications on how to securely design and build networks. The policy MUST specify in which cases zones are to be segmented, which communication relationships and protocols are permitted, how traffic for administration and monitoring is to be separated, which cross-site communication is allowed, and what encryption is required. The policy MUST be known to all employees responsible for network design and MUST be regularly checked for correctness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy should be maintained in a central, version-controlled document management system (DMS). Communication to the responsible employees can be ensured through regular training and a commitment to acknowledge receipt by signature. Checklists can be created to verify implementation, which are used for every significant network change.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether an up-to-date, approved, and dated security policy for the network exists. It is verified that the policy covers the required aspects (zoning, segmentation, protocols, etc.). Furthermore, through interviews with network administrators and review of training materials, it is checked whether the policy is known to the relevant personnel and whether regular reviews take place and are documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network security policy is fully integrated into the change management process. Any deviation from the policy requires a formal, documented, and ISB-approved exception request. The policy is reviewed at least annually and whenever there is a significant change in the network infrastructure or threat landscape, and updated as necessary. The results of the review are documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Integration into the change management process is carried out through a suitably configured IT Service Management (ITSM) tool. Exception requests are managed via a standardized form in the ITSM tool. The annual review is entered as a recurring task in the task management of the ISB or the network team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation of the change management for the integration of the security policy. Change tickets and exception requests are checked on a random basis for correct processing and approval. The protocol of the last review of the policy is inspected and checked for completeness and comprehensibility of the results.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the security policy is continuously monitored by automated configuration and compliance management tools. Deviations from the defined target configuration automatically trigger an alarm or an incident management process. The policy is dynamically adapted based on current threat intelligence and the results of vulnerability scans and penetration tests.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Specialized Network Configuration and Change Management (NCCM) or Security Policy Management (SPM) tools are used. These tools are coupled with the SIEM system and the institution's threat intelligence feed. The dynamic adaptation of the policy follows a defined process that includes a risk analysis of the proposed changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and reports of the compliance management tool used. The configuration of the automated alerting in the SIEM system is verified. The process for dynamic adaptation of the policy is traced based on the documentation and random examples (e.g., after the publication of a critical vulnerability). An automated audit could parse the configuration backups of the network devices against the policy definitions and report deviations (`diff /config/backup/firewall.conf /policy/firewall_template.conf`).

controls.title: Documentation of the network (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A complete documentation of the network MUST be created. It MUST include a network map. The documentation MUST be sustainably maintained. The initial actual state recording, including network performance, as well as all changes made to the network, MUST be included in the documentation. The logical structure of the network MUST be documented, in particular how the subnets are assigned and how the network is zoned and segmented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The documentation should be maintained in a central system such as a wiki or a document management system (DMS) to ensure versioning and access control. Specialized tools such as Microsoft Visio or draw.io are suitable for creating network maps. Changes to the documentation must be part of the change management process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the network documentation and compares it with the actual configuration of randomly selected network components (e.g., switches, routers, firewalls). It is checked whether the documentation is complete (logical structure, subnets, zoning) and whether the last changes made have been comprehensibly documented. An automated check can verify the completeness of the IP address documentation by comparing the documented IPAM with a live scan of the network (`nmap -sL -n 192.168.1.0/24 | diff - documented_ips.txt`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network documentation is supported by automated tools that regularly capture the actual state of the network and compare it with the documentation. The documentation includes not only the logical and physical topology but also configuration details of the active network components and dependencies between services and network segments. Every change in the documentation goes through a formal approval process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools for network discovery and visualization are used (e.g., NetBox, SolarWinds Network Topology Mapper). These tools are configured to scan the network at regular intervals (e.g., nightly). The results are used to validate and update the manual documentation. The approval process is mapped via the ITSM tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration and reports of the automated discovery tools. It is verified whether a process exists to handle the detected discrepancies. The approval process for documentation changes is randomly checked using tickets and logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network documentation is fully automated and updated in real-time. It serves as a "Single Source of Truth" for all network operations and automation processes (Infrastructure as Code). The documentation is directly linked to Configuration Management (CMDB), IP Address Management (IPAM), and network automation workflows. Any manual change to a component that does not follow the defined IaC process is automatically detected, reported, and ideally reverted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A combination of tools such as NetBox (as a source of truth for IPAM/DCIM), Ansible/Terraform (for Infrastructure as Code), and a Git repository (for versioning configurations) is used. CI/CD pipelines are used to test and automatically roll out changes to the documentation/configuration. A Network Configuration and Change Management (NCCM) tool monitors configurations for unauthorized changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the CI/CD pipeline for network changes and the configuration of the automation tools. It is verified that the documentation in NetBox corresponds to the deployed state by comparing the live configuration of a component with the code used in the pipeline. The alarm logs of the NCCM tool are checked for unauthorized changes. An automated audit job could periodically query the API of the SoT tool and compare it with the live configuration of the devices.

controls.title: Requirement specification for the network (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the security policy for the network, a requirements specification MUST be created. This MUST be maintained sustainably. All essential elements for network architecture and design MUST be derivable from the requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirements specification is a separate, versioned document that translates the general provisions of the security policy into concrete, technical requirements. For example, it describes what bandwidths are needed for which connections, what redundancy levels are required for certain components, or which specific firewall rule sets should serve as a basis. This document serves as a basis for tenders and concrete planning tasks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence, timeliness, and completeness of the requirements specification. It is verified that the specification is based on the valid security policy and that the elements of the network architecture and design (e.g., network plans, firewall concepts) are traceably derived from this specification. This can be done by comparing the documents and interviewing the network planners.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements specification is maintained in a structured format (e.g., requirements catalog in a database or a specialized tool). Each requirement is uniquely identifiable, prioritized, and has a clearly defined responsible person. The specification is reviewed regularly, at least annually, and adapted to new business or security requirements. A formal process for incorporating new requirements is established.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools such as Jira or Confluence with special templates or dedicated requirements management tools are used to manage the requirements. New requirements are submitted via a ticket system and evaluated and approved by a defined body (e.g., architecture board).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process for managing requirements. Requirements from the catalog are selected at random and their history (creation, modification, approval) and their implementation in the network architecture are tracked. The minutes of the last review of the specification are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements specification is fully integrated into the enterprise architecture. Each requirement is linked to business processes and protection goals (traceability). Changes in business processes or risk assessment lead to an automated review of the affected network requirements. The fulfillment of the requirements is validated by automated tests as part of a CI/CD pipeline before changes go into production.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Enterprise Architecture Management tools (EAM tools) are used to model the link between business processes, applications, data, and the network infrastructure. The network requirements are maintained as artifacts in this tool. Test cases for validating the requirements are implemented in a test framework (e.g., Pytest with Batfish for network analysis) and integrated into the pipeline for network changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the EAM model for completeness and correctness of the links. Using an example (e.g., introduction of a new online service), the entire process from the business requirement to the technical implementation in the network infrastructure and the automated testing is traced. The results of the automated tests are inspected and evaluated. An automated audit could use the API of the EAM tool to check the consistency of the relationships.

controls.title: Network separation into zones (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire network MUST be physically separated into at least the following three zones: internal network, demilitarized zone (DMZ), and external connections. The zone transitions MUST be secured by a firewall. This control MUST follow the principle of local communication (allowlist). Untrusted networks (e.g., Internet) and trusted networks (e.g., Intranet) MUST be separated by at least a two-stage firewall structure. To separate the Internet and external DMZ in terms of network technology, at least a stateful packet filter MUST be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The physical separation is realized by using different, dedicated firewall systems or at least by dedicated physical interfaces on a firewall cluster for the respective zone. The two-stage firewall structure consists of an outer firewall to the Internet and an inner firewall to the internal network. The DMZ is located between these two firewalls. The firewall rules are configured according to the default-deny principle; only explicitly allowed connections are possible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network plan and the firewall configurations. It is verified that the three zones exist and that the transitions are controlled by firewalls. The firewall rule sets are checked for compliance with the allowlist principle. It is checked whether a two-stage firewall architecture is implemented to separate the Internet and Intranet. An automated test could use a port scanner (e.g., nmap) from one zone to try to reach unauthorized ports in another zone.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The zoning is refined by further, specialized zones, e.g., a management zone, a database zone, or a zone for highly sensitive data. A P-A-P structure (Packet filter-Application-Layer-Gateway-Packet filter), in which traffic is routed through application-specific proxies or gateways, is implemented whenever the security policy requires it. All data traffic between the zones is logged and regularly checked for anomalies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The additional zones are set up as separate segments behind the inner firewall and separated from each other by corresponding firewall rules. The P-A-P structure is realized by using Application-Level Gateways (ALGs) such as Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) or e-mail relays in the DMZ. The logging is done by sending the firewall logs to a central SIEM system, in which corresponding correlation rules for detecting anomalies are defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network plan and firewall rules for the existence and correct protection of the refined zones. The configuration of the ALGs and proxies in the DMZ is checked. In the SIEM system, the configuration of the log collection and the existence of rules for analyzing the zone traffic are verified. Log entries are randomly checked for suspicious communication attempts.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The concept of zones is supplemented by end-to-end micro-segmentation within the zones. Each server or small group of servers forms its own isolated segment. Communication between the micro-segments is blocked by default and only released on the basis of a strict need-to-know principle (zero-trust approach). The segmentation is enforced by host-based firewalls or distributed firewalls in the virtualization platform. All communication attempts (allowed and blocked) are logged in detail and automatically analyzed to detect attack attempts in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For micro-segmentation, technologies such as VMware NSX, Cisco ACI, or host-based firewall solutions (e.g., iptables/nftables under Linux, Windows Defender Firewall) with central management (e.g., via Ansible or Group Policies) are used. The communication policies are defined at the application level. A SIEM system with UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) functions is used to analyze the traffic flows.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the micro-segmentation solution. It is verified that the 'Default Deny' principle is implemented between the micro-segments. Using examples, it is checked whether the allowed communication paths correspond to the documented target state. The effectiveness of the segmentation is checked by targeted penetration tests. An automated audit could analyze the flow logs of the virtualization platform and compare them with the defined zero-trust policy.

controls.title: Client-server segmentation (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Clients and servers MUST be placed in different network segments. Communication between these network segments MUST be controlled by at least a stateful packet filter. Dedicated network segments MUST be set up for guest access and for network areas where there is insufficient internal control over the end devices. Exceptions that allow clients and servers to be positioned in a common network segment SHOULD be regulated and documented in the corresponding application- and system-specific modules.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Separation is typically achieved by assigning different VLANs for client and server networks. Routing between these VLANs is controlled by a central firewall or a Layer 3 switch with Access Control Lists (ACLs). The ACLs are configured to allow clients to access only the explicitly required server ports. The guest network is completely isolated and only allows direct internet access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the switch and firewall configurations to ensure that clients and servers are in separate VLANs/subnets. The configuration of the stateful packet filter (firewall rules or ACLs) is checked for correctness and the principle of least privilege. It is verified that the guest network is properly isolated from the internal network. A scan from a client segment to the server segment can verify the effectiveness of the filtering rules (`nmap -p- <server-ip>`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The client networks are further segmented, e.g., by department, location, or endpoint trustworthiness. Similarly, the server networks are segmented by function or application criticality (e.g., web servers, database servers, application servers). Communication between all these segments is controlled by a firewall. Direct client-to-client communication is prevented at the network level wherever possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Further segmentation is realized through additional VLANs and more detailed firewall rule sets. To prevent client-to-client communication, technologies such as 'Private VLANs' or 'Client Isolation' are activated on the access switches. This forces communication between clients in the same VLAN to go through the gateway (and thus the firewall).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the extended network plan and firewall rules for the correct implementation of fine-grained segmentation. The configuration of the access switches is checked for the activation of client isolation features. Test connections are used to verify that a client cannot communicate directly with another client in the same segment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Identity-based segmentation is implemented. Network access for clients and servers is dynamically assigned based on user identity, device status (compliance), and the application (Zero Trust principle). Each communication request is individually authenticated and authorized. Communication is controlled and inspected at the application layer (Layer 7).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Network Access Control (NAC) solution (e.g., based on IEEE 802.1X) is used in combination with a Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW). The NAC solution dynamically assigns the correct VLAN to devices upon connection or applies specific filter rules based on information from the directory service (e.g., Active Directory). The NGFW inspects traffic at the application layer and can, for example, control access to specific URL paths or functions within a web application.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the NAC solution and the NGFW. Tests are conducted with different user and device identities to verify that the correct access rights are dynamically assigned. It is checked whether the Layer 7 controls are effective by attempting to access unauthorized application functions. The audit logs of the NAC and NGFW systems are analyzed for successful and failed access attempts.

controls.title: Endpoint segmentation in the internal network (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: ONLY endpoints with a similar security level MAY be placed in a network segment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Segmentation is achieved by grouping endpoints with similar security requirements into dedicated VLANs. For example, standard office clients, printers, VoIP phones, IoT devices (e.g., for building control), and servers are placed in separate VLANs. Communication between these VLANs is regulated by a firewall that allows only the absolutely necessary connections (e.g., a client may access a printer, but not vice versa).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network plan and documentation to understand the defined endpoint groups and their respective security levels. By inspecting the switch and firewall configurations, it is verified that the devices are correctly assigned to the intended segments and that the communication rules between the segments follow the principle of least privilege. Random scans from one segment to another confirm the effectiveness of the separation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The assignment of endpoints to network segments is automated by a Network Access Control (NAC) solution. The NAC solution classifies the endpoints upon connection based on characteristics such as MAC address, device profile (fingerprinting), or installed certificates and dynamically assigns them to the correct segment. Unclassifiable or non-compliant devices are moved to a quarantine network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A NAC solution such as Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass, or PacketFence is implemented. The solution is integrated with the network (switches, WLAN controllers) and ideally with the asset management system. Profiles and assignment rules are defined for the different device classes (clients, printers, IoT, etc.). The quarantine network has only limited access, e.g., to update servers, to restore compliance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the NAC solution, including the defined profiles and rules. Test cases are conducted by connecting different device types (known, unknown, non-compliant) to the network to check for correct dynamic assignment or quarantining. The audit logs of the NAC solution are analyzed for misclassifications or rule violations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: End-to-end micro-segmentation is implemented down to the level of individual endpoints. Each endpoint is logically in its own segment. Communication is no longer primarily controlled between VLANs, but between individual devices or device identities based on a central policy. This policy is dynamically adapted to the security context (user, location, time, application behavior). Any lateral movement between endpoints is blocked by default and only allowed when explicitly necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Micro-segmentation for endpoints is realized through the use of host-based firewalls, controlled by a central management system (such as an EDR system with firewall control). Alternatively or in addition, advanced network technologies such as Private VLANs or VXLAN with Group-Based Policies are used. The policies are defined in a central policy engine that uses information from various sources (EDR, IAM, SIEM) for context-based decision-making.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the central policy engine and the host-based firewalls. It is verified that the default policy blocks all direct communication between endpoints. Test cases are used to check the correct application of context-based exception rules. Targeted penetration tests attempt to move laterally from a compromised endpoint to another to validate the effectiveness of the micro-segmentation.

controls.title: Protection of sensitive information (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Sensitive information MUST be transmitted using secure protocols according to the current state of the art, unless communication takes place via trusted dedicated network segments (e.g., within the management network). If such protocols cannot be used, state-of-the-art encryption and authentication MUST be applied (see NET.3.3 VPN).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In practice, this means that unencrypted protocols such as Telnet, FTP, HTTP, or older SNMP versions must be replaced by their secure counterparts (SSH, SFTP/FTPS, HTTPS, SNMPv3). Where this is not possible, e.g., for legacy applications, the communication must be encapsulated in a VPN tunnel (e.g., IPsec or TLS) to ensure confidentiality and integrity. The definition of 'sensitive information' and 'trusted network segments' is made in the security policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the network configurations and application documentation for the use of insecure protocols. Passive network analysis (e.g., with Wireshark or a Network Intrusion Detection System) is used to examine live traffic for unencrypted transmissions of sensitive data. It is checked whether appropriate compensating measures such as VPN tunnels are in place for legacy systems. An automated scan could check the configuration of encryption protocols for vulnerabilities with `nmap --script=ssl-enum-ciphers -p <port> <host>`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An allowlist of permitted (secure) protocols and encryption algorithms (cipher suites) is defined and technically enforced. The use of all other protocols and algorithms is blocked. Certificate management for encrypted connections (e.g., TLS certificates) is standardized and centrally managed to ensure validity and trustworthiness. Encryption is also recommended within segments classified as trustworthy and implemented wherever possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The allowlist is configured on the firewalls and application servers. Next-Generation Firewalls can inspect traffic at the application layer and detect and block insecure protocols even on non-standard ports. For certificate management, an internal Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) or a centralized process for managing certificates from public CAs is established, including automatic renewal.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the firewalls and servers for the implementation of the allowlist for protocols and cipher suites. The certificate management process is reviewed, including the configuration of the PKI and the validity period of certificates. Vulnerability scans are performed to detect the use of outdated or weak encryption algorithms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All network traffic, both internal and external, is encrypted by default (Encrypt-by-Default principle). The encrypted traffic is decrypted at defined control points (e.g., on the firewall) for deep inspection (TLS inspection), checked for malware and attack attempts, and then re-encrypted. The integrity of the encryption is further enhanced by the use of hardware security modules (HSMs) for key management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: To enforce default encryption, technologies such as MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) for Layer 2 encryption or a comprehensive IPsec overlay network are used. TLS inspection is implemented on the Next-Generation Firewall or dedicated SSL inspection appliances. Private keys for critical services are stored and managed in a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 (or higher) certified HSM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the MACsec/IPsec infrastructure and the TLS inspection solution. It is verified that the inspection policies are compliant with data protection regulations (e.g., exceptions for banking, health data). The configuration and physical protection of the HSM are checked. Passive network analysis is used to verify that no unencrypted traffic actually remains on the network.

controls.title: Basic security of internet access (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Internet traffic MUST be routed through the firewall structure (see NET.1.1.A4 Network separation into zones). Data flows MUST be restricted by the firewall structure to the required protocols and communication relationships.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is technically implemented through a strict firewall rule base according to the 'Default Deny' principle. The rule set for outgoing traffic only allows explicitly approved services (e.g., HTTP/HTTPS on port 80/443, DNS on port 53) to defined destinations or destination categories. The rule set for incoming traffic blocks everything by default, with exceptions only for services that are hosted in the DMZ and are intended to be explicitly accessible from the internet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the perimeter firewall(s). It is verified that no uncontrolled internet access points (shadow IT, e.g., via LTE modems) exist. The firewall rule set is analyzed for compliance with the 'Default Deny' principle and for unnecessarily open rules (e.g., 'any/any'). The documentation of the firewall rules is checked for being up-to-date and comprehensible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Internet traffic is additionally routed through a web proxy with content filtering (URL filtering by categories, virus scan) and an email gateway with spam and malware filtering. The firewall performs application and user detection to define rules not only based on ports, but also based on applications (e.g., blocking file-sharing applications) and user groups. Egress filtering is implemented to prevent data from being sent to known malicious or unauthorized destinations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated web proxy solution (e.g., Squid, Forcepoint, Zscaler) and a Secure Email Gateway (e.g., Proofpoint, Cisco ESA) are implemented in the DMZ or as a cloud service. A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) is used to enable Layer 7 application control and user identification (e.g., through integration with Active Directory). Egress filtering uses threat intelligence feeds to block IP addresses and domains of C2 servers or phishing sites.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the web proxy, the email gateway, and the NGFW. It is tested whether access to blocked URL categories and applications is blocked. An attempt is made to download a test malware file and send it via email. The configuration of the egress filtering and the up-to-dateness of the threat intelligence feeds are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All internet traffic is subjected to deep inspection (TLS inspection). All downloaded and uploaded files are analyzed for suspicious behavior in a sandbox environment before being delivered to the end user or sent to the internet. Data Loss Prevention (DLP) techniques are used to detect and block the outflow of sensitive information. DNS requests are routed through a specialized, secure DNS service that blocks malicious domains at the DNS level (DNS filtering).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The functionalities TLS inspection, sandboxing, and DLP are realized through an advanced NGFW, a secure web gateway solution, or dedicated appliances. Cloud-based sandboxing services can be used to analyze unknown files. A secure DNS service such as Cisco Umbrella or Quad9 is configured as the primary DNS resolver for the entire organization.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the TLS inspection, the sandboxing engine, and the DLP policies. An attempt is made to download an unknown, potentially malicious file to trigger the sandbox analysis. An attempt is made to upload a file with test credit card numbers or other sensitive data to test the DLP rules. The DNS configuration of the clients is checked to ensure that they are using the secure DNS service.

controls.title: Basic security of communication with untrusted networks (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For each network, it MUST be determined to what extent it is to be classified as trustworthy. Networks that are not trustworthy MUST be treated like the internet and secured accordingly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The classification of the trustworthiness of networks (e.g., networks of partners, customers, service providers) must be documented in the security policy or a dedicated concept. A network is considered untrustworthy if the institution has no control over its security measures. The connection of such networks is always made via the perimeter firewall, usually in a separate segment of the DMZ, and is subject to the same strict filtering rules as internet access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation on the classification of connected third-party networks. The network topology and firewall configuration are analyzed to ensure that networks classified as untrustworthy are actually treated like the internet (i.e., connection to the firewall, restrictive rules). It is checked whether a risk assessment and an approval exist for each connection of a third-party network.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The connection of untrusted networks is made via dedicated extranet segments in the DMZ. Communication is restricted to the absolutely necessary systems and protocols. All data traffic with these networks is logged and monitored by an Intrusion Detection/Prevention System (IDS/IPS). Before a connection is established, partners must be contractually obligated to comply with minimum security standards.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate VLAN or subnet in the extranet area of the DMZ is set up for each partner or partner group. The firewall rules only allow the explicitly agreed-upon communication. The IDS/IPS is configured with specific rules for extranet traffic. The contractual agreements (e.g., as part of a data processing agreement) specify requirements such as the use of firewalls, antivirus software, and patch management on the partner's side.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the extranet segments and the associated firewall rules. The configuration and alerting of the IDS/IPS for extranet traffic are analyzed. Contracts with connected partners are randomly checked for the presence of IT security clauses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The connection of untrusted networks is generally avoided. Instead, access for partners is realized through a Zero Trust architecture, where the partner's users and devices must individually authenticate and authorize themselves to access specific, approved applications. The connection is always initiated by the partner and is encrypted end-to-end. A continuous check of the security status of the accessing partner endpoints takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access is realized via a modern VPN solution (e.g., SSL-VPN with Host-Checker) or a Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) / Software-Defined Perimeter (SDP) solution. These solutions ensure that only authenticated and authorized partners can access defined applications without gaining access to the entire network. The Host-Checker checks the compliance status of the partner's endpoint (e.g., up-to-date OS, running antivirus software).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the ZTNA/SDP solution and the associated access policies. It is tested whether a partner user can actually only access the applications approved for them. The functionality of the Host-Checker is verified by attempting to connect with a non-compliant test device. The audit logs are analyzed for suspicious access attempts by partners.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Most institutions today require data networks for their business operations and to fulfill their specialist tasks, over which, for example, information and data are exchanged and distributed applications are implemented. Not only conventional end devices, the extranet, and the internet are connected to such networks. They also increasingly integrate mobile end devices and elements that are attributed to the Internet of Things (IoT). Furthermore, cloud services and services for Unified Communication and Collaboration (UCC) are increasingly used via data networks. The resulting advantages are undisputed. But the risks also increase with the many end devices and services. Therefore, it is important to protect one's own network with a secure network architecture from the outset. For this, it must be planned, for example, how a local area network (LAN) or a wide area network (WAN) can be set up securely. Likewise, only partially trusted external networks, e.g., the internet or customer networks, must be connected appropriately.
To ensure a high level of security, additional security-relevant aspects must be considered. Examples include the secure separation of different tenants and device groups at the network level and the control of their communication by a firewall. Another important security element, especially for clients, is network access control.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to establish information security as an integral part of network architecture and network design.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design is to be applied to the entire network of an institution, including all subnets.
The module contains fundamental requirements that must be observed and fulfilled when planning, building, and operating networks. Requirements for the secure operation of the corresponding network components, including security components such as firewalls, are not the subject of this module. These are addressed in the module group NET.3 Network Components.
The focus of this module is on wired networks and data communication. However, general requirements for architecture and design, e.g., that zones always require a physical separation from network segments, must be observed and fulfilled for all network technologies.
Further specific requirements for network areas such as Wireless LAN (WLAN) or Storage Area Networks (SAN) are addressed in the module layer NET.2 Wireless Networks and in the module SYS.1.8 Storage Solutions, respectively. Furthermore, the topic of Voice over IP (VoIP) and its underlying security infrastructure is not discussed in this module but is handled in the corresponding module NET.4.2 VoIP.
Specific security requirements for Virtual Private Clouds and Hybrid Clouds are also not the focus of this module.
Network management is considered within the scope of zoning and segmentation; all further topics of network management are addressed in the module NET.1.2 Network Management.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Failure or insufficient performance of communication links
parts.prose: If communication links are insufficiently dimensioned or their performance is no longer adequate due to a technical failure or a Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack, clients may only be able to communicate with servers to a limited extent. This increases access times to internal and external services. These may then only be available to a limited extent or not at all. Institution-relevant information may also no longer be available. As a consequence, essential business processes or entire production processes can come to a standstill.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insufficiently secured network access points
parts.prose: If the internal network is connected to the internet and the perimeter is not sufficiently protected, e.g., because no firewall is used or it is misconfigured, attackers can access sensitive information of the institution and copy or manipulate it.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Improper structure of networks
parts.prose: If a network is improperly built or incorrectly extended, insecure network topologies can arise, or networks can be configured insecurely. This makes it easier for attackers to find security vulnerabilities, penetrate the institution's internal network, and steal information, manipulate data, or disrupt entire production systems. Attackers also remain undetected for longer in an improperly built network that security systems can only monitor to a limited extent.

controls.title: Planning of network management

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of network management is only done ad-hoc and is limited to the most urgent areas, such as monitoring critical servers. There is no formal planning document.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In practice, only basic monitoring tools like Ping are used to monitor the availability of individual systems classified as critical. There is a complete lack of planning for configuration management or central logging.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with the administrators whether there are informal planning approaches. It is checked whether basic monitoring mechanisms exist for selected critical systems, even if they are not anchored in a comprehensive plan.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic but not very detailed plan for network management. The plan lists the systems to be managed and the tools used, but does not define specific processes or configurations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A document describes at a high level that an SNMP server should be used for monitoring and a syslog server for logging. However, details on SNMP versions, access permissions, or the evaluation of logs are missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning document for network management. It is checked whether the essential components of network management (e.g., monitoring, logging) are named in it, even if the detailing of the processes and configurations is insufficient.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network management infrastructure MUST be planned appropriately. All points mentioned in the security policy and requirement specification for network management SHOULD be taken into account. At least the following topics MUST be considered: areas to be separated for network management, access options to the management servers, communication for management access, protocols used, requirements for management tools, interfaces for event or alarm messages, logging including interfaces to a central solution, reporting and interfaces to higher-level solutions, and corresponding requirements for the network components to be integrated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal planning document is created and maintained. This document contains a detailed breakdown of all points mentioned in the control text. For example, it specifies which network segments are intended for management (e.g., in-band vs. out-of-band), which protocols (e.g., SNMPv3, SSH) are to be used with which security settings, and how the connection to a central log management system is made.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence, completeness, and up-to-dateness of the planning document. It is checked whether all topic areas required in the control text (e.g., separation of areas, protocols, interfaces) are adequately and comprehensibly addressed in the plan. This can be done through a document review and interviews with the planning managers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The plan for network management is formalized, reviewed regularly (e.g., annually), and updated as needed. The plan defines clear interfaces and responsibilities for interaction with other IT management disciplines such as security and incident management. All "SHOULD" aspects of the basic requirement are mandatorily implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The plan is maintained in a document management system with version control. Regular meetings between network, security, and operations teams ensure that planning is integrated and up-to-date. The planning for logging explicitly includes the requirements for a SIEM connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks for the existence of revision histories and approval records for the planning document. It is verified through inspection of meeting minutes and interviews that regular, interdisciplinary coordination on network management planning takes place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network management planning is fully integrated into the enterprise architecture management process. Planning is dynamically adapted based on risk analyses, threat intelligence, and business requirements. Automated mechanisms exist to continuously check the conformity of the implemented infrastructure with the plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning is maintained in a specialized EA tool and is linked to the CMDB and risk management tools. Compliance scanning tools automatically check, for example, whether only the planned protocols are active on the management interfaces and whether the network segmentation corresponds to the plan. Deviations lead to automated alerts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports from the automated compliance tools to verify the conformity of the plan with reality. The link between the network management planning, the risk assessment, and the overarching ISMS is checked. Example command for checking: `compliance-scanner --policy /path/to/net-mgmt-plan.yml --target-network 10.1.0.0/16`.

controls.title: Requirement specification for network management

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Requirements for network management are only formulated informally and orally for individual components to be newly procured. A coherent specification does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before purchasing a new switch, the supplier is asked if the device supports SNMP, without specifying the version or required MIBs. This requirement is not documented in writing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews with administrators and purchasers whether any requirements for network management are considered during procurement, even if this is not formally documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a list of general requirements for network management that is used for procurement. However, this specification is not detailed and does not cover all essential elements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard checklist for purchasing network components includes the item "Must support network management". However, it does not specify which protocols, processes, or security features are required.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the requirement documents or checklists. It is checked whether a basic requirement specification exists, even if it is superficial and omits essential details.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the network management planning (NET.1.2.A1), requirements for the network management infrastructure and processes MUST be specified. All essential elements for network management MUST be taken into account. The policy for network management SHOULD also be observed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal requirements document is created. It is derived directly from the planning document and specifies concretely, for example: "All new switches must support SNMPv3 with AES-128 encryption", "The central management system must provide a syslog-NG-compatible input for logs", or "Access to the management GUI must be via HTTPS with TLS 1.2+".

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the requirement specification and checks on a random basis whether it is comprehensibly derived from the planning document. It is checked whether essential elements such as security protocols, interfaces, and processes are specified in a concrete and unambiguous manner.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirement specification contains measurable criteria for performance and security (e.g., maximum latency for alarm messages, supported cipher suites). Compliance with the specification is checked as part of acceptance tests for new components.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The specification states: "Alerting in case of a component failure must arrive at the central management system within 5 seconds". When commissioning a new system, this is checked and documented by means of a test case.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the requirement specification for measurable criteria. In addition, minutes of acceptance tests are inspected to verify that the specified requirements are actually checked when new systems are introduced.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirement specification is dynamically managed in a requirements management tool. Each requirement is linked to a risk analysis and a business process. Automated tests exist to continuously check the compliance of systems with the specification.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like Jira or a specialized RM tool is used. A requirement such as "Support for NTS for time synchronization" is directly linked to the risk "Manipulation of timestamps". An automated script regularly scans the network and checks which devices have NTS enabled and reports deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is given read access to the requirements management tool and verifies the links between requirements, risks, and processes. The results and configuration of the automated compliance tests are analyzed. Example command for checking: `nmap --script ntp-info <target>` to check NTP details.

controls.title: Regular data backup

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data backups of the network management are only performed irregularly and manually. Primarily configuration data of the network components are backed up, while system data of the management servers or log data are neglected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator occasionally copies the configuration files of important routers and switches to their local computer. There is no fixed schedule or defined procedure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews the administrators about their backup practices. The irregularity of the backups is understood by checking file timestamps in backup directories.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a regular, automated backup of network management data. However, it is not checked whether the backups were successful or whether they can be restored. The retention periods are not defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A daily backup script backs up the configurations of the network components and the database of the SNMP server. However, the log files of the backup job are not evaluated, and a test restore has never been performed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the backup automation (e.g., cron jobs, backup software configuration). They ask for records of recovery tests. If these are missing, this corresponds to the maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When backing up network management data, at least the system data for integrating the components or objects to be managed, event messages, statistical data, and data held for configuration management MUST be backed up.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central backup process is established that covers all data categories mentioned in the control text. The process is documented and includes a fixed schedule (e.g., daily incremental, weekly full), defined retention periods, and responsibilities. The backup target is a separate system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the data backup concept for network management. It is verified that the configuration of the backup software includes all required data sources (management server, configuration database, log directories). The backup logs of the last few weeks are checked for successful execution.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data backups of the network management are encrypted and stored in a physically separate, secure location. Recovery tests are performed and documented regularly (e.g., semi-annually).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backup software is configured to encrypt all backups with AES-256. The backups are replicated daily to a server in a different fire compartment. A complete restore of the management system from the backup is practiced in a test environment twice a year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the encryption configuration in the backup software. The logs of the recovery tests performed in the last cycles are requested and checked for completeness and success.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire process of data backup and recovery is fully automated. This includes checking the integrity of the backups and the regular, automated execution of recovery tests in an isolated sandbox environment. The results are visualized in a central dashboard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An automation script not only starts the backup every night, but also performs a hash check of the backup files afterwards. Once a month, a temporary VM environment is automatically created, the management system is restored from the backup, a set of functional tests is executed, and the environment is then destroyed again. Errors are automatically created as a ticket in the ticketing system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automation scripts and the configuration of the sandbox environment. The dashboards and the generated test reports or tickets from the last few months are reviewed to verify the continuous and automated verification of the backup process.

controls.title: Basic logging of events

parts.name: statement
