This procedure ensures that neither the content nor the time of the message can be manipulated unnoticed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture and configuration of the signature and timestamp infrastructure. The valid certificate of the external audit or certification of the archiving process is requested. The signature and timestamp of an archived log file are verified on a random basis.

controls.title: Integration of network management logging into a SIEM solution

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The log data from network management is forwarded to a SIEM solution. The requirement catalogs are adapted to ensure that the management solutions support the necessary interfaces and transfer formats.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The central log server is configured to forward all collected logs from the network devices to the SIEM system's data collector in real time. When procuring new management tools, care is taken to ensure that they support Syslog or other standardized formats for SIEM connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the log server or management tools for forwarding to the SIEM. It is checked in the SIEM whether the data from the network components is arriving. The requirement documents for procurements are checked for SIEM-relevant criteria.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network management logging SHOULD be integrated into a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) solution. The log data is parsed, normalized, and enriched with context information in the SIEM. Specific correlation rules are implemented that aim to detect attacks on or via the network infrastructure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the SIEM, parsers for the various log formats of the network manufacturers (Cisco, Juniper, etc.) are active. Incoming events are enriched with information from the CMDB (e.g., location, criticality of the device). A correlation rule triggers an alarm if a configuration change occurs on a switch outside of an approved maintenance window.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the parsers and enrichment rules in the SIEM. The implemented correlation rules related to network management events are evaluated for their functionality and purpose. The effectiveness is checked using simulated or past events.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integration with the SIEM is bidirectional and embedded in a SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) platform. Based on correlated events, the SIEM can trigger automated responses in the network infrastructure to contain attacks in real time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If the SIEM triggers an alarm about a client communicating with a known command-and-control server, it automatically starts a SOAR playbook. This playbook instructs the network management solution to activate an ACL on the access switch that blocks the port of the affected client, thus isolating it from the network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration of the SOAR platform and the playbooks running on it. The interfaces between SIEM, SOAR, and the network management systems are analyzed. The end-to-end process from detection to automated response is traced using test cases or logs of past incidents.

controls.title: Cross-site time synchronization

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: At all locations of the institution, the systems are synchronized with the same central, internal NTP servers to ensure a common time base.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NTP configuration on the devices at all locations (e.g., Berlin, Munich) points to the IP addresses of the two central NTP servers in the main data center. The firewalls between the locations are configured to allow NTP traffic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the NTP configuration of devices at different locations and verifies that they all point to the same central time sources. The firewall rules for cross-site NTP traffic are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Time synchronization SHOULD be ensured across all locations of the institution. A common reference time SHOULD be used for this purpose. A hierarchical and redundant NTP infrastructure is operated across all locations to increase accuracy and resilience.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Central Stratum 2 servers are operated at the main site. At each major branch site, there are local Stratum 3 servers that synchronize with the central servers. The devices at a site primarily use their local NTP servers. This reduces cross-site traffic and increases stability in the event of a WAN connection failure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the designed NTP hierarchy and compares it with the actual configuration. It is checked whether the stratum levels are configured correctly and whether the failover paths for NTP synchronization are designed sensibly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Independent, physical time sources (Stratum 1) are operated at several locations to create a highly precise and resilient common reference time. All cross-site NTP communication is cryptographically secured using NTS (Network Time Security) or equivalent mechanisms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate GPS-based time server is operated at both the Berlin and Munich sites. These serve as highly available Stratum 1 sources for the entire company. All NTP traffic, especially over WAN links, is secured with NTS to prevent manipulation of the time information.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the physical time sources at the various locations. The configuration of the NTS infrastructure (keys, certificates) is audited. The resilience of the time supply is assessed in a simulated failure of a site or a time source.

controls.title: Definition of contingency modes for the network management infrastructure

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Contingency procedures are defined that enable rapid restoration of the target states of software and configurations of the network management infrastructure. This is based on regular backups.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The emergency manual contains instructions on how to restore the configuration of a failed component from the backup to a replacement device.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the recovery procedures documented in the emergency manual and compares them with the existing backups.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Sufficiently good replacement solutions SHOULD be defined for a rapid restoration of the target states of software or firmware and the configuration of the components in the network management infrastructure. This includes keeping spare devices (cold spares) on hand.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For critical, non-redundant components (e.g., a special firewall type), an identical replacement device is kept in storage (cold spare). There is a documented and tested procedure for how to transfer the configuration from the failed device to the replacement device and put it into operation in the event of damage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the declared replacement devices through a physical inspection or by reviewing the inventory lists. The associated recovery instructions are checked. Logs from past tests or deployments are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A "black start" capability for network management has been established. This means that procedures and tools exist to rebuild the network management infrastructure from scratch without being dependent on the (potentially failed) production network. This capability is practiced regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an "emergency kit" that contains a laptop with all the necessary tools and configurations, as well as various console cables. The emergency manual describes how an administrator can use this kit to access the core components of the network (core switches, routers) via the serial console and apply a minimal basic configuration to make the network controllable again.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the contents of the emergency kit and the associated documentation ("black start" instructions). Logs from exercises where this scenario was practiced are requested. The currency of the configurations and tools in the kit is checked.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Reliable network management is a fundamental prerequisite for the secure and efficient operation of modern networks. This requires network management to comprehensively integrate all network components. Furthermore, suitable measures must be implemented to protect network management communication and infrastructure.
Network management includes many important functions such as network monitoring, component configuration, event handling, and logging. Another important function is reporting, which can be set up as a common platform for the network and IT systems. Alternatively, it can be implemented as a dedicated uniform platform or as part of the individual network management components.
The network management infrastructure consists of central management systems, such as an SNMP server, administration end devices with software for management access, and decentralized management agents. It also includes dedicated management tools, such as probes or specific measuring devices, as well as management protocols, such as SNMP or SSH. Management interfaces, such as dedicated Ethernet ports or console ports, are also part of a network management infrastructure.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to establish information security as an integral part of network management.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module NET.1.2 Network Management is to be applied to every network management system (management system and IT system to be managed) used in the information network. The IT systems to be managed are usually individual clients, servers, or active network components (network coupling elements).
This module considers the necessary components and conceptual tasks for network management. Requirements for system management for networked clients and servers are not described here.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unauthorized access to central network management components
parts.prose: If an attack succeeds in accessing network management solutions, e.g., through unpatched security vulnerabilities or insufficient network separation, all connected network components can be controlled and reconfigured. This can lead to access to sensitive information, redirection of network traffic, or sustained disruption of the entire network.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unauthorized access to individual network components
parts.prose: If an attack succeeds in accessing individual network components, the respective component can be controlled and manipulated. Any data traffic routed through the network component can thus be compromised. Furthermore, further attacks can be prepared to penetrate deeper into the institution's network.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unauthorized interference with network management communication
parts.prose: If network management communication is eavesdropped on and manipulated, active network components can be misconfigured or controlled. This can violate network integrity and restrict the availability of the network infrastructure. Furthermore, the transmitted data can be intercepted and viewed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficient time synchronization of network management components
parts.prose: If the system time of the network management components is insufficiently synchronized, it may not be possible to correlate the log data with each other. The correlation may also lead to incorrect statements because the different timestamps of events do not have a common basis. This means that it is not possible to react appropriately to events. Problems can also not be eliminated. As a result, security incidents and data exfiltration, for example, can remain undetected.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Wireless LANs (WLANs) can be used to set up wireless local networks or to extend existing wired networks. To this day, almost all WLAN components available on the market are based on the IEEE 802.11 standard and its supplements. A special role is played by the company consortium "Wi-Fi Alliance", which has created an industry standard called "Wi-Fi" based on the IEEE 802.11 standard. The Wi-Fi Alliance confirms with the Wi-Fi seal of approval that a device has passed certain interoperability and conformity tests.
Within institutions, WLANs can be used to work flexibly with mobile devices and to provide them with access to the institution's network. For this purpose, network access is set up within the institution via so-called Access Points. Due to the usually simple and fast installation, WLANs are also used to set up temporary networks, for example at trade fairs or smaller events. In addition, network access can be offered in public places, such as airports or train stations, via so-called hotspots. This enables mobile users to connect to the Internet or their institution's network. Communication then generally takes place between a central access point, the Access Point, and the WLAN component of the end device.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module systematically shows how WLANs can be securely set up and operated within an institution.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The NET.2.1 WLAN Operation module is to be applied to all communication networks that are set up and operated in accordance with the IEEE 802.11 standard series and its extensions.
The module contains fundamental requirements that must be observed and fulfilled when WLANs are set up and operated in institutions. However, requirements for the secure use of WLANs are not the subject of this module. The secure use of WLANs is covered in the NET.2.2 WLAN Usage module.
WLANs can be operated in two different modes, depending on the needs of the operating institution and the available hardware equipment. In ad-hoc mode, two or more WLAN clients communicate directly with each other. WLANs in ad-hoc mode can set up and configure themselves independently, i.e. without a fixed infrastructure. They can thus establish a fully meshed parallel network infrastructure. As a result, ad-hoc mode is unsuitable in an environment to be protected and will therefore not be considered further below. In most cases, WLANs are operated in infrastructure mode, i.e. communication between WLAN clients and the connection to wired LAN segments is via Access Points.
If corresponding services (e.g. RADIUS) are used for authentication on the WLAN, the corresponding IT systems on which the services are operated must be secured separately. For this purpose, the modules of layer SYS.1, such as SYS.1.1 General Server, can be used.
If a WLAN is operated, it should always be taken into account when implementing the modules NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design, NET.1.2 Network Management and DER.2.1 Handling of Security Incidents.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Failure or disruption of a wireless network
parts.prose: In wireless networks, information is transmitted by means of electromagnetic radio waves. If other electromagnetic sources radiate energy in the same frequency spectrum, they can interfere with wireless communication and, in extreme cases, prevent the operation of the WLAN. This can be caused by other radio systems and devices, such as Bluetooth, microwave ovens or other WLAN networks. In addition, denial-of-service attacks are also possible. For example, if certain control and management signals are sent repeatedly, this can lead to the wireless network no longer being available.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Missing or insufficient planning of WLAN deployment
parts.prose:
Errors in planning often turn out to be particularly serious because they can easily create widespread security vulnerabilities. If the use of WLANs is not planned or is planned inadequately, a variety of problems can arise, for example:

• Confidential data could be intercepted, for example if WLAN standards are used that are no longer state-of-the-art (e.g. WEP for encryption).

• The transmission capacity could be insufficient. This means that bandwidth-intensive applications cannot be used with the required quality of service.

• The WLAN coverage could be insufficient, so that no network is available in certain locations.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Missing or insufficient regulations for WLAN use
parts.prose: In a WLAN infrastructure that is not centrally administered, the Access Points are usually pre-configured in the default setting with no or only insufficient security mechanisms. If, for example, due to a lack of regulations, employees connect an unauthorized or unsecured Access Point to an internal network of the institution, this can lead to serious problems. This is because they practically undermine all security measures taken within the LAN, such as the firewall to protect against unauthorized external access.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unsuitable selection of authentication methods
parts.prose: If authentication procedures and mechanisms are missing or insufficient, security vulnerabilities can arise. For example, the IEEE 802.1X standard (Port Based Network Access Control) defines the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). However, some of the described EAP methods contain vulnerabilities. For example, EAP-MD5 is susceptible to man-in-the-middle and dictionary attacks. If EAP-MD5 is used, passwords can be guessed. In addition, the communication can be eavesdropped on.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Incorrect configuration of the WLAN infrastructure
parts.prose: Access Points and other WLAN components (e.g. WLAN Controller) offer a variety of configuration settings, which also concern security functions in particular. If these are configured incorrectly, either no communication via an Access Point is possible or the communication takes place unprotected or with too low a level of protection.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficient or missing WLAN security mechanisms
parts.prose: In their delivery state, WLAN components are often configured in such a way that no or only a few security mechanisms are activated. Some of the mechanisms are also insufficient and therefore do not offer sufficient protection. Even today, various WLAN components are still used that only support insufficient security mechanisms such as WEP. In some cases, these devices cannot even be upgraded to stronger security mechanisms. If such devices are used, attackers can easily eavesdrop on the entire communication and thus view confidential information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Eavesdropping on WLAN communication
parts.prose: Since radio is a medium that can be shared by multiple users ('shared medium'), the data transmitted via WLANs can be easily intercepted and recorded. If the data is not encrypted or is insufficiently encrypted, the transmitted user data can be easily viewed. In addition, wireless networks or the emitted radio waves often extend beyond the boundaries of the premises used by the owner. Thus, data is also broadcast into areas that cannot be controlled and secured by the users or an institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Spoofing a valid access point (Rogue Access Point)
parts.prose: Attackers can impersonate part of the WLAN infrastructure by installing their own access point with a suitably chosen name (SSID) near a WLAN client. This spoofed access point is called a 'Rogue Access Point'. If it offers the WLAN client a stronger signal strength than the real access point, the client will use it as a base station, provided they do not mutually authenticate. Additionally, the real access point could be disabled by a denial-of-service attack. Users log into a network that only pretends to be the target network. This allows attackers to eavesdrop on the communication. Through poisoning or spoofing methods, attackers can also fake a false identity or redirect network traffic to their IT systems, allowing them to intercept and control the communication. A rogue access point is a popular attack method, especially in public wireless networks (so-called hotspots).

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unprotected LAN access at the access point
parts.prose: If access points are visibly mounted and without physical protection, attackers can get between the access points and the switch infrastructure to eavesdrop on all network traffic. Even if the wireless communication is encrypted with WPA2, this poses a threat because these methods only secure the air interface, but do not further consider the Ethernet connection.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Hardware damage
parts.prose: Hardware damage can disrupt radio traffic. In the worst case, the WLAN can even fail completely. This particularly affects WLAN devices that are installed outside of protected rooms, e.g., to cover open squares. They are exposed to additional threats, such as intentional damage by attackers or environmental damage from weather or lightning strikes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Theft of an access point
parts.prose: If WLAN access points are installed unsecured in public areas, they can be stolen. This can be used, for example, to read out a shared secret key for authentication on the RADIUS server or the key used (for example, for WPA2-Personal). With this information, unauthorized access to the WLAN can then be gained.

controls.title: Defining a strategy for the use of WLANs (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of WLANs is ad-hoc for specific purposes, without a comprehensive strategy or formal planning. Responsibilities are not clearly defined and are assigned verbally as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this maturity level, WLANs are often introduced reactively to meet an immediate need. There is no documentation on the purpose, coverage area, or responsibilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask the IT managers if a document exists that describes the WLAN strategy. Check whether there is a list of the operated WLANs with a defined purpose and responsibilities. If these basic artifacts are missing, this maturity level can be assumed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal, basic idea about the use of WLANs, but it is not formally documented and approved. Essential aspects such as the exact coverage area or the interfaces between those responsible are only partially clarified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Typically, there are verbal agreements or e-mail correspondence that set the general direction for WLAN use. However, a formal strategy that is accessible and valid for everyone is missing. Responsibilities are roughly known, but not regulated in detail.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check for memos, e-mails, or minutes from meetings that discuss the use of WLANs. Ask different administrators about their responsibilities and compare the answers for consistency. If agreements exist, but they are not recorded in an official strategy document, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before WLANs are used, a general strategy is established. This defines in which organizational units, for which applications, and for what purpose WLANs are used and what information may be transmitted over them. The coverage area is defined. In addition, the responsibilities for administration and the interfaces between those responsible are documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution must create and adopt a formal strategy document for the use of WLANs. This document must cover the essential points: areas of use (Where?), use cases (What for?), data types (What?), geographical coverage, and administrative responsibilities (Who?).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the WLAN strategy document. Check whether the following points are documented: organizational units, permitted applications, purpose of use, classification of the information to be transmitted, defined coverage area, named administrators and their responsibilities, and defined communication channels.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The WLAN strategy is reviewed regularly, at least once a year, and updated if necessary. There is a formal process for requesting and approving new WLAN installations or significant changes to the existing infrastructure. The strategy is demonstrably linked to the institution's overarching IT security policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement a review cycle for the strategy document. Use a change management process to control changes to the WLAN landscape. The link to the IT security policy ensures that the WLAN strategy supports the institution's general security objectives.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the minutes of the last WLAN strategy reviews. Check the change management system for requests for new WLANs and whether they were approved according to the defined process. Compare the content of the WLAN strategy with the IT security policy for consistency and references.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The WLAN strategy is a living document managed in a central GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool. Changes to the strategy are subject to a formal, audited approval process. The strategy is continuously adapted to new technological developments (e.g. IoT, 6 GHz) and threat analyses. Future capacity and security requirements are proactively planned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Integrate the management of the WLAN strategy into the institution's GRC processes. Use automated workflows for changes and reviews. Conduct regular technology and threat analyses to proactively evolve the strategy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the change history and approval workflows of the WLAN strategy in the GRC tool. Request the results of the latest technology and threat analyses and compare them with the content of the current strategy. Automated check: `api-call-to-grc-tool --query 'policy_name=WLAN_Strategy' --show-history`.

controls.title: Selection of a suitable WLAN standard (B) [Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The WLAN standard is selected primarily based on availability or the manufacturer's specifications for the access points. No analysis of interference sources or formal comparison of security mechanisms is carried out. Insecure standards are tolerated for individual legacy devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this level, the latest or manufacturer-advertised standard (e.g. Wi-Fi 6) is often used without considering the specific security implications or environmental factors. Backward compatibility with insecure standards often remains enabled unnoticed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask for the reasoning behind the choice of the WLAN standard being used. Check the configuration of the access points to see if insecure standards such as WEP or WPA1 are still enabled, even if they are not primarily used. Look for documentation of a frequency analysis; if this is missing, this maturity level is likely.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A WLAN standard recognized as secure (e.g. WPA2 or WPA3) is deliberately selected for use. However, there is no formal, documented consideration of the security mechanisms or a systematic analysis of interference sources in the frequency band.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision for a secure standard is based on general knowledge or best practice recommendations. However, the process is not formalized. The risk of interference from other devices is considered, but not systematically investigated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the access points to verify that a secure standard such as WPA2/WPA3 is configured as the primary standard. Ask for the document that justifies the selection decision. If no such document exists, although a secure standard is in use, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of the WLAN planning, it is determined which operated devices can cause interference in the frequency bands used (2.4 GHz, 5 GHz). The security mechanisms of the available WLAN standards are systematically compared and the selection decision is documented. It is ensured that only generally recognized secure authentication and encryption methods are used. Devices that have to fall back on insecure methods are not used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Conduct an inventory of potential sources of interference (e.g. microwaves, Bluetooth, cordless phones). Create a comparison table of the security features of standards such as WPA2 and WPA3. Document the decision for a standard in a traceable manner. Deactivate insecure protocols and standards on all WLAN components.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the documentation on the analysis of interference sources and the comparison of WLAN standards. Check the configuration of the access points and the WLAN controller to ensure that insecure standards (WEP, WPA1) and authentication methods are disabled. Automated check: Perform a scan with a WLAN analysis tool (e.g., `inSSIDer`, `WiFi Analyzer`) and check the broadcasted beacons for supported security protocols.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The analysis and selection of WLAN standards is a periodic process that is repeated when new standards are published or serious security vulnerabilities become known. In addition to security, the selection criteria explicitly include performance and scaling aspects for future growth. The results of the frequency analysis are used to carry out optimized channel planning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Integrate the review of WLAN standards into your annual IT security review process. Use professional spectrum analyzers for a detailed investigation of the frequency bands to optimize not only interference but also channel usage.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the minutes of the last reviews of the standard selection. Request the channel planning documentation and compare it with the results of the frequency analysis. Check whether there is a process that triggers a re-evaluation in the event of new CVEs for WLAN standards.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection process for WLAN standards is partially automated. A central database of device properties and supported standards is maintained. Continuous configuration and vulnerability scans actively check whether devices are using or can fall back to insecure standards, and automatically isolate them from the network upon detection. The frequency bands are permanently monitored by sensors to detect interference and channel load in real time and dynamically adjust the channel plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use a WLAN management solution with integrated spectrum analysis and dynamic channel optimization (DCO/RRM). Integrate the WLAN infrastructure into a NAC solution that checks compliance with security standards on the end devices before network access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration and log data of the WLAN management system for evidence of dynamic channel adjustment. Request the configuration of the NAC rules that block or quarantine clients with insecure WLAN configurations. Automated check: `wlan-controller-cli --get-channel-history` and `nac-cli --get-policy --filter 'wlan-security=insecure'`.

controls.title: Selection of suitable cryptographic methods for WLAN (B) [Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Although WLAN encryption is enabled, outdated and insecure methods such as WEP or WPA1 are sometimes used, often for compatibility reasons with legacy devices. When using Pre-Shared Keys (PSK), simple, easy-to-remember passwords are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, the need for encryption is recognized, but the implementation is weak. Security is sacrificed in favor of functionality for outdated devices. The risks of weak keys are not sufficiently understood.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Scan the WLAN with an analysis tool and check the encryption protocols. Look for networks that use WEP or WPA(1)-TKIP. Ask for the PSK used; if it is short or not complex, this is an indicator. Automated check: `airodump-ng [interface]` and analysis of the `ENC` and `CIPHER` columns.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: WPA2 with Pre-Shared Key (WPA2-PSK) is used as the standard method. However, the keys used do not consistently meet the requirements for complexity and length and are rarely changed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The organization has taken a step in the right direction by using WPA2. However, key management is still immature. Often, the same, simple keys are used for long periods of time for many user groups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the WLAN configuration on the access points or in the controller. Verify that WPA2-PSK is being used. Ask for a PSK to be disclosed (for testing purposes) and evaluate its complexity and length. Check if there are policies for regular key changes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Communication over the air interface is consistently cryptographically secured. Cryptographic methods that are less secure than WPA2 are not used. When using WPA2-PSK, a complex key with a minimum length of 20 characters is used. Corresponding policies are documented and implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Ensure that all WLAN profiles exclusively use WPA2 or WPA3 with secure ciphers (such as AES/CCMP). Explicitly disable WEP and WPA1/TKIP. Define a mandatory policy for the creation of PSKs that specifies complexity and a minimum length of 20 characters, and document the currently used keys in a secure location.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the policy on WLAN encryption and key management. Check the configuration of all SSIDs in the WLAN controller and ensure that only WPA2/WPA3 with AES/CCMP is active. Request proof of the complexity and length of the PSKs used. Automated check: `wlan-controller-cli --get-ssid-config --all | grep -E 'security|preshared-key'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Where technically possible, WPA3 is preferred over WPA2. For the internal corporate WLAN, 802.1X-based authentication with a central RADIUS server is primarily used. WPA2/3-PSK is only used for dedicated networks such as guest WLANs, where the keys are rotated automatically and at short intervals (e.g. daily).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement a RADIUS server (e.g. FreeRADIUS, Microsoft NPS) and configure the access points and clients for 802.1X authentication (e.g. with PEAP-MSCHAPv2). For guest WLANs, use captive portal solutions that can dynamically generate and distribute unique or time-limited keys.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the corporate WLAN for 802.1X settings and the connection to a RADIUS server. Check the configuration of the guest WLAN and have the key rotation process demonstrated. Automated check: Check the RADIUS server logs for successful authentication attempts. Start `radiusd -X` in debug mode and perform a test login.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For access to all internal WLANs, WPA3-Enterprise with EAP-TLS (certificate-based authentication) is mandatory. The entire configuration is centrally managed and enforced via 'Policy as Code'. A continuous compliance monitoring system ensures that no devices with weaker crypto methods can connect; such attempts are automatically blocked and a security incident is triggered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Set up a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to issue client certificates for users and devices. Configure the RADIUS server and clients for EAP-TLS. Use a central configuration management tool (e.g., Ansible) to keep WLAN and RADIUS configurations consistent. Integrate the logs into a SIEM to create alerts for failed or insecure connection attempts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the PKI and RADIUS server configuration for EAP-TLS. Have the playbooks or configuration scripts of the 'Policy as Code' system shown to you. In the SIEM, check the WLAN security dashboard for alerts regarding insecure connection attempts. Automated check: `openssl s_client -connect <radius-server>:<port> -tls1_2` to verify server certificates and protocols.

controls.title: Proper positioning of access points (B) [Building services]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access points are placed where it is easiest or where reception is most urgently needed (e.g., on a desk or shelf). Aspects such as theft protection or targeted signal coverage are not considered, leading to insufficient coverage in some areas and strong signal bleeding in others.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This approach is typical for unplanned or hastily set up WLANs. The physical security of the devices and the control of signal propagation play no role.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Conduct a site survey and check the physical placement of the access points. Look for APs that are unsecured in easily accessible locations. Use a WLAN analysis tool on a mobile device to measure signal strength inside and outside the building and identify areas with strong signal bleeding.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access points are mounted on ceilings or walls to achieve better signal coverage. However, there are no special anti-theft brackets. Basic efforts are made to reduce transmission power to minimize signal propagation to the outside, but this is done without a formal site survey.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The placement is more thought out, but lacks professionalism in its implementation. Physical security is rudimentary, and transmission power optimization is done on a 'best guess' basis rather than based on measurement data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, check the mounting of the access points. Are they high up but attached with standard clips and easily removable? Ask the administrator how the transmission power is set. If the answer is 'we usually set it to medium' and no measurement logs exist, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access points are mounted to be access- and theft-proof. Based on a site survey, locations are chosen to provide sufficient coverage for the required areas and to minimize signal propagation into areas not to be serviced. Outdoor installations are protected from weather by suitable housings and from electrical discharges by lightning protection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Conduct a professional site survey before installation to determine the optimal locations and configurations for the APs. Use anti-theft mounting brackets or lockable enclosures, especially in public areas. For outdoor installations, APs with an appropriate IP rating (e.g., IP67) and suitable lightning protection components must be used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the site survey report. Check the physical mounting of the APs for the use of security hardware. Inspect outdoor installations for weatherproof housings and the presence of lightning protection measures. Automated check: `snmpwalk -v3 -u <user> -l authPriv -a SHA -A <pass> -x AES -X <pass> <ap-ip> RF-MIB::dot11PhyTxPower` to check the set transmission power and compare it with the target values from the site survey.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A professional RF site survey using specialized software is conducted to model and visualize signal propagation, strength, and interference before installation (predictive survey). A verification survey is performed after installation. The transmission power of the APs is actively managed to precisely control the signal footprint. Regular, documented physical inspections of the APs take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Commission a specialist or use professional tools like Ekahau or AirMagnet for predictive planning and a subsequent on-site validation survey. Implement a maintenance plan that includes regular physical checks of the APs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the heatmaps and reports from the site survey tool shown to you. Request the maintenance logs for the physical inspections. Compare the current transmission power configuration with the recommendations from the survey. Automated check: Many central WLAN management systems can generate heatmaps based on the actual data of the APs. Compare these with the original planning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AP placement and configuration is optimized by AI/ML-based planning tools. The WLAN system continuously monitors the RF environment and dynamically adjusts the transmission power and channel assignments of the APs (Adaptive Radio Management). The system can detect signal leakage outside the intended perimeter and trigger alarms. Physical manipulation of an AP (e.g., disconnection from the network) leads to the automatic blocking of the switch port and the triggering of a high-priority security incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Invest in a high-end WLAN solution with advanced RRM/ARM capabilities and integrated location detection. Configure port security measures on the switches that react to the disconnection of an AP (e.g., via LLDP/CDP), and integrate these alarms into your SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration and log data of the WLAN controller for events that indicate dynamic RF adjustments. Simulate a manipulation by disconnecting an AP from the switch and observe the reaction (port blocking, alarm in the SIEM). Automated check: `switch-cli --show port-security interface <interface-number>` and `siem-api --query 'event_type=tamper AND device_type=access_point' --time-frame 5m`.

controls.title: Secure basic configuration of the access points (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Individual default settings like the SSID are changed, but critical defaults like the administrator password or default SNMP community strings remain unchanged. Administration is done via the insecure default web interface (HTTP).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This is a very common and dangerous omission. Attackers know the default credentials of all manufacturers and can thus take control of the access points.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Try to log in to the web interface of an access point with the manufacturer's known default credentials. Check if the administration URL starts with `http://`. Automated check: Run a script that tries to log in to the APs with a list of default credentials via Telnet, SSH, and HTTP (e.g., with `hydra` or `nmap` NSE scripts like `http-default-accounts`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The default SSIDs and administrator passwords are always changed during commissioning. However, insecure administration access methods such as Telnet or HTTP often remain enabled, even if they are not actively used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The most basic mistakes are avoided, but complete hardening does not take place. The remaining open, insecure services still represent an unnecessary attack surface.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Verify that the default credentials no longer work. Run a port scan on an access point to check if insecure ports like 23 (Telnet) or 80 (HTTP) are open. Automated check: `nmap -p 23,80,161 <ap-ip>`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access points are not used in their factory default configuration. All default SSIDs, access passwords, and cryptographic keys are changed before production use. Insecure administration access (e.g., Telnet, HTTP, SNMPv1/v2c) is disabled. Administration of the access points is exclusively done via a suitably encrypted connection (e.g., SSH, HTTPS).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Create and use a mandatory checklist for the basic configuration (hardening) of new access points. This must include changing all default credentials, deactivating insecure services, and the exclusive use of encrypted management protocols.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the hardening checklist for access points. Check the configuration of an exemplary AP against this checklist. Run a port scan and verify that only secure management ports (e.g., 22, 443) are open. Automated check: `nmap -sV <ap-ip>` and check the open ports and services for secure versions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A standardized, hardened configuration template is created and rolled out to all access points from a central management solution. The configuration includes additional hardening measures such as deactivating unused physical ports on the AP, configuring a secure NTP service, and central logging of all events on a syslog server.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use the template functions of your WLAN controller or management software to ensure a uniform and secure configuration. Set up a central log server and configure all APs to send their logs there.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the configuration template in the WLAN management system shown to you. Check the configuration of an AP and compare it with the template. Check on the central syslog server if the logs of the access points are arriving there. Automated check: `wlan-controller-cli --get-config-template --name 'hardening_v1'` and on the log server `grep <ap-ip> /var/log/syslog`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration of the access points is fully automated through 'Policy as Code' or 'Infrastructure as Code' (e.g., using Ansible playbooks). A system for continuous compliance monitoring permanently checks the state of the APs against the defined security baseline. Any deviation automatically triggers an alarm and a configurable auto-remediation action that restores the secure state.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Develop scripts or playbooks that enable zero-touch provisioning and configuration of APs. Use configuration compliance software (or the features of your high-end WLAN solution) to continuously validate the configurations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the Ansible playbooks or scripts for AP configuration. Have the dashboard of the compliance tool shown to you. Simulate a manual, non-compliant change on an AP and observe the system's reaction (alarm, automatic correction). Automated check: Run the configuration playbook in `--check` mode to detect deviations: `ansible-playbook -i inventory.yml ap_config.yml --check`.

controls.title: Secure configuration of the WLAN infrastructure (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The WLAN is connected directly to the production LAN. Wireless clients are in the same network segment and broadcast domain as the wired clients and servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This configuration is extremely insecure as it extends the trust boundary of the physically secured LAN to the uncontrollable air interface. A compromised WLAN client has direct access to all resources on the LAN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Connect to the WLAN and check the received IP address. Compare it with the IP address of a wired client in the same office. If they are in the same subnet, this maturity level is met. Automated check: run `ip addr` or `ifconfig` on a WLAN client and analyze the subnet.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A separate VLAN is set up for the WLAN to separate it from the primary corporate LAN. However, there are no or only very broad filter rules (e.g., 'allow all') between the WLAN VLAN and other internal networks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Basic segmentation is in place, which is an improvement. However, without effective filtering at the interconnection point (router/firewall), this separation offers only limited protection against network-based attacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the switch configuration to ensure that the ports for the access points are assigned to a dedicated VLAN. Then check the configuration of the firewall or Layer 3 switch that handles routing for this VLAN. Look for the Access Control Lists (ACLs) or firewall rules. If no rules or only 'any-any-permit' rules exist, this state is reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is ensured that the WLAN represents its own security zone and is logically separated from other security zones (e.g., server network, client network, DMZ). Traffic between the WLAN zone and other zones is controlled at a central gateway (firewall) by defined packet filter rules according to the need-to-know principle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Define the WLAN as a separate zone in your security zone concept. Implement a ruleset on the central firewall that explicitly allows only the access to other zones required by WLAN users. The default rule must be 'deny all'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the network and security zone concept. Check the firewall configuration and the ruleset for traffic originating from the WLAN VLAN. Ensure that the rules are specific (e.g., defined source IPs, destination IPs, and ports) and that there is an implicit or explicit deny rule at the end. Automated check: `firewall-cli --get-rules --zone=wlan`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multiple SSIDs are used to map different security zones for different user groups and device types (e.g., Corporate, Guest, IoT). Each SSID is linked to its own VLAN and a dedicated, restrictive firewall ruleset. 'Client Isolation' is enabled on the access points to prevent direct communication between WLAN clients on the same network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Create separate SSIDs and VLANs for employees, guests, and insecure IoT devices. Create a separate, tailored ruleset on the firewall for each VLAN. In the WLAN controller's configuration, enable Client Isolation (also known as 'AP Isolation' or 'Private WLAN').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In the WLAN controller, check the number of configured SSIDs and their VLAN assignment. Check the firewall ruleset for each of these VLANs. Verify in the SSID configuration that Client Isolation is enabled. Automated check: `wlan-controller-cli --get-ssid-config --all | grep 'vlan|client-isolation'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Dynamic network segmentation is implemented. Based on the user's identity and the device's security status (Posture Assessment), a NAC (Network Access Control) solution dynamically assigns the appropriate VLAN to the client or applies individual firewall rules (micro-segmentation). The principle of least privilege is dynamically enforced for each individual connection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement a NAC solution that is integrated with your WLAN controller, RADIUS server, and your firewall. Define policies based on user attributes from Active Directory, the device type, and the results of a health check (e.g., current antivirus scanner, patch level).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the policy engine of the NAC solution demonstrated to you. Run a test by connecting with a compliant and a non-compliant device, and observe the different treatment (e.g., assignment to different VLANs, different access rights). Check the firewall logs to verify the dynamic application of rules. Automated check: `nac-cli --get-policy --user <testuser>`.

controls.title: Structure of a Distribution System (B) [Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access points are connected to available switch ports without a planned architecture. No conscious decision is made about physical or logical separation; the WLAN shares the infrastructure with the existing LAN.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this state, the Distribution System (the wired network connecting the APs) is not considered a separate component. This usually results in a flat, unsegmented network structure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the switch ports to which the APs are connected. Are they configured as simple access ports in the default VLAN? Ask the administrator if a decision on separation has been made. If not, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decision to use logical separation via VLANs has been made. However, the implementation is inconsistent across the network, and the VLAN configuration is sparsely documented or not documented at all.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The basic idea of separation is there, but a systematic plan is missing. Different administrators may configure the VLANs differently, leading to errors and inconsistencies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configurations of multiple switches to which APs are connected. Look for differences in VLAN assignment or configuration (e.g., native VLAN, tagged VLANs). Ask for the network documentation for the VLAN structure. If it is outdated, incomplete, or non-existent, this maturity level is met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before building the wired distribution system, a fundamental and documented decision is made as to whether the separation will be physical (separate switches) or logical (using VLANs on the access switches). The chosen method is implemented consistently throughout the entire network.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Analyze the pros and cons of both approaches in the context of your institution. A logical separation using VLANs is usually more flexible and cost-effective. Document the decision made in the network or WLAN concept. Ensure that all switch configurations comply with this decision.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the document in which the decision on the separation method is recorded (e.g., in the WLAN concept). Spot-check the configurations of the relevant switch ports to verify consistent implementation. Automated check: run and compare `switch-cli --show vlan brief` and `switch-cli --show interface <interface-number> switchport` on multiple switches.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decision for separation is part of the overarching network architecture documentation. The design for the distribution system is robust and planned in detail, including dedicated VLANs for AP management and separate VLANs for each SSID. The switch configurations are managed via standardized and versioned templates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Create detailed network diagrams and a VLAN table that describes the entire structure of the distribution system. Use configuration templates (e.g., text files with variables) to speed up the configuration of new switches and ensure consistency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the network architecture documentation and the configuration templates for the switches shown to you. Compare a running configuration of a switch with the corresponding template for deviations. Check whether the VLAN structure (management, user, guest VLANs) is implemented as documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network fabric automatically provisions the correct VLANs on switch ports where an access point is detected (e.g., via LLDP). The decision for logical separation is implemented in an automated network orchestration platform that ensures consistency and reduces manual errors. The architecture supports advanced overlay technologies (e.g., VXLAN) for dynamic and scalable segmentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement a modern network management or SDN (Software-Defined Networking) solution that supports automated port provisioning based on the detected device type. Define the segmentation logic centrally in the orchestration platform.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the configuration of the network orchestration platform demonstrated to you. Connect a new AP to an unconfigured port and observe the automatic provisioning process. Check the resulting configuration on the switch. Automated check: `orchestrator-api --get-port-profile --device-type 'access-point'`.

controls.title: Secure connection of WLANs to a LAN (S) [Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The transition from WLAN to LAN is unsecured. There are no packet filters or firewall rules that control traffic between the two network types.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This configuration negates the benefits of VLAN-based separation and poses a high security risk, as threats can spread unhindered from the potentially less secure WLAN to the LAN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Identify the gateway (router or Layer 3 switch) for the WLAN VLAN. Check its configuration for Access Control Lists (ACLs) or firewall policies. If there are no filter rules for traffic from the WLAN to the LAN, this state is met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: At the transition from WLAN to LAN, there is a packet filter, but it only applies very basic or broad rules (e.g., blocking known insecure ports). A detailed regulation based on the need-to-know principle is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A first step has been taken to control data traffic, but the filtering is not restrictive enough to provide effective protection. Often, only a few 'bad' services are blocked instead of only allowing the 'good' ones.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analyze the ACLs or firewall rules at the gateway. Are the rules very general (e.g., `permit ip any any`) with only a few specific `deny` rules? Is a `deny any any` rule missing at the end? If so, this maturity level is met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The transition between the WLAN and the LAN MUST be secured by a packet filter or a firewall. Defined rules must exist that control data traffic between the WLAN segment and other internal networks according to the principle of least privilege. The connection is implemented consistently with the established strategy for the distribution system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement a ruleset on the firewall or Layer 3 switch that handles routing between WLAN and LAN, which blocks all traffic by default ('default deny'). Then create explicit 'permit' rules only for the absolutely necessary protocols and destinations (e.g., access to intranet server on port 443).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the documentation of the firewall rule set for the WLAN zone. Review the configuration and ensure that it follows the 'default deny' principle and that the rules are specific. Automated check: `firewall-cli --list-all --zone=wlan` and analysis of the rules and the default behavior.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Stateful inspection firewall rules are used at the perimeter. In addition, egress filtering is applied to control where clients from the WLAN are allowed to establish connections to the internet. Separate, customized rule sets exist for different WLANs (e.g., guest vs. employee). All permitted and blocked traffic is logged for analysis purposes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use the stateful capabilities of your firewall to ensure that only responses to allowed requests from the LAN can return to the WLAN. Implement rules that restrict outgoing traffic to standard ports like 80/443 to make malware propagation more difficult. Configure the firewall to send all rule matches to a central Syslog server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check whether the firewall is operating in stateful mode. Analyze the egress filter rules for the WLAN zone. Compare the rule sets for the guest and employee WLANs. Check on the Syslog server whether the firewall logs are arriving. Automated check: `grep 'UFW BLOCK' /var/log/ufw.log | grep 'SRC=<wlan-subnet>'` (example for UFW).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) with Application-Layer Control (Layer 7) and an integrated Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) secures the perimeter. Policies are applied dynamically based on user identity and device status (via NAC integration). All traffic is inspected for malware and suspicious activities, and the results are forwarded in real-time to a SIEM for correlation and alerting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Deploy an NGFW that can filter traffic not only by ports but also by applications (e.g., 'Facebook', 'Dropbox'). Activate the IPS function to detect and block attacks at the network and application level. Integrate the firewall with your NAC and SIEM solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the NGFW configuration for application-based rules and active IPS signatures. Have the integration with the NAC solution demonstrated by showing how different users receive different application rights. Check the SIEM dashboard for alarms generated by the NGFW. Automated check: `ngfw-api --get-policy --user <test-user>`.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for the operation of WLANs (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no specific security policy for the operation of WLANs. Decisions are made ad-hoc or based on general, non-specific IT policies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Without a dedicated policy, there is no binding basis for secure operation. This leads to inconsistent configurations and an unclear security level.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask for the WLAN security policy. If none exists, or if reference is only made to a general 'IT Acceptable Use Policy' in which WLAN is not explicitly addressed, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are informal written rules or sections in other documents (e.g., network concept) that govern WLAN operation. However, these have not been adopted as a formal, standalone policy and are only partially known to those responsible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are approaches to regulation, but they lack formal anchoring and communication. The rules are often incomplete and not binding for all parties involved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Look for sections dealing with WLAN in the existing IT documentation. Ask different administrators what rules apply to them. If the statements are inconsistent and no formal policy document can be presented, this maturity level is met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the institution's general security policy, the key core aspects for the secure use of WLANs are specified in a separate policy. This policy is known to all those responsible for setting up and operating WLANs and serves as the basis for their work. Any detected deviations from the policy are dealt with appropriately.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Create a formal 'WLAN Security Policy' document. Derive the content from the higher-level IT security policy and the specific requirements of the BSI IT-Grundschutz. Make the document verifiably known to all involved employees (planning, operation, administration).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the WLAN security policy. Check whether it covers essential aspects such as authentication, encryption, network segmentation, and secure configuration. Ask for proof of promulgation (e.g., distribution list, entry in the intranet). Ask about the process that is triggered in case of non-compliance with the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The implementation of the content required in the policy is regularly checked (e.g., annually) by internal or external audits. The results of the review, including identified deviations and planned measures, are documented in a traceable manner and their implementation is tracked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Plan regular WLAN audits as part of your internal control system. Use the policy as a checklist for these audits. Document the results in an audit report and track the remediation of findings in an action plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the audit reports from the last WLAN reviews shown to you. Request the corresponding action plan and check the status of the open items. Automated check: Check the ticket or GRC system for entries related to the results of WLAN audits.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The WLAN security policy is managed in a GRC tool. Compliance checking is automated wherever possible. A compliance dashboard shows the current implementation status of the policy in real time. Deviations automatically lead to the creation of a ticket in the service management system and to escalation if not processed. The policy contains measurable key performance indicators (KPIs) for evaluating WLAN security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use configuration compliance tools that automatically compare your WLAN infrastructure settings with the policy requirements. Integrate this tool with your GRC and ticketing system. Define KPIs such as 'percentage of compliant access points' or 'number of detected rogue APs per month'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the compliance dashboard in the GRC tool or WLAN management solution demonstrated. Simulate a non-compliant change and observe the automated ticket creation. Request the KPI reports for the last few quarters. Automated check: `grc-tool-api --get-compliance-report --policy 'WLAN Security Policy'`.

controls.title: Appropriate selection of WLAN components (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: WLAN components are procured mainly based on price, availability, or marketing materials. A technical requirements list does not exist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This approach often leads to a heterogeneous, difficult-to-manage, and potentially insecure infrastructure, as important security and compatibility features are not considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask about the procurement process for the current WLAN components. Ask for the requirements list or specification sheet from that time. If such documents do not exist and the decision was made verbally or based on simple criteria, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During procurement, an informal evaluation takes place that focuses primarily on functional features and performance. Security aspects are mentioned, but not systematically evaluated against a requirements list.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a basic awareness of technical requirements, but the process is not formalized. Often, different products are 'tried out' without using clear, predefined criteria for the decision.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask for the documentation of the last WLAN procurement. If it consists of informal notes, emails, or a simple comparison table without predefined, weighted criteria, this maturity level is likely.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the results of the planning phase, a formal requirements list is created, which is used to evaluate the products available on the market. When procuring WLAN components, it is verifiably ensured that, in addition to functionality, attention is also paid to security, data protection, and compatibility of the components with each other.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Derive a detailed requirements specification or list from your WLAN strategy and security concept. This should include specific mandatory and optional criteria in categories such as security (e.g., WPA3 support, 802.1X), management, performance, and interoperability. Use this list to objectively compare offers and products.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the requirements list and the comparative product evaluation from the last WLAN procurement. Check whether criteria on security (e.g., supported protocols), data protection (e.g., handling of location data), and compatibility were explicitly included and evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements list is a formal, weighted checklist (utility analysis). A structured market analysis is carried out. Selected products from the shortlist are tested in a test environment (Proof of Concept) for fulfillment of the most important requirements before the final purchase decision. Recognized security certifications (e.g., FIPS, Common Criteria) are taken into account in the selection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Set up a lab environment to test potential new WLAN components. Define a test plan that covers the most important application and security cases. Make the request for security certifications a mandatory part of your tender documents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the documentation of the utility analysis, the results of the market analysis, and the test report from the proof of concept shown to you. Check the tender documents for the requirement of security certificates. Check whether the procured products actually have the specified certifications.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement process is integrated into a comprehensive supplier risk management. Continuous market observation for new technologies and vulnerabilities takes place. A key requirement for the components is the availability of APIs for deep integration into the existing management and security ecosystem (SIEM, NAC, SOAR). Suppliers must disclose their secure software development processes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Evaluate not only the product but also the manufacturer in terms of their security practices and how they handle vulnerabilities (PSIRT). Make API availability and integration capability a knockout criterion for strategic procurements. Use threat intelligence services to stay informed about new vulnerabilities in the products you use or evaluate.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the documentation for supplier risk management. Have the API documentation of the WLAN solution in use shown to you and check which integrations have actually been implemented. Ask about the process for monitoring vulnerability notifications for the WLAN components. Automated check: `api-client --test-connection --endpoint <wlan-controller-api>`.

controls.title: Use of a suitable WLAN management solution (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Each access point is configured individually and manually via its own web interface or command line. There is no central management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This approach is extremely inefficient, error-prone, and not scalable. Uniform configurations and fast, comprehensive changes (e.g., a new password) are practically impossible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask the administrator how they apply a configuration change to all access points. If the answer is 'I log into each one individually,' this maturity level has been reached. Check the configurations of two APs for unintentional differences.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple, often free management software from the manufacturer is used for basic tasks such as monitoring the online status or distributing simple configuration changes. Advanced features are missing or not used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A first step towards centralization has been taken, but the solution's capabilities are not fully utilized. Management is often still limited to a few basic parameters.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the management solution in use shown to you. Check which range of functions is actually used. If usage is limited to pure monitoring and changing the SSID, this maturity level is likely.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central management solution is used. The scope of services of this solution is in line with the requirements of the WLAN strategy and enables at least the central configuration, monitoring of the system status, and distribution of firmware updates to all access points.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Evaluate and procure a WLAN controller solution (hardware- or software-based/cloud) that meets the requirements defined in your strategy. Migrate the configuration of all access points to the central management and perform future changes only through this solution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the central management solution demonstrated. Verify that all productive access points are managed by the solution. Have the process for a central firmware update or a configuration change shown to you. Automated check: `wlan-controller-cli --get-managed-aps`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The central management solution is used for advanced functions such as detailed monitoring, reporting, alerting for failures or security problems, and enforcing configuration templates. It has role-based access control (RBAC) to assign different permissions to administrators.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use the advanced features of your management solution. Create configuration templates for different locations or use cases. Define meaningful alert rules (e.g., 'AP offline', 'High channel utilization'). Set up different administrator roles (e.g., 'WLAN Admin' with full access, 'Helpdesk' with read access).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration of the management solution for the use of templates and alert rules. Have the configuration of the role-based access control shown to you and check whether different roles exist and have been assigned. Request a sample report (e.g., on WLAN usage).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management solution is a feature-rich platform with extensive APIs that are deeply integrated into other systems such as NAC, SIEM, and 'Infrastructure as Code' tools. It offers advanced analytics, RF visualization, and predictive problem detection. Configuration and management are largely automated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Choose a management solution that supports open standards and APIs. Use these APIs to automate processes, e.g., the automatic inclusion of new APs in the management or the synchronization of data with a CMDB. Use AI-based analysis functions for proactive network optimization.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the implemented API integrations demonstrated (e.g., the display of WLAN data in another system). Check the dashboards of the management solution for analysis and prediction functions. Request the automation scripts that use the solution's API. Automated check: Run a test API call against the management solution to check its availability and functionality.

controls.title: Regular security checks in WLANs (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security reviews of the WLAN do not take place proactively, but only in reaction to a concrete suspicion or a security incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A reactive approach means that vulnerabilities and unauthorized devices often remain undetected for a long time and are only noticed when damage has already occurred.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask about the process and frequency for WLAN security checks. If there is no planned, regular process, this maturity level has been reached. Check if there are reports from past checks. If these are missing, this is another indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Occasionally, informal security checks are carried out. For example, an administrator manually checks the controller interface for foreign devices or performs a quick scan with a smartphone app. The results are not systematically documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an awareness of the need for checks, but there is a lack of system, regularity, and traceability. The checks depend on the initiative of individual employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask the administrator how they search for rogue APs. If the answer describes a manual, sporadic activity, this is an indication. Ask for the results of the last checks. If these do not exist or are only available as a note, the maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Regular security checks are carried out in the WLANs to specifically search for potential security vulnerabilities and unauthorized installed access points (Rogue APs). The results of these checks are documented in a traceable manner and compared with the target state.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Schedule regular (e.g., quarterly) security checks. Define a checklist that includes at least the search for rogue APs and a check for known configuration weaknesses. Use dedicated tools for this (e.g., Kismet, WiFi Pineapple in audit mode, or the functions of the WLAN controller). Keep a log of the checks performed and the results found.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the plan for the regular security checks. Have the logs of the last performed checks shown to you. Check whether the documentation is complete (date, auditor, results, identified deviations).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regular security checks also include planned vulnerability scans of the WLAN infrastructure components (controller, APs) and measurements of performance and coverage. Identified deviations from the target state are systematically investigated and tracked for remediation in a ticketing system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Integrate the IP addresses of your WLAN components into your regular vulnerability scans. Perform periodic verification site surveys to detect changes in the RF environment. Use your central ticketing system to record all findings and manage their processing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the reports of the last vulnerability scans for the WLAN infrastructure shown to you. Request the logs of the last performance and coverage measurements. Search the ticketing system for tickets that resulted from the security checks and check their processing status.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated Wireless Intrusion Detection/Prevention (WIDS/WIPS) solution performs continuous, automated security monitoring of the WLAN. The system scans the frequency spectrum 24/7 for rogue APs, misconfigurations, and known attacks, and can automatically trigger alarms or initiate countermeasures. Performance and coverage data are permanently recorded and analyzed to proactively identify the need for optimization.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement a WIDS/WIPS solution that is either integrated into your WLAN system or works as an overlay solution. Configure it to automatically react to critical events and send alarms to your SIEM or your operations team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the WIDS/WIPS dashboard demonstrated. Check the configuration of the automated alerting and response rules. Check the system's or SIEM's log data for detected events from the last few weeks. Automated check: `wids-cli --get-events --last 24h --type rogue_ap`.

controls.title: Regular audits of WLAN components (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Audits of the WLAN components do not take place. The assumption is that the initial configuration was correct and remains unchanged.

parts.name: guidance
