parts.prose: This assumption is dangerous because configurations can be changed by operational errors, failed updates, or unnoticed attacks ('Configuration Drift').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask for the audit plan or logs for WLAN components. If none exist, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Occasionally and in an unstructured manner, an administrator randomly checks the configuration of an access point to see if 'everything is still okay'. Physical checks do not take place. The results are not documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a basic understanding of the need for review, but a formal, regular, and traceable process is lacking. The checks are superficial and incomplete.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interview the administrator about their procedure for configuration checks. If this is done spontaneously and without a checklist, and no records are kept, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all components of the WLAN infrastructure, it is regularly checked whether all specified security measures have been implemented and the components are correctly configured. The audit results are documented in a traceable manner and compared with the target state.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Create a formal audit plan that specifies when (e.g., annually) and how the WLAN components are to be audited. Develop a detailed audit checklist based on your WLAN security policy and configuration specifications. Conduct the audit and create a formal report on the results.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the audit plan and audit checklist for the WLAN infrastructure. Have the audit reports from the last audit period shown to you. Compare the documented results with the target specifications from the security policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regular audits also include random physical checks of publicly installed access points for signs of tampering or opening attempts. All deviations found during the audits are systematically recorded in a ticketing system, their remediation is actively tracked and finally verified.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Expand your audit checklist to include 'Physical Inspection' for relevant APs. Integrate the audit process with your ticketing system so that a ticket is automatically created for each finding for remediation. The auditor should confirm the successful remediation at the end of the process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the audit checklist for the physical inspection item. Ask to see the logs of these inspections. Search the ticketing system for tickets resulting from the last audit and check their processing and verification status.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The audits are largely automated. A configuration compliance tool continuously compares the running configuration of all WLAN components with a defined and versioned 'Golden Configuration'. Any deviation ('drift') immediately triggers an alarm. The audit results and compliance status are visualized in a central GRC dashboard and are part of the continuous risk management.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement a solution for automated compliance checking. Define your security baseline as code (e.g., in YAML or JSON) and have the tool continuously check against it. Integrate the alarms into your SIEM and the reports into your GRC tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the compliance dashboard demonstrated to you. Request the 'Golden Configuration' baseline. Simulate a non-compliant configuration change on an AP and observe the automatic detection and alerting in the system. Automated check: Run the compliance tool manually or query its status via an API: `compliance-tool-cli --run-check --target-group wlan-aps`.

controls.title: Use of a VPN to secure WLANs (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of VPN to secure WLANs is not a considered option.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This requirement is relevant for high protection needs. In environments with normal protection needs, the absence of this measure is not necessarily a deficiency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask if the use of VPN over WLAN has been evaluated. If not, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The option to use a VPN over WLAN is known to employees and is used individually as needed, but is not centrally managed or enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees can manually connect to the corporate VPN when needed. However, there is no policy that requires this for specific use cases.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check if a VPN solution exists and if employees are informed about how to use it over WLAN. Check if there are policies that enforce its use. If these are missing, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of a VPN for additional security of WLAN communication has been evaluated and documented as a strategic option for use cases with high protection needs. There is a guide for users on how to securely use the VPN on the WLAN.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Conduct an assessment to determine for which data transmissions or user groups in the WLAN an additional VPN protection is useful. Ensure that a robust VPN solution is available and document its use for the target groups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the evaluation documentation on VPN use in the WLAN. Check the available instructions and configuration policies for VPN use. Ensure that the VPN solution itself is securely configured (current protocols, strong ciphers).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For access to all internal, classified as sensitive resources via the corporate WLAN, the use of a VPN is mandatory. This is enforced by firewall rules that block direct access from the WLAN segment to these resources and only allow access from the VPN address pool.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Identify sensitive systems (e.g., HR administration, development servers). Create firewall rules that allow access to these systems only from the IP addresses that your VPN gateway assigns to clients. Communicate this regulation clearly to users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the firewall rule sets. Look for rules that block access from the WLAN VLAN to sensitive zones but allow access from the VPN VLAN. Test access to a sensitive resource from the WLAN once directly and once with an active VPN. Automated check: `firewall-cli --list-rules --zone=internal | grep -E 'source=<wlan-vlan>|source=<vpn-vlan>'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An 'Always-on' VPN is configured for all corporate devices, which automatically routes all data traffic from the device (whether on WLAN or external) through an encrypted tunnel to the corporate network. The VPN solution is integrated into a Zero-Trust architecture and checks the device status (Device Posture) before establishing a connection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement an Always-on VPN solution (e.g., via Windows or MDM profiles). Integrate it with a NAC or Zero-Trust Network Access (ZTNA) solution to enable context-aware access control that goes beyond a mere network connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the configuration profiles on the end devices for the 'Always-on' setting. Have the integration configuration between the VPN gateway and the posture check solution shown to you. Observe the behavior of a non-compliant device when attempting to establish a VPN connection. Automated check: `vpn-gateway-cli --get-connection-logs --filter 'posture=failed'`.

controls.title: Additional security for connecting WLANs to a LAN (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No additional security measures are taken for WLANs with high protection needs at the transition to the LAN. The security is identical to that for WLANs with normal protection needs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If the protection needs are not differentiated, sensitive data or systems may not be adequately protected if they are accessible via the WLAN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Compare the firewall rule sets for the standard WLAN and a potential high-security WLAN (e.g., for administrators or executives). If they are identical, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For WLANs with high protection needs, slightly more restrictive firewall rules are applied, but they do not go beyond standard packet filtering.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an awareness of the increased protection needs, but the implemented measures are only a slight tightening of the standard measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Analyze the firewall rules for the high-security WLAN. If they only block a few more ports than the standard WLAN but do not use advanced security features, this maturity level is likely.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The transition from WLANs with high protection needs to the LAN is secured by a firewall with stateful inspection and an explicitly restrictive rule set based on the 'Default Deny' principle. The measures are significantly stricter than for WLANs with normal protection needs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Define a separate security zone concept for high-security WLANs. Implement an extremely minimalistic rule set that only allows the absolutely necessary connections. Document and justify every single permission.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the rule set for the high-security WLAN. Check if it is based on the 'Default Deny' principle and if the permissions are very specific and minimal. Compare it with the rule set for the standard WLAN to determine the significant difference.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The transition is secured by a Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) with an activated Intrusion Prevention System (IPS). Traffic is controlled at the application level (Layer 7) and monitored for known attack patterns. Only explicitly allowed applications may communicate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Deploy an NGFW at the transition point of the high-security WLAN. Create a rule set that is not based on ports, but on application signatures (e.g., 'allow RDP', 'deny Facebook'). Activate a strict IPS profile to actively block attack attempts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the NGFW configuration. Look for application-based rules and an active IPS profile for traffic from the high-security WLAN. Check the IPS logs for blocked attacks. Automated check: `ngfw-cli --get-rules --zone=high-security-wlan | grep 'application|ips-profile'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All traffic from the high-security WLAN is routed through a dedicated security appliance or a chain of security functions (Service Chaining) before entering the LAN. This includes Deep Packet Inspection (DPI), SSL/TLS inspection, sandboxing for unknown files, and advanced malware analysis. The security policies are dynamically updated based on threat intelligence feeds.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement a 'Security DMZ' for your high-security WLAN. Route all traffic through specialized systems for content analysis. This is especially important if the internet is accessed from this WLAN. Subscribe to commercial threat intelligence feeds to keep your defense mechanisms up to date.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the network diagram shown to you that depicts the traffic flow from the high-security WLAN through the security components. Check the configuration of the SSL inspection and the sandbox. Check if and how threat intelligence feeds are integrated into the firewall or IPS rules. Automated check: `security-gateway-api --get-threat-intelligence-status`.

controls.title: Securing communication between access points (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Communication between the WLAN components (Access Points and Controller) is unencrypted over the LAN. Wireless mesh connections are not used or are used unencrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Unencrypted management communication is a significant risk, as an attacker on the LAN could read or manipulate sensitive configuration data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Perform a packet capture on the switch port of an access point (port mirroring). Filter for the management protocol (e.g., CAPWAP, PAPI) and check if the packet contents are readable. Automated check: `tshark -i <interface> -Y 'capwap' -c 10` and analyze the output for unencrypted data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management communication between AP and controller is encrypted, but may use weak, manufacturer-preset keys or certificates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The encryption is active, but the basis of trust is weak. If all devices from the same manufacturer use the same key, the security is low.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the manufacturer's documentation on how AP-controller communication is secured. Check if factory default certificates are used and if there is a way to replace them with your own. Verify in the controller settings that encryption is active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is ensured by a deliberate configuration decision that the management communication between access points and the WLAN controller is encrypted over the LAN. Whether this encryption is active is checked regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Ensure that you use a WLAN solution that supports encrypted management protocols such as CAPWAP with DTLS or IPsec tunnels. Explicitly enable this feature in the controller's configuration. Include the verification of encryption in your regular WLAN audits.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the global configuration of the WLAN controller and ensure that management encryption (e.g., 'AP data security' or 'Control Plane Security') is enabled. Confirm this with a packet capture, where the traffic must be identifiable as encrypted (e.g., DTLS).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All management communication between the access points and the central WLAN controller must be strongly encrypted (e.g., using CAPWAP over DTLS 1.2 with strong cipher suites). For wireless mesh connections between APs, the backhaul communication is also secured with WPA2/WPA3 and a strong key.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Explicitly configure the secure protocol versions and cipher suites to be used for management communication on the WLAN controller. Disable outdated or weak algorithms. If you operate mesh WLANs, ensure that the same high security standards apply to the connections between APs as to client connections.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the advanced security settings of the WLAN controller for the DTLS parameter configuration. Have the mesh network configuration shown to you and check the configured encryption method. Automated check: `wlan-controller-cli --get-security-config | grep 'dtls|cipher'`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The encryption of communication between all WLAN components is secured by mutual certificate-based authentication. Only APs and controllers with valid certificates issued by the internal PKI can establish a secure connection. The integrity of the communication channels is continuously monitored, and any attempt to establish an unencrypted or unauthenticated connection is blocked and reported as a security incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Set up a certificate enrollment process for your access points (e.g., via SCEP). Configure the controller to only accept connections from APs with valid certificates and to also identify itself to the AP with a certificate. Integrate the corresponding logs into your SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the WLAN controller configuration for certificate-based AP authentication. Check the certificates on an AP and the controller for their validity and origin from the internal PKI. Simulate connecting an unprovisioned AP and ensure that it is rejected and an alarm is generated in the SIEM.

controls.title: Use of Wireless Intrusion Detection/Wireless Intrusion Prevention Systems (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No systems for detecting or preventing intrusions into the WLAN are used. The detection of attacks is purely coincidental.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Without specialized monitoring, most WLAN-specific attacks (such as Evil Twins, deauthentication attacks) go unnoticed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Ask about the WIDS/WIPS solution in use. If none exists and the basic functions integrated in the WLAN controller are also not used, this maturity level has been reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The basic functions for detecting rogue APs, which are included in most modern WLAN management solutions, are used. No further attack or anomaly detection takes place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The simplest form of monitoring is active. This provides basic protection against unauthorized installed devices, but not against active attacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Check the WLAN controller configuration for the activation of rogue AP detection. Have the list of detected (and, if applicable, classified) foreign APs shown to you. Check whether additional IDS/IPS functions are available and active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of a WIDS (Wireless Intrusion Detection System) or WIPS (Wireless Intrusion Prevention System) has been evaluated as a strategic option to increase WLAN security, and a decision on its use has been documented. If no dedicated solution is used, the advanced IDS functions of the WLAN controller are actively used and monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Evaluate the added value of a dedicated WIDS/WIPS solution compared to the integrated functions of your controller. Document the decision. If you use the integrated functions, configure them completely and set up a regular review of the detected events.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the evaluation documentation and the decision on the use of WIDS/WIPS. If a solution (dedicated or integrated) is in use, have the recently detected events shown to you. Check whether these events have been responded to.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Wireless Intrusion Detection System (WIDS) is in use. It continuously monitors the frequency spectrum for anomalies and known attack vectors (e.g., rogue APs, evil twins, deauthentication attacks). When a critical event is detected, the security team is automatically alerted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Implement a WIDS solution that either works as an overlay with dedicated sensors or uses the scanning capabilities of your production APs (hybrid mode). Configure the alerting rules so that critical alerts (e.g., 'potential evil twin detected') are immediately sent to the responsible team via email or another notification system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the WIDS dashboard and configuration shown to you. Check the configured signatures and alerting rules. In a test environment, perform a simulated attack (e.g., a deauth attack with `aireplay-ng`) and verify that an alarm is triggered and delivered. Automated check: `wids-cli --get-alerts --last 7d`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A Wireless Intrusion Prevention System (WIPS) is in use, which not only detects attacks but also automatically initiates active countermeasures. This can include the targeted disconnection of a client from a rogue AP or the automatic blocking of the switch port to which a rogue AP is connected. The WIPS is fully integrated into the SIEM/SOAR ecosystem to enable correlated threat analysis and automated response.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Use a WIPS solution that can take active intervention. Be cautious when configuring automated countermeasures to avoid disrupting legitimate devices (e.g., through misclassification). Integrate WIPS alerts into your SOAR platform to automate complex response chains (e.g., WIPS detects rogue AP -> SOAR queries switch for MAC address -> SOAR blocks port -> SOAR creates ticket).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Have the configuration of the automatic countermeasures in the WIPS shown to you ('Containment' functions). Simulate the connection of a rogue AP to the LAN and observe whether the corresponding switch port is automatically blocked. Check the associated playbook and the log entries in the SOAR platform.

controls.title: Creation of a usage policy for WLAN (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are rudimentary regulations for WLAN use, possibly only communicated orally or incompletely documented. These only cover individual aspects, such as the password for the guest WLAN, and are not systematically enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This state is often found in organizations where WLAN has grown "organically" without a central security concept. The rules are often only known to a small circle of IT staff.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD determine through interviews with employees and IT staff whether regulations for WLAN use are known. It SHOULD be checked whether a written policy exists. The absence of a comprehensive, written, and communicated policy indicates this level of maturity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic WLAN usage policy exists and is documented. It contains the most important prohibitions (e.g., no private devices in the production WLAN), but lacks detailed specifications on aspects such as the use of external hotspots or data classification. Regular monitoring of compliance does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is typically created when WLAN is introduced but is not actively maintained or adapted to new threats thereafter. Communication to employees is done once, e.g., upon hiring.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD verify the existence of the WLAN usage policy. The content SHOULD be checked for completeness according to the basic requirements (NET.2.2.A1). It SHOULD be determined whether there is a process for regular review and updating of the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A WLAN usage policy MUST be created that specifies the essential core aspects for secure WLAN use. The policy MUST describe the specifics of WLAN use (e.g., whether, how, and with which devices hotspots may be used), contain information on permitted/prohibited data types, define the handling of client-side security solutions, and include a clear prohibition of unauthorized access points. It MUST also be pointed out that the WLAN interface should be deactivated when not in use. The implementation of the policy MUST be regularly reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy should be anchored as an official document in the Information Security Management System (ISMS) and made accessible to all employees, e.g., in the intranet. The review can be carried out through random audits of client configurations and user surveys.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD request the WLAN usage policy. It SHOULD be checked whether all required aspects (hotspot usage, data classification, client security, prohibition of rogue APs, deactivation of the interface) are included. Evidence of regular reviews of compliance with the policy (e.g., audit reports) SHOULD be inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Building on the defined policy (Level 3), the results of the regular reviews are systematically documented and used to improve the policy and technical measures. The policy is proactively adapted to new technologies (e.g., WPA3) and known threat scenarios. It also contains specific requirements for different user groups (e.g., administrators, guests).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The documentation of the review results is done in a ticket system or a dedicated ISMS tool. The adjustments to the policy are controlled via a formal change management process. For different roles, there may be appendices or separate but coordinated policy documents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD inspect the documentation of the last reviews of policy compliance (e.g., audit reports, minutes). It SHOULD be verified that the findings from these reviews have led to concrete improvement measures. It SHOULD be checked whether the policy is up-to-date and addresses new technical developments and threats.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the WLAN usage policy is largely monitored automatically. Technical systems such as Network Access Control (NAC) enforce the policy's requirements (e.g., permitted devices, configuration baselines) in real time. Deviations lead to automated responses, such as quarantining the affected client. The policy is fully integrated into the ISMS process and is dynamically adapted to any significant change in the IT infrastructure or threat landscape.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A NAC solution is used that checks the state of clients (e.g., patch level, activated firewall) before network access is granted. Violations of the policy are reported to a SIEM system, which triggers automated response workflows. The policy itself is managed in a GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD check the configuration of the NAC solution to ensure that it correctly implements the requirements of the WLAN policy. The logs of the NAC and SIEM systems SHOULD be analyzed to verify the effectiveness of the automated monitoring and response. An attempt can be made to connect with a non-compliant client to test the system's response.

controls.title: Awareness and training of WLAN users (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Awareness for WLAN security takes place only sporadically and unstructured, for example, through a one-time circular email or a notice on the intranet. There is no formal training program.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Often, the topic is only briefly mentioned when a security incident has occurred. The information is not prepared and does not reach all relevant users.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD determine through interviews with users whether they are aware of the risks of WLAN use and whether they have ever received information or training on it. The absence of training materials and proof of participation is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general IT security basic training for all employees has been established. This covers the topic of WLAN security as one of many points, but does not go into specific application scenarios or the detailed meaning of security settings. A dedicated WLAN training is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The topic 'Secure WLAN' is covered with one or two slides in the general security awareness training. This conveys a basic awareness, but not actionable knowledge for specific situations such as using hotel WLANs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD review the documents of the general IT security training and assess how in-depth the topic of WLAN is covered. It SHOULD be checked whether the content is sufficient to meet the requirements of NET.2.2.A2, which will generally not be the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Users of WLAN components MUST be specifically made aware of and trained on the measures of the usage policy. Suitable training content MUST be defined that explains the importance of WLAN-specific security settings and points out the dangers of bypassing them. The training content MUST be adapted to the respective deployment scenarios and must also cover the security policy and the dangers of third-party WLANs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The training is established as a mandatory part of the onboarding process for new employees. Existing employees are trained at regular intervals (e.g., annually). The training can be conducted as an in-person event, an e-learning module, or through targeted informational materials. Participation is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD review the training materials for WLAN usage. It SHOULD be verified whether the content covers all required aspects (security settings, dangers, policy, third-party WLANs). Proof of participation (e.g., attendance lists, certificates from e-learning systems) SHOULD be spot-checked for various employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined basic training, role-specific training modules are offered (e.g., for travelers, administrators). Training success is verified through knowledge tests. Regular awareness measures, such as simulated phishing attacks via fake WLANs (e.g., 'Free_Airport_WiFi'), are conducted to maintain a high level of awareness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: E-learning platforms are used to manage the training and tests. The results of the tests are incorporated into the improvement of the training content. The simulated attacks are carried out by IT security in a controlled manner and are subsequently debriefed with the affected individuals.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD have the different, role-specific training materials presented to them. The results of the knowledge tests and awareness campaigns (e.g., click rates in phishing simulations) SHOULD be reviewed to evaluate the effectiveness of the measures.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training and awareness program is fully integrated into the security processes and is dynamic. If a security system (e.g., NAC, SIEM) detects insecure behavior by a user on the WLAN, a short, context-related learning module can be automatically assigned to them. Gamification approaches are used to continuously increase motivation and learning success.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The integration of the e-learning system with the SIEM is implemented. For example, if a user repeatedly connects to an insecure public WLAN, a reminder and a link to the relevant training content are automatically sent. A 'Security Champion' program with rewards promotes proactive security behavior.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD check the configuration of the integration between the SIEM and the learning platform. Log files SHOULD be analyzed to determine whether automated training measures were actually triggered upon detection of policy violations. The effectiveness of the gamification program SHOULD be evaluated based on metrics (e.g., reported incidents, achieved scores).

controls.title: Securing WLAN use at hotspots (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of public hotspots is neither explicitly permitted nor prohibited and is not regulated by technical or organizational measures. Employees use hotspots at their own discretion, often without a VPN connection to access company data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, employees connect directly to public WLAN at a hotel or airport to check emails or access cloud services, where data can be transmitted unprotected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD inquire about the procedures of traveling employees when using public WLANs through interviews. It SHOULD be checked whether there is a clear policy and technical enforcement (e.g., Always-On-VPN) for the use of hotspots. The absence of both indicates this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic instruction to use a VPN for accessing internal resources from public WLANs. Other aspects of hotspot security, such as disabling automatic connection or deleting known networks, are not addressed. Compliance with VPN usage is not monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A VPN client is installed on the laptops, but users decide for themselves when to activate it. It is often used only for accessing the intranet, but not for general internet traffic or cloud services.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD check the VPN client configuration for split tunneling. It SHOULD be verified through interviews and by reviewing the WLAN policy whether other security measures for hotspots (besides VPN) are defined and communicated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If the use of hotspots is permitted, it MUST be ensured that every user knows their security requirements and acts accordingly. Sensitive data MAY ONLY be transmitted if appropriate encryption is enabled on the client. Users MAY ONLY access the institution's internal resources via publicly accessible WLANs through a Virtual Private Network (VPN). If the WLAN interface is not used for an extended period, it MUST be deactivated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The organization provides a VPN solution to all employees who are allowed to use hotspots and trains them in its use. The requirements are clearly defined in the WLAN usage policy (see A1). The interface can be deactivated manually by the users, supported by regular reminders.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD spot-check the configuration of clients intended for hotspot use. It must be verified whether a VPN client is installed and configured. The users' knowledge of the security rules for hotspots SHOULD be determined through interviews. It SHOULD be checked whether the VPN connection is configured to tunnel all traffic (no split tunneling).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Building on the defined baseline security (Level 3), the connection between the hotspot and the client SHOULD be cryptographically secured according to the state of the art (e.g., using WPA3 if supported by the hotspot, otherwise covered by the VPN). Automatic connection to WLANs SHOULD be disabled. WLANs that are only used sporadically SHOULD be deleted from the history of known networks. It SHOULD be ensured that no users with administrative privileges log on to external WLANs from their clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Disabling automatic connection is enforced on clients via a configuration policy (e.g., GPO or MDM profile). Users are instructed and regularly reminded to remove unneeded WLAN profiles. The use of administrative accounts in insecure networks is prohibited by policy and spot-checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD check the client configuration to ensure that automatic connection to WLANs is disabled. On Windows, this can be checked with `netsh wlan show profile name="PROFILE_NAME"`, where the 'Connection mode' should be set to 'Manual'. The list of known networks SHOULD be checked for outdated hotspot entries. It SHOULD be verified through interviews and log analysis (if possible) that no administrative logons occur from external networks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security of hotspot usage is fully automated. An 'Always-On' VPN connection is technically enforced as soon as the client establishes a network connection outside of defined, trusted corporate networks. The client firewall is configured to block all non-VPN-tunneled traffic. The use of accounts with separate, restrictive permissions for use in external networks is technically enforced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A modern VPN solution with 'Always-On' and 'Trusted Network Detection' is used. It automatically detects whether the client is in a secure (corporate) or insecure (hotspot) network and establishes the tunnel accordingly. The client configuration is centrally managed via an MDM system and cannot be changed by the user. Separate user accounts with severely restricted rights are used for working on the go.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD verify the configuration of the 'Always-On' VPN-solution and the associated firewall rules on a client. An attempt SHOULD be made to establish a connection to an internet service while actively connected to an external test WLAN without the VPN tunnel being active; this must fail. It SHOULD be checked which user accounts are set up on the mobile devices and which rights these possess.

controls.title: Rules of conduct for WLAN security incidents (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no defined procedure for users in the event of a WLAN security incident. Reactions are ad-hoc, depend on individual experience, and are often incorrect (e.g., ignoring warnings, restarting the device without further reporting).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Users often try to solve the problem themselves instead of reporting it, out of fear of having made a mistake or because they do not know the correct contact person.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD determine through interviews with the helpdesk and users whether an established process for reporting WLAN incidents exists. The absence of tickets on this topic or reports of unresolved issues indicates this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general instruction to contact the User Help Desk for any type of IT problem. However, specific instructions for WLAN incidents, such as immediately deactivating the interface or documenting error messages, are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The user reports 'The WLAN is not working anymore' but provides no further information. Important forensic traces are lost because the user restarts the device multiple times or continues to work.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD review the instructions and processes of the User Help Desk. It SHOULD be checked whether there are specific questionnaires or instructions for accepting reports of WLAN security incidents. Existing tickets SHOULD be analyzed to assess the level of detail of the initial report by the user.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the event of WLAN security incidents, users SHOULD save their work, terminate WLAN access, deactivate the WLAN interface, document error messages and deviations, and notify IT operations via an appropriate escalation level (e.g., User Help Desk).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: These rules of conduct are taught as part of the security training (see A2). A simple checklist or an 'emergency leaflet' is provided to the users. The contact information for the User Help Desk is easily accessible on all devices (e.g., as a desktop sticker or wallpaper).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD check users' knowledge of the correct procedure in the event of a WLAN security incident by interviewing them. It SHOULD be verified whether the procedure is documented and made available to users (e.g., on the intranet or as part of training materials). Test scenarios can be run through (e.g., 'What do you do if you receive a warning that the WLAN certificate is invalid?').

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the defined procedure (Level 3), the reporting process is supported by a dedicated form in the self-service portal that guides the user through the necessary documentation. The User Help Desk is trained to ask specific questions when WLAN incidents are reported in order to make a qualified initial assessment and classify the incident correctly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the intranet or ticket system, there is a 'Report WLAN Security Incident' form that asks for fields for error messages, time, location, and observed behavior. The helpdesk works with a checklist to gather the necessary information before escalating the ticket to the security team.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD check the reporting form for WLAN incidents for completeness and user-friendliness. They SHOULD inspect the process documentation and the checklists of the User Help Desk. The quality of the created tickets for reported WLAN incidents SHOULD be evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The client devices are equipped with an Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solution that automatically saves relevant system information and network data upon detecting a potential WLAN attack (e.g., Rogue AP, ARP spoofing). Simultaneously, the WLAN interface is isolated, and the user receives a clear instruction on the screen guiding them to report the incident. The reporting process is simplified by a prominent 'panic button' on the desktop, which instructs the EDR agent to secure data and create a ticket.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An EDR solution with network monitoring functions is used. This is configured to react to typical WLAN attack vectors. The 'panic button' is a script that calls the EDR API, takes a screenshot, collects log files, and automatically generates an email or a ticket with this information.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor SHOULD verify the configuration and detection rules of the EDR solution regarding WLAN attacks. The functionality of the 'panic button' or a similar automated reporting mechanism SHOULD be tested. The reports and alerts generated by the EDR solution in connection with WLAN activities SHOULD be analyzed. A controlled test attack, e.g., with tools like 'airgeddon', can be carried out to observe the system's reaction.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs) can be used to set up wireless local networks or to extend existing wired networks. To date, almost all commercially available WLAN components are based on the IEEE 802.11 standard and its amendments. The 'Wi-Fi Alliance' industry consortium plays a special role here, having created an industry standard called 'Wi-Fi' based on the IEEE 802.11 standard. The Wi-Fi Alliance confirms with the Wi-Fi seal of approval that a device has passed certain interoperability and conformity tests.

WLANs offer an increase in convenience and mobility. However, their use also poses additional potential threats to information security, as communication is wireless. It is therefore important that, in addition to IT operations, users are also made aware of the potential dangers that can arise from the improper use of WLANs. Users must have the necessary knowledge to correctly understand and apply security measures. In particular, they must know what is expected of them in terms of information security and how they should react in certain situations when using WLANs.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module aims to show how WLANs can be used securely.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The NET.2.2 WLAN Usage module is to be applied to all IT systems (WLAN clients) that use WLANs.

The module contains fundamental requirements that must be observed and fulfilled when using WLANs in order to counter the specific threats. However, requirements that help to operate WLANs securely are not the subject of this module, but are described in the NET.2.1 WLAN Operation module. Furthermore, the module does not address general aspects of clients. Such aspects are covered in the SYS.2.1 General Client module and in the operating system-specific modules of the SYS IT Systems layer. The NET.2.2 WLAN Usage module should generally be taken into account when implementing the ORP.3 Information Security Awareness and Training and DER.2.1 Handling of Security Incidents modules.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient knowledge of regulations
parts.prose: If users do not know the rules for the correct handling of WLANs, or do not know them well enough, they cannot adhere to them. If, for example, clients are carelessly connected to foreign wireless networks, unencrypted information transmitted over them can be eavesdropped on. In addition, the operator of the wireless network can collect information about the users, such as websites visited.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Disregard of security measures
parts.prose: Due to negligence and a lack of controls, it repeatedly happens that people do not implement the security measures recommended or ordered for them, or only partially implement them. If, for example, a WLAN client is used in ad-hoc mode, although this is expressly forbidden in the usage policy, another client can communicate directly with the WLAN client. It can then, for example, gain unauthorized access to confidential documents that may be shared on the client.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Eavesdropping on WLAN communication
parts.prose: Since radio is a medium that can be shared by multiple users ('Shared Medium'), the data transmitted via WLANs can be easily eavesdropped on and recorded. If the data is not encrypted or is insufficiently encrypted, the transmitted payload data can be easily read. In addition, radio networks or the emitted radio waves often extend beyond the boundaries of the premises used. This means that data is also broadcast into areas that cannot be controlled and secured by the users or the institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Analysis of connection data in wireless communication
parts.prose: In WLANs based on IEEE 802.11, the MAC address of a WLAN card is sent with every data transmission. Since it is transmitted unencrypted, movement profiles of mobile users can be created, e.g., when they connect to public hotspots.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Spoofing a valid access point (Rogue Access Point)
parts.prose: Attackers can pose as part of the WLAN infrastructure by installing their own access point with a suitably chosen WLAN name (SSID) in the vicinity of a WLAN client. This fake access point is called a "rogue access point". If this offers the WLAN client a stronger transmission power than the real access point, the client will use it as a base station if they do not authenticate each other. In addition, the real access point could also be shut down by a denial-of-service attack. The users log on to a network that only pretends to be the target network. This makes it possible for the attackers to eavesdrop on the communication. Attackers can also fake a false identity or redirect network traffic to their IT systems using poisoning or spoofing methods. This allows them to listen in on and control the communication. A rogue access point is a popular means of attack, especially in public wireless networks (so-called hotspots).

controls.title: Secure basic configuration of a router or switch (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic hardening measures are only implemented for critical or exposed routers and switches, such as those at the internet gateway. Internal devices are largely operated with the manufacturer's default configuration, which does not include disabling unneeded services or ports.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, the administration focuses on fixing the most obvious vulnerabilities on the most important devices. There is no systematic process for hardening all network components. Often, only default passwords are changed, but insecure protocols remain active.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly selects several internal switches and routers and compares their configuration with the configuration of an external router. It is checked whether insecure default settings (e.g., active insecure services, default passwords) are present on internal devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All routers and switches are configured according to a basic, uniform checklist. This includes changing default passwords and disabling known insecure services. Unused ports are administratively shut down.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple configuration template or checklist is used for all new devices. However, the documentation of configuration changes is still irregular. The assignment of unused ports to a dedicated 'Unassigned-VLAN' is not yet done.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the configuration checklist and compares it with the configurations of several devices on a sample basis. It is verified whether all ports not in use have the status 'administratively down'. It is checked whether basic insecure services like Telnet are disabled.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before a router or switch is deployed, it MUST be securely configured. The integrity of the configuration files MUST be protected in an appropriate manner. Routers and switches MUST be configured so that only strictly necessary services, protocols, and functional extensions are used. Unnecessary services, protocols, and functional extensions MUST be disabled or completely uninstalled. Unused network ports MUST be disabled whenever possible. Information about the internal configuration and operating state MUST be hidden from the outside, and unnecessary information services MUST be disabled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined and documented hardening process is applied to all routers and switches. Access passwords are stored using a strong hashing algorithm. Configuration files are stored on a central, access-protected server. Unused physical ports are disabled. This process is repeatable and is applied to every new device.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented hardening procedure. Based on a sample of devices, it is verified that the configurations comply with the procedure. In particular, it is checked whether only the explicitly required services are active, whether unused ports are disabled, and whether information services (e.g., SNMP with public community string, CDP/LLDP on external interfaces) have been switched off.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All configuration changes SHOULD be documented in a traceable manner. Before access passwords are saved, they MUST be secured using a modern cryptographic method. Unused network ports are not only disabled, but SHOULD be assigned to a dedicated Unassigned-VLAN. If functional extensions are used, it SHOULD be justified and documented why such extensions are being used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A change management process is established for all configuration changes and documented in a ticket system. A dedicated 'dead VLAN' with no routing and services is configured for unused ports, to which all unused but active ports are assigned. The decision to use extensions is made and documented within an architecture board.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the change management system for recent configuration changes to network components and checks the completeness of the documentation. The configuration of the switches is checked to ensure that unused ports are assigned to an isolated Unassigned-VLAN. The auditor questions the administrators about the process for approving and documenting functional extensions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The secure basic configuration is automatically rolled out to all devices and monitored using configuration management tools (e.g., Ansible, Salt). Deviations from the target configuration are automatically detected and reported or corrected. The integrity of the configuration files is monitored in real-time by a File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Ansible playbooks or equivalent automation scripts define the 'golden image' for each device class. A central tool like Oxidized or Git is used for versioning and monitoring all configuration changes. A FIM solution that evaluates syslog messages from the devices alerts on unauthorized changes in the 'running-config'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the automation scripts and the configuration of the configuration management tool. It is checked whether a compliance report from the tool is available and how reported deviations are handled. The configuration and alerting logs of the FIM system are reviewed for their effectiveness. An automated audit can be simulated with `show running-config | compare golden_config.txt`.

controls.title: Protection of the administration interfaces (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only the administration interfaces of routers at the internet gateway are restricted by source IP filters. Administrative access to internal switches and routers is possible from the entire internal network without restrictions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The focus is exclusively on protecting the external attack surface. Internal threats from compromised clients or malicious insiders are not considered in this approach.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to establish a connection (e.g., via Telnet, SSH, HTTP) from a standard client network to the management IPs of internal core switches or routers. If this is successful, the control is not sufficiently implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative access to all routers and switches is restricted by Access-Control Lists (ACLs). However, these allow access from the entire administrators' subnet, not from individual IP addresses. Unencrypted protocols like Telnet or HTTP are still partially active as a fallback.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 'management access-class' is configured on the VTY lines, which refers to an ACL. This ACL typically contains a single 'permit' statement for an entire /24 network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the management ACLs on the devices. It is verified whether the permitted source address ranges are as restrictive as possible. A port scan from an allowed IP address is used to check whether insecure administration protocols are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administration and management access to routers and switches MUST be restricted to individual source IP addresses or address ranges. It MUST be ensured that administration interfaces cannot be accessed directly from untrusted networks. All services not required for the management interface MUST be disabled. If a network component has a dedicated hardware interface, unauthorized access to it MUST be prevented in an appropriate manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The management ACLs are configured to only allow the IPs of dedicated admin workstations or jump servers. Unnecessary services like HTTP server, SNMP (if not used for monitoring), or Telnet are globally disabled on the devices. Physical access to console ports is ensured by locked server cabinets.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the management ACLs and compares the entries with the list of authorized admin systems. It is checked via `show control-plane host open-ports` or equivalent commands which services are listening on the devices and whether they are all needed. The physical protection of the devices is checked by an inspection of the data center.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To administer routers and switches, only suitably encrypted protocols such as SSHv2 or HTTPS SHOULD be used. The management interfaces and administration connections MUST be protected by a separate firewall. Appropriate time limits, e.g., for timeouts, MUST be set for the interfaces. If unencrypted protocols must be used, a separate administration network (out-of-band management) MUST be utilized.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SSH is configured to allow only version 2 and to use strong cipher suites. All management traffic is moved to a separate management VLAN or a physically separate out-of-band network. The transition from admin workstations to this network is controlled by a firewall with restrictive rules. VTY and console sessions are configured with a short inactivity timeout (e.g., 15 minutes).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the SSH configuration of the devices for the protocol version and allowed algorithms. The firewall rules for the management network are analyzed. The configuration of the VTY and console lines is checked for the existence and value of `exec-timeout`. An `ssh -v <device-ip>` from a client shows the negotiated protocol version and cipher.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All administrative access is exclusively handled through a central Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution (bastion host). The PAM solution enforces Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), performs detailed logging of all commands, and can record sessions. The direct login credentials for the network devices are not known to the administrators and are managed and rotated by the PAM solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A PAM solution such as CyberArk, Teleport, or an open-source alternative is implemented. The management ACLs on the network devices are configured to exclusively allow connections from the PAM solution. Device authentication is handled via TACACS+ or RADIUS, with the PAM solution acting as a proxy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the PAM solution, particularly the MFA requirements and logging settings. It is verified whether the ACLs on the network devices exclusively allow the PAM servers as a source. The audit logs of the PAM solution are spot-checked for suspicious activities.

controls.title: Protection against fragmentation attacks (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Protection mechanisms against fragmentation attacks are only enabled on routers at the internet perimeter. These protection features are not configured on internal Layer 3 switches that also perform routing tasks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration focuses on protection against external attacks. The possibility that such attacks could also be launched from the internal network (e.g., from a compromised client) is not considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of one or more internal core or distribution Layer 3 switches. It is verified whether mechanisms for controlling IP fragments (e.g., `ip virtual-reassembly` on Cisco) are enabled. If this is not the case, the control is insufficient.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On all routers and Layer 3 switches, the basic protection mechanisms against fragmentation attacks are enabled with the manufacturer's default settings.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On Cisco devices, for example, the `ip virtual-reassembly in` command is configured on all relevant interfaces. However, there is no adjustment of the thresholds or timeouts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor spot-checks the configurations of routers and L3 switches to verify the activation of the protection feature. It is checked whether the command is present globally or on all relevant interfaces.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: On the router and Layer 3 switch, protection mechanisms MUST be enabled to defend against IPv4 and IPv6 fragmentation attacks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined configuration standard is implemented for all routers and L3 switches, which mandates the activation of protection mechanisms against fragmentation attacks for IPv4 and IPv6. This may include virtual reassembly of packets for inspection or dropping fragments via ACLs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configurations of the relevant devices to ensure that fragmentation protection measures are implemented for both IPv4 and IPv6. This can be done by checking interface configurations (`ip virtual-reassembly`) and Access Control Lists (ACLs that block `fragments`).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The parameters of the protection mechanisms against fragmentation attacks, such as the maximum number of concurrent reassemblies, buffer sizes, and timeouts, are adapted to the specific requirements of the network to ensure both security and performance. The occurrence of fragmentation attacks is logged and monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default values for `ip virtual-reassembly` are analyzed and adjusted if necessary (e.g., `ip virtual-reassembly in max-reassemblies <number> timeout <seconds>`). Explicit rules are created on border firewalls that log fragmented packets and drop them if a threshold is exceeded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the fragmentation protection parameters and asks the administrators for the reasoning behind the chosen values. The log configuration is checked to ensure that relevant events are captured and sent to a central system. The automatic check can be performed with `show ip virtual-reassembly`.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) is used to analyze network traffic in real time. It actively detects and blocks complex and evasive fragmentation attacks based on signatures and anomaly-based heuristics that go beyond the capabilities of standard routers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) or a standalone IPS device is placed at the network perimeter or at critical internal segmentation points. The corresponding protection profiles (e.g., 'DoS Protection') are activated and fine-tuned. The IPS is integrated into the SIEM process to correlate alarms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration and placement of the IPS/NGFW. The effectiveness of the protection profiles is analyzed. It is checked whether alarms for fragmentation attacks are generated by the IPS and are visible in the SIEM system. A penetration test can attempt to bypass the protection mechanisms with tools like 'hping3' or 'scapy'.

controls.title: Emergency access to routers and switches (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Local access via the console port is physically possible, but the necessary passwords are not documented or are known only to a single person. In an emergency, this can lead to significant delays.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The console port is not explicitly configured or protected. The access credentials may be the manufacturer's default settings or were set once and not securely stored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: As part of a simulated emergency drill, the auditor asks to establish access to a device via the console. The time required to provide the necessary credentials and equipment (cable, laptop) is measured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the data center, there is a 'crash cart' with a laptop and various console cables. The passwords for console access are stored in a password manager to which multiple administrators have access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A password is set for the console port (`line con 0`) and a basic configuration (e.g., timeout) is in place. However, the process is purely manual and requires the physical presence of an administrator in the data center.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and functionality of the crash cart. It is checked whether the console passwords for a sample of devices are current and correctly stored in the central password manager.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST always be possible for administrators to directly access routers and switches, so that they can still be administered locally even if the entire network fails.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined and documented process for emergency access exists. This ensures that access is possible at all times via the physical console port (e.g., with a laptop and a serial cable). The necessary passwords are securely stored and accessible to the on-duty personnel. The procedure is practiced regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation for emergency access. As part of an exercise, an administrator is asked to establish access to a sealed-off device (disconnected from the network) according to the documentation. The time required for the process and any difficulties encountered are logged.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated Out-of-Band (OOB) console server is used, which is accessible via a separate network (e.g., LTE modem or separate DSL line). This allows remote access to the console ports without being physically on-site. Access to the console server is protected by strong authentication.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A console server (e.g., from Raritan, Vertiv, Opengear) is installed and all console ports of the critical network devices are connected to it. The console server is equipped with its own internet connection, independent of the production network. Access is authenticated via RADIUS or TACACS+.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the architecture of the OOB network and the configuration of the console server. It is tested whether access via the console server is still possible after disconnecting a device from the production network. The authentication and logging configuration of the console server is analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The Out-of-Band console server is fully integrated into the central PAM (Privileged Access Management) solution. Access requires MFA, and all console sessions are recorded and logged. The solution provides redundant design to ensure the availability of the emergency access itself.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The console server is configured as a resource in the PAM solution. Administrators do not connect directly to the console server, but via the PAM portal, which tunnels and monitors the connection. Redundancy is achieved through a second console server at another location with separate connectivity.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of the console server into the PAM solution and checks the MFA requirements. A session recording is spot-checked. The failover functionality of the redundant OOB solution is checked as part of a test.

controls.title: Logging on routers and switches (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging is enabled on the devices, but the log messages are only kept in the local, volatile memory (RAM buffer) with a limited size. In case of a restart, all log data is lost.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The `logging on` command is active, but no `logging host` or `logging buffer` with sufficient size is configured. The manufacturer's default settings are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor logs into a device and executes the `show logging` command. It is checked whether the logs are only stored in the local buffer and how old the oldest entries are. After a (planned) reboot, it is checked whether the logs are still present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All routers and switches are configured to send their log data to a central syslog server. However, only standard events (severity level 'warnings' or higher) are logged, not all required event types.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A `logging host <server-ip>` is configured on all devices. However, the `logging trap` level is left at the default value, which often does not include informative events such as configuration changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the logging configuration on a device and compares it with the incoming logs on the syslog server. It is checked whether a manually performed configuration change is logged on the syslog server. If this is not the case, the configuration is insufficient.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A router or switch MUST be configured to log, among other things, the following events: configuration changes (if possible, automatically), reboots, system errors, status changes per interface, system and network segment, as well as login errors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The devices are configured to send logs with a sufficient level of detail (e.g., level 'informational' or 'notifications') to a central syslog server. This ensures that all required events are captured. The device clocks are synchronized via NTP to ensure correlatable timestamps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the logging configuration policy. Using a sample of devices, it is verified whether the configured logging level is sufficient to capture the required events. On the syslog server, it is checked whether events such as interface status changes (up/down) and failed login attempts are received. The NTP configuration is checked using `show ntp status` or equivalent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The log data is sent to a redundant cluster of syslog servers to minimize the loss of log data. The transmitted data is secured via TLS (Secure Syslog). Basic correlation rules and alerts for critical events (e.g., more than 5 failed logins in one minute) are set up on the central system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two or more syslog-ng or rsyslog servers are configured as targets. The `logging host` configuration on the network devices is adapted to use TCP and the corresponding port for Secure Syslog. In the log management tool, simple rules are created that trigger an email notification for specific event patterns.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the logging configuration on the end devices and the syslog servers to verify the redundant and secure transmission. The alerting rules are checked for their appropriateness and functionality. A failed login is provoked to see if an alarm is triggered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All log data from routers and switches is fed into a central Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. There, it is correlated with other data sources (e.g., from firewalls, servers, clients) to detect complex, multi-stage attacks. The integrity of the log data is ensured by digital signatures or blockchain-based mechanisms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The syslog data is received by a log aggregator (e.g., Logstash), parsed, and forwarded to the SIEM (e.g., Splunk, ELK Stack, QRadar). In the SIEM, complex use cases and dashboards for network security are implemented (e.g., detection of port scanning distributed across multiple switches).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the data flows into the SIEM system and analyzes the implemented correlation rules and dashboards. It is checked whether the entire process from collection to alerting works for a simulated security incident. The mechanisms for securing log integrity are verified.

controls.title: Regular data backup (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Configuration backups are only created manually and irregularly before major planned changes. There is no automated or regular process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Administrators execute `show running-config` before an update and copy the content to a text file on their local machine. The storage is not centralized and not protected against loss.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the configuration backup of a specific device from three months ago. If this cannot be provided, or only with great effort, the control is inadequate. The file systems on the admin workstations are checked for scattered configuration files.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automated script backs up the configurations of all devices nightly to a central file server. However, there is no verification of the successful backup and no versioning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple shell script that uses `expect`, or a TFTP server-based process, is run via cron job. The configuration files are overwritten every day.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the backup script and the target files on the server. It is verified that the timestamps of the files are current. The content of a backup file is randomly compared with the live configuration to check for completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The configuration files of routers and switches MUST be backed up regularly. The backup copies MUST be stored in such a way that they can be accessed in an emergency.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined process ensures that the configurations of all network components are regularly (e.g., daily) stored on a central, secured, and redundant storage system. Access to the backups is restricted to authorized administrators. The backups are versioned to allow for reverting to older versions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the data backup concept for network components. It is checked whether current backups for all relevant devices are available on the backup server. It is randomly checked whether a configuration from a week ago can be restored. The access permissions to the backup directory are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated Network Configuration Management (NCM) tool is used. This not only backs up configurations on a scheduled basis, but also on an event-driven basis, i.e., immediately after any detected change. The tool provides a graphical interface for comparing configuration versions (diff).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Oxidized, RANCID, or commercial NCM solutions (e.g., from SolarWinds, ManageEngine) are implemented. These tools are configured to listen for syslog messages about configuration changes and then immediately trigger a backup. The configurations are stored in a Git repository.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the NCM tool. A small change is made to a test device and it is observed live whether the tool detects the change and creates a new backup. The versioning history in the tool or in the Git repository is checked. The check can be automated by querying the API of the NCM tool.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The NCM tool is fully integrated with the Change Management System (ITSM) and the SIEM. Backed-up configurations are automatically checked for compliance with security policies (Compliance Checking). The process for restoring a configuration from backup is regularly tested and automated as part of emergency drills.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The NCM tool is configured to allow or confirm configuration changes only if a valid change ticket number is present. Compliance violations in configurations are sent as alarms to the SIEM. Ansible playbooks or similar scripts are developed to enable the restoration of a configuration at the push of a button.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the integrations between NCM, ITSM, and SIEM. A compliance report is requested from the NCM tool and analyzed. The logs from the last emergency drills are reviewed to verify the successful execution of the recovery test.

controls.title: Operational documentation (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are only outdated network diagrams. Important operational information such as IP address allocation, VLAN configuration, or standard procedures are not documented in writing and exist only as 'knowledge in the heads' of the administrators.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Documentation is seen as a tedious duty and is only created during the initial setup, but never updated. This leads to a high risk of personal dependency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the documentation for a specific device or service. They compare the documentation with the live configuration. Major discrepancies or the absence of documentation indicate a deficient implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The basic configuration parameters such as IP addresses, VLANs, and port assignments are documented in a central file or a wiki. However, instructions for recurring operational tasks are missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Excel spreadsheet or a simple wiki page is used to document the network configuration. It is updated manually and is often not part of the standard process for changes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the central documentation source for completeness and timeliness. They ask for the documentation for a standard operational task (e.g., 'Setting up a new switch port for a client'). If this is not available, the control is only implemented at a basic level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The most important operational tasks of a router or switch MUST be appropriately documented. This includes Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for recurring activities such as commissioning new devices, configuring ports, or performing updates.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In a central, versioned system (e.g., Confluence, SharePoint), SOPs for all important operational tasks are maintained in addition to network topology and configuration data. New team members can familiarize themselves with this documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the operational documentation, which should include network topology diagrams, configuration details, and SOPs for tasks like 'replacing a faulty switch' or 'firmware update'. The documentation is checked for clarity, completeness, and timeliness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All configuration changes and security-relevant tasks SHOULD be documented. The documentation SHOULD be protected from unauthorized access. Updating the documentation is an integral part of the change management process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The operational documentation is stored on a platform with fine-grained access control. Every configuration change in the ITSM system (Change Request) must include a reference to the updated documentation before the change can be closed. Security-relevant tasks (e.g., response to a security incident) are documented in playbooks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the access permissions to the documentation platform. Based on several completed change tickets, it is verified whether the documentation was actually updated as part of the process. The existence and quality of security playbooks are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A significant part of the operational documentation is automatically generated and kept up-to-date ('Documentation as Code'). Network and configuration monitoring tools dynamically generate current network diagrams, port assignments, and configuration overviews. Manually created documentation and automatically generated data are consolidated in a central portal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like NetBox are established as the 'Source of Truth' for network documentation. It is used by other systems (monitoring, automation) via API. Automation scripts (e.g., Ansible) use the data from NetBox to configure devices and, in turn, update the status in NetBox. Topology maps are dynamically generated from LLDP/CDP data from monitoring systems like LibreNMS or PRTG.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the architecture of the 'Documentation as Code' toolchain. The consistency of the data between the 'Source of Truth' (e.g., NetBox) and the live devices is checked on a random basis. An automated audit can query the NetBox API and compare it with the output of `show` commands on the devices.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the institution's general security policy, a specific security policy SHOULD be created.
