parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the defined RBAC model and its implementation via groups in the directory service and policies on the VPN gateway. They request the logs of the last permission recertifications.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire account and access management process is integrated into an Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) solution. Access is granted dynamically based on attributes (Attribute-Based Access Control, ABAC) and context to ensure just-in-time and least-privilege access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An IGA tool controls VPN access. A developer gets access to a specific production system only if they belong to the correct role, log in during an approved maintenance window, AND have a valid ticket for this task. After the task is completed, access is automatically revoked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the ABAC policies in the IGA system. They test various access scenarios with different attributes (e.g., with and without a valid ticket) to verify the correct functioning of the dynamic and just-in-time access control.

controls.title: Integration of VPN components into a firewall (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VPN component is a separate device that forwards traffic uninspected to the internal network ('tromboning') or is placed in front of the firewall.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standalone VPN gateway is set up in the data center and connected directly to the core switch. All traffic coming from the VPN is routed to the internal network without inspection by the central firewall.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the network plan and routing tables and determines that the traffic from the VPN gateway is not routed through and filtered by the firewall.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VPN components SHOULD be integrated into the firewall. This SHOULD be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: VPN termination is activated as a function on the central perimeter firewall. The decrypted traffic from VPN clients is thus automatically inspected by the same firewall rules and policies as all other traffic. The configuration is documented in the firewall concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies from the firewall configuration that the VPN functionality is active on the device and that the decrypted VPN traffic is processed by the firewall's rule set. They check whether this configuration is documented in the firewall concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The firewall policy for VPN traffic is specifically hardened and logically separated from other rule sets. Logging for this traffic is enhanced to enable detailed monitoring.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated zone or policy package is created on the firewall for VPN traffic. Stricter rules apply here than for internal traffic. All allowed and blocked connection attempts from the VPN are logged in detail and sent to a central log management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rule set and confirms the existence of a separate, hardened rule set for VPN traffic. They check the logging configuration of the firewall and verify the presence of detailed VPN traffic logs in the log management system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrated VPN/firewall solution is a Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) that performs Deep Packet Inspection (DPI), Intrusion Prevention (IPS), and antimalware scans on all decrypted VPN traffic. The configuration is managed as code and tested automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An NGFW terminates the VPN tunnels. IPS, Application Control, and Antivirus profiles are enabled for all traffic from the VPN. Any malware or unauthorized application usage (e.g., BitTorrent) is blocked and reported. The firewall configuration is managed in a Git repository, and changes are validated and rolled out via a CI/CD pipeline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the NGFW configuration and ensures that the security profiles (IPS, AV, etc.) are active for VPN traffic. They may attempt to transfer a test malware (e.g., EICAR test file) over a VPN connection and verify that it is blocked by the firewall. They conduct a review of the configuration pipeline.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) can be used to transmit sensitive data over untrusted networks, such as the internet. A VPN is a virtual network that operates within another network but is logically separate from it. The VPN uses the network merely as a transport medium but is itself independent of the structure and design of the network used. VPNs can protect the integrity and confidentiality of data using cryptographic methods. VPNs also enable the secure authentication of communication points when multiple networks or IT systems are interconnected via leased lines or public networks.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The module defines requirements with which a VPN can be planned, implemented, and operated in a targeted and secure manner.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
This module is to be applied to every method of accessing the institution's network via a VPN endpoint.
The module does not cover the fundamentals of secure networks and their structure (see NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design). Nor does this module cover all processes related to operating a VPN. VPNs should always be considered in the context of the modules ORP.4 Identity and Access Management, OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management, OPS.1.2.5 Remote Maintenance, OPS.1.1.2 Proper IT Administration, and CON.1 Cryptographic Concept.
Recommendations on how to configure the operating systems of VPN endpoints are also not part of this module. Corresponding requirements can be found in module SYS.1.1 General Server or SYS.2.1 General Client, as well as in the respective operating system-specific modules of the IT-Grundschutz Compendium.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Lack of or insufficient planning for VPN use
parts.prose:
If a VPN is not carefully planned, set up, or configured, security vulnerabilities can arise that could affect all IT systems connected to the VPN. This can enable attackers to access the institution's confidential information.
For example, insufficient VPN planning can lead to users not being properly trained. As a result, they might use the VPN in an insecure environment or log in from insecure clients. This could potentially allow attackers to access the entire institutional network.
Also, if the regular monitoring of VPN access is inadequately planned, attacks might not be detected in time. This prevents a timely response, and attackers could go unnoticed while stealing data or sabotaging entire processes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Insecure VPN service providers
parts.prose: If an institution has not carefully selected its VPN service providers, the institution's entire network could become insecure. For example, a VPN access insecurely offered by the service providers could be used for attacks to specifically steal information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Insecure configuration of VPN clients for remote access
parts.prose: If a VPN client is not configured securely, users might use its security mechanisms incorrectly or not at all. They might also change the VPN client's configuration. An insecure configuration also makes it possible for software installed by the users to compromise the security of the VPN client.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Insecure default settings on VPN components
parts.prose: In their default settings, VPN components are usually preconfigured with no or only inadequate security mechanisms. Often, more attention is paid to user-friendliness and seamless integration into existing IT systems than to security. If VPN components are not or are only inadequately adapted to the specific security needs of the institution, vulnerabilities and thus dangerous points of attack can arise. For example, if factory-default passwords are not changed, the entire VPN and thus the institution's internal network could be attacked.

controls.title: Justified decision for the use of NAC

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decision to use NAC is made only on an ad-hoc basis for individual, isolated projects or particularly critical network areas. There is a lack of an institution-wide, documented justification and a clear definition of the scope.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, NAC is introduced, for example, only for a new server VLAN, while the existing client networks are disregarded. The decision is often only recorded in project emails.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether there are isolated areas with NAC implementations. The auditor asks for the basis of the decision and finds that it is not formally documented and is not of an institution-wide nature.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general, institution-wide intention to use NAC. However, this decision is not formally documented, and the exact scope and justification are unclear. The handling of different device types, such as third-party devices, is not regulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT management has decided to introduce NAC orally or in a brief note. The IT department begins implementation without clear specifications regarding the scope (e.g., which network areas, which device types).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds evidence of a fundamental decision (e.g., in meeting minutes), but cannot identify a formal, approved document with a clear justification and a defined scope.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST fundamentally decide if and to what extent NAC will be used. The decision made MUST be documented in an appropriate place along with a justification. If NAC is used, the network areas and network components for which NAC is to be implemented, the handling of internal and external endpoint devices, and the consideration of NAC in the procurement of new IT systems MUST be addressed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An official document is created and approved by management. This document states: 'NAC will be introduced in all client networks (LAN and WLAN) for all company-owned and third-party endpoint devices to prevent unauthorized access and enforce network segmentation. 802.1X capability is a mandatory requirement for all future switch procurements.'

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the official decision document for the NAC deployment. It is checked whether the document contains a clear justification and whether the scopes defined therein (network areas, device types, procurement) are complete.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documented decision for NAC is formally integrated into the overarching IT security strategy and procurement policies. The decision and its justification are reviewed regularly, for example annually, and adapted to the current threat landscape and organizational changes as needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The requirement for NAC compatibility is an integral part of the checklists in the procurement process. The scope of NAC deployment (e.g., expansion to production networks) is reviewed annually as part of IT strategy planning to determine if adjustments are necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the NAC requirements are anchored in the official procurement policy. Minutes of strategic meetings or reviews are inspected to prove that the NAC decision is regularly reviewed and confirmed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decision-making process for the scope of NAC deployment is data-driven and based on continuous risk assessments, threat intelligence feeds, and business impact analyses for various network areas. The documentation is anchored in a GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) tool and linked to the corresponding risks and controls.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: New threat intelligence about attacks on IoT devices leads to a reassessment of the risk in the IoT network. The GRC tool triggers a workflow to review the expansion of NAC to this network and to document the decision.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the process in the GRC tool. It is checked whether decisions about NAC deployment are directly traceable to documented risk analyses and whether a traceable process exists for adapting the scope based on new threats. An automated way to check is to generate reports from the GRC tool that show the link between risks, assets, and the NAC decision.

controls.title: Planning the deployment of NAC

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning is limited to the selection and procurement of NAC software. Important aspects such as process adaptation, the creation of a detailed concept, or migration planning are ignored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A team is assigned to 'introduce NAC'. Software is purchased and an attempt is made to install it without first defining requirements or planning a migration path.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the project plan for the NAC introduction and finds that it consists of only one item 'procure software' and does not contain any of the aspects mentioned in the requirement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic technical plan is in place, focusing on the placement of RADIUS servers and basic switch configuration. However, there is no formal, detailed planning of operational and incident processes or a structured migration plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A network architect creates a diagram of how the NAC components will be connected. The configuration is planned rudimentarily, but how the help desk should handle NAC-related inquiries is not defined.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds technical planning documents (e.g., network diagrams), but cannot find any documentation on the adapted operational processes or a detailed migration plan (e.g., with pilot phases).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of NAC SHOULD be planned comprehensively and in detail. The planning SHOULD include at least the creation of requirements catalogs, the review and supplementation of IT asset management, the creation of a specific NAC concept, the definition of procurement, operational, and incident processes, migration planning, and the monitoring and logging of the NAC solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal project plan is created that includes work packages for all mentioned aspects. For example, there is a work package 'WP3: Create NAC concept', which aims to create the concept according to NET.3.4.A4, and a 'WP5: Plan migration', which defines a phased introduction (e.g., first monitor mode, then a pilot area, then full rollout).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the overall plan for the NAC deployment. It is checked whether this plan addresses all aspects mentioned in the control text (requirements catalog, asset management, concept, processes, migration, monitoring) and whether the planning is sufficiently detailed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning is carried out as a formal project according to a recognized project management methodology (e.g., PRINCE2, PMBOK). The plan contains detailed resource and time schedules, explicit risk management for the project, defined key performance indicators (KPIs), and test and rollback plans for the migration.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The project plan is managed in a project management tool (e.g., Jira, MS Project). It includes an explicit test plan that states: 'In Phase 2, the rollout will be tested with 50 pilot users from the finance department. The success criterion is that less than 5% of users open a ticket with the helpdesk. A detailed rollback plan describes how to reset the configuration in case of failure.'

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies not only the existence of the plan but also its quality. It is checked whether a project risk register exists, whether clear milestones and KPIs are defined, and whether formal test and rollback procedures are documented. It could be automatically checked whether all planning artifacts are marked as present and approved in the PM tool.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning is fully integrated into a change management system and uses automated tools for support. Automated discovery tools are used for inventory and dependency analysis. The plan is a living document that is continuously adapted during implementation based on feedback from the implementation phases and monitoring results.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A network discovery tool scans the network and automatically populates the IT asset management with the relevant devices. The migration plan is modeled in the change management system so that the configuration changes for each area are treated as a separate change request with automated pre- and post-checks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the process in the change management system. It is checked whether the planning is based on automatically collected asset data and whether a formal feedback loop exists that incorporates findings from the implementation into further planning. It can be automatically checked whether change requests for the NAC introduction are linked to entries from a discovery tool.

controls.title: Creation of a requirements catalog for NAC

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A few high-level requirements are informally recorded in an email or a short document. There is no structured catalog, and the requirements do not cover all relevant NAC components.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An email states: 'We need a NAC solution that supports 802.1X and has a RADIUS server'. Requirements for endpoints or scalability are missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the requirements catalog and receives an email or a short memo. It is noted that this is not a structured catalog and essential components (e.g., endpoints) are not considered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic list of functional requirements is created that addresses the main components. However, this list is not formally coordinated with all affected departments and committees and is not regularly updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The network department creates an Excel sheet with requirements for switches and the RADIUS server. This is used for procurement, but the help desk or the client management department were not involved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds a requirements catalog but cannot find any evidence (e.g., minutes, signatures) of coordination with all relevant stakeholders (especially outside the network department).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements for the NAC solution SHOULD be collected in a requirements catalog. The catalog SHOULD cover the basic functional requirements and address all NAC components (e.g., endpoints, access switches, and RADIUS servers). It SHOULD be coordinated with all affected departments, committees, and policies, be regularly updated, and be taken into account for procurements and tests of the solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal document 'NAC Requirements Catalog' is created. It contains chapters for endpoints (e.g., 'Must support EAP-TLS'), switches (e.g., 'Must support RADIUS Change of Authorization'), and RADIUS servers (e.g., 'Must support connection to Active Directory via LDAPS'). The document is verifiably sent to the heads of IT Operations, Clients, and Security for approval.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the requirements catalog and checks it for completeness with regard to the components. Furthermore, approval evidence from stakeholders and minutes of updates are requested. In the case of a recent procurement of switches, it is checked whether the tender referred to the catalog.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements catalog is expanded to include non-functional requirements. These include explicit specifications for performance (e.g., maximum authentication latency), scalability (e.g., number of endpoints to be supported), and high availability. The catalog is versioned and formally signed by all stakeholders.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Under 'Non-functional Requirements', the catalog states: 'NFR-01: The RADIUS solution must be able to support 10,000 endpoints.' and 'NFR-02: The average authentication time must not exceed 200ms.' The document is stored in a DMS with version control.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the catalog contains a section on non-functional requirements and whether these are quantifiable. The version history of the document and the formal approval evidence are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements catalog is managed in a dedicated requirements engineering tool. Each requirement is uniquely identifiable and is tracked throughout its entire lifecycle (traceability), from the original requirement through implementation in the concept to specific test cases. For new procurement projects, it is automatically checked whether the tender covers all relevant NAC requirements from the tool.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A tool like Jira or a specialized RE tool is used. The requirement 'NAC-REQ-101: Switch must support CoA' is linked to the test case 'NAC-TC-205: Test CoA function' and the concept chapter '3.4.2 Dynamic Authorization'. A new switch tender triggers an automated workflow that checks the coverage of the requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has a report generated from the RE tool that shows the traceability matrix between requirements, concept, and test cases. It is checked whether the process for reviewing procurements against the requirements is automated. An automated test could be an API query to the RE tool to verify the completeness of the links.

controls.title: Creation of a NAC concept

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the decision (A1) and the requirements (A3), a NAC concept SHOULD be created. This SHOULD be coordinated with the segmentation concept and should define at least the following aspects: network areas for NAC, authentication and authorization, use of additional functions, configuration specifications for all components, structure of the RADIUS infrastructure and rule set, as well as the connection to external security components and directory services. The concept SHOULD describe all technical and organizational specifications, be regularly reviewed and updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed concept document is created. It contains a chapter 'Authentication' which states: 'EAP-TLS with machine-based certificates is used for company-owned Windows clients. MAC authentication is used for printers.' Another chapter 'RADIUS Infrastructure' describes the setup of a high-availability RADIUS cluster and defines the RADIUS clients (switches) with their IP addresses and shared secrets.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the NAC concept and compares its table of contents and content with the aspects mentioned in the requirement. It is checked whether the concept is consistent with the general network architecture and segmentation concept and whether a process for regular review of the concept exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The NAC concept is expanded to include detailed descriptions of failure scenarios and the corresponding fallback mechanisms (RADIUS-down policies). The concept is formally reviewed and approved by a committee (e.g., IT security management). A fixed review cycle (e.g., annually) is established for the concept and its compliance is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The concept contains a chapter 'Emergency Operation' which states: 'In the event of failure of both RADIUS servers, already authenticated clients remain in the network. Newly connected clients are moved to a quarantine VLAN with internet-only connectivity.' The document is versioned and the approval is noted in the minutes of the IT Security Board.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the chapter on failure scenarios. The approval minutes and the evidence of compliance with the review cycle (e.g., meeting invitations, updated document versions) are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The NAC concept is implemented as an executable model as part of an Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) approach. The configurations for switches, RADIUS servers, and firewalls are described in code templates (e.g., Ansible Playbooks, Terraform models). The human-readable documentation is automatically generated from these code templates and comments. The concept provides for dynamic adjustment of policies based on external threat intelligence feeds.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RADIUS client definitions are maintained in an Ansible variable file. A playbook reads this file and configures the RADIUS server accordingly. A script generates HTML documentation from the variable file and Markdown templates. An integration with a threat feed ensures that when a critical vulnerability is discovered, a policy is automatically rolled out that isolates affected systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the IaC repository (e.g., in Git). It is checked whether the production configuration can be verifiably derived from the code templates and whether a process for automatic documentation generation exists. The consistency between the code repository and the running configuration can be automatically verified by running a read-only Ansible playbook in check mode.

controls.title: Adaptation of processes for endpoints with regard to NAC

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the endpoints that are to be integrated into the NAC solution, NAC SHOULD be appropriately considered in all relevant processes. In particular, the processes for commissioning, replacement, changes, and incidents SHOULD be adapted. For supplicant software, configuration, and identity features (e.g., certificates) required for NAC on the endpoints, a process SHOULD be defined to manage the endpoints centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The checklist for commissioning a new laptop is expanded to include the items 'Installation of the 802.1X supplicant' and 'Application for and installation of the device certificate'. The troubleshooting manual for the help desk is supplemented with a chapter 'Troubleshooting NAC problems'. The central software distribution is used for the distribution of the supplicant and configuration updates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process documentation for the endpoint lifecycle (commissioning, incidents, etc.) and checks whether it has been supplemented with NAC-specific steps. It is checked whether a documented process for the central management of the supplicant software exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The adapted processes are mapped in an IT Service Management (ITSM) tool. The workflows in the tool are adapted to include NAC-related tasks (e.g., automatically requesting a certificate when a new device is ordered) and ensure their completion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the ITSM tool, the 'New Employee' workflow is expanded to automatically generate a ticket for the PKI department to create a device certificate as soon as the laptop is registered in asset management. The incident ticket for 'Network Problems' receives a separate category 'NAC authentication failed' with a linked resolution workflow.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the process models in the ITSM tool. It is checked whether the workflows for the endpoint lifecycle contain explicit NAC-related tasks or steps. An automated report can be generated from the ITSM tool that lists the process steps for relevant service requests.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire endpoint lifecycle management is highly automated (Zero-Touch Provisioning). The ITSM system fully automatically orchestrates all NAC-related process steps, from ordering a device through automatic installation and configuration (incl. supplicant and certificate) to secure decommissioning with automatic revocation of the certificate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A new device is unpacked and connected to the network. It authenticates in an onboarding VLAN, is recognized by the client management solution (e.g., Intune, Jamf), which automatically rolls out all software, the 802.1X configuration, and a certificate via SCEP. After successful configuration, the device is restarted and authenticates in the production network. When decommissioned, the device is set to 'disposed' in asset management, which automatically triggers the revocation of the certificate in the PKI.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the automated onboarding and offboarding process demonstrated. The logs of the involved systems (client management, PKI, NAC) are analyzed to verify the fully automated orchestration. The process can be automatically checked by an API query to the client management system, which returns the status of the onboarding process.

controls.title: Definition of emergency processes for NAC

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be considered to temporarily disable the NAC security mechanisms if the operational chain is disrupted. In the emergency measures defined in the emergency process, productivity and information security SHOULD be weighed against each other. The options for emergency measures (RADIUS-down policies) SHOULD be considered and aligned with the relevant security policies, such as maintaining existing connections, making a fixed assignment of network segments, or completely disabling NAC.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An emergency manual is created which states: 'In the event of a total failure of the RADIUS cluster, the RADIUS-down policy 'Fail-Open in Guest-VLAN' is activated. This is done by executing the script 'enable_nac_fallback.sh' on the central switch management server. Activation must be approved by the Head of IT Operations.' The decision for this policy has been documented, weighing the risks (limited productivity) against security (no uncontrolled access to internal networks).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the emergency manual for NAC. It is checked whether the various options for RADIUS-down policies are documented, whether a clear decision has been made for one of the options, and whether the trade-off between security and productivity is comprehensible. In addition, the switch configuration is checked to see if the selected fallback policy is technically implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The emergency process contains clear activation criteria, a communication plan for those affected (incl. helpdesk and users), and clearly defined roles and responsibilities. The fallback configurations are preconfigured on the switches and are tested regularly (e.g., as part of emergency drills) to ensure they are functional.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The emergency manual defines: 'The emergency process is activated if the monitoring system reports a failure of both RADIUS servers for >5 minutes.' There is an email template for informing the helpdesk. As part of the annual emergency drill, the failure of the RADIUS servers is simulated and the fallback mechanism is tested live. The results are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the emergency manual for activation criteria and communication plans. Emergency drill logs are requested to verify that the fallback mechanisms are tested regularly and successfully.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The emergency failover is automated. The monitoring system detects a critical NAC failure and automatically activates the predefined, secure fallback state on the relevant network components. At the same time, the security and network teams are alerted. As soon as the problem is resolved, the system detects this and automatically switches back to normal operation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central monitoring tool (e.g., Nagios, Prometheus) performs a synthetic RADIUS login every 30 seconds. If this fails three times in a row, the tool triggers the activation of the fallback configuration via an API connection to the switch management system and creates a Prio-1 ticket in the ticketing system. As soon as the synthetic login is successful again, the normal configuration is also automatically restored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the monitoring and automation tool. It is checked whether the failover and failback process is fully automated. The process is tested by a simulated failure of the RADIUS service, using the logs of the monitoring, automation, and network management systems to verify the automatic switchover. An automatic test could be an API query to the monitoring system to check the configuration of the failover rule.

controls.title: Use of secure authentication methods

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Endpoints SHOULD use state-of-the-art secure authentication methods and be authenticated automatically based on certificates or access accounts. Insecure authentication methods SHOULD only be used in justified exceptional cases and the decision SHOULD be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The default configuration for Windows and macOS clients is set to use EAP-TLS with device certificates for 802.1X authentication. For a list of old printers that do not support 802.1X, an exception for MAC authentication in a separate, highly restricted VLAN is documented and approved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration on the RADIUS server and the client configurations (e.g., GPOs for Windows) to determine which authentication methods are permitted. The list of documented exceptions for insecure methods is requested and their justification is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy enforces the exclusive use of secure EAP types, especially EAP-TLS. The use of weaker methods such as MAC authentication or EAP-MD5 is generally prohibited and requires a formal risk acceptance process by information security management. Validation of the RADIUS server certificate is enforced on all clients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RADIUS server configuration only allows EAP-TLS as the authentication method. For MAC authentication of printers, a formal application with risk analysis must be submitted and approved by the CISO. The client configurations (via MDM/GPO) enforce server certificate validation and specify the name of the expected RADIUS server to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the RADIUS configuration to verify the permitted EAP types. The process for risk acceptance of exceptions is checked. In addition, the client configuration is examined to see if server certificate validation is enforced. This can be checked automatically by a script on a test client that tries to connect with a fake server certificate, which must fail.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For authentication, only hardware-based certificates are used, which are securely stored in a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) or a comparable Secure Enclave on the endpoints. The issuance, renewal, and revocation of these certificates are fully automated and integrated into a PKI and Mobile Device Management solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The certificate templates in the Microsoft PKI are configured so that the private key is created and stored in the client's TPM ('Key Attestation'). The distribution and renewal of the certificates is done automatically via SCEP/NDES, which is controlled by the MDM system. Insecure authentication methods are completely disabled on the RADIUS server.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the certificate templates on the PKI and the SCEP/MDM configuration. On a sample client, it is checked whether the private key of the certificate is actually marked as non-exportable and hardware-bound. The RADIUS logs are analyzed to see if authentications are taking place exclusively with certificate-based methods.

controls.title: Definition of NAC-specific roles and permissions for the RADIUS server

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the roles and permissions concept for the RADIUS server, the various groups that need to access a RADIUS server because of NAC SHOULD be taken into account. At a minimum, the respective organizational units that administer access switches (RADIUS clients), those responsible for endpoint groups, those who manage identities, and first-level support SHOULD be considered in order to administer them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A permissions concept is created for the RADIUS server. It defines the following roles: 'RADIUS-Admin' (full access, 2 people), 'Switch-Admin' (may only create/change RADIUS clients, members of the network team), 'MAC-Admin' (may only maintain MAC addresses in certain groups, e.g., Facility Management for printers), 'Helpdesk-User' (read-only access to logs for troubleshooting).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the permissions concept for the RADIUS server. It is checked whether the aforementioned groups are taken into account and whether the principle of least privilege is applied. A sample of the user accounts on the RADIUS server is compared with the concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The role and permissions concept is implemented in a granular way. Teams can only manage the objects (e.g., RADIUS clients, MAC address groups) for which they are responsible. All administrative actions on the RADIUS server are centrally logged and the logs are reviewed regularly, e.g., weekly, for unauthorized or unusual activities.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A rule is implemented on the RADIUS server that allows the 'Production IT' team to only manage switches whose IP addresses are in the 10.100.0.0/16 range. Every configuration change is sent to the central syslog server with a timestamp and the executing admin. A weekly report on all changes is generated and reviewed by the IT security officer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the granular implementation of the permissions by logging in as a member of a restricted team and trying to change objects outside of their responsibility. It is checked whether administrative logging is activated and the review protocols of the log analysis are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Administrative access to the RADIUS server is fully integrated into a central Identity and Access Management (IAM) solution. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enforced for all administrative roles. The assignment of permissions is dynamic based on the employee's role in the IAM and is regularly checked through automated access reviews (recertification campaigns).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Logging into the RADIUS admin interface is done via SAML or OpenID Connect against the organization's central Identity Provider, which enforces MFA. If an employee leaves the network team, their group membership in the IAM system is changed, which automatically and immediately revokes their access to the RADIUS server. An automatic recertification campaign is started every three months, during which managers must confirm the permissions of their employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the IAM connection and the MFA requirement. Reports from the IAM system on the last access review campaign for the RADIUS administrators are requested. The configuration can be checked automatically by an API query to the Identity Provider to verify the MFA requirement for the RADIUS admin application.

controls.title: Definition of a customized NAC rule set

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the NAC solution, a NAC rule set SHOULD be defined that implements the NAC concept. In this, it SHOULD be specified for each endpoint or endpoint group whether it is allowed unrestricted access to the network, whether access is denied, or whether only segments with restricted communication possibilities are accessible. The rule set SHOULD also specify the basis on which access control is carried out by defining the authentication methods used and the conditions for successful authentication for all endpoints.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy list is configured on the RADIUS server: 1. 'IF (User-Authentication-Type == EAP-TLS) AND (Client-Certificate-Issuer == Corp-PKI) THEN Permit-Access AND Assign-VLAN=10 (Clients)'. 2. 'IF (Calling-Station-Id IN Group:Printers) THEN Permit-Access AND Assign-VLAN=20 (Printers)'. 3. 'DEFAULT Deny-Access'. These rules directly implement the concept.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the policy set on the RADIUS server. This is compared with the specifications from the NAC concept to verify correct implementation. It is checked whether a rule exists for each relevant endpoint group and whether a 'Default Deny' rule is at the end.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy set is highly granular and assigns specific microsegments to endpoints based on a combination of attributes such as user group, device type, and authentication level. The policy set is versioned, and every change to it follows a formal change management process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RADIUS policy is extended: 'IF (User-Group == 'Finance') AND (Device-Type == 'Corporate-Laptop') AND (Authentication-Method == 'EAP-TLS') THEN Assign-VLAN=11 (Finance-Clients) AND Apply-ACL='ACL-Finance-Standard''. All changes to the policy set are versioned in a Git repository and require an approved change request.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the complexity and granularity of the policy set. The change management system is audited to verify that changes to the policy set are traceable and approved. The version history of the policy set is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The NAC policy set is dynamic and context-sensitive. Access rights are determined in real-time based on the current state of the endpoint (e.g., compliance status from an MDM/EDR system), the user context, and the current threat landscape. The policy set is fully managed via an Infrastructure-as-Code approach, and changes are automatically tested and deployed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each login, the RADIUS server queries the device's compliance status from the EDR system via API. 'IF (EDR-Status == 'compromised') THEN Assign-Quarantine-VLAN'. The entire policy set is stored as code in a Git repository. A change in the code triggers a CI/CD pipeline that validates the policy set in a test environment and, if successful, automatically rolls it out to production.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the API connections to external systems (EDR, MDM). The CI/CD pipeline for policy set management is audited. A test case is run in which a device is reported as 'non-compliant' to verify that the dynamic rule change takes effect in real-time. An automated test could check the configuration of the API endpoints and authentication data in the RADIUS server.

controls.title: Secure use of identities

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Individual identities SHOULD be used for NAC authentication. Identities used by more than one endpoint SHOULD only be used in justified exceptional cases. All information required for successful authentication SHOULD be secured against unauthorized access in accordance with the current state of the art.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each endpoint receives its own device certificate as its identity. The use of shared secrets for RADIUS clients is limited to the bare minimum, and the secrets are stored securely on the RADIUS server and not in plain text in scripts or documents. The use of a shared identity for a group of test devices is documented and approved as an exception.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor examines the configuration of the RADIUS server and the endpoints to verify that individual identities (e.g., unique certificates) are the standard practice. The documentation of exceptions for shared identities is checked. It is checked how and where RADIUS secrets are stored.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A policy strictly prohibits the use of shared identities. Any exception requires a formal risk acceptance process by the CISO. Authentication information such as RADIUS secrets or private keys is stored in a dedicated, hardened Secure Vault (e.g., HashiCorp Vault), which only the RADIUS service itself can access. All access to the vault is logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The RADIUS software is configured to retrieve the shared secrets for communication with the switches from a central vault via an API at startup. The secrets are no longer present in the RADIUS server's configuration file itself.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the policy prohibiting shared identities and checks the risk acceptance process. The configuration of the RADIUS server and the Secure Vault is analyzed to ensure that secrets are not stored in plain text on the file system. The vault's access logs are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unique, cryptographically strong identities are used for each endpoint, with their private keys generated and stored in hardware (TPM) (see A7). The concept of shared identities is technically prevented. Instead of shared secrets, certificate-based authentication is used wherever possible for communication between NAC components (e.g., between switch and RADIUS server using RADSEC).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Communication between switches and the RADIUS server is switched to RADSEC (RADIUS over TLS). Both the switches and the RADIUS servers receive certificates from the internal PKI and authenticate each other. This completely eliminates the need to configure shared secrets.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of RADSEC on switches and RADIUS servers. A network analysis (e.g., with Wireshark on a mirrored port) is performed to confirm that the RADIUS traffic is TLS-encrypted. It is checked whether no more shared secrets are defined in the RADIUS configuration.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Network Access Control (NAC) secures network access in the end device area through identity verification (authentication) and regulation (authorization). In this module, end devices are understood to be all IT systems connected at the access layer of a campus network. NAC can be used in both wired and wireless networks. An identity can be securely verified, for example, via accounts with certificates. Through the subsequent authorization, end devices are assigned appropriate network segments and permissions via authorization rules, thus defining access rules. Likewise, end devices can be denied network access.

For example, a printer can be identified as such via NAC and securely authenticated with a valid certificate. Once the printer has been successfully authenticated, it is then assigned to the network segment intended for the printer by means of NAC authorization.

NAC solutions use either the techniques described in the IEEE 802.1X standard (Port Based Network Access Control) or so-called MAC address authentication. With IEEE 802.1X, authentication takes place via the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) between a software on the end device, the so-called supplicant, and the so-called authenticator, which is realized by an access switch, WLAN access point, or WLAN controller. For authentication, a central RADIUS server (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is also used. The RADIUS server is also referred to as an Authentication Server or AAA server (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting). With MAC address authentication, the end device is authenticated via its MAC address.

An NAC solution according to IEEE 802.1X thus comprises the following components:

• Authentication Server or RADIUS server
• Supplicant on an end device
• Authenticator on an access switch or a WLAN component (WLAN access point or WLAN controller)
• Central NAC identity management, which can be implemented as integrated identity management on the server or draws on existing directory services

In this module, an NAC solution comprises all the components described above. If a single component of the NAC solution is meant, e.g., the RADIUS server, then this component is actually named as such. The central components of an NAC solution in this module are the RADIUS server and the NAC identity management.

For an NAC solution to be used meaningfully and for network access to be adequately secured, many points must be defined and the mentioned components of the solution must be coordinated. Furthermore, NAC-specific processes (e.g., measures to resolve disruptions) must be defined and existing processes (e.g., commissioning of end devices) must be adapted.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to establish information security as an integral part of NAC. An NAC solution should ensure that access to the network is regulated by identity-dependent authorization rules. This protects information that is processed, stored, and transmitted over networks.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The NET.3.4 Network Access Control module is to be applied to the elements of an NAC solution. This includes affected networks, clients, and central components.

To create an IT-Grundschutz model for a specific information domain, the entirety of all modules must generally be considered. As a rule, several modules must be applied to the topic or target object.

This module deals with NAC solutions based on the IEEE 802.1X standard and MAC address authentication via RADIUS. The focus is on the following sub-aspects of an NAC solution:

• General specifications for NAC for both the central components and the end devices
• Requirements for authentication and authorization
• Specifications for the management and operation of an NAC solution

Following contents are also important and are treated elsewhere:

• Directory services (see APP.2.1 General Directory Service)
• Network architecture and design (see NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design)
• WLAN-specific aspects (see NET.2.1 WLAN Operation and NET.2.2 WLAN Use)
• General operational aspects (see modules of the OPS Operation layer)

This module does not cover the following contents:

• Port Security and general aspects for network components (see NET.3.1 Routers and Switches)
• Proprietary NAC implementations not based on IEEE 802.1X
• The implementation of a RADIUS server on network components (access switch, WLAN access point, or WLAN controller)
• Administrative authentication on network components using RADIUS
• General aspects for end devices (see modules of the layers SYS.2 Desktop Systems, SYS.3 Mobile Devices, and SYS.4 Other Systems)
• General aspects for servers (see SYS.1.1 General Server) and virtualization (see SYS.1.5 Virtualization)
• General aspects for identity and access management (see ORP.4 Identity and Access Management)

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Inadequate planning of the NAC solution
parts.prose:
If not all IT systems and information relevant to NAC are recorded in an IT asset management system, a NAC solution cannot be adequately planned. Endpoints may then receive no network access or access to the wrong network segment.

If the requirements for the NAC solution have not been sufficiently recorded and analyzed, this can also lead to inadequate planning. For example, it is then possible that the switches in use cannot meet the requirements of the planned NAC solution or that the planned RADIUS server is incorrectly sized. Another consequence could be policies for the authentication and authorization methods used that are either too strict or too lenient. This could result in endpoints being denied network access or insecure authentication methods being used, even though secure methods would be possible. This could also potentially lead to overly broad communication permissions being granted.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Inadequately coordinated integration of end devices into the NAC solution
parts.prose:
Missing or inadequately implemented orchestration tools, security policies, requirements catalogs, and resources for registering all endpoints can lead to endpoints being integrated into the NAC solution in an uncoordinated manner. This makes it difficult to implement a secure and operationally-friendly authentication method for each endpoint group and to design a corresponding commissioning process. This could negatively impact the communication capabilities of the endpoints. Furthermore, devices that need protection may be accidentally placed in the wrong network segments.

If endpoints are insufficiently standardized or if NAC-specific endpoint requirements are inadequately supported, this can also lead to the use of insecure authentication methods, even though strong authentication would be fundamentally possible.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Use of insufficiently secure protocols in NAC
parts.prose: If secure EAP authentication methods are not technically supported, it may be necessary to use insecure authentication protocols such as EAP-MD5 or MAC authentication. In this case, spoofing, replay, or man-in-the-middle attacks are easier to carry out, and it cannot be ruled out that unauthorized IT systems could gain access to the network. If no restrictions are placed on which destinations and via which protocols endpoints with weak authentication protocols may communicate, unauthorized IT systems that gain access through one of the aforementioned attacks could also obtain extensive communication capabilities.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Incorrect Configuration of the NAC Solution
parts.prose:
Due to human error, inadequate processes, or insufficient personnel capacity and the resulting lack of time, NAC-specific parameters on endpoints, access switches, or RADIUS servers (NAC rule set) may be configured incorrectly. This can cause the entire NAC solution to behave in unintended ways, for example, by preventing endpoints from reaching required resources or from gaining network access.

If MAC addresses are deliberately registered incorrectly, too many resources can be made accessible by assigning incorrect network segments or other false authorization parameters.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Insufficient Validation of Configuration Changes
parts.prose: Inadequate change processes that do not validate configuration changes, or do so insufficiently, encourage configuration errors. This can result in endpoints being able to access too many or too few sensitive resources, or being denied network access altogether. For example, if NAC is disabled on switch ports without a compelling reason, unauthorized endpoints may gain unrestricted access to the network. If new software on endpoints is insufficiently validated, this can lead to interference between software components and affect the functionality of the supplicant.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Inadequately Protected Network Access
parts.prose:
If NAC is temporarily or permanently disabled on switch ports, network access is insufficiently protected. This makes it possible for unauthorized individuals to access the network or for insecure IT systems to receive overly broad communication permissions. As a consequence, information can be accessed without authorization, manipulated, or deleted. Furthermore, malware can be introduced in this way.

If endpoint compliance is inadequately checked, this can also lead to insufficiently protected network access, for instance, if an endpoint has inadequate antivirus protection and malware is introduced as a result.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Failure or Insufficient Availability of Central NAC Components
parts.prose: An inadequate or inadequately implemented NAC concept, malfunctioning NAC components or a malfunctioning network, insufficient requirements analysis, lack of processes, or Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks can lead to the failure or unavailability of central NAC components. This impacts the ability of endpoints to communicate. For example, depending on the switch configuration, if all RADIUS servers fail, endpoints will either have no network access or unrestricted network access.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. User Tracking
parts.prose: An inadequate administration concept, insufficient implementation of the concept, excessively long retention periods, or a lack of coordination with the works council and data protection officer could lead to personal log data being inadequately protected. This could allow for the creation of user profiles that enable employees to be tracked over time.

controls.title: Requirements analysis and planning for PBX systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A requirements analysis is only carried out sporadically and informally for immediate, obvious needs. There is no documented plan that considers future growth, expandability, or specific security features.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, decisions are often made ad hoc, for example, a small PBX system is purchased because the old one has failed, without a systematic survey of the actual needs of all departments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the responsible persons if a requirements analysis or a planning document exists. The absence of such documents or their purely informal character indicates this stage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic requirements analysis is performed, primarily covering the number of required lines and the most basic telephony functions (e.g., calling, holding, forwarding). The results are recorded in a simple document.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A list is created with the number of employees and the required telephones. The choice of system is based on these basic key figures. Security aspects or support contracts are only mentioned peripherally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the requirements analysis document and checks whether it covers basic aspects such as the number of lines and basic functions. It is checked whether the procured system meets these basic requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before procuring or expanding a PBX system, a requirements analysis MUST be performed. As part of this analysis, the functions the PBX system should offer MUST be defined. In addition to the specific features of the PBX system, the number of required connections and lines MUST also be determined. Possible expandability and basic security functions MUST also be considered during planning. Based on the determined requirements, the deployment of the PBX system MUST then be planned and documented. The planning MUST be coordinated with the responsible IT personnel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal document is created that summarizes the results of the requirements analysis. This includes function lists, capacity planning, basic security requirements (e.g., need for encryption), and considerations for support and maintenance contracts. This document serves as the basis for procurement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and completeness of the requirements and planning document. It is checked whether all aspects mentioned in the control text (functions, capacity, expandability, basic security) are covered and whether the planning has been coordinated with the IT department.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements analysis is formalized and established as an integral part of the procurement process. It includes detailed security requirements derived from the overarching security policies, such as specific requirements for encryption protocols or access control mechanisms. Support and maintenance contracts are evaluated against defined Service Level Agreements (SLAs). The planning is formally reviewed and approved by the Information Security Officer (ISO).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The analysis is carried out using a standardized template or a checklist-based process. SLAs for maintenance contracts, e.g., response times in the event of faults, are clearly defined. The approval by the ISO is recorded in the planning document.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the documented analysis and planning process. It is verified whether detailed security requirements have been defined and SLAs have been evaluated. The formal approval by the ISO is proven by signatures or entries in a ticket system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements analysis is embedded in a continuous, strategic technology management process. It is based on a detailed threat modeling for the specific operational context and considers the entire lifecycle of the system, including Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). The planning is fully integrated into the organization's risk management and procurement system and is regularly adapted to the changing threat landscape.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Formal modeling tools are used for the analysis. The results are automatically incorporated into tender documents and risk assessments. The plan is regularly reviewed and updated as part of security audits and strategy meetings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the integration of the planning process into the overarching ISMS. It is checked whether a current threat modeling and TCO analysis exist and whether their results have demonstrably been incorporated into the planning and procurement decisions. The regular updating of the plan is traced using logs and version histories.

controls.title: Selection of telecommunications service providers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A telecommunications service provider is selected mainly on the basis of price or a personal recommendation. A formal review of security aspects or contractual conditions does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection is often made by a single person without a formal process. Standard contracts for private customers or small businesses are accepted without adjustments or negotiations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the criteria for vendor selection. If no formal criteria exist and the contract contains no security-relevant clauses, this level is reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When selecting the telecommunications service provider, basic criteria such as costs, availability in the geographical area, and the range of basic services offered are considered. The main contract terms are reviewed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple comparison table is created with the offers from two to three providers. The contract is reviewed for commercial aspects such as term and price.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the comparison documents or decision proposal and checks whether basic criteria have been compared. The contract is checked for the written specification of the main services.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In order to be able to make phone calls to people whose telephones are not connected to the institution's own telecommunications system, a telecommunications service provider MUST be commissioned. The requirements for the telecommunications system, the security policy, as well as contractual and financial aspects MUST be taken into account. All agreed services MUST be clearly recorded in writing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection process is based on the results of the requirements analysis (NET.4.1.A1). A written contract is concluded that clearly regulates all essential services, costs, and responsibilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a written contract exists with the telecommunications service provider. It is checked whether the contract clearly describes the agreed services and whether the previously defined requirements (including security aspects) were demonstrably taken into account during the selection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection process for telecommunications service providers is formalized, e.g., through a tender (RFP). The selection criteria explicitly include security aspects such as guaranteed availability (SLAs), data protection regulations, and proof of the provider's security certifications (e.g., ISO 27001). Before being finalized, the contract is reviewed and approved by the legal department and the Information Security Officer (ISO).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal catalog of criteria with weighting is used. The provider must complete a self-assessment questionnaire regarding its security measures. The review by the legal and ISO departments is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the tender documents and the catalog of criteria. It is checked whether security requirements have been explicitly and assessably formulated. The approval notes of the responsible departments (Legal, ISO) are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of the telecommunications service provider is based on a comprehensive risk assessment of the supply chain. The provider must prove its security measures through third-party audits and submit regular reports. The contract contains audit rights for the own organization and severe penalties for non-compliance with security SLAs. The provider's security posture is continuously monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Services for monitoring third-party risks are used. The contract specifies concrete key performance indicators (KPIs) for security performance. Regular meetings are held with the provider to discuss the security situation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the supply chain risk analysis. Audit reports from the provider and minutes of the regular security meetings are reviewed. The contractual embedding of audit rights and penalties is checked.

controls.title: Logging in telecommunications systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging is enabled on the telecommunications system, but it uses the manufacturer's default settings. The logs are not actively evaluated and are overwritten after a short time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Logging is active by default, but no one checks the log files. The storage capacity for logs is limited, so only events from the last few hours or days are available.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the logging configuration on the telecommunications system. If only default settings are active and no process for evaluating or archiving the logs exists, this level is met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Logging is configured to capture essential events such as administrative logins (successful and failed) and critical system errors. The logs are stored locally on the system for a defined period.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrator has increased the logging level to capture relevant security events. The log files are stored locally and rotation is configured to retain the data for, e.g., 30 days.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the logging configuration and verifies that it goes beyond the default settings to log administrative access. The log rotation configuration is checked for an appropriate period.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In telecommunications systems, suitable data MUST be recorded and, if necessary, evaluated. All system-technical interventions involving program changes, as well as evaluation runs, data transmissions, and data access, MUST also be logged. All administration work on the telecommunications system MUST also be logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A logging concept is created that specifies which events (who, what, when) must be recorded for audits and error analysis. This includes configuration changes, failed login attempts, and the use of critical features.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a logging concept. Spot checks are used to verify that the events defined in the concept, particularly administrative activities and configuration changes, are actually recorded in the logs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logged information SHOULD be checked regularly. The log data of the telecommunications system is forwarded to a central log management system (e.g., SIEM). There are defined procedures for the regular, at least weekly, manual or semi-automated evaluation of the logs. In case of suspicious events, notifications are automatically generated to the responsible administrators.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The telecommunications system is configured to send its logs via syslog to a central server. Basic correlation rules and alerts are defined in the SIEM, e.g., for multiple failed login attempts. An administrator reviews a summary report weekly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the connection of the telecommunications system to the central log management system. The configuration of the alerting rules and the logs of the regular evaluations (e.g., weekly reports, tickets) are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The log data is analyzed in real time and correlated in the SIEM with information from other security sources (network, endpoints). The analysis uses advanced methods such as User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) and anomaly detection to proactively identify fraud patterns, unauthorized access attempts, or misuse. The integrity and authenticity of the log data are ensured by cryptographic measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Complex SIEM use cases are implemented that, for example, detect calls to known malicious numbers or unusual call volumes. Logs are digitally signed or transmitted via a secure channel to an audit-proof archive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the implemented SIEM correlation rules and their complexity. It is checked whether mechanisms for securing log integrity (e.g., hashing, signatures) are implemented. Samples of alarms are examined for their correct processing.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for telecommunications systems

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are basic, informal rules for the use of the telecommunications system. These may be part of a general IT user policy, but are not specifically formulated for telecommunications.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The general IT policy contains a sentence like 'The IT systems, including the telephone system, must be used securely.' Specific instructions are missing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for a specific policy for telecommunications systems. If none exists, the general IT policy is checked for corresponding, but non-specific, sections.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the institution-wide security policy, a separate security policy for the telecommunications system SHOULD be created. This security policy for the telecommunications system SHOULD contain basic statements on confidentiality, availability, and integrity. It SHOULD be known to all persons involved in the procurement, setup, implementation, and operation of the telecommunications system and form the basis for their work.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standalone document 'Security Policy for Telecommunications Systems' is created. It defines the protection goals, the scope, and the basic rules for secure operation and use. The document is made available to the relevant groups of people (IT operations, administrators).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the specific security policy for telecommunications systems. It is checked whether it contains the required basic statements and whether a process exists to make it known to the relevant persons (e.g., publication on the intranet, email distribution list).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy for telecommunications systems is a formally adopted, versioned document. It contains detailed and binding specifications for configuration hardening, the assignment of authorizations, the use of features (e.g., call forwarding), and the reporting channels for security incidents. The policy is reviewed and updated at least annually or in the event of significant changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is managed in a document management system with version control. It contains concrete checklists or configuration specifications. The review process is scheduled and the results are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the formal status of the policy (version, release date). It is checked whether the policy contains concrete, implementable specifications and whether the defined review process is demonstrably adhered to (e.g., through minutes).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is a dynamic document that is fully integrated into the ISMS. Its compliance is, wherever technically possible, monitored by automated configuration and compliance checks. The content of the policy is based on a detailed, specific risk assessment for the telecommunications environment and is regularly adapted based on new threat information and experience from incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Scripts or configuration management tools check the configuration of the telecommunications system against the policy's specifications daily. Deviations lead to automatic alarms. The results of the risk assessment and the threat intelligence feed flow directly into the updating of the policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the results of the automated compliance checks. The process for updating the policy based on risk analyses and threat intelligence is checked by tracing the connection between an identified risk and an adapted rule in the policy.

controls.title: Appropriate installation of the telecommunications system

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The telecommunications system is housed in a lockable room, such as a general IT or technical room, to which several people have access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The system is located in a server cabinet in a shared server room. The room is locked, but not specifically secured for the PBX system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the installation site and checks whether the room is at least lockable to prevent unauthorized access by the general public or any employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The PBX system SHOULD be housed in a suitable room. The interfaces on the PBX system, especially unused interfaces, SHOULD be adequately protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room for the PBX system is deliberately chosen to restrict physical access (e.g., a locked server room). Unused physical ports on the system are disabled through software configuration or fitted with blanking caps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the installation site and assesses its suitability with regard to access protection. A random check is carried out to see whether unused interfaces on the system are deactivated or physically covered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The PBX system is housed in a dedicated, access-controlled server room with appropriate environmental conditions (cooling, early fire detection). Access is restricted to a small, named group of people. Unused network ports on the switch to which the system is connected are deactivated (port security).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The system is located in a 19-inch rack in the air-conditioned server room. Access to the room is via an electronic locking system. The switch ports are administratively shut down and MAC address filtering is active.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of access authorizations for the server room. The switch configuration is checked for deactivated ports and port security settings for the PBX system connection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The PBX system is located in a high-security zone with multi-level access control (e.g., man-trap, biometrics) and video surveillance. All physical access is logged and regularly audited. The system housing and critical cable connections are fitted with tamper-evident seals.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The system is located in a lockable server cabinet within the high-security server room. Access logs are evaluated automatically. Numbered seals are attached to the housing screws and patch cables, and their condition is checked regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the implementation of the multi-level access control and reviews the recordings of the video surveillance and the access logs. The condition and documentation of the seals used are checked on a random basis.

controls.title: Restriction and blocking of unnecessary or security-critical features

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Obviously insecure features, such as remote maintenance access with default passwords or unprotected conference rooms, are deactivated during commissioning. However, most other functions remain active in their default state.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During the initial setup, a short checklist is used to close the best-known security gaps. A in-depth analysis of which functions are really needed does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the procedure during commissioning and checks whether at least the critical default settings known by the manufacturer have been changed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The scope of available features SHOULD be limited to the necessary minimum. Only the required features SHOULD be enabled. Features that are not required or are classified as critical due to their potential for misuse SHOULD be disabled as far as possible on the central system. Additional protective measures SHOULD be taken for confidential data stored and retrievable on the end devices.

parts.name: guidance
