parts.prose: The auditor asks for a demonstration of the 'factory reset' process. It is checked whether a corresponding instruction for the staff exists. It is checked on a decommissioned device whether the configuration has actually been deleted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When VoIP components are decommissioned or replaced, all security-relevant information (e.g., configuration, phone books, call lists, credentials) SHOULD be deleted from the devices. Confidential information SHOULD also be deleted from associated backup media. All labels SHOULD be removed before disposal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented process for decommissioning VoIP components is established. This process prescribes the secure deletion of the configuration (e.g., through factory reset and, if necessary, overwriting), the removal of labels, and the deletion of the device from central management and backups.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests and has the decommissioning process demonstrated. It is checked whether the execution of the deletion is logged. It is checked whether the corresponding entries in the VoIP system and in the backup system have been removed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: After the deletion process, it SHOULD be checked and documented whether the data has actually been successfully and irretrievably removed. It SHOULD be clarified with manufacturers or service companies at an early stage which measures for deleting security-relevant information are compatible with the contractual and warranty conditions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The deletion process is verified by a four-eyes principle. The successful deletion is confirmed in a handover protocol. For rented devices, the requirements for data deletion at the end of the contract are already specified in the contract.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the decommissioning protocols and checks whether the verification of the deletion is documented. In the case of rental agreements, it is checked whether they contain clauses on data security at the end of the contract.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The decommissioning process is fully audited and traceable. For devices containing sensitive data, cryptographic erasure (Crypto Erase) or physical destruction of the storage media is applied. A certificate of destruction is obtained from a certified service provider for each disposed device. All associated accounts, configurations, and firewall rules are automatically removed from the management systems (de-provisioning).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A certified disposal company is commissioned with the data destruction. The decommissioning process is integrated into an automated script or a workflow in the IT service management tool, which ensures that all digital traces of the device are removed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests a sample of destruction certificates. The automated de-provisioning process is analyzed and tested. It is checked whether references to the decommissioned device still exist in configurations or databases after the process has been executed.

controls.title: Requirements for a firewall for the use of VoIP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: VoIP traffic is routed through the firewall using very broad or non-specific rules, e.g., a rule that allows all traffic to or from the VoIP server. There is no specific adaptation of the firewall to the needs of VoIP.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Often, the VoIP system is placed in a 'server zone' for which a general, permissive rule already exists, or an 'ANY ANY from PBX_IP' rule is created to circumvent problems with RTP's dynamic port allocation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rules affecting the VoIP server. They look for overly permissive rules that open more than the required SIP and RTP ports.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The existing firewall is configured with specific packet filter rules for the necessary VoIP protocols and ports (e.g., TCP/UDP 5060/5061 for SIP, UDP 10000-20000 for RTP). However, it does not have application-specific intelligence for VoIP (Application Layer Gateway - ALG).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrator has manually opened the necessary ports for SIP and a defined RTP port range in the firewall. This is a static configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the firewall configuration and determines whether the rules are restricted to the specific VoIP ports. It is checked whether the firewall operates as a pure packet filter or has VoIP-specific functions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be checked whether the existing firewall is suitable for the use of VoIP and can be adapted accordingly. This includes the ability to handle VoIP protocols such as SIP and RTP.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the introduction of VoIP, a formal assessment of the existing firewall is carried out. If the firewall understands VoIP protocols (e.g., via a SIP-ALG module), it is configured and tested. If not, the risks are assessed and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documentation of the firewall assessment. The firewall configuration is checked to determine whether it has been adapted for VoIP (e.g., activation of SIP-ALG) and whether the configuration meets the requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If the existing firewall is not sufficient for secure VoIP operation (e.g., because it does not have a stable SIP-ALG or cannot detect VoIP-specific attacks), an additional, specialized firewall or a Session Border Controller (SBC) SHOULD be procured and installed for this purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Due to the shortcomings of the existing firewall, a dedicated Session Border Controller (SBC) is used as a VoIP firewall at the network perimeter. The SBC handles the secure termination of SIP trunks and external clients.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the network topology to verify the existence and correct placement of the SBC. The basic configuration of the SBC is checked to ensure that it functions as the primary security component for VoIP.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated, high-availability cluster of Session Border Controllers (SBCs) is used as the sole security instance for all external VoIP traffic. The SBCs perform deep packet inspection, implement topology hiding, transcoding, and provide protection against denial-of-service attacks and fraud scenarios (e.g., toll fraud).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An SBC cluster is operated in active/standby or active/active mode. The advanced security features of the SBC, such as call rate limiting, detection of irregular call patterns, and SIP header validation, are configured and actively used. All security-relevant events from the SBC are forwarded to a SIEM for correlation and alerting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the SBC cluster for high availability and the configuration of the advanced security features. It is checked whether logging to the SIEM works. VoIP-specific penetration tests can be carried out to validate the effectiveness of the SBC's protective measures.

controls.title: Encryption of signaling

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Signaling is consistently protected using TLS between the endpoints and the VoIP server. However, default cryptography settings are used and only the server identity is verified by a certificate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: SIP over TLS is activated on the telephone system and the clients. The telephone system uses a valid TLS certificate (e.g., from Let's Encrypt).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor records the signaling traffic and verifies with Wireshark that it runs over TLS (default port 5061). The server certificate is checked for validity and trustworthiness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The integrity and confidentiality of signaling information SHOULD be guaranteed by suitable cryptographic methods, such as Transport Layer Security (TLS). Not only the payload data in the signaling, but also the authentication data SHOULD be transmitted encrypted throughout.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy is established that mandates the use of SIP over TLS for all signaling. The configuration ensures that authentication methods such as SIP Digest also take place within the TLS tunnel and are therefore protected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the server and clients to verify the enforcement of SIP over TLS. A network capture confirms that no signaling data is transmitted unencrypted. It is checked whether authentication attempts take place within the TLS session.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the VoIP gateway SHOULD be restricted as much as possible by validating VoIP addresses (e.g., SIP-URI) and identities (e.g., H.323-ID). In addition, end-to-end security mechanisms for signaling (e.g., through S/MIME in SIP messages) SHOULD be considered. It SHOULD be documented how the signaling is protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VoIP server is configured to only accept calls from registered and authorized SIP-URIs. The possibility of using end-to-end encrypted signaling is evaluated and, if possible, activated for particularly sensitive communication. The entire configuration of the signaling protection is documented in detail.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the VoIP server's configuration to verify the access restriction mechanisms. It is checked whether call attempts from unauthorized addresses are rejected. The documentation on signaling protection is checked for completeness and correctness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Mutual TLS (mTLS) is enforced for TLS connections, requiring both the client and the server to authenticate with a valid, trusted certificate. Only strong and modern cipher suites are permitted. The validity of the certificates is actively checked using OCSP Stapling or CRLs. All aspects of the protection are documented and regularly audited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An internal Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is used to issue client certificates for all VoIP endpoints. The VoIP server is configured to only accept connections from clients with a valid certificate from this PKI. The configuration of the TLS protocol is hardened to disable outdated protocol versions (e.g., SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1) and weak ciphers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the PKI and server configuration for the enforcement of mTLS. A test with a client without a valid certificate must fail. The configuration of the permitted cipher suites is checked with tools like `testssl.sh` or `sslyze`: `testssl.sh <voip_server_ip>:<tls_port>`. The configuration of the OCSP/CRL check is verified.

controls.title: Secure media transport with SRTP

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: SRTP is enabled as the preferred method for all calls. However, if an endpoint does not support SRTP, an unsecured fallback to RTP is allowed to ensure compatibility. Standard key exchange mechanisms are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the telephone system configuration, SRTP is set to 'optional' or 'preferred'. Key exchange often occurs via SDES, where the keys are transmitted in the unencrypted or transport-encrypted SIP/SDP messages.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor makes a test call with a client that explicitly does not support SRTP and checks with a network sniffer whether the call is established and the media stream is transmitted as unencrypted RTP.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Media data (voice, video) transmitted via the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP) SHOULD be protected in an appropriate manner. The payload data SHOULD be protected by using the Secure Real-Time Transport Protocol (SRTP). The associated control channel SHOULD be protected using the Secure Real-Time Control Protocol (SRTCP).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy is established that mandates the use of SRTP/SRTCP for all media data streams. The VoIP components are configured to use SRTP/SRTCP for all calls.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes a sample of calls with a network sniffer (e.g., Wireshark). It is checked whether the media data is transmitted as SRTP and not as RTP. Wireshark can detect SRTP packets and mark them as such.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of SRTP is enforced ('Encrypt-or-Drop'), so that no calls with unencrypted RTP can be established. Secure key exchange mechanisms such as DTLS-SRTP are used. The security-relevant options of the SRTP implementation, such as the selected crypto profiles, SHOULD be documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The VoIP system and the clients are configured so that SRTP is mandatory ('mandatory'). DTLS-SRTP is configured as the key exchange method, as this is more secure than SDES. The selected SRTP profiles (e.g., AES_CM_128_HMAC_SHA1_80) are recorded in the configuration documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor makes a test call with a client that explicitly does not support SRTP; the call must fail. The configuration of the key exchange mechanism is checked. The documentation of the crypto profiles is compared with the actual configuration.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: End-to-end encryption of media data is enforced using advanced key exchange mechanisms such as ZRTP or PERC. The system is configured to use only the strongest available crypto profiles for SRTP. Regular, automated checks are performed to ensure that no fallback to insecure RTP occurs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Clients and servers are configured for the use of ZRTP, which enables an opportunistic key exchange independent of the SIP infrastructure. The configuration only allows crypto profiles with AES-256. A monitoring script regularly checks the system configuration and active calls for the use of unencrypted RTP and alerts in case of violations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration and function of ZRTP by comparing the Short Authentication String (SAS) between two endpoints. The configuration of the allowed crypto profiles is analyzed. The logs of the monitoring script are reviewed to assess its effectiveness.

controls.title: Separation of the data and VoIP network

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dedicated VLAN is set up for VoIP traffic. The primary goal is to ensure Quality of Service (QoS) by prioritizing voice traffic. The security aspects of the separation are secondary and there are few or no restrictive rules for communication between the VLANs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A new VLAN (e.g., VLAN 10) for voice is created on the network switches. The switch ports for telephones are assigned to this VLAN. QoS settings (e.g., CoS, DSCP) are configured to prioritize voice traffic. There are often 'allow any' rules between the voice VLAN and the data VLAN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the switch configuration to confirm the existence of the voice VLAN. The router or Layer 3 switch configuration is checked for the inter-VLAN routing rules. A test PC in the data VLAN attempts to establish a connection to a telephone in the voice VLAN to demonstrate the lack of restriction.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VoIP network SHOULD be appropriately separated from the general data network. This is typically achieved by using a separate logical network (VLAN) for VoIP components.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A network segmentation policy is established that mandates a separate VLAN for VoIP. The switches are configured accordingly to place VoIP endpoints in this VLAN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network policies and switch configurations to ensure that a separate VLAN for VoIP exists and is in use. It is checked on a random basis whether the VoIP endpoints are assigned to the correct VLAN.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The VoIP VLAN is secured by strict Access Control Lists (ACLs) on the router or Layer 3 switch. These only allow absolutely necessary communication (e.g., signaling to the VoIP server, DHCP, provisioning) and block all other traffic by default, especially direct communication from the data VLAN to the voice VLAN. There SHOULD be a policy for handling devices like PCs with softphones that need to access both networks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: ACLs are configured on the L3 switch to filter traffic into and out of the voice VLAN. For example, only traffic on port 5061 to the VoIP server and on port 67/68 to the DHCP server is allowed. For softphone clients, either specific firewall rules on the client PC or a VPN solution is used for access to the voice network.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the ACLs applied to the voice VLAN for their restrictiveness. Penetration tests are conducted to attempt to access services in the voice network from a client in the data network. The solution for softphone clients is evaluated for its security.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The separation is achieved through a physically separate network infrastructure or, if logical, secured by using 802.1X port-based network access control (PNAC) to prevent unauthorized devices from connecting to the voice VLAN. VoIP endpoints in a VoIP network SHOULD ONLY be able to establish the intended VoIP connections to other IT systems; all other outgoing traffic is blocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A RADIUS server is used for 802.1X authentication. Only devices with a valid certificate or known MAC address (MAB as a fallback) are granted access to the voice VLAN. Outgoing traffic from the voice VLAN is filtered by a firewall so that the phones can only communicate with the VoIP server, provisioning server, and NTP server, but cannot freely browse the internet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the RADIUS server and the switches for 802.1X. An attempt is made to connect an unauthorized device (e.g., a laptop) to a port designated for VoIP to check if access is denied or the device is moved to a quarantine VLAN. A test from a VoIP phone, e.g., a ping to an external internet address, must fail.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: Voice over IP (VoIP) refers to making phone calls over data networks, especially over the Internet. Special signaling protocols are used to transmit signaling information, for example, during a call. The actual payload data such as voice or video is transmitted using a media transport protocol. Both protocols are required to establish and maintain a multimedia connection. Some methods require only one protocol for both signaling and media transport.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module considers the security aspects of VoIP endpoints and mediation units (middleware). The components described here are similar in their functionality to the telecommunication systems described in module NET 4.1 PBX systems.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The NET.4.2 VoIP module is to be applied to all communication networks in which VoIP is used. Since VoIP is operated over data networks, the requirements of the NET.1.1 Network Architecture and Design or NET.3.2 Firewall modules should also be taken into account in addition to this module.
This module examines the security aspects of VoIP components and voice transmission via VoIP. If circuit-switched PBX systems exchange information with each other via a data network, this module should also be applied.
The specific threats and requirements of classic PBX systems and hybrid systems are covered in the NET 4.1 PBX Systems module.
VoIP software is often not run on dedicated hardware, but on standard IT. If softphones are installed on clients, the requirements of the SYS.2.1 General Client module and the operating system-specific modules should be taken into account. If software for VoIP is operated on servers, the requirements of the SYS.1.1 General Server module should be met in addition to the requirements of the operating system-specific modules.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Incorrect configuration of the VoIP middleware
parts.prose:
A VoIP-based telephone system can be affected by misconfigurations in a similar way to a circuit-switched telephone solution. For example, telephone users could be assigned incorrect telephone numbers or the entire telephone infrastructure could fail. Even seemingly non-critical errors, such as a misspelled name in the phone book, cannot be ruled out.
When communicating via VoIP, several IT systems are usually involved. If SIP is used as the initialization protocol, systems such as registrars, SIP proxy servers, and location servers are usually required for communication. If the VoIP infrastructure changes, all IT systems must be adapted. This can easily lead to configuration errors. Even if all services are located on one server, they often have to be configured individually. If only one system is changed incorrectly, the entire telephone infrastructure may no longer be usable.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Incorrect configuration of the VoIP components
parts.prose:
Regardless of whether VoIP components are dedicated hardware ('appliances') or software-based systems, the configuration is crucial for the error-free functioning of the system. In addition to the signaling settings defined during the planning phase, the transmission method for the media streams plays an important role. A compression method can be used to reduce the size of the data packets containing the voice information.
Incorrect configuration of the transmission method can lead to transmission problems. If an unsuitable method is used and voice information is compressed too much, the voice quality often deteriorates. If, on the other hand, a method is chosen that provides too little compression, the message stream is not sufficiently reduced and the data network can become overloaded.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Eavesdropping on telephone conversations
parts.prose:
If telephone calls or data are transmitted unencrypted, attackers could in principle listen in or read along. For example, they could tap the telephone cables directly or listen in on a PBX system that mediates between the callers. With VoIP, telephone calls and data transmissions can be eavesdropped on even more easily than with classic PBX systems. All voice information is transmitted within a media stream, for example with the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). Through techniques such as spoofing and sniffing, VoIP also provides attackers with all the possibilities of attacks in data networks.
With many PBX systems, callers can leave messages for recipients if they are not available by phone at the time of the call. Some answering machines, especially on VoIP systems, send this information as an audio file in an e-mail. The content of this e-mail could be directly intercepted and listened to by an attacker.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Misuse of freely accessible telephone lines
parts.prose:
Often, telephones are operated that are not personally assigned to any user. Some of these telephones, such as those in printer rooms, are only accessible to a limited group of people. On the other hand, telephones are often found in areas that are freely accessible to visitors. These include, for example, parking garages or areas in front of access control systems. If these telephones have an electronic phone book in which internal telephone numbers are stored, these numbers could be unintentionally leaked to the outside world.
When using VoIP telephones in freely accessible areas, other aspects may be relevant. This is because they have a high software component and are often operated in data networks that are also used for other IT applications. Attackers could therefore try to exploit vulnerabilities in the VoIP software or install malicious software themselves by directly accessing device information.
VoIP telephones must be connected to a data network. Attackers could connect a mobile IT system to this network connection and thus possibly gain access to the internal network, which is protected from the outside by a firewall. They may be able to use this access for attacks on confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

controls.title: Appropriate placement of a fax machine (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fax machine is present and connected, but the location was chosen without considering security aspects. It may be in a freely accessible area, allowing faxes to be viewed by unauthorized persons.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The device was placed wherever there was space, for example, in an unsecured hallway or reception area. Network and telecommunication connections are used without physical protection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through an on-site inspection that the fax machine is in an unsecured area and received documents are freely visible to unauthorized persons.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The fax machine is set up in a general office space that is not freely accessible to the public. It is connected to an available network and telephone jack. Care is taken to ensure that the printout is not directly facing a public corridor.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installation is carried out to the best of one's knowledge and belief in a general office area, but without a specific, documented security analysis of the location. Standard network sockets are used.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the fax machine is in a lockable office and not in a public area like a hallway. It is checked whether it is connected to a functioning jack.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Fax machines MUST be set up in such a way that incoming faxes cannot be viewed or taken by unauthorized persons. The location MUST have a suitable network connection for the fax machine. Fax machines MUST NOT be connected to network jacks not intended for them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The location is a lockable room (e.g., a printer or server room) to which only a defined group of people has access. The network connection used is documented in the network plan and designated for the fax machine. Physical access to the connection is controlled by the room's security.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the physical location of the fax machine through an on-site inspection. It is verified that the location effectively prevents access by unauthorized persons (e.g., through door locks, privacy screens). The network documentation is reviewed to check if the used connection is intended for the fax machine.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, the location SHOULD be selected so that there are sufficiently dimensioned telecommunication lines or channels. The room SHOULD be secured by an electronic access control system that logs access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before installation, capacity planning for the telecommunication connection is carried out to avoid bottlenecks. An electronic access control system is installed and logs all access attempts to the room where the fax machine is located. The logs are reviewed regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the capacity planning for the telecommunication connection. The functionality of the access control system is tested, and the logs are checked for unauthorized access attempts or anomalies.

controls.title: Information for employees about fax usage (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no formal information or guidance on fax usage. Employees use the device on a 'trial and error' basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: It is assumed that the operation is self-explanatory. Neither instructions nor notices are available.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes that there is no user manual or usage instructions at the fax machine and that employees have not received formal training.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A user manual from the manufacturer is available at the fax machine. If necessary, employees are verbally instructed by colleagues.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No proactive training is provided, but the original manufacturer's manual is available. Questions are answered by experienced colleagues or IT on an as-needed basis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks for the existence of the user manual at the device.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees MUST be informed about the specifics of information transmission by fax. They MUST also be informed that the legal validity of a fax transmission is severely limited. A comprehensible user manual MUST be available at the fax machine. In addition, instructions for correct fax usage MUST be available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A leaflet is created and distributed to all employees, e.g., upon hiring. This leaflet contains the most important information on risks and correct handling. A laminated, one-page quick start guide for operation and the most important security rules is attached to the device.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether instructions for fax usage and a user manual are available at the device. Through random interviews with employees, it is verified whether they have been informed about the risks and correct usage and where they can find this information.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, users SHOULD receive at least a quick start guide for the fax server's client software. The information on secure fax usage is integrated into a mandatory annual security training, and participation is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department creates a PDF quick start guide for the fax client software and makes it centrally available on the intranet. The topic 'Secure Fax Usage' is included as a permanent component in the e-learning module on information security. Completion of the module is mandatory for all employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the availability of the quick start guide for the fax client software. The training materials and the participation certificates or lists of the security trainings are reviewed to verify the regular, mandatory awareness training.

controls.title: Secure operation of a fax server (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The fax server is installed and the basic functions are manually checked. Unneeded services are manually stopped during installation but not permanently disabled, so they could run again after a restart.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installation is carried out according to the manufacturer's standard instructions. A manual check of the running services is performed once during installation. There is no regular check.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the fax server is generally functional. A check of the running services (e.g., with 'netstat -an') is performed at the time of the audit to determine if unnecessary services are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that the fax server exclusively offers fax services and is not used for other services. All unneeded features and access points of the communication interfaces used MUST be deactivated. Furthermore, the connection from the fax server to the PBX or the public telephone network MUST be regularly checked for functionality.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The fax server is installed on a dedicated system (physical or virtual) according to a documented hardening procedure. This procedure permanently deactivates all unneeded ports, services, and protocols. A maintenance plan prescribes a monthly functional check of the connection, which is logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the fax server (e.g., using `systemctl list-units --all` or `Get-Service`) to verify that only fax-related services are enabled. The documentation of the hardening process is reviewed. The logs of the regular functional checks are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, a test phase SHOULD take place before commissioning. Configuration parameters and all changes to the configuration of a fax server SHOULD be documented. The archiving and deletion of fax data SHOULD be regulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before production use, the fax server is operated in a separate test environment. All configuration changes are versioned in a configuration management system (e.g., Git). A data retention policy explicitly regulates the handling and deletion periods of fax data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the test phase. The configuration management system is inspected to check the traceability of changes. The data retention policy is checked and it is verified on a random basis that old fax data has been deleted according to the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The fax server is managed by an automated configuration management tool that continuously monitors compliance with the hardened state and automatically corrects deviations or raises alerts. The functional check of the connection is automated by regularly sending and receiving test faxes to a control service, with the results being centrally logged and monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tools like Ansible, Puppet, or Chef are used to declare and enforce the desired configuration state. A monitoring system like Nagios or Zabbix is extended with a script that checks fax connectivity every minute via an end-to-end test and raises an alarm in case of errors.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration playbooks/manifests of the configuration management tool. The configuration and logs of the monitoring system are inspected to verify the continuous, automated monitoring of the fax server's functionality and configuration.

controls.title: Creation of a security policy for fax usage (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No written regulations or policies exist for the use of fax machines or servers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Usage is unregulated and based on the individual assumptions of employees. There is no awareness of the need for a policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: By interviewing and requesting documents, the auditor determines that no security policy for fax usage exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are informal, unstructured instructions for fax usage, for example in the form of emails or short memos. These cover some aspects, such as handling confidential faxes, but do not constitute a comprehensive or approved policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The team leader has sent an email with the most important rules of conduct to his team. There is no central, officially approved document.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews employees and managers about existing regulations and asks to be shown relevant emails or notes. It is determined that no formal, complete policy exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before a device is approved, a security policy for fax usage SHOULD be created. This policy SHOULD define the type of use. Furthermore, it SHOULD regulate how incoming and outgoing faxes are to be handled. A regulation for handling undeliverable faxes SHOULD also be created. In addition, the policy SHOULD contain information and instructions for emergency preparedness and resilience of fax operations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal document 'Fax Usage Security Policy' is created, approved by the responsible body (e.g., Information Security Officer), and published on the intranet for all employees to access. The policy clearly defines responsibilities and the required processes.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the security policy for fax usage and reviews it for completeness regarding the required points (type of use, handling of incoming/outgoing faxes, undeliverable faxes, emergency preparedness). It is checked whether the policy is officially approved and accessible to employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy for fax usage is reviewed annually and updated as needed. It also contains clear specifications on which data classifications (e.g., 'STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL') may not be transmitted by fax. Compliance with the policy is checked on a random basis and the results are documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An annual review process for the policy is established in the ISMS. The policy is extended with an appendix containing a clear matrix for data classification and permitted transmission channels. The subject matter expert conducts a quarterly review of the fax journals for compliance with the policy and reports to the ISO (Information Security Officer).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the annual policy reviews. The policy is checked for the additional specifications on data classification. The records of the random checks are inspected.

controls.title: Procurement of suitable fax machines and fax servers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During procurement, functional requirements and price are primarily considered. Security aspects are not systematically used as a criterion, but may be covered coincidentally by selecting a brand-name product.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Procurement is based on a simple request such as 'We need a new fax machine'. A standard model is ordered from the office supply catalog.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement documents and determines that no explicit security requirements were formally defined and evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before fax machines or fax servers are procured, a list of requirements SHOULD be created. Based on this list, the potential systems or components SHOULD be evaluated. The list of requirements for fax machines SHOULD also include security-relevant aspects, such as the exchange of a subscriber identification, the output of transmission reports, as well as error logging and journaling. For a fax server, all requirements for the IT system, including the operating system, communication components, and application software, SHOULD be identified and considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement department uses a standardized checklist for procuring fax systems. This checklist contains a dedicated section on security requirements, which is reviewed by the Information Security Officer (ISO) or a subject matter expert before each procurement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the requirements lists and procurement documents for recently acquired fax machines or servers submitted. It is checked whether security-relevant aspects (subscriber identification, transmission reports, logging) were systematically considered. The involvement of the ISO in the process is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined requirements, appropriate additional security functions SHOULD be considered based on the protection requirements. The possibility that a fax server can be integrated into an existing data network and into a groupware system SHOULD be considered if necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement process includes a formal protection requirement assessment for the intended purpose. Based on this, advanced security functions such as encryption of the internal storage or connection to a central SIEM system are defined as a requirement. The ability to integrate into the existing infrastructure is verified by a proof-of-concept before the final purchase decision.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the protection requirement assessment in the context of fax procurement. It is verified that the selection decision comprehensibly considers the results of the protection requirement assessment and the requirements for advanced security functions. If applicable, the proof-of-concept protocols are reviewed.

controls.title: Appropriate labeling of outgoing faxes (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For most faxes, a cover sheet is used that contains the sender and recipient. However, there is no fixed template or regulation, so completeness and consistency vary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees use personal or department-specific templates for fax cover sheets. There is no company-wide standard template.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly checks the transmission logs and archived faxes for the use of cover sheets and finds inconsistent handling.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The source and destination of every fax transmission SHOULD be visible on all outgoing faxes. If this information cannot be determined from the transmitted document, a standardized fax cover sheet SHOULD be used. In general, the fax cover sheet SHOULD list at least the name of the sender's institution, the name of the contact person, the date, the number of pages, and an urgency note. It SHOULD also contain the names and institution of the recipients.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A company-wide, standardized template for fax cover sheets is created and made mandatory for all employees. The template is available on the intranet or directly in the fax software. The use of the cover sheet is prescribed in the fax policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and availability of the standardized fax cover sheet template. The fax policy is reviewed to check the mandatory regulation. Samples of outgoing faxes are checked to see if the standardized cover sheet has been used correctly and completely.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, the fax cover sheet SHOULD be adapted for each outgoing fax if necessary. The fax software enforces the use of a cover sheet and automatically fills in fields such as sender, date, and time from the system or user data to minimize errors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The fax server software is configured to technically prevent sending without a completed cover sheet. The cover sheet template is equipped with dynamic fields that are populated from Active Directory (for the sender) and system settings (date/time).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the fax server software to verify the enforced use of the cover sheet and the automatic population of fields. A test is made to send a fax without a cover sheet to check the effectiveness of the block.

controls.title: Appropriate disposal of fax consumables and spare parts (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Consumables such as used toner cartridges or ink ribbons are collected and disposed of in general office waste or a general recycling collection. There is no specific procedure for data protection-compliant disposal.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Empty cartridges are placed in their original box next to the trash can and disposed of by the cleaning staff. There is no awareness that these may contain residual information.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the responsible employees about the disposal process for fax consumables and determines that no data protection aspects are considered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All fax consumables from which information about sent and received fax documents can be obtained SHOULD be rendered illegible or disposed of by a reliable specialized company before disposal. The same procedure SHOULD also be followed for replaced information-bearing spare parts. Maintenance companies that inspect or repair fax machines SHOULD be obligated to handle them accordingly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a contract with a certified disposal service provider for the destruction of data carriers. All information-bearing consumables (e.g., toner cartridges, drum units) and spare parts (e.g., hard drives) are collected in locked security containers and picked up by this service provider for destruction. The contractual agreements with maintenance companies contain a clause on confidential handling and secure disposal of replaced parts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract with the disposal service provider and the associated handover and destruction certificates. The contracts with maintenance companies are checked for corresponding data protection clauses. An inspection shows the existence and use of the security containers.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, it SHOULD be regularly checked whether the defined handling for disposal is complied with by all parties involved, including external service providers. The entire lifecycle of information-bearing components is documented from procurement to certified destruction.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In an inventory system, information-bearing spare parts (e.g., hard drives from fax machines) are recorded with their serial numbers. Their whereabouts are tracked until disposal and cross-referenced with the certificate of destruction. At least once a year, unannounced checks are conducted to verify that employees and maintenance technicians are correctly disposing of consumables and spare parts in the security containers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the inventory lists and the complete lifecycle documentation for randomly selected components. The logs of the internal controls of the disposal process are reviewed.

controls.title: Use of transmission and reception logs (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logging functions of the fax machine or server are enabled, as this is the default setting. However, the logs are not regularly evaluated or archived and are only used manually for troubleshooting when needed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logs remain on the device until the memory is full and they are overwritten. An evaluation only takes place reactively when a user reports a problem.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the device configuration to see if logging is active. By interviewing the administrators, it is determined that no regular or proactive evaluation takes place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The transmission processes of incoming and outgoing fax transmissions SHOULD be logged. The communication journals of commercially available fax machines SHOULD be used for this purpose. If the fax machines have logging functions, these SHOULD be enabled. For a fax server, logging SHOULD also be enabled. The communication journals and log files SHOULD be evaluated and archived regularly. Unauthorized persons SHOULD not be able to access the communication journals and the logged information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logging functions of all fax systems are enabled. An operating concept defines which information is logged. The logs are collected weekly on a central log server and archived in accordance with legal and operational requirements. Access to the logs is restricted to a few administrators.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the fax systems for active logging. The operating concept is checked for the regulations on logging. The auditor verifies the central collection and the access permissions for the log files on the log server. The archiving processes are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined logging, the logs SHOULD be randomly checked for irregularities. It SHOULD be decided exactly what information is to be logged in order to meet data protection requirements (data minimization) and at the same time ensure sufficient traceability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process is defined according to which the fax logs are checked for anomalies (e.g., an unusual number of failed attempts, faxes to unknown numbers) on a monthly basis by an IT administrator. The results are logged. The logging is configured to record only metadata (time, source, destination, status) and no content, unless absolutely necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the logs of the monthly random evaluations. The configuration of the logging is verified to ensure that it complies with the principle of data minimization. The defined evaluation process is checked for its appropriateness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The fax logs are forwarded in real time to a central Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. The SIEM system correlates the fax events with other system logs and automatically alerts the security team in case of predefined suspicious patterns (e.g., fax spam attempts, transmission to high-risk numbers, unauthorized configuration changes).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The fax servers are configured as a log source in the SIEM (e.g., Splunk, ELK Stack, QRadar). Specific correlation rules and dashboards have been created for fax events, enabling proactive monitoring and rapid response to security incidents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the log forwarding from the fax server to the SIEM. In the SIEM system, the correlation rules, dashboards, and generated alarms for fax events are reviewed to assess the effectiveness of the automated monitoring.

controls.title: Control of programmable destination addresses, logs, and distribution lists (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Destination addresses and distribution lists are programmed once during setup. There is no regular review or deletion of numbers that are no longer needed. Changes are only made when an error is noticed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The speed dial keys and address books grow organically over time without old or incorrect entries being removed. There is no responsible 'gardener' for the data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the address book or speed dial list of the fax machine displayed and determines by questioning the employees that some entries are outdated or unknown and that there is no process for review.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Programmable speed-dial keys or stored destination addresses SHOULD be checked regularly to ensure that the desired fax number matches the programmed number. Fax numbers that are no longer needed SHOULD be deleted. It SHOULD be documented in a suitable manner when a new entry is added or a destination number is changed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A process is established whereby an authorized employee (e.g., a key user or administrator) checks all stored destination addresses and distribution lists every six months. The check is carried out and signed off using a printed list. All changes are documented in a logbook at the device or in a central file.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the logs of the last checks of the destination addresses. A random check is carried out to see whether the stored numbers are correct and whether changes have been documented in a traceable manner.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to regular review, the ability to change destination addresses and distribution lists is restricted to a very small, authorized group of people. For fax servers that are connected to groupware, the central address book of the groupware is used and its maintenance processes also apply to the fax numbers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The configuration of the fax machine or server is password-protected so that only administrators can change address book entries. Changes can be requested by users via a ticket system. Fax numbers are maintained as an attribute in the central Active Directory or groupware address book, whereby the general maintenance process for user accounts also covers the fax numbers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the access permissions for the configuration of the address book. The process for requesting and implementing changes (e.g., via the ticket system) is verified. If a central address book is used, its maintenance process and integration with the fax server are checked.

controls.title: Protection against fax machine overload (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Sufficient communication lines or channels SHOULD be available. For a fax server, the prospective fax volume SHOULD be estimated. Accordingly, high-performance components SHOULD be selected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During procurement and setup, an estimate of the expected fax volume (number of faxes per day, average number of pages) is carried out. Based on this, the number of required ISDN channels or the bandwidth of the FoIP connection as well as the performance of the fax server (CPU, RAM, storage) are dimensioned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the documentation for capacity planning and estimation. The configuration of the telephone system and the fax server is reviewed to compare the actual resources provided with the planning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logs of fax servers SHOULD be checked regularly to counteract bottlenecks due to overloads in a timely manner. Fax data that is no longer needed SHOULD be deleted from the fax server promptly to avoid storage overload.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An administrator checks the performance logs of the fax server (e.g., CPU utilization, queue length, memory usage) on a monthly basis. An automated routine has been set up to move or delete successfully delivered faxes from the server's active memory to an archive after 30 days.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the logs of the monthly performance checks. The configuration of the automated deletion or archiving routine is verified and a random check is carried out to see whether old fax data has actually been removed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The utilization of the fax server and the communication channels is continuously monitored by a monitoring system. When predefined thresholds are reached (e.g., 80% channel utilization for 10 minutes), a warning is automatically sent to the administrators. For critical applications, a high-availability fax server solution with load balancing is used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The monitoring system (e.g., Zabbix, PRTG) is configured to query the relevant performance parameters of the fax server and the PBX in real time. Escalation chains for alerting have been defined. A fax server cluster with an upstream load balancer is operated to distribute the load across multiple instances and ensure failover.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the monitoring system, including the thresholds and alerting rules. The architecture of the high-availability fax server setup is verified using network and system plans. The effectiveness of the load balancing and failover is tested (if possible).

controls.title: Blocking of specific source and destination fax numbers (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unwanted fax addresses SHOULD be blocked (blacklisting). Alternatively, only specific numbers SHOULD be allowed (whitelisting). It SHOULD be checked which approach is suitable in which situation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For general fax reception, a blacklist is maintained on the fax server or in the telephone system. Known spam fax numbers are added to this list after being reported by users. For special, high-security fax connections, a whitelist is used that only allows communication with predefined partners. The decision for black- or whitelisting is documented for each connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the filter lists (blacklist/whitelist) on the fax server or the PBX. The documentation that justifies the decision for the respective approach is reviewed. The process for reporting and adding numbers to the blacklist is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The filter lists for fax numbers are regularly reviewed and updated, e.g., semi-annually. Rules are used to block entire number blocks (e.g., for expensive service numbers or known spam source countries) instead of just individual numbers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The blacklist is extended with rules that block outgoing faxes to 0900 numbers or known foreign premium services. As part of a semi-annual review, the entries are checked for currency and the effectiveness of the filters is evaluated based on the logs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the filter rules for the use of number block locks. The logs of the semi-annual reviews of the filter lists are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A commercial or open-source service is subscribed to that provides current blacklists for spam fax numbers. These lists are automatically imported into the fax server configuration to ensure proactive protection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The fax server is configured to download a current blacklist from a trusted third-party provider daily and automatically update its filter rules. This minimizes manual maintenance effort and increases the detection rate.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the contract with the blacklist provider and the configuration of the automatic update on the fax server. The log files of the update process are inspected to verify regular and successful updates.

controls.title: Definition of authorized fax users (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only a few employees SHOULD be selected to have access to the fax machine. These employees SHOULD distribute incoming faxes to the recipients. The employees SHOULD be taught how to handle the device and how to implement the necessary security measures. Every authorized user SHOULD be informed about who is allowed to operate the fax machine and who is responsible for the device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each fax machine with an increased protection requirement, a list of authorized operators is created and maintained. These individuals receive verifiable instruction in operation and security procedures (e.g., distribution of confidential faxes in sealed envelopes). The responsibilities are clearly documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the list of authorized operators and the associated training and instruction records. Interviews are conducted to verify whether the authorized persons are aware of their tasks and the responsible contact persons.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the fax machine or fax server functions is technically enforced. Only authorized users can authenticate themselves at the device (e.g., via PIN or card) to send or receive faxes. The distribution of incoming faxes is handled via a traceable process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The fax machine is configured to require authentication via PIN, employee ID card, or by connecting to Active Directory before fax functions can be used (Secure Fax Release). On a fax server, access to the fax sending function is controlled via authorization groups in the groupware.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the access control on the fax machine or fax server. An attempt is made to use a fax function without authorization. The assignment of permissions is verified based on the authorization groups and the list of authorized persons.

controls.title: Making copies of incoming faxes (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Faxes printed on thermal paper that are needed for a longer period SHOULD be copied onto plain paper or scanned. It SHOULD be taken into account that the color on thermal paper fades faster and thus becomes illegible. The copies or scanned faxes SHOULD be archived in a suitable manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a clear work instruction for the responsible fax operators that all incoming faxes on thermal paper that are subject to a retention obligation must be immediately copied to plain paper. The original is then destroyed in a data protection-compliant manner. The copy is fed into the regular archiving process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the corresponding work instruction. By interviewing the responsible persons, it is verified that this process is known and followed. Spot checks in the archive are carried out to see whether there are any illegible thermal paper faxes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process of copying or scanning thermal paper faxes is integrated into the organization's digitization workflow. Incoming thermal paper faxes are scanned directly, provided with metadata, and archived in the document management system (DMS), instead of just being physically copied.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated scanner is available at the fax station. The work instruction describes the scanning process, the naming convention for the files, and the storage location in the DMS. After successful and quality-assured digitization, the thermal paper original is destroyed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the defined digitization process for thermal paper faxes. Faxes archived in the DMS are spot-checked for their quality and correct metadata. The process for destroying the originals is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of fax machines with thermal paper is generally prohibited for all applications with retention requirements. Instead, only laser printing fax machines or fax servers are used, which ensure long-term stable and archivable output.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement policy states that no more thermal paper fax machines may be purchased. Existing devices have been replaced with suitable systems as part of an exchange program. All faxes are received directly as PDF from the fax server or printed on plain paper.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the procurement policy. A walk-through is carried out to verify that no more thermal paper fax machines are in use, especially in areas with documents subject to retention.

controls.title: Announcement and reassurance in handling fax transmissions (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Important faxes SHOULD be announced to the recipients before they are sent. For this purpose, it SHOULD be specified which documents are to be registered in advance. Employees who wish to send confidential fax documents SHOULD be instructed to have the complete receipt confirmed by the recipients. For important or unusual faxes, recipients SHOULD in turn have the senders confirm that the fax document originates from them and has not been forged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security policy for fax use contains a chapter that regulates the handling of important and confidential faxes. It is defined that faxes with content of the protection requirement category 'HIGH' must always be announced by telephone and their receipt confirmed. The telephone is specified as the form of communication.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the corresponding passage in the security policy. Through interviews with employees who regularly send confidential information, it is checked whether this process is known and applied. Transmission logs with confidential faxes are spot-checked and evidence of the reassurance is requested (e.g. telephone note).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process of announcement and reassurance is formalized. For each fax transmission with a high protection requirement, a cover sheet must be filled out on which the telephone announcement and the confirmation of receipt are documented with a time stamp and the name of the conversation partner. This sheet is archived together with the transmission report.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A form 'Proof of confidential fax transmission' is created and made available to the employees. The completed forms are collected centrally and kept for a defined period to meet the verification obligation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly requests the archived proof forms and compares them with the entries in the transmission log. The completeness and plausibility of the entries are checked.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
This module covers the security aspects of transmitting information via commercially available fax machines and fax servers. The transmitted information is referred to as a fax (short for telefax) or, less commonly, as a telefacsimile or remote copy. With a conventional fax machine, the content on a master document is scanned point by point by the sending device and transmitted to the receiving devices. The receiving device reconstructs this content point by point and usually outputs it directly to paper.
A fax server, on the other hand, is a service that is installed on a server, thus enabling other IT systems in a data network to send and receive faxes. Fax servers are often integrated into existing email or groupware systems. This makes it possible for incoming fax documents to be delivered to users by the fax server via email. Documents to be sent are transferred to the fax server either via a printer queue or by email. As a rule, the document is sent or received between the fax server and the clients in the data network as an image file. The transmitted image file cannot be further processed directly in word processing systems. This usually first requires text recognition (OCR, Optical Character Recognition). Documents received and processed by a fax server can usually be easily archived, for example by the fax server service itself, by document management systems, or by the groupware that is directly connected to the fax server service.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: One goal of this module is to protect the information transmitted and processed via fax transmissions. Another goal is to protect fax machines and fax servers from manipulation by unauthorized persons. The transmission medium plays no role in the application of the module, so the requirements of the module should also be implemented for Fax over IP (FoIP).

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose: The NET.4.3 Fax Machines and Fax Servers module is to be applied to every fax machine and every fax server in the information domain.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Insufficient or incorrect supply of consumables
parts.prose: Fax machines receive documents and usually print them directly onto paper. For the smooth and uninterrupted operation of a fax machine, consumables such as paper and toner must be available in sufficient quantities. If this is not the case, it is often not possible to receive fax documents. In addition, no transmission confirmations can be printed, which may be mandatory.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Faulty fax transmission
parts.prose:
Numerous disruptions can occur on the transmission path between the sending device and the receiving device of a fax document. This can result in the fax documents to be transmitted being incomplete or illegible, or not arriving at the recipient at all. Decisions that depend on this information can be flawed and thus cause high damages.
Time delays that arise because the problems first have to be identified and the document has to be resent can lead to further complications. Often, the senders or recipients have no way of influencing the transmission path, so they have to wait until the disruption is resolved by a third party. Often, the senders even believe that the fax document was properly transmitted to the intended recipients, and the resulting problems are only recognized very late.
In addition, it cannot be ruled out that a fax document was transmitted to the wrong receiving device, for example, because of a misrouting in the public telecommunications network. It is also conceivable that for fax machines, numbers are dialed incorrectly or speed dial keys are programmed incorrectly. If a fax server is used, the numbers can also be entered incorrectly or stored incorrectly in the address book. This can lead to confidential information being transmitted to unauthorized persons.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Manipulation of address books and distribution lists
parts.prose:
Address books and distribution lists can often be kept in fax machines. If a fax server is used, similar address books and distribution lists can usually be kept in a central location via the groupware, which can be used by several users. The address books can store numbers of recipients so that they do not have to be re-entered for each fax transmission. It is also possible to create a group of recipients via distribution lists and thus send fax transmissions to several people at the same time.
Often, once programmed numbers of recipients or distribution lists are no longer checked when a fax document is to be sent. If unauthorized persons change the address books or distribution lists on the fax machine or in the groupware, confidential information can thus reach the wrong recipients. It can also happen that the intended recipients do not receive urgently needed information. For example, a fax number in the address book could be replaced or further recipients could be added to the distribution list without this being noticed by the responsible persons in the respective institution.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Unauthorized reading of fax transmissions
parts.prose: In almost all cases, it is most economical for several users to share a fax machine. Therefore, these are usually set up in rooms that all employees of an institution can enter, such as printer rooms. As a result, the fax machines are freely accessible to all employees, meaning all employees can also read received faxes and thus gain access to confidential information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Analysis of residual information in fax machines and fax servers
parts.prose:
Depending on the technical process by which fax machines store, process, or print information, varying amounts of residual information may remain in the fax machine after a fax has been sent and received. Unauthorized persons who gain possession of the device or its components may be able to recover this information.
On the hard drive of a fax server, faxes are stored at least until they can be delivered to their destination. Furthermore, modern operating systems use swap files, which may also contain residual information. This information could be illicitly analyzed if this fax server is accessed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Spoofing a false sender in faxes
parts.prose: Faxes are a popular medium for transmitting documents that are only valid with a signature. However, in the same way that a false sender can be faked with a false name and a false letterhead, a fax can also be manipulated. For example, signatures can be scanned from other documents and copied onto the fax document. It is generally not possible to tell the difference between a real signature and a reproduced graphic file. Damage occurs when recipients consider the information contained therein to be authentic or even legally binding.

controls.title: Planning of building security (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The building security is planned on an ad-hoc basis only for individual areas considered particularly critical, without pursuing a holistic approach.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In this phase, often only reactive measures are taken, for example, installing a better lock after a break-in, without analyzing the overall situation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether there is any form of planning for building security at all, even if it is only selective and undocumented. This can be done by interviewing those responsible and inspecting the areas identified as critical.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a basic, written concept for building security that covers the most important areas such as fire protection and access control. However, the various security aspects are considered in isolation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are separate documents for fire protection and access control regulations. There is no systematic coordination between these concepts, e.g., how a fire door affects access control.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing planning documents and checks whether the basic security aspects (personal protection, protection of assets, IT security) have been taken into account. It is checked whether the documents are known and implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Depending on the (planned) use of a building and the protection requirements of the business processes operated there, it MUST be determined how the building is to be secured. For a building, security aspects for the protection of persons in the building, the protection of economic assets and IT MUST be considered, from fire protection to electrics to access control.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The specifications are documented in a central building security concept. This document is consulted when planning construction measures or changes in use. Responsibilities for the individual security areas are clearly named.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and completeness of the building security concept. It is checked whether the specifications adequately reflect the protection requirements of the business processes and cover all relevant aspects (people, economic assets, IT). The implementation of the specifications is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security requirements from the various areas (fire protection, access, IT, etc.) MUST be coordinated with each other. The resulting, integrated security concept is reviewed regularly, at least every two years, and updated if necessary.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Interdisciplinary workshops are held to analyze the interactions between different security measures (e.g., escape route control vs. intrusion protection). The security concept is versioned and changes are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the coordination meetings and the revision history of the security concept. It is assessed whether the coordination of the measures is logical and consistent and whether the review process is formalized and verifiably carried out.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of building security is a fully integrated, risk-based process that is linked to the overarching Information Security Management System (ISMS) and Business Continuity Management (BCM). Changes in protection requirements or the threat landscape lead to an automated review and adaptation of the concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: GRC software (Governance, Risk, Compliance) is used to model the dependencies between business processes, IT systems and physical security measures. Threat modeling is carried out regularly to optimize planning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the processes and risk assessments mapped in the GRC software. It is verified whether the process for adapting the security concept is triggered automatically and whether the results of the threat modeling are demonstrably incorporated into the planning. Automated check: `check_grc_config --asset-type 'building' --verify-isms-link`.

controls.title: Adapted distribution of electrical circuits (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The distribution of electrical circuits follows no clear logic. Critical and non-critical consumers are often connected to the same circuit. A review of the design does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For example, the coffee machine in the break room is on the same fuse as the servers in the next room. The circuit protection is often oversized to avoid tripping, which increases the fire hazard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly inspects the fuse boxes and tries to trace the assignment of consumers to circuits. Obvious planning errors, such as the joint protection of IT and household appliances, are documented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The electrical circuits were fundamentally divided by area (e.g., offices, server room) during the original installation. However, there is no regular review or adaptation to new needs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The original planning is available, but over the years new consumers have been added without checking the circuit load. The documentation (circuit diagrams) is outdated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the current conditions with the original installation plans. It is checked whether subsequent changes could overload the original design without a formal review having taken place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be regularly checked whether the protection and design of the electrical circuits still meet the actual needs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A review is carried out by a qualified electrician at least once a year or in the event of major changes to the electrical installation (e.g., connection of new IT racks). The results are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the regular checks of the electrical circuits. It is verified that the checks have taken place and that identified deficiencies have been rectified. It is checked whether the intervals are appropriate.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The electrical circuits are logically separated according to protection requirements and function (e.g., separate circuits for IT, general consumers, security technology). The design of the electrical circuits is documented in detail and the plans are always up to date.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Dedicated electrical circuits connected to an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) are used for critical IT systems. The documentation is available digitally and is managed via a configuration management system (CMS).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the logical separation of the electrical circuits using the current circuit diagrams and through a physical inspection. It is checked whether the documentation in the CMS is up to date and whether changes are made according to a defined process.
