parts.prose: The zone concept is already taken into account during the planning of new buildings or conversions in order to achieve an optimal spatial arrangement. The transitions between the zones are designed as controlled security airlocks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During space planning, care is taken to ensure that zones with high protection needs are located inside the building and are only accessible via zones with lower protection needs. The transition from the internal zone to the protected zone (e.g., server room antechamber) is realized by a mantrap or a two-door airlock.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the building plans and assesses whether the zone concept has been optimally implemented. The design and function of the zone transitions (airlocks) are checked on-site.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The zone concept is dynamic and linked to the respective risks and processes. Access rights for zones are linked not only to persons, but also to specific times and conditions (e.g., approval by a second person). Compliance with the zone rules is monitored automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Access to the data center is only possible during service hours and after prior registration in the ticket system (conditional access). Access requires the simultaneous presence and authentication of two authorized persons (four-eyes principle). Video analysis monitors whether persons enter zones without authorization (tailgating).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the extended access rules (conditional access, four-eyes principle) in the access control system. The effectiveness of the anti-tailgating measures is tested. The logs are checked for rule violations and the subsequent alarms. Automated check: `check_access_control_system --zone 'data_center' --verify '4_eyes_principle_active,conditional_access_enabled'`.

controls.title: Automatic drainage (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no measures for automatic drainage in areas at risk from water.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the basement, which also houses the archive, there is no floor drain or lifting station.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection of endangered areas (basement, under water pipes), the auditor determines that no drainage facilities are available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Passive drainage facilities such as floor drains are available. However, active systems such as pumps are missing or not maintained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a floor drain in the server room in the basement. A pump for the event that the sewer is overloaded (backflow) does not exist. The function of the drain is never checked and it could be clogged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and condition of passive drainage facilities. They ask for maintenance records for any pumps that may be present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All areas at risk from water SHOULD be equipped with automatic drainage. It SHOULD be checked regularly whether the active and passive drainage facilities are still functioning.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In basement rooms with valuable assets (IT, archive), floor drains and redundant lifting stations (pumps) are installed. The function of the pumps and the patency of the drains are checked and documented annually as part of a maintenance plan.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the maintenance plan and logs for the drainage systems. It is checked whether maintenance is carried out regularly and whether the systems are sufficiently dimensioned for the potentially accumulating amount of water.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to drainage, water detectors are installed in critical areas to trigger an early alarm in the event of a water leak.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Water sensors are installed in the raised floor of the server room. These are connected to the hazard alarm system and report an alarm to the building services and the ISO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the positioning and function of the water detectors. A test (e.g., with a damp cloth) verifies the correct triggering and forwarding of the alarm.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The system is fully automated. When water is detected, not only is an alarm triggered, but countermeasures are also automatically initiated, such as closing main water shut-off valves and starting pumps. The pumps are connected to the emergency power supply.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Water detectors, motorized shut-off valves, and pumps are integrated into the building management system. A control logic is implemented that automatically closes the main valve for this part of the building in case of an alarm in the server room. The power supply for the pumps is ensured by the data center's UPS.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the control logic in the building management system. The function of the automatic countermeasures is checked as part of a planned test. The connection of the pumps to the emergency power supply is verified. Automated check: `check_bms_rule --trigger 'water_detected_dc1' --verify 'main_valve_closed,pumps_active'`.

controls.title: Appropriate site selection (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Site selection is based exclusively on economic criteria such as rental price and transport links. Environmental conditions and natural hazards are not taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A building is rented in a known flood zone because the rent is low. The potential risks are ignored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the criteria for the site selection and finds that security aspects played no role.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Obvious hazards such as location in a flood-prone area are avoided during site selection. However, a systematic analysis of all potential environmental hazards does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A flood map is checked to see if the location is at risk. Other risks such as proximity to chemical plants, flight paths or the local crime rate are not investigated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses which environmental hazards were considered in the site selection and which were not. It is determined that the analysis was only superficial.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When planning and selecting the building location, it SHOULD be checked which environmental conditions could have an influence on information security. There SHOULD be an overview of site-related hazards.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before selecting a new site, a formal site risk analysis is carried out. This takes into account natural hazards (floods, storms, earthquakes), environmental hazards (e.g. proximity to industrial plants, airports, railway lines) and social factors (e.g. crime, political instability). The results are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the site risk analysis and assesses its completeness and methodology. It is checked whether the results of the analysis have had a comprehensible influence on the site decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: These hazards SHOULD be counteracted with additional compensatory measures. The analysis is supported by external experts or specialized service providers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If a site has to be chosen despite known risks (e.g. flood risk), specific countermeasures are planned and budgeted (e.g. no use of the basement, installation of mobile flood protection walls). Geodata service providers and security consultants are commissioned for the analysis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor evaluates the planned and implemented compensation measures for their appropriateness and effectiveness. The reports of the external service providers are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Site risk analysis is a continuous process that is also repeated regularly for existing sites in order to identify changed environmental conditions (e.g. due to new construction projects in the neighborhood or climatic changes). The results flow directly into Business Continuity Management (BCM) and the adaptation of security measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every two years, the site risk assessment for all important sites is updated. For this purpose, current data on natural hazards and crime statistics are procured. If an increased risk is identified, the emergency plans and structural protection measures are adapted accordingly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the process for regular reassessment of site risks has been established and is being carried out. It is checked whether the results of the reassessment have demonstrably led to adjustments in BCM and in the security concepts.

controls.title: Gate or security service (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no reception or security service. Visitors can enter the building unchecked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The entrance door is open during the day. Strangers are not approached by the employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through an inspection and a test (social engineering) that uncontrolled access for strangers is possible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a reception, but its main task is not security control. The tasks are not clearly documented. Visitors are not always accompanied.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The reception staff is mainly responsible for the telephone switchboard and mail distribution. Visitors register, but are often only verbally directed to their destination without the person they are visiting picking them up.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the reception staff about their security duties and finds that they are unclear. The handling of visitors is observed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The tasks of the gate or security service SHOULD be clearly documented. The gate service SHOULD monitor all movements of people at the gate and at all other entrances and, depending on the security concept, control them. Visitors SHOULD be accompanied to the person they are visiting or picked up at the gate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a written service instruction for the gate service that regulates the processes for visitor registration, ID checks and accompaniment. All visitors are recorded in a list and receive a visitor's pass. It is clearly regulated that visitors must always be accompanied in the non-public area.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the service instruction for the gate service. The visitor lists are checked for completeness. Observation and test visits are used to verify whether the process for accompanying visitors is being adhered to.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees and visitors SHOULD be able to identify themselves to the gate service. The gate service SHOULD be informed in good time if access authorizations change.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All employees visibly wear an employee ID card. Visitors must present an official photo ID, which is checked against the registration. There is a process to ensure that the gate service receives an updated employee list immediately when employees join or leave.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether the employees are wearing their ID cards and whether an ID check is carried out for visitors. The process for updating the employee information for the gate service is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A digital visitor management system is used. Visitors must register online in advance and are automatically activated in the system after approval by the host. The gate service monitors the monitors of the hazard alarm systems (intrusion detection system, fire alarm system) and video surveillance and initiates defined measures in the event of an alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The visitor management system prints a pass with a barcode on arrival, which may be activated for defined doors. The gate service is qualified and trained as an intervention point for all security alarms. The alarm plans are available directly at the workplace.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the process in the digital visitor management system from pre-registration to check-out. The qualification of the gate service as an intervention point is checked and the alarm plans are reviewed. The reaction of the service is observed by means of a test alarm.

controls.title: Selection of a suitable building (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A building is selected without considering security requirements. Its suitability is not checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A building is rented and only afterwards is it discovered that the electrical installation is insufficient for the operation of the IT.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for the checklist or criteria catalog for the building selection and finds that security aspects were not included.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During the selection process, basic security aspects such as a solid overall impression are taken into account. However, a detailed check based on a checklist does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Care is taken to ensure that the building does not look run-down. However, it is not systematically checked whether, for example, the fire barriers are correctly installed or whether there is a sufficient power supply for the planned data center.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses whether the building selection was based on a systematic check of security-relevant properties or rather on subjective impressions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When selecting a suitable building, it SHOULD be checked whether all security requirements relevant for later use can be implemented. For each building, the existing hazards and the required measures to prevent or reduce damage SHOULD be documented in advance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before renting or purchasing a building, a due diligence check is carried out with regard to information security. Based on a comprehensive checklist, aspects such as structural condition, fire protection, burglary protection, power supply, etc. are assessed. The result is a report that documents the current state, the gaps to one's own requirements (target), and the estimated effort to close the gaps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the due diligence report for the building. It is assessed whether the check was comprehensive and whether the results had a comprehensible influence on the selection decision and the budget planning for necessary upgrades.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The inspection of the building is carried out by an interdisciplinary team of in-house experts (construction, IT, security) and, if necessary, by external experts (e.g. for fire protection, statics).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the inspection of the potential building, a team is formed that covers all relevant competencies. For critical aspects that cannot be assessed internally, expert opinions are obtained from external specialists.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the composition of the assessment team and reviews the external expert reports. It is assessed whether the expertise was sufficient for a well-founded decision.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of the building is fully integrated into the site selection process. The results of the site risk analysis and the building due diligence are combined to create an overall risk assessment for the potential options and to objectively select the best alternative.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A scoring model is used that weights various criteria (cost-effectiveness, functionality, security, site risks) and leads to an overall rating for each building in question. The decision is made on the basis of this objective assessment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the scoring model used, including the criteria and their weighting. It is checked whether the selection process is documented in a transparent, objective and comprehensible manner.

controls.title: Moving out of buildings (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The move-out is unplanned. There is no check to see if confidential information or valuable hardware is left behind.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During the move-out, old file folders or decommissioned hard drives are forgotten in the rooms. Keys are not returned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the process for a secure move-out and finds that none exists. If possible, an inspection of the old premises is carried out after the move-out.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an instruction that no documents may be left behind. However, there is no systematic check or inventory list.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees are instructed to empty their lockers. Whether this is done completely is not checked. It is not clear which IT assets were in the building at all.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses whether the move-out process goes beyond a simple instruction and whether mechanisms are in place to check for completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Prior to the move, an inventory SHOULD be created of all items relevant to information security for the move, such as hardware, software, data carriers, folders, or documents. After the move, all rooms SHOULD be searched for any items left behind.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the move, an inventory of all relevant objects is carried out. This inventory list is used to plan the move and to check for completeness at the new location. After the old property has been completely vacated, a responsible person carries out a formal final inspection and documents it in a report.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the inventory list and the final inspection report. It is checked whether the process was carried out systematically and whether deviations (e.g. missing objects) were documented and clarified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All data carriers left behind (if any) are securely erased or physically destroyed. Keys and access cards are demonstrably returned. The final inspection is carried out by at least two people according to the four-eyes principle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A deletion or destruction certificate is created for all data carriers that were not moved. The return of all issued keys and transponders is checked against the issuance list and documented. The final inspection is carried out jointly by a representative of the departing institution and the landlord.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the destruction certificates and the documentation of the key return. The final inspection report is checked for compliance with the four-eyes principle.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before the final handover of the building, a professional inspection for eavesdropping devices or hidden data carriers (Technical Surveillance Counter-Measures, TSCM) is carried out in sensitive areas. All IT and network components are reset to their factory settings to leave no configuration data behind.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized service provider conducts a 'sweep' of the former meeting and server rooms. A 'factory reset' is performed for all network switches, routers, and firewalls and documented in the inventory system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the report from the TSCM service provider. It is checked on a random basis whether the reset of the IT components has been demonstrably carried out (e.g. through console logs or screenshots).

controls.title: Firestop registry (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is not known where firestops are located or what types have been installed. There is no registry.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If a new cable needs to be laid, a hole is drilled in the wall at any point.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks for an overview of the firestops and finds that none exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The location of the firestops is shown in the building plans. However, there is no detailed information about type, approval, or current occupancy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: It is known which walls contain firestops. However, if a subsequent installation is made, it is not documented and it is not checked whether the firestop is suitable for it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the building plans with reality and determines that the documentation is insufficient for a correct subsequent installation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A firestop registry SHOULD be maintained. In this, all types of firestops SHOULD be recorded individually. After work on firestops, the changes SHOULD be entered in the registry.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A registry (e.g. as an Excel list or in a simple database) is maintained. For each firestop, the location, type, approval number, and a photo are documented. Each firestop has a unique identifier on site. Subsequent installations are noted in the registry.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the firestop registry and compares it on a random basis with the marking and condition of the firestops on site. It is checked whether recently installed cable runs are documented in the registry.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The changes in the registry SHOULD be entered within four weeks at the latest. The registry also contains information about the current percentage occupancy of the firestop and the manufacturer's specifications for subsequent installation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process for updating the registry is clearly defined and compliance with the deadline is monitored. The registry serves as a planning basis to decide whether a firestop still has capacity for more cables. The approval notices and processing instructions are stored digitally in the registry.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the timeliness of the entries in the registry and checks compliance with the four-week deadline. It is verified whether the stored information is sufficient for professional planning and execution of subsequent installations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The firestop registry is maintained in specialized CAFM software or a BIM model. Each firestop is marked with a QR code or NFC tag. Technicians can scan the code on-site with a mobile device, retrieve all relevant information, and document changes made directly in the system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The process of subsequent installation is completely digitized. The technician scans the firestop, the app shows them the approval and the free capacities. After the work is done, they take a photo, which is automatically assigned to the firestop in the registry with a time stamp and GPS coordinates.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the digital process demonstrated live. The data consistency between the mobile client and the central system is checked. The quality and traceability of the mobile documentation (incl. photos) is assessed. Automated check: `check_cafm_asset --type 'fire_stop' --verify 'qr_code_linked,last_update_recent'`.

controls.title: Hazard alarm system (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No hazard alarm system (HAS) is present, or only individual, non-networked detectors (e.g. a battery-powered smoke detector).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Hazards such as burglary or water are not technically detected. Reliance is placed on accidental discovery by employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through inspection and review of documents that no HAS is installed to detect relevant hazards (burglary, fire, water, etc.).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are stand-alone systems for different hazards that are not integrated (e.g. a separate burglar alarm system and a separate fire alarm system). The alarms are received at different locations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The burglar alarm system alerts a security service, the fire alarm system only a local siren. There is no central point that receives all hazard notifications. Maintenance is carried out in an uncoordinated manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the various alarm systems and their alarm routes. It is assessed whether the lack of integration leads to gaps or delays in alarm processing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There SHOULD be a hazard alarm system appropriate to the premises and the risks. The hazard alarm system SHOULD be regularly tested and maintained. It MUST be ensured that those who receive hazard notifications are able to react to the alarm appropriately, both technically and in terms of personnel.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An integrated hazard alarm system (HAS) is installed, which combines different trades (e.g. burglary and fire alarms) in one central unit. The system is serviced annually by a specialist company in accordance with manufacturer and standard specifications. There is an alarm and intervention plan that specifies who is informed in the event of an alarm and what measures are to be taken. The staff of the alarm receiving center is trained accordingly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the concept of the HAS, the maintenance contracts and reports. The alarm and intervention plan is checked for completeness and plausibility. The training records of the staff are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hazard alarm system is connected to a permanently staffed, qualified center (e.g. VdS-certified emergency call and service control center, ARC) that ensures immediate alarm follow-up.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All critical alarms from the HAS are reported to an external ARC via a secure transmission path. The intervention times and measures are clearly defined in the contract with the ARC.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract with the ARC and checks its certification. A test alarm is used to verify whether the alarm transmission and the response of the ARC correspond to the agreements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hazard alarm system is fully integrated into a higher-level physical security information management (PSIM) or building management system (BMS). In the event of an alarm, not only can alarms be forwarded from there, but active countermeasures and controls (e.g. video activation, emergency door release, ventilation control) can also be triggered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: If a burglar alarm is triggered, the PSIM automatically switches to the nearest camera, moves it to a predefined position, and starts recording. In the event of a fire alarm, the fire control matrices are automatically activated. All actions are logged in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configured control rules and workflows in the PSIM/BMS. The automated responses are checked by triggered test alarms. The logging is checked for completeness and tamper-proofing. Automated check: `check_gms_workflow --trigger 'burglar_alarm_zone_3' --verify 'cctv_linkage_active,door_lockdown_initiated'`.

controls.title: Perimeter security (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no perimeter security. The property line is not secured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Anyone can enter the property unhindered and approach the building.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor determines that there are no measures to secure the property (fencing, lighting, etc.).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple enclosure (e.g. a low fence or a hedge) is present to mark the property line. However, it does not offer any significant protection against being overcome.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A 1.20 m high chain-link fence surrounds the property. There are no measures to detect climbing over.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the height and nature of the enclosure in terms of its protective effect. It is checked whether there are any obvious weaknesses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Depending on the protection requirements of the building and depending on the terrain, it SHOULD have perimeter security. At a minimum, an outer enclosure or fence and security measures against unintentional and intentional non-violent overcoming of the property line SHOULD be considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A solid fence (e.g. a picket fence at least 2 meters high) is installed. The fence is designed to make it difficult to climb over (e.g. with a serrated top rail). Gates and driveways are normally closed and only opened when necessary.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the design and condition of the fence. It is checked whether the measures to make it difficult to overcome are effective and whether the regulations for gates and driveways are being complied with.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Measures to make it difficult to intentionally and violently overcome the property line, as well as open-area security measures (e.g. person and vehicle detection, video surveillance), SHOULD be considered and implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The fencing is additionally equipped with an anti-crawl barrier. The open area is illuminated at night. At critical sections of the perimeter, motion detectors and/or video cameras are installed, which trigger an alarm with a security service upon approach to the fence.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the effectiveness of the additional security measures. The illumination of the site and the configuration and function of the detection systems (motion detectors, cameras) are inspected. An alarm activation test is performed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Perimeter protection is a multi-layered, intelligent system. A combination of different detection technologies (e.g., fence detection system, infrared light barriers, video analytics, ground sensors) ensures highly reliable detection with a low false alarm rate. In case of an alarm, countermeasures such as switching on floodlights and broadcasting loudspeaker announcements are automatically triggered. All events are recorded for evidence purposes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A sensor system mounted on the fence detects climbing or cutting attempts. Intelligent video analytics distinguishes between humans, vehicles, and animals. In the event of an alarm, a PTZ (Pan-Tilt-Zoom) camera automatically tracks the intruder. The event data is reported to a central hazard management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the interaction of the various detection and response systems. The configuration of the intelligent video analytics is checked. The effectiveness of the overall system is tested through various realistic attack scenarios (e.g., a climbing attempt at a blind spot). Automated check: `check_perimeter_security_system --verify 'multi_sensor_fusion_active,ptz_autotracking_enabled,automated_response_configured'`.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
A building encloses all stationary workplaces, the information being processed, and the installed information technology. It thus provides protection against external influences. Therefore, it is necessary to consider not only the structure itself, i.e., walls, ceilings, floors, roof, windows, and doors, but also all building-wide infrastructure and supply facilities such as electricity, water, gas, heating, and cooling.
A building used by one or more organizational units of an institution is considered. These may have different security requirements. In addition, all considerations must take into account that a building is almost always entered by persons external to the institution, such as visitors, customers, or suppliers. If a building is used by different parties, then the design and equipment of the building and the usage concept for the building must be compatible. An optimal environment for the people working there should be ensured. Unauthorized persons should not be granted access where they could compromise security. The technology installed in the building should also be operable safely and efficiently.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module describes the requirements that must be met to optimally protect a building from an information security perspective. The measures resulting from the requirements depend on the type and size of the institution as well as the type and size of the building. Requirements from this module can also be applied to large properties with multiple buildings or to the use of individual parts of buildings in multi-party buildings.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The INF.1 General Building module must be applied once for each building.
This module addresses technical and non-technical security aspects in the planning and use of typical buildings for companies and public authorities. It considers the entire life cycle of buildings from an information security perspective, starting from the creation of a requirements catalog, through a concept, setup, and use, to conversions or moving out.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Fire
parts.prose:
Buildings and furnishings can be severely damaged by fire, and people can be seriously injured or killed. In addition to the damage caused directly by the fire, consequential damage must also be considered. For example, the recommissioning of areas damaged by fire usually takes weeks or even months. A very great danger in a fire is toxic smoke. Most personal injuries are therefore caused by smoke inhalation. But fire smoke can also cause severe damage to furnishings and IT systems.
When PVC burns, chlorine gases are produced, which, together with air humidity and fire-fighting water, form hydrochloric acid. If the hydrochloric acid vapors are distributed via the air conditioning system, this can also cause damage to sensitive electronic devices located in a part of the building far from the fire's location.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Lightning
parts.prose:
During a thunderstorm, lightning strikes are the greatest danger to buildings and information technology. Lightning reaches currents of up to 200,000 amperes at voltages of several 100,000 volts. This enormous electrical energy is released and dissipated within 50 to 100 microseconds. A lightning strike with these values that hits at a distance of about two kilometers still causes voltage peaks on electrical lines in the building that can lead to the destruction of sensitive electronic devices. These indirect damages increase the closer the lightning strikes the building.
If lightning strikes a building directly, the dynamic energy of the lightning can cause major damage. This can include, for example, damage to the roof and facade, as well as damage from fires or overvoltage damage to electrical devices.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Water
parts.prose: Water can cause damage to a building and its furnishings from the outside, for example through rain, floods, or inundations, or from the inside, for example through defective water-bearing pipes.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Damage from natural hazards and natural disasters
parts.prose: Depending on its location, a building is exposed to the risks of damage from natural hazards and natural disasters to varying degrees. Causes of natural disasters can be seismic, climatic, or volcanic phenomena, such as earthquakes, floods, landslides, tsunamis, avalanches, or volcanic eruptions. Examples of extreme meteorological phenomena are severe weather, hurricanes, or heavy rain.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Environmental hazards
parts.prose: Buildings can also be damaged by events in the immediate vicinity, for example, if toxic substances are released. Rescue work, road closures, or evacuations can also make it possible that the building can only be used to a limited extent or not at all.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Unauthorized access
parts.prose:
If unauthorized persons gain access to a building or individual rooms, this can lead to various other hazards. On the one hand, unauthorized persons can cause damage through deliberate actions such as theft or manipulation of information, IT systems, or IT components, and on the other hand, through unintentional misconduct, e.g., due to a lack of expertise.
Non-obvious manipulations can cause far greater damage than direct destruction. Property damage can already occur through unauthorized intrusion. Windows and doors are forced open and damaged in the process. Repairing or replacing them usually takes time and financial resources, during which they do not provide their protective function or only to a limited extent.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Violation of laws or regulations
parts.prose: When a building is constructed, many laws and regulations must be observed that concern, for example, fire protection or other aspects of structural safety. If these laws are violated, this may not be noticed for a long time, but can have catastrophic consequences, for example if firestops were not installed as intended.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Inadequate firestops
parts.prose:
Every building in which IT is operated is traversed by a multitude of cables and pipes, such as fresh and waste water pipes, heating pipes, or lines for energy supply or data transmission. It is unavoidable that such pipe and cable routes have to cross fire walls and floor ceilings. If suitable firestops are not installed at such points, fires and smoke may spread uncontrollably.
The high dynamics of IT also make it necessary to re-lay cables across firestops in the wiring network from time to time. The correct way to do this depends directly on the existing firestop and can vary greatly. If changes are made to a firestop that are not in accordance with the specifications of the respective company that manufactures the firestop, it may fail in the event of a fire. The fire could then spread to areas that would actually be protected by the firestop.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Power failure
parts.prose: In the event of a power outage, entire buildings or parts of them can become unusable. Not only the obvious, direct power consumers such as IT or lighting are dependent on the power supply. All infrastructure facilities are also directly or indirectly dependent on electricity today, e.g., elevators, air conditioning, hazard alarm systems, security locks, automatic door closing systems, sprinkler or PABX systems. Even the water supply in high-rise or basement floors is dependent on electricity due to the necessary pumps.

controls.title: Secure use of meeting, event, and training rooms (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only individual, particularly valuable devices in meeting rooms are sporadically secured against theft. Rules for the use of external devices exist, but are not consistently communicated or enforced, leading to inconsistent security practices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The implementation is limited to attaching Kensington locks to projectors or high-value displays. There is an email template that is sent when booking external meetings, which refers to the usage rules, but compliance is not checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly interviews employees to see if they are familiar with the rules for external devices. An inventory list is compared with the physically existing locks on devices to document the incomplete implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All existing equipment in the rooms is basically secured against theft. There are general rules for the use of external devices and access to network resources, but they are not specifically tailored to individual rooms or occasions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All IT devices are equipped with standard anti-theft locks. A general policy for the use of guest Wi-Fi and brought-in devices is published on the intranet and applies to the entire building.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts a complete walk-through of all meeting rooms and verifies that every device has a physical lock. The existence and availability of the general usage policy is checked on the intranet.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Equipment present in the rooms MUST be adequately secured against theft. In addition, it MUST be specified who administers the IT and other systems permanently present in the rooms. It MUST also be specified whether and under what conditions IT systems brought in by external persons may be used. Furthermore, it MUST be specified whether and which network access points and telecommunication interfaces external persons may access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal policy defines the anti-theft measures (e.g., Kensington locks, lockable media cabinets), the responsible administrators (IT operations, facility management), and the specific rules for guests. For guests, only access to a separate guest Wi-Fi or dedicated guest LAN ports is permitted, which is clearly defined in the policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the corresponding policy and checks it for completeness. During a walk-through, the implementation of the anti-theft measures is checked on a random basis. Furthermore, it is checked whether the configuration of the network sockets in the rooms corresponds to the policy (e.g., assignment to the guest VLAN).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policies for the use of rooms and equipment are regularly reviewed and updated. Compliance with network access rules for external devices is supported by a technical solution, such as Network Access Control (NAC) based on MAC addresses. An inventory list for the equipment in each room is actively maintained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A rudimentary NAC system is used, which moves unknown devices to a quarantine network. The inventory lists are maintained in a central system and checked during each maintenance. The policies are reviewed annually by the CISO.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the logs of the policy reviews for the last two years. A test is conducted to see what happens when an unregistered device is connected to a network socket. The correctness of the inventory lists is checked on a random basis in several rooms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully automated NAC system (e.g., 802.1X) regulates network access for all devices and users. All access attempts, both successful and failed, are centrally logged and automatically monitored for anomalies. The physical security of the room equipment is an integral part of regular, internal security audits.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An 802.1X-based NAC is implemented throughout the area and is coupled with Active Directory. Network logs are sent to a SIEM system, which generates alarms for suspicious activities (e.g., port scanning from the guest network). The infrastructure security of the meeting rooms is audited by the internal audit team at least once a year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the NAC and SIEM systems. Test attacks are carried out (e.g., connecting an unauthorized device, attempting to access internal resources from the guest network) and the correct logging and alerting in the SIEM is checked. The audit reports from recent years are reviewed.

controls.title: Closed windows and doors (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are irregularly reminded to close doors and windows. Doors are only locked for rooms explicitly declared as high-security, but not consistently in all rooms with sensitive information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Notices on the doors remind people to close them. There are no formal checks; closing them relies on the personal responsibility of the employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts a walk-through after business hours and documents the number of open or unlocked doors and windows in meeting rooms.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A general clean desk policy requires closing windows and doors when leaving work areas, including meeting rooms. However, locking is not explicitly required for all rooms with IT systems. Informal checks take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The clean desk policy is published on the intranet. The security service is instructed to look for open doors during their rounds, but does not keep a formal log of this.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the clean desk policy and questions the security service about their routines and observations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The windows and doors of the meeting, event, and training rooms MUST be closed when leaving. For rooms containing IT systems or sensitive information, the doors MUST be locked when leaving. In addition, it MUST be checked regularly whether the windows and doors have been closed after leaving the rooms. It MUST also be ensured that fire and smoke protection doors are actually closed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal policy prescribes closing and locking. A locking service or security personnel conduct daily, logged control rounds after business hours. The instruction to keep fire doors closed (unless a hold-open system is in place) is part of the general security briefing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the relevant policy and the control logs of the locking service from the past few weeks. During a walk-through, the condition of fire and smoke protection doors is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The checks by the security service take place at irregular times to encourage employees to comply with the regulations. Identified violations are documented and reported to the supervisors. Doors to rooms with particularly sensitive information are equipped with automatic door closers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The duty roster of the security personnel provides for variable control times. There is a defined process for reporting violations via a ticket system. Selected rooms are equipped with overhead door closers of the GEZE or Dorma type.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the reports of violations in the ticket system and checks whether follow-up action is taken. The function of the automatic door closers is physically tested.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Electronic access control systems log which person last left a room to establish clear accountability. In highly sensitive areas, magnetic contacts are used to monitor the closed state of windows and doors, which trigger an alarm to the security control center if they are found open without authorization after business hours.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All relevant rooms are equipped with a networked locking system (e.g., Salto, SimonsVoss). The alarm logic is configured in the building management system and is tested regularly. The logs of the access control system are kept for 90 days.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration of the alarm rules. A test alarm is triggered (e.g., by opening a window after simulated end of business hours) to check the entire chain from detection to notification. The access logs are checked for plausibility and completeness.

controls.title: Planning of meeting, event, and training rooms (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The location of meeting rooms is informally considered during planning. There is no formal classification system; the suitability of a room for confidential discussions is based on experience and word-of-mouth.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees know from experience that 'Room 301 has good soundproofing' or 'the conference room on the ground floor is visible from outside'. There are no written guidelines.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor interviews several employees to find out what criteria they use to select a meeting room for a confidential discussion, and documents the lack of a formal process.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general recommendation to use rooms in less frequented areas for sensitive discussions. However, there is no formal classification or enforcement of this recommendation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A short note in the room overview on the intranet reads: 'For confidential meetings, rooms on the upper floors are recommended.' The room booking tool has no corresponding filters or notices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the room usage documentation for corresponding recommendations and compares them with the functions of the booking system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When planning meeting, event, and training rooms, the location of the rooms SHOULD be given special consideration. In particular, rooms that are often used together with or exclusively by external persons SHOULD NOT be located in parts of the building where confidential information is regularly discussed and processed. It SHOULD be determined for each room how confidential the information discussed or processed there may be.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented room concept defines various security zones. Each meeting room is assigned a classification (e.g., 'Public', 'Internal', 'Confidential'). This classification takes into account the location, soundproofing, and visibility. The room booking tool displays this classification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the room concept and checks the classification of the rooms for plausibility. It is checked whether this information is visible to the employees in the room booking system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The formal room classification system is directly integrated into the room booking system. Rooms for confidential conversations are equipped with additional physical or technical protective measures, such as improved soundproofing or special, secure networks. The classification is reviewed regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The booking tool allows filtering by security level. 'Confidential' rooms have walls and doors with a certified sound insulation class and are defined as a separate security zone in the access control system. A review of the room classifications is carried out annually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the functionality of the room booking system. The soundproofing specifications and the configuration in the access control system for a room classified as 'Confidential' are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire building concept is based on a detailed zone model that strictly separates meeting rooms physically and logically according to their classification. In rooms classified for top-secret information, Technical Surveillance Counter-Measures (TSCM Sweeps) are regularly carried out to detect eavesdropping devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The building plan shows clearly defined red, yellow, and green zones. Access to red zones is severely restricted. There is a contract with a specialized service provider who performs quarterly TSCM inspections in the executive areas and specially secured project rooms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the security zone concept and the access logs for the high-security zones. The reports of the last TSCM inspections are requested and checked for completeness and findings.

controls.title: Trailing cables (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basically, care is taken to avoid tripping hazards from cables, mostly by running the cables along walls. However, professional cable bridges are not used as standard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees use gaffer tape to fix cables to the floor. There are no formal guidelines or provided material.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During a walk-through, the auditor looks for loose or improperly secured cables in the meeting rooms and traffic routes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Power outlets SHOULD be located where projectors, laptops, or other electronic devices are set up. Cabling that runs across the floor SHOULD be properly covered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During room planning, attention is paid to a sufficient number and sensible placement of sockets. For unavoidable, temporary floor cabling, professional cable bridges are available and their use is prescribed in the house rules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether cable bridges are available and whether the house rules prescribe their use. During a walk-through, the implementation in practice is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All meeting rooms are equipped with floor boxes or media ducts that provide power and network connections directly at the tables. This largely eliminates the need for 'trailing cables'. A sufficient supply of cable bridges for special cases is managed centrally.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Retractable connection panels for power, HDMI, and network are integrated into the conference tables. The facility management team manages a stock of cable bridges of various sizes, which can be requested via a ticket system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the equipment in the conference rooms and verifies the existence of and the process for requesting cable bridges.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room design consistently includes integrated cable management solutions in furniture, floors, and ceilings. Wherever possible, wireless presentation systems (e.g., ClickShare, Miracast) are used to eliminate cables. Regular safety inspections by the Occupational Safety Specialist explicitly include checking the cabling.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Professional wireless presentation systems are installed in all rooms and established as the primary connection method. The protocols of the regular inspections by the Occupational Safety Specialist are documented and measures are tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the functionality of the wireless presentation systems. He reviews the inspection protocols of the Occupational Safety Specialist for the last 12 months and checks the processing of identified deficiencies.

controls.title: Setting up secure network access (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A guest VLAN is set up for WLAN guests. However, the configuration of the wired network sockets in meeting rooms is inconsistent; some incorrectly allow access to the internal network. A simultaneous connection to the internet and intranet (multi-homing) is not actively prevented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate guest WLAN with a password exists. The switch ports for the sockets in the rooms are configured manually, but there is no consistent documentation or regular review of the configuration.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor connects a laptop to network sockets in several meeting rooms on a random basis and checks which network he gets access to. The switch configurations are checked for inconsistencies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that brought-in IT systems cannot be connected to the institution's internal IT systems via the data network. Only designated IT systems SHOULD be able to access the institution's LAN. A data network for external persons SHOULD be separated from the institution's LAN. Network access SHOULD be set up in such a way that third parties are prevented from reading internal data exchange. Network connections SHOULD be secured and a simultaneous connection to the intranet and internet SHOULD be prevented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A separate guest network (LAN and WLAN) is separated from the internal network by a firewall. All network sockets in meeting rooms are assigned to this guest network by default or are deactivated. Activation for the internal network requires a ticket. Client Isolation is enabled on the guest WLAN to prevent communication between guests. On the clients, simultaneous connection to LAN/WLAN is prevented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the firewall rules between the guest and internal network. He tests a network socket in a meeting room to verify the default assignment to the guest network. It is checked whether a guest client can reach other guest clients in the same WLAN.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Network access is controlled by a Network Access Control (NAC) solution based on certificates or user accounts. Devices are automatically assigned to the correct VLAN (Guest or Internal). The power supply for the media technology in the rooms is secured via a separate sub-distribution board to avoid interference with other areas.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A NAC solution (e.g., Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass) is in use in 'Monitor Mode' or with MAB (MAC Authentication Bypass) for known devices. The electrical planning provides for a separate power circuit for the media technology in each larger conference room, which is documented in the building plans.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the configuration of the NAC solution. It is tested whether an unknown device correctly lands in the guest network and a known, internal device gets access to the internal network. The electrical plans are inspected to confirm the separate power supply.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The guest network is completely separated from the internal network ('air-gapped') or runs over a separate internet uplink with its own dedicated security infrastructure (Firewall, IPS). All network traffic in the guest and internal network is monitored for anomalies. An 802.1X-based NAC solution rigorously authenticates every user and device before granting network access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The guest WLAN uses its own DSL/fiber optic connection. All data traffic is routed through a Next-Gen Firewall with an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS). 802.1X is rolled out comprehensively in 'Enforced Mode' and requires valid computer and user certificates. SIEM rules correlate network and authentication logs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the network diagram to verify the physical or logical separation. Penetration tests are conducted from the guest network. The 802.1X configuration on switches and RADIUS server is checked in detail. A test with an invalid certificate must fail.

controls.title: Secure configuration of training and presentation computers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The presentation computers are based on a standard client configuration that is not specially minimized. Although they are in their own organizational unit in Active Directory, they are still connected to the regular LAN.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The same Windows image is used for the presentation PCs as for office workstations. Only different group policies for desktop shortcuts are applied. The computers are in the same VLAN as other clients.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the OU membership and the applied GPOs of a presentation computer. An `ipconfig` or `ifconfig` command is executed to determine the VLAN membership and compare it with that of standard clients.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Dedicated training and presentation computers SHOULD be provided with a minimal configuration. It SHOULD be specified which applications can be used on training and presentation computers in the respective event. The training and presentation computers SHOULD only be connected to a separate data network, separated from the institution's LAN.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A hardened base image is created for presentation computers, containing only the operating system and absolutely necessary applications (browser, office suite, PDF reader). These computers are members of a dedicated VLAN, which is separated from the internal LAN and has only filtered internet access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the documentation of the hardened image and the list of installed software shown to him. The VLAN membership of the computer is checked and the firewall rules for this VLAN are analyzed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The allowed applications are technically enforced by an application whitelisting solution. The computer's configuration is centrally managed and enforced via a configuration management tool to prevent configuration drift.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A solution such as AppLocker (Windows) or comparable third-party software is used to only allow the execution of defined programs. The configuration is distributed via Group Policies or a tool like Ansible/Puppet and is regularly checked for compliance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor attempts to execute an unapproved application (e.g., a portable tool from a USB stick). The configuration of the application whitelisting solution is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The presentation computers are designed as non-persistent systems. They boot from a read-only master image at every startup, so that all changes made during a session are discarded upon restart. Physical interfaces such as USB ports are disabled via BIOS/UEFI and policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The computers use software like 'Deep Freeze' or boot over the network (PXE boot) from a read-only image. The BIOS/UEFI settings are password-protected and prohibit booting from external media and the use of USB storage devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor saves a file to the desktop, restarts the computer, and verifies that the file has disappeared. An attempt is made to connect and access a USB stick. The BIOS/UEFI settings are checked for their protection and configuration.

controls.title: Creation of proof of use for rooms (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central room booking system is mandatory for all employees to use. This system logs who has booked a room and at what time. There is no additional requirement to log the actual participants of a meeting.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room booking is integrated into the calendar software (e.g., Microsoft Exchange, Google Calendar). Every employee must book a room before using it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the booking history for a specific room and period exported from the calendar system and checks it for completeness and plausibility.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Depending on the type of use of the meeting, event, and training rooms, it SHOULD be apparent who used the rooms and at what time. For rooms where IT systems training or particularly confidential meetings are held, proof of use SHOULD also be provided. It SHOULD be considered to also introduce corresponding proof of use for rooms that are accessible to every employee.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room booking system serves as the basic proof of use. A policy mandates that for meetings classified as 'Confidential' or for IT training, the organizer must keep an attendance list and retain it for a defined period.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy for maintaining attendance lists. They select a past 'confidential' meeting from the booking system and request the corresponding attendance list from the organizer for review.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room booking system is linked to the physical access control system. Access to rooms classified as 'Confidential' or higher requires a valid booking. The log from the access control system serves as precise proof of who entered the room and when.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An interface between the calendar system and the access control system (e.g., via middleware) provisions temporary access rights for the booked period to the organizer and, if applicable, the invited participants. The access logs are regularly reviewed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor books a test room and verifies that their badge only works at the door of this room for the booked period. The access logs are compared with the booking data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The proof of use is fully automated. For high-security meetings, a two-factor check-in is required (e.g., badge and entry of a meeting PIN at the door reader). The access and usage data automatically flow into a SIEM system for correlation with other security-relevant events and for long-term archiving.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The door readers in high-security areas have a keypad. The room booking system generates a unique PIN for each meeting. The log data from the access control system is forwarded to the SIEM via Syslog and archived there according to compliance requirements.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the entire process demonstrated, from booking a high-security meeting and PIN generation to the check-in procedure. It is verified in the SIEM whether the log events are correctly received, processed, and archived.

controls.title: Resetting of training and presentation computers (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A documented procedure is in place to reset training and presentation computers to a predefined state after use. All changes made and data saved by the user are removed. The process is carried out manually by IT staff upon request or on a fixed schedule.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard operating procedure (SOP) exists for re-imaging the computers using a central software distribution solution. The process includes the deletion of all user profiles and temporary files.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the SOP. They save a file on a presentation computer, request a reset from IT, and then check whether the computer is in a clean initial state and the file has been removed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A procedure SHOULD be established to reset training and presentation computers to a predefined state after use. Changes made by users SHOULD be completely removed. The reset process is automated and runs, for example, on a time-controlled basis (e.g., nightly).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A scheduled task or a script controlled by a central management tool triggers the reset process every evening. The process restores the system from a clean snapshot or image backup and ensures that all user data is securely deleted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the automated reset mechanism (e.g., the cron job or the Scheduled Task). They leave a computer overnight after making changes and verify the clean state the next morning.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The computers use a technology that automatically resets the system to its defined, clean initial state at every restart. The process is fully automated and requires no manual interaction. This ensures a guaranteed clean state for every user.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The computers are equipped with 'instant recovery' software like Faronics Deep Freeze or Reboot Restore Rx, or they boot from a non-persistent VDI image. This setting is protected by an administrator password.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor saves a file to the desktop, creates a bookmark in the browser, and changes the background image. Then, they perform a restart and verify that all changes have been undone without exception. The protection of the configuration software is checked.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: As a rule, every institution has one or more rooms in which meetings, training courses, or other events can be held. Specially equipped rooms are often provided for this purpose. Meeting, event, and training rooms are essentially characterized by the fact that they are generally used by changing persons or internal or external groups of persons for only a limited period of time. Brought-in IT systems are often operated together with the institution's devices, such as external laptops with permanently installed projectors. These different usage scenarios result in a special threat situation that does not exist in this way in other rooms of the institution.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The aim of the module is to protect the information processed in meeting, event, and training rooms, as well as the IT systems operated in these rooms. It also deals with the recommended handling of external persons who use the corresponding rooms.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module INF.10 Meeting, Event, and Training Rooms is to be applied to every meeting, event, or training room.
This module considers all technical and non-technical security aspects for the use of meeting, event, and training rooms. Detailed recommendations on how the IT systems in these rooms can be configured and secured are not covered in this module. They can be found in SYS.2.1 General Client and in the operating system-specific system modules. Other security aspects relevant to meeting rooms, such as for WLANs or video conferencing systems, are covered in the modules of the NET.2 Wireless Networks and NET.4 Telecommunications layers, respectively. The cabling in these rooms is considered separately in module INF.12 Cabling. Requirements for fire protection can be found in module INF.1 General Building. Requirements for supervising visitors and for prohibiting the carrying of mobile phones can be found in module ORP.1 Organization.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Missing or inadequate regulations
parts.prose: If, for example, employees do not close the windows and doors after leaving a meeting, event, or training room, or if confidential information is not removed from a whiteboard or flip chart, this information can be viewed without authorization. In general, employees should therefore be provided with appropriate regulations so that such security gaps cannot occur. However, merely establishing regulations does not ensure that they will be observed and that operations will be trouble-free. Many problems arise when regulations exist but are not known to the employees. Often, for example, employees do not know that windows and doors must be locked after meetings or how to handle the work equipment available in the meeting room (e.g., technology or flip chart).

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Incompatibility between external and internal IT
parts.prose: IT systems are becoming increasingly mobile and are used in a growing number of different environments. People often encounter scenarios in which their own IT systems cannot be used as planned because they are not compatible with the third-party IT systems. For example, older devices do not have the same ports and connectors as newer devices. In addition, some devices are not compatible with other devices without a suitable adapter. So, if a suitable adapter is not available, a laptop prepared with all the important data for a meeting cannot be connected to a projector. Furthermore, attempts to connect the IT systems anyway can lead to damage to the devices or the stored data.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. "Flying" or temporary cabling
parts.prose: In meeting, event, and training rooms, both the people and the way the rooms are used change frequently. As a result, the equipment and thus the cabling in these rooms are constantly being changed. Depending on the location of the connection points in the room (power and data network sockets), cables may be temporarily laid across the room, including across traffic routes. Not only are people endangered by these tripping hazards, but IT systems can also be damaged if people pull the 'trailing' cables along with them.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Theft
parts.prose:
If data carriers, IT systems, accessories, software, or data that are partly stationary in a meeting, event, or training room are stolen, this results in costs for replacement and for restoring a workable state. On the other hand, the meeting, event, or training room can only be used to a limited extent afterwards due to the lack of availability of the devices. This may cause bottlenecks in room occupancy. Furthermore, confidential information can be stolen, misused, or disclosed.
In addition to expensive IT systems, mobile devices that are inconspicuous and easy to transport are also frequently stolen. If the meeting, event, or training rooms are not supervised or the IT systems are not adequately secured, the technology can be stolen quickly and discreetly. This is especially true if, for example, the rooms are not locked during meeting breaks.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Loss of confidentiality of information requiring protection
parts.prose: Confidential information can be disclosed through technical failure, carelessness, ignorance, and also through deliberate actions. This information can be present in various places, e.g., on storage media within IT systems (such as hard drives), on removable storage media (such as USB sticks or optical media), in printed form on paper, and on whiteboards or flip charts. If information is read or disclosed without authorization, this can have serious consequences for the institution, such as violations of laws, competitive disadvantages, or financial repercussions.

controls.title: Planning and Procurement (B) [Subject Matter Experts, Procurement Office, Data Protection Officer]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procurement of vehicles is done on an ad-hoc basis and is primarily based on functional requirements. Information security or data protection aspects are not systematically considered. Locking systems are adopted in the manufacturer's standard state without an assessment of their adequacy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, there is typically no formal procurement process for vehicles that explicitly includes security requirements. Decisions are often made by individual departments without central oversight or standardized criteria.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether a documented process for vehicle procurement exists. By interviewing those responsible and examining procurement documents from recent years, it is verified whether security and data protection requirements have been systematically collected and evaluated. The absence of such documentation indicates this level of maturity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A basic procurement process exists in which functional requirements for vehicles are documented. Security requirements are treated superficially, for example, the existence of a locking system is required without specifying its properties. Aspects such as the vehicle lifecycle or data transmission to third parties are not systematically analyzed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple procurement checklist might exist, but it covers security aspects only in general terms (e.g., 'Does the vehicle have an alarm system?'). The vehicle's data interfaces are not evaluated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing procurement policies and checklists. It is assessed whether the requirements for information security and data protection are detailed enough to enable an informed decision. If security features are only checked off as present without evaluating their quality, this level of maturity is reached.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before vehicles are procured, the purpose of use MUST be planned. The functional requirements, the information security requirements, and the data protection requirements for the installed IT components MUST be determined. The operational scenarios, the operating environment, and the entire lifecycle of the vehicles MUST be taken into account. The vehicles MUST have adequate locking systems unless they are otherwise continuously protected. During the planning phase, the possible transmission of data to third parties SHOULD be considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal requirements catalog is created, which, in addition to functional aspects, contains explicit chapters on information security (e.g., encryption, access control to systems) and data protection (e.g., deactivatability of telemetry services). The assessment of locking systems is risk-based.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and application of a detailed requirements catalog for vehicle procurement. It is checked whether a documented collection and evaluation of security and data protection requirements has taken place for current procurement processes. In particular, it is checked whether the aspects of lifecycle, operating environment, and locking systems have been evaluated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process is formalized and repeatable. Consideration of data transmission to vehicle manufacturers and third parties is mandatory and is evaluated in a documented manner. A formal, documented process for evaluating the data processing practices of providers is established and applied. A standardized checklist for security and data protection requirements is used for all procurements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution requests detailed data sheets from the manufacturers on the functioning of the IT systems and their data interfaces (Data Processing Agreements, DPIA). The results are demonstrably incorporated into the purchasing decision. The checklist used is updated annually or on an ad-hoc basis.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement files and checks whether a systematic and documented analysis of the vehicle's data flows has taken place. It is verified whether contracts or agreements with manufacturers regulate data processing and whether the internal checklists are consistently applied and maintained.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fully integrated procurement and lifecycle management process is established. The institution actively tests and validates manufacturers' security promises before purchase, for example, through penetration tests on test vehicles.
