parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The power supply is installed without special consideration for electromagnetic compatibility (EMC). The grid type (e.g., TN-C or TN-S) is not consistently known or documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During renovations, new outlets are simply connected to the existing, often outdated electrical installation without checking whether a continuous protective conductor is present.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that there is no documentation on the structure of the power distribution network. Measurements at outlets show inconsistent or missing protective conductor connections, which indicates an unsafe TN-C or mixed network.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In new buildings or during major renovations, a TN-S system is implemented as the standard for the power supply. However, detailed EMC planning, such as maintaining separation distances or measures against radiated interference, is not systematically carried out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hired electrician is instructed to implement the installation as a TN-S system. However, the cables are often laid directly next to data cables without considering the normatively required separation distances.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies, using the electrical plans, that a TN-S system was planned. During an inspection, random checks are made to see if the separation distances between power and data lines are being maintained.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The power supply MUST be EMC-compliant. For this, the power distribution network MUST be set up as a TN-S system. During construction and operation, the separation distances recommended in the relevant standards MUST be maintained as far as possible. Basic precautions MUST be taken against external radiation, radiation from the power line, and for the detection of equalizing currents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The entire electrical planning is based on the EMC standards series (e.g. DIN EN 61000). This includes the consistent implementation of a TN-S system from the service entrance, compliance with separation distances or the use of separators and shielded power cables in critical areas. A central equipotential bonding is professionally installed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the electrical planning documents and checks them for conformity with EMC requirements. It is verified that a TN-S system is documented and implemented. Measurements of the protective earth system and the equipotential bonding are carried out to confirm correct installation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the EMC-compliant design, line filters and/or special EMC-shielded distributors are used at critical points, such as in server rooms or for sensitive equipment, to further reduce interference. Regular measurements are taken to monitor compliance with EMC parameters during operation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The data center's power supply is fed through special EMC filters. The power distribution units in the rack are metal-enclosed. A measurement of the power quality and equalizing currents is carried out annually by a specialist company.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation and specifications of the line filters and special distributors used. The reports of the regular EMC measurements are inspected and checked for anomalies or trends.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The power supply is part of a comprehensive EMC protection concept that integrates all infrastructure areas (lightning protection, grounding, cabling). The power quality and potential interference variables are monitored in real time by a permanent monitoring system. In the event of deviations, alarms are triggered automatically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Power Quality Analyzers (PQA) are installed at the central power supply feed-in points, which permanently measure voltage, current, frequency and harmonics. The data is collected and evaluated in a central management system. In the event of critical deviations, IT operations are notified automatically.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the overall EMC concept for consistency and completeness. The configuration of the PQA monitoring system is checked, including the defined threshold values and the alerting chain. It is verified that the live data is recorded correctly and that alarms are responded to appropriately.

controls.title: Requirements analysis for cabling (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of the cabling is based exclusively on the immediate, current need. Future developments or protection goals such as confidentiality are not taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For a new office for 10 employees, exactly 10 network connections are ordered. The possibility that more connections or higher bandwidths will be needed in the future is ignored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews, the auditor determines that no strategic planning for the cabling exists. Project documentation confirms that the dimensioning always reflects only the status quo.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When planning the cabling, a flat-rate reserve for future growth is included. The basic protection goals of availability and integrity are implicitly addressed by using standard components.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The rule is: 'Always install twice as many connections as are currently needed'. A more detailed analysis, e.g. of future technologies (WLAN, VoIP) or security requirements, does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and application of the flat-rate planning rules. It is assessed whether this approach is sufficient to cover medium-term demand and whether basic protection goals are at least implicitly met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Fundamentally, the requirements that influence a future-proof, needs-based, and economical implementation of the cabling SHOULD be analyzed. In this requirements analysis, the short-term use SHOULD first be estimated. Based on this, the longer-term development SHOULD be estimated. Furthermore, the protection goals of availability, integrity, and confidentiality MUST be considered in the requirements analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before major cabling projects, a workshop is held with representatives from IT, building services, and users. A document records the current demand, the forecast demand for the next 5-7 years (e.g., due to new technologies like Wi-Fi 7, IoT), and the specific protection requirements (e.g., the need for shielded cables in development departments). This document is the basis for detailed planning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the requirements analysis. It is checked whether both short- and long-term aspects have been considered and whether the protection goals of availability, integrity, and confidentiality have been addressed. The traceability of the demand forecast is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements analysis is a formalized and recurring process. It is based on structured capacity forecasts and a detailed risk analysis. The results are incorporated not only into technical planning, but also into budget planning and strategic IT alignment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cabling infrastructure is also assessed annually as part of IT strategy planning. Trend analyses (e.g., increase in data traffic, number of end devices) are used to model future demand. A risk analysis assesses threats such as physical manipulation or eavesdropping and derives concrete requirements for the cabling from this (e.g., the need to secure cable routes).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the requirements analysis process is firmly embedded in the IT planning processes. The quality of the capacity forecasts and the risk analysis is assessed. It is checked whether the results of the analysis have demonstrably been incorporated into concrete planning and budget decisions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirements analysis is supported by an automated system that continuously collects usage and performance data from the network infrastructure. With the help of AI-supported forecasting models, future demand is dynamically predicted and proactive suggestions for necessary expansions or modernizations are generated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A network monitoring system, coupled with a DCIM tool, permanently records port occupancy, bandwidth utilization and the growth of connected devices. The system reports when the capacity of a route is expected to reach 80% in 6 months and automatically creates a ticket with a proposal for an expansion.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and effectiveness of the automated analysis and forecasting system. The accuracy of the prediction models is checked against historical data. It is checked whether the suggestions generated by the system are processed promptly and appropriately.

controls.title: Acceptance of the cabling (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no formal acceptance of the cabling work. The service is considered rendered upon payment of the invoice.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After the installer has finished their work, it is checked whether the connected devices have a network connection. If this is the case, the work is considered complete.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that no acceptance reports or measurement reports for cabling work exist. The responsibility for the quality of the installation lies implicitly solely with the contractor.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal acceptance process, which usually consists of a visual inspection and a simple functional test. The contractor hands over simple documentation, which, however, is not checked in detail.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The internal IT employee walks through the newly cabled areas with the installer. It is checked whether all outlets are installed. The installer hands over a folder with simple patch lists, which are placed in the filing cabinet.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds informal acceptance notes (e.g., e-mails). It is checked whether these at least provide evidence of a basic check of the service rendered. The quality of the handed-over documentation is assessed as superficial.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There SHOULD be a defined acceptance process for the cabling. The acceptance SHOULD take place when all agreed tasks have been completed. The contracting institution MUST provide written proof, at the latest by the acceptance date, that all standards and regulations have been complied with. During acceptance, the actual scope of the services MUST be checked. The acceptance report MUST be signed by the responsible parties in a legally binding manner and SHOULD be based on a checklist.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal acceptance date is agreed for each cabling measure. The basis for the acceptance is a checklist that includes, among other things, the completeness of the installation, the handover of qualified measurement reports for each individual link, and the updated documentation (route plans, patch lists). The report is signed by the client and contractor and archived digitally.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the acceptance reports and the associated checklists and measurement reports. It is checked whether the process was carried out correctly in formal terms, whether all required evidence is available, and whether the report was signed by the authorized persons. The consistency between the measurement report, documentation, and visible installation is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The acceptance process is supplemented by an independent verification measurement by the client or a contracted third party. In this process, the contractor's measurements are verified on a random basis (e.g., 10% of the links) with a separate, calibrated measuring device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before the final acceptance, the in-house technical services or a contracted engineering firm carries out its own certification measurements on a representative sample of ports. The results are compared with the installer's reports. Formal acceptance only takes place if they match.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and results of the verification measurements. It is checked whether a clearly defined process exists for selecting the samples and for the procedure in case of deviations. The calibration certificates of the measuring devices used are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The acceptance process is fully integrated into a digital workflow system. The installer uploads measurement reports and documentation directly to the system, where they are automatically checked for formal correctness and plausibility. The release is done digitally and directly triggers the update of the central infrastructure database (e.g., DCIM).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An online portal is used to process cabling orders. Measurement reports in a standardized format (e.g., Fluke LinkWare) are uploaded. The system automatically checks whether all limit values have been met and whether the number of measurements corresponds to the order. After digital approval by the responsible person, the ports are marked as 'ready for operation' in the DCIM system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the acceptance process mapped in the workflow system. The configuration of the automated check rules is controlled. Using log data, the end-to-end digital and media-disruption-free process from ordering and installation to final documentation is traced.

controls.title: Surge protection (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Surge protection is only available selectively, e.g., in the form of power strips with integrated protection for individual devices considered important. A systematic concept is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An expensive UPS with surge protection was purchased for the main server. However, the normal office workstations and the network switches are connected unprotected to the regular power supply.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor determines that a comprehensive surge protection concept is missing. Protection is limited to a few isolated solutions. There is no documentation describing the protection requirements and the measures implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A coarse protection device (Type 1) for the power supply is installed at the building entry point. However, a further, coordinated protection concept for medium and fine protection (Type 2, Type 3) is either missing or has been implemented incompletely.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The energy supplier installed a combined Type 1+2 arrester when installing the building's service connection. However, there are no further protection stages in the sub-distribution boards and at the end devices, which means that the protective effect of the coarse protection is not fully effective.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the surge protection at the building entry point by inspecting the documentation of the electrical installation and by visual inspection. It is determined that the subsequent protection stages in the sub-distribution boards and at the end devices are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every electrically conductive network SHOULD be protected against surges. For this purpose, a corresponding surge protection concept MUST be created that complies with the applicable standards. The concept MUST cover all relevant networks (power, data, telecommunications). Emergency power systems (EPS) and uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) MUST be included in the concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a holistic surge protection concept that was created by a qualified electrician. It provides for a multi-stage protection system (Type 1, Type 2, Type 3) for the power supply. In addition, surge arresters are installed for incoming telecommunications and data lines. The protection devices are coordinated with each other.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented surge protection concept and checks it for completeness and conformity with the relevant standards (e.g. DIN VDE 0100-443 and -534). During an inspection, the correct installation of the protective devices in the main distribution board, the sub-distribution boards and near the end devices is verified on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The surge protection concept is regularly reviewed for its currency and effectiveness, e.g. every 2 years, and adjusted if necessary. The functionality of the installed surge protection devices (SPDs) is regularly checked by measurements or by devices with a status display.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Surge protection devices with remote signaling are used. The status of all devices is centrally recorded and monitored in the building management system. If a protective device fails, a maintenance ticket is automatically created. In addition, the overall concept is reviewed by an external specialist every 2 years.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the logs of the regular reviews of the protection concept. The functionality of the remote signaling is verified, e.g. by inspecting the building management system or by checking the log files. It is checked whether failures of protective devices are responded to promptly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An intelligent surge protection system continuously monitors the condition of the protective devices and simultaneously measures occurring surge events. The collected data is analyzed to dynamically optimize the protection concept and proactively identify potential weaknesses.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Modern, networked surge protection devices (SPDs) not only report their own status, but also the number and strength of the surges they have diverted. This data is collected and correlated in a central database, for example, to determine whether certain parts of the building or systems are affected particularly frequently. Targeted improvement measures are derived from this.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the intelligent protection system and the collected data. It is assessed whether the analysis of the data has led to demonstrable improvements in the protection concept. The completeness and integrity of the recorded event data is checked.

controls.title: Removing and deactivating cables that are no longer needed (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cables that are no longer needed are not removed and remain unused and undocumented in the cable trays. This leads to a lack of clarity and increases the fire load.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During an office move, the patch cords at the switch and at the end device are removed, but the permanently installed cables in the wall and ceiling remain untouched. Nobody knows where these cables lead.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During the inspection of distribution rooms and cable trays, the auditor finds a large number of 'dead' cables that are no longer connected at one or both ends. The documentation is outdated and does not reflect the actual situation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cables that are no longer needed are marked as 'unused' at the end points (e.g. on the patch panel), but are not physically removed. Fire protection is not systematically taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a connection is no longer needed, the patch cord is removed from the switch and the port on the patch panel is marked with a red sticker. The permanently installed cable remains in place so that it can possibly be reused later.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds numerous marked but not removed cables in the distributors. It is checked whether this marking is consistent. It is assessed whether the amount of old cables already has a significant negative impact on clarity and fire load.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If cables are no longer needed, they SHOULD be professionally and completely removed. After cables have been removed, the firestops MUST be properly sealed. Cables that remain as a reserve SHOULD be kept operational and MUST be marked accordingly at the end points. In principle, an overview of cables that are no longer needed SHOULD be drawn up and it SHOULD be noted in the documentation which cables have been removed or deactivated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a defined process for decommissioning cabling. When a connection is decommissioned, a decision is made as to whether the cable will be retained as a strategic reserve or removed. Removed cables are deleted from the documentation. Remaining reserve cables are clearly marked as 'Reserve' at both ends. After each removal, a check is carried out to ensure that cable penetrations through fire walls have been correctly sealed again.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation and checks whether a process for decommissioning cables is defined. The lists of removed/deactivated cables are inspected. During an inspection, random checks are carried out to see whether reserve cables are correctly marked and whether firestops have been properly sealed after cable removal.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is proactive management of unused cabling. A review of the entire cable inventory is carried out regularly, e.g. annually, in order to systematically identify cables that are no longer needed and to initiate the process for their removal or deactivation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Once a year, a report is generated from the network monitoring system and the DCIM system that lists all ports that have been inactive for more than 12 months. This list is reviewed and a decision is made as to which cables can be removed from it. The removal is carried out as a separate small project with documentation adjustment and fire protection inspection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the annual review process. The reports of the inactive ports and the resulting logs of cable removals are inspected. It is checked whether the process consistently leads to a reduction in old cables and an increase in clarity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The lifecycle of each cable is managed in an Automated Infrastructure Management (AIM) system. If a port is deactivated, a workflow is automatically started that plans, commissions, and tracks the removal of the cable, including updating all plans and confirming firestop integrity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When a port is set to 'decommissioned' in the AIM system, a removal order is automatically generated for the responsible technician. The technician scans the barcodes at both ends of the cable to confirm correct removal. The system then updates the documentation independently. The order is only closed when the fire protection officer has also confirmed the inspection of the sealing material in the system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the workflow for cable removal configured in the AIM system. Using the system logs, a complete removal process from decommissioning to final documentation adjustment is traced. It is checked whether the process is free of media breaks and is audit-proof.

controls.title: Fire protection in cable trays (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cable trays are planned and operated without considering fire protection aspects such as overfilling or ventilation. The fire load is not assessed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Cable ducts are filled with cables until no more can physically fit. Possible heat development or the high concentration of combustible material (cable sheaths) is ignored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor finds massively overfilled cable trays. In some cases, cables are attached to the outside of the trays with cable ties because there is no more space inside. Fire protection concerns have obviously not been taken into account.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When planning cable trays, care is taken to ensure that they are not overfilled. However, there is no active ventilation or a detailed consideration of the fire load.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installation guideline states that cable trays may only be filled to a fill level of 60%. This rule is observed for new installations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the guideline on the fill level. During a visual inspection, the fill level is assessed at several points on the cable trays. It is checked whether the rule is also adhered to over time through subsequent installations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Trays SHOULD be sufficiently dimensioned to avoid overfilling and thus an increased fire load. They SHOULD have sufficient ventilation to prevent heat build-up.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning of cable trays is carried out taking into account the standards for fire protection and heat load. In closed trays or in areas with high cable density, ventilation openings are provided or the trays are deliberately oversized. The calculation of the fire load is part of the planning documentation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning documentation and checks whether the aspects of fill level, fire load and ventilation have been taken into account. During an inspection, the implementation is checked, e.g. by checking the existence of ventilation openings and measuring the temperature in critical tray sections.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In critical areas such as escape and rescue routes or server rooms, additional fire protection measures for cable trays are implemented. This can include the use of cables with an improved fire performance class (e.g., B2ca), the installation of fire detectors directly in the cable trays, or the use of special I or E channel systems for functional integrity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The main cable trays in the data center are equipped with an aspirating smoke detection (ASD) system, which enables very early fire detection. In all escape routes, only cables of class B2ca-s1a,d1,a1 are installed to minimize fire and smoke development.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the implementation of the extended fire protection measures. The specifications of the cables and fire protection systems (e.g., ASD) used are checked. The effectiveness of the fire detectors in the cable trays is also checked as part of the regular fire alarm test.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The temperature and smoke status in all critical cable trays are permanently monitored by a dense sensor network. The data is fed into the building management system and an AI system for anomaly detection. In the event of critical heating, proactive measures such as increasing room ventilation are triggered even before a fire breaks out.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Temperature sensors (e.g., fiber-optic linear heat detectors) and smoke detectors are installed at regular intervals in the main cable trays. The measured values are continuously reported to a management system. If the temperature exceeds a defined threshold, a pre-alarm is sent to the building services, and the ventilation system in that area increases its output.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the sensor network and the management system. The thresholds and automated responses are checked for appropriateness. The reliability of the system and its response to past events (e.g., test alarms) are evaluated based on historical data.

controls.title: Documentation and Labeling of Cabling (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cabling documentation does not exist or is severely outdated and incomplete. Cables and connections are not labeled or are labeled inconsistently.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: To find out which switch port belongs to which outlet in the office, a technician has to trace the line with a cable tracer. No diagrams exist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines that no usable cabling documentation is available. A visual inspection in a distribution cabinet reveals a chaotic scene with no readable or traceable labels on the cables and patch panels.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic documentation exists, mostly in the form of Excel spreadsheets and simple diagrams. Labeling of the connections is present, but not always systematic or up-to-date. Changes are only updated irregularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an Excel spreadsheet that assigns a room number and an outlet number to each port on the patch panel. However, the patch cords between the switch and the patch panel are not documented. When new connections are added, the list is sometimes, but not always, updated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the existing documentation. A spot check in the distribution cabinet reveals that the labels on the patch panels match the documentation, but the documentation has not been updated for over a year and recent changes are missing.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An institution SHOULD ensure that it has both internal (detailed) and external (neutral labeling of connections) documentation for its cabling. The internal documentation MUST contain all records of installation and operation. Any change in the network SHOULD be documented, and the master documentation MUST be updated no later than 4 weeks after completion of the work. The documentation SHOULD be regularly reviewed and updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cabling is documented in a CAFM or DCIM system. This includes cable tray layouts, cable schedules, and patch lists (end-to-end connection). Every cable and every port is uniquely labeled according to a uniform scheme. Changes are first documented in a working version and transferred to the master documentation within the 4-week period after completion of the work. The documentation is reviewed annually for currency.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the cabling documentation in the management system. It is checked whether the level of detail is sufficient and whether an update process is defined and followed. Change requests from recent months are used to check whether the 4-week update deadline has been met. On-site spot checks verify the correctness of the labeling and documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The cabling documentation is linked to other management systems, such as network monitoring or asset management. The consistency of data between the systems is regularly checked automatically. The cables are labeled with durable, machine-readable labels (e.g., barcodes).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the DCIM system, not only the cable is documented, but also which switch (from asset management) is connected to which port and which MAC address (from network monitoring) is active at the corresponding outlet. A nightly reconciliation checks these links and reports inconsistencies. All cables and ports are labeled with barcodes that can be scanned with a mobile device when changes are made.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the interfaces between the management systems and the configuration of the consistency checks. The logs of these checks are reviewed. During an on-site inspection, the functionality of the barcode-based data capture is tested on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documentation and labeling are fully automated by an Automated Infrastructure Management (AIM) system. Any physical change to the cabling is detected in real time by sensors on the patch panel, and the documentation is updated immediately without manual intervention. Unauthorized changes trigger an alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Intelligent patch panels with RFID or contact sensors register the plugging and unplugging of every patch cord. The AIM system updates the connection database in real time. If a technician changes a patch cord without a corresponding work order in the system, a security alert is generated for IT operations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the AIM system, especially the alarm rules. The audit trail integrity of the automatically generated logs is assessed. A test change (unplugging and plugging in a cable) is used to verify the real-time update of the documentation and the triggering of an alarm live.

controls.title: Neutral Documentation in Distribution Cabinets (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the distribution cabinets, there are no or only unstructured, handwritten notes on the port assignments.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: On the inside of the distribution cabinet door, there are several sticky notes with notes like 'Port 5 = Accounting Printer'.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During the inspection of the distribution cabinets, the auditor finds that structured on-site documentation is missing. Information is outdated, illegible, and unreliable.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the distribution cabinets, there are printed lists describing the port assignments. These often contain sensitive information such as the function of the connection (e.g., 'Management PC'). The lists are rarely updated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A printed Excel list in the distribution cabinet shows all patch panel ports with the corresponding room numbers and the name of the user or the function of the device. The list is six months old.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds the printed lists and assesses the content for potentially sensitive information. The currency of the lists is checked by comparing them with the visible state.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In each distribution cabinet, there SHOULD be documentation that reflects the current status of patching and line assignments and enables safe switching. This documentation SHOULD be kept as neutral as possible and list only existing and used connections as well as terminating spare cables. Information on the type of use (e.g., end device, user) SHOULD only be provided if this is explicitly required. All further information SHOULD be kept in separate as-built documentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In each distribution cabinet, there is a laminated list or a notice that specifies the unique, neutral destination ID for each port on the patch panel (e.g., Room-Number.Outlet-Number.Port-Letter, like 'E01-114.D1.A'). There is no information about users or connected devices. The list is reprinted and replaced with every change.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and content of the on-site documentation in several distribution cabinets. It is checked whether the documentation is kept neutral and does not contain sensitive information. The consistency of the list with the physical labeling of the patch panels is verified by spot checks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The neutral documentation in the distribution cabinet is supplemented by the use of machine-readable codes (e.g., QR codes) on the patch panels. Authorized technicians can scan these codes with a mobile device to directly access the detailed (but still neutral) connection information in the central database.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A small QR code is attached next to each port on the patch panel. If a technician scans this code with a special app, it displays the port's destination ID and its current status (active/inactive, VLAN assignment) from the DCIM system. The app requires authentication.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the functionality of the QR code system. It is checked whether access to the information requires authentication and whether the displayed data is correct and neutral. The physical attachment and readability of the codes are assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An Automated Infrastructure Management (AIM) system with LED indicators on the ports makes separate documentation in the distribution cabinet superfluous. To identify a connection or execute a work order, the corresponding ports on the patch panel and switch are automatically lit up by the system via LED.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A technician receives a work order on their tablet, e.g., 'Patch port E01-114.D1.A to Switch 3, Port 24'. When they start the job, the LEDs on the corresponding patch panel port and the target switch port start blinking, enabling fast and error-free execution. After the cable is plugged in, the LED turns off and the system marks the job as completed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the process of port-specific control via LED demonstrated live. The reliability of the system is tested by simulating several work orders. The logging of these guided patching operations in the AIM system is checked.

controls.title: Inspection of Electrical Systems and Existing Connections (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Inspections of electrical systems and equipment do not take place or only occur upon explicit request after an incident. There is no preventive inspection process.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Electrical devices are operated until they fail. Periodic electrical safety testing does not take place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds no inspection reports or inspection stickers on electrical systems and equipment. Interviews confirm that no regular inspection cycle has been established.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Portable electrical equipment (e.g., monitors, power supplies) is tested at irregular intervals. Fixed installations such as the electrical distribution system are rarely or never tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every few years, a service provider is commissioned to test the electrical devices at the workstations. However, the permanently installed electrical infrastructure in the walls and distribution boards is omitted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds inspection stickers on many end devices, but cannot view any inspection reports for the electrical distribution boards or fixed installations. The inspection deadlines for the end devices have been partially exceeded.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All electrical systems and equipment SHOULD be regularly tested in accordance with DGUV Regulation 3. All irregularities MUST be documented immediately and reported to the responsible organizational units. These units MUST rectify the defects promptly enough to rule out any danger to persons. The required level of availability MUST be ensured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A responsible qualified electrician has been appointed. There is a test concept with defined test intervals for all fixed and portable electrical systems and equipment. The tests are carried out by qualified personnel and documented in an inspection report. Identified defects are recorded in a list of defects and their rectification is tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the test concept and the risk assessment on which the test intervals are based. The inspection reports from the last test cycles are reviewed. The existence of inspection stickers is checked on a random basis. The list of defects is checked for open, critical items and for the speed of defect rectification.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of tests, deadlines, and reports is handled by a specialized software solution. This automatically sends reminders for upcoming tests and escalates overdue tests. Defects are recorded directly in the software and forwarded as workflows to the responsible technicians for rectification.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Software for maintenance planning (e.g., a CAFM module) manages all electrical assets and their inspection deadlines. The auditor records the test results on site on a mobile device directly in the software and prints out the inspection sticker. A detected defect automatically creates a ticket in the facility management's ticket system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the testing and defect rectification process mapped in the software. The configuration of the reminder and escalation mechanisms is checked. The system data is used to evaluate compliance with inspection deadlines and the average time to repair (Mean Time to Repair).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Critical electrical systems are permanently monitored by monitoring systems (e.g., insulation monitoring, residual current monitoring). This enables the detection of creeping faults long before they lead to a hazard or failure and reduces the need for tests that require a shutdown.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Residual Current Monitors (RCMs) are installed in the power distribution units of the data center, which permanently measure fault currents. A slow deterioration in the insulation of a device is thus detected at an early stage. The measured values are logged and analyzed centrally. If pre-warning thresholds are exceeded, maintenance is informed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the design and installation documentation of the permanent monitoring system. The configuration of the thresholds and alarms is checked. Based on the recorded measurement data, the effectiveness of the system for early detection of faults is evaluated.

controls.title: Avoidance of electrical ignition sources (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of private electrical appliances and multiple sockets is not regulated and is tolerated. These devices are not tested.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees bring their own coffee machines, fans, and chargers. At many workstations, several cheap power strips from the hardware store are connected in series to connect all devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor notes widespread use of untested private devices and improper use of power strips (cascading). This represents a significant fire hazard.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an instruction that restricts the use of private electrical appliances. The use of power strips is permitted as long as they have a CE marking. There is no systematic monitoring or testing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The house rules state that private fan heaters are prohibited. The coffee machine in the kitchenette is tolerated. Employees are advised not to plug power strips into one another, but this is not monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the house rules. During an inspection, it is checked to what extent the rules are known and observed. Improperly used power strips are still found, although less frequently.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of private electrical appliances within the institution SHOULD be clearly regulated. All electrical appliances MUST be tested and found to be safe by a qualified electrician before they are used. The use of power strips SHOULD be avoided as much as possible. Missing sockets SHOULD be professionally installed by a qualified electrician.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a clear policy: Private electrical appliances are generally prohibited; exceptions must be approved and the device must be tested by the internal qualified electrician (E-Check). The use of power strips is only permitted for IT workstations and only high-quality strips procured by the company may be used. Cascading is strictly prohibited. If more sockets are permanently needed in one location, an order is placed for retrofitting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy on the use of electrical appliances. It is checked whether a process for testing and approving devices exists. During an inspection, specific attention is paid to compliance with the rules, in particular the ban on cascading power strips and the presence of inspection stickers on all permitted devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the rules for avoiding ignition sources is proactively checked through regular, announced inspections by the qualified electrician or the fire safety officer. Employees are regularly made aware of the dangers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Quarterly inspections of all office areas are carried out, specifically looking for prohibited devices and incorrect use of power strips. Identified defects are documented and must be rectified immediately. Avoiding fire hazards from electricity is a fixed component of the annual safety briefing.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports of the regular inspections and the documentation of the safety briefings. It is assessed whether the checks are carried out consistently and lead to a demonstrable improvement in the situation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Technical measures are used to actively prevent the creation of ignition sources due to overload or fault currents. In critical areas, Arc Fault Detection Devices (AFDDs) are widely used, which detect dangerous arcs and switch off the circuit before a fire can start.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All circuits in server rooms, archives, and kitchenettes have been retrofitted with AFDDs (Arc Fault Detection Devices). These devices detect series and parallel arc faults, which are not detected by conventional circuit breakers, and thus offer significantly improved protection against electrically ignited fires.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the electrical plans and verifies the installation of the AFDDs in the defined critical areas by inspecting the distribution boxes. The test reports of the AFDDs (if available) are reviewed.

controls.title: A-B power supply (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be checked whether a dual-path A-B power supply should be created instead of a single-path power supply to supply important IT components and other consumers. The basic planning for such a supply is created, but without permanent monitoring of its functionality.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An A-B power supply is planned for the server room. This means that two completely separate power supply paths are built from the main distribution board to the racks. Each path is secured by its own UPS. The racks are equipped with two separate PDUs (Power Distribution Units), one for the A-path and one for the B-path. Servers with redundant power supplies are connected to both PDUs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning documents for the electrical installation for the server room. It is verified that two independent supply paths (A and B) from the feed-in to the PDUs in the racks are planned and documented. A visual inspection confirms the separate cable routing and the dual equipment with UPSs and PDUs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A dual-path A-B power supply is implemented for all important IT components. The functionality of both power supply paths is permanently monitored by suitable technical facilities. The monitoring includes the UPS systems and the PDUs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The implemented A-B power supply is monitored by a monitoring system. The UPS systems and the intelligent PDUs are connected to the network and report their status (load, remaining autonomy time, errors) to a central monitoring console. In the event of a failure of a supply path or a component, an alarm is automatically triggered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the implementation of the A-B power supply through an on-site inspection. The configuration of the monitoring system is checked. A simulated failure (e.g., switching off a circuit breaker on the A-path) is used to test whether the monitoring works correctly, the consumers continue to be supplied, and the alarm is triggered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The A-B power supply is consistently redundant down to the individual components and is realized by two physically separate grid connections fed from different sources. The switchover in the event of a fault is fully automatic and is tested regularly. The load distribution between the A and B paths is actively managed to ensure even utilization.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The building has two independent utility connections supplied by different substations. Each supply path (A and B) is fed by one of these connections, a separate emergency power system, and its own UPS farm. The PDUs in the racks permanently measure the load, and the management system can provide recommendations for redistributing consumers in case of an imbalance. Automated failover tests are performed monthly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contracts with the energy supplier and the planning documents to verify the independence of the two grid connections. The configuration of the load management and the automated failover tests is checked. The test protocols are reviewed and checked for successful and uninterrupted switchovers.

controls.title: Physical security of cabling (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Consideration SHOULD be given to securing cables and distributors against unauthorized access. The number and extent of locations where power supply facilities and data network access points are accessible to unauthorized persons SHOULD be kept as low as possible. Main and floor distributors are housed in lockable rooms or cabinets.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All central distribution cabinets for power and data supply are housed in dedicated, lockable technical rooms. The keys to these rooms are issued in a controlled manner to a limited group of people (IT, facility management). In publicly accessible areas, cables are laid under plaster or in closed cable ducts, if possible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor verifies that the distribution cabinets are locked and located in secure areas. The regulations for key management for the technical rooms are inspected and their effectiveness is assessed. It is checked whether cables are laid open and unprotected in public areas such as corridors.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to locking the rooms and cabinets, they are monitored with intruder alarm systems (IAS) or opening contacts. Cable routes that run through areas that are not permanently monitored are designed as closed, lockable sheet steel ducts. Network sockets in public areas are deactivated when not in use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The doors of the technical rooms and the distribution cabinets themselves are equipped with magnetic contacts that are connected to the IAS. Unauthorized opening triggers an alarm. Cable routes in the basement or in underground garages are designed as tamper-proof ducts. Network ports in conference rooms or foyers are deactivated by default via the network management system (port security) and must be enabled when needed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the IAS and the opening contacts. It is tested whether an alarm is triggered in the event of an unauthorized opening attempt. The configuration of port security for sockets in public areas is checked in the network management system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The entire critical cabling infrastructure is permanently monitored by a cable route monitoring system. Special monitoring cables or fibers, which are laid together with the data cables, detect manipulation attempts such as drilling into or opening the cable route and trigger an alarm immediately. Access to all distributors is controlled via an electronic access control system with logging.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The main cable routes between the data centers and the floor distributors are designed as fiber-optic-based alarm systems (e.g., LIOS system). Any unauthorized vibration or opening of the route is reported with location details. Access to the distribution cabinets is only possible with a personal transponder card, with every access being logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the design of the cable route monitoring and the electronic access control system. The effectiveness of the system is verified by a simulated manipulation attempt on a test section. The access logs of the distribution cabinets are analyzed for unauthorized or unusual access attempts.

controls.title: Use of cabinet systems (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Electrotechnical connections and distributors SHOULD be set up in or built into cabinet systems. When dimensioning the cabinet systems, the expected growth for the planned period of use SHOULD be taken into account by planning sufficient reserve space for future expansions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: All active and passive network components as well as the associated power distributions are housed in standardized 19-inch cabinet systems (racks). When planning a new distributor, a cabinet system is chosen that offers at least 30% unused rack units (U) as a reserve for future growth.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor verifies that all distributor components are properly installed in cabinet systems. Based on the documentation and a visual inspection, the available reserve space in the cabinets is assessed. It is checked whether there is a planning guideline for the dimensioning of new cabinets.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The cabinet systems are systematically planned and managed. This includes a well-thought-out concept for air conditioning, power supply (e.g., redundant PDUs), and cable management within the cabinet. The occupancy of the cabinets is documented in detail in a DCIM or CAFM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a standardized design concept for the cabinet systems in the data center. This defines, for example, the position of the switches, patch panels, and cable guides to ensure optimal air circulation (hot/cold aisle) and clean cabling. Every rack unit and the exact position of each component is recorded in a DCIM tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the concept for the design of the cabinet systems and the documentation in the management tool. It is compared whether the actual design of the cabinets corresponds to the defined standard and the documentation. In particular, attention is paid to tidy cable management and the correct implementation of the air conditioning concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The cabinet systems are equipped with comprehensive sensors for monitoring temperature, humidity, access, and power consumption. The data is collected and analyzed centrally to optimize operation and proactively manage risks. The planning and management of rack space is fully automated via a DCIM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each rack is equipped with sensors that monitor the temperature at several points (front/back, top/bottom) as well as the door openings. The intelligent PDUs report the power consumption per outlet. The DCIM system uses this data to create a 'heatmap' of the data center and warns if the temperature limits in a rack are exceeded or the power supply is in danger of being overloaded. When planning a new server installation, the system suggests the optimal installation location based on available space, power, and cooling capacity.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration of the rack sensors and the DCIM system. It is checked whether the collected live data is correct and the defined alarms are functioning. The logs and evaluations (e.g., energy efficiency, temperature history) are assessed for their significance and for the response to past events.

controls.title: Redundancy for IT cabling (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be checked whether a redundant primary IT cabling should be created, which is routed via independent paths. Likewise, it SHOULD be checked whether connections to IT or telecommunications providers should be designed to be redundant. A basic plan for this will be drawn up, but not necessarily implemented or checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Redundant cabling is planned for connecting the central server room to the floor distributors. This means that two separate fiber optic or copper backbone cables are laid. Ideally, these cables are routed through different riser shafts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning documents of the cabling infrastructure. It is checked whether a redundant design was planned for critical connections (backbone, provider connection). An on-site inspection verifies whether the planned redundant paths were implemented physically separate from each other.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Redundant cabling for the primary and secondary levels is implemented and is routed via physically separate paths (e.g., different fire compartments). If redundant cabling is used, its functionality SHOULD be checked regularly. This also applies to redundant provider connections.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The backbone cabling is fully redundant and the two cable paths run in different building wings and fire compartments. The redundant connections are connected to separate switches that use protocols such as Spanning Tree or Link Aggregation (LACP) to manage redundancy. A failover test is performed annually, in which one of the primary connections is physically disconnected to test the automatic switchover to the redundant path.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the physically separate and fire-compartment-spanning layout of the redundant cable paths using plans and an on-site inspection. The configuration of the network protocols for managing redundancy is checked on the switches. The logs of the annual failover tests are inspected and checked for a successful, uninterrupted switchover.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The redundancy extends to all cabling levels, including the tertiary cabling to highly critical workstations or systems. The functionality of both paths is permanently monitored by the network management system. If one path fails, an automatic switchover and alarm are triggered. The provider connections are not only redundant but also come from different carriers and are implemented via various building entry points.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The administrator's workstation for the central security systems is equipped with two network sockets connected to two different floor distributors, which in turn are supplied via the redundant backbones. The network management system continuously monitors the latency and availability of both paths. The internet connection is provided via a fiber optic connection from Telekom (north building entry point) and a radio relay link from Vodafone (south roof entry point).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the end-to-end redundancy concept from the provider connection to the end device for defined, highly critical systems. The configuration of the permanent monitoring of the redundant paths is checked. The contracts and technical documents of the different carriers are inspected to confirm the diversity of the connections. The system's response to a simulated failure of one of the paths is tested live.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
The proper and standards-compliant execution of the cabling is the basis for secure IT operations. A fundamental distinction must be made between electrical cabling and IT cabling.
The electrical cabling of IT systems and other devices includes all cables and distributions in the building from the feed-in point of the distribution network operator (DNO) to the connections of the end devices.
The IT cabling in an institution includes all communication cables and passive components such as distribution or splice panels or patch panels. It thus forms the physical basis of the internal communication networks. The IT cabling extends from the handover points from an external network to the connection points of the network participants. Handover points are, for example, the connection of a telecommunications company or the DSL connection of an internet provider.
Despite this distinction, the basic requirements for both types of cabling are identical. Therefore, the cabling within an institution should always be considered as a whole.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The goal of this module is to protect all electrotechnical and IT cabling from failure, manipulation, and interference.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose: The INF.12 Cabling module is to be applied once to cabling in buildings and rooms, in addition to the INF.1 General Building module. The requirements of the module must always be applied to both IT and electronic cabling.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Cable fire
parts.prose: Cable fires can cause considerable damage to an information system. A cable fire causes, for example, short circuits or breaks conductors. As a result, protective devices also fail. In addition, depending on the materials of the insulation, aggressive gases can be produced during cable fires.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficient dimensioning of the cabling
parts.prose: When workstations, server rooms, or data centers are planned, these plans are often based exclusively on current needs. However, future new requirements often also demand further capacities of the power grid and the data cables. This can become necessary, for example, as soon as additional servers are used or technical standards change. The cabling can, however, only be extended to the extent that the already existing and laid cables and cable routes allow.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficient documentation of the cabling
parts.prose:
If the exact location of cables is not known because it has been inadequately documented, these cables can be damaged during construction work outside or inside a building. Inadequate documentation also makes it difficult to inspect and repair cables.
Furthermore, it cannot be assumed that all cables in the installation zones are installed according to currently valid standards.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Insufficiently protected distributors
parts.prose: Occasionally, distributions of the power supply or data network are installed unlocked in areas that are generally accessible. Unauthorized persons can open and manipulate such distributors, causing failures in the power or data supply.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Cable damage
parts.prose: The more unprotected a cable is laid, the greater the risk that it will be damaged intentionally or unintentionally. Damage not only causes direct connection failures, but can also lead to malfunctions later on. Damaged insulation may only affect a cable's functional properties after a significant time delay.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Voltage fluctuations, overvoltage, undervoltage
parts.prose: Fluctuations in the supply voltage can occur in all areas of the networks. Extremely short and small events have little or no effect on IT systems. However, larger fluctuations lead to malfunctions. The connected systems can be damaged, even up to total failures. Destructive overvoltages can also occur.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Use of low-quality power strips
parts.prose:
Often, the permanently installed sockets are not sufficient for the devices to be operated. To compensate for this, power strips are often used. However, if these power strips are of insufficient quality, they can become a source of ignition and thus a major fire hazard.
In many cases, several power strips are connected in series (daisy-chained) to provide slots for all devices. With such a series connection, there is a risk of overload. The result can be an incomplete short circuit with a high risk of fire.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Impermissible cable connections
parts.prose:
In some cases, cable connections are made between IT systems or other technical components that are not intended and are impermissible. This can cause security problems or operational disruptions.
Such cable connections may, for example, allow unauthorized access to data networks, IT systems, information, or applications. Impermissible cable connections can also cause information to be transmitted to the wrong recipients. In addition, the connection can be disrupted.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Line impairments
parts.prose: The electrical signal transmission in communication cables can be negatively affected by electric and magnetic fields. A special form of this cable interference is crosstalk. In this case, currents and voltages from adjacent lines are transmitted as interference signals to the communication cable.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Eavesdropping and tampering with cables
parts.prose:
Eavesdropping attacks on data cables are a threat to information security that should not be neglected. In principle, there are no eavesdropping-proof cables. The cables differ in their quality only with regard to the effort that must be expended to eavesdrop on the line. Whether a cable is actually being eavesdropped on can only be determined with great technical measurement effort.
In addition, deliberate manipulations of cables up to their destruction represent a danger for the institution. Malfunctions of cables can be deliberately induced with manipulative intent. Such manipulations often have the goal of disrupting IT operations or damaging the institution.

controls.title: Assessment of the as-is state when taking over existing buildings (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When taking over existing buildings, a sporadic and unstructured survey of individual technical building systems considered critical is carried out. A comprehensive assessment of the overall condition or the documentation does not take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The survey typically focuses on obviously important systems such as the main heating system or the power supply. The results are recorded in informal notes or emails, without a standardized process.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should check on a random basis whether any survey has taken place at all for recently acquired buildings. It is checked whether the information gathered is sufficient to ensure basic operation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When taking over existing buildings, the technical building systems and the building structure are recorded using a simple checklist. The existing documentation is collected, but not checked for completeness or up-to-dateness.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standardized checklist is used to record the most important components (e.g., manufacturer, model, age). The collected documents are stored in a central location, for example on a network drive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should inspect the checklists used and check whether they have been completed for all acquired buildings. The existence of the central document archive is verified, but not its content.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When taking over existing buildings, the technical building equipment (TBE), building structure and facilities installed in the building, as well as existing documentation, MUST be recorded and assessed with regard to their condition (age, support status, future viability, completeness of documentation, etc.).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A defined process for building takeovers is established. This process includes a structured recording and assessment of all relevant systems and documents. The results are documented in a standardized report that serves as a basis for further planning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should inspect the defined takeover process and the associated assessment reports for recently acquired buildings. It is checked whether all aspects of the requirement (age, support status, etc.) have been systematically addressed in the assessment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The as-is assessment is supplemented by a systematic risk analysis for the identified defects and vulnerabilities. The collected data is transferred to a central asset management or CAFM system to track the lifecycle of the systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The results of the assessment are used to create a prioritized action plan for remedying defects and for modernization. The support status of software components is actively requested from the manufacturer and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should check the risk analyses performed and the resulting action plans. It is verified whether the collected system data has been correctly and completely imported into the central management system (e.g., CAFM).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The as-is assessment is highly automated through integration into a BIM (Building Information Modeling) model. Physical inspections are supplemented by automated scans for vulnerability detection in networked TBE components. A detailed lifecycle cost analysis is performed for all essential systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A digital twin of the building is created or updated. Automated discovery tools are used to identify all networked devices. The results are directly incorporated into strategic maintenance planning and budgeting.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should verify the integrity of the BIM model and its connection to the real system data. The reports from the automated vulnerability scans are analyzed. It is checked whether the lifecycle cost analysis is used as a basis for investment decisions.

controls.title: Regulation and documentation of responsibilities and accountabilities in the building (B) [Institutional management, Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Responsibilities are only informally known for the internal building services operation. Accountabilities of external service providers or other organizations in the building are not systematically recorded or documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple contact list for the building services staff exists. Contracts with external service providers are held by the purchasing department but are not directly accessible to technical staff.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should try to identify the person responsible for a specific system (e.g., elevator) that is maintained by an external service provider. The time and effort required to obtain this information are assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A central documentation of responsibilities and accountabilities exists in the form of a list of contact persons and the trades they manage. However, the exact rights, duties, and escalation paths are not described in detail.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Excel spreadsheet or an intranet page is used to list which service provider or internal department is responsible for which trade (heating, ventilation, electrical, etc.), including emergency numbers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should inspect the central list of accountabilities and check its timeliness on a random basis (e.g., by calling a listed number). It is checked whether the documentation is easily accessible to operational staff.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The corresponding rights, duties, tasks, competencies, and associated processes for all areas in the building MUST be regulated and documented. This includes organizational structures, requesting and operating organizations, interfaces, and reporting channels, including escalation. The entire documentation MUST always be up-to-date and available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An organizational handbook for Technical Facility Management (TFM) is created and maintained. For external service providers, responsibilities are contractually defined according to module OPS.2.3 (Use of Outsourcing). The documentation is stored in a central, version-controlled location (e.g., DMS, CAFM) to which all involved parties have regulated access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should inspect the TFM organizational handbook. It is checked whether the documentation contains clearly defined processes, interface descriptions, and escalation paths. The contracts with important external service providers are randomly checked for the regulation of responsibilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documented responsibilities and processes are technically mapped in the relevant IT systems (e.g., CAFM, ticketing system). Roles and permissions in these systems are derived directly from the accountability matrix. Regular, planned reviews of the documentation take place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The accountability matrix is linked to the ticketing system so that reports are automatically routed to the correct entity. An annual review process for the organizational handbook is established and its execution is logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should check the configuration of the ticketing system or CAFM system and compare it with the documented accountability matrix. The logs of the annual documentation reviews are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of responsibilities, rights, and duties is fully integrated into HR and procurement processes. Changes in personnel or contracts automatically trigger a workflow to update the accountability documentation and system permissions. Compliance with the defined processes is enforced by the system and is fully auditable.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An Identity and Access Management (IAM) solution is linked to the HR systems and the CAFM system. Workflows in a process management tool (BPMS) control the update processes. All changes to the accountability matrix are logged with a timestamp and the responsible person.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should trace the automated workflow for a personnel change (e.g., an employee leaving). It is checked whether the system permissions and the accountability documentation were automatically and correctly adjusted. The system's audit logs are checked for completeness and traceability.

controls.title: Documentation of Building Facilities (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Documentation for building facilities exists only sporadically, mostly in paper form in the respective technical rooms. There is no central collection or organization.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Manuals and plans from the manufacturer are stored in a folder in the technical room after installation. There is no guarantee that they are current or complete.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should try to find the technical documentation on-site for a randomly selected critical system (e.g., a UPS system). The completeness and readability are assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All important documentation for building facilities is collected centrally in one place, for example on a network drive. However, the documents are not systematically organized or supplemented with TFM-specific information.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Scanned plans, manuals, and acceptance protocols are stored in a folder structure on a file server. The folder structure is usually based on the trades.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should check the folder structure on the network drive and randomly open documents for various systems. It is assessed whether documents are available for all essential facilities.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All TBE building facilities, including building automation (BA), MUST be documented. In this process, all existing documentation MUST be consolidated, organized from a TFM perspective, and supplemented with TFM-specific information. The entire documentation, including the associated contact information, MUST always be up-to-date and available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Document Management System (DMS) or a CAFM system is used to manage the documentation. A uniform structure is defined that includes technical plans as well as maintenance contracts, inspection reports, and contact information. There is a process to ensure that the documentation is updated after changes are made to systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should inspect the documentation system and check the organizational structure. For a recently modified system, it is verified whether the corresponding documentation (e.g., the circuit diagram) has been updated. It is checked whether access to the documentation is regulated for the operating personnel.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The documentation of the building facilities is fully versioned and has a formal approval process. The documents are linked to the corresponding assets in the CAFM system, allowing direct navigation from the system to the documentation. Critical parameters from the documentation (e.g., maintenance intervals) are stored as data in the CAFM system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The check-in/check-out functionality of the DMS is used to prevent uncontrolled changes. QR codes on the systems allow on-site personnel to directly access the digital documentation via a mobile device.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor should trace the change process for a document, including the version history and approval log. It is checked on-site whether the QR codes on the systems work and lead to the correct, current documentation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All building facilities and their documentation are managed in a central BIM (Building Information Modeling) model as a 'single source of truth'. The model is linked to real-time operational data from the Building Management System (BMS) and the CAFM system. Changes in reality are automatically tracked in the model and vice versa.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A continuous BIM2FM process is established. The documentation is no longer static but a living digital twin of the building. Simulations based on the model are used for planning conversions or optimizing operations.
