parts.prose: Annual 'Black Building' tests are conducted, where the power supply to the entire building is cut off to test the response of all redundant systems (power, climate, security technology) under full load. These tests are planned and executed as a formal project with detailed Methods of Procedure (MOP) and the involvement of all stakeholders.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The annual Black Building test is planned months in advance. A detailed MOP describes every step, every expected reaction, and every rollback plan. All involved teams (IT, Facility Management, security service) are on-site and communicate via a dedicated channel. The results are analyzed and lead to concrete improvement measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the project documentation for the last Black Building test, including the MOP, participant lists, communication plans, and the final report with the 'Lessons Learned'.

controls.title: Systems for extinguishing or preventing fires (S) [Building services, Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A water sprinkler system, as is common for office spaces, is installed in the data center. Its activation would destroy the IT systems with the extinguishing water and cause a total failure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The data center is located in a normal office building, and the building's standard sprinkler system was simply extended into the room. No risk analysis regarding water damage was carried out.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Visual inspection of the ceiling for the presence of sprinkler heads. Request the fire protection concept to verify the type of extinguishing system. Check whether consequential damage from water has been assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A pre-action sprinkler system is installed. This reduces the risk of accidental activation, as it requires two trigger criteria (e.g., smoke and heat) to release water. However, in an emergency, it still represents a last resort with high damage potential.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dry-pipe sprinkler system is installed. Only when the fire alarm system reports a smoke alarm is the pipe system flooded with water (pre-action). However, water is only released when the glass ampoule of a sprinkler head bursts due to heat.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the technical specification of the extinguishing system to confirm that it is a pre-action system. Check the logic of the two-stage release.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A data center SHOULD be equipped with an automatic extinguishing or fire prevention system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on a protection needs analysis, it was decided to install an automatic extinguishing system. The planning and budgeting for a gas extinguishing system have been completed, and implementation is planned for the next quarter.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the protection needs analysis and the planning and approval documents for the extinguishing system. Review the project plan for implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic gas extinguishing system is installed (e.g., with Inergen, Argonite, or Novec 1230). This extinguishes fires without damaging the electronic devices and is therefore well-suited for use in data centers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A Novec 1230 extinguishing system is installed in the IT operations room and in the raised floor. It is triggered by the early fire detection system. The staff is trained on how to behave in case of an activation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the planning, acceptance, and maintenance documentation for the gas extinguishing system. Check the training records of the staff.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A fire prevention system using oxygen reduction (hypoxic air) is installed. This system permanently maintains the oxygen level in the air at a level where a fire cannot ignite in the first place. This proactively prevents fires instead of just fighting them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A fire prevention system keeps the oxygen content in the data center constant at 15.0%. Redundant sensors continuously monitor this value and control the supply of nitrogen. The system prevents fires in their initial phase and thus offers the highest protection for availability and assets.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the planning and safety documentation for the fire prevention system. Review the historical data of the oxygen sensors to check the stability of the set value. Check the maintenance logs of the system.

controls.title: Alternate data center (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are only external data backups, without a predefined recovery site or provisioned hardware. A recovery would take an indefinite, long time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Backups are written to tapes and collected by a service provider. In the event of a disaster, a new site would have to be found and new hardware procured first.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the backup concept. Ask about the plan for recovery at another site. If no such plan exists, the requirement is not met.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A detailed disaster recovery plan exists and data backups are regularly stored off-site. However, recovery would require the procurement of new hardware, which can take several days to weeks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The DR plan describes the system recovery sequence. Contracts with hardware suppliers assure fast delivery but do not guarantee it.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request for the DR plan. Review of the plans and contracts for emergency hardware procurement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A contract exists for a cold or warm site as a disaster recovery data center. Data backups are periodically transported or replicated to this site. A manual recovery process is planned and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A contract exists with a DR service provider for a cold site (empty room with power/cooling). In an emergency, delivered hardware would be installed there. The recovery time is estimated at several days.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request for the contract for the DR site. Review of the recovery plan and the documented, estimated recovery time.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A warm site with pre-installed hardware and network connectivity is maintained. Data is restored periodically or replicated asynchronously. The switchover to the disaster recovery data center is a manual process that can be completed within 24-48 hours and is practiced regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A second, smaller server room in another building serves as a warm site. The most important systems are installed there. Data is replicated nightly. A failover test for a non-critical system is performed once a year.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request for the documentation of the warm site and the replication technology. Review of the logs from the last failover tests.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A geographically separate disaster recovery data center SHOULD be established. The disaster recovery data center SHOULD be sized to maintain all of the institution's processes. It SHOULD also be constantly ready for use. All of the institution's data SHOULD be regularly mirrored to the disaster recovery data center. The switchover to the emergency data center SHOULD be tested and practiced regularly. The transmission paths to the disaster recovery data center SHOULD be appropriately secured and designed with corresponding redundancy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A second, fully equipped data center (hot site) is located 50 km away. All critical data is mirrored synchronously. The switchover can be largely automated and completed within a few hours. A full failover and failback test is conducted semi-annually. The connection between the sites is provided by two redundant dark fiber links from different carriers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request for the architecture and operating concepts for the disaster recovery data center. Review of the specification of the mirroring technology and the network connection. Analysis of the logs and results of the last full failover tests.

controls.title: Implementation of dust protection measures (H) [Building Services]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Construction or maintenance work is carried out in or near the data center without any dust protection measures. This leads to heavy contamination of the IT equipment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Workers drill into a wall in the server room without covering the area or vacuuming up the dust. The server fans suck the drilling dust directly in.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Visual inspection of the IT equipment and the room for excessive dust accumulation. Review of work instructions for contractors for dust protection requirements.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Simple dust protection measures such as covering racks with plastic sheeting are implemented. However, these measures are often not completely sealed and are insufficient to prevent the spread of dust.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Before drilling, a painter's drop cloth is hung over the adjacent rack. However, it remains open at the sides and bottom, allowing dust to spread anyway.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the dust protection measures used during construction work for their effectiveness and completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During construction projects, basic but planned dust protection measures are implemented. This includes the use of dust protection doors and the sealing of ventilation slots. After completion of the work, the area is thoroughly cleaned.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The work area is separated from the rest of the room by a dust protection door with a zipper. After the work, the area is cleaned with a HEPA filter vacuum cleaner.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request for the process description for construction work in the data center. Verification of whether dust protection measures and final cleaning are part of the process. Monitoring of the implementation during an ongoing construction project.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For construction work in a data center, suitable dust protection measures SHOULD be defined, planned, and implemented. This includes the creation of sealed enclosures (dust protection walls) around the work area and the creation of negative pressure in this area to prevent dust from escaping. After completion, the air quality is measured.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The work area is completely enclosed with a dust protection wall system. An air purification device is set up inside the enclosure, which creates a slight negative pressure. After the work is completed, a particle counter is used to check compliance with the cleanroom class according to ISO 14644-1.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request for the planning documents for dust protection measures during construction work. Review of the technical implementation of the enclosure and negative pressure generation. Checking of the measurement logs from the particle count.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Persons who are not themselves involved in the construction work SHOULD check at sufficiently close intervals whether the dust protection measures are functioning properly and whether the dust protection regulations are being complied with. A detailed Method of Procedure (MOP) is required for each job, describing all dust protection measures. The air quality is continuously monitored with real-time particle counters throughout the entire duration of the work.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated safety officer checks the integrity of the dust protection enclosure hourly. The MOP mandates the use of sticky mats at the entrance of the enclosure and the use of HEPA vacuums. A particle counter with an alarm function monitors the air in the data center and triggers an alarm if a threshold is exceeded.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request and review of a MOP for a recently completed construction project. Request for the inspection logs of the safety officer. Analysis of the historical data from the real-time particle counter during the construction phase.

controls.title: Appropriate structure of the cabling in the data center (H) [Building Services]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is 'cable spaghetti' in the data center. Power and data cables are laid together in a disorganized manner. This causes interference, complicates maintenance, and increases the fire load.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Cables are run directly across the floor or through the racks via the shortest route. Old, unused cables are not removed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Visual inspection of the cabling in the data center, especially under the raised floor and in the racks. Check for order, separation of power and data cables, and removal of deadwood cables.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cables are run in cable trays to create a basic order. However, power and data cables share the same trays, and clear labeling of the cables is missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A wire mesh tray under the ceiling is used to route all cables. There are no separating partitions. The cables are not labeled, which makes troubleshooting difficult.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Visual inspection of the cable trays. Check whether there is a physical separation of power and data cables within the trays. Random check to see if cables are labeled at both ends.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Power and data cables are consistently run in separate cable trays to avoid electromagnetic interference. Cable management systems in the racks ensure clean and orderly cabling. All cables are clearly labeled at both ends.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are separate cable trays for high-voltage, low-voltage, and data lines (copper and fiber optic). Horizontal and vertical cable management panels are used in the racks. Each cable is labeled with a tag indicating its start and end point. The cabling is documented in a database.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the physical separation of the cable trays. Check of the order and labeling of the cables in the racks. Request for the cabling documentation and random comparison with reality.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cable trays in data centers SHOULD be carefully planned and executed. Trays SHOULD be designed in terms of arrangement and dimensioning so that a separation of voltage levels and a sensible distribution of cables on the trays is possible and that there is sufficient space for future increases in demand.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cable trays were planned with a capacity reserve of at least 30%. The planning takes future expansions into account and ensures that new cables can be laid without affecting the existing ones. The cabling concept is part of the overall security concept of the data center.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request for the planning documents for the cable trays. Review of the utilization of the trays and the planned reserves. Check whether the cabling concept is documented and up-to-date.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the optimal supply of IT hardware that has two power supply units, a dual-path A-B supply SHOULD be set up for the IT operating areas, starting from the low-voltage main distribution board. Redundant lines (e.g., of the A and B power supply) SHOULD be routed via separate trays to ensure maximum availability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The data center has two completely separate power supply paths (A and B path), from the main distribution board via the UPS to the PDUs (Power Distribution Units) in the racks. The cable tray for the A path runs on the left side of the rack rows, the one for the B path on the right side. A failure of a complete supply path does not lead to a failure of the IT systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request for the single-line diagram of the power supply to check for continuous A/B redundancy. On-site inspection of the physical separation of the cable paths. Check whether the power supplies of the servers in the racks are correctly distributed between the A and B PDUs.

controls.title: Use of video surveillance systems (H) [Data Protection Officer, Building Services, Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Dummy video cameras are used that have no real surveillance function. Securing evidence is not possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Empty camera housings are mounted at the entrances to create a deterrent effect.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Visual inspection of the cameras. Check if cables lead to the cameras. Request access to the video management system to verify the existence of live images or recordings.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A CCTV system with live images is in place, but no recordings are stored. A subsequent evaluation of incidents is not possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monitor at the gate shows the live images from several cameras. However, no video recorder (NVR/DVR) is connected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the video surveillance system. Request for recorded material from a specific point in time in the past.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Video cameras are installed at entrances and exits as well as at other strategic points. The recordings are stored for a defined period (e.g., 72 hours) before being overwritten. The use of video surveillance has been coordinated with the data protection officer and employees have been informed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Cameras monitor the entrance area, the loading bay, and the aisles between the racks. The recordings are stored on a Network Video Recorder (NVR). The works council has given its consent, and the data protection officer has approved the corresponding procedural documentation. Warning signs are in place.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the approval documentation from the data protection officer. Review the NVR configuration regarding the recording duration. On-site check of the warning signs.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access control and intrusion detection SHOULD be supplemented by video surveillance systems. Video surveillance SHOULD be integrated into the overall security concept. The data protection officer MUST always be involved in the planning, design, and any evaluation of video recordings. The central technical components required for video surveillance SHOULD be installed in a protected manner. It SHOULD be checked regularly whether the system is functioning correctly and whether the agreed viewing angles are being maintained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Video surveillance is an integral part of the security concept. The NVR is housed in a separate, lockable rack. Any evaluation of video material is carried out according to the four-eyes principle and with the involvement of the data protection officer or works council and is documented. The correct alignment of the cameras is checked annually.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the security concept and review the chapter on video surveillance. Request the protocols of video evaluations. Review the inspection logs for camera alignment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A high-resolution video surveillance system is coupled with the access control system. When an access card is used or an intrusion alarm is triggered, the relevant cameras automatically record in higher quality and mark the event. The video material is monitored for anomalies (e.g., a person staying in an area for a suspiciously long time, objects left behind) using AI-based analysis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For each door transaction, a bookmark is set in the video recording that shows a still image of the person. A video analytics software is configured to trigger an alarm if a person stays in the cold aisle for more than 10 minutes without performing any activity at the rack ('loitering detection').

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the configuration of the coupling between access control and video surveillance. Request the specification and configuration of the video analytics software. Analyze the alarm logs of the video analytics.

controls.title: Redundant design of uninterruptible power supplies (H) [Planner]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: No UPS is in use. The IT systems are directly connected to the public power grid and fail immediately in the event of any disruption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The PDUs in the racks are directly connected to the normal building electrical installation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the single-line diagram of the power supply. Visual inspection of the power distribution in the racks and technical rooms for the presence of UPS systems.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single (non-redundant) UPS system is installed. It does not have a maintenance bypass, which means that the entire connected IT must be shut down for maintenance work.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A monolithic UPS supplies the data center. For the annual battery replacement or maintenance, a nighttime maintenance window with a complete shutdown must be planned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review of the UPS architecture. Check whether an external or internal maintenance bypass is available that allows for uninterruptible service.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single UPS system is installed, but it has an internal or external maintenance bypass. This allows maintenance work to be carried out on the UPS without having to shut down the connected loads, although they are unprotected during maintenance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UPS is equipped with a manual bypass switch. During maintenance, the load is transferred directly to the grid. This is planned and communicated in advance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the documentation of the UPS and the bypass circuit diagram. Review the process description for maintenance work in bypass mode.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: UPS systems SHOULD be modular and designed in such a way that a failure is compensated for by a redundant module without interruption (N+1 redundancy). This increases availability and significantly simplifies maintenance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A modular UPS is in use, consisting of four power modules, although three would be sufficient for the maximum load. If one module fails or is removed for maintenance, the UPS continues to operate without interruption with the remaining three modules.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the configuration of the UPS system. Compare the number of installed power modules with the number required for the load to verify N+1 redundancy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: If a dual-path A-B supply is set up for the IT operational areas, each of the two power paths SHOULD be equipped with an independent UPS system (2N redundancy). This represents the highest level of fault tolerance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The data center is supplied by two completely independent power supply paths (A and B). Each path has its own main distribution board, its own emergency power system, and its own UPS system. Servers with two power supplies are connected to both paths. The failure of a complete path (e.g., due to a fire in the A distribution) has no impact on operation.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the single-line diagram of the power supply. Check for end-to-end 2N redundancy from the feed-in to the PDU in the rack. Visual inspection of the separate routing of the A and B power paths.

controls.title: Redundant design of emergency power systems (H) [Planner]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no emergency power system (EPS). The bridging time depends solely on the capacity of the UPS.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: After the UPS batteries are depleted, an uncontrolled failure of the IT systems occurs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the power supply planning documents for the presence of an emergency power system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a contract with a service provider to rent a mobile emergency power system in an emergency. However, the guaranteed delivery time is long (e.g., 24 hours) and may exceed the autonomy time of the UPS.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A framework agreement ensures the availability of a mobile emergency power system. However, it has not been tested how quickly it can actually be on-site and operational.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the rental agreement for the emergency power system. Review the contractually guaranteed delivery times and compare them with the UPS autonomy time.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single, permanently installed emergency power system (N configuration) is in place. It is regularly maintained and tested. However, a failure of the EPS itself during a power outage would lead to a total failure.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A single emergency power system supplies the entire data center. There is a maintenance contract, and regular tests are carried out. The system represents a single point of failure.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the documentation and test logs of the emergency power system. Analyze the power supply architecture to identify single points of failure.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Emergency power systems SHOULD be designed redundantly (e.g., N+1). Regarding maintenance, redundant EPS MUST also be treated in accordance with INF.2.A14 Use of an emergency power system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two emergency power systems are installed, one of which is sufficient to carry the load, while the other serves as a reserve (N+1 redundancy). Both EPS are subjected to the same rigorous maintenance and testing regime.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Review the design of the emergency power system for N+1 redundancy. Check the maintenance and test logs for all installed EPS modules.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Multiple independent emergency power systems are installed in a 2N configuration, where each system can carry the full load of the data center. These are assigned to the redundant A and B power supply paths and ensure maximum fault tolerance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two identical but physically separate emergency power systems supply the A and B power buses. Each EPS has its own, separate fuel tank. A failure of one EPS or its fuel supply has no effect on the supply of the data center.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the single-line diagram and site plans to verify the 2N architecture and the physical separation of the EPSs and their supply. Review the test logs that demonstrate the independent operation of each EPS under load.

controls.title: Use of higher-grade hazard alarm systems (H) [Planner]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hazard detectors from the consumer sector (e.g., battery-operated smoke detectors from a hardware store) are used. These do not offer sufficient reliability for a data center.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Simple, non-certified smoke and water detectors are installed in the server room.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Visual inspection of the installed detectors. Check the type plates for certifications (e.g. VdS, EN).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A commercial, but not VdS or comparably certified, hazard alarm system is installed. Its reliability and tamper-proofness have not been proven.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A proprietary alarm system from a local installer is in use. The system has no recognized certification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the technical documentation of the hazard alarm system. Check whether the system or its components have recognized certificates.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A hazard alarm system is used whose components are certified according to relevant EN standards. The system offers a defined and traceable security level.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The installed intrusion alarm system is certified according to EN 50131 Grade 2. This represents a solid basic level of protection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the declarations of conformity and certificates for the components of the hazard alarm system. Check for compliance with the relevant EN standards.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A hazard alarm system certified by VdS (Vertrauen durch Sicherheit) of classes A or B is used. These offer higher reliability and better protection against sabotage than non-certified systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A VdS-certified intrusion alarm system of class B is installed. The installation was carried out and accepted by a VdS-approved installer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the VdS certificate for the installed hazard alarm system. Check whether the installation was carried out by a certified installer.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For data center areas with increased protection requirements, only hazard alarm systems of VdS Class C (according to VdS guideline 2311) SHOULD be used. This class offers the highest level of security, reliability, and sabotage protection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The intrusion alarm system that secures the entire data center is certified to VdS Class C. This is often a requirement from insurance companies for highly critical risks. The system has extended monitoring functions for all components and transmission paths.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Request the VdS attestation confirming the Class C certification of the system. Review the system documentation for the implementation of the specific requirements of Class C, such as extended sabotage monitoring.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Today, almost all strategic and operational functions and tasks are significantly supported by information technology (IT) or cannot be performed without IT. As a result, the demands on the performance and availability of IT systems and their connection to the network environment are constantly increasing. In order to meet this performance requirement, to maintain appropriate reserves and to be able to operate IT economically, institutions of all sizes are concentrating their IT landscape in data centers.
A data center (DC) is defined as follows:
1. If an IT-using institution has only one central IT operating area, this, together with the necessary support areas, must always be treated as a DC in accordance with the protection requirements. 'IT operating area' refers to rooms in which the hardware is set up and operated that is used to provide services and data. The DC includes the IT operating area and all other technical support areas (e.g. power supply, cooling supply, extinguishing technology, security technology) that serve the intended operation and security of the IT operating area.
2. If the institution's IT is operated in several areas distributed within a building or property and these areas are connected to each other and to the IT users via in-house LAN connections, at least the functionally most important of these areas must be treated as a DC. Furthermore, areas on whose proper operation 50% or more of IT users are dependent or from which 50% or more of services and data (measured against the totality of the areas) are provided must be treated as a DC.
3. If the IT-using institution is located at several spatially separate locations and these are linked to each other by connections other than in-house LAN connections, each of the locations must be considered and treated separately in accordance with (1).
4. An IT operating area in which IT required for critical business processes (processes whose disruption or failure leads to significant impairments in the performance of an institution's primary tasks) is located is always to be treated as a DC, regardless of size or the share rules from number (2).
5. IT operating areas from which services are provided to third parties are always to be regarded as part of a DC. It is irrelevant whether this is done for a fee or not.
6. If there is a justified interest in treating an IT operating area together with its support area as a server room in deviation from the aforementioned regulations, this must be justified, including the resulting reductions in security requirements.
The list of the six points does not mean that all points must be met jointly for an area to be considered a data center. Rather, various possibilities are described as to when an area is to be regarded as a DC. If a data center deviates from this definition, the IT operating area in question is referred to as a server room. This definition is based exclusively on the importance of the IT structure for the fulfillment of the tasks of the using institution and is therefore in methodological harmony with DIN EN 50600.
If a server room is to be secured, the requirements of this module can be reduced accordingly. However, this must be plausibly and comprehensibly justified (6) and at least the basic requirements must be implemented.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This building block is aimed, on the one hand, at institutions that operate a data center and wish to check as part of a review whether they have implemented suitable security measures. On the other hand, the building block can also be used to estimate the security measures that must be implemented if IT is to be centralized in a data center. The ultimate goal of the requirements described in this building block is to ensure the secure operation of the data center.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The INF.2 Data Center and Server Room module is to be applied to every data center and every server room.
This module is not suitable for small information domains with, for example, only one or very few servers or IT systems. An example of this is a small institution with a few IT workstations and a server that is operated in a separate room. In such cases, it is often sufficient to implement the INF.5 Room and Cabinet for Technical Infrastructure module.
Requirements for buildings and cabling in general are not part of this module. These can be found in the INF.1 General Building and INF.12 Cabling modules, which are always to be applied to rooms and buildings or cabling.
To keep the module manageable, technical details and planning figures have been deliberately omitted. Further information can be found in relevant standards and other BSI publications.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Flawed planning
parts.prose: If a data center is designed without considering how to secure it against elementary threats, there is a very high risk of failure. For example, site risks such as air traffic, earthquakes, or floods can jeopardize operational security and availability. Similarly, it can have a massive impact on the operation of a data center if, due to flawed design, there is not enough bandwidth available or the power supply at the chosen location is insufficient.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Missing or faulty access controls
parts.prose: If access controls are missing or inadequate, the risk increases that unauthorized persons enter the data center and cause damage either negligently, e.g., due to a lack of expertise, or intentionally. Attackers can, for example, steal sensitive data, steal devices, or manipulate servers. Inadequate access controls thus affect the availability, confidentiality, and integrity of data and IT components.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Insufficient monitoring
parts.prose: If the IT and infrastructure operated in the data center are insufficiently monitored and maintained, components can fail unnoticed. This can severely impair the availability and flawless functioning of the data center. Failures also often occur gradually. Without active monitoring, they might be noticed too late. It is then often no longer possible to react in time.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Inadequate air conditioning in the data center
parts.prose: IT components require specific operating conditions to function reliably. They also convert the electrical power they consume into additional heat. If the temperature, humidity, or airborne particulate matter in an IT operations area are not kept within the limits specified by the equipment manufacturers, this can lead to technical components no longer functioning correctly or failing.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Fire
parts.prose: Fire is a hazard that occurs rather infrequently. However, if a fire does occur, it usually has serious consequences, as fire and smoke can cause great damage. While electrical fires are the most common cause of fire within the IT operations area, a fire outside the IT operations area, and especially in support areas such as the power supply (including emergency power generator and UPS) or the air conditioning system, can have numerous other causes. If the IT operations area or the support areas and other neighboring areas have no or insufficient fire protection, a fire can spread quickly. In addition, fires originating outside could spread to the data center.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Water
parts.prose: Water can enter the data center through leaky water pipes, floods, burst pipes, or defective sprinkler or air conditioning systems. This can damage equipment and cause it to stop working. It can also trigger a short circuit, which could cause individual areas of the data center to fail or a fire to start.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Missing or inadequate protection against burglary
parts.prose: Even if a well-functioning access control system is in place, unauthorized persons can break into a data center if it is not adequately protected against burglary. Perpetrators could, for example, steal or manipulate IT components and gain access to confidential information. They could also destroy the devices or damage the data center as a whole.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Power failure
parts.prose: If the power fails, the operation of a data center and thus of the institution can be significantly disrupted. For example, in the event of a power outage, the IT services provided by the data center may suddenly become unavailable. Data can also be lost. In addition, it is possible that IT systems, telecommunication systems, or monitoring technology could be damaged by a sudden power failure.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Contamination
parts.prose: Dust and other contaminants in a data center can cause technical components (e.g., fans) to stop working. Contamination causes devices to wear out sooner and fail more frequently.

groups.title: INF.5 Room and cabinet for technical infrastructure

controls.title: INF.5.A1 Planning of room security (B) [Planner]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Initial, incomplete planning sketches for securing the room exist. However, these only consider individual, obvious threats such as unauthorized access, but disregard essential aspects such as environmental influences or legal regulations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, often only a checklist from the internet is used, without adapting it to the specific conditions of the room and the technology located therein. The planning is not formally documented or approved.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether any planning documents exist at all. It is checked whether basic aspects (e.g., a door with a lock) have been considered, even if a systematic and comprehensive approach is lacking.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Basic planning for securing the room has been carried out and documented. It covers the most important threats such as burglary and fire and considers basic legal requirements. However, a detailed risk analysis for specific threats is still missing.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning is based on standard specifications and best practices but has not yet been fully tailored to the specific risk situation of the organization. The documentation consists of basic plans and guidelines.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of a formal planning document. It is checked on a random basis whether the planning covers essential legal requirements (e.g., fire protection) and obvious dangers (e.g., burglary).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For a room containing technical infrastructure, appropriate technical and organizational specifications MUST be defined and implemented. The protection level to be achieved for the room MUST be taken into account. During planning, legal regulations and provisions as well as potential threats from environmental influences, burglary, and sabotage MUST be considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal planning document is created based on a qualitative risk analysis. It defines technical measures (e.g., type of door, fire extinguishers) and organizational rules (e.g., access control policy). The planning is reviewed and approved by the responsible departments (e.g., building services, information security officer).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning document for room security and compares it with the implemented measures. It is verified that the planning considers all aspects mentioned in the requirement (legal regulations, environmental influences, burglary, sabotage) and corresponds to the defined protection level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning of room security is reviewed and updated regularly, at least annually, and on an ad-hoc basis. The planning also considers less obvious threat scenarios and is supported by a formal risk and threat analysis. The results are documented in an audit-proof manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A structured process for reviewing the planning is established. Changes to the infrastructure or the threat landscape automatically trigger a reassessment. The planning is versioned and managed in a document management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the minutes of the regular planning reviews. It is checked whether the planning is based on a current and documented risk analysis and whether a process for ad-hoc updates has been established.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The planning process for room security is fully integrated into the organization's overall ISMS and risk management. The planning is validated through regular, practical exercises and simulations (e.g., break-in attempts, fire drills). The findings from these are continuously fed into the improvement of the planning and the implemented measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Where appropriate, the planning is supported by quantitative risk analyses. Tools are used to simulate threats (e.g., smoke propagation, temperature development) to validate the effectiveness of the planned measures. The results of the exercises are systematically recorded and tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation and results of the exercises and simulations performed. It is verified that a closed control loop (Plan-Do-Check-Act) has been established for room security and that findings demonstrably lead to the optimization of security precautions.

controls.title: INF.5.A2 Location and size of the room for technical infrastructure (B) [Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room is occasionally used as a passageway to shorten routes. It is cramped and work areas are not clearly defined, which makes maintenance work difficult.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room was selected purely based on availability, without considering security or work-related aspects. There is no marking of escape routes or work areas.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through observation and questioning whether the room is used as a passageway. A visual inspection shows whether there is sufficient space for safe work and escape routes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room is not an official passageway, but the door is not consistently kept closed. The basic space requirements for work and escape routes are met, but there are no reserves for future expansions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is an instruction not to use the room as a passageway, but it is not always followed. The room size was determined for the current needs, without forward-looking planning.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the room is not designated as an official passageway. A visual inspection confirms that the minimum distances for work and escape routes are maintained in accordance with occupational safety regulations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room for technical infrastructure MUST NOT be a passageway. It MUST be ensured that there is sufficient space for escape routes and work areas.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During planning, a location is explicitly chosen that does not require through traffic. The room size is dimensioned to comply with all legal requirements for work and escape routes (e.g., from ASR A2.3). This is documented in the construction and furnishing plans.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor ensures by means of building plans and an on-site inspection that the room is not a passageway. The dimensions of the work areas in front of the cabinets and the escape routes are checked and compared with the applicable regulations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The location of the room is chosen based on a risk analysis that also considers hazards from adjacent areas (e.g., water pipes, fire loads). The size of the room is planned to accommodate future expansions of the technical infrastructure without modifications. Escape routes and work areas are marked on the floor.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room planning includes a buffer of, e.g., 30% for future growth. The floor markings are applied with durable paint or tape. The risk analysis for the location is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the risk analysis for the room's location. It is checked whether capacity reserves were planned for when dimensioning the room. The existence and visibility of the floor markings are verified on site.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The selection of the room's location and size is the result of a comprehensive site analysis that evaluates physical security, environmental risks, expandability, and logistical aspects (e.g., delivery of equipment). The arrangement of components in the room is planned using 3D modeling for optimal workflows, cooling, and security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The site analysis and the 3D models are part of the central building documentation. The planning also considers aspects such as the load-bearing capacity of the floor for heavy components like UPS systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the site analysis and the 3D planning. It is verified that a holistic planning approach was pursued that goes beyond the mere minimum requirements and ensures long-term, secure, and efficient use of the room.

controls.title: INF.5.A3 Access regulation and control (B) [Building services, IT operations]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The door to the room is lockable, but the key is a standard key that many people have. There is no formal regulation or documentation about who has access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room is secured with a simple warded or cylinder lock. There is no list of authorized key holders. Keys are issued on an as-needed basis and without formal approval.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by questioning who has a key to the room. It is checked whether a regulation for access exists, even if it is informal.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room is secured by a lock. There is a list of people who have received a key. A further regulation on access times or purposes is missing. Access is not logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple key list is maintained in a spreadsheet. Key issuance requires the approval of a supervisor. There is no system for recording access.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the key list and checks its currency. It is verified that the circle of authorized persons is restricted to the necessary minimum.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room for technical infrastructure MUST be protected against unauthorized access. It MUST be regulated which persons are allowed to enter the room, for which period, for which areas, and for what purpose. It MUST be ensured that no unnecessary or overly broad access rights are granted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal access policy is created and communicated. The granting of access rights follows a documented approval process based on the need-to-know principle. Temporary access for external service providers is regulated separately and usually requires an escort.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the access policy and checks the process documentation for rights assignment. On a random basis, it is verified for selected individuals whether their access right is justified and documented. It is checked whether the rights assignment follows the principle of least privilege.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All access to the room for technical infrastructure SHOULD be individually recorded by the access control system. Access SHOULD be controlled and logged by an electronic access control system (ACS). The logs SHOULD be reviewed regularly, at least monthly, for implausible events.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ACS with personalized transponders or cards is used. The access logs are stored centrally and protected against manipulation. The review of the logs can be supported by automated scripts that, for example, report access outside of normal working hours.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the access logs for the last three months. It is checked whether all accesses have been recorded without gaps. The documentation of the regular log evaluation is reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The electronic access control system requires two-factor authentication (e.g., card and PIN or a biometric feature). The ACS is linked to a video surveillance system that records an image sequence for each access attempt. Access attempts outside defined time windows or denied attempts trigger an immediate alarm at a constantly staffed location.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ACS is used that employs modern cryptography for communication between the reader and the transponder. Alarms are forwarded to a Security Operations Center (SOC) or a security service provider. Access rights are dynamically obtained from a central Identity and Access Management (IAM) system and are regularly recertified.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the two-factor authentication and the alarm triggering. The link to the video surveillance system is verified. The integration into the IAM and the process for recertifying rights are checked using logs.

controls.title: INF.5.A4 Protection Against Burglary (B) [Planners, Building Services]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The door to the room has a simple lock. Other vulnerabilities such as unsecured windows, thin walls, or ceilings are not considered.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard residential door lock is used. Ground-floor windows have no bars or other protective measures. The walls are made of simple plasterboard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor assesses the mechanical stability of the door, walls, lock, and any windows through a visual inspection. It is determined whether obvious vulnerabilities for a burglary exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room MUST be protected against burglary. This is implemented by using a solid door with a security lock. The structural components (walls, ceiling) provide basic protection but are not certified to a specific resistance class.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A solid-leaf door with a drill-proof lock cylinder and a security strike plate is installed. Any existing windows are permanently sealed or fitted with bars.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the type of door, lock, and strike plate. It is checked whether basic burglary protection measures have been taken on all openings of the room.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room MUST be protected against burglary. Depending on the required security level of the room, suitable structural components such as walls, ceilings, and floors, as well as windows and doors with appropriate resistance classes according to DIN EN 1627, SHOULD be selected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on the protection needs assessment, a target resistance class (e.g., RC 2) is defined for the room's envelope. Doors, windows, and other components are procured and professionally installed according to this standard. The selection is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documents in which the required resistance class is specified. It is verified using manufacturer certificates and installation documentation whether the installed components (door, windows, etc.) comply with the specified resistance class.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to mechanical protection according to a defined resistance class (e.g., RC 2 or RC 3), an intruder alarm system (IAS) according to VdS class A or B is installed. The IAS monitors all openings and the interior for unauthorized intrusion.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IAS is planned and installed by a specialized company. It includes opening detectors on doors and windows as well as motion detectors in the room. A local alarm (siren, strobe light) is activated upon triggering.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the planning and installation documents of the IAS. The certification of the IAS (e.g., VdS certificate) is inspected. The function of the detectors and the alarm system is tested on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room is designed with a high resistance class (e.g., RC 4) or as a strongroom. An intruder alarm system according to VdS class C is installed and connected to a 24/7 manned alarm receiving center (ARC) that triggers an intervention chain. All components, including ventilation ducts, are included in the protection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The burglary protection is planned and implemented as an integrated system in which mechanical security and electronic surveillance are optimally coordinated. The contract with the ARC ensures that defined response times are met. Ventilation grilles are equipped with anti-saw protection and penetration monitoring.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the certification of the room envelope and the IAS according to the highest classes. The contract with the ARC is inspected. A test call is made to the ARC to verify the alarm transmission chain.

controls.title: INF.5.A5 Avoidance of and protection against electromagnetic interference fields (B) [Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When choosing the location of the room, electromagnetic interference fields are not taken into account. The room happens to be located near sources of interference such as a large electric motor.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room planning is carried out without knowledge or consideration of potential EMI sources in the building.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor identifies obvious, strong electromagnetic sources (e.g., main distribution boards, elevator motors, transformers) in the immediate vicinity of the room.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: During planning, care is taken not to place the room directly next to very strong, known sources of interference such as elevator motors or main transformers. A precise distance is not calculated but determined based on experience.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In the building plans, a minimum distance to the largest sources of interference is drawn and taken into account during installation. Less obvious sources such as high-voltage power lines are not considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor compares the location of the room on the building plan with the locations of the main EMI sources and assesses whether a plausible distance has been maintained.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Electromagnetic fields MUST be avoided in the immediate vicinity of the room for technical infrastructure. A sufficient distance from large machines such as elevator motors MUST be maintained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During the planning phase, all known, significant sources of interference in the building are identified and noted in the plans. Based on manufacturer specifications or general technical rules (e.g., DIN EN 50174-2), specific minimum distances to these sources are defined and adhered to when selecting the room's location.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the planning documents and checks whether an analysis of interference sources has been carried out and whether defined distance rules have been complied with. This is verified on-site by measuring the distances.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to maintaining distances, sensitive data and control lines are run in shielded cable ducts or as shielded cables (e.g., S/FTP) to minimize interference coupling. The shielding is properly connected to the equipotential bonding system at both ends.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Metallic cable trays are used, the parts of which are conductively connected to each other. During installation, care is taken to separate power and data cables.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the cabling on a random basis. It is checked whether shielded cables and ducts are used and whether the shield connection is properly executed. This can be done through a visual inspection and resistance measurement of the shield connection.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before commissioning and thereafter at regular intervals, professional EMC measurements are carried out in the room to verify compliance with the limit values according to EN 61000. In case of deviations, targeted measures are taken to shield the room or the sources of interference.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An external, specialized service provider is commissioned to carry out the EMC measurements. The results are documented. Possible measures in case of exceeded limit values are the subsequent installation of EMC wallpapers or the installation of line filters.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the protocols of the EMC measurements and checks whether they were carried out by qualified personnel and whether the measured values are within the permissible limits. If measures have been taken, their effectiveness is checked on the basis of subsequent measurements.

controls.title: INF.5.A6 Minimization of Fire Loads (B) [Employees, Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Combustible materials such as cardboard from new equipment, cleaning supplies, or old documents are regularly stored temporarily in the room. There is no rule for minimizing fire loads.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The room is misused as a storage room for convenience. There is no awareness of the resulting fire hazard.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor determines whether and what combustible materials are stored in the room. It is clarified by questioning whether this is a permanent condition.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal instruction not to store combustible materials in the room. However, this is not consistently enforced, so that fire loads temporarily accumulate again and again. The building materials of the room itself have not been selected for their flammability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An e-mail from the supervisor or a notice on the door indicates the storage ban. However, there are no regular checks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks on-site whether fire loads are present. It is inquired whether a regulation exists and how its compliance is ensured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Fire loads within and in the immediate vicinity of the room for technical infrastructure MUST be reduced to a minimum. Combustible materials for structural components MUST be avoided.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: During the planning and construction of the room, non-combustible (building material class A according to DIN 4102) or flame-retardant materials are explicitly selected for walls, floors, and ceilings. A binding policy is issued that prohibits the storage of any materials in the room. Compliance is monitored through regular, documented inspections (e.g., by the fire safety officer).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the construction documents to verify the building material classes of the materials used. The protocols of the control inspections are reviewed and the current condition of the room is checked on-site.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All cables and wiring installed in the room must have a low fire load and be low-smoke and halogen-free in case of fire (LSZH - Low Smoke Zero Halogen). Cable penetrations through walls and ceilings are sealed with certified firestops to prevent the spread of fire.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The use of LSZH cables is explicitly required in the tender for cabling work. The installation of the firestops is carried out by certified specialist companies and is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor randomly checks the labeling on the cable jackets for the LSZH property. The documentation and the visible execution of the firestops (e.g., identification plate) are checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room is designed as a separate, fire-resistant fire compartment (e.g., F90). An automatic early fire detection system (e.g., aspirating smoke detection system) and an automatic extinguishing system suitable for technical rooms (e.g., gas extinguishing system) are installed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The design of the fire compartment and the extinguishing system is carried out as part of a comprehensive fire protection concept by a specialist engineer. The systems are regularly maintained and inspected.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the fire protection concept and the acceptance protocols of the fire alarm and extinguishing system. The maintenance records of the last few years are checked.

controls.title: INF.5.A7 Prevention of misuse (B) [Employees, Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room is regularly used as storage for non-technical items such as office supplies, cleaning supplies, or personal effects. There is no awareness that this is a problem.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Due to a lack of space elsewhere, the server room is seen as a welcome storage area. There are no rules or controls.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor determines which and how many inappropriate items are stored in the room. Interviewing employees provides insight into the reasons and regularity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a verbal instruction or a notice not to misuse the room. However, compliance is not actively monitored, which is why violations occur repeatedly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The rule was communicated by a supervisor, but no responsibilities for monitoring were defined. Inappropriate items are only removed if they are in the way during maintenance work.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether inappropriate items are present and asks about the existence of a regulation. It is assessed whether the regulation is known and (even if only passively) implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room for technical infrastructure MUST NOT be used for other purposes, e.g., as a storage room or for cleaning supplies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A clear, written policy on the use of the room is issued, which is part of the general house rules or a specific IT policy. Compliance is checked as part of regular, documented inspections by a responsible body (e.g., facility management or IT).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the corresponding policy and the logs of the control inspections. During an on-site inspection, the current state of the room is compared with the policy.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room's designated purpose is emphasized by clear labeling on the door (e.g., 'Technical Room - Access for Authorized Personnel Only - No Storage'). Security training for employees and external service providers explicitly points out the prohibition of misuse.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The signage is professionally created and clearly displayed. The instruction on the correct use of the room is included in the annual safety briefing and in the induction for external companies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and visibility of the labeling. Based on training materials and external company briefings, it is checked whether the topic is actively communicated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the prohibition of misuse is part of the internal control system (ICS) and is regularly audited. Identified violations lead to an escalation process and an analysis of the root causes (e.g., lack of storage space elsewhere) to solve the problem systematically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The checks are planned and documented in an audit tool. In the event of violations, measures are recorded in the ticket system and their processing is tracked. The results are incorporated into the management review.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit planning and reports of the ICS regarding the use of technical rooms. The process for tracking measures and for root cause analysis is reviewed.

controls.title: INF.5.A8 Prevention of uncontrolled electrostatic discharge (S) [Planners]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The issue of electrostatic discharge (ESD) is not considered. The room has a highly chargeable floor covering such as carpet.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The flooring was selected purely for aesthetic or cost reasons. There is no awareness of the danger of ESD to electronic components.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor identifies the type of flooring and assesses its potential for electrostatic charging. They ask whether ESD protection measures are in place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A non-chargeable or low-chargeable flooring (e.g., linoleum, PVC without special ESD properties) is installed. Mobile ESD protection mats and wrist straps are available for maintenance work.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The flooring was not specifically selected as an ESD floor, but happens to have favorable properties. The use of mobile protective equipment is the responsibility of the respective technician.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and condition of the mobile ESD protective equipment. By interviewing the technicians, it is determined whether and how it is used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the room for technical infrastructure, a dissipative floor covering according to DIN EN 14041 SHOULD be installed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When planning the room, a floor covering that meets the requirements of DIN EN 14041 for dissipative floor coverings is explicitly specified and installed. The covering is professionally installed and connected to the building's equipotential bonding system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the product data sheets and the acceptance protocol for the flooring to check for conformity with DIN EN 14041. A visual inspection of the connection to the equipotential bonding system is carried out.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the dissipative flooring, fixed connection points for ESD wrist straps are installed. The personnel working in the room are regularly trained in handling ESD-sensitive components and using the protective equipment. The conductivity of the floor is periodically measured and documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The ESD training is part of the mandatory briefings for technicians. The flooring is measured with a special measuring device in accordance with the specifications of the relevant standards.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the technicians' training records. The logs of the periodic measurements of the flooring are inspected. The permanently installed connection points are checked for correct function.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room is set up as a complete ESD protected area (EPA) in accordance with DIN EN 61340-5-1. In addition to the flooring, this includes ESD-compliant work surfaces, chairs, tools, and packaging materials. Compliance with EPA requirements is ensured by an access control system with mandatory testing of personal ESD equipment (footwear, wrist strap).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An ESD coordinator is appointed who is responsible for setting up and monitoring the EPA. A personnel grounding tester is installed at the entrance to the zone. All items brought into the zone must be ESD-compliant.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the conformity of the entire facility with DIN EN 61340-5-1. The ESD control plan is checked. The function of the personnel grounding tester at the entrance is tested.

controls.title: INF.5.A9 Power supply (B) [Facility Management]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room is powered from any socket in the building. The mains system type is unknown or it is an outdated TN-C system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No separate electrical planning was carried out for the room. The wiring may be undersized and not designed for continuous operation of IT loads.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines the mains system type by inspecting the electrical plans or, if not available, by taking a measurement. The origin of the power supply is traced back.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room has its own circuit from a sub-distribution board. The installation is basically a TN-S system, but this was not explicitly planned or documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The electrical installation was carried out by an electrician according to current standards, which usually implies a TN-S system. However, there was no explicit requirement or verification of the mains system type.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies by measurements (e.g., resistance between N and PE conductor) that it is de facto a TN-S system. It is checked whether a separate circuit is present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The power supply network that supplies the room for technical infrastructure and the connected end devices MUST be set up as a TN-S system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The electrical planning for the room explicitly requires the installation of a TN-S system from the main distribution board to the sockets in the room. The implementation is confirmed by an acceptance protocol (E-Check) from a qualified electrician. The documentation (circuit diagrams) is created accordingly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the electrical planning documents and the acceptance protocol. It checks whether the TN-S system was explicitly requested and its correct installation confirmed. The plans are compared with the on-site installation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room for technical infrastructure has its own, dedicated sub-distribution board. All circuits in this room are supplied exclusively from this sub-distribution board. The sub-distribution board and the circuits are clearly and permanently labeled.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A small distribution box is installed near the room, which is fed directly from a main distribution board. All fuses and connections in this box are clearly assigned to the respective sockets or devices in the technical room.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the dedicated sub-distribution board. By tracing the cables or by test shutdown, it is ensured that all consumers in the room are supplied from there. The quality of the labeling is assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room's power supply is designed redundantly (A/B feed). Two independent TN-S systems from different main distribution boards or transformers supply the room. Intelligent Power Distribution Units (PDUs) monitor the power consumption per outlet and enable remote switching of consumers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Two separate supply lines are run into the room. Devices with redundant power supplies are connected to both feeds. The PDUs are integrated into the central monitoring system and report limit violations or failures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the physical separation of the two power supply paths from the source to the consumer. The function of the PDUs and their integration into the monitoring system is tested. A simulated failure of one feed is carried out to verify the switchover.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
A room for technical infrastructure contains technical components that rarely need to be operated directly on site. However, they are indispensable for the building infrastructure and thus also for the IT infrastructure. These can be, for example, distributors for the power supply, fuse boxes, ventilation systems, parts of telecommunication systems, patch panels, switches, or routers. This room is not a permanent workstation and is usually only entered or opened for maintenance.
If the technical infrastructure to be protected cannot be housed in a separate room or if the room cannot be set up according to the described requirements, the technical infrastructure can also be housed in a specially equipped cabinet. This can also be useful if a cabinet is the most economical alternative for housing the technical infrastructure. The requirements for the room must then be transferred to the cabinet and its enclosure with as equivalent an effect as possible.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose:
The objective of this module is to protect a room or cabinet for technical infrastructure in terms of information security through structural, mechanical, and electronic means. While a room generally refers to a room or cabinet within a building, it can also encompass, by analogy, a container outside a building or a tent with technical infrastructure. The protection should be designed in such a way that the functions of the technical components located therein cannot be impaired if possible.
Hereinafter, only the term 'room' for technical infrastructure will be used. However, the requirements of this module are also applicable to cabinets.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose: The module INF.5 Room and Cabinet for Technical Infrastructure is to be applied to rooms in which technical infrastructure is operated. The module is also to be applied when stationary containers, in the sense of a large cabinet, are operated.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Flawed planning
parts.prose: If a room for technical infrastructure is poorly planned, several problems can arise. For instance, water can enter or IT components can overheat due to solar radiation if the room's location is poorly chosen. An unsuitable location may also increase the likelihood of a break-in. Bottlenecks can also occur if the power supply is inadequately sized. If inferior materials are used, IT components are often more susceptible to failures and malfunctions. Lastly, regulations and rules may not be considered and complied with during the planning phase. If non-permissible deviations have to be rectified later, unnecessarily high costs can arise.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Unauthorised access
parts.prose: If there is no access control or burglar protection, or if these are too weak, unauthorised persons may be able to enter the room for technical infrastructure. They could cause damage there, either unintentionally, e.g., due to a lack of expertise, or intentionally, e.g., by stealing, replacing, tampering with, or destroying equipment.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Inadequate ventilation
parts.prose: If a room for technical infrastructure is inadequately ventilated, the permitted temperature range for the installed equipment may not be maintained. As a result, this equipment could fail or be permanently damaged.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Fire
parts.prose: A room for technical infrastructure can be severely damaged or completely destroyed by a fire, causing the business processes or specialised tasks that depend on it to fail. In a room with power cables and electricity consumers, there is a risk of fire, for example, if circuit breakers or device fuses do not trigger during excessive currents. On the other hand, negligence can also lead to fires, for example, if smoking occurs in the room and cables and equipment made of flammable material catch fire. Furthermore, sparks can form due to overvoltages or overheating, leading to a fire. A fire in the technical infrastructure room can also spread to other parts of the building. Conversely, a fire in the building can also spread to the technical infrastructure room.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Water
parts.prose: Flooding within the room for technical infrastructure can cause water damage to both the components operated there and the room itself. In addition to damage to the room, this water damage can also lead to short circuits in electrical devices. As a consequence, mould and corrosion can occur. A leak in a water pipe could also flood the room. Rainwater entering the building through overloaded storm drains during heavy rain can also lead to flooding of the room.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Power supply failure
