parts.prose: If the power supply to the room for technical infrastructure fails, multiple electrically operated components are usually affected. This can lead to a halt of all associated operational processes. A sudden interruption of the power supply can also cause damage to electrotechnical components, which may persist even after the power supply is restored. Lastly, consequential damage can occur if a critical component, such as the ventilation system, is not operational. If the room heats up, other devices can be damaged or even fail as a result.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Lightning strikes and overvoltages
parts.prose: In addition to the effects of a direct lightning strike, the induction effect of indirect lightning can cause overvoltage peaks even several hundred metres from the point of impact. Induction also occurs near the conductors of the lightning protection system. These inductive overvoltage peaks can potentially cause overvoltages on cable trays and at electrotechnical devices within the room for technical infrastructure, leading to functional disruptions or complete device failure.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.8. Electromagnetic interference fields
parts.prose: An interference source, such as elevator motors, transmission systems, or conductors of lightning protection systems, can emit electromagnetic fields. These can potentially interfere with switches, controllers, or IT systems. This interference voltage can cause electrotechnical components to malfunction or even fail. The devices within the room for technical infrastructure can also interfere with each other.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.9. Electrostatic discharge
parts.prose: Uncontrolled electrostatic discharges can damage or destroy devices with sensitive electronic components in the room for technical infrastructure. This can lead to the devices no longer functioning reliably or failing completely.

controls.title: Portable fire extinguisher

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is only a single portable fire extinguisher, its location is not known to all relevant employees. There are no regular inspections or training sessions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The measure is limited to the passive provision of a single fire extinguisher without organizational integration. It is usually a universal ABC extinguisher.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines whether a fire extinguisher exists. By questioning employees, it is determined whether its location and operation are known.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Suitable portable fire extinguishers are placed at several strategic points in and around the data media archive. However, the maintenance intervals are only adhered to irregularly. Basic instruction in their use is given on request.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The locations of the fire extinguishers are marked. Maintenance is often only carried out as part of general building inspections, not specifically for the archive.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and marking of portable fire extinguishers. The maintenance tags are checked on a random basis. It is checked whether documents for briefings exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the event of a fire, suitable portable fire extinguishers MUST be easily accessible in the data media archive. These portable fire extinguishers MUST be regularly inspected and maintained. Employees working near a data media archive MUST be trained in the use of portable fire extinguishers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A plan for the locations of the portable fire extinguishers is drawn up, paying attention to their suitability for IT fires (e.g., CO2 extinguishers). Inspections, maintenance, and training are documented. The fire protection officer is responsible.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the locations and types of fire extinguishers against the fire protection concept. The maintenance and training records for the required period are inspected and checked for completeness. An automated check can be performed by querying the service provider's maintenance database.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined measures, automatic fire detectors (e.g., smoke detectors) are installed and connected to an internal alarm point. The type of fire extinguishers is specifically adapted to the stored media (e.g., CO2 extinguishers to avoid damage to electronics).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The fire alarm system is integrated into the building management system. Regular tests of the alarm chain are carried out and logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the functionality of the fire detectors by means of a test alarm. The specifications of the extinguishers are checked for their suitability for IT environments. Alarm logs are inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic gas extinguishing system that is harmless to IT media is installed. The system is regularly inspected and is connected to the central security management system to trigger immediate reactions and an automatic shutdown of ventilation systems in the event of an alarm.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The gas extinguishing system is VdS-certified. The triggering is linked to the access control system to prevent endangering people. The maintenance and testing of the entire system are carried out by specialized companies.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the certification and maintenance documents of the gas extinguishing system. The logs of the last system tests, including the correct control of peripheral systems (ventilation, alarms), are checked. An automated check can query the status of the extinguishing system via the central security management system.

controls.title: Access regulation and control

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the archive room is secured by a simple standard lock. A list of key holders exists, but it is not regularly updated or checked for necessity.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple cylinder lock key is issued to a large group of employees. There is no physical reinforcement of the door or frame.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the locking mechanism and requests the key list. Through interviews, the timeliness of the list and the need of the key holders are checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A security lock is installed. Access is restricted to a defined group of people and specified in a policy, but there is no logging of access.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A locking cylinder with a security card is used to prevent unauthorized key duplication. The policy is communicated to the authorized persons.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the type of lock and the existence of the access policy. The list of authorized persons is compared with the actual key or card holders.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to the data media archive MAY ONLY be possible for authorized persons. Access MUST be reduced to a minimum number of employees. Therefore, access MUST be regulated and controlled. A concept for access control MUST be developed. The access control measures defined therein SHOULD be regularly reviewed for their effectiveness. The entire room MUST have a mechanical resistance adequate for the protection requirement, which MUST not be less than RC2 (according to DIN EN 1627).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An access control concept is created and approved. It defines the authorized roles and applies the need-to-know principle. The resistance class RC2 is ensured for doors, windows, and walls and proven by manufacturer declarations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the access control concept and the list of authorized persons. The evidence for the achieved resistance class (e.g., certificates for doors) is checked. The logs of the authorization reviews are inspected. An automated audit can compare the configured permissions in an electronic access control system with the specifications from the concept.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An electronic access control system (e.g., card reader) is used, which logs all access attempts (both successful and failed). The logs are regularly checked for anomalies, at least monthly. The mechanical resistance of the room is increased to RC3.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system like Salto or SimonsVoss is implemented. The log data is forwarded to a central SIEM system for analysis. The review of the logs is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the configuration of the access control system and requests the logs for the last four weeks. It is checked whether the documented reviews have taken place. The evidence for the RC3 class is checked. SIEM rules that react to anomalous access attempts can be checked automatically.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A two-factor authentication system (e.g., card and PIN or biometrics) is used for access. The access control system is linked to video surveillance, which starts a recording for every access attempt. An intruder alarm system connected to a security service secures the room outside of business hours.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Biometric readers are combined with card readers. The cameras are positioned to completely cover the entrance area. The contract with the security service contains clear instructions for alarm situations. The mechanical resistance is at least RC4.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the two-factor authentication. The link between the access system and video recording is checked. The alarm chain to the security service is verified (e.g., by a test alarm). The certification of the intruder alarm system (e.g., VdS class) and the evidence for the RC4 class are checked.

controls.title: Protection against dust and other contamination

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The room is occasionally cleaned as part of general office cleaning. A smoking ban is mentioned in the general house rules but is not explicitly enforced for the archive.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There are no specific cleaning instructions or materials for the archive room. The data media are stored on open shelves.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a visual inspection of the room for cleanliness. It is checked whether there are specific instructions for protection against contamination.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are regular cleaning schedules for the archive. A strict no smoking, eating, and drinking policy is indicated by signs at the entrance and is generally followed. Data media are stored in simple plastic boxes to protect them from direct dust.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cleaning schedule includes a weekly dry cleaning. The boxes are not sealed but offer basic protection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the cleaning schedule and checks the labeling of the room. The storage of the data media in boxes is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that the data media in the data media archive are adequately protected from dust and contamination. The requirements for this MUST be analyzed already in the planning phase. A strict smoking ban MUST be observed in data media archives.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy for the data media archive defines measures for protection against contamination. This includes the type of storage (e.g., in closed cabinets), cleaning procedures (e.g., use of dust-binding cloths), and a strict ban on eating, drinking, and smoking, which is actively communicated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the corresponding policy and the planning documents. An on-site inspection verifies the implementation of the measures (clean, closed cabinets, no signs of contamination). Compliance with the smoking ban is verified.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The archive room is equipped with a dedicated air filtration system to control airborne particles. Data media are stored in sealed, antistatic special containers. The room is maintained at a slight overpressure relative to the rest of the building.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A ventilation system with filters of class F7 or higher is installed. The containers for the data media are specially certified for long-term archiving. The overpressure is generated by the ventilation system and regularly checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the specification of the ventilation and filter system as well as the certificates of the storage containers. The maintenance logs of the system are checked. The overpressure can be measured with a manometer.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The archive is designed as a cleanroom environment with a particle lock, positive air pressure, and a HEPA (High-Efficiency Particulate Air) filter system. The environmental parameters, including the particle concentration in the air, are continuously monitored and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The structural implementation is carried out according to cleanroom standards. Special cleanroom clothing (gowns, overshoes) must be worn before entering. The monitoring sensors are connected to a central management system that issues alarms in case of deviations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the construction and planning documents of the cleanroom. The logs of the environmental monitoring are analyzed. Compliance with the rules of conduct (e.g., use of the airlock) is observed. The sensor data from the management system can be evaluated automatically.

controls.title: Closed windows and locked doors

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are verbally reminded to lock the door when leaving. There are no formal rules or regular checks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This measure relies solely on the sense of responsibility of individuals. The door often remains unlocked during working hours.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts unannounced inspections to check if the door is locked. Employees are asked about the applicable instructions.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a written instruction that doors and any existing windows must be closed and locked when leaving the room. Compliance is checked randomly during general inspection rounds.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A notice on the door serves as a reminder of the locking obligation. The instruction is part of the general security guidelines.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the written instruction and checks if it is known to the employees. The results of the inspection rounds are reviewed, if available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In a data media archive, there SHOULD, if possible, be no windows. If there are windows, they MUST be closed when leaving the data media archive. Likewise, the door MUST be locked when leaving. Fire and smoke protection doors MUST also be closed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The locking obligation is formally anchored in the usage regulations for the archive and is verifiably brought to the attention of all authorized persons. The absence of windows is defined as a planning requirement for new archives.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence of the usage regulations and the evidence of acknowledgment by the employees. During an inspection, the condition of doors and windows is checked. Planning documents for new archives are checked for the requirement (no windows).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Self-closing and self-locking doors are installed. Sensors on windows and doors report their status (open/closed) to a central monitoring system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Door closers and motorized locks are installed. Magnetic contacts are attached to doors and windows and connected to the intrusion detection or building management system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the function of the self-closing/self-locking door. The status of the sensors is verified in the monitoring system by opening and closing doors and windows. The status of the sensors can be queried periodically and automatically and compared with the expected states (e.g., always closed at night).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The door and window status is fully integrated into the building's security system. An alarm is automatically triggered if the room remains unsecured outside of business hours or for an extended period. The alarm system can only be armed when doors and windows are properly closed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The logic for the alarm is configured in the intrusion alarm control panel (forced operation). The alarm is sent to a permanently staffed location (security service).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the system behavior by attempting to arm the alarm system with a door open. A test alarm is triggered to check the entire notification chain. The configuration of the intrusion alarm control panel is reviewed and checked for correctness.

controls.title: Use of protective cabinets

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only a few particularly sensitive data carriers are kept in a lockable office cabinet. The majority of the media are stored on open shelves.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is no clear regulation as to which data carriers must be secured separately; the decision is left to the discretion of the employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor carries out a visual inspection of the storage methods and questions employees about the criteria for separate storage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All data carriers and media are stored in standard, lockable steel sheet office cabinets.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Standard filing cabinets are used, which offer basic protection against unauthorized access, but no certified burglary or fire protection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies by means of an inspection that all data carriers are stored in locked cabinets and checks on a random basis whether they are actually locked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The data carriers and media in data media archives SHOULD be stored in suitable protective cabinets.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Based on a protection needs analysis, protective cabinets with a defined resistance class against burglary (e.g., according to EN 1143-1) are procured and used. The selection criteria are documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation on the protection needs analysis and the selection decision for the cabinets. It is checked on site whether the procured cabinets are used and whether the corresponding type plates with certifications are present.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Protective cabinets with certified fire protection (e.g., S 60 DIS or S 120 DIS according to EN 1047-1) are used for digital data carriers. Access to the cabinets is also regulated and logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cabinets are specially designed and certified for storing electronic media. Access can be granted via separate electronic locks, the logs of which are regularly evaluated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the certification of the fire protection on the basis of the type plates. If available, the access logs of the cabinet locks are inspected and checked for plausibility.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: High-security safes are used that offer both a high level of burglary protection (e.g., resistance grade III according to EN 1143-1) and certified fire protection. In addition, the cabinets are air-conditioned or contain desiccants to ensure optimal humidity for long-term storage.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cabinets are firmly anchored to the building. Access requires two-factor authentication. The climate data within the cabinets is permanently monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the certificates for burglary and fire protection as well as the evidence of professional anchoring. The function of the access control and climate monitoring is tested. The log data from the climate monitoring can be evaluated automatically.

controls.title: Avoiding water-carrying pipes

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The existence of water pipes in or above the archive room is known, but no specific protective measures are taken.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The risk is considered low or ignored. There are no precautions to detect or respond to leaks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: During an inspection, the auditor identifies water pipes and asks what measures are in place to protect against water damage.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Water pipes are visually inspected for leaks and corrosion as part of general, regular building inspections.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: This check is part of a checklist for the janitor, but is not specifically documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor questions the janitor about the inspection routines and reviews the general checklists for building inspections.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In data media archives, unnecessary water pipes SHOULD generally be avoided. If water pipes are nevertheless routed through the data media archive, they SHOULD be checked regularly to ensure they are still sealed. In addition, precautions SHOULD be taken to detect water leakage at an early stage. For a data media archive with high availability requirements, there SHOULD be response plans that specify exactly how to proceed in the event of a leak.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When planning new archives, avoiding water pipes is defined as a requirement. For existing archives, the pipes are recorded in a register and regular, documented inspections are carried out. A simple response plan is drawn up, which defines contact persons and initial steps.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the pipe register, the inspection logs and the response plan. Planning documents for new archives are checked for compliance with the requirement.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Water detectors are installed on the floor of the archive room and are coupled to an alarm system. Where possible, the pipes are provided with a secondary seal or drip pans.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The water detectors are placed at strategic low points. Alarms are sent via email or SMS to the building services. The response plans are regularly practiced.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the function of the water detectors (e.g., by moistening) and the alarm chain. The structural implementation of the secondary sealing is assessed. The protocols of the exercises are reviewed. The status of the water detectors can be queried automatically via a connected system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An automatic shut-off valve, which is coupled to the water detectors, is installed at the entry point of the water-carrying pipes into the archive area. The alarm is sent to a 24/7 staffed location. The response plans are detailed and are practiced at least annually under realistic conditions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The solenoid valve is installed in such a way that it interrupts the water supply for the relevant area in the event of an alarm. The connection to the permanently staffed location (e.g., security service) is contractually regulated. The exercises also include the evacuation of media from the endangered areas.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the entire chain of action from the triggering of the sensor to the closing of the valve and the alerting of the staffed location by means of a simulated alarm. The documentation of the annual exercises is checked in detail.

controls.title: Compliance with climatic conditions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A thermometer is installed in the room. The values are read occasionally, but there are no defined setpoints or systematic logging.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple household thermometer is used. The climate is not regulated; only the current state is passively observed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a visual inspection and questions those responsible about the specifications for temperature and humidity.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A simple air conditioning system is installed to regulate the temperature in summer. The temperature and humidity are recorded manually in a list on a daily basis.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A split air conditioning unit is used. Logging is done on paper. Humidity is not actively regulated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the manually kept log lists for completeness and plausibility and inspects the air conditioning system.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It SHOULD be ensured that the permissible maximum and minimum values for temperature and humidity as well as the particulate matter content in the room air in the data media archive are observed. The values of air temperature and humidity SHOULD be recorded and documented several times a year for a period of one week. Any deviations from the setpoint value SHOULD be rectified promptly. The air conditioning units used SHOULD be serviced regularly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The setpoints for climate and purity are defined based on the recommendations of the storage media manufacturers. Data loggers are used for periodic recording. A maintenance contract exists for the air conditioning units.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the defined setpoints. The logs of the data loggers and the maintenance records of the air conditioning units are checked. It is verified whether action was taken in response to logged deviations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A permanent environmental monitoring system is installed that continuously records temperature and humidity. The system automatically sends warnings via email or SMS if predefined thresholds are exceeded or not met. Redundant air conditioning units are in place.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Sensors are distributed at several points in the room to detect hot spots. The alarm thresholds are set slightly tighter than the maximum permissible values to allow for an early response. The redundant air conditioning units operate in a load-sharing mode.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the recorded climate data for trends and limit violations. The configuration of the alarm is checked and verified by a test. The function of the redundant air conditioning units is checked. The measured values and alarms from the monitoring system can be read and evaluated automatically.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The environmental monitoring system is fully integrated into the building management system. Climate control is fully automated, with redundant units that allow for immediate failover. Historical data is analyzed to predict maintenance needs and optimize energy consumption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Precision air conditioning units that can precisely regulate both temperature and humidity are in use. The climate data is analyzed by specialized software that detects anomalies before they lead to limit violations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the reports of the trend analysis. The failover function of the air conditioning units is tested by simulating a failure of one unit. The integration into the building management system and the automation rules stored there are checked.

controls.title: Secure doors and windows

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The archive door is a solid wood door with a security strike plate and a lock with drill protection. Any existing windows are lockable and not on the ground floor.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Standard components from DIY stores or specialist retailers are used, which offer a basic increase in security compared to standard doors but do not have a certified resistance class.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor performs a visual inspection of the door, lock, strike plate, and windows to assess the basic security features.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security measures such as windows, doors, and walls SHOULD be equivalent and appropriate with regard to burglary, fire, and smoke. Depending on the protection requirements, a suitable resistance class according to DIN EN 1627 SHOULD be met. All security doors and windows SHOULD be checked regularly to ensure they are still functioning correctly. The entire room SHOULD have mechanical resistance adequate for the protection requirements, which is in no case lower than RC3 (according to DIN EN 1627).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: For the room, resistance class RC3 is defined as the target based on the protection requirements. Doors and windows are procured and installed that are certified for this class according to DIN EN 1627. The walls are checked or upgraded for corresponding resistance. There is a plan for the regular inspection of the locking mechanisms and fittings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the certificates and installation instructions for the doors and windows to verify compliance with RC3. The inspection logs of the security components are checked. An automated procedure is not applicable here; it requires physical inspection and document review.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All components of the room (doors, windows, walls, ceiling, floor) are demonstrably certified according to resistance class RC4 of DIN EN 1627. In addition, all openings are equipped with intruder detection sensors (e.g., magnetic contacts, glass break sensors) that are part of an intruder alarm system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Certified RC4 elements are installed by a specialist company. The intruder alarm system is certified according to VdS Class A or B. The sensors are regularly checked for their functionality.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the certificates for the RC4 components and the intruder alarm system. The functionality of the sensors is verified through tests (e.g., opening the door when the system is armed). The logs of regular system maintenance are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The archive room is designed as a certified room-in-room system (modular strongroom) with a resistance class of RC5 or higher. All openings are monitored not only by opening and glass break sensors, but also by structure-borne sound sensors on walls and ceiling. The intruder alarm system has a VdS Class C certification.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning and construction of the strongroom are carried out by a specialized, certified company. The connection of the highly sensitive sensors to the intruder alarm control panel is designed redundantly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the complete certification documentation of the room-in-room system and the VdS Class C system. The test reports from the installer and the regular maintenance reports are analyzed in detail. A penetration test by an external service provider can be commissioned to validate the overall security.

controls.title: Hazard alarm system

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Battery-operated standalone smoke detectors and a simple door magnetic contact are installed, which triggers a local alarm (siren) when opened.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The devices are from retail and are not networked with each other or connected to an external entity. The batteries must be checked manually and regularly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor tests the function of the smoke detectors and the door contact. They inquire how the regular checking of the batteries is ensured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An appropriate hazard alarm system SHOULD be installed in data media archives. This hazard alarm system SHOULD be regularly tested and maintained. It SHOULD be ensured that the persons who receive hazard notifications are able to react appropriately to alarm messages.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A hazard alarm system that reports at least burglary and fire is installed. The alarm notifications are sent to an internal department (e.g., gatehouse, IT department). A documented plan exists that specifies who takes what steps in the event of an alarm. The system is maintained according to the manufacturer's specifications.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the concept of the hazard alarm system, the maintenance contracts, and the alarm plan. The notification chain to the internal department is checked by a test alarm. It is verified through interviews whether the recipients of the notification know their tasks.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An integrated hazard alarm system is installed, covering burglary (opening and motion detectors), fire (smoke and heat detectors), and water ingress. The system is connected to a 24/7 staffed security control center (internal or external). The response procedures are documented in detail and are regularly practiced.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The system is certified according to VdS Class A or B. The contract with the security control center regulates the intervention times and measures. The exercises and their results are logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the certification of the system and the contract with the security control center. The logs of the last exercises are analyzed. Triggering a test alarm serves to check the entire notification and intervention chain. The configuration of the system can be automatically checked for compliance with the defined security policies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The hazard alarm system is certified according to VdS Class C. It integrates multiple, redundant sensor types (e.g., light barriers, structure-borne sound sensors, early-stage fire detection through aspirating smoke detection systems). Alarms are automatically correlated with the recordings of the video surveillance system and provided to the intervention personnel. The integrity of the system and its communication paths is permanently monitored (sabotage protection).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The planning and installation are carried out by a VdS-certified installer. The correlation of alarm and video data is realized via a hazard management software. The transmission to the control center is carried out via at least two independent, monitored paths.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the complete VdS attestation of the system. The configuration of the hazard management system is checked. The sabotage security is tested by simulating a line interruption. The correlation of alarm and video image is verified by triggering various sensors.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: Data media archives are closed rooms within an institution where data media of any kind are stored. This includes not only data media on which digital information is stored, but also paper documents, films, or other media.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This building block describes the typical threats and information security requirements for a data media archive. The goal is to protect the information located on the data media and other media archived there.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The INF.6 Data Media Archive building block is to be applied to all rooms used as a data media archive.
This building block considers technical and non-technical security requirements for data media archives. Recommendations for correct archiving are not covered in this building block. Information on this can be found in the OPS.1.2.2 Archiving building block.
Within the framework of IT Baseline Protection, no increased fire protection requirements are placed on the archive rooms. However, additional fire protection requirements can be met by the containers in which the data media are stored.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Impermissible temperature and humidity
parts.prose: When storing long-term digital storage media, temperature fluctuations or excessive humidity can lead to data errors and reduced storage life.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Missing or inadequate regulations
parts.prose: If employees do not close or lock the windows and doors after leaving the data media archive, data media or other information can be stolen. Sensitive information could then be viewed or passed on by unauthorized persons. If employees are not sufficiently aware of the relevant regulations, security vulnerabilities can occur. Simply establishing regulations is not enough. They must be observed to ensure smooth operation. Many problems arise when regulations exist but are not known.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unauthorized access to restricted areas
parts.prose: If access controls are missing or inadequate, unauthorized persons can enter a data carrier archive and view, steal, or manipulate sensitive information. This can compromise the availability, confidentiality, and integrity of the archived information. Even if no immediate damage is apparent, business operations can be disrupted.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Theft
parts.prose: Since many data carriers are very portable, it is all the easier to slip them unnoticed into a bag or under clothing and take them away. If there are no copies of the information, the information stored on the stolen data carriers is lost. Furthermore, the persons who stole the data carriers could view and disclose confidential information. This can cause further damage. In most cases, this damage is significantly more severe than the cost of replacement data carriers.

controls.title: Suitable selection and use of an office space (B) [Supervisors]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: An informal check of the suitability as an office space is only carried out for individual areas considered critical. There is no systematic process for the selection and furnishing of office spaces, and aspects such as public traffic are not consistently taken into account.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The selection of office spaces is done ad-hoc, mostly based on availability rather than a security assessment. The Workplace Ordinance is only consulted reactively in case of complaints or obvious defects.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the responsible persons if a process for room selection exists. It is checked on a random basis whether a documented suitability assessment exists for office spaces where sensitive data is processed. The absence of any documentation indicates this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All office spaces are generally selected and furnished in such a way that the Workplace Ordinance is implemented. A basic differentiation according to the protection requirements of the processed information takes place, but is not anchored in a formal concept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a checklist for setting up standard office spaces. For rooms in security-relevant areas (e.g., with public traffic), there are verbal or informal instructions not to use them for processing highly sensitive data.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects a selection of office spaces and compares their furnishing with the requirements of the Workplace Ordinance. It is checked whether there is a basic, understandable logic as to why certain activities take place in certain rooms, even if this is not written down.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only suitable rooms may be used as office spaces. The office spaces must be appropriately selected and furnished for the protection requirements or the protection level of the information processed there. Office spaces with public traffic must not be located in security-relevant areas. The Workplace Ordinance must be implemented for the workplace and for the setup of an office space. This process is defined and is applied repeatably.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A documented procedure for the selection and furnishing of office spaces is established. This procedure considers the protection requirement level of the information to be processed in the respective rooms and contains clear specifications on how the Workplace Ordinance is to be implemented. It is clearly defined which areas are considered security-relevant and therefore may not be used for offices with public traffic.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the documented procedure for room selection. It is checked whether the selection and furnishing of a representative sample of office spaces correspond to this procedure. In particular, it is verified that rooms with public traffic are not located in security-relevant zones and that the furnishing corresponds to the protection requirements of the data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The process for selecting and using office spaces is formalized and is regularly reviewed and adjusted as needed. The suitability of a room is reassessed not only at the initial setup but also periodically or when the protection requirements of the information processed there change. The results of these assessments are documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A room register is maintained in which the maximum permissible protection level of the information to be processed is stored for each office space. Changes in the use or protection requirements of processes trigger an automatic review of the room's suitability. Compliance with the Workplace Ordinance is checked through regular inspections by the occupational safety specialist.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the room register and the documentation of the regular reassessments. It is checked whether a corresponding reassessment of the used premises has taken place in the event of a recent change in the protection requirements of an information domain. The logs of the security inspections are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The management of office spaces is integrated into the central Information Security Management System (ISMS). The selection and furnishing of rooms is a fully automated process coupled with dynamic risk assessment. Physical security measures of the room (access control, alarm system) are technologically linked to the protection requirements of the data processed there.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A building management system controls the allocation of rooms based on the roles of the employees stored in the HR system and the protection requirements of the business processes defined in the ISMS tool. Technical sensors permanently monitor relevant environmental parameters (e.g., unauthorized presence outside of business hours) and report deviations to a SIEM.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the configuration of the building management system. By simulating a change in the protection requirement of a process in the ISMS tool, it is verified live whether the system automatically generates a warning regarding the room's suitability. The SIEM logs are analyzed for relevant alarms from the room monitoring system. The audit can largely be carried out by evaluating system configurations and log data.

controls.title: Closed windows and locked doors (B) [Employees, Building Services]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are occasionally verbally reminded to close windows and lock doors when leaving the offices. There is no formal instruction or regular review.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Closing and locking is done at the discretion of individual employees. There is no uniform practice. Awareness is usually only raised after an incident (e.g. theft).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks employees if they are aware of an instruction to lock offices. An inspection after working hours shows on a random basis whether offices are open or unlocked. The absence of a policy is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a written instruction that requires all employees to close the windows when leaving the office. If confidential documents are in the room, the door must also be locked. However, compliance is not actively monitored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The instruction is given to employees upon hiring or is available on the intranet. It is relied upon that employees will implement the instruction on their own responsibility.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the written instruction shown to them and checks how it has been communicated. During an inspection, the behavior of the employees is observed. It is checked whether the basic expectation has been clearly communicated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A suitable instruction specifies that employees must close all windows when leaving their offices. If confidential information is in the office, the doors must be locked upon leaving. It is regularly checked manually whether the requirements are being met. It is also ensured that fire and smoke protection doors are actually closed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: An official policy on "Behavior when leaving the workplace" is available and all employees are demonstrably informed about it. Supervisors or a security service conduct sporadic but regular inspection rounds after closing time and document their observations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the corresponding instruction and checks its content and distribution list. In addition, the logs of the inspection rounds are viewed. An independent physical inspection of selected areas after closing time verifies the effectiveness of the implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy for locking windows and doors is detailed and part of the regular security briefings. The checks take place according to a fixed schedule, are systematically documented, and violations are followed up on. In areas with public traffic or high protection requirements, self-closing doors are used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Regular e-learning courses on physical security are mandatory for all employees. The inspection rounds are supported by a checklist, and the results are incorporated into a report to security management. The procurement policy for doors provides for self-closing mechanisms as standard for certain zones.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the training materials and participant lists of the security briefings. The system for inspections and the procedure for following up on violations are checked based on the documentation. It is checked whether self-closing doors are actually installed and functioning correctly in designated zones.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The monitoring of windows and doors is largely automated. Technical sensors on windows and doors are linked to the building management system or the alarm system. The system automatically reports open windows or unlocked doors after business hours or when the alarm system is armed. Compliance with the requirements is verified continuously and without gaps.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Magnetic contacts on windows and latch contacts on doors report the status to a central console. When the last employee leaves a zone (detected by the access control system), the system automatically checks the locking status and, in case of deviations, generates an alarm to the security service. This procedure is defined in the security policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the configuration of the monitoring system shown to them. It is tested live whether an open window triggers an alarm after the monitoring is activated. The alarm logs of the last few months are checked for plausibility and correct handling of the incidents. The audit is primarily carried out by analyzing the system configuration and log data.

controls.title: Trailing cables (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Cables are laid on an ad-hoc basis to connect devices. Only cables that pose an obvious and immediate tripping hazard in main traffic routes are temporarily fixed to the floor with adhesive tape.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The cabling is unstructured and does not follow any planning. The responsibility lies with the individual employee. Multiple socket outlets and extension cords are often used improperly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts a visual inspection of the office spaces. Exposed cables, especially in walkways, and the improper use of extension cords are indicators of this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All cables that must run across traffic routes on the floor are covered with simple cable bridges. However, there is no forward-looking planning of connection sockets in the room design, which often leads to long cable runs.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a stock of standard cable bridges that are used by employees or facility management as needed. However, there is no comprehensive cable management policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks whether cable bridges are used for all cables laid on the floor in traffic routes. It is checked whether the placement of the connection sockets is the cause of a high number of "flying" cables.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The power connections and data network access points in the office space are ideally located where the IT equipment is set up. Cables that run across the floor are suitably covered with cable bridges or ducts to avoid tripping hazards and to protect the cables from damage.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When planning office workstations, the position of network and power connections is taken into account. Where floor installation is unavoidable, professional cable management systems (e.g. robust cable ducts) are used. There is an instruction that prescribes the proper installation of cables.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor conducts a visual inspection of the office spaces. It is checked whether the positioning of the connections is sensible and whether suitable covers are used for all floor cabling. The existence and knowledge of the corresponding instruction is randomly checked among the employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a comprehensive cable management concept. When planning offices, structured cabling via underfloor, wall, or ceiling ducts is provided as standard to minimize floor cabling. Temporary cabling requires approval and is removed after a short time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department and facility management work closely together in office design. Floor boxes or cable ducts in the desks are used to enable direct and clean cabling of the workstations. Temporary cable installations for events or conversions are documented and their removal is tracked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor is shown the cable management concept. The implementation of the structured cabling is checked on the basis of construction plans or inspections. The records of temporary cabling are reviewed to verify their proper approval and removal.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The office design generally provides for sufficient power and network connections at each designated workstation, so that flying cabling is completely avoided. Where appropriate, wireless technologies (e.g. WLAN, wireless charging) are used to further reduce the number of cables. Regular safety and occupational health inspections automatically check compliance with the specifications.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The office equipment standards require a high density of permanently installed connection points. The use of extension cords is only permitted in explicitly approved exceptional cases. During safety inspections, photos of cabling are taken and automatically analyzed for violations using AI image recognition.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the office equipment standards. An inspection verifies the almost complete absence of floor cabling and extension cords. The logs and analysis results of the automated review of safety inspections are viewed. Conformity can be demonstrated to a high degree through inspection and document review.

controls.title: Ergonomic workstation (S) [Central Administration, Supervisors]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Ergonomic aspects are only considered superficially and only in response to an explicit complaint from an employee. There is no proactive design or policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Standard office furniture is procured and set up without considering individual needs. Adjustments are only made if health problems are reported.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the process for ergonomic workplace design. The absence of a proactive process and the sole reaction to complaints are indicators of this maturity level. A survey of employees can confirm this.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees receive a standardized basic ergonomic setup such as adjustable chairs. Instructions for correct adjustment are provided, but implementation is up to the employee. The positioning of screens to prevent snooping (shoulder surfing) is not done systematically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Upon hiring, employees receive a leaflet on ergonomics. The office furniture meets basic ergonomic standards but is not individually adapted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that all workstations are equipped with basic ergonomic equipment and that instructions are available. A visual inspection shows whether the positioning of the monitors systematically prevents unauthorized viewing or whether this is left to chance.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The workstations of all employees are ergonomically set up. The screens are positioned in such a way that ergonomic and undisturbed work is possible and they cannot easily be viewed by unauthorized persons. The Display Screen Equipment Regulation is demonstrably implemented and the workstations are individually adjustable for error-free operation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy exists for the design of VDU workstations, which specifies both ergonomic aspects and protection against visual eavesdropping (e.g., through clever positioning or partition walls). Compliance with the VDU workstation regulation is documented as part of the risk assessment. Employees are instructed on how to individually adjust their work equipment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the workplace design policy and the risk assessment documentation. During a walk-through, random checks are performed to determine whether the workstations comply with the requirements, especially the positioning of monitors for protection against visual eavesdropping.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees are proactively offered ergonomic consultations at their workstation. In areas with high public traffic or in open-plan offices, privacy screen filters are used on monitors as a standard measure to increase protection against visual eavesdropping.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The occupational safety specialist or an external service provider regularly conducts consultations and assists with the individual adjustment of workstations. The procurement policy requires the use of privacy screen filters for laptops and for monitors in defined zones.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the records of ergonomic consultations that have been conducted. It is verified whether privacy screen filters are in use as required in the designated areas (e.g., reception, open-plan office spaces).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The ergonomic setup and review of the workstation is a fixed, mandatory part of the onboarding process for new employees. Regular, mandatory training on ergonomics and information security at the workplace (including shoulder surfing) is conducted. Privacy screen filters are standard on all mobile devices and at all workstations in non-enclosed offices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A specialized service provider sets up each workstation individually before a new employee starts. Participation in annual e-learning courses is automatically monitored. The IT department ensures that all procured monitors and laptops are equipped with privacy screen filters.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the process description for onboarding and the training records. A sample of devices is checked for the presence of privacy screen filters. The completeness of the implementation can be verified by inspecting the procurement and onboarding documentation.

controls.title: Tidy Workstation (S) [Employees, Supervisors]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The expectation of a tidy workstation is communicated informally, but there is no policy and no checks. Confidential documents are often left out in the open.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Tidying up is left to the discretion of each individual. There is no awareness-raising for the associated information security risks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: A walk-through of the office premises during the absence of employees (e.g., during the lunch break) shows whether confidential documents, passwords, or data carriers are openly accessible. The absence of a policy confirms this maturity level.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a written "Clean Desk Policy" that instructs all employees to lock away confidential information at the end of the workday and leave their workstation tidy. However, compliance is not checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is published on the intranet and is mentioned during hiring. Implementation is based on trust in the employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the Clean Desk Policy. A walk-through after business hours serves as a random check to assess the actual implementation by employees, even if no internal checks are conducted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees are instructed to leave their workstation tidy and to ensure that unauthorized persons cannot view confidential information. This means that sensitive information is locked away when not in use. Supervisors sporadically check whether sensitive information is openly accessible at workstations.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A clear Clean Desk Policy is established and is part of regular awareness measures. Supervisors are instructed to ensure compliance as part of their supervisory duties and to conduct random checks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the Clean Desk Policy and checks its level of awareness. By interviewing supervisors, it is verified whether they are performing their control function. A physical inspection of workstations serves to review the actual implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the Clean Desk Policy is verified through regular, planned, and documented inspection rounds by security services or supervisors. Identified violations are systematically recorded and reported to the respective supervisors for follow-up. The policy is part of the employee performance review.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a fixed schedule for clean desk checks. The results are summarized in a monthly security report and presented to management. In case of repeated violations, discussions are held with the employees concerned.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the logs of the inspection rounds and the monthly security reports. The procedure for reporting and following up on violations is examined for its effectiveness. The documentation must prove systematic and consistent implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organization follows a "Clear Screen and Clean Desk Policy" that is strictly enforced. The use of paper documents is actively minimized through digitization workflows. The checks are integrated into the daily closing-down procedures and are carried out comprehensively. Violations have defined and communicated consequences.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to locking away documents, locking the screen when leaving the desk is strictly required and technically supported (e.g., through short timeout periods). The security service uses a daily checklist for all offices. In case of a violation, a notification is left at the workstation, and a report is triggered to the supervisor and the HR department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the digitization policies and the checklists of the closing-down service. The system configurations for the automatic screen lock are verified. The records are used to demonstrate the consistent follow-up of violations. The high process maturity should be demonstrable through comprehensive documentation and automation.

controls.title: Appropriate Storage of Official Documents and Data Media (S) [Employees, Facility Management]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Lockable containers are available (e.g., in mobile pedestals), but there are no instructions as to which documents or data media must be stored in them. Their use is inconsistent and left to chance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The decision of what to lock away is made by each employee individually, without any criteria. Often, only personal belongings are locked up, but not official documents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects workstations and checks whether confidential documents are left in the open, even though lockable furniture is available. The absence of a corresponding policy or instruction is a clear indicator.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees are instructed to store confidential documents and data media in the designated, standard-issue lockable desk containers when not in use. However, what qualifies as 'confidential' is not clearly defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every workstation is equipped with a mobile pedestal with a lock. A general instruction for its use is communicated, but there is no information classification that would allow for clear assignment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that all workstations are equipped with lockable containers and that a general instruction exists. By interviewing employees, it is determined whether there is uncertainty about which specific documents must be locked away.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are instructed to keep confidential documents and data media locked away when not in use. Suitable lockable containers are provided in the offices or their vicinity for this purpose. This instruction is checked as part of clean desk inspections.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy exists that clearly defines what is considered confidential information and how it must be stored. Every employee has access to a personal, lockable container. Additionally, larger, lockable cabinets are available for departments.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor has the relevant policy presented to them. It is checked whether the provided containers are appropriate for the type and volume of documents. The logs of the clean desk inspections are reviewed to see if correct storage is also being checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on an information classification policy, it is clearly regulated which type of information must be stored in which type of security container (e.g., lockable cabinet, burglar-proof safe). The availability and correct use of these containers are regularly audited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In addition to standard office furniture, high-security cabinets or safes (e.g., for personnel documents or contracts) are provided depending on the protection requirements. Key management for these containers is formally regulated and documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the information classification policy and the key management concept. It is checked on a random basis whether documents with high protection requirements are actually stored in the prescribed, higher-grade security containers. The documentation of key issuance is inspected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Access to security containers is managed and logged via an electronic locking system. An inventory of the stored, highly confidential physical documents and data media is maintained. The organization actively pursues a strategy to reduce paper documents ("paperless office") to minimize the risks of physical documents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Cabinets and safes are equipped with electronic locks that are managed via the central access control system. Access is granted on a personal basis, and every opening event is logged. Workflows for digitizing incoming mail and for digital record-keeping are established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor analyzes the configuration and log files of the electronic locking system. The inventory of physical documents is compared with the contents of a sample of security containers. The progress of the "paperless" strategy is reviewed using key performance indicators.

controls.title: Use of Anti-Theft Devices (H) [Employees]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Anti-theft devices such as cable locks are available on request for individual, particularly exposed devices, but are not used systematically.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A few laptops or PCs, e.g., at a trade fair booth, are secured with a Kensington lock. This is not used in normal office operations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the availability and use of anti-theft devices. An inspection of publicly accessible areas shows whether devices there are unsecured. The absence of a policy and only sporadic use are indicators.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All desktop PCs in areas with public access are secured with cable locks by default. For other devices such as laptops or in internal areas, there is no binding regulation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The IT department secures new desktop PCs with a lock when they are set up in reception or consultation areas. Laptops used by employees are not secured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks all devices in areas with public access and verifies whether the desktop PCs are secured. It is checked whether a clear demarcation of the areas in which security is mandatory exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In areas with public access or if access to rooms cannot be adequately restricted, anti-theft devices are used for all IT systems (including laptops and peripheral devices). This is stipulated in a policy and employees are obliged to use them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a policy that defines in which zones (e.g., all freely accessible areas) and for which devices (e.g., desktops, laptops, projectors) anti-theft devices are to be used. Corresponding cable locks are issued to all affected employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests to see the policy on the use of anti-theft devices. During an inspection of the defined zones, random checks are carried out to determine whether all relevant devices are secured as prescribed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a comprehensive, company-wide policy that stipulates that all stationary IT equipment and all laptops that remain in the office overnight must be secured with a physical anti-theft device, regardless of the zone. Compliance is checked through regular inspections.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Every IT workstation is equipped with a cable lock for the PC/docking station and the monitor by default. Employees with laptops also receive a lock. The clean desk inspections also include checking the correct use of the anti-theft devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the company-wide policy and the logs of the inspection rounds. During an inspection, it is checked in various areas (not just publicly accessible ones) whether the devices are secured accordingly.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the universal use of physical anti-theft devices, all valuable IT assets are marked with tamper-proof labels and recorded in an asset management system. A technical system (e.g., NAC or WLAN tracking) triggers an alarm if a device is unexpectedly disconnected from the network or removed from its assigned area.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Each device is inventoried upon procurement and provided with an asset tag. The Network Access Control (NAC) system is configured to associate the physical switch port with a device identifier (MAC address). If the device is connected to another port, access is blocked and a security incident is triggered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the asset management system and compares the entries with a physical sample of devices. The configuration of the NAC system or a comparable tracking solution is analyzed. A device is removed on a trial basis to verify the correct triggering of the alarm.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose: An office space is the area within an institution where one or more employees are located to perform their duties. This module describes the typical threats and information security requirements for an office space.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The objective of the module is to protect the information that is processed in office spaces.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The INF.7 Office Workspace module is to be applied to every room in the information network that is used as an office workstation.
This module considers technical and non-technical security requirements for office spaces. Recommendations on how the IT systems in these rooms can be configured and secured are not covered in this module. Information on this can be found, among other places, in the SYS.2.1 General Client module and in the operating system-specific modules.
Requirements for buildings in general are not part of this module. These can be found in the INF.1 General Building module, which must always be applied to rooms and buildings. The cabling of office spaces is also not addressed. For this, the INF.12 Cabling module must be considered.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Unauthorized access
parts.prose: If access controls are missing or inadequate, unauthorized persons can enter an office space and steal sensitive data, steal devices, or manipulate them. This can compromise the availability, confidentiality, or integrity of devices and information. Even if no immediate damage is apparent, business operations can be disrupted. For example, it must be investigated how such an incident was possible, whether damage occurred, or whether manipulations were carried out.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Impairment due to unfavorable working conditions
parts.prose: An office space not set up according to ergonomic principles or an unfavorable working environment are problematic. Both can lead to employees being unable to work undisturbed or to use the IT provided not at all or not optimally. Disturbances can be noise, heavy customer traffic, unfavorable lighting, or poor ventilation. This can limit workflows and the potential of employees. Errors can also creep into the work, which can reduce the integrity of data.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Manipulation by cleaning and external personnel or visitors
parts.prose: For smaller or shorter meetings, it is usually more efficient to receive the visitor in the office. However, the visitor, as well as cleaning and external personnel, could view internal information in various ways, endanger business processes, and manipulate IT systems. Anything is possible, from improper handling of technical equipment to attempting to "play" with IT systems to theft of documents or IT components. For example, a plug connection could be accidentally disconnected by cleaning staff, or water could get into the IT. Documents can also be misplaced or even disposed of with the waste.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Manipulation or destruction of IT, accessories, information, and software in the office space
parts.prose: Attackers may try to manipulate or destroy IT systems, accessories, and other data carriers for various reasons. The later they are discovered by employees or the institution itself, the more comprehensive the perpetrators' knowledge, and the more profound the consequences for a work process, the more effective the attacks are. For example, sensitive data of employees could be viewed without authorization. Data carriers or IT systems could also be destroyed. Significant downtime and process restrictions could be the result.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Theft
parts.prose:
As IT devices become more and more portable, it is all the easier to slip them into a bag unnoticed. The theft of data carriers, IT systems, accessories, software, or information incurs costs for replacement. But resources are also needed to restore a workable state. On the other hand, losses can also arise due to a lack of availability. In addition, the person who stole the IT devices could view and disclose confidential information. This can cause further damage. In many cases, this damage weighs significantly more heavily than the purely material loss of the IT device.
In addition to expensive IT systems, mobile devices that can be transported inconspicuously and easily are also frequently stolen. If the office spaces are not locked, not supervised, or the IT systems are not sufficiently secured, the technology can be stolen quickly and inconspicuously.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Flying cabling
parts.prose: Depending on where the connection points for sockets, power supply, and the data network are located in the office space, cables could be laid across the room, even over traffic routes. Such "flying" cables are not only tripping hazards where people can get injured. If people get caught on them, IT devices can also be damaged.

controls.title: Securing official documents at the home office workstation (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Official documents and data carriers at the home office workstation are only sporadically kept safe from theft, for example in a drawer without a lock. There is no consistent regulation or implementation thereof.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this level, the risk of theft or unauthorized access to documents is recognized, but addressed only sporadically and inconsistently. No lockable containers are provided or their use mandated.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through an interview with the employee and an inspection of the workstation that no systematic precautions have been taken for the secure storage of documents and that they are partially openly accessible.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Lockable containers are available at the home office workstation. There is a basic instruction to secure sensitive documents, but compliance with a consistent "Clean Desk Policy" is not checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution provides simple lockable mobile pedestals or cabinets. The responsibility for consistent use and adherence to a clean desk policy lies entirely with the employee, without any control mechanisms.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that lockable containers are available. Through an interview, it is determined whether the employee knows the instruction to use them. A random check can show that the implementation is not always consistent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Official documents and data carriers MUST be stored at the home office in such a way that unauthorized persons cannot access them. Therefore, sufficient lockable containers (e.g., lockable mobile pedestals or cabinets) MUST be available. All employees MUST leave their workstations tidy and ensure that no confidential information is freely accessible (Clean Desk Policy).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal policy on secure storage and the clean desk policy for the home office workstation is created and communicated to all relevant employees. The institution ensures that the containers provided have an appropriate lock quality. Adherence to the policy is stipulated as part of the teleworking agreement.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the existence and communication of the storage and clean desk policy. By reviewing the teleworking agreement and interviewing the employee, they verify that the requirements are known. A random, announced video inspection of the workstation at the end of the workday can be used to check implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the clean desk policy is regularly checked through documented self-assessments by employees. The provided lockable containers meet a defined security class. Access to documents with high protection needs is regulated by separate, specially secured containers.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees complete a quarterly checklist on compliance with security regulations at the home office workstation. Cabinets with certified security locks are procured for storage. Documents are classified and assigned to different storage requirements depending on their protection needs.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the completed self-assessment checklists. They check the specifications of the locking systems used and compare them with the internal requirements. In addition, it is checked whether the classification of documents and the corresponding storage rules are implemented consistently.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Only certified high-security safes (safes) are used for the storage of official documents and data carriers. The workroom itself is access-controlled, for example, by a smart lock system with logging. All printed confidential documents are automatically watermarked to trace their origin.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution procures and installs high-security safes according to EN 1143-1 at the home office workstation.
