The access control system for the workroom is linked to central monitoring. The printing infrastructure is configured to apply invisible watermarks (e.g., user ID, timestamp) to all printouts.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the certificates of the high-security safes. They check the log data of the access control system for unauthorized access attempts. Randomly selected printed documents are examined for the presence and correctness of the digital watermark. An automated test could check the print logs for the successful application of the watermark policy.

controls.title: Transport of work material to the home office workstation (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no specific regulations for the transport of work material. Employees transport data carriers and documents at their own discretion, often unsecured and visible to third parties.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: At this stage, there is a lack of awareness of the risks of transport. Materials are, for example, carried loosely in a car or in an open bag on public transport.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through questioning, the auditor determines that the employee is not aware of any transport guidelines and that no special means of transport (e.g. lockable bags) have been provided.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general instruction to keep work materials protected during transport, for example in a closed bag. However, electronic data carriers are not encrypted by default.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A simple, non-lockable laptop bag or backpack is used for transport. The instruction is part of the general security briefing, but its compliance is not monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks about the known transport instructions. They randomly check whether the hard disk encryption (e.g., BitLocker) is active on carried laptops and find that this is not consistently the case.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be regulated which data carriers and documents may be processed at the home office workstation and transported back and forth between the institution and the home office workstation. In general, data carriers and other documents MUST be transported securely. These regulations MUST be communicated to the employees in a suitable manner.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal policy defines which types of information may leave the workplace. Lockable bags or cases are provided for transport. It is mandatory that all mobile data carriers (laptops, USB sticks) must be encrypted by default and verifiably.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the transport policy and checks whether the employees have demonstrably received and understood it (e.g., through training records). They verify the issuance of lockable transport containers. The encryption of mobile devices is checked via a central management tool (MDM/UEM) or by a manual spot check. An automated script could query and report the encryption status of all managed devices.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The transport regulations are differentiated according to the protection needs of the data. For the transport of documents with high protection needs, tamper-evident or tamper-proof containers (e.g., security bags with seals) are used. The transport of critical data carriers is logged.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The transport policy contains a matrix that prescribes the respective means of transport and security measures based on the data classification. The institution procures tamper-evident seals or bags. A formal handover protocol is kept for the transport of, for example, backup data carriers.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the differentiated transport policy for its traceability. They check the use of seals and randomly review the transport logs for completeness and correctness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The physical transport of documents with high protection requirements is generally prohibited; access is exclusively via secure remote connections. For all other necessary transports, lockable, GPS-trackable cases are used. Access to data media is protected by multi-factor authentication in addition to encryption.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy explicitly prohibits physical transport. The transport cases used are equipped with an IoT module for location tracking, which sends an alarm to a central office if opened without authorization. For example, accessing encrypted USB drives requires a combination of a password and a hardware token.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the policy enforces the transport ban and that no exceptions are made. They check the functionality of the GPS tracking and the alarm function of the cases. Furthermore, the configuration of the multi-factor authentication for data media is checked. An automated test could query the tracking platform to verify the conformity of the case locations.

controls.title: Protection against unauthorized access at the home office (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are verbally reminded to lock the front door, but there are no formal instructions to protect the specific work area from unauthorized access by third parties (e.g., family members, visitors).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Protection is limited to the general measures that the employee takes privately anyway. It is not taken into account that in the home environment, non-malicious third parties (e.g., children) could also gain unsupervised access to company devices or documents.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through questioning that no specific rules for access protection of the workplace exist or have been communicated.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a written regulation that the workplace must be secured when leaving it (e.g., locking the computer). Measures for the physical protection of the room or apartment (doors, windows) are mentioned, but not further specified or checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The telework agreement contains a clause that generally obliges the employee to protect the workplace. No specific requirements are made for the locking technology of doors or windows.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the telework agreement. They ask the employee how they secure the workplace and find that the measures are based on a basic level (e.g., standard front door lock).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees MUST be informed which regulations and measures for burglary and access protection are to be observed. It MUST be pointed out that windows must be closed and doors locked when the home office is unoccupied. It MUST be ensured that unauthorized persons cannot enter the home office and access official IT and documents at any time.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A detailed policy is created and verifiably brought to the attention of the employees. This policy requires that the workplace, if it is not in a separate, lockable room, must be secured when leaving so that third parties (including family members) cannot access IT and documents (e.g., by locking away the devices). These measures MUST be reviewed at reasonable time intervals, but at least when domestic circumstances change.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy on access protection and the proof of acknowledgment by the employees. They conduct a survey or a self-assessment in which the employee confirms the implementation of the measures. Changes in domestic circumstances (e.g., moving) are tracked as a trigger for a new review.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It is mandatory that the home office be set up in a separate, lockable room. The quality of the locks on doors and windows of the room or apartment must meet a defined minimum standard (e.g., RC2 classification). The presence of non-company personnel in the workroom during working hours is prohibited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The telework agreement prescribes a separate room and requires proof of the quality of the burglary protection (e.g., through a manufacturer's certificate or a craftsman's invoice). Employees are explicitly instructed not to receive visitors in the study while they are working.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests evidence for the separate room (e.g., floor plan, photos) and the burglary protection. Compliance with the rule prohibiting outside persons is addressed and randomly checked during employee performance reviews.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The workroom is equipped with a burglar alarm system and/or video surveillance connected to a central monitoring station, which is active when the employee is absent. Access to the room is controlled via a biometric or smart lock system with central logging. The physical security of the workplace is regularly audited by an external security service provider.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution commissions the installation and maintenance of the burglar alarm system and the access control system. The logs of the access system are automatically analyzed for anomalies. There is a contract with a security service provider for regular, including unannounced, physical checks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the audit reports of the external security service provider. They check the configuration and alarm logs of the burglar alarm system as well as the access logs of the locking system. An automated test could check the log data of the access system for compliance with the working time models.

controls.title: Suitable furnishing of the home office (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution provides recommendations for ergonomic furnishing but leaves the implementation entirely to the employee. Basic security aspects such as burglary protection are not systematically addressed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A leaflet with ergonomic tips is provided. There is no financial support or provision of office furniture. The employee uses their private furnishings.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the leaflet has been distributed. No further check of the actual furnishings takes place.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The home office SHOULD be separated from the private areas of the apartment by a suitable room layout. The home office SHOULD be furnished with office furniture that meets ergonomic requirements. Likewise, the home office SHOULD be protected against burglaries by suitable technical security measures. The protective measures SHOULD be adapted to the local conditions and the existing protection requirements.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The institution offers a catalog of ergonomic office furniture (chair, desk) from which employees can choose, or provides a budget for it. A policy is created that defines minimum requirements for spatial separation and basic burglary protection (e.g., lockable windows and doors). The implementation is confirmed by a self-declaration from the employee.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the policy for furnishing the workplace. They verify the processes for providing furniture or budgets. The self-declarations of the employees are randomly checked for plausibility, e.g., by requesting photos of the workplace.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal risk assessment for the home office is carried out, which includes ergonomics, lighting, noise, and psychological stress factors. Based on the assessment, specific, binding measures are implemented. The requirements for burglary protection are clearly defined (e.g., resistance class RC2 for windows/doors on the ground floor).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The risk assessment is carried out by an occupational safety specialist (or a similarly trained person) using a standardized checklist, possibly via video. Necessary equipment, such as special lighting or improved locks, is procured and financed by the institution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documented risk assessments and the resulting action plans. They randomly check whether the defined measures (e.g., proof of RC2 windows) have been implemented.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The home office is approved by an external, certified auditor for occupational safety and building security before commissioning. All furnishings and security installations are provided, professionally installed, and regularly maintained by the institution to ensure a consistently high standard.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a framework agreement with a service provider that handles the complete furnishing, acceptance, and maintenance of home offices. This also includes the installation of burglar alarm systems or special soundproofing measures, if required.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the acceptance protocols and certificates of the external auditor. They check the maintenance contracts and records. The effectiveness of the measures is verified through regular, including unannounced, on-site audits.

controls.title: Disposal of confidential information at the home office (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are instructed not to dispose of confidential documents in household waste, but to bring them to the institution for destruction. However, no special containers or deadlines are specified for this.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The responsibility for the secure temporary storage and transport of the documents to be destroyed lies entirely with the employee. This can lead to an insecure accumulation of confidential material in the home office.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks the employee about the disposal process and finds that while it is known, there are no supporting resources or controls.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Confidential information SHOULD be disposed of securely. A special security policy SHOULD therefore regulate how sensitive material is to be disposed of. The necessary disposal options SHOULD be available.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A data destruction policy is created. Employees are either provided with a shredder that meets an appropriate security level (e.g., P-4 according to DIN 66399), or sealable collection containers are issued, which are regularly exchanged for empty ones at the institution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the data destruction policy. They verify the provision of shredders or collection containers. The security level of the shredders is checked through questioning and inspection of procurement documents. An automated system could manage the inventory and assignment of the devices to the employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The disposal requirements are differentiated according to the protection needs of the information. For information with a high protection need, the use of a shredder with a higher security level (e.g., P-5) or the mandatory return in sealed containers is prescribed. The destruction is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy includes a matrix that specifies the required particle size (security level) of the shredder depending on the data classification. Employees working with highly confidential data receive appropriate devices. The return of sealed containers is logged.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the differentiated policy. They check the specifications of the shredders in use and compare them with the requirements. The logs for the return of collection containers are checked for completeness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A certified external service provider is commissioned to regularly collect sealed security containers with confidential materials directly from employees' homes and verifiably destroy them. The private purchase and use of shredders is prohibited to ensure a consistently high quality of destruction.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: There is a contract with a disposal company certified according to DIN 66399. The service provider supplies the security containers and handles all logistics. The employees receive a certificate of destruction for each collection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the contract and the certifications of the disposal service provider. They check the destruction certificates for completeness and correctness on a random basis. Employee satisfaction with the process is determined via surveys.

controls.title: Handling of official documents with high protection needs at the home office (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When processing information with high protection needs, consideration SHOULD be given to refraining from using a home office entirely. Otherwise, the home office SHOULD be protected by extended, high-quality technical security measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A formal process for risk assessment and approval for processing data with high protection needs in the home office is established. The approval is linked to the implementation of defined additional security measures, such as the use of a dedicated, lockable room and a security safe.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the approval process and the risk assessments carried out. They verify that the defined additional protective measures have been implemented for approved cases, e.g. by inspecting evidence or photos.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The processing of information with high protection needs at the home office is only permitted after a documented, positive security check of the workplace. The prescribed, extended security measures must include an intruder alarm system, certified burglary protection for doors and windows (e.g. RC3) and the use of privacy screens on all monitors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The security check is carried out and documented by the Information Security Officer (ISO) or a specialist commissioned by them. The institution finances and organizes the installation of the required security technology. The correct application of the privacy screens is checked.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor inspects the records of the security checks. They check the evidence of the installation of the intruder alarm system and the certified components. The installation and effectiveness of the privacy screens are verified during an on-site inspection or via video review.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The processing of information with very high protection needs at the home office is strictly prohibited. Exceptions require approval at management level and are only possible if the home office has been certified by an external auditor as a physical security zone (comparable to a server room). This includes measures such as biometric access control, video surveillance and, if necessary, protection against eavesdropping.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A policy explicitly prohibits the processing and defines a strict, multi-stage exception approval process. For approved exceptions, an external security service provider is commissioned with the design, implementation and certification of the required high-security measures. This can also include the setup of a dedicated, monitored network connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks compliance with the general prohibition. They check the exception approvals for compliance with the defined process. The certificates and audit reports of the external security auditor for the upgraded workplaces are inspected and evaluated.

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Teleworkers, freelancers, or self-employed individuals typically work from home offices. Unlike the workplace in the office, these employees use a workplace in their own property. It must be possible to sufficiently separate the professional environment from the private one. If employees use home offices permanently, various legal requirements must also be met, for example, the workplaces must comply with occupational health and ergonomic regulations.
At a home office, the same infrastructural security cannot be assumed as is found in the office premises of an institution. For example, the workplace is often also accessible to visitors or family members. Therefore, measures must be taken to achieve a level of security comparable to that of an office space.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: This module shows how the infrastructure of a home office can be set up and operated securely. The core objective of the module is to protect the institution's information at the home office.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The INF.8 Home Office module is to be applied to all rooms that are used as a teleworking place.
The module contains fundamental requirements that must be observed and fulfilled to counteract the threats to a home office. However, it only defines specific requirements for the infrastructure of a fixed workplace with access by third parties. Security requirements for the IT systems used, e.g., clients and multifunction devices, and especially for the technical aspects of teleworking, e.g., communication links, are not the subject of this module. They are described in the OPS.1.2.4 Teleworking module or in the respective system-specific modules.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.1. Missing or inadequate regulations for the home office
parts.prose: Since a home office is located outside the institution, employees there are largely on their own. As a result, missing or inadequate regulations for the home office environment can lead to IT problems with longer downtimes. If IT problems cannot be resolved via remote administration, for example, a person from IT operations at the institution must first drive to the home office to fix the problems there. If the handling of internal and confidential information at the home office is not regulated in a comprehensible manner, employees could store such information incorrectly. If it cannot be prevented that information is spied on or modified, the confidentiality and integrity of the information may be at risk.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.2. Unauthorized access to sensitive rooms of the home office
parts.prose:
Rooms of a home office in which sensitive information is stored and processed or in which sensitive devices are stored or operated become sensitive rooms. If unauthorized persons can enter these rooms unsupervised, the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of this data and information are significantly endangered.
Examples:
• A home office is located in a separate study, but is not consistently locked. When small children were briefly unsupervised, they played in the unlocked study. In the process, important documents were used as drawing paper.
• While a person was engrossed in project work at the home office, a visitor arrived unexpectedly. While the person was making coffee in the kitchen, the visitor wanted to quickly look something up on the internet on the unlocked client and accidentally infected it with malware.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.3. Impairment of IT use due to unfavorable working conditions at the home office
parts.prose: A home office not set up according to ergonomic principles or an unfavorable working environment can lead to people not being able to work there undisturbed. The IT used may also not be usable or not be used optimally. Noise, disturbances from family members, and poor lighting or ventilation can have an adverse effect. This limits the workflows and potential of employees. Errors could also creep into the work. In addition, the protection of the integrity of data can be diminished.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.4. Unsecured transport of files and data carriers
parts.prose:
When documents, data carriers, or files are transported between the institution and the home office, this data and information can be lost. They could also be stolen, read, or manipulated by unauthorized third parties. The transport of files and data carriers can be inadequately secured in various ways:
• If unique copies are transported and there is no corresponding backup, goals and tasks cannot be achieved as planned if the unique copy is lost.
• If unencrypted data carriers fall into the wrong hands, this can lead to a serious loss of confidentiality.
• If there is insufficient access protection during transport, files or data carriers can be copied or manipulated unnoticed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.5. Improper Disposal of Data Carriers and Documents
parts.prose: If it is not possible to dispose of data carriers and documents appropriately at the home office, they might simply be thrown into the household trash. However, valuable information can be extracted from this, which can be specifically misused for blackmail attempts or corporate espionage. The consequences range from loss of knowledge to existential threats to the institution, for example, if important contracts are not secured or business partnerships fail as a result.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.6. Manipulation or Destruction of IT, Accessories, Information, and Software at the Home Office
parts.prose: IT devices, accessories, information, and software used at the home office can sometimes be more easily manipulated or destroyed than within the institution. The home office is often accessible to relatives and family visitors. Also, the institution's central protective measures, such as gatekeeping services, are not present here. If IT devices, accessories, information, or software are manipulated or destroyed, employees at the home office are often only able to work to a limited extent. Furthermore, destroyed IT components, information, and software solutions may need to be replaced, which requires both financial and time resources.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: 2.7. Increased Risk of Theft at the Home Office
parts.prose: The home office is usually not as well-secured as a workplace in a company or a public authority. Due to elaborate precautions such as security doors or a gatekeeping service, the risk of someone breaking into the building without authorization is much lower there than in a private home. During a burglary, items that can be sold quickly and easily are usually stolen first. This can also include work-related IT equipment. However, the information on the stolen work-related IT systems often has a higher value than the IT systems themselves. Third parties could try to achieve a higher profit through blackmail or by passing the data on to competing companies than by selling the hardware.

controls.title: INF.9.A1 Suitable selection and use of a mobile workplace (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no regulations whatsoever regarding the selection and use of mobile workplaces. The responsibility lies entirely with the individual employee, who acts at their own discretion and may neglect security aspects.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No specific measures are taken. There is complete reliance on the "common sense" of the employees, without supporting them with guidelines or assistance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviews with employees and managers reveal that there are no policies, instructions, or tools for the secure selection and use of mobile workplaces.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are basic, mostly undocumented instructions for using mobile workplaces. Employees are verbally advised not to have confidential conversations or leave documents exposed in obviously insecure environments, such as public places.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The instructions are usually passed on verbally during the onboarding of new employees. There is no formal documentation, no checklists, and no systematic review of compliance.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor asks a selection of employees whether they have received instructions on security for mobile work and what these instructions are. It is checked whether there is a basic awareness of the main risks, but without verifying the existence of formal processes.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST require its employees to select and use mobile workstations in an appropriate manner. Properties and exclusion criteria for mobile workstations MUST be defined. At a minimum, it MUST be regulated under which workplace conditions information requiring protection may be processed, how employees can protect themselves from unauthorized viewing by third parties, whether a permanent network and power supply must be available, and which workplace environments are completely prohibited.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The regulations are clearly documented in a policy for mobile working. The criteria for working environments are described in detail (e.g. noise level, lighting, ergonomics, lockable rooms). A checklist is provided to employees for evaluating potential mobile workplaces.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the binding policy for mobile working and the associated checklists. Through interviews and inspections of the workplaces used, it is checked on a random basis whether employees know and apply the regulations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to the defined regulations, the criteria for suitable workplaces are reviewed regularly, at least annually, and updated based on new threats or experiences. Employees are actively and repeatedly trained to recognize unsafe environments. There is a formal process to approve exceptions for working in potentially unsafe environments (e.g. at trade fairs) by defining additional protective measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The policy is reviewed and adapted annually or on an ad hoc basis. Training is offered as e-learning courses, the completion of which is tracked. A form for applying for exceptions is available on the intranet and the approval process is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the existence and up-to-dateness of the policy, the training materials, and the proof of participation. The processes and documentation for granted exceptions are inspected and checked for plausibility.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution provides a curated and maintained list of audited and approved mobile work locations (e.g. co-working spaces with security certification). The use of mobile devices is technically restricted so that certain high-security applications can only be run when the device is in a trusted network or at a GPS-verified, secure location.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The list of approved work locations is maintained and kept up to date through regular on-site security audits. The technical enforcement of location-based security is implemented via a Mobile Device Management (MDM) or Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) solution with geofencing capabilities.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the list of approved work locations and the corresponding audit reports. The configuration of the MDM/UEM solution is checked to verify the correct implementation of the geofencing rules. An automated test is performed by attempting to launch a protected application from an unauthorized location.

controls.title: INF.9.A2 Regulations for mobile workplaces (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no regulations whatsoever as to which information or IT components may leave the institution. Employees decide at their own discretion what to take with them for their work.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken. There is no awareness of the risks of uncontrolled information transport.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Interviews reveal that there are no policies or informal rules about carrying company property and information.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is an informal, undocumented rule that "particularly secret" documents should not be taken home. However, there are no clear criteria for what is considered "particularly secret" and the rule is not actively communicated or enforced. A log of devices taken off-site is not kept.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The rule is passed on verbally from supervisors to employees. There are no awareness-raising measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews, the auditor determines that there is a vague understanding of how to handle sensitive data outside the office, but that this is not based on a documented regulation and is not consistent.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For all work on the go, it MUST be regulated which information may be transported and processed outside the institution and what protective measures must be taken. It MUST be regulated which IT systems and data carriers may be taken along and by whom. It MUST be logged when and by whom which mobile devices were used off-site. Users MUST be made aware of the value of the information and systems and trained accordingly.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The regulations are part of the security policy for mobile working. An issue log, e.g. in the form of an Excel list or a simple tool, is maintained by the IT department. Awareness and training are provided as part of the general security awareness training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the relevant policy and checks the issue log for completeness and up-to-dateness. By interviewing employees, it is checked on a random basis whether the regulations are known and whether they have participated in the relevant training courses.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The regulations for data transport and processing are linked to the protection needs assessment and data classification. For each data class, it is clearly defined whether and under what conditions (e.g., only with encrypted devices) processing outside the institution is permitted. The issuance log is digital and automatically reminds about overdue returns of loaner devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The data classification policy contains an appendix with instructions for mobile working. The issuance log is maintained via an IT asset management system that can send automated notifications. The training is mandatory for all mobile employees and concludes with a test.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the regulations against the data classification policy. The functionality of the digital issuance log, including the notification feature, is verified. The training records and test results are reviewed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with data transport regulations is technically enforced by a Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solution. The DLP solution prevents, for example, the copying of data classified as "strictly confidential" to unencrypted USB drives. Access to internal resources from outside is only possible for devices that pass a positive compliance and security state check (Posture Assessment) via a UEM solution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A client- and network-based DLP solution is implemented and the rules are configured according to the data classification. The UEM solution checks the device status (e.g., patch level, enabled encryption, activated antivirus protection) before establishing a VPN connection.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the DLP and UEM solution and the defined rules. Practical tests are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the technical controls (e.g., attempting to send a protected file or to connect from a non-compliant device).

controls.title: INF.9.A3 Physical and Logical Access Control (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no instructions for the physical protection of devices and documents or for locking IT systems at the mobile workplace. Devices and documents are often left unattended and unlocked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken for physical and logical access control at the mobile workplace. People are relying on luck.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through observation and interviews, it is determined that there are no rules and that insecure behavior is the norm.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are verbally instructed to lock their screen when they leave their desk. There is no formal regulation or verification. The rule to secure items when absent (e.g., on a train) is known, but not documented and is followed inconsistently.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The instruction to lock the screen is part of the informal onboarding process. There are no technical enforcement measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews that the instruction to lock the screen is known. However, random observations show inconsistent implementation.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees MUST be informed of the regulations for burglary and access protection to be observed at the mobile workplace. When the mobile workplace is unoccupied, windows and doors MUST be locked. If this is not possible (e.g., on a train), employees MUST securely store or carry all documents and IT systems with them. If the workplace is left even for a short time, the IT systems in use MUST be locked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The regulations are documented in a policy for mobile working and are verifiably brought to the employees' attention. The screen lock is realized by a simple key combination (e.g., Win+L), the use of which is trained.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy. Through interviews and unannounced observations (where possible), random checks are made to see if employees know the rules and consistently lock their devices when they leave their desk.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All mobile IT systems are configured to lock automatically after a short period of inactivity (e.g., maximum 5 minutes). This policy is enforced centrally. Employees are also equipped with physical security measures such as Kensington locks and are trained in their use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The automatic screen lock is configured via a Mobile Device Management (MDM) solution or Group Policy Objects (GPOs) and cannot be disabled by the user. The issuance of cable locks is documented.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the central configuration of the automatic screen lock in the management console. It is checked whether the relevant employees are equipped with physical security devices and know how to use them.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unlocking devices requires strong multi-factor authentication that includes at least one biometric factor (fingerprint, facial recognition). The MDM solution is capable of remotely locking or wiping (Remote Lock/Wipe) a device if it is reported lost or is located in an unsafe place for an extended period. The use of privacy screens is mandatory for all mobile devices.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The MFA requirement is enforced via MDM policies. The process for Remote Lock/Wipe is defined and tested, and the responsible personnel are trained. Privacy screens are issued as standard equipment to all mobile employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the MDM configuration regarding MFA requirements and the remote wipe function. It is verified that the remote wipe process has been documented and tested. The provision of privacy screens on devices is checked on a random basis.

controls.title: INF.9.A4 Working with third-party IT systems (B)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no regulations for the use of third-party IT systems. Employees use private or public computers (e.g., in internet cafes or hotels) for business purposes without being aware of the risks.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken. The use of third-party systems is common practice.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews with employees, it is determined that the use of third-party systems for business purposes is common and that there are no policies regarding this.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general, verbally communicated instruction to avoid using third-party IT systems whenever possible. However, there are no specific instructions on how to behave if use is unavoidable, or how to delete temporary data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The instruction is passed on informally. There are no training sessions or technical aids.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through interviews that employees have been instructed to avoid third-party systems but have no further knowledge or tools for emergencies.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution MUST regulate how employees are allowed to work with non-institutional IT systems. All mobile employees MUST be educated about the dangers of third-party IT systems. The regulations MUST specify whether and how information worthy of protection may be processed on third-party IT systems. It MUST also be ensured that all temporary data created during this process is deleted after use.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The regulations are documented in the security policy for mobile working. The education is provided through awareness campaigns. Instructions are provided on how to securely delete browser caches and temporary files in common operating systems.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the corresponding regulations in the security policy. It is checked whether the employees have been informed about the risks (e.g., through proof of awareness measures). Through interviews, the knowledge about the secure deletion of temporary data is queried on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For cases where working on a third-party system is absolutely necessary, a secure, containerized work environment is provided. This environment ensures that no data remains on the host system.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees are provided with a bootable USB stick with a hardened live operating system (e.g., a customized Linux distribution) and encrypted persistent storage. All network connections from this environment are mandatorily routed through the institution's own VPN.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the concept and technical implementation of the secure work environment on the USB stick. It is verified that this solution has been issued to the relevant employees and that they have been trained in its use.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The processing of information worthy of protection on third-party IT systems is generally technically prevented. Access to business data and applications from a third-party system is only permitted via a central Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) or a comparable terminal server solution. This ensures that no data is stored on the third-party end device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A VDI solution (e.g., based on Citrix or VMware Horizon) is implemented. Access is via a web browser or a thin client. The VDI policies are configured to prevent data copying between the virtual and local session and access to local drives of the third-party system.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the architecture and configuration of the VDI solution. In particular, the policies governing data exchange with the end device are reviewed. A practical test is conducted to verify that no data can be stored on a third-party system.

controls.title: INF.9.A5 Timely Loss Reporting (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no defined process for reporting losses or thefts. Such incidents, if reported at all, are reported only casually and with significant delay.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No action is taken. The organization does not react proactively to losses.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews with management and employees, it is determined that no process for loss reporting exists and responsibilities are unclear.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees know that they should report the loss of their laptop to their direct supervisor. However, there is no central point of contact, no availability outside of business hours, and no formalized process for what happens after the report.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Reporting to the supervisor is an informal, unwritten rule. The supervisor then decides ad hoc how to proceed.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In interviews, the auditor finds that employees would name the supervisor as the contact person, but have no knowledge of a formal, institutionalized reporting channel.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees MUST immediately report to their institution if information, IT systems, or data carriers have been lost or stolen. For this purpose, there MUST be clear reporting channels and defined contact persons within the institution who are also available outside of usual business hours.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A central reporting point (e.g., IT helpdesk or ISO) is designated and its contact details are made known to all employees. The reporting channel is described in the security policy for mobile working. For reports outside of business hours, there is an on-call service or an emergency hotline.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that a reporting channel and contact person are defined and documented. It is checked whether the contact details are easily accessible (e.g., on an emergency card or on the intranet). The employees' knowledge of the reporting channel is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A 24/7 security incident hotline is established and known to all employees. The reporting process is formally documented and includes a checklist of information that the reporting person should have ready (e.g., when, where, what exactly was lost, last known use). The report triggers a predefined incident response workflow.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The hotline number is printed on the devices and employee ID cards. The incident response process, which includes, for example, locking accounts and initiating remote wipe measures, is mapped in an incident management tool.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the documentation of the incident response process and the functionality of the hotline. The checklist for loss reports is inspected. Compliance with the documented workflow is checked based on past incidents.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The reporting process is integrated into a mobile app or a self-service portal. Reporting a loss via this platform can be initiated by the employee themselves and immediately and automatically triggers the locking of the device (remote lock) and the associated user accounts. The process is regularly tested through unannounced exercises.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A self-service function for loss reports is implemented in the UEM portal or a dedicated security app. The automation of immediate measures (locking, etc.) is realized via scripts and API connections of the involved systems (UEM, Active Directory). An annual plan for conducting tests exists.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the function of the self-service platform and the underlying automation. The documentation and the results of the conducted exercises are reviewed. The response times from the report to the automated locking are analyzed.

controls.title: INF.9.A6 Disposal of confidential information (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no rules for disposing of information on the go. Confidential documents, drafts, and notes are carelessly disposed of in public trash cans (e.g., in a hotel, at the train station).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken. The risk of dumpster diving is not considered.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through questioning, it is determined that there are no instructions for disposal and that employees dispose of confidential documents in the regular trash.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees are verbally instructed not to throw sensitive documents into public trash cans. However, there are no instructions for handling defective data carriers or a clear regulation for their return transport.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The instruction is an informal rule that is not documented or trained. No aids for secure transport are provided.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: In interviews, the auditor determines that there is a basic awareness of the insecure disposal of paper documents, but that no comprehensive regulations exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be regulated that confidential information is not disposed of insecurely while on the move. Before obsolete or defective data carriers and documents are destroyed, it MUST be checked whether they contain sensitive information. If this is the case, the data carriers and documents MUST be securely transported back to the institution and disposed of or destroyed there via the institution's own secure methods (e.g., shredder).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The regulation for return transport is stipulated in the security policy for mobile working. Employees are informed about the central disposal options (e.g., data protection bin, shredder) in the institution.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the corresponding policy. Through questioning of employees, it is verified whether the regulation for return transport and central disposal is known and understood.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees who work remotely on a regular basis are equipped with suitable aids for the secure return transport of sensitive documents. They are also trained in how to securely delete temporary digital information on their mobile devices to avoid data clutter.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees are provided with lockable and opaque document bags or folders. There are instructions and, if necessary, tools for securely deleting files (e.g., using tools like 'sdelete' or the system's own functions).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies that the aids (e.g., document bags) have been issued. The existence and quality of the instructions for securely deleting digital data are checked. The employees' knowledge of this is checked on a random basis.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For business trips where a large amount of sensitive paper material is expected, employees are equipped with portable shredders (at least protection class 3, security level P-4). All temporary digital data on mobile devices must be stored in a specially encrypted container, which is automatically and securely deleted after a trip or project is completed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Suitable portable shredders are procured and issued as needed. The container solution is managed via the UEM platform. The deletion process is linked to predefined events (e.g., 'business trip finished' in the travel expense tool).

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the procurement records and the issuing procedure for the portable shredders. The configuration of the container solution and the automated deletion process in the UEM platform is audited. The effectiveness of the deletion process is technically verified.

controls.title: INF.9.A7 Legal framework for mobile working (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no specific legal or contractual agreements for mobile working. It is tacitly tolerated without considering aspects such as working hours, data protection, or occupational health and safety.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken. The organization is fully exposed to the legal risks of unregulated mobile work.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by reviewing employment contracts and questioning the HR department that no specific regulations for mobile working exist.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The standard employment contract contains a general clause that mobile working is possible by arrangement. However, specific conditions regarding working hours, availability, data protection responsibility, or cost coverage are not formulated.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A standard sentence is included in the employment contracts, which, however, does not establish detailed and legally sound regulations.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the employment contracts and finds that while mobile working is mentioned, it is not sufficiently legally structured.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For mobile working, labor law and occupational health and safety frameworks MUST be observed and regulated. All relevant points MUST be clearly regulated either through company agreements or through individual agreements made in addition to the employment contract between the mobile employee and the institution.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: In cooperation with the HR department, the works council (if applicable), and possibly the legal department, a formal supplementary agreement for mobile working or a company agreement is drawn up. This regulates aspects such as place of work, working hours, availability, data protection obligations, insurance coverage, and equipment.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the valid company agreement or the standard supplementary agreement for mobile working. It is checked whether these agreements have been concluded with all mobile employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The legal agreements are reviewed regularly, at least annually, by the legal department or external specialized lawyers to ensure conformity with current legislation and case law. The agreement contains specific and detailed clauses on data protection responsibility (especially compliance with GDPR) and liability.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A fixed process for the annual review of legal documents is established. The results of the review are documented, and necessary adjustments are implemented promptly.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the evidence of the regular legal reviews of the agreements. In particular, the clauses on data protection are checked for their appropriateness and up-to-dateness.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The agreements are fully integrated into the digital HR onboarding process. Before being enabled for mobile working, employees must complete a mandatory e-learning module on the legal and data protection aspects and pass a test. For employees who regularly work abroad, there are special regulations tailored to the respective national law.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The HR system manages the status of the agreements and the training and controls the release of technical permissions for mobile working. The content of the e-learning modules is created and kept up-to-date in cooperation with the legal department.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the onboarding process for mobile work mapped in the HR system. The training materials and test results are reviewed. The existence and application of country-specific regulations for foreign assignments are checked on a random basis.

controls.title: INF.9.A8 Security policy for mobile workstations (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is no specific security policy for mobile workstations. The topic is not addressed in any way.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken. There are no written security guidelines.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines by searching the document management system and by questioning the ISO that no corresponding policy exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security rules that are also relevant for mobile working are distributed across various documents (e.g., a general IT usage policy, a password policy). However, there is no consolidated document geared towards the specific risks of mobile working.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Existing general policies are not supplemented with the specific aspects of mobile work. Employees have to find the relevant information themselves.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that while general security policies exist, they do not explicitly and cohesively address the specifics of mobile workstations (e.g., public environments, risk of theft).

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All relevant security requirements for mobile workstations MUST be documented in a security policy that is mandatory for mobile employees. It MUST be coordinated with the institution's existing security policies and with all relevant departments. The policy MUST be updated regularly, and employees MUST be made aware of and trained on the current policy.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A dedicated security policy for mobile working is created, adopted, and communicated to all relevant employees. The policy is reviewed at least every two years or when relevant changes occur. Training is provided as part of awareness measures.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor requests the valid security policy for mobile workstations and checks the approval and modification date. It is verified that the policy is consistent with other relevant documents. The implementation of awareness and training measures is checked using attendance lists or other evidence.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security policy is published prominently on the intranet. Employees must formally confirm annually that they have read and understood the policy. The policy is supplemented with concrete examples, checklists, and best-practice guides to increase comprehensibility and feasibility.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A system for tracking acknowledgment (e.g., via the LMS or a simple form) is implemented. The supporting materials (checklists, guides) are published together with the policy and actively promoted.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the evidence of annual acknowledgment of receipt by the employees. The quality and usefulness of the provided supporting materials are assessed.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the essential points of the policy is actively and technically monitored (e.g., through configuration checks of the UEM solution). In addition, regular, random, and unannounced audits are conducted on mobile employees. The content of the policy is dynamically adapted based on current threat intelligence feeds and the results of audits and incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UEM solution is used to check compliance rules (e.g., encryption active, OS patched). A plan for internal audits is created and implemented. A process for evaluating threat intelligence and adapting the policy is established.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the technical compliance checks and the resulting reports. The planning and results of the internal audits are inspected. The process for updating the policy based on new findings is audited.

controls.title: INF.9.A9 Encryption of portable IT systems and data carriers (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Encryption is not used on portable IT systems and data carriers. Confidential data is transported without protection.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken to encrypt mobile devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines through a technical inspection of some sample devices that no disk encryption or other encryption mechanisms are active.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The encryption functions integrated into the operating system (e.g., BitLocker, FileVault) are known, but their activation is left to the users' discretion. This leads to inconsistent implementation, with only some devices being encrypted.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Employees receive instructions on how to activate encryption manually. There is no central administration or verification.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks several mobile devices on a random basis and finds that encryption is not activated on all devices. It is determined that no central policy on encryption exists.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: It MUST be ensured that portable IT systems and data carriers are secured in accordance with internal policies. Mobile IT systems and data carriers MUST be encrypted. The cryptographic keys for recovery MUST be stored securely and separately from the encrypted device.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Disk encryption is mandatory for all mobile devices. The recovery keys are managed centrally and securely by the IT department, e.g., in Active Directory or a dedicated database. The regulation is documented in the security policy.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the encryption policy. The process for securely storing the recovery keys is checked. It is verified, using inventory lists and random technical checks, that all devices classified as mobile are encrypted.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Disk encryption is centrally enforced and monitored on all mobile devices via a management solution (UEM, GPO). The encryption algorithm used (e.g., AES-256) and the key length are documented and comply with the state of the art. The secure storage of recovery keys in a central management console is implemented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The UEM solution or group policies are configured so that encryption is automatically activated when a device is commissioned and cannot be deactivated by the user. Compliance (i.e., the encryption status) is continuously monitored.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration in the management console to verify the enforcement of encryption. The compliance monitoring reports are reviewed. The documentation of the selected encryption standard is checked.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Hardware-based encryption (e.g., via a Trusted Platform Module, TPM 2.0) is enforced to provide the best possible protection for the keys. In addition to disk encryption, a second layer of encryption is used for particularly sensitive data, for example, through encrypted containers or file-based encryption. The use of external data carriers (e.g., USB sticks) is technically restricted so that only the use of hardware-encrypted and centrally managed models is possible.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: When procuring devices, the presence of a TPM 2.0 is considered and its use is enforced via the management solution. A container solution (e.g., VeraCrypt) or an enterprise solution for file encryption is also rolled out. The UEM solution is configured to block all unauthorized USB storage devices.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor verifies the procurement policies and the UEM configuration regarding TPM usage. The configuration of the second encryption layer is checked. The technical implementation of the USB lock is audited through a practical test.

controls.title: INF.9.A10 Use of anti-theft devices (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Physical anti-theft devices are not considered or provided. The risk of theft is disregarded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken. Devices are left unsecured.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews and observation, it is determined that no anti-theft devices are used or even available.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Anti-theft devices such as cable locks are available from the IT department upon request. However, there is no policy that dictates when and where they must be used.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A small number of cable locks are kept on hand for when they are needed. Usage is left to the individual responsibility of the employees.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor finds that although anti-theft devices are available, their use is not regulated and they are therefore only used sporadically.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When mobile IT systems are left unattended, even for a short time, in publicly accessible or poorly secured areas (e.g., at trade fair stands, in co-working spaces, hotel rooms), they MUST be secured with a suitable physical anti-theft device (e.g., a Kensington lock). This regulation is documented and known to the employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The obligation to use anti-theft devices in defined scenarios is specified in the security policy for mobile working. All mobile employees receive an anti-theft device if required.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the relevant policy. Through interviews, it is checked whether the employees know the regulation and have the appropriate equipment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees who work on the move regularly are equipped with high-quality cable locks as standard. The security policy clearly and unambiguously defines the situations (e.g., hotel rooms, conference rooms, trains) in which the use of a lock is mandatory. Compliance is regularly addressed as part of awareness-raising measures.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The issuance of cable locks is part of the onboarding process for mobile employees and is documented. The awareness campaigns include visual examples of the correct use of the locks.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor checks the issuance logs for the anti-theft devices. The content of the awareness campaigns is reviewed to ensure that the topic of anti-theft protection is covered.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In addition to cable locks, devices used in particularly exposed locations are equipped with permanent asset tags and alarm security software. This software triggers a loud alarm and sends a notification to a security service if the device is removed from a predefined area (geofence) without authorization or the charging cable is disconnected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A software-based alarm solution (e.g., integrated into the UEM solution or as a standalone product) is installed and configured on the devices. The processes for alerting and response are defined and coordinated with an external service provider.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the configuration of the alarm security software and the contracts with the security service provider. The alerting and response process is tested for its functionality, e.g., through a simulated theft.

controls.title: INF.9.A11 Prohibition of the use of insecure environments (H)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There are no rules regarding the work environment. Even highly sensitive information is processed in unprotected public environments such as cafés or trains.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken. The choice of work environment is left solely to the employee, without security aspects playing a role.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: Through interviews, it is determined that there are no restrictions on the choice of work environment, even for processing highly sensitive data.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: There is a general, undocumented understanding that top-secret projects should not be worked on in a public café. However, there are no clear criteria for what constitutes an 'insecure environment' and for which types of information this applies.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: Managers give verbal and non-specific instructions on protecting information in public.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor determines in interviews that a basic awareness exists, but there are no formal, classification-based rules for the choice of work environment.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Criteria for the work environment MUST be established that must at least be met for information with an increased need for protection to be processed on the move. The criteria MUST at least cover the following topics: protection against viewing and unauthorized access by third parties, availability of closed and, if necessary, lockable or guarded rooms, secure communication options, and a sufficient power supply.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The criteria are clearly defined in the security policy for mobile working. Employees are given a checklist to evaluate potential work environments based on these criteria.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the defined criteria and the checklist in the security policy. Through random interviews, it is checked whether employees who work with highly sensitive data know and apply these criteria.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A formal classification of environments (e.g., "Trusted", "Controlled", "Public") is established. The data classification policy is linked to this environment classification and clearly defines which data class may be processed in which type of environment. The processing of data with high or very high protection needs is explicitly prohibited in "public" environments.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The classification matrix (data vs. environment) is published as an appendix to the security policy and is part of the mandatory security training.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the classification matrix for completeness and logic. It is verified whether this matrix is known to and understood by the relevant employees.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the environment policies is enforced through technical controls. Access to applications that process highly sensitive data is automatically blocked if the device connects to a network identified as insecure (e.g., public Wi-Fi) or if its location (via GPS) is in a zone classified as "Public".

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A UEM solution with Network Access Control (NAC) and geofencing capabilities is deployed. The Conditional Access policies are configured to control access based on network and location information.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor audits the configuration of the UEM and Conditional Access policies. The effectiveness of the block is verified through a practical test, attempting to access a protected application from a public hotspot.

controls.title: INF.9.A12 Use of a privacy screen (S)

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Privacy screens are not considered. The risk of "shoulder surfing" is ignored.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: No measures are taken. Screen content is freely visible to bystanders.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes that no privacy screens are present or required.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The institution provides privacy screens on request. However, their use is not mandatory and is at the discretion of the employees.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: A small number of privacy screens are kept in the IT storage and are issued when needed. There is no active communication about their availability or benefits.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor notes that although privacy screens exist, they are rarely used due to a lack of regulations.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Employees MUST use a privacy screen for the displays of their IT systems in public or uncontrolled environments such as trains, airplanes, or co-working spaces. This rule is documented.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The obligation is stipulated in the security policy for mobile working. Employees who work remotely on a regular basis can request a privacy screen from IT.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the policy. Through interviews, it is randomly checked whether mobile employees are aware of the rule and have a privacy screen.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: All employees who regularly work remotely are equipped with a privacy screen by default. The security policy explicitly requires its use in all environments outside the institution's secure premises or a secure home office.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The privacy screen is part of the standard equipment for mobile employees and is provided during device issuance. The rule is actively taught in security training sessions.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the issuance logs for the standard equipment. It is checked whether the training materials include the correct use of privacy screens.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The use of privacy screens is mandatory for all portable devices in the institution. When procuring new devices, models with an integrated, electronically switchable privacy screen (such as HP Sure View) are preferred. Compliance with the mandatory use is verified through regular, unannounced checks (e.g., walk-throughs in office and break areas).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose: The procurement policy is updated to include the requirement for integrated privacy screens. A plan for regular checks is created and implemented by the Information Security Officer.

parts.name: assessment-method
parts.prose: The auditor reviews the procurement policy and the logs of the checks performed. It is randomly checked whether the devices in use comply with the requirements and whether the filters are actively used (where applicable).

parts.name: introduction
parts.title: Introduction
parts.prose:
Good network coverage and powerful IT devices, such as laptops, smartphones, or tablets, enable employees to work from almost any location or from anywhere. This means that work-related tasks are often no longer performed solely in the rooms and buildings of the institution, but at changing workstations in various environments, e.g., in hotel rooms, on trains, or at the customer's premises. The information processed in this context must be adequately protected.
On the one hand, mobile working changes the duration, location, and distribution of working hours. On the other hand, it increases the requirements for information security, as a secure IT infrastructure, such as is found in an office environment, cannot be assumed in environments with mobile workstations.

parts.name: objective
parts.title: Objective
parts.prose: The module describes security requirements for mobile workstations. The objective is to create a security situation for such workstations that is comparable to that of an office environment.

parts.name: usage
parts.title: Delimitation and Modeling
parts.prose:
The module INF.9 Mobile Workstation is to be applied to all spaces that are frequently used as mobile workstations.
The module contains fundamental requirements that must be observed and fulfilled when employees not only work within the institution but also frequently at changing workstations outside.
The module primarily covers the organisational, technical, and personnel requirements for fully or partially mobile work. To secure IT systems, data media, or documents used in mobile work, all relevant modules such as SYS.3.1 Laptops, SYS.3.2 General Smartphones and Tablets, SYS.4.5 Removable Media, NET.3.3 VPN, and SYS.2.1 General Client must be considered separately.
Security requirements for VDU workstations outside the institution's buildings that are permanently set up by the institution (teleworking places) are not the subject of this module. These are described in the module OPS.1.2.4 Teleworking. Likewise, security requirements for the infrastructure of the teleworking place are not addressed. This topic is covered in the module INF.8 Home Office.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Missing or inadequate regulations for mobile workstations
parts.prose: If mobile working is not regulated or is inadequately regulated, the institution may suffer financial damage, among other things. For example, if it is not regulated which information may be transported and processed outside the institution and which protective measures must be observed, confidential information can fall into the wrong hands. This information could then potentially be used against the institution by unauthorised persons.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Impairment due to changing operating environment
parts.prose:
Since mobile data media and end devices are used in very different environments, they are exposed to many threats. These include, for example, harmful environmental influences such as excessively high or low temperatures, dust, or moisture. Transport damage can also occur.
In addition to these influences, the operational environment with its varying security level must also be considered. Smartphones, tablets, laptops, and similar mobile end devices are not only portable but can also communicate with other IT systems. In the process, malware can be transmitted or sensitive information can be copied, for example. It may also become impossible to perform tasks, appointments with customers may be missed, or IT systems may be damaged.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Manipulation or destruction of IT systems, accessories, information, and software at the mobile workstation
parts.prose: IT systems, accessories, information, and software used in a mobile context can potentially be tampered with or destroyed more easily than within the institution. The mobile workstation is often accessible to third parties. Also, the institution's central protective measures, such as gate services, are not present here. If IT systems, accessories, information, or software are tampered with or destroyed, employees at the mobile workstation are often only able to work with limited capacity. Furthermore, destroyed IT components or software solutions may need to be replaced, which requires both financial and time resources.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Delays due to temporarily limited accessibility
parts.prose: Most of the time, employees at mobile workstations do not have fixed working hours and are also harder to reach when on the move. This can significantly delay the flow of information. Even if information is transmitted via email, this does not necessarily shorten the response time, as it cannot be guaranteed that mobile employees will read the emails promptly. The impact of this temporarily limited availability varies depending on the situation and the institution, but it can severely restrict the availability of information.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Unsecured transport of files and data carriers
parts.prose:
When documents, data carriers, or files are transported between the institution and mobile workstations, this information and data can be lost or stolen, read, or manipulated by unauthorized persons. This can result in significant financial damage to the institution. The transport of files and data carriers can be inadequately secured in various ways:
• If unique copies are transported and there is no corresponding data backup, objectives and tasks cannot be achieved as planned if the unique copy is lost.
• If unencrypted data carriers fall into the wrong hands, this can lead to a serious loss of confidentiality.
• If there is insufficient access protection during transit, files or data carriers can be copied or manipulated unnoticed.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Improper disposal of data carriers and documents
parts.prose: If it is not possible to dispose of data carriers and documents appropriately at the mobile workstation, they usually end up in the household trash. Also, when working on the go, employees often throw drafts and other supposedly useless documents directly into the nearest wastebasket. Or they simply leave them behind, whether in a hotel or on a train. However, if data carriers or documents are not disposed of properly, third parties can extract valuable information from them, which can be specifically misused for blackmail attempts or corporate espionage. The consequences range from loss of knowledge to an existential threat to the institution, for example, if important contracts are not secured or partnerships fail as a result.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Loss of confidentiality of sensitive information
parts.prose: At a mobile workstation, it is easier for third parties to access confidential information located on hard drives, removable storage media, or paper, especially if they act professionally. They can also eavesdrop on communication links. If information is read or disclosed without authorization, this has serious consequences for the entire institution. Among other things, the loss of confidentiality can lead to the institution violating laws or suffering competitive disadvantages and financial damage.

parts.name: risk
parts.title: Theft or loss of data carriers or documents
parts.prose: The mobile workstation is not as well-secured as a workstation in a company or public authority. Official IT systems and documents can therefore be stolen more easily, for example, during a train journey, from a hotel room, or from external conference rooms. In addition, mobile IT systems or IT components can be lost. Besides the purely material damage from the immediate loss of the mobile IT system, further financial damage can also arise, for instance, if sensitive data such as emails, meeting notes, addresses, or other documents are disclosed. The institution's reputation could also be damaged.
